p. 1

HISTORIAE — HISTORY

PHILOSOPHIAE — OF PHILOSOPHY

EPITOME. — IN EPITOME

§. I.

§. I.

Philosophiae origo & progressus á mundo condito usque ad Christi D. adventum.

The origin and progress of Philosophy from the creation of the world to the coming of Christ our Lord.

1 Philosophia idem sonat ac Studium, seu amor sapientiae. „Sapientia autem est (uti ex veterum sententia loquitur Tullius s1), „rerum divinarum, & humanarum, causarumque, quibus hae res continentur scientia. In Philosophia namque, res cùm ad Deum, tùm ad alia extra Deum posita, pertinentes, rationis naturalis adminiculo scilicèt, exiguntur, causae quoque earundem ex principiis aut certis omninò, aut verosimilimis admodùm concinna, atque suis è legibus perfecta consecutione ducuntur. Ipsam hanc qui expetunt, Philosophi nominantur, adpellatione jam inde à Pithagorae modesto responsò studiosiùs retenta, ut postea dicemus.

hilosophy means the same as Study, or Love of Wisdom. “Wisdom, 1 P moreover, is (as Tully says, following the opinion of the ancients (a)) the knowledge of things divine and human, and of the causes by which these things are held together.” For in Philosophy, things pertaining both to God and to other things placed outside God are examined, namely with the help of natural reason, and their causes are derived, by a well-ordered consequence complete according to its own laws, from principles either altogether certain or highly probable. Those who seek it are named Philosophers, a name retained all the more carefully ever since the modest answer of Pythagoras, as we shall say later.

2 Philosophiam ab Omnipotenti Deo numeris omnibus absolutam sine ullo labore accepisse dicitur primus hominum parens Adamus. Sed quum ob violatam Dei legem (ait Purchotius s2)

2 Adam, the first parent of mankind, is said to have received from Almighty God, without any labor, a Philosophy complete in every respect. But when, as Purchot says (b), for violating the law of God he

Lib. 2. de Offic.

Bk. 2 of On Duties.

p. 2

ab eo, in quo positus erat, deliciarum horto fuisset expulsus, inter ceteras peccati poenas, quibus obnoxius esse coepit, ignorantiae tenebris traditus, in eas posteritatem secum traxit omnem. Quare nulla propemodùm excellentis illius, caelestisque doni in hominum animis vestigia supererant, quum nonnulli, excussâ ceterorum socordiâ, rerum pulcherrimarum admiratione commoti, & frequenti effectuum singularium observatione, quae experientia dicitur, edocti, eam à fundamentis instaurare omni ope ac studio sunt adgressi.

had been expelled from the garden of delights in which he had been placed, then, given over to the darkness of ignorance among the other penalties of sin to which he became subject, he dragged all his posterity with him into that darkness. Hence almost no traces of that excellent and heavenly gift remained in men’s minds, when some, shaking off the sloth of the rest, moved by admiration of the most beautiful things and taught by frequent observation of particular effects, which is called experience, set about restoring it from its foundations with every effort and zeal.

3 Id autem ferè apud omnes constat, scientiae naturalis, liberaliumque artium studium in Graecia potissimùm viguisse, sed quod ait Diogenes Laertius in Proemio ad vitas Philosophorum, Philosophiam in Graecia natam esse, non secùs ac homines ipsos, à vero prorsùs est alienum. Nam ut omittam quod ait Josephus s1 Sethi nepotes Caelorum ordinem, ac siderum cursus observasse: „neve inventa sua ex hominum notitia dilaberentur, quum Adamus generalem Mundi interitum, unum incendio, diluvio alterum praedixisset, duas excitasse columnas, alteram lateritiam, alteram lapideam, & utrique sua inventa insculpsisse, ut si lateritia diluvio periret, superstes esset lapidea, quae hominibus discendi copiam faceret“: Ut haec; inquam, omittam; quae vulgò nota sunt: (quamquam Ethnicis magna ex parte fuerint ignota) nemo sanè inficias ibit, Hebraeorum Patriarchas ac duces, ut Abrahamum, Mosen, & alios, rerum naturalium scientiâ fuisse informatos, non secus ac Salomonem Judaeorum Regem, qui, ut testantur Sacrae Literae s2, „disputavit super lignis à cedro, quae est in libano, usque ad hyssopum, quae egreditur de pariete, & disseruit de jumentis, & volucribus, & reptilibus, & piscibus.“ Illud insuper ipsorum Ethnicorum testimonio certum est, Assyrios, & Chaldaeos in Astronomia cum laude fuisse versatos, invitante scilicèt eos plana patentique regione, quam incolebant, ex qua siderum cursus liberè observare poterant. Hinc Tullius s3 Chaldaeos cognitione astrorum, solertiâque ingeniorum antecelluisse memorat.

3 It is agreed among nearly all, moreover, that the study of natural science and of the liberal arts flourished above all in Greece; but what Diogenes Laertius says in the Proem to the Lives of the Philosophers, that Philosophy was born in Greece just as men themselves were, is altogether foreign to the truth. For, to pass over what Josephus says (c), that the grandsons of Seth observed the order of the Heavens and the courses of the stars, “and, lest their discoveries should slip out of men’s knowledge, since Adam had foretold a general destruction of the World, the one by fire, the other by flood, set up two columns, one of brick, the other of stone, and carved their discoveries on both, so that if the brick one should perish in the flood, the stone one would survive and give men the means of learning”: to pass over these things, I say, which are commonly known (although they were for the most part unknown to the Heathen), no one will indeed deny that the Patriarchs and leaders of the Hebrews, such as Abraham, Moses and others, were instructed in the science of natural things, just like Solomon, King of the Jews, who, as the Sacred Scriptures testify (d), “treated about trees from the cedar that is in Libanus, unto the hyssop that cometh out of the wall: and he discoursed of beasts, and of fowls, and of creeping things, and of fishes.” This moreover is certain from the testimony of the Heathen themselves, that the Assyrians and Chaldeans were laudably versed in Astronomy, invited, namely, by the flat and open region they inhabited, from which they could freely observe the courses of the stars. Hence Tully (e) records that the Chaldeans excelled in the knowledge of the stars and in the shrewdness of their minds.

4 Ab Assyriis, autem, & Chaldaeis, teste Josepho s4 Arithmetica per Abrahamum translata est ad AEgyptios, qui necessitate compulsi Geometriae pariter studuerunt: quoniam per anniversariam Nili inundationem, ut Proclus refert, agrorum termini apud illos sic turbarentur, ut discerni postea sine Geometria non possent.

4 From the Assyrians and Chaldeans, moreover, as Josephus witnesses (f), Arithmetic was carried by Abraham to the Egyptians, who, compelled by necessity, likewise studied Geometry: since, as Proclus reports, the boundaries of their fields were so confounded by the annual flooding of the Nile that they could not afterwards be distinguished without Geometry.

5 Tandem ab AEgyptiis ad Phoenices simul, & ad Graecos

5 Finally, from the Egyptians, at once to the Phoenicians and to the Greeks across the

In Praef. ad suas Instit. Philos. ex qua nonnulla quae ad hanc primam Hist. Philosoph. partem spectant, paucis immutatis excerpsimus, uti & reliqua ex operibus Brukerii, Stanlei, Klausi, aliorumque.

In the Preface to his Institutiones Philosophicae, from which we have excerpted, with a few changes, some things that pertain to this first part of the History of Philosophy, as also the rest from the works of Brucker, Stanley, Klausius and others.

Lib. 1. Antiq. Judaic. c. 3.

Bk. 1 of the Jewish Antiquities, ch. 3.

Lib. III. Reg. cap. 4.

Bk. III of Kings, ch. 4.

De Divinat. Lib. 1.

On Divination, bk. 1.

Antiquit. Judaicar. cap. 9.

Jewish Antiquities, ch. 9.

p. 3

trajecto mari, delata est Geometria; quam videlicet in AEgypto didicit Thales Milesius, & in Graeciam intulit, ut narrat ipse Diogenes Laertius in ejus vita.

the sea, Geometry was carried; which Thales of Miletus, namely, learned in Egypt and brought into Greece, as Diogenes Laertius himself narrates in his life.

6 Itaque non Graecis solis acceptam referre debemus Philosophiam; sed quemadmodum apud eos extitére viri ingenio, & rerum naturalium cognitione praecellentes qui Sapientes primùm, postea Philosophi sunt adpellati: ita ceteris quoque nationibus sui fuerunt veritatis interpretes, ac doctores; Hebraeis quidem Rabbini, Babylonis, & Assyriis Chaldaei; Persis Magi; Indis Brachmanes, seu Gymnosophistae; imò & in extremis Orientis oris apud Sinas fuere disciplinarum humanarum, & liberalium Artium cultores, in quibus maximè celebratur Confucius, qui ideò Sinensis Philosophus adpellatur. Item apud AEgyptios Hierophantae, apud Gallos Druidae floruerunt.

6 Therefore we must not credit Philosophy to the Greeks alone: but just as among them there arose men excelling in ingenuity and in the knowledge of natural things, who were first called Wise Men, afterwards Philosophers, so the other nations too had their own interpreters and teachers of truth: among the Hebrews, indeed, the Rabbis; of Babylon and Assyria, the Chaldeans; among the Persians, the Magi; among the Indians, the Brahmans, or Gymnosophists; nay, even on the shores of the farthest East, among the Chinese, there were cultivators of the human disciplines and of the liberal Arts, among whom Confucius is most celebrated, who is therefore called the Chinese Philosopher. Likewise among the Egyptians the Hierophants flourished, and among the Gauls the Druids.

7 Praecipua autem Philosophiae gloria Graecis ideo tribuitur, quòd ii diligentiùs incubuerint in singulas illius partes, eamque in quoddam veluti corpus digestam Scriptis suis ad posteros transmiserint. Quamobrem illustriores Philosophorum sectae, de quibus mentio fit in Scholis, á Graecis sunt repetendae.

7 The chief glory of Philosophy, however, is attributed to the Greeks because they applied themselves more diligently to each of its parts, and, having arranged it as it were into a kind of body, handed it down to posterity in their Writings. Wherefore the more illustrious sects of Philosophers, of which mention is made in the Schools, are to be traced back to the Greeks.

§. II.

§. II.

Illustriores Philosophorum Sectae.

The More Illustrious Sects of Philosophers. 8

8 Secta autem est quaedam hominum multitudo quae ab aliis quodammodò secta & divisa certum doctrinae genus sub aliquo Duce sectatur. Hinc vel à secando, vel à sectando nominata est secta.

A sect, moreover, is a certain multitude of men which, in some way cut off and divided from others, follows a certain kind of doctrine under some Leader. Hence it was named secta either from secando [cutting] or from sectando [following].

9 Porrhò primi Graecorum Philosophi in duas sectas dividuntur, scilicet in Dogmaticam, & Academicam.

9 Further, the first Philosophers of the Greeks are divided into two sects, namely the Dogmatic and the Academic.

10 Secta Dogmatica eos comprehendit Philosophos, qui veritatem adsecutos esse se, saltem in pluribus, contendunt: quae iterum duplex est, Jonica, & Italica.

10 The Dogmatic sect comprises those Philosophers who contend that they have attained the truth, at least in most things; and it is in turn twofold, the Ionic and the Italic.

11 Ionicae sectae dux fuit Thales, dictus Milesius, sive quia Miletum, quae Urbs est Ioniae caput, patriam habuit; sive quia quum ex Phaenicia oriundus esset, inter Cives Milesios, ut quidam tradunt, fuit adscriptus. Ipsum anno primo Olympiadis 35. natum esse memorat Apollodorus apud Diogenem Laertium in ejus vita, mortuum verò anno aetatis septuagesimo. Annus autem ille primus Olympiadis 35. est 639. ante aeram vulgarem Christianorum, & à mundo condito 3365. s1 Thaletem sectati sunt Anaximander,

11 The leader of the Ionic sect was Thales, called the Milesian, either because he had as his native city Miletus, which is the capital City of Ionia, or because, although he was of Phoenician origin, he was enrolled, as some relate, among the Citizens of Miletus. Apollodorus, in Diogenes Laertius’s life of him, records that he was born in the first year of the 35th Olympiad, and died in the seventieth year of his age. That first year of the 35th Olympiad, moreover, is the year 639 before the common era of the Christians, and 3365 from the founding of the world. () Thales was followed by Anaximander,

p. 4

Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, Heraclítus, Demócritus, & alii, qui omnes praeceptoris sui Philosophiam illustrarunt, & ad Socratem usque, ac Platonem perduxerunt.

Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, Heraclitus, Democritus, and others, all of whom made the Philosophy of their master illustrious, and carried it down as far as Socrates and Plato.

12 Italicae princeps fuit Pythagoras Samius, qui quum Pherecydis Syri fuisset discipulus, ac AEgyptum & Babyloniam doctrinae comparandae gratia perlustrasset, tandem recepit se in Italiam, tempore Servii Tullii Romanorum Regis; & Crotone non longe à Tarento Philosophiae per annos circiter viginti operam navavit; indeque postea Metapontum profectus, testante Justino s1, diem ibi supremum obit anno 4 Olympiadis 70. Ab eo primùm Philosophi nomen usurpatum est. Quippe quum per Peloponnesum transiens interrogatus esset à Leonte Sicyoniorum, vel Phliasiorum Tyranno (erant autem Sicyon, & Phlius urbes Peloponnesi) quem se profiteretur: respondit se Philosophum esse, hoc est, Sapientiae studiosum; modestiore scilicet, adpellatione usus, inquit Diogenes Laertius in Proemio ad vitas Philosophorum, ut retunderet fastum ac superbiam Graecorum, qui se Sapientes praedicabant: quia solus Deus vere Sapiens dici potest; homines verò potius Sapientiae amatores sunt nominandi, quàm Sapientes.

12 The chief of the Italic sect was Pythagoras of Samos, who, having been a disciple of Pherecydes the Syrian, and having traveled through Egypt and Babylonia for the sake of acquiring learning, at length betook himself to Italy, in the time of Servius Tullius, King of the Romans; and at Croton, not far from Tarentum, he devoted himself to Philosophy for about twenty years; and having afterwards gone from there to Metapontum, as Justin testifies (g), he died there in the 4th year of the 70th Olympiad. By him the name of Philosopher was first used. For when, passing through the Peloponnese, he was asked by Leon, Tyrant of the Sicyonians, or of the Phliasians (Sicyon and Phlius, moreover, were cities of the Peloponnese), what he professed himself to be, he answered that he was a Philosopher, that is, one devoted to Wisdom; using, namely, a more modest appellation, says Diogenes Laertius in the Proem to the Lives of the Philosophers, in order to beat down the arrogance and pride of the Greeks, who proclaimed themselves Wise Men: because God alone can truly be called Wise, whereas men are rather to be named lovers of Wisdom than Wise.

13 Pythagorae dogmata inter ceteros amplexi sunt Timaeus Locrensis, Archytas Tarentinus, Philolaus Crotoniata, Parmenides, & Zeno ambo Eleatae, quorum hic Dialecticae auctor dicitur á Diogene Laertio, ac Melissus Samius: qui omnes Physicae seu naturali scientiae praecipuam dederunt operam ad institutionem usque veteris Academiae, cujus Princeps fuit Socrates: quo tempore Philosophi animum á rebus Physicis ad morum scientiam Socratis exemplo converterunt.

13 Among others, the doctrines of Pythagoras were embraced by Timaeus of Locri, Archytas of Tarentum, Philolaus of Croton, Parmenides and Zeno, both of Elea, the latter of whom is called the author of Dialectic by Diogenes Laertius, and Melissus of Samos: all of whom gave their chief attention to Physics, or natural science, right up to the institution of the old Academy, whose Chief was Socrates; at which time the Philosophers, following the example of Socrates, turned their minds from Physical things to the science of morals.

14 Secta Academica nomen suum desumpsit ab Academia hoc est a loco nemoroso in suburbio Athenarum sito, quem heros nobilis, Academus nomine, Philosophorum exercitationibus consecrarat. Hujus sectae Philosophi adsensum omnem cohibebant: nihil omnino adfirmabant: ipsaque rursus in veterem, mediam, & novam Academiam fuit divisa.

14 The Academic sect took its name from the Academy, that is, from a wooded place situated in a suburb of Athens, which a noble hero, Academus by name, had consecrated to the exercises of the Philosophers. The Philosophers of this sect withheld all assent; they affirmed nothing whatever: and the sect itself was in turn divided into the old, the middle, and the new Academy.

15 Veteris Academiae Principes fuere Socrates, & ejus discipulus Plato. Unde veteres Academici, iidem Platonici dicti sunt, ut & Sceptici seu Inquisitores: quod licet ignotam esse veritatem arbitrarentur, de ea tamen invenienda non desperarent; ideoque ejus inquisitioni constanter vacarent. Pyrrhonici quoque vocati sunt, à Pyrrhone Academico.

15 The Chiefs of the old Academy were Socrates and his disciple Plato. Hence the old Academics were called by the same token Platonists, and also Sceptics, or Inquirers: because, although they judged truth to be unknown, they nevertheless did not despair of finding it, and therefore devoted themselves constantly to the inquiry after it. They were also called Pyrrhonists, from Pyrrho, an Academic.

16 Socrates in Attica natus est anno 4. Olympiadis 77. Secundum Diogenem Laertium in ejus vita: hoc est anno mundi juxta calculum Usserianum 3536. Mortuus verò ann. 1 Olympiadis 95. aetatis septuagesimo. „Primus ille à rebus occultis, (ut ait Cic.) s2 & ab ipsa natura involutis, in quibus omnes ante eum

16 Socrates was born in Attica in the 4th year of the 77th Olympiad, according to Diogenes Laertius in his life; that is, in the year of the world 3536 according to Ussher’s calculation. He died, however, in the 1st year of the 95th Olympiad, in the seventieth year of his age. “It was he who first, from things hidden (as Tully says (h)) and wrapped up by nature herself, in which, before him, all

Olympias spatium est quatuor annorum. Olympias prima celebrata est anno mundi 3250.

An Olympiad is a space of four years. The first Olympiad was celebrated in the year of the world 3250.

Lib. XX. Historiar. cap. 4.

Bk. XX of the Histories, ch. 4.

p. 5

Philosophi occupati fuerant, avocavit Philosophiam, & ad vitam communem adduxit, ut de virtutibus, & vitiis, omninoque de bonis rebus, & malis quaereret: caelestia autem vel procul esse á nostra cognitione censeret, vel si maximè cognita essent, nihil tamen ad benè vivendum conferre. Hic in omnibus ferè sermonibus, qui ab iis, qui illum audierunt, perscripti varie, & copiosè sunt, ita disputabat, ut nihil adfirmaret ipse, refelleret alios, nihil se scire diceret, nisi id ipsum.

the Philosophers had been occupied, called Philosophy away and brought it to common life, so that it should inquire about virtues and vices, and in general about good and evil things; and he held that heavenly things were either far removed from our knowledge, or, even if they were known as fully as possible, still contributed nothing to living well. In nearly all the discourses which were written down, variously and copiously, by those who heard him, he disputed in such a way that he affirmed nothing himself, refuted others, and said that he knew nothing, except that very thing.”

17 Operam Socrati dedere Crito, Aristippus, Cebes, Xenophon, Euclides, &c. Sed inter eos omnes eminebat Plato Atheniensis, qui & Socrati in Academia successit, ejusque methodo insistens nihil adfirmabat, sed, ut ait idem Tulliuss1 ,, multa in ejus libris in utramque partem disseruntur, de omnibus quaeritur, nihil certi dicitur ,,. Plato autem discipulum inter ceteros habuit Aristotelem Peripateticae sectae postea Principem, & sibi adversarium.

17 Crito, Aristippus, Cebes, Xenophon, Euclid and others were followers of Socrates. But among them all Plato the Athenian was eminent, who also succeeded Socrates in the Academy and, keeping to his method, affirmed nothing, but, as the same Tully says (i), “in his books many things are argued on both sides, everything is inquired into, nothing certain is said.” Plato, moreover, had among his other disciples Aristotle, afterwards the Chief of the Peripatetic sect, and his own adversary.

18 Post mortem Platonis, & Speusippi, ceteri Socratis successores in Academia timidam illam Philosophandi methodum abjecere; & in Dogmaticorum partes translati triplicem constituere Sectam, Peripateticorum, Stoicorum, & Epicureorum.

18 After the death of Plato and of Speusippus, the other successors of Socrates in the Academy cast off that timid method of philosophizing; and, having passed over to the party of the Dogmatics, they established a threefold Sect, that of the Peripatetics, of the Stoics, and of the Epicureans.

19 Peripatetici praeceptore gloriantur Aristotele. Hic natus Stagyrae opido Macedoniae circa annum mundi 3621 scilicet anno primo Olympiadis 99, patre Nicomacho, matre Phaestide, septimum decimum annum agens Platonem audivit. Philosophicis disciplinis ipsos viginti annos excultus, magistro é vivis sublato, ad Hermiam Aternensium in Mysia tyrannum se contulit Aristoteles, apud quem triennio ubi versatus fuisset, in Macedoniam ad erudiendum Alexandrum profectus, exactis cum eo annis octo, Athenas rediit: hic Xenocratem Speusippi successorem in Acedemia quum reperisset, Lyceum (in suburbio locus fuerat à Pericle conditus, ut lectum recens militem ipse in eo bellicis artibus instrueret) sibi delegit: qua in statione, quoniam de rebus philosophicis inambulando disseruit, factum iccircò, ut Schola ab inambulandi consuetudine PERIPATETICA vocaretur.

19 The Peripatetics glory in Aristotle as their master. He was born at Stagira, a town of Macedonia, about the year of the world 3621, namely in the first year of the 99th Olympiad, his father being Nicomachus and his mother Phaestis, and in his seventeenth year he heard Plato. When he had been trained in the Philosophical disciplines for full twenty years and his master had been taken from among the living, Aristotle betook himself to Hermias, tyrant of the Atarneans in Mysia; and having stayed with him for three years, he set out for Macedonia to instruct Alexander, and, after spending eight years with him, returned to Athens. Here, since he found Xenocrates, the successor of Speusippus, in the Academy, he chose for himself the Lyceum (a place in the suburb, which had been built by Pericles so that he himself might train newly levied soldiers in it in the arts of war); and since in that station he discoursed on philosophical matters while walking about, it came about that the School was called Peripatetic, from its custom of walking about.

20 Auctor est Strabos2 & in eo mirè consentiunt Historiae Philosophiae Scriptores, Aristotelem scripta sua & Bibliothecam discipulo suo Theophrasto tradidisse, cui & Scholam reliquit. Theophrastum pariter & suos, & Aristotelis libros testamento legasse Neleo Scepsio, qui fuerat illius, & Aristotelis Auditor, ut testatur Diogenes Laertiuss3. Igitur Neleus Bibliothecam illam in oppidum Scepsin transtulit, eamque haeredibus ineruditis hominibus moriens reliquit. Illi autem ubi Attalicorum Regum, quibus Scepsis

20 Strabo is our authority (k), and the Writers of the History of Philosophy agree wonderfully with him on this, that Aristotle handed over his writings and his Library to his disciple Theophrastus, to whom he also left his School; and that Theophrastus likewise bequeathed by will both his own books and Aristotle’s to Neleus of Scepsis, who had been a hearer of him and of Aristotle, as Diogenes Laertius testifies (l). Neleus, therefore, carried that Library over to the town of Scepsis, and at his death left it to his heirs, unlearned men. But they, when they learned of the zeal of the Attalid Kings, to whom Scepsis

Academic. quaest. Lib. 1.

Academic Questions, bk. 1.

Loco sup. citat.

In the place cited above.

p. 6

parebat in libris undequaque ad instruendam Pergami Bibliothecam conquirendis studium intellexissent: suos ne auferrentur in terram defoderunt. ubi diù relicti ac quodammodo sepulti jacuere. Tandem ab illorum successoribus éruti sunt, humore & blattis vitiati & corrossi, ac Apelliconi Tejo, librorum magis quam scientiae studioso magnâ pecuniâ venditi. Apellicon verò, facta imperita exesarum partium instauratione, in nova libros transtulit exempla, quae tamen mendis adhuc plurimis, & plurimis etiam relictis lacunis, scatebant.

was subject, in seeking out books from every quarter to furnish the Library of Pergamum, buried their own in the ground lest they be carried off; and there they lay a long time, abandoned and, as it were, entombed. At length, dug up by the successors of those men, damaged and gnawed by damp and by moths, they were sold for a great sum of money to Apellicon of Teos, a man more devoted to books than to learning. Apellicon, for his part, after an unskilled restoration of the eaten-away parts, transcribed the books into new copies, which nevertheless still teemed with very many faults, and with very many gaps also left unfilled.

21 At statim post mortem Appelliconis bibliotheca illius, quae erat in Piraeo à L Sulla, ut Plutarchus in ejus vita commemorat, subducta est, ac Romam asportata, ubi Grammaticus quiddam Tyrannio, Aristotelicorum librorum usum sibi permitti petiit: eaque facultate obtentâ, plurima in iis intervertit ipse, & cum Andronico quodam Rhodio exempla communicavit, à quo similiter interpolata, tandem in lucem emissa sunt. Ex quo satis superque constat Aristotelis libros miserè foedatos esse, multisque locis hiulcos, ita ut nullus pro certo adfirmare possit qualia sint verba ipsiusmet Aristotelis; quid suppleverit Appellicon, quid Tyrannio & Andronicus. Qui de hoc plura velit legat Stanleyums1. Nos ad reliqua gradum facimus.

21 But immediately after the death of Apellicon his library, which was at Piraeus, was carried off by L. Sulla, as Plutarch records in his life, and taken to Rome, where a certain Grammarian, Tyrannio, asked to be allowed the use of the Aristotelian books; and, having obtained this permission, he himself corrupted a great many things in them, and shared copies with a certain Andronicus of Rhodes, by whom, after they had been likewise interpolated, they were at length brought out into the light. From this it is more than sufficiently clear that the books of Aristotle were wretchedly defiled and full of gaps in many places, so that no one can affirm for certain which are the words of Aristotle himself, and what Apellicon supplied, what Tyrannio and Andronicus. Whoever wishes to know more of this, let him read Stanley (m). We pass on to the rest.

22 Stoicorum Dux fuit Zeno Cittieus, sive è Cittio Cypri oppido oriundus, qui Athenis in Porticu severioris Philosophiae dogmata magna cum nominis celebritate tradebat circa Olympiadem 130.

22 The Leader of the Stoics was Zeno of Citium, that is, a native of Citium, a town of Cyprus, who at Athens, in the Portico, taught the doctrines of a severer Philosophy, with great celebrity of name, about the 130th Olympiad.

23 Epicurei ità vocati sunt ab Epicuro hujus sectae Patrono; qui in hortis, ubi suos agebat conventus, Demócriti placita, quae propria fecerat, explicabat. Obiit annó secundo Olympiadis 127, post mund. condit. 3735, quum vixisset annos 72. Epicuri Philosophiam latinis carminibus in sex libros distributis scripsit Lucretius Cicerone duodecim annis minor. Reprehenditur Epicurus à Tullios2 quod Logicam contempserit, multò autem maximè, quod ,, ex animis hominum extraxerit radicitùs Religionem cum Diis immortalibus :::::: re tollens, oratione relinquens Deos ,,. Unum hoc adnectimus: Epicuri Scholam serie continua & rara consensione ad Augusti aetatem usque pertinuisse quatuordecim Magistris spatium annorum 237 explentibus.

23 The Epicureans were so called from Epicurus, the Patron of this sect, who in the gardens where he held his gatherings expounded the tenets of Democritus, which he had made his own. He died in the second year of the 127th Olympiad, in the year 3735 after the founding of the world, having lived 72 years. Lucretius, twelve years younger than Cicero, wrote out the Philosophy of Epicurus in Latin verses divided into six books. Epicurus is censured by Tully (n) for having despised Logic, but far most of all because “he tore Religion up by the roots from the minds of men, abolishing it, together with the immortal Gods, in reality, while leaving the Gods in words.” We add this one thing: that the School of Epicurus lasted, in a continuous succession and with a rare agreement, down to the age of Augustus, fourteen Masters filling a space of 237 years.

24 Interea verò Socratis methodus ab Arcesila revocata fuerat circa Olympiadem 120; unde ipse secundae, seu mediae Academiae Princeps nominatur. Is autem Socratis opinioni hoc addidit, ut non modò nihil sciri adfirmaret cum Socrate, sed ne posse quidem rem ullam sciri contenderet. Hinc novi Academici, iidem Acataleptici sunt vocati, quasi diceres, qui nihil omninò comprehendere se posse profiterentur.

24 Meanwhile, however, the method of Socrates had been revived by Arcesilaus about the 120th Olympiad, whence he himself is named the Chief of the second, or middle, Academy. He, moreover, added this to the opinion of Socrates: that he not only affirmed with Socrates that nothing is known, but contended that nothing whatever can even be known. Hence the new Academics were also called Acataleptics, as if you were to say, men who professed that they could comprehend nothing at all.

p. 7

25 Arcesilae suffragati sunt Lacydes, novae, seu tertiae Academiae Auctor, Evander, & praecipuè Carneades, qui Romae magna cum eloquentia novorum Academicorum doctrinam explicuit, ibique discipulos habuit Clitomachum, Philonem, & Antiochum, à quibus eruditus est M. T. Cicero, qui & ipse Academicus fuit, ac Platonicae methodi strenuus adsertor.

25 Arcesilaus was supported by Lacydes, the Author of the new, or third, Academy, by Evander, and above all by Carneades, who at Rome expounded the doctrine of the new Academics with great eloquence, and there had as disciples Clitomachus, Philo and Antiochus, by whom M. T. Cicero was taught, who himself also was an Academic and a vigorous champion of the Platonic method.

§. III. — §. III

De Eclectica Philosophia, deque Philosophia post Christum natum.

On the Eclectic Philosophy, and on Philosophy after the Birth of Christ.

26 Quae Philosophia Graecis Eclectica, Latinis Electiva dicitur. Hanc philosophandi rationem Clemens Alexandrinus explicat, dum, ubi multa in laudem Philosophiae disseruisset, addit, se omnia haec in Philosophiam non Stoicam, nec Platonicam, nec Epicuream, aut Aristotelicam pronunciasse; sed quaecumque ab his sectis rectè dicta sunt, quae docent justitiam cum pia scientia, hoc totum electum, Philosophiam se adpellare aits1. Quasi (ut subdit Stanleyuss2 ,, ne nomine quidem Philosophiae dignum censeret studium eorum, qui superstitiosè in unius verba magistri jurare non dubitant ,,. Eclectici nempè apes imitantur, quae (Senecae sunt verbas3 ,, vagantur, & flores ad mel faciendum idoneos carpunt, deinde quidquid attullere disponunt, ac per favos digerunt, utque Virgilius ait:

26 This Philosophy is called Eclectic by the Greeks, Elective by the Latins. This manner of philosophizing is explained by Clement of Alexandria when, after discoursing at length in praise of Philosophy, he adds that he had declared all this not of the Stoic Philosophy, nor of the Platonic, nor of the Epicurean or the Aristotelian; but whatever things have been rightly said by these sects, which teach justice together with pious knowledge, this whole selection, he says, he calls Philosophy (o). As if (as Stanley adds (p)) “he judged the study of those who do not hesitate superstitiously to swear by the words of a single master not worthy even of the name of Philosophy.” The Eclectics, namely, imitate the bees, which (these are Seneca’s words (q)) “wander about and pluck the flowers fit for making honey, then arrange whatever they have brought in, and distribute it through the combs, and, as Virgil says:

..........................liquentia mella

……………………the liquid honey

Stipant, & dulci distendunt nectare cellas.

They pack, and swell the cells with sweet nectar.”

27 Hujus Philosophiae Princeps Potamon Alexandrinus fuit, illustresque fama nactos auditores habuit haec philosophandi ratio (neque enim Sectae nomine isthaec philosophandi methodus venire potest). Viri etiam Sanctimonia inclyti Eclecticam philosophiam studiosiùs propugnare contenderunt, cum primis quidem Clemens Alexandrinus, & Gregorius Thaumaturgus, non alia videlicet causâ eam professi ,, nisi, ut veritatem, quae in una secta reperiri non poterat, ex pluribus derivarent ,, quod innuit Lactantius, adfirmans unà ,, eos omnes sapientiam sibi adimere, qui sine ullo judicio inventa majorum probant, & ab aliis pecudum more

27 The Chief of this Philosophy was Potamon of Alexandria, and this manner of philosophizing (for this method of philosophizing cannot come under the name of a Sect) had hearers who had won illustrious fame. Men renowned for Holiness also strove to defend the Eclectic philosophy with especial zeal, foremost among them Clement of Alexandria and Gregory Thaumaturgus, having professed it, namely, for no other reason “than that they might draw from many sects the truth which could not be found in one”; which Lactantius intimates, affirming at the same time that “all those deprive themselves of wisdom who without any judgment approve the discoveries of their forefathers, and, like cattle, by others are

dicuntur; nec putant fieri posse, ut aut ipsi plus sapiant, quia minores vocantur, aut illi desipuerint, quia majores nominanturs1.

are led; nor do they think it possible either that they themselves should be wiser, because they are called the younger, or that those others should have been foolish, because they are named the elders (r).”

28 Sequentibus temporibus post Christi adventum doctrina Platonis ad octavum circiter Ecclesiae seculum primas semper obtinuit, eique plurimi SS. Patres studium, & vigilias suas consecrarunt. Eandem inter Latinos Patres diligentissimè excoluit S. Augustinus, qui ut erat acerrimo ingenio, multis eam partibus illustravit, & ad refellendos Ethnicorum errores, adserendamque Religionis Christianae veritatem feliciter adhibuit.

28 In the following ages after the coming of Christ, the doctrine of Plato always held first place until about the eighth century of the Church, and very many of the Holy Fathers consecrated their study and their vigils to it. Among the Latin Fathers it was most diligently cultivated by St. Augustine, who, being of a most penetrating wit, illustrated it in many parts and happily employed it to refute the errors of the Heathen and to assert the truth of the Christian Religion.

29 Quod verò Philosophiam Aristotelicam adtinet, certum est, illam primis Ecclesiae seculis nullum unquam obtinuisse dominatum, quinimo SS. Patres innumeris conviciis eam derisere. Illos legere est apud Cl. Petaviums2 Eorum agmen ducit S. Justinus Martyr (sive quis alius Christianus Doctor, qui librum inscripsit: Quorundam Aristotelicarum dogmatum eversio) Clemens Alexandr. sequitur ita scribens.s3 ,, Sed nec molestum fuerit meminisse etiam Peripateticorum, cujus quidem sectae qui pater est, nihil de eo Patre qui est Supremus intelligens errores plurimos docet ,,. Iraeneus Lugdunensis Episcopuss4 duo ab Aristotele refutat accepta nimirùm minutiloquium, & subtilitatem, quibus Christianae Fidei simplicitas, & candor corrumpitur. Hoc ipsum in Aristotele reprehendunt Origeness5, Lactantius Firmianuss6, Eusebius Caesariensiss7, Athanasius Alexandr. Episcopuss8 Basiliuss9, Gregorius Nicenuss10, Ambrosiuss11, Johann. Chrisostomuss12, Augustinuss13, Hieronymuss14 qui testatur quod Ariana haeresis argumentationum rivos de fontibus Aristotelis mutuatur, quod & confirmat S. Ambrosiuss15 inquiens: ,, Sic enim Arianos in perfidiam ruisse cognovimus, relinquunt Apostolum,

29 As for the Aristotelian Philosophy, it is certain that in the first ages of the Church it never held any dominion; nay rather, the Holy Fathers derided it with countless reproaches. These may be read in the celebrated Petavius (s). Their file is led by St. Justin Martyr (or whatever other Christian Doctor wrote the book entitled The Overthrow of Certain Aristotelian Doctrines). Clement of Alexandria follows, writing thus (t): “But it will not be irksome to recall also the Peripatetics, the father of whose sect, understanding nothing about that Father who is Supreme, teaches very many errors.” Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons (u), refutes two things received from Aristotle, namely hair-splitting talk and subtlety, by which the simplicity and candor of the Christian Faith are corrupted. This very thing is censured in Aristotle by Origen (x), Lactantius Firmianus (y), Eusebius of Caesarea (z), Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria (a), Basil (b), Gregory of Nyssa (c), Ambrose (d), John Chrysostom (e), Augustine (f), and Jerome (g), who testifies that the Arian heresy borrows the streams of its argumentations from the fountains of Aristotle; which St. Ambrose (h) also confirms, saying: “For thus we know that the Arians rushed headlong into perfidy: they abandon the Apostle,

Divin. Instit. Lib. 2. cap. 8.

Divine Institutes, bk. 2, ch. 8.

sequuntur Aristotelem ,,. Gregorius quoque Nazianzenuss1 dolet irrepsisse in Ecclesiam captiones sophisticas & pravum artificium Aristoteleae artis velut AEgyptiacas quasdam plagas. S. Augustinus ita Pelagianos compellats2 ,, Ad hoc redacta est haeresis vestra, ut gemant Sectatores vestri non inveniri Dialecticos Judices in Ecclesia de Scholis Peripateticorum à quibus possitis absolvi ,,. S. Vincentius Ferrerius quaerulus exclamats3, Aristotelem & Averroem fuisse phialas irae Dei projectas super aquas sapientiae Christianae, unde factae sunt amarae, ut absynthium. Plura qui velit, legat Cl. Guidonem Grandi. Historiam sequamur.

they follow Aristotle.” Gregory Nazianzen too (i) laments that the captious arguments of the sophists and the depraved artifice of the Aristotelian art had crept into the Church like certain Egyptian plagues. St. Augustine addresses the Pelagians thus (k): “Your heresy has been brought to this, that your followers groan that no Dialectician Judges from the Schools of the Peripatetics are to be found in the Church by whom you might be acquitted.” St. Vincent Ferrer exclaims querulously (l) that Aristotle and Averroes were vials of the wrath of God poured out upon the waters of Christian wisdom, whence they were made bitter as wormwood. Whoever wishes more, let him read the celebrated Guido Grandi. Let us follow our History.

30 Occidentales interea Provincias haud paulò alia rerum facies habuit. Arabes namque sub finem octavi seculi, & noni principium subactis antea amplissimis regionibus per Africam latè & Hispaniam dominationem adepti, Aristotelis doctrinam ex Graeco Arabicè,& ex Arabico Latinè redditam, commentariisque illustratam exsuscitarunt, atque in scholas publicas invexére; quae quidem ratio ipsos penè quingentos annos tenuit, linguarum Graecae ac Latinae intelligentia ferè consepultâ. Haec philosophandi methodus per Arabes in Hispaniam invecta ad Anglos & Gallos transmigravit, latèque diffussa est, Platonis tùm facundus & uberior in sermone stylus negligi, acumen dialecticum vigére coepit, Aristotelis interpretibus subtile, minutum, contentiosum, nimiùm loquax disserendi genus studiosè consectantibus: quos inter praecipui numerantur Avicenna, Alpharabius, Alchindus, omnium autem facile princeps Averroes, Cordubensis, nuncupatione singulari Commentator adpellatus. Hinc nata Philosophia disputatrix, & contentiosa, quae sermonis barbariem secum in Scholas invexit, & Scholastica vocata est, eo quod in Scholis ad nostra usque tempora sit usurpata: quamvis tamen variam diversis temporibus fortunam experta sit, de qua si longiùs orationem protrahere mens foret exscribenda mihi essent integra volumina Bruckerii, aliorumque; aliqua tamen capita delibabimus.

30 The Western Provinces, meanwhile, presented a far different face of things. For the Arabs, toward the end of the eighth century and the beginning of the ninth, having previously subdued very extensive regions and obtained dominion far and wide through Africa and Spain, revived the doctrine of Aristotle, rendered from Greek into Arabic and from Arabic into Latin and illustrated with commentaries, and brought it into the public schools; and this system indeed held them for nearly five hundred years, the understanding of the Greek and Latin languages being almost buried along with it. This method of philosophizing, brought by the Arabs into Spain, migrated to the English and the French and was spread far and wide; then the eloquent and richer style of Plato’s discourse began to be neglected and dialectical acumen to flourish, the interpreters of Aristotle zealously pursuing a subtle, minute, contentious, excessively talkative manner of discoursing: among whom are reckoned as chief Avicenna, Alfarabi, Alkindi, but easily the prince of all Averroes of Córdoba, called by the singular title of the Commentator. Hence was born the disputatious and contentious Philosophy, which brought barbarism of speech with it into the Schools, and was called Scholastic, because it has been in use in the Schools down to our own times; although it has met with varied fortune at different times, and if I had a mind to draw out my discourse on it at greater length, whole volumes of Brucker and others would have to be copied out by me; we shall, however, touch on some chief points.

31 Anno 1209. Parisiensis Concilii Decreto praecipui Aristotelis libri combusti sunt, & eorum lectio interdicta. Anno 1591 Franciscus Patricius Gregorio XIV. suadet ut é Scholis Christianorum Aristotelis Philosophia tollatur. Postea vero Petrus Ramus Parisis defendit Theses contra Aristotelis doctrinam Dein Johann. Picus Mirandulanus Philosophiam Pythagoricam restituere conatus est. Besarion & Marcilius Ficinus Platonicam, Gaspar Sciopius Stoicam, Bernardinus Telesius illam quae Parmenidis adpellatur.

31 In the year 1209, by Decree of the Council of Paris, the principal books of Aristotle were burned and the reading of them forbidden. In the year 1591 Francesco Patrizi urges Gregory XIV to remove the Philosophy of Aristotle from the Schools of Christians. Afterwards Peter Ramus defended Theses at Paris against the doctrine of Aristotle. Then John Pico della Mirandola attempted to restore the Pythagorean Philosophy, Bessarion and Marsilio Ficino the Platonic, Caspar Scioppius the Stoic, Bernardino Telesio that which is called the Parmenidean.

32 Scholasticae Philosophiae Principem alii Lanfrancum Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem statuunt. Nonnulli, inter quos Naudaeus à D. Johann. Damasceno primam originem repetunt, á quo ad
