ELEMENTORUM RECENTIORIS PHILOSOPHIAE

OF THE NEWER PHILOSOPHY

PARS I. ELEMENTA LOGICES. — PA RT I . ELEMENTS OF LOGIC

p. 1

ELEMENTA — ELEMENTS

RECENTIORIS PHILOSOPHIAE.

OF THE NEWER PHILOSOPHY.

PROLEGOMENA.

PROLEGOMENA .

1 Philosophia, cujus praecipuas partes veluti in núcleo exhibebimus, est cognitio veri, boni, atque honesti solo naturae lumine, & ratiocinio inde ducto comparata. Ratiocinium, seu recta ratio est expedita facultas veritates alias ex aliis cum quibus connectuntur eliciendi. Ex quo facilè patet philosophiam Scepticam, quia nihil certò cognosci posse profitétur, Philosophiae nomen haud meréri, sed Dogmaticam.

hilosophy, whose principal parts we shall set forth as it were in a nut1 P shell, is the knowledge of the true, the good and the honorable, acquired by the light of nature alone and by reasoning drawn from it. Reasoning, or right reason, is the ready faculty of eliciting truths from other truths with which they are connected. From this it is easily seen that Sceptical philosophy, since it professes that nothing can be known with certainty, does not deserve the name of Philosophy, whereas Dogmatic philosophy does.

2 Neque obscurum est, id vocabulum adtribuendum non esse scientiae veri, & boni, quam vel à majoribus per manus traditam accepimus, vel ex docti cujusdam praeceptis repétimus. Unde éxsulat Philosophia Traditionaria, & Sectaria, quum nulla harum ex recta ratione derivétur. Prima enim tota nítitur auctoritate majorum, secunda verò auctoritate unius hominis, qui sectariis pro oraculo est. Hinc divisiones Philosophiae, quas vulgò adferunt minus adcuratae sunt, nam Scepticam, & Sectariam non magis adcuratè dixeris Philosophiam quàm statuam hominem.

2 Nor is it obscure that this name is not to be attributed to a knowledge of the true and the good which we have either received from our elders, handed down from hand to hand, or draw from the precepts of some learned man. Hence Traditionary and Sectarian Philosophy are banished, since neither of them is derived from right reason. For the first rests wholly on the authority of the elders, the second on the authority of one man, who is an oracle to his sectaries. Hence the divisions of Philosophy that are commonly offered are less than accurate; for you would no more accurately call Sceptical and Sectarian philosophy Philosophy than call a statue a man.

3 Quod verò adtinet ad Philosophiam illam Eclecticam, latinè Electivam ea est, in qua sapientiam ratione tantùm quaérimus, rationem autem régimus sensuum experimentis, & observationibus, ìntima conscientia, ratiocinatione, & auctoritate círca ea, quae alia via sciri nequeunt. In hac ratione philosophandi non quaéritur, quis quidpiam dixerit, sed quàm rectè, id est, quàm rationi conforme. Ita autem philosophandum esse praeclarè demonstrat Lactantius, cujus locum integrum ponam; est enim lectu dignissimus.

3 As for that Eclectic Philosophy, in Latin Elective, it is the one in which we seek wisdom by reason alone, and govern reason by the experiments of the senses and by observations, by inner consciousness, by reasoning, and by authority in those things that cannot be known by any other way. In this manner of philosophizing one does not ask who said a thing, but how rightly, that is, how conformably to reason. That one must philosophize in this way is splendidly demonstrated by Lactantius, whose passage I shall give whole; for it is most worthy of being read.

4 ,, Quare oportet, inquit, in ea re maximè, in qua vitae ratio versátur, sibi quemquam confídere, suoque judicio, ac suis sénsibus niti, ad investigandam & perpendendam veritatem, quàm credentem alienis erroribus décipi, tamquam

4 “Wherefore,” he says, “in that matter above all in which the conduct of life is at stake, each man ought to trust himself and rely on his own judgment and his own senses for investigating and weighing the truth, rather than, by believing, be deceived by the errors of others, as if he himself

p. 2

ipsum rationis expertem. Dedit omnibus Deus pro virili portione sapientiam, ut & inaudita investigare possent, & audita perpéndere. Nec quia nos majores nostri temporibus antecessérunt, sapientia quoque antecessérunt, quae si omnibus aequaliter datur; occupári ab antecedentibus non potest. Illibábilis est, tamquam lux & claritas solis: quia ut sol oculorum, sic sapientia lumen est cordis humani. Quare cum sápere, id est veritatem quaérere, omnibus sit innatum, sapientiam sibi ádimunt, qui sine ullo judicio inventa majorum probant, & ab aliis pécudum more ducuntur. Sed hoc eos fallit, quod majorum nomine posito, non putant fieri posse, ut aut ipsi plus sapiant, quia minores vocantur; aut illi desipuérint, quia majores nominantur.

were devoid of reason. God has given wisdom to all according to each one’s share, so that they might both search out things unheard and weigh things heard. Nor, because our elders went before us in time, did they also go before us in wisdom; for if wisdom is given to all equally, it cannot be seized beforehand by those who came first. It cannot be diminished, like the light and brightness of the sun: for as the sun is the light of the eyes, so wisdom is the light of the human heart. Wherefore, since to be wise, that is, to seek the truth, is innate in all men, those deprive themselves of wisdom who without any judgment approve the discoveries of their elders and are led by others in the manner of cattle. But what deceives them is this: once the name of elders is set before them, they do not think it can happen either that they themselves are wiser, because they are called younger, or that those others were foolish, because they are named elders.”

5 Quae omnia de scientiis naturalibus, ut est, ex. gr. Philosophia intelligenda sunt. Nam de eo, qui adrogantissimè brevi humana ratione Dei auctoritati, id est summae rationi insultat, ¿ quid ego dicam aliud, nisi omnem rationem excútere? Quod qui éfficit, is non Philosophus, sed ne rationalis quidem est. In naturali ergò scientia eam libertatem commendámus. quae nullam ab Ecclesia, nullam ab ejus dogmátibus probat alienationem. Haec est Eclectica Philosophia, in qua omni cura, omnique studio incumbendum vobis esse reor. Est enim illa, ut cum Tullio loquar, cujus studium qui vituperat haud sanè intelligo, quidnam sit, quod laudandum putet.

5 All these things are to be understood of the natural sciences, such as, for example, Philosophy is. For of him who most arrogantly, with his brief human reason, insults the authority of God, that is, the highest reason, what else am I to say than that he casts off all reason? He who does this is not a Philosopher; he is not even rational. In natural science, therefore, we commend that freedom which approves no estrangement from the Church, none from her dogmas. This is the Eclectic Philosophy, to which I judge you must apply yourselves with all care and all zeal. For it is that philosophy, to speak with Tully, whose study, if anyone disparages it, I truly do not understand what it is that he thinks worthy of praise.

6 Quum porrò ad veram hominis utilitatem comparata sit Philosophia, talis que sit finis qualia sunt media: cónsequens est, ut subtiliores speculationes Peripateticorum de rebus, quae vel humana ratione indagari nequeunt, vel saltim nihil emolumenti generi humano adferre possunt, tantò minus ad sapientiae studium pertinébunt, quantò minus conjunctae sunt cum verâ hominis felicitate, quam in cognoscendo Deum naturae conditórem, atque omnis veri, boni, & honesti principium & finem sitam esse, cum melioris notae Theologis censémus.

6 Since, further, Philosophy is designed for the true utility of man, and the end is of the same kind as the means: it follows that the subtler speculations of the Peripatetics about things that either cannot be searched out by human reason, or at least can bring no profit to the human race, will belong to the study of wisdom the less, the less they are joined with the true happiness of man, which, with the Theologians of better note, we judge to consist in knowing God, the founder of nature, and the beginning and end of everything true, good and honorable.

7 Quia denique Philosophia in veri & boni cognitione consistit: ea Philosophiae pars, quae mentem ad veri cognitionem praeparat Instrumentalis, seu Logica, quae eamdem cognitione illa imbuit, Theoretica, quae deniquae illam ad verum bonum perdúcit Practica solet adpelari. Theoretica, quum mentem cognitione veri imbuat, aut veritates de Deo, spiritibus, & ente inquirit, aut quid circa rerum naturalium causas, verum sit, investígat. Priore casu Metaphysica, posteriore Physica nuncupatur. Denique quum Practica viam ad bonum ostendat: ea, vel quid generatim bonum, vel in specie quid justum, decorum, vel utile

7 Since, finally, Philosophy consists in the knowledge of the true and the good: that part of Philosophy which prepares the mind for the knowledge of the true is usually called Instrumental, or Logic; that which imbues it with that knowledge, Theoretical; and that which finally leads it to the true good, Practical. The Theoretical, since it imbues the mind with the knowledge of the true, either inquires into truths about God, spirits and being, or investigates what is true concerning the causes of natural things. In the former case it is called Metaphysics, in the latter Physics. Finally, since the Practical shows the way to the good: it is either what is good in general, or in particular what is just, becoming, or useful, that it

p. 3

sit docet. De bono in genere Ethica, de justo, honesto & decóro Jus naturale, de utili Politica, & Oeconomica agunt. Quum verò angustiae temporis non sinant me in omnibus Philosophiae partibus explicandis diutiùs immorari, Logicam; Metaphysicam, Ethicam paulò fortè quàm oportéret breviùs; Physicam multò liberiùs explicabo.

teaches. Of the good in general Ethics treats; of the just, the honorable and the becoming, Natural Law; of the useful, Politics and Economics. But since the narrowness of time does not allow me to linger too long in explaining all the parts of Philosophy, I shall explain Logic, Metaphysics and Ethics somewhat more briefly, perhaps, than was fitting; Physics much more fully.

8 Sed antequam opus incipiam Creatorem, & Gubernatorem rerum omnium Deum demissè ínvoco, & rogo, mihi scribenti ne desit, sed mentem sua luce perfundat, ne in hisce lucubrandis abérrem; quin potius praeceptiones eas tradam, quae puerorum mentes non modò ad ista, quae mundo adspectabili continentur penitùs intelligenda, sed, quod maximè curare debemus, ad caelestia illa, & beatum adspectum Conditoris, quodammodò perducant, neu sinat, ut aliquid quod à Romana Ecclesia vel à Legibus sancítis alienum sit, nobis imprudentibus excíderit.

8 But before I begin the work, I humbly invoke God, the Creator and Governor of all things, and I beg him not to fail me as I write, but to flood my mind with his light, lest I go astray in these lucubrations; rather, that I may hand down such precepts as will lead the minds of boys not only to a thorough understanding of these things contained in the visible world, but also (what we ought most of all to care for) in some manner to those heavenly things and to the blessed vision of the Maker; and that he not permit anything alien to the Roman Church or to the sanctioned Laws to slip from us unawares.

9 Quod si per humanam infirmitatem erravérimus, quidquid dixérimus, condemnamus: ac nos, nostraque omnia Pontificis Maximi judicio libentissimè submíttimus. Quod si interdùm nos auctorem aliquem haereticum laudábimus, hominis eruditionem laudamus, improbitatem detestámur, nec legendum propónimus nisi quibus gravissimi judices ad quos pertinet, legendi copiam fécerint.

9 But if through human infirmity we shall have erred, whatever we have said we condemn: and we most willingly submit ourselves and all that is ours to the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff. And if at times we shall praise some heretical author, we praise the man’s learning and detest his wickedness, nor do we propose him for reading except to those to whom the most grave judges whose office it is have granted leave to read.

10 Vos autem Adolescentes lectissimi, eo & moneo, & hortor demissé Deum invocétis, qui vobis bonam mentem largiatur, enixèque Angelicum Magistrum D. Thomam Aquinátem adprecémini, qui vobis à D. O. M. intelligendi acúmen obtineat. Nisi enim antè Dei praeceptis mentem vestram imbuéritis nunquàm (mihi credite) vos veram Philosophiam adsequémini, Faxit Deus, ut quemadmodùm vestri gratia, & ut vos ad optima studia perdúcerem, hujusmodi laborem adgredior; vicissim vos mihi, meisque conatibus respondéatis.

10 But you, most excellent Young Men, I both admonish and exhort humbly to call upon God, that he may grant you a good mind, and earnestly to pray to the Angelic Master St. Thomas Aquinas, that he may obtain for you from God, Best and Greatest, sharpness of understanding. For unless you first imbue your mind with the precepts of God, never (believe me) will you attain the true Philosophy. God grant that, just as I undertake a labor of this kind for your sake and to lead you to the best studies, you in turn may answer to me and to my efforts.

p. 4

ELEMENTORUM

OF THE ELEMENTS

RECENTIORIS PHILOSOPHIAE

OF THE NEWER PHILOSOPHY

PARS I. LIB. I.

PART I. BOOK I .

ELEMENTA LOGICES — ELEMENTS OF LOGIC

CAPUT. I. — CHAPTER I

De Logicae natura, & constitutione.

On the nature and constitution of Logic. 1

1 Quum Philosophia sit cognitio veri, & ad illam cognitionem intellectum praéparet Logica: definiri ea potest quamoptimè, Disciplina quae mentem perpolit, ut in omni loco, & tempore verum consequatur, vel breviùs: Scientia de invenienda proponendaque veritate. Quumque véritas vel certò constet, vel tantùm probabíliter, de utróque Logicum solícitum esse oportet.

Since Philosophy is the knowledge of the true, and Logic prepares the intellect for that knowledge, it can very well be defined as the Discipline that refines the mind so that it may attain the truth in every place and time, or more briefly: the Science of finding and setting forth the truth. And since the truth is established either with certainty or only probably, the Logician must be concerned with both.

2 Et quamvis, omnes homines, nisi morbo impediantur, recta ratione, id est, facultate ratiocinandi pólleant, & hinc negári non possit dari Logicam naturalem; inde tamen non séquitur, ut Artificialis sit negligenda, quia ars naturam pérficit, & intellectus non solum facultate, sed & promptitudine ratiocinandi, quin & methodo cogitationes, ratiocinationesque disponendi instructus esse debet. Nam & facultate numerandi ex. gr. solâ naturâ duce gaudet homo, & potentiâ saltandi, loquendi, persuadendi, nec quisquam tamen dúbitat, quin Arithmetica, Ars Saltatoria, Grammatica, Rethorica utilissimae sint. Utilitas ergò Logicae in omni genere eruditionis planè admiranda est. ¿Quem enim alium studiorum omnium finem nobis propónimus, quàm ut veritatem inveniámus, ac inventam communicémus cum aliis?

2 And although all men, unless hindered by disease, are strong in right reason, that is, in the faculty of reasoning, so that it cannot be denied that there is a natural Logic, it does not follow from this that the Artificial is to be neglected; for art perfects nature, and the intellect must be furnished not only with the faculty but also with readiness in reasoning, and indeed with method in arranging thoughts and reasonings. For man enjoys, for example, the faculty of counting under the guidance of nature alone, and the power of dancing, of speaking, of persuading; and yet no one doubts that Arithmetic, the Art of Dancing, Grammar and Rhetoric are most useful. The utility of Logic in every kind of learning is therefore altogether to be admired. For what other end of all our studies do we set before ourselves than to find the truth and, having found it, to communicate it to others?

3 Magnâ curâ Logicam olim excoluit Zeno Eleates, cui originem hujus scientiae acceptum vulgò réferunt. Excoluerunt etiam Megarici, Stoici, Epicurei. Nos in id acri studio

3 Zeno of Elea, to whom the origin of this science is commonly credited, once cultivated Logic with great care. The Megarians, Stoics and Epicureans also cultivated it. We shall apply ourselves to it with keen zeal,

p. 5

incumbémus, ut optima quaevis praecepta, quae à Recentioribus trádita accépimus eo ordine proponámus, qui naturae hujus disciplinae nobis videtur quàm convenientíssimus; commodíssimum autem videtur primò considerare naturam intellectus humani, deinde naturam veritatis, ac demùm quomodo ea invenienda, proponendaque sit disquirere.

so that we may set forth all the best precepts that we have received as handed down by the Moderns, in the order that seems to us most suited to the nature of this discipline; and it seems most convenient to consider first the nature of the human intellect, then the nature of truth, and finally to inquire how truth is to be found and set forth.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II. On the Nature of the human intellect, and on the operations of

De Natura intellectus humani, deque mentis operationibus.

the mind.

Circa Verum intellectus, circa Bonum voluntas magis occupata est. Quum ergò Logica tradat rationem inveniendi, proponendique veritatem; facilè patet eam docéri non posse, nisi vires animi, seu intellectus humani, ejusque operationes probè perspectas habeamus.

The intellect is occupied rather with the True, the will with the Good. Since, therefore, Logic teaches the method of finding and setting forth the truth, it is easily seen that it cannot be taught unless we have thoroughly examined the powers of the mind, or human intellect, and its operations.

5 Corpore, & Spiritu constat hoc ánimans, quem vocamus Hominem. In corpore haec omnia insunt: extensio, divisibilitas, soliditas, figurabílitas, partium mobílitas, &c. Contra verò Spiritus est id, quod in homine est, & corpus non est, nec ab ullo videtur: conjícimus autem adesse aliquod principium incorpóreum dírigens, ex rebus quae in máchina corporea fiunt sat spectabílibus; quod verò adtinet ad internas animi operationes, illae ex íntima demùm ipsiusmet hominis convictione constant. Etenim experímur esse in nobis rem aliquam, quae cognóscit, & vult. Nam & amicos cognóscimus, & bona illis optámus, & membra nostra pro lubitu nostro torquémus. Etenim certò scio me brachium movére, si volo, si verò nolo, non movére. Proinde, est in me aliquid, quod praeest machinationi huic eamque regit & moderatur.

5 This living being which we call Man consists of Body and Spirit. In the body all these are found: extension, divisibility, solidity, figurability, mobility of parts, etc. Spirit, on the other hand, is that which is in man and is not body, nor is seen by anyone: we infer, however, that some incorporeal directing principle is present from the things, conspicuous enough, that take place in the bodily machine; while as for the internal operations of the mind, these are established, in the end, by the innermost conviction of man himself. For we experience that there is in us something that knows and wills. For we both know our friends and wish them well, and we turn our limbs at our pleasure. For I know for certain that I move my arm if I will to, and do not move it if I do not will to. Accordingly, there is something in me that presides over this machinery and rules and governs it.

6 Vicissim & corpus nostrum si adpulsu externi corporis adfícitur, id ope organorum machinationis nostrae, quos sensus vocant, animus sentit: si enim cutículae ignem admoveas, haec corporis adfectio ab animo sentítur. Dolorem item sentio, cum digitum mihi pungit spína. Corpus itaque menti obtémperat, eaque, quae illa ímperat exséquitur, & vicissim animus quidquid sensuum ope percípitur, sentit ipse. Alterum

6 In turn, if our body is affected by the impact of an external body, the mind feels it by means of those organs of our machinery which are called senses: for if you bring fire near the skin, this affection of the body is felt by the mind. Likewise I feel pain when a thorn pricks my finger. The body, therefore, obeys the mind and carries out what the mind commands, and in turn the mind itself feels whatever is perceived by means of the senses. But that the one

p. 6

autem ab altero movéri & pendére, illud ipsum est, quod vocatur complexio, seu commercium animi, & corporis.

is moved by the other and depends on it, this is the very thing that is called the complexion, or commerce, of the mind and the body.

7 Quidquid ergò illud sit, quod intelligit, & vult, (de quo alio loco erit dicendum) illud certum est, esse in homine rem aliquam, quae cognoscit, & vult, quam vocamus animum, mentem, animam rationalem, spiritum, &c. Certum denique est, corpus, & animum duas esse substantias omninò distinctas. Animus percipit rerum formas, discernit, júdicat, ratiocinatur, sentit, adfectibus commovetur, &c. quae nemo corpori tribuerit, nisi stultè: anima igitur non est corpus.

7 Whatever, then, that may be which understands and wills (of which we shall have to speak in another place), this much is certain: that there is in man something which knows and wills, which we call the soul, the mind, the rational soul, the spirit, etc. Finally, it is certain that body and mind are two altogether distinct substances. The mind perceives the forms of things, discerns, judges, reasons, feels, is stirred by passions, etc., things which no one would attribute to the body except foolishly: the soul, therefore, is not body.

8 Nobis etiam compertum est, animum nostrum peculiare hoc habere, ut intélligat, ita ut intelligendo alias & alias cognitiones rectè atque ordine eliciat, tùm etiam liberè operétur. Nimirum cùm mens objectam rem presentem sibi facit, eam pércipit. Quid autem sit idea, quid perceptio magna dissentio est. 2 Ut autem aequivocatio omnis è medio tollatur, constituimus primò, nos ideae nomine, perceptionem quamcumque cujusvis rei adpelare. Igitur omnis notio, vel comprehensio, vel perceptio quaecumque sit, idea à nobis dicitur. Hinc ex. gr. notio, perceptio ve figurae, plantae, animalis, voluptatis, &c. idea est.

8 We have also found that our mind has this peculiar to it, that it understands, so that in understanding it elicits one cognition after another rightly and in order, and also that it acts freely. That is to say, when the mind makes an object present to itself, it perceives it. But what an idea is, and what a perception, is a matter of great disagreement. (a) In order, however, that all equivocation be removed, we lay down first that by the name of idea we mean any perception whatever of any thing whatever. Every notion, therefore, or comprehension, or perception, whatever it may be, is called by us an idea. Hence, e.g., the notion or perception of a figure, a plant, an animal, a pleasure, etc., is an idea.

9 Res externas percípimus, quae organa nostra sensoria adficiunt. Ea autem est sensationum lex, ut quotiès ab objecto sensibili mutatio quaedam producitur in órgano sensorio ritè

9 We perceive the external things that affect our sense organs. Now this is the law of sensations, that whenever some change is produced by a sensible object in a duly

Sunt, qui idéas & perceptiones idem esse censeant, & dicunt, consistere in motibus sensuum, & cérebri. Ita Hobbesius Leviath. P. 1. cap. 3. 4. & in Elem. Philosoph. cap. 25. art. 2. Sunt, qui idéas & perceptiones eamdem mentis cognitionem dicant: ita tamen, ut eadem cognitio dum ad mentem fertur, quae percipit; adpeletur perceptio: dùm ad objectam rem, cujus est imago, & quae percípitur; idèa. Ita Arnaldus & Lockius Essai sur l' Entendement Humain in Praefat. & lib. 2. c. 8. §. 7. 8. Alii omninò perceptiones ab ideis sejungunt, & putant, Deum humanae menti idéas rerum imprimere. Ita Malebranche. Recherche de la Veritè lib. 3. Postremo alli ideas materiales ajunt esse adfectiones sensuum, & cérebri: intellectuales verò, quae materialibus respondent, esse perceptiones materialium. Ita Vvolff. à quo non dissentiunt Scholastici, qui tamen idéam materialem vocant intellectionem. In tanta doctissimorum hominum dissentione, aliquid certi velle proferre adrogantis esset.

There are those who hold that ideas and perceptions are the same thing, and say that they consist in motions of the senses and of the brain. So Hobbes, Leviathan, pt. 1, ch. 3, 4, and in Elem. Philosoph. ch. 25, art. 2. There are those who say that ideas and perceptions are the same cognition of the mind, yet in such a way that the same cognition, inasmuch as it is referred to the mind which perceives, is called perception; inasmuch as it is referred to the object of which it is the image, and which is perceived, idea. So Arnauld and Locke, Essai sur l’Entendement Humain, in the Preface, and bk. 2, ch. 8, §. 7, 8. Others altogether separate perceptions from ideas, and think that God impresses the ideas of things on the human mind. So Malebranche, Recherche de la Verité, bk. 3. Lastly, others say that material ideas are affections of the senses and of the brain, while intellectual ones, which correspond to the material, are perceptions of material things. So Wolff, from whom the Scholastics do not dissent, though they call the material idea an intellection. Amid so great a disagreement among the most learned men, it would be arrogant to wish to put forward anything as certain.

p. 7

constituto, totiès in anima oriatur sensatio quaedam particularis, huic mutationi respondens. Itaque motiones sensuum cérebrum adficiunt, & illi aliquid ímprimunt, ex quo mens pércipit res quae sensum pulsant, 2 quod plurimis exemplis confirmat Hallerius 2 in notis ad Boerhaavium. Haec perceptio mentis vocatur idea.

constituted sense organ, so often there arises in the soul a certain particular sensation corresponding to this change. Thus the motions of the senses affect the brain and impress something on it, from which the mind perceives the things that strike the sense, (b) as Haller (c) confirms with very many examples in his notes to Boerhaave. This perception of the mind is called an idea.

10 Quando idéas simplices adquírit intellectus, id est, cum objectam rem praesentem sibi facit, eamque pércipit, quin ad aliam réferat, ex. gr. cum solem, aut equum cognoscit, haec cognitio vocatur simpliciter perceptio, vel ut Scholastici loquuntur Simplex apraehensio, seu cognitio nihil adfirmans vel negans; cum verò intellectus binas ideas inter se cómparat, unamque ad aliam refert, & pércipit conveníre álteri, aut non; ex. gr. cum dicit Sol est lucidus, Sol non est equus, haec cognitio est judicium, seu actus intellectus, quo aliquid de objecto adfirmamus aut negamus. Quando intellectus tres idéas interse confert Ratiocinari dicitur. Raciocinatio autèm, seu discursus est actio mentis, quâ plures ideas, quarum una ab alia dependet compónimus, ut quod latebat detegámus. Quaeritur ¿utrum aër sit gravis? Non statim id liquidò adpáret; utor ergò ratiocinio hoc modo: quidquid lanci impositum eam deprimit illud est grave, aer lanci impositus eam dèprimit: ergo aer est gravis.

10 When the intellect acquires simple ideas, that is, when it makes an object present to itself and perceives it without referring it to another, e.g. when it knows the sun, or a horse, this cognition is called simply perception, or, as the Scholastics put it, Simple apprehension, that is, a cognition affirming or denying nothing; but when the intellect compares two ideas with each other, refers one to the other, and perceives that it agrees with the other, or not, e.g. when it says The sun is bright, The sun is not a horse, this cognition is judgment, or the act of the intellect by which we affirm or deny something of an object. When the intellect compares three ideas with one another, it is said to Reason. Reasoning, or discourse, is the action of the mind by which we put together several ideas, of which one depends on another, so as to uncover what lay hidden. The question is asked: is air heavy? This is not at once clearly apparent; I therefore use reasoning in this way: whatever, placed on a scale-pan, presses it down is heavy; air placed on a scale-pan presses it down: therefore air is heavy.

11 Praeterea, animus noster plures idéas rerum longè differentium compónit: ut cùm humano capiti, leoninum corpus & alas adjungit, ac novum animal fingit. Interdùm è contrario ideam unam ab alia mens veluti disjúngit: ut cum albitúdinem parietis cogitamus, quin de pariete cogitémus. Aliquando cogitationes, & ratiocinia sua ordine dispónit, quò faciliùs perspiciat, an ex aliis in alia sit procedendum. Haec mentis operatio vocatur Methodus. Aliquando posteaquam in utramque partem disputatum, controversumque est, nec planè intellectum

11 Further, our mind puts together several ideas of things very different from one another, as when it joins a lion’s body and wings to a human head and feigns a new animal. Sometimes, on the contrary, the mind as it were disjoins one idea from another: as when we think of the whiteness of a wall without thinking of the wall. Sometimes it arranges its thoughts and reasonings in order, the more easily to see whether one ought to proceed from some to others. This operation of the mind is called Method. Sometimes, after the matter has been argued and disputed on both sides, and it is not clearly understood

Id ita se habére, vel ex hoc apertè effícitur, quod morbus capitis acutissimus, vel cranii fractúra, vel ejusmodi morbi, qui in cérebro & capite evenérunt, interdùm memoriam rerum delerunt omnem, interdûm verò rerum intelligentiam abstulérunt. Quod etiam in dementibus, & vesánis évenit, qui cérebri vitio incónditè, & inconsultè loquuntur. Quumque animus nec aegrescat, nec mutetur, quoniam hae adfectiones corporeae sunt; relínquitur, aliquid in cérebro ímprimi, ex quo nos rerum formas, & idéas percípimus.

That this is so is plainly shown even from this: that a very acute disease of the head, or a fracture of the skull, or diseases of that kind which have occurred in the brain and the head, have sometimes destroyed all memory of things, and sometimes taken away the understanding of things. This also happens in the demented and the insane, who through a defect of the brain speak incoherently and senselessly. And since the mind neither falls sick nor is changed, because these affections are bodily, it remains that something is impressed in the brain, from which we perceive the forms and ideas of things.

Tom. 4. §. 581.

Vol. 4, §. 581.

p. 8

è qua parte stet veritas, dubitàt mens, seu à judicando supersédet. Postremò, ut alia omittam, cùm mens rem iteratò percipit, & insuper conscia est, eamdem sibi jam pridem cognitam esse, haec operatio vocatur Memoria.

on which side the truth stands, the mind doubts, or suspends judgment. Finally, to pass over other things, when the mind perceives a thing again and is moreover conscious that it had known that same thing long before, this operation is called Memory.

12 Ex quo manifestum fit, plures quàm vulgares Logici Aristotelici suspicantur, esse mentis operationes, á quibus rectè definítur intellectus: facultas mentis, quae percipit, judicat, ratiocinatur, disponit, &c. Probè tamen memoriâ tenenda est potestas, ac diversitas nominum, quae facultates mentis significant, & pássim occurrunt. Phantasia, seu Imaginatio est, vis illa mentis, quâ res omnes corporea imagine expraesas nobis repraesentámus. Ingenium est mentis solertia in inveniendo, & excogitando. Judicium est facultas seligendi ea quae recta sunt, iisque pro rei dignitate utendi. Et ea quidem quae compónit ingenium non semper re ipsa existunt. Possem enim facilè in mente conjúngere idéas auri, & montis, & mihi formare imáginem montis aurei, qui tamen extra cogitationem non existit. Ejusmodi idaee vocantur chimaericae, vel entia rationis.

12 From this it becomes manifest that there are more operations of the mind than the common Aristotelian Logicians suppose; and by them the intellect is rightly defined: the faculty of the mind which perceives, judges, reasons, disposes, etc. One must, however, keep well in mind the force and the variety of the names that signify faculties of the mind and occur here and there. Phantasy, or Imagination, is that power of the mind by which we represent to ourselves all things expressed by a bodily image. Ingenuity is the mind’s skill in discovering and devising. Judgment is the faculty of selecting the things that are right and of using them according to the worth of the matter. And indeed the things that ingenuity composes do not always exist in reality. For I can easily join in my mind the ideas of gold and of a mountain, and form for myself the image of a golden mountain, which nevertheless does not exist outside thought. Ideas of this kind are called chimerical, or beings of reason.

13 Ex quo autem patet haec entia rationis non confundenda esse cum non entibus, quae planè non sunt objecta mentis, de quibus quippe nihil cogitari potest. Sic circulus quadratus est non ens, quia de eo, ne cogitari quidem quidquam potest. Quum itaque, quae componit ingenium non semper re ipsâ existant: judicio opus est, quod rem ab umbra, chimaeram ab ipsa re adcuratè secernat. Hinc quò rectiùs est hominis judicium, eò magis ad veritatem inveniendam, atque proponendam idóneus erit. Hinc etiam perspicuum est, cur illi, qui ingenio ádmodùm valent, judicio plerùmque non itèm: nam ingenium in excogitando, & componendo quodlibet occupatur: contrà judicium in separando recta à non rectis, quae longè interse discrepant.

13 From this, moreover, it is plain that these beings of reason are not to be confused with non-beings, which are not objects of the mind at all, since nothing can be thought about them. Thus a square circle is a non-being, because nothing whatever can even be thought about it. Since, therefore, the things that ingenuity composes do not always exist in reality, there is need of judgment to distinguish accurately the thing from the shadow, the chimera from the reality itself. Hence the more correct a man’s judgment is, the fitter he will be for finding and setting forth the truth. Hence it is also clear why those who are very strong in ingenuity are generally not so in judgment: for ingenuity is occupied in devising and composing anything whatever, whereas judgment is occupied in separating the right from the not right, which differ widely from each other.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

¿Quomodo se habeant sensus ad ideas acquirendas?

How are the senses related to the acquiring of ideas?

14 Licet non omnes omninò ideae à sensu proficiscantur, ut existimat Lockius; 2 tamen si de majori earum parte loquimur verum est, sensus fenestras esse

14 Although not all ideas whatsoever proceed from sense, as Locke holds (d), it is nevertheless true, if we speak of the greater part of them, that the senses are the windows of the mind, through

p. 9

animi, per quas in eum primaevae notiones ingrediuntur, ipseque cétera, quae extra sunt intelligit. Quoniam verò quàm facilè id fiat, nisi fabricationis sensuum rudem aliquam ideam habeamus, cognosci non potest; paucula praemittémus, quae ad ea, quae sequuntur viam sternant.

through which the first notions enter into it, and by which it understands the other things that are outside it. But since how easily this comes about cannot be known unless we have some rough idea of the construction of the senses, we shall set down beforehand a very few things to pave the way for what follows.

15 Quinque sunt sensus machinationis humanae, per quos rerum ideae cum cérebro, & cum mente communicantur: Visus, Auditus, Odoratus, Gustatus, Tactus, quibus nominibus quinque órgana diversa designámus. Et ut à visu ordiamùr, oculi, quibus ille percipitur, peculiarem eamque mirabilem fabricationem habent, quam minutè dilucidare non est hujus loci: tantùm dicimus oculum esse globum ex tribus membraneis praecipuis coagmentátum, nimirùm cornea, uvea, retina; quarum quaelibet humórem suum claudit. Humor qui in medio est, & vocatur crystallinus utrinque est convéxus, & lentis figuram praesefert. Radii lucis ab objecto corpore reflexi, dùm transeunt hanc lentem refringuntur, & inverso situ imaginem 2 objecti in fundo interioris membranae, quam vocant retinam depíngunt. Retina est expansio partis intimae medullaris nervi óptici, qui usque ad sensorium commune pertingit, ut optimè explicat Vvinslouv 2 in expositione anatomica corporis humani.

15 There are five senses of the human machine, by which the ideas of things are communicated to the brain and to the mind: Sight, Hearing, Smell, Taste, Touch, by which names we designate five different organs. And to begin with sight: the eyes, by which it is perceived, have a peculiar and wonderful structure, which it is not the place here to elucidate minutely; let us say only that the eye is a globe composed of three principal membranes, namely the cornea, the uvea and the retina, each of which encloses its own humor. The humor that is in the middle, which is called the crystalline, is convex on both sides and has the shape of a lens. The rays of light reflected from the object body are refracted while they pass through this lens, and paint an inverted image (e) of the object on the back of the inner membrane, which they call the retina. The retina is an expansion of the innermost medullary part of the optic nerve, which reaches as far as the common sensorium, as Winslow (f) explains very well in his anatomical exposition of the human body.

16 Pulso igitur oculo à luce, quae pulsatio cérebro imprimitur ope illius nervi; protinùs habetur, idea, ac perceptio ex. gr. figurae triangularis, vel quadratae, &c. Has verò perceptiones sequitur judicium, quo enuncio, extáre corpus figurae triangularis, vel quadratae, &c. & hoc judicium reliquas sensuum perceptiones conséquitur.

16 When, therefore, the eye has been struck by light, and this impulse has been impressed on the brain by means of that nerve, there is at once an idea and perception, e.g. of a triangular figure, or of a square one, etc. These perceptions are followed by the judgment by which I declare that there exists a body of triangular figure, or of square, etc.; and this judgment follows upon the other perceptions of the senses as well.

17 Auditus organum est instar cochléae cujus in fundo est membrana quaedam tensa, quod Tympanum vocant. Post tympanum sunt quatuor ossícula mobilia, & aër intra quamdam thecam contortam, quae duo forámina habet ad labyrinthum pertinentia, hoc est ad tortuosum meatum in ipsa ossis substantia excavátum: in cujus labyrinthi extrema parte fibrae nervi auditorii dilatantur, qui nervus ad cérebrum proténditur. Fac pulses aes aliquod; motus & fremitus aeris aërem exteriorem

17 The organ of Hearing is like a snail’s shell, at the bottom of which is a certain stretched membrane, which they call the Tympanum. Behind the tympanum are four movable little bones, and air within a certain twisted case which has two openings leading to the labyrinth, that is, to a tortuous passage hollowed out in the very substance of the bone; in the far part of this labyrinth the fibers of the auditory nerve spread out, and this nerve extends to the brain. Suppose you strike some piece of bronze: the motion and vibration of the bronze strike the outer air.

Essai concernant l' Entendement Humain lib. 1.

Essai concernant l’Entendement Humain, bk. 1.

Hanc imagínulam nihil ad visionem fácere, quatenus imago est, jam vel Cartesii aevo, non suspicabantur modò, sed penè evicerant Philosophi Recentiores. Ipse enim ille Renatus Des-Cartes quaerit, ¿quo demum alio occello praedicta imagúncula videatur?

That this little image contributes nothing to vision insofar as it is an image, the Modern Philosophers had, already in the age of Descartes, not only suspected but all but proved. For René Descartes himself asks: by what other little eye, then, is the aforesaid little image to be seen?

Cours d' Anatomie Volum. V.

Cours d’Anatomie, vol. V.

p. 10

pulsat. Aër pulsus, & in cochléa, contractus fertur ad tympanum auris, & illud cómmovet. Porrò tympanum pulsat ossícula, & aërem qui labyrinthum ingrediens, tremórem ipsum cum fibris nervi auditorii commúnicat: qui nervus in cérebro eamdem impressionem facit. En idea sonus, quae varia est, pro diverso tremóre córporum. Cl. Bernardus Nievventtyt 2 ex quo haec desúmpsimus innumera alia de aure refert.

The air, thus struck and compressed in the cochlea, is carried to the tympanum of the ear and sets it in motion. The tympanum in turn strikes the little bones and the air, which, entering the labyrinth, communicates that very tremor to the fibers of the auditory nerve; and this nerve makes the same impression in the brain. Here you have the idea of sound, which varies according to the different tremor of bodies. The celebrated Bernard Nieuwentyt (g), from whom we have taken these things, reports innumerable others about the ear.

18 Vvillis, qui copiosè de saporibus disputat s2 putat Gustum praecipuè situm esse in área superiori linguae. At lingua quibusdam membranis obvólvitur: exterior una, quae dicitur Epidermis: secunda quae multis foraminibus pertúsa est: tertia quae papillis plurimis est conspersa, quae secundam pervádunt, & in epidérmide consistunt. Hae autem prominentiae, sunt quaedam expansiones subtilissimorum nervorum; atque in hisce papillis linguae sapor percípitur, quod hoc ferè modo à plurimis Anatomicis explicatur, & fit. Salinae particulae, itemque spiritus quidam tenuissimus, quibus corpora omnia sápida abundant, acúmine suo feriunt insénsiles nervos, ex quibus papillae illae constant. Motus iste cum cérebro communicatur. Hinc animus sentit hunc motum: hoc est habet perceptionem sapóris.

18 Willis, who treats of flavors at length (h), thinks that Taste is situated chiefly in the upper surface of the tongue. Now the tongue is wrapped in certain membranes: an outer one, which is called the Epidermis; a second, which is pierced with many holes; a third, which is sprinkled with very many papillae, which pass through the second and end in the epidermis. These prominences are certain expansions of very fine nerves; and it is in these papillae of the tongue that flavor is perceived, which is explained by most Anatomists in roughly this way, and so it comes about. Saline particles, and likewise a certain very thin spirit, with which all flavorful bodies abound, strike with their sharpness the sensitive nerves of which those papillae consist. This motion is communicated to the brain. Hence the mind feels this motion, that is, has the perception of flavor.

19 Simili modo Odoratus: membrana illa villosa, quae interiorem narium partem vestit, contexta est plurimis nervis epidermide denudatis; quod in causâ est, cur exquisiti sensus sit, adeó ut vix tacta ingentem commotionem progignat. Et hoc est organum Odoratus: nam particulae subtilissimae tùm olei, tùm salis volatilis, ut vocant, quae à corporibus exhalantur, in istam membranam incurrentes alio, & alio modo véllicant papillas nerveas, quae titillatio per nervos, cérebro imprímitur, ideo sentítur.

19 In like manner Smell: that villous membrane which lines the inner part of the nostrils is woven of very many nerves stripped of epidermis, which is the reason why it is of so exquisite a sense that, when barely touched, it produces a great commotion. And this is the organ of Smell: for the very fine particles, both of oil and of volatile salt, as they call it, which are exhaled from bodies, running into that membrane, twitch the nervous papillae in one way and another; and this titillation is impressed on the brain through the nerves, and so is felt.

20 Tactus demùm proprium hoc est, quod non certum locum ut reliqui sensus habet, sed in toto corpore est: proptereaquod quamcumque corporis partem scalpámus, sentitur contactus corporis. Verumtamen in extremis digitis manus, peculiari modo résidet tactus ad plurima distinguenda. Porrò sub cúticula seu epidermide, hoc est, sub membrana exteriori carnis, exténditur membrana reticulosa & cutis, quae innumeris papillis nerveis conspersa est, & quae papillae ex cute instar subtilissimorum pennicillorum exurgentes, epidermidem ipsam contingunt. Hinc quum tangis carnem, nervum tangis, quumque nervi

20 Finally, this is proper to Touch, that it does not have a definite place, as the other senses do, but is in the whole body: so that whatever part of the body we scratch, the contact of a body is felt. Nevertheless, touch resides in a peculiar manner in the tips of the fingers of the hand, for distinguishing very many things. Further, under the cuticle or epidermis, that is, under the outer membrane of the flesh, there extend the reticular membrane and the skin, which is sprinkled with innumerable nervous papillae; and these papillae, rising out of the skin like very fine little brushes, touch the epidermis itself. Hence when you touch flesh you touch a nerve, and since all the nerves

L' Existence de Dieu demontreè par les merveilles de la Nature. Contempl. XIV.

L’Existence de Dieu demontreè par les merveilles de la Nature, Contempl. XIV.

De anima Brutorum, cap. 12.

De Anima Brutorum, ch. 12.

p. 11

omnes à cérebro, vel à cerebéllo & spinali medúlla ducantur, facillimè eumdem motum in cérebro éxcitant, ex quo mens percipit contactum, id est, adquirit ideam tactus, ut optimè explicat Hallerius, Faye, & Verdier, 2

are led from the brain, or from the cerebellum and the spinal marrow, they very easily excite the same motion in the brain, from which the mind perceives the contact, that is, acquires the idea of touch, as Haller, Faye and Verdier (i) explain very well.

21 Hinc manifestum fit organorum munus esse excipere impressionem corporum, eamque ad cérebrum transmíttere: idque mediis nervis, qui hisce peragendis sunt quàm aptissimi: mentem verò esse quae rerum ideas pro varietate sensuum élicit. Dicimus autem oculum videre, aurem audire, &c. quod secùs est. Nam oculus tantùm excipit cum imagine motum quendam, ut ita dicam, quem cùm cérebro commúnicat; mens verò per talem motum occasionalitèr admonita sibi eformat ideam rei visae. Sed quum motum illum organi, sequatur mentis perceptio, idcircò utrumque confúndimus; & existimamus oculum videre, &c.: quamvis nos lateat omninò quo pacto sensuum adfectiones ad cérebrum perveniant, easque motitationes, quae in cerebro imprimuntur mens nostra percipiat. Itaque in omnibus penè sensationibus, ut optimè notat Mallebranche, 2 quatuor licet diversa confunduntur, quia scilicet simul, & velut uno temporis puncto aguntur.

21 Hence it becomes manifest that the office of the organs is to receive the impression of bodies and to transmit it to the brain, and to do so by means of the nerves, which are most apt for accomplishing this; but that it is the mind which elicits the ideas of things according to the variety of the senses. We say, however, that the eye sees, the ear hears, etc., which is not so. For the eye only receives, together with the image, a certain motion, so to speak, which it communicates to the brain; while the mind, prompted on the occasion of such a motion, forms for itself the idea of the thing seen. But since the perception of the mind follows that motion of the organ, we therefore confuse the two, and think that the eye sees, etc.; although it is altogether hidden from us how the affections of the senses reach the brain, and how our mind perceives those motions that are impressed in the brain. Thus in almost all sensations, as Malebranche (j) very well notes, four things, though different, are confused, namely because they take place together, and as it were in one point of time.

22 Primum quod confunditur est actio corporis externi, hoc est, in calore ex. gr. impulsio, & motus particularum ligni in fibras manus. Secundum est passio organi sensus, hoc est, agitatio fibrarum manus orta ex impulsione particularum ignis, quae agitatio ad cérebrum usque pervenit. Tertium est sensatio aut perceptio mentis, hoc est, id quod quilibet sentit quum ad ignem accedit. Quartum est judicium, quo mens judicat, id quod sentit esse in manu sua & in igne.

22 The first thing that is confused is the action of the external body, that is, in heat, for example, the impulse and motion of the particles of the wood against the fibers of the hand. The second is the passion of the sense organ, that is, the agitation of the fibers of the hand arising from the impulse of the particles of fire, which agitation reaches all the way to the brain. The third is the sensation, or perception of the mind, that is, what anyone feels when he approaches the fire. The fourth is the judgment by which the mind judges that what it feels is in its hand and in the fire.

23 Haec quatuor, ut videre est, longè diversa sunt, nec tamen vulgò distinguuntur; nemo tamen est, qui ad rem adtendens non videat ex hisce quatuor, quae in nobis aguntur, quum aliquo externo corpore adficimur, duo priora ad corpus, duo posteriora ad mentem duntaxat pertinére. His obiter dictis, quo pacto animus noster claras, distinctas, atque adaequatas ideas sibi formet, paulò adcuratiùs erit considerandum.

23 These four, as may be seen, are very different, and yet they are not commonly distinguished; yet there is no one who, attending to the matter, does not see that of these four, which take place in us when we are affected by some external body, the first two pertain to the body, the last two to the mind alone. These things having been said in passing, we shall have to consider somewhat more accurately how our mind forms for itself clear, distinct and adequate ideas.

p. 12

CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

Divisio Idearum. — The Division of Ideas.

24. Idea, ut jam diximus, est objecti cujusvis genuina imago, quam mens immediatè contemplatur, vel est quaelibet de re quavis cogitatio. Aliquando rem ita percipimus, ut eam quum iterùm se offert ab aliis facilè secernamus; haec vocatur idea clara: si non possum sic distinguere rem ab alia, haec idea est confusa; íta ex. gr. Lunae claram ideam unusquisque etiam ex plebe habet, non item Jovis, Martis, Saturni, quas stellas plebejus facilè cum stellis fixis confundet.

24 An idea, as we have already said, is the genuine image of any object whatever, which the mind contemplates immediately, or any thought whatever about any thing. Sometimes we perceive a thing in such a way that, when it presents itself again, we easily distinguish it from others; this is called a clear idea: if I cannot so distinguish a thing from another, the idea is confused. Thus, e.g., everyone, even among the common people, has a clear idea of the Moon, but not likewise of Jupiter, Mars and Saturn, stars which a man of the people will easily confuse with the fixed stars.

25 Verùm etiam si rem aliquam ab aliis facilè distinguam, evenit aliquandò, ut notas omnes, quae rem à ceteris secernunt, singilatim enumerare valeam, aliquandò non item; primo casu idea clara, est distincta, secundo indistincta: ex. gr. quum sciam triangulum ab aliis figuris numero linearum, quibus inclusum est distingui posse, ejus non modò claram, sed & distinctam habere ideam dicor. Contrà si videns magnetem ferrum ad se trahere, ex hac nota secerno magnétem ab aliis lapidibus, sed nequeo singilatìm numerare ceteras notas omnes quae magnétem ab aliis lapidibus sejungunt; habeo ideam claram, sed confusam magnétis. Igitur plus éxprimit idea distincta, quam clara, & rectè idea clara dividitur in distinctam, & confusam.

25 But even if I easily distinguish some thing from others, it sometimes happens that I am able to enumerate one by one all the marks that separate the thing from the rest, and sometimes not; in the first case the clear idea is distinct, in the second indistinct. E.g., when I know that a triangle can be distinguished from other figures by the number of the lines by which it is enclosed, I am said to have not only a clear but also a distinct idea of it. On the other hand, if, seeing that a magnet draws iron to itself, I separate the magnet from other stones by this mark, but cannot enumerate one by one all the other marks that set the magnet apart from other stones, I have a clear but confused idea of the magnet. A distinct idea therefore expresses more than a clear one, and a clear idea is rightly divided into distinct and confused.

26 Quòd si non modò rem ejusque notas in numero habeo, sed & harum ipsarum notarum, quae illam distinctam notionem ingrediuntur, ideam distinctam habeo, idea haec erit adaequata, quod ubi secùs se habet, idea distincta quidem, sed inadaequata erit. Sic ex. gr. notae quibus ignem ab aliis materiis discerno, sunt lux, calor, potentia incendendi, &c. Harum rerum omnium, si quis habet ideam distinctam, notionem ignis adaequatam habebit, sin minus inadaequatam. Igitur plus éxprimit idea adaequata quàm distincta; nec póssumus acquirere ideas adaequatas omnium rerum, non enim habemus ideam distinctam adjunctorum omnium, quibus unaquaeque res constat, imò paucissimae ideae adequatae comparari possunt in hac vita, ut rectè hoc loco monet Vvolffius.

26 But if I not only have the thing and its marks enumerated, but also have a distinct idea of those very marks which enter into that distinct notion, this idea will be adequate; where it is otherwise, the idea will indeed be distinct, but inadequate. Thus, e.g., the marks by which I discern fire from other materials are light, heat, the power of setting on fire, etc. If anyone has a distinct idea of all these things, he will have an adequate notion of fire; if not, an inadequate one. An adequate idea therefore expresses more than a distinct one; nor can we acquire adequate ideas of all things, for we do not have a distinct idea of all the adjuncts of which each thing consists; indeed, very few adequate ideas can be obtained in this life, as Wolff rightly warns on this point.

p. 13

27 Praeterea ideae vel sunt Substantiarum, vel Modorum, vel Relationum. Nam omnia quae cognoscimus, vel à singulis modis seorsùm esse possunt, & id vocamus substantiam, vel sunt modi alicujus rei, & haec vocamus accidentia, seu modos: ex modis autem, vel est aliquid, quod ad aliud fingitur referri, & id vocamus relationem. Haec divisio adaequata est; etenim planè impossibile est dari aliquam perceptionem, quae nec sit perceptio substantiae, nec perceptio modi, nec perceptio alicujus relationis.

27 Further, ideas are either of Substances, or of Modes, or of Relations. For all the things we know either can exist apart from each single mode, and this we call substance; or they are modes of some thing, and these we call accidents, or modes; and among modes, again, there is something that is conceived as referred to another, and this we call relation. This division is adequate; for it is plainly impossible that there be any perception which is neither a perception of substance, nor a perception of a mode, nor a perception of some relation.

28 Totum claret exemplo: lignum quadratum est res, quae seorsùm à figura quadrata potest existere: nam fieri potest rotundum, & id vocamus substantiam. Contrà quadraturam, & rotunditatem nusquàm in corporibus naturalibus invenies separatim, id autem vocamus accidens, seu modum substantiae, quòd si quadraturam concipio ut modum proprium corporis, necessariò id me ducit in cognitionem corporis, & hoc vocamus relationem.

28 The whole is made clear by an example: a square piece of wood is a thing that can exist apart from the square figure, for it can be made round; and this we call substance. On the other hand, you will nowhere find squareness and roundness separately in natural bodies, and this we call an accident, or mode of substance; and if I conceive squareness as a mode proper to a body, it necessarily leads me to the knowledge of the body, and this we call relation.

29 Ex dictis fit manifestum non habere nos ideam claram & distinctam substantiae, sed valdè obscuram. Nam ideae, quas habemus singularum substantiarum sensu acquiruntur; at sensus adtingunt tantùm modos, qui substantiam ornànt, substantiae verò naturam non itèm: propterea substantia ab aliis rebus nequit clarè sejungi. Ex. gr. ferrum offert nobis ideam corporis gravis, duri, quod non nisi magno igne liquefít, quodque rubígine consúmitur, & omninò est adcommodatum ad corpora secanda, &c. & quamvis conemur ferri naturam penitùs cognoscere, nihil efficiemus. Verùm haec idea nihil aliud repraesentat, nisi modos ferri. ¿Quis ením audeat dicere, aliud se praeter ista in ferro reperire? Ergò idea ferri, quam habemus est composita ex ideis omnium modorum. Quia tamen certò scimus, adjuncta illa posse mutari ex. gr. figuram quadratam in rotundam, &c. fieri duriùs, & dividendis lignis accommodatiùs, quin ipsa natura ferri mutetur, colligimus praeter adjuncta, & proprietates, aliud in ferro esse, quod nos vocamus substantiam, & subjectum. Quid verò illud sit, & in quo ab aliis secernatur nescímus.

29 From what has been said it becomes manifest that we do not have a clear and distinct idea of substance, but a very obscure one. For the ideas we have of particular substances are acquired by sense; but the senses reach only the modes that adorn the substance, not likewise the nature of the substance: hence substance cannot be clearly separated from other things. E.g., iron offers us the idea of a heavy, hard body, which is melted only by a great fire, which is consumed by rust, and which is altogether suited to cutting bodies, etc.; and however much we try to know the nature of iron thoroughly, we shall achieve nothing. For this idea represents nothing other than the modes of iron. Who indeed would dare to say that he finds anything else in iron besides these? Therefore the idea of iron that we have is composed of the ideas of all its modes. Since, however, we know for certain that those adjuncts can be changed, e.g. the square figure into a round one, etc., and that iron can become harder and better suited to splitting wood, without the very nature of iron being changed, we conclude that there is something in iron besides its adjuncts and properties, which we call substance and subject. But what that is, and in what it is distinguished from other things, we do not know.

30 Itaque notio substantiae, ut rectè monet Lockius, est idea rei nobis prorsùs incognitae, seu idea rei obscurissimae, quam nos fingimus esse subjectum accidentium. Idea verò singularum substantiarum, ut ferri, & ligni est idea composita ex ideis proprietatum omnium. Malè itaque philosophantur, qui censent ex iis, quas cognoscimus proprietatibus, naturam rei planè cognosci. Nam & si nonnullas proprietates noscamus, certò adfirmare non póssumus, nullas superesse proprietates, quae nobis cognitae non sint. Quare ex proprietatibus, quas

30 Thus the notion of substance, as Locke rightly warns, is the idea of a thing altogether unknown to us, or the idea of a most obscure thing, which we feign to be the subject of accidents. But the idea of particular substances, as of iron and of wood, is an idea composed of the ideas of all their properties. Those, therefore, philosophize badly who hold that the nature of a thing is fully known from the properties we know. For even if we know some properties, we cannot affirm with certainty that no properties remain which are not known to us. Wherefore from the properties which we know

p. 14

novimus, res alias ab aliis sejúngere possumus, & quò plures proprietates internoscimus, eò magis ad cognítionem naturae accedimus, id tamen longè distat à clarâ, & distinctâ, & multò magis ab adaequata essentiae, seu naturae perceptione.

we can separate things from one another, and the more properties we discern, the more nearly we approach the knowledge of the nature; yet this is far removed from a clear and distinct perception of the essence, or nature, and much farther still from an adequate one.

31 Relationes, ut diximus sunt ideae, quarum una ad alteram se refert, ut una sine altera intelligi nequeat, vel ut unius consideratio considerationem alterius involvat. Ex quo inferimus haud parùm errare, qui de idea relativa aliquid absolutè adfirmant, vel negant, nec fundamentum relationis ritè expendunt. Quae observatio quantae utilitatis sit ad evitandas logomachias, quin & adfectus tristiores sedandos, dici non potest. Sic multi se pauperes esse dolent, quum nulla re necessaria indigeant. Et ¿curverò nisi quòd fundamentum relationis ponunt homines admodùm divites, quibuscum comparati sibi pauperrimi videntur? Eleganter Seneca, 2

31 Relations, as we have said, are ideas of which one refers to the other in such a way that one cannot be understood without the other, or that the consideration of the one involves the consideration of the other. From this we infer that those err not a little who affirm or deny something absolutely of a relative idea, and do not duly weigh the foundation of the relation. How useful this observation is for avoiding logomachies, and indeed for calming the sadder passions, cannot be told. Thus many grieve that they are poor, though they lack nothing necessary. And why so, unless because they take very rich men as the foundation of the relation, compared with whom they seem to themselves very poor? Elegantly says Seneca, (k)

Ferre, quam sortem patiuntur omnes

To bear the lot that all men suffer

Nemo recusat.

No one refuses.

Nemo se credit miserum, licet sit.

No one believes himself wretched, though he be.

Tolle felices, removeto multo

Take away the fortunate, take far away

Divites auro, removeto, centum

The rich in gold, take away those who

Rura qui scindunt opulenta bubus;

Cleave rich fields with a hundred oxen;

Pauperi surgent animi jacentes,

The poor man’s downcast spirits will rise.

Est miser nemo, nisi COMPARATUS.

No one is wretched, except by Comparison.

CAPUT V.

CHAPTER V.

De ideis singularibus, particularibus, universalibus, ubi de quinque praedicabilibus.

On singular, particular and universal ideas, where also of the five predicables. 32

32 Ideae aliae nobis rem ipsam repraesentant in individuo, ex. gr. Alexandrum, aliae quod res cum aliis quibusdam commune habet, ex. gr. regiam ejus dignitatem: aliae quod res cum omnibus ejusdem naturae commune habet, ex. gr. humanitatem. Primi generis ideae singulares,

Some ideas represent to us the thing itself in the individual, e.g. Alexander; others what the thing has in common with certain others, e.g. his royal dignity; others what the thing has in common with all things of the same nature, e.g. humanity. Ideas of the first kind are called singular, of the second particular

In Troad. V. 1016.

In Troad. V. 1016.

p. 15

secundi particulares; tertii universales adpelantur. Universalia igitur non sunt extra mentem, seu ut Scholastici loquuntur aparte rei. Homo universalis non est nisi idéa, homines enim qui existunt, singulares sunt.

particular, of the third universal. Universals, therefore, are not outside the mind, or, as the Scholastics put it, a parte rei [on the side of the thing]. Universal man is nothing but an idea; for the men who exist are singular.

33 Peripatetici secundum Porphyrium quinque universalium classes fecére, Genus, Speciem, Differentiam Specificam, Proprium, & Accidens. Genus à Porphyrio dicitur: notio universalis, quae de pluribus praedicatur specie differentibus, cum quid sit quaeritur: ex. g. animal, hominis & equi genus est, quia notionem utríque communem designat, & adferri solet ab eo, qui respondet interroganti, quid homo, quid equus sit. Species est universalis notio, quae de pluribus dicitur numero differentibus, tamquam tota essentia, ut homo, qui enuntiatur de Petro, & Paulo, & aliis naturae humanae individuis. Individuum autem est id, quod in plura talia quale ipsum est, dividi nequit: ex. gr. Petrus. Differentia specifica, est notio universalis, quae de pluribus dicitur numero differentibus tamquam forma metaphysica, determinans genus ad talem speciem ex. gr. rationalitas.

33 The Peripatetics, following Porphyry, made five classes of universals: Genus, Species, Specific Difference, Property and Accident. Genus is defined by Porphyry as a universal notion which is predicated of many things differing in species, when it is asked what a thing is: e.g. animal is the genus of man and of horse, because it designates the notion common to both, and it is what is usually offered by one who answers someone asking what a man, what a horse is. Species is a universal notion which is said of many things differing in number, as their whole essence, as man, which is predicated of Peter, and Paul, and the other individuals of human nature. An Individual, moreover, is that which cannot be divided into several things such as it is itself: e.g. Peter. Specific Difference is a universal notion which is said of many things differing in number, as a metaphysical form, determining the genus to such a species, e.g. rationality.

34 Proprium quatuor dicitur modis: primò, quod soli speciei accidit, sed non toti, ut esse Medicum. Secundo è converso, quod toti speciei accidit, sed non soli, ut esse bipedem. Tertio, quod soli, & toti speciei accidit, sed non semper, ut in homine sermocinari. Quarto quod toti speciei, & semper accidit, talis est in homine facultas sermocinandi, seu colloquendi, nam ut egregiè ait Cicero: hoc enim uno praestamus, vel maxime feris, quod colloquimur inter nos, & quod exprimere dicendo sensa possumus. Accidens est notio universalis, quae pluribus adesse potest, vel abesse incolumi eorum natura, seu ut loquuntur Scholastici: quod potest adesse, vel abesse absque subjecti corruptione, talis est in Petro albedo. Haec in praesentia indicare satis fuerit.

34 Property is said in four ways: first, what belongs to one species alone, but not to the whole of it, as to be a Physician. Second, conversely, what belongs to the whole species, but not to it alone, as to be two-footed. Third, what belongs to one species alone and to the whole of it, but not always, as in man to be conversing. Fourth, what belongs to the whole species, and always: such in man is the faculty of discourse, or of conversing; for, as Cicero excellently says: for in this one thing above all we excel the beasts, that we converse with one another, and that we can express our thoughts by speaking. Accident is a universal notion which can be present to or absent from many things while their nature remains intact, or, as the Scholastics put it: that which can be present or absent without the corruption of the subject; such in Peter is whiteness. It will be enough to have indicated these things for the present.

CAPUT VI. — CHAPTER VI

De Antepraedicamentis, & Cathegoriis Peripateticorum.

On the Antepredicaments and the Categories of the Peripatetics. 35

35 Peripatetici vocant cathegorias, seu Praedicamenta Dogma philosophicum, quod in Philosophia vocari nequit in dubium. ¡Nugae! Nam nihil aliud sunt

The Peripatetics call the categories, or Predicaments, a philosophical Dogma, which cannot be called into doubt in Philosophy. Nonsense! For the predicaments are nothing other

p. 16

praedicamenta, nisi nomenclatura, quae ostendit, quo nomine Aristoteles quaedam entia nominaverit: re autem vera inepta divisio est, ut infra ostendemus; sed priùs aliqua de antepraedicamentis explicabimus.

than a nomenclature, which shows by what name Aristotle named certain beings: in actual fact it is an inept division, as we shall show below; but first we shall explain a few things about the antepredicaments.

36 Antepraedicamenta quatuor numeravit Aristoteles: Univoca, Aequivoca, Analoga, & Denominativa. Univoca sunt, quorum nomen est commune, ratio vero significata per nomen est omnino eadem in omnibus. Verba illa omnino eadem, non significant identitatem, sed similitudinem. Aequivoca sunt ea quorum nomen est commune, ratio vero significata per nomen est omnino diversa. Vulgare est exemplum Canis, qui pro animali domestico, & pro sidere accipitur. Analoga sunt quorum nomen est commune ratio vero significata per nomen partim est eadem, partim diversa, vel uni convenit propriè, alii impropriè, sic risus est analogus respectu hominis, & prati. Denominativa sunt, quae ab aliquo nomine derivantur, sic fortis à fortitudine, &c. Et haec sunt antepraedicamenta. Si autem res ipsas consideramus, sine labore intelligemus, ideas omnes ad tres veluti classes posse revocari, Substantiam, Adjuncta, Relationes, quod & superiùs diximus.

36 Aristotle counted four Antepredicaments: Univocals, Equivocals, Analogues and Denominatives. Univocals are things whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is altogether the same in all. Those words altogether the same signify not identity, but likeness. Equivocals are those whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is altogether different. A common example is Dog, which is taken for the domestic animal and for a star. Analogues are things whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is partly the same, partly different, or belongs properly to one, improperly to another; thus laughter is analogous with respect to a man and to a meadow. Denominatives are those which are derived from some name, as brave from bravery, etc. And these are the antepredicaments. But if we consider the things themselves, we shall understand without effort that all ideas can be reduced to three classes, as it were: Substance, Adjuncts, Relations, as we also said above.

37 Aristoteles verò refert omnia quae sunt in decem classes, quas cathegorias vocat, alii Praedicamenta. Una est substantiae, seu rei quae per se existere potest: alia accidentium, seu earum rerum quae per se existere non possunt. In prima classe substantiae duas numerat. Secunda Quantitas, vel discreta, ut numeri, vel continua: eaque, vel permanens, ut corpus, vel successiva, ut motus. Tertia Qualitas, vel animi, ut virtutes, scientiae, vel corporis, ut calor, &c. Quarta Relatio, qua una res ad aliam cognoscendam ducit. Quinta Actio, vel quae in agente, ut amor, vel quae in alio recipitur, ut calefactio. Sexta Passio contraria actioni ut calefieri. Septima Ubi, seu locus, ut esse Romae, esse domi, esse ruri, &c. Octava Tempus, ut quandò verbis tempus significantibus, respondemus cras, &c. Nona Situs, quod exprimitur hisce verbis stat, cubat, &c. Decima Habitus: id est, ea que corpus vestiunt, ut palium, &c. En praedicamenta. En dogma Philosophicum, quod temerarium existimant Peripatetici in dubium vocare.

37 Aristotle, however, refers all things that exist to ten classes, which he calls categories, and others Predicaments. One is that of substance, or of a thing that can exist by itself; the others are those of accidents, or of those things that cannot exist by themselves. In the first class he counts two substances. The second is Quantity, either discrete, as numbers, or continuous; and this either permanent, as a body, or successive, as motion. The third is Quality, either of the mind, as virtues and sciences, or of the body, as heat, etc. The fourth is Relation, by which one thing leads to the knowledge of another. The fifth is Action, either that which is in the agent, as love, or that which is received in another, as heating. The sixth is Passion, the contrary of action, as being heated. The seventh is Where, or place, as to be at Rome, to be at home, to be in the country, etc. The eighth is Time, as when, to words signifying time, we answer tomorrow, etc. The ninth is Position, which is expressed by these words: stands, lies, etc. The tenth is Habit, that is, the things that clothe the body, as a cloak, etc. Behold the predicaments. Behold the Philosophical dogma which the Peripatetics judge it rash to call into doubt.

38 Alitèr tamen Sapientissimi Recentiores existimarunt, quibus illa divisio, vel distributio paulò liberius efficta videtur, quippe quae, ut advertit Cl. Auctor Artis cogitandi, è viri cujuspiam imaginatione prodivit, penes quem jus nullum erat ad leges aliis scribendas, qui non minus quam ille uti poterunt suo jure ad objecta cogitationum suarum tali methodo disponenda, quae suae philosophandi rationi sit maximè consentanea.

38 Otherwise, however, have the most learned Moderns judged, to whom that division, or distribution, seems to have been devised somewhat too freely; for, as the celebrated Author of the Art of Thinking observes, it came forth from the imagination of some man who had no right to write laws for others, who could, no less than he, use their own right to arrange the objects of their thoughts by whatever method is most in keeping with their own way of philosophizing.

39. Et re vera talis distributio inepta prorsus videtur, quum plurima certe contineat, quae non vera entium genera, sed solae denominationes extrinsecae dici debent, ut Relatio, Ubi, Tempus; quòd si denominationes omnes, & modi extrinseci admitti deberent, jam non decem, sed infinita penè entium genera admitterentur. Desunt etiam multa, ex. gr. plures species accidentium, tum corporis, ut quies, tùm spirituum, ut cognitio, &c. In hoc ulterius reprehenditur, quod hominem sub corpore tamquàm sub genere collocet, quum similiter contineri possit sub mente, nec minori jure dicatur Mens, quàm Corpus. Falsa & pugnantia habet: nam refert longitudinem, latitudinem, & pondus ad quantitatem, deinde objecta sensuum ad qualitates, quum tamen extensio, & motus incurrant etiam in visum, pondus, & motus in tactum; adeoque Quantitas sit simul Qualitas. Ut alia hujus generis flagitia omittam.

39 And in fact such a distribution seems altogether inept, since it certainly contains a great many things that ought to be called not true genera of beings but only extrinsic denominations, as Relation, Where, Time; for if all denominations and extrinsic modes were to be admitted, then not ten but almost infinite genera of beings would have to be admitted. Many things are also missing, e.g. several species of accidents, both of body, as rest, and of spirits, as cognition, etc. It is further faulted in this, that it places man under body as under a genus, although he could equally be contained under mind, and could with no less right be called Mind than Body. It contains things false and conflicting: for it refers length, breadth and weight to quantity, and then the objects of the senses to qualities, although extension and motion also fall under sight, and weight and motion under touch; and so Quantity would be at the same time Quality. To pass over other enormities of this kind.

40 Adcuratius itaque Recentiores Philosophi septem entium genera, vel cathegorias numerant, ut sub communi, supremoque entis genere, duplex substantiae species, corpus nimirum, & spiritus, sive mens, atque insuper etiam quinque modorum species, nitida, perfecta que serie contineantur. Hinc in illorum sententia,

40 More accurately, therefore, the Modern Philosophers count seven genera, or categories, of beings, so that under the common and supreme genus of being there are contained, in a neat and perfect series, two species of substance, namely body and spirit, or mind, and in addition five species of modes. Hence, in their view,

Mens, Mensura, Quies, Motus, Positura, Figura

Mind, Measure, Rest, Motion, Position, Figure

Sunt cum Materia cunctarum exordia rerum.

Are, with Matter, the beginnings of all things.

41 Persuassum namque est hujus Philosophiae sectatoribus his septem rebus omnem naturam exhauriri. Nomine Mentis intelligitur substantia spiritualis, ut Deus, Angeli, & Anima rationalis. Mensura quantitatem significat. Quies permanentiam corporis in loco in quo reperitur. Motus est translatio sive migratio corporis ex uno in alium locum. Positura significat partium dispositionem, illam praesertim, quae intima est, quaeque variari non potest, quin eadem substantia varietur. Figura est illa partium dispositio quae exterius adparet, quaeque salva rei substantia variari potest. Materia denique corpus, aut corpoream substantiam significat, quidquid demum corporis, sive materiae nomine intelligatur. Haec verò septem entium genera cunctarum exordia rerum dicuntur, quia nihil concipi potest, quod in ejusmodi rerum generibus non includatur, aut nulla denique singularis substantia reperiatur, in qua plures, aut omnes etiam ex modis ipsis distingui sive reperiri non possint. Verùm ut omnia inlustrius adpareant sequentem tabulam vobis offero, ut ab aliquibus Recentioribus depicta est.

41 For the followers of this Philosophy are persuaded that the whole of nature is exhausted by these seven things. By the name of Mind is understood spiritual substance, as God, the Angels and the rational Soul. Measure signifies quantity. Rest, the permanence of a body in the place in which it is found. Motion is the translation or migration of a body from one place to another. Position signifies the disposition of the parts, above all that which is innermost and which cannot be varied without the substance itself being varied. Figure is that disposition of the parts which appears outwardly, and which can be varied while the substance of the thing remains intact. Matter, finally, signifies body or corporeal substance, whatever in the end may be understood by the name of body or matter. And these seven genera of beings are called the beginnings of all things because nothing can be conceived that is not included in these genera of things; or, finally, no singular substance is found in which several, or even all, of these modes cannot be distinguished or found. But so that everything may appear more clearly, I offer you the following table, as it has been drawn by some of the Moderns.

p. 18

CAPUT VII. — CHAPTER VII

De Definitionibus, & Divisionibus.

On Definitions and Divisions.

42 Qui sibi ideas rerum distinctas, & adaequatas adquisivit, ei jam facile erit, res non modò descrivere, sed & definire, & dividere. Quibus sanè instrumentis carére non potest, qui véritatis investigandae studio tenetur. Si enim distinctam habemus ideam, rem definire possumus, si adaequatam nihil facilius erit, quàm eam dividere.

hoever has acquired for himself distinct and adequate ideas of 42 W things will now find it easy not only to describe things, but also to define and divide them. And indeed one who is bound to the study of investigating the truth cannot do without these instruments. For if we have a distinct idea, we can define the thing; if an adequate one, nothing will be easier than to divide it.

43 Definitio ergò est oratio rem ita determinans ut ab aliis omnibus semper distingui possit. Descriptio à definitione ita differt, quod licet utraque vera sit, illa tamen rei non nisi certis sub circunstantiis; haec semper cómpetat. Ex. gr. si dico: horologium est machínula hoc vel illo modo facta, quae vel stilo, vel percussione ostendit quota sit hora diei: haec est definitio horologii: si dico est theca rotunda, quae pendet ex caténa propè lectum, haec propositio tametsi clara, est descriptio horologii.

43 Definition, then, is a statement so determining a thing that it can always be distinguished from all others. Description differs from definition in this, that although both are true, the former applies to the thing only under certain circumstances, the latter always. E.g. if I say: a clock is a little machine made in this or that way, which, either by a hand or by striking, shows what hour of the day it is, this is the definition of a clock; if I say: it is a round case that hangs from a chain near the bed, this proposition, though clear, is a description of a clock.

44 Quum ergò definitio semper competere debeat rei, consequens est, ut primo id quo cum aliis ejusdem naturae rebus convenit, ac deinde ideam quae ad essentiam rei primario pertinet, & qua à reliquis omnibus distinguitur, comprehendere debeat, adeoque constare ex genere, & differentia specìfica.
