Ex. gr. triangulum est figura tribus lineis circunscripta. Quod si differentiam illam specìficam desumo à nota aliqua, qua rem mihi obviam ab aliis omnibus semper discernere possim, definitio illa dicetur nominalis: ex. gr. circulus est figura, cujus peripheria à centro ubique aequaliter distat. Si differentiam in eo ponam, ut ostendam modum, quomodo illa res oriatur, vel quomodo possibilis sit, definitio realis emerget, ex. gr. circulus ést figura, quae radio circa punctum circumacto describitur.

44 Since, then, a definition must always apply to the thing, it follows that it must comprehend first that in which the thing agrees with other things of the same nature, and then the idea which belongs primarily to the essence of the thing and by which it is distinguished from all the rest; and so it must consist of genus and specific difference. E.g. a triangle is a figure bounded by three lines. But if I take that specific difference from some mark by which I can always tell the thing I meet apart from all others, that definition will be called nominal: e.g. a circle is a figure whose periphery is everywhere equally distant from the center. If I place the difference in showing the manner in which the thing arises, or how it is possible, a real definition will result; e.g. a circle is a figure described by a radius turned about a point.

45 Si tamen definitio nominis adcurata omninò sit, ita ut rem ipsam nomine significatam ab alia qualibet re distinguat, nihil interest tales definitiones vel rei vel nominis adpelari, ut optime advertit Cl. Jacquier. Ex quibus facile patet primò definitionem non debére esse negativam, quià ita res à re non distinguitur, per id quod ad essentiam pertinet. Secundò cum definito reciprocari debere, sive, ut Scholae loquuntur, quod

45 If, however, the definition of the name is altogether accurate, so that it distinguishes the very thing signified by the name from any other thing whatever, it makes no difference whether such definitions are called definitions of the thing or of the name, as the celebrated Jacquier very well observes. From this it readily appears, first, that a definition ought not to be negative, since in that way a thing is not distinguished from a thing by what belongs to its essence. Second, that it ought to be reciprocal with the thing defined, or, as the Schools say, that the thing defined and the definition be mutually

p. 19

mutuo convertantur definitum & definitio. Tertió eamdem constare debére verbis propriis, perspicuis, aut certè jam antea definitis. Quartò quod definitum non ingrediatur definitionem, seu quod non explicetur idem per idem, ex. gr. circulus est circulus. Quinto definitionem convenire debere omni & soli definitio, unde vitiosa est illa definitio hominis: animal bipes sine plumis. Ex quibus regulis fluunt quatuor in Scholis recepta axiomata: cui convenit definitio, convenit & definitum, & è contrario: item cui repugnat definitio, repugnat & definitum, & è converso.

convertible. Third, that it ought to consist of proper and perspicuous words, or at least of words already defined beforehand. Fourth, that the thing defined should not enter into the definition, that is, that the same should not be explained by the same, e.g. a circle is a circle. Fifth, that the definition ought to apply to all of the thing defined and to it alone; hence that definition of man is faulty: a two-footed animal without feathers. From these rules flow four axioms received in the Schools: to whatever the definition belongs, the thing defined belongs also, and conversely; likewise: to whatever the definition is repugnant, the thing defined is repugnant also, and vice versa.

46 Duo tamen hic curemus oportet. Primum, ut obscura nomina, quae in controversiam veniunt, adcurate definiamus, ne ex ambiguo disputemus. Peccant in hanc legem nonnulli Philosophi, qui quòd vocabula non definiant, ad convicia, atque pugnos usque altercantur inter se, & si eadem ambo disputantes dicant aliis & aliis verbis. Secundum: ne quum nomina definimus, putemus nos rem ipsam definire. In hanc regulam etiam peccant illi ipsi Philosophi: quum enim certa vocabula arbitratu suo definiant persuadent sibi, se naturas rerum significatarum penitus cognoscere, & definire: ex. gr. interroges eos, ¿quid sit arbor? Ajunt esse vivens insensitivum. ¿Quit sit fulmen? Reponunt, esse exhalationem in nube accensam, quae tendit deorsum. Verum hae explicationes tantum declarant; quae res iis nominibus significentur, at rerum naturas non aperiunt, nisi prius distincte cognoscam, quid sit vivens insentivum, exhalatio, nubes, accensio, cetera. Sed jam de divisione pauca dicamus.

46 Two things, however, we must take care of here. First, that we define accurately the obscure names that come into controversy, lest we dispute from an ambiguity. Some Philosophers sin against this law, who, because they do not define their terms, wrangle with one another even to abuse and fisticuffs, even if both disputants are saying the same things in different words. Second: that when we define names, we should not think that we are defining the thing itself. Against this rule those very Philosophers also sin: for when they define certain words at their own discretion, they persuade themselves that they thoroughly know and define the natures of the things signified: e.g. ask them, what is a tree? They say it is a living insensitive thing. What is lightning? They answer that it is an exhalation kindled in a cloud, which tends downward. But these explanations declare only what things are signified by those names; they do not lay open the natures of the things, unless I first know distinctly what a living insensitive thing, an exhalation, a cloud, kindling and the rest are. But now let us say a few things about division.

47 Divisio est propositio, quae resolvit totum in partes, quo facilius quid contineat intelligatur, aut meliùs: ideae universalis in plures particulares solutio. Id quod resolvitur, dicitur divisum, partes in quas dividitur, membra dividentia. Alia est divisio Physica, ut quum dividimus lignum in partes, alia Logica, ut quum mente divido substantiam in corpus, & spiritum. Hae partes vocantur inferiora.

47 Division is a statement that resolves a whole into its parts, so that what it contains may be more easily understood; or better: the resolution of a universal idea into several particular ones. That which is resolved is called the thing divided; the parts into which it is divided, the dividing members. One division is Physical, as when we divide wood into parts; another Logical, as when I divide substance in my mind into body and spirit. These parts are called inferiors.

48 Lex prima divisionis est, quod membra dividentia adaequent totum divisum. Vitiose igitur dividunt Aristotelici ens in decem cathegórias, quia plures constitui possunt. Secunda, quod unum membrum non contineatur in alio, quare numerus non rectè dividitur in parem, & imparem, & binarium: nam binarius continetur in pari. Logicus itaque pro sua sapientia rem ita dividat, ut clarior inde rei cognitio habeatur, quo facilius, & adcuratius eam definiat. Atque illud caveat studiosè, quod supra de definitione monuimus, ne quum dividit significationem nominis, existimet se rem ipsam dividere: quod flagitium

48 The first law of division is that the dividing members be equal to the whole divided. Faultily, therefore, do the Aristotelians divide being into ten categories, since more can be established. The second, that one member not be contained in another; hence number is not rightly divided into even, odd and binary: for the binary is contained in the even. Let the Logician, therefore, in his wisdom so divide a thing that a clearer knowledge of the thing may be had from it, so that he may define it the more easily and accurately. And let him carefully beware of what we warned above concerning definition, lest, when he divides the signification of a name, he think he is dividing the thing itself: an enormity which Aristotle

p. 20

Aristoteles ipse, & Veteres nonnulli imprudentes admiserunt. Quae de divisione monuimus, eadem & de subdivisionibus intelligenda, quamvis danda sit opera, ne subdivisiones praeter necessitatem multiplicentur. Quò magis enim magnum saxum in pulverem conteritur, eò minus ejus magnitudinem animo comprehendimus.

himself and some of the Ancients imprudently committed. What we have warned concerning division must be understood of subdivisions as well, although care must be taken that subdivisions are not multiplied beyond necessity. For the more a great rock is ground into dust, the less do we grasp its size with the mind.

CAPUT VIII. — CHAPTER VIII

De Judiciis, & propositionibus, de que propositionis materia, forma, quantitate, qualitate: de oppositione, aequipollentia, & conversione propositionum.

On Judgments and Propositions, and on the matter, form, quantity and quality of a proposition: on the opposition, equipollence and conversion of propositions.

49 Quando mens binas ideas adcuratè perceptas interse comparat, easque velnectit, vel divellit nascitur inde judicium quod est: perceptio convenientiae, aut disconvenientiae, quae reperitur inter duas ideas. Judicium autem verbis expressum Propositio, vel enunciatio adpelatur. Propositio autem est: oratio adfirmans, vel negans aliquid de aliquo. Respondet enim judicio, quod vel duas ideas connectit, vel disjungit.

hen the mind compares two ideas, accurately perceived, with 49 W each other, and either connects them or pulls them apart, there arises from this judgment, which is: the perception of the agreement or disagreement that is found between two ideas. Judgment expressed in words is called a Proposition, or enunciation. A proposition, moreover, is: a statement affirming or denying something of something. For it corresponds to judgment, which either connects or disjoins two ideas.

50 Omnis propositio constat subjecto, & praedicato, seu adtributo, quos terminos inter se jungit copula est, quamvis haec aequè ac subjectum saepè in praedicato latitet, adeoque tota propositio uno, vel binis vocabulis constet. ex. gr. Petrus amat, morior, in quibus subaudiuntur hae: Petrus est amans, ego sum moriens. Subjectum est id de quo aliquid dicitur. Praedicatum, quod dicitur de subjecto. Copula est nexus, sivè unio subjecti & praedicati. Per copulam, seu per verbum est, vel non est vis judicandi significatur, idest, ostenditur praedicatum in subjecto includi, vel non includi. Haec enim propositio: Deus est justus, hoc dicere vult, in idea Dei inclusa est idea justitiae. Haec altera, homo non est equus, hoc vult dicere, in idea hominis non inclusa est idea equi. Nulla enim propositio adfirmans est vera, nisi quia totum praedicatum in subjecto includitur, nulla

50 Every proposition consists of a subject and a predicate, or attribute, terms which the copula is joins together; although this, just like the subject, often lies hidden in the predicate, and so the whole proposition consists of one or two words, e.g. Peter loves, I die, in which these are understood: Peter is loving, I am dying. The subject is that of which something is said. The predicate, what is said of the subject. The copula is the link, or union of subject and predicate. By the copula, or by the verb is, or is not, the force of judging is signified, that is, it is shown that the predicate is included, or not included, in the subject. For this proposition, God is just, means this: in the idea of God the idea of justice is included. This other, a man is not a horse, means: in the idea of man the idea of horse is not included. For no affirmative proposition is true except because the whole predicate is included in the subject; no negative

p. 21

negans verò nisi quia totum non includitur, ex. gr. quum dico ego sum vivens pronomine ego designo ideam complexam mei individui, & volo dicere meum individuum est vivens; quod valet, in idea cómplexa mei individui includitur idea viventis.

one, except because the whole is not included. E.g. when I say I am living, by the pronoun I I designate the complex idea of my individual self, and I mean my individual self is living; which amounts to: in the complex idea of my individual self the idea of living is included.

51 Materia propositionis sunt illae voces quibus eadem propositio veluti partibus componitur. Rationae materiae propositio dicitur necessaria, quando praedícatum necessario convenit subjecto, ut homo est animal; contingens quando contingenter convenit, ut Joannes est albus; impossibilis, quando ei repugnat, ut Sempronius est lapis. Sed haec item ad necessariam refertur: nam illa dicitur necessario vera: haec necessario falsa.

51 The Matter of a proposition is those words of which the same proposition is composed, as it were of parts. By reason of its matter a proposition is called necessary when the predicate agrees necessarily with the subject, as man is an animal; contingent when it agrees contingently, as John is white; impossible when it is repugnant to it, as Sempronius is a stone. But this too is referred to the necessary: for the former is called necessarily true, the latter necessarily false.

52 Forma propositionis est ipsa copula, quae conjungit praedicatum cum subjecto. Ratione formae dividitur propositio in adfirmativam, quae adtribuit unum alteri, & in negativam, quae negat unum de alio: Ubi obiter nota, propositionem negativam esse, quando particula non, cadit supra verbum. Dividitur etiam in Cathegorematicam, quae sine conditione adfirmat vel negat, & in hypotheticam, que adfirmat sub conditione, ut si Sol lucet, dies est. Propositio complexa, est quae pluribus propositionibus constat, ut Magister docet, & discipulus capit.

52 The Form of a proposition is the copula itself, which joins the predicate with the subject. By reason of its form a proposition is divided into affirmative, which attributes one thing to another, and negative, which denies one thing of another. Note here in passing that a proposition is negative when the particle not falls upon the verb. It is divided also into Categorematic, which affirms or denies without condition, and hypothetical, which affirms under a condition, as if the Sun shines, it is day. A complex proposition is one that consists of several propositions, as the Master teaches, and the disciple learns.

53 Quantitas propositionis est extensio subjecti formalis ad significanda plura, vel pauciora. Inde propositio est universalis, si subjectum sit universale, ut omnis homo est animal, particularis si subjectum est particulare, ut aliquis homo currit, singularis, si subjectum singulare sit, ut Petrus currit. His accedit propositio indefinita, cujus subjectum est commune & non coarctatur, ut homo legit, non enim dicitur omnis, aut aliquis, aut hic, sed indefinitè homo legit.

53 The Quantity of a proposition is the extension of the formal subject to signify more or fewer things. Hence a proposition is universal if the subject is universal, as every man is an animal; particular if the subject is particular, as some man runs; singular if the subject is singular, as Peter runs. To these is added the indefinite proposition, whose subject is common and is not restricted, as man reads; for one does not say every, or some, or this, but indefinitely man reads.

54 Qualitas propositionis dicitur veritas vel falsitas, quia propositió in communi praescindit ab eo quod sit vera vel falsa, sed si reduplicative sumatur ut vera vel falsa, tunc veritas, vel falsitas, utpotè forma denominans propositionem illi convénit essentiáliter: ast propositioni specificative sumptae solum convenít contingenter. Propositiones modales dicuntur illae in quibus explicatur modus, quo praedicatum adfirmatur, vel negatur de subjecto, ut quum dicitur: necesse est hominem esse animal.

54 The Quality of a proposition is said to be its truth or falsity, because a proposition in general abstracts from being true or false; but if it is taken reduplicatively as true or false, then truth or falsity, being a form that denominates the proposition, belongs to it essentially; whereas to a proposition taken specificatively it belongs only contingently. Those propositions are called modal in which the mode is expressed in which the predicate is affirmed or denied of the subject, as when one says: it is necessary that man be an animal.

55 Hinc omnes propositiones ad quatuor classes referuntur. Id exprimunt Scholastici quatuor literis A. E. I. O. A. vniversalis adfirmans, ut omnis homo est justus E universalis negans, ut nullus vitiosus est beatus. I particularis adfirmans, ut aliquis vitiosus est dives. O particularis negans, ut aliquis vitiosus non est dives; sed ut facilius memoriae haec inhaereant his versiculis comprehensa sunt.

55 Hence all propositions are referred to four classes, which the Scholastics express by four letters, A. E. I. O. A, the universal affirmative, as every man is just; E, the universal negative, as no vicious man is happy; I, the particular affirmative, as some vicious man is rich; O, the particular negative, as some vicious man is not rich; but so that these may stick more easily in the memory, they have been comprised in these little verses.

p. 22

Asserit A, negat E. verum generaliter ambae.

A affirms, E denies, but both universally.

Asserit I, negat O, sed particulariter ambae.

I affirms, O denies, but both particularly.

56 Oppositio est repugnantia duarum propositionum, quae eodem subjecto, & praedicato constant. Quadruplex vulgò statui solet oppositio propositionum: contradictoria, contraria, subcontraria, & subalterna. Oppositio contradictoria est inter duas propositiones, quarum una est universalis, altera particularis, una adfirmans, altera negans ex. gr. omnis homo est albus, aliquis homo non est albus. Contradictoriae quoque dicuntur propositiones singulares, quarum una negat, quod adfirmat altera: ex.gr. Aristoteles est Philosophorum princeps, Aristoteles non est Philosophorum princeps. Contradictio enim est adfirmatio & negatio ejusdem praedicati de eodem subjecto, & secundum idem tempus.

56 Opposition is the incompatibility of two propositions that consist of the same subject and predicate. Opposition of propositions is commonly held to be fourfold: contradictory, contrary, subcontrary and subalternate. Contradictory opposition is between two propositions of which one is universal, the other particular, one affirmative, the other negative, e.g. every man is white, some man is not white. Singular propositions are also called contradictory when one denies what the other affirms: e.g. Aristotle is the prince of Philosophers, Aristotle is not the prince of Philosophers. For contradiction is the affirmation and negation of the same predicate of the same subject, and at the same time.

57 Propositionum contradictoriarum, una semper est vera, altera falsa. Oppositio contraria est inter duas propositiones universales, quarum una est adfirmans, altera negans, ut omnis homo est albus, nullus homo est albus. Oppositio subcontraria est inter duas propositiones particulares, quarum una est adfirmans, altera negans, ut aliquis homo est albus, aliquis homo non est albus. Oppositio subalterna (quae rigorosa oppositio non est) versatur inter duas propositiones, quarum una est universalis, altera particularis, sed utraque vel est adfirmans, vel negans, ut omnis homo est albus, aliquis homo est albus, nullus homo est albus, aliquis homo non est albus, quae ut clarius inrelligatis in subjectum paradigma oculos conjicite.

57 Of contradictory propositions, one is always true, the other false. Contrary opposition is between two universal propositions, of which one is affirmative, the other negative, as every man is white, no man is white. Subcontrary opposition is between two particular propositions, of which one is affirmative, the other negative, as some man is white, some man is not white. Subalternate opposition (which is not opposition in the strict sense) is found between two propositions of which one is universal, the other particular, but both either affirmative or negative, as every man is white, some man is white; no man is white, some man is not white; and to understand these more clearly, cast your eyes on the diagram below.

A Omnis homo est albus. CONTRARIAE. E Nullus homo est albus. SUBALTERNAE CONTRA (DIC) TORIAE CONTRA (DIC) TORIAE SUBALTERNAE I Aliquis homo est albus. SUBCONTRARIAE O Aliquis homo non est albus.

A: Every man is white. — E: No man is white. — I: Some man is white. — O: Some man is not white. Above: Contraries. Below: Subcontraries. At the sides: Subalterns. Across: Contradictories.

p. 23

58 Accipite demum certissimas regulas ad oppositionem dignoscendam: quae nec simul verae, nec simul falsae esse possunt, contradictoriae sunt, quae non simul verae, sed tamen possunt esse simul falsae, contrariae sunt, quae non possunt esse simul falsae, & possunt esse simul verae, subcontrariae. Propositionum subalternarum, aliquando una est vera, & altera falsa, aliquando utraque falsa, aliquando utraque vera: ex. gr. omnis homo est animal, aliquis homo est animal.

58 Take, finally, these most certain rules for recognizing opposition: those which can be neither true together nor false together are contradictories; those which cannot be true together, but can nevertheless be false together, are contraries; those which cannot be false together, and can be true together, are subcontraries. Of subalternate propositions, sometimes one is true and the other false, sometimes both are false, sometimes both true: e.g. every man is an animal, some man is an animal.

59 Aequipollentia, seu aequivalentia propositionum est reductio oppositarum propositionum ad eumdem sensum ope particulae non, quae in contradictoriis praeponitur subjecto, in contrariis post ponitur, in subalternis verò praeponitur simul atque postponitur, ut hoc versiculo demonstratur.

59 Equipollence, or equivalence, of propositions is the reduction of opposite propositions to the same sense by means of the particle not, which in contradictories is placed before the subject, in contraries is placed after it, and in subalterns is placed both before and after, as is shown by this little verse:

Prae contradic: post contra, prae postque subalter.

Before for contradic., after for contra., before and after for subalter.

60 Conversio propositionum est reciproca mutatio subjecti in praedicatum, & praedicati in subjectum, quando nimirum praedicatum ponitur loco subjecti, & subjectum ipsum loco praedicati, remante tamen propositionis illius veritate, quamvis aliquando propositionis extensio, sive quantitas varietur. Conversio autem propositionum ex Grammatica potius, quam ex Logica est colligenda. En mysteria Veterum Logicorum adcuratius quàm illi faciunt explicata. Noluimus tamen ea omittere, ne ereptam juventuti rem utilem, aut fructuosam fortassè Veteres suspicentur.

60 Conversion of propositions is the reciprocal change of the subject into the predicate and of the predicate into the subject, namely when the predicate is put in the place of the subject, and the subject itself in the place of the predicate, the truth of that proposition nevertheless remaining, although sometimes the extension, or quantity, of the proposition is varied. The conversion of propositions, however, is to be gathered from Grammar rather than from Logic. Here are the mysteries of the old Logicians, explained more accurately than they themselves explain them. We did not wish, however, to omit them, lest the Ancients should perhaps suspect that something useful or fruitful had been snatched away from the youth.

CAPUT IX. — CHAPTER IX

De Ratiocinatione, vel syllogismo, & variis argumentationum generibus.

On Reasoning, or the Syllogism, and the various kinds of argumentation.

61 Ratiocinatio, vel Syllogismus est operatio intellectus, qua ille constituta duarum idearum comparatione cum tertia, jungendae ne istae sint, an separandae cognoscit, vel ut Scholastici loquuntur. Ratiocinatio est cognitio, quae ex una, vel duabus propositionibus aliam infert. Si ex una tantum propositione aliam inferat, ex. gr. cogito: ergo existo, vocatur Enthymema, si autem ex duabus propositionibus inferatur alia, ex. gr. omne quod cogitat existit, sed ego cogito: ergo existo dicitur Syllogismus.

easoning, or Syllogism, is the operation of the intellect by which, having set 61 R up a comparison of two ideas with a third, it learns whether they are to be joined or to be separated; or, as the Scholastics put it, Reasoning is the cognition that infers another proposition from one or from two propositions. If it infers another from one proposition only, e.g. I think: therefore I exist, it is called an Enthymeme; but if another is inferred from two propositions, e.g. everything that thinks exists; but I think: therefore I exist, it is called a Syllogism.

p. 24

62 Quum ergo, ut diximus tres sint ideae in Syllogismo comparandae; consequens est, ut simul ac quatuor ideas in unum Syllogismum compingimus, vitiosa emergat ratiocinatio, quod plerumque fit, ubi vocabulum aliquod, aequivocatione laborat. Hinc male quis ratiocinaretur: Spiritus est substantia cogitans; sed spiritus vini est spiritus: ergo spiritus vini est substantia cogitans, nam quatuor ideae in unum Syllogismum compinguntur. Tres illae ideae, si verbis exprimuntur, termini vocantur, & is quidem de quo aliquid quaeritur terminus minor, quod de eo quaeritur major; & is quocum hi duo termini comparantur medius adpelari solet. Si eg. scire vellim, an aer sit gravis, & hinc has ideas comparem cum pressione corporum: aër erit terminus minor, quia de eo aliquid quaeritur, gravis terminus major, quia hoc ipsum est quod de aëre quaeritur, pressio corporum erit terminus medius, quia cum hac idea duae reliquae comparantur.

62 Since, then, as we have said, there are three ideas to be compared in a Syllogism, it follows that as soon as we cram four ideas into one Syllogism, a faulty reasoning results; which mostly happens when some word suffers from equivocation. Hence one would reason badly thus: Spirit is a thinking substance; but spirit of wine is spirit: therefore spirit of wine is a thinking substance; for four ideas are crammed into one Syllogism. Those three ideas, if they are expressed in words, are called terms; and the one about which something is asked is usually called the minor term, that which is asked about it the major, and that with which these two terms are compared the middle. E.g. if I wished to know whether air is heavy, and therefore compared these ideas with the pressure of bodies: air will be the minor term, because something is asked about it; heavy the major term, because this is the very thing that is asked about air; the pressure of bodies will be the middle term, because the other two are compared with this idea.

63 Tribus propositionibus Syllogismus constat, quarum prima, quae ex majori & medio termino componitur dicitur major, secunda, quae ex minore & medio, minor, tertia demum, quae ex minore, & majore, conclusio adpelatur. Sic si Syllogismum construam ex terminis paulò ante propositis: quod premit corpora inferiora est grave; aer premit corpora inferiora: ergo aer est gravis; prima propositio erit major, secunda minor, postrema conclusio seu consequentia adpelatur. In Enthymemate, prima dicitur antecedens, secunda consequentia.

63 A Syllogism consists of three propositions, of which the first, which is composed of the major and the middle term, is called the major; the second, composed of the minor and the middle, the minor; the third, finally, composed of the minor and the major, is called the conclusion. Thus if I construct a Syllogism from the terms proposed a little earlier: what presses on lower bodies is heavy; air presses on lower bodies: therefore air is heavy, the first proposition will be the major, the second the minor, and the last is called the conclusion or consequent. In an Enthymeme the first is called the antecedent, the second the consequent.

64 Dilemma est argumentatio ex duabus interrogationibus in quarum qualibet capitur respondens, ex. gr. vel qui peccat recordatur inferni vel non? Si concedis: ergo est stultus; si negas: ergo etiam est stultus, quia tantae poenae non recordatur.

64 A Dilemma is an argumentation from two questions, by either of which the respondent is caught, e.g. does he who sins remember hell, or not? If you grant it: then he is a fool; if you deny it: then he is a fool too, because he does not remember so great a punishment.

65 Inductio est argumentatio à singularibus sufficienter enumeratis ad universale, ut si dicas: aurum liquari potest, stannum, plumbum, & ferrum liquari possunt: ergo omne metallum liquari potest. Haec argumentatio erit mala & roboris expers, si vel unam partem ex numerandis non examinet. Exemplum seu paritas est argumentatio ab uno ad aliud simile in eadem linea. Demonstratio est argumentatio, quae constat præmissis evidentibus. Hinc per demonstrationem res manifeste nobis vera adparet. Illud quippe verè evidenterque cognoscitur, quod ex claris, perspicuisque principiis eruitur. Ceterum, aut effectum ex sua causa demonstramus, aut causam ex suo effectu. Prior demonstratio à priore, posterior à posteriore dicitur.

65 Induction is argumentation from singulars sufficiently enumerated to the universal, as if you say: gold can be melted; tin, lead and iron can be melted: therefore every metal can be melted. This argumentation will be bad and devoid of strength if it fails to examine even one part of those that are to be enumerated. Example, or parity, is argumentation from one thing to another similar thing in the same line. Demonstration is argumentation that consists of evident premises. Hence through demonstration a thing manifestly appears true to us. For that is truly and evidently known which is drawn out from clear and perspicuous principles. For the rest, we demonstrate either the effect from its cause, or the cause from its effect. The former demonstration is called a priori, the latter a posteriori.

66 Sic ex. g. si rotunditatem telluris demonstro ex umbra ejus in Eclipsibus Lunaribus, demonstro causam ex effectu,

66 Thus, e.g., if I demonstrate the roundness of the earth from its shadow in Lunar Eclipses, I demonstrate the cause from the effect, so

p. 25

adeoque ea demonstratio erit à posteriore. Contra ubi mentis immortalitatem ex ejus spiritualitate, hanc ex cogitatione demonstro, demonstratio erit à priore. Cognitio, quae demonstrationis ope adquiritur scientia vocatur. Definitur autem scientia: cognitio certa & evidens rei necessariae ex demonstratione proveniens.

that this demonstration will be a posteriori. On the other hand, when I demonstrate the immortality of the mind from its spirituality, and this from thought, the demonstration will be a priori. The cognition that is acquired by means of demonstration is called science. Science, moreover, is defined: certain and evident cognition of a necessary thing, proceeding from demonstration.

67 Dicitur cognitio certa, hoc est firma & stabilis, penitúsque inconcusa, & per hoc scientia differt ab opinione, quae non est nisi probabilis rei cognitio. Dicitur cognitio evidens, clara scilicèt & planè perspicua, atque hinc discernitur à fide, quae tota in obscuris versatur. Dicitur rei necessariae, ut inde pateat nullam de iis rebus dari posse scientiam, propriè loquendo, quae aliter esse possunt, ac cognoscuntur. Dicitur postremò ex demonstratione proveniens, ut discernatur ab intelligentia, nempè à cognitione primorum principiorum, Horum enim notio à demonstratione non dependet, quum ex suis terminis sint evidentissima, ex. gr. totum est majus sua parte, &c. Sicut demonstratio, alia est à priore, alia à posteriore, ita duplex scientia distinguitur: perfectissima, scilicèt, & minus perfecta. Illa per demonstrationem à priore adquiritur, haec verò per demonstrationem à posteriore.

67 It is called certain cognition, that is, firm and stable and altogether unshaken, and by this science differs from opinion, which is nothing but probable cognition of a thing. It is called evident cognition, namely clear and plainly perspicuous, and hence it is distinguished from faith, which is wholly concerned with obscure things. It is said to be of a necessary thing, so that it may thence be plain that, properly speaking, no science can be had of those things which can be otherwise than as they are known. It is said, lastly, to be proceeding from demonstration, so that it may be distinguished from understanding, namely from the cognition of first principles. For the notion of these does not depend on demonstration, since they are most evident from their own terms, e.g. the whole is greater than its part, etc. Just as one demonstration is a priori and another a posteriori, so a twofold science is distinguished: namely most perfect and less perfect. The former is acquired through demonstration a priori, the latter through demonstration a posteriori.

CAPUT X. — CHAPTER X

De forma, & figura Syllogismi.

On the Form and Figure of the Syllogism.

68 Forma Syllogismi est dispositio terminorum, in ordine ad conclusionem rectè inferendam: haec forma duplex est, modus scilicét, & figura. Modus est dispositio propositionum in ordine ad adfirmationem, aut negationem, universalitatem, aut particularitatem, & quùm medium tripliciter disponi possit in propositionibus, ex hoc resultat triplex figura Syllogismi, ut his versiculis demonstratur.

he Form of a Syllogism is the disposition of the terms with a view to cor68 T rectly inferring the conclusion: this form is twofold, namely mode and figure. Mode is the disposition of the propositions with respect to affirmation or negation, universality or particularity; and since the middle can be disposed in the propositions in three ways, from this there results the threefold figure of the Syllogism, as is shown by these little verses:

Prima prius subjicit medium, dein praedicat ipsum

The first first subjects the middle, then predicates it;

Altera bis dicit, bis tertia subjicit ipsum.

The second twice predicates, the third twice subjects it.

69 Prima figura ponit medium in majori tanquam subjectum. & ipsum medium tanquam praedicatum in minori. Secunda figura tam in majori, quàm in minori ponit medium ut praedicatum. Tertia demum, tam in majori, quàm in minori ponit medium

69 The first figure puts the middle in the major as subject, and the middle itself as predicate in the minor. The second figure puts the middle as predicate both in the major and in the minor. The third, finally, both in the major and in the minor, puts the middle

p. 26

ut subjectum. En exempla. Prim. fig. quod cogitat est spiritus; mens cogitat: ergo mens est spiritus. Secund. fig. corpus non cogitat; mens cogitat: ergo mens non est corpus. Tert. fig. quidquid cogitat est spiritus, aliquid quod cogitat in homine est: ergo spiritus aliquis in homine est: Omnes autem modi undeviginti his barbaris vocibus continentur.

as subject. Here are examples. First fig.: what thinks is spirit; the mind thinks: therefore the mind is spirit. Second fig.: body does not think; the mind thinks: therefore the mind is not body. Third fig.: whatever thinks is spirit; something that thinks is in man: therefore some spirit is in man. All the modes, moreover, nineteen in number, are contained in these barbarous words:

Barbara, Celarem, Darii, Ferio, Baralipton,

Barbara, Celarem, Darii, Ferio, Baralipton,

Celantes, Dabitis, Fopesmo, Frisesomorum,

Celantes, Dabitis, Fopesmo, Frisesomorum,

Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco, Darapti,

Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco, Darapti,

Felapton, Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison.

Felapton, Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison.

70 Ubi observatum volunt Peripatetici, quod omnes dictiones triplici syllaba constant, si excipias Baralipton & Frisesomorum, quibus metri causa, ut ipsi dicunt, additur una & altera syllaba, quae non pertinent ad figùram. In memoriam revocáte, quod A dénotat universalem adfirmativam, &c. Undè syllogismus in Barbara ex. gr. constat triplici propositione universali adfirmativa. In Celarem majori negativa, minori adfirmativa, & consequentia negativa, omnibus universalibus. Novem priores modi in duobus primis versibus contenti, ad primam figuram spectant, quatuor posteriores ad secundam, & reliqui ad tertiam. Nunc agendum erat de syllogismi reductione: nos verò Peripateticos circunspectiores sequentes, hujusmodi tractationem consultò relinquimus: nam plerumquè, ut ait S. Augustinus, citius videt ingeniosus non esse rectam conclusionem, quam praecepta ejus capit: tardus autem non eam videt, sed multo minus, quod de illa praecipitur.

70 Here the Peripatetics would have it observed that all the words consist of three syllables, if you except Baralipton and Frisesomorum, to which, for the sake of the meter, as they themselves say, one or two syllables are added that do not pertain to the figure. Recall to memory that A denotes the universal affirmative, etc. Hence a syllogism in Barbara, e.g., consists of three universal affirmative propositions; in Celarem, of a negative major, an affirmative minor and a negative consequent, all universal. The first nine modes, contained in the first two verses, belong to the first figure, the next four to the second, and the rest to the third. Now we ought to treat of the reduction of the syllogism; but we, following the more circumspect Peripatetics, deliberately leave aside a treatment of this kind: for generally, as St. Augustine says, a man of wit sees sooner that a conclusion is not right than he grasps its precepts; a slow man does not see it, and much less what is prescribed concerning it.

CAPUT XI. — CHAPTER XI

Tráditur universale principium dignoscendi, legitimusne sit syllogismus, an vitiosus, quin ulla prorsùs vulgarium regularum ratio habeatur.

A universal principle is handed down for recognizing whether a syllogism is legitimate or faulty, without any account at all being taken of the common rules.

71 Haec est célebris illa regula ab Auctore Clariss. Artis cogitandi inventa, nempè quod ut conclusio rectè inferatur dèbet contineri in aliqua praemissarum, & hoc ipsum debet ostendi, seu indicari per alteram, quae adplicata, vel indicativa vocatur, sicut prima dicitur

his is that celebrated rule devised by the most illustrious Author of 71 T the Art of Thinking: namely that, for the conclusion to be rightly inferred, it must be contained in one of the premises, and this very thing must be shown, or indicated, by the other, which is called the applicative, or indicative, just as the first is called the containing one.

p. 27

continens, In syllogismis adfirmativis nihil planè interest, an majorem, an minorem dicamus esse continentem, vel adplicatam, quia útraque aliquomodo conclusionem cóntinet, útraque etiam mutuò ostendit illam in altera continéri. Nam ex. gr. si dúbito, ¿an homo impius sit miser?, sic argumentabor. Quicumque servit cupiditatibus, est miser, sed impius servit cupiditatibus: ergo impius est miser. Quamcumque praemissarum designáveris, poterit dici conclusionem continére, idque ab altera ostendi. Nam conclusio continetur in majori, quia serviens cupiditatibus, impium sub se continet, & à minori ósténditur, quia serviens cupiditatibus, in sua idea comprehendit ideam miseri.

In affirmative syllogisms it makes no difference at all whether we call the major or the minor the containing or the applicative, since each in some way contains the conclusion, and each also mutually shows it to be contained in the other. For e.g. if I doubt whether an impious man is wretched, I shall argue thus: Whoever is a slave to his desires is wretched; but the impious man is a slave to his desires: therefore the impious man is wretched. Whichever of the premises you designate, it can be said to contain the conclusion, and this to be shown by the other. For the conclusion is contained in the major, because one who is a slave to his desires contains the impious man under itself; and it is shown by the minor, because one who is a slave to his desires comprehends in its idea the idea of the wretched.

72 Nihilominus in syllogismis adfirmativis, quum major ferè semper sit universalior, ut plurimum haberi poterit pro continente, & minor pro adplicante. In syllogismis verò negativis, praemissa negans est semper propositio continens, & adfirmans est propositio adplicans, quia quum consequentia sit negativa, aequius est, ut in praemissa negativa contineatur, quàm in adfirmante, quum negatio solùm in negatione includatur. Sed principium adplicemus.

72 Nevertheless, in affirmative syllogisms, since the major is almost always the more universal, it can for the most part be taken as the containing premise, and the minor as the applicative. In negative syllogisms, however, the negative premise is always the containing proposition, and the affirmative is the applicative proposition, because, since the consequent is negative, it is more reasonable that it be contained in the negative premise than in the affirmative, since a negation is included only in a negation. But let us apply the principle.

73 Dubito ex. g. ¿an iste syllogismus rectè concludat? Evangelium salutem spondet Christianis; quidam impii sunt Christiani: ergo Evangelium salutem spondet qnibusdam impiis, Consideratis ergo praemissis, evidens est, conclusionem in majori propositione minimè contineri, quamvis prima facie, in minori videatur comprehensa. Etenim Evangelium non omnibus christianis salutem promittit, sed iis tantùm, qui Christi D, mandata observant, quod non faciunt impii. Igitur syllogismus est illegitimus. Eadem ratione nullus est, qui sequitur: omnis homo est animal; equus non est homo: ergo equus non est animal. Conclusio namquè in praemissa negante non comprehenditur. At è contrario isti sunt optimi: Miseri sunt, qui cupiditatibus serviunt; avari cupiditatibus serviunt: ergo avari sunt miseri. Nulla substantia carens partibus destrui potest ab agente creato; anima rationalis est substantia carens partibus: ergo anima rationalis à nullo agente creato destrui potest. Utriusque enim conclusio in majori continetur, quemádmodum minor ipsa propositio palám facit.

73 I doubt, e.g., whether this syllogism concludes rightly: The Gospel promises salvation to Christians; some impious men are Christians: therefore the Gospel promises salvation to some impious men. Having considered the premises, then, it is evident that the conclusion is by no means contained in the major proposition, although at first sight it seems to be comprehended in the minor. For the Gospel does not promise salvation to all Christians, but only to those who observe the commandments of Christ the Lord, which the impious do not do. Therefore the syllogism is illegitimate. By the same reasoning this one is null: every man is an animal; a horse is not a man: therefore a horse is not an animal. For the conclusion is not comprehended in the negative premise. On the contrary, these are excellent: They are wretched who are slaves to their desires; the avaricious are slaves to their desires: therefore the avaricious are wretched. No substance lacking parts can be destroyed by a created agent; the rational soul is a substance lacking parts: therefore the rational soul can be destroyed by no created agent. For the conclusion of each is contained in the major, as the minor proposition itself makes plain.

74 Ope etiam hujus principii facili negotio détegi potest fallacia hujus syllogismi: qui dicit te esse animal, dicit verum; sed qui dicit te esse anserem, dicit te esse animal: ergo qui dicit te esse anserem dicit verum. Respondére namque sufficit, neutram praemissarum continére conclusionem. Animal enim in majori sumitur particulariter, quia est praedicatum hujus propositionis: tu es animal. Hinc etiam peti potest solutio sophismatis, quod Sanctus Augustinus refert: non es, quod ego sum; ego sum homo: ergo tu non es homo: nam

74 By the help of this principle, too, the fallacy of this syllogism can be detected with little trouble: he who says you are an animal says what is true; but he who says you are a goose says you are an animal: therefore he who says you are a goose says what is true. For it suffices to answer that neither of the premises contains the conclusion. For animal in the major is taken particularly, since it is the predicate of this proposition: you are an animal. Hence, too, may be sought the solution of the sophism that St. Augustine reports: you are not what I am; I am a man: therefore you are not a man: for each

p. 28

útraque praemissa loquitur de re singulariter mihi propria, itàque non potest continere conclusionem, quae procedit de re tibi propria.

premise speaks of a thing singularly proper to me, and so it cannot contain the conclusion, which proceeds about a thing proper to you.

75 Ad hanc normam, facilemque regulam omne ratiocinium exígite, nec operosa, & prorsùs inutili syllogismorum reductione vobis erit opus, si hanc omnibus communem, & penè in conspectu positam argumentandi legem sequemini. Hujus enim principii lumine cujusvis argumentationis bónitas deprehendi fácile potest, ut aliae proindè leges, vel obscuriores, vel minùs ùniversales, vel inutiles etiam censéri possint; imò verò debeant.

75 To this norm and easy rule submit every reasoning, and you will have no need of the laborious and altogether useless reduction of syllogisms, if you follow this law of arguing, which is common to all and placed almost before one’s eyes. For by the light of this principle the goodness of any argumentation whatever can easily be detected, so that the other laws can accordingly be deemed either more obscure, or less universal, or even useless; nay rather, they must be.

CAPUT XII. — CHAPTER XII

De fallaciis Syllogismi.

On the Fallacies of the Syllogism.

76 Fallacia Syllogismi, quae ex multiplici capite venit, vitium est, & cognoscendum, & vitandum. Primò igitur Syllogismus fallit ex aequivocatione alicujus nóminis, ex. gr. Gallus est avis; sed vir Francus est Gallus: ergo vir Francus est avis. Secundò quum fit transitus à genere ad speciem, ut Sempronius est animal, sed asinus est animal: ergo Sempronius est asinus. Tertia fallacia dicitur ignoratio elenchi, quando nimirùm aliud impugnatur, quàm quod est in quaestione, quia vel adtribuitur adversario, quod ipse non ádserit, vel ignoratur status quaestionis. Hùc pértinet mutatio medii, quando probaturus ex. gr. Deum esse amandum quia Bonus, relicto medio Bonitatis adsumis Sapientiam, aut Omnipotentiam. Quarta est petitio principii, quando supponitur id quod probari debebat. Ad hoc sophisma revocari possunt rationes illae, quibus probatur ignotum per aequè ignotum, incertum per aequè incertum, aut incertius.

allacy of a Syllogism, which comes from many sources, is a fault both 76 F to be recognized and to be avoided. First, then, a Syllogism deceives by the equivocation of some name, e.g. a gallus [cock] is a bird; but a Frenchman is a Gallus [Gaul]: therefore a Frenchman is a bird. Second, when there is a passage from genus to species, as Sempronius is an animal, but an ass is an animal: therefore Sempronius is an ass. The third fallacy is called ignoratio elenchi, namely when something other is attacked than what is in question, because either something is attributed to the adversary which he himself does not assert, or the state of the question is ignored. Here belongs the change of the middle, when, intending to prove, e.g., that God is to be loved because He is Good, you abandon the middle of Goodness and take up Wisdom or Omnipotence. The fourth is petitio principii, when that is supposed which ought to have been proved. To this sophism can be brought back those reasons by which the unknown is proved by the equally unknown, the uncertain by the equally uncertain, or by the more uncertain.

77 Latè patet sophisma petitionis principii: quicumque enim ponit sine ulla probatione véluti perspícuum, quod probatione omninò índiget, is quidem petit concedi sibi principium aliquod, quod erat probandum. Id verò vel proximè, vel remotè fit. Proximè, ut si pro ratione ponat conclusionem probandam, vel eisdem, vel sinónimis verbis, vel per círculum. Remotè, ut si rem apertè falsam, vel mera verba, vel aliquid hujúsmodi

77 The sophism of petitio principii extends widely: for whoever, without any proof, sets down as if perspicuous what altogether needs proof asks that some principle be granted him which was to be proved. This happens either proximately or remotely. Proximately, as when one puts forward as a reason the conclusion to be proved, either in the same words or in synonymous ones, or by a circle. Remotely, as when one brings forward a thing openly false, or mere words, or something of this kind

p. 29

ádferat ad probandam thesim: nam etiam tali casu petit sibi concédi principium, quod ei probandum erat, ut propósitum éfficeret. Quum praemissarum altera, vel plane dubia, vel plane falsa, pro ratione adfertur, hoc sophisma vocatur etiam petitio principii. Id plurimis modis fieri potest, ut supra dixímus. Aristoteles probat inerrantia sidera scintilláre, quia plurimum distant à nobis, s1 & plurimum distare quia scintillent. s2 En circulus.

to prove the thesis: for in such a case too he asks that the principle be granted him which he had to prove in order to accomplish what was proposed. When one of the premises, either plainly doubtful or plainly false, is adduced as a reason, this sophism too is called petitio principii. This can happen in very many ways, as we said above. Aristotle proves that the fixed stars twinkle because they are very far distant from us (l), and that they are very far distant because they twinkle (m). Behold a circle.

78 Quum adsignant pro causa physica mera verba, quae nihil reapsè significant, dari petitionem principii supra díximus, En exemplum. Philosophi nimis multi, dum res ab ipsa natura involútas explicare conantur, quum id firmis, & perspicuis argumentis nequeant efficere, & inscitiam suam nolint profitéri, ad verba inania recúrrunt, & plaudunt sibi, quasi tale mysterium reserassent. Hinc horror vacui, virtus soporifera, & id genus vocábula, sonóra illa quidem, & ampullósa, sed quae nullam sententiam habent, nec nos faciunt doctiores.

78 When they assign as a physical cause mere words that in reality signify nothing, we have said above that there is a petitio principii. Here is an example. Very many Philosophers, while they try to explain things wrapped up by nature herself, since they cannot accomplish this with firm and perspicuous arguments and are unwilling to confess their ignorance, have recourse to empty words and applaud themselves as though they had unlocked some such mystery. Hence horror of the vacuum, soporific virtue, and words of that kind, sonorous indeed and bombastic, but which have no meaning and do not make us more learned.

79 Quinta fallacia est non causae ut causa, ex. gr. Petrus in studiis bona dissipavit, & nihil ipsi profuit: ergo tempus in studiis non debet impendi. Ad hoc sophisma revocanda est, vulgaris illa mentis humanae fallacia: post hoc: ergo propter hoc. Sexta est imperfecta partium enumeratio. Sic pessimè ratiocinatur, qui integro Collegio tribuit peccatum aliquorum ex ipso. Septima est fallacia accidentis quando de natura rei judicatur ex eo, quod illi cónvenit per accidens; sic Medicinae omnia mala tribuuntur, quae proveniunt à circulatorum erroribus. Octava est, quando arguitur à secundum quid, ad simpliciter ex. gr. Aethiops est albus secundum dentes: ergo est albus.

79 The fifth fallacy is non-cause as cause, e.g. Peter squandered his fortune on studies, and they did him no good: therefore time ought not to be spent on studies. To this sophism must be brought back that common fallacy of the human mind: after this: therefore because of this. The sixth is imperfect enumeration of the parts. Thus he reasons very badly who attributes to a whole College the sin of some of its members. The seventh is the fallacy of the accident, when one judges of the nature of a thing from what belongs to it by accident; thus all the evils that come from the errors of quacks are attributed to Medicine. The eighth is when one argues from what holds in some respect to what holds simply, e.g. an Ethiopian is white as to his teeth: therefore he is white.

80 Nona est paritas inepta: quando nimirùm, ex eo quod duae res in uno, vel áltero praedicato, sunt símiles, collígimus álteram álteri esse simíllimam. Ejusdem sophísmatis auctores sunt illi, qui, ut aliquid álteri faciendum persuadeant, vitia astùtè praetereunt, cómmoda verò in caelum extollunt, ex. gr. Scholastici Philósophi, ut nobis persuadeant, Logicam suam ceteris esse praeferendam, cum jactatione ponunt, se ex Aristotelis Dialéctica disputáre, esse eam utilem ad Theologiam Scholasticam addiscendam: tùm demùm neminem sine ea in abstrusioribus disciplinis posse disputare. Illud autem tacent: talem Dialecticam esse artem cavillandi, & sine ullo fine contendendi, non trádere viam indagandi verum, tùm certum, tùm probabile: nihil de

80 The ninth is inept parity: namely when, because two things are similar in one or another predicate, we conclude that the one is very like the other. Authors of the same sophism are those who, in order to persuade someone that something is to be done, cunningly pass over its faults and extol its advantages to the skies; e.g. the Scholastic Philosophers, in order to persuade us that their Logic is to be preferred to the others, boastfully state that they dispute out of Aristotle’s Dialectic; that it is useful for learning Scholastic Theology; and finally that no one can dispute in the more abstruse disciplines without it. But they are silent about this: that such Dialectic is the art of caviling and of contending without any end; that it does not hand down the ways of searching out the true, whether the certain or the probable; that it contains nothing on the art

De Caelo. 2. cap. 8.

On the Heavens, 2, ch. 8.

Analyt. Prior. 1. cap. 13.

Prior Analytics, 1, ch. 13.

p. 30

arte critica continére, tùm deniquè nihil utilitatis humano generi adferre, ut in céteris disciplinis rectè sermocinetur, quod tacendum non fuit.

of criticism; and finally that it brings the human race no utility toward reasoning rightly in the other disciplines: which ought not to have been passed over in silence.

81 Decimà fallacia est: quando non alio argumento infirmamus propositionem veram, nisi auctorem irridendo. Peccant in hoc freqüenter Scholastici cum Recentioribus Philosophis disputantes. Verùm haec confutandi ratio infirma est prorsùs. Cogendi ergò sunt ii, ut theses non cachinnis, & dicteriis, sed argumentis firmis & perspicuis confútent. Fádem viâ cum iis agemus, qui querélis, éjulatu, jurejurándo falsum aliquid nobis persuadére conantur, quia ejusdem sophismatis rei sunt. Dicta sufficiant.

81 The tenth fallacy is: when we weaken a true proposition by no other argument than by ridiculing its author. The Scholastics often sin in this when disputing with the Modern Philosophers. But this way of refuting is altogether weak. They must therefore be compelled to refute theses not with guffaws and witticisms, but with firm and perspicuous arguments. In the same way shall we deal with those who try to persuade us of something false by complaints, wailing and oaths, because they are guilty of the same sophism. Let what has been said suffice.

LIBER II. — BOOK II

De Veritate.

On Truth.

82 Si quis intellectus operationibus rectè utitur, benè sanè utitur ratione, cónseqüensque est, ut hoc modo procédens, inveniat veritatem, de qua jam agendum paulò adcuratiùs. Veritas est, vel Metaphysica, vel Moralis, vel Logica. Metaphysicè verum dicitur, quidquid habet essentiam sibi convenientem. Etiam dicitur metaphysicè verum omne ens, vel existens, vel posibile, quum est consentaneum ideae, quam Deus habet de eo. Quare hoc sensu, Petrus, est verus Petrus, quia respondet ideae Dei, Haec veritas metaphysica vocatur etiam realis. Veritas moralis est, convenientia verborum, signorumque externorum cum cogitationibus mentis. Hinc, qui quod sentit, eloquitur, Verum, qui aliud sentit, aliud loquitur, Falsum dícere perhibetur. Nos verò ágimus de veritate Logica, quae est convenientia idearum nostrarum cum objecto. Hinc, si mihi ex. gr. concipio turrim, vel aliquid rotundum, & ea verè talia sunt, veritatem dicor adsequutus. Conveniunt enim ideae cum objecto. Contrà falsum est disconvenientia idearum cum objecto. Alia deinde veritas est certa, alia probabilis. Certa, quum penitùs sum persuassus, rem ita se habére. Probabilis, quum ita sum persuassus, ut timeam ne id ipsum sit falsum.

f anyone uses the operations of the intellect rightly, he certainly uses 82 I reason well, and it follows that, proceeding in this manner, he will find the truth, of which we must now treat a little more accurately. Truth is either Metaphysical, or Moral, or Logical. Whatever has the essence befitting it is called metaphysically true. Every being, too, whether existing or possible, is called metaphysically true when it is in conformity with the idea that God has of it. Hence in this sense Peter is a true Peter, because he corresponds to the idea of God. This metaphysical truth is also called real. Moral truth is the agreement of words and of external signs with the thoughts of the mind. Hence one who speaks out what he thinks is said to speak the True; one who thinks one thing and says another, the False. We, however, are dealing with Logical truth, which is the agreement of our ideas with the object. Hence if, e.g., I conceive a tower, or something round, and these things truly are such, I am said to have attained the truth. For the ideas agree with the object. Conversely, the false is the disagreement of ideas with the object. Further, one truth is certain, another probable. Certain, when I am thoroughly persuaded that the thing is so. Probable, when I am so persuaded that I fear lest it be false.

p. 31

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De veri & falsi criterio.

On the Criterion of the True and the False.

83 Sunt autem charactéres nonnulli, seu certae adsentiendi notae, quae item Criteria veritatis vocantur, quibus verum à falso secernitur: & in quae intuentes nos, veritatem quam quaérimus, invenímus. Quaéritur ergò, ¿quo tandem argumento tuti esse possímus ea, quae adfirmatè judicamus, sic se habere, ut judicamus, nulloque pacto in iis nos décipi?: in quo constituendo non mediocritèr Recentiores dissentiunt.

here are, moreover, certain characters, or definite marks of assent, 83 T which are likewise called Criteria of truth, by which the true is distinguished from the false, and by looking upon which we find the truth we seek. It is asked, then, by what argument, in the end, we can be safe that the things we judge affirmatively are as we judge them to be, and that we are in no way deceived in them: in establishing which the Moderns disagree not a little.

84 Petrus Daniel Huet existimat solam Dei locutionem eam esse, quae certos nos facit non errare. s1 Quae opinio falsa est; nam si ratione nihil possumus certò definire, ¿quomodo certiores érimus, Deum id nobis dixisse? Non omnes Divino Spiritu adflantur, deinde homines saepissimè in judicando decipiuntur. Qua propter, nequeunt plane constituere, an à Deo fiant certiores, an alitèr. Non nego, Prophetas dum Dei numine erant adflati, saepè nullo alio indiguisse argumento, quo convincerentur sibi Deum loqui: at non omnes erant Prophetae: maxima ergò tùm hominum pars, nihil sciebat: ut hodie, quum non sint Prophetae saltèm quos Ecclesia pro talibus habeat, omnes in omnium rerum ignoratione versentur, necesse est. Quicumque igitur hanc sententiam tuentur, nos in foedissimum Pyrrhonismum conjiciunt.

84 Pierre Daniel Huet holds that the speech of God alone is what makes us certain that we do not err (n). This opinion is false; for if we can determine nothing with certainty by reason, how shall we become certain that God has said this to us? Not all are breathed upon by the Divine Spirit; and then men are very often deceived in judging. Therefore they cannot plainly establish whether they are made certain by God, or otherwise. I do not deny that the Prophets, while they were inspired by the divine power, often needed no other argument by which to be convinced that God was speaking to them: but not all were Prophets; the greatest part of men, therefore, knew nothing at that time; so that today, since there are no Prophets, at least none whom the Church holds as such, all must necessarily be sunk in ignorance of all things. Whoever, then, defends this opinion casts us into the foulest Pyrrhonism.

85 Benedictus Spinosa origine Judaeus, quem Pantheistae, & Fanatici recentiores sequuntur, existimat, s2 humanam rationem esse veri criterium, non aliam ob rem, nisi quod ipsa sit ipsissima Dei ratio, quia mens nostra est particula mentis Divinae. Quae adeò sunt portentosa, ut qui velit ea resellere, is etiam cum ratione insaniat. Nam Dei ratio simplex est, & infinita: partiri ergò nequit: ergo ubicumque adest, eadem est.

85 Benedict Spinoza, a Jew by origin, whom the Pantheists and the more recent Fanatics follow, holds (o) that human reason is the criterion of the true for no other reason than that it is the very reason of God itself, because our mind is a particle of the Divine mind. These things are so monstrous that whoever would refute them would himself be going mad by reason. For the reason of God is simple and infinite: therefore it cannot be divided: therefore wherever it is present, it is the same.

Traitè de la foiblesse del' Esprit Humain.

Traité de la foiblesse de l’Esprit Humain.

p. 32

Quod si ratio nostra ipsa est Dei ratio, nulla ignorabimus; infinitae enim rationi omnia aperta sunt. ¿An quisquam est adeò amens, ut hunc in modum sibi aduletur, persuadeatque sibi, nihil esse, quod ignoret? Spinosismus s1 ergò ineptissimis deliramentis scatet.

Now if our reason is itself the reason of God, we shall be ignorant of nothing; for to infinite reason all things are open. Is anyone so mad as to flatter himself in this way, and to persuade himself that there is nothing he does not know? Spinozism (p), therefore, teems with the most inept ravings.

86 Nicolaus Malebranche Presbyt. Congreg. Orat. Gallicani, existimat, mentem nostram essentialiter Deo conjungi, atque in Dei idéa, & lumine nos omnia percípere, sive Dei lumen esse criterium veri, quia mens nostra omnia videt in Deo. s2 Sed si vera haec sunt, non video, quid discriminis intersit beatorum inter, & viatorum statum, ubi mens humana tot erroribus obnoxia saepè saepiùs à veritate aberrat. Mitto alia, ne longior sim quàm quod Elementorum limites patiuntur. At illud certè non omittam, quod unio haec substantialis mentis cum Deo nequit intelligi nisi in Spinosistico systémate. Enim verò, si Deus locus est mentium, ut spatium corporum, aut Dei partes erunt, aut modi, aut Deus ipse. Plura de hoc argumento Clariss. Genovesi. s3

86 Nicolas Malebranche, Priest of the French Congregation of the Oratory, holds that our mind is essentially joined to God, and that we perceive all things in God’s idea and light, or that the light of God is the criterion of the true, because our mind sees all things in God (q). But if these things are true, I do not see what difference there is between the state of the blessed and that of wayfarers, in which the human mind, subject to so many errors, very often strays from the truth. I pass over other things, lest I be longer than the limits of Elements allow. But this I shall certainly not omit, that this substantial union of the mind with God cannot be understood except in the Spinozist system. For indeed, if God is the place of minds, as space is of bodies, they will be either parts of God, or modes, or God himself. More on this subject in the celebrated Genovesi (r).

Tract. Theolog. Polit. cap. 1.

Theological-Political Treatise, ch. 1.

Spinosismus error est, non admittentium nisi unicam substantiam infinitis adtributis praéditam, quae inter numerantur infinita cogitatio, atque infinita extensio: eorum unumquodque aeternam, & infinitam essentiam habet, entia verò infinita oriri finguntur ex necessaria modificatione adtributorum istíus substantiae, animas scilicèt ex modificatione infinitae cogitationis, & corpora ex modificatione extensionis infinitae. Spinosa Deum non distinguit à mundo, Deum facit mutabilem, extensum, & tamen intelligentem. Impiae hypotheseos básim, & fundamentum adsúmit Spinosa non posse dari duas substantias ejusdem essentiae, quia si eamdem habeant essentiam, inquit, sunt una, & eadem substantia. Nullus autèm est, qui statim non videat, duas substantias habere non posse eamdem essentiam identitate numerica, (ut ajunt) posse verò identitate vel generica vel specifica. Nullus quoque est homo sensu communi praéditus, qui ex eo, quod Petrus, & Paulus sint homines, ideoque habeant eamdem essentiam, sive similes sint ratione humanitatis, conclúdat, Petrum, & Paulum esse unum, & eumdem hominem numericè, seu esse unicum individuum. Sed de his oportuniùs in Ethica.

Spinozism is the error of those who admit only a single substance endowed with infinite attributes, among which are numbered infinite thought and infinite extension: each of these has an eternal and infinite essence, while finite beings are imagined to arise from the necessary modification of the attributes of this substance, namely souls from the modification of infinite thought, and bodies from the modification of infinite extension. Spinoza does not distinguish God from the world; he makes God mutable, extended, and yet intelligent. As the basis and foundation of his impious hypothesis Spinoza assumes that there cannot be two substances of the same essence, because if they have the same essence, he says, they are one and the same substance. But there is no one who does not see at once that two substances cannot have the same essence by numerical identity (as they say), but can by identity either generic or specific. Nor is there any man endowed with common sense who, from the fact that Peter and Paul are men, and therefore have the same essence, or are alike by reason of humanity, would conclude that Peter and Paul are numerically one and the same man, or are a single individual. But of these things more opportunely in the Ethics.

Recherche de la Veritè lib. 1. cap. 2. §. 4.

Recherche de la Vérité, bk. 1, ch. 2, §. 4.

Disciplin. Metaphys. Elem. tom. 3. cap. 3.

Disciplin. Metaphys. Elem., vol. 3, ch. 3.

p. 33

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De vero probabili, ubi de probabilitate Hermeneutica, Morali, & Physica.

On the Probable True, where also on Hermeneutic, Moral and Physical Probability.

87 Quod non nihil dubitationis in mente relinquit, id probabilitèr tantum est verum. Fundamentum probabilitatis est sola hypothesis id est, propositio, quam ideò pro vera adsúmimus, quia proprietates, & effectus rei, indè cómmodè explicantur. Ex. gr. si pro vero sumo materiam subterráneam inflammabilem, maximè nitrósam, & sulphúream esse causam terraemotus, haec hypothesis, usque donec certior adpareat, pro falsa haberi nequit: nam ex ea omnia phaenómena, & facilè, & verosimilitèr expóni possunt. Aut verò pro hypothesi adsúmo verborum significationem, pósitum, connexionem cum fine auctoris conspirantem, aut testis cujusdam auctoritatem. Si primum fit, probabilitas illa Hermeneutica, seu probabilis interpretatio dicitur; si secundum Historica, quae speciatim fides nuncupatur.

hat leaves some doubt in the mind is true only probably. The sole 87 W foundation of probability is a hypothesis, that is, a proposition that we assume as true for this reason, that the properties and effects of a thing are conveniently explained from it. E.g. if I assume as true that a subterranean inflammable matter, chiefly nitrous and sulphurous, is the cause of earthquakes, this hypothesis, until something more certain appears, cannot be held to be false: for from it all the phenomena can be explained both easily and plausibly. Or else I assume as a hypothesis the signification of the words, their position, and a connection in agreement with the aim of the author, or the authority of some witness. If the first, that probability is called Hermeneutic, or probable interpretation; if the second, Historical, which is specifically named faith.

88 Fundamentum itaque probabilitatis Hermeneuticae est hujusmodi. Quod cum verborum significatione, positu, connexione, itemque cum Auctoris fine convenit: id probabiliter pro sensu auctoris habendum. Fundamentum probabilitatis Historicae est hujusmodi: Quod verum esse testatur homo fidedignus, id probabiliter verum est.

88 The foundation, therefore, of Hermeneutic probability is of this kind: What agrees with the signification, position and connection of the words, and likewise with the Author’s aim, is to be held probably as the Author’s meaning. The foundation of Historical probability is of this kind: What a trustworthy man testifies to be true is probably true.

89 Quod traditum nobis ab hominibus, id primùm, aut à praesentibus, vel coaevis traditur, aut ab absentibus, & recentioribus. 2. testes vel plures sunt, vel unus: itemque 3. vel oculis rem percepérunt, vel ab aliis narrari audiverunt, quin & 4. vel scientiae suae rationem reddunt, vel non, & 5. vel rem in se possibilem referunt, vel mirabilem, vel plane impossibilem. Deinde 6. vel noti, vel ignoti sunt. 7. vel neutrius, vel unius tantum partis studio feruntur. 8. vel prudentes, vel vecordes, vel probi, vel improbi, & mendaces. Ex quibus divisionibus facilè intelliguntur régulae ex quibus de gradibus humanae fidei potest judicari. I. est: Quo magis certus sum auctorem noluisse me decipere, eo majorem ei fidem habere teneor. II. An quis voluerit me decipere, saepe ex ipsis narrationis circunstantiis judicandum est.

89 What is handed down to us by men is, first, handed down either by those present, or contemporaries, or by those absent and later. 2. The witnesses are either several or one; and likewise 3. they either perceived the thing with their eyes, or heard it narrated by others; nay, and 4. they either give a reason for their knowledge, or not; and 5. they report a thing either possible in itself, or marvelous, or plainly impossible. Further, 6. they are either known or unknown; 7. they follow the zeal either of neither party or of one party only; 8. they are either prudent or foolish, honest or dishonest, and liars. From these divisions are easily understood the rules by which one can judge of the degrees of human faith. I. is: The more certain I am that the author did not wish to deceive me, the greater the faith I am bound to have in him. II. Whether anyone has wished to deceive me must often be judged from the very circumstances of the narration.

p. 34

90 Certissimum itaque est 1. uni testi rem mirabilem narranti, parùm fidei haberi, etiam si aliàs non adeo suspectus sit, maxime ubi res ita comparata est, ut testis facilè décipi imaginatione potuerit. 2. majorem esse probabilitatis gradum si rem, ut ut mirabilem, non tamen impossibilem, pluresque interim testes, licèt non per omnia eodem modo, iisdemque circunstantiis réferant. 3. multò probabílius esse, quod plures fidedigni iisdem circunstantiis réferunt, eamque probabilitatem haud parum augéri, si testes sint oculati, si personae publicae, si jurati. Plurimae aliae hujus probabilitatis regulae videri possunt apud Clariss. Anton. Genovesii s1

90 It is therefore most certain, 1. that little faith is to be had in a single witness narrating a marvelous thing, even if he is otherwise not much suspected, especially when the matter is such that the witness could easily have been deceived by his imagination; 2. that the degree of probability is greater if several witnesses report a thing that, however marvelous, is yet not impossible, even if not in every respect in the same manner and with the same circumstances; 3. that what several trustworthy men report with the same circumstances is much more probable, and that this probability is increased not a little if the witnesses are eyewitnesses, if they are public persons, if they are sworn. Very many other rules of this probability can be seen in the celebrated Antonio Genovesi (s).

91 Probabilitas moralis tunc habetur, quando ex signis quibusdam, quae homines praeseferunt, aliquid vel ocultum declaramus, vel praedícimus futurum. Haec pro rebus, quas praedícit adpelatur vel Practica vel Politica. Ex. gr. video Titium facie subtristi adspernantem licitas voluptates, déditum lucro, adtrita & sórdida veste, qui perpetuò clamitat se esse páuperem. Hinc probabiliter ínfero, Titium esse avarum. Haec autem divinandi ratio, quae ex signis externis ratiocinando, animi propensiones investígat, vocatur Probabilitas moralis, seu Practica. Aliquando verò ex hominum consiliis futurum aliquem eventum praedícimus, & haec divinatio peculiari vocábulo nominatur. Probabilitas Politica. Sed hae consecutiones, sunt magis, & minus probabiles, non secus ac judicandi vis, & usus rerum in iis, qui conjectant, qui, si multum prospiciunt, multò veriùs, & probabiliùs judicant.

91 Moral probability is had when, from certain signs that men display, we either declare something hidden or predict something future. According to the things it predicts, this is called either Practical or Political. E.g. I see Titius with a sad face spurning lawful pleasures, given over to gain, in a worn and sordid garment, perpetually crying out that he is poor. Hence I probably infer that Titius is avaricious. This way of divining, then, which by reasoning from external signs investigates the propensities of the mind, is called moral Probability, or Practical. Sometimes, however, we foresee some future event from the counsels of men, and this divination is named by a word of its own, Political Probability. But these consequences are more or less probable, just as the force of judging and the experience of things are greater or less in those who conjecture; those who see far ahead judge much more truly and more probably.

92 Probabilitas Physica tunc datur, quùm ex observatione phaenomenórum, & sensationum, hypothesim aliquam cogitamus, quae phaenómena omnia dilucidè explicet, & peritè. Quod si hypóthesis, quam pono est talis, ut ex ea nequeam probare, rem ita se habére; non est hypothesis, sed fictio. Ex. gr. quum dicunt Peripatetici horrorem vacui esse causam, cur antlia hauriat aquam, est mera fictio, quia talia verba non explicant, cur aqua 32 pedes adscendat, ultrò non adscendat in antlia mille pedes longa.

92 Physical Probability is given when, from the observation of phenomena and of sensations, we think out some hypothesis that explains all the phenomena lucidly and skillfully. But if the hypothesis that I posit is such that from it I cannot prove that the thing is so, it is not a hypothesis but a fiction. E.g. when the Peripatetics say that the horror of the vacuum is the cause why a pump draws water, it is a mere fiction, because such words do not explain why water rises 32 feet and rises no further in a pump a thousand feet long.

In Elem. Art. Logico-Critic.

In the Elem. Art. Logico-Critic.

p. 35

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

Regulae humanam mentem dirigentes in iis credendis doctrinis, quae tam Divinae, quam humanae auctoritati innituntur.

Rules directing the human mind in believing doctrines that rest on Divine as well as on human authority.

93 Auctoritate ducimur, quùm in ferendo de rebus judicio, dictis aliorum stamus. Divina, vel Humana est illa auctoritas, quae ad adsensum nos movet. Divina auctoritate nos falli impossibile prorsùs est, ut dicémus. Auctoritate verò humana posse nos décipi, nèminem fugit. Interest ergò quàm maximè, ut in hac parte nos rectè instituamus, En itaque regulae, quae in credendis doctrinis usui nobis esse possunt.

93 We are led by authority when, in passing judgment on things, we abide by the sayings of others. That authority which moves us to assent is either Divine or Human. That we should be deceived by Divine authority is utterly impossible, as we shall say. But that we can be deceived by human authority escapes no one. It matters very greatly, therefore, that we instruct ourselves rightly in this respect. Here, then, are the rules that can be of use to us in believing doctrines.

94 Reg. I. Ea omnia adsensu firmissimo admittenda sunt, quae Divinae auctoritati innituntur. Magis quippe repugnat Deum falli, aut fállere, quàm vera ea non esse, quae ratio vel evidentissima ostendit. In iis ergò quae sunt Fidei Divinae aequissimum est, quemadmodùm ait Apostolus: in captivitatem redigere intellectum in obsequium Christi, vidélicèt, ut ne quidem levissimè de earum veritate dubitemus, quae divina auctoritate nobis credenda traduntur. Reg. II. Firmo, constanti que animo admittenda sunt, quae nobis ab Ecclesia divina fide credenda proponuntur. Fieri enim non potest ut Ecclesia in iis definiendis, quae ad fidem pértinent, decipiatur, nosque in errorem indúcat, quum Christus D. apertè dixerit nunquam fore, ut deficeret fides Petri, nec ut portae inferi contra Ecclesiam praevalerent.

94 Rule I. All those things are to be admitted with the firmest assent which rest on Divine authority. For it is more repugnant that God should be deceived, or deceive, than that those things should not be true which reason shows most evidently. In those things, therefore, which belong to Divine Faith it is most just, as the Apostle says, to bring into captivity the understanding unto the obedience of Christ, namely, so that we do not doubt even in the slightest of the truth of those things which are handed down to us to be believed on divine authority. Rule II. Those things are to be admitted with a firm and constant mind which are proposed to us by the Church to be believed with divine faith. For it cannot happen that the Church should be deceived in defining those things which pertain to faith, and lead us into error, since Christ our Lord said openly that it would never come about that the faith of Peter should fail, nor that the gates of hell should prevail against the Church.

95 Reg. III. Magnopere curandum est, ut id teneamus, quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est. Nam illud est hujusmodi, ut ab ipsomet Christo D. ore tenùs tráditum Apóstolis fuerit, atque per illos in nos constanti traditione s1

95 Rule III. Great care must be taken that we hold that which has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. For that is of such a kind that it was handed down by word of mouth by Christ our Lord himself to the Apostles, and derived through them to us by constant tradition (t).

p. 36

derivatum. Reg. IV. Non omnis sententia ex eo praecissè censenda est tuta, quod Ecclesia haudquaquam illam proscripserit. Ecclesia enim non omnes apertè damnat errores, sed eos tantùm, qui faciunt strépitum. Tandiu enim, (inquit S. August.) sustinetur peccatum, aut error cujuslibet, donec, aut accusatorem inveniat, aut pravam opinionem pertinaci animositate defendat. Reg. V. Firmiter tenendum est tanquam certum, quod in materia fidei, & morum, omnes SS. Patres docent. Quum enim SS. Patres fuerint á Deo missi, ut Ecclesiam erudirent, fieri nequaquam potuit, ut in iis, quae ad Religionem spectant, omnes erraverint. Dixi omnes; non enim eorum quilibet tanta fuit infallibilitate donatus, ut nulla prorsus in re errare potuerit, quemadmodum expressè docet S. August.

Rule IV. Not every opinion is to be deemed safe precisely because the Church has by no means proscribed it. For the Church does not openly condemn all errors, but only those that make a stir.
