158 Quum hactenùs de operationibus intellectus humani, ipsaque natura veritatis, de fallaciis sensuum, voluntatis, & mentis, quae veri adsecutionem impediunt, satis pro Elementorum ratione actum sit: proximum est, ut quomodo his intellectus operationibus ad investigandam, communicandamque veritatem utendum sit, dicamus paulò adcuratiùs. Agemus itaque primò de Methodo, quâ verum inveniendum est, tum de illa, quâ verum nobis notum, céteris est explicandum; quibus deinde pauca de methodo Studendi, & Disputandi, nonullaque de Pedantismo philosophico profligando subjiciémus.

ince enough has now been said, as the plan of Elements allows, about 158 S the operations of the human intellect and the very nature of truth, and about the fallacies of the senses, of the will and of the mind which impede the attainment of truth, the next thing is that we should say a little more accurately how these operations of the intellect are to be used for investigating and communicating truth. We shall treat, therefore, first of the Method by which the truth is to be found, then of that by which a truth known to us is to be explained to others; to which we shall then append a few things on the method of Studying and of Disputing, and some on routing philosophical Pedantry.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De Methodo Logico-analytica, sive inventionis.

On the Logico-analytic Method, or method of invention.

159 Ratio illa & méthodus abscónditae, optataeque veritatis investigandae, Methodus Analytica nuncupatur, seu methodus inventionis, quae definiri potest: ars disponendi cogitationes nostras, ut quantum humana conditio patitur, verum, quod nos latet detegamus. Dicitur Análytica, nempè resolutionis, quia ut quod in abdito delitescit, apertum nobis fiat, omne totum dividi debet in suas partes, omne compositum resolvendum est in sua principia, omnisque effectus ad suam causam est revocandus.

hat manner and method of investigating hidden and desired truth 159 Tis called the Analytic Method, or method of invention, which can be defined: the art of disposing our thoughts so that, as far as the human condition allows, we may uncover the truth that is hidden from us. It is called Analytic, that is, of resolution, because, in order that what lies concealed in hiding may become open to us, every whole must be divided into its parts, every composite must be resolved into its principles, and every effect must be referred back to its cause.

160 Peripatetici Philosophi praeclarissimam hanc, imò potissimam sanè Philosophiae partem, vix, aut ne vix quidem

160 The Peripatetic Philosophers scarcely, or not even scarcely, touched this most excellent, nay truly the most important, part of Philosophy,

p. 53

adtingerunt, quamvis eadem praecipuus sit scopus, praestantissimae hujus disciplinae, quae arduam provinciam emendandae, regendaequae mentis sibi súscipit gubernandam. Nos quaecumque à Recentioribus hac in re literis consignata sunt, seligémus, quàmque fieri póterit brevissimè, nitidè que explicábimus.

although it is the chief aim of this most excellent discipline, which takes upon itself the arduous charge of correcting and ruling the mind. We shall select whatever the Moderns have committed to writing on this subject, and shall explain it as briefly and as neatly as can be done.

161 Antequam autem opus adgrediamur, animadvertendum est, eam esse hujusce mentis nostrae naturam, ut non quaecumque ei incomperta sunt, ádsequi possit, prae oculis ergo habendum est, nos ignorare rerum essentias, itaque ignorare essentiam materiae, quo posito fiunt quaestiones indisolubiles quibus respondére non possumus, ut sunt illae, quae dependent à cognitione essentiae, dequibus non loquimur. Ne quis ergo fortè tempus incautè perdat in iis méthodo Análytica inquirendis, quae crassis semper involúta ténebris homines latebunt, oportunum dúximus vos praemonére, ut ab earum inquisitione abstineatis.

161 Before we approach the work, however, it must be noted that the nature of this mind of ours is such that it cannot attain everything that is unknown to it. It must therefore be kept before our eyes that we are ignorant of the essences of things, and so ignorant of the essence of matter; and this being posited, there are insoluble questions which we cannot answer, such as those which depend on knowledge of essence, of which we are not speaking. Lest anyone, then, should perhaps incautiously waste his time in inquiring by the Analytic method into those things which, wrapped always in thick darkness, will lie hidden from men, we have thought it fitting to forewarn you to abstain from inquiring into them.

162 Sunt etiam quaestiones inutiles, ut sunt ferè omnes, quae à Peripateticis aeternis disidiis pertractantur, ex. gr. an copula sit terminus? An privatio sit principium compositi in facto? An materia adpetat formas corruptas? aliasque multò etiam vaniores, quas pudéret me dicere non intelligere, si ipsi intelligerent, qui háec tractant: quae quidem quaestiones, aut nunquam dírimi poterunt, sicuti certè adhùc in utramque partem à Scholasticis disputantur, aut si fortassè dírimi perfectè possent, nihilò tamen nos doctiores efficerent; ut absurdum proindè sit methodi Analyticae leges, aut ingenii vim, aut pretiosi temporis partem dirimendis illis adhibére.

162 There are also useless questions, such as are nearly all those that are handled by the Peripatetics in endless quarrels, e.g. whether the copula is a term? Whether privation is a principle of the composite as already made? Whether matter desires corrupted forms? and others emptier still by far, which I should be ashamed to say I do not understand, if those who treat them understood them themselves: questions which either can never be settled, just as they are certainly still disputed on both sides by the Scholastics, or, if perhaps they could be settled perfectly, would nevertheless make us not a whit more learned; so that it is accordingly absurd to apply the laws of the Analytic method, or the force of the mind, or any part of precious time, to settling them.

163 Habemus praeterea quaestiones solubiles, nec inutiles, quae in tres classes cómmodè dividuntur, nam in quacumque quaestione dato adtributo, quaeritur cui subjecto cómpetat? aut subjecto posito, inquiritur, quod determinatum praedicatum illi competat? aut deniquè posito praedicato, & subjecto interrogatur, an unum álteri cómpetat. Tria igitur sunt, nec plura esse possunt summa quaestionum omnium génera. Primi generis est ex. gr. haec quaestio: quaenam est terraemotus causa? In hac enim quaestione dato adtributo, nempè causam terremotus, quaeritur, ¿quodnam sit subjectum cui adtributum illud conveniat? nimirum, ¿quidnam id sit, cui adtributum hoc cómpetat, quod terraemotum pariat? & sic de réliquis. En itaque regulae, quibus in veri investigatione procedamus oportet.

163 We have, besides, questions that are soluble and not useless, which are conveniently divided into three classes; for in any question whatever, either, an attribute being given, it is asked to what subject it belongs? or, a subject being posited, it is inquired what determinate predicate belongs to it? or finally, a predicate and a subject being posited, it is asked whether the one belongs to the other. There are, therefore, three highest genera of all questions, nor can there be more. Of the first kind is, e.g., this question: what is the cause of earthquakes? For in this question, an attribute being given, namely the cause of the earthquake, it is asked what the subject is to which that attribute belongs? that is, what is that thing to which this attribute belongs, that it produces the earthquake? and so of the rest. Here, then, are the rules by which we must proceed in the investigation of the truth.

164 Reg. I. Perpende utrum ita sis animo praeparatus, ut ei veritati inveniendae, aut solvendae quaestioni aptus sis, ne aut inutiliter divageris; aut inepta & ridicula effutias. Agitur ex. gr. de re Theologica, Medica, Astronomica, quas res ignoras. ¿Nonné

164 Rule I. Weigh whether you are so prepared in mind as to be fit for discovering that truth or for solving the question, lest you either wander about to no purpose, or blurt out inept and ridiculous things. Suppose, e.g., the matter in hand is Theological, Medical, Astronomical, things of which you are ignorant. Will you not be utterly ridiculous

p. 54

perridiculus eris, qui hujusmodi facultates ignorans, in scenam prodis, Theologum, Medicum, Astronomum acturus? Hùc adferri potest Horatianum illud.

who, ignorant of such faculties, come forth upon the stage to play the Theologian, the Physician, the Astronomer? To this may be applied that saying of Horace:

Sumite materiam vestris, qui scribitis aequam

Take, you who write, a matter equal to your strength,

Viribus, & versate diù, quid ferre recúsent.

and turn over long what your shoulders refuse to bear,

Quid valeant húmeri.

what they can carry.

165 Quòd si rei de qua agitur, ideas habeamus, aptique simus quaestioni solvendae, tum séquitur Reg. II. Expendito simplex ne qnaestio sit, an composita: quod si fuerit composita eam adcurate in omnes simplices divídito, minutatim examinato, & in eam primum inquirito, quae lucem aliis praeferre possunt. Ex. g. Quaesitum est, ¿quinam usus, & constructio partium oculi? Duae proponuntur quaestiones: earum secunda omnium primùm examinábitur: nisi enim sciatur, quaenam sint oculi partes, explicari non potest, quinam sint earumdem usus. Reg. III. Propositae quaestionis nodum, quam clarissimis verbis explicato. Siquidem nisi statuatur apertè, quid quaerendum sit, in incerto omnis vagabitur disputatio. Reg. IV. Quaestionem intellige, & exactè, ac quamsimplicissime exprime, id est, resecato ab ea quaecumque minimè ad eam faciunt. Quo circa, si quae sunt in quaestione proposita, quae demi possunt salva quaestione, prudentiae est ea resecare.

165 But if we have ideas of the thing in question, and are fit to solve the question, then follows Rule II. Weigh whether the question is simple or compound: and if it is compound, divide it accurately into all its simple questions, examined minutely, and inquire first into that one which can carry light before the others. E.g. It is asked, what is the use and the structure of the parts of the eye? Two questions are proposed: of these the second will be examined first of all; for unless it is known what the parts of the eye are, it cannot be explained what their uses are. Rule III. Explain the knot of the proposed question in the clearest words. For unless it is plainly established what is to be sought, the whole disputation will wander in uncertainty. Rule IV. Understand the question, and express it exactly and as simply as possible, that is, cutting away from it whatever does not at all bear upon it. Concerning which, if there are things in the proposed question that can be removed while the question remains intact, it belongs to prudence to cut them away.

166 Reg. V. Dividatur quoad fieri potest omne genus in suas species, eaque omnia separentur, atque in certas classes distribuantur. Reg. VI. Constituto quod investigandum est, adtente observare debemus, quidnam ea ipsa in re nobis innotescat. Mens quippe nostra ignotis in tantum capiendis par est, in quantum diversimodè illa participant, de eorum natura, quae nobis priùs nota erant. Reg. VII. Plurimum interest, (ut egregiè monet Cartesius) cogitationes nostras certo ordine promovere, incipiendo scilicet ab his rebus, quae cognitu nobis sunt faciliores, atque ex his paulatim, ac veluti per gradus ad difficiliorem investigationem progrediendo. Reg. VIII. & postrema. Si diu perquisiveris, nec veritatem repereris, examen redintegrato. Si iterum frustra tentaveris, ne pronunciato rem, aut falsam, aut minus possibilem, ex hoc tantum qnod non intelligis, nisi adèo sis perridiculus, ut mentem tuam veri, & falsi mensuram putes.

166 Rule V. Let every genus be divided, as far as can be done, into its species, and let them all be separated and distributed into definite classes. Rule VI. Having established what is to be investigated, we must attentively observe what, in that very thing, becomes known to us. For our mind is equal to grasping unknown things only insofar as they participate in diverse ways in the nature of those things which were previously known to us. Rule VII. It is of the greatest importance (as Descartes excellently advises) to advance our thoughts in a fixed order, beginning, namely, with those things which are easier for us to know, and from these proceeding little by little, and as it were by steps, to the more difficult investigation. Rule VIII, and last. If you have searched long and have not found the truth, renew the examination. If you have tried again in vain, do not pronounce the thing either false or less than possible merely because you do not understand it, unless you are so utterly ridiculous as to think your own mind the measure of the true and the false.

p. 55

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De Méthodo Logico-synthetica, sive Doctrinae tradendae.

On the Logico-Synthetic Method, or the Method of Imparting Doctrine.

167 Veritas análytica méthodo quaesita, & inventa synthetica methodo aliis demonstratur. Est igitut synthesis methodus doctrinae tradendae, seu veritatis quâmcommodissimé fieri possit demonstrandae. Demonstrare autèm est tam aptè ad suadendum raciotinari, ut adsensum denegare seriò, & ex animo minimè possit is quocum disputamus. Ut verò ineluctabilis aliorum suasio obtineatur, quatuor hae leges serventur necessè est.

ruth sought by the analytic method and found is demonstrated to 167 T others by the synthetic method. Synthesis, therefore, is the method of imparting doctrine, or of demonstrating the truth as conveniently as can be done. To demonstrate, moreover, is to reason so aptly for persuading that the person with whom we are disputing can in no way seriously and sincerely refuse his assent. But in order that the persuasion of others may be obtained beyond escape, these four laws must be observed.

168 Reg. I. Nullam vocem, locutionemve, quae ambigua, aut obscura sit, vel esse possit, indefinitam adhibeas, sed determinatum sensum, praecissamque significationem in quam hujusmodi voces, locutionesve accipi vis, luculentissime explica. Reg. II. Praedefinitas semel voces, & locutiones, ne inter argumentandum, in alium sensum per incuriam detorqueas. Reg. III. Nullam illationem deducito, quae non sit necessario vinculo, & immediato adnexa cum iis propositionibus, exquibus eam colligis. Reg. IV. & postréma. Omnis propositio ex qua aliquid per consequens colligendum, inferendumve est, vel simplicis intuitionis esto, vel ex aliis praemissis per necessarium consequens deducta. Hae leges, non modò necessariae sunt ad demonstrationem conficiendam, sed solae sufficiunt, ut optimè probat Cl. Soría. s1

168 Rule I. Use no word or expression that is, or can be, ambiguous or obscure, left undefined; but explain most lucidly the determinate sense and the precise signification in which you wish such words or expressions to be taken. Rule II. Do not, through carelessness, twist words or expressions once defined into another sense in the course of arguing. Rule III. Draw no inference that is not connected by a necessary and immediate bond with the propositions from which you gather it. Rule IV, and last. Every proposition from which something is to be gathered or inferred by you must either be self-evident by simple intuition, or be deduced from other premises as a necessary consequence. These laws are not only necessary for constructing a demonstration, but they alone suffice, as the celebrated Soria excellently proves. (y)

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

De Méthodo studendi.

On the Method of Studying.

169 Methodum studendi eam voco, qua studia nostra dirigenda sunt, ut ex librorum lectione disciplinam quam cupimus proprio etiam marte ediscamus. Profectó nonnisi defectu rectae methodi factum árbitror,

ethod of studying I call that by which our studies are to be directed, 169 M so that from the reading of books we may thoroughly learn the discipline we desire by our own efforts as well. Truly, I judge that it has come about only through lack of a right method

Elem. Logic.

Elem. of Logic.

p. 58

donec ocurrat cujus ambae à respondente concedantur. Proprium est Paedigogorum, quos Hispanè Pedantes adpellamus, quum thesin refutandam sibi sumunt, non antithesin probare, & bona fide agere, sed ad stratagémata confúgere, & vel ea, quae obiter neque consultò, & ex animi sententia dicuntur infirmare, vel interrogatiunculis ineptis respondentem transversum ageré, deridere vel argumentis ab instituto alienissimis tironem fatigare, vel tandem eadem argumenta etiam atque etiam obtrúdere, quasi nihil adversarius iis respondisset.

until one occurs both of whose premises are granted by the respondent. It is characteristic of Pedagogues, whom in Spanish we call Pedantes, when they take it upon themselves to refute a thesis, not to prove the antithesis and to act in good faith, but to resort to stratagems: either to weaken things that are said in passing, and not deliberately and as one’s real opinion; or to drive the respondent off course with inept little questions, to mock him, or to weary the beginner with arguments utterly foreign to the matter in hand; or finally to thrust forward the same arguments again and again, as though the adversary had made no reply to them.

Respondentis propria.

THINGS PROPER TO THE RESPONDENT.

176 Respondens ab opponente propositum adsumat syllogismum, hoc est, repetat, ut adpareat, ipsum opponentis mentem fuisse adsequutum. Praemissas iterata vice repetat, notans, ad singulas, num eas concedat, an probationem ulteriorem desideret, an interea transire permittat, donec altera fuerit sufficienter probata, utendo ex. gr. his fórmulis: concedo majorem, nego minorem, nego antecedens, transeat major, &c. Si praemissas alio respectu concedat, alio neget, utatur distinctione, eamque ad argumentum adplicet, quo in casu opponentis est, vel probare praemissam sub limitatione qua negatur, vel limitationem tanquam ineptam, impugnare. Quum Praeses vices respondentis in se suscipiat, eadem quae respondentis ejus sunt officia.

176 The respondent should take up the syllogism proposed by the opponent, that is, repeat it, so that it may appear that he has grasped the opponent’s meaning. Let him repeat the premises a second time, noting at each one whether he grants it, or desires a further proof, or allows it to pass for the meantime until the other has been sufficiently proved, using, e.g., these formulas: I grant the major, I deny the minor, I deny the antecedent, let the major pass, etc. If he grants the premises in one respect and denies them in another, let him use a distinction and apply it to the argument; in which case it is the opponent’s part either to prove the premise under the limitation under which it is denied, or to attack the limitation as inept. When the President takes upon himself the part of the respondent, the same duties are his as are the respondent’s.

CAPUT V.

CHAPTER V.

De Pedantismo philosophico profligando.

On Banishing Philosophical Pedantry.

177 Haec vox Pedantismus originem ducit a Paedagogis: qui quòd pédites sequantur nobiles puérulos, Pedanti Italica voce nuncupantur. Hi homines ex diuturno puérulis imperandi usu, eam auctoritatem adfectant, ut etiam cum aliis hominibus, atque de rebus aliis loquentes, voce, vultu, gestuque ipso auctoritatem praeseferant. Quumque vel Humanioribus literis, vel Philosophia leviter, aut ne vix quidem leviter erudíti sint, sic mentem ineptissimis opinionibus imbuunt, omninò ut judicium deprávent,

his word Pedantry takes its origin from Pedagogues, who, because 177 T they follow noble boys on foot, are called Pedanti in the Italian tongue. These men, from long habit of commanding boys, affect such authority that even when speaking with other men and about other matters they display authority in their voice, their look, and their very gestures. And since they are educated in humane letters or in Philosophy only lightly, or not even lightly, they so imbue their minds with most inept opinions as utterly to deprave their judgment,

p. 59

& judicandi aciem retundant: imò, (quod maximè dolendum) frequenter etiam iis, quorum educationi dant operam, eadem vitia instíllant. Ex quo putidissimus Pedantismus, id est generalis ineptia judicii nascitur: quae, quasi bonarum artium pestis, in adolescentium perniciem longè latèque serpit, & cùm humaniores literas, tùm graviores disciplinas contáminat.

and blunt the edge of their judging: nay (what is most to be lamented), they frequently instill the same vices even in those to whose education they devote their labor. From this is born that most rotten Pedantry, that is, a general ineptitude of judgment: which, like a plague of the liberal arts, creeps far and wide to the ruin of young men, and contaminates both humane letters and the weightier disciplines.

178 Atque hinc manifestum fit, idem Recentioribus esse pedantam, quod Latinis erat ineptus. Ineptum autèm illi vocabant eum, qui ad benè de rebus judicandum non erat aptus. Haec autem ineptia judicii non angustis regionibus finitur, sed perlatè patet. Nos tamen eam uno Pedantismi Philosophici nomine designamus; propterea quod ab imprudentia judicandi dimanat, quae prudentiae recte cogitandi, id est Logicae, cujus in omníbus disciplinis praecipuus usus est, proximè repugnat.

178 And hence it becomes manifest that a pedant is to the Moderns the same as an ineptus [inept man] was to the Latins. They called ineptus the man who was not apt for judging well about things. This ineptitude of judgment, however, is not confined within narrow regions, but extends far and wide. We nevertheless designate it by the single name of Philosophical Pedantry, because it flows from imprudence in judging, which is most directly opposed to the prudence of thinking rightly, that is, to Logic, whose chief use is in all the disciplines.

179 Hinc meritò illi condemnantur, qui jurant in verba magistri, & religioni ducunt, ab ipsius sententiis vel minimum declinare. Hic Pedantismus veteres Pythagoréos infuscavit: qui tantùm praeceptori suo tribuebant, ut semper in ore haberent, ipse dixit: quod illis erat pro demonstratione Geometrica. Id ipsum Arabes cum Aristotele suo, & Galeno factitarunt. Id illi qui ab Arabibus doctrinam acceperant ab XII. seculo tanto studio priestiterunt, ut non, quid esset verum, sed quid Aristoteles dixerit, anxiè explorarent: imò non, quid Aristoteles, vir non ineptus dixerit; sed quid Arabes, qui Philosophi sententias perperàm interpretati fuerant, eidem adfinxerint, investigarent. Ex quo illae disputationes, quae tot secula invaluerunt: & impedimento fuere hominibus, ne praeclarum aliquid in bonis studiis molirentur. Et nisi vergente ad finem superiori seculo tale jugum Philosophi penitùs excussissent, adhùc in illa barbarie, & squalóre disciplinae omnes jacérent.

179 Hence those are deservedly condemned who swear by the words of a master, and make it a matter of conscience to depart even in the least from his opinions. This Pedantry darkened the old Pythagoreans, who attributed so much to their teacher that they always had in their mouths he himself said it; which for them stood in place of a Geometrical demonstration. The Arabs did this very thing with their Aristotle, and with Galen. Those who had received their doctrine from the Arabs practiced it from the twelfth century on with such zeal that they anxiously explored, not what was true, but what Aristotle had said; nay, they investigated not what Aristotle, a man not inept, had said, but what the Arabs, who had wrongly interpreted the Philosopher’s opinions, had foisted upon him. From this came those disputations which prevailed for so many centuries, and stood in men’s way, so that they attempted nothing distinguished in good studies. And unless, as the last century was drawing to its close, the Philosophers had thoroughly shaken off such a yoke, all the disciplines would still be lying in that barbarism and squalor.

180 Hinc eodem Pedantismo laborant ii, qui quum animum ad aliquam disciplinam adplicant, non animadvertunt, quo illud, quod disputatur pertineat, quemque fructum mens humana ex talibus disciplinis cápere debeat. Hujusmodi sunt qui sine ulla methodo disciplinis vacant, nec de polienda mente judicioque formando cogitant. Horum sanè infinitus est numerus. Ad eandem classem referuntur illi, qui in unam disciplinam toto pectore incumbunt, quin ea, ex quibus lucem ipsa accipit adtingant. Quis ferat homines qui Naturali philosophiae dant operam, quin Geometriam animo rectè percipiant?

180 Hence those labor under the same Pedantry who, when they apply their mind to some discipline, do not notice to what end the matter disputed pertains, and what fruit the human mind ought to gather from such disciplines. Of this kind are those who give themselves to the disciplines without any method, and take no thought for polishing the mind and forming the judgment. Of these the number is truly infinite. To the same class are referred those who apply themselves to one discipline with their whole heart without so much as touching those things from which it receives its light. Who would bear men who devote themselves to Natural philosophy without rightly grasping Geometry in their minds?

181 In eodem numero ponuntur illi, qui res, quas ipsi, nedum alii non intelligunt, magna vocis, & láterum contentione disputant. Id faciunt frequenter illi qui de quidditatibus,

181 In the same number are placed those who dispute, with loud voice and straining of lungs, about things which they themselves, to say nothing of others, do not understand. This is frequently done by those who wrangle among themselves about quiddities,

p. 60

haecceitatibus, formalitatibus, de appetitu materiae primae, & sexcentis hujusmodi altercantur inter se. Nempè intelligunt ii quidem voces, & interdùm ideas abstractas, quas vocibus adjungunt. Sed quùm talibus ideis nullae res tales respondeant; disputant de nihilo. Proinde ut multas voces fundunt, nihil re vera dicunt, ideoque se non intelligunt, tùm quod nihil dicunt, tùm quod saepissime diversas ideas vocibus subjiciunt.

haecceities, formalities, the appetite of prime matter, and six hundred things of this kind. They understand, to be sure, the words, and sometimes the abstract ideas which they join to the words. But since no such things correspond to such ideas, they are disputing about nothing. Accordingly, though they pour out many words, they say nothing in truth, and therefore do not understand themselves, both because they say nothing and because they very often put different ideas under the same words.

182 Referuntur etiam inter pedantas illi qui de aliorum scriptis judicium confidenter faciunt, quin ea quae necessaria sunt, ut aptè judicent, habeant ¡Quàm enim temerarium est de Recentiorum philosophorum sententiis judicare, priùs quàm eorum placita, & historiam Litterariam vel à límine salútent! Quis ferat eos, qui nulla verae Theologiae eruditione imbúti, nulla Artis criticae notitia tincti, nonnullorum sententias, tanquam si essent Catholicae fidei repugnantes, magno supercilio repudiant, quas ii non dicam non expendunt, sed ne intelligunt quidem.

182 Among the pedants are also reckoned those who confidently pass judgment on the writings of others without having the things that are necessary in order to judge aptly. For how rash it is to judge of the opinions of the Modern philosophers before having so much as greeted their tenets and the History of Letters from the threshold! Who would bear those who, imbued with no learning in true Theology, tinged with no knowledge of the Critical Art, repudiate with great haughtiness the opinions of certain authors as though they were repugnant to the Catholic faith, opinions which they, I will not say do not weigh, but do not even understand?

183 Meritò etiam ejus farinae homines (ut festiviùs loquamur) inter Archipedantas retúleris, quibus curae cordique est ad subsellia feminarum de recta philosophandi methodo & Recentiore Philosophia decérnere: scilicèt, magnum auctoritatis momentum Peripateticae Scholae accedere in dies ex ipso illo FEMINATUSCONSULTO debet: quasi verò non dedeceat viros, ubi consilio, labore, alacritate, & optimarum artium institutione opus erat, ad garrulas feminas & rudiorem plebeculam confúgere. Sed haec satis.

183 Deservedly, too, you would count among the Archpedants men of that stamp (to speak more merrily) whose heart’s concern it is to pronounce, before the benches of the women, on the right method of philosophizing and on the Newer Philosophy: forsooth, a great weight of authority must accrue day by day to the Peripatetic School from that very Decree of the Women’s Senate: as if it were not unbecoming for men, where there was need of counsel, labor, alacrity, and training in the best arts, to take refuge with chattering women and the ruder rabble. But enough of this.

184 Pedantibus etiam accensentur Consequentiarii: ii nimirum, qui, dùm aliorum sententias confútant, non eversis fundamentis contrariae opinionis, ad consequentias confugiunt; quò adversariorum honorem, & nominis existimationem in discrimen vocent. Existimantes se, sin minus rationibus, saltim per minas & convicia adversarios suos de gradu, & causa esse dejecturos. Ex. gr. Laudet quis investigationem philosophicam Boylei, Leibnitzii, Nevvtoni, Leeuvvenockii, Clarkii, Derhami, ceterorumque haereticorum, qui Philosophiam in bono lumine collocarunt. Infert consequentiarius: esse Haereticum, vel de haeresi suspectum: non esse audiendum: & quidquid eruditionis indè profluit, tanquam perniciosum, esse explodendum.

184 To the Pedants are also added the Consequence-mongers: those, namely, who, while they refute the opinions of others, without overturning the foundations of the contrary opinion, take refuge in consequences, by which to bring the honor and good name of their adversaries into jeopardy; thinking that, if not by reasons, at least by threats and abuse, they will dislodge their adversaries from their ground and their cause. E.g. someone praises the philosophical investigation of Boyle, Leibniz, Newton, Leeuwenhoek, Clarke, Derham, and the other heretics who have set Philosophy in a good light. The consequence-monger infers: that he is a Heretic, or suspect of heresy; that he is not to be listened to; and that whatever learning flows from that source is to be hissed off the stage as pernicious.

185 Jam verò haec ratiocinatio: Laudat investigationem philosophicam Haereticorum: ergo est Haereticus: est falsa. Adeoque, quae inde ducuntur, ceterae eodem vitio laborant. Nam non omnia, quae Haeretici dixére; sunt falsa: nec omnia quae Catholici scripserunt vera sunt. Utrique & bona, & mala scripsére, quae expendenda sunt ad oraculum Vaticani: & si per

185 Now this reasoning: He praises the philosophical investigation of Heretics: therefore he is a Heretic, is false. And so the other things that are drawn from it labor under the same vice. For not everything the Heretics have said is false, nor is everything Catholics have written true. Both have written things good and bad, which are to be weighed by the oracle of the Vatican: and if by Pontifical

p. 61

Pontificias leges extare legique licet, utique temerè repreheduntur argumentis ab invidia ductis. Eodem jurè argumentaremur hoc modo: tuetur mordicus dogmata Aristotelis, adhaeret placitis Galeni, Avicenae, Averroesii: ergo est Ethnicus, aut Mahumedanus. Quod tamen ineptissimum argumentandi genus est.

laws they may exist and be read, they are surely censured rashly with arguments drawn from envy. By the same right we might argue in this way: he stubbornly defends the dogmas of Aristotle, adheres to the tenets of Galen, Avicenna, Averroes: therefore he is a Heathen, or a Mohammedan. Which, however, is a most inept kind of arguing.

186 Etiam cum pedantibus junguntur illi, qui non alia ratione politissimorum Recentiorum laudem se se consecuturos esse arbitrantur, quàm si Philosophiam scripturi centonem ex sententiis repugnantibus consuant: ut si quis ex. gr. scripturus Physicam, posteaquam systema Scholasticorum de formis substantiali, & accidentali mórdicùs tuetur, tamen in quibusdam phaenomenis explicandis, Gassendi, Cartesii, Nevvtoni opiniones amplexatur. Is quidem pedanta est & sine ullo judicio scribit.

186 Joined with the pedants, too, are those who think they will win the praise of the most polished Moderns in no other way than if, when about to write a Philosophy, they stitch together a patchwork of conflicting opinions: as if someone, e.g., about to write a Physics, after stubbornly defending the system of the Scholastics on substantial and accidental forms, nevertheless, in explaining certain phenomena, embraces the opinions of Gassendi, Descartes, Newton. He indeed is a pedant, and writes without any judgment.

187 Postremò accensentur pedantibus illi, qui puerorum mentes multitudine obruunt praeceptorum, ac toti sunt in eo, ut longas disputationes contexant, quin prius examinent, an ad finem, quem sibi ponunt, conducant. Ex quo existit, ut tiro, quamlibet tricis illis & cavillationibus benè excultus, si ad aliquam controversiam reducitur, de qua in schola non diputatur, quid constituere debeat, ignoret.

187 Lastly, those are counted among the pedants who overwhelm the minds of boys with a multitude of precepts, and are wholly bent on weaving long disputations, without first examining whether they conduce to the end they set themselves. From this it comes about that the beginner, however well trained in those trifles and quibbles, if he is brought to some controversy that is not disputed in the school, does not know what he ought to decide.

188 Quod ne à me, Adolescentes, invidiosè, aut alia de causa dictum putetis, vobis pro certo adfirmo, me nullo partium studio agi ista disputantem, & scribentem. Peccarem certè, & ridendus essem meritò, si ego, qui tironibus auctor sum, ne ex praejudicatis sententiis dijudicent, ipse poenitendo praejudicio de aliorum sententiis pronunciarem: Nolo ego judex esse in hac causá: judicent doctissimi homines, qui in Peripatetica philosophia diu multumque se torserunt, qui; si viri boni sunt, fatéri debent, hanc, quam ipsi callent Logicam vulgatam quamque laudibus ad caelum férunt, divinumque vocant inventum; istam ipsam nihil juvare se, ut de rebus, quae in Scholis non traduntur, disputent.

188 Lest you should think, young men, that this has been said by me out of ill-will or for any other cause, I affirm to you for certain that in disputing and writing these things I am moved by no partisanship. I should certainly sin, and deservedly be laughed at, if I, who counsel beginners not to judge from prejudiced opinions, should myself pronounce on the opinions of others with a prejudice to be repented of. I do not wish to be judge in this cause: let those most learned men judge who have long and greatly tormented themselves in the Peripatetic philosophy; who, if they are honest men, must confess that this common Logic in which they are versed, and which they extol to the skies with praises and call a divine invention, that very Logic helps them not at all to dispute about matters that are not taught in the Schools.

189 Et haec sunt praecipua pedantismi genera, ad quae cetera facili negotio reducuntur. Supersedémus reliquis, ne infinitè excùrrat oratio. Ex iis, quae diximus sat manifestum est, praepósterum, absurdum, ineptum ratiocinandi morem, & verae Philosophiae inopiam in causa fuisse, quamobrem, in pedantismum incidamus: id est, in nulla disciplina finem, atque adjumenta commodè cognoscamus, modumque teneamus. Quae si rectè agnosceremus, caveremus profecto ab ineptiis, quae nos doctiorum, & prudentium ludibrio exponunt: quod ipsum est in unaquaque re esse Philosophum. Cl. Verney, ex quo haec excerpsimus plura alia de pedantismo disserit. Ipsum consulite.

189 And these are the chief kinds of pedantry, to which the rest are easily reduced. We pass over the others, lest our discourse run on without end. From what we have said it is sufficiently manifest that a preposterous, absurd, and inept manner of reasoning, and the want of true Philosophy, have been the cause of our falling into pedantry: that is, of our failing, in any discipline, properly to recognize its end and its aids, and to keep due measure. If we rightly recognized these, we should surely beware of the inepties that expose us to the mockery of the learned and the prudent; and this is the very thing that being a Philosopher in each matter means. The celebrated Verney, from whom we have excerpted these things, discourses of many others concerning pedantry. Consult him.

p. 60

haecceitatibus, formalitatibus, de appetitu materiae primae, & sexcentis hujusmodi altercantur inter se. Nempè intelligunt ii quidem voces, & interdùm ideas abstractas, quas vocibus adjungunt. Sed quùm talibus ideis nullae res tales respondeant; disputant de nihilo. Proinde ut multas voces fundunt, nihil re vera dicunt, ideoque se non intelligunt, tùm quod nihil dicunt, tùm quod saepissime diversas ideas vocibus subjiciunt.

haecceities, formalities, the appetite of prime matter, and six hundred things of this kind. They understand, to be sure, the words, and sometimes the abstract ideas which they join to the words. But since no such things correspond to such ideas, they are disputing about nothing. Accordingly, though they pour out many words, they say nothing in truth, and therefore do not understand themselves, both because they say nothing and because they very often put different ideas under the same words.

182 Referuntur etiam inter pedantas illi qui de aliorum scriptis judicium confidenter faciunt, quin ea quae necessaria sunt, ut aptè judicent, habeant ¡Quàm enim temerarium est de Recentiorum philosophorum sententiis judicare, priùs quàm eorum placita, & historiam Litterariam vel à límine salútent! Quis ferat eos, qui nulla verae Theologiae eruditione imbúti, nulla Artis criticae notitia tincti, nonnullorum sententias, tanquam si essent Catholicae fidei repugnantes, magno supercilio repudiant, quas ii non dicam non expendunt, sed ne intelligunt quidem.

182 Among the pedants are also reckoned those who confidently pass judgment on the writings of others without having the things that are necessary in order to judge aptly. For how rash it is to judge of the opinions of the Modern philosophers before having so much as greeted their tenets and the History of Letters from the threshold! Who would bear those who, imbued with no learning in true Theology, tinged with no knowledge of the Critical Art, repudiate with great haughtiness the opinions of certain authors as though they were repugnant to the Catholic faith, opinions which they, I will not say do not weigh, but do not even understand?

183 Meritò etiam ejus farinae homines (ut festiviùs loquamur) inter Archipedantas retúleris, quibus curae cordique est ad subsellia feminarum de recta philosophandi methodo & Recentiore Philosophia decérnere: scilicèt, magnum auctoritatis momentum Peripateticae Scholae accedere in dies ex ipso illo FEMINATUSCONSULTO debet: quasi verò non dedeceat viros, ubi consilio, labore, alacritate, & optimarum artium institutione opus erat, ad garrulas feminas & rudiorem plebeculam confúgere. Sed haec satis.

183 Deservedly, too, you would count among the Archpedants men of that stamp (to speak more merrily) whose heart’s concern it is to pronounce, before the benches of the women, on the right method of philosophizing and on the Newer Philosophy: forsooth, a great weight of authority must accrue day by day to the Peripatetic School from that very Decree of the Women’s Senate: as if it were not unbecoming for men, where there was need of counsel, labor, alacrity, and training in the best arts, to take refuge with chattering women and the ruder rabble. But enough of this.

184 Pedantibus etiam accensentur Consequentiarii: ii nimirum, qui, dùm aliorum sententias confútant, non eversis fundamentis contrariae opinionis, ad consequentias confugiunt; quò adversariorum honorem, & nominis existimationem in discrimen vocent. Existimantes se, sin minus rationibus, saltim per minas & convicia adversarios suos de gradu, & causa esse dejecturos. Ex. gr. Laudet quis investigationem philosophicam Boylei, Leibnitzii, Nevvtoni, Leeuvvenockii, Clarkii, Derhami, ceterorumque haereticorum, qui Philosophiam in bono lumine collocarunt. Infert consequentiarius: esse Haereticum, vel de haeresi suspectum: non esse audiendum: & quidquid eruditionis indè profluit, tanquam perniciosum, esse explodendum.
