Ejusmodi principium quod dat esse rei vocatur essentia, natura, constitutivum ejusdem rei, hoc uno discrimine, quod ubi concipitur tanquam fons, & origo proprietatum, vocatur essentia; ubi verò concipitur tanquam fons & origo operationum, quae à tali re producuntur, dicitur natura, plerumque tamen, natura, & essentia promiscuè usurpantur.

19 Accordingly essence, to begin with it, is nothing other than the first attribute that is conceived in a thing, and from which all the rest proceed as from a root. In the Schools it is commonly defined: that through which a being is, or is conceived to be; or that which intrinsically composes a thing; or that which intrinsically gives being to a thing. Such a principle, which gives being to a thing, is called the essence, the nature, the constitutive of that same thing, with this one difference, that where it is conceived as the source and origin of properties it is called essence, but where it is conceived as the source and origin of the operations which are produced by such a thing it is called nature; most often, however, nature and essence are used indiscriminately.

20 Hinc dirimi breviter poterunt celeberrimae quaestiones illae, quae tanto adparatu in Scholis agitari solent; utrum nempè essentiae rerum sint aeternae ac invariabiles, utrum Deus contradictoria efficere possit? Quamvis enim plurimi existiment rerum essentias ita, reluctante licet intellectu nostro, à Deo variari posse, ut circulus in figura angulis praedita, sive quadrata redduci possit, ut Deus efficere possit bis duo non esse quatuor &c, longè tamen verisimilius videtur rerum essentias ita certas ac invariabiles esse, ut nec à Deo variari possint.

20 Hence those most celebrated questions which are wont to be agitated in the Schools with so much apparatus can be briefly settled: namely, whether the essences of things are eternal and invariable, and whether God can bring about contradictories? For although very many think that the essences of things can be varied by God, even against the resistance of our intellect, in such a way that a circle could be turned into a figure endowed with angles, or into a square one, and that God could bring it about that twice two is not four, etc., yet it seems far more probable that the essences of things are so certain and invariable that they cannot be varied even by God.

p. 8

21 Quum enim essentiae nomine nihil aliud intelligatur, nisi adtributum illud, aut illa perfectio, quae dat esse rei, impossibile est certe ut principium illud varietur quin ipsa quoque res, quae recipit esse variari debeat, ut ex. gr. si radiorum aequalitas, & angulorum privatio auferatur, circulus etiam auferri debebit, sive circulus amplius concipi vel haberi non poterit. Et certè ejusmodi rerum essentiae nihil aliud sunt quam archétypae rerum ideae, vel imagines illae, quae ab aeterno Deus in mente habuit, & ad quarum similitudinem res in tempore creavit, ideòque sicuti imagines illae, vel divinae ideae immutabiles sunt, sic ipsae rerum essentiae invariabiles etiam censeri debent.

21 For since by the name of essence nothing else is understood but that attribute, or that perfection, which gives being to a thing, it is certainly impossible for that principle to be varied without the thing itself, which receives its being, having to be varied as well; as, e.g., if the equality of the radii and the privation of angles are taken away, the circle too will have to be taken away, or a circle can no longer be conceived or had. And certainly such essences of things are nothing other than the archetypal ideas of things, or those images which God had in his mind from eternity, and in whose likeness he created things in time; and therefore, just as those images, or divine ideas, are immutable, so the essences of things themselves must also be deemed invariable.

22 Existentia communiter definitur: positio entis aut essentiae extra nihil & omnes causas; ideòque inter essentiam & existentiam discrimen illud reperitur, quod essentia possibilibus etiam rebus conveniat, quae in causae primae, sive secundae potentia continentur, existentia vero iis solum rebus conveniat, quae extra causam primam sive secundam positae sunt. Quandoquidem verò essentia & existentia aequaliter substantiis omnibus, & accidentibus convenit, ut accidentia non minus quàm substantiae, si possibilia fuerint, habeant esse, si producta fuerint habeant existere, & accidentia tamen seu modi á substantiis maximè distinguuntur, in subtantiis ipsis praeter essentiam, & existentiam accidentibus quoque communem concipi, vel admitti debet alia perfectio, quae accidentibus convenire non possit, ut illae proinde substantiae ab accidentibus veluti constanti, clarissimoque discrimine distinguantur.

22 Existence is commonly defined: the placing of a being or essence outside nothing and all causes; and therefore between essence and existence there is found this difference, that essence applies also to possible things, which are contained in the power of the first or of a second cause, whereas existence applies only to those things which have been placed outside the first or second cause. Since, however, essence and existence apply equally to all substances and to accidents, so that accidents no less than substances, if they are possible, have being, and, if they have been produced, have existing, and since accidents or modes are nonetheless very greatly distinguished from substances, in substances themselves, besides essence and existence, which are common to accidents as well, another perfection must be conceived or admitted which cannot apply to accidents, so that those substances may accordingly be distinguished from accidents as by a constant and most clear difference.

23 Haec nova perfectio substantiis solum conveniens dicitur hypostasis, vel subsistentia, ultima nempè perfectio, forma, vel actus, quo res, aut natura, vel essentia ita perficitur, terminatur, completur, vel redditur sui juris non modò, ut non indigeat alio ad essendum, & operandum, sed etiam ut sibi tribuantur operationes suae, sive ut sit ac operetur independenter ab alio, quod soli certae substantiae convenire potest, quae per se subsistit, & substat, sive subjicitur accidentibus. Subjectum verò, substantia, sive compositum quod hac ultima perfectione donatur, sive quod per se subsistit ac operatur dicitur suppositum, & si spiritualis & incorporeae cognitionis capax sit ut in Deo, Angelis, & hominibus vocatur persona, quae proinde à Boethio definitur: rationalis naturae individua substantia.

23 This new perfection, which applies to substances alone, is called hypostasis, or subsistence: namely the ultimate perfection, form or act by which a thing, or nature, or essence, is so perfected, terminated, completed, or made its own master, not only so that it does not need another for being and operating, but also so that its operations are attributed to it, or so that it is and operates independently of another; which can belong only to a certain substance, which subsists by itself, and stands under, or is subjected to, accidents. The subject, moreover, the substance or composite, that is endowed with this ultimate perfection, or that subsists and operates by itself, is called a suppositum; and if it is spiritual and capable of incorporeal knowledge, as in God, the Angels and men, it is called a person, which is accordingly defined by Boethius: an individual substance of a rational nature.

24 Hinc in divinis tres hypostases, vel subsistentiae reperiuntur, ideòque etiam tres personae: quumque subsistentia Divini Verbi, subsistentiae creatae, vel humanae vices in Christo Domino suppleverit, sive terminaverit naturam humanam, quae propria creata, vel humana subsistentia terminari debebat, clarissimè adparet quod in Christo Domino duplex quidem natura: divina, scilicèt, ac humana, ideoque duplex voluntas ut à VI Synodo contra

24 Hence in divine things three hypostases, or subsistences, are found, and therefore also three persons: and since the subsistence of the Divine Word took the place of the created, or human, subsistence in Christ the Lord, or terminated the human nature, which ought to have been terminated by its own created or human subsistence, it appears most clearly that in Christ the Lord there is found a twofold nature, divine, namely, and human, and therefore a twofold will, as the Sixth Synod against the Monothelites

p. 9

Monothelitas definitum est, reperitur: unica tamen hypostasis, vel subsistentia divina, ideòque unica persona divina in illo reperiebatur.

defined; but only one hypostasis, or divine subsistence, and therefore only one divine person, was found in him.

25 Quumque non natura, sed persona sit illa, quae aliquid operari vel pati dicitur, juxta commune principium illud: operationes sunt suppositorum, operationes aut merita Christi D. infiniti valoris, ac dignitatis, ideoque infinitis hominibus à scelerum culpa, vel poena redimendis pares esse debebant, quippè quae ab infinita persona, sive Supposito divino producebantur. Sed haec Theologis pro rei dignitate explicanda relinquimus, ne nos falcem in alienam messem immitamus.

25 And since it is not the nature but the person that is said to operate or to suffer something, according to that common principle, operations belong to supposita, the operations or merits of Christ the Lord had to be of infinite value and dignity, and therefore equal to redeeming infinite men from the guilt or the punishment of their crimes: since they were produced by an infinite person, or divine Suppositum. But these things we leave to the Theologians, to be explained according to the dignity of the matter, lest we put our sickle into another’s harvest.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

De aliis proprietatibus vel adtributis Entis, sive de Unitate, Veritate, & Bonitate.

On the other properties or attributes of Being, or on Unity, Truth, and Goodness.

26 Proprietates illae vel adtributa entis, quae sup. cap. sunt explicatae, non cuilibet enti, sed singulis entis generibus convenire possunt, sed essentia quidem in entibus omnibus etiam possibilibus, existentia verò in iis rebus, quae extra omnem causam positae sunt, subsistentia denique in substantiis tantummodò reperitur. Alia tamen sunt adtributa quae sic universaliter enti conveniunt, ut omnes entium fines vel terminos transcendant, vel excedant, unde transcendentalia vocantur, ideòque non aliqua solum, sed singula prorsùs entium genera complectuntur, solentque tria praesertim à Philosophis enumerari Vnitas, nempè, Veritas, & Bonitas.

he properties or attributes of being which were explained in the chap26 T ter above can apply not to every being, but to the individual genera of being: essence, indeed, is found in all beings, even possible ones, existence in those things which have been placed outside every cause, and subsistence, finally, in substances only. There are, however, other attributes which apply to being so universally that they transcend, or exceed, all the bounds or limits of beings, whence they are called transcendentals; and therefore they embrace not some only, but absolutely all the genera of beings; and three in particular are commonly enumerated by the Philosophers: namely Unity, Truth and Goodness.

27 Vnitas nihil est aliud quàm carentia sive privatio divisionis, nec alia de causa conceptus entis unicus, & simplex est, nisi quod ille varias in partes dividi non potest. Quoniam ergo unitas divisioni opponitur, totidem unitatis genera distingui possunt, quot sunt divisiones ipsae, vel distinctiones quae inter entia reperiuntur. Distinctio verò sive divisio triplex â Philosophis numeratur; generica nempè, specifica, & numerica. Distinctio generica, dicitur illa, quae reperitur inter entia, quae sub diverso genere, sive cathegoria continentur, ut inter circulum, & lineam rectam, circulus enim sub figurae curvilinae, linea verò recta, neque ad curvilineum genus, neque ad quodvis aliud genus figurae pertinet.

27 Unity is nothing other than the lack or privation of division, and for no other reason is the concept of being one and simple except that it cannot be divided into various parts. Since, therefore, unity is opposed to division, as many kinds of unity can be distinguished as there are divisions themselves, or distinctions, found among beings. Distinction or division is reckoned threefold by the Philosophers: namely generic, specific and numerical. Generic distinction is said to be that which is found between beings that are contained under a different genus or category, as between a circle and a straight line; for the circle is contained under the genus of curvilinear figure, whereas the straight line belongs neither to the curvilinear genus nor to any other genus of figure.

28 Specifica reperitur inter entia, quae quum sub eodem genere contineantur diversae tamen speciei sunt, ut inter circulum & triangulum, qui sub eodem figurae genere collocantur, ad varias tamen figurae species pertinent. Numerica denique est illa, quae reperitur

28 Specific distinction is found between beings which, though they are contained under the same genus, are yet of a different species, as between a circle and a triangle, which, though placed under the same genus of figure, yet belong to different species of figure. Numerical distinction, finally, is that which is found

p. 10

inter individua ejusdem speciei, vel inter illa quae sub eadem specie continentur, & solis circunstantiis & conditionibus individuantibus distinguuntur, ut circulus A, circulus B. Distinctio generica atque specifica desumi concipitur à forma, natura, vel essentia rerum, unde illa quae specificè sive genericè differunt diversam essentiam habere debent.

between individuals of the same species, or between those that are contained under the same species and are distinguished only by individuating circumstances and conditions, as circle A, circle B. Generic and specific distinction is conceived to be drawn from the form, nature, or essence of things; whence those things that differ specifically or generically must have a different essence.

29 Distinctio verò numerica quae materialis etiam vocari solet, ut plurimi existimant à sola materia, quae proindè principium individuationis vocatur, vel à circunstantiis materialibus desumi debet; unde Thomistae arbitrantur in Angelis quia materia carent, hanc numericam distinctionem admitti, sive plures Angelos in unica specie reperiri non posse, sed potius Angelos singulos specificè inter se differre. Quemadmodùm tamèn rationales animae, etsi incorporeae sint, numericè inter se distinguuntur ex ordine, vel habitudine qua singulae ad proprium corpus diriguntur; ita quoque Angeli numericè distingui possunt ex accidentibus vel circunstantiis spiritualibus quibus adfecti sunt, aut certè ex varia actione Dei qua creati fuerint, vel conserventur.

29 Numerical distinction, on the other hand, which is also commonly called material, must, as very many think, be drawn from matter alone, which is accordingly called the principle of individuation, or from material circumstances; whence the Thomists hold that in Angels, because they lack matter, this numerical distinction is not admitted, or that several Angels cannot be found in a single species, but rather that individual Angels differ specifically from one another. Yet just as rational souls, though they are incorporeal, are numerically distinguished from one another by the order or habitude by which each is directed to its own body, so too Angels can be numerically distinguished by the spiritual accidents or circumstances with which they are affected, or at any rate by the varied action of God by which they were created or are conserved.

30 Distinctio realis est illa quae reperitur in re independenter ab intellectu. Distinctio rationis est illa quae pendet ab intellectu. Distinctio realis dividitur in entitativam, modalem, & virtualem. Realis entitativa quae etiam major vocari solet, dicitur illa quae reperitur inter varias res, quarum entitates ita distinctae sunt, ut una ab alia separari, vel saltem una sine alia perfectè concipi possit, ut inter Lunam & Solem, aurum, & argentum &c. Realis minor seu modalis dicitur illa quae datur inter rem & modum rei, qui modus ab ipsa re separari, vel sine ipsa perfecte concipi non potest, ut inter figuram & corpus figuratum. Virtualis denique, quam potius fundamentum distinctionis, quàm distinctionem dixeris, quae reperitur in re, quae quamvis unica & simplex sit, pluribus tamen aequívalet, ideòque occasionem praebet intellectui, ut plures in illa partes concipiat, ut in Deo, ejusque adtributis & perfectionibus, adtributa ipsa veluti distincta cóncipimus, ut Justitiam à Misericordia.

30 Real distinction is that which is found in the thing independently of the intellect. Distinction of reason is that which depends on the intellect. Real distinction is divided into entitative, modal and virtual. Real entitative distinction, which is also commonly called major, is said to be that which is found between various things whose entities are so distinct that one can be separated from the other, or at least one can be perfectly conceived without the other, as between the Moon and the Sun, gold and silver, etc. Real minor, or modal, distinction is said to be that which obtains between a thing and a mode of the thing, which mode cannot be separated from the thing itself, or perfectly conceived without it, as between figure and the figured body. Virtual distinction, finally, which you might rather call the foundation of a distinction than a distinction, is that which is found in a thing which, although it is one and simple, is yet equivalent to several, and therefore gives the intellect occasion to conceive several parts in it; as in God and in his attributes and perfections we conceive the attributes themselves as distinct, e.g., Justice from Mercy.

31 Praeter haec distinctionis genera Scotus distinctionem aliam admittit, quam dicit esse formalem, actualem ex natura rei, formalem quia non reperitur inter rem & rem, sive inter rem & modum entis, sed inter varias formalitates seu perfectiones ejusdem rei, ut inter adtributa Dei, inter animalitatem & rationalitatem hominis &c. actualem verò & ex natura rei, quia actualiter de facto independenter ab intellectu reperitur in rebus. Hinc gravissima exorta est quaestio inter Thomistas, & Scotistas, quo nimirùm distinctionis genere distinguantur gradus metaphysici ejusdem rei, ut ex. gr animalitas & rationalitas quae reperiuntur in homine, gradus vegetandi & sentiendi qui reperitur in brutis, atque universaliter genus & differentia, quae in singulis rebus, sive speciebus continentur.

31 Besides these kinds of distinction Scotus admits another distinction, which he says is formal, actual, and from the nature of the thing: formal, because it is found not between thing and thing, or between a thing and a mode of being, but between various formalities or perfections of the same thing, as between the attributes of God, between the animality and rationality of man, etc.; actual, and from the nature of the thing, because it is found in things actually and in fact, independently of the intellect. Hence arose a most weighty question between the Thomists and the Scotists: by what kind of distinction, namely, the metaphysical grades of the same thing are distinguished, as, e.g., the animality and rationality that are found in man, the grade of vegetating and of sensing that is found in brutes, and universally the genus and difference that are contained in individual things or species.

p. 11

32 Thomistae existimant inter haec omnia distinctionem solum virtualem sufficere. Scotistae praeter hanc virtualem, formalem etiam admittunt, qua gradus ipsi non veluti duae res aut modi (alioquin distinctio foret realis) sed veluti duae formalitates concipiantur, ideòque formalis illa distinctio minor est reali, major autem virtuali, sive inter utramque media. Sed haec Scholastici viderint. Distinctio rationis in majorem, minorem; ac minimam dividi solet. Prima vocatur illa, qua in unica, eadémque re varii conceptus distinguuntur, quorum unus non continetur in alio, ut justitia & misericordia quae distinguutur in Deo. Distinctio rationis minor quando conceptus ipsi impliciter mutuò includuntur, ut unum, bonum, verum, quae concipiuntur in ente.

32 The Thomists think that among all these only a virtual distinction suffices. The Scotists, besides this virtual one, admit also a formal one, by which the grades themselves are conceived not as two things or modes (otherwise the distinction would be real) but as two formalities; and therefore that formal distinction is less than the real, but greater than the virtual, or midway between the two. But let the Scholastics see to these things. Distinction of reason is commonly divided into major, minor and minimal. The first is the name given to that by which, in one and the same thing, various concepts are distinguished, of which one is not contained in the other, as justice and mercy, which are distinguished in God. Distinction of reason is minor when the concepts themselves mutually include each other implicitly, as one, good, true, which are conceived in being.

33 Distinctio denique rationis minima vocatur illa, quae sine ullo fundamento, & ex solo intellectus arbitrio, sive potius infirmitate aut prava consuetudine unum ab alio distinguit ut ex. gr. Deum à Divinitate hominem ab humanitate &c. Unde haec distinctio vocatur rationis ratiocinantis, quòd nempè à sola ratione dependeat, quum distinctio rationis major, aut minor nomine rationis ratiocinatae vocari soleat, quasi nimirùm ratio quaedam aut fundamentum distinctionis in ipsa re reperiatur. Sed haec aliaque id genus, quae fusè à Peripateticis explicantur tanti certè non sunt, ut uberiùs exponi debeant. Innuenda tamen hic fuerant, quòd frequentissimus illorum usus in Theologiam ipsam irrepserit; ideòque plura intelligi nequeant, nisi haec vocum significatio explicetur.

33 Minimal distinction of reason, finally, is the name given to that which, without any foundation, and by the mere choice of the intellect, or rather by its weakness or by a bad habit, distinguishes one thing from another, as, e.g., God from the Divinity, man from humanity, etc. Hence this distinction is called a distinction of reasoning reason, because, namely, it depends on reason alone, whereas the major or minor distinction of reason is commonly called by the name of reasoned reason, as if, namely, some ground or foundation of the distinction were found in the thing itself. But these and other things of the kind, which are explained at length by the Peripatetics, are certainly not of such worth that they should be set forth more fully. They had to be hinted at here, however, because the very frequent use of them has crept into Theology itself; and therefore many things cannot be understood unless this meaning of the words is explained.

34 Altera proprietas entis est Veritas, aptitudo nempè ut ens ipsum ab intellectu cognoscatur. Distinguitur in transcendentalem & formalem. Prima, est entitas ipsa rei, quatenùs ab intellectu praesertim Divino concipitur, quum nempè entitas ipsa & essentiae rerum in Deo vel archétypis ipsius ideis & imaginibus expraessa contineatur, potest à Deo cognosci, ideòque concipi velut objectum aut terminus Divinae cognitionis, quae ipsi rei vel ideae cognitae perfectissimè respondet, ideòque veritatem ab illa sortítur, & vicissim illi communicat, ut idea vera, vel vera cognitio dicatur. Veritas autem formalis est eadem conformatio intellectus cognoscentis cum re cognita.

34 The second property of being is Truth, namely the aptitude of being itself to be known by the intellect. It is divided into transcendental and formal. The first is the very entity of the thing, insofar as it is conceived by an intellect, especially the Divine one: for since the very entity and essences of things are contained, expressed, in God, or in his archetypal ideas and images, it can be known by God, and therefore conceived as the object or term of the Divine knowledge, which corresponds most perfectly to the thing itself, or to the idea known, and therefore derives its truth from it, and in turn communicates it to it, so that it is called a true idea, or true knowledge. Formal truth, however, is that same conformity of the knowing intellect with the thing known.

35 Quae denique de veritate jam diximus, de ultima quoque centis adfectione de Bonitate nimirum intelligi facilè poterunt, nisi quod veritas ad intellectum, bonitas autem ad voluntatem refertur. Bonitas autem transcendentalis est ipsum ens, quatenus adpeti vel amari potest à voluntate; bonitas formalis quae moralis etiam vocatur, est conformatio objecti vóliti & amáti cum legibus morum, praeceptis nimirùm, & archétypa boni imagine quae in Deo reperiuntur. Et haec quae ex Cl. Corsinio excerpta sunt dicta sufficiant.

35 What we have said, finally, about truth can easily be understood also of the last affection of being, namely of Goodness, except that truth is referred to the intellect, and goodness to the will. Transcendental goodness, then, is being itself, insofar as it can be desired or loved by the will; formal goodness, which is also called moral, is the conformity of the object willed and loved with the laws of morals, namely with the precepts and with the archetypal image of the good, which are found in God. And let these things, which have been excerpted from the distinguished Corsini, suffice as said.

p. 12

METAPHYSICES — METAPHYSICS

PARS ALTERA.

SECOND PART.

PSYCHOLOGIA,

PSYCHOLOGY,

sive

OR

De Anima rationali.

On the Rational Soul.

36 Quid prodesse nobis possunt sublimiores scientiae, Adolescentes optimi, si nos metipsos ignoremus? Si nesciamus quid sit anima nostra, an spiritualis, & immortalis, quodnam inter ipsam & corpus commercium intercedat? Hae autem cognitiones omnes, ¿quid nobis prosunt, si animam ipsam perdamus, si ejusdem facultatibus ad veram immortalitatem, aeternam scilicet beatitudinem consequendam non utamur? In duas ergo Dissertationes alteram hanc Metaphysices partem dividemus. Prima erit de origine, spiritualitate, & immortalitate mentis humanae. Secunda de admirabili commercio quod inter ipsam mentem, & corpus est.

hat can the loftier sciences profit us, excellent young men, if we are 36 W ignorant of ourselves? If we do not know what our soul is, whether it is spiritual and immortal, and what commerce intervenes between it and the body? And all these cognitions, what do they profit us, if we lose the soul itself, if we do not use its faculties to attain true immortality, namely eternal beatitude? We shall therefore divide this second part of Metaphysics into two Dissertations. The first will be on the origin, spirituality and immortality of the human mind; the second on the admirable commerce that exists between the mind itself and the body.

DISSERTATIO I. — DISSERTATION I

De Origine, spiritualitate, & immortalitate mentis humanae.

On the Origin, spirituality, and immortality of the human mind.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De Animae origine, & quo tempore corpori infundatur.

On the origin of the Soul, and at what time it is infused into the body. 37

37 Ut vera creationis habeatur notio, (ait celebr. Clarkius s1) non oportet eam sibi effingere tanquam generationem alicujus rei erutae ex nihilo considerato ut materia, Creare est

That a true notion of creation may be had (says the celebrated Clarke (d)), one must not picture it to oneself as the generation of some thing drawn out of nothing considered as matter. To create is to give existence

p. 13

existentiam dare rei, quae prius illam non habeat, hoc est, efficere, ut existat res quae prius non existebat. Omnes Philosophi admittunt, quod nullum agens creatum potest quidquam eorum efficere, quae non nisi per creationem esse possunt. Soli quippe Deo convenit creandi virtus. Neque enim fas est, inquit S. Augustinus s1, ullius naturae, quamlibèt minimae, mortalisque, creatorem, nisi Deum, credere ac dicere. His positis.

to a thing that did not have it before; that is, to bring it about that a thing exists which did not exist before. All Philosophers admit that no created agent can bring about any of those things which cannot be except through creation. For the power of creating belongs to God alone: For it is not lawful, says St. Augustine (e), to believe or to say that the creator of any nature, however small and mortal, is anyone but God. These things being laid down,

38 Dico 1: rationalis anima à Deo solo creatur, quum corpusculo infunditur. Prob.: creare est efficere ut existat res quae prius non existebat; sed Deus facit ut anima existat, quae prius non existebat: ergo. Prob. 2: creare est aliquid efficere, nullo quod ad ipsum intrinsecùs pertineat, priùs existente; sed ita facit Deus animam: ergo. Prob. min.: mens humana est substantia simplex, carens partibus, compositionis, & divisibilitatis expers: ut in sequentibus videbimus: ergo efficitur sine ulla partium successione nulloque quod ad ipsam intrinsecùs pertineat priùs existente: ergo sola creatione fit; sed creatio soli Deo competit, ut dictum est jam: ergo anima rationalis â Deo Creatore conditur.

38 I say 1: the rational soul is created by God alone when it is infused into the little body. It is proved: to create is to bring it about that a thing exists which did not exist before; but God brings it about that the soul exists, which did not exist before: therefore. It is proved 2: to create is to make something when nothing that intrinsically pertains to it exists beforehand; but it is thus that God makes the soul: therefore. Proof of the minor: the human mind is a simple substance, lacking parts, devoid of composition and divisibility, as we shall see in what follows: therefore it is made without any succession of parts, and with nothing that intrinsically pertains to it existing beforehand: therefore it comes to be by creation alone; but creation belongs to God alone, as has already been said: therefore the rational soul is made by God the Creator.

39 Prob. 3: anima rationalis non est generabilis, sed quod non est generabile per creationem fit: ergo. Prob. maj.: quod generabile est, est corruptibile, ut omnes fatentur; sed anima rationalis est incorruptibilis quia est immortalis, ut posteriùs Cap. III. ostendetur: ergo. Prob. 4: natura non extenditur nisi ad generandum, sed quod non est, non generatur, non enim est unde generetur, ut optimè ait Hippócrates s2 ergo creatio excedit naturae potentiam: ergo nequit fieri nisi â Deo.

39 It is proved 3: the rational soul is not generable; but what is not generable comes to be by creation: therefore. Proof of the major: what is generable is corruptible, as all admit; but the rational soul is incorruptible, because it is immortal, as will be shown later in Ch. III: therefore. It is proved 4: nature extends only to generating; but what is not is not generated, for there is nothing from which it might be generated, as Hippocrates says very well (f); therefore creation exceeds the power of nature: therefore it cannot be done except by God.

40 Christianus Wolff s3 celebris nostri seculi philosophus fatetur quidem animam rationalem à solo Deo per creationem fieri, verùm Libnitzium sequutus contendit animas omnium hominum, initio simul conditas a Deo fuisse, easque singulas suis inclusas corpusculis. Animae, inquit, praeexistunt in corpusculis organicis praeexistentibus ex quibus fetus in utero formatur.

40 Christian Wolff (g), a celebrated philosopher of our age, admits indeed that the rational soul comes to be by creation from God alone; but, following Leibniz, he contends that the souls of all men were made by God together at the beginning, and each of them enclosed in its own little body. Souls, he says, pre-exist in pre-existing organic corpuscles, from which the fetus is formed in the womb.

41 Dico 2: contra Leibnitzium, & Wolfium: animae rationales non fuerunt omnes simul initio temporis à Deo creatae, iisque organicis corpusculis inclusae, quae tunc itidèm à Deo condita in útero matris delitescunt. Prob. 1: ex Concilio Lateranensi V. s4 ubi expraessè definitum fuit, animam rationalem pro corporum, quibus infunditur multitudine singulariter esse multiplicabilem, multiplicatam, & multiplicandam: ergo animae omnium hominum, qui ad finem usque mundi nascituri sunt non fuere initio temporis à Deo creatae, quia tunc licet sint multiplicatae, non sunt tamen

41 I say 2, against Leibniz and Wolff: rational souls were not all created together by God at the beginning of time and enclosed in those organic corpuscles which, likewise made by God at that time, lie hidden in the mother’s womb. It is proved 1: from the Fifth Lateran Council (h), where it was expressly defined that the rational soul, according to the multitude of the bodies into which it is infused, is singly multipliable, multiplied, and to be multiplied: therefore the souls of all men who are to be born until the end of the world were not created by God at the beginning of time, because at that time, although they are multiplied, they are not, however, to be multiplied:

De l' Existence de Dieu tom. 1. c. 11.

De l’Existence de Dieu, vol. 1, ch. 11.

Lib. 12. de Civit. Dei. c. 24.

Bk. 12, City of God, ch. 24.

Lib. 1. de Diaeta num. 5.

Bk. 1, On Regimen, no. 5.

Psycholog. Rat. §. 704. & seq.

Psychologia Rationalis, §. 704 ff.

p. 14

multiplicandae: ergo animarum praexistentia apertè refragatur Concilio Lateranensi, ac proindè propugnari minimè potest.

therefore the pre-existence of souls is openly contrary to the Lateran Council, and consequently can by no means be defended.

42 Probatur 2. ab absurdo: hac opinione positâ non posset indiscriminatim singulis feminis Virginitas suadéri, quippe quum non constet quae feminae animatis corpusculis praeditae sint, nequit virginitas singulis feminis suaderi, quin verum sit, optionem in nobis esse, ut tot pereant animae, quot animata corpuscula illae complectuntur. Eandem quoque ob causàm nulli feminae licèret perpetuo se virginitatis voto obstríngere, nisi certò ei primò constiterit corpuscula animata suo in sinu minimè contineri, quae omnia, quum non minus falsa, quàm absurda sint sequitur, Wolffianam opinionem penitùs à Viro Catholico rejiciendam esse.

42 It is proved 2. from absurdity: once this opinion is granted, Virginity could not be urged upon all women indiscriminately; for since it is not known which women are endowed with animated corpuscles, virginity cannot be urged upon individual women without its being true that it lies in our choice that as many souls should perish as those animated corpuscles contain. For the same reason, too, no woman would be permitted to bind herself by a perpetual vow of virginity unless it were first certainly established for her that no animated corpuscles are contained in her womb; and since all these things are no less false than absurd, it follows that the Wolffian opinion is to be utterly rejected by a Catholic man.

43 Pro secunda quaestionis parte sciendum est, in hoc convenire antiquos omnes Philosophos, nempè, animam rationalem non illicò à conceptione infundi, sed post aliquod tempus. Communissima opinio defendit animam rationalem post quadraginta dies fetum informare, quia tunc, & non antea perfectè organizatum est corpusculum. Ita Galenus 3. Hippocrates s2 sive quisquis Auctor est libri de Natura pueri, differentiam docens inter fetus masculos, & femineos illos triginta, hos duobus supra quadraginta diebus dearticulari dixit, hoc est, perfectè organizari. Multò autem breviorem terminum ad hujusmodi perfectionem adsignavit idem Hippocrates lib. de Carnibus, num. 10. inquiens in septem diebus habet quaecumque, corpus habere debet, atque hoc pacto si corpus in septem diebus absolutum est, in septimo animari, ex sententia Hippocratis videtur consentaneum. Alii adserunt fetum humanum triduo perfici, ac tertia die rationalem animam recipere. Aristoteles s3 adseruit hominem vivere vita plantae, vita animalis, & hominis, adeoque animam rationalem post aliquot tempus fetui advenire, licet illud tempus non definierit. His positis.

43 For the second part of the question, it should be known that all the ancient Philosophers agree in this, namely that the rational soul is not infused immediately upon conception, but after some time. The most common opinion holds that the rational soul informs the fetus after forty days, because then, and not before, the little body is perfectly organized. So Galen (i). Hippocrates (j), or whoever is the author of the book On the Nature of the Child, teaching a difference between male and female fetuses, said that the former are articulated in thirty days, the latter in forty-two, that is, perfectly organized. But the same Hippocrates, in the book On Flesh, no. 10, assigned a much shorter term for perfection of this kind, saying in seven days it has whatever the body ought to have; and in this way, if the body is complete in seven days, it seems consistent with the opinion of Hippocrates that it is animated on the seventh. Others assert that the human fetus is completed in three days, and receives the rational soul on the third day. Aristotle (k) asserts that man lives the life of a plant, the life of an animal, and that of a man, and hence that the rational soul comes to the fetus after some time, although he did not define that time. These things being laid down,

44 Dico 3: cum Cl. Paulo Zacchia s4 & aliis magni nominis Auctoribus, quos laudat, & sequitur Illmus. D. Feijoo s5: in primo conceptionis momentó infunditur fetui anima rationalis. Prob. eficacissimis rationibus: negari nullomodo potest, fetum illicò, atque conceptus est vivere, nutriri, & augeri: sed haec omnia habere non potest ab alia anima quàm à rationali: ergo Prob. min.: absurdum est dicere ut Aristoteles adfirmabat fetum priùs vivere anima vegetativa, postea sensitiva, & tandem rationali; alioquin eae tres simul animae in homine essent, quod nemo sanus dixerit: ergo vita, nutritio, & augmentum fetus non possunt provenire nisi

44 I say 3: with the distinguished Paolo Zacchia (l) and other authors of great name, whom the Most Illustrious Don Feijóo (m) praises and follows: the rational soul is infused into the fetus at the first moment of conception. It is proved by most effective reasons: it can in no way be denied that the fetus, as soon as it is conceived, lives, is nourished, and grows; but it cannot have all these things from any other soul than from the rational one: therefore. Proof of the minor: it is absurd to say, as Aristotle affirmed, that the fetus lives first by a vegetative soul, then by a sensitive one, and finally by a rational one; otherwise those three souls would be in man at once, which no one in his right mind would say: therefore the life, nutrition, and growth of the fetus cannot come except

Sub Leone X. Sess. 8. Tom. 19. Collect. Concil. Labb.

Under Leo X, Sess. 8, vol. 19 of Labbe’s Collection of the Councils.

Lib. 15. de Usu. n. 5.

Bk. 15, De Usu, no. 5.

De Natur. pueri n. 10.

On the Nature of the Child, no. 10.

Lib. 2. de Generat. animal. c. 7.

Bk. 2, On the Generation of Animals, ch. 7.

p. 15

ab unica anima rationali; sed à primo instanti conceptionis vivit, nutritur, & augetur, ut omnes consentiunt: ergo in ipso instanti anima rationali donatur. Prob. 2: Deus, & natura semper operantur propter finem, Deus quidem ex sua libera voluntate, natura autem ex necessitate; sed retardatio infussionis animae rationalis nullum potest habere finem: ergo.

from the rational soul alone; but from the first instant of conception it lives, is nourished, and grows, as all agree: therefore at that very instant it is endowed with the rational soul. Proof 2: God and nature always act for an end, God indeed from his own free will, nature from necessity; but the delay of the infusion of the rational soul can have no end: therefore.

45 Prob. min.: talis finis, vel esset corporis perfectio, vel ad hoc, ut suis operationibus fungi rectè posset. Non primum: quia oporteret multò serius animam rationalem infundi, quum corpus in termino quadraginta dierum non sit adsequutum suam perfectionem, ita ut oculis pateat, quinimò nihil amplius habet post aliquot menses, nisi rudem quandam, & vix Lynceis oculis perceptibilem partium delineationem. Non secundum: nam quod spectat ad operationes proprias animae rationalis, nec post quadraginta dies, nec postquam infans jam nono exacto mense in lucem prodit, earum ullam exercére anima apta est: ergo retardatio infussionis animae rationalis, nullum potest habere finem. Concludendum igitur ex his, quod quum fetus conceptus illicò vivat, nutriatur, & augeatur, id ab alia anima quàm à rationali habere non possit, quae & vegetare, & nutrire, & vitam communicare potest, quum omnibus facultatibus necessariis ad haec peragenda sit instructa, eamque in ipso instanti conceptionis à Deo creari, & fetui infundi, ac per se ipsam conceptum nutrire, & augere, illique vitám, & sensum communicare.

45 Proof of the minor: such an end would be either the perfection of the body, or this, that it might be able to perform its operations rightly. Not the first; for then the rational soul would have to be infused much later, since at the term of forty days the body has not attained its perfection so as to be evident to the eyes; indeed, after some months it has nothing more than a certain rough delineation of the parts, scarcely perceptible even to the eyes of a Lynceus. Not the second: for as regards the operations proper to the rational soul, neither after forty days, nor after the infant, the ninth month completed, has come forth into the light, is the soul fit to exercise any of them: therefore the delay of the infusion of the rational soul can have no end. We must therefore conclude from these things that, since the conceived fetus lives, is nourished, and grows immediately, and cannot have this from any other soul than the rational one, which can vegetate, and nourish, and communicate life, since it is furnished with all the faculties necessary for accomplishing these things, it is created by God at the very instant of conception and infused into the fetus, and by itself nourishes and increases the conceptus, and communicates life and sense to it.

46 Confirmatur conclusio: vel anima rationalis potest vitam & sensum conceptui communicare vel non: si primum nihil obstat, quominùs idem possit ante quadraginta dies, non enim à corpore eas facultates adipiscitur, sed eas ex sua natura possidet. Si secundum: ergo corpus etiam anima rationali praesente, ab alia anima vitam, augmentum, nutritionem, sensum recipit, quia non est verisimile ea omnia ánte quadragessimum diem ab alia anima, & post quadraginta à rationali praestari. Confirmatur ulterius: si homo ante quadraginta dies non recipit animam rationalem, ante praedictum terminum non erit homo, nam ¿quomodo esset homo, non habens formam hominis? Erit igitur planta, vel vermis, vel insectum, vel aliud animal, vel bestia quaedam ad nullum genus, vel ad nullam viventium speciem certam reducibile, & ex se constituet novam speciem animalis? ¿Quaenam igitur erit haec species? Haec circa fetus humani animationem, quae probabiliter dici posse mihi vissa sunt, dicta sufficiant.

46 The conclusion is confirmed: either the rational soul can communicate life and sense to the conceptus, or it cannot: if the first, nothing prevents it from being able to do the same before forty days, for it does not acquire those faculties from the body, but possesses them from its own nature. If the second: then the body, even when the rational soul is present, receives life, growth, nutrition and sense from another soul; for it is not likely that all these things are supplied before the fortieth day by another soul, and after forty by the rational one. It is further confirmed: if man does not receive the rational soul before forty days, he will not be a man before the said term; for how would he be a man, not having the form of a man? Will he then be a plant, or a worm, or an insect, or some other animal, or some beast reducible to no genus, or to no definite species of living things, and will he constitute of himself a new species of animal? What, then, will this species be? Let what has been said about the animation of the human fetus suffice: these are the things that seemed to me could be said with probability.

Argumenta contra primam conclusionem.

Arguments against the first conclusion. 47

47 Opp. 1. Creatio est productio rei ex nihilò, sed ex nihilo nihil fit: ergo anima rationalis non creatur. Dist. min.: nihil fit, hoc est aliquid non eruitur ex nihilo, tanquam

Obj. 1. Creation is the production of a thing out of nothing; but out of nothing nothing comes: therefore the rational soul is not created. I distinguish the minor: out of nothing nothing comes, that is, something is not drawn out of nothing as

Quaestion. Medico-Legal.-Lib. 9. tit. 1. quaest. postrem.

Quaestiones Medico-Legales, bk. 9, tit. 1, last question.

Teatro Critico tom. 8. Discurso 11.

Teatro Crítico, vol. 8, Discourse 11.

p. 16

ex causa materiali, & praejacente, conc, hoc est non potest effici, ut existat id, quod priùs non existebat, subdist: si loquamur de agente, cujus vires finitae sunt, conc; si sermo habeatur de agente cujus potestas sit infinita, qualis est Deus, nego, & consequentiam. Dices cum Tolando, & Gildono. Deus communicavit materiae divisibilitatem, & figuram, licet easdem in se Deus non habeat: ergo etiam â substantia non intelligente, qualis est materia, substantía intelligens nempè, anima, emanare potest: ergo non est creata à Deo. Nego conseq. & est disparitas, quia Deus eminentissimè in se continet quidquid boni, & perfecti in materia est, & sua potentia in materia omnia producit: materia autem nec formaliter, nec virtualiter, nec eminenter potest continére veras, & simplices perfectiones animae; quum in ente corporeo, inertique, cujusmodi est materia, entis intelligentis, liberèque agentis, adaequata ratio esse non possit, quae solùm in ente libero, agente, intelligente reperitur.

from a material and pre-existing cause, I grant; that is, it cannot be brought about that what did not exist before should exist, I subdistinguish: if we speak of an agent whose powers are finite, I grant; if the discussion is of an agent whose power is infinite, such as God is, I deny; and I deny the consequence as well. You will say with Toland and Gildon: God communicated divisibility and figure to matter, although God does not have them in himself: therefore an intelligent substance too, namely the soul, can emanate from a non-intelligent substance, such as matter is: therefore it is not created by God. I deny the consequence, and there is a disparity, because God contains in himself most eminently whatever good and perfection there is in matter, and by his power produces all things in matter; but matter can contain neither formally, nor virtually, nor eminently the true and simple perfections of the soul; since in a corporeal and inert being, such as matter is, there cannot be the adequate ground of an intelligent and freely acting being, which is found only in a free, acting, intelligent being.

48 Opp. 2: cum Antonio Rocco: anima omninò dependet à corpore seu materia: ergo producitur dependenter à materia: ergo non creatur. Antec. prob. 1, quia haec anima ab hujus corporis temperie pendet, aliàs quaelibet anima in quodlibet corpus ingredi posset. 2: quia si anima non dependéret à corpore, pereunte ac disoluto corpore invita non recederet: ergo. Ad argumentum dist. antec.: dependet à corpore, ut sit, nego, ut exerceat munus formae corpus vivificantis, ac moventis, conc., atque ideò liberum non est animae ingredi quodcumque corpus, quoniam huic regendo, ac vivificando à Deo Conditore destinatur, & producitur hac lege, ut unà cum hoc corpore constituat hominem individuum: Quod autem resoluto corpore anima recédat invíta, poena est originalis peccati. Exemplo nautae felicissimè, aptèque explicat Cl. Berti s1, quomodo anima sit à corpore dependens, & independens, quod non ingratum vobis audire erit.

48 Obj. 2. with Antonio Rocco: the soul depends entirely on the body, or matter: therefore it is produced dependently on matter: therefore it is not created. The antecedent is proved 1. because this soul depends on the temperament of this body; otherwise any soul could enter any body. 2. because if the soul did not depend on the body, it would not depart unwillingly when the body perishes and is dissolved: therefore. To the argument I distinguish the antecedent: it depends on the body in order to be, I deny; in order to exercise the office of a form that vivifies and moves the body, I grant; and therefore the soul is not free to enter any body whatever, since it is destined by God its Creator to rule and vivify this one, and is produced under this law, that together with this body it should constitute an individual man. That the soul departs unwillingly when the body is dissolved, however, is a penalty of original sin. The distinguished Berti (n) explains most happily and aptly, by the example of a sailor, how the soul is both dependent on the body and independent of it, which it will not be unwelcome to you to hear.

49 Nauta homo est ad regendam navim destinatus. Quatenùs homo non opus habet navigio, quo est ipse longè nobilior, nam & vitam interdùm ágere aliter, quàm navigando potest; at quatenùs nauta, cujus est maria navigatione tranare utique indiget navi. Hac dissolutá, cógitur, aut in litore misserrimam vitam ducere, aut feliciorem in portu. Refectâ autem navi ad patriam tandèm revertitur. Anima pariter est spiritualis substantia, sed corporis forma, & quasi navicularia, nam illud, regit, & movet, & exploratè ad portum tentat adpellere. Ut spiritualis substantia, praestantior est corpore, neque aliquid commodi ab illo captat: ut forma corporis ab eo dependet, non quidem ut sit, sed ut mare perambulet, vitam nempè mortalem. Morte corpus, ut navis tempestate dissolvitur, atque anima pro meritis vitam agit sive miseram, sive tranquillam. Resurget mortale corpus ad vitam perennem, & haec ipsa resurrectio, quasi dirútae navis instauratio est.

49 A sailor is a man destined to steer a ship. Insofar as he is a man, he has no need of the vessel, than which he himself is far nobler, for he can at times lead his life otherwise than by sailing; but insofar as he is a sailor, whose business is to cross the seas by navigation, he certainly needs a ship. When this is broken up, he is forced to lead either a most wretched life on the shore, or a happier one in port. But when the ship has been repaired, he at length returns to his homeland. The soul likewise is a spiritual substance, but it is the form of the body and, as it were, its shipmaster, for it steers and moves it, and, having taken its bearings, tries to bring it into port. As a spiritual substance it is more excellent than the body, and gains no advantage from it: as the form of the body it depends on it, not indeed in order to be, but in order to travel the sea, namely the mortal life. By death the body is dissolved, like a ship by a storm, and the soul, according to its merits, leads a life either wretched or tranquil. The mortal body will rise again to everlasting life, and this resurrection itself is, as it were, the restoration of the wrecked ship.

De Theolog. Discipl. tom. 1.

De Theologicis Disciplinis, vol. 1.

p. 17

50 Opp. 3: cum eodem: Si anima rationalis crearetur, non contraheret ex semine Adae originale peccatum; sed contrahit: ergo. Nego maj.: non ideò originalis labes á filio contrahitur, quia ipsius anima, ex infecta anima patris, veluti pars ex toto in illius generatione deciderit, ut pertinaciter contendit Roccus, & Pomponatius, sed rationalis anima originali culpa ex eo polluitur, quod corruptae carni conjungatur, sicut aqua viciato in vase corrumpitur. Id vero quo pacto fiat, Theologi ad quos spectat clarissimè explicant. Sed insistit Roccus: accidentia sine subjecto non traducuntur; sed peccati originalis subjectum est anima: ergo si anima ex semine Adae non propagatur, neque peccatum propagatione diffunditur. Nego maj: nam ut optimè respondet AEstius transeunt de uno in alterum subjectum, subjecto non transfuso haereses, vitia, lepra, aliaque morum, & morborum contagia.

50 Obj. 3. with the same: If the rational soul were created, it would not contract original sin from the seed of Adam; but it does contract it: therefore. I deny the major: original stain is not contracted by the son because his soul fell away from the infected soul of the father in his generation, like a part from a whole, as Rocco and Pomponazzi stubbornly contend; rather, the rational soul is polluted by original guilt from this, that it is joined to corrupted flesh, as water is corrupted in a tainted vessel. How this comes about, indeed, the Theologians, to whom it belongs, explain most clearly. But Rocco insists: accidents are not transmitted without their subject; but the subject of original sin is the soul: therefore if the soul is not propagated from the seed of Adam, neither is sin spread by propagation. I deny the major: for, as Estius very well replies, heresies, vices, leprosy, and other contagions of morals and of diseases pass from one subject into another without the subject being transferred.

51 Opp. tandem: homo generat sibi simile, sed similitudo non consistit in materia, sed in specie, natura, & forma: ergo etiam forma quae est anima ab homine generatur: ergo non creatur â Deo. Ad argumentum respondeo, hominem generare sibi simile, quatenùs ita materiam disponit, ut ei Deus inferat animam, qua species, & natura humana perficiatur. Nam inserta anima corpori filius gerit imaginem, & similitudinem Patris, tametsi anima non sit ab ipso per generationem propagata. Neque patrocinatur Rocco illud Genes. 2 cunctae ánimae quae ingrésse sunt cum Jacob in AEgiptum, & egressae sunt de foemore illius. Horum quippè verborum sensus est: cuncti homines qui â Jacob per generationem descenderunt &c. Sufficit enim quod filius tantùm quoad corpus descendat de foemore patris, ut totus filius descendisse dicatur, etsi enim corpus non sit in homine pars princeps, ea tamen est, quae in nobis immediatè occurrit quaeque â nobis conspicitur, sicuti etiam statua dicitur opus artificiis, quamvis non nisi quoad formam â statuario dependeat.

51 Obj. finally: man begets his like; but likeness consists not in matter, but in species, nature and form: therefore the form too, which is the soul, is begotten by man: therefore it is not created by God. To the argument I reply that man begets his like insofar as he so disposes matter that God may put into it the soul by which the human species and nature are perfected. For once the soul has been put into the body, the son bears the image and likeness of the Father, even though the soul is not propagated from him by generation. Nor does that text of Genesis (o) support Rocco: All the souls that went with Jacob into Egypt, and that came out of his thigh. For the sense of these words is: all the men who descended from Jacob by generation, etc. For it suffices that the son descend from the thigh of the father as regards the body alone for the whole son to be said to have descended; for although the body is not the principal part in man, it is nevertheless what meets us immediately in ourselves and what is seen by us; just as a statue too is called the work of the artist, although it depends on the sculptor only as regards its form.

Argumenta contra ceteras conclusiones.

Arguments against the other conclusions. 52

52 Opp. contra secundam cum Wolffio s2 & Sennerto: Deum quievisse die septimo ab universo opere quod patrarat, legitur Genes. 2. ℣. 2: ergo hodie nihil amplius creat: ergo creatio animarum in prima creatione â Deo facta est. Hoc est praecipuum Wolffii argumentum. Sed cum magno Augustino s3 respondemus, Deum requievisse á condendis generibus

Obj. against the second, with Wolff (p) and Sennert: that God rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done, we read in Gen. 2, v. 2: therefore today he creates nothing more: therefore the creation of souls was accomplished by God in the first creation. This is Wolff’s chief argument. But with the great Augustine (q) we reply that God rested from founding kinds of creatures,

Genes. cap. 46. ℣. 26.

Gen. ch. 46, v. 26.

p. 18

creaturae, quia ultrà jam non condidit aliqua genera nova. Itaque dum dicitur, Deum animam creare, non aliquid facere dicitur quod ante non fecerat. Jam enim sexto die fecerat hominem ad imaginem suam, quod utique secundum animam intelligitur. Hoc & nunc facit non instituendo quod non erat, sed multiplicando quod erat. Vnde, & illud verum est, quod â rebus quae non erant instituendis requievit. Et hoc verum est, quod non solum gubernando quae fecit, verùm etiam non quod nondum, sed quod jam creaverat numerosius creando usque nunc operatur.

because beyond that he no longer founded any new kinds. And so, when God is said to create a soul, he is not said to do something that he had not done before. For already on the sixth day he had made man to his own image, which is certainly understood according to the soul. And this he does now, not by instituting what was not, but by multiplying what was. Hence both that is true, that he rested from instituting things that were not; and this is true, that he works until now, not only by governing what he made, but also by creating in greater number, not what he had not yet created, but what he had already created.

53 Opp. contra tertiam: Ex motu embrionis magis, ac certiùs deprehenditur animae praesentia, quàm ex aliis operationibus; sed ante quadragesimum diem non movetur embrio, & praeterea seriùs movetur femella quam mas: ergo ante quadragesimum non recipit embrio animam rationalem, & mas, & femella non eodem conceptionis momento eam recipiunt. Nego maj. argumenti: quia aliae operationes motum praecedentes alteri agenti tribui non possunt nisi animae rationali, & perinde est elicere ex motu praesentiam animae rationalis, quàm deducere ex vita, ex nutritione augmentatione, unde quum fetus in utero illicò vivat nutriatur augescat, sentiat; illicò animam rationalem illum habere necesse est. Adhaec: ¿quamnam dependentiam habet motus ab anima rationali, ut rationalis est? Oportuit ergo adfirmare, tunc fetum animam rationalem recipere, quum aliquam operationem rationali animae, ut rationali pertinentem edit, non quando moveri incipit. Minor autem argumenti absolutè loquendo falsa est. ¿Quis enim adfirmare audebit non habere embrionem ante quadragesimum diem, motum aliquem inobservabilem? Neque etiam si omnis motus abesset, inde inferri deberet animam rationalem praesentem non esse.

53 Obj. against the third: The presence of the soul is detected more, and more certainly, from the motion of the embryo than from its other operations; but before the fortieth day the embryo does not move, and moreover the female moves later than the male: therefore before the fortieth the embryo does not receive the rational soul, and male and female do not receive it at the same moment of conception. I deny the major of the argument: because the other operations that precede motion cannot be attributed to any other agent than the rational soul, and it is all one to elicit the presence of the rational soul from motion and to deduce it from life, from nutrition, from growth; hence, since the fetus in the womb immediately lives, is nourished, grows, and feels, it must immediately have a rational soul. Besides: what dependence does motion have on the rational soul as rational? One ought therefore to have affirmed that the fetus receives the rational soul when it performs some operation pertaining to the rational soul as rational, not when it begins to move. The minor of the argument, moreover, is false, absolutely speaking. For who will dare to affirm that the embryo does not have some unobservable motion before the fortieth day? Nor, even if all motion were absent, ought one to infer from this that the rational soul is not present.

54 Multò ergo rationabilius inferri debet praesentia animae in embrione ex vitae operationibus, & ex formatione ipsius fetus, neque enim aliquid eorum ab aliqua causa dependére potest quàm ab intrinseca, neque in fetu ulla alia intrinseca causa imaginari potest, quàm ipsa anima. Differentia autèm inter masculum, & femellam quoad primum motum in utero materno excitatum (si vera sunt quae narrantur) in eo fortè consistit, quia materia ex qua producitur mas majori spirituum copia turget, & calorem vividiorem obtinet. Praeterea observatum est, mares nonnullos ob eorum imbecillitatem seriùs movéri, quàm femellas, & alia ex parte femellas nonnullas ob earum robur citiùs moveri, quàm mares, unde inclusa minoris absolutè loquendo falsa omninò est.

54 Much more reasonably, therefore, ought the presence of the soul in the embryo to be inferred from the operations of life and from the formation of the fetus itself; for none of these can depend on any cause other than an intrinsic one, nor can any other intrinsic cause be imagined in the fetus than the soul itself. The difference, moreover, between the male and the female as to the first motion excited in the mother’s womb (if what is reported is true) perhaps consists in this, that the matter from which the male is produced swells with a greater abundance of spirits and obtains a livelier heat. Besides, it has been observed that some males, because of their weakness, move later than females, and on the other hand that some females, because of their strength, move sooner than males; whence the included minor, absolutely speaking, is altogether false.

55 Opp. 1. Fetus non debet recipere animam rationalem nisi perfectè organizatus sit: sed haec organizatio non eodem tempore in singulis perficitur, ob temperamentorum, & virium varietatem: ergo anima non infunditur in ipso conceptionis momento. Pluribus modis responderi potest ad argumentum. Primò: concedendo organizationem requiri, ut anima operetur, negando verò eam

55 Obj. 1. The fetus ought not to receive the rational soul unless it is perfectly organized; but this organization is not completed at the same time in every individual, because of the variety of temperaments and powers: therefore the soul is not infused at the very moment of conception. The argument can be answered in several ways. First: by granting that organization is required for the soul to operate, but denying that it is necessary

In Princip. Philos. § 705.

In Princip. Philos. § 705.

Lib. IV. de Genes. ad litt.

Bk. IV, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis.

p. 19

necessariam esse ut informet. Secundo: dicendo Deum non debere subjici naturae, ita ut spectare debeat antequàm animam infundat, fetus organizationem ab ipsa natura machinatam. Sed alia via ex Recentiorum mente placet argumento satisfacere. Communissima inter Recentiores est opinio de perfecta delineatione embrionis in corpusculis in utero matris delitescentibus, qua posita negari potest fetum non esse perfectè organizatum ante quadragesimum.

for it to inform. Second: by saying that God ought not to be subject to nature, so that before he infuses the soul he must wait for the organization of the fetus contrived by nature itself. But it is preferable to satisfy the argument in another way, according to the mind of the Moderns. The most common opinion among the Moderns is that of the perfect delineation of the embryo in the corpuscles lying hidden in the mother’s womb; and once this is granted, it can be denied that the fetus is not perfectly organized before the fortieth.

56 Si autem per organizationem perfectam intelligant adversarii, organizationem omnibus numeris ita absolutam, ut per eam fetus habeat quidquid embrionem habere oporteat, ita ut oculo teste omnibus membris atque necessariis organis sit instructus, negabimus, hanc organizationem necessariam esse ad recipiendam animam, nam si ita esset, oporteret animae receptionem retardari ad plures menses, unde quum Angelicus Magister ait s1 animam rationalem infundi quum corpus est dispositum, non est intelligendus de hac ultima dispositione, alioquin ipse S. Doctor contradictoria adsereret, quod vel cogitare nefas est.

56 But if by perfect organization our adversaries understand an organization so complete in every respect that by it the fetus has whatever an embryo ought to have, so that, as the eye bears witness, it is furnished with all its members and necessary organs, we shall deny that this organization is necessary for receiving the soul; for if it were so, the reception of the soul would have to be delayed for several months; hence, when the Angelic Master says (r) that the rational soul is infused when the body is disposed, he is not to be understood of this final disposition; otherwise the holy Doctor himself would be asserting contradictory things, which it is wrong even to think.

57 Ipse enim Sapientissimus Magister s2 adserit, quod quum anima sit proprius corporis actus, & forma necessariò simul cum corpore produci debet, at corpus illicò producitur cum concipitur: ergo ex mente Doctoris Angelici etiam anima rationalis tunc infunditur; infusa autem illicò operatur, & sic in primo momento conceptionis ipsius embrionis praesens est, nam aliàs semper esset verum dicere corpus ante produci, quàm animam, contra id quod Theologi docent cum Angelico Mag. s3

57 For the most wise Master himself (s) asserts that, since the soul is the proper act and form of the body, it must necessarily be produced together with the body; but the body is produced immediately when it is conceived: therefore, according to the mind of the Angelic Doctor, the rational soul too is infused then; and once infused it operates immediately, and thus it is present at the first moment of the conception of the embryo itself; for otherwise it would always be true to say that the body is produced before the soul, contrary to what the Theologians teach with the Angelic Master (t).

58 Sed dices: anima fuit inspirata in faciem Adae quum ejus corpus perfectum esset: ergo in quemlibet hominem debet introduci quum corpus est omnimodò perfectum. Respondeo, argumentum nihil probare: nam quamtuncumque perfectum velint adversarii esse embrionem in quadragesimo, nunquam tam perfectum erit, quàm corpus Adae, quum Deus in illud animam inspiravit. Adhaec: magna differentia esse debet inter opus ab ipso Deo immediatè emanans, & opus commissum naturae in hominis generatione.

58 But you will say: the soul was breathed into the face of Adam when his body was perfect: therefore it ought to be introduced into any man when the body is perfect in every way. I reply that the argument proves nothing: for however perfect our adversaries may wish the embryo to be on the fortieth day, it will never be as perfect as the body of Adam when God breathed the soul into it. Besides: there must be a great difference between a work emanating immediately from God himself and a work entrusted to nature in the generation of man.

59 Opp. 3: Si anima rationalis in primo instanti conceptionis praesens esset, abortu sequuto ante quadragesimum, juberent Canones illum fetum baptizari; sed non jubent: ergo quia animâ rationali ante quadragesimum non informatur. Respondeo quod in his abortibus impossibile est ob eorum debilitatem, non illicò à corpore animam separari, & iccirco Sacri Canones, baptismatis nullam faciunt mentionem, satisque fuit, si quandocumque aliquod

59 Obj. 3. If the rational soul were present at the first instant of conception, then when an abortion occurred before the fortieth day the Canons would order that fetus to be baptized; but they do not so order: therefore it is because it is not informed by the rational soul before the fortieth. I reply that in these abortions it is impossible, because of their weakness, that the soul should not be separated from the body at once, and for that reason the Sacred Canons make no mention of baptism; and it was enough if, whenever they give some sign of life

P. 1. quaest. 100. art. 1. ad 2.

Pt. 1, q. 100, art. 1, ad 2.

P. 1. quaest. 90. art. 4.

Pt. 1, q. 90, art. 4.

P. 1. quaest. 91. art. 4. ad 3.

Pt. 1, q. 91, art. 4, ad 3.

p. 20

vitae signum ex motu praebent, etiam si ante quadragessimum id fieret, baptismatis lavácro emundentur saltim sub conditione: sed hoc nihil obstat quominus cum Cl. Feijoo adfirmemus, in quocumque tempore abortus contingat, fetum baptizari debere sub conditione, nam juxta omnes tunc baptismo ablui debet quum probabile sit fetum esse animatum, sed ex dictis valdè probabile est, cùm probabilitate intrinseca rationum, tum extrinseca Auctorum magni nominis fetum ab ipso instanti conceptionis anima rationali informatum esse: ergo quocumque tempore abortus contingat baptizari saltem sub conditione debet.

by motion, even if this happened before the fortieth, they should be cleansed in the laver of baptism, at least conditionally; but this in no way prevents us from affirming with the distinguished Feijóo that, at whatever time the abortion occurs, the fetus ought to be baptized conditionally; for according to everyone it ought to be washed in baptism when it is probable that the fetus is animated; but from what has been said it is highly probable, both by the intrinsic probability of the reasons and by the extrinsic probability of authors of great name, that the fetus is informed by the rational soul from the very instant of conception: therefore, at whatever time the abortion occurs, it ought to be baptized, at least conditionally.

60 Opp. tandem: Leges tam Canonicae quam Civiles distinguunt fetum animatum ab inanimato, illumque non nisi post quadraginta dies animari statuunt, atque hac de causa poenam majorem, aut minorem delinquentibus, & abortum procurantibus imponunt, in quarum confirmationem emanavit denique Constitutio Sixti V. Pontif. Maximi, in qua abortum animati fetus procurantes, iisdem poenis subjici determinatur, quibus veri homicidae subjiciuntur: ergo conclusio nostra contraria est auctoritati Legum Ecclesiasticarum, & Secularium. Ad argumentum respondeo cum supra laudato Zacchia, tam Canones, quam Leges non ex propria scientifica cognitione in laudatis textibus loqui, sed ex placitis Sapientium illius seculi Philosophorum, & Medicorum, uti alias consueverunt facere in iis, quae ad alios professores pertinent. Ergo quum de ea re praedicti Sapientes consulti fuissent, eorum determinationem Canones, & Leges in hoc sequi volentes, poenas delinquentibus modò majores, modò minores imposuerunt pro ea quam illi differentiam faciebant inter fetum non animatum anima rationali, & animatum. Verùm adhuc his positis contendimus Canonum, & Legum determinationes secundum justitiam emanasse, easque sarctas tectas remanere debere, firma etiam nostra opinione remanente de animatione fetus in primo conceptionis momento.

60 Obj. finally: the Laws, Canon as well as Civil, distinguish the animated fetus from the inanimate, and declare it animated only after forty days, and for this reason impose a greater or a lesser penalty on offenders and on those who procure abortion; in confirmation of which the Constitution of Sixtus V, Supreme Pontiff, was finally issued, in which it is determined that those who procure the abortion of an animated fetus are subject to the same penalties as true homicides: therefore our conclusion is contrary to the authority of the Ecclesiastical and Secular Laws. To the argument I reply, with Zacchia, praised above, that both the Canons and the Laws speak in the texts cited not from their own scientific knowledge, but from the opinions of the wise men of that age, Philosophers and Physicians, as they have been accustomed to do elsewhere in matters that belong to other professions. Therefore, since the aforesaid wise men had been consulted on that matter, the Canons and Laws, wishing to follow their determination in this, imposed on offenders penalties now greater, now lesser, according to the difference that those men made between the fetus not animated by the rational soul and the animated one. But even with these things granted, we contend that the determinations of the Canons and Laws issued in accordance with justice, and must remain safe and intact, while our opinion on the animation of the fetus at the first moment of conception also remains firm.

61 Canones enim, & Leges Civiles in imponendis poenis semper sequuntur mitiorem sententiam; quum ergo in dubium verteretur, an semper, & quocumque tempore procurans abortum eadem poena esset plectendus, & aliqui mitiùs sentientes judicassent, minori poena plectendum fetu teneriori existente, & ante quadragesimum, contrà aliis sentientibus, priori sententiae Canones adhaeserunt, atque summa cum ratione statuunt majorem poenam procuranti abortum post quadraginta dies, quàm ante, quia multò majorem vim infert ille tam fetui, quàm matri, quàm inferat hic. Tenerioris enim fetus abortus ob ligamentorum debilitatem, facilè & cum minimo matris incommodo succedit, at provectioris fetus abortus non nisi cum matris evidenti periculo fit, undè ex Hyppocrate s1 & ex quotidiana experientia scimus tutiores esse

61 For the Canons and Civil Laws always follow the milder opinion in imposing penalties; since, therefore, it was called into doubt whether one who procures abortion always, and at any time whatever, should be punished with the same penalty, and some, of the milder opinion, had judged that he should be punished with a lesser penalty when the fetus is more tender and before the fortieth, while others thought the contrary, the Canons adhered to the former opinion, and with the greatest reason they establish a greater penalty for one who procures abortion after forty days than before, because the former inflicts much greater violence both on the fetus and on the mother than the latter does. For the abortion of a more tender fetus, because of the weakness of the ligaments, takes place easily and with the least discomfort to the mother, whereas the abortion of a more advanced fetus does not take place without evident danger to the mother; whence from Hippocrates (u) and from daily experience we know that abortions are safer

p. 21

abortus in primo quadragenario, in sequentibus autem difficiles, ac multò minus tutos. Haec pro argumenti responsione dicta sufficiant. Clariss. verò Feijoo ultrà contendit, eum qui post duos, aut tres á conceptione dies abortum procuraverit, incurrere poenam irregularitatis à Gregorio XIV. statutam contra procurantes abortum animati fetus, ut videre est apud ipsum. s1

in the first forty days, but difficult in the following ones, and much less safe. Let what has been said in reply to the argument suffice. The most distinguished Feijóo, however, contends further that one who has procured an abortion two or three days after conception incurs the penalty of irregularity established by Gregory XIV against those who procure the abortion of an animated fetus, as may be seen in his work (x).

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

Expenditur an humana mens sit substantia spiritualis, num verò corporea?

It is examined whether the human mind is a spiritual substance, or rather a corporeal one?

62 Mens humana est id quod in unoquoque nostrum cogitat. A Scholasticis vulgò definitur: actus primus corporis physici, & organici potentia vitam habentis. Ignotum scilicet per ignotiùs explicant. Nos autem eam definimus: principium quo homo cogitat, seu quo verum intelligit, bonumque vult, suarumque insupèr perceptionum ac volitionum conscius existit. Dicitur mens, quoniam cogitandi vis in anima eminent. Dicitur anima rationalis, seu animus, quoniam incorporeae cognitionis aut rationis capax est.

he human mind is that which thinks in each of us. By the Scholastics it is 62 T commonly defined: the first act of a physical organic body having life in potency. They explain, namely, the unknown by the more unknown. We, however, define it: the principle by which man thinks, or by which he understands the true and wills the good, and is moreover conscious of his own perceptions and volitions. It is called mens [mind], because the power of thinking is preeminent in the soul. It is called anima rationalis [rational soul], or animus, because it is capable of incorporeal knowledge, or reason.

63 Ejusmodi vero principium, sive animam in nobis existere evidentissimum est: nihil enim magis perspicuum esse potest, quàm nos cogitare dum cogitamus, aliquid velle quum volumus, percipere, dubitare, recordari, quum percipimus, dubitamus, recordamur: principium ergo illud in nobis existit, quo singulae operationes, & actus illi in nobis peraguntur.

63 That a principle of this kind, or a soul, exists in us is most evident; for nothing can be more manifest than that we think while we think, that we will something when we will, that we perceive, doubt, remember, when we perceive, doubt, remember: therefore that principle exists in us by which each of these operations and acts is carried out in us.

64 Per corpus seu materiam intelligimus substantiam extensam, divisibilem, solidam, ex variis partibus, variarum figurarum contextam. Per spiritualem verò substantiam, intelligimus substantiam expertem materiae, seu quae extensionem, divisibilitatem, soliditatem excludit. Quaestio est igitur utrum id quod in unoquoque nostrum cogitat, sit substantia expers extensionis, divisibilitatis, soliditatis, &c.?

64 By body, or matter, we understand an extended, divisible, solid substance, woven together from various parts of various figures. By a spiritual substance, on the other hand, we understand a substance devoid of matter, or one that excludes extension, divisibility, solidity. The question, therefore, is whether that which thinks in each of us is a substance devoid of extension, divisibility, solidity, etc.?

65 Materialistae increduli, nempè, perversissimique homines, tuentur nihil praeter physicam sensibilitatem in homine esse, adeòque per eam quae quid materiale est, & â materia dependet, hominem intelligere, cogitare, ratiocinari, ac proindè animum nostrum esse materiam. Perniciosissimum hunc errorem tuentur

65 The Materialists, namely unbelieving and most perverse men, maintain that there is nothing in man besides physical sensibility, and hence that it is through this, which is something material and depends on matter, that man understands, thinks, reasons, and consequently that our mind is matter. This most pernicious error is maintained by Spinoza,

In Lib. de Nat. Pueri.

In the book On the Nature of the Child.

Teatro Critico. Tom. 8. Discurso 11. num. 27.

Teatro Crítico, vol. 8, Discourse 11, no. 27.

p. 22

Spinosa, Hobbesius, Tolandus s1 neque ab illo admodùm abhorret Lockius. Inter Materialistas Recentiores recensentur Johann. Jac Rousseau, Voltaire aliique Philosophi Galli perniciosissimis libellis quibus Religionem, moresque corrumpunt, à quorum lectione uti decet Christianum philosophum vos semper abstinere debetis. Contra hos ergo incredulos perditosque homines.

Hobbes, Toland (y), nor is Locke very far removed from him. Among the more recent Materialists are counted Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Voltaire and other French Philosophers, with most pernicious little books by which they corrupt Religion and morals; from reading these, as befits a Christian philosopher, you must always abstain. Against these unbelieving and lost men, then:

66 Dico 1. Mens humana est substantia spiritualis, seu â materia, vel corpore distincta, atque díversa. Prob. prima pars, scilicèt, mentem humanam esse substantiam.
