Experimur cogitationes in nobis continuò mutari, alias aliis fluxu perpetuo succedere; sed mutabilia, quae enti insunt, modi dicuntur, & sine subjecto esse non possunt: ergo id quod in nobis cogitat, nempè anima est subjectum cogitationum. Subjectum autèm, alio subjecto non indiget ad existendum; ideòque substantia est: ergo anima est substantia.

66 I say 1. The human mind is a spiritual substance, or one distinct and different from matter, or body. The first part is proved, namely that the human mind is a substance. We experience that our thoughts are continually changed in us, and that they succeed one another in a perpetual flux; but the changeable things that are in a being are called modes, and cannot be without a subject: therefore that which thinks in us, namely the soul, is the subject of thoughts. A subject, moreover, does not need another subject in order to exist; and therefore it is a substance: therefore the soul is a substance.

67 Prob. secunda pars: principium operationum quae ad materiam pertinere non possunt est substantia prorsus distincta a materia, ac proindè spiritualis; sed anima est principium cogitationum, quae ad materiam nullomodo possunt pertinere: ergo est substantia spiritualis. Prob. min.: si cogitatio pertineret ad materiam esset intrinseca materiae modificatio; quum enim cogitatio sit subjecti cogitantis actio interna, intrinseca est subjecti cogitantis modificatio, sed cogitatio non potest esse intrinseca materiae modificatio: ergo nullomodo potest ad materiam pertinere. Prob. min.:

67 The second part is proved: the principle of operations that cannot belong to matter is a substance altogether distinct from matter, and consequently spiritual; but the soul is the principle of thoughts, which can in no way belong to matter: therefore it is a spiritual substance. Proof of the minor: if thought belonged to matter, it would be an intrinsic modification of matter; for since thought is an internal action of the thinking subject, it is an intrinsic modification of the thinking subject; but thought cannot be an intrinsic modification of matter: therefore it can in no way belong to matter. Proof of the minor:

Spinosa. Part. 2. Ethic. prop. 13. & Coroll. prop. 17. Hobbes. Phys. Part. 2. cap. 25. num. 10., & in Leviath. sive de Republica. Part. 1. de Homine. Cap. 3. Tolandus. Leç. 3. sur le mouvement. Auctor operis inscript. Epitres Philosophiques. Ep. 3. & 25. num. 53. Auctor Op. inscript. La Philosophie du Bon Sens (vulgò Marchio d' Argens) Tom. 2. Reflex. 4. §. 10. & seq. Auctor impii libelli editi Postdami ann. 1748. & inscript. Discours sur la vie heureuse. Auctor alterius impii libelli inscript. L' Esprit (vulgò Helvetius.) Disc. 1. cap. 1. Bayle. Dictionnaire Historique, & Critique. Art. Leucippe. remarq. E. & art. Rorarius. remarq. D, & F. Rouseau. Discours su l' inegalitè parmi les hommes, edit. Amstelaedam. ann. 1755. Auctor libelli inscript. Oracles de la Raison (vulgò Gildon) pag. 186. Auct. Op. inscript. Epitres Juives (vulgò Marchio d' Argens), alique multi hujus farinae homines, qui nihil nisi materiale, in nobis esse conatu planè irrito conantur ostendere. His omnibus accensendus etiam est Voltaire, qui tam contra spiritualitatem, quàm contra immortalitatem animae apertè pugnat, tum tom. 6. Opp. Lettre â Monsieur de Genoville, pag. 140. tùm tom. 9. de l' Ame, & des Idees, pag. 58, & 91. tùm tom. 7. cap. 35. sur l' Ame, pag. 283. edit. Paris. ann. 1757, & alibi in suis Opusculis.

Spinoza, Pt. 2 of the Ethics, prop. 13, and Cor. to prop. 17. Hobbes, Phys. Pt. 2, ch. 25, no. 10, and in the Leviathan, or On the Commonwealth, Pt. 1, On Man, ch. 3. Toland, Leç. 3, sur le mouvement. The author of the work entitled Epitres Philosophiques, Ep. 3 and 25, no. 53. The author of the work entitled La Philosophie du Bon Sens (commonly said to be the Marquis d’Argens), vol. 2, Reflex. 4, §. 10 ff. The author of the impious little book published at Potsdam in the year 1748 and entitled Discours sur la vie heureuse. The author of another impious little book entitled L’Esprit (commonly said to be Helvétius), Disc. 1, ch. 1. Bayle, Dictionnaire Historique, & Critique, art. Leucippe, rem. E, and art. Rorarius, rem. D and F. Rousseau, Discours sur l’inégalité parmi les hommes, Amsterdam ed., year 1755. The author of the little book entitled Oracles de la Raison (commonly said to be Gildon), p. 185. The author of the work entitled Epitres Juives (commonly said to be the Marquis d’Argens), and many other men of this stamp, who try, with an utterly vain effort, to show that there is nothing in us but what is material. To all these must also be added Voltaire, who openly fights against both the spirituality and the immortality of the soul, both in vol. 6 of his Works, Lettre à Monsieur de Genonville, p. 240, and in vol. 9, de l’Ame, & des Idées, pp. 58 and 91, and in vol. 7, ch. 35, sur l’Ame, p. 283, Paris ed., year 1757, and elsewhere in his minor works.

p. 23

si esset intrinseca materiae modificatio, esset ipsa materia modificata, sed cogitatio nec est, neque esse potest materia modificata ergo.

if it were an intrinsic modification of matter, it would be matter itself modified; but thought neither is nor can be matter modified: therefore.

68 Prob. min.: si ita esset, cogitatio haberet proprietates materiae, esset proindè extensa, divisibilis in partes, & figurata: sed hoc evidentissimè repugnat: ergo. Prob. min.: ¿quis enim tam amens est, ut credat actum intellectus ex. gr. adsensum, vel dissensum esse certo loci spatio difussum, posse scindi in duas, quatuor ve partes, & habere figuram rotundam, quadratam, aut triangularem? Ergo cogitatio non habet, nec habere potest proprietates materiae: ergo anima est principium operationum, quae ad materiam pertinere non possunt: ergo est spiritualis, & non materia.

68 Proof of the minor: if it were so, thought would have the properties of matter; it would consequently be extended, divisible into parts, and figured; but this is most evidently repugnant: therefore. Proof of the minor: for who is so mad as to believe that an act of the intellect, e.g. assent or dissent, is spread out over a certain space of place, that it can be cut into two or four parts, and have a round, square, or triangular figure? Therefore thought does not have, nor can it have, the properties of matter: therefore the soul is the principle of operations that cannot belong to matter: therefore it is spiritual, and not matter.

69 Sed rem hanc cum Clariss. Valsechio s1 paulò adtentius contemplemur, videamusque num possímus nobis metipsis persuadére materiam cogitare posse? Ego cogito, meamque cogitationem considero, compono plures notiones, eas séparo, eas conjungo. Dicto citiùs é caelo ad terras migro, & plurimas remotissimas res animo pervolvo. Harum rerum naturam, proprietates, relationes perpendo: metior motus, spatia, tempora: cónfero res has cum illis, ex apertis, clarisque, ad occultas, & latentes ratiocinando gradum facio. Nec immoror his tantum rebus, quae subjectae sunt sensibus, sed etiam illas pervolvo, quae longe sensus meos exsuperant. Novi, & sermocinor, de Ente, de Ordine, de Virtutibus, de Veritate, de Ratione, de Deo.

69 But let us contemplate this matter a little more attentively with the most distinguished Valsecchi (z), and see whether we can persuade ourselves that matter can think. I think, and I consider my thought; I compose several notions, I separate them, I join them. Quicker than it can be said, I pass from heaven to earth, and turn over in my mind a great many most remote things. I weigh the nature, the properties, the relations of these things: I measure motions, spaces, times: I compare these things with those; from the open and clear I make my way by reasoning to the hidden and latent. Nor do I dwell only on the things that are subject to the senses, but I also turn over those that far surpass my senses. I know, and I discourse, about Being, about Order, about the Virtues, about Truth, about Reason, about God.

70 Horum & his similium operationum, quae cogitationes dicuntur, conscientiam habeo, hoc est sensum intimum, maximè vividum, per quem ea novi; novi etiam me, qui cogito, & â quo eae operationes dimanant, esse non posse frustum stupidae, inertisque carnis, sed substantiam se moventem, praeditam agendi vi, & efficacitate, & ea virtute, cujus non est materies capax.

70 Of these and similar operations, which are called thoughts, I have consciousness, that is, an inner and most vivid sense, through which I know them; I know also that I, who think, and from whom these operations flow, cannot be a lump of stupid and inert flesh, but a self-moving substance, endowed with a power and efficacy of acting, and with that virtue of which matter is not capable.

71 Ad hanc materiam interea memet converto, ejus anâlysim adcurate instituo, neque in ea quicquam reperio aliud, quam extensionem, soliditatem, figuram, quietem, aut motum. In plurimas tenuissimas partes éam seco. His, omnes, quas quidem possim configurationem do, has impello omnibus directionibus, omnibus motus gradibus: at nihil unquam in his internosco, quod vel tantillum simile sit ei, quod clarè cognosco, quum dico cogitare: imò natura ipsa ab adscribendo illis hoc adtributum me retrahit: volentemque adserere, pulverem tenuissimum, ferventemque sanguinem posse eas cogitationes, & ratiocinia elicere major me vis absterret, quàm si dicerem, circulum esse quadratum: audientemque cogitationem esse duram, aut mollem, triangularem, aut pentágonam, haec monstrosa conjunctio magis me cómmovet, quàm aut hircocervus, aut chimaera.

71 Meanwhile I turn to this matter; I carefully carry out an analysis of it; and I find in it nothing other than extension, solidity, figure, rest, or motion. I cut it into a great many very fine parts. I give them every configuration I can, I impel them in every direction, with every degree of motion: but I never discern in them anything that is in the slightest degree like what I clearly know when I say to think; indeed nature itself draws me back from ascribing this attribute to them: and when I wish to assert that the finest dust and boiling blood can elicit those thoughts and reasonings, a greater force deters me than if I were saying that a circle is square; and when I hear that thought is hard or soft, triangular or pentagonal, this monstrous conjunction disturbs me more than either a goat-stag or a chimera.

72 Ut breviter dicam, intimo sensu cogitationem novi, clarè extensionem novi, & tantum abest, ut illam in hac inspiciam, aut

72 To speak briefly, I know thought by an inner sense, I know extension clearly, and so far am I from perceiving the former in the latter, or vice versa,

Dei fondamenti della Relligione, & de i fonti dell' Empietà.

Dei fondamenti della Religione, & dei fonti dell’Empietà.

p. 24

vice versa, ut potius conferens unam cum alia, talem esse inter eas discrepantiam, diversitatem, distantiamque video, ut licet summoperè enitar, ne fingere quidem, eas inter se conjungi possim.

that rather, comparing the one with the other, I see that there is such a discrepancy, diversity and distance between them that, however hard I strive, I cannot even imagine them joined to each other.

73 Ob oculos idem argumentum ponit Franciscus Lamy Ordin. S. Benedicti. s1 Integrum locum ponam è Gallico in Latinum sermonem conversum ,, ¿Quodnam ergo harum operationum principium est? (inquit laudatus Monachus) erit ne corpus, an anima corporea? Potest ne unquam concipi, corpus, hoc est, massam carnis configuratam, hoc vel illo modo elicere posse spirituales notiones, percipere justitiam, sapientiam, veritatem, percipere, & cognoscere se ipsam.

73 The same argument is set before our eyes by François Lamy, of the Order of St. Benedict (a). I shall give the whole passage, turned from French into Latin: “What, then, is the principle of these operations? (says the Monk just praised) Will it be the body, or a corporeal soul? Can it ever be conceived that a body, that is, a mass of flesh configured in this or that way, can elicit spiritual notions, perceive justice, wisdom, truth, and perceive and know itself?

74 ,, Quis seriò credere potest, ventum, vaporem, spirituum animalium fumum, qui diffunditur per meam carnem, qui per mea commeat organa, posse judicare, hoc est, percipere relationes, quae inter res sunt? An ille ebulliens, discurrensque per caput meum in causa est, cur spiritus animales connectant inter se demonstrationes, admirabilem illum illationum ordinem, qui interdùm uno intuitu conspicitur.

74 “Who can seriously believe that a wind, a vapor, a smoke of animal spirits, which is diffused through my flesh and passes through my organs, can judge, that is, perceive the relations that exist between things? Is that thing, boiling and running about through my head, the cause why the animal spirits connect demonstrations with one another, that admirable order of inferences which is sometimes beheld in a single glance?

75 ,, Est ne tandem verisimile, hanc organorum corporeorum, animaliumque spirituum complexionem, considerare, discutere, praevidere, perpendere, velle, desiderare, bonum eligere posse? Ens hoc luteum aptum esse ad solvendas quaestiones, & problémata? Atqui si res ita se habet, cur in solvendis quaestionibus, quae sint aliquantò abstractiores, difficilioresque, obstruuntur, quantum per nos licet organa sensuum, materia nosmet expedimus, ejus motus impedimus, efficimusque, ut per eos nullum ipsa in nobis excitet impulsum ex ea parte, quae ad quaestionum enodationem incumbit? Nonne ex hoc evidenter colligimus, eam partem corpoream non esse? Hactenus ille.

75 “Is it, finally, likely that this complex of corporeal organs and animal spirits can consider, discuss, foresee, weigh, will, desire, choose the good? That this being of clay is fit for solving questions and problems? And yet, if the matter is so, why, in solving questions that are somewhat more abstract and difficult, do we stop up the organs of the senses as far as we can, free ourselves from matter, impede its motions, and bring it about that through them it excites in us no impulse from that part which applies itself to the unravelling of the questions? Do we not evidently gather from this that that part is not corporeal?” Thus far he.

76 Dico 2. cogitatio non est formaliter posita in eo quod objecta in organa nostra agant, aut in certa quadam motione tenuissimae maximèque mobilis substantiae, in cérebro nobis excitata â rebus circa quas cogitando versamur. Prob.: si per hoc intelligeremus, quod objecta in organa nostra ágerent, movendo scilicet illam tenuissimam substantiam cérebri, non alia ratione imago objectorum in nobis imprimeretur, ac ista vel illa figura in cera imprimatur: ergo sicuti cera suae figurae conscia non est; ita & nos quoque eorum quae cognoscimus conscii esse non possemus; sed hoc ad evidentiam usque falsum est: ergo.

76 I say 2. Thought does not formally consist in this, that objects act on our organs, or in a certain motion of a most subtle and highly mobile substance, excited in our brain by the things with which we are occupied in thinking. Proof: if by this we understood that objects act on our organs, namely by moving that most subtle substance of the brain, the image of the objects would be impressed on us in no other way than this or that figure is impressed in wax: therefore, just as wax is not conscious of its figure, so we too could not be conscious of the things we know; but this is false to the point of evidence: therefore.

77 Dico 3. animus noster est aliquid omninò diversum ab ea tenuissima maximèque mobili substantia, quae ex puriori sanguine in cérebro elaboratur. Prob. 1.: quia quantumvis tenuissima ponatur illa substantia, materia est; sed anima nequit esse materia, quum sit principium operationum quae ad materiam nullomodo possunt

77 I say 3. Our mind is something altogether different from that most subtle and highly mobile substance which is elaborated in the brain from the purer blood. Proof 1: because, however subtle that substance be supposed, it is matter; but the soul cannot be matter, since it is the principle of operations that can in no way belong to matter,

De la Connoissance de soi meme.

De la Connoissance de soi-même.

p. 25

pertinere, ut est demonstratum: ergo. Prob. 2.: nequit anima in illa vivida substantia collocari, quin ipsa itidem cogitatio in certa corpusculorum motione quae in cerebro fiat formaliter statuatur; sed demonstravimus, cogitationem ab omni corporea motione quae fiat in cérebro toto caelo differre: ergo anima rationalis est omninò aliud ab ea vivida substantia, quae ex puriori sanguine in cérebro perficitur.

as has been demonstrated: therefore. Proof 2: the soul cannot be placed in that living substance without thought itself being likewise placed formally in a certain motion of corpuscles that takes place in the brain; but we have demonstrated that thought differs by the whole breadth of heaven from every corporeal motion that takes place in the brain: therefore the rational soul is something altogether other than that living substance which is perfected in the brain from the purer blood.

78 Dico 4: absurdissima est Johannis Lockii opinio adserentis impossibile non esse ut materia cogitet, imò Dei potentia effici posse ut materia vi cogitandi donetur. Prob.: cogitatio aut vis percipiendi intrinsecè repugnat materiae, aut corpori, ut probatum manet; sed potentia Dei quamtumvis nullis limitibus circunscribatur, tamen ad impossibilia, & contradictoria extendi non potest, quum nequeat facere, ut idem simul sit, & non sit: ergo absurdissima est opinio. Lockii.

78 I say 4: most absurd is the opinion of John Locke, who asserts that it is not impossible that matter should think, nay, that it can be brought about by the power of God that matter be endowed with the power of thinking. Proof: thought, or the power of perceiving, is intrinsically repugnant to matter, or body, as stands proved; but the power of God, however true it is that it is circumscribed by no limits, nevertheless cannot extend to impossible and contradictory things, since it cannot make the same thing at once be and not be: therefore Locke’s opinion is most absurd.

79 Advertendum verò hic est, quod quamvis Divina revelatione certissimè constet animae spiritualitas, eamque probare possemus luculentissimis, Sanctarum Scripturarum, & Patrum testimoniis, illis abstinemus, quia negotium nobis est cum incredulis perditisque hominibus, Divinam revelationem floccifacientes, ideò in eos urgéri debent demonstrationes Philosophicae, nec haec arma ex nostris manibus éripi permittendum est, ut eis utamur contra infensissimos Christianae nostrae Religionis hostes. Postremò vos moneo, quod aliqui Scriptores Ecclesiastici, humanam animam, Angelos, Deum ipsum, corpus interdùm vocarunt quia nimirum ut Clariss. Jacquier animadvertit, quum incorpoream quamdam substantiam concipere vix possent, quidquid existeret, ut â nihilo distingueretur, corpus vocabant, ita ut corporis nomine, entia â nihilo sécernere duntaxat intenderint. At corpus illud á materia perspicuè distinguebant, ideòque nominis abusu duntaxat errarunt. Levitici etiam Cap. 17. dicitur animam omnis carnis in sanguine esse. Sed hoc ita dictum est, ait S. Augustinus, quomodo dictum est: petra erat Christus, scilicèt non quia hoc erat, sed quia hoc significabatur.

79 It must be noted here, however, that although the spirituality of the soul is most certainly established by Divine revelation, and we could prove it by the most splendid testimonies of the Holy Scriptures and of the Fathers, we abstain from them, because our business is with unbelieving and lost men who set Divine revelation at naught; therefore Philosophical demonstrations must be pressed against them, nor must we allow these weapons to be snatched from our hands, so that we may use them against the most bitter enemies of our Christian Religion. Lastly, I warn you that some Ecclesiastical Writers have at times called the human soul, the Angels, God himself, a body, because, namely, as the most distinguished Jacquier remarks, since they could scarcely conceive an incorporeal substance, they called whatever existed a body in order to distinguish it from nothing, so that by the name of body they intended only to separate beings from nothing. But they clearly distinguished that body from matter, and therefore erred only by an abuse of the name. In Leviticus, ch. 17, too, it is said that the soul of all flesh is in the blood. But this was said in such a way, says St. Augustine, as it was said: the rock was Christ; not, namely, because it was this, but because this was signified by it.

Materialistarum argumenta solvuntur.

The arguments of the Materialists are answered. 80

80 Opp. 1. contra primam: sine ulla ratione negatur, cogitationem materiae convenire, nisi omnes materiae modificationes cognoscamus, sed non omnes cognoscimus: ergo. Nego majorem: nam & si non cognoscamus omnes materiae modos, tamen certò scimus, materiae convenire non posse modos contradictorios. Porrò si materia cogitaret, ipsi convenirent modi contradictorii, nam cogitatio excludit partes, extensionem, figuram, divisionem. Haec autem omnia includit materia: ergo materia haberet proprietates contradictorias, si vi cogitandi praedita esse posset.

Obj. 1. against the first: it is denied without any reason that thought belongs to matter, unless we know all the modifications of matter; but we do not know them all: therefore. I deny the major: for even if we do not know all the modes of matter, we nevertheless know for certain that contradictory modes cannot belong to matter. Now if matter thought, contradictory modes would belong to it, for thought excludes parts, extension, figure, division. But matter includes all these: therefore matter would have contradictory properties, if it could be endowed with the power of thinking.

p. 26

81 Inst. 1: licet motus, & quies non sint aliquod extensum, & divisibile tamen sunt modificationes materiae: ergo licet cogitatio non sit extensa, dividua, & figurata, tamen potest esse modificatio materiae. Nego conseq. & est disparitas: quia materia potest habere modificationes purè extrinsecas, ut sunt motus, & quies, quae neque sint extensae, neque divisibiles, quia sunt meri respectus, merae relationes nihil mutantes in ipsa re: at materia non potest habere modificationes intrinsecas, quae neque sint extensae, neque divisibiles &c.: quum ergo cogitatio sit subjecti cogitantis modificatio intrinseca, non potest convenire materiae nisi ipsa cogitatio sit divisibilis, & extensa, quod absolutè repugnat, ut probatum manet.

81 Inst. 1: although motion and rest are not something extended and divisible, they are nevertheless modifications of matter: therefore, although thought is not extended, divisible and figured, it can nevertheless be a modification of matter. I deny the consequence, and there is a disparity: because matter can have purely extrinsic modifications, such as motion and rest, which are neither extended nor divisible, because they are mere respects, mere relations that change nothing in the thing itself; but matter cannot have intrinsic modifications that are neither extended nor divisible, etc.: since, therefore, thought is an intrinsic modification of the thinking subject, it cannot belong to matter unless thought itself is divisible and extended, which is absolutely repugnant, as stands proved.

82 Inst. 2. anima laeso corpore laeditur ergo operationes animae sunt modificationes materiae. Dist. antec: laeditur sed diverso modo, concedo; eodem modo, nego, & conseq. Laeditur enim corpus, quatenus nexus partium, aut dissolvitur, aut vehementer impellitur, anima verò laeditur quatenus ex lege conjunctionis in ea excitatur sensatio gravis & molesta. Dices: concipi non potest quomodo, quod spirituale est recipiatur in corpore, quod extensionem habet, & potest in plures partes secari: ergo anima non est spiritualis, sed ejusdem naturae, ac corpus in quo recipitur.

82 Inst. 2. When the body is injured the soul is injured: therefore the operations of the soul are modifications of matter. I distinguish the antecedent: it is injured, but in a different way, I grant; in the same way, I deny, and the consequence. For the body is injured insofar as the connection of its parts is either dissolved or violently disturbed, whereas the soul is injured insofar as, by the law of union, a grievous and troublesome sensation is excited in it. You will say: it cannot be conceived how what is spiritual is received in a body, which has extension and can be cut into several parts: therefore the soul is not spiritual, but of the same nature as the body in which it is received.

83 Nego conseq. quae non infertur. Etenim nunquid ideò (ait S. Augustinus) negandum est, quod apertum est, quia comprehendi non potest, quod occultum est? ¿Nunquid propterea, dicturi sumus, non ita esse, quod ita esse perspicimus, quoniam cur ita sit non possumus invenire? Profectò animo comprehendi non potest, quomodo materialis substantia valeat cogitare: igitur etiam Materialismus hac una de causâ falsa est hypothesis. Sed dices: inter corpus, & spiritum nulla datur proportio: ergo si anima est substantia spiritualis, corpori copulari nequiret, sed unitur: ergo non est substantia spiritualis.

83 I deny the consequence, which does not follow. For is that which is open (says St. Augustine) to be denied because that which is hidden cannot be comprehended? Shall we, on that account, say that what we perceive to be so is not so, because we cannot find out why it is so? Assuredly the mind cannot comprehend how a material substance is able to think: therefore Materialism too, for this one reason, is a false hypothesis. But you will say: between body and spirit there is no proportion: therefore, if the soul is a spiritual substance, it could not be coupled to the body; but it is united to it: therefore it is not a spiritual substance.

84 Dist. antec. nulla datur proportio hoc est, similitudo in natura, concedo: nulla datur proportio, hoc est, habitudo formae, ad subjectum, seu perfectivi ad perfectibile, nego, & conseq. Verùm est corpus, & spiritum esse substantias genere diversas; ac proinde, inter corpus, & spiritum eam non haberi proportionem, quam habent inter se duo entia ejusdem generis, & ordinis. At falsum est, inter corpus, & spiritum proportionem illam haberi non posse, quae satis est, ut corpus â spiritu perficiatur, totumque per se unum ex illorum unione consurgat.

84 I distinguish the antecedent: there is no proportion, that is, likeness in nature, I grant; there is no proportion, that is, the relation of a form to its subject, or of what perfects to what is perfectible, I deny, and the consequence. It is true that body and spirit are substances different in genus; and consequently that between body and spirit there is not that proportion which two beings of the same genus and order have to each other. But it is false that between body and spirit there cannot be that proportion which suffices for the body to be perfected by the spirit, and for a whole one by itself to arise from their union.

85 Objicies 2: una eademque tùm animae, tùm corporis est conditio: ergo. Prob. antec.: anima non agit in pueris, viget in juvenibus, debilitatur in senibus, easdem ac nostrum corpus adfectiones subit, & diversimodè mutatur: ergo. Dist. antec: & haec omnia contingunt propter arctam conjunctionem qua unita est corpori, concedo; ex naturâ ipsius animae quatenùs est substantia

85 You will object 2: the condition of the soul and that of the body are one and the same: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: the soul does not act in children, is vigorous in young men, is weakened in old men, undergoes the same affections as our body, and is changed in various ways: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: and all these things happen because of the close conjunction by which it is united to the body, I grant; from the nature of the soul itself insofar as it is a spiritual substance,

p. 27

spiritualis, nego, & conseq. Sicuti mirari quisquam non debet, si artifex, quamvis nullam mutationem quoad scientiam subierit, propter defectum instrumentorum sua praeclara opera perficere non possit; ita quoque nullus admirationi locus esse debet, si, dum organa corporea non dum suam perfectionem acquisierint, vel impedita quavis ratione fuerint, anima quoque, quoad ea potissimum in quibus ab iisdem organis pendet, vel nullomodo agere possit, vel cum magna difficultate agat.

I deny, and the consequence too. Just as no one ought to wonder if an artisan, although he has undergone no change as regards his knowledge, cannot accomplish his splendid works for want of instruments, so too there ought to be no room for wonder if, while the corporeal organs have not yet acquired their perfection, or have been impeded for whatever reason, the soul too, chiefly in those things in which it depends on those same organs, either cannot act at all or acts with great difficulty.

86 Unde quamvis mutatio non in anima, sed in corporeo ordine contingat; tamen etiam anima ob unionem, quam habet cum organis corporeis, particeps illius esse videtur. Ceterùm quàm multa sunt, quae anima nostra videt, licet organa corporea malè adfecta sint? ¿Anne dum membra corporis patiuntur, de rebus sublimioribus, quae sunt positae supra sensus, anima cogitare non potest? ¿Nonne harum rerum contemplatione dolorem mitigat, & lenit, atque contra eum se munit, & defendit? Verùm mirandum non est, si Materialistae animam cum corpore interire contendant, nisi enim hanc falsam opinionem induant, conscientiae stimulos, quibus aeterna mala sibi parata esse monentur, aliqua saltem ex parte sedare nunquam possunt.

86 Hence, although the change takes place not in the soul but in the corporeal order, nevertheless the soul too, because of the union it has with the corporeal organs, seems to share in it. Besides, how many things are there that our soul sees, although the corporeal organs are badly affected? Can the soul not think about loftier things, placed above the senses, while the members of the body are suffering? Does it not mitigate and soothe its pain by the contemplation of these things, and fortify and defend itself against it? But it is no wonder if the Materialists contend that the soul perishes with the body; for unless they put on this false opinion, they can never quiet, at least in some part, the goads of conscience by which they are warned that eternal evils are prepared for them.

87 Objic. 3: contra secundam cum Helvetio in impio opere, Gallicè inscripto L' Esprit. Per physicam sensibilitatem, quae est facultas recipiendi diversas impressiones causatas ab exterioribus objectis, & per memoriam, quae est facultas conservandi impraessiones quas objecta in nos causant, omnes ideae, & cogitationes produci possunt: imò ut planiùs loquamur, solâ physicâ sensibilitate omnes cogitationes producuntur: ergó omnis cogitatio in eo est formaliter posita quod objecta in organa nostra agant: ergo nulla datur anima spiritualis. Prob. antec. quoad primam partem, quia quando rei alicujus reminiscimur, tunc interiora nostra organa, ferè in eodem statu esse debent, ac quando res illa in nos sensibiliter agit. Hic autem status organorum necessariò producere debet sensationem: ergo reminisci idem est, ac sentire.

87 Obj. 3: against the second, with Helvétius in the impious work entitled in French L’Esprit. By physical sensibility, which is the faculty of receiving the various impressions caused by external objects, and by memory, which is the faculty of preserving the impressions that objects cause in us, all ideas and thoughts can be produced: nay, to speak more plainly, all thoughts are produced by physical sensibility alone: therefore all thought consists formally in this, that objects act on our organs: therefore there is no spiritual soul. Proof of the antecedent as to the first part: because when we remember some thing, our interior organs must then be in nearly the same state as when that thing acts sensibly on us. But this state of the organs must necessarily produce sensation: therefore to remember is the same as to sense.

88 Prob. altera pars: quando de magnitudine vel colore objecti mihi propositi judico, evidens est meum judicium esse sensationem, quia illud refertur ad diversas impraessiones, quas objecta causarunt in meis organis: unde possum aequaliter dicere: ego judico, ac ego sentio. Itemque possum aeque dicere, duo objecta unum album, nigrum alterum in me producere diversas impraessiones: ergo judicare idem est ac sentire. Ita pro suo more ineptit perniciosus Materialista. Sed his omnibus nihil ineptiùs, aut absurdiùs fingi potest Et ad primum quod adtinet.

88 Proof of the other part: when I judge of the size or color of an object set before me, it is evident that my judgment is a sensation, because it is referred to the various impressions that the objects have caused in my organs: whence I can equally say I judge and I sense. And likewise I can equally say that two objects, one white, the other black, produce different impressions in me: therefore to judge is the same as to sense. Thus, after his fashion, the pernicious Materialist talks nonsense. But nothing more inept or absurd than all this can be devised. And as regards the first:

89 ¿Undenam novit Helvetius, nostra interiora organa, quando alicujus rei reminiscimur, ferè in eodem statu esse debere, ac quando res illa in nos sensibiliter agit? Profectò recordatione voluptatum, quas degustavimus, non semper cum gaudio recordamur,

89 Whence did Helvétius learn that our interior organs, when we remember something, must be in nearly the same state as when that thing acts sensibly on us? Surely, in recollecting the pleasures we have tasted, we do not always remember them with joy,

p. 28

sed saepè etiam cum tristitia & dolore, & tunc potissimum quando ex iis plura nobis mala parta esse videmus. Voluptatis autem recordatione semper laetaremur, si tunc organa nostra interiora eodem ferè modo se haberent, ac quando sensibiliter voluptate fruimur. ¿Quid verò continget quando multorum simul reminiscimur, quae contraria inter se sunt, uti sunt dolor, & voluptas; Praeterea: quàm multa sunt, quibus nullomodo sensibiliter adfici possumus, & tamen eorum reminiscimur? ¿Anne veritas, & falsitas adficit sensus nostros? ¿Turpitudo, vel honestas actionum adficit tactum, oculos, palátum, vel nares?

but often also with sadness and grief, and then especially when we see that many evils have come to us from them. We would, however, always rejoice in the recollection of pleasure, if our interior organs were then disposed in nearly the same way as when we sensibly enjoy the pleasure. And what will happen when we remember at the same time many things that are contrary to one another, such as pain and pleasure? Besides: how many things are there by which we can in no way be sensibly affected, and yet we remember them? Do truth and falsity affect our senses? Does the turpitude or honorableness of actions affect touch, the eyes, the palate, or the nostrils?

90 Et ad secundum quod spectat, profectò si idem, est, judicare, ac sentire, inde necessariò sequitur, ut dum judico de sapore, sentiam saporem: ergo ut plures sapores quisque pro suo libito succesivè sentiat, satis erit, ut de iisdem judicet, nam quando duo inter se non distinguuntur, sed sunt unum, & idem, quod uni convenit, alteri convenire debet: ergo qui judicat de coloribus ex. gr. videt colores; qui judicat de odoribus, odores sentit. ¿Cuinam tandem haec risum non moveant?

90 And as regards the second, surely, if to judge is the same as to sense, it necessarily follows from this that while I judge of a taste, I sense the taste: therefore, for anyone to sense several tastes in succession at his pleasure, it will be enough for him to judge of them; for when two things are not distinguished from each other but are one and the same, what belongs to the one must belong to the other: therefore one who judges of colors, e.g., sees colors; one who judges of odors senses odors. Whom, then, would these things not move to laughter?

91 Diversitatem igitur judiciorum quae formantur de rebus sensui nostro subjectis, licet ad diversitatem impraessionum referri, & nos quoque concedamus; tamen judicium esse idem cum impraessione, quae fit in nostros sensus hoc verò est, quod nullomodo dare [?] possumus. Tunc enim nos judicium ferre dicimur, quando aliquid alteri convenire vel non convenire adfirmamus: quare notio ejus, cui aliquid convenire, vel non convenire, notio ejus, quod convenire, vel non convenire dicitur, & facultas quae utramque notionem simul comparet,atque determinet,quid alicui enti conveniat, vel non conveniat, ad judicium faciendum, simul conveniant oportet, quod quidem per solam sensuum impraessionem haberi non potest; quum impraessio sensuum sit determinata, atque peculiaris, quae namque visionem adficiunt, ad aurem pertinere non possunt, per impraessionem quae fit in auribus, judicare non possumus de impraessione quae fit in paláto: ergo per impraessionem sensuum, unum cum altero comparari non potest, neque determinari quid alicui enti conveniat, vel non conveniat.

91 Although, then, we too grant that the diversity of the judgments formed about the things subject to our sense is referred to the diversity of impressions, yet that judgment is the same as the impression made on our senses is something we can in no way admit. For we are said to pass judgment when we affirm that something agrees or does not agree with another: wherefore the notion of that with which something agrees or does not agree, the notion of that which is said to agree or not to agree, and the faculty that compares both notions together and determines what agrees or does not agree with some being, must concur together in order to make a judgment; and this indeed cannot be had through the impression of the senses alone, since the impression of the senses is determinate and peculiar; those that affect vision cannot belong to the ear; through the impression made in the ears we cannot judge of the impression made on the palate: therefore, through the impression of the senses, one cannot be compared with another, nor can it be determined what agrees or does not agree with some being.

92 Opp. 4. contra 4. cum Lockio: ideò negamus per Dei potentiam fieri non posse, ut materia cogitet, quia id comprehendere non possumus; sed haec ratio prorsùs insufficiens est: ergo. 2: quamvis in idea Medici non includatur idea Musici tamen hae duae res possunt in homine conjungi: ergo quamvis idea cogitationis in idea materiae non includatur, materia cogitare poterit. Ad primum nego causalem: haec enim non est ratio nostrae persuasionis, non enim ita putamus, quia quomodo hoc fieri posse non videamus, sed quia fieri non posse certissimâ ratione perspicimus. Ad secundum respondeo, quod esse medicum, & musicum non repugnat essentiae hominis, at cogitatio, materiae repugnat, quia

92 Obj. 4. against the 4th, with Locke: we deny that it can be brought about by the power of God that matter should think, because we cannot comprehend it; but this reason is altogether insufficient: therefore. 2: although the idea of a Musician is not included in the idea of a Physician, nevertheless these two things can be joined in a man: therefore, although the idea of thought is not included in the idea of matter, matter will be able to think. To the first I deny the causal proposition: for this is not the reason for our persuasion; we do not think so because we do not see how this can be done, but because we perceive by a most certain reason that it cannot be done. To the second I reply that to be a physician and a musician is not repugnant to the essence of man, but thought is repugnant to matter, because

p. 29

materia extensa debet esse, habere partes, &c. Substantia verò cogitans nihil horum habere potest, uti jam demonstravimus.

matter must be extended, have parts, etc. But a thinking substance can have none of these things, as we have already demonstrated.

93 Opp. 5. In idea materiae continetur notio substantiae extensae, atque solidae, non verò vegetationis: ergo sicut Deus vim vegetandi substantiae extensae, atque solidae unire potest, ita etiam vim cogitandi. 2: Quamvis ignoremus, qua ratione vis vegetandi in plantis, sentiendi in brutis inesse possit, tamen hoc â Deo fieri posse non negamus: ergo. Ad primum nego conseq. & ratio est, quia vegetatio, ut ipsi Materialistae fatentur, per motum, diversam dispositionem, atque configurationem partium perfici potest. At verò cogitatio per motum atque configurationem non potest materiae convenire, ut jam probavimus. Ad secundum eadem est responsio: quamvis enim illa ignoremus, tamen illud quoque simul cognoscimus, nullam contradictionem sequi si ea admittamus.

93 Obj. 5. In the idea of matter is contained the notion of an extended and solid substance, but not of vegetation: therefore, just as God can unite the power of vegetating to an extended and solid substance, so too can he unite the power of thinking. 2: Although we do not know in what way the power of vegetating can be present in plants, and that of sensing in brutes, nevertheless we do not deny that this can be done by God: therefore. To the first I deny the consequence, and the reason is that vegetation, as the Materialists themselves admit, can be accomplished through motion and the diverse disposition and configuration of the parts. But thought cannot belong to matter through motion and configuration, as we have already proved. To the second the reply is the same: for although we do not know those things, we nevertheless know at the same time this as well, that no contradiction follows if we admit them.

94 Opp. 6. Si dicamus Deum efficere non posse, ut materia cogitet, quia hoc impossibile nobis adparet, Dei Omnipotentiam nostris ideis coarctatam esse consequitur; sed hoc est absurdum: ergo. 2. Nos non habemus ideam claram, & distinctam substantiae, ut diximus in Logica: ergo adfirmare non possumus cogitationem extensioni convenire non posse. Ad primum nego antec.: quia sicut Divinae virtuti nihil derogatur, dum dicitur numerum binarium, atque ternarium simul unitum, numerum senarium, constituere non posse, ita quoque quoniam perspectum habemus materiam extensam esse debere, divisibilem, &c.; cogitationi autem hoc repugnare, nihil Divinae potentiae derogatur, si materiae cogitationem tribui non posse adfirmemus. Per hoc autem Divinam Omnipotentiam in nostris ideis non concludimus, sed ei rationis lumini subjicimur, quod nobis Deus ipse dedit, quo profectò abuteremur, si ideas evidenter incompatibiles, simul unire posse adfirmaremus.

94 Obj. 6. If we say that God cannot bring it about that matter should think, because this appears impossible to us, it follows that the Omnipotence of God is confined by our ideas; but this is absurd: therefore. 2. We do not have a clear and distinct idea of substance, as we said in the Logic: therefore we cannot affirm that thought cannot belong to extension. To the first I deny the antecedent: because, just as nothing is taken away from the Divine power when it is said that the number two and the number three united together cannot constitute the number six, so too, since we have perceived that matter must be extended, divisible, etc., and that this is repugnant to thought, nothing is taken away from the Divine power if we affirm that thought cannot be attributed to matter. By this, moreover, we do not enclose the Divine Omnipotence within our ideas, but submit ourselves to that light of reason which God himself has given us, and which we would surely abuse if we affirmed that evidently incompatible ideas can be united together.

95 Ineptissimè ergo ita argumentatur Voltaire 2 Deus est Omnipotens: ergo negare, eum posse vim cogitandi dare materiae, est impium. At ego respondeo: imò id asserere est amentiae. Essentiae rerum non sunt objectum Divinae Omnipotentiae, sed existentia. Potest Deus efficere, ut triangulum existat, aut non existat; at efficere nequit, ut triangulum sit rotundum. Quid ita? Quia hoc implicat contradictionem, nam hoc in casu, & esset, & non esset triangulum. Atqui inter materiam, & cogitationem, id ipso Voltaire fatente 2 est contradictio: non potest igitur efficere Deus, ut materia cogitet. Ut contradictio tolleretur mutandae essent naturae, ut materia non esset amplius materia, aut cogitatio non esset amplius cogitatio: tunc autem quaestio nulla esset. Haec notá sunt cuicumque, vel prima limina Metaphysicae salutavit.

95 Most ineptly, therefore, does Voltaire (b) argue thus: God is Omnipotent: therefore to deny that he can give the power of thinking to matter is impious. But I reply: nay, to assert it is madness. The essences of things are not the object of the Divine Omnipotence, but their existence is. God can bring it about that a triangle exist or not exist; but he cannot bring it about that a triangle be round. Why so? Because this implies a contradiction, for in this case it would both be and not be a triangle. But between matter and thought, as Voltaire himself admits (c), there is a contradiction: God therefore cannot bring it about that matter should think. For the contradiction to be removed, the natures would have to be changed, so that matter would no longer be matter, or thought would no longer be thought: but then there would be no question. These things are known to anyone who has so much as greeted the first threshold of Metaphysics.

Metaphysique & Lett. XIII. Sur Mr. Locke.

Métaphysique, and Lett. XIII, Sur Mr. Locke.

In Elem. Phys. Newton.

In the Elem. Phys. Newton.

p. 30

96 Ad secundum respondeo verum esse nos non habere ideam claram, & distinctam substantiae, sed tamen quae corporeae substantiae necessariò conveniunt, & quae incorporeae repugnant, certissimè novimus. Dices: Deus creare potest tam substantiam materialem, quam spiritualem omni agendi vi destitutam: ergo Deus aequalem agendi vim iisdem tribuere potest, ita ut substantia materialis cogitet. Respondeo quod ea quae à Deo alicui substantiae tribuuntur, inter se repugnare non debent, at materiam cogitantem esse repugnat.

96 To the second I reply that it is true that we do not have a clear and distinct idea of substance, but we nevertheless know most certainly what necessarily belongs to corporeal substance and what is repugnant to incorporeal substance. You will say: God can create both a material and a spiritual substance devoid of all power of acting: therefore God can attribute an equal power of acting to them, so that a material substance may think. I reply that the things attributed by God to any substance must not be repugnant to one another; but it is repugnant that matter should be thinking.

97 Opp. tandem: in idea Divinae Justitiae non concipitur Misericordia, & tamen sunt una res indistincta: ergo licet in idea materiae non includatur cogitatio non repugnat materiam posse cogitare. Nego conseq. Idea enim Justitiae non repraesentat rem, ut in se est, sed prout connotat extrinsecum objectum; ac proinde sat est si objectum Justitiae diversum sit ab objecto Misericordiae, ut utriusque idea, & conceptus distinguatur. At per ideam corporis concipio substantiam extensam, divisibilem, & figuratam, & nihil horum percipio in idea cogitationis, ideoque diversa corporis, seu materiae, & cogitationis perceptio infert discrimen materiam inter & cogitationem, id est non inter objecta duntaxat, sed inter unam, aliamque substantiam. Ita Cl. Berti.

97 Obj. finally: in the idea of Divine Justice Mercy is not conceived, and yet they are one undistinguished thing: therefore, although thought is not included in the idea of matter, it is not repugnant that matter can think. I deny the consequence. For the idea of Justice does not represent the thing as it is in itself, but insofar as it connotes an extrinsic object; and consequently it is enough that the object of Justice be different from the object of Mercy for the idea and concept of each to be distinguished. But through the idea of body I conceive an extended, divisible and figured substance, and I perceive none of these in the idea of thought; and therefore the different perception of body, or matter, and of thought implies a distinction between matter and thought, that is, not merely between objects, but between one substance and another. So the distinguished Berti.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

¿An anima nostra sit immortalis, num vero in morte unà cum corpore pereat?

Whether our soul is immortal, or rather perishes together with the body at death?

98 Princeps totius Psychologiae argumentum tractandum suscipimus, quum de immortalitate rationalis animae disserimus; ut quod ad conformandos rectè mores, & ad timorem juxtà, cultumque Supremi Numinis fovendum, momenti permultum habet. Quo quidem argumento obedientissimè; ut par est respondebimus sapientissimae praeceptioni qua Lateranense V. Concilium s1 mandat omnibus Philosophiae Professoribus hanc de immortalitate animae assertionem manifestam omni conatu facerent, & naturali ratione, pro viribus stabilirent.

he principal argument of the whole of Psychology is the one we un98 T dertake to treat when we discuss the immortality of the rational soul, as something of very great moment for rightly forming morals, and likewise for fostering the fear and worship of the Supreme Deity. In this argument we shall most obediently, as is fitting, respond to the most wise precept by which the Fifth Lateran Council (d) commands all Professors of Philosophy to make this assertion of the immortality of the soul manifest with every effort, and to establish it, as far as they can, by natural reason.

99 Et rectè quidem, cum enim ii, (ut egregiè, advertit Doctissimus Cano, s2 qui animae immortalitatem inficiantur, nec

99 And rightly so; for since those (as the most learned Cano excellently remarks (e)) who deny the immortality of the soul believe neither in Christ the

Ann. 1533 sub Julio II, & Leone X. celebratum. Sess. 8.

Held in the year 1513 under Julius II and Leo X. Sess. 8.

p. 31

Christo Domino, nec Evangelio credant; Ecclesiae verò, Sanctorumque fidem pro nihilo putent, ita supervacaneum videtur esse, ex iis locis, quae auctoritatem fidei continent, argumenta depromere. In hac ergo dissertatione non Sacris auctoritatibus, sed principiis naturae lumine notis insistendum pro viribus est adversus Epicúrum, Lucretium, aliosque Recentiores Philosophos perniciosissimos, veritatum Sacrosanctae nostrae Religionis inimicos, qui humanam animam mortalem, unàque cum corpore interituram conatu planè irrito ostendere nituntur. Sed priusquam ad quaestionem accedamus aliqua claritatis gratiâ explicemus oportet.

the Lord nor in the Gospel, and hold the faith of the Church and of the Saints as nothing, so it seems superfluous to draw arguments from the places that contain the authority of faith. In this dissertation, therefore, we must take our stand, as far as we can, not on Sacred authorities but on principles known by the light of nature, against Epicurus, Lucretius, and other most pernicious modern Philosophers, enemies of the truths of our most holy Religion, who strive with an utterly vain effort to show that the human soul is mortal and will perish together with the body. But before we approach the question, we must explain some things for the sake of clarity.

100 Immortalitas absoluta, quae intrinseca dici potest, convenit enti viventi nullum habenti in se, & ex natura sua principium interitus. Immortalitas relativa, quae extrinseca dici potest, convenit enti viventi, quod non potest ab alio extrinseco destrui, vel annihilari. Soli Deo convenire immortalitatem tùm absolutam, tùm relativam certum est: anima autem rationalis non habet immortalitatem relativam in omni sensu; quamvis enim non possit destrui. vel annihilari ab alio ente creato, potest tamen absolutè annihilari â Deo.

100 Absolute immortality, which can be called intrinsic, belongs to a living being that has in itself, and from its own nature, no principle of perishing. Relative immortality, which can be called extrinsic, belongs to a living being that cannot be destroyed or annihilated by another, extrinsic, being. It is certain that immortality both absolute and relative belongs to God alone; the rational soul, however, does not have relative immortality in every sense; for although it cannot be destroyed or annihilated by another created being, it can nevertheless absolutely be annihilated by God.

101 Quum ergo quaeritur: ¿an anima nostra sit immortalis? Quaestio non est, an à Deo absolutè annihilari possit, sed quaeritur duntaxat primò: ¿an anima rationalis nullum habeat in se, & ex natura sua principium interitus? Secundo: an nulla in toto mundo existat causa extrinseca creata mentem potens destruere? Tertio: ¿an Deus nolit eam annihilare, aut eam mutare unquam, ita ut facultates vitales, quas in ea depraehendimus amittat? Hic est status quaestionis, qui quidem probè attendi debet. Fide autem certum est mentem humanam non interituram cum corpore, sed in aeternum duraturam viventem. Hinc Christus Dominus 2 Nolite inquit timere eos, qui occidunt corpus, animam autem non possunt occidere, & alibi. 2 Qui odit animam suam in hoc mundo, in vitam aeternam custodit eam. Sed quoniam rationibus naturalibus, ut supra diximus stabilienda est quaestio

101 When, therefore, it is asked whether our soul is immortal, the question is not whether it can absolutely be annihilated by God; rather, it is asked only, first: whether the rational soul has in itself, and from its own nature, no principle of perishing? Second: whether there exists in the whole world no created extrinsic cause able to destroy the mind? Third: whether God wills never to annihilate it, or ever to change it so that it should lose the vital faculties we detect in it? This is the state of the question, which must indeed be carefully attended to. By faith, moreover, it is certain that the human mind will not perish with the body, but will endure, living, for eternity. Hence Christ the Lord (f) says: Fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul; and elsewhere (g): He that hateth his life in this world, keepeth it unto life eternal. But since, as we said above, the question must be settled by natural reasons:

102 Dico 1. Anima rationalis nullo corruptionis genere naturaliter interire potest, adeòque naturâ sua est immortalis. Prob. conclusio. Substantia spiritualis nullomodo perire, aut corrumpi naturaliter potest, sed anima rationalis est substantia spiritualis, ut superiori capite probátum manet: ergo. Prob. major.: Substantia spiritualis est substantia simplex seu nullis constans partibus, ut fatentur omnes; sed substantia simplex nullomodo perire, aut corrumpi naturaliter potest: ergo. Prob. minor: primo perire non potest, aut corrumpi, divisione, aut dissolutione, quum sit partium expers, & realiter indivisibilis. „ In animi namque cognitione, (ut

102 I say 1. The rational soul cannot naturally perish by any kind of corruption, and hence it is immortal by its nature. The conclusion is proved. A spiritual substance can in no way perish or be corrupted naturally; but the rational soul is a spiritual substance, as stands proved in the preceding chapter: therefore. Proof of the major: a spiritual substance is a simple substance, or one consisting of no parts, as all admit; but a simple substance can in no way perish or be corrupted naturally: therefore. Proof of the minor: first, it cannot perish or be corrupted by division or dissolution, since it is devoid of parts and really indivisible. “For in the knowledge of the mind (as

Lib. XII. de Loc. Theolog. Cap. postrem.

Bk. XII, De Locis Theologicis, last ch.

Matth. 12. ℣. 28.

Matt. 10, v. 28.

Joann. 12. ℣. 29 [?].

John 12, v. 25.

p. 32

eleganter Cicero 2 dubitare non possumus, nisi planè in physicis plumbei sumus, quin nihil sit animus admixtum, nihil concretum, nihil copulatum, nihil coagmentatum, nihil duplex. Quod quum ita sit. certè nec secerni, nec dividi, nec discerpi, nec distrahi potest: nec interire igitur. Est enim interitus quasi discessus, & secretio, ac diremptus earum partium, quae ante interitum junctione aliqua tenebantur. „ Secundo se ipsam perimere, aut annihilare non potest, nec à quocumque agente creato destrui potest. Primo quia nihil in rerum natura sibimetipsi contrarium est: Secundo: quia nullum agens creatum humanum animum creare potest: ergo nec ipsum annihilare: ergo anima rationalis nullo corruptionis genere naturaliter interire potest, adeoque naturâ sua est immortalis,

Cicero elegantly puts it (h)), we cannot doubt, unless we are altogether leaden in physics, that there is nothing mixed in the mind, nothing concrete, nothing coupled, nothing joined together, nothing twofold. And since this is so, it certainly can be neither separated, nor divided, nor torn apart, nor pulled asunder: nor, therefore, can it perish. For perishing is, as it were, a departure, a separation and a disjunction of those parts which before perishing were held together by some bond.” Secondly, it can neither destroy nor annihilate itself, nor be destroyed by any created agent whatever. First, because nothing in the nature of things is contrary to its very self; Secondly: because no created agent can create the human mind: therefore it cannot annihilate it either: therefore the rational soul cannot perish naturally by any kind of corruption, and hence is immortal by its nature.

103 Argumentis moralibus probatur etiam conclusio nostra. Primo ex firmissimo omnium populorum consensu, constantique omnium nationum sententiâ. Nulla enim gens tam barbara unquam fuit, cujus mentem non imbuerit immortalitatis animae opinio, quod is tantum ignorare potest, qui planè hospes in Historiis est, quique Veterum caerimonias, ritus atque leges prorsùs ignorat. Secundo: quia si nulla nobis post mortem futura sit vita, nunquam expleri in nobis poterit illud felicitatis desiderium, quod ipsa nobis natura impraesit, deteriorisque essemus conditionis, quàm cetera viventia.

103 Our conclusion is also proved by moral arguments. First, from the most firm consent of all peoples and the constant opinion of all nations. For there was never any nation so barbarous that its mind was not imbued with the opinion of the immortality of the soul, which only he can be ignorant of who is an utter stranger to histories, and who knows nothing at all of the ceremonies, rites and laws of the Ancients. Secondly: because if there were to be no life for us after death, that desire for happiness which nature itself has impressed on us could never be fulfilled in us, and we would be of a worse condition than the other living things.

104 Tertio: Quia negari non potest huic universo Summum praesse Guvernatorem rerum omnium Deum, qui justas criminibus poenas, debitamque virtuti mercedem rependat, quod utique fieri non posset si mens nostra unà cum corpore interiret, nam hìc videmus insontes saepius indigére, & ópprimi, improbos verò deliciis adfluere, quod quidem à Christo Domino in paupere Lazaro, & Epulone divite expraessum est 2 Recordare quia recepisti bona in vita tua, & Lazarus similiter mala: nunc autem hic consolatur, tu verò cruciaris. Ex quibus inferendum est, caecitatem Materialistarum deplorandam esse, quum ex absurdissima sua opinione nihil emolumenti sperare unquam possint. Si enim toti intereunt, ut sibi vesanè fingunt, hujus suae confidentiae nulla eos merces manet, si animus immortalis est, ut certè est, aeternas daturi sunt poenas, quòd tantâ pervicaciâ, religione omni abjecta manifestis testimoniis refragari sustinuerint.

104 Thirdly: because it cannot be denied that over this universe there presides God, the Supreme Governor of all things, who repays crimes with just punishments and virtue with its due reward; which certainly could not be done if our mind perished together with the body, for here we see the innocent more often in want and oppressed, and the wicked abounding in delights; which indeed was expressed by Christ our Lord in the poor man Lazarus and the rich glutton (i): Remember that thou didst receive good things in thy lifetime, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted; and thou art tormented. From which it is to be inferred that the blindness of the Materialists is to be deplored, since from their most absurd opinion they can never hope for any profit. For if they perish entirely, as they madly imagine, no reward awaits them for this confidence of theirs; if the mind is immortal, as it certainly is, they will pay eternal penalties, because with such obstinacy, having cast off all religion, they have dared to resist manifest testimonies.

105 Dico 2: Anima rationalis à Deo in morte nequaquam annihilatur, sed illius voluntate corpori post mortem superest sine fine victura. Prob. 1: „ Neque enim (ut optimè ait Leibnitzius 2 adversus Puffendorfium scribens) „ Neque enim dubitari

105 I say 2: The rational soul is in no way annihilated by God at death, but by His will survives the body after death, to live without end. Prob. 1: “For (as Leibniz (k), writing against Pufendorf, excellently says) it cannot be doubted

Tusc. Lib. 1. cap. 28.

Tusculan Disputations, bk. 1, ch. 28.

Luc. 6. ℣. 25.

Luke 16, v. 25.

p. 33

test, Rectorem Universi Sapientissimum, eumdemque potentissimum, bonis praemia, malis poenas destinasse, & éxsequi destinata in futura vita, quando in hac praesente pleraque impunita transmitti constat „. Ex quo clare infertur, nunquam futurum esse, ut animae á Deo destruantur. Secundo: est in nobis naturalis inclinatio, ob quam semper esse adpetimus, & ita esse, ut semper felices in nostro fine immutabiliter quiescamus: ergo ad futurum vitae statum consequitur etiam immortalitas animorum.

that the most wise and likewise most powerful Ruler of the Universe has appointed rewards for the good and punishments for the wicked, and executes what He has appointed in the future life, since it is agreed that in this present one most things pass unpunished.” From which it is clearly inferred that it will never come to pass that souls are destroyed by God. Secondly: there is in us a natural inclination by which we desire always to be, and so to be that we may rest always happy, immutably, in our end: therefore to the future state of life there follows also the immortality of souls.

106 Et re vera: „ creatura intellectualis (ut sapientissimè loquitur Angelicus Praeceptor S. Thomas s1 „ non pervenit ad ultimum finem, nisi quando ejus desiderium naturaliter quietatur, sicut autem desiderat felicitatem, ita naturaliter desiderat felicitatis perpetuitatem. „ Probatur tertio: substantiis spiritualibus, ex sui naturâ convenit, ut incorruptibiles sint, ut probatum manet; ergo neque etiam Dei potentiâ ordinaria eae destrui debent. Prob. conseq. „ Deus (ut ait S. Thom. s2) qui est institutor naturae, non subtrahit rebus quod est proprium naturis earum „: ergo si substantiae spirituales ex sui naturâ habent, ut semper sint, Deus easdem semper conservare debet: ergo animae nostrae immortales sunt, etiamsi quoad sui principium spectentur. Haec adversus Libertinos, qui verbo Dei non credunt.

106 And in truth: “an intellectual creature (as the Angelic Teacher St. Thomas most wisely says (l)) does not reach its ultimate end except when its desire is naturally set at rest; but just as it desires happiness, so it naturally desires the perpetuity of happiness.” It is proved thirdly: it belongs to spiritual substances by their own nature to be incorruptible, as has been proved; therefore neither ought they to be destroyed by the ordinary power of God. The consequence is proved: “God (as St. Thomas says (m)), who is the institutor of nature, does not withdraw from things what is proper to their natures”: therefore if spiritual substances have it from their own nature that they always exist, God must always conserve them: therefore our souls are immortal, even if they are considered with respect to their principle. So much against the Libertines, who do not believe the word of God.

107 Nos autem qui Scripturis Sanctis ita firmiter adhaeremus, ut pro illarum defensione sanguinem nostrum effundere parati simus, constanter credimus animorum immortalitatem: constat namque certissimo Dei Oraculo s3 pulverem, sive corpus, reversurum esse in terram suam unde erat; spiritum verò rediturum ad Deum, qui dedit illum. Justorum animas esse in manu Dei, neque umquam fore, ut tormentum mortis eas adtingat. Christum Dominum s4 dicturum justis in die judicii, ut ad eum veniant benedicti á Patre, regnumque accipiant, quod à constitutione mundi illis paraverat; impiis autem ex adverso, ut eant maledicti in ignem aeternum, quem diabolo, ejusque Angelis, tunc itidem constituit justissimus judex, ut alia praetereamus innumera id genus oracula, quibus Deus nos certos reddit, animam nostram in aeternum esse duraturam.

107 But we, who adhere so firmly to the Holy Scriptures that we are ready to shed our blood in their defense, constantly believe in the immortality of souls: for it is established by the most certain Oracle of God (n) that the dust, or body, shall return into its earth from whence it was, but the spirit shall return to God, who gave it; that the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and that it will never be that the torment of death shall touch them; that Christ our Lord (o) will say to the just on the day of judgment that they should come to Him, blessed of the Father, and receive the kingdom which He had prepared for them from the foundation of the world; but to the impious, on the contrary, that they should go, cursed, into everlasting fire, which the most just judge then likewise appointed for the devil and his Angels: to pass over other innumerable oracles of that kind, by which God makes us certain that our soul is to endure forever.

Libertinorum argumenta solvuntur.

The arguments of the Libertines are answered. 108

108 Libertini innumera propemodum Scripturae Sacrae testimonia, quibus eorum impietas apertissimè convincitur, negligunt, & parvipendunt; unum aut alterum quo facilius apud imperitos abuti possunt studiosè requirunt. Opponunt

The Libertines neglect and make light of the almost innumerable testimonies of Sacred Scripture by which their impiety is most plainly refuted: they studiously seek out one or another which they can more easily abuse among the unskilled. They object, therefore,

Epist. ad Gerh. Wolth. quae est 16. Volum. II. Epistolar. ad divers.

Letter to Gerh. Wolth., which is no. 16, vol. II of the Epistolae ad diversos.

III. Cont. Gent. Cap 51. num. 2.

III Contra Gentiles, ch. 51, no. 2.
