II Contra Gentiles, ch. 55, no. 17.

Eccles 12. ℣. 7. Sap. 3. ℣. 1.

Eccles. 12, v. 7. Wisd. 3, v. 1.

Math. Cap. 25. ℣. 34, & seq.

Matt., ch. 25, v. 34 ff.

p. 34

itaque primò: unum esse interitum hominis, & jumentorum scribit, Ecclesiastes 2. Resp. unum esse interitum hominum & jumentorum, quantum adtinet ad vitam corpoream communem omnibus animantibus. Itaquè nihil habet homo jumento ampliùs ratione corporis, quoniam cuncta ad eandem terrae conditionem redeunt, unde facta sunt. Mens ergo in terram nòn revertitur, quum ex terra non sit producta. Praeterea responderi potest his omnibus in locis non loqui Salomonem ex sententia propriâ; sed impiorum, refert nimirùm. quod iniqui tenent animo, non autem quod ipse sentit, ut egregiè observat S. Gregorius Magnus s2, & Doctissimus Episcopus Huet. s3

first: that Ecclesiastes (p) writes that the death of man and of beasts is one. Reply: the death of men and of beasts is one as regards the bodily life common to all animals. Thus man has nothing more than the beast by reason of the body, since all things return to the same condition of earth from which they were made. The mind, therefore, does not return into the earth, since it was not produced from earth. Moreover, it can be answered that in all these places Solomon does not speak from his own opinion but from that of the impious; that is, he relates what the wicked hold in their minds, not what he himself thinks, as St. Gregory the Great (q) and the most learned Bishop Huet (r) excellently observe.

109 Opp. 2. Sapientiae Cap. 20. legitur: post hoc, id est, post mortem spiritus diffunditur tanquam mollis aër: ergo anima rationalis homine moriente evanescit. Secundo: Ecclesiastes s4 ait: „ ¿quis novit si spiritus filiorum Adae ascendat sursum, & si spiritus jumentorum descendat deorsum? „ Ergo aequalis est conditio hominis, & jumenti etiam quoad spiritum. Ad primum respondeo ibi loqui ex sententia impiorum, ut capitis initium declarat. Dixerunt impii cogitantes apud se non rectè, & ℣. 2. subjungit: haec cogitaverunt impii, & erraverunt, nec judicaverunt honorem animarum sanctarum, quoniam creavit Deus hominem inexterminabilem. Ad secundum respondeo: verba illa esse reprehendentis impios, quorum animus non nisi terrena sapit. Si enim omnia velímus metiri sensibus: quis novit si spiritus filiorum Adae, &c. Pariter quod dicitur in VI. Synodo OEcumenica, animam non naturâ, sed gratiâ Dei esse immortalem eo sensu intelligendum est, quod anima immortalitatem habeat Deo volente, & conservante, quae conservatio est ex sola gratia. Itaque immortalitas intrinseca animae rationali naturalis est; gratuita vero immortalitas extrinseca.

109 Obj. 2. In Wisdom, ch. 2, we read: after this, that is, after death, the spirit is poured abroad as soft air: therefore the rational soul vanishes when a man dies. Secondly: Ecclesiastes (s) says: “Who knoweth if the spirit of the children of Adam ascend upward, and if the spirit of the beasts descend downward?” Therefore the condition of man and of beast is equal, even as regards the spirit. To the first I reply that it speaks there from the opinion of the impious, as the beginning of the chapter declares: The wicked said, reasoning with themselves, but not right; and in v. 2 it adds: These things the wicked thought, and were deceived, nor esteemed the honor of holy souls, for God created man incorruptible. To the second I reply: those words are those of one reproving the impious, whose mind savors nothing but earthly things. For if we wish to measure all things by the senses: who knoweth if the spirit of the children of Adam, etc. Likewise, what is said in the Sixth Ecumenical Council, that the soul is immortal not by nature but by the grace of God, is to be understood in this sense, that the soul has immortality by God’s willing and conserving it, which conservation is from grace alone. Thus intrinsic immortality is natural to the rational soul; but extrinsic immortality is gratuitous.

110 Opp. 3 cum Lucretio totaque veterum Epicureorum familia: anima rationalis cum corpore nascitur: ergo cum corpore debet interire, nam id omne corrumpitur quod generatur. Dist. antec.: cum corpore nascitur per generationem, nego antec: per creationem, conc: Perit ergo corpus quia sola partium dissolutione interimitur: anima verò veluti substantia simplex perire non potest, quin in sui nihilum redigatur, quod autem perire nequit, nisi per annihilationem immortale est ex sua natura. Dices: quum perit subjectum quod perficitur â forma, perit forma; sed anima est forma perficiens corpus: ergo pereunte corpore, anima perire debet. Dist. minorem: est forma corporis ita, ut sine illo existere queat naturâ sua, & operari, conc., ita ut ab illo cùm in existendo, tùm in operando intrinsecùs ac proindè necessariò dependeat, nego; & conseq.

110 Obj. 3, with Lucretius and the whole family of the ancient Epicureans: the rational soul is born with the body: therefore it must perish with the body, for everything that is generated is corrupted. I distinguish the antecedent: it is born with the body by generation, I deny the antecedent; by creation, I concede it. The body, therefore, perishes because it is destroyed by the mere dissolution of its parts: but the soul, as a simple substance, cannot perish without being reduced to its own nothing; and what cannot perish except by annihilation is immortal by its own nature. You will say: when the subject that is perfected by a form perishes, the form perishes; but the soul is the form perfecting the body: therefore when the body perishes the soul must perish. I distinguish the minor: it is the form of the body in such a way that it can exist and operate by its own nature without it, I concede; in such a way that it depends on it intrinsically, and therefore necessarily, both in existing and in operating, I deny; and the consequence.

111 Inst. Mens humana est pars hominis ideoque substantia

111 Inst. The human mind is a part of man, and therefore an incomplete substance:

Cap. 3. ℣. 19.

Ch. 3, v. 19.

Lib. 1. Dialog. Cap. 4.

Bk. 1 of the Dialogues, ch. 4.

Demonstrat. Evangelic. Op. 4.

Demonstratio Evangelica, Prop. 4.

Cap. 3. ℣. 21.

Ch. 3, v. 21.

p. 35

incompleta: ergo intrinsecùs dependet à corpore, ita ut ejus essentia sit ut actu conjungatur corpori. Dist. antec.: est substantia incompleta hoc est, est apta ad corpus informandum, & hominem unà cum corpore constituendum, conc., hoc est, est dimidia substantia, cui deest aliquid ad rationem sustantiae, nego; & conseq. Dices: mens humana non producitur nisi dependenter à corpore: ergo ab illo intrinsecùs pendet. Dist. antec. nisi dependenter â corpore tanquam ab occasione, conc., tanquam à subjecto in quo & per quod existat, nego, & conseq.

therefore it depends intrinsically on the body, so that its essence is to be actually joined to the body. I distinguish the antecedent: it is an incomplete substance, that is, it is apt to inform a body and to constitute a man together with the body, I concede; that is, it is half a substance, which lacks something of the notion of substance, I deny; and the consequence. You will say: the human mind is not produced except dependently on the body: therefore it depends on it intrinsically. I distinguish the antecedent: except dependently on the body as on an occasion, I concede; as on a subject in which and through which it exists, I deny; and the consequence.

112 Rotunditas cerae ex. gr. producitur dependenter à cera in qua recipitur, ideo pendet à cera, ut existat, ac pereunte cera, rotunditas perit: anima autem producitur tantum dependenter a corpore tanquam ab occasione, quatenùs scilicèt Deus determinat animam creare corpori conjungendam, nec propter solum corpus ipsam creat, sed propter semetipsum. Itaque anima non magis pendet à corpore, ut existat, quàm paries aliquis ab alio pariete praeexistente ad cujus occasionem construitur ut cum illo domum efficiat. Inst.: mens humana pendet à corpore, ut operetur: ego ut existat. Dist. antec: pendet tanquam ab occasione, hoc est, propter legem conjunctionis inter ipsam, & corpus, conc., pendet tanquam à principio suarum operationum, nego, & conseq.

112 The roundness of wax, e.g., is produced dependently on the wax in which it is received; hence it depends on the wax in order to exist, and when the wax perishes the roundness perishes: but the soul is produced dependently on the body only as on an occasion, inasmuch, namely, as God determines to create the soul to be joined to the body; nor does He create it on account of the body alone, but on account of itself. Thus the soul depends no more on the body in order to exist than some wall depends on another, pre-existing wall, on the occasion of which it is built so as to make a house together with it. Inst.: the human mind depends on the body in order to operate: therefore also in order to exist. I distinguish the antecedent: it depends on it as on an occasion, that is, on account of the law of union between itself and the body, I concede; it depends on it as on the principle of its operations, I deny; and the consequence.

113 Corpus non cogitat, non percipit, non vult, non sentit, non est ergo principium operationum animae, sed propter leges commercii, quod est inter illas substantias tam dispares, mens determinatur ad cogitandum ex occasione motuum qui fiunt in corpore. Inst. anima separata à corpore non potest ullas sensationes habere: ergo dependet à corpore ut existat. Dist. antec.: si per sensationem intelligas perceptionem alicujus impraessionis factae in corpus, conc., si intelligas interiorem adfectionem animae, qualis ipsae advenire solet ex occasione corporis, nego, & conseq. Anima separata à corpore iisdem perceptionibus immediatè adfici potest Deo volente, quibus adficitur mediante corpore dum illi est unita.

113 The body does not think, does not perceive, does not will, does not sense; it is not, therefore, the principle of the soul’s operations; but on account of the laws of the commerce that exists between those substances so unlike each other, the mind is determined to think on the occasion of the motions that take place in the body. Inst. The soul separated from the body cannot have any sensations: therefore it depends on the body in order to exist. I distinguish the antecedent: if by sensation you understand the perception of some impression made in the body, I concede; if you understand the interior affection of the soul, such as usually comes to it on the occasion of the body, I deny; and the consequence. The soul separated from the body can, if God wills, be immediately affected by the same perceptions by which it is affected by means of the body while it is united to it.

114 Opp. 4: mens humana obnoxia est innumeris mutationibus, quum sit capax diversarum operationum: ergo naturaliter interire debet. Dist. antec.: obnoxia est mutationibus accidentalibus, semper tamen retinens totam suam essentiam, conc., mutationibus substantialibus, nego, & conseq. Praeterea modificationes oppositae, ut sunt amor, & odium, volitiones, & nolitiones sibi succedunt in eadem anima, sed sine ulla divisione, & separatione partium in subjecto, quod non evenit in modificationibus corporis: igitur diversae, & oppositae modificationes, quae possunt materiam mutare, & perimere, idem non possunt in substantiam spiritualem, & simplicem qualis est anima.

114 Obj. 4: the human mind is subject to innumerable changes, since it is capable of diverse operations: therefore it must naturally perish. I distinguish the antecedent: it is subject to accidental changes, while always retaining its whole essence, I concede; to substantial changes, I deny; and the consequence. Moreover, opposite modifications, such as love and hatred, volitions and nolitions, succeed one another in the same soul, but without any division or separation of parts in the subject, which does not happen in the modifications of the body: therefore diverse and opposite modifications, which can change and destroy matter, cannot do the same to a spiritual and simple substance such as the soul is.

115 Opp. 5. anima non est immortalis, quia est substantia, quum plures substantiae pereant, sed neque quia spiritualis est, quum gratia, & habitus ipsius animae sint spirituales, & tamen pereant:

115 Obj. 5. The soul is not immortal because it is a substance, since many substances perish; nor yet because it is spiritual, since grace and the habits of the soul itself are spiritual, and yet they perish:

p. 36

ergo nullo jure defenditur immortalis. Respondeo: animam esse immortalem non praecisse quia est substantia, sed quia est talis substantia, simplex nimirum, & cogitans. Quia enim est substantia simplex carens partibus, per actionem creati agentis perire non potest, quia est substantia cogitans; illius est naturae, ut operari, ac proinde vivere etiam sejuncta á corpore possit. Quae vero dependent à dispositione subjecti, ut accidentia spiritualia ex. gr. habitus corrumpi possunt quia educuntur ex subjecto disposito, & ab eo dependent tùm in fieri, tùm in conservari, unde sublatis subjecti dispositionibus, pereunt: at vero anima rationalis non educitur ex corpore, neque ab eo dependet in fieri & conservari. Dices: quod habet initium, habet finem, sed anima habet initium: ergo & finem. Dist. antec, quod habet initium per generationem transeat, per creationem, nego, & conseq.

therefore it is maintained with no right to be immortal. I reply that the soul is immortal not precisely because it is a substance, but because it is such a substance, namely simple and thinking. For because it is a simple substance lacking parts, it cannot perish by the action of a created agent; because it is a thinking substance, it is of such a nature that it can operate, and hence also live, separated from the body. But the things that depend on the disposition of the subject, as spiritual accidents, e.g. habits, can be corrupted, because they are educed from a disposed subject and depend on it both in coming to be and in being conserved; whence, when the dispositions of the subject are removed, they perish: but the rational soul is not educed from the body, nor does it depend on it in coming to be and in being conserved. You will say: what has a beginning has an end; but the soul has a beginning: therefore also an end. I distinguish the antecedent: what has a beginning by generation, let it pass; by creation, I deny; and the consequence.

116 Opp. 6: Anima separata à corpore esset in statu violento: ergo naturaliter non potest existere á corpore separata: ergo perire debet. Resp. 1: permisso antec, nego conseq. quae non infertur nam animae damnatorum quae simplices substantiae sunt, etiamsi in statu violento versentur, non tamen ideò pereunt, sed dolori suo in perpetuum vivunt. Resp. 2: negando antec: siquidem propensio quam habet anima ad corpus, non ita eam solicitat, quin facillimè carere possit corporis praesentiâ. Et certè animae beatae, & intimè cum Deo conjunctae minimè sunt in statu violento, qui earum obstaret faelicitati.

116 Obj. 6: The soul separated from the body would be in a violent state: therefore it cannot naturally exist separated from the body: therefore it must perish. Reply 1: granting the antecedent, I deny the consequence, which does not follow; for the souls of the damned, which are simple substances, even though they are in a violent state, do not on that account perish, but live forever for their pain. Reply 2: by denying the antecedent: since the propensity which the soul has toward the body does not so solicit it that it cannot most easily do without the presence of the body. And certainly the blessed souls, intimately joined with God, are by no means in a violent state, which would stand in the way of their happiness.

117 Opp. 7: inter homines atque bruta maximam similitudinem esse, experientiâ novimus; sed brutis non convenit immortalitas: ergo. Dist. antec, quoad ea, quae sensus adficere possunt, conc, quoad ea per quae animae nostrae immortalitatem probavimus, nego. Mirum non est, si bruta quoad ea quae sensus adficere possunt, hominibus quodammodo adsimilari videantur; nam quum animalem naturam cum nobis communem habeant, iis rebus oportet, ut adficiantur, quae animalem naturam adficiunt; nunquam tamen negare possunt Materialistae, talem in solis hominibus addiscendi capacitatem esse, ut tùm metaphysica, tum moralia principia, vel sublimiora nosse possint. Maximum ergo discrimen inter homines atque bruta interesse, semper constat, unde non una utrorumque conditio esse potest.

117 Obj. 7: we know by experience that there is the greatest similarity between men and brutes; but immortality does not belong to brutes: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: as regards the things that can affect the senses, I concede; as regards those through which we have proved the immortality of our soul, I deny. It is no wonder if brutes, as regards the things that can affect the senses, seem in some way to resemble men: for since they have an animal nature in common with us, they must be affected by the things that affect animal nature: yet the Materialists can never deny that in men alone there is such a capacity for learning that they can know both metaphysical and moral principles, or more sublime ones. It is always evident, therefore, that there is the greatest difference between men and brutes, whence the condition of both cannot be one and the same.

118 Adhaec. Plures inlustres Theologi & Physici s1

118 Moreover, many illustrious Theologians and Physicists (t) maintain

p. 37

dunt Brutorum animas esse principium activum immateriale, sive spiritum, id est, non esse corpus ejusdem rationis ac corpora omnia quae ministerio sensuum cognoscimus. Persuasum namque illis est, conditum esse substantiae spiritualis genus quoddam, quae sensationis quidem, & perceptionis simplicis capax sit, aliis tamen facultatibus, quibus mens humana pollet instructa non sit, viribus naturae, atque à nulla causa creata destrui queat, in nihilium; ab eo duntaxat, qui condidit, tum agenda, ubi organico jam corpore ad vitae functiones haud idoneo, illa suo sentiendi munere, veluti defuncta fuerit. Quae quidem uti digna sunt, quae pluribus disceptentur; ita sermonem nostrum, explicationem reposcerent.

that the souls of brutes are an immaterial active principle, or spirit, that is, not a body of the same nature as all the bodies we know through the ministry of the senses. For they are persuaded that there has been created a certain kind of spiritual substance which is capable indeed of sensation and of simple perception, yet is not furnished with the other faculties in which the human mind is strong; which cannot be destroyed by the forces of nature, nor by any created cause, but is to be reduced to nothing only by Him who created it, when, the organic body being no longer fit for the functions of life, it shall have, as it were, discharged its office of sensing. These things indeed, as they deserve to be discussed at greater length, so would they call for a discourse and an explanation of their own.

119 Ad rem vero quod adtinet dico, quod etsi hoc Systema admittatur, nullum argumentum ex eo deducitur ad evertendam animae rationalis immortalitatem. Ex eo namque quod in illo Systemate brutorum anima his facultatibus praedita non est, quibus ornatur anima humana. hoc est, eo quod non ideas abstractas, sed sensationes tantùm percipere potest, sequitur in illa, nec libertatem esse, nec meritum, nec crimen, neque summum Bonum cognoscendi facultatem, & eo fruendi, in quo alterius vitae felicitas consistit. Quapropter, argumenta quae nobis persuadent animam humanam à corpore secretam in aeternum esse duraturam, animae brutorum, etiamsi spiritualis esse diceretur non sufragantur. Haec enim, quum ad finem pervenerit suum, qui est, ut corpus animet, ab eo qui eam condidit in nihilum revertetur.

119 But as for the matter at hand, I say that even if this System is admitted, no argument is deduced from it for overthrowing the immortality of the rational soul. For from the fact that in that System the soul of brutes is not endowed with the faculties with which the human soul is adorned, that is, from the fact that it cannot perceive abstract ideas but only sensations, it follows that in it there is neither liberty, nor merit, nor crime, nor the faculty of knowing the Supreme Good and of enjoying it, in which the happiness of the other life consists. Wherefore the arguments which persuade us that the human soul, separated from the body, is to endure forever do not support the soul of brutes, even if it were said to be spiritual. For this soul, when it has reached its end, which is to animate the body, will return to nothing by the act of Him who created it.

120 Opp. 8: Iisdem rebus aequè anima adficitur ac corpus: ergo est ejusdem naturae cum corpore: ergo sicut moritur corpus ita, & anima: Secundò: corpus in animam agit: ergo sunt ejusdem naturae, quia nulla res nisi corporea tangi potest à corpore. Haec sunt praecipua argumenta Lucretii quibus frustra conatur ostendere animum nostrum cum corpore perire. Sed ne videar totam quam habent vim illis detrahere, Eminentissimum Cardinalem Melchiorem de Polignac s1 audiamus illa proponentem, & doctissimè refutantem.

120 Obj. 8: The soul is affected by the same things equally with the body: therefore it is of the same nature as the body: therefore, just as the body dies, so too does the soul. Secondly: the body acts on the soul: therefore they are of the same nature, because nothing but a corporeal thing can be touched by a body. These are the principal arguments of Lucretius, by which he vainly tries to show that our mind perishes with the body. But lest I seem to take away from them all the force they have, let us hear the Most Eminent Cardinal Melchior de Polignac (u) proposing them and most learnedly refuting them.

Forsitam oppones, in nobis, foedere tanto,

Perhaps you will object that in us, by so close a bond,

Et mentem, et corpus jungi, ut non possit utrumque

Both mind and body are joined, that the two cannot

Discerni; proprio nimirùm edoctus ab usu

Be told apart; taught, namely, by our own experience

Nihil nisi per sensus ad mentem accedere nostram:

That nothing reaches our mind except through the senses:

Quos ubi sopivit somnus, vel fervida febris

And when sleep has lulled them, or a burning fever

Invertit, turbari animum, atque errare vagantem;

Overturned them, the mind is troubled and strays wandering;

Saepè etiam attonitum subito procumbere morbo.

Often, too, stunned by a sudden disease, it falls prostrate.

Anti-Lucret. Lib. V. à ℣. 712.
