p. 38

Insuper orbatos homines ratione videri,

Moreover, that men are seen bereft of reason,

Vel capite offenso, vel sic à matre creatos,

Either from a hurt to the head, or born so from the mother,

Omnis eos ut deficiat prudentia mentis,

So that all wisdom of mind fails them,

Partibus in cérebri certus quia deficit ordo.

Because the settled order fails in the parts of the brain.

Imò ad naturam depressos usque ferinam

Nay, sunk even to the nature of a beast,

Ut cum improviso morsu per sanguinis alveos

As when, through an unforeseen bite, along the channels of the blood

Tetra canum rabies hominem pervasit, & imis

The foul madness of dogs has invaded a man, and in his inmost

Visceribus, medioque infixit corde venenum;

Bowels, and in the midst of his heart, has fixed its venom;

Quid cane distat homo? Furor ambos abripit unus,

How does the man differ from the dog? One fury carries both away,

Mordendique fames, eademque insania vexat.

And a hunger for biting, and the same insanity torments them.

Verùm haec omnia, ut sapientissimè prosequitur Auctor Eminentissimus.

But all these things, as the Most Eminent Author most wisely continues,

Ostendunt unà mentem cum corpore jungi.

Show that the mind is joined together with the body.

Quis neget? Ast unam mentisque & corporis esse

Who would deny it? But that the nature of mind and of body

Naturam, non significant. Ita quilibet arte

Is one, they do not signify. Thus anyone skilled

Strenuus Aonia citharam pulsare sonantem

In the Aonian art of striking the sounding lyre

Mobilibus digitis, chordasque animare loquaces,

With nimble fingers, and of quickening the speaking strings,

Et lenocinio blandi modulaminis aures

And with the allurement of a sweet melody

Demulcere tuas, citharâ sic pendet ab ipsa,

Of soothing your ears, so depends on the lyre itself

Non ullos, ut possit ea sine promere cantus.

That without it he can bring forth no songs at all.

Nam si rupta silet, si qua temerata ruina est,

For if, broken, it is silent, if it is impaired by some damage,

Si chordae nimiùm tensae, nimiùmve remissae

If the strings, stretched too tight or let too slack,

Amisére tonum, vel si una aut altera desit;

Have lost their tone, or if one or another is missing;

Si caveam implerunt sordes, hebetantque sonorem;

If dirt has filled the hollow and dulls the sound;

Ecce manet citharoedus iners, frustraque peritus

Behold, the lyre player remains idle, and, skilled in vain,

Aut nihil, aut pravum canit, et nescire videtur.

Sings either nothing or badly, and seems not to know how.

Ergo artem museam ipsâ in testudine pones?

Will you then place the art of music in the lyre itself?

Ac tibi proptérea res una putabitur esse

And will you on that account think that one thing

Organum & organicus? Talis fit copula porrò

Are instrument and player? Such, further, is the bond

Corporis ac mentis: nisi quod déponere non quit

Of body and mind: except that the mind cannot lay aside

Adjunctum sibi mens, nec sponte resumere corpus.

The body joined to it, nor take it up again at will.

At dum vita manet nobis, haec semper eidem

But while life remains to us, it will always be joined

Cui sociata semel sociabitur instrumento.

To the same instrument with which it was once joined.

Cetera consimili penitùs ratione geruntur.

All else is managed in a wholly similar way.

Nam veluti quaedam citharae sunt propria, quae non

For just as certain things are proper to the lyre, which do not

p. 39

Organicum spectant, ut concamerata tabellis

Concern the player, as the hollow, vaulted with thin boards

Per commisuras laterum specus, unde sonando

Through the joinings of its sides, whence in sounding

Fit fremitus levis, & responsat textilis Echo;

A light murmur arises, and the woven Echo answers;

Nervorum pariter situs, & mensura frequentes

Likewise the position and the measure of the strings, frequent

Aut raros, celeres, aut tardos, tempore eodem

Or rare, swift or slow, in the same time,

Subsultus referunt, ex quo sonus exit acutus,

Give back their quiverings, from which the sound comes out high

Aut gravis. Haec cantor non efficit, utitur illis.

Or low. These the singer does not make; he uses them.

Nec non ipse quidem tenet in se multa vicissim,

And he himself in turn holds many things within himself,

Quorum ut sit compos citharâ non indiget ullâ,

To possess which he needs no lyre at all:

Nimirum est in eo modulandi parta facultas,

Namely, the acquired faculty of making melody is in him,

Atque omnis ratio harmoniae: nam cuncta per artem

And the whole theory of harmony: for by art he knows all things,

Et quae consona sunt, & quae sunt disona novit:

Both those that are consonant and those that are dissonant:

Et nihil à citharae nervis prodivit amoeni,

And nothing pleasing has come forth from the strings of the lyre

Quod non per digitos transmissum emanet ab ipso.

That does not flow from him, transmitted through his fingers.

Atque ita suave melos pariter debetur utrique:

And so the sweet melody is owed equally to both:

Et citharae quod det sonitus, quicumque cientur;

To the lyre, because it gives the sounds, whatever are stirred;

Et modulatori praesertim; quod sciat illos

And to the player above all, because he knows how to draw them

Elicere, ac mutis animam velut indere chordis.

Forth, and, as it were, to put a soul into the mute strings.

Haud secus in nobis addictam foedere certo

Not otherwise in us, the mass bound to it by a fixed compact

Mens agitat molem, et moles respondet agenti.

The mind moves, and the mass answers to its mover.

121 Ad secundum dico: quod tangere, & tangi contactu quantitatis nisi corpus nulla potest res; potest verò contactu virtutis. Solutio est D. Thomae. Atque haec dicta sufficiant.

121 To the second I say: that nothing but a body can touch and be touched by contact of quantity; but it can by contact of power. The solution is St. Thomas’s. And let what has been said suffice.

p. 40

DISSERTATIO II. — DISSERTATION II

De Commercio mentem inter & corpus. — On the Commerce between Mind and Body.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

Exponuntur celebriores Philosophorum sententiae.

The more celebrated opinions of the Philosophers are set forth.

122 Commercium mentis cum corpore dicitur mirabilis ille consensus, quem habent certae operationes mentis cum certis quibusdam motibus corporis, & vicissim certi motus corporis cum certis adfectionibus mentis, ratione cujus, modò mens corporis, modò corpus mentis veluti interpres existit. Duae sunt leges praecipuae, quibus mutuum hoc mentis cum corpore commercium continetur. Prima: si res extra nos constitutae in organa sensoria impressiones efficiant, earumdem, tum rerum notio in mente excitatur. Secunda: mens nostra ita corpori dominatur, ut si quaedam ipsius corporis partes moveantur, ad illius nutum tandiu perseverent in motu quandiu ipsa vult; atque á motu cessent, quám primum eidem placet, quod utrumque manifestâ proculdubio experientiâ docemur. Tria systemata excogitata sunt ad hunc commercium explicandum, scilicèt systema Influxus, Causarum occasionalium, & Harmoniae praestabilitae.

he commerce of the mind with the body is the name given to that won122 T derful consent which certain operations of the mind have with certain motions of the body, and in turn certain motions of the body with certain affections of the mind, by reason of which now the mind is, as it were, the interpreter of the body, now the body of the mind. There are two principal laws by which this mutual commerce of the mind with the body is maintained. The first: if things placed outside us make impressions on the sense organs, then the notion of those things is excited in the mind. The second: our mind so dominates the body that, if certain parts of the body itself are moved, they persevere in motion at its nod as long as it wills, and cease from motion as soon as it pleases it; both of which we are without doubt taught by manifest experience. Three systems have been devised to explain this commerce, namely the system of Influx, of Occasional Causes, and of Pre-established Harmony.

123 Systema influxus physici, situm est in verâ, ac mutuâ efficientiâ, quae animae adversus corpus, & huic adversus animam adtribuitur. Peripatetici nimirum, hujus systematis defensores docent, naturas has (animam scilicèt, & corpus) plurimùm dissimiles, ita sibi esse adstrictas, ut altera in alteram verè, atque efficienter influat; neque tamen ea actione ex una in alteram quidquam transferri; sed impraessis in sensu motionibus, & nervorum ope ad cerebrum usque propagatis, mentem ad informandas rerum notiones determinari, & vicissim suborta in animo voluntate membri cujuspiam commovendi, nervos continuò impelli, motusque in eo membro voluntarios consequi.

123 The system of physical influx consists in a true and mutual efficiency, which is attributed to the soul with respect to the body and to the body with respect to the soul. The Peripatetics, namely, the defenders of this system, teach that these natures (the soul, namely, and the body), most unlike as they are, are so bound to each other that the one truly and efficiently flows into the other; and yet that by this action nothing is transferred from the one into the other; but that, when motions are impressed on the sense and propagated by means of the nerves as far as the brain, the mind is determined to form the notions of things; and in turn, when a will to move some limb has arisen in the mind, the nerves are at once impelled, and voluntary motions follow in that limb.

114 [?] Quare opinantur hi Philosophi, saepè in humano corpore inchoari motus, qui causam in corpore ipso antecedentem non

114 Wherefore these Philosophers think that motions often begin in the human body which have no antecedent cause in the body itself,

p. 41

beat, sed ex animi adpetitu, & movendi facultate progignatur; saepè item ad mentis arbitrium motiones in membris extingui nullo in natura corporea motu consequente.

but are produced from the appetite of the mind and its faculty of moving; and likewise that motions in the limbs are often extinguished at the mind’s will, without any motion following in the corporeal nature.

125 Cartesiani cum P. Malebranchio systematis causarum occasionalium defensores, adserunt, mentem in corpus nullomodo agere, verùm ex occasione cogitationum animae, á Deo corpus moveri, quemadmodum ex occasione motionum corporis, mentem idem ille modificat. Volo globum projicere, Deus extendit brachium meum, manum globo adplicat, digitos claudit, ut globum adprehendam &c. Eodem modo ubi corpora extranea in nervos agunt, Deus perceptionum inde oriendarum immediatus auctor est. Dum manus globo adplicatur, non globum sentio, sed Deus mihi dat perceptionem ipsius contactus.

125 The Cartesians, with Fr. Malebranche, defenders of the system of occasional causes, assert that the mind in no way acts on the body, but that on the occasion of the thoughts of the soul the body is moved by God, just as on the occasion of the motions of the body that same God modifies the mind. I wish to throw a ball: God extends my arm, applies my hand to the ball, closes my fingers so that I may grasp the ball, etc. In the same way, when external bodies act on the nerves, God is the immediate author of the perceptions that are to arise therefrom. While my hand is applied to the ball, I do not sense the ball, but God gives me the perception of the contact itself.

126 Aër percutit tympanum auris, sonum ego percipio, sed sensatio haec non ab aëris agitatione, & inde secuto nervi motu, propriè pendet, sed Deus perceptionem hanc immediatè menti imprimit. En systema causarum occasionalium perspicuè dilucidèque à Cl. SGravessande 2 explicatum. Unde adparet in hoc systemate animam destitui vi activa, quâ motus in corpore producitur, & tantummodo per suas volitiones, occasiones praebere Deo hos motus producendi: similiter corpus per motus occasionem Deo praebet producendi has in anima ideas.

126 The air strikes the tympanum of the ear, I perceive a sound; but this sensation does not properly depend on the agitation of the air and on the motion of the nerve that follows from it, but God immediately impresses this perception on the mind. There you have the system of occasional causes, clearly and lucidly explained by the celebrated ’s Gravesande (x). Whence it appears that in this system the soul is deprived of the active force by which motion is produced in the body, and only through its volitions provides God with occasions of producing these motions: similarly the body, through its motions, provides God with the occasion of producing these ideas in the soul.

127 Leibnitzius novum systema protulit à Wolfio plurimum illustratum, quod harmonia praestabilita s2 vulgò adpellatur. In hoc systemate anima statuitur illius naturae „ ut vi propria (verba sunt Wolffi s3) „ omnes perceptiones & adpetitiones continua serie independenter ab omni principio externo producat, & praesentia idearum materialium in cerebro, nihil prorsus ad eas producendas conferat, adeò ut perceptiones, & adpetitiones in anima eodem modo, quo nunc, consequerentur etiamsi corpus non existeret. Deinde corpus organicum ponitur machina eo modo conformata, ut vi mechanismi ex impressionibus sensibilium nascantur motus volitionibus, & adpetitionibus animae respondentes citra ullam determinationem extrinsecam immediatam ab anima pendentem, qui eodem quo nunc modo consequerentur etiam si anima non existeret.

127 Leibniz put forward a new system, much illustrated by Wolff, which is commonly called pre-established harmony (y). In this system the soul is laid down to be of such a nature that by its own force (the words are Wolff’s (z)) “it produces all its perceptions and appetitions in a continuous series, independently of every external principle, and the presence of material ideas in the brain contributes absolutely nothing to producing them, so that the perceptions and appetitions in the soul would follow in the same way as now even if the body did not exist. Next, the organic body is laid down to be a machine so formed that by the force of mechanism, from the impressions of sensible things, motions arise corresponding to the volitions and appetitions of the soul, without any immediate extrinsic determination depending on the soul; and these would follow in the same way as now even if the soul did not exist.

Introduct. ad Philosoph. n. 230, & seq.

Introductio ad Philosophiam, no. 230 ff.

Leibnitzius in quadam Epist. ad Psaffium data, ait, se harmoniam praestabilitatam veluti fabulam philosophicam jocandi causâ excogitasse. Verùm tam seriò, tamque vehementer postea pro ea pugnavit, ut suspicionem ingerat lectori eum ex animi sententiâ id judicasse, & saltim ex consuetudine eam legendi, & tractandi, nubem pro Junone fuisse amplexatum. Act. Erudict. Lips. 1728.

Leibniz, in a certain letter written to Pfaff, says that he devised the pre-established harmony as a kind of philosophical fable, for the sake of jesting. But afterwards he fought for it so seriously and so vehemently that he suggests to the reader the suspicion that he judged it so in earnest, and that at least, from the habit of reading and handling it, he embraced a cloud in place of Juno. Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensia, 1728.

Psychol. Rat. Sect. 3. cap. 4. & in Ephemerid. Paris. 1695.

Psychologia Rationalis, sect. 3, ch. 4; and in the Paris Ephemerides, 1695.

p. 42

128 „ Quare duo haec automata (pergit Wolffius) „ spirituale alterum, alterum materiale ea lege junguntur, ut singuli motus qui mechanismi efficientia fiunt in corpore, consentiant singulis perceptionibus atque adpetitionibus, & aversionibus animae eodem prorsus ordine sese invicem consequentes, quo animae modificationes sese invicem excipiunt.

128 “Wherefore these two automata (Wolff continues), the one spiritual, the other material, are joined by this law, that the single motions which take place in the body by the efficiency of mechanism agree with the single perceptions, appetitions and aversions of the soul, following one another in exactly the same order in which the modifications of the soul succeed one another.

129 „ Nempè Deus harmoniam praestabilivit, quatenus animae junxit corpus, in quo existere potest series motuum perceptionibus, & adpetitionibus animae consentientium, & eum fecit rerum materialium nexum, ut motus isti ad actum producantur per continuas in organa sensoria impressiones extrinsecùs factas „. Hactenùs Wolffius. Concipite ergo mentem, & corpus, quae conveniant inter se ita, ut hujus motus cum perceptionibus, & determinationibus illius respondeant, & habebitis integrum harmoniae praestabilitae Systema.

129 “That is, God pre-established the harmony inasmuch as He joined to the soul a body in which there can exist a series of motions agreeing with the perceptions and appetitions of the soul, and made such a connection of material things that those motions are brought into act through continuous impressions made from without on the sense organs.” Thus far Wolff. Conceive, then, a mind and a body which agree with each other in such a way that the motions of the latter correspond with the perceptions and determinations of the former, and you will have the whole System of pre-established harmony.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

Exploditur causarum occasionalium Systema, & harmoniae praestabilitae.

The System of occasional causes, and that of pre-established harmony, is exploded.

130 Dico 1: Sustineri non potest causarum occasionalium systema quia gravissimis difficultatibus est implicatum. Nam primò: vel omnes omninò animi adfectiones à Deo efficerentur, vel aliquae duntaxat? Si omnes, nulla in nobis erit libertas, imò nec anima, ¿unde enim eam esse demontrabimus? Si aliquas, cur aliquas? Cur non omnes? An plus requiritur efficacitatis ad efficiendas has, quam illas? Cur non internoscit anima eas, quas ipsa vi sua progignit, ab illis, quas in ea Deus imprimit? Cur eundem planèque similem de omnibus sensum habet?

say 1: The system of occasional causes cannot be maintained, because 130 I it is entangled in the gravest difficulties. For, first: would absolutely all the affections of the mind be effected by God, or only some? If all, there will be no liberty in us, nay, not even a soul; for whence shall we demonstrate that it exists? If some, why some? Why not all? Is more efficacy required to effect these than those? Why does the soul not distinguish those which it produces by its own force from those which God impresses on it? Why does it have the same and entirely similar sense of them all?

131 Secundò: hoc admisso systemate omnes animi, corporisque motus habendi erunt in miraculis ut quorum effectrix causa naturae universitate nequaquam contineatur. Neque eos é prodigiorum censu eximas propterea quod anima & corpus iis efficiendis occasionem suppeditent: nam & Lazari in vitam revocationi occasionem preces Sororum praebuere; ¿an iccirco minus habenda est prodigiosa?

131 Secondly: if this system is admitted, all the motions of the mind and of the body will have to be held as miracles, since their effecting cause is in no way contained in the whole of nature. Nor would you exempt them from the class of prodigies because the soul and the body supply the occasion for effecting them; for the prayers of his Sisters also furnished the occasion for the recalling of Lazarus to life: is it on that account to be held less prodigious?

132 Dico 2: Leibnitzianum systema nodos habet inexplicabiles, nec á Viro Catholico propugnari potest. Et primò: si mens humana ad rerum notiones sucesivè producendas per suam naturam determinata est, eas in semet necessariò producit, ita ut illarum

132 I say 2: The Leibnizian system has inexplicable knots, nor can it be defended by a Catholic Man. And first: if the human mind is determined by its nature to produce the notions of things successively, it produces them in itself necessarily, so that their production

p. 43

effectio impediri à nobis neutiquam possit; quo posito destruitur animus omni libertate in suas perceptiones. Pari modo si vi solius mechanismi motus corporis peraguntur, hi intrinsecùs necessarii sunt, atque adeò sic consequuntur, ut nullus eorum impediri à nobis queat, perinde ac motiones cordis, quae imperio mentis non subduntur. Nulla ergo actio hominem dignum reddet, qui illius causâ vel commendetur, vel reprehendatur.

can in no way be hindered by us; and, this being posited, the mind is stripped of all liberty over its perceptions. In like manner, if the motions of the body are carried out by the force of mechanism alone, they are intrinsically necessary, and so follow in such a way that none of them can be hindered by us, just like the motions of the heart, which are not subject to the command of the mind. No action, therefore, will render a man worthy of being either commended or blamed on its account.

133 Quid? Quod harmoniae praestabilitae systema apertam ad inhonestè vivendum sternat viam, siquidem in eo cura sensuum externorum ad cogitationes honestas in mente fovendas, turpesque repellendas nihil prorsus confert? Praeterea Scripturae Sacrae, & Sanctis Patribus contrarium apertè est dicere, (ut dicunt Harmonistae) mutationes quae ex rerum sensibilium adpulsu in organis sensoriis fiunt, ad perceptiones, adpetitionesque excitandas in anima nihil prorsus conferre, quum Scriptura, & SS. Patres doceant impediri posse, ne humana mens cognoscat res sensibiles, atque hinc ne in illas desiderio inordinato feratur, si externi sensus ita custodiantur, ut à rebus ipsis immutari nequaquam possint.

133 What of the fact that the system of pre-established harmony lays open a road to living dishonorably, since in it the care of the external senses contributes absolutely nothing to fostering honorable thoughts in the mind and repelling base ones? Moreover, it is plainly contrary to Sacred Scripture and to the Holy Fathers to say (as the Harmonists say) that the changes which take place in the sense organs from the impact of sensible things contribute absolutely nothing to exciting perceptions and appetitions in the soul, since Scripture and the Holy Fathers teach that it can be prevented that the human mind should know sensible things, and hence that it should be borne toward them by inordinate desire, if the external senses are so guarded that they can in no way be altered by the things themselves.

134 Etenim primò: Pepigi, (inquit Job 2 foedus cum oculis meis, ut ne cogitarem quidem de Virgine. Jeremias ait: ascendit mors per fenestras nostras. „ Mors quippè (exponit S. Gregorius s2) per fenestras ascendit, & domum ingreditur, quum per sensus corporis concupiscentia veniens, habitaculum intrat mentis. „ Secundò: docet Scriptura s3 avertendam esse faciem à muliere comptâ, & minimè circumspiciendam speciem alienam, quia scilicet propter speciem mulieris multi perierunt, & ex hoc, concupiscentia quasi ignis exardescit, quatenus nempe visionem comptae mulieris consequuntur in anima inhonestae cogitationes, concupiscentia per eam accenditur, & turpia desideria excitantur.

134 For, first: I made a covenant (says Job (a)) with my eyes, that I would not so much as think upon a virgin. Jeremiah says: death is come up through our windows. “For death (St. Gregory (b) explains) comes up through the windows and enters the house when concupiscence, coming through the senses of the body, enters the dwelling of the mind.” Secondly: Scripture (c) teaches that the face is to be turned away from a woman dressed up, and that one should by no means gaze about upon another’s beauty, because, namely, many have perished by the beauty of a woman, and hereby lust is enkindled as a fire; inasmuch, that is, as dishonorable thoughts follow in the soul upon the sight of an adorned woman, concupiscence is kindled by it, and base desires are excited.

135 Ad haec: admiti nequit praestabilitae harmoniae systema, quin macerationes carnis, tanquam ad eam spiritui subigendam planè innutiles rejicere cogamur, ridendaquè erunt omnia quae de poenitentia, cùm ex Divina Scriptura, tùm ex SS Patribus Catholica tradit Ecclesia, nam in hoc systemate eadem iniqua desideria habitura est mens nostra illis macerationibus positis, ac haberet, si caro tot cruciatibus minimè aflictaretur: frustra ergo cum Apostolo s4 clamaret Ecclesia: „ mortificate membra vestra, quae sunt super terram, fornicationem, immuditiam, libidinem, concupiscentiam malam, & avaritiam „. Nullus quippè eorum motuum ad quos corpus nostrum per suam structuram jam determinatum est, impediri â nobis potest admisso Harmonistarum

135 Besides: the system of pre-established harmony cannot be admitted without our being compelled to reject mortifications of the flesh as altogether useless for subjecting it to the spirit; and all that the Catholic Church hands down concerning penance, both from Divine Scripture and from the Holy Fathers, will be laughable; for in this system our mind will have the same wicked desires when those mortifications are applied as it would have if the flesh were in no way afflicted by so many torments: in vain, therefore, would the Church cry out with the Apostle (d): “mortify your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil concupiscence, and covetousness.” For none of those motions to which our body is already determined by its structure can be hindered by us, once the system of the Harmonists is admitted.

Cap. 31. ℣. 1.

Ch. 31, v. 1.

Lib. 21. Moral. cap. 2.

Bk. 21 of the Morals, ch. 2.

Eccles. cap. 9. ℣. 8.

Eccles., ch. 9, v. 8.

p. 44

systemate. Fatalismo etiam favet. Sunt enim Fatalistae, qui omnia quae in mundo contingunt ne ipsis quidem exceptis humanis actionibus, inimpedibili necessitati subjiciunt.

It also favors Fatalism. For the Fatalists are those who subject all things that happen in the world, not even excepting human actions themselves, to an unimpedable necessity.

136 Ex his quae hactenùs dicta sunt ad evidentiam usque mihi probatum videtur omninò rejiciendum esse systema Leibnitzianum. Nec praeterire possum aliam difficultatem utrique systemati communem. Etenim Cartesiana, & Leibnitziana hypothesis omnem de corporum existentia philosophicam certitudinem evertunt. Deus enim in hypothesi causarum occasionalium, non corpus in anima nostra sensationes produceret: in Leibnitzi opinione anima per naturam suam, nullo existente corpore easdem sensationes haberet, quas nunc experitur. Ex his igitur hypothesibus aperta est via ad Idealismum, quo omnis materiae tanquam inutilis existentia negatur, & certè plures in hunc errorem prolapsi sunt, atque etiam in alium absurdiorem quem Egoismum vocant, delirantes scilicet, propriam duntaxat sui ipsius existentiam certò cognitam esse.

136 From what has been said thus far, it seems to me proved to the point of evidence that the Leibnizian system is to be altogether rejected. Nor can I pass over another difficulty common to both systems. For the Cartesian and the Leibnizian hypotheses overturn all philosophical certainty about the existence of bodies. For in the hypothesis of occasional causes God, not the body, would produce the sensations in our soul: in Leibniz’s opinion the soul, by its own nature, would have the same sensations it now experiences even if no body existed. From these hypotheses, therefore, the way lies open to Idealism, by which the existence of all matter is denied as useless; and certainly many have fallen into this error, and also into another, more absurd one, which they call Egoism, raving, namely, that only one’s own existence is known with certainty.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

Sententia Peripateticorum, ut verosimilior amplectitur rejectis Recentiorum opinionibus.

The opinion of the Peripatetics is embraced as the more probable, the opinions of the Moderns being rejected.

137 Qui Philosophorum nomine gloriantur, inquirendae veritatis desiderio accensi ita esse debent, ut nullae Sectae addicti, non Aristotelem, non Platonem, non Leibnitzium, aut Newtonum, sed veritatem sequentes, nullius debeant jurare in verba magistri. Nos igitur qui Philosophiam Eclecticam profitemur omni partium amore sublato, nec Philosophos antiquos impugnamus quia Veteres nec Recentiores laudamus quia Recentiores sunt, sed eo precissè quod juxta ingenioli nostri tenuitatem palmam antiquis in multis praeripere videntur, ut pluribus in locis probavimus, & magno rationum pondere in Physica etiam ostendemus. Ceterùm amor quo Recentiores amplectimur, non adeò nos abripit, ut illorum placita nullo discrimine posito exosculemur, quin potius ab eorum sententia libentissimè recedimus quum veritati contraria nobis videtur, quod in hac gravissima quaestione manifestum facimus, in qua rejectis Recentiorum opinionibus, veterum Peripateticorum sententiam amplectimur. Sit ergo conclusio nostra.

hose who glory in the name of Philosophers ought to be so inflamed 137 T with the desire of seeking out the truth that, addicted to no Sect, following not Aristotle, not Plato, not Leibniz or Newton, but the truth, they should swear by the words of no master. We, therefore, who profess the Eclectic Philosophy, setting aside all love of parties, neither attack the ancient Philosophers because they are Ancients, nor praise the Moderns because they are Moderns, but precisely because, according to the slenderness of our small talent, they seem to snatch the palm from the ancients in many things, as we have proved in several places, and shall show also in the Physics with great weight of reasons. But the love with which we embrace the Moderns does not so carry us away that we kiss their tenets without making any distinction; rather, we most willingly depart from their opinion when it seems to us contrary to the truth, as we make manifest in this most grave question, in which, rejecting the opinions of the Moderns, we embrace the opinion of the old Peripatetics. Let our conclusion, therefore, be:

138 Commercium mentis cum corpore consistit in illa adligatione animae vi cujus anima motionibus corporis adficitur, &

138 The commerce of the mind with the body consists in that binding of the soul by virtue of which the soul is affected by the motions of the body, and in turn

Ad Coloss. cap. 3.

To the Colossians, ch. 3.

p. 45

vicissim motus in corpore efficere physico, & vero influxu possit. Prob: Etsi concipere non possimus, quo modo spiritus ita adligetur corpori, ut nulla ratione cum libuerit ex eo exire possit, quia tamen talem statum animae nostrae experimur, talem adligationem admittere debemus; atqui etiam experimur, animam dolore, voluptateve adfici ex motibus corporis: ergo quamvis modum quo id fiat non adsequamur, id tamen admittere erit rationi consentaneum. Et sicut nemo dicit illam adligationem haberi per aliquam ideam aut adprehensionem animae, sed re vera per ipsum realem statum animae, ita eae perceptiones motuum corporeorum debebunt habere fundamentum in ipsis motibus realibus.

can effect motions in the body by a physical and true influx. Prob.: Although we cannot conceive how a spirit is so bound to a body that it can by no means leave it when it pleases, yet because we experience such a state of our soul, we must admit such a binding; but we also experience that the soul is affected with pain or pleasure by the motions of the body: therefore, although we do not attain the manner in which this happens, it will nevertheless be consonant with reason to admit it. And just as no one says that that binding is had through some idea or apprehension of the soul, but in truth through the real state of the soul itself, so those perceptions of bodily motions will have to have their foundation in the real motions themselves.

139 Quod autem anima etiam verè, & physicè moveat corpus, inde videtur sufficienter probari, quod talis potentia non sit supra vires, nec contra proprietates spiritus; activum enim esse, ex essentia competit spiritui, cur autem haec activitas constringatur tam arctis limitibus, ut numquam extra animum prodire possit, quum etiam corpora extra se agere possint? Praeterea si resistentia, aut impenetrabilitas esset conditio sine qua non ad agendum, ne quidem spiritus spiritum movère posset. Nec quis nitidè certòque ostendet incorporei animi motus, corpus ipsum movere non posse? Certè Dei substantia quamvis incorporea, corpus quo libuerit impellere profectò potest.

139 But that the soul also truly and physically moves the body seems sufficiently proved from this, that such a power is neither above the forces nor against the properties of a spirit; for to be active belongs to a spirit by its essence; and why should this activity be constrained within such narrow limits that it can never go forth outside the mind, when even bodies can act outside themselves? Moreover, if resistance or impenetrability were a condition sine qua non for acting, not even a spirit could move a spirit. And who will show clearly and certainly that the motions of the incorporeal mind cannot move the body itself? Certainly the substance of God, though incorporeal, can indeed impel a body whithersoever it pleases.

140 Quid ergo prohibet quominus Deus animis nostris quos regendo corpori destinavit, eam quoque vim concesserit, ut corpus ipsum movere possint, & voluntatis actus, qui in animo excitantur, in corpus ipsum, non corporeo quidem, sed physico tamen influxu agant, ideoque corporeum motum, incorporeo voluntatis actui consonum producant? Ergo dicendum, Deum posse efficere potentiam creatam motricem corporis, quum nullum in hoc privilegium, aut perfectionem infinitam videamus, ut soli Deo competat; quum autem id & sensus communis suadeat, & munus quo anima fungitur exigere videatur, quàm congruentissimè talem vim ei à Deo inditam dicemus. Qui ergo propter naturarum dissimilitudinem facultatem corpus movendi ab animo súbmovent, hi illam à Deo etiam submovére debent, eorum proinde oratio non jam á Philosopho sed à Censore opprimenda est.

140 What, then, prevents God from having granted to our souls, which He destined to rule the body, this force too, that they can move the body itself, and that the acts of the will which are excited in the mind act on the body itself, not indeed by a corporeal but nevertheless by a physical influx, and hence produce a bodily motion consonant with the incorporeal act of the will? It must therefore be said that God can make a created power that moves the body, since we see in this no privilege or infinite perfection such that it would belong to God alone; and since both common sense urges it and the office the soul performs seems to demand it, we shall most fittingly say that such a force has been put into it by God. Those, then, who on account of the dissimilarity of the natures remove from the mind the faculty of moving the body must also remove it from God; their discourse, therefore, is to be put down no longer by the Philosopher but by the Censor.

Argumenta solvuntur.

The arguments are answered. 141

141 Opp. 1: impossibile omninò est, substantiam simplicem, & inextensam qualis est anima agere in substantiam extensam, quale est corpus, ut per se patet: ergo impossibilis est influxus physicus. Nego antec: quamvis enim nesciamus quomodo mens simplex in corpus agat, non ideo tamen actio illa neganda est. Cartesianorum & Leibnitzianorum argumenta

Obj. 1: it is altogether impossible that a simple and unextended substance, such as the soul is, should act on an extended substance, such as the body is, as is self-evident: therefore physical influx is impossible. I deny the antecedent: for although we do not know how the simple mind acts on the body, yet that action is not on that account to be denied. The arguments of the Cartesians and Leibnizians demonstrate

p. 46

demonstrant, nec corpus in mentem, nec mentem in corpus agere, quemadmodum corpus in alterum corpus agit, sed non probant substantiam unam non posse agere in alteram aliquomodo, omnemque influxum esse impossibilem. Quamvis ergo physicas motuum leges in animae corporisque commercio non servari concedamus; inde tamen minimè sequitur, entia intelligentia, atque libera vim à Deo non accepisse motus aliquos in corporibus producendi, juxtà leges alias ipsorum naturae convenientes.

that neither does the body act on the mind nor the mind on the body in the way that a body acts on another body; but they do not prove that one substance cannot act on another in any way, and that all influx is impossible. Although, therefore, we grant that the physical laws of motion are not observed in the commerce of soul and body, yet it by no means follows from this that intelligent and free beings have not received from God the force of producing some motions in bodies according to other laws suited to their nature.

142 Dices: Systema influxus physici sustineri non potest, nisi concedatur ex animo in corpus, & vicissim quidpiam transfundi, id enim sonat ipsum influxus vocabulum: sed hoc est absurdum: ergo. Nego majorem argumenti: quum corpus in mentem agere, aut influere contendimus, pingui sit ingenio oportet, qui ita ut vult argumentum intelligat, id namque intelligimus vim duntaxat ac naturam mentis à commotionibus cerebri sic adfici, ac dirigi, ut repraesentationes in ea oriantur, minimè verò ideas rerum externarum ex corpore in mentem quasi commeare. Certum proindè est, agitationibus cerebri animo non communicari motum quendam corporibus proprium, sed eum modo naturae suae convenienti ad agendum determinari.

142 You will say: The system of physical influx cannot be maintained unless it is granted that something is transfused from the mind into the body, and conversely, for that is what the very word influx means: but this is absurd: therefore. I deny the major of the argument: when we contend that the body acts on, or flows into, the mind, he must be of dull wit who understands the argument as he pleases; for by this we understand only that the force and nature of the mind are so affected and directed by the commotions of the brain that representations arise in it, but by no means that the ideas of external things pass, as it were, from the body into the mind. It is certain, therefore, that by the agitations of the brain no motion proper to bodies is communicated to the mind, but that the mind is determined to act in a manner suited to its own nature.

143 Opp. 2: Systema influxus pugnat cum immortalitate animae: ergo sustineri nequit. Antec. probatur: nam hac opinione positâ anima mortuo corpore nihil operari poterit, quum illi desit adminiculum ad agendum necessarium. Argumentum hocce à nobis solutum jam est, sed explicationis gratia dicimus, quod quemadmodum ridiculus sis, si, quòd inclusus in carcere solem absque fenestra contueri nequeas, ex eo velis efficere nihil te quum è carcere exieris, posse cernere; ita quamvis animus propter corporis terreni consortium non queat sine ejusdem adjumento percipere, perperàm hinc colligas, eum quum liber evolaverit, circunjecta corpora non posse comprehendere, ut eleganter ait Tulius s1.

143 Obj. 2: The system of influx conflicts with the immortality of the soul: therefore it cannot be maintained. The antecedent is proved: for, this opinion being posited, the soul, once the body is dead, will be able to do nothing, since it will lack the aid necessary for acting. This argument has already been answered by us, but for the sake of explanation we say that, just as you would be ridiculous if, because when shut up in a prison you cannot look upon the sun without a window, you wished to conclude from this that you can see nothing when you have come out of the prison, so, although the mind, on account of its fellowship with the earthly body, cannot perceive without its help, you wrongly gather from this that, when it has flown away free, it cannot apprehend the surrounding bodies, as Cicero elegantly says (e).

144 Dices cum Bylffingero: admisso corporis in animam influxu, effectum causâ suâ majorem fore, quod perabsurdum est. Contendit enim Leibnitzianus iste, integrum ac plenum effectum respondentem viribus nostri corporis esse motiones cerebri, causam ergo ab effectu vinci, si perceptiones quae in mente formantur eisdem cerebri motionibus adtribuantur. Sed haec nihil negotii facescunt. Corpori, enim aliam à motu effectionem, nos quidem minimè adsignamus neque enim ideas in animo formari à corpore dicimus, sed à mente ipsa motione cerebri veluti admonita. Quare plenus corporis effectus motus est, animae verò perceptio.

144 You will say, with Bilfinger: if the influx of the body into the soul is admitted, the effect will be greater than its cause, which is quite absurd. For this Leibnizian contends that the entire and full effect corresponding to the forces of our body is the motions of the brain; the cause, therefore, is surpassed by the effect if the perceptions which are formed in the mind are attributed to those same motions of the brain. But these things cause no trouble. For we by no means assign to the body any effect other than motion; for we do not say that ideas are formed in the mind by the body, but by the mind itself, admonished, as it were, by the motion of the brain. Wherefore the full effect of the body is motion, but that of the soul is perception.

145 Opp. 3: cum Cartesianis: influxus physici hypothesis tanquam minus probabilis rejici debet, si causarum occasionalium systema, & facilius sit intellectu, & nullis incommodis obnoxium;

145 Obj. 3, with the Cartesians: the hypothesis of physical influx ought to be rejected as less probable if the system of occasional causes is both easier to understand and liable to no inconveniences;

Tusc. quaest. lib. 1. cap. 20.

Tusculan Disputations, bk. 1, ch. 20.

p. 47

sed ita est: ergo. Prob. minor: Licitum est, imò necessarium ad Deum recurrere si causae secundae non sufficiunt; nihil autem aliud fit in systemate causarum occasionalium; atque in hac hypotesi nullum admittitur miraculum propriè dictum, quum omnia fiant secundum leges naturales à Deo constitutas, ac proindè ordini naturae convenientes. Neque incerta redditur corporum existentia; Deus enim summè verax velle non potest, ut perpetuis illusionibus decipiamur. Tandem vim activam non detrahit voluntati hypothesis Cartesiana, ipsa etenim voluntas data motuum corporeorum occasione deinde agit, & suas operationes liberè elicit: ergo causarum occasionalium systema facillimè intelligitur, & nullis incommodis est obnoxium.

but so it is: therefore. The minor is proved: It is permitted, nay necessary, to have recourse to God if second causes do not suffice; and nothing else happens in the system of occasional causes; and in this hypothesis no miracle properly so called is admitted, since all things happen according to natural laws established by God, and hence suited to the order of nature. Nor is the existence of bodies rendered uncertain; for God, being supremely truthful, cannot will that we be deceived by perpetual illusions. Finally, the Cartesian hypothesis does not take active force away from the will, for the will itself, on the occasion of the bodily motions given, then acts, and freely elicits its operations: therefore the system of occasional causes is very easily understood and is liable to no inconveniences.

146 Ad singulas argumenti partes cum Cl. Jacquiero respondeamus. Et primò in effectuum naturalium explicatione ad primam tandem causam recurrendum est, verum id facere non debent Philosophi, si causae secundae suppetant, quae quidem omnes ad primam referuntur. Porrò in praesenti quaestione ad primam causam immediatè confugere, necessarium non est, nisi demonstretur, impossibilem esse influxum physicum quod quidem nulla ratione ostendi posse jam probatum est. Secundò: In hypothesi causarum occasionalium ex infinita Dei veracitate, & ex revelatione ostendi quidem potest corporum existentia, sed adimeretur aliud probationis genus quod ex nostris sensationibus oritur, quo certè convinci debent Idealistae, qui Revelationem parvipendunt.

146 Let us reply to the several parts of the argument with the celebrated Jacquier. And first: in the explanation of natural effects one must at last have recourse to the first cause; but Philosophers ought not to do this if second causes are available, all of which indeed are referred to the first. Further, in the present question it is not necessary to take refuge immediately in the first cause, unless it is demonstrated that physical influx is impossible, which, as has already been proved, can be shown by no reason. Secondly: in the hypothesis of occasional causes the existence of bodies can indeed be shown from the infinite veracity of God and from revelation, but another kind of proof would be taken away, that which arises from our sensations, by which the Idealists, who make light of Revelation, ought certainly to be convinced.

147 Tandem in eadem hypothesi explicarit nequit jus atque imperium illud, quod animae in corpus concessum fuit. Si enim corpus ipsum ab anima non veluti efficiente, sed occasionali solum causâ moveretur, corporis motus non ab anima, sed à Deo producerentur, huic autem difficultati accedit etiam, quod ubi voluntatis actus in anima excitatus fuerit, corporeus motus illi consonus aliquando facilius difficilius aliquando in corpore excitari conspicitur, quod optimè explicatur, si motus ille ab anima veluti efficiente causâ repetatur, quae modò languidius, modò vividius in corpore operari possit.

147 Finally, in the same hypothesis that right and command which was granted to the soul over the body cannot be explained. For if the body itself were moved by the soul not as by an efficient but only as by an occasional cause, the motions of the body would be produced not by the soul but by God; and to this difficulty is added also the fact that, when an act of the will has been excited in the soul, a bodily motion consonant with it is seen to be excited in the body sometimes more easily, sometimes with more difficulty; which is best explained if that motion is traced back to the soul as its efficient cause, which can operate in the body now more languidly, now more vigorously.

148 Vix autem concipi vel explicari potest, si motus ille produci dicatur à Deo, qui ea lege corpus, animamque conjunxerit, ut ipse solum â divina vi sua motum illum in corpore produceret, quem anima in corpore produci cuperet. Igitur actuum illorum efficiens causa non Deus, ut Cartesiani volunt, sed humana anima esse debet, aut explicent nobis Cartesiani, cur data volitionis alicujus occasione, Deus aliquando similem, aliquando verò dissimilem corporeum actum in corpore excitaret, quod explicare certè non poterunt. Si verò dicant motum corporeum ab anima verè produci, & animam dato aliquo corporeo motu verè, & propriè agere, jam tota lis in solo nomine posita est, & causae occasionalis nomen usurpent, per nos licet, at re vera in hypothesim influxus physici relabuntur.

148 But it can scarcely be conceived or explained if that motion is said to be produced by God, who joined body and soul by such a law that He alone, by His divine force, would produce in the body that motion which the soul desired to be produced in the body. Therefore the efficient cause of those acts must be not God, as the Cartesians will have it, but the human soul; or else let the Cartesians explain to us why, on the occasion of some volition being given, God would excite in the body now a similar, now a dissimilar bodily act; which they will certainly not be able to explain. But if they say that the bodily motion is truly produced by the soul, and that the soul, on the occasion of some bodily motion being given, truly and properly acts, then the whole dispute rests on a mere name; let them use the name of occasional cause, for all we care, but in reality they slip back into the hypothesis of physical influx.

p. 48

149 Opp. tandem cum Wolffianis, & Leibnitzianis: illa hypothesis longè probabilior est, & amplecti debet in qua evanescunt difficultates influxus physici, & causarum occasionalium hypothesibus communes, sed talis est harmoniae praestabilitae hypothesis: ergo. Prob. min.: in hoc sistemate jam explicato humanum corpus imdependenter ab anima motus suos, suorumque actuum seriem producit, perinde ac si nulli corpori conjuncta esset. Itaque duo illi corporeorum motuum, & cogitationum ordines simul, eodemque tempore peraguntur, non quòd anima in corpus aut corpus in animam influere possit. Evanescit ergo prima difficultas, concipiendi scilicèt, qua ratione corpus in animam, & anima in corpus agat. Deinde harmonia illa praestabilita est inter motus corporeos, & perceptiones animae, non verò inter adpetitiones ejus. Evanescit ergo difficultas altera de voluntatis humanae libertate: ergo.

149 Obj., finally, with the Wolffians and the Leibnizians: that hypothesis is far more probable, and ought to be embraced, in which the difficulties common to the hypotheses of physical influx and of occasional causes vanish; but such is the hypothesis of pre-established harmony: therefore. The minor is proved: in this system, already explained, the human body produces its motions and the series of its acts independently of the soul, just as if it were joined to no body. Thus those two orders, of bodily motions and of thoughts, are carried on together and at the same time, not because the soul can flow into the body or the body into the soul. The first difficulty therefore vanishes, namely that of conceiving in what way the body acts on the soul and the soul on the body. Next, that pre-established harmony is between the bodily motions and the perceptions of the soul, but not between its appetitions. The second difficulty, therefore, concerning the liberty of the human will vanishes: therefore.

150 Ad argumentum respondeo quod harmoniae praestabilitae hypothesis non solum communes habet, cum causarum occasionalium systemate difficultates, sed etiam longè graviores. Et certè immeritò supponitur futura in humano corpore constans quaedam ac invariabilis motuum series, dependenter á sola partium textura, externorumque corporum actione, quum experientia teste compertum sit, corporis nostri motus ab extrinsecis etiam subitisque causis mirificè variari, ita ut motuum nostrorum series, non ex intrinseco quodam, constantique principio, sed ex innumeris prorsùs, arbitrariisque causis oriatur. Accedit etiam, animum aliquando motibus, & adfectionibus illis adsentiri, quae excitantur in corpore, sed aliquando tamen iis resistere ac dissentiri, ita ut nulla constans, ac invariabilis similium motuum series, vel harmonia effingi possit, qua dum motus quidam in corpore excitatur, similis alteri, & cónsonum in anima producatur.

150 To the argument I reply that the hypothesis of pre-established harmony not only has difficulties in common with the system of occasional causes, but also far graver ones. And certainly it is undeservedly supposed that there will be in the human body a certain constant and invariable series of motions, depending solely on the texture of the parts and on the action of external bodies, since it is established by the testimony of experience that the motions of our body are wonderfully varied by extrinsic and sudden causes as well, so that the series of our motions arises not from some intrinsic and constant principle, but from altogether innumerable and arbitrary causes. Add, too, that the mind sometimes assents to those motions and affections which are excited in the body, but sometimes nevertheless resists and dissents from them, so that no constant and invariable series of similar motions, or harmony, can be feigned by which, while a certain motion is excited in the body, a similar and consonant one is produced in the soul.

151 Tandem: Perfecta libertatis idea requirit, ut humanus animus suorum actuum dominus, auctor, & causa esse debeat, non alia de causa illos exerat, nisi quòd illos exerere velit, eoque imperio, ac libertate corporis etiam motus sequi, aut iis resistere, eos efficere, aut ab iis abstineri possit. Haec igitur remanet semper gravissima difficultas, motus corporis esse necessarios in Leibnitziana hypothesi, utpote quia alii esse non possunt, quam qui existunt. Neque est quod dicant adversarii, inter motus corporeos duntaxat, & perceptiones animae, non verò inter adpetitiones ejus hanc harmoniam fuisse praestabilitam. Etenim hypotesim istam ideo excogitavit Leibnitzius, quòd nullam inter animam, & corpus dependentiam fingi posse crediderit: ac proinde non minus inter animae volitiones, quàm perceptiones, harmoniam praestabilitam admittere debet.

151 Finally: The idea of perfect liberty requires that the human mind, which must be the master, author and cause of its acts, should exert them for no other reason than that it wills to exert them, and that by that command and liberty it can also follow the motions of the body or resist them, effect them or abstain from them. This most grave difficulty, therefore, always remains, that the motions of the body are necessary in the Leibnizian hypothesis, inasmuch as they cannot be other than those which exist. Nor is there any ground for the adversaries to say that this harmony was pre-established only between the bodily motions and the perceptions of the soul, but not between its appetitions. For Leibniz devised that hypothesis precisely because he believed that no dependence could be feigned between the soul and the body: and therefore he must admit a pre-established harmony no less between the volitions of the soul than between its perceptions.

152 Neque tandem valet responsio motuum omnium seriem juxta liberam voluntatis determinationem â Deo fuisse praevissam,

152 Nor, finally, does the reply avail that the series of all motions was foreseen by God in accordance with the free determination of the will, and ordered.

p. 49

atque ordinatam. Etenim quum nullam inter animam & corpus actionem admittant Leibnitziani, nulla ratione praevidere, ac ordinare potuit Deus motuum omnium seriem cum libera voluntate consentientem. Si enim inter animam, & corpus nulla dependentia intercedere possit, hanc Deus praevidere, & ordinare non potuit; Si autem dependentia illa non repugnet, jam inutilis est Harmoniae praestabilitae hypothesis. Quae quum ita sint facilè patet, Recentiores Metaphysicos in explicanda corporis, animique societate nihilo feliciores fuisse Peripateticis, sed audaciores, Superest ergo, ut arcani hujus foederis leges infinita Dei potentia, & sapientia constitutas, ab intellectu nostro omninò clarè comprehendi non posse libentissimè fateamur.

ordered. For since the Leibnizians admit no action between the soul and the body, God could in no way foresee and order a series of all motions agreeing with the free will. For if no dependence can intervene between the soul and the body, God could not foresee and order it; but if that dependence is not repugnant, then the hypothesis of pre-established harmony is useless. These things being so, it is readily apparent that the modern Metaphysicians have been no more fortunate than the Peripatetics in explaining the society of body and mind, but more audacious. It remains, therefore, that we most willingly confess that the laws of this secret covenant, established by the infinite power and wisdom of God, cannot be comprehended altogether clearly by our intellect.

ADPENDIX. — APPENDIX

De Animi sede.

On the Seat of the Mind.

153 Scholastici putant animum nostrum per totum corpus non modò virtute & efficaciâ, sed re ipsa diffusum esse. Apud Cartesii adseclas saltem priores, in glandula pineali, quae est particula cerebri, residere dicitur. At si anima in omnibus membris resideat, eccur tamen judicia in cerebro peraguntur? Cur enim duos judicet esse globulos, si ita duobus digitis unicum contingat, ut talem situm nervi obtineant, quo extimi interiores fiant? [Log. §. 113.] Certè necessitas hujusmodi diffusionis nulla adparet. Imò qui fieri potest, ut dolére quidam putent sibi dudùm abscissam manum, ut si aquae nonnihil cérebro adfundatur, nullus sensus in organis externis habeatur?

he Scholastics think that our mind is diffused through the whole body, 153 T not only by power and efficacy, but in reality itself. Among the followers of Descartes, at least the earlier ones, it is said to reside in the pineal gland, which is a small part of the brain. But if the soul resides in all the members, why then are judgments carried out in the brain? For why would one judge that there are two globules, if one touches a single one with two fingers so placed that the nerves take up a position in which the outer ones become inner? [Log. §. 113.] Certainly no necessity for a diffusion of this kind appears. Indeed, how can it happen that some people think they feel pain in a hand long since cut off, and that, if a little water is poured over the brain, no sensation is had in the external organs?

154 Sed neque in glandula pineali apta sedes animi constitui videtur. Audiamus Anatomicos s1. ,, Fredericus olim hanc glandulam (pinealem) petrificatam vidit, tres calculos in eadem reperit. Sed mirabilius est, quod jam dudum nobis communicavit praeclarissimus Carolus Drelincurtius, quodque observaverat in virgine circiter 20 ann, quae postquam dira cephalaea s2 semestri discruciata fuisset, ac tandem occaecata, ac deincèps sensibus orbata, in mediis planctibus mortem obierat; ipsi scilicet pinealis glandula non tantum saxea fuit, sed etiam ad ovi gallinacei amplitudinem excreverat, qua sua mole nervorum opticorum thalamos s3 nec non reliquos tandem nervos compressit s4.

154 But neither does the pineal gland seem to be established as a fit seat for the mind. Let us hear the Anatomists (f). “Frederik once saw this gland (the pineal) petrified, and found three stones in it. But more wonderful is what the most distinguished Charles Drelincourt long ago communicated to us, and what he had observed in a virgin of about 20 years, who, after she had been tormented for six months by a dreadful cephalaea (g), and at length blinded, and thereafter deprived of her senses, had met her death amid lamentations: in her, namely, the pineal gland was not only stony, but had even grown to the size of a hen’s egg, and by its bulk had compressed the thalami (h) of the optic nerves and finally the remaining nerves as well (i).”

Ruysch. in Thes. Anat.

Ruysch, in the Thes. Anat.

Cephalaea est capitis dolor inveteratus, aegrè cedens, contumax & pertinax.

Cephalaea is an inveterate pain of the head, yielding with difficulty, stubborn and persistent.

Locum è quo nervi optici egrediuntur Galenus thalamus vocavit.

The place from which the optic nerves issue Galen called the thalamus.

Vid. Theatr. Anatom. Boneti tom. 2. p. 309.

See Bonet, Theatr. Anatom., vol. 2, p. 309.

p. 50

155 Recentiùs D. Dela Peyronie s1 sedem animae corpus callosum s2 constituit. Ostendit namque laesis reliquis cérebri partibus, solo illaeso corpore calloso, usum sensuum & rationis in diversis perstitisse integrum, laeso verò corpore calloso, unà sensationes, & rationis usum subtractum fuisse. His verò non obstantibus adserendum mihi videtur animam sedem propriam habere in solo cérebro, licet certò statui non possit in qua praecisè cerebri parte resideat. In ea enim sola corporis parte dicendum est animam residere, quae sola est in qua anima immediatè operetur; animum verò in solum cerebrum immediatè operari, apertissimè constat: etenim vitiato solo cérebro, sensuum omnium usus amittitur; hinc Apoplexia correpti, veluti fulmine percussi, omni sensu privantur, ita ut nihil sentiant. Corporis etiam adfectiones, quae non transmittuntur ad cérebrum, mentem prorsùs latent, ut in parálysi accidit. (Vide Phys. §. 560, & seq.)

155 More recently M. de La Peyronie (k) has placed the seat of the soul in the corpus callosum (l). For he showed that when the other parts of the brain were injured and the corpus callosum alone was unharmed, the use of the senses and of reason remained whole in various persons; but when the corpus callosum was injured, sensations and the use of reason were taken away together. Notwithstanding these things, however, it seems to me that it must be asserted that the soul has its proper seat in the brain alone, although it cannot be settled with certainty in precisely which part of the brain it resides. For the soul must be said to reside in that part of the body alone which is the only one in which the soul operates immediately; but that the mind operates immediately on the brain alone is most plainly evident: for when the brain alone is impaired, the use of all the senses is lost; hence those seized by Apoplexy, as if struck by lightning, are deprived of all sense, so that they feel nothing. The affections of the body, too, which are not transmitted to the brain, remain wholly hidden from the mind, as happens in paralysis. (See Phys. §. 560 ff.)

156 Peripatetici verò saltem ab XIII. Christiani nominis seculo, animum in toto corpore esse contendunt. Moventur talibus argumentis. Primo, quia quamcumque corporis partem tangamus, animus sentit, quod signum est, eum ibi esse. Deinde quia intelligi non potest, quo pacto animus sit forma substantialis corporis humani, ut definitum est in Concilio Viennensi s3, id est, sit id, quod corpus regit, nisi totum corpus occupet. Verum opus non est hujusmodi rationes ad Lydium lapidem revocare.

156 The Peripatetics, however, at least from the thirteenth century of the Christian name, contend that the mind is in the whole body. They are moved by arguments such as these. First, because whatever part of the body we touch, the mind feels, which is a sign that it is there. Next, because it cannot be understood how the mind is the substantial form of the human body, as was defined at the Council of Vienne (m), that is, is that which governs the body, unless it occupies the whole body. But there is no need to bring reasons of this kind to the Lydian touchstone.

157 Et ad primam quod adtinet dico cum Cl. Jacquiero, animam percipere impressionem factam in qualibet corporis parte, quia impressio illa ad cerebrum propagatur ope nervorum, qui à qualibet corporis parte ad cerebrum usque pertingunt; nimirùm à qualibet parte corporis, tensi sunt nervi usque ad cerebrum, unde quum nervi extremitas, quae est in pede ex. gr. vel in manu vellitur, pariter vellitur, seu movetur altera extremitas, quae est in cerebro, & vi istius motus in cerebro excitati admonetur anima, doloremque sentit, si impressio facta vehemens fuerit. Illud verò multis experimentis confirmatur. I. Si arctissimè stringatur pars aliqua corporis, cerébrum inter, & partem aliam corporis resecandam, aut pungendam, nullus, aut ferè nullus sentitur dolor: quia scilicèt nullus, aut ferè nullus pérvenit motus ad extremitatem nervi, quae est in cérebro. II. Si quis, ut aliquandò evenit, altè defixus sit in aliquam cogitationem, ut plurimùm, non percipit objecta externa, quae tamen feriunt sensus illius externos; quia nimirùm tunc nervi ita sunt tensi, ut non admittant alium motum, quo mens determinetur ad percipienda objecta externa.

157 And as regards the first, I say with the distinguished Jacquier that the soul perceives an impression made on any part of the body because that impression is propagated to the brain by means of the nerves, which reach from any part of the body all the way to the brain; namely, from any part of the body nerves are stretched as far as the brain, so that when the extremity of a nerve which is, e.g., in the foot or in the hand is plucked, the other extremity, which is in the brain, is likewise plucked or moved, and by the force of this motion excited in the brain the soul is alerted, and feels pain if the impression made was vehement. This is moreover confirmed by many experiments. I. If some part of the body is bound very tightly, between the brain and another part of the body that is to be cut off or pricked, no pain, or almost none, is felt; because, namely, no motion, or almost none, reaches the extremity of the nerve which is in the brain. II. If someone, as sometimes happens, is deeply fixed on some thought, he very often does not perceive external objects, which nevertheless strike his external senses; because, namely, the nerves are then so stretched that they do not admit another motion by which the mind might be determined to perceive external objects.

Ann. 1741.

In the year 1741.

Corticalis substantia cerebri, dicitur exterior substantia illius cinerei coloris ad differentiam interioris candidioris, quae medullaris, & callosum corpus dicitur.

The cortical substance of the brain is the name given to its outer substance, of an ashen color, as distinguished from the inner, whiter substance, which is called the medullary substance and the corpus callosum.

Sub Clem. V. Ann. 1311.

Under Clement V, in the year 1311.

p. 51

158 Sed instant. Quaecumque pars corporis laedatur, anima percipit dolorem, veluti existentem in illa ipsâ parte corporis, quae laeditur: ergo mens proximè praesens est parti cuilibet corporis. Nego conseq. Quamvis enim percipiatur ab anima dolor, velut existens in quacumque laesa corporis parte, non tamen anima dolorem percipit in illa ipsa corporis parte, quae laeditur.

158 But you will insist. Whatever part of the body is injured, the soul perceives the pain as existing in that very part of the body which is injured: therefore the mind is immediately present to every part of the body. I deny the consequence. For although the pain is perceived by the soul as existing in whatever part of the body is injured, the soul nevertheless does not perceive the pain in that very part of the body which is injured.

159 Et quidem caecus baculo explorans objecta externa, proprietates eorundem, liquiditatem ex. gr. vel duritiem percipit extremo baculo, ac extremo in baculo velut existentem quodammodò. Nemo tamen dixerit, animam hominis caeci residere in extremitate baculi. Sic etiam quamvis anima percipiat sensationem aliquam ex. gr. caloris, aut frigoris velut existentem in extremo digito, aut quâlibet alterâ corporis parte, non iccircò dicendum est animam agere in extremum digitum, & in eo proximè percipere sensationem, quâ adficitur; motus nimirùm extremo digito primùm communicatus, postmodùm per nervos ad cérebrum diffusus pervenit ad animae sedem, ubi fit sensatio, quam tamen anima naturaliter refert ad alteram extremitatem nervorum, ubi facta fuit prima impulsio.

159 And indeed a blind man exploring external objects with a stick perceives their properties, e.g. fluidity or hardness, at the end of the stick, and as it were existing in a certain manner at the end of the stick. Yet no one would say that the blind man’s soul resides at the extremity of the stick. So too, although the soul perceives some sensation, e.g. of heat or of cold, as existing in the tip of the finger or in any other part of the body, it must not therefore be said that the soul acts upon the tip of the finger and immediately perceives in it the sensation by which it is affected; namely, the motion first communicated to the tip of the finger, then spread through the nerves to the brain, reaches the seat of the soul, where the sensation takes place, which the soul nevertheless naturally refers to the other extremity of the nerves, where the first impulse was made.

160 Ad secundam objectionem quod spectat, dico animam esse posse veram corporis formam, (ut reverâ est) nempè principium á quo actiones humanae oriuntur, licet negemus eam in toto corpore esse diffussam. Quod quidem ut illustrius exponatur audiamus locum insignem ex Angelico Magistro S. Thoma s1 Spiritus (inquit S. Doct.) possunt alligari corpori, vel per modum formae, sicut anima corpori humano alligatur ut DET EI VITAM: vel etiam absque hoc, quod sit ejus forma, sicut Necromántici virtute daemonum spiritus alligatur imaginibus.

160 As regards the second objection, I say that the soul can be the true form of the body (as indeed it is), namely the principle from which human actions arise, although we deny that it is diffused through the whole body. That this may be set forth more clearly, let us hear a notable passage from the Angelic Master St. Thomas (n): Spirits (says the holy Doctor) can be bound to a body either by way of form, as the soul is bound to the human body to give it life; or else without this, that it be its form, as Necromancers by the power of demons bind spirits to images.

161 Porrò advertamus, quo tempore Clemens V. Synodum Viennensem coëgit, extitisse, qui docerent, animas nostras non aliâ ratione corporibus humanis uti, ac daemones iis corporibus, quae obsident s2. Haec satis docent, quid & Veteres Theologi, & Patres Viennenses sibi voluerint, quum docuere animas esse formas substantiales, nempè mentes humanas non obsidere humana corpora, velut quandoque daemones, sed informare, id est, vitam eis dare. Duae igitur sunt hìc secernendae quaestiones: prima: informet anima corpus, id est, ei vitam det, necne. Hoc dogma esse vult Synodus Viennensis, idque nos etiam docemus. Altera: si ut eum informet ac vivum reddat nécessum sit ut per totum corpus sit diffusa? Hoc Philosophiae juris est. Dicta sufficiant.

161 Let us note, moreover, that at the time when Clement V convened the Synod of Vienne there were those who taught that our souls make use of human bodies in no other way than demons make use of the bodies which they possess (o). These things show well enough what both the Ancient Theologians and the Fathers of Vienne meant when they taught that souls are substantial forms, namely that human minds do not possess human bodies, as demons sometimes do, but inform them, that is, give them life. There are therefore two questions to be distinguished here: the first, whether the soul informs the body, that is, gives it life, or not. The Synod of Vienne wills this to be dogma, and we too teach it. The other: if it informs it and renders it living, is it necessary that it be diffused through the whole body? This is a matter of Philosophy’s jurisdiction. Let what has been said suffice.

IV. Cont. Gent. cap. 90.

IV Contra Gentiles, ch. 90.

Abregé d’Histoire Ecclesiastique, Paris, 1751, under the year 1312.

METAPHYSICES — METAPHYSICS

PARS POSTREMA.

FINAL PART.

THEOLOGIA NATURALIS.

NATURAL THEOLOGY.

DISSERTATIO UNICA. — SINGLE DISSERTATION

Omni argumentorum genere, Existentia Supremi Numinis invictissimè demonstratur.

By every kind of argument the Existence of the Supreme Deity is most invincibly demonstrated.

162 De Deo quantum ad Metaphysicam spectat acturi, expendemus, an ratione naturali possit illius existentia ostendi; tempus enim non fert, ut in exponendis Divinae Essentiae adtributis immoremur, hoc enim, quum Sacrae Theologiae studio animum adplicueritis, oportunius expendetis.

f God, being about to treat of him so far as concerns Metaphysics, we 162 O shall weigh whether his existence can be shown by natural reason; for time does not allow us to dwell on setting forth the attributes of the Divine Essence; these, indeed, you will weigh more opportunely when you have applied your mind to the study of Sacred Theology.

163 Atheus s1 dicitur, qui Supremi Numinis existentiam inficiatur. Dei nomine intelligitur ,, ens à se, atque adeò necessariò existens, plenum rationis atque consilii, à quo adspectabilis mundus, quaeque in illo sunt, condita fuerint, & facta regantur ,,. Haec definitio nominalis est. In ea tamen consentire omnes, (ut ait Cl. à Brixia), arbitror inficiari posse neminem, ut enim habet Cicero s2 ,, Deus qui intelligitur à nobis, non alio modo intelligi potest, nisi mens soluta quaedam & libera,

163 He is called an Atheist (p) who denies the existence of the Supreme Deity. By the name of God is understood “a being from itself, and hence necessarily existing, full of reason and counsel, by whom the visible world and the things that are in it were founded and, having been made, are ruled.” This definition is a nominal one. Yet that all agree in it, no one, I think (as the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia says), can deny; for as Cicero has it (q): “God, who is understood by us, cannot be understood in any other way than as a certain mind, unfettered and free, separated from

p. 53

segregata ab omni concretione mortali, omnia sentiens, & movens, ipsaque praedita motu sempiterno ,,. His positis inquirendum est, an sit evidens evidentiâ physica, Deum existere? Loquimur de physicâ evidentiâ, nempè de ea, quae sufficit ad extorquendum adsensum constantem, atque firmum, non à protervo, deque omnibus dubitante, sed à viro veritatis amatore ingenuo, Rem quippè cum his agere, in animo mihi non est hoc loci, qui adeò inficiantur omnia, ut ne ipsa quidem prima cognitionis principia, etsi evidentissima sint, pro veris sine dubitatione admittant. Sat erit horum sophismata, & cavillationes convellere.

from all mortal admixture, perceiving and moving all things, and itself endowed with everlasting motion.” These things laid down, we must inquire whether it is evident with physical evidence that God exists. We speak of physical evidence, namely of that which suffices to extort a constant and firm assent, not from a wanton man who doubts of everything, but from an ingenuous lover of truth. For it is not in my mind in this place to deal with those who so deny everything that they do not admit as true without doubting even the first principles of knowledge themselves, most evident though they are. It will be enough to pull up their sophisms and cavils.

164 Dico igitur: evidens est, evidentiâ physicâ Deum existere. Prob. 1. ex perpetuo, constantique omnium nationum, populorumque consensu: qod enim natura universaliter confitetur, necesse est, verum esse. Naturam enim universaliter mentiri, impossibile est. Omnes porrò gentes, nationes omnes quantumvis feras, ac barbaras in id perpetuò consentire, ut supremum aliquod Numen admitterent, adeò apertum est, ut negari ab eo tantum possit, qui in Historiis planè hospes fuerit. ,, Nulla gens est ,, (inquit Tullius) s1, ,, neque tam immansueta, neque tam fera, quae non etiam si ignoret, qualem habere Deum deceat, tamen habendum sciat ,,.

164 I say, therefore: it is evident with physical evidence that God exists. Proof 1, from the perpetual and constant consent of all nations and peoples: for what nature universally confesses must necessarily be true. For it is impossible for nature universally to lie. Now that all races, all nations, however wild and barbarous, have perpetually agreed in this, that they admit some supreme Deity, is so plain that it could be denied only by one who is an utter stranger to History. “There is no race” (says Cicero (r)) “so untamed, nor so wild, that, even if it does not know what sort of God it ought to have, does not yet know that it ought to have one.”

165 Et sanè nisi id cognitum, comprehensumque animis haberemus inquit laudat. Cicero s2 ,, non tam stabilis opinio permanéret, nec confirmaretur diuturnitate temporis, nec unà seculis, aetatibusque hominum inveterari potuisset. Etenim videmus ceteras opiniones fictas atque vanas diuturnitate extabuisse. ¿Quis enim hyppocentaurum fuisse, aut chimaeram putat? ...... ......Opinionum enim commenta delet dies, naturae judicia confirmat ,,. Sed licet jam, ut cum eodem Tullio loquar, s3 (& haec erit secunda probatio) licet inquam ,, remota subtilitate disputandi, oculis quodammodò contemplari pulchritudinem rerum earum, quas Divinâ Providentiâ dicimus constitutas ,,.

165 “And surely, unless we had this known and grasped in our minds,” says the praised Cicero (s), “so stable an opinion would not have remained, nor would it have been confirmed by length of time, nor could it have grown old together with the centuries and ages of men. For we see that other opinions, feigned and empty, have wasted away with length of time. For who thinks that the hippocentaur existed, or the chimera? …… For time blots out the fictions of opinion, but confirms the judgments of nature.” But it is now permitted, to speak with the same Cicero (t) (and this will be the second proof), it is permitted, I say, “setting aside subtlety of disputation, to contemplate in a manner with our eyes the beauty of those things which we say were established by Divine Providence.”

166 ,, At principiò terra universa cernatur, locata in media mundi sede, solida & globosa, & undique ipsa sese nutibus suis conglobata, vestita floribus, herbis, arboribus, frugibus; quorum omnium incredibilis multitudo insatiabili varietate distinguitur. Adde hùc fontium gelidas perennitates, liquores perlucidos amnium, riparum vestitus viridissimos, speluncarum concavas altitudines, saxorum asperitates, impendentium montium altitudines, immensitatesque camporum. Adde etiam reconditas auri, argentique venas. ¿Quae verò, & quàm varia genera bestiarum vel cicurum, vel ferarum? ¿qui volucrum lapsus, atque cantus¿ ¿qui pecudum pastus? ¿quae vita silvestrium?

166 “And first let the whole earth be beheld, set in the middle seat of the world, solid and globular, and on every side gathered into a globe by its own tendencies, clothed with flowers, grasses, trees, crops: the incredible multitude of all of which is distinguished by an insatiable variety. Add to this the cool perennial flowings of springs, the transparent waters of rivers, the greenest clothing of the banks, the hollow depths of caverns, the roughness of rocks, the heights of overhanging mountains, and the immensities of the plains. Add also the hidden veins of gold and silver. And what kinds of beasts, and how varied, whether tame or wild! What flights and songs of birds! What pasturings of cattle! What life of the creatures of the woods!

Sint re verâ Athei, an non, magna quaestio est. Nullos extitisse Atheos, aliqui Viri docti putarunt, maximè verò antiquos Philosophos nullomodo Atheos dici posse, contendit Johann. Christophorus Wolffius in libro de Atheismi falsò suspectis, & alii post eum. E contrariò Veteres plures Atheos fuisse, defendit post alios Johan. Henricus Poppius. De Atheismo Philosophorum Gentilium celebriorum, & Buddeus de Spinosismo ante Spinosam.

Whether there really are Atheists or not is a great question. Some learned men have thought that no Atheists have existed, and Johann Christoph Wolf, in his book De Atheismi falso suspectis, and others after him, contend that the ancient Philosophers in particular can in no way be called Atheists. On the contrary, Johann Heinrich Poppius, after others, maintains that many of the Ancients were Atheists, in De Atheismo Philosophorum Gentilium celebriorum; and so does Buddeus in De Spinozismo ante Spinozam.
