167 ,, Quid jam de hominum genere dicam, qui quasi cultores terrae constituti, non patiuntur eam, nec immanitate belluarum efferari, nec stirpium asperitate vastari, quorumque operibus agri, insulae, litoraque collúcent distincta testis, & urbibus; quae si, ut animis, sic oculis vidére possémus, nemo, cunctam intuens terram, de divina ratione dubitaret. At verò ¿quanta maris est pulchritudo? ¿Quae species universi? ¿Quae multitudo, & varietas insularum? ¿Quae amaenitates orarum & litorum, quot genera, quámque disparia partim summersarum, partim fluitantium, & innatantium belluarum, partim ad saxa nativis testis inhaerentium? Ipsum autem mare sic terram adpetens, litoribus eludit, ut una ex duabus naturis conflata videatur ,,.

167 “What shall I now say of the race of men, who, set up as it were as cultivators of the earth, suffer it neither to grow wild with the savagery of beasts nor to be laid waste by the roughness of thickets, and by whose works the fields, the islands and the shores shine, studded with houses and cities? If we could see these things with our eyes as we can with our minds, no one, gazing upon the whole earth, would doubt of the divine reason. And truly, how great is the beauty of the sea! What an aspect of the whole! What a multitude and variety of islands! What delights of coasts and shores! How many kinds, and how unlike, of creatures, partly submerged, partly floating and swimming, partly clinging to the rocks with their native shells! And the sea itself, so making for the land, sports upon the shores that the two natures seem fused into one.

168 ,, Exindè mari finitimus aër die, & nocte distinguitur, isque tum fusus, & extenuatus sublime fertur, tùm autèm concretus in nubes cogitur, humoremque colligens terram auget imbribus, tum effluens hùc & illùc, ventus efficit. Idem annuas frigorum, & calorum facit varietates, idemque & volatum alitum sustinet, & spiritu ductus alit, & sustentat animantes Restat ultimus, & á domiciliis nostris altissimus, omnia cingens & coercens caeli complexus: qui idem aether vocatur, extrema ora, & determinatio mundi in quo cum admirabilitate maxima igneae formae cursus ordinatos definiunt ,,.

168 “Next, the air bordering on the sea is divided by day and night, and it is now borne aloft, spread out and thinned, and now, condensed, is gathered into clouds, and, collecting moisture, enriches the earth with rains, and now, flowing this way and that, makes wind. It too produces the yearly variations of cold and heat, and it also sustains the flight of birds, and, drawn in by breathing, nourishes and sustains living creatures. There remains the last and, from our dwellings, the highest, the embrace of heaven, girding and confining all things: which is also called the ether, the outermost border and boundary of the world, in which the fiery forms trace out their ordered courses with the greatest wonder.

169 ,, E quibus Sol cujus magnitudine multis partibus terra superatur, circum eam ipsam volvitur, isque oriens, & occidens diem, noctemque conficit; & modò accedens, tùm autèm recedens binas in singulis annis reversiones ab extremo contrarias facit, quarum intervallo, tùm quasi tristitiâ quadam contrahit terram, tùm vicissim laetificat, ut cum caelo hilarata videatur? Luna autèm quae est, ut ostendunt Mathematici, major quàm dimidia pars terrae, iisdemque spatiis vagatur, quibus Sol; sed tùm congrediens cum Sole, tùm digrediens, & eam lucem, quam à Sole accepit mittit in terras, & varias ipsa mutationes lucis habet; atque etiam tùm subjecta & opposita Soli radios ejus & lumen obscurat; tùm ipsa incidens in umbram terrae, quum est è regione Solis, interpositu interjectuque terrae, repentè deficit, iisdemque spatiis hae stellae, quas vagas dicimus, circum terram feruntur, eodemque modo oriuntur, & occidunt; quarum motus, tùm incitantur, tùm retardantur, saepè etiam insistunt. Quo spectaculo nihil potest admirabiliùs esse, nihil pulchriùs ,,. Hactenùs Romanae eloquentiae Princeps.

169 “Of these the Sun, by whose magnitude the earth is surpassed many times over, revolves around that very earth, and by rising and setting it makes day and night; and now approaching, now receding, it makes each year two returns from opposite extremes, in the interval of which it now as it were contracts the earth with a kind of sadness, now in turn gladdens it, so that it seems to be made joyful together with the sky. The Moon, moreover, which is, as the Mathematicians show, larger than half the earth, wanders through the same spaces as the Sun; but now coming together with the Sun, now parting from it, it both sends to the earth the light which it has received from the Sun and itself undergoes various changes of light; and sometimes, placed beneath the Sun and over against it, it darkens its rays and light; sometimes, falling itself into the shadow of the earth, when it is opposite the Sun, it suddenly fails, through the interposition and intervention of the earth; and through the same spaces those stars which we call wandering are borne around the earth, and in the same way they rise and set; and their motions are now quickened, now retarded, often they even stand still. Than which spectacle nothing can be more wonderful, nothing more beautiful.” Thus far the Prince of Roman eloquence.

170 Haec igitur, qui seriò animadverterit, adtentoque fuerit animo comtemplatus, non dubito, quin eò tandèm veniat, ut nobiscum fateatur, eximiam mundi machinam, quaeque in illo sunt corpora, sine ratione atque consilio fieri minimè potuisse. ,, An cum machinatióne quâdam, (inquit laudat. Elegantissim. Cicero)

170 Whoever, then, has seriously attended to these things and contemplated them with an attentive mind will, I do not doubt, at last come to confess with us that the excellent machine of the world, and the bodies that are in it, could by no means have come to be without reason and counsel. “Or when, by some contrivance,” (says the praised, most elegant Cicero) we

p. 55

,, 2 moveri aliquid videmus, ut sphaeram, ut horas, ut alia permulta non dubitamus, quin illa opera sint rationis; quum autem impetum caeli admirabili cum celeritate moveri, vertique videamus constantissimè conficientem vicissitudines anniversarias, cum summa salute, & conservatione rerum omnium, dubitamus, quin ea non solùm ratione fiant, sed etiam excelenti quâdam, divinâque ratione?

“(u) we see something being moved, as a sphere, as clocks, as very many other things, we do not doubt that those are works of reason; but when we see the onrush of the heaven moved with wonderful swiftness and turned round, most constantly bringing about the yearly alternations with the utmost safety and preservation of all things, do we doubt that these things are done not only by reason, but by a reason that is excellent and divine?”

171 Lubet itaque argumentum ita paucis conficere. Si est aliquid in rerum naturâ, quod hominis mens, quod ratio, quod vis, quod potestas humana efficere non possit, est certè quod illud efficit, homine meliùs. Atqui res caelestes, omnesque eae quarum est ordo sempiternus ab homine confici non possunt. Est igitur id, quo illa conficiuntur, homine meliùs. Id autem quòd potiùs dixeris quam Deum? Etenim si Deus non est, quid esse potest in rerum naturâ homine meliùs? In eo enim sola ratio est; quâ nihil potest esse praestantius. Esse autem hominem qui nihil in mundo melius esse, quam se, putet, desipientis adrogantiae est, ne dicam amentiae. Ergo est aliquid homine melius. Est igitur Deus.

171 It pleases me, therefore, to complete the argument thus in a few words. If there is something in the nature of things which the mind of man, which reason, which human force, which human power cannot bring about, that which brings it about is certainly better than man. But the heavenly things, and all those whose order is everlasting, cannot be brought about by man. That, therefore, by which they are brought about is better than man. And what would you call this rather than God? For if God does not exist, what can there be in the nature of things better than man? For in him alone is reason, than which nothing can be more excellent. But for a man to think that there is nothing in the world better than himself is the arrogance of a fool, not to say of a madman. Therefore there is something better than man. Therefore God exists.

172 Prob. 3: ex humani corporis structurâ, quae adeó mirabilis est, tamque stupenda, ut supremi opificis existentia planè ad evidentiam per eam, si considerata diligenter fuerit, optimèque perspecta contra Atheum evincatur. Age, circunspice humani corporis opificium, cujus admonitione perdisce, quis tam pulchrae imaginis conditor, quis oculorum pictor, quis nares, auresque tornavit, quis labia distendit oris, quis nervos tetendit, atque ligavit, quis irrigavit venas, quis ossa congesit solida, quis carnem pellicula tenui circumtexit, quis digitos, articulósque discrevit, quis fundamenta pedis extendit, quis perforavit poros, atque meatus aperuit, quis pulmonum exculpsit fistula?

172 Proof 3: from the structure of the human body, which is so wonderful and so astounding that by it, if it has been diligently considered and thoroughly examined, the existence of the supreme maker is plainly established against the Atheist to the point of evidence. Come, look around at the workmanship of the human body, and by its prompting learn thoroughly who is the founder of so beautiful an image, who the painter of the eyes, who turned the nostrils and the ears, who stretched the lips of the mouth, who drew taut the nerves and bound them, who watered the veins, who piled up the solid bones, who wove the flesh round with a thin skin, who parted the fingers and the joints, who laid out the foundation of the foot, who pierced the pores and opened the passages, who carved out the pipes of the lungs?

173 Vide quot Divinae Artis opera in unâ materiâ demonstrantur, singulaque pulchra, recteque dimensa, nec non propriis invicèm officiis differentia. ¿Quisnam singula finxit? ¿Nonnè haec solus ipse Deus cuncta, propria voluntate molitus est? Et quum statuam, & imaginem absque fabro, & pictore fieri, nullus adserere audeat, miram hominis fabricationem sine conditore constitisse putabimus? Ipsa demum humana mens, ejusque vires atque operationes, nonnè ostendunt, & quidem ad evidentiam usque Supremum extare Numen à quo cóndita tam sublimis substantia fuerit, in corpore posita eique ineffabiliter copulata? Certè animum, mentemque hominis, rationem, consilium, prudentiam, qui non divinâ curâ perfecta esse perspicit, his ipsis rebus mihi videtur prorsùs carére.

173 See how many works of Divine Art are displayed in a single matter, each of them beautiful and rightly measured, and also differing from one another in their proper functions. Who, then, fashioned each of them? Did not God himself alone contrive all these things by his own will? And when no one would dare assert that a statue and an image come to be without a sculptor and a painter, shall we think that the wonderful fabric of man came to stand without a founder? Finally, does not the human mind itself, with its powers and operations, show, and indeed to the point of evidence, that there exists a Supreme Deity by whom so sublime a substance was founded, placed in a body and ineffably coupled with it? Surely whoever does not perceive that the mind and intellect of man, his reason, counsel and prudence were perfected by divine care seems to me to be wholly lacking in these very things.

174 Prob. 4, & ab Atheis quaero cum Tullio s2, cur si

174 Proof 4. And I ask of the Atheists with Cicero (x) why, if they maintain that

volunt, naturalia quaeque composita, ipsumque mundum ornatissimum atque pulcherrimum ex témerè concursantibus átomis non tantùm fieri potuísse, sed factum esse re ipsâ; cur, inquam, ipsi quoque non dicant, si innumerabiles unius & viginti formae literarum aliquò conjiciantur posse ex his Annales Ennii ut deincèps legi possint effici? Id certè minus quàm unum vile animalculum, ne dicam quàm tota ipsa mundi machina operosum est. Cur non Annales Enni, sed unus tantùm Virgilii versus nunquam hac ratione effectus est? Praeterea, (ut egregiè idem Cicero argumentatur s1, si mundum efficere potest concursus atomorum, cur porticum, cur templum, cur domum, cur urbem non potest, quae sunt minus operosa. & multò quidem faciliora? Certè ita témerè Athei de mundo effutiunt, ut mihi quidem nunquam admirabilem hunc Caeli ornatum suspexisse videantur.

that all natural composites, and the most adorned and most beautiful world itself, not only could have come to be from atoms running together at random, but were in fact so made, why, I say, do they not also say that if innumerable forms of the one-and-twenty letters were thrown together somewhere, the Annals of Ennius could be produced from them, so that they could afterwards be read? That is certainly less laborious than a single paltry animalcule, not to say than the whole machine of the world itself. Why has not the Annals of Ennius, but even a single verse of Virgil, never been produced in this way? Moreover (as the same Cicero excellently argues (y)), if a concourse of atoms can make a world, why can it not make a portico, a temple, a house, a city, which are less laborious and indeed much easier? Surely the Atheists babble so rashly about the world that they seem to me never to have looked up at this wonderful adornment of the Heaven.

175 Adde cum Lactantio s2. Si fortuitis atomorum concursionibus nascuntur omnia, cur nunquàm fortuitò accidit, sic coire illa principia, ut efficerent animal ejusmodi, quod naribus potiùs audiret, odoraret oculis, auribus cérneret? Ceterùm eâ ipsâ quam usurpant ratione jugulantur Athei. Dicunt non repugnare ut mundus fieret ex atomorum concursione fortuitâ, & si non repugnat, nullam esse rationem cur hoc modo re ipsâ factum non fuerit. At contra ipsos ita hoc idem urgetur argumentum. Non repugnat ut existat causa plena rationis, quae ad eam combinationem, quae nunc habetur primigenias atomos determinaverit: ergo causa istiusmodi re ipsá existit.

175 Add, with Lactantius (z): If all things arise from chance concurrences of atoms, why has it never happened by chance that those principles came together so as to make an animal of such a kind that it would hear with its nostrils rather, smell with its eyes, see with its ears? Moreover, the Atheists have their throats cut by the very reasoning they employ. They say that it is not repugnant that the world should be made from a chance concurrence of atoms, and that if it is not repugnant, there is no reason why it should not in fact have been made in this way. But against them this same argument is urged thus: It is not repugnant that there should exist a cause full of reason which determined the primordial atoms to that combination which is now found: therefore a cause of this kind in fact exists.

176 Prob. 5. Ipsa namque rerum contingentia invictissimum omnium judicio argumentum est Deum existere. Hinc etenim fit, ut admittere, vel inviti cogamur Ens aliquod a se, & necessariò existens, à quo res quae existunt contingenter, suum deindè esse receperint. Certum est itaque repugnare ad evidentiam, ut omne ens sit ab alio. Quum enim extra collectionem omnium entium, nullum habeatur ens, collectio omnium entium esset à nihilo tanquam ab efficiente causa, si omne ens haberet ab alio ut existeret. Igitur aliquod datur ens non ab alio. Quod autem est non ab alio, & est, à se ipso est, ut patet: ergo aliquod necessariò datur ens, quod à se existit.

176 Proof 5. For the very contingency of things is, in the judgment of all, a most invincible argument that God exists. For hence it comes about that we are compelled, even against our will, to admit some Being from itself, and necessarily existing, from which the things that exist contingently have afterwards received their being. It is therefore certain that it is evidently repugnant that every being should be from another. For since outside the collection of all beings no being is found, the collection of all beings would be from nothing as from an efficient cause, if every being had from another that it should exist. Therefore there is some being not from another. But what is not from another, and is, is from itself, as is plain: therefore there necessarily is some being which exists from itself.

177 Similiter repugnat ut tota collectio entium sit contingens. Si enim tota est contingens, tota ita existit, ut non esse ex aequo potuerit, & si ex aequo potuit non esse, nulla est ratio cur ad existendum potiùs, quàm ad non existendum fuerit determinata, nisi fortè placeat dicere, illam collectionem determinasse se ipsam ad existendum, quo certè, (ut ait Cl. à Brixia) nihil magis absurdum est, nihilque risu magis dignum. Datur ergo ens

177 Likewise it is repugnant that the whole collection of beings should be contingent. For if the whole is contingent, the whole so exists that it could equally have not been; and if it could equally have not been, there is no reason why it was determined to existing rather than to not existing, unless perhaps one is pleased to say that that collection determined itself to existing, than which surely (as the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia says) nothing is more absurd, and nothing more worthy of laughter. There is, therefore, a necessary being,

necessarium, & quidem tale, ut in eo contineatur ratio, cur contingentia entia existunt. Plurae aliae sunt hujus dignissimi argumenti invictissimae demonstrationes, quas videre potestis apud Cl. Thomam Mariam Cerboni s1

and indeed such that in it is contained the reason why contingent beings exist. There are many other most invincible demonstrations of this most worthy argument, which you can see in the distinguished Tommaso Maria Cerboni (a).

Atheorum cavillationes refutantur.

The cavils of the Atheists are refuted.

178 Opp. 1. Existentia Dei est articulus fidei: ut enim habet Apostolus s2, accedentem ad Deum oportet credere quid est: ergo nequit ratione naturali demonstrari. Dist. antec.: est articulus fidei adeò nempè, ut nonnisi per revelationem cognosci possit, nego, hoc est, admitti debet per fidem, si per rationem non innotescat, conc, & nego conseq. Porrò nullam in eo esse repugnantiam ut existentia Dei per media cùm naturalia, tùm supernaturalia innotescere nobis possit, manifestum adeò est, ut demonstratione non indigeat. Praeterea, quum Fides Divina sit adsensus datus alicui propositioni ex revelatione Divinâ tanquam motivo, prius est hominem esse certum de existentiâ Dei, quam ipsum moveri ad adsentiendum ex auctoritate Dei revelantis. Hinc sensus testimonii supra laudati, hic est: quisquis accedit ad Deum, id est, quisquis vult amplecti veram Religionem, debet esse certus de existentiâ Dei.

bj. 1. The existence of God is an article of faith: for, as the Apostle has it 178 O (b), he that cometh to God must believe that he is: therefore it cannot be demonstrated by natural reason. I distinguish the antecedent: it is an article of faith in such a way, namely, that it can be known only through revelation, I deny; that is, it must be admitted through faith if it does not become known through reason, I grant; and I deny the consequence. Moreover, that there is no repugnance in the existence of God becoming known to us through means both natural and supernatural is so manifest that it needs no demonstration. Besides, since Divine Faith is an assent given to some proposition on account of Divine revelation as its motive, a man must be certain of the existence of God before he is moved to assent on the authority of God revealing. Hence the sense of the testimony praised above is this: whoever cometh to God, that is, whoever wishes to embrace the true Religion, must be certain of the existence of God.

179 Vel propter metum, vel propter ignorantiam causarum, vel propter fraudes imperantium, atque Legislatorum, vel demùm propter educationem factum fuisse ut omnes homines in aliquam Religionem consenserint Hobbesius s3, Spinosa s4, Bayle s5, Tolandus s6 & alii complures falsò & temerè contendunt.

179 That it came about either through fear, or through ignorance of causes, or through the frauds of rulers and Legislators, or finally through education, that all men have agreed in some Religion, is falsely and rashly contended by Hobbes (c), Spinoza (d), Bayle (e), Toland (f) and very many others.

180 Opponunt itaque 2[?]: homines quia natura sua infirmi sunt & rerum futurarum expectatione solliciti, res formidolosas facilè sibi fingunt: ergo probabile est, metu inductos fuisse, ut aliquod Supremum Numen admitterent. Nego conseq. Nam sicut multi in metum, ita etiam plures in audaciam naturaliter inclinant: ergo metus non potest esse causa universalis ob quam omnes in rem aliquam unanimiter consentiant. Deindè homines libertatis & dominii amantes esse ex sua ipsorum natura Athei fatentur cum Hobbesio s7; sed impossibile est apud omnes homines naturalem dominii, & libertatis cupiditatem ita obrutam esse inani metu, ut

180 They object, therefore, 1: men, because they are weak by their nature and anxious with the expectation of things to come, easily feign fearful things for themselves: therefore it is probable that it was induced by fear that they admitted some Supreme Deity. I deny the consequence. For just as many incline naturally to fear, so also more incline to boldness: therefore fear cannot be the universal cause on account of which all agree unanimously in some thing. Next, the Atheists confess with Hobbes (g) that men are lovers of liberty and of dominion by their very nature; but it is impossible that among all men the natural desire for dominion and liberty should be so overwhelmed by empty fear that

all should agree in feigning a Supreme Deity: therefore the Atheists, who posit both, contradict themselves.

181 Opp. 3: homines ab ipsa naturâ insitum habent investigare causas rerum: si autem veras adsequi non potuerint, supposititias sibi fingunt: hinc Deum existere, sibi falsò persuaserunt, ut primum principium rerum omnium se adsequutos esse gauderent: ergo ignorantia & error in causâ fuere cur Deus aliquis admitteretur ab hominibus. Nego antec. & conseq.: quae enim propter ignorantiam constituta sunt inanibus levibusque rationibus innituntur: ergo facilè refelli possunt: ergo impossibile est, ut peritissimi quique in eo consentiant. Quàm absurdum ergo est, & ab omni ratione alienum, cunctas nationes, easque inter se dissitas, nullamque invicem communicationem habentes convenire potuisse in uno eodemque errore, & genere fictionis.

181 Obj. 3: men have it implanted by nature itself to investigate the causes of things; but if they have been unable to attain the true ones, they feign supposititious ones for themselves: hence they have falsely persuaded themselves that God exists, so that they might rejoice at having attained the first principle of all things: therefore ignorance and error were the cause why some God was admitted by men. I deny the antecedent and the consequence: for things established on account of ignorance rest on empty and light reasons, and therefore can easily be refuted: therefore it is impossible that all the most skilled men should agree in them. How absurd, then, it is, and how foreign to all reason, that all nations, and those far removed from one another and having no communication with one another, should have been able to agree in one and the same error and kind of fiction!

182 Opp. 4. Quum intelligerent Legislatores fore ut cives in officio multò facilius continerentur si aliquod Supremum Numen existere crederent, à quo puniri possent dum malè agerent, eorum astutiâ factum est, ut Religio in populos introduceretur, atque propagaretur: ergo ab ipsis Legislatoribus, Religionis origo repetenda est. Nego antec. Opiniones namque, quae hominum calliditate disseminantur, praecipuè si indè fiat, ut haud leve gravamen omnibus imponatur, diutiùs non perdurare, experientiâ compertum est. Ergo quum haec consensio, quamvis homines propter eam pluribus legibus subjecti sint, semper perduraverit, suam ab astutiâ Legislatorum orginem habere non potuit. Deindè barbarae quoque gentes, quae nemini subjectae essent in aliquam Religionem semper consenserunt, ipsaque Religio unà cum humano genere suum ortum habuit.

182 Obj. 4. Since Legislators understood that citizens would be kept in their duty much more easily if they believed that there exists some Supreme Deity by whom they could be punished when they did wrong, it came about by their cunning that Religion was introduced among the peoples and propagated: therefore the origin of Religion must be sought from the Legislators themselves. I deny the antecedent. For it has been found by experience that opinions which are disseminated by the craft of men do not last very long, especially if it comes about from them that no light burden is laid upon all. Therefore, since this consent has always endured, although on account of it men are subjected to more laws, it cannot have had its origin from the cunning of Legislators. Next, barbarous nations too, which were subject to no one, have always agreed in some Religion, and Religion itself had its origin together with the human race.

183 Opp. 5. Saepissimè contingit, ut certissimum id habeamus, quod vanum atque inane in se est, cùm propter praejudicia, tùm etiam propter educationem, institutionemque, quam in pueritia habuimus: ergo etiam Religio ab hisce duobus principijs dimanassè potuit. Nego antec. Nam quod omninò diversum est, in unius, ejusdemque rei consensionem inducere non potest; sed educatio atque institutio apud gentes omninò diversa est, semperque fuit; indèque contigisse videmus, ut mores eorum, atque consuetudines diversae sint: ergo. Deindè educationis, atque institutionis praejudicia depelluntur si ad veritatem adsequendam animus seriò adjiciatur; sed licet omni aetate non defuerint, qui meditationi scientiarum operam dederint, nullus tamen fuit, (si unum aut alterum delirantem excipias) qui ab hac communi consensione recesserit: ergo.

183 Obj. 5. It very often happens that we hold as most certain what is vain and empty in itself, now on account of prejudices, now also on account of the education and instruction which we had in childhood: therefore Religion too could have flowed from these two principles. I deny the antecedent. For what is altogether diverse cannot lead to agreement in one and the same thing; but education and instruction among the nations is, and always was, altogether diverse; and hence we see it has come about that their morals and customs are diverse: therefore. Next, the prejudices of education and instruction are driven out if the mind is seriously applied to attaining the truth; but although in every age there have not been lacking those who devoted their effort to the study of the sciences, there was nevertheless no one (if you except one or another raving man) who departed from this common consent: therefore.

184 Dices: fuere Philosophi qui nullos Deos esse putarunt teste Tullio s1. Quatuor autem Atheistarum sectas physicas

184 You will say: there were Philosophers who thought that there are no Gods, as Cicero witnesses (h). Moreover, four physical sects of Atheists were distinguished by Cudworth therefore

De Cive cap. 1. §. 4.

De Cive, ch. 1, §. 4.

p. 59

Cudwortus s1 distinxit: ergo. Secundo: Deum nemo vidit unquam: ergo credimus Supremi Numinis existentiam ex praeceptorum institutione, & parentum educatione; Ad primum nego conseq. Ex eo namque quod nonnulli Philosophi contra hanc consensionem pugnaverint, majorem in ea vim inesse ad persuadendum rectè concluditur; ex hoc enim evincitur hanc universalem consensionem, non ab ignorantia, errore, educatione, aut aliquo praejudicio dimanasse, sed profluxisse ab interna voce naturae, ab ipsa ratione, quae unicuique congenita est, ab ipso naturali lumine, quod propter ineptias paucorum delirantium philosophorum nunquam obscurari potuit. Ad secundum dist. antec.; nemo vidit in se, conc., in ejus operibus, nego, & conseq. ¿Quis enim animum vidit unquam? Eum tamen agnosco ex ejus operibus, quia cogito, &c.

(i): therefore. Second: no one has ever seen God: therefore we believe the existence of the Supreme Deity from the instruction of our teachers and the education given by our parents. To the first I deny the consequence. For from the fact that some Philosophers have fought against this consent, it is rightly concluded that a greater force for persuading is in it; for from this it is established that this universal consent did not flow from ignorance, error, education or some prejudice, but proceeded from the inner voice of nature, from the reason itself which is inborn in each man, from the natural light itself, which on account of the follies of a few raving philosophers could never be obscured. To the second I distinguish the antecedent: no one has seen him in himself, I grant; in his works, I deny; and I deny the consequence. For who has ever seen the mind? Yet I acknowledge it from its works, because I think, etc.

185 Opp. 6. Gentium consensus si uti firmum ad suadendum argumentum admittatur, multa absurda consequuntur: ergo. Prob. antec. Polytheismus consensui gentium fuit constitutus; nam si Judaei excipiantur omnes in eum consenserunt. Secundo. Unaquaeque natio ob consensum majorum suorum Religionem suam Religioni alterius praeferri deberet. Tertio, Multos errores disseminatos, variasque superstitiones consensu gentium fuisse institutas, nullus ignorare potest: ergo. Respondeo cum distinctione: & in hisce omnibus consensus certus, atque universalis fuit, nego, inconstans, incertus, atque particularis, conc. Consensus ergo, ex quo ad rem aliquam suadendam firmissimum argumentum desumi posse contendimus, ejusmodi esse debet, ut omnes cunctarum nationum, omniumque temporum homines firmiter, constanterque, complectatur.

185 Obj. 6. If the consent of nations is admitted as a firm argument for persuading, many absurdities follow: therefore. Proof of the antecedent. Polytheism was established by the consent of nations; for, if the Jews are excepted, all agreed in it. Second. Each nation, on account of the consent of its forefathers, ought to prefer its own Religion to the Religion of another. Third. No one can be ignorant that many errors were disseminated and various superstitions instituted by the consent of nations: therefore. I reply with a distinction: that in all these things the consent was certain and universal, I deny; that it was inconstant, uncertain and particular, I grant. The consent, therefore, from which we contend that a most firm argument for persuading of some thing is drawn must be such that it embraces firmly and constantly all men of all nations and of all times.

186 Opp. 7. Oritur à praejudicio, quod dicamus aliquem esse ordinem in mundo, nimirùm, inquit Spinosa, ex eo, quod homines in se, & extra se multa invenerint sibi utilia ex. gr. oculos ad videndum, herbas, & alimenta ad nutritionem, Solem ad illuminandum, &c., indè factum est, ut statim judicaverint, ita omnia ab aliquo agente parata & disposita fuisse: ergo ex opificio, & ordine mundi non rectè probatur Deum existere. Neg. antec. Non magis enim praejudicio laborant homines dum judicant ex. gr. partes organicas oculorum ab opifice sapientissimo paratas, & dispositas fuisse, non autem fatali quadam necessitate coaluisse, quàm praejudicio laboraret ipse Spinosa (cujus est haec cavillatio) si vel considerando structuram aedificiorum, vel horologii fabricam, suspicaretur causas intelligentes, â quibus singulari industriâ fuerunt disposita; atqui praejudicio non laboraret Spinosa, si causas ejusmodi vel existere, vel extitisse suspicaretur: imò haberetur ut insanus, si haec omnia fatali quâdam necessitate disposita fuisse contenderet; quàm igitur potiori jure ex mirabili totius

186 Obj. 7. It arises from prejudice that we say there is some order in the world; namely, says Spinoza, from the fact that men found within themselves and outside themselves many things useful to them, e.g. eyes for seeing, plants and foods for nourishment, the Sun for giving light, etc., it came about that they at once judged that all things had thus been prepared and disposed by some agent: therefore from the workmanship and order of the world it is not rightly proved that God exists. I deny the antecedent. For men do not labor under prejudice when they judge, e.g., that the organic parts of the eyes were prepared and disposed by a most wise maker, and did not grow together by some fatal necessity, any more than Spinoza himself (whose cavil this is) would labor under prejudice if, in considering either the structure of buildings or the construction of a clock, he were to suspect intelligent causes by which they were disposed with singular industry; but Spinoza would not labor under prejudice if he suspected that causes of this kind either exist or have existed; nay, he would be held a madman if he contended that all these things had been disposed by some fatal necessity; with how much better right, then, from the wonderful disposition of the whole world

De Nat. Deor.

On the Nature of the Gods.

System. Intellect. cap. 3. §. 30.

Systema Intellectuale, ch. 3, §. 30.

p. 60

mundi dispositione sine praejudicio comperimus existere opificem summè intelligentem.

do we find, without prejudice, that there exists a supremely intelligent maker.

187 Non injocundum vobis fore existimo, si argumenta aliqua quae exponit P. Hieronymus Maria Buzzi in Accurata Synopsi Theologiae Cl. P. Joh. Laur. Berti totidem verbis exscripta vobis proponam: vel ex hoc namque cognoscetis quàm perspicuè omnia complectatur, quàm nitidè proponat, quamque utile Theologiae ejusmodi studium vobis postea futurum sit s1.

187 I think it will not be unpleasant for you if I set before you some arguments which Fr. Girolamo Maria Buzzi expounds in the Accurate Synopsis of the Theology of the distinguished Fr. Giovanni Lorenzo Berti, copied out in as many words; for even from this you will learn how clearly it embraces everything, how lucidly it sets things forth, and how useful a study of this kind will afterwards be to you in Theology (*).

188 Opp. 8. Mundum a Deo conditum non fuisse pluribus argumentis ostenditur: ergo ex ejus Opificio Dei existentia non probatur. Antec. prob. 1. Percipi enim nequit Deum Æternum mundum fecisse mortalem, idque repentè, quum tot seculis ante cessaverit. ¿Quam indè coeperit gloriam, aut gaudium, qui nunquam potuit gloria, aut felicitate carére? ¿Quibus instrumentis aut ministris sit usus? Si lucem postea creavit, quomodo non antea jacuerit in tenebris? Ergo Deus mundum non condidit. Secundo. Vel Sapientibus mundum Deus condidit, vel insipientibus; atqui neutris condidit, nam illi sunt pauci, isti prorsus indigni: ergo nulli condidit.

188 Obj. 8. It is shown by several arguments that the world was not founded by God: therefore the existence of God is not proved from his Workmanship. The antecedent is proved: 1. For it cannot be conceived that God, being Eternal, made a mortal world, and that suddenly, when he had rested for so many ages before. What glory or joy did he gain from it, who could never lack glory or happiness? What instruments or ministers did he use? If he created light afterwards, how did he not lie in darkness before? Therefore God did not found the world. Second. God founded the world either for the Wise or for the foolish; but he founded it for neither, for the former are few, the latter wholly unworthy: therefore he founded it for none.

189 Tertio. Nullus est ordo in ejus partibus, quarum aliae desertae, aliae belluis tantùm, aut volucribus aptae, ut aër, montes, mares, paludes. Agri verò non nisi labore improbo fruges emittunt, quae saepè grandine, aut illuvione pessumdantur: ergo à Deo Sapientissimo creatum non est. Quarto. Ferae péssimae, pestilentiae, fames, morbi, Dei Providentiam evertunt: ergo. Quinto Vagitus infantium, corporis nuditas, & calamitates innumerae, quibus homo quovis animalculo est miserior, satis probant mundum à Deo in ejus gratiam non fuisse constructum: ergo mundus à Deo non est conditus, ac proinde ex mundi Opificio non benè probatur Supremi Numinis existentia.

189 Third. There is no order in its parts, of which some are deserted, others suited only for beasts or for birds, as the air, the mountains, the seas, the marshes. The fields, moreover, put forth crops only with unremitting labor, and these are often ruined by hail or by flood: therefore it was not created by a most Wise God. Fourth. The most noxious wild beasts, pestilences, famines, diseases overthrow the Providence of God: therefore. Fifth. The wailing of infants, the nakedness of the body, and the innumerable calamities by which man is more wretched than any animalcule, prove sufficiently that the world was not built by God for his sake: therefore the world was not founded by God, and consequently the existence of the Supreme Deity is not well proved from the Workmanship of the world.

190 Respondeo neg. antec., & ad prim. prob. nego etiam antec., cui etiam Epicurei respondere debent, qui materiam aeternam statuunt licet mundo initium atque interitum tribuant. Porrò in aeternitate, ubi ait S. Augustinus s2 ,, nulla creatura est, cujus mutabilibus motibus tempora peragantur, tempora omninò esse non possunt, & alibi s3 ,,. Si ante Coelum & terram nullum erat tempus, cur quaeritur, quid tunc faciebas? ,, Neque Deus ministris, aut instrumentis indiguit, quae infirmitatem declarant artificis, neque in tenebris jacuit aliquando ille qui semper fuit lux vera. Ad 2. nego min. Deus enim primò propter se, deindè propter sapientes condidit universum. Quod verò alii sint

190 I reply: I deny the antecedent; and to the first proof I deny the antecedent as well, to which the Epicureans too must reply, who posit eternal matter although they attribute to the world a beginning and an end. Moreover, in eternity, where, as St. Augustine says (k), “there is no creature by whose changeable motions times are carried on, times can by no means exist,” and elsewhere (l): “If before Heaven and earth there was no time, why is it asked what thou wast doing then?” Nor did God need ministers or instruments, which betray the weakness of a craftsman; nor did he who always was the true light ever lie in darkness. To the 2nd I deny the minor. For God founded the universe first for his own sake, then for the sake of the wise. But that others are

Hac Synopsi utimur in Colleg. Salesiano ad studium Sac. Theologiae.

We use this Synopsis in the Salesian College for the study of Sacred Theology.

p. 61

mali, id non à Deo est, sed ab homine quem Deus posuit in manu consilii sui, melius esse ratus de malis benefacere, quàm mala nulla esse permittere.

wicked is not from God, but from man, whom God placed in the hand of his own counsel, judging it better to do good with evils than to permit no evils to exist.

191 Ad 3. neg. antec. Nulla enim est orbis pars, unde homini commodum non accedat. Montes puriorem aërem, saltus pascua, rupes metalla & marmora suppeditant. Flumina pisces alunt, hortos irrigant, urbes ornant, & muniunt. Mare nubes & imbres agrorum feracitati confert, mercesque è remotissimis oris transvehit. Calor & frigus etiam prosunt, is enim tellurem gravidat, ille fruges matúrat: ergo &c. Ad 4. & 5. nego antec. Ærumnae etenim & mors ipsa sunt originalis peccati stipendia. Sed quia haec Atheus irridet. Respondeo 2.: ex his induci homines ad terrenarum rerum contemptum, industriamque laudabilem: monéri ut parce vivant, nec nimia venere ac vino sibimortem accelerent. Ferarum verò nulla est, quae aut opem nobis, aut victum, voluptatem, aut medelam non praebeat. Ad ult. neg. antec. Melior est enim cum imbecillitate sapientia, quàm sine ratione, vel maxima fortitudo. Hactenùs P. Buzzi.

191 To the 3rd I deny the antecedent. For there is no part of the globe from which some advantage does not come to man. The mountains supply purer air, the woodlands pastures, the rocks metals and marbles. Rivers feed fish, water gardens, adorn and fortify cities. The sea contributes clouds and rains to the fertility of the fields, and carries goods across from the remotest shores. Heat and cold too are of use, for the latter makes the earth pregnant, the former ripens the crops: therefore, etc. To the 4th and 5th I deny the antecedent. For hardships, and death itself, are the wages of original sin. But since the Atheist mocks these things, I reply 2.: by these things men are led to contempt of earthly things and to praiseworthy industry; they are warned to live sparingly and not to hasten death upon themselves by excessive venery and wine. Of wild beasts, moreover, there is none which does not furnish us either help, or food, pleasure or remedy. To the last I deny the antecedent. For wisdom with weakness is better than even the greatest strength without reason. Thus far Fr. Buzzi.

192 Opp. 9. Non est certum adspectabilem mundum existere: ergo Dei quoque existentia incerta erit. Resp. 1. neg. antec. Non enim unum est argumentum, quo corporum existentia contra Idealistas evincitur. Resp. 2. neg. conseq. Demonstratur enim Supremi Numinis existentia ex eo etiam quod existat ens contingens, ipsa nimirùm humana mens, cujus existentiam inficiari nequit Idealista, quin velit neminem, ne quidem de propria existentia habere certitudinem posse, quod quàm falsum sit, ne dicam ampliùs, non est, cur longo sermone ostendam.

192 Obj. 9. It is not certain that the visible world exists: therefore the existence of God too will be uncertain. Reply 1: I deny the antecedent. For there is more than one argument by which the existence of bodies is established against the Idealists. Reply 2: I deny the consequence. For the existence of the Supreme Deity is demonstrated also from the fact that a contingent being exists, namely the human mind itself, whose existence the Idealist cannot deny without holding that no one can have certainty even of his own existence; and how false this is, not to say more, there is no reason for me to show at length.

193 Opp. 10. Ex eo quod existat ens contingens colligi certò nequit extare ens necessarium: ergo. Prob. antec.: potest existere ens necessarium, quin existat ens contingens: ergo vicissim potest existere ens contingens, quin existat ens necessarium. Resp. cum Cl. à Brixia neg. antec. ad cujus probationem permitto antec. & nego conseq. Ratio discriminis est evidens. Quum enim in ente contingente non detur ratio sufficiens cur ipsum existat potius, quàm non existat, nequit existere ens contingens quin detur etiam necessarium in quo sufficiens illius ratio contineatur. Contra verò res se habet loquendo de ente necessariò. Hoc enim tale est, ut rationem suae existentiae comprehendat.

193 Obj. 10. From the fact that a contingent being exists, it cannot be gathered with certainty that a necessary being exists: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: a necessary being can exist without a contingent being existing: therefore, in turn, a contingent being can exist without a necessary being existing. I reply with the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia: I deny the antecedent; to its proof I let the antecedent pass and deny the consequence. The reason for the difference is evident. For since in a contingent being there is no sufficient reason why it should exist rather than not exist, a contingent being cannot exist unless there is also a necessary being in which its sufficient reason is contained. The case is the contrary when we speak of the necessary being. For this is such that it comprises the reason of its own existence.

194 Dices: existentia entis contingentis non est necessariò connexa cum ente necessario, alioquin ens contingens necessariò existeret: ergo potest existere ens contingens quin existat ens necessarium. Dist. antec.: id est, non est hujusmodi ut haberi nequeat ens necessarium quin habeatur contingens, conc., hoc est potest extare ens contingens, quin existat necessarium, nego, & conseq. Verum est existentiam entis contingentis, non adeò esse connexam cum ente necessariò, ut extare nequeat ens necessarium; quin

194 You will say: the existence of a contingent being is not necessarily connected with the necessary being; otherwise the contingent being would exist necessarily: therefore a contingent being can exist without a necessary being existing. I distinguish the antecedent: that is, it is not of such a kind that a necessary being cannot be had without a contingent one being had, I grant; that is, a contingent being can exist without a necessary one existing, I deny; and I deny the consequence. It is true that the existence of a contingent being is not so connected with the necessary being that the necessary being could not exist unless there existed

Lib. XII. de Civit. Dei Cap. 15.

Bk. XII of The City of God, ch. 15.

Lib. XI. Confess. cap. 13.

Bk. XI of the Confessions, ch. 13.

p. 62

existat ens contingens. Non enim ens contingens necessariò producitur. At est falsum existentiam entis contingentis non ita connexam esse cum ente necessario, ut prorsus repugnet haberi ens contingens, quin necessarium habeatur. Quum enim ens necessarium rationem obtineat, cur existat contingens, contradictio est, ut existat ens contingens, quin existat necessarium; quemadmodùm evidens in eo est pugna, ut sit effectus, quin causa existat.

a contingent being. For a contingent being is not produced necessarily. But it is false that the existence of a contingent being is not so connected with the necessary being that it is altogether repugnant that a contingent being be had without a necessary one being had. For since the necessary being holds the reason why the contingent exists, it is a contradiction that a contingent being should exist without a necessary one existing; just as the conflict is evident in this, that there should be an effect without a cause existing.

195 Opp. demum. Evidenter non repugnat processus in infinitum in causis efficientibus: ergo evidenter non constat admittendam esse causam, quae sit omnium prima. Omisso antec. neg. conseq. Existentia siquidem Dei demonstrata à nobis ex eo non est, quod infinita causarum series repugnet. Sive enim repugnet, sive non, semper verum est causam á se existentem admitti oportere; quum fieri nequeat ut tota entium collectio eâ ratione sit, ut non esse ex aequo potuerit. Esse itaque Deum O. M. indubium est. Si enim (verbis Ciceronis perorabo) ,, Si enim ratio mecum facit, si eventa, si populi, si nationes, si Graeci, si Barbari, si majores etiam nostri, si denique hoc semper ita putatum est, si summi Philosophi, si Poetae, si Sapientisimi Viri, qui Respublicas constituerunt, qui urbes condiderunt: an dum bestiae loquuntur, expectamus, hominum consentiente auctoritate contenti non sumus ,,? s1. Atque haec de Theologia Naturali totaque Metaphysica dicta sufficiant.

195 Obj. finally. It is evidently not repugnant that there be a process to infinity in efficient causes: therefore it is evidently not established that a cause must be admitted which is the first of all. Passing over the antecedent, I deny the consequence. For the existence of God has not been demonstrated by us from the fact that an infinite series of causes is repugnant. For whether it is repugnant or not, it is always true that a cause existing from itself must be admitted, since it cannot be that the whole collection of beings should be in such a way that it could equally have not been. That God, the Best and Greatest, exists is therefore beyond doubt. For (I shall conclude in the words of Cicero): “For if reason is on my side, if events, if peoples, if nations, if Greeks, if Barbarians, if our forefathers too, if, finally, this has always been so thought, if the greatest Philosophers, if the Poets, if the Wisest Men, who established Commonwealths, who founded cities: are we waiting until the beasts speak, and are we not content with the agreeing authority of men?” (m). And let what has been said of Natural Theology and of the whole of Metaphysics suffice.

De Divin. Lib. 1. Cap. 19.

On Divination, bk. 1, ch. 19.

sivè

OR

PHILOSOPHIAE MORALIS — OF MORAL PHILOSOPHY

ELEMENTA. — THE ELEMENTS

PRAEFATIO. — PREFACE

Ethicam, sive Moralem Philosophiam dirigendis, perficiendisque moribus institutam esse, ut virtutis amore, vitiorumque fugâ veram felicitatem, ac beatitudinem consequamur, nemo est qui nesciat. Hinc ars bene vivendi, animi medicina, virtutis indagatrix, expultrixque vitiorum, ars vitae, morum magistra meritò solet adpellari. Definiri ea potest, quamoptimè: cognitio boni, vel scientia ostendens rationem ad summum bonum, ejusque fruitionem perveniendi. Quum verò nos non modò Philosophos, sed Catholicos etiam esse sentiamus ac mirificè gloriemur, meritò Eruditorum reprehensionem incurrerem si animi medicinam nec summis, ut ajunt, labris Adolescentibus degustandam proponerem.

thics, or Moral Philosophy, has been instituted for directing E and perfecting morals, so that by love of virtue and flight from vices we may attain true felicity and beatitude: there is no one who does not know this. Hence it is deservedly wont to be called the art of living well, the medicine of the mind, the investigator of virtue and the expeller of vices, the art of life, the mistress of morals. It can be defined, and very well: the knowledge of the good, or the science showing the way to arrive at the highest good and at the enjoyment of it. But since we feel that we are not only Philosophers but Catholics too, and glory in this wonderfully, I would deservedly incur the reproach of the Learned if I set the medicine of the mind before Youths not even to be tasted, as they say, with the tips of the lips.

p. 2

Innumera siquidem dicenda nobis occurrerent, si omnia complecti mens foret, quae à Veteribus, Recentioribusque Philosophis in adornanda Morum scientia explicari conspicimus: praecipua tamen, ac summa veluti capita seligémus, ut nobiliora morum praecepta breviori, clariorique ordine complectamur. Quum verò nemo possit ad summum bonum scilicèt Deum, ejusque fruitionem pervenire nisi officia erga Deum, erga seipsum, erga alios observet, si virtutem non colat, vitiaque detestetur, hinc omnis Ethica ad duo veluti supremà capita revocari optimè potest. Primò itaque de Officiis disseremus, tùm de virtute generatim ejusque causis & signis aliqua delibabimus. Longiùs enim orationem protahere praescripti Elementorum limites haud patiuntur. Sit itaque.

For countless things would present themselves for us to say, if we had a mind to embrace everything that we see explained by the Ancients and the Moderns in setting out the science of Morals; we shall, however, select the principal and, as it were, the chief heads, so as to embrace the nobler precepts of morals in a briefer and clearer order. Since, moreover, no one can attain the highest good, namely God, and the enjoyment of Him, unless he observes his duties toward God, toward himself and toward others, unless he cultivates virtue and detests vices, the whole of Ethics can very well be reduced to two, as it were, supreme heads. First, therefore, we shall discourse on Duties; then we shall touch on a few things concerning virtue in general and its causes and signs. For the prescribed limits of the Elements do not allow us to draw out the discussion any further. Let there be, then,

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De variis hominum officiis erga Deum, se ipsos, alios, & erga Rempublicam.

On the various duties of men toward God, toward themselves, toward others, and toward the Commonwealth. 1

1 „Quum multa sint in Philosophia gravia, & utilia, accuratè copiosèque à Philosophis disputata, latissimè patére videntur ea, quae de officiis tradita ab illis, & praecepta sunt. Nulla enim vitae pars, neque publicis, neque privatis, neque forensibus, nec domesticis in rebus, neque si tecum agas quid, neque si cum altero contrahas, vacare officio potest; in eoque edendo sita vitae est honestas omnis, & in negligendo turpitudo.„ ait Eloquentissimus Consularis Philosophus M. T. Cicero 3. Et rectè quidem: quum enim homo exlex non sit, prosequatur officia quaedam oportet, ut fini suo optimè respondeat.

“Although there are many weighty and useful things in Philosophy, discussed accurately and copiously by Philosophers, those things which they have handed down and prescribed concerning duties seem to extend most widely. For no part of life, neither in public nor in private affairs, neither in the courts nor at home, neither if you transact anything with yourself nor if you contract with another, can be free of duty; and in discharging it lies all that is honorable in life, and in neglecting it all that is base,” says the most eloquent consular Philosopher M. T. Cicero (a). And rightly indeed: for since man is not without law, he must pursue certain duties in order to answer best to his end.

2 Hujusmodi officia & à ratione, & à Revelatione ducuntur. Est enim in praesenti rerum providentia lumen rationis obscurum, ac debile, cui proindè ne erret, alterius luminis praesidum necessarium est. Jam verò, quae ex ratione & Revelatione officia praestare homo debet, vel Deum respiciunt, & sunt Religionis, vel ad hominem prout sui custos est, referuntur, vel hominem spectant, prout ad alios refertur, & Societatis adpellantur, vel prout ad Rempublicam, & officia Civis nuncupantur.

2 Duties of this kind are derived both from reason and from Revelation. For in the present providence of things the light of reason is dim and weak, and therefore, lest it err, it needs the protection of another light. Now the duties which man must perform by reason and Revelation either regard God, and are those of Religion; or are referred to man inasmuch as he is his own guardian; or regard man inasmuch as he is related to others, and are called those of Society; or inasmuch as he is related to the Commonwealth, and are named the duties of the Citizen.

3 Quantum ad Deum adtinet, certum imprimis est non solùm interno, & spirituali, sed etiam externo, & sensibili Religionis

3 As regards God, it is certain first of all that not only with an internal and spiritual, but also with an external and sensible worship of Religion

De Officiis Lib. 1. cap. 1.

On Duties, bk. 1, ch. 1.

p. 3

cultu esse adorandum. Religionis nomine intelligimus cultum amoris, obsequii, & servitutis, ei praestandum cui debetur. Atque hinc vera Religio quae Catholica est, omnem impietatem, & superstitionem excludit. Impietatem voco, & neglectum Religionis, & contemptum, quorum utrumque directè cum rationis lumine pugnat: superstitio verò vel est cultus ortus ex erroneis de Deo opinionibus, vel exhibitus rei, cui non debetur, vel Deo quidem exhibitus, sed modis, & ritibus ejus perfectionibus non consentaneis. Hinc & Atheismus, & Pantheismus, & Polyteismus, & superstitio Mahumedana, & pervicacia Judaica, & omnis omninò secta ab Ecclesia Catholica proscripta, eliminatur.

He must be adored. By the name of Religion we understand the worship of love, of obedience and of service, to be rendered to Him to whom it is due. And hence the true Religion, which is the Catholic one, excludes all impiety and superstition. I call impiety both the neglect and the contempt of Religion, each of which directly conflicts with the light of reason; superstition, on the other hand, is either a worship arising from erroneous opinions about God, or one shown to a thing to which it is not due, or one shown indeed to God, but in ways and rites not consonant with His perfections. Hence Atheism, and Pantheism, and Polytheism, and the Mahometan superstition, and Jewish obstinacy, and every sect whatever proscribed by the Catholic Church, are excluded.

4 Atque ex hoc conficitur summam esse obligationem amplectendi Religionem Catholicam, utpotè quae sola est vera Religio Revelata. In ea enim signa credibilitatis deprehenduntur, qualia sunt praecipua, sanctitas & unitas doctrinae, tum etiam vitae probitas praecipuorum, maximè primorum praedicatorum, ac propagatorum, signa quae loquentem Deum testantur, uti miracula, & prophetiae opere completae, Martyrum testimonium, continua succesivo Religionis Interpretum, ac controversiarum Judicum. Hujusmodi Religio nefariis perditissimorum hominum adgressionibus nequaquam victa, à primordio rerum usque ad haec quibus vivimus tempora, immobilis restitit, constansque: est ergo ipsa Dei opus.

4 And from this it follows that there is the highest obligation to embrace the Catholic Religion, inasmuch as it alone is the true revealed Religion. For in it are found the signs of credibility, of which the chief are: the holiness and unity of its doctrine; then also the probity of life of its principal, and above all of its first, preachers and propagators; the signs that testify that God is speaking, such as miracles and prophecies fulfilled in deed; the testimony of the Martyrs; the continual succession of the Interpreters of Religion and of the Judges of controversies. Such a Religion, in no way overcome by the wicked assaults of the most abandoned men, has stood immovable and constant from the beginning of things down to these times in which we live: it is therefore the work of God Himself.

5 Quis tamen induxisset animum ut hoc crederet, Ornatissimi Adolescentes, nisi res ipsa maximo cum nostrorum temporum dedécore id ipsum demonstrasset? Turba hominum emersit, qui statuerunt non antiquas superstitiones revocare, sed superstitioni oppositam impietatem disseminantes, post secula tot ex terrarum orbe eliminare Religionem, Deumque ipsum ejus auctorem é Caelo detrudere. Hujus consilii Hobbesius, Spinosa, Tolandus, Bayle recensentur inter insigniores duces. Hos veluti conductitia gens, sequuntur Collinius, Wolstonus, Marchio Argensis, Voltaire, Rouseau, Helvetius, aliique plurimi qui prae pudore non audentes nomen adponere suum pestiferis liberculis Epistolarum, Speciminum, Tractatuum, Cogitationum, Examinum, Ephemeridum 2,

5 Yet who would have brought his mind to believe this, most accomplished Young Men, had not the thing itself demonstrated it, to the very great disgrace of our times? A crowd of men has arisen who have resolved, not to call back the ancient superstitions, but, by disseminating the impiety that is the opposite of superstition, to eliminate Religion from the face of the earth after so many centuries, and to thrust God Himself, its author, down from Heaven. Among the more notable leaders of this design are counted Hobbes, Spinoza, Toland, Bayle. These are followed, like a hired band, by Collins, Woolston, the Marquis d’Argens, Voltaire, Rousseau, Helvétius, and very many others, who, not daring for shame to put their names to their pestilential little books of Letters, Specimens, Treatises, Thoughts, Examinations, Ephemerides (b), and to many

p. 4

pluribusque aliis hujus farinae operibus, quibus Europa scatèt, descenderunt in aciem.

other works of this stamp, with which Europe teems, have come down into the battle line.

6 Equidem dijudicare non aussim, (verbis utor Clariss. Valsechi), quinam potius in homine sapienti turbam hanc intuente excitari sensus debeat, num indignationis, an contemptus, an verò misericordiae. ¡Heu miseros! ¿Tantùmne vobis virium esse putatis, ut aliquot pagellis in lucem éditis, tot seculorum consensum vos refellere, erroris coarguere universum hominum genus, vocem naturae comprimere, Supremoque Numini bellum inferre posse arbitramini? ¿An Religionem illam, quam non tunc dominans idololatria, non Tyrannorum crudelitas, armis totius Romani imperii instructa, non acumen tot Philosophorum in disputandi artibus omnibus exercitatorum opprimere potuerunt, avaritia, voluptas, mos, gestus cupiditatibus omnibus orbis corrupti, effeminatique domabunt? Fabulae.

6 For my part I would not dare to decide (I use the words of the most distinguished Valsecchi) which feeling ought rather to be aroused in a wise man beholding this crowd, whether that of indignation, or of contempt, or rather of pity. Ah, wretched men! Do you think you have so much strength that you judge yourselves able, by bringing out a few little pages, to refute the consensus of so many centuries, to convict the whole human race of error, to stifle the voice of nature, and to wage war on the Supreme Deity? Will that Religion which neither idolatry, then dominant, nor the cruelty of Tyrants equipped with the arms of the whole Roman empire, nor the acumen of so many Philosophers practiced in all the arts of disputation could overwhelm, be subdued by avarice, pleasure, the manners and bearing of a world corrupted by every desire and made effeminate? Fables.

7 Quinimò ipsa omnium óbicum victrix, cordium triumphàtrix, ingeniorumque, multiplicavit victorias suas certaminibus, suosque adversarios post pugnam, propugnatores suos acerrimos est experta. ¿An Religionem, inquam, istam prosternet, delebitque omninò, infamis quaedam satyra, Libertinarum fabellarum collectio; delectus aliquot ambiguorum verborum, pueriliumque sophismatum? Nisi haec est summa audacia, imò insignis vesania nescio quaenam unquam possit esse. Et re vera satis est, vel obiter legere horum Magistrorum scriptiuncula, ut statim dignoscantur indicia levium, & delirantium. Ne, quaeso, putetis, vos in iis

7 Nay rather, Religion itself, victorious over all obstacles, triumphant over hearts and minds, has multiplied its victories by its contests, and has found its adversaries, after the battle, to be its keenest champions. Shall that Religion, I say, be laid low and utterly destroyed by some infamous satire, a collection of libertine little tales, a selection of a few ambiguous words and puerile sophisms? If this is not the height of audacity, nay, a signal madness, I do not know what ever could be. And in truth it is enough to read even in passing the little writings of these Masters for the marks of light-minded and raving men to be recognized at once. Do not, I beg you, think that in them you can find

reperire posse systema aliquod deductum benè, ut prima imis, media, & imis, & primis respondeant, & aptè inter se cohaereant, quo & Religioni, & Deo O. M. bellum inferatur.

some well-deduced system, in which the first things answer to the last, the middle ones both to the last and to the first, and all cohere aptly with one another, by which war might be waged both on Religion and on God, the Best and Greatest.

8 Nil nisi confusae audiuntur declamationes, & voces; veluti audiebantur in terra Senaar inter ingentis turris opifices, qui ne ipsi quidem mutuos sermones suos intelligébant. Evomit unusquisque infanda, & falsa, sed tam varia, tam contraria, ut non solum idem significent, sed haec, illa destruant.

8 Nothing is heard but confused declamations and voices, as they were heard in the land of Sennaar among the builders of the huge tower, who did not even understand one another’s speech. Each one spews out unspeakable and false things, but so various, so contrary, that not only do they not mean the same thing, but these destroy those.

9 Negat Atheus Deum esse: Deista 2 ait, esse, sed res humanas non curare. Naturalista contra utrumque pugnat, defenditque summa ope & Providentiam, & Deum. Hic autem quum nolit in Deo recognoscere, nisi quod ipse ingenio suo tam hebeti capere potest, & Athei, & Deistae telis se praebet confodiendum. Dat Helvetius homini animam ejusmodi, quàm equi, lupique habent, illamque libertate quàvis spoliat. Rousseau eam liberam facit, & spiritualem: at primaeva originalis conditio hominis, sententiâ ejus, nihil differt ab origine luporum, & equorum.

9 The Atheist denies that God exists; the Deist (c) says that He exists, but does not care for human affairs. The Naturalist fights against both, and defends with all his might both Providence and God. But this man, since he will recognize nothing in God except what he himself can grasp with so dull a wit, offers himself to be pierced by the weapons both of the Atheist and of the Deist. Helvétius gives man a soul of the same kind as horses and wolves have, and strips it of all freedom. Rousseau makes it free and spiritual: but the primeval, original condition of man, in his opinion, differs in nothing from the origin of wolves and horses.

10 Adserunt ii hominem totum perire, pereunte vitâ: alii putant, eum futurum immortalem. Inter hos tamen quidam sentiunt eum in altera vita nullis puniendum suppliciis; alii haec supplicia futura volunt, quae necessariò lex praescribit; irrídent alii has leges, has poenas tanquàm pura putaque Poetarum, & Regum commenta. Si hos audis, ab aeterno fuit mundus, si illos, initium habuit, ut placet unis à Deo, ut alteris à casu & fortuito concursu atomorum aeternarum, & errantium.

10 These assert that the whole man perishes when life perishes; others think that he will be immortal. Among the latter, however, some hold that in the other life he is to be punished with no torments; others will have it that there will be those torments which the law necessarily prescribes; others laugh at these laws, these penalties, as the pure and simple fictions of Poets and of Kings. If you listen to these, the world has been from eternity; if to those, it had a beginning: from God, as some hold; from chance and the fortuitous concourse of eternal and wandering atoms, as others do.

11 Quod tamen est non minus verum, quam mirandum, illud est, unumquemque eorum bello irrequieto in se saevíre, & semeptisum suis se armis confodere. Quot sint in Hobbesii operibus, quorum haec evertunt illa, ii unùm ignorant, qui ea non legerunt. Tota Spinosae Ethica innititur definitioni, quae duobus modis intelligi potest, quorum unus, qui verus est, alterum evertit; hic autem eversus librum totum, qui ex definitione pendet à principio ad finem usque, Geometricè destruit 2 Libertinorum grex

11 What, however, is no less true than astonishing is this: that each of them rages against himself in a restless war, and very often pierces himself with his own weapons. How many things there are in the works of Hobbes of which some overturn others, only those are ignorant who have not read them. The whole Ethics of Spinoza rests on a definition which can be understood in two ways, of which the one, which is true, overturns the other; and this other, once overturned, destroys geometrically the whole book, which depends on the definition from beginning to end (d). The herd of Libertines

Deista, sive Theista adpellatur, qui Deum existere quidem concedit, sed Religionem nullam, cultum nullum profitetur. Religionem omnem, Divinamque Revelationem tanquam meras fabulas fastidiosè traducunt Deistae, satisque esse garriunt; si Deus in naturae, cordisque simplicitate adoretur.

A Deist, or Theist, is the name given to one who indeed grants that God exists, but professes no Religion, no worship. The Deists disdainfully decry all Religion and divine Revelation as mere fables, and prattle that it is enough if God is adored in the simplicity of nature and of the heart.

hoc in capite duces suos praeclaros religiosè imitatur, à quibus quum mendacium didicerit etiam illud didicit, ut respuat, quod adprobavit sibique semper contradicat.
