Definitio cui innititur Spinosae systema est definitio substantiae his concepta verbis. Per substantiam intelligo id, quod in se est, & per se concipitur: hoc est, id, cujus conceptus non indiget conceptu alterius rei, à quo formari debeat (Ethic. P. 1. Def 3). Jam verò haec verba id quod in se est duplicem significationem habere possunt. I. quod est in se, hoc est, quod est ex se, exclusâ causâ, quae illud producat. II. id quod est in se, id est, quod est per se ipsum excluso subjecto, quod illud sustentet. Modi ut ex. gr. motus, figura &c. non existunt ex se, quoniam indigent causâ à qua producantur, sed neque existunt per se; requirunt enim subjectum, quo inhaereant, ut pila ex. gr. Ens autèm perfectissimum existit per se, & ex se. Non enim indiget subjecto, à quo sustentetur, sed ne habere quidem causam potest, á qua producatur. Equus per se existit, quum nullo subjecto inhaereat; at non existit ex se, quum habuerit causam à qua fuit productus. Spinosa usus est ambigua dictione existit in se, vultque proprium esse substantiae existere ex se ipsâ, exclusâ causa quae illam producat; sed hoc est, quod omnes negant, & quod nusquam in libro suo probavit Recutitus ille philosophus. Transeamus ad alias definitionis partes, & praeunte adlatae distinctionis face, illius fraudem detegemus. Per substantiam intelligo id, quod in se est, additque, & per se concipitur. Si credit Spinosa substantiae conceptum esse tam absolutum, ut nullam importet relationem cum subjecto, quod eam sustineat, ut motus eam importat ad mobile, verè sentit, sed hoc nihil Pantheismo opitulatur. ¿Quid ergo vult? Hoc nempè: conceptum substantiae ita esse absolutum, ut à se removeat quamcumque relationem ad causam, quae illam producat, sed hoc falsum omninò est, & hoc nunquam probaturus est. Idem dicendum de aliis verbis, quae sequuntur, quae impius Appella addit explicaturus adlatam substantiae definitionem, hoc est, substantia est id, cujus conceptus non indiget conceptu alterius rei, à quo formari debeat. Si enim significare vult conceptum substantiae debere à se excludere relationem ad aliam substantiam, ad quam ipsa referatur, veluti effectus ad causam, id negamus, neque ille unquam id probabit. Vafer tamen Haebreus hoc intelligebat; ex hoc enim uno falso principio derivavit totum suum Pantheisticum systema, volebatque in ea definitione includere tanquam fundamentum id, quod erat totius controversiae caput; hoc est, esse de essentia substantiae, ut existat ex se, exclusâ quacumque causâ, neque posse unquam concipi in substantia unâ relationem effectus ad aliam substantiam, tanquam ad causam ipsius procreatricem.

The definition on which Spinoza’s system rests is the definition of substance conceived in these words: By substance I understand that which is in itself and is conceived through itself: that is, that whose concept does not need the concept of another thing from which it must be formed (Ethics, Pt. 1, Def. 3). Now these words, that which is in itself, can have a twofold meaning. I. That which is in itself, that is, which is from itself, excluding a cause that produces it. II. That which is in itself, to that is, which is through itself, excluding a subject that sustains it. Modes, e.g. motion, shape, etc., do not exist from themselves, because they need a cause by which they are produced; but neither do they exist through themselves, for they require a subject in which to inhere, e.g. a ball. But the most perfect Being exists through itself and from itself. For it does not need a subject by which to be sustained, nor can it even have a cause by which it is produced. A horse exists through itself, since it inheres in no subject; but it does not exist from itself, since it has had a cause by which it was produced. Spinoza used the ambiguous expression exists in itself, and will have it proper to substance to exist from itself, excluding a cause that produces it; but this is what everyone denies, and what that circumcised philosopher nowhere proved in his book. Let us pass to the other parts of the definition and, with the torch of the distinction just given going before us, uncover his fraud. By substance I understand that which is in itself, and he adds, and is conceived through itself. If Spinoza believes that the concept of substance is so absolute that it implies no relation to a subject that sustains it, as motion implies one to the movable, he thinks truly, but this helps Pantheism not at all. What then does he mean? This, namely: that the concept of substance is so absolute that it removes from itself every relation to a cause that produces it; but this is altogether false, and this he will never prove. The same must be said of the other words that follow, which the impious Apella adds to explain the definition of substance just given, that is, substance is that whose concept does not need the concept of another thing from which it must be formed. For if he means that the concept of substance must exclude from itself a relation to another substance to which it is referred, as an effect to a cause, we deny it, nor will he ever prove it. The crafty Hebrew, however, understood this; for from this one false principle he derived his whole Pantheistic system, and he wished to include in that definition, as its foundation, that which was the head of the whole controversy: namely, that it is of the essence of substance that it exist from itself, excluding any cause whatever, and that there can never be conceived in a substance a relation of effect to another substance as to the cause that procreates it.

p. 7

Hierosolyma Romam, ab Augusti seculo ad Ludovici aetatem. A Caraibis Antillarum fit transitus ad Ottentotos Africae; ab his ad Groelandos Boreales; inde ad homines sylvestres aliarum regionum remotiorum. Hinc orbis plagarum adeò inter se dissitarum modò examinantur leges, modo conferuntur inter se mores, nunc enarrantur turpitudines, nunc plausibus celebratur irreligio. Antiquitates Sinenses majus pondus, quàm Sacra Genesis penès eos habent. Diodorus, Strabo, & Tacitus citantur Judaicarum antiquitatum Moyse ipso peritiores. Horatius, Petronius, Manilius, Lucretius, Poppius sapientiae incomparabiles praeceptores adferuntur.

to Rome, from the age of Augustus to the age of Louis. A passage is made from the Caribs of the Antilles to the Hottentots of Africa; from these to the northern Greenlanders; thence to the wild men of other remote regions. Hence the laws of regions of the world so unlike one another are now examined, now their customs are compared with one another, now their turpitudes are recounted, now irreligion is celebrated with applause. Chinese antiquities carry greater weight with them than sacred Genesis. Diodorus, Strabo and Tacitus are cited as more expert in Jewish antiquities than Moses himself. Horace, Petronius, Manilius, Lucretius, Poppius are brought forward as incomparable teachers of wisdom.

13 Totum tamèn id saepius fit, quin auctorum loca percenseant; ut plurimùm infideliter loca adferunt; semper autem sine arte Critica, satis namque est ut enuncientur voce impávidâ, censoria, quae sola potest, ut opinantur, dare pondus fabulis, & mendaciis.

13 Yet all this is mostly done without the passages of the authors being examined; for the most part they bring in those passages unfaithfully, and always without the art of Criticism; for it is enough that they be pronounced in a fearless, censorious voice, which alone, as they suppose, can give weight to fables and lies.

14 Haerent in obtutu Libertini juvenes tantae eruditionis congeriem, tantam rerum varietatem, tantam decidendi confidentiam legentes. Admirantur hujusmodi Philosophos velut sapientiae oracula. Religio, cujus neque fundamenta, neque systema meditati sunt unquam, in eorum mentibus vacillat. Praeceptores autem isti existimant re ipsâ se, quod intendebant fuisse consequutos, & rapidâ, turbulentaque loquacitate reverâ ostendisse Religionem Catholicam fictionem esse, Evangelium jocum, lymphatos ejus Martyres, Sanctos Patres nihil omninò scire, omnesque veros Catholicos gregem stolidorum, inutiles, imò Societati, & Reipublicae perniciosos esse.

14 Libertine youths stand fixed in their gaze as they read such a heap of erudition, such a variety of matters, such confidence in deciding. They admire Philosophers of this kind as oracles of wisdom. Religion, whose foundations and whose system they have never meditated, wavers in their minds. These teachers, for their part, think that they have in fact achieved what they intended, and by their rapid and turbulent loquacity have really shown that the Catholic Religion is a fiction, the Gospel a jest, its Martyrs madmen, that the Holy Fathers know nothing at all, and that all true Catholics are a herd of fools, useless, nay pernicious to Society and to the Commonwealth.

15 Quod si in farragine tantâ rerum inutilium & absurdarum, sophismata quaedam sunt intermixta, quae Religionem Naturalem & Revelatam adgrediantur, hoc tamen certissimum est, non semel, sed saepissimè à nostris Doctoribus & praecipuè ab Angelico Mag. D. Thoma Aquinate ea fuisse dissoluta, imò, ut ita dicam, in cinerem redacta & difflata.

15 But if in so great a farrago of useless and absurd things certain sophisms are mixed in which attack natural and revealed Religion, this nevertheless is most certain: that these have been resolved, not once but very often, by our Doctors, and especially by the Angelic Master St. Thomas Aquinas, nay, so to speak, reduced to ashes and blown away.

16 Intelligetis jam non sine gravi causâ me à principio dixisse, nullos alios quàm indignationis, contemptus miserationis sensus in homine prudenti excitari posse, quotiescumque hos intuetur Scriptores, qui artibus tam puerilibus se posse Religionem evertere confidunt; eam Religionem dico, cujus Divina origo, dógmatum veritas sanctitas praeceptorum, eximia virtus, & protectionis vis, quâ munitur, effecerunt, ut per tot seculorum cursus, post tot casus neque ferro vinceretur, neque scriptis concuteretur; neque superaretur superstitione, & impietate: uno verbo ut retunderet omnes hominum, daemonisque impetus.

16 You will now understand that it was not without grave cause that I said at the beginning that no other feelings than those of indignation, contempt and pity can be aroused in a prudent man whenever he looks upon these Writers, who trust that with such puerile arts they can overturn Religion: that Religion, I say, whose divine origin, the truth of its dogmas, the holiness of its precepts, and the eminent virtue and force of the protection by which it is defended, have brought it about that through the course of so many centuries, after so many vicissitudes, it has been neither conquered by the sword, nor shaken by writings, nor overcome by superstition and impiety: in a word, that it has beaten back all the assaults of men and of demons.

17 In tanta ergo pestilentissimorum colluvie librorum, quibus, (ut sapientissimè loquitur felic. record. Clemens Papa XIII. 3

17 In so great a cesspool, then, of most pestilential books, by which (as Pope Clement XIII of happy memory most wisely says (e)) men

p. 8

homines corrupti, & reprobi circa Fidem impudentissimâ licentiâ cum impunitate conjuncta absurdissimas, impiasque opiniones in imperitorum animos conantur infundere; necessarium omninò duxi commonere vos, ut ab hujusmodi librorum lectione, si (quod Deus non sinat) in manus fortassè vestras aliquandò inciderint omnino abstineatis, ne vos decipiant per philosophiam, & inanem fallaciam secundum traditionem hominum, & non secundum Christum, ut loquitur S. Paulus 3. Sed unde egressa fuit oratio revertatur.

corrupt and reprobate concerning the Faith, with a most impudent license joined with impunity, try to pour most absurd and impious opinions into the minds of the unlearned, I have thought it altogether necessary to warn you that, should books of this kind (which God forbid) perhaps at some time fall into your hands, you abstain altogether from reading them, lest they cheat you by philosophy, and vain deceit; according to the tradition of men, and not according to Christ, as St. Paul says (f). But let our discourse return to the point from which it set out.

18 Quantum ad Deum adtinet, quum praestantissimus ille sit, summumque jus, summamque auctoritatem in omnia jure ac meritò sibi vindicet, quisque intelligit, illum tanto obsequio ac veneratione prosequendum, quantum Optimo rerum Conditori, & Amantissimo Conservatori debeatur. Multa sunt quibus nostrum erga alios obsequium testificamur, & quidem amor, obsequii nostri praecipuum argumentum est. Fit enim illo, ut mirum in modum eos studio ac pietate colamus, quos benevolentiâ nostra dignos esse censemus. Dubium ergo esse non potest, quin Deus O. M. qui jure dominii à nobis colendus est, prae reliquis & amandus sit, & summoperè diligendus. Nec certè una tantum ratio est, qua ad id praestandum adigamur. Est namque Deus summum illud bonum, quod si oculis cerneretur, mirabiles, amores (ut de Sapientia ait Plato) excitaret sui. Quippè quidquid nobis in hac vita bene est, ab eo uno proficisci intelligimus, aeternam beatitudinem in altera ex ejus fruitione recepturi.

18 As regards God, since He is most excellent and rightly and deservedly claims for Himself the supreme right and the supreme authority over all things, everyone understands that He is to be honored with as great a homage and veneration as is owed to the Best Founder and the most Loving Preserver of things. There are many things by which we testify our homage toward others, and indeed love is the chief proof of our homage. For by it it comes about that we cultivate in a wonderful way, with zeal and devotion, those whom we judge worthy of our benevolence. There can therefore be no doubt that God, the Best and Greatest, who by right of dominion is to be worshipped by us, is to be loved above all else and cherished supremely. Nor indeed is there only one reason by which we are driven to do this. For God is that highest good which, if it were seen with the eyes, would arouse (as Plato says of Wisdom) wondrous loves of itself. For whatever is good for us in this life we understand to proceed from Him alone, and we are to receive eternal beatitude in the other life from the enjoyment of Him.

19 Hinc à Sacris Literis erùdimur Deum ex toto corde, ex tota anima, & totis viribus diligendum esse, 2 ut si cor nostrum perenni, ac irrequietâ veluti flammâ incensum, amoris victima consumi posset, vix, ac ne vix quidem amor ille par foret, ut aliquas amantissimi Patris amori vices rependeret. Omnibus itaque animi viribus nobis est enitendum, ut Deum super omnia diligamus, & quandoquidem Deus charitas, & ignis est, ignem venit mittere in terram, nec aliud vult nisi ut accendatur 2 ipsum lacrymis, effusisque votis rogare debemus, ut vehementius ille divinae charitatis ardor in nostris cordibus accendatur, adfectus omnes consumat, nosque demum placabilem, Deoque placentem hostiam efficiat.

19 Hence we are taught by Sacred Scripture that God is to be loved with the whole heart, with the whole soul, and with all one’s strength (g), so that, if our heart, kindled as it were by a perpetual and restless flame, could be consumed as a victim of love, that love would scarcely, nay not even scarcely, be equal to repaying in some measure the love of a most loving Father. With all the powers of the mind, therefore, we must strive to love God above all things; and since God is charity, and is a fire, and came to cast fire on the earth, and wills nothing else but that it be kindled (h), we ought to ask Him Himself with tears and outpoured prayers that the ardor of divine charity may be kindled more vehemently in our hearts, consume all our affections, and at last make us a victim acceptable and pleasing to God.

20 Supremum verò numen non amore solum, sed etiam timore veneramur. Quoniam autem, ut Scholae loquuntur, duplex est timor Dei, filialis, nimirum, ac servilis, praestat utrumque ad illud colendum adhibere. Primus ab ejus amore nascitur, nec potest ab hoc dulci vinculo separari. Alter oritur à poena, nec potest à servitute sejungi. Huic enim, & timori certissima quoque fides addenda est. ¿Quis enim non fidat ei, quem nec decipi, nec decipere posse certo sciat? Est

20 We venerate the Supreme Deity, however, not with love alone but also with fear. And since, as the Schools say, the fear of God is twofold, namely filial and servile, it is best to employ both in worshipping Him. The first is born of love for Him and cannot be separated from this sweet bond. The other arises from punishment and cannot be disjoined from servitude. To this love, moreover, and to fear, a most certain faith must also be added. For who would not trust Him whom he knows for certain can neither be deceived nor deceive? God is indeed
