Letter in the form of a Brief, given to Fr. Anton. Valsecchi on 21 March, in the year 1767.

Ad Coloss. Cap. 2. ℣. 8.

To the Colossians, ch. 2, v. 8.

Math. Cap. 22. ℣. 37.

Matthew, ch. 22, v. 37.

Luc. 12. ℣. 29.

Luke 12, v. 29.

p. 9

quidem Deus ipsa ratio suprema, ipsa bonitas, ipsaque veritas. De ejus ergo promissis, dictisque, ubi constet, dixisse, & promisisse, nemini licet dubitare. Ex fide necessariò consequitur Spes, qua & praemium virtuti constitutum expectare debemus, & auxilia etiam illa, quae cum virium nostrarum imbecillitatem adjuvent, sunt proinde ad illud consequendum omninò necessaria.

supreme reason itself, goodness itself, and truth itself. Concerning His promises and words, therefore, once it is established that He has spoken and promised, no one may doubt. From faith there necessarily follows Hope, by which we ought to expect both the reward appointed for virtue and also those helps which, since they assist the weakness of our powers, are therefore altogether necessary for attaining it.

21 Amor itaque ille filialis, quo Deum, veluti Patrem diligimus, excitare nos debet, ut ab illo bona cuncta nobis profutura certò sperare possimus: ideoque ab illo nobis opem, in adversis rebus auxilium petere, atque exorare debemus, ut Redemptor ipse saepissimè nos ad orandum, atque petendum invitat: petite, & accipietis, quaerite, & invenietis; pulsate, & aperietur vobis Divino tamen consilio nos admonet, ut in Christi ipsius nomine petamus Siquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo dabit vobis.

21 That filial love, therefore, by which we love God as a Father, ought to rouse us to hope with certainty from Him for all the goods that will profit us; and therefore we ought to ask and entreat of Him help, and aid in adversity, as the Redeemer Himself very often invites us to pray and to ask: Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. By divine counsel, however, He admonishes us to ask in the name of Christ Himself: If you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you.

22 Verum ne ab ipsa quidem invocatione Dei precibusque, velit nolit Rousseau, abstinere possumus. Haec enim officii nostri prima pars est, cui certè deesse non possumus, quin maxima nobis incommoda, & detrimenta importemus. Quippe quum tot, tantisque malis adflictemur, in iis recreari Supremi tantum Numinis potestate, ac sapientiâ datum est. Immortales quoque Deo non habendae solum, sed etiam agendae sunt gratiae. ¿Quis namque innumeris beneficiis cumulatus se ab hoc officio praestando immunem esse arbitretur? Quod si vel uno creationis, & conservationis adfecti beneficio Deo plurimum deberemus, quid de ea vitae conditione statuendum in qua nobis longè plura sunt impertita?

22 But not even from the invocation of God and from prayer can we abstain, whether Rousseau will or no. For this is the first part of our duty, in which we certainly cannot fail without bringing on ourselves the greatest inconveniences and losses. For since we are afflicted by so many and such great evils, it is granted to us to be refreshed in them only by the power and wisdom of the Supreme Deity. Immortal thanks, too, are not only to be felt toward God, but also to be rendered to Him. For who, heaped with innumerable benefits, would think himself exempt from performing this duty? And if, endowed with the single benefit of creation and conservation alone, we would owe God very much, what must we judge of that condition of life in which far more has been imparted to us?

23 At haec interna sunt Religionis officia. De externis autem haec veluti summatim nobis videntur statuenda. Deus non modò interno, & spirituali, sed etiam externo, & sensibili Religionis cultu est adorandus, ut supra diximus. Et sanè nihil est in nobis, quod Dei munus non sit, illique propterea omni ex parte subjectum. Igitur externa quoque corporis membra illi serviant oportet. Cui argumento alterum quoque accedit, & illud quidem gravissimum ex ipsa naturae nostrae conditione desumptum. Si enim agnitio numinis, Societatis naturalis, ac status civilis vinculum est necessarium, ejusdem quoque cultus utrique hominum conditioni erit summopere commendatus. Certum est autem nec Societatem, nec Civilem hanc formam absque sensibili operatione posse subsistere, quamobrem ad eam statuendam cultus etiam externus, ac sensibilis accedat necesse est. Ex lege externi cultus praestandi alia consequuntur officia. Primum est, ut de Deo, deque rebus Divinis, non nisi honorificentissimè colloquamur. Secundum, ut omnibus externis argumentis, interna officia ad aliorum exemplum manifestemus. Tertium, ut Divinorum etiam scientiam aliis explicemus, ut sic vicissim alter alteri prosit. Tandem, ut Dei gloriam omni pietate, & studio promoveamus.

23 But these are the internal duties of Religion. Concerning the external ones, the following seem to us to be laid down, as it were in summary. God is to be adored not only with an internal and spiritual, but also with an external and sensible worship of Religion, as we said above. And indeed there is nothing in us that is not the gift of God, and therefore subject to Him in every respect. Therefore the external members of the body too must serve Him. To this argument another is added, and that a very weighty one, taken from the very condition of our nature. For if the acknowledgment of the Deity is the necessary bond of natural Society and of the civil state, the worship of that same Deity will also be supremely commended to both conditions of men. But it is certain that neither Society nor this Civil form can subsist without sensible operation; wherefore, in order to establish it, an external and sensible worship must also be added. From the law of rendering external worship other duties follow. The first is that we speak of God and of Divine things only in the most honorable way. The second, that by all external signs we manifest our internal duties for the example of others. The third, that we also explain the knowledge of Divine things to others, so that in turn one may profit another. Finally, that we promote the glory of God with all piety and zeal.

24 Sed de officiis pertractemus, quae homini erga se ipsum sunt

24 But let us treat fully of the duties which are to be

p. 10

excolenda. Quae ad genus hoc officiorum pertinent, ea cùm animi; tùm corporis custodiâ, & culturâ continentur. Sed quamvis ad utrumque adigamur, eò tamen major, adcuratiorque animi perfectio esse debet, quò mens ipsa corpore praestantior est, atque nobilior. Jam vero animi cura, intellectus, & voluntatis emendatione perficitur. Quidquid igitur hanc emendationem spectare videatur, id maximè Christiano viro omni studio, ac diligentia praestandum est. Et quoniam vitia intellectus, studio disciplinarum removentur faciliùs, ut voluntatis errores tutiùs emendantur exercitatione virtutum, ad utramque, nobis erit confugiendum. Nihil autem ad animi culturam, relatis adjumentis, procurandam aptius dari & excogitari potest, quàm adtenta, ac vigil adfectuum nostrorum moderatio.

cultivated by man toward himself. The things that pertain to this kind of duties are contained in the custody and cultivation both of the mind and of the body. But although we are bound to both, the perfecting of the mind must nevertheless be greater and more careful, by as much as the mind itself is more excellent and nobler than the body. Now the care of the mind is perfected by the amendment of the intellect and of the will. Whatever, therefore, seems to regard this amendment must be performed by a Christian man above all, with all zeal and diligence. And since the vices of the intellect are more easily removed by the study of the disciplines, as the errors of the will are more safely amended by the exercise of the virtues, we shall have to take refuge in both. Nothing, however, among the aids just mentioned, can be offered or devised that is more apt for procuring the cultivation of the mind than an attentive and vigilant moderation of our affections.

25 Adfectus principes sunt, Amor, Odium, Desiderium, Laetitia, Spes, Tristitia, Diffidentia, Audacia, Desperatio, Voluptas, Ambitio, Avaritia, Ira, Pudor, Taedium. Invidia, Irrisio, Zelotypia, Immodicus sui amor, Aemulatio, quibus humanos animos allici, moveri, vel excitari conspicimus, ut exinde virtutes omnes, vel vitia, veluti ex uberrimis fontibus oriantur. [Vid. dict. in Log. Lib. 2. cap. 5.]. Hinc in omni vitae genere illud praeceptum nobis est, ut motus animi rationi non obtemperantes corrigamus. De corpore autem, quum nemo propriae vitae sit Dominus, quidquid effutiat Voltaire, nullum quoque absolutum ejus dominium potest in illud excercere. Et quidem tanta corporis custodia retinenda, quanta nec ad illud perimendum, nec ad illud labefactandum, requiritur. Quae tamen omnia, salvo semper Religionis negotio, intelligenda, & praestanda sunt.

25 The principal affections are Love, Hatred, Desire, Joy, Hope, Sadness, Distrust, Boldness, Despair, Pleasure, Ambition, Avarice, Anger, Shame, Weariness, Envy, Derision, Jealousy, immoderate Love of self, Emulation, by which we see human minds enticed, moved or excited, so that from them all the virtues or vices arise as from most abundant springs. [See what was said in the Logic, bk. 2, ch. 5.] Hence in every kind of life we have this precept: that we correct the motions of the mind that do not obey reason. As for the body, since no one is Lord of his own life, whatever Voltaire may blurt out, neither can anyone exercise an absolute dominion over it. And indeed such custody of the body must be kept as is required in order neither to destroy it nor to impair it. All of which, however, is to be understood and performed always without prejudice to the business of Religion.

26 Non defuere qui putarunt ad grave damnum evitandum & potissimum ad ignominiam ipsâ morte turpiorem effugiendam, licere sibi mortem consciscere. Sed haec nec cum juris naturae praescriptionibus, nec cum Christianis legibus ullomodo consentire certum est. Nulla enim est naturae necessitas, quamobrem, quod solius Dei proprium est, & Principum, Dei vices gerentium in terris, illud etiam imperium invito ipsomet domino nobis vindicemus. Accedit: in Providentiam injurios esse, ac nimis de Divina Bonitate diffidere, qui in summis rerum angustijs, se ab amantissimo luminum Patre dessertos esse conqueruntur, ut ne quid de virtute Fortitudinis dicam, quae certè in adversis, tantò magis elucescit, quantò fortius mala tolerantur.

26 There have not been lacking those who thought that, in order to avoid grave harm, and above all to escape an ignominy more shameful than death itself, it was lawful for them to inflict death on themselves. But it is certain that this in no way agrees either with the prescriptions of the law of nature or with Christian laws. For there is no necessity of nature why we should claim for ourselves, against the will of its very master, that dominion too which is proper to God alone, and to Princes, who act in God’s stead on earth. Add that those are injurious to Providence and distrust the Divine Goodness too much who, in the extreme straits of affairs, complain that they have been deserted by the most loving Father of lights; not to speak of the virtue of Fortitude, which certainly shines out in adversity the more, the more bravely evils are endured.

27 Reliqua hominis erga hominem officia servanda haec sunt. Hominum genus ad mutuam Societatem generari, quidquid in oppositum sentiat vivens adhuc hominum fabula Rousseau, compertum est apud omnes. ¿Quid enim aut organa ad loquendum apta proficiant, aut cuinam usui adfectus ad alios adjuvandos inserviant, nisi ab ipsa natura, nimirùm à Deo Sapientissimo naturae auctore ad magnam veluti Societatem ineundam destinemur? Mutuo ergo

27 The remaining duties to be observed by man toward man are these. That the human race is generated for mutual Society, whatever Rousseau, still living and the talk of men, may think to the contrary, is ascertained among all. For what would organs fit for speaking profit, or to what use would affections for helping others serve, unless we were destined by nature itself, namely by God, the most wise author of nature, to enter as it were into one great Society? We are therefore joined by a mutual bond of friendship

p. 11

amicitiae & benevolentiae vinculo conjungimur. Et quemadmodum in eo observando omnis honestas, ita in eo frangendo, violandoque deformitas, ac turpitudo omnis sita est.

and benevolence. And just as all that is honorable lies in observing it, so all deformity and baseness lies in breaking and violating it.

28 Ex hac autem amicitia duo officiorum genera deducuntur. Primum ut ne quem verbo, facto ve offendamus; alterum, ut nostri similibus, quoad possumus, beneficentiâ opitulemur. Et quidem aliorum laesio, quae naturali illa lege prohibetur: quod tibi non vis, alteri ne feceris, patére quamlatissime potest. Quum enim vel animi, vel corporis, vel fortunae bona sint; hinc tribus modis aliis detrimento esse quimus.

28 From this friendship, moreover, two kinds of duties are derived. The first, that we offend no one by word or deed; the second, that we help our fellows with beneficence as far as we can. And indeed the injury of others, which is forbidden by that natural law, what you would not have done to you, do not do to another, can extend very widely. For since there are goods of the mind, of the body and of fortune, we can be harmful to others in three ways.

29 Itaque ea honestatis praecipua pars est, neminem, aut pravis opinionibus, aut exemplis ad malum perpetrandum impellere. Aeque enim dictis, aut factis dociles labefactantur animi, & in eo qui peccant, non unius tantum criminis, sed plurium, sed multiplicium sed planè innumerabilium summa aequitate reprehenduntur.

29 Thus the chief part of what is honorable is to impel no one to commit evil, either by depraved opinions or by examples. For impressionable minds are undermined equally by words and by deeds, and those who sin in this are reproved with the greatest justice for the sum, not of one crime only, but of many, nay of manifold, nay plainly of innumerable ones.

30 Hinc multò majorem curam adhibere debent Parentes, Tutores, Curatores, Pedagogi, bonarum artium Magistri, aut quicunque tandem sint, quibus precipuè incumbit Adolescentûm educatio, ut in iis instituendis eam teneant disciplinae rationem, quae ad probitatis normam sit exactè composita. In hoc autem officio excolendo puerorum naturam, & conditionem sequendam esse, nemo est qui non videat.

30 Hence much greater care must be applied by Parents, Guardians, Curators, Pedagogues, Masters of the liberal arts, or whoever at length they may be on whom the education of youth chiefly falls, that in instructing the young they keep to that method of discipline which is exactly conformed to the norm of probity. In discharging this duty, moreover, there is no one who does not see that the nature and condition of the children must be followed.

31 In his autem, quae ad fortunae bona referuntur, paucis multa sic explico. Quaecumque in aliorum facultate sunt posita, & extrinsecus ad eos conservandos, nobilitandosque accersita, ea violari non nisi cum juris naturae transgressione possunt. Etsi enim nulla sint privatâ naturâ, veteri tamen occupatione, victoria, bello, pactione, conditione, sorte, fiunt hujusmodi.

31 As for those things that are referred to the goods of fortune, I explain much in few words thus. Whatever things are placed in the possession of others, and procured from outside for their preservation and advancement, cannot be violated except with a transgression of the law of nature. For although no things are private by nature, they nevertheless become so by ancient occupation, victory, war, compact, condition, lot.

32 Optimum ergo illud nomen, quod cuique virtutum exercitatione obtigit, nec privatim, nec publicè laedi ab altero potest. Qua quidem in re si falsò aliorum dicta, seu facta criminemur, & sumus calumniae rei, & contra justitiam peccamus. Sin vero, quod in altero vitii, peccatique est, quod quidem verum sit, sed occultum, manifestemus alteri, jam mutuae benevolentiae adversamur. Sed nihil turpius, faedius nihil in hominum Societate dictorum, pactorumque inconstantiâ. Quum enim praecipuum Justitiae fundamentum sit Fides, hac virtute sublata, Justitia quoque, & unâ simul cum illa Socialitas corruat oportet. Quamobrem si nemini data fides est violanda, pari ratione alterum quoque decipiendi mendacio facultas omnis erepta est. Quod quidem de omni mendacii genere ita intelligimus, ut sive cum alterius detrimento id fiat, sive ad tui aliorumque mentiaris utilitatem, utriusque juris, perfecti nimirum, & imperfecti laesor existimeris. De beneficentia, ac liberalitate existimo, universa, quae ex hoc capite derivantur officia, ea principio illo contineri: quodcumque ab aliis tibi fieri vis, & aliis facito. Itaque istorum omissio non ad injustitiam, sed ad

32 That excellent name, therefore, which has fallen to each man through the exercise of the virtues, can be injured by another neither privately nor publicly. In this matter, if we falsely charge the words or deeds of others as crimes, we are both guilty of calumny and sin against justice. If, on the other hand, we make manifest to another what is a vice and a sin in someone else, which is indeed true but hidden, we are already acting against mutual benevolence. But nothing is more shameful, nothing fouler in the Society of men, than inconstancy in words and compacts. For since the chief foundation of Justice is Faith, once this virtue is removed, Justice too, and together with it sociability, must collapse. Wherefore, if the faith given to anyone must not be violated, by the same reasoning every license of deceiving another by a lie has also been taken away. This indeed we understand of every kind of lie, so that whether it is done to the detriment of another, or you lie for the advantage of yourself and of others, you will be judged a violator of both rights, namely the perfect and the imperfect. Concerning beneficence and liberality, I think that all the duties derived from this head are contained in that principle: whatever you would have done to you by others, do also to others. Thus the omission of these is to be referred not to injustice, but to inhumanity

p. 12

inhumanitatem, & turpitudinem referenda est. In beneficiis conferendis multae cautiones adhibendae sunt, & imprimis videndum cum Tullio: ne obsit benignitas & iis ipsis, quibus benignè videbitur fieri, & ceteris; deinde, ne major benignitas sit, quàm facultas; tum, ut pro dignitate cuique tribuatur. Sed aliqua de officio hominis erga Rempublicam dicere necessum existimo.

and baseness. In conferring benefits many cautions must be applied, and first of all we must see to it, with Tully, that the kindness not harm the very persons to whom it will seem to be done kindly, nor others; next, that the kindness not be greater than one’s means; then, that to each be given according to his worth. But I judge it necessary to say something about the duty of man toward the Commonwealth.

33 Prudentis itaque & honesti Civis officium erit Patriam, & Principem ipsum sincero amore complecti, ipsius imperio, legibus, ministris humiliter parére, omnium animos eximia charitate, munificentiâ, morum suavitate, justitiâ, virtutibus omnibus promereri; ingenio, solertiâ, liberalibus artibus, fide, prudentia, familiae curâ, solicita liberorum educatione, pietate, religione ceteris praefulgere; a publicis honoribus, ac dignitatibus, quibus se quenquam imparem esse noverit, abhorrere, promeritas tamen, ac ultrò oblatas sedulò, diligenter, fideliter gerere; communi denique Civium, & Principis saluti, libertati, vel incolumitati, in secundis adversisque rebus consilio, viribus, opibus diligenter consulere; atque ubi injuncti muneris debitum, vel gravis calamitas postulaverit honores, fortunas, liberos, vitamque ipsam dulci ac decora morte constanter effundere. Haec atque alia principia non laxismum sapiunt, neque ê putidis Laxismi fontibus hausta sunt.

33 It will therefore be the duty of a prudent and honorable Citizen to embrace his Country and the Prince himself with sincere love; humbly to obey his rule, his laws and his ministers; to win over the minds of all by eminent charity, munificence, sweetness of manners, justice, and all the virtues; to outshine others in talent, skill, the liberal arts, good faith, prudence, care of the household, solicitous education of children, piety and religion; to shrink from public honors and dignities for which he knows himself to be unequal, but to administer those he has merited, and those offered of their own accord, sedulously, diligently and faithfully; finally, to provide diligently, by counsel, strength and resources, in prosperity and adversity, for the common welfare, liberty or safety of the Citizens and of the Prince; and, where the debt of the office laid upon him or a grave calamity shall have demanded it, steadfastly to pour out honors, fortunes, children, and life itself in a sweet and becoming death. These and other such principles do not savor of laxism, nor are they drawn from the putrid springs of Laxism.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De Virtute generatim, ejusque causis, & signis.

On Virtue in general, and its causes and signs.

34 „Omnis summa Philosophiae (inquit Tullius 2) ad beatè vivendum refertur, idque unum expetentes homines, se ad hoc studium contulerunt„. Virtutem necessariam esse ad benè beatèque vivendum agnoscunt omnes: eaque propter, quae ad virtutem generatim pertinent, ejusque effectrices causas tractare tantò lubentiùs suscepi, quantò res est quae naturae nostrae magis interest.

34 “The whole sum of Philosophy,” says Tully (i), “is referred to living happily, and men, seeking this one thing, have devoted themselves to this study.” All acknowledge that virtue is necessary for living well and happily; and on that account I have undertaken to treat the things that pertain to virtue in general, and its efficient causes, the more gladly as the matter is one that concerns our nature the more.

35 Virtus verò est, (inquit Clariss. Genovesi s2) quidquid naturam perficit, atque ad finem suum consequendum habiliorem reddit: ut contra vitium est, quod impeditiorem efficit ad finem suum, aut ab eo distrahit. Quoniam autem adfectus naturae humanae sunt quidam vehementiores impetus, à quibus in finem impellimur, tota natura virtutis, ejusque officium in hoc praesertim posita sunt,

35 Virtue, moreover, is (says the most distinguished Genovesi (k)) whatever perfects nature and renders it more apt for attaining its end; as, on the contrary, vice is what makes it more hindered with respect to its end, or draws it away from it. But since the affections of human nature are certain more vehement impulses by which we are driven toward our end, the whole nature of virtue and its function are placed chiefly in this, that

De Finib. 2.

On Ends, 2.

p. 13

ut eos témporet, modificet, ac ad summum naturae nostrae bonum regat.

that it temper them, modify them, and direct them to the highest good of our nature.

36 Fines porrò naturae nostrae, aut praesentem tantùm vitam spectant, aut futuram quoque. Quae homines perficiunt ad vitae futurae beatitudinem, atque ad eam regunt, virtutes Theologicae dicuntur, de quibus disserere Theologorum est: quae verò eumdem hominem ad societatem sanctè colendam servandamque instituunt, & societatis tranquillitatem securitatemque pariunt dicuntur virtutes Civiles: quaecumque demùm hominem perficiunt ad tranquillitatem vitae privatae aut solitariae virtutes Monasticae, & Ethicae adpellantur.

36 Now the ends of our nature regard either the present life only, or the future one as well. The virtues that perfect men for the happiness of the future life and direct them toward it are called Theological virtues, about which it is for Theologians to discourse; those, on the other hand, that train the same man for holily cultivating and preserving society, and produce the tranquillity and security of society, are called Civil virtues; and finally whatever virtues perfect man for the tranquillity of a private or solitary life are named Monastic and Ethical virtues.

37 Sed gravis hoc in loco vetusque nobis exoritur quaestio, acquiri ne possit virtus? Sunt enim qui existimant virtutem à natura totam esse, non ab arte quoque, disciplinâ, & exercitio. Nam natura nostra temperamentis necessariò agitur, ut ea nec extirpare possímus nec immutare. Sunt quidam, qui sanguineo temperamento praediti, in jocos, scurrilitatem, amores, aliasque corporis voluptates quasi inviti rapiuntur, quos qui fraenare velit, is totam eorum naturam immutet necesse est. Alii temperamento sunt praediti melancholico, ut idcircò perpetuò inquieti sint, minimè sibi satisfacientes, turbidi, truces, immanes. Eos qui cícures efficere velit, fibras, vasa, fluida, structuram omnem humani corporis, & naturae constitutionem pervertere debet. Sunt quidam naturâ timidi, & pusillamines, iracundi alii; quidam molles, & inertes: alii avari: alii naturâ ambitiosi: quidam súbdoli & fraudulenti. Hos ubi ad virtutem compónere velímus, á primis naturae Elementis exordiri oportet. Accedit, quod naturae humanae constitutiones diversae á climatibus, si non integrae nascuntur, at plurimum tamen pendeant. Ita isti concludere sibi videntur, virtutem, nisi á natura sit, acquiri nullo pacto posse, aut naturae esse dissimulationem.

37 But here a grave and ancient question arises for us: can virtue be acquired? For there are those who think that virtue comes wholly from nature, and not also from art, discipline and exercise. For our nature, they say, is necessarily driven by the temperaments, so that we can neither root them out nor change them. There are some who, endowed with a sanguine temperament, are carried away as if against their will into jests, buffoonery, love affairs and the other pleasures of the body; whoever would curb them must change their whole nature. Others are endowed with a melancholic temperament, so that on that account they are perpetually restless, least of all satisfied with themselves, turbid, grim, savage. He who would make them tame must overturn the fibers, the vessels, the fluids, the whole structure of the human body, and the constitution of nature. Some are by nature timid and pusillanimous, others irascible; some soft and inert; others avaricious; others by nature ambitious; some sly and fraudulent. When we wish to compose these to virtue, we must begin from the first Elements of nature. Add that the constitutions of human nature, so diverse according to climate, if they are not wholly born of it, yet depend on it very greatly. Thus these men think they conclude that virtue, unless it be from nature, can in no way be acquired, or else is a dissimulation of nature.

38 Falluntur tamen, eaque naturae humanae faciunt indomabilia, quorum nihil est non patiens fraeni. Principiò enim temperamenta magis vim habent ad excipiendum, quam ad moraliter agendum. Ratione, sensu, & phantasiâ naturam commovent, faciliùs quidem & promtiùs, aut tardiùs & difficilius, quàm si abessent: imperium rationis non semper elúdunt. Ac ut mollitudo aut durities in cera facilitas est, aut difficultas ad literas excipiendas, non vis scalpens; eodem modo temperamenta efficiunt, ut promtiùs & faciliùs, aut difficiliùs & tardiùs quibusdam rerum imaginibus agitemur, non autem ut perpetuò inviti impellamur. Deinde vim habeant physicè agendi: vim certè habere non possunt ad necessariò moraliter agendum: libertatem enim ad malitiam moralem non necessariò trahunt, etsi saepè non leviter adliciant.

38 They are mistaken, however, and they feign to be untamable those things in human nature of which none is not patient of the rein. For in the first place, the temperaments have more force for receiving than for acting morally. They move nature by reason, sense and imagination, more easily indeed and more promptly, or more slowly and with more difficulty, than if they were absent; they do not always elude the command of reason. And just as softness or hardness in wax is an ease or a difficulty in receiving letters, not the force that carves them, in the same way the temperaments bring it about that we are stirred more promptly and easily, or with more difficulty and more slowly, by certain images of things, but not that we are perpetually impelled against our will. Next, let them have the force of acting physically: they certainly cannot have the force of acting by moral necessity; for they do not necessarily drag freedom to moral malice, even though they often entice it not lightly.

39 Quamobrem si rationem emendare, si phantasiam purgare studeamus, si rerum bonitatem aut malitiam exactè dimetiamur, si veras rerum cum natura & finibus nostris relationes

39 Wherefore, if we strive to amend reason, to purge the imagination, if we measure exactly the goodness or malice of things, if we discern the true relations of things to our nature and our ends,

Dissert. de Virtute, quam paucis immutatis hìc damus.

Dissert. on Virtue, which we give here with a few changes.

p. 14

dispiciamus, poterimus quidem ab illis aut paulò vehementiùs commoveri erga vitia, aut retardari aliquantùm à virtute concipienda, nullo autem modò inviti ad illa adigi, aut ab his retrahi. Nec ullum majus argumentum esse potest evádere illa posse instrumenta virtutis, quàm quod experientia docet, plures sibi illa & rationi submisisse, ut sentirent quidem se aut vehementiùs agitari, aut impediri vi magna, interea vel fraenarent, vel stimulis agerent. Neminem esse ego ajo quamtumvis depravatum, qui, si ingenuus esse velit, se invítum ad vitia rapi fateatur: neminem scelestissimum, qui ad honestatem & virtutem flecti nequeat. Hinc eleganter admodùm, & praeclarè dixit Horatius 4, quod

we shall indeed be able to be stirred by them somewhat more vehemently toward vices, or to be held back somewhat from conceiving virtue, but in no way to be driven to the former, or drawn back from the latter, against our will. Nor can there be any greater argument that those things can become instruments of virtue than what experience teaches: that very many have so subjected them to themselves and to reason that, while they felt themselves either more vehemently agitated or hindered by a great force, they meanwhile either curbed them or drove them on with goads. I say that there is no one, however depraved, who, if he would be candid, would confess that he is carried to vices against his will; no one so very wicked that he cannot be bent to what is honorable and to virtue. Hence Horace said very elegantly and admirably (l) that

Invidus, iracundus, iners, vinosus, amator,

The envious man, the wrathful, the sluggard, the drunkard, the lover,

Nemo adeò ferus est, qui non mitescere possit,

No one is so savage that he cannot grow gentle,

Si modò culturae patientem accommodet aurem.

If only he lend a patient ear to cultivation.

40 Non equidem negaverim climata aliquid in temperamenta & mores influere; sed necessariò agere, id ego esse falsum adfirmo. D. de Montesquieu 2 probare nititur diversitatem climatis plus in nos posse, quam moralem, imò istam nihil ferè supra nos posse, & opinionem de metempsychosi climati Indorum eodem modo proportionatam esse, quo est proporcionata Hispanis Religio, quam profitentur. Alibi 2 adfirmat: per se adparere si humano more loqui velimus, à diversitate climatis terminos praescriptos esse Religioni cùm Christianae, tùm Mahometanae. In hoc opere clima idem praestat, ac motus in hac universitate rerum, estque causa eorum, quae á nobis fiunt. Tale verò quum sit fundamentum hujus Operis, qualia esse oportet, quae ex ea deducuntur?

40 I would not indeed deny that climates have some influence on temperaments and manners; but that they act necessarily, that I affirm to be false. M. de Montesquieu (m) strives to prove that the diversity of climate has more power over us than moral diversity, nay that the latter has almost no power over us, and that the opinion of metempsychosis is proportioned to the climate of the Indians in the same way as the Religion they profess is proportioned to the Spaniards. Elsewhere (n) he affirms that it appears of itself, if we wish to speak in human fashion, that limits have been prescribed by the diversity of climate both to the Christian Religion and to the Mahometan. In this Work climate performs the same office as motion in this universe of things, and it is the cause of the things that are done by us. Since such is the foundation of this Work, what must the things be that are deduced from it?

41 Verùm per diversitatem climatum nullam ut supra dixi, voluntati necessitatem inferri posse, experientiâ compertum est. ¿Quam enim diversa climata sunt, in quibus vel una eademque Religio servatur, vel modò una, modò altera Religio, vel subitò vera, abjectâ antiquâ & patria, aut è contrario in pretio fuit? ¿Nonne in uno eodemque climate Londini verbi causâ omnino inter se diversas Religiones homines constantissimè profitentur? ¿Quidquod non eosdem mores in eadem gente diversis temporibus reperimus? Nisi quis dicere velit Graecorum ac Romanorum, qui fuerunt olim, mores & studia, eadem nunc esse, iidem populi, qui olim barbarie, aut immanitate efferabantur, nunc humani sunt, ac virtuosi: contra aut immanes, qui humani fuere, aut molles, qui fortes, aut injusti, qui juris olim tenacissimi, aut impii, qui fuere pii. Atque haec dicta sufficiant.

41 But that no necessity can be brought upon the will by the diversity of climates, as I said above, has been found by experience. For how diverse are the climates in which either one and the same Religion is kept, or now one Religion, now another; or in which the true one has suddenly come into esteem, the ancient and ancestral one being cast aside, or the contrary? Do not men in one and the same climate, in London for example, most constantly profess Religions altogether different from one another? And what of the fact that we do not find the same manners in the same nation at different times? Unless someone wishes to say that the manners and pursuits of the Greeks and Romans who once were are the same now; that the same peoples who once ran wild in barbarism or savagery are now humane and virtuous; or, on the contrary, that those are savage who were humane, or soft who were brave, or unjust who once held most tenaciously to right, or impious who were pious. And let what has been said suffice.

Epistolar. 1. Ep. 1. Vid. etiam Cicer. Tusc. 4. cap. 37.

Epistles 1, Ep. 1. See also Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 4, ch. 37.

L' Esprit des Loix. Lib. 24. cap. 24.

L’Esprit des Loix, bk. 24, ch. 24.

Cap. 25.

Ch. 25.

p. 15

42 Sed quoniam virtutes non innascuntur nobiscum, ut perspicuum est, jure hoc in loco à nobis quaeretur, quae sint causae effectrices virtutum moralium? Ac videntur esse omninò quinque, Deus, ingenium seu temperamentum, educatio, exercitatio, praecepta. Ac principio verae & perfectae virtutis fons primus sola esse potest prima rerum omnium causa: à qua enim sunt essentia, & natura nostra, ab eadem & conservantur & perficiuntur, & ad fines suos potentissimè & sapientissimè ducuntur. Praeterea nemo adcuratissimè noscere potest praeter Deum, naturarum rationalium fines, media ad fines, mediorum cum fine proportionem, & vires ad id necessarias. Deus ergò tantùm verae perfectaeque virtutis dator primus esse potest.

42 But since the virtues are not born with us, as is evident, it will rightly be asked at this point: what are the efficient causes of the moral virtues? And there seem to be five in all: God, talent or temperament, education, exercise, precepts. And in the first place, the first source of true and perfect virtue can only be the first cause of all things: for from Him our essence and nature are, by the same they are both preserved and perfected, and they are led to their ends most powerfully and most wisely. Moreover, no one but God can know most accurately the ends of rational natures, the means to the ends, the proportion of the means to the end, and the powers necessary for this. God alone, therefore, can be the first giver of true and perfect virtue.

43 Ingenium, seu natura & temperies ad virtutem moralem duo potissimum confert. Primùm facultatem seu aptitudinem ad virtutem excipiendam, aliàs enim virtutem nunquam adsequeremur. Secundum impetum, & inclinationem erga virtutem, quae aptitudinis illius naturalis quaedam perfectio est. Tertia & quarta virtutis causae sunt educatio, & exercitatio; educatione enim, & exercitatione, ut tenellae plantae continuatâ culturâ ad fruges, ita natura nostra ad habitus virtuosos tandem inflectitur. Qui dixit hominem civilem nihil esse aliud, nisi habituum congeriem educatione, & exercitatione contractorum, dignum philosopho verbum pronunciavit. Scilicet homo Naturae tam differt à Civili, quàm animal, ut ita dicam ab homine.

43 Talent, or nature and temperament, contributes chiefly two things to moral virtue. First, the faculty or aptitude for receiving virtue, for otherwise we should never attain virtue. Second, the impulse and inclination toward virtue, which is a certain perfection of that natural aptitude. The third and fourth causes of virtue are education and exercise; for by education and exercise our nature is at length bent toward virtuous habits, as tender plants are brought to bear fruit by continued cultivation. He who said that the civil man is nothing other than a heap of habits contracted by education and exercise pronounced a word worthy of a philosopher. The man of Nature, namely, differs as much from the Civil man as an animal, so to speak, from a man.

44 Sed ad educationem & exercitationem conferunt plurimum praecepta doctrinae, quae quinta sunt virtutis causa. Ea enim praecepta si adtentè excipiantur, & recolantur saepissimè ita, ut in succum & sanguinem convertantur, tantam vim obtinent ad naturam reficiendam, ut altera esse videantur natura. Sed de his nunc adcuratiùs edisseramus. Praecepta ei observanda, qui se ad virtutem excitare, & exercere vult, duorum sunt generum, alia generalia, alia specialia. De his cap. superiori egimus. Generalia hìc proponemus.

44 But the precepts of doctrine, which are the fifth cause of virtue, contribute very greatly to education and exercise. For if those precepts are attentively received and very often gone over again, so that they are turned into sap and blood, they acquire such force for refashioning nature that they seem to be a second nature. But of these let us now discourse more accurately. The precepts to be observed by one who wishes to rouse and exercise himself to virtue are of two kinds, some general, others special. Of these we treated in the preceding chapter. The general ones we shall set forth here.

45 Primum praeceptum est, ut divinum auxilium, quo ad virtutem colendam vires recipiamus, adsiduis praecibus imploremus. Nam & prima causa virtutis effectrix est Deus, & timor Dei initium Sapientiae in divinis Scripturis adpellatur. Secundum praeceptum est, ut virtutis insignis pulchritudo, ac uberrimi fructus continenter ob oculos habeantur. Socrates dicere solebat, quod si honestas, & virtus vultum suum sine velo ostenderet, incredibiles in nobis amoris flammas accenderet. Inter fructus verò virtutis praecipui sunt. I. Animi tranquillitas, quae à sola virtute proficiscitur. II. Vera laus, & gloria, quae non à vitiis, sed à sola virtute expectari potest, etiam in hac morum pravitate, qua plerique omnes sumus. III. Vera utilitas, quandoquidem vitia utilitatem mentiri possunt, veram praestare nequeunt. IV. Vera nobilitas;

45 The first precept is that we implore with assiduous prayers the divine help by which we may receive strength for cultivating virtue. For God is also the first efficient cause of virtue, and in the divine Scriptures the fear of God is called the beginning of Wisdom. The second precept is that the signal beauty of virtue and its most abundant fruits be kept continually before our eyes. Socrates used to say that if honorableness and virtue showed their face without a veil, they would kindle incredible flames of love in us. Among the fruits of virtue, moreover, the chief are: I. Tranquillity of mind, which proceeds from virtue alone. II. True praise and glory, which can be expected not from vices but from virtue alone, even in this depravity of morals in which nearly all of us live. III. True utility, since vices can feign utility, but cannot furnish the true kind. IV. True nobility; for nobility

p. 16

nobilitas enim ex virtute primum nata est, & in virtute posita est essentialiter, ut qui avita nobilitate gloriantur, ipsi omni virtute vacui, nobilium magis filii, quam nobiles dicendi sunt. V. tandem virtus magnum hoc beneficium secum adfert, ut amorem etiam à barbaris extundat: hinc praeclarum illud Tullii, virtus etiam in hoste diligitur.

was first born of virtue, and is placed essentially in virtue, so that those who glory in ancestral nobility, while themselves wholly void of virtue, are to be called sons of nobles rather than nobles. V. Finally, virtue brings with it this great benefit, that it wrings love even from barbarians; hence that admirable saying of Tully: virtue is loved even in an enemy.

46 Tertium praeceptum est, ut non mediocria tantùm, aut factu faciliora, in virtute tibi proponas sequenda, sed ad summum ejus fastigium, ac virtutem, quae dicitur heroica semper adspires; quod ni feceris, vix in extrema ejus parte haerebis. Quartum praeceptum est, ut vitia omnia vivis coloribus perpetuò menti depingamus, atque adsuescamus exhorrére. Dici enim vix potest, quantam vim conferat ad virtutem constabiliendam horror vitiorum. Quintum praeceptum est, ut perpendamus, in quod vitium simus, aut ob temperamentum, aut ob educationem, aut ob seculi mores procliviores, ut ab eo nos longius abducamus. Atque in hoc praesertim homini virtutis amanti danda est opera. Eleganter Horatius 2

46 The third precept is that you set before yourself, to be pursued in virtue, not only middling things or things easier to do, but that you always aspire to its highest summit, and to the virtue that is called heroic; for unless you do this, you will scarcely cling to its lowest part. The fourth precept is that we perpetually paint all the vices to the mind in vivid colors, and accustom ourselves to shudder at them. For it can scarcely be told how much force the horror of vices contributes to establishing virtue. The fifth precept is that we weigh to which vice we are more prone, whether because of temperament, or of education, or of the manners of the age, so that we may draw ourselves farther away from it. And to this above all the man who loves virtue must give his effort. Elegantly Horace (o):

……………………… Denique te ipsum

……………………… Finally, shake out

Concute, num qua tibi vitiorum inseverit olim

Yourself, whether nature, or else bad habit, has at some time

Natura aut etiam consuetudo mala: namque

Sown in you any vices; for in neglected fields

Neglectis urenda filix innascitur agris.

Springs up the fern that must be burned.

47 Sextum praeceptum est ex superiori ductum. Nempè quoniam sunt quaedam vitia, quae aetatum sunt propria, ut in adolescentibus ac juvenibus intemperantia, & praecipitantia: in viris aetate maturis ambitio, in senibus avaritia, querimonia: haec in primis coercenda sunt, & vitanda, ne si nos semel invadant totam vitam moralem conturbent. Septimum praeceptum est, ut otium cane pejus & angue fugias: est enim ut vitiorum omnium sentina, ita praecipuè virtutis inimicum. Quocirca labori incumbendum est viro virtutis amanti. Quumque duplices sint labores, animi, & corporis; corporis quidem labores pro cujusque conditione suscipiendi: sed animus nunquam, aut rarò á seriis occupationibus removendus est. Homines ipsi literarum studio dediti operae pretium facient, si artem aliquam honestam illam, & ingenuis dignam discant, atque in ea subcisivis horis se exerceant. Egregios superioris aetatis philosophos cum voluptate exercuisse aut sculpturam, aut picturam, aut artem perspiciliorum, vel horologiorum ex eorum Vitis scimus. Inter animi autem labores studia sunt literarum, quibus qui seriò vacant, tempus, quod impendant in vitia, non habent. Fama est rogatum Newtonum, an amationibus unquam operam dedisset, respondisse, nullum sibi reliquum fuisse tempus à meditationibus philosophicis, quo ea de re cogitaret.

47 The sixth precept is derived from the preceding one. Namely, since there are certain vices proper to the ages of life, as intemperance and rashness in adolescents and youths, ambition in men of mature age, avarice and querulousness in the old, these must above all be restrained and avoided, lest, once they invade us, they throw our whole moral life into confusion. The seventh precept is that you flee idleness worse than a dog and a snake: for it is, as it were, the sink of all the vices, and so the especial enemy of virtue. Wherefore the man who loves virtue must apply himself to labor. And since labors are twofold, of the mind and of the body, the labors of the body are indeed to be undertaken according to each one’s condition; but the mind is never, or rarely, to be removed from serious occupations. Men devoted to the study of letters will themselves do something worth the effort if they learn some honorable art, worthy of the freeborn, and exercise themselves in it in their spare hours. We know from their Lives that excellent philosophers of the last age practiced with pleasure either sculpture, or painting, or the art of optical glasses, or of clocks. Among the labors of the mind, moreover, are the studies of letters; those who seriously give themselves to these have no time to spend on vices. It is reported that Newton, when asked whether he had ever given his attention to love affairs, answered that no time had been left him from his philosophical meditations in which to think about that matter.

Satyr. Lib. 1. Satyr. 3. à V. 34.

Satires, bk. 1, Sat. 3, from v. 34.

p. 17

48 Octavum praeceptum est, ut non solum historias virorum in virtute illustrium adtentissimè legamus, verum etiam eligamus amicos honestos, virtuosos, & sinceros, atque cum iis familiarissimè conversemur. Enim verò cùm ex lectione vitarum illustrium Virorum, tùm ex conversatione Virorum virtuosorum transmeat aliquid continenter in animum; quo paulatim ad virtutem componimur. Praeterea cum amicis virtuosis non possumus non esse virtuosi, ac perpetuò ad virtutem inflecti: omnes enim homines quantumvis impudentes verentur hominum gravium, & honestorum reprehensionem, ac judicia. Praeclare Seneca 3, Magna pars peccatorum tollitur, si testis peccaturis adsistat.

48 The eighth precept is that we not only read most attentively the histories of men illustrious in virtue, but also choose honorable, virtuous and sincere friends, and converse with them most familiarly. For indeed, both from reading the lives of illustrious men and from the conversation of virtuous men something continually passes over into the mind, by which we are gradually shaped to virtue. Besides, with virtuous friends we cannot fail to be virtuous, and to be perpetually bent toward virtue: for all men, however shameless, fear the reproof and the judgments of grave and honorable men. Excellently Seneca (p): The greater part of sins is taken away, if a witness stands by those about to sin.

49 Nonum praeceptum est, ut si testis morum sanctitate gravis, & qui pudorem, ac reverentiam incutiat, non semper habeatur praesens, saltem perfecta quaedam ejus imago menti perpetuò obversetur: plurimum enim animum à vitio retrahit, impellitque ad virtutem. Sed in re morali id in primis maximi momenti est, sedulò secum reputare coram Deo nos esse, & operari, Dei verò oculum vindicem esse, Deo enim plena sunt omnia. Decimum praeceptum est, ut vitiorum occasiones omnes fugiamus, atque eorum initiis vehementissimè resistamus: quòd scilicet semper faciliùs est, integrum hominem vitio jam irrepenti resistere, quàm hominem jam vitio correptum, ac debilitatum: vires enim paulatim decrescunt, atque in eadem ratione augescit vitium. Id verò cùm in omnibus vitiis adhibendum est, tùm praecipuè in iis, ad quae sumus naturâ procliviores. Alexander Macedo (ut refert Plutarchus), quum semel invisisset Darii Persarum Regis filias aetate florentes, ac formâ pulcherrimas, noluit secundò invísere, quia sibi ab illis metuebat: Dolores, inquit, oculorum sunt.

49 The ninth precept is that, if a witness grave in holiness of morals, and one who inspires shame and reverence, is not always present, at least some perfect image of him should perpetually hover before the mind: for it draws the mind very greatly away from vice and impels it toward virtue. But in moral matters this is above all of the greatest moment: to reflect carefully within oneself that we are, and act, in the presence of God, and that the eye of God is an avenger; for all things are full of God. The tenth precept is that we flee all occasions of vices, and most vehemently resist their beginnings: because, namely, it is always easier for a man still whole to resist a vice that is only creeping in than for a man already seized and weakened by vice: for his strength gradually decreases, and the vice grows in the same proportion. And while this is to be applied in all vices, it is so especially in those to which we are by nature more inclined. Alexander of Macedon (as Plutarch relates), having once visited the daughters of Darius, King of the Persians, in the flower of their age and most beautiful in form, refused to visit them a second time, because he feared for himself on their account: They are, he said, torments of the eyes.

50 Undecimum praeceptum est, ut quod de salute corporis perspectè pronunciavit Hippocrates, nihil parvum, nihil contemnendum existima, id potiori jure ad animum referamus; nam plerumque parva scintilla neglecta magnum excitavit incendium. Duodecimum praeceptum est, ut quotidie, & adcuratè factorum, dictorum, aut cogitatorum nostrorum examen instituamus. Testatur Seneca, se hoc praecepto totam vitam regere sólitum, nec unquam somnum capere, quin severus sui censor cuncta perpendisset dicta, facta, cogitata, ignoscentem aliis multa, sibi nihil. Extat in carmine aureo, quod Pythagorae tribuitur, locus super ea re insignis, quem operae pretium est immortali memoria tenére. Is sic latinè se habet.

50 The eleventh precept is that what Hippocrates wisely pronounced concerning the health of the body, consider nothing small, nothing to be despised, we should refer with better right to the mind; for very often a small spark neglected has stirred up a great conflagration. The twelfth precept is that we institute daily and carefully an examination of our deeds, words, or thoughts. Seneca testifies that he was accustomed to rule his whole life by this precept, and never to take sleep until, as a severe censor of himself, he had weighed all his words, deeds and thoughts, forgiving others much, himself nothing. There is in the golden poem which is attributed to Pythagoras a remarkable passage on this matter, which it is worth the effort to hold in undying memory. In Latin it runs thus:

E somno primum vigilans, quùm strata relinquis,

When first you wake from sleep, as you leave your bed,

Disponas animo luce expedienda futura,

Arrange in your mind what must be dispatched in the coming day.

Quando adimit rebus veniens nox atra colorem,

When black night, coming on, takes from things their color,

Ne prius admittas per dulcia lumina somnum,

Do not admit sleep through your sweet eyes

Epist. 11. ad Lucilium.

Letter 11, to Lucilius.

p. 18

Singula quàm elapsi ter volveris acta diei.

Before you have thrice gone over each act of the day now past.

Numquid deliqui? quid gessi in tempore? quid non?

Have I done wrong? What have I done in due time? What not?

Cur isti facto decus abfuit, aut ratio illi?

Why was honor lacking to this deed, or reason to that?

51 Postremum tandem praeceptum est, ut de nobis quammodestissime sentiamus, nec tam quò progressi simus, quàm quousque nobis adhuc sit progrediendum, cogitemus. Nihil enim tam progressibus in virtute obstat, quàm adrogantia, & multa nostri opinio: quandoquidem nemo eò pervenire contendet, quò se jam pervenisse putat. Itaque, quod Plato de virtutibus intellectualibus dixit, multi ad scientiam pervenissent, nisi se jam pervenisse putarent, id tu de virtute morali majori jure dicere potes. Eam obrem cavendum est, ne laudibus capiamur, atque à recto virtutis tramite superbientes deflectamus. Plura alia praecepta tradi possent, sed si quae in superioribus protulimus exercitatione ipsa in naturam convertantur, primae Adolescentiae, (cujus beneficio hunc suscipimus laborem) regendae sufficiunt. Illud autem nunc explicandum est, quibus argumentis cognoscere possímus, profecérimus, necne in virtute? En principaliora.

51 The last precept, finally, is that we think of ourselves most modestly, and consider not so much how far we have advanced as how far we still have to advance. For nothing so obstructs progress in virtue as arrogance and a great opinion of ourselves: since no one will strive to arrive where he thinks he has already arrived. Therefore what Plato said of the intellectual virtues, many would have arrived at knowledge, had they not thought they had already arrived, you can say with greater right of moral virtue. For this reason we must beware lest we be captivated by praises and, growing proud, turn aside from the right path of virtue. Many other precepts could be handed down; but if those which we have set out above are turned into nature by practice itself, they suffice for governing early Adolescence (for whose benefit we undertake this labor). But this must now be explained: by what arguments can we know whether we have advanced in virtue or not? Here are the principal ones.

52 Primum argumentum est, virtutis ipsius amor. Is scilicet se profecisse in virtute sciat, qui virtutem impensè amat. Agnoscet autem se virtutem amare, si occasionem exercendae impatienter quaerat, si magno ejus desiderio teneatur; si hominum virtuosorum conversatione delectetur, si ad praesentiam vitiorum exhorrescat: uno verbo, quibus indiciis cognoscitur, nos rem aliam quamlibet amare, iisdem dignoscitur, nos amare virtutem. Alterum indicium est, si ad aliorum irrisionem constanter perseveret in virtute, nec magnopere animô turbetur. Id autem ut obtineat, necessarium est non solum ut in virtute occalleat, verum etiam sedulò perpendere, majorem hominum partem vitiis esse corruptam, ac propterea necesse esse, ut virtuosus pluribus displiceat, ut eorum saepè invidentiae obnoxius sit, ut calumniis laceretur. In antecessum haec futura secum reputet, quominus, quum accidunt perturbetur.

52 The first argument is the love of virtue itself. He, namely, may know that he has advanced in virtue who loves virtue intensely. And he will recognize that he loves virtue if he impatiently seeks an occasion of exercising it; if he is held by a great desire for it; if he is delighted by the conversation of virtuous men; if he shudders at the presence of vicious ones: in a word, it is discerned that we love virtue by the same signs by which it is known that we love any other thing whatever. The second sign is if one perseveres constantly in virtue in the face of the mockery of others, and is not greatly disturbed in mind. And to obtain this it is necessary not only to grow hardened in virtue, but also to weigh carefully that the greater part of men is corrupted by vices; and that therefore the virtuous man must needs displease many, be often exposed to envy, be torn by calumnies. Let him reflect within himself beforehand that these things will come, so that he is the less disturbed when they happen.

53 Quinimo hinc tertium argumentum profectus in virtute deducere potest: displicére enim malis, magnum est bonitatis argumentum. Itaque Philosophus ille, de quo Laertius, quum relatum ei esset, se publicè laudari, me miserum, inquit, quid tantum mali commisi. Quartum indicium est, si laeto animo objurgationes, & reprehensiones auscultemus. Cujus ratio est, quia virtus animum non insolentem, trucem, ferocem, aliorum contemtorem efficit, sed mitem, ac facillimum. Itaque ubi mansuetudo deest, quod in nebulonibus videre licet, manifestum est argumentum, aut nihil, aut admodùm parùm in virtute profecisse. Eleganter Plutarchus, spicae plenae curvantur, vacuae eriguntur.

53 Indeed, from this a third argument of progress in virtue can be drawn: for to displease the wicked is a great argument of goodness. Thus that Philosopher of whom Laertius speaks, when it had been reported to him that he was being publicly praised, said: wretch that I am, what great evil have I committed? The fourth sign is if we listen with a glad mind to rebukes and reprehensions. The reason for this is that virtue makes the mind not insolent, fierce, savage, contemptuous of others, but gentle and most easy to deal with. Therefore where meekness is lacking, as may be seen in worthless fellows, it is a manifest argument that one has made either no progress, or very little, in virtue. Elegantly Plutarch: full ears of grain bend down, empty ones stand upright.

54 Jam quintum Signum, nos in virtute profecisse, est, si ad

54 Now the fifth sign that we have advanced in virtue is if, in the face of the difficulties

p. 19

difficultates, quas virtus in prospectu offert, non cedamus timidi, sed contra audentes eamus. Ad hunc ardorem accendendum considerandi perpetuò sunt fructus virtutis. Sextum indicium est, si res adversae, aequo animo ferantur. Enimverò, qui vel minimis malis ita conturbatur, ut miser sit, ne latum quidem unguem profecit. Atque hoc est, quod Stoici docebant, non cadere in Sapientem aegritudinem. Praeclare Cicero 2. „Necesse est, inquit, qui fortis sit, eumdem esse magni animi; qui magni animi sit, invictum; qui invictus sit, eum res humanas despicere, atque infra se positas arbitrari: despicere autem nemo potest eas res, propter quas aegritudine affici potest. Ex quo efficitur fortem virum aegritudine numquam affici. Omnes autem sapientes fortes, non cadit igitur in sapientem aegritudo.„

which virtue offers in prospect, we do not yield timidly, but go against them boldly. To kindle this ardor, the fruits of virtue must be perpetually considered. The sixth sign is if adversities are borne with an even mind. For indeed, he who is so disturbed by even the smallest evils that he is miserable has not advanced even a finger’s breadth. And this is what the Stoics taught, that distress does not befall the Wise man. Excellently Cicero (q): “He who is brave,” he says, “must likewise be great of soul; he who is great of soul, unconquered; he who is unconquered must look down upon human affairs and judge them to be placed beneath him: but no one can look down upon those things on account of which he can be affected by distress. From which it follows that the brave man is never affected by distress. But all wise men are brave; distress therefore does not befall the wise man.”

55 Septimum indicium est, sit virtuosus allicientia ad vitium contemnat: nam si facile de proposito suo dimoveatur, aut nihil, aut parum profecit. In primis autem solent homines vitiosi vitia sua pulcherrimis adspectibus ornare; quibus minus vitiosi videantur, atque vitii horrorem aliis demant: consuetudine cohonestare: humanae naturae imbecillitate excusare: virtutes velut aut imbecillium animorum, aut enthusiastarum commenta traducere, ac deridére: sapientes eos vocare, qui utilitatis privatae causa astutè alios decipere didicerint, stultos qui nesciant. Tu si ab illis capi minimè pateris, scito, te in virtute profecisse.

55 The seventh sign is if the virtuous man despises enticements to vice: for if he is easily moved from his purpose, he has made either no progress or little. For vicious men are above all wont to adorn their vices with the most beautiful appearances, so that they may seem less vicious, and to take away from others the horror of vice: to make it respectable by custom, to excuse it by the weakness of human nature; to traduce and deride the virtues as the figments either of weak minds or of enthusiasts; to call those wise who have learned to deceive others cunningly for the sake of private advantage, and those fools who do not know how. If you by no means allow yourself to be taken in by them, know that you have advanced in virtue.

56 Octavum signum profectus in virtute constituo, si literarum studiosi ea ex omnibus studiis avidiùs adripiant; quae sibi & Societati utilia sunt, cetera valére jubeant, vel in transitu salutent. Quis verò tam amens sit ut adfirmet sibi, aut Societati utiles fore quaestiones interminabiles quae tanta animorum contentione in Scholis disceptantur, & quae Arabum olent vetus oleum? Postremum signum, quo quis se grandem fecisse in virtute gradum cognoscere potest, hoc habeo, si nempè se ita animo pacato sentiat, tamque sit Divinae Providentiae securus, ut virtute contentus, nec anxius, nimiumque sollicitus quaerat, quid cras sit futurum, nec venturi temporis curâ admodùm turbetur. Tu igitur, si sapis, quid cras sit futurum fuge quaerere. ¿Virtutem colis? Cetera tranquillus esto.

56 I set down as the eighth sign of progress in virtue if those devoted to letters take up most eagerly, out of all studies, those that are useful to themselves and to society, and bid farewell to the rest, or greet them in passing. For who is so mad as to affirm that the interminable questions which are disputed in the Schools with such contention of minds, and which smell of the old oil of the Arabs, will be useful to himself or to Society? The last sign by which one can know that he has taken a great step in virtue I hold to be this: if, namely, he feels himself so peaceful in mind, and is so secure in Divine Providence, content with virtue, that he does not anxiously and over-solicitously ask what will be tomorrow, nor is much disturbed by care for the time to come. You therefore, if you are wise, forbear to ask what will be tomorrow. Do you cultivate virtue? For the rest, be tranquil.

57 Et haec quidem in praesenti sufficiant: pauca haec sunt sed pro Elementorum ratione plerisque jam nimis multa videbuntur. Nobis hanc operam navare visum est disciplinae pulcherrimae, nescio quo fato in Scholis Americae nostrae hactenùs neglectae non sine maximo Juventutis dispendio, & Philosophiae detrimento. Utiliora haec sunt quàm de Ente Rationis, de Connexione Dei cum possibilitate aut impossibilitate possibilium deque aliis sexcentis acriter dimicare.

57 And let these things suffice for the present: they are few, but for the scope of Elements they will already seem too many to most. It seemed good to us to devote this effort to a most beautiful discipline, neglected hitherto by I know not what fate in the Schools of our America, not without the greatest loss to Youth and detriment to Philosophy. These things are more useful than to fight sharply over the Being of Reason, over the Connection of God with the possibility or impossibility of possibles, and over six hundred other things.

Tusc. 3. Cap. 27.

Tusculan Disputations 3, ch. 27.
