AN EPITOME.

Typis edita primùm Genuae in gratiam Scholaris Juventutis, ann. MDCCLXVIII: recussa nunc pro iis, qui Physicae nostrae operam dabunt. Mexici MDCCLXXIV.

Printed first at Genoa for the benefit of the Scholastic Youth, in the year mdcclxviii: reprinted now for those who will apply themselves to our Physics. Mexico mdcclxxiv.

PRAEFATIO. — PREFACE

Quum in confesso sit apud veros optimarum artium cultores, sine Geometriae cognitione vix, aut ne vix quidem, boni quidquam in Physica unquam adferri posse; neque verò ad ceteras disciplinas, quae ad Naturae vestigationem Philosopho dignam spectabunt, aditum patére, nisi Geometriam plusquàm mediocriter

ince it is acknowledged among the true cultivators of the best S arts that without a knowledge of Geometry scarcely, or not even scarcely, can anything good ever be brought into Physics; and that access indeed does not lie open to the other disciplines which will bear upon an investigation of Nature worthy of a Philosopher, except to those more than moderately learned in Geometry:

p. 2

doctis: jam pridem in animum induxeram, pollicitusque vobis, optimi Adolescentes, fueram, me non ante de rebus physicis verba facturum, quàm Geometricas Institutiones, quales per angustias temporis oportebat, brevissimas quidem, vobis tradidissem. Fortè verò fortunâ mecum asportaveram ex Italia Libellum, mole quidem parvum, sed quem satis instituto nostro, & maximè ad rem physicam rectè atque ordine excolendam, augendam, vobis emolumento fore, crediderim. Nam qui de corporea natura seriò tractare volet, is denique Geometriam in primis quàm diligentissimè possit, perdiscat: aliter non Physicam ipse ille, nec Philosophiam; sed Philosophiaè fumum atque umbram consectabitur. Qui verò se Physicos, tanto nomine dignos, arbitrantur, quòd totos dies per longas, ex ordine, syllogismorum centurias, cérebrum hauriant, quasi Naturam rerum, & Naturae Summum Conditorem ipsi commentis suis, & stultis quaestionibus, implicare vellent; per summum dedecus atque ignaviam: viderint, an non satiùs iisdem fuisset, ab abstrusis, & multâ caligine obnubilatis, sibi temperasse. Turpe enim est, & Philosopho prorsùs indignum, de hoc disserere velle, quod nescias: turpius consuetudini parére malle, quàm veritatem in aprico sitam amplecti: porrhò turpissimum aliis, quibus non adeo laeva mens est, quique Adolescentûm tyrocinio praesunt, & rectae institutioni, acriter invidêre. Sed quidquid hoc erit, en vobis Auctoris Praefationem, statim vestris oculis subjiciendam. Sic enim ille.

I had long since resolved, and had promised you, excellent Young Men, that I would not speak on physical matters before I had handed down to you Geometrical Institutions, very brief indeed, such as the narrowness of the time required. By good fortune I had brought away with me from Italy a little Book, small indeed in bulk, but one which I should believe would be sufficient for our purpose, and of benefit to you above all for cultivating and advancing physical matters rightly and in order. For whoever will wish to treat seriously of corporeal nature, let him, in short, learn Geometry thoroughly above all things, as diligently as he can: otherwise he will be pursuing not Physics, nor Philosophy, but the smoke and shadow of Philosophy. But those who think themselves Physicists, worthy of so great a name, because all day long they exhaust their brains on long hundreds of syllogisms in a row, as though they wished to entangle the Nature of things, and the Supreme Maker of Nature, in their own fabrications and foolish questions, to their utmost disgrace and sloth: let them see whether it would not have been better for them to have kept away from things abstruse and clouded over with much darkness. For it is shameful, and wholly unworthy of a Philosopher, to wish to discourse about what you do not know; more shameful to prefer to obey custom rather than to embrace the truth that lies in the open sun; and most shameful of all to envy bitterly others, whose minds are not so perverse, and who preside over the apprenticeship of Young Men and over their right instruction. But be that as it may, here is the Author’s Preface, to be placed at once before your eyes. For thus he writes.

p. 3

ELEMENTA — ELEMENTS

GEOMETRIAE

OF GEOMETRY

UTILIORA.

OF GREATER USE .

Geometria Nomen exiguum, Munus habet amplissimum. Ejus Elementa, demonstrationum scilicet principia, collegit Euclides Alexandrinus Anno ante Christum ferè 280. Vir omni laude major; quibus ad universam Mathesim, ceterasque naturales disciplinas aditus aperiretur. Eorum tamen difficultate deterriti plerique adolescentes, Mathematicis institutis vix à limine salutatis; aut ingenii, aut constantiae minus compotes, terga vertunt, omnemque sibi spem praecidunt solidiores scientiae fructus adipiscendi, non solùm, quia primis, ac simplicissimis rerum naturalium demonstrationibus destituuntur; sed quia nil aequè mentis aciem exacuit, ac praeparat ad alias disciplinas faciliùs, & rectiùs percipiendas, (propter quem praecipuè usum addiscendam Geometriam ajebat Plato) quàm Geometrica exercitatio, quae certissimam aperit viam veritatis investigandae.

Geometry has a slight Name, but a most ample Office. Its Elements, namely the principles of demonstrations, were collected by Euclid of Alexandria, about the Year 280 before Christ, a Man greater than all praise, so that by them access might be opened to the whole of Mathematics and to the other natural disciplines. Most young men, however, deterred by their difficulty, having scarcely greeted Mathematical studies from the threshold, and lacking either in wit or in constancy, turn their backs and cut themselves off from all hope of obtaining the fruits of a more solid science; not only because they are left destitute of the first and simplest demonstrations of natural things, but because nothing so sharpens the edge of the mind, and prepares it for perceiving the other disciplines more easily and more rightly (for which use chiefly Plato said Geometry was to be learned), as Geometrical exercise, which opens the surest way of investigating truth.

Quà de causa Geometrica Elementa, praesertim ea, quae Naturali Philosophiae plurimo futura sunt usui (quod alii aliter egregiè praestitere) breviori, ac fortassis etiam clariori methodo exhibemus. Et primo libro figuras, quae rectis lineis continentur: secundo figuras curvilineas: tertio figurarum proportiones exponimus. Magna quidem juvandi spe (quod nostri est Instituti), quia multùm haec principia adolescentes juvasse docuit experimentum.

For this reason we set forth the Geometrical Elements, especially those which will be of very great use to Natural Philosophy (which others have furnished excellently in other ways), in a briefer, and perhaps also a clearer, method. And in the first book we set forth the figures which are contained by straight lines; in the second, curvilinear figures; in the third, the proportions of figures; with great hope indeed of being of help (which is the aim of our Institution), since experience has taught that these principles have helped young men much.

p. 4

LIBER I. — BOOK I

De Figuris rectilineis.

On Rectilinear Figures.

Ex Geometriae Elementis alia sunt Principia, quae sola nominum explicatione constant; alia ex iis deducta, ad praxim pertinentia, quae Problemata dicuntur: alia ad Veritatis cognitionem ordinata, quae Theoremata adpellantur. Primò igitur Liber hic Principia dabit; Secundò Problemata circa figuras Rectilineas; Tertiò Theoremata selectiora.

In the Elements of Geometry, some things are Principles, which consist solely in the explanation of names; others, deduced from them and pertaining to practice, are called Problems; others, ordered to the knowledge of Truth, are named Theorems. First, then, this Book will give the Principles; second, Problems concerning Rectilinear figures; third, the more select Theorems.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

Principia.

Principles.

Principia vel sunt definitiones, vel Communes notiones, quae aut circà veritatis considerationem versantur, & Axiomata dicuntur, aut circà Operis effectionem, & Postulata nuncupari solent. Singula hic proponimus, nonnullis, ubi opus fuerit, adjectis declarationibus: quibus & haec discentibus dilucidiora reddantur, & Theoremata deinde breviùs demonstrentur.

Principles are either definitions, or Common notions, which either concern the consideration of truth, and are called Axioms, or concern the carrying out of a Work, and are usually named Postulates. We propose each of them here, with explanations added to some, where there is need: so that by these, too, they may be rendered clearer to learners, and the Theorems may afterwards be demonstrated more briefly.

§. I.

§. I.

Definitiones.

Definitions.

In his nonnihil à communi Methodo discedimus, ut à notioribus initium faciamus.

In these we depart somewhat from the common Method, so as to begin from the things better known.

I. Corpus est, quod trinam habet dimensionem, Longitudinem scilicet, Latitudinem, & Profunditatem.

I. A Body is that which has a threefold dimension, namely Length, Breadth and Depth.

II. Extremum Corporis est superficies, in qua sola Longitudo, & Latitudo consideratur.

II. The Extremity of a Body is the surface, in which Length and Breadth alone are considered.

III. Extremum Superficiei est linea, in qua sola consideratur Longitudo.

III. The Extremity of a Surface is the line, in which Length alone is considered.

IV. Extremum Lineae est Punctum, in quo nec Longitudo, nec Latitudo, nec Profunditas consideratur.

IV. The Extremity of a Line is the Point, in which neither Length, nor Breadth, nor Depth is considered.

Et ideò definiri solet Punctum, in quo nulla est Pars.

And hence a Point is usually defined as that in which there is no Part.

V. Ex fluxu puncti fieri concipitur Linea: ex motu lineae in latitudinem Superficies: ex motu superficiei secundùm profunditatem generatur Corpus.

V. A Line is conceived to come about from the flowing of a point; a Surface from the motion of a line in breadth; from the motion of a surface according to depth a Body is generated.

p. 5

VI. Linea recta est ab uno puncto ad aliud Brevissima.

VI. A straight Line is the Shortest from one point to another.

Hinc Lineae rectae, quae iisdem punctis terminantur, sunt aequales, & omninò congruunt inter se. Et lineae curvae, aut quomodocumque inflexae majorem habent longitudinem, quàm Recta, si iisdem Punctis terminentur.

Hence straight Lines which are bounded by the same points are equal, and wholly coincide with each other. And curved lines, or lines bent in any manner whatever, have a greater length than a Straight one, if they are bounded by the same Points.

VII. Plana superficies est, cui ex omni parte Recta linea potest adcommodari: estque ab una linea ad aliam brevissima.

VII. A plane surface is one to which a Straight line can be fitted in every direction; and it is the shortest from one line to another.

VIII. Angulus in superficie est Duarum linearum post unum commune punctum mutua Inclinatio.

VIII. An Angle in a surface is the mutual Inclination of Two lines beyond one common point.

IX. Angulus Rectilineus dicitur, qui ex rectis lineis componitur: Curvilineus, qui ex curvis: Mixtus, qui ex una curva, altera recta.

IX. An Angle is called Rectilinear which is composed of straight lines; Curvilinear, which of curved ones; Mixed, which of one curved and the other straight.

X. Angulus Rectus est, quum Recta linea, quae Perpendicularis dicitur, aequaliter utrinque inclinatur super aliam Rectam.

X. An Angle is Right when a Straight line, which is called Perpendicular, is inclined equally on either side upon another Straight line.

XI. Angulus obtusus est major Recto.

XI. An obtuse Angle is greater than a Right one.

XII. Angulus Acutus est minor Recto.

XII. An Acute Angle is less than a Right one.

Quoniam verò in Angulorum cognitione plurima est discentium difficultas.

But since learners find very great difficulty in the knowledge of Angles,

Nota 1, quòd quum ad unum punctum duae solae lineae concurrunt, potest Angulus una litera designari. At quum saepe contingat, plures lineas ad idem punctum uniri; ob vitandam aequivocationem, solet Angulus tribus literis designari, quarum Media indicat Angulum; prima & tertia litera quomodocumque sumantur, designant lineas, continentes Angulum. Ut in I. Figura Theorematum, Iconismo II. Angulus D A B Rectus est; quia linea Perpendicularis B A aequaliter utrinque inclinatur per Quadrantem Circuli supra lineam D E: adeoque Mensura Anguli recti D A B est Quadrans D B Circuli sive majoris, sive minoris. Angulus D A G est Obtusus, cujus Mensura est Arcus D G major Quadrante. Angulus D A F est Acutus, cujus Mensura est Arcus D F minor Quadrante.

Note 1, that when only two lines meet at one point, the Angle can be designated by one letter. But since it often happens that several lines are united at the same point, to avoid equivocation the Angle is usually designated by three letters, of which the Middle one indicates the Angle; the first and third letters, taken in whatever order, designate the lines containing the Angle. As in Figure I of the Theorems, Plate II, the Angle DAB is Right, because the Perpendicular line BA is inclined equally on either side, by a Quadrant of a Circle, upon the line DE: and so the Measure of the right Angle DAB is the Quadrant DB of a Circle, whether larger or smaller. The Angle DAG is Obtuse, whose Measure is the Arc DG, greater than a Quadrant. The Angle DAF is Acute, whose Measure is the Arc DF, less than a Quadrant.

Nota 2, quòd quum quilibet Circulus dividatur à Mathematicis in 360. partes, quas gradus adpellant, Angulus rectus dici solet Angulus 90. graduum; (quae est quarta pars Circuli) Angulus obtusus major 90 gradibus; Angulus acutus minor 90. gradibus. Hinc Anguli recti sunt omnes inter se aequales; adeoque quum plures Anguli sunt uni, vel pluribus rectis similiter aequales, erunt & inter se aequales.

Note 2, that since every Circle is divided by Mathematicians into 360 parts, which they call degrees, a right Angle is usually called an Angle of 90 degrees (which is the fourth part of a Circle); an obtuse Angle, greater than 90 degrees; an acute Angle, less than 90 degrees. Hence right Angles are all equal to one another; and so, when several Angles are equal to one or to several right angles alike, they will also be equal to one another.

Nota 3, quòd lineae tunc majorem, vel minorem Angulum efficiunt, non quum longiores, vel breviores sunt; sed quum in eadem singularum longitudine magis, vel minus invicem recedunt. Hinc si duae linae A D, A L (in eadem Figura) singulae sint aequales duabus A E, A N; & earum extrema Puncta D, & L aequè distent inter se, ac E, & N; Anguli D A L, & E A N erunt aequales. Et è converso, si Anguli sint aequales extrema puncta aequè distabunt. Ex opposito autem quum D, & M magis inter se

Note 3, that lines make a greater or a lesser Angle, not when they are longer or shorter, but when, with the same length of each, they recede more or less from each other. Hence if two lines AD, AL (in the same Figure) are each equal to the two AE, AN, and their extreme Points D and L are as far apart from each other as E and N, the Angles DAL and EAN will be equal. And conversely, if the Angles are equal, the extreme points will be equally distant. On the other hand, when D and M stand farther apart from each other

p. 6

distent, quàm E, & N, erit Angulus D A M Rectus major Angulo E A N Acuto.

than E and N, the Right Angle DAM will be greater than the Acute Angle EAN.

XIII. Parallelae lineae sunt, quae pari ubique spatio distant inter se, & quantumvis producantur, nunquam concurrent ad Angulum efficiendum.

XIII. Parallel lines are those which stand apart from each other by an equal space everywhere, and, however far they are produced, never meet so as to make an Angle.

Ut in Eigura II. Theorem. Icon. II. sunt Lineae C D, A B, inter quas eadem incidit Perpendicularis C A, D B. Et si quaevis alia linea illas secet, ut linea G P; lineae Parallelae ex utravis parte aequaliter ad illam inclinantur: nam si magis ad mediam secantem inclinarentur ex alterutra parte, ex. gr. versus I, M; magis ex ea parte adcederent inter se; adeoque non essent Parallelae. Hinc Duo simul Anguli L, & N, sunt aequales Duobus simul Angulis I, & M: quia aequales sunt ex utravis parte Inclinationes.

As in Figure II of the Theorems, Plate II, are the Lines CD, AB, between which the same Perpendicular CA, DB falls. And if any other line cuts them, as the line GP, the Parallel lines are inclined equally toward it on either side: for if they were inclined more toward the middle secant on one side or the other, e.g. toward I, M, they would approach each other more on that side, and so would not be Parallel. Hence the Two Angles L and N together are equal to the Two Angles I and M together: because the Inclinations are equal on either side.

XIV. Figura est Quantitas, quae sub uno, vel pluribus terminis continetur.

XIV. A Figure is a Quantity which is contained under one or several bounds.

Scilicet, quae clauditur vel una Linea curva, ut Circulus: vel una curva, altera recta, ut Semicirculus: vel pluribus rectis, ut Triangulum.

That is, one which is enclosed either by one curved Line, as the Circle; or by one curved and the other straight, as the Semicircle; or by several straight ones, as the Triangle.

XV. Circulus est Figura plana, unius Lineae circuitu comprehensa, quae Circumferentia dicitur, seu Peripheria: ad quam omnes rectae lineae ductae ab uno medio Puncto sunt aequales.

XV. A Circle is a plane Figure, comprehended by the circuit of one Line, which is called the Circumference, or Periphery: to which all straight lines drawn from one middle Point are equal.

XVI. Hoc autem medium Circuli Punctum vocatur Centrum.

XVI. And this middle Point of the Circle is called the Center.

XVII. Diameter est Linea ducta ab uno puncto ad aliud circumferentiae, transiens per centrum, & secans Circulum in duas partes aequales.

XVII. A Diameter is a Line drawn from one point of the circumference to another, passing through the center, and cutting the Circle into two equal parts.

XVIII. Rectilineae Figurae sunt, quae rectis lineis continentur: Trilaterae, quae tribus: Quadrilaterae, quae quatuor: Multilaterae, quae pluribus.

XVIII. Rectilinear Figures are those which are contained by straight lines: Trilateral, which by three; Quadrilateral, which by four; Multilateral, which by more.

XIX. Triangulum, secundùm Latera consideratum, est Aequilaterum, quod tria latera habet aequalia; ut in Fig. V. Icon. II. A H I.

XIX. A Triangle, considered according to its Sides, is Equilateral, which has three equal sides; as in Fig. V, Plate II, AHI.

XX. Isosceles seu AEquicrure, quod duo tantùm latera habet aequalia; ut in eadem Figura, A B C.

XX. Isosceles, or Equal-legged, which has only two equal sides; as in the same Figure, ABC.

XXI. Scalenum, quod tria inaequalia habet latera; ut in eadem Figura, B A L.

XXI. Scalene, which has three unequal sides; as in the same Figure, BAL.

XXII. Triangulum, secundùm Angulos consideratum, est Rectangulum, seu Orthogonum, quod habet unum Angulum Rectum; ut in Fig. III. Icon. III. A C B.

XXII. A Triangle, considered according to its Angles, is Right-angled, or Orthogonal, which has one Right Angle; as in Fig. III, Plate III, ACB.

XXIII. Obtusangulum, seu Amblygonium, quod habet unum Angulum Obtusum; ut in eadem Fig. AEB.

XXIII. Obtuse-angled, or Amblygonal, which has one Obtuse Angle; as in the same Fig., AEB.

XXIV. Acutangulum, seu Oxygonium, cujus omnes Anguli sunt Acuti; ut in eadem Fig. ADB.

XXIV. Acute-angled, or Oxygonal, all of whose Angles are Acute; as in the same Fig., ADB.

XXV. Quadratum est, cujus omnia latera sunt aequalia, & Anguli recti, Fig. VI. Icon. I.

XXV. A Square is that whose sides are all equal, and its Angles right; Fig. VI, Plate I.

XXVI. Rhombus, cujus latera omnia aequalia, sed Anguli non recti; Fig. VII. Icon. I.

XXVI. A Rhombus, whose sides are all equal, but its Angles not right; Fig. VII, Plate I.

XXVII. Rectangulum altera parte longius, cujus Anguli

XXVII. A Rectangle longer on one side, whose Angles are right,

p. 7

recti sunt, sed bina tantùm opposita latera aequalia: Fig. VIII. Icon. I.

but only the two opposite sides equal: Fig. VIII, Plate I.

XXVIII. Rhomboïdes, cujus bina tantùm opposita latera aequalia sunt, & Anguli non recti; Fig. IX. Icon. I.

XXVIII. A Rhomboid, of which only the two opposite sides are equal, and the Angles not right; Fig. IX, Plate I.

XXIX. Atque istae quatuor Figurae Quadrilaterae communi vocabulo vocantur Parallelogramma; quia bina latera opposita habent parallela.

XXIX. And these four Quadrilateral Figures are called by a common name Parallelograms, because they have the two opposite sides parallel.

XXX. Ceterae verò Figurae quadrilaterae irregulares, quae neque bina latera opposita, neque oppositos Angulos habent aequales, Trapezia nuncupantur: ut in Fig. XII. Icon. I. LHMI.

XXX. But the other, irregular, quadrilateral Figures, which have neither the two opposite sides nor the opposite Angles equal, are called Trapezia; as in Fig. XII, Plate I, ## LHMI

§. II.

§. II.

Postulata.

Postulates.

I. A Quovis Puncto, ad quodvis punctum duci potest Linea Recta.

I. From any Point to any point a Straight Line can be drawn.

II. Linea recta potest in directum, quantum volueris continuari.

II. A straight Line can be continued in a straight line as far as you wish.

III. Quovis centro ad quodvis intervallum potest Circulus describi.

III. From any center at any interval a Circle can be described.

IV. Potest quaelibet linea dividi in partes AEquales, vel Inaequales.

IV. Any line can be divided into Equal or Unequal parts.

V. Potest cuilibet Rectae poni altera AEqualis, vel Inaequalis, Perpendicularis, vel Parallela.

V. To any Straight line another can be placed, Equal or Unequal, Perpendicular or Parallel.

§. III. — §. III

Axiomata.

Axioms.

I. Quae eidem sunt aequalia, inter se sunt aequalia.

I. Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other.

Et quae communem habent mensuram, sunt aequalia.

And things which have a common measure are equal.

Et quod uno aequalium majus, vel minus est, est etiam majus, vel minus altero aequalium.

And what is greater or less than one of equals is also greater or less than the other of the equals.

II. Si aequalibus aequalia, aut commune aliquid addas, vel auferas; quae supersunt, sunt aequalia.

II. If to equals you add equals, or something common, or take them away from them, the things that remain are equal.

III. Si aequalibus inaequalia addas, vel auferas; quae supersunt, sunt inaequalia.

III. If to equals you add unequals, or take them away from them, the things that remain are unequal.

IV. Quae ejusdem, aut aequalium sunt dupla, tripla, aut dimidia; inter se sunt aequalia.

IV. Things which are double, triple, or half of the same thing, or of equals, are equal to each other.

Et quotiescumque duo ab eodem aequaliter exceduntur, vel illud excedunt, sunt aequalia.

And whenever two things are equally exceeded by the same thing, or equally exceed it, they are equal.

V. Quae mutuò sibi congruunt, aequalia sunt.

V. Things which mutually coincide with each other are equal.

VI. Totum est majus sua Parte.

VI. The Whole is greater than its Part.

Et est aequale omnibus suis partibus simul sumptis. Et Pars, quae aequalis est caeteris omnibus partibus simul sumptis, est Dimidium totius.

And it is equal to all its parts taken together. And the Part which is equal to all the other parts taken together is the Half of the whole.

p. 8

VII. Duae rectae Lineae spatium non comprehendunt.

VII. Two straight Lines do not enclose a space.

Scilicet ad claudendum undique spatium, saltem tres Lineae rectae requiruntur.

That is, to enclose a space on all sides, at least three straight Lines are required.

VIII. Duae rectae Lineae non habent commune segmentum, seu Partem.

VIII. Two straight Lines do not have a common segment, or Part.

Scilicet duae rectae lineae, quae angulum efficiunt, non possunt continuari in unam rectam, nisi inflectantur.

That is, two straight lines which make an angle cannot be continued into one straight line unless they are bent.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

Problemata.

Problems.

Problemata sunt Propositiones, quae docent Opus aliquod faciendum circa Lineas, Angulos, aut Figuras. Praecipua, ad rectilineas Figuras pertinentia, hic proponuntur, eorumque demonstrationes solùm indicantur, exceptâ primâ: tum quia hae facilè ex positis Principijs, aut demonstrandis Theorematibus deducuntur; tum quia Problemata non sunt Principia ad ceteras veritates ostendendas; sed ut Hypotheses supponi possunt. Quae Methodus Discentibus videtur magis adcommodata, ne sub initium perturbentur; sed post demonstrata Theoremata in Problematum demonstrationibus inveniendis exerceantur.

Problems are Propositions which teach how to do some Work concerning Lines, Angles, or Figures. The principal ones, pertaining to rectilinear Figures, are proposed here, and their demonstrations are only indicated, except for the first: both because these are easily deduced from the Principles laid down, or from the Theorems to be demonstrated; and because Problems are not Principles for showing the other truths, but can be supposed as Hypotheses. This Method seems better suited to Learners, so that they may not be thrown into confusion at the beginning, but, once the Theorems have been demonstrated, may exercise themselves in finding the demonstrations of the Problems.

PROBLEMA I. (Icon. I. Fig. 1.)

Problem I. (Plate I. Fig. 1.)

Triangulum AEquilaterum efficere.

To make an Equilateral Triangle.

Aperiatur Circinus intervallo datae lineae AB; tum ab utraque lineae extremitate fiant, Circino invariato, duo arcus, se secantes in C: demùm ex Puncto C ducantur lineae CA, & CB, quae constituent Triangulum AEquilaterum ABC.

Let the Compass be opened to the interval of the given line AB; then from each end of the line, with the Compass unchanged, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at C; finally from the Point C let the lines CA and CB be drawn, which will constitute the Equilateral Triangle ABC.

Ad demonstrandum, perficiatur circulus A C F, & B C E.

For the demonstration, let the circles ACF and BCE be completed.

Demostratio. Linea A C est aequalis lineae A B, quia ductae sunt a centro ad circunferentiam ejusdem Circuli: ex definitione XV. Sed eidem lineae A B est etiam aequalis linea B C: propter eandem definitionem: ergò lineae C A & C B sunt aequales inter se: ex I. Axiomate; adeoque Triangulum A B C, constans ex tribus lineis aequalibus, est AEquilaterum.

Demonstration. The line AC is equal to the line AB, because they are drawn from the center to the circumference of the same Circle: from definition XV. But the line BC is also equal to the same line AB, by the same definition: therefore the lines CA and CB are equal to each other: from Axiom 1; and so the Triangle ABC, consisting of three equal lines, is Equilateral.

Ad efficiendum Triangulum Isosceles, aperiatur semel circinus majori, vel minori intervallo, quàm data linea; & deinde fiant arcus, ut supra. Si verò dum fiunt arcus, semper varietur circini intervallum, fiet Triangulum Scalenum.

To make an Isosceles Triangle, let the compass be opened once to a greater or a lesser interval than the given line; and then let arcs be made, as above. But if, while the arcs are being made, the interval of the compass is changed each time, a Scalene Triangle will be made.

p. 9

PROBLEMA II. (Fig. 2.) — Problem II. (Fig. 2.)

Lineam Bifariam dividere.

To bisect a line.

Ab extremis A, & B datae lineae fiant duo arcus, aequali circini intervallo, se secantes in C; & alii duo infra eandem lineam, se secantes in D. Linea C D dividet bifariam lineam A B. Demonstratur ex Theor. IV. hujus libri par. 2. si ex C, & D ducantur lineae ad extrema A, & B.

From the ends A and B of the given line let two arcs be made with the same opening of the compass, cutting each other at C; and two others below the same line, cutting each other at D. The line CD will bisect the line AB. It is demonstrated from Theor. IV of this book, pt. 1, if from C and D lines are drawn to the ends A and B.

PROBLEMA III. (Fig. 3.) — Problem III. (Fig. 3.)

Angulum Bifariam dividere.

To bisect an angle.

Ex puncto anguli A, ad libitum intervallum, abscindantur hinc inde aequalia latera in B, & C: tum ex punctis sectionis B, & C, aequali circini intervallo, fiant duo arcus, se secantes in D. Linea D A dividet angulum bifariam. Dem. ex eod. Theor. IV.; ductis ex B, & C lineis ad D.

From the vertex of the angle A, at any interval you please, let equal sides be cut off on either side at B and C; then from the points of section B and C, with the same opening of the compass, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at D. The line DA will bisect the angle. Dem. from the same Theor. IV, with lines drawn from B and C to D.

PROBLEMA IV. (Fig. 4.)

Problem IV. (Fig. 4.)

Lineam Parallelam ducere.

To draw a parallel line.

Sit ducenda lineae F G Parallela, quae transeat per punctum D. Primò ponatur unus Circini pes in D, alter in quovis puncto lineae F G, ut in A. Secundò ex A, invariato circini intervallo, secetur eadem linea in B. Tertiò ex punctis B, & D eadem circini diductione fiant duo arcus, se secantes in C. Linea D C erit Parallela lineae F G. Ex Theor. VI. Cor. 2.

Let a line parallel to FG be drawn, passing through the point D. First, let one foot of the compass be placed at D, the other at any point of the line FG, as at A. Second, from A, with the opening of the compass unchanged, let the same line be cut at B. Third, from the points B and D, with the same spread of the compass, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at C. The line DC will be parallel to the line FG. From Theor. VI, Cor. 2.

Alitèr. Quovis puncto, veluti medio E, fiat arcus D F, & alius ex altera parte G H: tum secetur arcus G H aequalis arcui D F. Linea D H erit Parallela quaesita.

Otherwise. From any point, such as the middle point E, let an arc DF be made, and another, GH, on the other side; then let the arc GH be cut equal to the arc DF. The line DH will be the parallel sought.

PROBLEMA V. (Fig. 5.)

Problem V. (Fig. 5.)

Lineam Perpendicularem ducere.

To draw a perpendicular line.

Si ex dato puncto F extra lineam sit ducenda Perpendicularis ad lineam B G: posito uno circini pede in F, secetur hinc inde linea, ulterius producta (si opus fuerit) in B, & G: deinde ex B, & G fiant duo Arcus, aequali circini intervallo, se

If from a given point F outside a line a Perpendicular is to be drawn to the line BG: placing one foot of the compass at F, let the line be cut on either side, extended further (if need be), at B and G; then from B and G let two Arcs be made, with the same opening of the compass, cutting

p. 10

secantes in H. Linea F H erit Perpendicularis quaesita. Ex Teor. IV. par. 2.

each other at H. The line FH will be the Perpendicular sought. From Theor. IV, pt. 2.

Advertendum tamen, quod non â quolibet puncto ad quodlibet lineae punctum potest duci Penpendicularis; sed necesse est quandoque datam lineam ulterius producere, ut ad illam ex dato puncto duci possit Perpendicularis.

It must be noted, however, that a Perpendicular cannot be drawn from any point whatever to any point whatever of a line; but it is sometimes necessary to produce the given line further, so that a Perpendicular can be drawn to it from the given point.

Si Perpendicularis ducenda sit ad datum punctum C, intra lineam B G, sive id punctum sit extremum lineae, sive non. Fiat ex puncto C ad libitum intervallum arcus fere semicirculi, & circino invariato abscindatur primò arcus G E, deinde arcus E D: tum etiam, invariato circino, ex punctis D, & E, fiant duo arcus, se secantes in F. Erit ducta Linea F C Perpendicularis quaesita. Ex eod. Theor.

If a Perpendicular is to be drawn at a given point C within the line BG, whether that point is the end of the line or not: from the point C let an arc of nearly a semicircle be made, at any interval you please, and, with the compass unchanged, let there be cut off first the arc GE, then the arc ED; then also, with the compass unchanged, from the points D and E let two arcs be made, cutting each other at F. The line FC, when drawn, will be the Perpendicular sought. From the same Theor.

PROBLEMA VI. (Fig. 6.)

Problem VI. (Fig. 6.)

Quadratum efficere.

To make a Square.

Ducatur ad extremum lineae A B perpendicularis illi aequalis C A: deinde, eodem datae lineae intervallo, ex C, & B fiant duo arcus, se secantes in D. Demum ex puncto D ducantur lineae ad B, & C; Et habebitur Quadratum. Ex Theor. VI. cor. 2.

Let a perpendicular CA, equal to the line AB, be drawn at its end: then, with the same interval of the given line, from C and B let two arcs be made, cutting each other at D. Finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and the Square will be had. From Theor. VI, Cor. 2.

PROBLEMA VII. (Fig. 7.)

Problem VII. (Fig. 7.)

Rhombum efficere.

To make a Rhombus.

Ad extremum datae lineae A B ducatur alia illi aequalis C A, ad quemcumque Angulum non rectum: deinde ab extremis C, & B, eodem datae linae intervallo, fiant duo arcus, se secantes in D. Demum ex puncto D ducantur lineae ad B, & C: & habebitur Rhombus. Ex eod. Theor.

At the end of the given line AB let another, CA, equal to it be drawn, at any Angle that is not right: then from the extremities C and B, with the same interval of the given line, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at D. Finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and the Rhombus will be had. From the same Theor.

PROBLEMA VIII. (Fig. 8.)

Problem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

Rectangulum oblongum efficere.

To make an oblong Rectangle.

Ad extremum A B ducatur perpendicularis major, vel minor illa: deinde ab extremo C fiat arcus, intervallo lineae A B, & ab extremo B fiat arcus, intervallo lineae C A, priorem arcum intersecans in D: demum ex puncto D ducantur lineae ad B, & C: & habebitur Rectangulum altera parte longius. Ex eod. Theor.

At the end of AB let a perpendicular greater or less than it be drawn: then from the end C let an arc be made with the interval of the line AB, and from the end B let an arc be made with the interval of the line CA, intersecting the former arc at D: finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and a Rectangle longer on one side will be had. From the same Theor.

p. 11

PROBLEMA IX. (Fig. 9.) — Problem IX. (Fig. 9.)

Rhomboidem efficere.

To make a Rhomboid.

Ad extremum lineae A B ducatur linea inaequalis C A, ad angulum non rectum: tum ab extremo C, intervallo lineae A B, fiat arcus; & ab extremo B, intervallo lineae C A, fiat alius, priorem intersecans in D. Demum ex puncto D ducantur lineae ad B, & C: & habebitur Rhomboides. Ex eod. Theor.

At the end of the line AB let an unequal line CA be drawn, at an angle that is not right: then from the end C, with the interval of the line AB, let an arc be made; and from the end B, with the interval of the line CA, let another be made, intersecting the former at D. Finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and the Rhomboid will be had. From the same Theor.

PROBLEMA X. (Fig. 10.) — Problem X. (Fig. 10.)

Efficere Triangulum alteri aequale.

To make a Triangle equal to another.

Sumatur linea D E aequalis lineae A B: deinde, intervallo lineae A C, ab extremo D fiat arcus: similiter, intervallo lineae B C, ab extremo E fiat arcus, qui priorem intersecet in F. Triangulum D E F erit aequale triangulo A B C. Patet ex ipsa constructione.

Let a line DE be taken equal to the line AB: then, with the interval of the line AC, let an arc be made from the end D; similarly, with the interval of the line BC, let an arc be made from the end E, which intersects the former at F. The Triangle DEF will be equal to the triangle ABC. It is evident from the construction itself.

Similiter fit Triangulum ex tribus lineis non conjunctis A, B, C; dummodo duae simul sumptae, quae angulum constituunt, sint majores una Recta; propter def. VI.

In like manner a Triangle is made from three lines not joined, A, B, C; provided that the two taken together which constitute an angle are greater than the one Straight line: by def. VI.

PROBLEMA XI. (Fig. 11.)

Problem XI. (Fig. 11.)

Angulum aequalem alteri efficere.

To make an Angle equal to another.

Ex dato Angulo A, quovis intervallo, fiat arcus B C: deinde ab extremo D lineae D E, ubi ponendus est Angulus aequalis, eodem circini intervallo fiat arcus, qui secet datam lineam in F: tum abscindatur arcus F G aequalis arcui B C. Linea ducta ex D per G, constituet in D angulum aequalem angulo A. Ex def. Anguli not. 1.

From the given Angle A, at any interval, let an arc BC be made: then from the end D of the line DE, where the equal Angle is to be placed, with the same interval of the compass, let an arc be made which cuts the given line at F: then let the arc FG be cut off equal to the arc BC. The line drawn from D through G will constitute at D an angle equal to the angle A. From the def. of an Angle, note 1.

PROBLEMA XII. (Fig. 12.)

Problem XII. (Fig. 12.)

Rectangulum, vel aliud Parallelogrammum efficere, dato Triangulo aequale.

To make a Rectangle, or another Parallelogram, equal to a given Triangle.

Ponatur Parallela C D Basi A K dati Trianguli: deinde dividatur Basis in E bifariam, & super lineam aequalem dimidiò Basis fiat Rectangulum, vel quodcumque Parallelogrammum F D B G, inter parallelam C D: & erit Parallelogrammum B D aequale dato triangulo A C K. Ex Theor. VIII.

Let a Parallel CD be placed to the Base AK of the given Triangle: then let the Base be divided in two at E, and upon a line equal to half the Base let a Rectangle, or any Parallelogram FDBG, be made, within the parallel CD: and the Parallelogram BD will be equal to the given triangle ACK. From Theor. VIII.

p. 12

Hinc patet, quomodo cuicumque Trapezio fiat aequale Parallelogrammum. Dividatur enim Trapezium in duo Triangula, ducendo lineam ad oppositos Angulos H I, cui ducantur Parallelae per verticem L, & M: tum divisa H I bifariam in N, inter easdem Parallelas super basi B G aequali dimidiae H N, fiat Parallelogrammum F B D G: quod erit aequale Trapezio L M, utpotè aequale duobus Triangulis H L I, & H M I, quae Trapezium componunt. Ex eod. Theor.

Hence it is evident how a Parallelogram may be made equal to any Trapezium whatever. For let the Trapezium be divided into two Triangles by drawing a line to the opposite Angles HI, to which let Parallels be drawn through the vertices L and M: then, HI having been bisected at N, between the same Parallels, upon a base BG equal to the half HN, let the Parallelogram FBDG be made: which will be equal to the Trapezium LM, inasmuch as it is equal to the two Triangles HLI and HMI, which compose the Trapezium. From the same Theor.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

Theoremata.

Theorems.

Theorema est Propositio, proprietatem aliquam quantitatis demonstrans. Tres praecipuae sunt ejus partes: Propositio ipsa, quae proponit veritatem ostendendam: Praeparatio, quae disponit lineas quandoqne necessarias ad demonstrationem: Demonstratio, quae ex positis Principiis, aut Theorematibus propositam veritatem concludit.

A Theorem is a Proposition demonstrating some property of quantity. Its principal parts are three: the Proposition itself, which proposes the truth to be shown; the Preparation, which arranges the lines sometimes necessary for the demonstration; the Demonstration, which concludes the proposed truth from the Principles laid down, or from Theorems.

Duodecim in hoc capite ex 1. & 2. Euclidis libro selecta Theoremata proponuntur, adjectis Corollariis, seu illationibus, quae ex Theorematibus facilè descendunt: quorum alia in Euclidis propositionibus continentur, alia extra Euclidem sunt; ejus Authoris ordine nonnihil variato, ad clariorem, si Superis placet, methodum retinendam. Initio quippe facto ab Angulis, & Lineis, ad Triangulorum proprietates, & ex iis ad figuras Quadrilateras demonstrandas devenimus.

Twelve Theorems selected from the 1st and 2nd books of Euclid are proposed in this chapter, with Corollaries, or inferences, added, which follow easily from the Theorems: some of these are contained in the propositions of Euclid, others lie outside Euclid; the order of that Author has been varied somewhat, so as to keep, if it please Heaven, a clearer method. For, beginning from Angles and Lines, we come to the properties of Triangles, and from these to demonstrating Quadrilateral figures.

Ne verò Numerus insigniorum Euclidis Propositionum, qualis passim à Mathematicis usurpatur lateat; illum ad paginae finem adponemus. Principia tamen, unde Demonstrationes descendunt, non semper indicabimus; quia tam clara sunt, ut animo praesentia supponantur.

But lest the Number of the more notable Propositions of Euclid, as it is commonly used by Mathematicians, should lie hidden, we shall place it at the foot of the page. The Principles, however, from which the Demonstrations descend, we shall not always indicate, because they are so clear that they may be supposed present to the mind.

THEOREMA I. (Icon. II. Fig. 1.)

Theorem I. (Plate II. Fig. 1.)

Linea recta, cadens in aliam rectam, ut G A in D E, facit angulos ex utraque simul parte aequales duobus Rectis. 3

A straight line falling upon another straight line, as GA upon DE, makes the angles on both sides together equal to two Right angles. (a)

Praeparatio. Facto ex centro A quovis Circulo, ducatur ad lineam D E Perpendicularis B C.

Preparation. A Circle having been made from the center A at any interval, let a Perpendicular BC be drawn to the line DE.

Euclidis lib. 1. Prop. 13.

Euclid, bk. 1, prop. 13.

p. 13

Demonstratio. Duo simul Anguli D A G, & G A E habent eandem Mensuram, ac duo Recti D A B, & B A E, scilicet duos Circuli quadrantes, juxtà def. Anguli, not. 1. Ergo duo simul Anguli D A G, & G A E sunt aequales duobus Rectis; ex 1. Axiomate.

Demonstration. The two Angles DAG and GAE together have the same Measure as the two Right angles DAB and BAE, namely two quadrants of a Circle, according to the def. of an Angle, note 1. Therefore the two Angles DAG and GAE together are equal to two Right angles: from Axiom 1.

Corollarium I. Si duae linae non sunt in directum positae, ut D A, A G, comprehendunt ex una parte arcum minorem, ex altera arcum majorem semicirculo, ut patet; unde solùm linea recta, ut D E, in quam cadat alia recta, comprehendit Angulos aequales duobus rectis. 2

Corollary I. If two lines are not placed in a straight line, as DA, AG, they comprehend on one side an arc less than a semicircle, on the other an arc greater, as is evident; whence only a straight line, as DE, upon which another straight line falls, comprehends Angles equal to two right angles. (a)

II. Si duae lineae se invicem secent, Anguli ad verticem oppositi, ut D A F, & E A I, sunt aequales. Nam arcus D B E est semicirculus; similiter arcus F G I est semicirculus, utpotè à diametris secti: ergo si auferatur ab utroque communis arcus F E, remanet arcus D F aequalis arcui E I, & Angulus D A F aequalis Angulo E A I. 2

II. If two lines cut each other, the vertically opposite Angles, as DAF and EAI, are equal. For the arc DBE is a semicircle; likewise the arc FGI is a semicircle, inasmuch as they are cut off by diameters: therefore if the common arc FE is taken away from each, there remains the arc DF equal to the arc EI, and the Angle DAF equal to the Angle EAI. (b)

III. Si plures rectae lineae supra eandem rectam in eodem puncto uniantur, faciunt angulos omnes aequales duobus rectis. Et si duae rectae, aut plures se invicem secent, faciunt omnes angulos, circa idem punctum, aequales quatuor rectis: nam duobus semicirculis omnes comprehenduntur. 2

III. If several straight lines are united upon the same straight line at the same point, they make all the angles equal to two right angles. And if two straight lines, or more, cut each other, they make all the angles about the same point equal to four right angles: for they are all comprehended by two semicircles. (c)

THEOREMA II. (Fig. 2.)

Theorem II. (Fig. 2.)

Si linea recta duas rectas Parallelas secet, fient I. duo simul Anguli Interni, L, & N, aequales duobus Angulis rectis. II. Anguli Alterni, I, & N, aequales inter se. III. Angulus Exterior, H, etiam aequalis Angulo N, Interiori opposito versus eandem partem. 2

If a straight line cuts two Parallel straight lines, then I. the two Internal Angles L and N together will be equal to two right Angles. II. The Alternate Angles I and N will be equal to each other. III. The Exterior Angle H will also be equal to the Angle N, the Interior opposite toward the same side. (d)

Dem. I. Quatuor simul Anguli I, & L, M, & N sunt aequales quatuor Angulis rectis: ex antec. Theor. sed duo simul Anguli interni L, & N, sunt aequales duobus simul internis ex altera parte I, & M: juxtà defin. 13. Parallel. Ergo duo simul Anguli interni L, & N ex una parte sunt aequales duobus Rectis; sicut duo interni ex altera I, & M.

Dem. I. The four Angles I and L, M and N together are equal to four right Angles: from the preceding Theor.; but the two internal Angles L and N together are equal to the two internal ones together on the other side, I and M: according to defin. 13, Parall. Therefore the two internal Angles L and N together on one side are equal to two Right angles, just as the two internal ones on the other side, I and M.

Dem. II. Duo simul Anguli L, & N sunt aequales duobus Rectis: ex modò demonstratis; sed etiam duo simul Anguli I, & L sunt aequales duobus Rectis; ex I. Theor. ergo, sublato communi Angulo L, remanet Angulus I, aequalis Angulo N alterno.

Dem. II. The two Angles L and N together are equal to two Right angles: from what has just been demonstrated; but the two Angles I and L together are also equal to two Right angles: from Theor. I; therefore, the common Angle L being taken away, there remains the Angle I equal to the alternate Angle N.

Dem. III. Duo simul Anguli L, & N sunt aequales duobus rectis: sed etiam duo simul Anguli L, & H sunt aequales duobus Rectis; ex I. Theor. ergo, sublato communi Angulo L, remanet

Dem. III. The two Angles L and N together are equal to two right angles: but the two Angles L and H together are also equal to two Right angles: from Theor. I; therefore, the common Angle L being taken away, there remains the Angle

Pr. 14.

Prop. 14.

Pr. 15.

Prop. 15.

Cor. pr. 15.

Cor. of prop. 15.

Pr. 29.

Prop. 29.

p. 14

Angulus exterior H aequalis Angulo N interiori, & opposito versus eandem partem.

the exterior H, equal to the Angle N, interior and opposite toward the same side.

Coroll. Facilè demonstratur Conversum hujus Theorematis; scilicet, quòd si Linea, secans alias duas lineas, faciat duos angulos internos ad eandem partem aequales duobus rectis, illae duae lineae erunt Parallelae: Nam aequè inclinabuntur ad mediam secantem, & inter se. Similiter si faciat angulos alternos, aut internum, & externum aequales 5.

Cor. The Converse of this Theorem is easily demonstrated; namely, that if a Line cutting two other lines makes the two internal angles on the same side equal to two right angles, those two lines will be Parallel: For they will be equally inclined to the middle secant, and to each other. Likewise if it makes the alternate angles, or the internal and the external, equal (a).

THEOREMA III. (Fig. 3.)

Theorem III. (Fig. 3.)

In quocumque Triangulo I. tres simul Anguli sunt aequales duobus Rectis. II. Angulus exterior, G, est aequalis duobus simul interioribus oppositis, A, & B. 3

In any Triangle I. the three Angles together are equal to two Right angles. II. The exterior Angle G is equal to the two interior opposite ones together, A and B. (b)

Praeparatio. Ducatur Linea D E Parallela Basi B C per verticem A.

Preparation. Let a Line DE be drawn Parallel to the Base BC through the vertex A.

Dem. I. Angulus B est aequalis angulo D alterno, ex antec. Theor. & Angulus C est aequalis angulo E, etiam alterno: sed Anguli D, E, & A simul sunt aequales duobus rectis, ex I. Theor. ergo si Angulis, B, & C, addatur etiam Angulus A, tres simul anguli B, C, & A sunt aequales duobus Rectis.

Dem. I. The Angle B is equal to the alternate angle D, from the preceding Theor., and the Angle C is equal to the angle E, likewise alternate: but the Angles D, E and A together are equal to two right angles, from Theor. I; therefore if to the Angles B and C the Angle A is also added, the three angles B, C and A together are equal to two Right angles.

Dem. II. Anguli B, & A cum C simul sunt aequales duobus Rectis: sed etiam duo simul Anguli C, & G exterior, sunt aequales duobus rectis; ergo, sublato communi Angulo C, remanet Angulus G exterior aequalis duobus simul Angulis interioribus oppositis A, & B.

Dem. II. The Angles B and A together with C are equal to two Right angles: but the two Angles C and G, the exterior, together are also equal to two right angles; therefore, the common Angle C being taken away, there remains the exterior Angle G equal to the two interior opposite Angles A and B together.

Coroll. I. Cognitis duobus Angulis alicujus Trianguli, jam tertius innotescit, residuus ad duos rectos.

Cor. I. When two Angles of any Triangle are known, the third at once becomes known, as the remainder up to two right angles.

II. Si duo Triangula habeant duos Angulos aequales, etiam tertium, residuum ad duos rectos, habebunt aequalem.

II. If two Triangles have two Angles equal, they will also have the third, the remainder up to two right angles, equal.

III. Ex eodem puncto ad eandem lineam rectam non potest duci, nisi una Perpendicularis; quia Triangulum non potest habere duos Angulos rectos.

III. From the same point to the same straight line only one Perpendicular can be drawn; because a Triangle cannot have two right Angles.

THEOREMA IV. (Fig. 4.)

Theorem IV. (Fig. 4.)

Duo Triangula sunt omninò aequalia, I. Si habeant duo latera singula singulis aequalia, & angulum iis comprehensum aequalem. II. Si habeant tria latera similiter aequalia. III. Si habeant duos angulos aequales, & latus iis

Two Triangles are wholly equal, I. If they have two sides equal, each to each, and the angle comprehended by them equal. II. If they have three sides likewise equal. III. If they have two equal angles, and the side comprehended by them

Eucl. lib. I. prop. 28. 27.

Eucl. bk. I, prop. 28, 27.

Prop. 32.

Prop. 32.

p. 15

comprehensum aequale. IV. Si habeant latus uni ex duobus aequalibus angulis oppositum aequale 2.

equal. IV. If they have a side opposite one of the two equal angles equal (a).

Dem. I. Si latus A B sit aequale lateri D E, & latus A C aequale lateri D F, & Angulus A aequali angulo D; Latus D E lateri A B superpositum congruet, & latus D F lateri A C, & puncta E, F punctis B, C: ergo & Bases, & reliqui ad Basim Anguli congruent, & erunt in utroque triangulo aequales: ex definitione VI. lineae rectae.

Dem. I. If the side AB is equal to the side DE, and the side AC equal to the side DF, and the Angle A equal to the angle D: the Side DE, superposed on the side AB, will coincide with it, and the side DF with the side AC, and the points E, F with the points B, C: therefore both the Bases and the remaining Angles at the Base will coincide, and will be equal in each triangle: from definition VI of the straight line.

Dem. II. Si distantia B C sit aequalis distantiae E F, & reliqua latera continentia Angulos A, & D, singula singulis aequalia; erit angulus A aequalis angulo D: ex definit. Anguli not. 3. ergo totum triangulum D E F erit aequale triangulo A B C: ex I. part. hujus.

Dem. II. If the distance BC is equal to the distance EF, and the remaining sides containing the Angles A and D are equal, each to each, the angle A will be equal to the angle D: from the definit. of Angle, no. 3; therefore the whole triangle DEF will be equal to the triangle ABC: from pt. I of this.

Dem. III. Si linea E F sit aequalis lineae B C; huic superposita, congruet & si angulus E, sit aequalis angulo A B C, etiam latus D E congruet lateri A B: (si enim latus D E caderet intra, ut in H, esset angulus E minor; si extra, ut in G esset angulus E major angulo A B C contra hypothesim) & si angulus F sit aequalis angulo A C B, ex eadem ratione latus D F congruet lateri A C: ergo erunt triangula A B C, EDF omninò aequalia.

Dem. III. If the line EF is equal to the line BC, then, superposed on it, it will coincide with it; and if the angle E is equal to the angle ABC, the side DE will also coincide with the side AB (for if the side DE fell inside, as at H, the angle E would be smaller; if outside, as at G, the angle E would be greater than the angle ABC, contrary to the hypothesis); and if the angle F is equal to the angle ACB, by the same reasoning the side DF will coincide with the side AC; therefore the triangles ABC, EDF will be wholly equal.

Dem. IV. Si linea E F sit aequalis lineae B C, & angulus E aequalis angulo A B C, & angulus A aequalis angulo D: erit etiam angulus F aequalis angulo A C B: ex III. Theor. ergo erunt triangula A B C, & D E F omninò aequalia: ex tertia parte hujus.

Dem. IV. If the line EF is equal to the line BC, and the angle E equal to the angle ABC, and the angle A equal to the angle D: the angle F will also be equal to the angle ACB: from Theor. III; therefore the triangles ABC and DEF will be wholly equal: from the third part of this.

Coroll. Hinc patet, quòd lineae, ab extremitatibus ejusdem Basis productae, quò magis propè Basim conjunguntur, eò efficiunt Angulum H majorem Angulo A, & Angulum A majorem Angulo G: quia quum anguli ad Basim H B C, & H C B, minores sint, quàm anguli A B C, & A C B, tertius H supra Basim, residuus ad duos rectos, debet esse major Angulo A. Ex Theor. III. s2

Cor. Hence it is plain that the nearer to the Base the lines produced from the extremities of the same Base are joined, the greater they make the Angle H than the Angle A, and the Angle A than the Angle G: because, since the angles at the Base HBC and HCB are smaller than the angles ABC and ACB, the third, H, above the Base, the remainder up to two right angles, must be greater than the Angle A. From Theor. III. (b)

THEOREMA V. (Fig. 5.)

Theorem V. (Fig. 5.)

Triangulum Isosceles, ut A B C habet angulos supra Basim, B, & C, aequales inter se. s3

An Isosceles Triangle, as ABC, has the angles above the Base, B and C, equal to each other. (c)

Praepar. Intelligatur Basis divisa Bifariam in L, & ducatur A L.

Prep. Let the Base be understood to be bisected at L, and let AL be drawn.

Dem. In Triangulis A B L, & A C L, linea B L est aequalis lineae L C: ex construct. Latus A B aequale lateri A C: ex supposit. Latus A L commune: ergo Triangulum A B L est omninò aequale

Dem. In the Triangles ABL and ACL, the line BL is equal to the line LC: from the construction. The side AB is equal to the side AC: from the supposition. The side AL is common: therefore the Triangle ABL is wholly equal

Eucl. lib. I. prop. 4. 8. 26.

Eucl. bk. I, prop. 4, 8, 26.

Eucl. lib. I prop. 21.

Eucl. bk. I, prop. 21.

Prop. 5.

Prop. 5.

p. 16

Triangulo A C L, & anguli B, & C, communi lateri oppositi, sunt aequales. Ex antec. Theor.

to the Triangle ACL, and the angles B and C, opposite the common side, are equal. From the preceding Theor.

Coroll. I. Etiam Anguli D, & E infra Basim sunt aequales; nam duo simul anguli B, & D, sunt aequales duobus rectis: nec non anguli C, & E: ex Theor. I. ergo sublatis aequalibus B, & C, remanent aequales anguli D, & E.

Cor. I. The Angles D and E below the Base are also equal; for the two angles B and D together are equal to two right angles, and no less the angles C and E: from Theor. I; therefore, when the equal angles B and C are taken away, the angles D and E remain equal.

II. Si anguli B, & C, erunt aequales, etiam latera A B, & A C, erunt aequalia; nam imposita C L super aequalem L B; anguli, & extrema puncta B, & C congruent; Punctum A est utrique lateri A B, & A C commune; ergo lineae A C, A B erunt aequales: ex defin. VI. lineae rectae. 3

II. If the angles B and C are equal, the sides AB and AC will also be equal; for when CL is placed upon the equal LB, the angles and the extreme points B and C will coincide; the Point A is common to both sides AB and AC; therefore the lines AC, AB will be equal: from defin. VI of the straight line. (a)

III. Si Triangulum A H I sit aequilaterum, erunt singuli tres anguli aequales, & ê converso si sint tres anguli aequales, erunt tria latera aequalibus angulis opposita etiam aequalia.

III. If the Triangle AHI is equilateral, each of its three angles will be equal; and conversely, if the three angles are equal, the three sides opposite the equal angles will also be equal.

IV. Linea A L si dividat Basim bifariam, etiam dividet angulum A bifariam: & si dividet angulum A bifariam, etiam dividet bifariam, & perpendiculariter Basim trianguli A B C Isoscelis; nam fiunt duo Triangula A B L, & A C L omninò aqualia: ex Theor. IV. & anguli ad L, utpote utrinque aequales, recti sunt.

IV. If the line AL bisects the Base, it will also bisect the angle A: and if it bisects the angle A, it will also bisect the Base of the Isosceles triangle ABC, and perpendicularly: for two Triangles ABL and ACL come out wholly equal, from Theor. IV; and the angles at L, being equal on either side, are right.

Coroll. V. In Triangulis majori lateri major angulus opponitur, & ê converso. Nam sit Triangulum H A I, aequilaterum, & aequiangulum, ex. gr. si crescit Latus H I in C, crescit etiam angulus A, & minuitur angulus C, (ex III. Theoremate) qui opponitur minori lateri A H: & si crescit angulus A, etiam crescit Latus H I in C, vel B. s2

Cor. V. In Triangles the greater angle is opposite the greater side, and conversely. For let the Triangle HAI be equilateral and equiangular: if, e.g., the Side HI grows to C, the angle A also grows, and the angle C diminishes (from Theorem III), which is opposite the smaller side AH: and if the angle A grows, the Side HI also grows to C, or B. (b)

VI. Perpendicularis A L est brevissima omnium, quae duci possunt ex eodem puncto A ad lineam B C: nam ceterae lineae, utpotè oppositae angulo L Recto majori, sunt majores; & quò magis recedunt á perpendiculari, eò majores sunt; quia oppositae angulis obtusioribus.

VI. The Perpendicular AL is the shortest of all the lines that can be drawn from the same point A to the line BC: for the other lines, being opposite the Right angle L, which is greater, are greater; and the farther they recede from the perpendicular, the greater they are, because they are opposite more obtuse angles.

Hinc omnes distantias metítur Linea Perpendicularis; quia omnium rectarum, quae duci possunt ab uno puncto ad eandem lineam, est brevissima; adeoque una & certa Mensura.

Hence the Perpendicular Line measures all distances; because of all the straight lines that can be drawn from one point to the same line it is the shortest, and therefore the one and certain Measure.

THEOREMA VI. (Fig. 6.)

Theorem VI. (Fig. 6.)

Diameter dividit Parallelogrammum in duo Triangula aequalia. s3

The Diameter divides a Parallelogram into two equal Triangles. (c)

Dem. Triangula A B C, & B D C habent latus B C commune, & Angulum A B C aequalem angulo B C D alterno, nec non

Dem. The Triangles ABC and BDC have the side BC common, and the Angle ABC equal to the alternate angle BCD, and also the angle

Eucl. bk. I, prop. 6.

Eucl. lib. I. prop. 18. 19.

D B C aequalem angulo A C B etiam alterno: ex Theor. II. ergo & latera aequalibus angulis opposita, & tota triangula sunt invicem aequalia, ex Theor. IV.

DBC equal to the angle ACB, likewise alternate: from Theor. II; therefore the sides opposite the equal angles, and the whole triangles, are equal to each other, from Theor. IV.

Coroll. I. Hinc sequitur, quod in Parallelogrammo anguli oppositi sunt aequales: nam quum anguli alterni circa diametrum sint aequales, ex modo demonstratis, reliqui duo oppositi erunt etiam aequales. ex III. Theor.

Cor. I. Hence it follows that in a Parallelogram the opposite angles are equal: for since the alternate angles about the diameter are equal, from what has just been demonstrated, the other two opposite angles will also be equal, from Theor. III.

II. In Figura Quadrilatera si lineae ex utraque parte oppositae, sint aequales, erunt etiam Parallelae; & si duae oppositae sint aequales, & Parallelae, etiam aliae duae erunt aequales, & Parallelae; nam ducta Diametro, fient duo Triangula aequalia. ex Theor. IV. 4

II. In a Quadrilateral Figure, if the lines opposite each other on either side are equal, they will also be Parallel; and if two opposite lines are equal and Parallel, the other two will also be equal and Parallel; for when the Diameter is drawn, two equal Triangles will be formed, from Theor. IV. (a)

III. Complementa A E, E D circa Diametrum habent superficiem aequalem. Nam Triangula A B C, & B C D, sunt aequalia; ex antec. Theor. ergo si ex iis subtrahantur Triangulum H B E aequale etiam Triangulo E B I, nec non Triangulum F E C ex eadem ratione aequale Triangulo E C G; quae remanent complementa A E, & E D, sunt aequalia. 2

III. The complements AE, ED about the Diameter have an equal surface. For the Triangles ABC and BCD are equal, from the preceding Theor.; therefore if from them we subtract the Triangle HBE, equal to the Triangle EBI, and also the Triangle FEC, for the same reason equal to the Triangle ECG, the complements that remain, AE and ED, are equal. (b)

THEOREMA VII. (Fig. 7.)

Theorem VII. (Fig. 7.)

Parallelogramma, in eadem Basi constituta, & inter easdem Parallelas, sunt aequalia, 2

Parallelograms constituted on the same Base and between the same Parallels are equal. (c)

Dem. Quoniam A G, & G F sunt Parallelogramma, constituta in eadem Basi C G, huic opposita latera A E, & F B erunt aequalia: ex antec. Theor. additâ communi linea E F, erunt latera A F, & E B aequalia, & latus C F est aequale lateri G B, & angulus externus A E C aequalis interiori opposito A B C; ex Theor. II. ergo Triangula A F C, & E B G sunt aequalia: ergo sublato communi Triangulo E L F, remanet Trapezium A E C L, aequale trapezio L G F B: ergo addito communi Triangulo L C G; fit Parallelogrammum A G aequale Parallelogrammo G F.

Dem. Since AG and GF are Parallelograms constituted on the same Base CG, the sides opposite it, AE and FB, will be equal, from the preceding Theor.; adding the common line EF, the sides AF and EB will be equal; and the side CF is equal to the side GB, and the exterior angle AEC equal to the interior opposite angle ABC, from Theor. II; therefore the Triangles AFC and EBG are equal: therefore, taking away the common Triangle ELF, there remains the Trapezium AECL, equal to the trapezium LGFB: therefore, adding the common Triangle LCG, the Parallelogram AG becomes equal to the Parallelogram GF.

Coroll. I. Etiam Parallelogramma A G, & E D, constituta in aequalibus Basibus, & inter easdem Parallelas, sunt aequalia inter se; nam ambo sunt aequalia eidem Parallelogrammo F G. s4

Cor. I. Parallelograms AG and ED constituted on equal Bases and between the same Parallels are also equal to each other; for both are equal to the same Parallelogram FG. (d)

II. Quoniam verò distantiam inter Parallelas A B, C D metitur perpendicularis A C; ex Theor. V. coroll. ult. Superficies Parallelogrammorum generantur ex ductu basis in perpendicularem: juxtà def. V. ita, ut si latus A C sit 9. palmorum ex. gr.; & G C 4; erit superficies, facta à motu lineae C G in lineam A C, & Parallelogrammum A G, vel huic aequale G F, 36. palmorum.

II. But since the distance between the Parallels AB, CD is measured by the perpendicular AC, from Theor. V, last cor., the Surfaces of Parallelograms are generated by drawing the base into the perpendicular, according to Def. V; so that if the side AC is, e.g., 9 palms, and GC 4, the surface made by the motion of the line CG along the line AC, and the Parallelogram AG, or GF equal to it, will be 36 palms.

III. Hinc si Parallelogramma sint aequalia super eadem, vel aequali Basi, manifestum est, etiam habere eandem perpendicularem altitudinem, seu esse inter easdem Parallelas.

III. Hence if Parallelograms on the same or an equal Base are equal, it is manifest that they also have the same perpendicular altitude, or are between the same Parallels.

THEOREMA VIII. (Fig. 8.) — Theorem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

Parallelogrammi dimidium est Triangulum constitutum in eadem Basi, & inter easdem Parallelas. s1

A Triangle constituted on the same Base and between the same Parallels is half of the Parallelogram. (a)

Dem. Triangulum B C G est dimidium Parallelogrammi F G: ex Theor. VI. sed Parallelogrammum F G est aequale Parallelogrammo A G: ex antecedenti; ergo Triangulum B C G etiam est dimidium Parallelogrammi A G, constituti in eadem Basi C G, & inter easdem Parallelas.

Dem. The Triangle BCG is half of the Parallelogram FG, from Theor. VI; but the Parallelogram FG is equal to the Parallelogram AG, from the preceding; therefore the Triangle BCG is also half of the Parallelogram AG, constituted on the same Base CG and between the same Parallels.

Coroll. I. Patet, etiam Triangulum B H D, constitutum in aequali basi, & inter easdem Parallelas, esse dimidium Parallelogrammi A G, quum sit dimidium aequalis Parallelogrammi F D.

Cor. I. It is plain that the Triangle BHD also, constituted on an equal base and between the same Parallels, is half of the Parallelogram AG, since it is half of the equal Parallelogram FD.

II. Manifestum quoque est, Triangula, quae sunt in basibus iisdem, aut aequalibus, & inter easdem Parallelas, esse inter se aequalia; quum sint dimidia aequalium Parallelogrammorum s2.

II. It is also manifest that Triangles which are on the same or equal bases and between the same Parallels are equal to each other, since they are halves of equal Parallelograms (b).

III. Quum autem dimidium Parallelogrammi A G fiat ex ductu dimidiae basis in Perpendicularem A C; superficies Triangulorum, quae est aequalis dimidio Parallelogrammo, ex Theorem. VI. etiam cognoscitur ex ductu dimidiae basis in eandem Perpendicularem altitudinem; unde si basis Trianguli B C G sit 4. palmorum; Perpendicularis altitudo B D, vel A C sit 9. palmorum, erit tota Trianguli B C G. Superficies 18. palmorum.

III. But since half of the Parallelogram AG is made by drawing half the base into the Perpendicular AC, the surface of the Triangle, which is equal to half the Parallelogram, from Theorem VI, is likewise known by drawing half the base into the same Perpendicular altitude; whence if the base of the Triangle BCG is 4 palms, and the Perpendicular altitude BD, or AC, 9 palms, the whole Surface of the Triangle BCG will be 18 palms.

IV. Triangula igitur aequalia super eadem, aut aequali basi, habent aequalem perpendicularem altitudinem, seu sunt inter easdem Parallelas s3.

IV. Equal triangles, therefore, on the same or an equal base, have an equal perpendicular altitude, or are between the same Parallels (c).

THEOREMA IX. (Fig. 9.)

Theorem IX. (Fig. 9.)

In Triangulo rectangulo Quadratum lateris, A C, subtendentis angulum rectum, B, est aequale duobus simul Quadratis laterum, A B, B C, continentium angulum rectum s4.

In a right-angled Triangle the Square of the side AC, subtending the right angle B, is equal to the two Squares together of the sides AB, BC, which contain the right angle (d).

Praep. Constructis octo Triangulis aequalibus, quae designantur numeris 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; intelligatur Quadratum H O supra lineam H I aequalem lineae A B; Quadratum D M lateris B C; & Quadratum A E lateris A C.

Prep. Eight equal Triangles having been constructed, which are marked by the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, let there be understood the Square HO upon the line HI, equal to the line AB; the Square DM of the side BC; and the Square AE of the side AC.

Dem. Duo simul Quadrata H O, & M B componuntur ex Quadrato L O, & quatuor aequalibus Triangulis 1, 8, 4, 5; Similiter Quadratum A E componitur ex eodem Quadrato L O, & quatuor Triangulis aequalibus 5, 3, 7, 8; ergo Quadratum A E est aequale duobus simul Quadratis H O, & B M, quum constent ex partibus aequalibus.

Dem. The two Squares HO and MB together are composed of the Square LO and four equal Triangles 1, 8, 4, 5. Likewise the Square AE is composed of the same Square LO and four equal Triangles 5, 3, 7, 8; therefore the Square AE is equal to the two Squares HO and BM together, since they consist of equal parts.

Coroll. In Quadrato quum Diameter opponatur angulo recto, erit Quadratum Diametri aequale duobus quadratis laterum aequalium, ac proinde duplum unius Quadrati.

Cor. In a Square, since the Diameter is opposite a right angle, the Square of the Diameter will be equal to the two squares of the equal sides, and consequently double one Square.

THEOREMA X. (Fig. 10.)

Theorem X. (Fig. 10.)

Si recta linea, A B, secetur utcumque in F, erit totum Quadratum lineae, A B, aequale duobus simul Quadratis partium, & duobus Rectangulis, quae fiunt ex iisdem partibus 3.

If the straight line AB is cut anyhow at F, the whole Square of the line AB will be equal to the two Squares of the parts together, and the two Rectangles which are made from the same parts (a).

Praeparat. Ducatur Perpendicularis F I Parallela lineae A C; secetur A H aequalis A F, & ducatur Perpendicularis H E Parallela lineae A B: ex quo omnes lineae in quadrato A D erunt ad angulos rectos, & oppositae fient aequales. ex Theor. VI. cor. 1. & 2.

Prep. Let the Perpendicular FI be drawn Parallel to the line AC; let AH be cut equal to AF, and let the Perpendicular HE be drawn Parallel to the line AB: from which all the lines in the square AD will be at right angles, and the opposite ones will be equal, from Theor. VI, cor. 1 & 2.

Dem. Quadratum A G super partem A F, Quadratum G D super G E aequalem lineae F B, duo Rectangula C G, & G B ex partibus lineae A B, sunt omnes partes totius Quadrati A D: ergo sunt illi aequalia.

Dem. The Square AG upon the part AF, the Square GD upon GE, equal to the line FB, and the two Rectangles CG and GB from the parts of the line AB, are all the parts of the whole Square AD: therefore they are equal to it.

Coroll. I. Si recta linea A B secetur utcumque in F, iisdem constructis, Rectangulum A I, cujus unum latus est aequale toti lineae A B, alterum parti A F; necnon Rectangulum F D, cujus unum latus est aequale toti A B, alterum alteri parti F B, sunt simul aequalia toti Quadrato A D, cujus sunt partes 2.

Cor. I. If the straight line AB is cut anyhow at F, with the same construction, the Rectangle AI, one side of which is equal to the whole line AB, the other to the part AF, and the Rectangle FD, one side of which is equal to the whole AB, the other to the other part FB, are together equal to the whole Square AD, of which they are the parts (b).

II. Si eadem linea secetur utcumque in F, similiter Quadratum A G ex ejus parte A F, & Rectangulum F E ex duabus partibus F B, & A F, seu aequali F G, sunt aequalia toti Rectangulo E A ex tota linea A B, & ejus segmento A F, quum illa duo sint partes omnes Rectanguli A E 2.

II. If the same line is cut anyhow at F, the Square AG from its part AF, and the Rectangle FE from the two parts FB and AF, or the equal FG, are likewise equal to the whole Rectangle EA from the whole line AB and its segment AF, since those two are all the parts of the Rectangle AE (c).

In Triangulis Obtusangulis Quadratum lineae, C A, quae opponitur Angulo Obtuso, C B A, continet, praeter Quadrata duorum laterum, C B, B A, duo rectangula, quae

In Obtuse-angled Triangles the Square of the line CA, which is opposite the Obtuse Angle CBA, contains, besides the Squares of the two sides CB, BA, two rectangles which

Praeparatio. Producatur alterutrum latus C B usque ad perpendicularem A D; tum fiant Quadratum C L totius lineae C D; Quadratum D F segmenti B D; Quadratum D O Perpendicularis D A: & producantur C F, F I, quae constituent Quadratum G I ex lateribus aequalibus lineae C B, ex Theor. VI. cor. 1 & 2.

Prep. Let the side CB be produced on one side as far as the perpendicular AD; then let there be made the Square CL of the whole line CD, the Square DF of the segment BD, and the Square DO of the Perpendicular DA; and let CF, FI be produced, which will constitute the Square GI from sides equal to the line CB, from Theor. VI, cor. 1 & 2.

Dem. Quadratum lateris C A est aequale duobus simul quadratis laterum C D, & D A, comprehendentium Angulum rectum D: ex Theor. IX & ex eadem ratione Quadratum lateris A B est aequale duobus simul Quadratis laterum A D, B D, cujus Quadratum E B continetur in toto Quadrato C L: sed Quadratum C L, praeter Quadratum B E, & Quadratum G I, continet duo rectangula C F, F L quae fiunt ex lineis C B, & B D; ergo Quadratum lateris C A continet, praeter quadrata laterum CB, B A, duo Rectangula, quae fiunt ex latere C B, & segmento B D, producto usque ad Perpendicularem A D.

Dem. The Square of the side CA is equal to the two squares together of the sides CD and DA, which comprehend the right Angle D, from Theor. IX; and by the same reasoning the Square of the side AB is equal to the two Squares together of the sides AD, BD, whose Square EB is contained in the whole Square CL: but the Square CL, besides the Square BE and the Square GI, contains two rectangles CF, FL, which are made from the lines CB and BD; therefore the Square of the side CA contains, besides the squares of the sides CB, BA, two Rectangles which are made from the side CB and the segment BD, produced as far as the Perpendicular AD.

THEOREMA XII. (Fig. 12.)

Theorem XII. (Fig. 12.)

In quocumque Triangulo Quadratum lateris, A C, oppositi angulo Acuto, A B C, superant Quadrata laterum A B, B C, duobus Rectangulis totius lateris, C B, & ejus segmenti, D B, quod est inter angulum acutum, B, & Perpendicularem, A D s2.

In any Triangle whatever, the Squares of the sides AB, BC exceed the Square of the side AC, opposite the Acute angle ABC, by two Rectangles of the whole side CB and its segment DB, which lies between the acute angle B and the Perpendicular AD (b).

Praepar. Ducatur ab Angulo A Perpendicularis A D, cujus fiat Quadratum D O, & segmenti D B Quadratum D N; & secta I E aequali D B, ducantur etiam ad angulos rectos F E, D L, quarum singula latera opposita erunt aequalia, ex Theor. VI. cor. 2.

Prep. From the Angle A let the Perpendicular AD be drawn, of which let the Square DO be made, and of the segment DB the Square DN; and, IE having been cut equal to DB, let FE, DL also be drawn at right angles, the opposite sides of which will each be equal, from Theor. VI, cor. 2.

Dem. Quadratum lateris C B, hoc est totum Quadratum C I, continet, praeter Quadrata C G, & G I, duo rectangula H G, G B; & Quadratum lateris A B est aequale Quadrato D O perpendicularis A D, & insuper alteri quadrato D N lateris D B, propter angulum rectum D: ex Theor. IX Sed, ex eodem, Quadratum lateris C A est solùm aequale Quadratis G C, D O: ergo Quadratum lateris C A superant duo Quadrata laterum C B, B A duplici Rectangulo H G, & duplici Quadrato G I: quae simul sunt aequalia duobus Rectangulis E I ex toto latere C B, & ejus segmento B D, ex Theor. X. cor. 2.

Dem. The Square of the side CB, that is, the whole Square CI, contains, besides the Squares CG and GI, two rectangles HG, GB; and the Square of the side AB is equal to the Square DO of the perpendicular AD together with the other square DN of the side DB, on account of the right angle D, from Theor. IX. But, by the same, the Square of the side CA is equal only to the Squares GC, DO: therefore the Squares of the sides CB, BA exceed the Square of the side CA by the double Rectangle HG and the double Square GI, which together are equal to the two Rectangles EI from the whole side CB and its segment BD, from Theor. X, cor. 2.
