PARS IV.

PART IV.

ELEMENTA PHYSICES. — ELEMENTS OF PHYSICS

PROLEGÓMENA. — PROLEGOMENA

§. I.

§. I.

De Physica ejusque scópo.

On Physics and its scope.

1 Disciplinae illius tractationem ordimur, cujus munus est naturam ejusque ordinem, ac leges, vires item, atque effectus naturales inquírire, singulorum oríginem, causas investigáre, quae proinde Physica nuncupatur, eaque definiri potest: Facultas, quae circa corpus naturale, quátenus naturale est, versatur. Dicitur etiam Scientia naturae, cognitio scilicèt rerum earum quae sensibibilem mundi máchinam constituunt. Physicus namque totus in eo est, inquit Claris. Gassendus, 2 ut explóret tùm ipsum, rerum omnium complexum, tùm quamlibet speciatim rem, disquirendo quantum fas est; an, & ex quibus principiis constet, an, & â quibus producta causis, & ob

e begin the treatment of that discipline whose task is to in1 W quire into nature and its order and laws, and likewise its forces and natural effects, and to investigate the origin and causes of each single thing; which is therefore called Physics, and may be defined: The faculty which is concerned with natural body, insofar as it is natural. It is also called the Science of nature, namely the knowledge of those things which make up the sensible machine of the world. For the physicist, says the illustrious Gassendi (a), is wholly occupied in exploring both that complex of all things itself and each thing in particular, by inquiring, so far as is permitted, whether it exists, and of what principles it consists, whether, and by what causes it has been produced, and for

p. 2

quem finem effecta, an, & quibus viribus, proprietatibusque donata, ceteraque hujusmodi, quae si perspecta fuerint, tùm res, rerumque natura perspectae, censentur.

what end it was made, whether, and with what forces and properties it is endowed, and other things of this kind; and once these have been seen through, then both the thing and the nature of things are deemed to be thoroughly known.

2 Díximus in definitione, Physicam versari circa corpus naturale prout naturale est, nimirùm prout sensibilium adfectionum subjectum est, earumque omnium mutationum capax, quas in mundo fieri conspicimus: & per hoc distinguitur corpus naturale â Mathemático, ipsaque Physica â Geometria, quae itidem circa corpus versatur.

2 We said in the definition that Physics is concerned with natural body insofar as it is natural, namely insofar as it is the subject of sensible affections and capable of all those changes which we observe taking place in the world; and by this natural body is distinguished from the mathematical, and Physics itself from Geometry, which is likewise concerned with body.

3 Objecta Physicae sunt Corpus, Spatium, & Motus, quid verò per haec intelligitur paucis indicábo. Quamcumque rem oculis intueri, vel manu comprehéndere, & palpáre possumus, quaeque pressioni resistit, Corpus adpelamus. Extensionem universi, in quo corpora ponuntur, & liberè moventur, Spatium. Translationem corporis ex una in aliam spatii partem, vocamus Motum.

3 The objects of Physics are Body, Space and Motion; what is understood by these I shall indicate in a few words. Whatever thing we can behold with the eyes, or grasp and feel with the hand, and which resists pressure, we call Body. The extension of the universe, in which bodies are placed and move freely, we call Space. The transfer of a body from one part of space into another we call Motion.

4 Omnes situs, motus, mutationes, & actiones corporum, quae sensibus observantur, sive uno, sive pluribus, adpelantur Phaenomena. Omnia corpora secundum certas leges, vel regulas movéri constat. Lex autem naturae, est norma illa secundum quam Deus voluit certos motus semper, id est in omnibus occasionibus péragi, hinc ex. gr. quaelibet planta suum prodúcit semen, unde iterum similis, non diversi, renascitur planta; hinc unumquodque animal ex sese sui simile gignit. Corpus grave sibi liberè commissum spontè cadit deorsum. Ope harum legum intelligimus quid naturalitèr, quid miraculosè contingit. Nam naturalia sunt phaenómena, quae constanter eodem modo observantur, positis corporibus in similibus occasionibus; miracula autem sunt, quum phaenómena legibus istis contraria eveniunt.

4 All the positions, motions, changes and actions of bodies which are observed by the senses, whether by one or by several, are called Phenomena. It is agreed that all bodies are moved according to certain laws or rules. A law of nature, moreover, is that norm according to which God willed certain motions to be performed always, that is, on all occasions; hence, e.g., every plant produces its own seed, from which a like plant, not a different one, is born again; hence every animal begets from itself one like itself. A heavy body freely left to itself falls downward of its own accord. By means of these laws we understand what happens naturally and what miraculously. For those phenomena are natural which are observed constantly in the same manner when bodies are placed on similar occasions; but there are miracles when phenomena occur contrary to those laws.

5 Si verò aliquid évenit secundum naturae leges, sed praeter sólitum, seu contra id quod tali naturae debetur, vocatur nonnaturale. Ut febris, quae quidem ita palpitationem & cordis & arteriarum ágitat, ut dicantur esse in statu nonnaturali. Quod súperat naturae vires ac leges, supernaturale vocatur. Ita quod Sol ex. gr. dum est in meridie ad orientem retrò volvatur, est supernaturale, quia nullis naturae viribus id éffici potest, ut évidens est. Quaedam verò res sunt, quae etiamsi supra naturam sint, tamen nonnisi ab homine bona Philosophia exculto, benèque exercitato judicari potest, an naturalia sint, an praeter naturam. Hinc de rebus insoléntibus cautè judicare debemus, ne ea pro miraculis habeamus, quae talia non sunt. Utilissimum est hoc mónitum ut occurramus ineptae multitudini indoctórum, & verò etiam eorum, qui cétera docti, tamen, quòd bonae Philosophiae expertes sint, proni sunt, qui gárrulae cuivis muliérculae miraculum aliquod narranti fidem habeant.

5 But if something happens according to the laws of nature, yet beyond what is usual, or contrary to what is owed to such a nature, it is called nonnatural: as a fever, which so agitates the beating both of the heart and of the arteries that they are said to be in a nonnatural state. What surpasses the forces and laws of nature is called supernatural. Thus if the Sun, e.g., while it is at noon, were rolled back toward the east, this is supernatural, because it cannot be brought about by any forces of nature, as is evident. There are, however, certain things which, even though they are above nature, can nevertheless be judged only by a man cultivated in good Philosophy and well practiced, whether they are natural or beyond nature. Hence we must judge cautiously of unusual things, lest we take for miracles things which are not such. This warning is most useful, so that we may meet the foolish multitude of the unlearned, and indeed also of those who, though learned in other matters, yet, because they are without good Philosophy, are prone to give credence to any chattering little woman who tells of some miracle.

In Proem. Physices.

In the Proem to the Physics.

p. 3

§. II.

§. II.

Utilitas Physicae.

The usefulness of Physics. 6

6 Dignitas certè ac praestantia Physicae vel ex eo intelligi satis superque potest, quod disciplinae hujus studium tantumdem pateat, quantum ipsa natura. Et sanè ¿quis negèt longè dignissimum esse contemplari modò caelorum amplitudinem, corporum certa in iis lege decurrentium molem, jam in tellúris abdita se penetráre, metallorum, lápidum oríginem, plantarum, animalium varietatem penè infinitam scrutari, ipsam denique in hac rerum universitate relucentem Dei majestatem considerare? Unde Seneca 3 hanc tanti fecit contemplationem, ut dícere non dubitáverit: nisi ad haec (naturae secretiora) admitterer, non fuerat opere pretium nasci.

The dignity, certainly, and the excellence of Physics can be understood amply enough even from this alone, that the study of this discipline extends as far as nature itself. And indeed, who will deny that it is by far the worthiest thing now to contemplate the vastness of the heavens and the mass of the bodies running their courses in them by a fixed law, now to penetrate into the hidden recesses of the earth, to search out the origin of metals and stones and the almost infinite variety of plants and animals, and finally to consider the majesty of God shining forth in this universe of things? Hence Seneca (b) valued this contemplation so highly that he did not hesitate to say: unless I were admitted to these things (the more secret things of nature), it would not have been worth while to be born.

7 Jocunditas deinde & suavissima voluptas hoc è naturae studio enascitur. ¿Quem enim non delectet scientia, in qua nunquam deest occasio, novos, eosque mirabiles effectus, velut tótidem summi rerum Conditoris testimonia luculenta & inveniendi & contemplandi? ¿Quis animalium innumerorum, terrestrium, aquatilium, volatilium, insectorum genera quàm diversissima, rerum ceterarum miram varietatem, pulchritudinem, ad certos usus habilitatem sine ingenua animi voluptate contueri possit? ¿Quid quod Physico jocundissimum praebeant spectaculum ea quoque, quae imperítos formídine complère solent? Ita dum vulgus rude inani metu eclipseos concútitur, Philosophi

7 Then delight and the sweetest pleasure spring from this study of nature. For whom would a science not delight in which there is never lacking the occasion both of discovering and of contemplating new and wonderful effects, as so many shining testimonies of the supreme Maker of things? Who could behold the most diverse kinds of innumerable animals, terrestrial, aquatic, flying, insects, the wondrous variety of the other things, their beauty and their fitness for definite uses, without a noble pleasure of mind? What of the fact that those very things which commonly fill the unskilled with dread afford the physicist a most delightful spectacle? Thus, while the rude multitude is shaken by an empty fear of eclipses, the Philosophers

Hunc solem & stellas; & decedentia certis Tempora momentis, sunt qui formidine nulla Imbúti spectent. s2

This sun, and the stars, and the seasons that pass at fixed Moments, there are some who, touched by no dread, Can behold. (c)

8 Quin gaudent amoénam tam sibi scenam aperiri [?], & occasionem parari, qua naturam caelestium corporum expendant. Physicus Cometarum facies aliis horríficas, tranquillo animo intuetur. Omnium rerum, (inquit Tullius s3) natura cognita, levamur superstitione, liberamur mortis metu, non conturbamur ignoratione rerum, è qua ipsa horribiles existunt saepè formídines.

8 Nay, they rejoice that so pleasant a scene is opened to them, and an occasion afforded of weighing the nature of the heavenly bodies. The physicist beholds with a tranquil mind the faces of Comets, which to others are horrifying. By the knowledge of the nature of all things (says Tully (d)) we are relieved of superstition, freed from the fear of death, and not disturbed by ignorance of things, from which very ignorance horrible terrors often arise.

9 His accedunt emolumenta plurima, quae è Physica per disciplinas reliquas omnemque vitae usum sese diffundunt. ¿Quae enim emolumenta in saluberrimam medendi artem è Physica profluunt? ¿quántas accessiones scientia nautica accepit usu acus magneticae, astrorum observatis motibus, rosae nauticae inventione? Praetereo

9 To these are added very many benefits, which spread from Physics through the remaining disciplines and every use of life. For what benefits flow from Physics into the most salutary art of healing? What great accessions has nautical science received from the use of the magnetic needle, from the observed motions of the stars, from the invention of the mariner’s compass card? I pass over the

utilitates, quas diversi generis horologia, tubi optici, microscopia perspicilla, aliaque innumera; quae Physicae in acceptis referenda sunt in vitam humanam praebent.

the advantages which clocks of various kinds, telescopes, microscopes, spectacles and innumerable other things, which must be credited to Physics, afford to human life.

§. III. — §. III

De Peripateticorum Physica.

On the Physics of the Peripatetics. 10

10 Hujusmodi verò & innumerae aliae utilitates, quae tacitus praetereo frustra in Peripateticorum Schola requiras, si adpelare possumus Physicam disciplinam illam in qua pléraque passím adversus naturae observationem, adversus perspicua experimenta tradi consueverunt. Sed audire juvat Mathematicum Physicumque egregium Thomam Vincentium Tosca, Hispaniae nostrae decus, ac Valentini Congregationis Oratorii ornamentum praeclarissimum. Hispánum hominem audiant ii, qui sputacílicis praejudiciis imbúti falsò putant Recentiorum Physicam ab haereticis tantum éxcoli, nefasque judicant studiosae juventúti propóni & commendari: genus hominum natum ad perniciem, interitumque bonarum artium.

Such advantages, however, and innumerable others which I silently pass over, you will seek in vain in the School of the Peripatetics, if we may call Physics that discipline in which most things have customarily been taught everywhere against the observation of nature and against plain experiments. But it is a pleasure to hear the excellent mathematician and physicist Tomás Vicente Tosca, the glory of our Spain and a most distinguished ornament of the Congregation of the Oratory of Valencia. Let them hear a Spaniard, those who, steeped in contemptible prejudices, falsely suppose that the Physics of the Moderns is cultivated only by heretics, and judge it impious that it should be set before studious youth and commended to them: a race of men born for the ruin and destruction of the good arts.

11 „Nescio certè (loquitur Clariss. Tosca 2 Nescio certè, quo fato, eoque satis infelici jam ab aliquibus retrò seculis, Peripateticorum Schola metaphysicis commentationibus ita est addicta, ut physicas res omninò neglígere videatur: ad nauseam usque prodeunt in dies libri, qui entis rationis ultimos apices prosequuntur; mirabilium verò naturae effectuum, quotidie in oculos occurrentium naturam, & causas omninò praetereunt. Nihil olim amoenius habebatur (ait Ludovicus Vives 2 contemplatione horti hujus naturae: nunc verò naturalium rerum inquisitio, ita metaphysicis abstractionibus implicatur, ut super eisdem, ceu debili fundamento, non nisi vastum aedificium assertionum, ac dissidentium sententiarum consurgat, seu potius crux erigatur, qua potius ingenia torqueantur, quàm tantâ rerum naturalium amoenitate delectentur.

11 “I know not, certainly (so speaks the most illustrious Tosca (e)), I know not, certainly, by what fate, and that an unhappy enough one, the School of the Peripatetics has now for some centuries back been so given over to metaphysical speculations that it seems to neglect physical things altogether: books come out daily, to the point of nausea, which pursue the last fine points of the being of reason, but pass over altogether the nature and causes of the wonderful effects of nature that meet our eyes every day. Nothing was once held more pleasant (says Luis Vives (f)) than the contemplation of this garden of nature: but now the inquiry into natural things is so entangled in metaphysical abstractions that upon them, as upon a weak foundation, there rises nothing but a vast edifice of assertions and of dissenting opinions, or rather a cross is set up, on which minds are tortured rather than delighted by so great a pleasantness of natural things.

12. "Dolendum certè maxime est, quibus ambágibus de tota philosophia labyrinthum fecerint ii, qui physicas res, non physicè ut par est, sed metaphysicis praecisionibus ab omni sensu, & experimento remotis, pertractant; dolendum iterum altas alioquin mentes, dum sciendi famem satiare cupiunt, toto saltim trienio, inani tantum entium rationis esca cibari, non sine maximo juventutis dispendio, detentis nimirum eorumdem íngeniis ad meliora ne pergant.

12 “It is surely most to be lamented by what windings those have made a labyrinth of the whole of philosophy who treat physical things not physically, as is fitting, but with metaphysical precisions remote from all sense and experiment; it is to be lamented again that minds otherwise lofty, while they desire to satisfy their hunger for knowledge, are fed for at least a whole three years on the empty food of beings of reason alone, not without the greatest loss to youth, their minds being held back, namely, lest they go on to better things.

In Phys. Praefat.

In the Preface to the Physics.

Lib. 5. de Caus. corrupt. art.

Bk. 5 De causis corruptarum artium.

p. 5

13 "Ad meliora dixi. Quis enim dubitet, rerum naturalium speculationem multò praestantiorem esse metaphysicis illis quaestionibus, ne dicam tricis, quibus perpetua lite, & plerumque de vocibus solet in Scholis acritèr decertari. Certè, cum Deus Jobo incomparabilem suae sapientiae eminentiam patefácere vellet, eidem quam plurima, eaque mirabilia quaesíta proposuit ex naturalis philosophiae promptuariis desumpta, ut toto capite 38. & 39 est manifestum, sed de iis, quae in Scholis tanti fiunt, nec verbum.

13 “To better things, I said. For who would doubt that the study of natural things is far more excellent than those metaphysical questions, not to say trifles, over which it is customary in the Schools to contend sharply in perpetual litigation, and for the most part about words? Certainly, when God willed to disclose to Job the incomparable eminence of his wisdom, he put to him a great many questions, and wonderful ones, taken from the storehouses of natural philosophy, as is manifest from the whole of chapters 38 and 39; but of those things which are made so much of in the Schools, not a word.

14 "Poterat autem eidem quamplurima de ente rationis interrogare, an nempe, & quomodo existat, qualis sit ejusdem fabrica, quae prentiae, quive actus ad ejusdem structuram concurrant: an insuper á Deo, an ab Angelis, an á sensibus corporeis effici possit? De praecissionibus autem inquirere poterat, an tantum formales sint, an etiam objectivae? De carentiis praeterea, an dentur? imò, an etiam carentiarum carentiae? an item rerum essentiae ab earumdem existentia realiter distinguantur? Verùm de his, aliisque similibus, altum silentium.

14 “He could, however, have asked him a great many things about the being of reason: namely, whether and how it exists, what its fabric is, what powers or what acts concur in its construction; whether, moreover, it can be produced by God, or by the Angels, or by the bodily senses? About precisions, too, he could have inquired whether they are only formal, or objective as well? About lacks, moreover, whether there are any? nay, whether there are even lacks of lacks? and likewise whether the essences of things are really distinct from their existence? But about these and other like things, deep silence.

15 "Praeterea Sapientiae cap. 7. Salomon scientiam sibi divinitus collatam non inde commendat, quod ingentem illam formalitatum, distinctionum, ac reflexionum turbam, illum Deus docuerit, sed potius inde, quod eidem patefécerit dispositionem orbis terrarum, & virtutes elementorum, initium, & consummationem, & medietatem témporum, vicissitudinum permutationes, & commutationes temporum, anni cursus, & stellarum dispositiones, naturas animalium, & iras bestiarum, vim ventorum &c.„ Hactenus Tosca. ¿Quid ad haec homines illi rerum physicarum parùm aut nihil studiosi? ¿Annon reprehensionem Isaïae 3 merentur: Opus Domini non respícitis, nec opera manuum ejus consideratis?

15 “Moreover, in Wisdom, ch. 7, Solomon commends the knowledge bestowed on him by God, not because God taught him that huge crowd of formalities, distinctions and reflexions, but rather because he disclosed to him the disposition of the whole world, and the virtues of the elements, the beginning, and ending, and midst of the times, the alterations of their courses, and the changes of seasons, the revolutions of the year, and the dispositions of the stars, the natures of living creatures, and rage of wild beasts, the force of winds, etc.” Thus far Tosca. What do those men say to these things, who are little or not at all studious of physical things? Do they not deserve the rebuke of Isaiah (g): The work of the Lord you regard not, nor do you consider the works of his hands?

16 Non deerunt ergò homines qui vos ipso in aditu dejicere, & ab institutis cogitationibus avocare sint conaturi, illud identidèm auribus, animisque vestris inculcando, genus hoc Physicae novum, obscurum, involúcris mathemáticis úndique obseptum esse, sed contempta obtrectantium dicacitate in pulcherrimum naturae studium sedulò incúmbite, & nolíte abdúci sermónibus imperitórum. Verum quidem est sine Geometriae praesidio dignos in Physica progressus éffici non posse, sed hoc vos praesidium satis in anteactis estis experti, quùm Geometricas Institutiones, quales oporrebat evolvistis. Sufficiunt enim ad pleniorem Physicae nostrae intelligentiam Elementa illa Geometriae superiùs quam brevissimè expósita.

16 There will not be lacking, therefore, men who will try to throw you down at the very entrance and to call you away from the reflections you have undertaken, by dinning again and again into your ears and minds that this kind of Physics is new, obscure, and wrapped on every side in mathematical coverings; but, despising the raillery of the detractors, apply yourselves diligently to the most beautiful study of nature, and do not let yourselves be led away by the talk of the unskilled. It is true indeed that without the aid of Geometry no worthy progress can be made in Physics; but you have sufficiently experienced this aid in what has gone before, when you went through such Geometrical Institutions as were needed. For those Elements of Geometry set out above as briefly as possible suffice for a fuller understanding of our Physics.

§. IV.

§ . I V.

De Studio Geometriae.

On the Study of Geometry.

17 Certè Geometria necessaria est Physico, ut enim ait Illustriss. Caramuel: Eminent inter céteros in philosophicis Scholis, qui Geometriam callent; serpunt, qui ignorant: loquor expertus: neque enim frustra foribus Academiae auream inscriptionem posuit Plato, qua ab illius ingressu arcébat eos, qui Geometriae essent prorsus ignari. NULLUS GEOMETRIAE EXPERS INTRATO. Et rectè quidem. Quandoquidem, cum Natura, (inquit clariss. Gulielminus, 4 ubique mathematica sit, idem est naturam absque mathési expiscári velle, ac sine cruribus ambulare, aut artificem instrumenta omnia ad artefactum necessaria abjicere, & nihilóminus suum opus promíttere.

17 Certainly Geometry is necessary to the physicist; for, as the illustrious Caramuel says: Those excel among the rest in the philosophical Schools who are versed in Geometry; those who are ignorant of it serve: I speak from experience. Nor was it in vain that Plato placed on the doors of the Academy the golden inscription by which he kept from entering it those who were wholly ignorant of Geometry: Let no one ignorant of geometry enter. And rightly indeed. Since, as Nature (says the most illustrious Guglielmini (h)) is everywhere mathematical, it is the same to wish to fish out nature without mathematics as to walk without legs, or for a craftsman to throw away all the instruments necessary for the work and nevertheless to promise his work.

§. V.

§ . V.

Auctores quos sequemur.

The authors we shall follow. 18

18 Sed quod in principio fieri ab omnibus Physicis consuevit, ut sectam, in quam jurassent, indicarent, erunt fortassè, qui & á nobis id fieri poscant, inquirentes ¿ Nùm Cartesium, an Leibnitzium, nùm Nevvtonum, an alium sequamur? Quibus his paucis respondébimus. Profitémur judicium nostrum fore liberum, sic ut in nullius Philosophi sectam simus juratúri, nullam enim putamus fuisse sectam, quae omne verum vidisset, nullam, quae non aliquid ex vero. Itaque veritatem sparsam per singulos, perque sectas diffusam in corpus colligere, id verò arbitramur proprie ad nostrum institutum pertinére. Sed juvat ipso in límine regulas philosophandi constituere.

But since it has been the custom of all physicists to indicate at the outset the sect to which they had sworn, there will perhaps be some who demand this of us as well, asking: Do we follow Descartes, or Leibniz, or Newton, or someone else? To them we answer in these few words. We profess that our judgment is free, so that we will swear to the sect of no Philosopher; for we think there has been no sect that saw every truth, and none that did not hold something of the truth. Therefore to gather into one body the truth scattered among individuals and dispersed through the sects, this we judge to belong properly to our undertaking. But it is well, on the very threshold, to set down the rules of philosophizing.

§. VI.

§. VI.

De Regulis philosophandi.

On the Rules of philosophizing. 19

19 Dum phaenomena explicare, dumque naturae leges investigare conamur, oportebit ad sequentes regulas philosophandi â Clariss. Nevvtono 3 praescriptas religiosè adténdere. Prima est hujusmodi.

While we try to explain phenomena and to investigate the laws of nature, it will be necessary to attend scrupulously to the following rules of philosophizing prescribed by the most illustrious Newton (i). The first is as follows.

Dissert. de Salibus. Praefat.

Dissertatio de Salibus, Preface. (i)

Lib. 3. Princip. Math. Philos.

Bk. 3 of the Mathematical Principles of Philosophy.

p. 7

20 Causae rerum naturalium, non plures admitti debent, quam quae & verae sint, & phaenómenis explicandis sufficiant. Si enim causa possibilis tantum sit, nunquam vera haberi poterit; quamvis alioqui producendo effectui apta fuerit, atque adcommodata. Eundem effectum ex pluribus causis oriri posse indubia res est, ex tot verò causis, non plus quàm una revera existit, & operatur, eaque sola â Physicis investiganda, quòd sola sit vera illius effectus causa. Spernendi utique sunt Philosophi illi, qui ex suis hypothesibus, & pro libitu fictis causis, naturales effectus derivare contendunt, parum de causarum illarum existentia soliciti. Hypotheses ergò ex Physica sunt proscribendae, nam ut optimè ait Musschembroek, 4 quidquid ex iis colligitur est inconstans, ex illis suscitantur controversiae inutiles, finguntur phaenómena, ut hypotheses roborentur, & defendantur.

20 No more causes of natural things ought to be admitted than such as are both true and sufficient to explain their phenomena. For if a cause is merely possible, it can never be held to be true, however apt and suited it may otherwise have been to producing the effect. That the same effect can arise from several causes is a matter beyond doubt; but of so many causes not more than one really exists and operates, and it alone is to be investigated by physicists, because it alone is the true cause of that effect. Those Philosophers are surely to be spurned who strive to derive natural effects from their own hypotheses and from causes feigned at pleasure, little concerned about the existence of those causes. Hypotheses, therefore, are in that case to be banished from Physics; for, as Musschenbroek very well says (j), whatever is gathered from them is inconstant; from them useless controversies are stirred up; phenomena are feigned so that the hypotheses may be strengthened and defended.

21 Nisi forte Clariss. Viro Perraultio, 3 adsentiendum sit, qui non omninò absonè de hypothesibus in hunc maxime modum decernit. Ad veritatis inquisitionem hypótheses certis adstrictas legibus adcommodatas esse contendit, ea ratione ductus, quod è praestitutis hypothesibus ordine quàm aptissimo ad thésim connitámur, palamque sit, complura, quae in praesens certa tenémus, olim hypothesium è número fuisse. Leges porrò, quibus arctari hypothesium ratio debeat heae fuerint praecipuae, scilicet: E rebus naturalibus fluat hypóthesis, atque è phaenómenis identidem observatis enascatur, minimè verò ex libidine confingatur positio quaedam, ad quam, nescio, quibus offuciis natura ipsa pertrahatur; adsumpta non citra fundamentum propositio non uni duntaxat alterique phenómeno, sed omnibus eo in genere examússim respondeat; adhaec â nullo alterius generis, quod compertum quidem sit, & exploratae certitudinis phaenómenon, & nullo item evidente principio dissentiat; demum consectaria ejuscemodi generet, quae sobria, consentanea saniorum Philosophorum placitis habeantur, certa consecutione ex adsumpto doctrinae fundamento proficiscantur. Altera philosophandi regula haec est.

21 Unless perhaps we must agree with the most illustrious Perrault (k), who, not altogether unreasonably, rules on hypotheses very much in this manner. He contends that hypotheses bound by fixed laws are suited to the investigation of truth, being led by this reason: that from hypotheses laid down beforehand we strive in the most fitting order toward the thesis, and it is plain that a great many things which at present we hold as certain were once among the number of hypotheses. Now the laws by which the method of hypotheses ought to be restricted would chiefly be these, namely: Let the hypothesis flow from natural things and arise from phenomena observed again and again, but let no position be fashioned at whim, toward which nature herself is dragged by I know not what tricks; let the proposition, assumed not without foundation, correspond exactly not to one or another phenomenon only, but to all of that kind; let it, moreover, dissent from no phenomenon of another kind that has been ascertained and is of tested certainty, and likewise from no evident principle; finally, let it generate conclusions of such a kind as are held sober and consonant with the tenets of the saner Philosophers, and proceed by sure consequence from the assumed foundation of the doctrine. The second rule of philosophizing is this.

22 Effectuum naturalium ejusdem generis eaedem sunt causae. Haec regula ex prima facilè deribatur. Etenim (per primam regulam) natura simplex est, neque superfluis causis redundat, effectus ergò ejusdem generis, sive omninò similes, diversis causis tribui, naturae simplicitati omninò repugnat. Ita gravium descensus in Europa, & America eidem causae tribuendus est. Pari ratione quum in omnibus hominibus eadem respirationis instrumenta demonstrent observationes anatómicae, eamdem esse in singulis respirandi causam, meritò conclúdimus. Sed cavendum est diligenter, ne ex charactéribus merè externis de perfecta effectuum similitudine audacter pronunciemus. Ita plantae quaedam lethales, externam plantarum salúbrium speciem

22 Of natural effects of the same kind the causes are the same. This rule is easily derived from the first. For (by the first rule) nature is simple and does not abound in superfluous causes; therefore to attribute effects of the same kind, or wholly alike, to different causes is altogether repugnant to the simplicity of nature. Thus the descent of heavy bodies in Europe and in America is to be attributed to the same cause. By like reasoning, since anatomical observations show the same instruments of respiration in all men, we rightly conclude that the cause of breathing is the same in each. But one must carefully beware lest from merely external characters we pronounce boldly on the perfect likeness of effects. Thus certain lethal plants imitate the external appearance of wholesome plants,

Elem. Physic. tom. 1. cap. 1.

Elementa Physicae, vol. 1, ch. 1.

Perrault. Essais de Physique.

Perrault, Essais de Physique.

p. 8

imitantur, sed principio quodam interno & non facilè perspicuò inter se maximè differunt. Quod, ut alia praetéream, in Cicuta aquâtica & Petroselino verissimum est. Summòpere itaque curandum est; ut nempe certò compertas habeamus omnes effectuum partes, conditionesque singulas, tunc enim haec analogiae regula extra omnem dubitationem posita est. Tertia ita se habet.

but differ greatly from one another by a certain internal principle that is not easily perceived. Which, to pass over other examples, is most true of water hemlock and parsley. The greatest care must therefore be taken that we have all the parts of the effects, and each of their conditions, certainly ascertained; for then this rule of analogy is placed beyond all doubt. The third runs thus.

23 Qualitates corporum, quae intendi, & remitti nequeunt, (hoc est, neque augeri, neque minui) & quae omnibus in quibus experimenta instituere licet, corporibus cómpetunt; pro corporum universorum qualitatibus haberi possunt. Hoc est, quae eaedem semper & invariatè in corporibus persevérant, utcumque sit temporis & loci variata conditio, quamcumque etiam mutationem, alterationemve corpora patiantur, cujusmodi sunt soliditas, figurabílitas: nam aliae sunt qualitates quae intendi, & remitti possunt: hujus generis sunt grávitas, & vis aatractionis. Diminúta enim corporis distantia â centro, ad quod vel gravitate, vel adtractione tendit, gravitatis, & adtractionis vires augentur, eaedemque minuuntur ex aucta distantia, ut in ferro ad magnétem adtracto experiri licet. Haec sunt philosophandi regulae, quibus usuri deiceps sumus.

23 The qualities of bodies which cannot be intended and remitted (that is, neither increased nor diminished) and which belong to all bodies on which it is possible to make experiments, are to be held for qualities of all bodies universally. That is, those which persist always the same and invariable in bodies, however the condition of time and place may vary, and whatever change or alteration bodies may undergo; such as solidity and figurability: for there are other qualities which can be intended and remitted, and of this kind are gravity and the force of attraction. For when the distance of a body from the center toward which it tends, either by gravity or by attraction, is diminished, the forces of gravity and of attraction are increased, and they are diminished when the distance is increased, as can be found by experiment in iron attracted to a magnet. These are the rules of philosophizing which we shall use from here on.

§. VII. — §. VII

Physices divisio.

Division of Physics. 24

24 Recepta in praesens apud Viros hac in tradenda disciplina exercitatissimos méthodo, consuevit duplici tractatione definíri Physica, Generalis scilicet nomine, & Particularis. Generalis corpus generatim sumptum, compositorum natúralium principia considerat, & phaenómena pariter istùc pertinentia, uti & causas eorumdem comprehendit. Particularis singula corporum genera expendit, eorumque vires, proprietates, & operátiones demonstrat. Nos utrumque simul praestábimus, quoniam multi esse nec debemus, nec verò póssumus.

Following the method now accepted among men most practiced in teaching this discipline, Physics has customarily been marked out in a twofold treatment, namely under the name of General and of Particular. The General considers body taken generally and the principles of natural composites, and likewise comprehends the phenomena pertaining to them, as also their causes. The Particular examines the single kinds of bodies and demonstrates their forces, properties and operations. We shall perform both at once, since we neither ought, nor indeed are able, to be lengthy.

p. 9

PHYSICES PARS I — PHYSICS, PART I

DE NATURA,

ON THE NATURE

ATQUE PRINCIPIIS CORPORUM. — AND PRINCIPLES OF BODIES

DISSERTATIO I. — DISSERTATION I

De Corpore physico generatim sumpto.

On physical Body taken generally.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De Natura Corporis. Philosophorum opiniones exponuntur, & refutantur.

On the Nature of Body. The opinions of the Philosophers are set out and refuted. 1

1 Id primum in hac dissertatione quaerendum occúrreret, ¿utrum corpora existant? ut constaret priùs existere id, cujus naturam inquírendam suscipimus. Verùm cum conscientia nostra illorum existentiam nobis suadeat, hoc veluti postulatum ab adversariis concedendum propónimus, pro certo habentes, supervacanea inquisitione rem certissimam obscuriorem éffici. Corpora igitur existunt. Verùm circa eorum esséntiam, non una, eademque est Philosophorum opinio.

The first thing to be asked in this dissertation would be whether bodies exist, so that it might first be established that the thing whose nature we undertake to inquire into exists. But since our consciousness persuades us of their existence, we propose this, as a kind of postulate, to be granted by our adversaries, holding it for certain that a most certain matter is only made more obscure by a superfluous inquiry. Bodies, therefore, exist. But concerning their essence the opinion of Philosophers is not one and the same.

2 Egregius Philosophus, atque in Mathematicis disciplinis mirificè versatus Renatus Des-Cartes corporeae substantiae naturam in extensione collocavit: ait enim: 3 percipiemus naturam materiae sive corporis in universum spectati non consistere in eo, quod sit res dura, vel ponderosa, vel colorata, vèl alio aliquo modo sensus afficiens, sed tantum in eo quod sit res extensa in longum, latum, & profundum: quod etiam adfirmavit Aristoteles, nam Lib. 3. Phys. text. 43: corpus est, inquit, quod omniquaque habet dimensionem. Sed statum quaestionis proponámus. Quaestio ergo inquirit, ¿quaenam sit ratio formalis corporis physici? hoc est: ¿quodnam ex iis omnibus adtributis, quae corpori insunt, (ut impenetrabilitas, extensio, divisibilitas, &c.) sit ita primum in ipso corpore, ut ex illo veluti ex radíce, cetera omnia proveniant? Illud enim adtributum est ratio formalis rei, per

2 The excellent Philosopher René Descartes, wonderfully versed in the mathematical disciplines, placed the nature of corporeal substance in extension; for he says (l): we shall perceive that the nature of matter, or of body regarded in general, does not consist in its being a thing hard, or heavy, or colored, or affecting the senses in any other way, but only in its being a thing extended in length, breadth and depth: which Aristotle also asserted, for in Bk. 3 of the Physics, text 43, body is, he says, that which has dimension in every direction. But let us set out the state of the question. The question, then, asks: what is the formal reason of physical body? that is, which of all those attributes that belong to body (as impenetrability, extension, divisibility, etc.) is so first in the body itself that from it, as from a root, all the rest proceed? For that attribute is the formal reason of the thing, through

p. 10

quod res ipsa est id quod est, atque à ceteris omnibus primò distinguitur. His positis.

which the thing itself is what it is, and is first distinguished from all others. These things being laid down:

3 Dico primo contra Cartesium, & Aristotelem: essentia corporis in actuali extensione, vel triplici dimensione nequaquam posita est. Probatur. ¿Quis negabit Deum Opt. Max. destruere posse totam aëris molem, quae à terris ad Lunam usque intercípitur? sed tunc eadem prorsùs extensio remanéret, neque tamen substantia ulla corporea relinquerétur: ergo. Sed negat id fieri posse Cartesius: existimat enim, quod si ex. gr. aër hujus cubiculi destruatur, parietes ipsi sese mutuò contingent, quum illa se conjúngere dicantur, quae nullo interjecto corpore disjunguntur, aut in hac hypóthesi manifestissimam repugnantiam contineri putat, quum spatium illud vacuum quidem foret, ut suppónitur, & simul non vacuum, quia semper haberetur in illo trina dimensio, adeoque corpus ipsum.

3 I say first, against Descartes and Aristotle: the essence of body is by no means placed in actual extension, or in threefold dimension. It is proved. Who will deny that God, Best and Greatest, can destroy the whole mass of air which is enclosed between the earth and the Moon? But then the very same extension would remain, and yet no corporeal substance would be left: therefore. But Descartes denies that this can happen: for he thinks that if, e.g., the air of this little room were destroyed, the walls themselves would touch one another, since those things are said to be joined which are separated by no intervening body; or he thinks that in this hypothesis a most manifest contradiction is contained, since that space would indeed be void, as is supposed, and at the same time not void, because there would always be threefold dimension in it, and therefore body itself.

4 Verùm ¿quis non videat Cartesium hac in parte nobis impónere, quum probat idem per idem, atque principii loco id adsúmit, quod in controversia positum fuerat? Non alia siquidem ratione vacuum à Deo fieri non posse contendit, quàm quia semper in illo spatio corpus remanéret, remanente nimirùm extensione, quae juxta ipsum est essentia corporis, quod idem illud est, de quo disseritur. Deinde: licet sit certum quod duo corpora se tangunt, quum nullum alium corpus intérjacet, sed non est necesse ea se contingere, quae nullo corpore disjunguntur. Cartesius igitur corpus physicum cum mathemático confundit. Verùm ¿quis non videat aliud esse oportére corporis physici, aliud corporis mathemátici constitutivum, sive aliam esse naturam corporis, quod in sola imaginatione nostra continetur, aliam illius, quod in ipsa quoque rerum natura reperitur? Sic lineae Geometricae constitutivum est, ut longitudinem habeat sine latitudine, neque tamen essentia lineae, quae realitèr, & physicè in rerum natura reperítur in sola longitudine sine latitudine consístere debet.

4 But who does not see that Descartes here imposes upon us, since he proves the same by the same, and assumes in place of a principle what had been placed in controversy? For he contends that a void cannot be made by God for no other reason than that body would always remain in that space, extension, namely, remaining, which according to him is the essence of body; and that is the very thing under dispute. Next: although it is certain that two bodies touch each other when no other body lies between them, yet it is not necessary that those things touch which are separated by no body. Descartes, therefore, confuses physical body with mathematical body. But who does not see that what constitutes physical body must be one thing, and what constitutes mathematical body another; or that the nature of the body which is contained in our imagination alone is one, and that of the body which is also found in the very nature of things is another? Thus what constitutes a Geometrical line is that it have length without breadth; and yet the essence of a line which is found really and physically in the nature of things need not consist in length alone without breadth.

5 Repónere quidem possent Cartesiani, corpus mathemáticum plurimum à corpore physico differri, sed non ratione extensionis, quae utrique essentialiter communis est. Sed illud etiam animadvértere debent, quod tunc non póterit extensio ampliùs haberi tamquam essentia perfecta corporis physici, ut ipsi contendunt: quemadmodum quia figura circulo & triangulo communis est, non potest haec sola alterutrius essentia haberi; essentialiter igitur corpus physicum aliquid aliud habere debet, per quod à simplici extensione, & à corpore mathemático distinguatur.

5 The Cartesians could indeed reply that mathematical body differs very greatly from physical body, but not by reason of extension, which is essentially common to both. But they ought also to take note of this: that then extension could no longer be held to be the complete essence of physical body, as they themselves contend; just as, because figure is common to the circle and to the triangle, it cannot be held to be the sole essence of either of them. Essentially, therefore, physical body must have something else, by which it is distinguished both from simple extension and from mathematical body.

6 Petrus Gassendus vult 3 corporis essentiam pòsitam esse in actuali impenetrabilitate contra quem. Dico secundò: impenetrabilitas actualis non est formalis ratio corporis physici. Prob.: in eo posita non est formalis ratio corporis, quo corpus ipsum privari potest;

6 Pierre Gassendi would have (m) the essence of body placed in actual impenetrability; against whom I say secondly: actual impenetrability is not the formal reason of physical body. Proof: the formal reason of body is not placed in that of which the body itself can be deprived

Part. 2. Princip. n. 4.

Pt. 2 of the Principles, no. 4.

p. 11

quin désinat esse corpus; sed potest corpus actuali impenetrabilitate destitui, quin désinat esse corpus: ergo. Prob. min. Certum est duo corpora compenetrari divinitùs posse, quin illorum essentia mutetur: ergo &c.

without ceasing to be body; but body can be deprived of actual impenetrability without ceasing to be body: therefore. Proof of the minor. It is certain that two bodies can be compenetrated by divine power without their essence being changed: therefore etc.

Satis fit Objectionibus.

THE OBJECTIONS ARE ANSWERED.

7 Opp. 1. pro opinione Cartesii: intellectâ trina dimensione céteris omnibus praecisis, quae corpori insunt, intelligitur corpus, non enim intelligitur spiritus, ut est perspicuum: at inter corpus & spiritum non datur medium: ergo formalis ratio corporis est trina dimensio. Argumentum in adversarios retorqueri optimè posset, & contra ipsos probare formalem corporis rationem in impenetrabilitate consistere. Resp. dist. antec. Intelligitur corpus secundum magis obviam illius proprietatem, conc. secundum illius essentiam nego, & conseq. Sanè intelligitur corpus hoc ipso quod concipiatur substantia in partes integrales divisibilis, neque tamen dicent Cartesiani, divisibilitatem in partes ita pertinere ad corpus, ut á formali illius ratione minimè discernatur.

7 Obj. 1, for the opinion of Descartes: when threefold dimension is understood, all the other things that are in body being cut away, body is understood; for spirit is not understood, as is evident; and between body and spirit there is no middle: therefore the formal reason of body is threefold dimension. The argument could very well be turned back against the adversaries, and prove against them that the formal reason of body consists in impenetrability. Reply: I distinguish the antecedent. Body is understood according to its more obvious property, I grant; according to its essence, I deny; and I deny the consequent. Body is surely understood by the very fact that a substance divisible into integral parts is conceived; and yet the Cartesians will not say that divisibility into parts so belongs to body that it is in no way to be distinguished from its formal reason.

8 Opp 2. quicumque ad ideam corporis adténdere volunt, fatéri coguntur, non aliter se concípere corpus, quàm ut substantiam quoquoversùs extensam: ergo formalis corporis ratio à trina dimensione diversa non est. Argumentum nimis probat: etenim in idea corporis non trina tantùm extensio, sed etiam actualis impenetrabilitas sese offert. Resp. neg. conseq. etenim quum major idearum pars sensu adquiratur [§. 14. Log.] certòque constet ministerio sensuum íntima rerum adtributa immediatè nobis minimè innotéscere [§. 29, Log.], relinquitur, rationem formalem corporis non esse illud ejusdem adtributum, quod in idea ipsius corporis, quam infantiae tempore háusimus, nobis occurrit, sed tantùm magis obviam corporis proprietatem dici adtributum illud rectissimè posse.

8 Obj. 2. Whoever are willing to attend to the idea of body are forced to admit that they conceive body in no other way than as a substance extended in every direction: therefore the formal reason of body is not different from threefold dimension. The argument proves too much: for in the idea of body not only threefold extension, but also actual impenetrability presents itself. Reply: I deny the consequent; for since the greater part of our ideas is acquired by sense [§. 14, Log.], and it is certain that the inmost attributes of things become in no way known to us immediately through the ministry of the senses [§. 29, Log.], it remains that the formal reason of body is not that attribute of it which occurs to us in the idea of body that we drew in in the time of infancy, but that attribute can most rightly be called only the more obvious property of body.

9 Opp. 3. S. Augustinus Evodium ádloquens inquit 3: Abs te quaero: utrum corpus ullum esse putes, quod non pro modo suo habeat longitudinem, latitudinem, & profunditatem? ..... Si hoc demas corporibus quantum mea opinio est, neque sentiri possunt, neque corpora rectè existimari: ergo. Resp. haec verba intelligi debére de corporibus quoad existentiam, quum certè sine extensione aliqua nullum corpus possit esse sensíbile, non verò quoad essentiam, sicuti exístere quidem non potest corpus sine figura, & tamen illius essentia in figura positam esse nemo dixerit. Non inficiamur autèm, extensionem esse ex proprietatibus corporis unam, sed conténdimus tantùm, non esse adtributum primum in corpore.

9 Obj. 3. St. Augustine, addressing Evodius, says (n): I ask you whether you think there is any body that does not, in its own measure, have length, breadth and depth? ….. If you take this away from bodies, in my opinion they can neither be perceived by the senses nor rightly be judged to be bodies: therefore. Reply: these words must be understood of bodies as to existence, since certainly without some extension no body could be sensible; but not as to essence: just as body cannot indeed exist without figure, and yet no one would say that its essence is placed in figure. We do not deny, however, that extension is one of the properties of body; we contend only that it is not the first attribute in body.

10 Opp 4. nullum corpus sine triplici dimensione exístere, vidéri, vel cóncipi potest: ergo extensio est ratio formalis corporis.

10 Obj. 4. No body can exist, be seen, or be conceived without threefold dimension: therefore extension is the formal reason of body.

Sect. 1. Phys. Lib. 3. c. 6.

Sect. 1, Phys., bk. 3, ch. 6.

Lib. de quant. animae. n. 6.

Bk. On the Magnitude of the Soul, no. 6.

p. 12

Conseq. non infertur, quia nec etiam corpus aliquod finitum sine figura, nec homo sine capacitate scientiae cóncipi potest, & tamen haec ad illorum essentiam pertinére minimè debent. Dices: si essentia corporis in trina dimensione constituitur. clarissimè probatur spiritualitas animae rationalis, ut ostensum est in Psychologia: ergo Resp. in nostra de essentia corporis sententia eamdem habere vim argumentum pro animi spiritualitate; quemadmodùm enim, ex eo quod anima rationalis extensionem actualem habére non possit, rectè infert Cartesius esse incorpoream, ita nos ex eo quod anima rationalis extensionem habére non éxigat, optimè inférimus, quod illa sit diversae naturae ac corpus.

The consequent does not follow; because neither can any finite body be conceived without figure, nor man without the capacity for knowledge, and yet these ought by no means to pertain to their essence. You will say: if the essence of body is constituted in threefold dimension, the spirituality of the rational soul is most clearly proved, as was shown in the Psychology: therefore. Reply: in our opinion on the essence of body the argument for the spirituality of the soul has the same force; for just as, from the fact that the rational soul cannot have actual extension, Descartes rightly infers that it is incorporeal, so we, from the fact that the rational soul does not require to have extension, very well infer that it is of a different nature from body.

11 Opp 5. quum ipsum nihil, quod ante mundi creationem fuit, mente concípere vólumus, extensionem quamdam fingimus: ergo extensio ipsa non ut proprietas, sed ut ratio formalis corporis à nobis concipitur. Disting. antec. & ex imaginationis nostrae phantásmate benè colligitur essentia, sive ratio formalis corporis, nego, & pérperam collígitur, conc. & nego conseq. Argumentum probat ante mundi creationem darj jam materiam existentem: nam concipimus extensionem: ergo juxta Cartesianos concipimus corpus: ergo corpus illud erat existens ab aeterno, quod absurdum est.

11 Obj. 5. When we wish to conceive in the mind that very nothing which was before the creation of the world, we imagine a certain extension: therefore extension itself is conceived by us not as a property, but as the formal reason of body. I distinguish the antecedent; and from the phantasm of our imagination the essence, or formal reason, of body is well gathered, I deny; is wrongly gathered, I grant; and I deny the consequent. The argument proves that matter was already existing before the creation of the world: for we conceive extension: therefore, according to the Cartesians, we conceive body: therefore that body was existing from eternity, which is absurd.

12 Sed instant Cartesiani: nihili nulla est extensio, nulla proprietas, nulla qualitas; sed quando concípimus ipsum nihil, quod antè mundi creationem fuit, illud concípimus, ut extensum: ergo concípimus aliquid, non verò ipsum nihil, ac proinde aliquod corpus concípimus. Sed in hoc argumento, (ut optimè notat Illustriss. Petrus Daniel Huet 4 hallucinatur Cartesius: animadvértere enim debebat, proprietates, sive qualitates duplicis esse géneris, positivas alias, alias negativas, nihili proprietates positivas nullas esse, negativas multas. Dicimus enim, nihilum esse incorruptum, nihilum nihilo simile esse, nihilum esse contrarium enti, ex nihilo mundum â Deo esse creatum, &c. Sed hae proprietates sunt merae negationes, corruptionis nempe, discrepantiae â nihilo, &c. Similitèr, quum fingimus in nihilum à Deo redigi vinum, quod vase aliquo continetur, nullo alio admisso corpore in vini locum, dicendum est, vacuum manére spatium, quod à vino occupabatur, ejusdemque id fore amplitúdinis, & extensionis, ac priùs erat vinum, meritòque vacuo huic spatio extensionem tribuemus, at negativam: nam quum dicam spatium illud inane, quod intra vas est, esse pedis unius quadrati, perindè erit ac si dicerem, in spatio illo pedali nullum esse corpus; & pedális haec extensio vacui, sive nihili, erit negatio corporis in spatio pedáli.

12 But the Cartesians insist: of nothing there is no extension, no property, no quality; but when we conceive that very nothing which was before the creation of the world, we conceive it as extended: therefore we conceive something, and not nothing itself, and consequently we conceive some body. But in this argument (as the Most Illustrious Pierre Daniel Huet (o) very well notes) Descartes is deluded: for he ought to have observed that properties, or qualities, are of two kinds, some positive, others negative; that of nothing there are no positive properties, but many negative ones. For we say that nothing is incorruptible, that nothing is like nothing, that nothing is contrary to being, that the world was created by God out of nothing, etc. But these properties are mere negations, namely of corruption, of difference from nothing, etc. Likewise, when we imagine that the wine which is contained in some vessel is reduced to nothing by God, no other body being admitted into the place of the wine, it must be said that the space which was occupied by the wine remains void, and that it will be of the same amplitude and extension as the wine was before; and we shall deservedly attribute extension to this void space, but a negative one: for when I say that that empty space which is inside the vessel is of one square foot, it will be just as if I said that in that space of a foot there is no body; and this extension of a foot, of the void, or of nothing, will be the negation of body in a space of a foot.

13 Opp. 6 modus non potest cóncipi sine re, cujus est modus, sed extensio optimè percipi potest sine lapide ex. gr. ergo extensio non est proprietas, aut modus corporis, sed ipsius

13 Obj. 6. A mode cannot be conceived without the thing whose mode it is; but extension can very well be perceived without, e.g., a stone: therefore extension is not a property or mode of body, but its very essence.

Censura Philosoph. Cartes. cap. 5. n. 3.

Censura Philosophiae Cartesianae, ch. 5, no. 3.

p. 13

essentia. Dist. min. extensio lapidis potést concipi sine illa, nego; extensio generatim sumpta subdist. potest concipi praecisè sine lapide, conc. sine ullo corpore cujus sit extensio, nego, & conseq. Dices pro opinione Gassendi: statim ac concipitur substantia aliqua actu impenetrabilis, concipitur corpus: ergo. Conseq. non infertur; etenim statim ac concipitur ignis, concipitur substantia aliqua, quae calorem actualem habeat, & tamén nemo dixerit essentiam ignis in actuali calore positàm esse, nam ignis Babilónicus adplicatus extitit sine combustione.

I distinguish the minor. The extension of the stone can be conceived without it, I deny; extension taken generally, I subdistinguish: it can be conceived precisely without the stone, I grant; without any body whose extension it is, I deny; and I deny the consequent. You will say, for the opinion of Gassendi: as soon as some actually impenetrable substance is conceived, body is conceived: therefore. The consequent does not follow; for as soon as fire is conceived, some substance is conceived which has actual heat, and yet no one would say that the essence of fire is placed in actual heat, for the Babylonian fire, when applied, was without burning.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

Sententia nostra exponitur, & probatur.

Our opinion is set out and proved.

14 Dico cum plurimis Recentioribus: ratio formalis corporis physici optimè constituitur in naturali[?] impenetrabilitate, sive (quod idem est) in exigentia naturali occupandi locum impenetrabiliter. Prob. concl. in eo ratio formalis corporis physici rectè constituitur, ex quo adtributa cetera tamquam ex radíce ducúntur, ut omnes consentiunt; sed adtributum ejuscémodi est naturalis impenetrabilitas, sive quod idem est, impenetrabilitas radicalis: ergo. Prob. min: ex ea profluit extensio corporis entitativa, illud namque dicitur entitativè extensum, quod compléctitur plures partes interse unitas, ita ut, unius éntitas extra entitatem alterius tota existat; sed hac ratione conjungi interse plura non possunt, nisi sint naturalitèr impenetrabilia: ergo.

say, with very many of the Moderns: the formal reason of physical 14 I body is best constituted in natural impenetrability, or (what is the same) in the natural exigency of occupying place impenetrably. Proof of the conclusion: the formal reason of physical body is rightly constituted in that from which the other attributes are derived as from a root, as all agree; but such an attribute is natural impenetrability, or, what is the same, radical impenetrability: therefore. Proof of the minor: from it flows the entitative extension of body; for that is called entitatively extended which comprises several parts united among themselves in such a way that the whole entity of one exists outside the entity of another; but several things cannot be conjoined among themselves in this way unless they are naturally impenetrable: therefore.

15 Séquitur soliditas, vi cujus, aut cómprimi non possunt corpora, aut ad certum duntaxat gradum viribus nostris coarctari, Mobilitas deinde; quia si corpora non resisterent corporibus, motum vix cogitáre possémus, quem in rebus experímur. Deinde divisibilitas, mensurabilitas, & capacitas recipiendi quamvis figuram ex naturali impenetrabilitate consequuntur. Secundò: videtur perspicuum, istiusmodi exigentiam non posse a priori de corpore demonstrari; nihil est enim in compore, ex quo tamquam ex principio, sive radíce, naturalis illius impenetrabilitas, queat dedúci, nam non ideo corpus est impenetrabile, quia extensum, sed è contrario, ideo est entitativè extensum, quia impenetrabile.

15 There follows solidity, by virtue of which bodies either cannot be compressed, or can be constrained by our forces only to a certain degree. Then mobility; because, if bodies did not resist bodies, we could scarcely think of the motion which we experience in things. Then divisibility, measurability, and the capacity to receive any figure whatever follow from natural impenetrability. Secondly: it seems evident that such an exigency cannot be demonstrated of body a priori; for there is nothing in body from which, as from a principle, or root, its natural impenetrability could be deduced; for body is not impenetrable because it is extended, but on the contrary it is entitatively extended because it is impenetrable.

Satisfit Objectionibus.

THE OBJECTIONS ARE ANSWERED.

16 Opp. 1. Impenetrabilitas convenit etiam Angelis. Potest enim Angelus ita esse in loco, ut corpus quodcumque ab illo

16 Obj. 1. Impenetrability belongs also to Angels. For an Angel can be in place in such a way that it excludes any body whatever from it;

p. 14

excludat: ergo impenetrabilitas nequit esse formalis ratio corporis. Dist. antec. Si impenetrabilitas sumatur pro naturali exigentia occupandi locum cum exclusione alterius, prout sumitur in quaestione, nego; si sumatur pro potentia libera non penetrationis, conc. Corporis impenetrabilitas istiusmodi est, ut illius causa, nequeat corpus naturae viribus, simul cum alio in eodem loco consistere, utque semper suaptè essentia requirat locum, in quo existit, cum exclusione alterius cujusque corporis occupare. At verò Angelus ejus est naturae, ut locum non repleat, tametsi corpus quodcumque à loco, in quo est, vi sua repéllere liberè possit.

therefore impenetrability cannot be the formal reason of body. I distinguish the antecedent. If impenetrability is taken for the natural exigency of occupying place with the exclusion of another, as it is taken in the question, I deny; if it is taken for a free power of non-penetration, I grant. The impenetrability of body is such that, because of it, a body cannot by the forces of nature subsist together with another in the same place, and by its very essence it always requires to occupy the place in which it exists with the exclusion of every other body. But an Angel is of such a nature that it does not fill place, although it can freely repel any body whatever, by its own force, from the place in which it is.

17 Opp. 2. corpus non est impenetrabile ab Angelo: ergo per impenetrabilitatem non distinguitur corpus ab spiritu, ac propterà non benè collocatur ratio formalis corporis in impenetrabilitate naturali. Dist. antec. corpus non est impenetrabile ab Angelo defectu sui, nego; ratione Angeli, conc. & nego conseq. Corpus petit naturâ suâ id omne â suo loco exclúdere, quod locum replet. Hinc, quum substantia spiritualis non sit loci repletiva, hujusmodi quoque ipsa nón est, ut eam á suo loco expellere corpus possit. Ceterùm quum perspicuum sit ex traditis superiori loco, impenetrabilitatem, quae inest corpori non compétere Angelis, dubium esse nequit, quin corpus â spiritu per impenetrabilitatem radicalem satis discernatur.

17 Obj. 2. Body is not impenetrable by an Angel: therefore body is not distinguished from spirit by impenetrability; and for that reason the formal reason of body is not well placed in natural impenetrability. I distinguish the antecedent. Body is not impenetrable by an Angel through its own defect, I deny; by reason of the Angel, I grant; and I deny the consequent. Body by its nature seeks to exclude from its place everything that fills place. Hence, since a spiritual substance is not repletive of place, neither is it of such a kind that body could expel it from its place. Moreover, since it is evident from what was taught in the preceding place that the impenetrability which is in body does not belong to Angels, there can be no doubt that body is sufficiently distinguished from spirit by radical impenetrability.

18 Opp. 3. Unum corpus potest divina virtute esse simul cum alio in eodem loco: ergo potest corpus impenetrabilitate privari, adeoque &c. Nego conseq. nam etsi corpus aliquod per miraculum impenetrabilitate actuali spolietur, semper tamen illam exigit habére, nec hujusmodi exigentia auferri ab illo unquàm potest: eo prorsùs modo, quo etsi calor actualis ab igne, motus deorsùm à lapide auferri, vel impedíri possit à Deo, potentia tamen, imò & exigentia relínquitur, qua remoto óbice proprium effectum actualiter illa corpora prodúcant.

18 Obj. 3. One body can by divine power be together with another in the same place: therefore body can be deprived of impenetrability, and so etc. I deny the consequent; for although some body may by a miracle be stripped of actual impenetrability, yet it always requires to have it, nor can such an exigency ever be taken away from it; in exactly the same way as, although actual heat may be taken away from fire, and downward motion from a stone, or be impeded by God, yet the power, nay even the exigency, remains, by which, once the obstacle is removed, those bodies would actually produce their proper effect.

19 Opp. 4. extensum non nisi ex extensis potest consúrgere: ergo extensio est adtributum corporis priùs impenetrabilitate. Dist. antec. & haec extensa sunt apta ad componendum corpus ratione impenetrabilitatis ipsarum, conc. & non ita sunt, nego. Enimverò sicut hoc non tollit quominùs extensum ex suo genere sit aliquid compósitum, ita non ímpedit quominùs aptitudo partium ad illud componendum, nempè naturalis earum impenetrabilitas sit adtributum ipsius compositi priùs quàm entitativa ejusdem extensio: impenetrabilitas enim naturalis nihil est aliud, quam naturalis exigentia occupandi locum cum exclusione alterius, partes verò corporis per hanc ipsarum impenetrabilitatem aptae redduntur ad extensum constituendum.

19 Obj. 4. An extended thing can arise only from extended things: therefore extension is an attribute of body prior to impenetrability. I distinguish the antecedent: and these extended things are apt for composing body by reason of their impenetrability, I grant; and they are not so, I deny. For indeed, just as this does not prevent the extended thing from being, of its own kind, something composite, so it does not prevent the aptitude of the parts for composing it, namely their natural impenetrability, from being an attribute of the composite itself prior to its entitative extension: for natural impenetrability is nothing other than the natural exigency of occupying place with the exclusion of another, and the parts of body are rendered apt for constituting an extended thing through this impenetrability of theirs.

20 Dices: principia, ex quorum unione consurgit totum entitativè extensum, non sunt corpus si divisim sumantur, sed principia corporis: ergo formalis ratio substantiae corporeae non est

20 You will say: the principles from whose union the entitatively extended whole arises are not body if taken separately, but principles of body: therefore the formal reason of corporeal substance is not

p. 15

diversa ab extensione, sed est ipsamet extensio. Nego ant. quia partes constituentes extensum divisim sumptae, sunt substantia materialis, sive corporea; (non enim sunt spiritus): ergo formalis ratio substantiae corporeae ab entitativa extensione diversa est: ergo si ratio substantiae materialis, diversa est ab extensione, ratio quoque corporis ab eadem erit planè diversa.

different from extension, but is extension itself. I deny the antecedent; because the parts constituting the extended thing, taken separately, are material, or corporeal, substance (for they are not spirits): therefore the formal reason of corporeal substance is different from entitative extension: therefore, if the reason of material substance is different from extension, the reason of body too will be plainly different from it.

21 Opp. 5. meliùs, quam per naturalem impenetrabilitatem explicatur essentia corporis per collectionem omnium adtributorum, ita ut corpus dicatur substantia natura sua impenetrabilis, extensa, divisibilis, mobilis, atque apta ad figuram quamvis recipiendam: ergo. Dist. ant.: & hic est status quaestionis, nego, & non est, conc. Explico solutionem: quantumvis memoratae proprietates sint adfectiones propriae corporum, atque ita collectae corpori duntaxat conveniant, hoc non ímpedit, quominùs adferatur: ex ipsis iis relatis unum aliquod esse adtributum, quod príncipe loco in corporibus occurrit, & ex quo reliquae proprietates in ipsis repertae fluunt. Certè in controversiam venire nequit, proprietates generales corpori ita inesse, ut rei ab eo distinctae haudquaquam cómpetant, quum id, ne in dubium quidem vocari queat, haecque notio, uti obvia cuivis, ita pluribus à Philosopho non est discutienda.

21 Obj. 5. The essence of body is explained better through the collection of all its attributes than through natural impenetrability, so that body is called a substance by its nature impenetrable, extended, divisible, mobile, and apt to receive any figure whatever: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: and this is the state of the question, I deny; and it is not, I grant. I explain the solution: however much the properties mentioned may be proper affections of bodies, and, thus collected, may belong to body alone, this does not prevent its being asserted that among those very ones listed there is some one attribute which occurs in the first place in bodies, and from which the remaining properties found in them flow. Certainly it cannot come into controversy that general properties so inhere in body that they in no way belong to a thing distinct from it, since that cannot even be called into doubt; and this notion, as it is obvious to anyone, so need not be discussed at length by a Philosopher.

DISSERTATIO II. — DISSERTATION II

De Principiis corporis naturalis.

On the Principles of natural body.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

Notiones generales principiorum.

General notions of principles. 22

22 Principia intrinseca compositi naturalis ea omnia dicuntur, ex quibus compositum ipsum essentialiter constituitur. Sic anima rationalis, & corpus sunt principia hominis intrínseca. Haec, vel primaria sunt, vel secundaria. Primaria sunt illa ex quibus ipsum compositum ita constituitur, ut ea simul ex aliis, in quae resolvi possint, minimè componantur, seu ut loquuntur Scholastici: quae neque ex se invicem, neque ex aliis, sed omnia ex ipsis fiunt. Principia secundaria ea vocantur, quae constituunt quidem compositum naturale, verum & ipsa ex aliis essentialiter coalescunt. Sic corpus organicum est principium hominis secundarium, quum ita hominem constituat, ut ipsum quoque, simul ex

Intrinsic principles of a natural composite are all those from which the composite itself is essentially constituted. Thus the rational soul and the body are intrinsic principles of man. These are either primary or secondary. Primary are those from which the composite itself is so constituted that they themselves are in no way composed, together, of others into which they could be resolved; or, as the Scholastics say, which are made neither from one another, nor from others, but all things are made from them. Those are called secondary principles which do indeed constitute a natural composite, but themselves too coalesce essentially from others. Thus the organic body is a secondary principle of man, since it so constitutes man that it itself too, together with

p. 16

aliis essentialiter componatur. Insupèr principia rerum intrinseca, vel metaphysica sunt, vel artificiosa, vel sensibilia.

others, is essentially composed. Moreover, the intrinsic principles of things are either metaphysical, or artificial, or sensible.

23 Metaphysica sunt ea, quae metaphysicarum rerum instar, sensu non adtingi possunt, sed tantùm intellectu comprehendi. Artificiosa sunt, quae miro quodam naturae artificio dispósita, & conjuncta, corpus naturale componunt ea ratione, ut omnes illius sensibiles adfectiones, operationesque, ex partium magnitudine, figura, motu, &c. proveniant, atque ex his adcommodatè explicari queant. Sensibilia demum, seu Physica vocantur ea quae à se mutuo reapse per veram corporum resolutionem, possunt separari, sensuumque adminiculo discerni. Incomperto est apud omnes Philosophos tam Veteres, quàm Recentiores, quodvis compositum naturale, quod viribus naturae produci, ac destrui potest, duplici constare principio essentiali; quorum alterum determinabile est, & materia dicitur, alterum detérminans, & forma compellatur. Certum quippe est fieri mutationes naturales compositi unius in aliud quoad substantiam; ¿quis enim neget cibum ex. gr. mutari in chílum, hunc in sánguinem, sánguinem in alias corporis orgánici partes, quorum profectò unum in aliud ea lege convértitur, ut nihil sensibile remáneat, ex quo utrumque essentialiter coalescit.

23 Metaphysical are those which, after the manner of metaphysical things, cannot be reached by sense, but only grasped by the intellect. Artificial are those which, disposed and conjoined by a certain wonderful artifice of nature, compose natural body in such a way that all its sensible affections and operations arise from the magnitude, figure, motion, etc. of the parts, and can be suitably explained from these. Sensible, finally, or Physical, are called those which can really be separated from one another by a true resolution of bodies, and be discerned with the aid of the senses. It is established among all Philosophers, the Ancients as well as the Moderns, that any natural composite which can be produced and destroyed by the forces of nature consists of a twofold essential principle; of which one is determinable and is called matter, the other determining, and is named form. For it is certain that natural changes of one composite into another as to substance take place: for who would deny that food, e.g., is changed into chyle, this into blood, and blood into the other parts of the organic body; of which one is surely converted into another on such terms that nothing sensible remains out of which each of them essentially coalesces?

24 Jam verò certum est, compositum, quod naturae viribus mutatur, neque creatione fieri, neque in nihilum rédigi. Certum igitur est dari quidpiam ex quo existente fiunt omnia, adeòque cunctis commune, quod principium determinabile, seu materia rectè indigitatur. Haud absimili ratione, quoniam, ut liqüet composita naturalia inter se differunt quoad substantiam; per eam vero partem, quae omnibus ex aequo communis est, haudquaqüam discriminentur; manifestum redditur, aliud quiddam esse in corporibus, quod principium determinans, id est forma vocatur. Quare si materia sumatur pro subjecto, ex quo praevie existente naturalia composita producuntur: forma verò praecise pro eo, quo unumquodque compositum, est id ipsum, quod est, atque a céteris quoad essentiam distinguitur, patet sanè de existentia horum principiorum Peripateticos inter, & Recentiores quaestionem movéri haud posse. Verùm sicut eadem illa sic accepta notionibus abstractis cóntinentur, & Physicae considerationis neutiquam sunt; ita ad rerum physicarum naturam, adfectiones, operationesque explicandas minimè faciunt.

24 Now it is certain that a composite which is changed by the forces of nature is neither made by creation nor reduced to nothing. It is certain, therefore, that there is something from which, as existing, all things are made, and which is therefore common to all; and this is rightly designated as the determinable principle, or matter. In a not dissimilar way, since, as is plain, natural composites differ from one another as to substance, but are in no way distinguished by that part which is equally common to all, it is made manifest that there is something else in bodies which is called the determining principle, that is, form. Wherefore, if matter is taken for the subject from which, as previously existing, natural composites are produced, and form precisely for that by which each composite is the very thing that it is, and is distinguished from the rest as to essence, it is plain indeed that no question can be raised concerning the existence of these principles between the Peripatetics and the Moderns. But just as these same principles, so taken, are contained in abstract notions and are by no means objects of Physical consideration, so they contribute nothing to explaining the nature, affections and operations of physical things.

25 Totum igitur quod hac in re negotium facessit, positum in eo est, ut palam fiat, quae sit horum principiorum physica natura, nimirùm ¿quid physicè sit illud, ex quo praeexistente tamquam ex subjecto determinabili composita naturalia a causis creatis producuntur, quidque illud, per quod unumquodque compositum est id quod est, & â quovis alio essentialiter distinguitur? Peripatetici nihil dedere hac super re, materiam, atque formam metaphysicè considerasse contenti. Recentiores verò scholasticis subtilitatibus rejectis in eo sunt toti, ut physicam horum principiorum naturam in aperto ponant, unde adparet, quam falsò dicant vulgares

25 The whole business, therefore, that this matter involves consists in this: that it be made plain what the physical nature of these principles is; namely, what physically is that from which, as pre-existing, as from a determinable subject, natural composites are produced by created causes, and what is that by which each composite is what it is, and is essentially distinguished from any other? The Peripatetics gave us nothing on this matter, content to have considered matter and form metaphysically. But the Moderns, having rejected the scholastic subtleties, are wholly engaged in setting out openly the physical nature of these principles; whence it appears how falsely the common Peripatetics

p. 17

Peripatetici, neque materiam, neque formam â Recentioribus admitti. His itaque constitutis systéma metaphysicum Peripateticorum videamus.

say that neither matter nor form is admitted by the Moderns. These things, then, being established, let us look at the metaphysical system of the Peripatetics.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

Exponitur systéma Metaphysicum Peripateticorum.

The Metaphysical system of the Peripatetics is set out.

26 Supponendum est, corpus quodlibet naturale dupliciter considerari posse, & quatenus generatur, sive ut Peripatetici loquuntur in fieri, & quatenus jam genitum est, sive, ut ipsi dicunt in facto esse. Principia corporis naturalis, quatenus generatur, sunt tria juxta Aristotelem 5 materia, forma, & privatio: generatio enim est, transitus quidam â non esse substantiali ad illud esse substantiale, in quo transitu tria necessario concurrunt, nempe terminus á quo, seu privatio illius esse, illud esse quod adquiritur, quod est forma, & illud ex quo res constituta per illud esse fit, quod est materia. Principia corporis naturalis jam facti, seu in facto esse, tantum sunt duo, nempe materia, & forma, ut supra dictum est. Adhaec, ajunt unionem esse formam quandam, seu modum substantialem, partem ut quo, cujus est facere, ut ex materia, & forma totum quoddam completum substantiale constituatur. Thomistae ferè negant, hanc unionem esse â materia, & forma distinctam, ceteri contrà statuunt, & pro vera entitate modali ipsam agnoscunt. Imò verò sunt quibus unio alia ejus ipsius unionis, quam unitionem vocant, adserenda videatur. Haec autem sicuti alia pléraque, tanti non sunt, ut fusius â me exponi debeant.

t must be supposed that any natural body can be considered in two ways: 26 I both inasmuch as it is generated, or, as the Peripatetics speak, in fieri, and inasmuch as it has already been generated, or, as they themselves say, in facto esse. The principles of natural body, inasmuch as it is generated, are three according to Aristotle (p): matter, form, and privation: for generation is a certain passage from substantial non-being to that substantial being, in which passage three things necessarily concur, namely the terminus a quo, or the privation of that being; that being which is acquired, which is form; and that from which the thing constituted through that being is made, which is matter.
