The principles of natural body already made, or in facto esse, are only two, namely matter and form, as was said above. In addition, they say that union is a certain form, or substantial mode, a part ut quo, whose office is to bring it about that a certain complete substantial whole is constituted from matter and form. The Thomists generally deny that this union is distinct from matter and form; the others hold the contrary, and acknowledge it as a true modal entity. Nay, indeed, there are some to whom another union of that very union, which they call unition, seems to need asserting. But these things, like most others, are not of such importance that they ought to be set out by me at greater length.

27 Docent praeterea Peripatetici materiam primam esse substantiam simplicem, incompletam, primum rerum corporearum fundamentum, primumque subjectum naturalium transmutationum. Eam ita definit Aristoteles 3 materia secundum se neque est quid, nec quantum, nec quale, nec aliquid eorum quibus ens determinatur, neque utique negationes. Ipsum nihil meliori definitione explicare non posset Aristoteles, lepidè inquit Hispanus noster D. Martinus Martinez 3. Non est quid, id est, secundum se non est homo nec lapis, nec lignum, &c. Non est quantum, id est nullam habet determinatam magnitudinem, nec quale, quia nec calida est, nec frigida,

27 The Peripatetics teach, besides, that prime matter is a simple, incomplete substance, the first foundation of corporeal things, and the first subject of natural transmutations. Aristotle defines it thus (q): matter of itself is neither something, nor a quantity, nor a quality, nor any of those things by which being is determined; nor yet negations. Aristotle could not have explained nothing itself with a better definition, as our Spaniard Don Martín Martínez wittily says (r). It is not something, that is, of itself it is not a man, nor a stone, nor wood, etc. It is not a quantity, that is, it has no determinate magnitude; nor a quality, because it is neither hot nor cold, nor

Lib. 1. Phys. cap. 6. & 7.

Bk. 1 of the Physics, ch. 6 and 7.

p. 18

neque aliquid eorum, &c. quia non est ulla forma, cujus est ens determinare ád hanc, aut illam speciem physicam. Denique non est negationes, sive entium carentiae, quia est entitas positiva.

any of those things, etc., because it is not any form, whose office it is to determine a being to this or that physical species. Finally, it is not negations, or privations of beings, because it is a positive entity.

28 Ex dictis inferunt: materiam primam esse subjectum ad multiplices formas indifferentem, & quidem non modalem, sed absolutam, nam si accidens esset, in alio subjecto reciperetur, ac proinde non esset primum subjectum: esse simplicem, id est, non compositam ex subjecto & forma: nam tunc non esset primum principium, hoc tamen non impedit, esse compositam integraliter ex partibus extensis. Inferunt etiam esse incompletam, hoc est, esse ordinatam ad constituendum totum cum alia parte substantiali: esse ingenerabilem & incorruptibilem, nam quum generatio sit productio rei ex praesupposito subjecto; corruptio verò desitio rei permanente subjecto, materiaque, quae est primum subjectum, nec praesupponi á se possit, nec possit destructa manére, inde nec generari, nec corrumpi potest. Esse naturaliter indestructibilem, quia Deus nullam destruit substantiam nisi ad inimici fortioris exigentiam, & nihil est in rebus inimicum materiae.

28 From what has been said they infer: that prime matter is a subject indifferent to many forms, and indeed not modal, but absolute; for if it were an accident, it would be received in another subject, and consequently would not be the first subject: that it is simple, that is, not composed of subject and form, for then it would not be the first principle; this, however, does not prevent its being composed integrally of extended parts. They infer also that it is incomplete, that is, that it is ordered to constituting a whole together with another substantial part: that it is ingenerable and incorruptible; for since generation is the production of a thing from a presupposed subject, and corruption the ceasing of a thing while the subject remains, and since matter, which is the first subject, can neither be presupposed by itself nor remain when destroyed, it can therefore neither be generated nor be corrupted. That it is naturally indestructible, because God destroys no substance except at the demand of a stronger enemy, and there is nothing in things hostile to matter.

29 Quod ad formam spectat eam esse dicunt substantiam incompletam, quae tanquam actus primus materiam complet, informat, ut corpus naturale in determinata specie constituat. Dicitur incompleta, quia cum materia determinatur ad constituendum compositum; actus dicitur, quia determinat potentiam materiae ad certum complementum, & certam compositi speciem: vocatur autem primus actus, ut ab accidentibus discernatur, qui actus sunt materiae, sed secundarii. Ex materia & forma ita explicatis omnia composita constare adfirmant Peripatetici. Ex dictis inferunt 1. quod differentia specifica corporum non à materia, ut quae in omnibus eadem est specie, sed à forma desumatur. 2. quod forma substantialis in omni generatione, de novo producatur, & in corruptione (excepta anima rationali) destruatur, remanente materia prima, quae est incorruptibilis 3. quod, omnes formae (anima rationali excepta) educantur ex potentia materiae, vel à causa creata, si adsit proportionata, vel á solo Deo, ut auctore naturae. Hactenus Peripateticorum systema.

29 As regards form, they say that it is an incomplete substance, which as first act completes and informs matter, so as to constitute natural body in a determinate species. It is called incomplete, because together with matter it is determined to constituting the composite; it is called act, because it determines the potency of matter to a certain complement and to a certain species of composite: and it is called first act, that it may be distinguished from accidents, which are acts of matter, but secondary ones. The Peripatetics affirm that all composites consist of matter and form so explained. From what has been said they infer: 1. that the specific difference of bodies is taken not from matter, as being the same in species in all, but from form. 2. that substantial form is produced anew in every generation, and destroyed in corruption (the rational soul excepted), prime matter remaining, which is incorruptible. 3. that all forms (the rational soul excepted) are educed from the potency of matter, either by a created cause, if a proportionate one is present, or by God alone, as author of nature. So far the system of the Peripatetics.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

Quambrevissimè exponitur & refutatur Systema Leibnitzii.

The System of Leibniz is very briefly set out and refuted. 30

30 Leibnitzius admittit in natura vim aliquam insensibilem, & entia abstracta: atque hac de causa in classe eorum est, qui metaphysica, sive insensibilia corporum

Leibniz admits in nature some insensible force, and abstract beings: and for this reason he is in the class of those who, as the principles of bodies, metaphysical, or insensible, ones

Haec est celebris materiae definitio ab Aristotele tradita lib. 1. Metaphys. cap. 3. qua in re Aristotelem derisit S. Justinus Martyr, & S. Basilius.

This is the celebrated definition of matter handed down by Aristotle in bk. 1 of the Metaphysics, ch. 3; on which point St. Justin Martyr and St. Basil derided Aristotle.

Filosofia Sceptica en Diálogos.

Filosofía escéptica en diálogos.

p. 19

principia statuerunt. Elementa omnium rerum juxta ipsum sunt mónades, sive substantiae simplices, ingenerabiles, & incorruptibiles à Deo creatae. Quaevis monas repraesentat totum universum, adeoque est quodammodo omnia, sed sicut remota non satis oculis discernimus, ita fit, ut non omnia, quae quavis in monade insunt, distinctè repraesententur. Ejus integrum systéma in Actis Eruditorum Lipsiensibus 4 publicatum fuit. Sed ¿quis mente adsequatur, quod monas quaevis, ens videlicet partium expers rerum universitatem repraesentet? Nec animus est Leibnitzio objectare usum in explicanda sua opinione vocabulorum, quibus nulla subsit idea distincta, quod Hartsoeker explevit 3: neque monadologiam ab idealismi errore haud alienam commonstrare, quod ex institituto factum à Jac. Frider. Mullero. Haec pauca delibasse satis fuerit.

have laid down. The elements of all things, according to him, are monads, or simple, ingenerable and incorruptible substances created by God. Every monad represents the whole universe, and so is in a certain way all things; but just as we do not sufficiently discern remote things with our eyes, so it comes about that not all the things that are in any given monad are distinctly represented. His complete system was published in the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig (s). But who could grasp with his mind that any monad whatever, that is, a being devoid of parts, represents the whole totality of things? Nor is it my intention to reproach Leibniz with the use, in explaining his opinion, of words beneath which no distinct idea lies, which Hartsoeker has done in full (t); nor to show that the monadology is not far removed from the error of idealism, which has been done expressly by Jac. Frider. Müller. It will be enough to have touched upon these few things.

CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

Praemittuntur axiomata ad confutanda, vel stabilienda systemata prorsùs necessaria.

Axioms altogether necessary for refuting or establishing systems are set out beforehand. 31

31 Antequam refutationem systematis Peripateticorum adgrediamur, axiomata quaedam universalia Physicae propria, atque ex generalibus requisitis ad cujusvis Scientiae systema stabiliendum necessariis deducta, premittenda putamus, quae cùm in dijudicandis aliorum systematibus, tùm in nostro constituendo, facem veluti praeferant, & quibus tanquam fundamentis tota Physica deinceps nitatur. Ea autem sunt hujusmodi.

Before we approach the refutation of the system of the Peripatetics, we think we must first set out certain universal axioms proper to Physics, deduced from the general requisites necessary for establishing the system of any Science, which may carry a torch before us, as it were, both in judging the systems of others and in constituting our own, and on which, as on foundations, the whole of Physics may henceforth rest. They are, moreover, of this kind.

32 Axioma I. In Physicis illud systema, aut opinio, seu falsa rejici debet, quae contra Theologiam Sacram, vel sanam metaphysicam, aut certam experientiam quidpiam docet vel adsumit. Axioma II. Illud systema praeferendum est aliis, quod simplicius est, & ex paucioribus principiis corporis naturalis proprietates, effectus & phaenómena explicat. Entia profectò non sunt multiplicanda citra necessitatem, non debet item per plura fieri, quod fieri potest per pauciora, ut omnes Philosophi consentiunt. Qua propter nec principia rerum, nec effectuum causae multiplicandae sunt, nisi ratio haud dubia id poscat, ut supra dictum est [§. 20.] Axioma III. Illud systema melius censendum est, quod plura, quae apud Physicos in considerationem duci debent, evolvit. Physica enim tota in eo versatur, ut rerum naturalium adfectiones, effectus &c. quàm plurimi, & quam optimè explicentur.

32 Axiom I. In Physics that system or opinion must be rejected as false which teaches or assumes anything contrary to Sacred Theology, or to sound metaphysics, or to certain experience. Axiom II. That system is to be preferred to the others which is simpler, and explains the properties, effects and phenomena of natural body from fewer principles. Beings, assuredly, are not to be multiplied beyond necessity; likewise, what can be done by fewer things ought not to be done by more, as all Philosophers agree. Wherefore neither the principles of things nor the causes of effects are to be multiplied, unless an undoubted reason demands it, as was said above [§. 20.]. Axiom III. That system is to be judged the better which unfolds the more of the things that must be taken into consideration among Physicists. For the whole of Physics is engaged in this: that the affections, effects, etc. of natural things be explained, as many of them as possible, and as well as possible.

Supplem. tom. 7. Sect. 11. ann. 1721.

Supplement, vol. 7, sect. 11, year 1721.

Cours de Physique Lib. 1. cap 1. art. 3.

Cours de Physique, bk. 1, ch. 1, art. 3.

p. 20

33 In adlata hujus axiomatis ratione fundatur Axioma IV. Systema illud praeferendum est ceteris, quod non modò generalibus notionibus utitur ad explicanda rerum phaenómena, sed speciatim etiam naturam corporum, adfectiones, & causas effectuum quoad ejus fieri potest perspicuè, ac dilucide proponit. Ideae enim generales pariunt duntaxat notitiam obscuram rerum particularium, resque naturales optimè non explicant, quod munus est Physicae. Hinc, si quaerenti ex. gr. ¿cur calor rarefaciat corpora, frigus adstringat? respondeatur: hanc esse caloris, hanc frigoris naturam, haud dignum Philosopho responsum datur. Similiter, interrogantem de variis naturae effectibus, generali qualitatis termino expedire, parvi est, atque humilis ingenii, ut Clariss. Rohault 3 loquitur. Hinc consequitur Axioma V. Illa doctrina reliquis praestat, quae nihil adserit, vel ponit, quod cogitatione comprehendi, aut explicari satis nequeat. Physica enim quantum fieri potest exhibére nobis debet naturam ad vires intelligentiae nostrae adcommodatam, & sublatis involúcris naturam rerum explicare.

33 On the reason given for this axiom is founded Axiom IV. That system is to be preferred to the rest which not only uses general notions to explain the phenomena of things, but also sets forth in particular the nature of bodies, their affections, and the causes of effects, as far as this can be done, perspicuously and lucidly. For general ideas produce only an obscure knowledge of particular things, and do not explain natural things in the best way, which is the task of Physics. Hence, if to someone asking, e.g., why does heat rarefy bodies and cold contract them? the answer is given that this is the nature of heat, and that the nature of cold, a response unworthy of a Philosopher is given. Similarly, to dispatch someone who asks about the various effects of nature with the general term quality is the mark of a small and lowly wit, as the most illustrious Rohault (u) says. Hence follows Axiom V. That doctrine excels the rest which asserts or posits nothing that cannot be sufficiently grasped in thought or explained. For Physics, as far as this can be done, ought to exhibit nature to us accommodated to the powers of our intelligence, and to explain the nature of things with its wrappings removed.

34 Axioma VI. Systema illud in Physica obtineat necesse est, quod rerum naturalium doctrinam adcommodatè ad naturam ac rationem disciplinae hujus persequitur. Hùc quoque ceu regulae quaedam aliae perquam utiles revocari possunt sequentes. I. Non est recurrendum ad causam primam seu Deum, quando haberi potest causa secunda. II. Dum nobis ignotae sunt causae sensibiles effectuum, insensibilis quaedam, & perinde ignota haud quaquam adstruatur. III. In his quaestionibus, aut immorandum non est, aut ab iis tractandis omninò abstinendum, quarum solutio vel nunquam reperietur, vel si fortè reperiatur nihilo nos doctiores reddit. IV. Idem dicendum de iis controversiis, quae ab imperscrutabili Dei consilio pendent, & illi soli cognitae sunt, qui fecit omnia, quae proinde rectè ait Tertullianus, aut à Deo discenda esse, aut à nullo. His constitutis.

34 Axiom VI. That system must prevail in Physics which pursues the doctrine of natural things in a manner suited to the nature and method of this discipline. To this may also be referred, as certain further rules, the following, which are extremely useful. I. One must not have recourse to the first cause, or God, when a second cause can be had. II. While the sensible causes of effects are unknown to us, let no insensible and equally unknown cause whatever be asserted. III. On those questions one must not dwell, or must altogether abstain from treating them, whose solution either will never be found, or, if perchance it is found, makes us none the more learned. IV. The same is to be said of those controversies which depend on the inscrutable counsel of God and are known to Him alone who made all things, and which therefore, as Tertullian rightly says, are to be learned either from God or from no one. These things being established,

CAPUT V.

CHAPTER V.

Refutatur Systéma metaphysicum Peripateticorum.

The metaphysical system of the Peripatetics is refuted.

35 Dico primo: principia corporis naturalis, prout ab Aristotele exponuntur, nihil ferè ad Philosophiam naturalem adipiscendam deserviunt. Veritas hujus adsertionis satis patebit, si consideremus corporis naturalis principia, materiam scilicet, & formam nonnisi

say, first: the principles of natural body, as they are set forth by Aristotle, 35 I serve almost nothing toward acquiring natural Philosophy. The truth of this assertion will be sufficiently plain if we consider that the principles of natural body, namely matter and form, were only metaphysically and

In Phys. Praefat.

In the Preface to his Physics.

p. 21

metaphysicè & in abstracto fuisse ab Aristotele adsignata, & cuncta, quae de eisdem adserit, & determinat, solummodo esse metaphisicas quasdam praecisiones, quibus physicae res nunquam satis exponuntur, itaque ad cognitionem particularium corporum, diversorumque phaenomenorum explicationem nihil conferunt, proindeque nihil ferè ad Physicam adipiscendam deserviunt, nec in Physicae systemate locum habere possunt ex Axiom. VI.

and in the abstract assigned by Aristotle, and that everything he asserts and determines about them is merely certain metaphysical abstractions, by which physical things are never sufficiently set forth; and so they contribute nothing to the knowledge of particular bodies or to the explanation of the various phenomena, and therefore serve almost nothing toward acquiring Physics, nor can they have a place in the system of Physics, by Axiom VI.

36 Quod ut clarius fiat hunc casum supponite. Quaerat aliquis ex. gr. ¿ex quibus, ceu intrinsecis principiis domus coalescat? Respondeam autem ego coalescere ex materia & forma domus: materiam autem esse id ex quo domus fit, formam verò esse actum, quo materia determinata est, ut domum componat. Hac certè responsione verum dixi, sed interrogantem doctiorem non feci, ideoque meritò rursum inquiret ¿quid nempè sit materia illa ex qua facta sit domus, quidve similiter sit actus ille, qui forma domus adpelatur. Non ergo ex Aristotelis Schola doctiores evadimus in iis, quae ad rerum naturalium primordia spectant, proindeque metaphysicum Peripateticorum systema nihil ferè ad Philosophiam naturalem adipiscendam deservit, non ex eo quod falsum sit, sed è contrario quod nimis verum, nihilque doceat praeter ea quae ignorari non possunt. ¿Quis enim unquam dubitare potest ex materia, & forma omnia composita esse? : at postquam haec didicimus nullius phaenomeni causam reddere possumus: nihil ergò deservit ad Physicam perdiscendam.

36 To make this clearer, suppose the following case. Let someone ask, e.g., from what, as from intrinsic principles, does a house come together? And let me answer that it comes together from the matter and the form of the house: that the matter, moreover, is that from which the house is made, and the form the act by which the matter is determined to compose a house. With this answer I have certainly spoken the truth, but I have not made the questioner more learned; and therefore he will rightly ask again what, namely, that matter is from which the house has been made, or likewise what that act is which is called the form of the house. We do not, therefore, come away from the school of Aristotle more learned in those things which pertain to the first beginnings of natural things; and therefore the metaphysical system of the Peripatetics serves almost nothing toward acquiring natural Philosophy, not because it is false, but on the contrary because it is too true, and teaches nothing beyond those things which cannot be unknown. For who can ever doubt that all composites are made of matter and form? But after we have learned these things we can give the cause of no phenomenon: therefore it serves nothing toward learning Physics thoroughly.

37 Dico secundo: Systema Peripateticum de principiis corporis naturalis negligendum omninò est in Physica. Prob: nam si in Philosophia naturali systema illud rectè negligitur, in quo res naturales, aut non explicantur, vel ignotum per aequè ignotum proponitur, Peripateticum certè systema locum in Physica habere non potest ex Axiom. III. & IV. ac proinde negligendum omnino est. Prima hujus propositionis pars, licet à nobis probata jam superiùs sit, plenius & ad evidentiam usque probatur. Pone etenim in quaestionem venire ¿cur ignis ex. gr. certis, quas experimur qualitatibus donetur, aqua ex adverso alias adfectiones sortiatur? Non alium responsum à Peripatetico excipies, quam hoc: videlicet eo ex capite, ista cónsequi, quod ignis aliam formam substantialem habeat, aqua aliam; quod si quis instet quaerendo ¿quid formae illae sint, qua lege diversos effectus producant, diversa exposcant accidentia? Reponunt hi philosophi continuò: naturam hanc esse formae ignis, ut tales exigat adfectiones, aliam contra esse naturam formae ipsius aquae, quod quidem est contra Axiom. IV.

37 I say secondly: the Peripatetic system of the principles of natural body is to be altogether neglected in Physics. Proof: for if in natural Philosophy that system is rightly neglected in which natural things either are not explained or the unknown is set forth through the equally unknown, the Peripatetic system certainly cannot have a place in Physics, by Axioms III and IV, and therefore it is to be altogether neglected. The first part of this proposition, although it has already been proved by us above, is proved more fully and to the point of evidence. For suppose the question arises why fire, e.g., is endowed with certain qualities which we experience, while water, on the other hand, obtains other affections? You will receive no other answer from a Peripatetic than this: namely, that these things follow from the fact that fire has one substantial form, water another; and if someone insists by asking what those forms are, by what law they produce diverse effects and demand diverse accidents? these philosophers reply at once that this is the nature of the form of fire, that it requires such affections, and that on the contrary the nature of the form of water itself is another; which is indeed against Axiom IV.

38 Secunda pars propositionis constat, nam dum â Peripatetico quaeritur ¿cur calor & frigus ex. gr. diversam sensationem producant? non aliam indigitant causam, quam qualitates has diversas, omninò esse diversae naturae. ¿Quis verò negabit his loquendi modulis rerum phaenomena neutiquam explicari, &

38 The second part of the proposition is evident; for when a Peripatetic is asked why heat and cold, e.g., produce a diverse sensation? they point to no other cause than that these qualities are diverse, of an altogether diverse nature. But who will deny that by these little ways of speaking the phenomena of things are by no means explained, and that the unknown

p. 22

ignotam controversiae materiam responso perinde ignoto expediri? ergo in Peripatetico systemate ignotum per aeque ignotum proponitur, generalibusque utitur notionibus ad explicanda rerum phaenomena contra Axiom. IV. ac proinde in Physica negligendum omnino est.

matter of the controversy is dispatched with an answer just as unknown? Therefore in the Peripatetic system the unknown is set forth through the equally unknown, and it uses general notions to explain the phenomena of things, contrary to Axiom IV, and therefore it is to be altogether neglected in Physics.

39 Adhaec dum Peripatetici in eo sunt unicè ut formas substantiales interíre, atque generari propugnent ¿qua ratione novam formam substantialem ignis ex. gr. exoriri commonstrabunt, iisdem omnibus manentibus, quibus constitutis eadem forma destrui solet. Eadem est candela, (verbis utor Clariss. Casati 2) cum eodem ardente ellychnio flammam edens: insufflas, flamma perit: iterum insufflas, flamma reviviscit: ortus & interitus eadem est causa, scilicet idem flatus, aedem dispositiones, idem subjectum, quod flamma privatur, & flammam recipit. Praetereo quam plurima argumenta adversus systema Peripateticum, speciatim ea, quibus Henricus Wiber materiam, & formam valide exagitat. s2 Systema hoc haudquaquam veluti ab Aristotele excogitatum spectamus, sed Peripateticum vulgare dicimus, quod fortasse aptiùs Arabicum ab Arábibus Stagyritae interpretibus nuncupari posset. Aristotelis quippe mentem longè aliam fuisse multis ostendunt Gassendus, s3 Sturmius, s4 Stephanus Pace, s5 alliique.

39 Moreover, while the Peripatetics are intent solely on maintaining that substantial forms perish and are generated, by what reasoning will they show that a new substantial form, e.g. of fire, arises while all the same things remain by which, once they are established, the same form is wont to be destroyed? The candle is the same (I use the words of the most illustrious Casati (x)), giving out flame with the same burning wick: you blow on it, the flame perishes; you blow again, the flame comes back to life: the cause of the arising and of the perishing is the same, namely the same breath, the same dispositions, the same subject, which is deprived of flame and receives flame. I pass over a great many arguments against the Peripatetic system, especially those by which Henricus Wiber vigorously assails matter and form (y). We by no means regard this system as devised by Aristotle, but call it the common Peripatetic system, which might perhaps more aptly be named Arabic, after the Arabs, the interpreters of the Stagirite. For that Aristotle’s mind was far different is shown at length by Gassendi (z), Sturm [a], Stephanus Pace (b), and others.

CAPUT VI. — CHAPTER VI

Systémata Artificiosa. Exponitur, & refutatur Atomistarum systéma.

Artificial Systems. The system of the Atomists is set forth and refuted.

40 Petrus Gassendus Vir célebris, & Philosophiae studiis mirificè commendatus, & cum eo tota Atomistarum Schola, censet unicum rerum principium esse atomos. Atomus autem juxta hos Philosophos est corpusculum inséctile, sive indivisíbile, figuratum tamen, trinèque mensurabile, extensum, solidum, & impenetrabile. Hae atomi sunt materia prima juxta ipsos. Figura in his, eaque diversissima est, ut aliquae habeant figuram cubi, sphaerae, cylindri,

ierre Gassendi, a celebrated man, wonderfully commended for his studies 40 Pin Philosophy, and with him the whole school of the Atomists, holds that the only principle of things is atoms. An atom, moreover, according to these Philosophers, is a corpuscle that cannot be cut, or indivisible, yet having figure and measurable in three dimensions, extended, solid and impenetrable. These atoms are prime matter, according to them. There is figure in them, and that most diverse, so that some have the figure of a cube, a sphere, a cylinder, a pyramid, a

De igne, Diss. 9.

Phys., bk. 7, sect. 1, ch. 3.

La Fisica de’ Peripatetici al paragone della vera Fisica d’Aristot.

p. 23

pirámidis, prismatis, &c. Phaenómena, & mutationes corporum naturalium per explicatas átomos exponunt. Hoc est antiquissimum Epicúri systema á Clariss. Gassendo renovatum. Sed plurima quae in Deum, Providentiam, Religionemque Epicúrus impiè congesserat expunxit, ceteraque uberrimè exornavit. Etenim Epicúrus posuit atomos aeternas, increatas, infinitas.

a prism, etc. They set forth the phenomena and changes of natural bodies through the atoms thus explained. This is the most ancient system of Epicurus, renewed by the most illustrious Gassendi. But he expunged the very many things which Epicurus had impiously heaped up against God, Providence and Religion, and adorned the rest most richly. For Epicurus posited atoms eternal, uncreated, infinite.

41 Verúm Gassendus, & cum eo Atomistae Recentiores, Epicúrum errasse fatentur, dum átomos ipsas increatas, per se mobiles, admisit, atque illud etiam pérditae insaniae in Epicúro fuisse demonstrat, quod mundum ex fortuito atomórum concursu génitum fore, nulloque Divinae mentis consilio, vel Providentia regi credíderit; nam ut est á Cicerone observatum: nihil tam arcànum, admirabile, divinumque est, quod non apud istos atomorum turba conficiat. 2 Etsi itaque negari non possit plurima in Atomistarum sententia felicitèr, atque utilitèr esse excogitata, Atomistarum tamen systéma, sive hypothesis universè recipienda non videtur, quùm incertum prorsús sit, an ejusmodi corpuscula dari possint, quae extensa sint, simulque indivisibilia, proindeque est contra Axiom. V.

41 But Gassendi, and with him the more recent Atomists, acknowledge that Epicurus erred when he admitted the atoms themselves as uncreated and mobile of themselves; and he shows that this too was a mark of desperate madness in Epicurus, that he believed the world to have been generated from a fortuitous concourse of atoms and to be governed by no counsel of the Divine mind, or Providence; for, as Cicero observed, there is nothing so hidden, so admirable and divine, that among these men the throng of atoms does not accomplish it (c). Although, therefore, it cannot be denied that a great many things in the opinion of the Atomists have been devised happily and usefully, yet the system, or hypothesis, of the Atomists does not seem acceptable as a whole, since it is altogether uncertain whether there can be corpuscles of this kind which are extended and at the same time indivisible; and therefore it is contrary to Axiom V.

CAPUT VII. — CHAPTER VII

Exponitur Cartesii Systéma, & refutatur.

The system of Descartes is set forth and refuted.

42 Primò ponit Cartesius s2 creatam à Deo materiam simplicem, homogeneam, trine mensurabilem, & undìque extensam. Hanc materiam divisit Deus in particulas inter se quàmproximè aequales, cubicas, ita ut contactu immediato, ac omnem vacuum excludente se omni ex parte contingerent. Pártibus sic divisis Cónditor Deus impressit vehementissimum motum duplicem, unum quo singulae portiones circa proprium centrum, alterum quo plures simul circa commune centrum moverentur. Portionibus materiae ita in girum actis Cartesius à vertendo nomen vórticum adtribuit, atque hinc, secundò docet ex agitatione illa, motuque duplici materiae adtrítis particularum ángulis, tria diversi generis provenisse elementa, quorum primum minutissimas continet partes, secundum glóbulos, in quos quadrátae particulae ablatis ángulis sunt conformatae: tertium sunt partes crassiores, & variis ángulis irregulares

irst, Descartes (d) posits a matter created by God, simple, homogeneous, 42 F measurable in three dimensions, and extended everywhere. This matter God divided into particles as nearly equal to one another as possible, cubical, so that they touched one another on every side with an immediate contact excluding all void. On the parts thus divided God the Creator impressed a most vehement twofold motion: one by which the individual portions were moved about their own center, the other by which several together were moved about a common center. To the portions of matter thus driven round in a circle Descartes gave the name of vortices, from vertendo [turning]; and hence, secondly, he teaches that from that agitation and twofold motion of matter, the angles of the particles having been worn away, three elements of different kinds arose, of which the first contains the most minute parts; the second, globules, into which the square particles were shaped once their angles were removed; the third consists of the coarser parts, irregular, with various angles.

43 Quod ut ad vivum exhibeant Cartesii Intérpretes in

43 To exhibit this to the life, the interpreters of Descartes turn their attention to the turner’s

Tusc. I. c. 2.

Tusculan Disputations I, ch. 2.

Princip. part. 3. n. 45.

Principles, pt. 3, no. 45.

p. 24

Tornatóris Officinam animum advertunt, ubi ex cubo rapidissimè circumacto globus effingitur: ut enim ex ligni cúbici adtrítu trium specierum partes adpárent, aliae nimírum minutissimae, rursús quaedam majores, sed irregulares, nec figura, nec mole similes, ac tandem ipse globus efformatur; ita primum elementum minimis illis partibus, tertium majoribus, secundum globo ipsi cómparant.

workshop, where a globe is shaped out of a cube turned round very rapidly: for just as, from the wearing of a cubic piece of wood, parts of three kinds appear — some, namely, most minute; others again larger, but irregular, alike neither in figure nor in bulk; and finally the globe itself is formed — so they compare the first element to those smallest parts, the third to the larger ones, the second to the globe itself.

44 Tertiò statuit tria haec elementa materiam esse, ex qua corpora omnia réliqua componuntur, ex primo quidem Sol, & Stellae fixae: ex secundo corpora diáphana, fluidaque omnia, ex tertio corpora opáca, ut sunt terra, aër, reliquaque corpora mixta. Tertium elementum vocant etiam materiam striatam, id est, crassiorem. Sed jam Cartesianos vortices, utpotè ad phaenomenorum explicationem ímpares, ineptosque paucis rejiciamus.

44 Thirdly, he lays down that these three elements are the matter of which all the remaining bodies are composed: from the first, indeed, the Sun and the fixed Stars; from the second, all diaphanous and fluid bodies; from the third, opaque bodies, such as earth, air, and the remaining mixed bodies. The third element they also call striated matter, that is, coarser matter. But let us now reject in a few words the Cartesian vortices, as unequal to the explanation of the phenomena, and unfit.

45 Dico igitur: Cosmogonia Cartesii (hoc est mundi efformatio á Cartesio excogitata) sive systéma vórticum locum in Physica habere nequit. Prob. etenim in hac hypothesi multa inter se parum cohaerent, atque adeò naturae phaenómena connexo ordine explicari in eo non possunt: ergo. Antec. constat. In primis namque systéma hoc in primo illo elementorum trium exortu deficit. Si enim vacuum nullum, ut vult Cartesius vel Divínitus est possíbile, quùm materia in partes cúbicas divisa fuit, earumque partium singulae, circa proprium axem, & universi centrum movebantur, cóncipi certè non potest, quomodo spatium aliquod vacuum inter ejusmodi partes, tunc non interciperetur, quod nulla scilicet subtíli materia tunc repleretur, quùm non dum haec ex angulorum adtritione prodiisset.

45 I say, therefore: the Cosmogony of Descartes (that is, the formation of the world devised by Descartes), or the system of vortices, cannot have a place in Physics. Proof: for in this hypothesis many things cohere poorly with one another, and so the phenomena of nature cannot be explained in it in a connected order: therefore. The antecedent is evident. For in the first place this system fails at that first origin of the three elements. For if no void is possible, as Descartes would have it, even by Divine power, then, when matter was divided into cubic parts and each of those parts was moving about its own axis and about the center of the universe, it certainly cannot be conceived how some empty space would not then be intercepted between parts of this kind, a space, namely, that would not then be filled by any subtle matter, since this had not yet come forth from the wearing of the angles.

46 Praeterea verò: omninò necessarium videtur, ut rapidissimo, jugique motu, & adtritu elementa haec á Cartesio excogitata suam naturam amítterent saltim post aliquot secula: ex. gr. globuli in materiam subtílem, & partes ramosae heterogenae tertii elementi in glóbulos tandem abirent. Ergo vel compensationem quandam fieri oportebat explicatu difficíllimam, & nusquam (quod víderim) á Cartesio aptis naturae legibus explicatam; vel mundi máchina corruisse post annos plus jam sex mille debuit. ¿Quid ad haec Cartesiani?

46 Moreover, it seems altogether necessary that, through so very rapid and continual a motion and wearing, these elements devised by Descartes should lose their nature, at least after some centuries: e.g., the globules would at length pass into subtle matter, and the branching heterogeneous parts of the third element into globules. Therefore either some compensation had to take place, most difficult to explain and nowhere (so far as I have seen) explained by Descartes by apt laws of nature; or the machine of the world must have collapsed after more than six thousand years by now. What do the Cartesians say to this?

ADPENDICULUS. — APPENDIX

Systéma Newtonianum leviter adtingitur.

The Newtonian system is touched upon lightly. 47

47 De Clariss. Newtoni systémate aliqua licet brevissimè exponere necessum est. A Cartesii elementis praeter alia in primigeniis corporum particulis differt, utpote quas Cartesius friábiles, Newtonus, duras ac solidas, ita ut nullis naturae viribus frangi possint adstruit. 2 Systématis Newtoniani

Of the system of the most illustrious Newton it is necessary to set forth some things, though very briefly. It differs from the elements of Descartes, besides other things, in the primordial particles of bodies, inasmuch as Descartes asserts them to be friable, Newton hard and solid, so that they cannot be broken by any forces of nature (e). Of the Newtonian system the principal head

p. 25

praecipuum caput est vis adtractrix: per hanc íntelligunt virtutem, seu principium actionis illius, quae per vires corporum ordinarias, pressionem nempè, & percussionem explicari nequeat; actio autem illa propterquam corpora accedunt, adtractio iis dicitur. Hanc universalem esse, mutuamque tùm magnorum corporum, tùm minimarum materiae particularum volunt.

head is the attractive force: by this they understand the virtue, or principle, of that action which cannot be explained by the ordinary forces of bodies, namely pressure and impulse; and the action itself by which bodies approach one another is called by them attraction. This they hold to be universal and mutual, both of great bodies and of the smallest particles of matter.

48 Nonnulli Philosophi, Galli praesertim dicunt, quod quamvis Newtoni systema vagas, incertasque hypótheses ex Philosophia exturbatas velit [§ 20]: Newtonianorum tamen aliqui nihil minus praestant, vim adtractricem recipiendo Neque enim sciunt vim hujusmodi esse causam effectum, nec ope illius phaenomenorum rationem reddere possunt. Et ad primum quod adtinet Clariss. ipse Newtonus s1: quam ego, inquit, attractionem appello, fieri sanè potest ut ea[?] efficiatur impulsu, vel alio aliquo modo nobis ignoto. Hanc vocem attractionis ita hic áccipi velim, ut in universum solummodo vim aliquam significare intelligatur, qua corpora ad se mutuo tendant, cuicunque demum causae attribuenda sit illa vis.

48 Some philosophers, the French especially, say that although Newton’s system would have vague and uncertain hypotheses driven out of Philosophy [§ 20], some of the Newtonians nevertheless do no less themselves, by admitting an attractive force. For they do not know whether a force of this kind is a cause or an effect, nor can they by its help give the reason of the phenomena. And as regards the first, the most illustrious Newton himself (f): “What I call Attraction may be perform’d by impulse, or by some other means unknown to me. I use that Word here to signify only in general any Force by which Bodies tend towards one another, whatsoever be the Cause.”

49 Et álibi s2 ita loquitur: voces autem attractionis, impúlsus, vel propensionis cujuscunque in centrum indifferenter, & pro se mutuo promiscuè usurpo; has vires non physicè, sed mathematicè tantum considerando. Unde caveat Lector, ne per hujusmodi vires cógitet, me speciem, vel modum actionis, causamve, aut rationem physicam alicubi definire, vel centris, quae sunt puncta mathematica, vires verè, & physicè tribuere, si fortè aut centra trahere, aut vires centrorum esse dixero. Ut ea propter dixerit Nolletus s3: adtractionem, ubi è Newtoni manibus ad Sectatores transmissa est, simplicitate sua magnoperè fuisse expoliatam.

49 And elsewhere (g) he speaks thus: “I use the words attraction, impulse, or propensity of whatever kind toward a center indifferently and promiscuously for one another, considering these forces not physically but only mathematically. Hence let the Reader beware of thinking that by words of this kind I anywhere define the species or mode of action, or the physical cause or reason, or that I attribute forces truly and physically to centers, which are mathematical points, if perchance I should say that centers attract, or that there are forces of centers.” So that for this reason Nollet (h) said that attraction, once it passed from the hands of Newton to his followers, was greatly despoiled of its simplicity.

50 Et ad secundum quod spectat, videlicet adtractionis ope phaenomenorum rationem reddi haud posse plurimis nititur osténdere D. Pluche s4. Explicent, inquit, adtractionis ope; ¿eccur ingens moles aedificii cujusdam, quae comparatè ad plumam vi adtractrice penè infinita pollet, volitantem in aëre plúmulam ad sese non adducit? aut ¿cur lapis ponè turrim décidens potius à tellúre adtrahatur, quam à turri, quae vicinior est? Licet enim, (ut inquiunt Newtoniani) adtractionem quamvis aliam immensum quantum excedat vis adtractrix telluris, ¿quis tamen abnuat, si virtuti hujus augmentum adjiciatur, ipsam majori nisu acturam? Addatur ergò viribus adtrahentibus telluris vis adtractrix montis praerupti tanquam partis globo terraqüeo adnexae. ¿Ecquid causae fuerit, quod summa haec virium adtrahentium non accéleret motum lapidis juxta montem decidui, eumque non promoveat

50 And as regards the second, namely that by the help of attraction the reason of the phenomena cannot be given, M. Pluche (i) strives to show it by very many arguments. Let them explain, he says, by the help of attraction: why does the huge mass of some building, which compared with a feather possesses an almost infinite attractive force, not draw to itself a little feather fluttering in the air? or why is a stone falling beside a tower attracted by the earth rather than by the tower, which is nearer? For although (as the Newtonians say) the attractive force of the earth exceeds any other attraction by an immense amount, who will deny that, if an increase is added to this virtue, it will act with a greater effort? Let there be added, then, to the attracting forces of the earth the attractive force of a steep mountain, as of a part joined to the terraqueous globe. What cause could there be why this sum of attracting forces does not accelerate the motion of a stone falling beside the mountain, and does not drive it on faster

velocius, quam si eadem ex altitudine in plano aliquo nullis móntibus áspero delabatur?

than if it fell from the same height on some plain not rough with any mountains?

51 Nec refert vim adtractrícem montis, comparatè ad alteram telluris haud esse sensibilem, ut enim demus insensibilem illam haberi, si cum hac conferatur, ¿an tamen talis censenda, si relatè ad corpus in aëre péndulum, à cacúmine, atque adeo à parte globi terraquei haud remotum, si junctim cum tellure in eumdem motum deorsum conspírans spectétur? Deinde: si tellus ímpedit adtractionem aliam omnem, ¿qui fieri potest ut in harum virium praesentia aestuans mare â Luna adtrahatur? quùm tamen, & aquae telluri sint viciniores, quam etiam ceu pars terraquei componunt, & moles globi hujus, lunarem exsúperet? Sed dicta sufficiant, ut systema adtractionis Newtonianum summis, ut ajunt, labris degustétis. Neque enim mens fuit, (quod impossibile esset) paucis pagellis illud in universum expéndere: mysterium nempè est impervium iis, qui sublimiori mathési initiati haud sunt. Newtonii systéma jure, meritòque defendunt plurimi Clariss. gravissimique Philosophi, quos consúlere debetis, si bonae Philosophiae amatores estis.

51 Nor does it matter that the attractive force of the mountain is not sensible in comparison with the other force, that of the earth; for, granting that it is held insensible when compared with that, is it nevertheless to be reckoned such if it is regarded relative to a body hanging in the air from the summit, and hence not far from a part of the terraqueous globe; if it is regarded as conspiring jointly with the earth in the same downward motion? Then: if the earth impedes every other attraction, how can it happen that, in the presence of these forces, the surging sea is attracted by the Moon? when yet the waters are both nearer to the earth, and also compose it as a part of the terraqueous globe, and the mass of this globe exceeds that of the Moon. But let what has been said suffice for you to have tasted the Newtonian system of attraction, as they say, with the tips of your lips. For it was not my intention (which would be impossible) to weigh it in its entirety in a few little pages: it is indeed a mystery impenetrable to those who are not initiated in the higher mathematics. The system of Newton is defended rightly and deservedly by very many most illustrious and most weighty philosophers, whom you ought to consult if you are lovers of good Philosophy.

CAPUT VIII. — CHAPTER VIII

Systémata Physica elementria, seu sensibilia, & Chymicum systéma.

The elementary, or sensible, physical systems, and the chemical system.

52 Elementarii, Veteres quidam fuere, qui unum duntaxat elementum, dixerunt esse primum rerum naturalium principium. Ex his Thales Milesius aquam, sive humidum rerum principium esse censuit 2. Xenóphanes terram s2. Anaxímenes, aërem s3. Heraclitus, ignem s4. Alii duo statuerunt elementa. Inter Recentiores Elérus Academiae Berolinensis Sodális, aquam pro principio passivo ex quo aër, & terra fiant, ignem pro activo habet s5. Praecipuum systéma Elementariorum cóndidit Empédocles. Is pro materia prima quatuor elementa vulgaria adsumpsit, terram, nimirum, aquam,

52 There were some of the Ancients, called Elementarians, who said that one element only was the first principle of natural things. Of these Thales of Miletus held water, or the moist, to be the principle of things (j); Xenophanes, earth (k); Anaximenes, air (l); Heraclitus, fire (m). Others laid down two elements. Among the Moderns, Eller, Fellow of the Berlin Academy, holds water as the passive principle, from which air and earth come to be, and fire as the active (n). The principal system of the Elementarians was founded by Empedocles. He took as prime matter the four common elements, namely earth, water, air, and

Histoire du Ciel. Tom. 2. Cosmogon. §. 9.

Histoire du Ciel, vol. 2, Cosmogon., §. 9.

p. 27

aërem, & ignem, pro forma verò eorum combinationem 2. Alii aliter opinabantur: nihil enim, (ut ait Cicero) tam absurdum excogitari potest, quod non sit dictum ab aliquo Philosophorum.

and fire, but as their form, their combination [o]. Others held otherwise: for nothing (as Cicero says) can be thought up so absurd that it has not been said by some one of the philosophers.

53 Chymia, quae â Recentioribus etiam Chemia vocatur, id est ars resolvendi corpora, ab Hérmete dicitur inventa, ac propterea Hermética quoque dicitur. Eam non solum in ordine ad parandas medicínas, sed etiam ad explicanda rerum naturalium principia Theophrastus Paracelsus Pater Chymicorum dictus plurimùm inlustravit, Chymici itaque Spargyrici, aut Empirici sunt, qui in corporum analysi occupantur, nec aliud arte sua, & operationibus inquírunt, nisi ut conjuncta, & colligata in corporibus mixtis principia evolvant, evolúta sensibus ipsis subjiciant. Objectum artis hujus est corpus omne sensibile, dividitúrque in tres classes, seu regna, vel familias, ut ipsi loquuntur, nempè animale, vegetabile, & minerale. Quae autem ex his ope potissimum ignis, & per menstrua, seu dissolventia eliciunt, ea illis corporum principia sunt juxta axioma ipsorum: quod ex iis partibus quodlibet constituatur, in quas resolvitur. Principia eorum quinque numerantur videlicet, Mercurius, Sulphur, Sal, Aqua, & Terra. Priora tria, activa dicuntur, duo postrema, passiva.

53 Chymia, which by the Moderns is also called Chemia, that is, the art of resolving bodies, is said to have been invented by Hermes, and is therefore also called Hermetic. It was greatly illustrated, not only with a view to preparing medicines but also to explaining the principles of natural things, by Theophrastus Paracelsus, called the Father of the Chemists. The chemists, then, are the Spagyrists, or Empirics, who are occupied with the analysis of bodies and seek nothing else by their art and operations than to unfold the principles joined and bound together in mixed bodies and, once unfolded, to subject them to the senses themselves. The object of this art is every sensible body, and it is divided into three classes, or kingdoms, or families, as they themselves speak, namely the animal, the vegetable and the mineral. And what they draw out of these, chiefly by the help of fire and through menstrua, or dissolvents, those are for them the principles of bodies, according to their axiom: that anything is constituted of those parts into which it is resolved. Their principles are numbered five, namely Mercury, Sulphur, Salt, Water and Earth. The first three are called active, the last two passive.

54 Mercurius, sive spiritus est liqüor subtílis, penetrans, & volátilis, qui primus è corporibus adplicato igne exire solet, â quo etiam pro majore, vel minore dosi incrementum corporum, & corruptio pendet; & â quo mixtorum omnium motus immediatè proveniunt. Unde patet, mercurium Chymicorum longè aliam esse substantiam, quam sit argentum vivum, quod alias etiam mercurius, dicitur. Sulphur vocant substantiam quamdam pinguem, oleaginósam, per quam habent mixta, quae ea abundant, ut flammam concipiant. Sal est substantia sápida, [quia est sapórum origo], quae per aquam dilui, & igne liqüefieri potest. Dividitur in fixum, & volátilem, ácidum, & álkali; prior igne non ávolat, licet dissolvatur, & fundatur, alter calore ávolat, & dissipatur. Dicitur ácidum, quod linguae impositum eam certo quodam acrimoniae sensu omnibus noto adficit, ac véllicat. Alkali, quod rarioris texturae est, saporisque véluti urentis, multisque meatibus interruptum, unde si cum acido misceatur magnam ebullitionem efficit. Alkálicum idcirco vocatur illud omne corpus, quod miscéri cum ácido haud potest, quin magnam effervescentiam éxcitet.

54 Mercury, or spirit, is a subtle, penetrating and volatile liquor, which usually comes out of bodies first when fire is applied; on which, according to its greater or lesser dose, the growth and corruption of bodies depend; and from which the motions of all mixed bodies immediately proceed. Hence it is plain that the mercury of the chemists is a substance far different from quicksilver, which is otherwise also called mercury. Sulphur they call a certain fat, oily substance, through which mixed bodies that abound in it are able to catch flame. Salt is a savory substance [because it is the origin of savors], which can be diluted by water and liquefied by fire. It is divided into fixed and volatile, acid and alkali: the former does not fly off in the fire, though it is dissolved and melted; the latter flies off and is dissipated by heat. It is called acid because, placed on the tongue, it affects and twitches it with a certain sense of sharpness known to all. Alkali is that which is of a looser texture and of a taste as it were burning, and broken up by many passages; whence, if it is mixed with an acid, it produces a great ebullition. Therefore every body is called alkaline which cannot be mixed with an acid without exciting a great effervescence.

55 Aqua, quae etiam phlegma â Chymicis vocatur, est substantia fluida, maximè humida, inodóra insípida. Terra demum damnata, quae, & caput mortuum dicitur, non admodum curae est Chymicis, qui eam fere negligunt, estque substantia árida, fixa, insípida, sólida, ac pulvérea, quae post extractos liqüores dictos, & salia fixa rémanet. Haec sunt quinque Chymicorum elementa, quae

55 Water, which is also called phlegm by the chemists, is a fluid substance, extremely moist, odorless, insipid. Earth, lastly, the damned earth, which is also called caput mortuum, is not much the concern of the chemists, who almost neglect it; it is a dry, fixed, insipid, solid and powdery substance, which remains after the said liquors and the fixed salts have been extracted. These are the five elements of the chemists, which

ab ipsis tanquam principia corporum admittuntur. Hic óbitèr animadverto, negligendas minimè esse, neque verò floccifaciendas Chymicorum operationes. Quid verò de Elementariorum, & Chymicorum systémate statuendum sit, postea vidébimus.

are admitted by them as the principles of bodies. Here I note in passing that the operations of the chemists are by no means to be neglected, nor indeed to be held of no account. For it must be confessed, as Du Hamel says [p], that Physics has taken great increases from the labors and experiments of the chemists. Hence many arts very useful for life have flowed. What is to be determined about the system of the Elementarians and of the chemists we shall see later.

CAPUT IX. — CHAPTER IX

Expónitur nostra de principiis corporum internis doctrína.

Our doctrine on the internal principles of bodies is set forth. 56

56 Dico primo. Physica materiae natura in eo sita videtur, quod sit substantia impenetrabiliter extensa, constans partibus primigeniis exilissimis, iisdemque quoad substantiam homogeneis, quoad molem, figuram, motum, similesque adfectiones inaequalibus, ac diversis. Prob. per partes. In eo posita est physica natura materiae corporum naturalium, per quod habet, ut possit tanquam primum subjectum accedente forma compositum naturale constituere, & quod cognoscitur habere, tum ratione, tum quoad liceat sensuum experientia; sed hoc ipso quod materia sit substantia impenetrabiliter extensa habet, & habere intelligitur, quidquid requiritur, ut possit tanquam primum subjectum accedente forma compositum naturale constituere; ergo. Minor patet: hoc etenim constituto capax est motus, & quietis [?], variae dispositionis, compositionis, textúrae & aliarum ejusmodi adfectionum; ex quo resultat, ut deinceps patebit, forma substantialis cum qua compositum naturale constituit.

I say, first: The physical nature of matter seems to consist in this, that it is a substance impenetrably extended, consisting of primordial parts that are most minute, and these homogeneous as regards substance, but unequal and diverse as regards bulk, figure, motion and like affections. Proof, by parts. The physical nature of the matter of natural bodies is placed in that by which it has the capacity, as first subject, with a form supervening, to constitute a natural composite, and which it is known to have both by reason and, so far as is permitted, by the experience of the senses; but by this very fact, that matter is a substance impenetrably extended, it has, and is understood to have, whatever is required for it to be able, as first subject, with a form supervening, to constitute a natural composite: therefore. The minor is plain: for, this being established, it is capable of motion and rest, of varied disposition, composition, texture, and other affections of this kind; from which results, as will be plain hereafter, the substantial form with which it constitutes the natural composite.

57 Secunda pars propositionis constat: nam quoniam materia in compositione corporum esse intelligitur quiddam primum, uti est de ratione principii primi, idcirco primigeniis constare particulis rectè adfirmatur. Has particulas exilissimas esse stupenda corporum divisibilitas posthac perpendenda ad evidentiam commostrat: nunc verò in hujus rei confirmationem duo tantummodo experimenta adhibeamus.

57 The second part of the proposition is evident: for since matter in the composition of bodies is understood to be something first, as belongs to the notion of a first principle, it is therefore rightly asserted to consist of primordial particles. That these particles are most minute the stupendous divisibility of bodies, to be weighed hereafter, demonstrates to evidence; but now, in confirmation of this matter, we shall employ only two experiments.

58 Observat Clariss. Boyle 2, unum granum 2 cupri in

58 The most illustrious Boyle observes [q] that one grain [] of copper, dissolved in spirit

Tract. 1. Phys. Gen. Diss. 3. c. 5.

[p] Tract. 1, General Physics, Diss. 3, ch. 5.

p. 29

spiritu salis ammoniaci dissolutum, tantam aquae copiam caerúleo colore, & quidem conspicuo, saturoque imbuisse, ut partes 256806. illi gránulo aequales comprehenderet. Doctiss. P. Franciscus de Lanis testatur 4 gumma lacca quae juglandis córtici implendo sufficiat, eam aquae copiam intenso colore tingi, quae satis est ad mille folia papyrácea ex utraque parte, eodem colore imbuenda. Cùm ergò in quolibet folio mille milliones punctorum coloratorum commodè designari possint, erunt in illis omnibus foliis 1,000,000,000,000 puncta visibilia colorata, ac inter se distincta. Haec certè probant exlissimas esse partes materiae. Deinde partes has minimas magnitudine sua inaequales, figura, motu, diversas esse ex eo manifestum fit, quod inaequalitas haec ac divérsitas exilissimarum partium adstrui debeat, ut sensibiles cujusvis naturalis corporis qualitates, & operationes rectè, & commodè explicentur.

spirit of sal ammoniac, imbued so great a quantity of water with a blue color, and that a conspicuous and saturated one, that it contained 256806 parts equal to that little grain. The most learned Fr. Francesco Lana testifies [r] that as much gum lac as would suffice to fill a walnut shell tinges with an intense color such a quantity of water as is enough to imbue a thousand paper leaves on both sides with the same color. Since, then, on any one leaf a thousand millions of colored points can conveniently be marked, there will be on all those leaves 1,000,000,000,000 visible colored points, distinct from one another. These things certainly prove that the parts of matter are most minute. Next, that these smallest parts are unequal in their magnitude, and diverse in figure and motion, is manifest from this, that this inequality and diversity of the most minute parts must be asserted in order that the sensible qualities and operations of any natural body may be rightly and conveniently explained.

59 Hae demum exilissimae corporum partes homogeneae utique esse possunt, nec quoad substantiam diversae, quùm minimè requiratur, quod sint substantialiter diversae, ut ex illarum unione emergant corpora, quorum sensibiles qualitates diversae sint inter se, & operationes planè dissímiles. Possunt autem ex primigeniis illis partibus materiae fieri composita, quorum sensibiles qualitates, atque operationes planè diversae sint inter se, quamvis ipsae partes quoad substantiam minimè inter se differant: nam quùm sint inaequalis magnitudinis, & diversae figurae, possunt diversa ratione artificiosè disponi inter se, possunt denique earum aliquae secundum diversas directiones moveri in toto, quod constituunt, & aliae in illo quiescere, quod planè sufficit, ut ex illis componi queant corpora, quae dissimilibus qualitatibus praedita sint: ergo partes illae, homogeneae esse utique possunt.

59 These most minute parts of bodies, finally, can certainly be homogeneous, and not diverse as regards substance, since it is by no means required that they be substantially diverse in order that from their union bodies may emerge whose sensible qualities are diverse from one another, and whose operations are quite dissimilar. For composites can be made from those primordial parts of matter whose sensible qualities and operations are quite diverse from one another, although the parts themselves differ not at all from one another as regards substance: for since they are of unequal magnitude and diverse figure, they can be artfully disposed among themselves in diverse ways; finally, some of them can be moved in diverse directions within the whole that they constitute, and others be at rest in it, which quite suffices for bodies endowed with dissimilar qualities to be capable of being composed of them: therefore those parts can certainly be homogeneous.

60 Dico secundo: Forma essentialis, seu substantialis corporum naturalium vitae expertium, si physicé spectetur nihil diversum est â dispositione illa, convenientia & proportione illarum particularum ex quibus ipsa corpora intrinsecùs, & quoad essentiam componuntur. Prob: posita certâ dispositione, proportione, &c. partium materiae, & omni alio sublato, quamoptimé intelligitur ens corporeum, seu compositum substantiale ab aliis specifice distinctum; sed per formam substantialem nihil aliud intelligitur, quam ratio illa, quâ hoc compositum est actu tale ab aliis specificè diversum, & ratione cujus hos habet speciales effectus, & proprietates: ergo. Prob. maj. exemplo plantae: praecisè positâ in materiae particulis certâ dispositione, organisatione, &c. optimè habetur ratio, qua succus alimentitius exugatur, distribuatur, &c. & cur tale corpus végetans sit planta, non vero lapis &c. quin opus unquam sit ad aliquid aliud recúrrere, ut explicentur haec phaenómena, haec adtributa plantae: ergo.

60 I say, second: The essential, or substantial, form of natural bodies devoid of life, if it is regarded physically, is nothing different from that disposition, congruence and proportion of the particles of which the bodies themselves are composed intrinsically and as to their essence. Proof: given a certain disposition, proportion, etc., of the parts of matter, and everything else taken away, a corporeal being, or a substantial composite specifically distinct from others, is understood perfectly well: but by substantial form nothing else is understood than that ground by which this composite is actually such, specifically different from others, and by reason of which it has these special effects and properties: therefore. The major is proved by the example of a plant: given precisely a certain disposition, organization, etc., in the particles of matter, an excellent account is had of how the nutritive sap is sucked up, distributed, etc., and why such a vegetating body is a plant and not a stone, etc., without there ever being need to recur to anything else in order to explain these phenomena, these attributes of the plant: therefore.

De mira subtilitat. effluvior. cap. 3.

[q] De mira subtilitate effluviorum, ch. 3.

Uncia continet. 480 grana.

Magist. Nat. & Art. Tom. 1. tract. 1. cap. 1. Obs. 3.
