creatum, sed hoc non est dicendum: ergo. Conseq. prob.; nam agens creatum, non producit de novo materiam, quum illam praesupponat, nec formam quae non generatur, nec producitur: ergo nihil producit. Respondeo agentia creata, nec materiam, nec formam producere, sed tantum compositum: creaturae enim, ut optimè ait S. Bonaventura 2 solum faciunt, ut quod erat uno modo, sit alio modo.

but this must not be said: therefore. Proof of the conseq.: for a created agent does not produce matter anew, since it presupposes it; nor the form, which is neither generated nor produced: therefore it produces nothing. I reply that created agents produce neither matter nor form, but only the composite: for creatures, as St. Bonaventure excellently says (z), only bring it about that what was in one mode comes to be in another mode.

107 Opp. 8. Singula entia naturalia vitae expertia habent suas peculiares operationes ex. gr. in igne reperitur particularis operatio calefaciendi, & sic de aliis; sed hujusmodi operationes nequeunt oriri â materia, quae ex se iners est, nullamque habet vim operatricem, eademque est specie in omnibus compositis naturalibus: ergo proveniunt ab uniuscujusque speciali forma: ergo haec est aliquid entitativè â materia distinctum. Dist. min. praedictae operationes nequeunt oriri â materia secundum se spectata, conc. â materia, ut modificata, nego, & conseq.

107 Obj. 8. Each natural being devoid of life has its own peculiar operations; e.g., in fire is found a particular operation of heating, and so of the rest; but operations of this kind cannot arise from matter, which of itself is inert and has no operative force, and is the same in species in all natural composites: therefore they proceed from the special form of each: therefore this is something entitatively distinct from matter. Dist. min.: the aforesaid operations cannot arise from matter considered in itself, I grant; from matter as modified, I deny; and the conseq.

108 Opp. tandem: nostra opinione posita, nullum datur discrimen inter alterationem, & generationem; sed datur, nam in alteratione, qualitates tantum producuntur, in generatione forma substantialis debet produci: ergo forma substantialis est semisubstantia á materia distincta, ut ex Arabum sententia contra doctrinam Aristotelis propugnant Peripatetici. Resp. neg. maj.: in alteratione enim, idem manet corpus sensibile, quod antea fuit, quum pauca tantum ex eo pereant accidentia, pauca recens adveniant, ut quum aqua ex cálida fit frigida, vel quum cera ex flava, fit candida, aut ex moli dura. At verò in generatione, aut omnia pereunt accidentia, aut si nonnulla supersint, ea non sufficiunt, ut corpus sensibile, dici possit idem: ex. gr. quum cera in fumum soluta est, corpus idem adpelari nequit, tametsi quaedam fortassè accidentia, quae prius erant in cera, ex. gr. odor in fumo remaneat, quia pauca haec accidentia ad ceram constituendam non sufficiunt.

108 Obj. finally: once our opinion is posited, there is no difference between alteration and generation; but there is one, for in alteration only qualities are produced, in generation a substantial form must be produced: therefore the substantial form is a semi-substance distinct from matter, as the Peripatetics maintain, following the opinion of the Arabs, against the doctrine of Aristotle. Reply: I deny the maj.: for in alteration the same sensible body remains which was there before, since only a few accidents perish from it and a few newly arrive, as when water from hot becomes cold, or when wax from yellow becomes white, or from soft hard. But in generation either all the accidents perish, or, if some remain, they are not enough for the sensible body to be called the same: e.g., when wax has been dissolved into smoke, it cannot be called the same body, although perhaps certain accidents which were before in the wax, e.g. the odor, remain in the smoke, because these few accidents are not enough to constitute wax.

109 Inst. Si res ita se habet, generatio, & alteratio non distinguuntur nisi secundum magis, & minus; sed magis & minus non mutant speciem, ut vulgari Scholarum fertur axiomate: diversae autem formae, diversas species constituunt: ergo forma substantialis corporis vitae expertis non est artificiosa partium dispositio. Dist. min: magis, & minus non mutant speciem, ubi pauca duntaxat pereunt accidentia, conc., ubi omnia, aut fere omnia intereunt, nego Quum autem nova datur forma, omnia ferè quae priori subjecto inerant accidentia destruuntur, & nova succedunt, ut quum ex ligno fit ignis, ex cera, fumus &c. Unde nova tunc species resultat, nam fumus diversae speciei est â cera, & ignis â ligno, ea enim inter se specie censentur differre, in quibus adparet tanta

109 Inst. If the matter stands so, generation and alteration are not distinguished except according to more and less; but more and less do not change the species, as the common axiom of the Schools has it: whereas diverse forms constitute diverse species: therefore the substantial form of a body devoid of life is not an artificial disposition of the parts. Dist. min.: more and less do not change the species where only a few accidents perish, I grant; where all or nearly all perish, I deny. But when a new form is given, nearly all the accidents which were in the former subject are destroyed, and new ones succeed, as when from wood comes fire, from wax smoke, etc. Hence a new species then results; for smoke is of a different species from wax, and fire from wood; for those things are judged to differ among themselves in species in which there appears so great a diversity

In 2. Dist. 18. art. 4. q. 1.

On 2, Dist. 18, art. 4, q. 1.

p. 45

diversitas, ut quod de uno essentialiter probatum est, id alteri convenire non debeat. Haec dicta sufficiant.

that what has been proved essentially of the one need not belong to the other. Let these things that have been said suffice.

CAPUT XI. — CHAPTER XI

De Principiis secundariis, seu Sensibilibus.

On the Secondary, or Sensible, Principles.

110 Antequam sententiam nostram proponamus, adfirmare juvat: tria ê vulgaribus elementis ignem, aquam, & terram, nihil diversum videri â totidem Chymicorum principiis, mercurio, scilicet, phlegmate, ac capite mortuo. Et ad mercurium, quod adtinet Willis, 2 Sennertus 2, Boerhaavius s3, & Lemery s4 compluresque alii asserunt mercurium Chymicorum illud esse principium, quod ignis elementaris, seu substantia quaedam subtilissima & ab aere, & â flamma, igneque vulgari prorsus diversa: aquam vero â phlegmate terram â capite mortuo non discriminari, laudati supra Auctores cum aliis ostendunt. His positis sit conclusio.

efore we propose our opinion, it is useful to affirm that three of the com110 B mon elements, fire, water and earth, seem nothing different from as many principles of the Chemists, namely mercury, phlegm and caput mortuum. And as regards mercury, Willis (a), Sennert (b), Boerhaave (c), Lémery (d) and many others assert that the mercury of the Chemists is that principle which is elemental fire, or a certain most subtle substance, wholly different from air, and from flame and common fire; but that water is not discriminated from phlegm, nor earth from caput mortuum, the Authors praised above show, with others. This laid down, let the conclusion be:

111 Sensibilia corporum principia praeter vulgaria quatuor Elementa, Chymicorum quoque gemina, sal, & sulphur rectè constituuntur. Prob. ex eo, quod resolutionis ope élici queant memorata principia ê singulis corporibus, quod quidem de vegetabilibus, & animalibus nemo in controversiam vocaverit, qui multiplices Chymicorum operationes, & diversa partium per eas solutarum conditionem spectaverit. Obvia certè experientia in ligni virentis combustione, id ipsum declarat, spirituosae enim, maximèque ágiles particulae vinculis velut exsolutae in flammam concitantur, & â ceteris avulsae ávolant penitùs: sulphureae, sive oleosae flammam alunt, sensímque sublevantur in fúliginis partem concrescentes: salinae, partim in fumum abeunt, oculos acriter pungentes, partim in cineribus résident; aquosae, principio statim gemmarum instar exilissimarum erumpunt in vaporem dissipandae; terra demùm salibus eductis superstes manet.

111 The sensible principles of bodies, besides the four common Elements, are rightly held to be also the twin principles of the Chemists, salt and sulphur. Proof: from the fact that the said principles can be drawn out of individual bodies by means of resolution; which indeed, as regards vegetables and animals, no one will call into controversy who has observed the manifold operations of the Chemists and the diverse condition of the parts dissolved by them. An obvious experience in the burning of green wood declares this very thing: for the spirituous and most agile particles, released as it were from their bonds, are roused into flame and, torn away from the rest, fly off entirely; the sulphurous, or oily, ones feed the flame, and are gradually raised up, concreting into the part of soot; the saline ones partly go off into smoke, sharply stinging the eyes, partly settle in the ashes; the watery ones burst forth at the very beginning like the tiniest buds, to be dispersed into vapor; earth, finally, remains as survivor once the salts have been drawn out.

112 Hoc ipsum de regno minerali, exemplo ferri demonstrari potest. Cl. Boerhaave s5 loquens de ferro in vino Rhenano soluto hoc, inquit, summum remedium mihi hactenus cognitum in

112 This very thing can be demonstrated of the mineral kingdom by the example of iron. The celebrated Boerhaave (e), speaking of iron dissolved in Rhenish wine, says: this is the highest remedy known to me so far in the art and

De Ferment. cap. 2.

De Fermentatione, ch. 2.

Opp. cap. 11.

Works, ch. 11.

Elem. Chem. Tom. 1.

Elementa Chemiae, vol. 1.

In Chem.

In the Chemistry.

p. 46

arte, & natura ad instaurandam vim haematopoieticam [?] (vis nempè convertendi chylum in sanguinem) corpori humano, quoties haec sola ex debilitate nimis laxorum solidorum, & humorum minus levi, aquosa, frigida, inerti, indole exoritur. Addit medicatam metallorum potestatem hoc potissimum experimento demonstrari; neque enim ulla rei vegetabilis, animalis ve virtute, nulla victus regula, id quis efficiet in casu dicto, quod hoc marte conficitur.

and in nature for restoring the haematopoietic force (namely the force of converting chyle into blood) to the human body, whenever this arises solely from the weakness of over-lax solids, and from a not very light, watery, cold and inert character of the humors. He adds that the medicinal power of metals is demonstrated chiefly by this experiment: for by no virtue of anything vegetable or animal, by no rule of diet, will anyone bring about in the said case what is accomplished by this Mars.

113 Quae profectò indicant in ferro peculiares quasdam dótes, actuosam, subtilem unà substantiam residere, cui spiritus rectoris nuncupationem tribuunt Chymici, quamque nos, consentaneae ad superiora dicta, elementare ignis fluidum ceteris principiis, certa ratione, quantitate, plexu ferrum constituentibus illigatum, putamus: saltem metallo huic tale principium inesse eadem solutio manifestat atque hinc aquam pariter, ut, quam salium genera omnia evaporant, legitima ratiocinatione comprehendi deducimus. Sulphur ex odore incalescentis per tunsionem ferri percipitur: ê terra demum coagmentari, & durities ipsa, & vitriolum in ferro contentum, quod ipsum ê terreis moleculis conflatum est, ostendunt.

113 These things surely indicate that there reside in iron certain peculiar endowments, an active and at the same time subtle substance, to which the Chemists give the name of spiritus rector, and which we, consistently with what was said above, think to be the elemental fluid of fire, bound up in a certain ratio, quantity and texture with the other principles constituting iron: at least the same solution shows that such a principle is present in this metal; and hence we deduce by legitimate reasoning that water likewise is comprised in it, as being what all kinds of salts give off in evaporation. Sulphur is perceived from the odor of iron growing hot under pounding: finally, both its very hardness and the vitriol contained in iron, which is itself made up of earthy molecules, show that it is compacted of earth.

114 Aërem demùm sensibile principium corporum esse, facilè suadebitur, si compertum habeatur, aëri ea competere, quae ad rationem elementi corporum mixtorum exposcuntur. Etenim in omni penè compositorum análysi, ceteras inter aëreae sese particulae produnt: vix ullus est humor, ait Boerhaavius, cujus non immisceat se aër partibus, vix solidum, unde aliqua arte educi nequeat, quibus constitutis deducimus, sensibilia rerum corporearum principia rectè haberi, mercurium quem ab igne, seu subtilissimo fluido non secérnimus, aërem deindè, salem, sulphur, aquam, & terram.

114 Finally, it will easily be shown convincingly that air is a sensible principle of bodies, if it be ascertained that those things belong to air which are required for the character of an element of mixed bodies. For in almost every analysis of composites, among the rest, aerial particles betray themselves: there is scarcely any humor, says Boerhaave, with whose parts air does not mingle itself, scarcely any solid from which it cannot be drawn out by some art; these things being established, we deduce that the sensible principles of corporeal things are rightly held to be mercury, which we do not distinguish from fire, or the most subtle fluid; then air, salt, sulphur, water and earth.

Solvuntur argumenta.

The arguments are answered.

115 Opp. 1. Elementa Chymicorum non reperiuntur in mixtis ea forma, qua ipsi nobis expónunt: ergo non debent esse principia sensibilia corporum. Antecedens probatur, nam ignis actione sua efficit, ut corporis partes alia forma, statuque post resolutionem sese exhibeant, ac fuerint in mixto; ac proinde veluti novae substantiae ab igne productae censéri debent: ergo. Resp. negando antec. probationis: Nam ut suo loco dicemus tota caloris natura, in corpusculis céleri, perturbato, & expansivo motu adfectis posita est; nihilque aliud, nisi expansio primùm, tùm perturbata partium agitatio in corpore, quum calorem concipit efficitur. Evidens est autèm, ope motus perturbati, & expansivi exilium corpusculorum, quae naturalis compositi poros subeunt nullam novam substantiam, entitativè posse produci, sed texturam tantùm laxari, & nexum solvi, quo componentes ipsius compositi particulae simul unitae detinentur, ac proinde, naturalis

115 Obj. 1. The Elements of the Chemists are not found in mixed bodies in the form in which they themselves set them out to us: therefore they ought not to be sensible principles of bodies. The antecedent is proved: for fire by its action brings it about that the parts of a body show themselves after the resolution in another form and state than they were in the mixture; and therefore they must be considered as new substances, as it were, produced by fire: therefore. Reply by denying the antec. of the proof: for, as we shall say in its place, the whole nature of heat consists in a swift, disturbed and expansive motion impressed on corpuscles; and nothing else is effected but, first, an expansion, then a disturbed agitation of the parts in the body, when it conceives heat. Moreover it is evident that by means of the disturbed and expansive motion of the corpuscles which enter the pores of a natural composite no new substance can be entitatively produced, but only that the texture is loosened and the bond dissolved by which the component particles of the composite itself are held united together; and therefore the destruction of a natural composite,

Elem. Chem. Tom. 2. p. 445.

Elementa Chemiae, vol. 2, p. 445.

p. 47

compositi destructio, quae ignis, sive caloris actione per se efficitur consistit, non in productione alicujus novae substantiae, sed tantùm in solutione nexus, quo componentes partes colligatae sunt inter se.

which is effected per se by the action of fire, or heat, consists not in the production of some new substance, but only in the dissolution of the bond by which the component parts are tied together.

116 Dixi: ignem, sive calorem non aliud efficere per se quum naturale compositum destruit, nisi partes componentes dissolvere. Non inficior enim haud raro contingere, ut nova aliqua substantia, quae in composito non fuerat, caloris actione producatur. Verùm id omnino per accidens est, fit namque nova substantia, si calor sit vehementior quàm solutio partium requírat. Particulae siquidem â nimio calore ultra modum agitatae, miscentur adeò inter se quae diversi sunt generis, ut novae concretiones inde emergant, ac proinde ut novae substantiae hinc produci videantur, sed hoc non officit quominus substantiae praedictae in mixtis reperiantur, etenim ex corporibus ejusdem speciei, sal, sulphur, & mercurius ejusdem itidem rationis perpetuò extrahuntur, quod profectò tanta constantia non fieret, si illae substantiae â calore entitativè producerentur; contingit siquidem raro, quod fortuitò efficitur.

116 I said that fire, or heat, effects nothing else per se, when it destroys a natural composite, than to dissolve the component parts. For I do not deny that it happens not rarely that some new substance, which had not been in the composite, is produced by the action of heat. But this is entirely per accidens; for a new substance comes to be if the heat is more vehement than the dissolution of the parts requires. For the particles, agitated beyond measure by too great a heat, are so mingled together, those of diverse kinds, that new concretions emerge from it, and hence new substances seem to be produced; but this does not prevent the aforesaid substances from being found in mixed bodies; for from bodies of the same species salt, sulphur and mercury, likewise of the same character, are perpetually extracted, which would surely not happen with such constancy if those substances were produced entitatively by heat; for what is effected by chance happens rarely.

117 Opp. 2. Si sal, sulphur, & mercurius sunt principia secundaria compositi, principia planè innumera erunt, tot nempè, quot sunt rerum earundem species; sed hoc est absurdum: ergo. Maj. prob. nam ut de sale solo mentionem faciamus, propè totidèm sales inter se diversi erunt, quot corpora composita; etenim sal ê ligno fraxineo extractus, causticus est, hoc est carnem, cui adplicatur adurendo corródit, ex aliis lignis extractus non itèm: ergo. Dist. maj.: planè innumera erunt principia ex quibus essentiale rerum ipsarum discrimen desumitur, conc. maj, ex quibus specificè distinguntur, nego maj. & dist. min.: absurdum est tot principia per quae res differunt, constituere, quot sunt species rerum ipsarum, nego; tot constituere genera omnium principiorum quot sunt genera compositorum, conc. min. & neg conseq.

117 Obj. 2. If salt, sulphur and mercury are secondary principles of the composite, the principles will be plainly innumerable, namely as many as there are species of those same things; but this is absurd: therefore. Maj. proved: for, to make mention of salt alone, there will be nearly as many salts differing from one another as there are composite bodies; for salt extracted from ash wood is caustic, that is, it corrodes by burning the flesh to which it is applied; extracted from other woods, it is not so: therefore. Dist. maj.: the principles from which the essential difference of the things themselves is taken will be plainly innumerable, I grant the maj.; those by which they are specifically distinguished, I deny the maj.; and dist. the min.: it is absurd to constitute as many principles by which things differ as there are species of the things themselves, I deny; to constitute as many genera of all the principles as there are genera of composites, I grant the min.; and I deny the conseq.

118 Sed ex hoc argumento nihil colligitur quod non Scholasticam principiorum hypothesim prorsùs evertat Scholastici enim, tot ponunt essentialium formarum, sive formalium principiorum genera, quot sunt composita quae speciè inter se differunt.

118 But from this argument nothing is gathered which does not utterly overturn the Scholastic hypothesis of principles. For the Scholastics posit as many genera of essential forms, or formal principles, as there are composites that differ from one another in species.

119 Opp. 3. ferrum quoque inter principia secundaria admitti debet: ergo. Prob. antec. etenim in plurimarum plantarum cineribus reperiuntur granula, quae ad magnétem accedunt, speculi caustici ope funduntur, non secùs ac ramenta ferri, quae demùm in metallicas confluunt sphaerulas, ut testatur Clariss. Geofroy 2: ergo Argumentum tantùm probat partes componentes nexu tam arcto alligatas esse invicèm, ut integram ferri in partes licet exilissimas divisi, naturam referant, ac tueantur, sed non probat ferrum inter secundaria corporum principia admitti debere; etenim ut

119 Obj. 3. Iron too must be admitted among the secondary principles: therefore. Proof of the antec.: for in the ashes of very many plants granules are found which go to the magnet and are fused by means of a burning mirror, no otherwise than iron filings, which at length flow together into metallic spherules, as the most renowned Geoffroy attests (f): therefore. The argument proves only that the component parts are bound to one another by so tight a bond that, even when divided into the most minute parts, they retain and preserve the integral nature of iron; but it does not prove that iron must be admitted among the secondary principles of bodies; for, as is attested by

p. 48

testatur Magnus Boerhaavius ferrum coalescit, ex ipsis principiis quae a nobismet adstruuntur, ut adeò metallum hoc non inter principia seu elementa, sed mixta inter corpora locum habet.

the great Boerhaave, iron coalesces out of the very principles which are established by us, so that this metal has its place not among the principles or elements, but among mixed bodies.

120 Et[?] quid autem vetat dicere, potius sub ipso combustionis actu partes pingues, salinas, àcidi vitriolici, & terreas, quae elementa sunt ferri in unum fusas, ac conjunctas in verum ferrum coaluisse? Ut proindè eductio ferri ex cineribus, & argilla, sit vera confectio. Argumento, hanc in rem fortasse fuerit quod Monumenta Academiae Regiae Scientiarum Paris, 2 memorant: ea scilicèt composita, quae minus promptè cremantur, & fumum copiosiùs reddunt, ut herbae, ac duriora ligna, majori copia ferrum suis in cineribus largiri, quàm quae subito conflagrant flammamque nitidiùs lucentem edunt.

120 And what forbids us to say, rather, that in the very act of combustion the fatty, saline, vitriolic-acid and earthy parts, which are the elements of iron, fused into one and joined together, coalesced into true iron? So that, consequently, the extraction of iron from ashes and clay is a true making of it. An argument for this may perhaps be what the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Paris (g) record: namely, that those composites which burn less readily and give off smoke more copiously, such as herbs and the harder woods, yield iron in their ashes in greater quantity than those which flare up suddenly and give off a more brightly shining flame.

121 Neque aliunde repetenda fortasse origo granulorum ferri, quae è calculo humano per Clariss. Listerum calcinato educta, Societati Regiae Londíni exhibita fuere. s2 Ut ea propter Clariss. Boerhaave in hanc quidem sententiam oportunè descendit: Si illum, inquit, metallum mutabile, si destructibile ullum, certè hoc erit. s3 Neque tamen idem de elementis per nos constitutis, de resolutione in universum omni adfirmare licebit. Praepóstere enim á singularibus prorsùs, quae intercurrunt quandoque circunstantiis, generalem duci consecutionem, nemo est, qui ignoret.

121 Nor perhaps is the origin to be sought elsewhere of the granules of iron which, drawn out of a calcined human calculus by the most renowned Lister, were exhibited to the Royal Society of London (h). So that for this reason the most renowned Boerhaave opportunely came down to this opinion: If any metal, he says, is changeable, if any destructible, it will certainly be this one (i). Yet it will not be permitted to affirm the same of the elements established by us, concerning every resolution universally. For no one is unaware that it is wholly preposterous to draw a general consequence from singular cases, in which circumstances sometimes intervene.

122 Opp. 4. Experientia constat sulphur potissimùm, atque mercurium in terram, & aquam resolvi, ut testantur Viri Clariss. Du-Hamel, s4 & Du Clós: ergo sulphur, & mercurius non sunt ejus conditionis, cujus necessario debent esse, ut pro rerum principiis haberi jure ac merito possint. Pretermisso antec. nego conseq. Quum enim illa secundaria naturalis compositi principia statuantur, illorum ex aliis compositio non impedit, quominùs pro ejusmodi principiis haberi legitime possint. Ut ut igitur de salis, sulphuris, atque mercurii compositione res sit, nostra in tuto erit assertio, hoc ipso duntaxat, quod naturale quodcumque mixtum in terram, aquam, salem, &c. quum caloris actione corrumpitur, per solam eorumdem separationem resolvatur.

122 Obj. 4. It is established by experience that sulphur especially, and mercury, are resolved into earth and water, as the most renowned men Du Hamel (j) and Du Clos attest: therefore sulphur and mercury are not of that condition of which they must necessarily be in order to be rightly and deservedly held for principles of things. Passing over the antec., I deny the conseq. For since those are laid down as secondary principles of a natural composite, their composition from others does not prevent them from being legitimately held for principles of this kind. However the matter may stand, then, concerning the composition of salt, sulphur and mercury, our assertion will be safe by this alone: that any natural mixture whatever, when it is corrupted by the action of heat, is resolved into earth, water, salt, etc., by their mere separation.

123 Opp. 5. Nostra opinione posita, sequitur, ut quaelibet mixti particula, sit mixta ex sale, sulphure, &c & sic in infinitum, sed hoc repugnat: ergo. Resp. quod si de quavis omninò particula quae in mixto est sermo habeatur, verum est, quod illarum quaelibet non ex iis omnibus constat, ex quibus mixtum ipsum essentialiter consurgit. Velle autem, nullam esse particulam in mixto, quae non sit mixta, perindè est, ac petere principium. Quaerere enim: an ex terra, aqua,

123 Obj. 5. Our opinion being posited, it follows that any particle whatever of a mixture is mixed of salt, sulphur, etc., and so to infinity; but this is repugnant: therefore. Reply: if the talk is of absolutely any particle that is in the mixture, it is true that each of them does not consist of all those things from which the mixture itself essentially arises. But to will that there is no particle in the mixture which is not mixed is just the same as begging the question. For to ask whether a natural mixture is so composed of earth, water,

Histoire de l'Academ. Royal. 1704. p. 37.

Histoire de l’Académie Royale, 1704, p. 37.

Memoir. de l' Acad. 1705. p. 363.

Mémoires de l’Académie, 1705, p. 363.

Journal des Scavans 1719. p. 378.

Journal des Sçavans, 1719, p. 378.

Elem. Chem tom 2. p. 447.

Elementa Chemiae, vol. 2, p. 447.

Tom. 4. Philosoph. cap. 20. num. 9.

Vol. 4, Philosophia, ch. 20, no. 9.

p. 49

sale, &c. ita componatur mixtum naturale, ut illarum substantiarum particulae in eo sint formaliter, ¿ecquid est aliud, nisi quaerere: an naturale quodcumque mixtum ejus sit naturae, ut aliquae in ipso habeantur particulae, quae non sint mixtae?

salt, etc., that the particles of those substances are formally in it, what else is it but to ask whether any natural mixture whatever is of such a nature that there are in it some particles which are not mixed?

124 Praeterea argumentum ab Scholasticis responderi etiam debet. Etenim si nulla in mixto potest esse pars, quae non sit mixta, nulla quoque essentialis pars in composito esse poterit, quae essentialiter non sit composita: ergo materia, & forma ex aliis principiis essentialiter componantur necesse est, quae itidem ex aliis essentialiter componi debent, atque ita deinceps, ut scilicet verum sit, nullam esse partem compositi, quae non sit composita; sed hoc est absurdum: ergo absurdum est etiam, nullam penitùs esse partem in mixto, quae non sit mixta. In fine adverte: non omnia sensibilia principia in quolibet composito reperiri, neque semper aequali copia, quoniam experientia nos édocet corpora alia sale ex. gr. abundare, minus verò olei, mercuriique continere, in aliis terra principem habet locum, aliorum pars potissima est sulphur.

124 Moreover, the argument must also be answered by the Scholastics. For if there can be no part in a mixture which is not mixed, there could also be no essential part in a composite which is not essentially composite: therefore matter and form must necessarily be composed essentially of other principles, which likewise must be essentially composed of others, and so on, so that it would be true, namely, that there is no part of a composite which is not composite; but this is absurd: therefore it is absurd also that there is absolutely no part in a mixture which is not mixed. Finally, note: not all the sensible principles are found in every composite, nor always in equal quantity, since experience teaches us that some bodies abound in salt, e.g., but contain less oil and mercury; in others earth holds the chief place; of others the greatest part is sulphur.

125 Opp. 6. quatuor tantùm vulgaria elementa statui debent, ut principia corporis naturalis: ergo superfluunt Chymica. Prob. antec.: tot esse debent elementa, quot sunt primae, & principes qualitates; sed eae sunt quatuor, calor nempè, frigus, humiditas, siccitas: ergo. Disting. maj. prob.: si ex iis tantum qualitatibus adfectiones omnes, vires, & phaenómena in compositis occurrentia derivari possint, conc., si non ita possint, ut re vera non possunt, nego, & conseq. Etenim ut optimè argumentatur, Sennertus 3 quae â qualitatibus manifestis fit alteratio, & laesio, tam subito quod venena faciunt, hominem interímere non potest. Praeterea in minima quantitate, venena, illaesa in corpore latére possunt, tandemque longo post tempore vires suas éxserunt.

125 Obj. 6. Only the four common elements should be laid down as principles of natural body: therefore the Chemical ones are superfluous. Proof of the antec.: there must be as many elements as there are first and principal qualities; but these are four, namely heat, cold, moisture, dryness: therefore. I distinguish the maj. of the proof: if from those qualities alone all the affections, forces and phenomena occurring in composites can be derived, I grant; if they cannot be so, as in truth they cannot, I deny; and the conseq. For, as Sennert (k) argues excellently, an alteration and injury arising from manifest qualities cannot kill a man as suddenly as poisons do. Moreover, poisons in the least quantity can lie hidden unharmed in the body, and at length after a long time put forth their forces.

126 Sic exigua sputi canis rábidi quantitas illaesa in corpore manére, & contra caloris nostri actionem sese tueri[?] potest, tandemque post menses non solum sex, sed longè plures etiam, gravissimas corpori nostro mutationes inducit Et quod de venenis diximus, de aliis rebus plurimis dici potest, quarum vires sunt longè majores, & nobiliores, quàm ut ad qualitates primas referri possint ¿Quis actiones magnetis ad qualitates primas commode reducet? ¿Ecquis deindè colores multiplices, odores, sapores &c. â dictis quatuor qualitatibus répetet? Sola itaque quatuor haec elementa totidèm qualitatibus praedita rem non expediunt

126 Thus a tiny quantity of the saliva of a rabid dog can remain unharmed in the body and protect itself against the action of our heat, and at length, after not only six but even many more months, induces most grievous changes in our body. And what we have said of poisons can be said of very many other things, whose forces are far greater and nobler than that they could be referred to the first qualities. Who will conveniently reduce the actions of the magnet to the first qualities? Who, again, will derive the manifold colors, odors, flavors, etc. from the said four qualities? These four elements alone, then, endowed with as many qualities, do not settle the matter.

127 Neque valet dicere, ex plurium mixtione plerumque fieri, ut vires emergant, quae in miscibilibus ante mixtionem minime habebantur, etenim concedimus quidem, (inquit Sennertus laudatus, plus esse in composito, quàm in quolibet simplici seorsim sumpto. Interim non sequitur, quod plus sit in

127 Nor does it avail to say that from the mixture of several things it mostly comes about that forces emerge which were not at all present in the miscibles before the mixture; for we grant indeed (says the praised Sennert) that there is more in the composite than in any simple taken separately. Meanwhile it does not follow that there is more in the composite

Apud Klaus. tom. 1. Phys. pag. 150.

In Klaus, vol. 1, Phys., p. 150.

p. 50

composito, quàm in simplicibus omnibus, quae in compositionem ingrediuntur. Si plures colores miscentur, fit quidem color alius ab omnibus seorsim sumptis simplicibus, sed tamen solum color idem sit; nunquam verò excoloribus quocumque modo mixtis, fiet odor, vel sapor, vel alia diversae speciei qualitas. Ita temperamentum è quatuor qualitatibus primis aliud quidem est, quàm simplices qualitates seorsim sumptae, non tamen alia alterius speciei qualitas inde oritur, & quocumque modo qualitates primae misceantur, nunquam ex iis fiet color, vel alia specie differens qualitas.

than in all the simples which enter into the composition. If several colors are mixed, there arises indeed a color other than all the simples taken separately, but still only a color; never, however, from colors mixed in whatever way, will there come an odor, or a flavor, or another quality of a different species. So the temperament made of the four first qualities is indeed something other than the simple qualities taken separately, yet no other quality of another species arises from it; and however the first qualities are mixed, never will a color, or any other quality differing in species, come from them.

DISSERTATIO III. — DISSERTATION III

De proprietatibus corporum.

On the properties of bodies.

128 Constitutis corporum principiis, eorumdemque natura exposita, eae jam adfectiones expendendae veniunt, quae ex natura corporis proximè ducuntur, atque sunt magnitudo, figura, situs, divisibilitas, ac praecipuè motus, substantia quippe natura sua impenetrabilis quendam extensionis modum, sive magnitudinem nanciscitur, estque in partes divisibilis, figuram item aliquam, & inter alias substantias extensas posituram obtinet, habilitate denique ad motum, & quietem praéditam esse intelligitur. Praeterea debet esse in loco, & tempore de quibus etiam Physici agere solent. Utiliora dabimus.

he principles of bodies having been established and their nature set 128 T forth, those affections now come to be weighed which are derived most proximately from the nature of body; and they are magnitude, figure, situation, divisibility, and above all motion: for a substance by its nature impenetrable acquires a certain mode of extension, or magnitude, and is divisible into parts; it likewise obtains some figure, and a position among other extended substances; and finally it is understood to be endowed with an aptitude for motion and rest. Moreover, it must be in place and time, of which Physicists are also wont to treat. We shall give the more useful things.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

DE CORPORIS MAGNITUDINE.

ON THE MAGNITUDE OF BODY.

Ostenditur in quonam formaliter magnitudo corporis posita sit.

It is shown in what the magnitude of body formally consists.

129 Rem certam puto, corporis magnitudinem in eo formaliter consistere, per quod unum corpus, si alteri conferatur, dicitur illi aequale, vel inaequale, quemadmodùm nomine qualitatis, id venit,

think it certain that the magnitude of a body formally consists in that 129 I by which one body, if compared with another, is said to be equal or unequal to it; just as by the name of quality is meant that by reason

p. 51

ratione cujus unum alteri simile, vel dissimile nuncupatur. Hoc constituto.

of which one thing is called similar or dissimilar to another. This established:

130 Dico primo contra plures Scholasticos: magnitudo corporis non consistit formaliter in illius impenetrabilitate. Prob.: apertè constat duo quaelibet corpora, ita convenire in impenetrabilitate, ut si penes illam spectentur, discerni unum ab altero nullatenus possit: ergo vel magnitudo corporis in impenetrabilitate posita formaliter non est, vel duo quaelibet corpora sunt inter se aequalia; sed hoc manifestè adversatur veritati: ergo magnitudo corporis in illius impenetrabilitate nequaquam consistit.

130 I say, first, against many Scholastics: the magnitude of body does not consist formally in its impenetrability. Proof: it is plainly established that any two bodies agree in impenetrability in such a way that, if they are considered in respect of it, one can in no way be discerned from the other: therefore either the magnitude of body is not formally placed in impenetrability, or any two bodies whatever are equal to each other; but this manifestly opposes the truth: therefore the magnitude of body by no means consists in its impenetrability.

131 Dico secundo: magnitudo corporis nihil est diversum ab entitativa ipsius corporis extensione. Prob.: corporis magnitudo est id formaliter, penès quod unum corpus si comparetur alteri, dicitur illi aequale, vel inaequale; sed per extensionem entitativam unum corpus dicitur alteri aequale, vel inaequale: ergo corporis magnitudo nihil est ab entitativa ejusdem extensione diversum. Maj. constat.: ideò namque duo corpora palmaris longitudinis censentur aequalia, quia eadem utriusque extensio est, corpora vero quorum alterum palmaris, alterum bipalmaris sit longitudinis, inaequalia nuncupantur, quia eadem non est utriusque extensio, sed unum ab altero penès illam superatur. Confirm. concl. Convenit penès omnes, rarefactionem esse motum ad majorem, & condensationem esse motum ad minorem quantitatem, sed rarefactio est motus ad majorem extensionem, ad minorem vero condensatio: ergo.

131 I say, secondly: the magnitude of body is nothing different from the entitative extension of the body itself. Proof: the magnitude of body is formally that in respect of which one body, if compared with another, is said to be equal or unequal to it; but it is by entitative extension that one body is said to be equal or unequal to another: therefore the magnitude of body is nothing different from its entitative extension. The maj. is evident: for two bodies a palm in length are judged equal for this reason, that the extension of both is the same; whereas bodies of which one is a palm and the other two palms in length are called unequal, because the extension of both is not the same, but the one is exceeded by the other in respect of it. Confirmation of the concl. It is agreed among all that rarefaction is motion toward greater, and condensation motion toward lesser quantity; but rarefaction is motion toward greater extension, and condensation toward lesser: therefore.

132 Respondent: Corporis magnitudinem consistere quidem in extensione, sed solida sive impenetrabili. Contra tamèn quia praecissa impenetrabilitate, & sola posita extensione, habetur fundamentum aequalitatis, & inaequalitatis: ergo impenetrabilitas ad formalem magnitudinis rationem nullatenùs pertinet; sicuti eandem omninò ob causam certum est ad magnitudinem non spectare corporis duritiem. Profectò ideo durities non pertinet ad formalem rationem magnitudinis, quia duo corpora possunt esse inaequalia, & simul aeque dura: ergo neque ad magnitudinem aliquomodò spectat impenetrabilitas, quia inaequalia possunt esse duo corpora, & simul ex aequo impenetrabilia.

132 They reply: the magnitude of body consists indeed in extension, but in solid, or impenetrable, extension. But against this: because, when impenetrability is prescinded and extension alone is posited, the foundation of equality and inequality is had: therefore impenetrability in no way pertains to the formal notion of magnitude; just as, for altogether the same cause, it is certain that the hardness of a body does not concern magnitude. Surely hardness does not pertain to the formal notion of magnitude for this reason, that two bodies can be unequal and at the same time equally hard: therefore neither does impenetrability concern magnitude in any way, since two bodies can be unequal and at the same time equally impenetrable.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De Figura, & Situ corporum.

On the Figure and Situation of bodies.

133 Extensio cujusvis corporis terminis, sive superficiebus, quae materiam corporis propriam includunt, limitatur. Ordo ille, & positio quam inter se habent superficies, volumen corporis terminantes,

he extension of any body is limited by terms, or surfaces, which en133 T close the matter proper to the body. That order and position which the surfaces bounding the volume of the body have among themselves

p. 52

figura dicitur, qua corpus dicitur esse sphaericum, cúbicum &c. Exterior itaque corporis conformatio vocatur figura, quae nempè ad rei naturam intrinsecùs non pertinet, & communis esse potest corporibus omninò diversis; figura, autem ipsarum partium corpus certum suo in genere constituens, quae in cera ex. gr. haud dubie alia esse debet quam in ferro, configuratio vocatur. Situs est certa quaedam positura, ordo, combinatio, textura, sive artificiosa ipsarum molecularum dispositio in toto, quod ex illis intrinsecus constituitur.

is called figure, by which a body is said to be spherical, cubical, etc. The exterior conformation of a body, then, is called figure, which namely does not pertain intrinsically to the nature of the thing, and can be common to altogether diverse bodies; but the figure of the parts themselves, constituting a body definite in its kind, which in wax, e.g., must doubtless be other than in iron, is called configuration. Situation is a certain posture, order, combination, texture, or artificial disposition of the molecules themselves in the whole which is intrinsically constituted of them.

134 Superficies corporum modis omninò multiplicibus variari potest. Prodigiosa autem haec figurarum varietas innumeris Physicorum experimentis comprobatur, quorum utiliora seligemus. Super fragmentum vitri aliquas guttas aceti optimi détine per aliquod horas, ut pro parte évaporent, inde eas intuere microscopio, innumeros sales observabis ferè omnes acuminatos. Si acetum in vase aliquo detineas aëri expositum post aliquod hebdomadas, & aestivo tempore citiùs, innumeras veluti exilissimas anguillas hùc illùc discurrentes microscopio videbis. Ex iis verò patet aceti saporem acrem, non ab anguillis, ut nonnulli putarunt, sed à salibus diversis originem dúcere.

134 The surfaces of bodies can be varied in altogether manifold ways. This prodigious variety of figures, moreover, is confirmed by innumerable experiments of the Physicists, of which we shall select the more useful. Keep some drops of the best vinegar on a fragment of glass for some hours, so that they partly evaporate; then look at them through a microscope: you will observe innumerable salts, nearly all pointed. If you keep vinegar in some vessel exposed to the air for some weeks, and more quickly in summertime, you will see with the microscope innumerable, as it were, most tiny eels running about hither and thither. From these, however, it is plain that the sharp taste of vinegar draws its origin not from the eels, as some have thought, but from diverse salts.

135 Super vitrum pone aquae purae guttam, & in ea pauxillum salis communis in pulverem redacti probè solve, postquam sponté omnis aqua evaporavit microscopio observa guttam, videbis salem in crystallos redactum figurae cúbicae. Si eadem ratione saccharum solvas, observabis crystalla figurae feré rotundae. Richardus Mead in mechanica expositione venenorum, minimam partem succi venenosi, qui emittitur à dente viperae quum mordet super vitrum collocavit, & brevi temporis spatio mutatus est in crystallos tenuissimas, & maximè acutas, quae adeò erant rigidae, ut per mensem absque ulla mutatione permánserint. Ex figura itaque & duritie hujus veneni repetenda est indomabilis ejus natura, quae vix remediis oportunè adhibitis quandòque cedit. Si aliqua portio píperis contúsi, in vase aqua pleno, per aliquot dies servetur, innumera diversi generis, diversaeque figurae animalcula microscopio observantur.

135 Put a drop of pure water on glass, and in it dissolve thoroughly a little common salt reduced to powder; after all the water has evaporated of its own accord, observe the drop with the microscope: you will see the salt reduced into crystals of cubical figure. If you dissolve sugar in the same way, you will observe crystals of nearly round figure. Richard Mead, in his Mechanical Account of Poisons, placed upon glass a very small part of the venomous juice which is emitted from the tooth of a viper when it bites, and in a short space of time it was changed into most slender and extremely sharp crystals, which were so rigid that they remained for a month without any change. From the figure and hardness of this poison, then, is to be derived its untamable nature, which sometimes scarcely yields to remedies opportunely applied. If a portion of crushed pepper is kept for some days in a vessel full of water, innumerable animalcules of diverse kind and diverse figure are observed with the microscope.

136 Aliis modis figurata insecta deprehenduntur in aqua stagnante injectis feni concissi, palearum, plantarumque variarum frustis, dùm animalcula quaedam globulis similia, alia longiora, seque in gyrum agentia spectantur, in nonnullis pedes distinguuntur, quaedam vermium instar annulata cernuntur, & jocundo spectaculo saepè observantur majora insequi minora, ut ea dévorent.

136 Insects figured in other ways are detected in stagnant water into which bits of cut hay, of chaff and of various plants have been thrown: certain animalcules are seen like globules, others longer and turning themselves round in a circle; in some, feet are distinguished; some are seen ringed like worms; and, in a pleasant spectacle, the greater are often observed to pursue the lesser so as to devour them.

137 Si colligas partes emissas spontè, aut beneficio ignis arte eductas à corporibus, animadvertes ejusdem esse naturae, & eosdem ac corpora ipsa producere effectus. Ita vapor aquae collectus dat aquam, vapor sulphuris, & cámphorae, sulphur, & cámphoram denuò restituunt. Haec verò non evenirent, si corporum partes non

137 If you collect the parts emitted spontaneously, or drawn out of bodies by art with the help of fire, you will notice that they are of the same nature, and produce the same effects, as the bodies themselves. Thus the vapor of water, collected, gives water; the vapors of sulphur and of camphor restore sulphur and camphor anew. But these things would not happen if the parts of bodies did not

p. 53

haberent, nec solutae conservarent eandem figuram. Aquae, & aliorum vaporum partes observari possunt, si corpora évaporent in cubiculo úndique clauso, in quo nonnisi solis radius transeat, qui vapores illuminet. Hac ratione innotuit partes aquae esse perfectè rotundas. Plura alia notatu digna reperiuntur in scriptis Leuwenhoek, Roberti Boyle, Martini Lyster, Erasmi Bartholini, Johannis Freind, quos Auctores ubi copia erit, & otium suppetit consúlere potestis.

have, and when released did not preserve, the same figure. The parts of water and of other vapors can be observed if bodies evaporate in a small room closed on all sides, into which only a ray of the sun passes to illuminate the vapors. In this way it became known that the parts of water are perfectly round. Many other things worth noting are found in the writings of Leeuwenhoek, Robert Boyle, Martin Lister, Erasmus Bartholin and John Freind, which Authors you will be able to consult when you have the means and the leisure.

138 Quum quaelibet ergo materiae, seu corporis pars peculiarem figuram habeat, necessariò dùm actu separantur partes alicujus corporis, superficies ejusdem augeri debet. Nam quum sejunguntur partes, & quaelibet propria contineatur superficie, quia figuram habet, superficies illae internae corporis, quibus se mutuò tangebant partes, redduntur conspicuæ, & corporis in partes secti superficiem integram componunt, unà cum superficie veteri sub qua totum corpus continebatur. Quum itaque corpus aliquot in partes dividitur, ejus superficies augetur manente eadem massa, seu soliditate. Quare quum eadem remaneat materia, & superficies corporis augeatur continua partium separatione, superficies majorem acquiret ad materiam corporis rationem.

138 Since, then, any part whatever of matter, or of body, has its peculiar figure, necessarily, while the parts of some body are actually separated, its surface must be increased. For when the parts are disjoined, and each is contained by its own surface, because it has figure, those internal surfaces of the body by which the parts touched one another become visible, and, together with the old surface under which the whole body was contained, compose the entire surface of the body cut into parts. When, therefore, a body is divided into several parts, its surface is increased while the same mass, or solidity, remains. Wherefore, since the same matter remains and the surface of the body is increased by the continued separation of the parts, the surface will acquire a greater ratio to the matter of the body.

139 Ex hoc verò plura exponuntur phaenómena quae sepissimè observantur, quum fluidum aliquod, veluti aër, ignis, aqua agunt in corpora. Fluidorum actio sequitur rationem superficiei corporis; quò enim major est corporis superficies, eò major fluidi quantitas in corpus agit. Hinc optimè explicatur cur ventus qui nequit adtollere pedem cubicum mármoris, plures evehat momento temporis ad insignem altitudinem pedes cúbicos arenae, nempè, pondus céntuplo majus primo. Nam pes cúbicus arenae idem est ac pes cúbicus marmoris in partes totidem sectus, quot sunt arenae grana; at ventus in pulverem marmoris majorem exercére potest vim, quàm in pedem cubicum ejusdem, adtollet itaque pedem cubicum arenae, imò plures arenae pedes, & elevare non poterit integrum marmoris.

139 From this, moreover, are explained several phenomena which are very often observed when some fluid, such as air, fire or water, acts upon bodies. The action of fluids follows the ratio of the surface of the body; for the greater the surface of the body, the greater the quantity of fluid that acts upon the body. Hence it is excellently explained why a wind which cannot lift a cubic foot of marble carries up in a moment of time several cubic feet of sand to a remarkable height, namely a weight a hundred times greater than the first. For a cubic foot of sand is the same as a cubic foot of marble cut into as many parts as there are grains of sand; but the wind can exert a greater force on marble in powder than on a cubic foot of the same; it will therefore lift a cubic foot of sand, nay several feet of sand, and will not be able to raise a whole foot of marble.

140 Exponitur eodem modo vis maxima medicata argenti vivi, seu mercurii ad morbos pertinaces depellendos. Gutta mercurii facilè resolvitur in innumeros exilissimos globulos, ut patebit si radios solis speculo cóncavo, aut lente crystallina collectos, contra eam projicias. Quare ejus superficies citò intra corpus mirum in modum augebitur, hac vero aucta, faciliùs mercurius in vasa impelletur à fluidis corporis, atque vi acquisita materiam morbosam ab ipsis expellet; aut in minora vasa áditum sibi facilè aperiet, atque ita haec saltem deplebit, unde expeditior fiet circuitus fluidorum, ex quo convalescet corpus à morbis diuturnis. Non itaque mercurius, ut plerique putant proprio póndere, sed divisibilitate operatur.

140 In the same way is explained the very great medicinal force of quicksilver, or mercury, for driving out stubborn diseases. A drop of mercury is easily resolved into innumerable most tiny globules, as will be plain if you throw upon it the rays of the sun collected by a concave mirror or a crystal lens. Wherefore its surface will quickly be increased to a wonderful degree within the body, and, this being increased, the mercury will more easily be driven by the fluids of the body into the vessels, and with the force acquired will expel the morbid matter from them; or it will easily open for itself an entrance into the smaller vessels, and so will at least deplete them, whence the circulation of the fluids will become more unimpeded, by which the body recovers from long-lasting diseases. Mercury, then, does not operate by its own weight, as most think, but by its divisibility.

141 Ex figura, & situ corporum multa possunt explicari

141 From the figure and situation of bodies many phenomena can be explained

p. 54

phaenómena; eaque non minus utilia quam scitu jocunda, quorum aliqua tantum exponemus, ut ex iis quae nunc â nobis exponentur plurimum lucis accédat iis quae de Statica, & Hydrostatica postea dicemus. Corpora ergo omnia gravitatem quandam habere videntur, hinc fit, ut lapides ex. gr. tandiù descendant, donec aliorum corporum occursu sustineantur. Sustineri autem incipiunt, quum ipsorum centrum gravitatis descéndere prohibetur. Est autèm centrum gravitatis: punctum in quolibet corpore grave positum, per quod si suspendatur corpus, omnes illius partes quemcumque iis déderis situm, hunc servabunt: adeòque futurae sunt in aequilibrio. ex. gr. Si baculus, aut virga ferrea media sui parte filo suspendatur, ac utraque illius pars sit in aequilibrio, punctum illud undè suspendetur, erit illius gravitatis centrum, quoniam illius partes utrimque aequalis erunt pónderis.

and these no less useful than pleasant to know, of which we shall set forth only some, so that from those which are now to be set forth by us very much light may come to what we shall afterwards say on Statics and Hydrostatics. All bodies, then, are seen to have a certain gravity; hence it comes about that stones, e.g., descend until they are held up by meeting other bodies. They begin to be held up, moreover, when their center of gravity is prevented from descending. The center of gravity, moreover, is the point placed in any heavy body by which, if the body is suspended, all its parts will keep whatever situation you have given them, and so will be in equilibrium. E.g., if a staff or an iron rod is suspended by a thread at its middle part, and each part of it is in equilibrium, that point from which it will be suspended will be its center of gravity, since its parts on either side will be of equal weight.

142 Sed si virga illa non sit ubique homogenea, seu ejusdem naturae, puta si altera sui parte sit ferrea, altera lignea, centrum illius gravitatis non erit in medio extensionis, sed ab eo recedet versùs eam materiae partem, quae est densior. Qua propter centrum gravitatis, & centrum magnitudinis, seu extensionis, non in idem semper punctum confluunt, sed tantùm quum materia corporis gravis est homogenea: ex. gr. in globo ferreo centrum extensionis, seu punctum illius medium, quod â singulis superficiei punctis ex aequo distat, concipi etiam potest centrum gravitatis, quum materia in globo ferreo, ubique sit homogenea.

142 But if that rod is not everywhere homogeneous, that is, of the same nature, suppose if in one part it is of iron and in the other of wood, its center of gravity will not be in the middle of its extension, but will recede from it toward that part of the matter which is denser. Wherefore the center of gravity and the center of magnitude, or of extension, do not always coincide in the same point, but only when the matter of the heavy body is homogeneous: e.g., in an iron globe the center of extension, or its middle point, which is equally distant from the individual points of the surface, can also be conceived as the center of gravity, since the matter in the iron globe is everywhere homogeneous.

143 Jam quum corpus grave deorsum tendit, nempè ad terrae centrum, quod ideo centrum gravium adpelant, quoniam ad illud gravia omnia nituntur, ipsius motus, vel descensus per quamdam lineam, cui centrum gravitatis semper insistit dirigitur, eaque iccircò linea directionis, vocatur, ac definitur, linea recta, quae â gravitatis centro, ad centrum gravium porrigi intelligitur. Jam vero Axiomata haec sunt. Primum. Quiescit corpus grave alteri insistens, si prohibeat corpus cui incumbit, quo minus illius centrum gravitatis deorsum moveatur. Quum enim tota corporis gravitas sit veluti in uno puncto collecta, fieri nequit ut deorsum moveatur corpus, si illius centrum gravitatis deorsum moveri non possit.

143 Now, when a heavy body tends downward, namely to the center of the earth, which they therefore call the center of heavy things, since all heavy things strive toward it, its motion, or descent, is directed along a certain line on which the center of gravity always stands; and for this reason it is called the line of direction, and is defined: the straight line which is understood to be stretched from the center of gravity to the center of heavy things. Now the Axioms are these. First: A heavy body resting on another remains at rest, if the body on which it lies prevents its center of gravity from being moved downward. For since the whole gravity of the body is as it were collected in one point, it cannot happen that the body moves downward if its center of gravity cannot move downward.

144 Secundum: labitur corpus grave alteri insistens, si illius centrum gravitatis ab eo, cui corpus ipsum insistit minimè sustineatur. Etenim si centrum gravitatis non sustinetur, nihil prohibet, quo minus prout exigit naturae lex, centrum ipsum deorsum tendat, ac proindè quo minus totum corpus deorsum moveatur. Corpus ergo grave numquam decídere potest, nisi ipsius gravitatis centrum décidat. Non potest autem illud centrum décidere quandiu corpus in plano horizontali, sic collocatum est, ut linea directionis intra illius basim transire concipiatur. Axioma tertium: Centrum gravitatis ponderosi cujusque corporis non nisi violenter potest ascendere; est enim contra legem naturae, ut corpus grave sua veluti sponte sursum tendat.

144 Second: a heavy body resting on another slips, if its center of gravity is not supported by that on which the body itself rests. For if the center of gravity is not supported, nothing prevents the center itself from tending downward, as the law of nature requires, and consequently the whole body from moving downward. A heavy body, then, can never fall unless its center of gravity falls. But that center cannot fall as long as the body is so placed on a horizontal plane that the line of direction is conceived to pass within its base. Third axiom: The center of gravity of any heavy body cannot ascend except violently; for it is against the law of nature that a heavy body should tend upward as it were of its own accord.

p. 55

145 Horizontali plano D E (Fig. I) insistat secundum planam superficiem m n x solidum grave A, cujus linea directionis a b intra illius basim m n x cadat. Dico fieri tunc nullatenus posse, ut corpus A deorsum labatur: Etenim perspicuum est centrum gravitatis a sustineri à plano D E, cui corpus A insistit: cádere autem nequit corpus, si ejus centrum gravitatis deorsum moveri non pòssit [§. 43]: ergo corpus A deorsum non cadet. Sed aliud sit corpus H G (Fig. II.) cujus linea directionis Cd cadat extra basim F G, id in partem e statim lapsurum intelligitur, quia dum totum corpus motu circulari fertur circa F ipsius centrum gravitatis C semper descendit: ergo cadat necesse est [§. 144]. Praeterea centrum grávitatis C non sustinetur à plano D E, quum linea directionis Cd extra basim F G excurrat: ergo necesse est ut corpus H G deorsum ruat [§. 144.]

145 Let a heavy solid A rest on the horizontal plane D E (Fig. I) by its plane surface m n x, and let its line of direction a b fall within its base m n x. I say that it can then in no way happen that the body A slips downward. For it is evident that the center of gravity a is supported by the plane D E on which the body A rests; but a body cannot fall if its center of gravity cannot move downward [§. 43]: therefore the body A will not fall down. But let there be another body H G (Fig. II) whose line of direction Cd falls outside the base F G; it is understood that it will at once fall toward the side e, because, while the whole body is carried with a circular motion about F, its center of gravity C is continually descending: therefore it must needs fall [§. 144]. Moreover, the center of gravity C is not supported by the plane D E, since the line of direction Cd runs outside the base F G: therefore it is necessary that the body H G should tumble down [§. 144].

146 Hinc ratio adparet, cur aliquae turres inclinatae non cadant, cujusmodi sunt Bononiensis, & Pisana à me observatae dum Italiam anno 1767 peragrarem Bononiensis est turris quadrata altitudinis 130 pedum 3. Pisana est turris rotunda altitudinis 138 pedum. Bononiensis turris perpendiculum distat à basi intervallo 9 pedum, perpendiculum verò turris Pisanae per spatium 15 pedum extra basim excurrit, Firmae tamen, & stabiles persevérant, quia utriusque linea directionis intra basim est, & ideò neutra ruere deorsum potest. Hinc etiam sequitur, exilia corpora, ut acus ex. gr. stare super cuspide sua minimè posse, nimis enim angusta ejus basis est, undè quaevis vel minima inclinatio, quivis vel minimus aëris impulsus súfficit, ut illius linea directionis extra basim excurrat.

146 Hence the reason appears why some leaning towers do not fall, such as those of Bologna and Pisa, observed by me while I was traveling through Italy in the year 1767. The Bologna tower is square, 130 feet high. The Pisa tower is round, 138 feet high. The plumb line of the Bologna tower stands off from the base by an interval of 9 feet, while the plumb line of the tower of Pisa runs outside the base over a space of 15 feet. Yet they remain firm and stable, because the line of direction of each is within the base, and therefore neither can tumble down. Hence it also follows that slender bodies, such as a needle, for example, can by no means stand upon their point, for its base is too narrow; whence any inclination, however slight, any impulse of the air, however small, suffices for its line of direction to run outside the base.

147 Hinc etiam colligitur cur situla A (Fig. III.) aqua plena, baculo B C, è mensa cui imponitur suspensa, non cadat, dummodo alter baculus G D infra ansam, & prioris baculi extremum C in situlae fundo ad perpendiculum erigatur. Nam quum ambo baculi simul cum situla unum & idem corpus efficiant, cádere non potest situla, quin adtollatur pars extrema B baculi B C describendo

147 Hence it is also gathered why a bucket A (Fig. III) full of water, suspended from a rod B C laid on a table, does not fall, provided another rod G D is set upright below the handle and against the end C of the first rod, perpendicular to the bottom of the bucket. For since both rods together with the bucket make one and the same body, the bucket cannot fall without the end B of the rod B C being raised, describing, namely,

Longitudo, & divisio mensurae linearum, non est eadem ubique gentium: aliquas celebrium mensurarum varietates expónet Tabula sequens in particulis istiusmodi, qualium Pes Regius Parisinus est 1440. Cóntinet is nempè 12 póllices, pollex verò 12 lineas, linea 10 particulas, seu puncta, adeòque pes ínteger Parisinus continebit particulas 1440. Pes Regius Parisinus ...1440 Vénetus... 1540. Hispánus... 1240. Bononiensis... 1691. Románus... 1320. Viennensis... 1399. Londinénsis... 1351. Holländicus... 1391.

: The length and division of the measure of lines is not the same among all nations: the following Table will set out some varieties of the well-known measures in particles of the kind of which the Royal Paris Foot is 1440. That foot, namely, contains 12 inches, the inch 12 lines, the line 10 particles, or points, and so the whole Paris foot will contain 1440 particles. Royal Paris Foot 1440. Venetian 1540. Spanish 1240. Bolognese 1691. Roman 1320. Viennese 1399. London 1351. Dutch 1391.

p. 56

nimitum arcum B L. Eadem autem adtolli non potest, quin simul centrum gravitatis i, quod est in situla describat arcum i M, quod describere nequit quin sursum ascendat contra gravium nissum (Axioma 3. §. 144.) ergo situla decidere non poterit, sed necessario è baculo immota dependet.

the arc B L. But it cannot be raised without the center of gravity i, which is in the bucket, describing at the same time the arc i M, which it cannot describe without ascending upward against the tendency of heavy bodies (Axiom 3, §. 144): therefore the bucket will not be able to fall, but will necessarily hang motionless from the rod.

148 Ope motus centri gravitatis explicatur etiam, qui fieri possit, ut corpus aliquod ascendendo, adsiduè descendat, quod prima fronte Paradoxum videtur Tribus lignis triangulum A B C (Fig. IV.) construatur, cujus basis C B sit aequalis axibus duorum conorum, qui simul juncti sint per bases G F. Subjiciantur basi C B duo sustentacula C D, B E radio basis conorum G F breviora. Si coni illi duo ponantur super extremitatem A, videbuntur ascendere in C B ubi maxima est elevatio, centrum tamen gravitatis descendet.

148 By means of the motion of the center of gravity it is also explained how it can happen that a body, while ascending, continually descends, which at first sight seems a Paradox. Let a triangle A B C (Fig. IV) be constructed of three pieces of wood, whose base C B is equal to the axes of two cones joined together by their bases G F. Under the base C B let two supports C D, B E be placed, shorter than the radius of the base of the cones G F. If those two cones are set upon the extremity A, they will seem to ascend into C B, where the elevation is greatest; yet the center of gravity will descend.

149 Ut hoc planiùs intelligatur considerate planum A B b (Fig. V.) in quo centrum gravitatis a duorum conorum reperitur. Centrum hoc elevatum est supra horizontem quantum linea a b, quae aequalis est p F. Si conus incéderet super F D centrum gravitatis a describeret lineam a p horizonti F D parallelam. Conus autem in IV. figura ita movetur per duo plana B A, A C ut ejus vertex x x sit in B C, vel in C (Fig. V.) ergo in motu coni centrum gravitatis a describit a C, nempè adsiduè descendit, ita ut quando perveniat in C, centrum gravitatis ejusdem descenderit quantum notatur à p C, sed motus corporum determinatur à motu centri gravitatis ipsorum: ergo si centrum conorum descendit, ut est demonstratum, conus ascendere debet. Duplex itaque conus per duo plana IV. figurae ascendat necesse est.

149 That this may be understood more plainly, consider the plane A B b (Fig. V) in which the center of gravity a of the two cones is found. This center is raised above the horizon by as much as the line a b, which is equal to p F. If the cone advanced upon F D, the center of gravity a would describe the line a p parallel to the horizon F D. But the cone in the IV. figure moves along the two planes B A, A C in such a way that its vertex x x is in B C, or in C (Fig. V): therefore in the motion of the cone the center of gravity a describes a C, that is, it continually descends, so that when it arrives at C, its center of gravity will have descended by as much as is marked by p C; but the motion of bodies is determined by the motion of their center of gravity: therefore if the center of the cones descends, as has been demonstrated, the cone must ascend. It is necessary, then, that the double cone should ascend along the two planes of the IV. figure.

150 Cognitio centri gravitatis, & lineae directionis apta est aliis pluribus explicandis: Homo ex. gr. qui ita sedeat, ut cum femoribus crura angulum rectum constituant, fémora quoque cum trunco sint ad angulum rectum, súrgere non poterit, nisi priùs humeros inclinet aut pedem retróferat, ut linea directionis intra basim pedum décidat. Si humeris, & calcaneis parietem adtingens, ac pedum tantummodo extremitatibus terra innixus homo stet, infléctere se non poterit, nisi pedem anteferat, alias quum se inflectit, cadat necesse est, quia tunc linea directionis extra basim décidit.

150 The knowledge of the center of gravity and of the line of direction is suited to explaining many other things. A man, for example, who sits in such a way that his legs make a right angle with his thighs, and his thighs too are at a right angle with his trunk, will not be able to rise unless he first inclines his shoulders or draws his foot back, so that the line of direction may fall within the base of the feet. If a man stands touching a wall with his shoulders and heels, and resting on the ground only with the tips of his feet, he will not be able to bend himself unless he puts a foot forward; otherwise, when he bends, he must needs fall, because the line of direction then falls outside the base.

151 Verum haec leviter adtigisse satis est: nam si omnia, quae à figura & situ partium ducuntur, referre esset animus omnia ferè, & naturae, & artis phaénomena hùc essent congerenda: qualitates enim penè omnes à figura, & situ partium oriuntur.

151 But it is enough to have touched on these things lightly: for if it were my intention to report all the things that are derived from the figure and situation of the parts, almost all the phenomena both of nature and of art would have to be heaped together here: for nearly all qualities arise from the figure and situation of the parts.

p. 57

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

De divisibilitate corporum.

On the divisibility of bodies.

152 Divisibilitatem esse adfectionem corporibus omnibus propriam; uti indubium est, ita in quaestionem hic venire minimè debet, id duntaxat Physici considerant ¿quorsum divisibilitas illa se extendat? Quae quidem comtemplatio summi in Physica est momenti, atque ea de causa Recentiores Physici experimenta plurima instituerunt, scriptisque editis argumentum hoc illustrarunt. ¿Num verò materia, corpus, sive continuum physicum dividi in infinitum queat, vel an tandem sit in partibus insectibilibus sistendum? Controversia est, quae ut ait P. Regnault 2 jam indè ab exortu Philosophiae célebris elegantissima citrà fructum torsit ingenia. Nos eo consilio rem adgrediemur, ut controversiae statu proposito, quod certum in illa videri possit ingenuè exponamus.

hat divisibility is an affection proper to all bodies, as it is beyond 152 T doubt, so it ought by no means to come into question here; the Physicists consider only this: how far does that divisibility extend? This contemplation is indeed of the highest moment in Physics, and for that reason the modern Physicists have instituted very many experiments and have illustrated this subject in published writings. But can matter, body, or the physical continuum be divided to infinity, or must one at last come to a stop at indivisible parts? It is a controversy which, as Fr. Regnault says (m), has from the very rise of Philosophy tormented famous and most elegant wits without fruit. We shall approach the matter with this design: that, having set forth the state of the controversy, we may candidly expound what can seem certain in it.

153 Continuum ergo dicitur illud, quod resultat ex partibus ita conjunctis, ut illarum extrema sint unum, hoc est, quae ad eandem prorsus substantiam pertinent, ut sunt partes ligni, quae eandem, & unicam ligni substantiam componunt. Contiguum verò dicitur illud, cujus partes extremae sunt simul, ut quum manus, aut duo corpora sese tangunt Partes etiam alicujus compositi deinceps positae, vel juxta positae dicuntur, quum inter illas alterius corporis particulae ex. gr. aëris intérjacent, ut sunt grana in acervo tritici. Partes aliquotae dicuntur, quae aliquoties repetitae adaequant praecisse totum. Sic pes est pars aliquota Hexapedae, quia sexies repetitus Hexapedam pracisse adaequat.

153 That, then, is called a continuum which results from parts so joined that their extremities are one, that is, belong to altogether the same substance, as are the parts of wood, which compose the same single substance of the wood. That, however, is called contiguous whose extreme parts are together, as when hands, or two bodies, touch each other. The parts of some composite are also said to be placed in succession, or placed side by side, when particles of another body, e.g. of air, lie between them, as are the grains in a heap of wheat. Those parts are called aliquot which, repeated some number of times, exactly equal the whole. Thus the foot is an aliquot part of the fathom, because, repeated six times, it exactly equals the fathom.

154 Partes aliquantae dicuntur, quae nunquam aliquoties repetitae adaequant praecisse totum, sed vel excedunt, vel ab eo deficiunt: sic pars quatuor pedes extensa, est pars aliquanta hexapedae, quia si bis sumatur excedit hexapedam, semel verò sumpta non dum adaequat. Partes proportionales sunt, quae in continua proportione decrescunt, sic hexapeda dividi pótest in duas medietates, & quaelibet ex his in alias duas, & sic deinceps. Continui physici partes in infinitum divisibiles esse arbitrantur Peripatetici, & Cartesiani plurimi. Qui Epicurum, & Gassendum sequuntur contrariam tuentur sententiam.

154 Those parts are called aliquant which, repeated any number of times, never exactly equal the whole, but either exceed it or fall short of it: thus a part four feet long is an aliquant part of the fathom, because if it is taken twice it exceeds the fathom, while taken once it does not yet equal it. Proportional parts are those which decrease in continued proportion; thus the fathom can be divided into two halves, and either of these into two others, and so on. The Peripatetics and very many Cartesians judge the parts of the physical continuum to be divisible to infinity. Those who follow Epicurus and Gassendi defend the contrary opinion.

155 Primae sententiae defensores ita arguunt. Omne extensum est divisibile in partes; sed omne corpus quantumvis tenue

155 The defenders of the first opinion argue thus. Everything extended is divisible into parts; but every body, however thin, is always

Entret. Physiques. Entret. I.

Entret. Physiques. Entret. I.

p. 58

semper extensum est: ergo omne corpus semper, & in infinitum est divisibile. Respondent Epicuréi disting. maj. omne extensum mathematicè sumptum, concedunt, physice sumptum, negant. Id mathematicè extensum dicitur, quod ratione suarum dimensionum duntaxàt consideratur, non inspecta subjecti extensi conditione, ac natura: physice verò extensum vocatur, quod tanquam substantia quaedam physica, certa natura ac conditione donata consideratur, quidquid extensum est, mathematicè, ac per mentem dividi potest; at non semper re ipsa, & physice, quum esse possit substantia quaedam simplex non ex partibus composita, scilicet atomus, quae primum est subjectum ex quo omnia corpora sensibilia constant, & ultimum in quod resolvuntur Hactenus Epicúrei, & Gassendistae.

extended: therefore every body is always, and to infinity, divisible. The Epicureans reply by distinguishing the major: everything extended taken mathematically, they grant; taken physically, they deny. That is said to be extended mathematically which is considered only by reason of its dimensions, without regard to the condition and nature of the extended subject; that, however, is called extended physically which is considered as a certain physical substance endowed with a definite nature and condition. Whatever is extended can be divided mathematically and by the mind, but not always in reality itself and physically, since there can be a certain simple substance not composed of parts, namely the atom, which is the first subject of which all sensible bodies consist, and the last into which they are resolved. Thus far the Epicureans and Gassendists.

156 Hi autèm contra Peripateticos sic arguunt: Si materia in infinitum esset divisibilis, corpus exiguum, ut granum tritici, infinitas actu partes in se continéret, nàm corpus in ea tantum quae continet divisibile cogitatur; sed hoc manifeste repugnat: ergo materia sive continuum non est in infinitum divisibile. Respondent Peripatetici disting. maj. si materia esset divisibilis secundum partes alíquotas, corpus exiguum haberet, &c. concedunt, si sit tantum divisibilis in partes proportionales quarum unaquaeque infinitas alias in se includit, negant. Habetis quaestionis statum.

156 These, moreover, argue thus against the Peripatetics: If matter were divisible to infinity, a tiny body, such as a grain of wheat, would contain within itself infinite parts in act, for a body is conceived as divisible only into those parts which it contains; but this is manifestly contradictory: therefore matter, or the continuum, is not divisible to infinity. The Peripatetics reply by distinguishing the major: if matter were divisible according to aliquot parts, a tiny body would have, etc., they grant; if it is divisible only into proportional parts, each of which includes infinitely many others within itself, they deny. You have the state of the question.

157 Sed haec omnia (ut optimè advertunt Purchot, & Klaus) 2 sunt hujusmodi, ut si rationes duntaxat, non responsiones ponderentur, demonstrationum vim obtinére ex utráque parte videantur. Ut iccircò unum hoc liceat pronunciare; incertum esse an corporea magnitudo dividi semper possit, an verò in insecabilibus partibus omnis tandèm illius divisio definiatur, quod quidem eò adserimus oportunius, quò certiùs novimus, ad incrementa Physicae perinde prorsùs esse, sive indivisibiles ponantur continui partes, sive divisibiles in infinitum, nam ad principia corporis naturalis, & ad phaenómena in universum explicanda commostrare sufficit corpora quaevis in partes adeò minutas dispésci posse, ut vel ipsa ratio obstupescat, quod sequenti propositione â nobis probandum quàmclarissime est.

157 But all these things (as Purchot and Klaus very well observe) (n) are of such a kind that, if only the reasons, and not the replies, are weighed, they seem on both sides to carry the force of demonstrations. So that it may therefore be permitted to pronounce this one thing: it is uncertain whether corporeal magnitude can always be divided, or whether all its division at last terminates in indivisible parts; which we assert all the more fittingly as we know the more certainly that for the advancement of Physics it is altogether the same whether the parts of the continuum are posited as indivisible or as divisible to infinity; for, for the principles of natural body and for explaining the phenomena in general, it suffices to show that any bodies whatever can be split into parts so minute that reason itself is astonished, which is to be proved by us as clearly as possible in the following proposition.

158 Dico igitur: corpora in partes omnino exilissimas stupendum prorsùs in modum actu divisa sunt, dividique possunt. Primò quidem odoris diffusio subministrat argumentum summae subtilitatis, ad quam substantia odorifera pervenire potest.
