Ultrà ea quae diximus (§ 58.) exemplo sit càlculus exhalationum fumosarum, quem P. de Lanis s2 exequitur, & ab exiguo thuris grano egredientium, & singula cubiculi puncta occupantium. Laudatus igitur Pater posito cubiculo 20 pedes longo, totidem lato, & in altitudinem ad 15 pedes adtolli, càlculo facto adfirmat, forè

158 I say, therefore: bodies are actually divided, and can be divided, into utterly minute parts in an altogether stupendous manner. First, indeed, the diffusion of odor furnishes an argument of the extreme subtlety to which an odoriferous substance can attain. Beyond what we have said (§. 58), let an example be the calculation which Fr. Lana Terzi (o) carries out of the smoky exhalations that issue from a tiny grain of incense and occupy every point of a small room. The said Father therefore, supposing a room 20 feet long, as many wide, and rising to a height of 15 feet, affirms, having made the calculation, that the particles

Part. 2. Physic. Gener. num. 128.

Pt. 2, General Physics, no. 128.

p. 59

particularum fumi in cubiculo reipsa contentarum 75,000,000,000,000, quae omnes uno exiguo thuris granulo conclusae antea, adhuc tamen tantae sunt, ut olfatum hominis adficere queant.

of smoke actually contained in the room will be 75,000,000,000,000, all of which, though previously shut up in one tiny grain of incense, are nevertheless still so many that they can affect a man’s sense of smell.

159 Reple Phialam A (Fig. VI.) colli recurvi quae Aeolypila dicitur, aqua rosarum, aut alia qualibet odóra, suppone ignem, vel thecam B, in qua sit spiritus vini cum ellychnio accenso, brevè evaporabit aqua per exíle collum, & odor per integrum, & si latum cubiculum diffundetur. Post duo, aut tria minuta rémove ab igne phialam, & obtúra, vix sensibilis erit aquae diminutio, ita ut minima ejus quantitas per totum aërem cubiculi dispersa sit. Jam verò calculo facto ab erudito P. Johanne de Turre 2 Viro in rimandis naturae arcanis perspicacissimo compertum est, quod illa minima aquae portio quae tempore trium minutorum evaporavit, resolvitur in particulas naribus sensibiles 3,583,180,800, quod sanè omnem superat captum.

159 Fill the vial A (Fig. VI) with a bent neck, which is called an Aeolipile, with rose water or any other fragrant water; put a fire under it, or the case B, in which there is spirit of wine with a lighted wick; the water will soon evaporate through the slender neck, and the odor will be diffused through the whole room, however large. After two or three minutes remove the vial from the fire and stop it up: the diminution of the water will scarcely be sensible, so that a very small quantity of it has been dispersed through the whole air of the room. Now, by a calculation made by the learned Fr. Giovanni della Torre (p), a man most perspicacious in searching out the secrets of nature, it has been ascertained that that very small portion of water which evaporated in the space of three minutes is resolved into 3,583,180,800 particles sensible to the nostrils, which truly surpasses all comprehension.

160 Odóres fragrantium camporum insulae Ceylán ad decem etiam leucarum distantiam versus navigia appropinquantia deferuntur. Exigua moschi particula odore ita imbuit alia corpora majora, vestes, chyrothécas, libros, ut per longissimum tempus odorem servent, & tamen continuò nunquam non partes odoriferas exibeant. Plura similia referuntur á Boyleo, Keilio, S'Graversandio, & aliis Physicis Quum verò tot perpetuò diffluentibus particulis odoratis, nullum sensibile substantiae dispendium in pluribus observari possit, incredibiliter subtilia, effluvia haec esse oportebit.

160 The odors of the fragrant fields of the island of Ceylon are carried toward approaching ships even at a distance of ten leagues. A tiny particle of musk so imbues other larger bodies — clothes, gloves, books — with its odor that they keep the odor for a very long time, and yet continually never cease to give off odoriferous parts. Many similar things are related by Boyle, Keill, ’s Gravesande, and other Physicists. Since, then, with so many odorous particles perpetually flowing off, no sensible loss of substance can be observed in many cases, these effluvia will have to be incredibly subtle.

161 Secundò ostenditur ex tincturis. Laudatus Boyle expertum se refert, quod si granum cupri dissolutum, & spiritu vini permixtum infundatur lampadi cujus ellychnium ex plumóso alúmine efformatum non consumitur, per semihoram integram flamma caeruleo colore tincta producitur, adeòque semper novae cupri particulae sibi succedunt, eundemque in flamma colorem efficiunt: ita ut mirari satis non possimus, qua ratione particula illa cupri tam minutim concídi potuerit, ut novum semper colorem, hoc est novas semper particulas suppéditet.

161 Secondly, it is shown from tinctures. The said Boyle relates that he found by experience that if a grain of copper, dissolved and mixed with spirit of wine, is poured into a lamp whose wick, made of plume alum, is not consumed, a flame tinged with a blue color is produced for a whole half hour; and so new particles of copper continually succeed one another and produce the same color in the flame: so that we cannot sufficiently wonder by what means that particle of copper could have been cut up so minutely as to supply always new color, that is, always new particles.

162 Tertiò idem evincitur ex ductilitate auri, nam ut celeberrimus Physicus Reaumurius s2 testatur: uncia auri cubica in tenuissima folia quadrata, plusquam quingenties centena millia à bracteatoribus contunditur, sed quod omnem prorsus imaginationis vim superat, si unum ex his foliis argenteo cylindro circumvolvatur, & totum illius superficiem ambiat, deindè cylindrus ejusmodi per plura foramina sensim, ac successivè angustiora trajiciatur, donec ad tenuissimi fili, vel capilli crassitiem redigatur, ubique tamen haec longissimi fili superficies inaurata adparebit, quod

162 Thirdly, the same is proved from the ductility of gold; for, as the most celebrated Physicist Réaumur (q) testifies, a cubic ounce of gold is beaten out by the gold-beaters into more than five hundred times a hundred thousand square leaves of the utmost thinness; but, what altogether surpasses every power of the imagination, if one of these leaves is wrapped round a silver cylinder and covers its whole surface, and the cylinder is then drawn gradually through several successively narrower holes until it is reduced to the thickness of a very fine thread, or of a hair, the surface of this very long thread will nevertheless appear gilded everywhere, which

Magist. Nat. & Art. Tract. 1. Lib. 1. cap. 1. Obs. 4.

Magist. Nat. & Art., Tract. 1, bk. 1, ch. 1, Obs. 4.

Elem. Physic. Tom. 1. n. 135.

Elem. Physic., vol. 1, no. 135.

p. 60

certè fieri non potest, ut inito cálculo demonstratur nisi unicum granum auri ad duas circiter leucas extendatur.

certainly cannot happen, as is shown when the calculation is made, unless a single grain of gold is extended to about two leagues.

163 Quartò ex observationibus microscopicis abyssus exilitatis materiae demonstratur. Observatum â se refert P. de Lanis 2, animalculum albissimum, quod oculis licèt perspicacissimis invisibile fuerat, microscopio viginti septem millionibus vicium augente objectum, grano triticeo videbatur aequale: velocissimo motu per duodecim minuta secunda temporis, vix grani triticei longitudinem confécit. ¿Quaenam ergo in ejusmodi animalculo passuum, quaenam pedum, quae oculorum, quae pupillae, quae sanguinis, quae spirituum animalium mira subtilitas esse debet! Idem dicendum de tenuissimis illis animalculis, qui in caseo, ope microscopii cernuntur. Quantula autèm est eorum animalculorum pupilla, per quam tamen longè tenuiores luminis radii transeunt? ¿Quantulae sunt eae partes quae spiritus animales possunt nominari? Haec si consideremus, fateamur necessè est, ampliùs quiddam, ac quod nostra nobis imaginandi facultas sistere queat, in minimis recondi.

163 Fourthly, an abyss of minuteness in matter is demonstrated from microscopic observations. Fr. Lana Terzi (r) relates that he observed a very white animalcule which had been invisible to even the most perspicacious eyes, and which, placed under a microscope magnifying twenty-seven million times, appeared equal to a grain of wheat: with a very swift motion it scarcely covered the length of a grain of wheat in twelve seconds of time. What, then, must be the wondrous subtlety of the steps, of the feet, of the eyes, of the pupil, of the blood, of the animal spirits in an animalcule of this kind! The same must be said of those very fine animalcules which are seen in cheese with the help of a microscope. How tiny, moreover, is the pupil of those animalcules, through which nevertheless far finer rays of light pass? How tiny are those parts which can be called animal spirits? If we consider these things, we must needs confess that something greater, and more than our faculty of imagining can present to us, lies hidden in the smallest things.

164 Solertissimus Naturae indagator Lewenhoek in aqua per aliquot dies adservata, exquisiti microscopii ope, minima observavit animalcula, quorum millia, vulgaris arenae globuli magnitúdinem non excedunt. Jam quum animalculum quodvis sit corpus organicum, perpendamus paulispèr; quàm delicatae, & subtiles debent esse partes ad ipsum constituendum, & ad vitalem actionem conservandam necessariae. Haud facilè concipitur, quo pacto in tam angusto spatiolo comprehendi possint cor, quod vitae fons est, músculi ad motum necessarii, glandulae, ventriculus, & intestina, aliaque membra innumera, sine quibus animal esse non potest. Praeterea, quum singula memorata membra sint etiam corpora organica, aliis carére non possunt partibus ad suas actiones necessariis. Constabunt ergo ex fibris, membránulis, túnicis, venis, arteriis, nervis, & his similibus canaliculis, quorum éxilitas imaginationis vires longè superat. At his infinitae propèmodum minores esse debent partes fluidi, quod per canaliculos decurrit, nempè sanguis, lympha, & spiritus animales. ¡Quanta in vilissimo animalculo portenta, Divinaeque Omnipotentiae argumenta!

164 That most skillful investigator of Nature, Leeuwenhoek, observed in water kept for some days, with the help of an exquisite microscope, very small animalcules, thousands of which do not exceed the size of a globule of common sand. Now since any animalcule whatever is an organic body, let us weigh for a little how delicate and subtle must be the parts necessary to constitute it and to preserve its vital action. It is not easily conceived how in so narrow a little space there can be comprised the heart, which is the fount of life, the muscles necessary for motion, the glands, the stomach and intestines, and innumerable other members without which an animal cannot exist. Moreover, since each of the members mentioned is also an organic body, they cannot lack other parts necessary for their actions. They will therefore consist of fibers, little membranes, tunics, veins, arteries, nerves, and similar little canals, whose minuteness far surpasses the powers of the imagination. But almost infinitely smaller than these must be the parts of the fluid which runs through the little canals, namely the blood, the lymph and the animal spirits. What prodigies in the meanest animalcule, and what proofs of the Divine Omnipotence!

165 Nec tantum naturae opera admirabilem materiae subtilitatem manifestò demonstrant, artis etiam opera celebratissima idem evincunt, admirationeque nos complére jure merito debent. Cl. Derham, 2 P. Klaus, 2 & Sigaud de la Fond s4 referunt, quod Oswaldus Nerlinger conformavit è grano píperis scyphum in quo inserti erant mille ducenti caliculi eburnei, quorum singuli

165 Nor do the works of nature alone manifestly demonstrate the admirable subtlety of matter: the most celebrated works of art also prove the same, and must with full justice fill us with admiration. The distinguished Derham (s), Fr. Klaus (t) and Sigaud de la Fond (u) relate that Oswald Nerlinger fashioned out of a peppercorn a cup in which were set twelve hundred little ivory cups, each of which was furnished with a stand

Memoires de l' Academ. 1713.

Memoires de l’Academ., 1713.

Magist. Nat. & Art. Praefat.

Magist. Nat. & Art., Preface.

p. 61

sustentaculo instructi, & inaurato margine ornati erant, tanto adhuc relicto spatio, ut quatuor centum alii consimiles potuerint ímponi.

and adorned with a gilded rim, so much space being still left over that four hundred others like them could have been put in.

166 Atque haec pauca è multis quae adjici possent ad commonstrandam summam continui divisibilitatem, exilitatemque materiae à nobis proposita, iis verbis concludimus, quibus suam de insectis tractationem ordítur Plinius s1: rerum, scilicèt, naturam nusquam magis, quàm in minimis sitam esse. Àgnoscimus etiam, & cum Magno Augustino s2 profitemur: Deum ita esse magnum in operibus magnis, ut minor non sit in minimis.

166 And these few things, out of the many that could be added, which we have put forward to show the extreme divisibility of the continuum and the minuteness of matter, we conclude with those words with which Pliny (x) begins his treatment of insects: that the nature of things, namely, is nowhere more to be found than in the smallest things. We acknowledge also, and profess with the great Augustine (y), that God is so great in his great works that he is not less in the least.

CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

De Corporum porositate.

On the porosity of bodies.

167 Per poros corporum intelligimus, intervalla, cavitates, atque foramina, sivè visibilia, sivè invisibilia, quae passim occurrunt in omnibus corporibus, sive ea sint fluida, sive sint mollia sive dura. Oriuntur autem pori ex coagmentatione minimorum corpusculorum corpora visibilia constituentium. Ea enim ob suas figuras vix unquam sic jungi possunt, ut omninò congruant inter se, neque ullas cavitates, atque forámina relinquant ab aliqua materia subtili corpori extranea occupanda. Finge ex. gr. minima corpuscula quae corpus aliquod componunt, sphaerica esse, jam singulae tres sphaerae tangent se in tribus punctis, atque relinquent in medio spatium triangulare, quapropter in corpore erunt innumeri ejusmodi pori triangulares à materia aliqua subtilissima repleti.

y the pores of bodies we understand the intervals, cavities and openings, 167 B whether visible or invisible, which occur everywhere in all bodies, whether these be fluid, or soft, or hard. Pores arise, moreover, from the joining together of the smallest corpuscles that constitute visible bodies. For these, on account of their figures, can scarcely ever be so joined that they fit one another altogether and leave no cavities and openings to be occupied by some subtle matter foreign to the body. Imagine, e.g., that the smallest corpuscles which compose some body are spherical: then every three spheres will touch one another in three points and will leave a triangular space in the middle; wherefore there will be in the body innumerable triangular pores of this kind, filled with some very subtle matter.

168 Idem erit si corpuscula minima componentia aliarum figurarum esse statuantur, nisi quod poros etiam longè diversarum figurarum ex eorum corpusculorum coagmentatione suboriri necesse est. Pori autem ut plurimum sunt adeò minimi, ut sensibus non percipiantur. Sensuum igitur judicio standum non est, ut determinemus, quantum materiae solidae in quolibet corpore inveniatur. Fieri enim potest, ut duo corpora mole aequalia, sub eorum superficie eandem materiae quantitatem continére videantur, & tamen in altérutro ex his vix aliquid materiae inveniatur. His positis.

168 It will be the same if the smallest component corpuscles are laid down to be of other figures, except that pores of very different figures as well must necessarily arise from the joining together of those corpuscles. Pores, moreover, are for the most part so very small that they are not perceived by the senses. We must not, therefore, abide by the judgment of the senses in determining how much solid matter is found in any body. For it can happen that two bodies equal in bulk seem to contain the same quantity of matter beneath their surface, and yet in one of the two scarcely any matter is found. These things laid down,

169 Dico: Corpora omnia sive magna, sive parva, dura aeque, ac liquida innumeris poris pertusa sunt. Probatur: admittenda est summa illorum corporum porósitas, quam facta in unoquoque

169 I say: all bodies, whether large or small, hard as well as liquid, are pierced through with innumerable pores. Proof: the greatest porosity of those bodies must be admitted which experiments made in each body demonstrate:

Thelogie Physique. Lib. 8. c. 4. not. 11.

Théologie Physique, bk. 8, ch. 4, note 11.

Phys Gener. Part. 2. n. 127.

Phys. Gener., pt. 2, no. 127.

Leçons de Physique. Tom. 1. pag. 64.

Leçons de Physique, vol. 1, p. 64.

Hist. Nat. Lib. 11. cap. 2.

Natural History, bk. 11, ch. 2.

Lib. 21. cont. Faust. cap. 5.

Bk. 21, Against Faustus, ch. 5.

p. 62

corpore experimenta demonstrant; sed experimenta plurima ostendunt corpora omnia innumeris poris esse pertusa: ergo Probatur minor: & ut à corporibus diaphanis incipiamus, de eorum summa porositate satis superque constat ex eo, quod ipsa lucem transmittunt, quum tamen si corpora ista innumeris poris non essent pertusa, transitum lucis radiis forent denegatura. Quapropter aër; aqua, vitrum, crystallum, ádamas reliquique lapides pellucidi innumeris poris referti esse debent, nam pelluciditas intelligi non potest, nisi ad opposita superficierum puncta radiis lucis pateat facilis transitus. Hinc evidens est, crystallum ex. gr. nihil ferè materiae omninò solidae continere.

demonstrate: but very many experiments show that all bodies are pierced through with innumerable pores: therefore. The minor is proved; and, to begin with diaphanous bodies, their very great porosity is more than sufficiently established from the fact that they transmit light, whereas, if these bodies were not pierced through with innumerable pores, they would deny passage to the rays of light. Wherefore air, water, glass, crystal, diamond and the other pellucid stones must be filled with innumerable pores; for pellucidity cannot be understood unless an easy passage lies open for the rays of light to the opposite points of the surfaces. Hence it is evident that crystal, e.g., contains almost nothing whatever of solid matter.

170 Jam verò quoniam partes minimae omnium corporum adparent aliquomodò pellucidae ut microscopio observatur; inde fit, ut corpora etiam opaca suis poris destituta non sint, nam si partes minimae ex quibus ea coalescunt, sunt porosae, porosa quoque sint oportet, corpora ex illis partibus minimis composita. Jam de singulis corporibus dicamus.

170 Now, since the smallest parts of all bodies appear in some measure pellucid, as is observed with the microscope, it follows that opaque bodies too are not devoid of their pores; for if the smallest parts of which they grow together are porous, the bodies composed of those smallest parts must also be porous. Let us now speak of particular bodies.

171 Ligna quamtumvis compacta, & dura, porosa esse arguit nutritionis ratio, quae fieri non posset, nisi fibrae lignae essent perforatae, ut nempè, transitum succo è radicibus adscendenti permittere possint. Testae quamvis coctae, & durae adeò sunt porosae, ut liquoris immissi particulas facilè bibant, & odorem ejus diutissimè servent. Adsunt etiam lapides crassi, compactique, qui aquam transmittunt, & ex illis fiunt mortaria per quae aqua percolatur, ut lutulentis partibus purgetur Effluvia magnetica transeunt per lignum, vitrum, & metalla: nam si super lamina aliqua vitrea, lignea, aut metallica statuatur ferrum, aut chálybis fragmenta exigua, magnes vero infra laminam quocumque modo moveatur, videbitis ferrum agitari ad motum magnetis.

171 That woods, however compact and hard, are porous is argued by the manner of their nourishment, which could not take place unless the woody fibers were perforated, so that, namely, they can allow passage to the sap ascending from the roots. Earthenware vessels, though baked and hard, are so porous that they easily drink in the particles of a liquid poured into them, and keep its odor a very long time. There are also thick and compact stones which transmit water, and from them are made mortars through which water is strained, that it may be purged of its muddy parts. Magnetic effluvia pass through wood, glass and metals: for if iron, or small fragments of steel, are placed on some plate of glass, wood or metal, and the magnet is moved in any way whatever below the plate, you will see the iron stirred by the motion of the magnet.

172 Durissima etiam marmora â fluidis plurimis penetrantur, â spiritu vini, à spiritu terebinthinae, ut in Monumentis Academiae Regiae Parisiensis testatur Clariss. Dufay 2. Clariss. Homberg s2 detexit salem expressum ê mixturis calcis vivae, aceti distillati, salis petrae, salis marini, & sulfuris communis penetrare ferrum non secùs, atque aqua papyrum permeat.

172 The hardest marbles, too, are penetrated by very many fluids, by spirit of wine, by spirit of turpentine, as the most distinguished Dufay testifies in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (z). The most distinguished Homberg (a) discovered that a salt extracted from mixtures of quicklime, distilled vinegar, saltpeter, sea salt and common sulfur penetrates iron no otherwise than water permeates paper.

173 Clariss. item Reaumurius modum ostendit ova recentia conservandi, hocque suggerit consilium, ut pori minimi, & innumeri in córtice ovi existentes crusta tali obducantur, quae ab aqua dissolvi nequeat, consistentiamque habeat, ut ne â particulis, quae ex ovo erúmpere nituntur, & evaporarent, solvatur. Huic usui oportuna erit pinguedo vérvecum, cera ad liquiditatem calefacta, aut vernix communis aliquoties superinducta. Certè Nolletus s3

173 The most distinguished Réaumur likewise shows a method of preserving fresh eggs, and suggests this plan: that the very small and innumerable pores existing in the shell of the egg be covered over with a coating that cannot be dissolved by water and has such consistency that it is not loosened by the particles which strive to burst out of the egg and would evaporate. Suitable for this use will be mutton fat, wax heated until liquid, or common varnish laid on several times. Certainly Nollet (b) found by experience,

Memoires de l' Academ. 1728. 1732.

Memoires de l’Academ., 1728, 1732.

Histoire de l' Academ. 1713.

[a] Histoire de l’Academ., 1713.

p. 63

expertum se scribit ova hoc modo sex etiam mensium spatio conservatá fuisse, ne minimo quidem ingrato sapore vitiata. Servit haec praxis longiori tempore mare navigantibus, & ad adsportandas etiam in nostra regna aves peregrinas, quae vivae non sine summa molestia per tot terrarum, & aequoris tractus transveherentur.

he writes, that eggs were preserved in this way even for the space of six months, without being spoiled by even the least unpleasant taste. This practice serves those who sail the sea for a longer time, and also for bringing into our kingdoms foreign birds, which would not be carried alive across so many stretches of land and sea without the greatest trouble.

174 Describam etiam vobis, ut magis adpareat corporum porositas atramentum quod simpaticum vulgò â Chymicis nuncupatur. Hoc autèm modo parari solet. Lithargyri uncia una sumatur, quae cum aceti distillati uncis quinque vel sex misceatur, & per chartam de more percoletur. Hoc liquore, qui acetum saturni, sive impregnatio saturni facta cum aceto distillato á Chymicis adpellatur, utendum est ad exarandos charactéres, quos non magis conspicietis, quàm si aqua scripséritis, verùm si adhibeatur liquor alius mox dicendo artificio comparandus, jam charactéres fiunt conspicui. Capiatur itaque auripigmenti uncia una, quae cum calcis vivae uncis duabus misceatur, mixturae immitatur aqua, habebitur liquor alter, quo imbuenda est charta aliqua charactéribus antea descriptis exarata, centum etiam interpositis chartarum foliis, statim hujus liquoris particulae multa permeant chartae folia, & charactéres, qui antea oculos fugiébant praeclarè nigros legétis, atque mirabimini.

174 I will also describe for you, so that the porosity of bodies may appear more clearly, the ink which is commonly called sympathetic by the Chemists. It is usually prepared in this way. Let one ounce of litharge be taken and mixed with five or six ounces of distilled vinegar, and let it be filtered through paper in the usual way. This liquor, which is called by the Chemists vinegar of Saturn, or impregnation of Saturn made with distilled vinegar, is to be used for tracing characters, which you will no more perceive than if you had written with water; but if another liquor is applied, to be prepared by an artifice presently to be described, the characters at once become visible. Let one ounce of orpiment therefore be taken and mixed with two ounces of quicklime; let water be poured onto the mixture: there will be had a second liquor, with which some paper inscribed with the characters previously traced is to be moistened; even with a hundred sheets of paper placed in between, the particles of this liquor at once pass through the many sheets of paper, and you will read, splendidly black, the characters which before escaped the eyes, and you will marvel.

175 Magis autèm mirabimini ipsum quoque hydrargyrum per poros ligni transire: etenìm si fiat vasculum cylindricum C B A (Fig. VII.) eique tubus vitreus immitatur trium circiter pedum, còchlea E in D instructus qui per aperturam in basi vasculi cochlea lignea munitam hydrargyro repletur, aperto foraminulo in D cóchlea E remota, ut aëris externi pressio in hydrargyrum non intercipiatur, jocundo spectaculo mercurius per poros ligni in G F erumpit, quod si pars G F unde hydrargyrum effluit microscopio observetur, non minori jucunditate sese expectanda praebent foraminula rotunda ordine disposita, ut refert Thumigg in Institutionibus Philosophiae Wolffianae s1

175 But you will marvel more that quicksilver itself also passes through the pores of wood: for if a little cylindrical vessel C B A (Fig. VII) is made, and a glass tube about three feet long, furnished with a screw E at D, is inserted into it, which is filled with quicksilver through an opening in the base of the little vessel fitted with a wooden screw, then, the little hole at D being opened and the screw E removed, so that the pressure of the external air upon the quicksilver may not be intercepted, the mercury bursts out through the pores of the wood at G F in a delightful spectacle; and if the part G F from which the quicksilver flows out is observed with a microscope, little round holes arranged in order present themselves, to be looked at with no less delight, as Thümmig reports in the Institutions of the Wolffian Philosophy (c).

176 Fluidorum etiam porositas indè facilè colligitur, quod fluida quaedam se invicem imbibant. Repleatur vas ad tres pollices altitudinis oleo vitrioli, cui addatur tantundem aquae, indè claudatur, ne aliquid in eorumdem effervescentia évaporet, fermentatione sedata, non sex pollices altitudinis, sed minores numero habebitis: Praeterea si intra vas quodlibet sint duo pollices altitudinis arenae, & iis admisceatis duos pollices altitudinis aquae, habebitis non quatuor, sed duos tantum pollices materiae. Longus essem si phaenomena omnia, quae presens argumentum exornare possent, hìc vellem describere.

176 The porosity of fluids too is easily gathered from the fact that certain fluids imbibe one another. Let a vessel be filled to a height of three inches with oil of vitriol, let as much water be added to it, then let it be closed, so that nothing may evaporate in their effervescence: when the fermentation has subsided, you will have not six inches of height, but a smaller number. Moreover, if within any vessel there are two inches’ height of sand, and you mix with them two inches’ height of water, you will have not four, but only two inches of matter. I should be long if I wished to describe here all the phenomena that could adorn the present subject.

177 Tantum advertam, contingere interdùm, ut aliqua corpora transitum nonnullis effluviis praebeant, aliis dénegent: id quod contingere putandum est, tum ex peculiari quadam pororum

177 I will only note that it sometimes happens that some bodies afford passage to certain effluvia and deny it to others: which must be thought to happen both from a certain peculiar configuration of the pores,

Leçons de Physique. Tom. 1.

Leçons de Physique, vol. 1.

Instit. Philosoph. Exp. §. 247. & seq.

Instit. Philosoph. Exp., §. 247 ff.

p. 64

configuratione, tum ex effluviorum magnitudine, atque figura. Sic si oleum de cera extractum, sulphuris quinta essentia ambo sanè odoratissima, ampulla vitrea diligenter adserventur, quanquam magnopere ampullam agitaveris, aut ad ignis praesentiam calefacias, tamen nullum, vel tenuissimi odoris halitum praebent. Quod si odores vitrum non prevadunt, desinamus mirari si minus subtiles aquae partes vitri poros non subeant, ut â sapientissimis Academiae Florentinae viris, luculentissimo experimento comprobatum est.

and from the size and figure of the effluvia. Thus, if oil extracted from wax and quintessence of sulfur, both certainly very odorous, are carefully kept in a glass flask, even though you shake the flask a great deal or warm it before the fire, they nevertheless give off no exhalation, even of the faintest odor. And if odors do not penetrate glass, let us cease to wonder if the less subtle parts of water do not enter the pores of glass, as has been proved by a most splendid experiment by the very learned men of the Florentine Academy.

178 Pororum igitur multiplex est necessitas, & usus in natura. Primò in generationibus plantarum, dum calore, & humore plántulae semen subeunte illud evolvitur, similiter in animalium productionibus, nempè, gallina ovo incubans non alia ratione, quàm calore poros corticis subeunte, & penetrante pullum excludit. Secundo, in nutritionibus, siquidem per eos conveniens alimentum, & succi in partes singulas amandantur. Tertio, ut cetera omittam, fermentationes, nempè diversas rarefactiones, motus magneticos aliosque effectus ad quos praestandos, explicandosque minima haec interstitia mirum quantùm conducunt, maximi ea usus sunt ad excernendos in animalibus noxios, & superfluos humores, quod perspiratione efficitur de qua in cap. seq. agemus. Atque hactenùs de porositate, quae est proprietas corporibus omnibus communis.

178 Manifold, therefore, is the necessity and use of pores in nature. First, in the generation of plants, while the little seed of the plant is unfolded by the heat and moisture entering it; similarly in the production of animals: namely, a hen sitting on an egg hatches the chick by no other means than by the heat that enters and penetrates the pores of the shell. Secondly, in nourishment, since through them suitable nourishment and juices are sent off to the single parts. Thirdly, to omit the rest — fermentations, namely, various rarefactions, magnetic motions and other effects, for producing and explaining which these minute interstices contribute wonderfully — they are of the greatest use for excreting harmful and superfluous humors in animals, which is effected by perspiration, of which we shall treat in the following chapter. And thus far of porosity, which is a property common to all bodies.

Argumenta solvuntur.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

179 Opp. 1. Si corpora omnia innumeris poris pertusa sunt, jam absoluta corporum pondera non cognoscimus: ignota enim est materiae quantitas, ac proinde, & ignotum pondus quod materiae quantitati proportinale est; atqui id repugnare videtur: ergo. Conc. maj. neg. min.: nullum etenim inveniri potest corpus perfectè solidum, ut ex dictis fit manifestum, quod quidem si invenire licéret, jam innótesceret quantitas materiae in singulis corporibus, illorumque proindè pondus absolutum, conferendo scilicet datam aliquam materiae portionem, cum pari volumine diversorum corporum.

179 Obj. 1. If all bodies are pierced through with innumerable pores, then we do not know the absolute weights of bodies: for the quantity of matter is unknown, and hence also the weight, which is proportional to the quantity of matter; but this seems contradictory: therefore. I grant the major, deny the minor: for no perfectly solid body can be found, as is manifest from what has been said; and if one could indeed be found, the quantity of matter in each body, and hence its absolute weight, would at once become known, namely by comparing some given portion of matter with an equal volume of different bodies.

180 Quamobrem, quum tali corpore perfectè solidum nusquam inveniatur, superfluis conjecturis indulgent otiosi Philosophi, qui ficititiis hypothesibus materiae quantitatem determinare conantur, imò totum hoc universum ex materiae quantitate valdè exigua constare, probabilissimum est. Sed dices: saltim aurum erit corpus perfectè solidum: ergo falsum est quod hactenùs diximus. Nego antec. aurum enim aquam nedum mercurium, cujus partes proculdubio subtiliores sunt, per se transmittit, ut testatur Clariss. Martini s1 nam globus aureus concavus aqua repletus, ac deincèps magna vi

180 Wherefore, since such a perfectly solid body is nowhere found, those idle Philosophers indulge in superfluous conjectures who attempt to determine the quantity of matter by fictitious hypotheses; nay, it is most probable that this whole universe consists of a very small quantity of matter. But you will say: at least gold will be a perfectly solid body: therefore what we have said thus far is false. I deny the antecedent: for gold of itself transmits water, not to say mercury, whose parts are doubtless subtler, as the most distinguished Martini testifies (d); for a hollow golden globe filled with water, and then, with great force compressed,

p. 65

compressus exudavit undiquè aquam, innumerisque guttulis exiguis, tanquam rorulentus undiquè stillavit, tametsi aurum ipsum interea nulla sui parte rimas égerit. Praeterea aurum á tenuissimis aquae regiae particulis penetratur facillimè, quod fieri non posset nisi poros habeat.

compressed, exuded water on every side, and dripped everywhere with innumerable tiny droplets as though bedewed, although the gold itself meanwhile had cracked in no part of it. Moreover, gold is very easily penetrated by the very fine particles of aqua regia, which could not happen unless it had pores.

181 Opp. 2. Si tanta sit corporum porositas, in errorem nos perpetuò índucerent sensuum organa, falsisque sensationibus nos perpetuo deciperet Deus O. M. sed haec illusio Divinae veracitati repugnat: ergo. Nego maj. plurimae enim sensuum fallaciae per ratiocinationem philosophicam ad examen revocari, atque emendari possunt, nec sensibus témerè credendum est, ut diximus in Logica. Non est judicium veritatis in sensibus, ait S. Augustinus. Itaque Deus O. M. ad sensuum errorem nos minimè cogit, nam infinitae ejus Bonitati placuit eas tantùm hominibus cóncedere cognitiones, quae ad justas vitae hujus utilitates, & ad finem ultimum, vitam scilicet, aeternam perducere possunt.

181 Obj. 2. If the porosity of bodies were so great, the organs of the senses would perpetually lead us into error, and God, Best and Greatest, would perpetually deceive us by false sensations; but this illusion is contrary to the Divine veracity: therefore. I deny the major: for very many fallacies of the senses can be called back to examination and corrected by philosophical reasoning, and the senses must not be rashly believed, as we said in the Logic. The judgment of truth is not in the senses, says St. Augustine. God, Best and Greatest, therefore by no means drives us into the error of the senses; for it pleased his infinite Goodness to grant to men only those cognitions which can lead to the just uses of this life and to the ultimate end, namely eternal life.

CAPUT V.

CHAPTER V.

De transpiratione corporum.

On the transpiration of bodies.

182 Corporis effluvia dicuntur corpuscula quaedam subtilissima, quae ex corporis poris erumpunt, & quoquoversus veluti in orbem disperguntur. Motus autem quo corpus effluvia emittit, Transpiratio nuncupatur. Transpirare namque dicitur corpus quod subtilissimam substantiam exhalat. Atmosphaéra corporis est spatium ab illius effluviis veluti in orbem circa ipsum corpus diffusis occupatum; ut si corpus X. (Fig. VIII.) effluvia extra se diffundat, quae repleant spatium A B C D, ipsumque proinde corpus circumambiant, spatium éxtima superficie A B C D comprehensum, erit ipsius corporis atmosphéra (nempè halituum, aut vaporis sphaera). Omnia ergo corpora quae effluvia emittunt atmosphaéra praédita sunt. His constitutis.

he effluvia of a body are said to be certain very subtle corpuscles 182 T which burst out of the pores of the body and are scattered in every direction as if in a circle. The motion, moreover, by which a body emits effluvia is called Transpiration. For a body is said to transpire which exhales a very subtle substance. The Atmosphere of a body is the space occupied by its effluvia diffused as if in a circle around the body itself; so that, if the body X (Fig. VIII) diffuses outside itself effluvia which fill the space A B C D and hence surround the body itself, the space comprised by the outermost surface A B C D will be the atmosphere of that body (namely, the sphere of its exhalations, or of vapor). All bodies, therefore, which emit effluvia are endowed with an atmosphere. These things being established,

183 Dico igitur: nullum propè videtur esse corpus mixtum in natura, quod vel continuò non transpiret, vel (quamquam non idem est) ex quo profluvia quaedam non ávolent. Dixi non idem esse transpirare, & profluvia emittere: quoniam primum solum convenit corporibus vita animali, aut vegetabili praéditis, alterum etiam vitae expertibus. Probatur observationibus, & experimentis. Sicuti enim nullum est corpus sensibile quod poris careat, quodque aliquid subtilissimae substantiae non complectatur: ita nullum

183 I say, therefore: there seems to be scarcely any mixed body in nature which does not either continually transpire, or (though it is not the same thing) from which certain outflowings do not fly off. I said that to transpire and to emit outflowings are not the same: because the first belongs only to bodies endowed with animal or vegetable life, the other also to those devoid of life. It is proved by observations and experiments. For just as there is no sensible body which lacks pores and which does not contain something of a very subtle substance, so likewise none

Instit. Philosoph. Rat. tom. 1. n. 59.

Instit. Philosoph. Rat., vol. 1, no. 59.

p. 66

quoque videtur esse ex cujus poris aliqua illius substantiae portio continuò non erumpat spontè, vel ab ipso auferatur impetu alterius corporis incurrentis. Sed hoc ipsum speciatim de diversis corporibus evincamus. Quoad animalia patet ex canum sagacitate qui feram longiùs etiam absentem ob effluvia per viam relicta consequúntur, magis etiam patebit ex adducendis infra Sanctorii, & Dodarti observationibus. De plantis idem adfirmant Physici cum P. de Lanis, & Malpighi.

seems to exist from whose pores some portion of its substance does not continually burst out of its own accord, or is not carried off from it by the impetus of another body running against it. But let us prove this very thing specifically of different bodies. As regards animals, it is plain from the sagacity of dogs, which follow a wild beast even when it is far away by the effluvia left along its path; it will be still more plain from the observations of Sanctorius and Dodart to be adduced below. The Physicists affirm the same of plants, with Fr. Lana Terzi and Malpighi.

184 Profectò non alia redditur ratio, cur plantae dum aër vehementius calet, inclinentur, & flaccescant, aëre verò refrigerato vigére, recrearique incipiant, quàm quod occulta haec expiratio ab aestu effecta, ingentem corpusculorum copiam plantis eripiat: quo fit, ut exhauriantur, & laxentur fibrae, firmitatem suam amittant defectuque corpusculorum, ac spirituum, qui túbulos fibrarum sustentant, gravitatis tandem viribus cédere cogantur, quod maximè in heliotropio elucescit. Ut nihil de odore, quem corpora maximè vegetabilia quaquaversùm diffundunt vobis commémorem.

184 Truly no other reason is given why plants, while the air is very hot, droop and wither, but, when the air has cooled, begin to flourish and revive, than that this hidden expiration, brought about by the heat, robs the plants of a huge quantity of corpuscles; whence it comes about that the fibers are exhausted and slackened, lose their firmness, and, through the lack of the corpuscles and of the spirits which sustain the little tubes of the fibers, are at length forced to yield to the forces of gravity; which shines forth most of all in the heliotrope. Not to mention to you the odor which vegetable bodies above all diffuse in every direction.

185 Quod adtinet ad complura mixta, ex. gr. vinum, spiritum vini, aliaque ejusmodi, quae actuosa abundant substantia, evidens est, si per notabile tempus libero aëri exposita fuerint, multum talia mixta debilitari manifesto indicio, multum actuosae substantiae per avolationem subtilissimi vaporis depérditum fuisse. Pondus verò in aliquibus etiam sensibiliter minui, experimentis compluribus ostendit laudatus P. de Lanis 2. De cámphora ita loquitur vir eximius Robertus Boyle s2. Quum in exacta bilance cámphoram librassem, paucarum horarum spatio visibilem ponderis sui jacturam passa fuit corpusculorum avolatione: memorat etiam insignem evaporationem, quam observavit in pomis, nec non in corporibus firmiori tegumento obductis, ut sunt ova, quae in dies manifestò leviora reddebantur, & in aliis corporibus quae diù in bilancibus, observato ponderis eorum decremento detinuerat.

185 As regards very many mixed bodies, e.g. wine, spirit of wine, and others of this kind which abound in active substance, it is evident that, if they have been exposed to the free air for a considerable time, such mixtures are much weakened, a manifest sign that much active substance has been lost through the flying off of a very subtle vapor. That the weight too is in some cases sensibly diminished, the said Fr. Lana Terzi (e) shows by many experiments. Of camphor that eminent man Robert Boyle (f) speaks thus. When I had weighed camphor in an exact balance, in the space of a few hours it suffered a visible loss of its weight through the flying off of corpuscles: he also records a remarkable evaporation which he observed in apples, as well as in bodies covered with a firmer integument, such as eggs, which became manifestly lighter from day to day, and in other bodies which he had kept long in the balances, observing the decrease of their weight.

186 Effluvia per exhalationem emanantia, ut plurimum eundem colorem, sapórem, & odórem rétinent, quae corpora ipsa â quibus ávolant habent. Sic ut cetera omittam, fatetur P. de Lanis, quum salem ex absynthio pararet, manuque linguam tángeret, licèt antea manus absynthium nullomodo contrectasset, eundem tamen prorsùs saporem se percepisse, qui ipsius plantae esse solet, ex salis videlicet halitibus manui adhaerescentibus. Alius, qui singulos in dies pauxillum de spiritu vitrioli potioni suae admixtum sumpserat advertit, claves probè levigatas ad nitórem, quas secum gestabat, ut nunquàm à spiritu hoc contactas, nigredinem, ac rubiginem traxisse. Puella morbo icterico pressa mali citrei colorem vestibus, quibus induebatur, numisque argenteis, quos deferebat ad usum, induxit.

186 Effluvia emanating by exhalation for the most part retain the same color, taste and odor which the bodies themselves from which they fly off possess. Thus, to omit the rest, Fr. Lana Terzi confesses that when he was preparing a salt from wormwood and touched his tongue with his hand, although his hand had previously in no way handled the wormwood, he nevertheless perceived exactly the same taste which belongs to the plant itself, namely from the exhalations of the salt adhering to his hand. Another, who had taken every day a very little spirit of vitriol mixed into his drink, noticed that the keys he carried with him, well polished to brightness, had contracted blackness and rust, although they had never been touched by this spirit. A girl afflicted with jaundice imparted the color of a citron to the clothes she wore and to the silver coins she carried for use.

Magist. Nat. & Art. tom. 2. Lib. 2. c. 1. exp. 129. n. 1.

Magist. Nat. & Art., vol. 2, bk. 2, ch. 1, exp. 129, no. 1.

De atmosphaera corpor. consist.

De atmosphaera corpor. consist.

p. 67

187 Ex dictis infertur 1. Nullum ferè esse corpus mixtum, quod sua atmosphaera non cingatur. Illud enim omne corpus atmosphaera praeditum est, quod effluvia emittit. Infertur 2. nullum existere corpus mixtum, cujus internae subtiliores particulae jugi motu non sint adfectae, licet motus hujusmodi sit exilissimus, sensibusque percipi haud possit. Quum enim materia aetherea jugi in motu constituta, corpus etiam maximè compactum permeet, partes tenues evéllat, & exhalationem quandam excitet, perspicuum videtur, inesse corporibus subtilium quarumdam partium intestinam agitationem, neque haec in solis illis minimis particulis, quae primum per corpus effluunt conquiescit, verùm & aliae, impulsum recipiunt; materia quippe subtilis per poros ingressa, & agitata, particulas alias látera pororum efformantes continuò urget, atque impellit, quo fit, ut modò hanc, modo aliam particulam à reliquo corpore avellat, vinculoque abrupto secum ávehat.

187 From what has been said it is inferred, 1. That there is scarcely any mixed body which is not surrounded by its own atmosphere. For every body that emits effluvia is endowed with an atmosphere. It is inferred, 2. That there exists no mixed body whose internal, subtler particles are not affected with a continual motion, although a motion of this kind may be very slight and can hardly be perceived by the senses. For since the ethereal matter, placed in continual motion, permeates even the most compact body, plucks away its fine parts and excites a certain exhalation, it seems evident that there is in bodies an intestine agitation of certain subtle parts; nor does this come to rest in those smallest particles alone which first flow out through the body, but others too receive an impulse; for the subtle matter, having entered through the pores and being agitated, continually urges and impels other particles that form the sides of the pores, whence it comes about that it plucks away now this, now that particle from the rest of the body and, the bond being broken, carries it off with itself.

188 Infertur 3. Cum Roberto Boyle s1 & de Lanis s2: nullum esse compositum naturale, cujus omnes partes planè quiescant. Patet & ex dictis, & ex eo, quia quum nullum sit corpus, quod sua veluti sponte tandem non corrumpatur; nullum certè horum est, cujus internae subtiliores partes jugiter non moveantur. Sed de transpiratione insensibili in corpore humano ex doctissimo Sanctorio s3 pauca dicamus.

188 It is inferred, 3., with Robert Boyle (g) and Lana Terzi (h): that there is no natural composite all of whose parts are entirely at rest. It is plain both from what has been said and from this, that since there is no body which is not at length corrupted as if of its own accord, there is certainly none of these whose internal, subtler parts are not continually moved. But let us say a few things about insensible transpiration in the human body from the most learned Sanctorius (i).

189 Sanctorius perspirationem insensibilem corporis humani primùm ad calculos revocavit, 30 annis ei observandae insumptis, ex cujus observationibus, quaedam adnotare placuit. Perspiratio insensibilis, magis aufert à corpore 24 horarum spatio, quàm omnes sensibiles evacuationes simul per 15 dies. Hic est aphorismus 4 Sect. 1. Medicinae Staticae Sanctorij. Homines valentes, per hyemem intra 24 horas, 50 uncias transpirant, item intra idem tempus ex assumpto 8 librarum cibo, perspiratio 5 libras aufert. Aphor. 6. Quantitas perspirationis insensibilis aliquam varietatem pátitur, pro varietate naturae, regionis, temporis, aetatis, morborum. Aphor. 7. Quodvis frigus, minimum quidem, quod noctu dormiendo pátimur, impedit perspirationem. Aph 50. Una ex frequentibus causis, quae tempore aestivo impedit perspirationem, est crebra in lecto corporis agitatio. Aph 51.

189 Sanctorius was the first to reduce the insensible perspiration of the human body to calculation, having spent 30 years in observing it; from his observations it has pleased us to note down some things. Insensible perspiration carries off more from the body in the space of 24 hours than all the sensible evacuations together in 15 days. This is aphorism 4 of Sect. 1 of the Medicina Statica of Sanctorius. Healthy men in winter transpire 50 ounces within 24 hours; likewise, within the same time, out of 8 pounds of food taken, perspiration carries off 5 pounds. Aphor. 6. The quantity of insensible perspiration suffers some variety according to the variety of nature, region, season, age, and diseases. Aphor. 7. Any cold, even the slightest, which we suffer while sleeping at night, impedes perspiration. Aph. 50. One of the frequent causes which in summertime impede perspiration is frequent agitation of the body in bed. Aph. 51.

190 In aestate, si corpus jaceat detectum prohibetur perspiratio, unde capitis gravitas, & corporis confractio. Aph. 113. Somnus plácidus adeò favet perspirationi, ut 7 horis, 50 unciae cocti perspirabilis in robustis saepè exhalent. Sect. 4. Aph. 1. Integrum Sanctorij volumen exscriberem, si omnes utilissimas observationes explicare vellem. Erunt fortassè viri planè hospites in Physica, qui

190 In summer, if the body lies uncovered, perspiration is checked, whence heaviness of the head and a feeling of the body being broken. Aph. 113. Placid sleep so favors perspiration that in 7 hours 50 ounces of digested perspirable matter are often exhaled in robust persons. Sect. 4, Aph. 1. I should copy out the whole volume of Sanctorius if I wished to set forth all his most useful observations. There will perhaps be men, plain strangers in Physics, who will confidently
