p. 68

confidenter adferant, parùm, aut nihil utilitatis in his rebus esse, sed iterum vobis dico nolite adduci sermonibus imperitorum. Eo autem unde digressi fuimus, revertamur.

assert that there is little or no usefulness in these matters; but again I say to you: do not be led by the talk of the unskilled. Let us, however, return to the point from which we digressed.

191 Clariss. Dodart 2 Academiae Regiae Parissinae Socius, & Regis Galliae medicus experimentis 33 annorum spatio confectis, stabilivit, majorem longè esse transpirationem in juventute, quàm in alia quavis aetate s2 Ex dictis manifestum est in corporibus nostris velocissimam mutationem cóntingere, atque huic perpetuae vicissitudini obnoxias esse durissimas corporis nostri partes; & quidem nullum est in corpore animali os tàm durum, tàm compactum, quod non nutriatur, ac proinde quod non mutetur, & partem sui amittat, novamque recúperet.

191 The most distinguished Dodart (j), Member of the Royal Academy of Paris and physician to the King of France, established by experiments carried out over a space of 33 years that transpiration is far greater in youth than in any other age (k). From what has been said it is manifest that a very rapid change takes place in our bodies, and that the hardest parts of our body are subject to this perpetual vicissitude; and indeed there is no bone in the animal body so hard, so compact, that it is not nourished, and hence that it is not changed, and does not lose part of itself and recover a new one.

192 ; Ecquis ergo non mirabitur Omnipotentis Dei manum, quae in corporis nostri structura, tot subtilissima disposuit instrumenta ad nutritionem, & evaporationem necessaria! At singulos aetatis humanae gradus diversosque corporis nostri status paulò adtentius contemplemur, magis enim haec utilitatis habent, quàm de adpetitu materiae, aliisque nugis vulgaris philosophiae acriter rixari. In puerili aetate partes sunt tenellae, aqua abundant, infinitisque canaliculis perforatae, quos quidem in ossibus, membranis, cartilaginibus tendinibus, & in cute ipsa demonstrant injectiones anatomicae. Hinc fit, ut vis, quae in corpore animali motus principium est, molliores partes faciliùs extendat. Progressu temporis robustiores fiunt partes, atque solidantur, idque tandiù fit, donec tandem extendendis solidis haud amplius satis sint cordis vires.

192 Who, then, will not marvel at the hand of Almighty God, which in the structure of our body has disposed so many very subtle instruments necessary for nourishment and evaporation! But let us contemplate a little more attentively the single stages of human life and the different states of our body; for these things have more usefulness than quarrelling sharply about the appetite of matter and other trifles of the common philosophy. In childhood the parts are very tender, abound in water, and are perforated with innumerable little canals, which anatomical injections indeed demonstrate in the bones, membranes, cartilages and tendons, and in the skin itself. Hence it comes about that the force which is the principle of motion in the animal body extends the softer parts more easily. With the progress of time the parts become more robust and are solidified, and this goes on until at length the forces of the heart are no longer sufficient for extending the solids.

193 Attamen facile adhuc flexibilis manet cellularis textura multisque in locis pinguedinem, sanguinemque admittit, hinc pinguiores fiunt adulti ad certum usque tempus, nec tamen crescunt. Provecta aetate textura cellularis fit crassior, rigescunt senum ossa, vasa excretoria comprimuntur, secretiones minuuntur, sanguis exsiccatur, & in singulis corporis partibus terrestrem veluti humorem deponit. Hinc partes omnes duriores observantur, hinc crustae osseae in ossium superficie, & maximè in vértebris deprehenduntur.

193 Nevertheless the cellular tissue still remains easily flexible and in many places admits fat and blood; hence adults become fatter up to a certain time, and yet they do not grow. In advanced age the cellular tissue becomes thicker, the bones of old men stiffen, the excretory vessels are compressed, the secretions are diminished, the blood is dried up and deposits a kind of earthy humor in the single parts of the body. Hence all the parts are observed to be harder; hence bony crusts are found on the surface of the bones, and above all in the vertebrae.

Apud Ozanam. Recreat. Mathematiques. Tom. 3.

In Ozanam, Recreat. Mathematiques, vol. 3.

De eodem Dodarto refert Ozanam citatus, factum hìc non incongruè adferendum: quod nempè initio Quadragesimae Dodart 116 libras, & unciam 1. adpénderit, tum sacri jejunii tempus exégerit leguminibus potissimùm victitans. Sabatho dein majoris Hebdomadae rursùs pondus sui corporis exáminans reperit illud non excedere 107 lib. & 12 unc., hoc est 46 dierum spatio amisisse se 8 lib. cum 5 unc. nempè 1/14 partem suae substantiae. Resumpto postea consueto vivendi modo post dies 4, póndere 4 librar. auctus est, Uudè patet, eum 8, vel 9. diebus prístini sui pónderis integritatem recepturum fuisse, atque adeò reparari facilè, id quod jejunio est dissipatum.

Of the same Dodart the said Ozanam relates a fact not unfittingly to be brought forward here: namely that at the beginning of Lent Dodart weighed 116 pounds and 1 ounce, then spent the time of the holy fast living chiefly on legumes. Then on the Saturday of Holy Week, examining the weight of his body again, he found that it did not exceed 107 lb. and 12 oz.; that is, in the space of 46 days he had lost 8 lb. with 5 oz., namely the 1/14 part of his substance. Having afterwards resumed his accustomed manner of living, after 4 days he had gained 4 pounds in weight. Whence it is plain that in 8 or 9 days he would have recovered the integrity of his former weight, and that what is dissipated by fasting is thus easily repaired.

p. 69

His gradibus ad senectutem, mortemque ipsam pérgimus. Solvitur tandem fragilis haec corporis nostri máchina iterum reparanda, & ad meliorem (faxit Deus) aeternamque vitam revocanda. Atque hactenùs de transpiratione.

By these stages we proceed to old age and to death itself. At length this fragile machine of our body is dissolved, to be repaired again and recalled (God grant it) to a better and eternal life. And thus far of transpiration.

Argumenta solvuntur.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

194 Opp. 1. Si omnia corpora mixta continuò transpirant, futurum est, ut pondere, ac mole sensim decrescant, sed hoc experimentis quampluribus adversatur: ergo. Secundo: per ipsos quoque corporis humani poros, necessaria quoque ad vitam fluida erúmperent, sed hoc non est dicendum, nam tunc nunquam homo valetudinem haberet: ergo. Ad 1. nego maj. cum P. de Lanis, quia quum corpus effluvia emittit, amissio haec per alia similia in aëre dispersa compensatur, quae ab alijs corporibus decerpta in hujus corporis poros invehuntur, praesertim quum homogeneae particulae invicem facillimè conjungantur, quod Auctor citatus confirmat magnétis phaenomenis, de quo constat, in virtute roborari non obstante continua effluviorum emanatione.

194 Obj. 1. If all mixed bodies continually transpire, it will come about that they gradually decrease in weight and bulk; but this is contradicted by very many experiments: therefore. Secondly: through the very pores of the human body the fluids necessary for life would also burst out; but this is not to be said, for then a man would never have good health: therefore. To 1. I deny the major, with Fr. Lana Terzi, because when a body emits effluvia, this loss is compensated by other similar ones dispersed in the air, which, plucked from other bodies, are carried into the pores of this body, especially since homogeneous particles join with one another very easily; which the cited Author confirms by the phenomena of the magnet, of which it is established that it is strengthened in its virtue notwithstanding the continual emanation of effluvia.

195 Ad 2. nego etiam maj.: quod enim per corporis humani poros necessaria ad vivendum fluida non erumpant, id repetendum est ex diversa fluidorum, pororumque figura, cujus eam oportuit esse varietatem, ut in sani corporis statu necessariis fluidis exitum prohiberet. Itaque rursùs semperque laudanda est Divina Bonitas, quae admirabilem corporis nostri structuram ita composuit, ut vivere possimus, & quantum ipse Deus vellet, viveremus, ad immortalem vitam deinde transituri.

195 To 2. I also deny the major: for the fact that the fluids necessary for living do not burst out through the pores of the human body is to be traced back to the different figure of the fluids and of the pores, whose variety had to be such as to prevent the exit of the necessary fluids in the state of a healthy body. Therefore the Divine Goodness is to be praised again and always, which so composed the admirable structure of our body that we might live, and live as long as God himself willed, to pass thereafter to immortal life.

196 Opp. 2. de fide est omnes homines in propria carne resurrecturos, ante Divini judicis Tribúnal sistendos, ut boni donentur praemio, improbi autem supplicio mancipentur; sed hoc componi nequit cum corporis humani transpiratione, nam ¿quomodo eae corporis particulae, quae per insensibilem transpirationem adsiduè evanescunt in idem corpus iterùm coalescent? Ergo. Neg min: quamvis enim corporis nostri materia per insensibilem transpirationem avolaverit; quamvis etiam in belluae carnivorae, aut barbari hominis substantiam transiverit, Deus eandem discernet, & corpori cujus erit restituet. Particulae omnes quae ab ortu ad mortem usque, corpus nostrum per diversas aetates constituerunt, nobiscum non resurgent, tum enim enormis magnitudinis monstra excitaremur.

196 Obj. 2. It is of faith that all men will rise again in their own flesh, to be set before the Tribunal of the Divine judge, so that the good may be rewarded and the wicked consigned to punishment; but this cannot be reconciled with the transpiration of the human body; for how will those particles of the body which continually vanish through insensible transpiration grow together again into the same body? Therefore. I deny the minor: for although the matter of our body has flown off through insensible transpiration, although it has even passed into the substance of a carnivorous beast or of a barbarous man, God will discern it and restore it to the body whose it will be. Not all the particles which from birth until death constituted our body through its different ages will rise again with us; for then we should be raised up as monsters of enormous size.

197 Deus eam nobis restituet, quam ipse decrevit magnitudinem, de qua quidem magnitudine nihil fides docet, nihil autem â ratione alienum est, imò ratio ipsa demonstrat, Deum Omnipotentem dispersas materiae particulas, quae uniuscujusque

197 God will restore to us that size which he himself has decreed, about which size faith indeed teaches nothing; but it is in no way foreign to reason, nay, reason itself demonstrates, that Almighty God can gather the scattered particles of matter which made up each man’s

p. 70

nis substantiam per totum vitae decursum componebant, collígere, & elígere posse, atque in eam quam velit magnitudinem revocare, & quod alicui defuerit, supplebit ille, qui etiam de nihilo potuit quod voluit operari, ut ait S. Augustinus s1. Corporum resurrectio solius divinae potestatis opus est cujus causas, & rationem témerè quis investigabit. Certa ergo fide tenendum omninò est, quod ad adventum Christi D., omnes homines resúrgere habent cum corporibus suis, & reddituri sunt de factis propriis rationem, & qui bona egérunt, ibunt in vitam aeternam, qui verò mala, in ignem aeternum. s2

substance through the whole course of life, and pick them out, and recall them to whatever size he wishes; and what may be lacking to anyone, He will supply who was able to make even out of nothing whatever he willed, as St. Augustine says (l). The resurrection of bodies is the work of the divine power alone, whose causes and reason one would investigate rashly. It must therefore be held altogether with sure faith that at the coming of Christ the Lord all men shall rise again with their bodies, and shall give an account of their own deeds; and they that have done good shall go into life everlasting, and they that have done evil into everlasting fire (m).

CAPUT VI. — CHAPTER VI

De Rarefactione, & Condensatione corporum.

On the Rarefaction and Condensation of bodies.

198 Corpus rarum dicitur, quod sub mognis dimensionibus parum continet materiae: densum verò, quod multum habet materiae sub parvis dimensionibus, sic aqua medium implens vásculum, igni admota ebulliens, rara dicitur, quia pro tanta quam habet tunc extensione, re ipsa parum est materiae aqueae: contrà cera antea calefacta, postea frigescens, densa est, quia ad minus spatium contrahitur. Unde rarefactio est motus, quo corpus eadem manente materiae quantitate ad majus spatium exiénditur. Nam si aliquid ejusdem materiae adjiciatùr, ex. g: aqua, bullienti aquae, non rarefactio, sed aumentatio erit. Condensatio est motus quo corpus ad minus spatium redigitur, quin aliquid de ejus materia dematur, nam si de cèra ex. gr. quidquam auferatur, non condensatio, sed diminutio erit.

body is called rare which under great dimensions contains little matter; dense, 198 A however, which has much matter under small dimensions; thus water filling half a little vessel and boiling when brought near the fire is called rare, because for so great an extension as it then has there is in reality little aqueous matter; wax, on the contrary, first heated and afterwards cooling, is dense, because it contracts into a smaller space. Hence rarefaction is the motion by which a body, the same quantity of matter remaining, is extended into a greater space. For if something of the same matter is added, e.g. water to boiling water, it will not be rarefaction but augmentation. Condensation is the motion by which a body is reduced to a smaller space without anything of its matter being taken away; for if anything is taken away from wax, e.g., it will not be condensation but diminution.

199 Corpus rarum, & tensum in eo conveniunt, quod sub majori extensione parum materiae contineant, differunt tamen in eo, quod tensum ad minorem extensionem éxigit redúci: non verò rarum, precisè scilicet ob raritatis statum. Similiter corpus densum, & compressum in eo conveniunt, quod sub parva extensione multum habent materiae. Compressum verò majorem exigit extensionem, non verò densum, ratione nempè densitatis. Compressum majorem exigit extensionem: nam particulae illud componentes per causam extrinsecam ad minus spatium sunt reductae, densum verò ab aliqua causa intrinsecùs ita constituitur, ut majorem extensionem non éxigat, haec autem causa potest esse colligatio, novaque implexio, ac fixatio paticularum corpus illud componentium, qua pósita, etiam

199 A rare and a stretched body agree in this, that under a greater extension they contain little matter; they differ, however, in this, that the stretched body requires to be brought back to a smaller extension, but not the rare body, precisely, that is, on account of its state of rarity. Similarly a dense and a compressed body agree in this, that under a small extension they have much matter. But the compressed body requires a greater extension, not, however, the dense, namely by reason of its density. The compressed body requires a greater extension: for the particles composing it have been reduced to a smaller space by an extrinsic cause; but the dense body is so constituted by some intrinsic cause that it does not require a greater extension; and this cause can be the binding together, the new interweaving and the fixing of the particles composing that body; and once this is in place, even with

In Enchirid. cap. 20

In the Enchiridion, ch. 20.

Ex Symbol. tribut. S. Athanasio.

From the Creed attributed to St. Athanasius.

p. 71

nullo repágulo extrinsecùs adhibito, pristinam extensionem non répetunt. His ita constitutis.

with no restraint applied from outside, they do not regain their former extension. These things being thus established,

200 Dico: rarefactio corporum in eo sita est, quod pori corporis dilatentur: condensatio autem in eo, quod ejusdem pori constringantur, ad quam dilatationem ingressus particularum, & corpusculorum insensibilium, uti ad constrictionem expulsio earumdem conséquitur. Prob.: corpus tum raréscere dicitur, si non aucta materia ejus volumen crescat, & majus spatium óccupet, densari verò, si non imminuta materia volúmen decrescat, & corpus spatio minori congruat [§. 198]; sed evidens est augeri volumen corporis, quin crescat materia illius, hoc ipso quod pori dilatentur in eo; decréscere autem volumen corporis, quin de materia quidpiam auferatur hoc ipso quod pori coarctentur; ergo. Quod verò in sensu physico esse non possit rarefactio sine ingressu corpusculorum insensibilium, igneorum, aethereorum, aut aliorum patet, quia quum ex dicendis nullum detur vacuum sensibile, adeòque sensibile quodvis spatium plenum sit materia aliqua subtilissima, cónsequens est, ut quando dilatantur pori, mole totius corporis sensibiliter aucta, haec materia utpotè subtilissima eos subeat, repleatque. Eodem proportionaliter modo de condensatione ratiocinandum est.

200 I say: the rarefaction of bodies consists in this, that the pores of the body are dilated; condensation, however, in this, that the same pores are constricted; upon which dilatation there follows an entry of particles and of insensible corpuscles, as upon the constriction their expulsion. Proof: a body is said to rarefy when, its matter not being increased, its volume grows and occupies a greater space; to be condensed when, its matter not being diminished, its volume decreases and the body fits a smaller space [§. 198]; but it is evident that the volume of a body is increased without its matter growing, by the very fact that the pores in it are dilated, and that the volume of a body decreases without anything being taken away from its matter, by the very fact that the pores are narrowed: therefore. That in the physical sense, moreover, there cannot be rarefaction without the entry of insensible corpuscles, fiery, ethereal or others, is plain; because, since (as will be said) there is no sensible void, and so every sensible space is full of some very subtle matter, it follows that when the pores are dilated, the bulk of the whole body being sensibly increased, this matter, being very subtle, enters and fills them. One must reason about condensation in the same way, proportionally.

201 Confirm.: Illa sententia in rebus physicis praeferenda est ceteris, quae captu est facilis, nec mysteria humanum intellectum ferè superantia invehit, & in qua facillimè redditur ratio phaenomenorum in motu rarefactionis, & condensationis occurrentium [Axiom. III. IV. & V. §§. 32. & 33.]; sed talis est nostra sententia: ergò. Min. tum ex hactenùs dictis, tum ex solutione objectionum elucéscet, & etiam inductione experimentorum, eorumdemque explicatione probatur. Explicatur enim cur aqua in glaciem concréta majus spatium occupet, quàm in statu suo naturali. Academici Florentini ut id exactè examinarent, tubum vitreum elegérunt, altera extremitate clausum, quem aqua ad medietatem implevérunt, tum nivi minutim contritae immerserunt, donec aqua in glaciem verteretur, quo fiebat, ut aqua dilatata adsúrgeret in tubo, & majus in illo spatium, quàm quum fluida esset occuparet.

201 Confirm.: In physical matters that opinion is to be preferred to the others which is easy to grasp, does not bring in mysteries almost surpassing the human intellect, and in which an account is most easily given of the phenomena occurring in the motion of rarefaction and condensation [Axiom. III, IV & V, §§. 32 & 33]; but such is our opinion: therefore. The minor will shine forth both from what has been said thus far and from the solution of the objections, and is also proved by induction from experiments and by their explanation. For it is explained why water congealed into ice occupies a greater space than in its natural state. The Florentine Academicians, to examine this exactly, chose a glass tube closed at one end, which they filled with water to half its height, then immersed it in finely crushed snow until the water was turned into ice; whereby it came about that the dilated water rose in the tube and occupied a greater space in it than when it was fluid.

202 Praeterea exactissima bilance examinarunt aquae pondus ante glaciationem; & ejusdem jam glaciatae, & repererunt, plus ponderasse non glaciatam, quàm post glaciationem. Horum autem ratio est, quia quum aquae particulae ex una parte invicem congelatione adhaereant, mutuoque strictiùs compléctantur, innumeros, eosque satis notabiles poros ex alia parte relinquunt, qui materia praecípuè aërea sunt repleti, quae quum per poros strictiores aquae quae glaciatur exire nequeat, dilatatur; quo fit, ut glacies quae quoddam adgregatum est ex aqua coagulata, & ex aëre sic dilatato in illis búllulis incluso extensior evadat, quàm erat ipsa aqua ante glaciationem.

202 Moreover, with a most exact balance they examined the weight of water before freezing, and of the same water once frozen, and found that the unfrozen water weighed more than after freezing. The reason of these things, moreover, is this: since the particles of water on one side adhere to one another by congelation and embrace one another more tightly, they leave on the other side innumerable and quite notable pores, which are filled chiefly with aerial matter; and since this cannot escape through the narrower pores of the water that is freezing, it is dilated; whence it comes about that ice, which is a kind of aggregate of coagulated water and of air thus dilated and enclosed in those little bubbles, becomes more extended than the water itself was before freezing.

p. 72

203 Dùm enim dilatatur aër, nec erumpit, totam aquae molem in qua continetur, augéri necesse est, & consequenter sub majori mole constituta, eandemque aquae materiam cóntinens, sed plurimis praesertim igneis particulis destitutam, levior evadit. Existimo tamen, aquam si â búllulis separata posset existere sub eodem volumine, post glaciationem reddendam fore graviorem; patet enim grándinem, in qua nullae adparent búllulae, esse graviorem aqua pluviali, in hac siquidem mérgitur, quum è contrario glacies vulgaris, & búllulis conspicuis plena eidem aquae supérnatet; fit enim ex aqua tantillum condensata, & ex aëre plurimum dilatato, quoddam adgregatum leviùs aqua antè glaciationem. Omitto plura alia, quae ex his nullo admodùm negotio exponuntur. Momenta nùnc à diversis phaenómenis petita paucis discutiamus.

203 For while the air is dilated and does not burst out, the whole bulk of the water in which it is contained must necessarily be increased; and consequently, being set under a greater bulk and containing the same matter of water, but deprived of very many particles, especially fiery ones, it becomes lighter. I think, however, that water, if it could exist separated from the little bubbles under the same volume, would be rendered heavier after freezing; for it is plain that hail, in which no little bubbles appear, is heavier than rain water, since it sinks in it, whereas, on the contrary, common ice, full of conspicuous little bubbles, floats on the same water: for out of water condensed a little and air very greatly dilated there is made an aggregate lighter than the water before freezing. I omit many other things which are set forth from these with no trouble at all. Let us now discuss in a few words the difficulties drawn from various phenomena.

Argumenta solvuntur.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

204 Opp. 1. in nostra sententia non potest reddi congrua ratio phaenomenorum, quae observantur in vase, quod ex cupro conflatur formam, piri, vel pomi réferens, pro cáudiculo habens tubum exiguo forámine terminatum, quod vas Aeolípila nuncupatur. Haec spiritu vini ad certam quantitatem impleta, ignique superimposita, fontem ex spiritu vini salientem exhibebit, cui si candélam, admoveas liquor prosiliens inflammábitur (Fig. IX.). Similiter, si ad dimidium aqua repleatur, & carbonibus admoveatur, vapórem per canaliculum magna vehementia, & sónitu ejiciet (Fig. X.): imò vapor aquam in Aeolípila contentam ad altitudinem 20 pedum propellet. His autèm constitutis ita argumentum efformatur.

204 Obj. 1. On our opinion no fitting account can be given of the phenomena observed in a vessel which is made of copper, has the shape of a pear or an apple, and has for its little stem a tube ending in a tiny opening; this vessel is called an Aeolipile. Filled with spirit of wine to a certain quantity and set upon a fire, it will exhibit a fountain of spirit of wine leaping up, and if you bring a candle near it, the liquor springing out will be set alight (Fig. IX). Similarly, if it is filled to half with water and set near coals, it will throw out vapor through the little canal with great vehemence and noise (Fig. X): nay, the vapor will drive the water contained in the Aeolipile to a height of 20 feet. These things being established, the argument is formed thus.

205 Si rarefactio habetur per dilatationem pororum, tunc quando in aeolipilà rarescit aqua, vel spiritus vini, tantundem etiam rarefiat necesse est ipsum vasculum, quum propiùs sit igni, quàm liquor in eo contentus; sed hoc adversatur experientiae: ergo. Neque aptiùs complura alia explicantur, ut quod globus vitreus (Fig. XI.) gutta aquae, vel spiritu vini plenus, & undique clausus, igni aproximatus cum fragóre dissiliat; similiter castaneae non incisae prunis immissae sonitu rumpantur, praesertim quum dici non possit, quod aër externus, qui rarefácere aquam déberet, vitrei globuli poros permeet. Sed haec argumenta citra difficultatem explanari possunt. Equidèm aeolípila calore nonnihil dilatari, & rarefieri quoque ádsero, at quum solidior sit, magisque compacta materia constet, habet partes magis cohaerentes, sibique invicèm infixas, unde ut pori ejus tantoperè, ac liquor contentus rarefierent, major vis caloris requiritur, quam sit illa quae ad poros aquae, vel spiritus vini, corporum nempè liquidorum, ideoque minus sibi cohaerentium dilatandos sufficit.

205 If rarefaction takes place through the dilatation of the pores, then, when water or spirit of wine is rarefied in the aeolipile, the little vessel itself must necessarily be rarefied just as much, since it is nearer to the fire than the liquor contained in it; but this is contrary to experience: therefore. Nor are several other things explained more aptly: as that a glass globe (Fig. XI), full of a drop of water or of spirit of wine and closed on all sides, bursts with a crash when brought near the fire; similarly, that chestnuts not cut open, put into live coals, burst with a noise; especially since it cannot be said that the external air, which would have to rarefy the water, permeates the pores of the glass globule. But these arguments can be explained without difficulty. I indeed assert that the aeolipile is somewhat dilated, and also rarefied, by heat; but since it is more solid and consists of more compact matter, it has parts more cohering and fixed into one another; whence, for its pores to be rarefied as much as the liquor contained, a greater force of heat is required than that which suffices for dilating the pores of water or of spirit of wine, bodies, namely, that are liquid and therefore cohere less among themselves.

p. 73

206 Nec minus alia explicari queunt. Certè difractio globi vitrei ab aquae rarefactione, seu vapore oritur. Castanae in ignem injectae disruptio similiter ab humidis particulis intra córticem inclusis calore rarefactis, & exitum quaerentibus efficitur. Neque miremini vim á nobis tantam tribui vapori, quum constet vaporem rarefactum majori pollére vi, quam pulverem pyrium qui simili globulo vitreo, & ejusdem ponderis, cujus est gutta aquae inclusus globum quidem diffringit, sed fragóre longè minori; quumque insuper ex Nolleto s1 innotuerit aquam in vaporem conversam 14000 vicibus majus volumen formare.

206 Nor can the other phenomena be explained any less easily. Certainly the bursting of a glass globe arises from the rarefaction of water, or from vapor. The bursting of chestnuts thrown into the fire is likewise brought about by moist particles shut up within the shell, which are rarefied by the heat and seek an outlet. Nor should you wonder that so great a force is attributed by us to vapor, since it is established that rarefied vapor has a greater force than gunpowder, which, shut up in a like little glass globe and of the same weight as the drop of water, does indeed shatter the globe, but with a far smaller crash; and since, moreover, it is known from Nollet (n) that water converted into vapor forms a volume 14000 times greater.

207 Opp. 2. in condensatione excluditur materia subtilis; ergo tunc non intromittitur aliqua subtilis materia. Nego conseq.: quum enim materia subtilis quae introducitur, partes corporis invicèm strictiùs conjungat, ac nectat, in causa est, ut pori constringantur: & consequenter alia materia subtilis, quae in ipsis continebatur, foras erumpat, quae autèm excluditur plus est, quàm quae de novo adjicitur, ideòque corpus densum minus spatium occupat, quàm antè condensationem occupabat. Alia argumenta quae Scholastici movére solent, distinguendo duplicem significatum raritatis, & densitatis; alterum quo metaphysicè, & insensibiliter, alterum quo physicè, & sensibiliter corporum gemina haec mutatio usurpatur facillimè diluuntur.

207 Obj. 2. In condensation subtle matter is excluded; therefore no subtle matter is then introduced. I deny the consequence: for since the subtle matter which is introduced joins and binds the parts of the body more tightly to one another, it is the cause of the pores being contracted, and consequently of the other subtle matter, which was contained in them, bursting out; but what is excluded is more than what is newly added, and therefore the dense body occupies less space than it occupied before condensation. The other arguments which the Scholastics are wont to raise are very easily dissolved by distinguishing a twofold signification of rarity and density: one in which this twin change of bodies is taken metaphysically and insensibly, the other in which it is taken physically and sensibly.

208 Opp. tandem: quum scintilla ignis in acervum pulveris, pyrij delapsa eum accendit, & rarefacit, motus ille aut rarefactio, nec à pororum dilatatione, nec á materia subtili proficisci potest. ¿Quid est enim quod eam impellat materiam, aut tanta vi agitet, ut vel solo contactu tantam pulveri pyrio agitationem impertiatur? ¿Unde illius vis ut arces ipsas disjiciat, ut in cuniculis videmus? Respondeo, eum effectum pororum dilatationi, & vi elasticae accensi pulveris potissimùm esse referendum, etenim accensus pulvis qui majorem locum postulat, omni ex parte parietibus innixus, qua parte minus obsistitur, ea erumpit: dilatatio successiva pulveris, vim percussionis auget. Vis etiam pulveris qua globum è tormento bellico propellit, particulis etiam igneis, adjuncta aëris, & nitri elasticitate tribuenda est, hi enim tot elatéres in omnem partem summa vi nituntur, quumque minor sit resistentia globi, quàm ex parte posteriori tormenti bellici, idcircò etiam globum aliquot librarum ad notabilem distantiam éjicit. Atque tantorum effectuum in pulvere, princeps causa est sal nitri ob suam elasticitatem, unde ut ait Kircherus, si tormentum pulvere, ex solo sulphure, & carbonibus citra nitrum confecto impleatur, pulvisque accendatur, is non ejiciet globum ex tormento, deficiente nempè elaterio.

208 Obj. finally: when a spark of fire falling on a heap of gunpowder kindles and rarefies it, that motion or rarefaction can proceed neither from the dilatation of the pores nor from subtle matter. For what is it that impels that matter, or agitates it with such force that by mere contact it imparts so great an agitation to the gunpowder? Whence comes its force, so that it throws down citadels themselves, as we see in mines? I reply that this effect is to be referred chiefly to the dilatation of the pores and to the elastic force of the kindled powder; for the kindled powder, which demands a greater place, pressing against the walls on every side, bursts out on the side where it is less resisted: the successive dilatation of the powder increases the force of the percussion. The force of the powder by which it propels a ball from a cannon is also to be attributed to the fiery particles, joined with the elasticity of the air and of the niter; for these so many springs strive in every direction with the utmost force, and since the resistance of the ball is less than that of the hinder part of the cannon, it therefore hurls even a ball of several pounds to a notable distance. And of such great effects in the powder the principal cause is saltpeter, on account of its elasticity; whence, as Kircher says, if a cannon is filled with powder made of sulphur and charcoal alone, without niter, and the powder is kindled, it will not expel the ball from the cannon, the spring, namely, being wanting.

Leçons de Physique. Tom. 4. Lect. 12. Sect. 2. Exp. 7.

Leçons de Physique, vol. 4, lesson 12, sect. 2, exp. 7.

p. 74

DISSERTATIO IV. — DISSERTATION IV

Aliae corporum proprietates brevitèr exponuntur, & principaliora phaenomena quamclarissimè explicantur.

OTHER PROPERTIES OF BODIES ARE BRIEFLY SET FORTH, AND THE PRINCIPAL PHENOMENA ARE EXPLAINED AS CLEARLY AS POSSIBLE

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De Fermentatione corporum.

On the Fermentation of bodies.

209 Nihil aliud videtur esse fermentatio, quàm motus intestínus mixti, quo subtiliores partes illius, magisque actuosae texturam laxant, crassiores particulas adtenuant, & exágitant ita, ut in toto mixto effervescentia quaedam, & ebullitio observetur. A duobus principiis répeti optimè potest fermentationis explicatio: à salibus nempè acidis, & alkalicis: quum enim acidi salis particulae ob suam rigiditatem non nisi cum violentia in poros salis alkalici, & materias alkalicas se intrudant, magnam partem impellente materia aetherea, igneasque, & aëreas particulas in poris latentes cómprimant, violentis his concussionibus, & accedente, tum ignis, tum aëris elaterio, fit, ut meatus in quos rapidè irruerunt effringantur, aëris rarefacti, ignisque adminiculo impellantur, & in omnem partem disjiciantur particulae alkalicae, quam disjectionem partium diversarum sequitur illa intumescentia in fermentationibus observata, quae si bullas vaporum instar efformet, ebullitio, si cum calore sensibili conjungatur, effervescentia dicitur.

ermentation seems to be nothing other than an intestine motion of a mixed 209 F body, by which its subtler and more active parts loosen its texture, attenu‐ ate the coarser particles, and agitate them in such a way that a certain effervescence and ebullition is observed in the whole mixture. The explanation of fermentation can best be derived from two principles, namely from acid and alkaline salts: for since the particles of an acid salt, on account of their rigidity, intrude themselves only with violence into the pores of an alkaline salt and into alkaline materials, the ethereal matter impelling a great part of them, and compress the fiery and airy particles lying hidden in the pores, it comes about through these violent concussions, with the spring both of the fire and of the air coming to their aid, that the passages into which they rapidly rushed are broken open, and that the alkaline particles are impelled by the help of the rarefied air and of the fire and are scattered in every direction; and this scattering of the diverse parts is followed by that swelling observed in fermentations which, if it forms something like bubbles of vapor, is called ebullition, and if it is joined with sensible heat, effervescence.

210 In universum dici potest: motum illum intestínum fermentationis, excitari à spirituosis particulis, quae intra crassiores, & solidiores contentae, & compressae, illis disjectis, & concissis, aperto velut cárcere erumpunt, sese liberiùs explicant, suoque motu alias partes ágitant, variè permiscent, ac perturbant. Sed ex P.

210 In general it can be said that that intestine motion of fermentation is excited by spirituous particles which, contained and compressed within coarser and more solid ones, burst out, when these are scattered and cut to pieces, as from an opened prison, unfold themselves more freely, and by their motion agitate the other parts, variously mix them together, and disturb them. But I am pleased to note, following Father Regnault (o)

p. 75

Regnault s1 adnotare placet fermentationem pulveris fulminantis.

(o), the fermentation of fulminating powder.

211 Pulvis fulminans est mixtura composita ex tribus partibus nitri, duabus salis tártari, & una sulphuris, separatim in pulverem redactis, & commixtis. Haec in cochleari ferreo candelae sive prunis admota, & ad certum gradum calefacta, repentè cum horribili detonatione, dissipatur, & interdùm cochlear disrúmpit. Actio nempè igneorum corpusculorum se insinuantium defert spícula nitri in salem tartari, & dilatatio aëris interni violentam illam agitationem efficit, ex qua detonatio oritur. Disrupti cochlearis causam reddit P. Regnault, quod vis pulveris non modo in omnem partem feratur, sed illa insupèr in cochleare impellatur ab aëre superiore resistente, tantò potentius, quantò majori celeritate, & vehementia pulvis dissipatus aërem ímpetit, àc commovet. Ex quibus phaenomena fermentationis explicantur.

211 Fulminating powder is a mixture composed of three parts of niter, two of salt of tartar, and one of sulphur, each reduced separately to powder and then mixed together. This, put in an iron spoon over a candle or live coals and heated to a certain degree, is suddenly dissipated with a horrible detonation, and sometimes bursts the spoon. The action, namely, of the fiery corpuscles insinuating themselves carries the spicules of the niter into the salt of tartar, and the dilatation of the internal air brings about that violent agitation from which the detonation arises. Father Regnault gives as the cause of the bursting of the spoon that the force of the powder is not only borne in every direction, but is moreover driven into the spoon by the resisting upper air, the more powerfully the greater the speed and vehemence with which the dissipated powder strikes and moves the air. From these things the phenomena of fermentation are explained.

212 Primò: si spiritus nitri adfundatur mercurio stannovè, effervescentia, & ebullitio benè calida sequetur; acidae quippe spiritus nitri particulae aëris interni elaterio adjutae, rapidè irruunt in particulas alkalicas mercurij, aut stanni; hinc agitationem communicant in omnem partem, unde effervescentia, ebullitio, calor sensibilis. Secundò: si misceatur óleum tartari cum spiritu nitri in quo antea sint soluta ramenta ferri, fermentatio ignem concipiet; nam acidae particulae, alkalicis communicant motum & agitationem omnem in partem, qui motus major est eo, qui à simplici calore producitur, hic autèm motus in omnem partem producitur à spiritu nitri, qui in ramenta ferri offendit plurima obstacula, quae ab eo vinci debent. Aliae explicationes phaenomenorum videri possunt in Lexic. Physices, Gallicè edito à P. Paulian s2

212 First: if spirit of niter is poured onto mercury or tin, an effervescence and a very hot ebullition will follow; for the acid particles of the spirit of niter, aided by the spring of the internal air, rush rapidly into the alkaline particles of the mercury or of the tin; hence they communicate agitation in every direction, whence effervescence, ebullition, sensible heat. Secondly: if oil of tartar is mixed with spirit of niter in which iron filings have previously been dissolved, the fermentation will take fire; for the acid particles communicate motion and agitation in every direction to the alkaline ones, and this motion is greater than that which is produced by simple heat; this motion in every direction, moreover, is produced by the spirit of niter, which meets in the iron filings a great many obstacles that must be overcome by it. Other explanations of the phenomena can be seen in the Dictionary of Physics published in French by Father Paulian (p).

213 Tertio: fermentatio calcis vivae dum aqua adfunditur hac de causa exóritur: in calcis confectione, calor fibras petrae rumpit, poros ampliat, novosque éfficit, interstitia haec, & pori materia subtili, igneisque corpusculis replentur, dum deindè refrigerare íncipit, aër exterior in multos meatus pénetrat, & per alium, atque alium succedentem condensatur; itaque si aqua adfundatur, illa calcem siccissimam violentè pervadit, cujus agitatione igneae particulae, & sal mineralis in poris latens, ac post calcinationem relictus, solvuntur, cárcereque liberantur, unde igniculis majori vi agentibus, ácidis etiam salium particulis, in alkali poros se ingerentibus, partes calcis cédere coactae separantur, disjiciuntur; hinc effervescentia, & calor sensibilis. De hac materia inter alios videri possunt Willis s3, Boerhaave s4, Franciscus Bayle s5 & P. de Lanis s6.

213 Thirdly: the fermentation of quicklime when water is poured on it arises for this reason. In the making of lime the heat breaks the fibers of the stone, enlarges the pores, and makes new ones; these interstices and pores are filled with subtle matter and fiery corpuscles; then, when the lime begins to cool, the outer air penetrates into its many passages and is condensed by more and more air coming in after it; and so, if water is poured on, it violently pervades the very dry lime, and by its agitation the fiery particles and the mineral salt lying hidden in the pores and left behind after calcination are loosed and freed from their prison; whence, the little fires acting with greater force, and the acid particles of the salts also thrusting themselves into the pores of the alkali, the parts of the lime, forced to yield, are separated and scattered: hence the effervescence and sensible heat. On this matter, among others, Willis (q), Boerhaave (r), François Bayle (s) and Father Lana (t) may be consulted.
