214 Hinc etiam quarto explicari potest phaenómenon pulveris ardentis, qui etiam dicitur pulvis Pyróbola. Ponatur in disco terreo pulvis aluminis, cum tertia parte sui ponderis mellis, vel farinae, vel sácchari, & posito disco super carbones, diù moveantur hi pulveres, donec probe exsiccentur, & fusci fiant. Tunc contundantur in mortario, & iterum exsiccentur, & hoc donec partes pulveris non amplius uniantur, sed maneant sejunctae. Tunc ponatur hic pulvis in parvo matracio s1 longi colli, quod sepeliatur usque ad collum in arena, leniter charta obturato matracio, exponatur vas igni per gradus aucto, usque dum inferior pars colli rubeat, nec amplius prodeat fumus: extincto igne ponatur pulvis in phiala probè clausa ne aëri exposita sit, & ad usus servetur.

214 Hence, fourthly, can also be explained the phenomenon of the burning powder, which is also called the pyrophorus powder. Let powdered alum be put in an earthen dish with a third part of its weight of honey, or flour, or sugar, and, the dish being set over coals, let these powders be stirred for a long time until they are thoroughly dried and turn dark. Then let them be pounded in a mortar and dried again, and this until the parts of the powder no longer unite but remain separate. Then let this powder be put in a small long-necked matrass (u), which is buried up to the neck in sand; the matrass being lightly stopped with paper, let the vessel be exposed to a fire increased by degrees, until the lower part of the neck glows red and no more smoke comes forth; when the fire is put out, let the powder be placed in a phial well closed, so that it is not exposed to the air, and kept for use.

215 Proprietas hujus pulveris est, ut vel minima ejus portio aëri exposita incendatur spontè absque strepitu. Tractu temporis tamèn hanc vim amittit, & quum non citò incenditur saepè eam ore humectando, incenditur. Ratio horum redditur. Quum igni exponitur ut torrefiat; tunc intimè pervaditur ab igne, acquiritque vim detinendi ignem, ut alkali. Statim ac aëri exponitur, ejus humiditatem trahit, atque ita ignis latens compressus acquirit vim se expandendi, & sensibilis redditur, ut calx aqua humectata; hinc tractu temporis vim hanc amittit, quia avolat ignis, & si nimiùm humidum in aëre non fuerit, ore humectata incenditur.

215 The property of this powder is that even the smallest portion of it, exposed to the air, takes fire spontaneously, without noise. In the course of time, however, it loses this force, and when it does not take fire quickly, it often takes fire when it is moistened with the breath. The reason of these things is given. When it is exposed to the fire to be roasted, it is then intimately pervaded by the fire, and acquires the power of retaining fire, as an alkali does. As soon as it is exposed to the air, it draws in the air’s moisture, and so the latent, compressed fire acquires the force of expanding itself and is rendered sensible, as in lime moistened with water; hence in the course of time it loses this force, because the fire flies off; and if there has not been too much moisture in the air, it takes fire when moistened with the breath.

216 Preatermittere tamèn non possum hac de re differens vegetationes chymicas. Has inter celebratissimae sunt arbor Martis, & arbor Dianae, sivè Philosophica. Primam exponit Lemery filius in Monumentis Academiae Regiae Parisiensis s2. In vase vitreo (Fig. XIII.) in quo sit scobs ferri pone super hanc spiritum nitri, ingens fiet effervescentia, & ebullitio. Spiritus tingetur colore intensè rubro ob ferrum solutum, & plures orientur fumi rubri. Sedáta effervescentia, qua partes ferri adtolluntur ad superiora, prójice in liquorem oleum tartari per deliquium, orietur mediocris effervescentia, qua liquor plurimum inflabitur, paulo post ad ejus látera, & labrum innumeri orientur rami, & arbusta, quae absque ulla visibili effervescentia superabunt liquorem, & labrum, atque externè décident, ut exhibetur in figura. In alia vegetatione loco spiritus nitri adhibuit Lemery spiritum productum à vapore rubro, quem emittit spiritus nitri in effervescentia, & hoc usus est in alio experimento ad solvendum ferrum, & vegetatio magis

216 I cannot, however, pass over the different chemical vegetations that belong to this subject. Among these the most celebrated are the tree of Mars and the tree of Diana, or Philosophical tree. The first is set forth by Lemery the son in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (x). Into a glass vessel (Fig. XIII.) in which there are iron filings, pour spirit of niter upon them; a huge effervescence and ebullition will arise. The spirit will be tinged with an intensely red color on account of the dissolved iron, and many red fumes will arise. When the effervescence, by which the parts of the iron are raised to the upper regions, has subsided, throw into the liquor oil of tartar per deliquium; a moderate effervescence will arise, by which the liquor will be greatly swollen; a little after, on its sides and on the lip, countless branches and shrubs will arise, which without any visible effervescence will rise above the liquor and the lip, and fall down on the outside, as is shown in the figure. In another vegetation Lemery employed, in place of the spirit of niter, a spirit produced from the red vapor which spirit of niter gives off in effervescence, and he used this in another experiment to dissolve iron, and a more distinct vegetation

Matracium est ampúlla vitrea longo, & recto collo instructa. Aliud est matracium ad adtenuandos lentè igne liquores. Componitur ex phiala vitrea A (Fig. XII.) colli longi, cum alia phiala parva B lutata cum prima: liquor adscendit in B, iterum reddit in A &c. atque per hunc circuitum adtenuatur, & faeces deponit in fundo phialae A.

A matrass is a glass flask furnished with a long and straight neck. Another kind of matrass serves for attenuating liquors over a gentle fire. It is composed of a glass phial A (Fig. XII.) with a long neck, with another small phial B luted to the first: the liquor ascends into B, returns again into A, etc., and through this circulation it is attenuated and deposits its dregs at the bottom of phial A.

p. 77

distincta orta est, quia vapor ruber imbibitur sulphure ferri, quod citiùs, & in partes minores ferrum dividit.

arose, because the red vapor is imbibed by the sulphur of the iron, which divides the iron more quickly and into smaller parts.

217 Ut haec phaenómena exponantur, observandum est, spiritum nitri dividere ferrum in partes minimas, & cum iis consociari, quae partes eò minores sunt, quò magis spiritus sulphure ferri abundat. Sulphur autem metalla dividere posse incompertò est, accedat modò oleum tartari, quod est alkali terreum; partes accidi nitrosi non adeò cohaerent cum iis ferri, ut non possint cum suis acuminibus ingredi cavitates alkali, hinc oritur effervescentia, quam ostendunt ampullae aëris adsiduè à liquore erumpentes, quum tamen partes acidae cum ferro unitae sint, ideò non maxima vi irruere possunt in alkali, ideoque effervescentia non est sensibilis, ut ea quae oritur, si in simplici spiritu nitri ponatur oleum tartari per deliquium; in nostro verò experimento acidae nitri particulae pro parte ingrediuntur álkali, pro parte cohaerent cum ferri particulis.

217 That these phenomena may be explained, it must be observed that spirit of niter divides iron into very small parts and associates itself with them, and these parts are the smaller the more the spirit abounds in the sulphur of the iron. That sulphur, moreover, can divide metals is well established. Now let oil of tartar, which is an earthy alkali, be added: the parts of the nitrous acid do not cohere so closely with those of the iron that they cannot enter with their points into the cavities of the alkali; hence arises the effervescence, which the bubbles of air continually bursting from the liquor display. Since, however, the acid parts are united with the iron, they cannot rush into the alkali with very great force, and therefore the effervescence is not so sensible as that which arises if oil of tartar per deliquium is put into simple spirit of niter; but in our experiment the acid particles of the niter partly enter the alkali, partly cohere with the particles of the iron.

218 Ferri verò particulae pressae ab ácido, & álkali magis dividuntur, & sulphur ferri adtenuatur, & magis volátile redditur, ita ut hoc secum deferat, & sursum adtollat maximo impetu versùs superficiem vasis particulas ferri unitas cum salinis, quae quàm primùm expeditae sunt à liquore, determinata ratione coherent, & áridae factae, figuram referunt arbustorum.

218 The particles of the iron, however, pressed by the acid and by the alkali, are divided still more, and the sulphur of the iron is attenuated and rendered more volatile, so that it carries with it and lifts upward with very great impetus toward the surface of the vessel the particles of iron united with the saline ones; and these, as soon as they are freed from the liquor, cohere in a determinate manner and, having become dry, take on the figure of shrubs.

219 Arbor Dianae facilè & expeditè producitur methodo tradita ab Hombergio in Monumentis Academiae Regiae Parisiensis s1. Sume drachmas quatuor scobis argenteae s2, & amalgáma s3 fiat absque igne, cum drachmis duobus mercurii. Solve amalgama in quatuor unciis aquae fortis, & projice solutionem in vase cum 18 unciis aquae communis, indè ágita aquam, eamque in phiala benè obturata repóne. Quoties ea uti volueris ad arborem producendam, sume unciam hujus aquae, & repone in alia phiala, in hanc pone amalgama commune auri, aut argenti ad magnitudinem pisi, quod sit semifluidum, seu in consistentia bútyri, post duo, aut tria minuta ex subsidente ad fundum vasis amalgámate prodire incipient fila, quae ramos emittent laterales, & paulatim crescent, & formabuntur in parva arbusta argentea, ut depingitur in Figura XIV, & hoc intra horae quadrantem, & amalgáma, cui inhaerent indurescet, & album fiet. En brevi confecta arbor Dianae, quam prius longa perficiebatur operatione.

219 The tree of Diana is produced easily and expeditiously by the method handed down by Homberg in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (y). Take four drachms of silver filings (z), and let an amalgam (a) be made with two drachms of mercury, without fire. Dissolve the amalgam in four ounces of aqua fortis, and throw the solution into a vessel with 18 ounces of common water; then shake the water, and put it away in a well-stopped phial. Whenever you wish to use it to produce the tree, take an ounce of this water and put it in another phial; into this put a common amalgam of gold or of silver of the size of a pea, which should be semifluid, or of the consistency of butter: after two or three minutes threads will begin to come forth from the amalgam that has settled to the bottom of the vessel, which will put out lateral branches, will grow little by little, and will be formed into small silver shrubs, as is depicted in Figure XIV; and within a quarter of an hour this, together with the amalgam to which they adhere, will harden and become white. Behold the tree of Diana made in a short time, which was formerly completed only by a long operation.

220 Ut haec vegatio exponatur, notandum est, aquam nulli ampliùs vegetationi esse posse idoneam, & pisum amalgámae non minui in pondere post operationem. His positis; certum est

220 That this vegetation may be explained, it must be noted that the water can no longer be fit for any further vegetation, and that the pea of amalgam is not diminished in weight after the operation. These things being laid down, it is certain that the silver

Memoires de l' Academ. Royal. A. 1706, & 1707.

Mémoires de l’Académie Royale, for the years 1706 and 1707.

Memories de l' Academ. A. 1692.

Mémoires de l’Académie, year 1692.

Drachma est octava pars unciae.

A drachm is the eighth part of an ounce.

Amalgamatio fit quum aliquod metallum cum alio, vel cum minerali intimè unitur.

Amalgamation takes place when some metal is intimately united with another, or with a mineral.

p. 78

argentum cum mercurio, & nitro in aqua solutum esse causam vegetationis. Quum solutio dilúta fuerit ab aqua partes nitri non ampliùs maxima vi consociatae sunt cum argenteis, ideòque ponendo in aqua novum amalgama ad hoc feruntur, & relinquunt super amalgama partes argenti, & mercurii, vel rectiùs circa ipsum ramos formant partes nitri cum mercurialibus, & argenteis. Id comprobatur ex diversitate arbustorum: nam si argentum, & mercurius pura fuerint, arbores pulcherrimae oriuntur.

dissolved with the mercury and the niter in water is the cause of the vegetation. When the solution has been diluted by the water, the parts of the niter are no longer associated with the silver ones with very great force, and therefore, when a new amalgam is put into the water, they are borne toward it and leave the parts of silver and of mercury upon the amalgam; or, more correctly, the parts of the niter form branches around it together with the mercurial and silver parts. This is confirmed by the diversity of the shrubs: for if the silver and the mercury have been pure, most beautiful trees arise.

221 Si solutio sit nimis dilúta lentius producentur arbores, sed rami magis erunt conspicui. Si solutio sit fortior, tunc densiores, minusque perfectè orientur arbores. Si amalgáma positum ad magnitudinem pisi, fuerit durum, resolvetur à solutione, & arbor orietur ut in Fig. XV. Etiam fit vegetatio ope aquae pluviae, quae in sententia nostra optimè explicari potest. Tempore pluvio, & tonitruoso cóllige determinatam quantitatem aquae defluentis à tecto. Hanc serva: post plures dies deponet materiam viridescentem ad altitudinem duarum linearum, quae tempore calido, vel exposita propè camínum, inflabitur, ampullas producet, inde filamenta, & ramos virides, quorum nonnulli usque ad aquae superficiem adscendent, cessante calore iterum deponentur ad fundum, redeunte calore iterum germinabunt.

221 If the solution is too dilute, the trees will be produced more slowly, but the branches will be more conspicuous. If the solution is stronger, then the trees will arise denser and less perfect. If the amalgam put in, of the size of a pea, is hard, it will be dissolved by the solution, and the tree will arise as in Fig. XV. A vegetation is also made by means of rainwater, which can be very well explained on our view. In rainy and thundery weather collect a determinate quantity of water running down from a roof. Keep it: after several days it will deposit a greenish matter to the height of two lines, which in hot weather, or when placed near a fireplace, will swell, will produce bubbles, then filaments and green branches, some of which will rise as far as the surface of the water; when the heat ceases they will settle again to the bottom; when the heat returns they will sprout again.

222 Singuli rami habebunt in extremitatibus ampullas aëris veluti esset fructus. Vegetatio haec nisi fortè velis (quod per me licet), verissima semina simul cum aqua in terram decídere; facilè exponitur ope effervescentiae; materia enim primò inflatur, & ob effervescentiam excluditur aër, qui visibilis est, & hic elevat, & distribuit, materiam in ramos, & arbusta, quae ob venustum colorem viridem mirè imittantur naturalem plantarum vegetationem. Haec curiosiora sunt. Plura alia apud Cl. Auctores à me saepius laudatos comperietis.

222 Each branch will have at its extremities bubbles of air, as though they were fruit. This vegetation, unless perhaps you prefer (which I allow) that very true seeds fall to the earth together with the water, is easily explained by means of effervescence; for the matter is first inflated, and on account of the effervescence air is expelled, which is visible, and this raises and distributes the matter into branches and shrubs, which, on account of their charming green color, wonderfully imitate the natural vegetation of plants. These things are rather curious. You will find many others in the celebrated Authors often praised by me.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De Tempore.

On Time.

223 Perturbatum hìc á nobis fortassè rerum ordinem suspicari quis posset, quòd inter corporum proprietates, temporis quoque ac loci naturam enumeremus, verùm quum concipi non possit corporum motus, nisi temporis etiam, locique natura adcuratè cognita fuerit, iccircò quum plurima de Motu, qui universalis corporum adfectio censeri potest inferiùs dicturi simus, rem instituto nostro

erhaps someone might suspect that the order of things has been disturbed 223 P by us here, in that among the properties of bodies we also enumerate the nature of time and of place; but since the motion of bodies cannot be conceived unless the nature of time and of place has also been accurately known, therefore, since we are going to say a great many things below about Motion, which can be considered a universal affection of bodies, we shall seem to be doing something quite

p. 79

satis adcomodam facturi videmur, si antequàm motus naturam, leges, & proprietates omnes explicemus, illa de tempore ac loco (Scholarum subtilitatibus rejectis) brevissimè compléctamur ex quibus pro ceteris oportuniùs explicandis lux quaedam adfulgeat.

in keeping with our plan if, before we explain the nature, the laws, and all the properties of motion, we embrace very briefly (the subtleties of the Schools being set aside) those things concerning time and place from which some light may shine forth for explaining the rest more conveniently.

224 Tempus itaque, ut ab illo exordiamur, facillimè quidem concipitur, sed à nobis explicari, vel definiri vix potest. „Quid enim, (ait Magnus Augustinus) s1 Quid enim familiarius, & notiùs in loquendo commemoramus, quàm tempus; & intelligimus quidèm cùm id loquimur, intelligimus etiam cùm aliquo loquente id audimus? Quid est ergo tempus? Si nemo ex me quaerat scio; si querenti explicare velim, nescio: fidenter enim dico scire me, quod si nihil praeteriret, non esset praeteritum tempus; & si nihil esset, non esset praesens tempus.“ Aristoteles autèm tempus definirè volens, ait illud esse numerum motus secundum prius, & posterius s2. Quae quidem definitio à Recentioribus reprehendi meritò solet, etenim verosimiliùs dici potest, quod motus ipse sit numerus, & mensura temporis; quum certè nos, temporis durationem aliquo motu, ut horologii, vel solis numerare, vel mensurare consuevérimus

224 Time, then, to begin with it, is indeed very easily conceived, but can scarcely be explained or defined by us. “For what,” says the great Augustine (b), “what do we mention more familiarly and more knowingly in speaking than time? And we understand it, surely, when we speak of it; we understand it also when we hear another speaking of it. What, then, is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one who asks, I do not know: yet I say confidently that I know that if nothing passed away there would be no past time, and if nothing were, there would be no present time.” Aristotle, however, wishing to define time, says that it is the number of motion according to before and after (c). This definition is deservedly wont to be censured by the Moderns; for it can more probably be said that motion itself is the number and measure of time, since we are certainly accustomed to number or to measure the duration of time by some motion, such as that of a clock or of the sun.

225 Res etiam non modò quum moventur, sed etiam dum quiescunt, tempori subjiciuntur, atque aliquo tempore continentur, ideoque tempus dici deberet aequaliter numerus, & mensura motus, & quietis, & quemadmodùm tempus dicitur ab Aristotele numerus cujuscumque motus, ita quoque dici deberet numerus cujuscumque quietis. Quid quòd numerus, sive mensura rerum non est res ipsa numerata, aut mensurata, quemadmodum digiti per quos dies numerantur non sunt dies ipsi, nec ulna qua mensuratur pannus est ipse pannus, ut alia plura omittam, quae videri possunt in Philosophia Sceptica Hispáno idiomate conscripta á Doctore Martinez s3. Unde meritò reprehenditur, Aristotelica temporis definitio tanquam vitiosa, vel obscura, vel potius falsa.

225 Things, moreover, are subject to time not only when they are moved but also while they are at rest, and are contained in some time; and therefore time ought to be called equally the number and measure of motion and of rest; and just as time is called by Aristotle the number of any motion whatever, so it ought also to be called the number of any rest whatever. What of the fact that the number or measure of things is not the thing itself numbered or measured, just as the fingers by which days are numbered are not the days themselves, nor is the ell by which cloth is measured the cloth itself? — to omit many other things, which can be seen in the Philosophia Sceptica written in the Spanish language by Doctor Martínez (d). Hence the Aristotelian definition of time is deservedly censured as faulty, or obscure, or rather false.

226 Clariùs itaque describi poterit tempus: successiva rerum mutabilium duratio, ex qua definitione intelligitur insigne discrimen inter aeternitatem, & tempus: nam in aeternitate partes aliquae distingui non possunt, nam omnes temporum differentias admirabili modo compléctitur, unde satis adcommodè ab omnibus Theologis cum Boethio definiri solet: Interminabilis vitae tota simul, & perfecta possessio. Nos quidem vitam hanc nostram mortalem totam simul haud possidémus: nam quae praeteriit possessa quidem â nobis fuit, & quae futura superst, possidebitur, solumque labile illud instans, quod nobis praesens est, á nobis possidetur, & quemadmodùm sphaéra super aliquod planum revolúta, semper illud

226 More clearly, then, time can be described as the successive duration of mutable things; from which definition is understood the notable difference between eternity and time: for in eternity no parts can be distinguished, since it embraces all the differences of times in an admirable way; whence it is quite fittingly defined by all Theologians, with Boethius: the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of interminable life. We, indeed, by no means possess this mortal life of ours all at once: for what has passed was indeed possessed by us, and what remains to come will be possessed, and only that fleeting instant which is present to us is possessed by us; and just as a sphere rolled over some plane always touches it

Confess. Lib. 11. n. 17. al. cap. 14.

Confessions, bk. 11, no. 17, otherwise ch. 14.

Phys. 5. cap. 16 text. 7.

Physics 5, ch. 16, text 7.

Dialogo 6. pag. 126. & 127.

Dialogue 6, pp. 126 and 127.

p. 80

in puncto contingit, sic ferè brevis vita nostra, per plura veluti instantia temporis, quibus existit, celerrimè transigitur, nam ut eleganter canit Ovidius s1.

at a point, so our brief life is passed very swiftly through the many instants, as it were, of time in which it exists; for, as Ovid elegantly sings (e),

……Velut unda impellitur unda

……As wave is driven onward by wave,

Urgeturque eadem veniens, urgetque priorem,

And, coming on, is pressed by the next, and presses the one before,

Tempora sic fugiunt pariter, pariterque sequuntur.

So the times flee, and alike they follow.

227 Deo autèm immortali tota ejusdem interminabilis vita, ita praesens est, ut ejusdem nihil praeterierit, nihilque unquàm praetéritum sit Aevum quod inter aeternitatem, ac tempus ipsum concipitur, egregiè describitur: duratio entis creati permanentis, & á Deo dependentis, suaptè natura incorruptibilis. Talis est duratio Angeli, & animae rationalis.

227 But to the immortal God the whole of His interminable life is so present that nothing of it has passed away, and nothing of it is ever past. Aevum, which is conceived as lying between eternity and time, is excellently described as the duration of a created, permanent being, dependent on God, and by its own nature incorruptible. Such is the duration of an Angel and of the rational soul.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

Ostenditur quid sit corporum locus.

It is shown what the place of bodies is.

228 Aristoteles 4. Phys. locus est (inquit) corporis ambientis terminus immobilis primus, id est superficies prima & interior corporis aliud corpus continentis. Haec superficies interior, vocatur cóncava, exterior verò convexa. En exemplum: Globus terraqueus undique ab aëre circunscribitur: ubi tria consideranda sunt, & aër ipse, & ejusdem cóncava superficies, & globi terraquei superficies convexa, quae superficiei concavae aëris contigua est: ait itaque Aristoteles: Telluris locum non esse aërem illum ambientem, neque telluris convexam superficiem, sed cóncavam illam aëris superficiem, tellurem ambientem. Aristotelis sententiam Cartesius amplexatus est Expressè namque & ipse docet s2, externum locum corporis sumi posse pro superficie, quae proximè ambit locatum.

ristotle, in Physics 4: place is (he says) the first immobile boundary of the sur228 A rounding body, that is, the first and interior surface of a body containing another body. This interior surface is called concave, and the exterior convex. Here is an example. The terraqueous globe is circumscribed on every side by the air: here three things are to be considered, the air itself, its concave surface, and the convex surface of the terraqueous globe, which is contiguous to the concave surface of the air. Aristotle therefore says: the place of the Earth is not that surrounding air, nor the convex surface of the earth, but that concave surface of the air which surrounds the earth. Descartes embraced the opinion of Aristotle. For he too expressly teaches (f) that the external place of a body can be taken for the surface which most closely surrounds the thing located.

229 Ambientem hanc superficiem vocat locum externum, ut ipsum discernat ab interno, scilicet à spatio, quod ejus sententia, non re, sed sola cogitatione à locati corporis substantia distinguitur. Re vera enim, ait Cartesius s3 extensio in longum latum, & profundum, quae spatium constituit, eadem planè est cum illa, quae

229 This surrounding surface he calls the external place, so as to distinguish it from the internal, namely from space, which in his opinion is distinguished from the substance of the located body not in reality but by thought alone. For in truth, says Descartes (g), the extension in length, breadth and depth which constitutes space is plainly the same as that which constitutes body.

Metamorph. XV. V. 181.

Metamorphoses XV, v. 181.

Part. 2. Princip. num. 15.

Pt. 2 of the Principles, no. 15.

p. 81

stituit corpus. Contrà vero Demócrito, & Epicúro adstipulatus olim fuit S. Augustinus s1 locus enim, ait Sanctus Doctor, in spatio est, quod longitudine, & latitudine, & altitudine corporis occupatur. Non secùs de loco sentiunt Gassendus s2, Newtonus s3, Keil, s4 iique demùm omnes Recentiores, quibus mihi magis cordi est, quàm in nullius verba jurare Nonnullis itaque positis, quid de loci natura sentiendum putem, brevitèr dicam. Nihil enim hac in re determinari legitimè potest, nisi primò quod certum est, ab incerto discernatur.

body. On the other hand, St. Augustine formerly agreed with Democritus and Epicurus (h): for place, says the Holy Doctor, is in space, which is occupied by the length, breadth and height of a body. Not otherwise do Gassendi (i), Newton (j), Keill (k) think about place, and, in short, all the Moderns, to whom nothing is more at heart than to swear by the words of no master. Having laid down these few things, then, I shall say briefly what I think should be held about the nature of place. For nothing can legitimately be determined in this matter unless what is certain is first distinguished from what is uncertain.

230 Certum in primis puto: nullum re ipsa esse corpus, quod aliquo in loco non existat. An verò Divinitus possit fieri, ut corpus aliquod núllibi existat, vulgares Philosophi, qui possibilium philosophia maximè delectantur, ad trúcinam révocent. Pro re comperta itidem habeo, locum non esse in loco, atque adeò, locum non esse ex illis unum, quae in loco existunt. Si namque ita esset, eadem ratione & locus loci, atque ita deinceps in infinitum esset in loco. In comperto etiam est: nullum eorum haberi posse pro loco corporum, quod localiter movetur. Id enim duntaxat moveri potest localiter, quod in loco existit. Arbitror postremò: in eo statuendum esse locum corporum in quo ita singula ipsa corpora existunt, ut unam illius partem repleant, eorum extensioni omninò aequalem, moveantur in ipso prorsùs immobili, ab eoque primo & per se mutuò sese excludant, adeò nempè, ut in eadem simul plura componi naturae viribus nequaquam possint. Omnes namque fatentur, corpora replére locum, quem singula occupant, ipsum aequare, atque ob id esse impenetrabilia, quòd eorum quodlibet ab eo loco, in quo est, aliud excludat. Nomine spatii non aliud intelligitur, nisi negativa, penitusque immobilis secundum trinam dimensionem extensio, in qua existentia corpora modo posita sint, quamque si in nihilum redigerentur, ipsa relinquerent. Negativa haec extensio dicitur à S. Augustino spatiosum nihil, ab aliis intervallum. His positis.

230 I hold as certain, in the first place, that no body really exists which does not exist in some place. Whether, however, it can be brought about by Divine power that some body should exist nowhere, let the common Philosophers, who take the greatest delight in the philosophy of possibles, weigh in the scales. I likewise hold as an ascertained matter that place is not in a place, and so that place is not one of those things that exist in a place. For if it were so, by the same reasoning the place of the place also would be in a place, and so on to infinity. It is ascertained also that none of those things which are moved locally can be held for the place of bodies. For only that which exists in a place can be moved locally. I judge, finally, that the place of bodies is to be set in that in which the bodies themselves singly so exist that they fill one part of it altogether equal to their extension, are moved in it while it is itself wholly immobile, and by it, primarily and of themselves, mutually exclude one another, so far, namely, that several cannot by any means be placed together in the same part by the forces of nature. For all admit that bodies fill the place which each occupies, that they equal it, and that they are on that account impenetrable, because each of them excludes another from that place in which it is. By the name of space nothing else is understood but a negative extension, wholly immobile according to its threefold dimension, in which existing bodies are now placed, and which, if they were reduced to nothing, they would leave behind. This negative extension is called by St. Augustine a spacious nothing, by others an interval. These things being laid down:

231 Dico 1. admittendum re ipsa est spatium, si illud esse possibile evincatur. Probatur: nam quum spatium non sit aliquod reale positivum, sed purum nihil, nequit esse terminus actionis productivae: ergo, si non existit, neque profectò potest esse possibile; quum quod non est re ipsa & est possibile, à Deo saltem possit produci. Quamobrem vel possibile non est spatium, vel si est possibile, illud re ipsa existere, necesse est ipsi dicamus.

231 I say 1. Space is really to be admitted, if it is shown to be possible. It is proved: for since space is not something real and positive but a pure nothing, it cannot be the term of a productive action; therefore, if it does not exist, it certainly cannot be possible either, since what does not really exist and is possible can be produced, at least by God. Wherefore either space is not possible, or, if it is possible, we must necessarily say that it really exists.

232 Dico 2.: possibile est spatium, in quo nullum planè corpus existat. Prob.: potuit Deus antequam Mundi machinam cónderet, creare duo tantum sphaerica corpora, eaque ita collocare;

232 I say 2. Space is possible in which no body at all exists. Proof: God could, before He founded the machine of the World, have created only two spherical bodies, and have placed them in such a way

Loc. cit. num. 10.

Loc. cit., no. 10.

Lib. 83. Quaest. quaest. 20, & lib. 4. sup. Genes. n. 34.

Bk. of 83 Questions, q. 20, and bk. 4 on Genesis, no. 34.

Sect. 1. Phys. Lib. 2. cap. 6.

Sect. 1 of the Physics, bk. 2, ch. 6.

Princip. Schol. ad Def. 8.

Principia, Schol. to Def. 8.

Introduct. ad ver. Philosoph. Lect. 2. & 6.

Introductio ad veram Philosophiam, lect. 2 and 6.

p. 82

ut sese mutuò tángerent. In hoc nulla adparet, vel minima repugnantia. Itaque sint duo hujuscemodi corpora A B (Fig. XVI.) quae se tangant in puncto C. Quoniam ergo res est certissima, duarum spherarum contactum in uno duntaxat puncto posse fieri, apertum manet, fore, ut duo corpora A B, non nisi in puncto C. sese mutuò tangant, ac proinde, ut à se mutuò distent convexae eorum superficies, sive ut à puncto a ad punctum b duci possit recta a b, & sic de aliis. Inter convexas autèm hujuscemodi superficies nullum re ipsa haberetur corpus, quum scilicet positum fuerit duo tantum corpora A & B fuisse à Deo creata: ergo inter illas superficies purum tunc haberetur intervallum, sive spatium, & ideo possibile est spatium, in quo nullum planè corpus existat.

that they touched each other. In this no repugnance, not even the least, appears. Let there be, then, two such bodies A, B (Fig. XVI.), which touch each other at the point C. Since, therefore, it is a most certain thing that the contact of two spheres can take place at one point only, it remains evident that the two bodies A, B will touch each other only at the point C, and consequently that their convex surfaces will be distant from each other, or that a straight line can be drawn from the point a to the point b, and so of the others. Between such convex surfaces, however, no body would really be had, since it has been supposed, namely, that only the two bodies A and B were created by God: therefore between those surfaces there would then be a pure interval, or space; and therefore space is possible in which no body at all exists.

233 Dico 3. admittendum re ipsa est spatium, negativa scilicet, extensio à corporea substantia omninò diversa. Prob.: re ipsa admittendum est spatium si illud esse possibile evincatur [§. 231.]; sed constat evidenter evidentia mathematica spatium esse possibile: [§. 232.] ergo re ipsa est admittendum. Praeterea existentia spatii non obscurè ex eo etiam colligitur, quod extensio mundi non sit infinita. Nec enim finita esse potest, nisi extra illius fines detur spatium, quod ab aliis corporibus occupari queat. Limitibus porrò minimè carére mundum, eorum omnium sententia est, qui habent pro re comperta, nullum ens praeter Deum esse infinitum Ex dictis manifestum fit, quod omnia corpora in spatio existunt, unam illius partem replent singula, eorum extensioni planè aequalem in eoque moventur prorsùs immobili.

233 I say 3. Space is really to be admitted, namely a negative extension, altogether different from corporeal substance. Proof: space is really to be admitted if it is shown to be possible [§. 231.]; but it is established with mathematical evidence that space is possible [§. 232.]; therefore it is really to be admitted. Moreover, the existence of space is clearly gathered also from the fact that the extension of the world is not infinite. For it cannot be finite unless outside its bounds there is space which could be occupied by other bodies. That the world is by no means without limits is the opinion of all those who hold it for an ascertained matter that no being besides God is infinite. From what has been said it becomes manifest that all bodies exist in space, that each fills one part of it, plainly equal to its extension, and that they are moved in it while it is wholly immobile.

234 Constat etiam, quod quum duo quaelibet corpora sibi mutuò re ipsa resistant, videtur aliquid necessariò admitti oportére, in quo dum unum illorum existit, alterum esse naturae viribus minimè possit. Id autèm non esse nisi spatium, videtur perspicuum, quum etiam non existente imò repugnante quavis circumambiente superficie, duo quaelibet corpora sint naturaliter impenetrabilia, utpotè quae adhuc sunt corpora. Non inficior secundariò, & per accidens haud posse duo corpora, quia impenetrabilia una eademque cóncava superficie contineri, sed spatium in quo corpora existunt, illud unicè est à quo ipsa corpora primò, & per se ratione naturalis suae soliditatis, mutuò sese excludunt.

234 It is established also that, since any two bodies really resist each other, it seems that something must necessarily be admitted in which, while one of them exists, the other can by no means be by the forces of nature. That this, however, is nothing other than space seems perspicuous, since, even if no surrounding surface whatever existed, nay, if one were impossible, any two bodies would be naturally impenetrable, inasmuch as they would still be bodies. I do not deny that secondarily and accidentally two bodies, because they are impenetrable, cannot be contained by one and the same concave surface; but space, in which bodies exist, is the only thing from which the bodies themselves primarily and of themselves, by reason of their natural solidity, mutually exclude each other.

235 Dico 4. contra Peripateticos: corpora non idèo sunt in loco, quòd á cóncava alterius corporis superficie circunscribantur. Prob.: si ita esset, núllibi corpus illud existeret quod á nulla circumambiente superficie contineatur: ergo quum ultimum Caelum á nullo externò corpore comprehendatur, illud est re ipsa extra nihil sui quin aliquo in loco existat; sed falsum est existere corpus posse quin sit alicubi [§ 230.] ergo corpora non ideo sunt in loco quod &c. Ultimum porrò Caelum nullibi esse, Aristotelis admissa sententia, inficiari nemo Scholasticorum potest, quin ipsimet Aristoteli apertissimè refragetur. Haec enim habet

235 I say 4, against the Peripatetics: bodies are not in a place because they are circumscribed by the concave surface of another body. Proof: if it were so, that body which is contained by no circumambient surface would exist nowhere: therefore, since the outermost Heaven is comprehended by no external body, it really is outside its own nothingness without existing in any place; but it is false that a body can exist without being somewhere [§ 230.]: therefore bodies are not in a place because, etc. That the outermost Heaven, moreover, is nowhere, once the opinion of Aristotle is admitted, none of the Scholastics can deny without most openly opposing Aristotle himself. For this is what the Prince of the Peripatetics (l)

p. 83

Peripateticorum Princeps s1 Caelum non est alicubi, nec ullo in loco est, siquidem nullum corpus ipsum continet. Quare, ut ait Clariss. Gassendus s2: mirùm dictu est in quas redigantur angustias Peripatetici, qui dum superficiem desérere nolunt, coguntur locum denegare corpori nobilissimo, eidemque amplissimo, cui ratio suadet principem locum assignare.

(l) has: Heaven is not somewhere, nor in any place, since no body contains it. Wherefore, as the most illustrious Gassendi says (m): it is wonderful to tell into what straits the Peripatetics are driven, who, while they are unwilling to abandon the surface, are forced to deny place to the noblest body, and at the same time the most ample, to which reason persuades us to assign the principal place.

236 Confirmatur: posita Aristotelis opinione, dicendum est tandiù corpus in eodem loco existere, quandiù ab eadem circumambiente superficie continetur, quod falsum est; ex hoc enim sequitur idem corpus existere simul posse in eodem loco, & localiter moveri, ut patet de aqua vitreo vase contenta. Movetur enim unà cum vase, quum vas ipsum alio transfertur, neque tamen mutatur superficies, qua circunscribitur: ergo corpus non ideo est in loco quod, &c. 2.: etiam concava ambientis corporis superficies, in loco existit, simulque, & ipsa, movetur quum corpus alio transfertur: ergo nequit in ea statui corporum locus quin dicere cogamur, immobilem localiter non esse locum, simulque in loco, & ipsum locum existere contra ea quae diximus. [§. 230.]

236 It is confirmed: once the opinion of Aristotle is laid down, it must be said that a body exists in the same place as long as it is contained by the same circumambient surface, which is false; for from this it follows that the same body can at the same time exist in the same place and be moved locally, as is evident in the case of water contained in a glass vessel. For it is moved together with the vessel when the vessel itself is carried elsewhere, and yet the surface by which it is circumscribed is not changed: therefore a body is not in a place because, etc. 2. The concave surface of the surrounding body also exists in a place, and it too is moved at the same time when the body is carried elsewhere: therefore the place of bodies cannot be set in it without our being forced to say that place is not locally immobile, and that place itself at the same time exists in a place, contrary to what we have said [§. 230.]

237 Dico 5.: locus corporum est spatium ab ipsis corporibus occupatum. Prob: unumquodque corpus reipsa existit in spatio, unam illius partem replet sibi aequalem, in eoque movetur prorsus immobili [§. 230.] sed nomine loci non aliud intelligitur, nisi id in quo unumquodque corpus hoc modo est [§. 230.]: ergo. Confirmatur: in eo statuendus est locus corporum, in quo corpora ipsa ita existunt, ut unumquodque ab eo in quo est, aliud quodcumque ratione naturalis suae soliditatis primò, & per se excludat [§. 230.]. Id autem non est nisi spatium, quod singula occupant [§§. 233, & 234]: ergo. Secundo: cóncava ambientis corporis superficies haberi nequit pro continentis corporis loco [§. 235]; sed hac rejecta, unum manet spatium, quod pro loco adsumi possit: ergo locus cujusque corporis est ipsum spatium.

237 I say 5. The place of bodies is the space occupied by the bodies themselves. Proof: each body really exists in space, fills one part of it equal to itself, and is moved in it while it is wholly immobile [§. 230.]; but by the name of place nothing else is understood than that in which each body is in this manner [§. 230.]: therefore. It is confirmed: the place of bodies is to be set in that in which the bodies themselves so exist that each, by reason of its natural solidity, primarily and of itself excludes any other whatever from that in which it is [§. 230.]. But this is nothing but the space which each occupies [§§. 233 and 234]: therefore. Secondly: the concave surface of the surrounding body cannot be held for the place of the contained body [§. 235]; but when this is rejected, space alone remains which can be taken for place: therefore the place of each body is space itself.

Argumenta solvuntur.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

238 Opp. 1. contra tertiam cum Cartesio: spatium dicitur extensio in longum latum, & profundum; sed haec non distinguitur à corpore: ergo. Disting. maj: spatium dicitur extensio &c., negativa, concedo, positiva, nego, & distinguo min. Extensio positiva non distinguitur &c, concedo, negativa nego, & conseq. Corpus est extensio non qualiscumque, sed positiva, & solida, eaque ratione divisibilis, ut illius partes divelli possint à se mutuò, ac penitùs separari. Spatium autèm dicitur

bj. 1, against the third conclusion, with Descartes: space is called exten238 O sion in length, breadth and depth; but this is not distinguished from body: therefore. I distinguish the major: space is called extension, etc., negative, I grant; positive, I deny; and I distinguish the minor: positive extension is not distinguished, etc., I grant; negative, I deny; and the consequence. Body is not any extension whatever, but a positive and solid one, and divisible in such a way that its parts can be torn from one another and entirely separated. Space, on the other hand, is indeed called extension,

Lib. 4 Phys. tex 45.

Bk. 4 of the Physics, text 45.

Sect. 1. Phys. Lib. 2. cap. 6.

Sect. 1 of the Physics, bk. 2, ch. 6.

p. 84

quidem extensio, sed negativa, penetrabilis & omninò indiscerptibilis: corpus namque, & spatium adtributa sibi vindicant, non diversa solùm, sed ita contraria, ut impossibile sit illa, tanquam uni, & eidem inhaerentia subjecto, concipere, maxima itaque corporis à spatio differentia in eo consistit, quod omne corpus tria quidem habet spatiorum (hoc est dimensionum) genera, non tamen quidquid tria habet spatiorum genera, est corpus.

extension, but negative, penetrable, and altogether indiscerptible: for body and space claim for themselves attributes not only diverse, but so contrary that it is impossible to conceive them as one thing and as inhering in the same subject. The greatest difference of body from space, therefore, consists in this: that every body indeed has the three kinds of spaces (that is, of dimensions), yet not whatever has the three kinds of spaces is body.

239 Opp. 2.: Spatium vel est aliquid reale, vel purùm nihil. Si secundum: ergo perperam vocatur extensum, mensurabile &c., quia nihili nullae sunt proprietates Si primùm: ergo aliquid praeter Deum est immensum, interminatum; sed hoc est absurdum: ergo non datur spatium. Respondeo: spatium non esse aliquod reale positivum, sed ut ait S. Augustinus spatiosum nihil. Reale dici potest, quatenùs ab intellectu non dependet. Nullo quippè cogitante intellectu, distant à se mutuo puncta a b Fig. XVI. Extensum dicitur spatium, mensurabile &c., eodem planè sensu, quo extensa, & mensurabilis vocatur umbra, quatenùs nempè extensum & mensurabile corpus potest in illo spatio collocari. Nihili autem ut diximus [§. 12] nullae sunt proprietates positivas, negativas multas. Quae quum ita sint, frustra quaeritur, ab Scholasticis: ¿nùm spatium sit substantia, vel accidens? Manifestum est enim, nihil nisi reale positivum esse, quod duntaxat in substantiam, & accidens potest jure distribui. Nec eos juvat, spatium non esse aliquod fictum ab intellectu, etenim neque umbra aliquod hujusmodi est, & tamen Scholasticorum nemo, dicet eam esse substantiam vel accidens. Neque etiam officit spatium, imaginarium nuncupari, quatenus ab imaginatione dependeat, nam ideò ita dicitur, quia illius dimensiones instar corporearum dimensionum, quae in sensum cadunt, imaginémur.

239 Obj. 2: Space is either something real or a pure nothing. If the second: then it is wrongly called extended, measurable, etc., because of nothing there are no properties. If the first: then something besides God is immense and unbounded; but this is absurd: therefore there is no space. I reply that space is not something real and positive, but, as St. Augustine says, a spacious nothing. It can be called real inasmuch as it does not depend on the intellect. For with no intellect thinking, the points a, b (Fig. XVI.) are distant from each other. Space is called extended, measurable, etc., in plainly the same sense in which a shadow is called extended and measurable, inasmuch, namely, as an extended and measurable body can be placed in that space. Of nothing, moreover, as we have said [§. 12], there are no positive properties, but many negative ones. Since these things are so, it is vainly asked by the Scholastics whether space is a substance or an accident. For it is manifest that only the real and positive is that which can rightly be divided into substance and accident. Nor does it help them that space is not something feigned by the intellect, for neither is a shadow anything of this kind, and yet none of the Scholastics will say that it is a substance or an accident. Nor does it stand in the way that space is called imaginary, as though it depended on the imagination; for it is so called because we imagine its dimensions after the manner of corporeal dimensions, which fall under the senses.

240 Opp. 3. Contra quartam, & quintam: indubia res est locum debere esse aliquod reale, sed hujuscemodi non est spatium: ergo. Disting. maj.: aliquod reale nempè, non fictum ab intellectu, conc. hoc est ens aliquod positivum, quod produci per realem actionem possit, nego, & eadem solut. distincta min., nego conseq. Verùm enim est, locum esse non posse aliquod prorsùs imaginarium, at ex hoc non sequitur debere esse aliquod ens reale positivum: sequeretur enim, vel aliquod ens reale extare posse, quin sit álicubi, vel ipsum quoque locum in loco existere. Ea igitur realitas inest spatio, quae loco convenire legitimè potest.

240 Obj. 3. Against the fourth and fifth: it is an undoubted thing that place must be something real, but space is not of this kind: therefore. I distinguish the major: something real, namely not feigned by the intellect, I grant; that is, some positive being which can be produced by a real action, I deny; and, the minor being distinguished by the same solution, I deny the consequence. For it is true that place cannot be something altogether imaginary, but from this it does not follow that it must be some real positive being: for it would follow either that some real being could exist without being anywhere, or that place itself also exists in a place. That reality, therefore, is in space which can legitimately belong to place.

241 Opp. 4.: locus dicitur récipere rem locabilem, eam continere, & ab ea repleri, sed haec non conveniunt spatio, sed enti positivo: ergo. Dist. maj. & ab ea repleri, perindè prorsùs, atque vas liquorem recipit, ipsum continet, & ab illo repletur, nego, ita nimirùm, ut sit sensus, quod res existat in loco, & quidem adeò, ut nihil ipsius rei extra locum habeatur, neque sinat loquendo de corporibus, ut ab altera re simul occupetur, conc, & dist.

241 Obj. 4: place is said to receive the locable thing, to contain it, and to be filled by it; but these things do not belong to space, but to a positive being: therefore. I distinguish the major: and to be filled by it exactly as a vessel receives a liquor, contains it, and is filled by it, I deny; in such a way, namely, that the sense is that the thing exists in the place, and indeed so that nothing of the thing itself is had outside the place, and that, speaking of bodies, it does not allow the place to be occupied at the same time by another thing, I grant; and I distinguish the

p. 85

min: haec munera non conveniunt spatio si primo modo sumitur, conc, si sumatur secundo modo, nego, & conseq. Solutio est manifesta.

minor: these functions do not belong to space if it is taken in the first way, I grant; if it is taken in the second way, I deny; and the consequence. The solution is manifest.

242 Opp. demum: corpus refertur ad ea quae circum ipsum sunt, videlicèt judicamus corpus tandiù esse in eodem loco, quamdiù eandem à circunstantibus corporibus distantiam servat: ergo haec relatio erit corporis locus. Dist. antec.: refertur, ut illius situs definiatur, conc ut certi simus ipsum corpus esse in loco, nego, & conseq. Corporis situs nihil est aliud, nisi respectus quidam ex eo resultans, quod certam positionem corpus ipsum habeat inter illa quibus confertur, quaeque veluti immobilia spectantur, determinatamque distantiam ab illis obtineat; at falsum est referendum esse corpus ad corpora circunstantia, ut certò nobis constet, ipsum in loco existere. Sicuti enim ab illis non dependet, ut sit extra nihil sui, ita iisdem opus non habet ut aliquo in loco existat. Propterea Recentiores dividunt locum in absolutum, & relativum, primum vocant eam spatii partem, quam corpus occupat. Secundum verò quem modo situm diximus etiam adpelant adparentem, & sensibilem. Ex dictis sequentia Corollaria deducuntur.

242 Obj. finally: a body is referred to the things which are around it; that is, we judge that a body is in the same place as long as it keeps the same distance from the surrounding bodies: therefore this relation will be the place of the body. I distinguish the antecedent: it is referred so that its situation may be defined, I grant; so that we may be certain that the body itself is in a place, I deny; and the consequence. The situation of a body is nothing else but a certain respect resulting from the fact that the body itself has a certain position among those things with which it is compared, and which are regarded as immobile, and holds a determinate distance from them; but it is false that the body must be referred to the surrounding bodies in order that it may be certain to us that it exists in a place. For just as it does not depend on them in order to be outside its own nothingness, so it has no need of them in order to exist in some place. Therefore the Moderns divide place into absolute and relative; the first they call that part of space which the body occupies. The second, which we have just called situation, they also call apparent and sensible. From what has been said the following Corollaries are deduced.

243 Primum: Locus corporum absolutus, nihil est reale positivum. Spatium quippè nihil hujuscemodi est. Secundum: Potest corpus mutare locum absolutum, quin mutet relativum. Homo enim sedens in navi, quae moveatur, eundem in illa, ut patet situm retinet, at simul continuò mutat locum absolutum, quum una cum navi in qua est, diversam spatii partem singulis momentis corpus ipsum occupet. Tertium: Divisio loci in naturalem, & violentum de loco duntaxat relativo intelligenda est. Quum enim spatium sit sibi perpetuò uniformè, perindè est corpori quamcumque illius partem teneat, & ideò quilibet locus absolutus, est corpori naturalis. Contra verò est in loco violento, si inter alia corpora eum situm non servet, quem servare debet, ut stet illa eorumdem dispositio, quam initio temporis Deus constituit. Sic terra esset in loco violento, si suprà aquam existeret, quum constitutio mundi requirat, ut infra illam habeatur.

243 First: The absolute place of bodies is nothing real and positive. For space is nothing of this kind. Second: A body can change its absolute place without changing its relative place. For a man sitting in a ship which is moving keeps the same situation in it, as is evident; but at the same time he continually changes his absolute place, since together with the ship in which he is his body occupies a different part of space at each moment. Third: The division of place into natural and violent is to be understood of relative place only. For since space is perpetually uniform with itself, it is all the same to a body whatever part of it it holds, and therefore any absolute place whatever is natural to a body. On the contrary, a body is in a violent place if among other bodies it does not keep that situation which it ought to keep so that that disposition of them may stand which God established at the beginning of time. Thus the earth would be in a violent place if it existed above the water, since the constitution of the world requires that it be held below it.

CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

De Vacuo.

On the Vacuum.

244 Loci natura exposita, reliquum est, ut de vacuo non nulla dicamus. Hinc constabit apertiùs, quod superiori capite demonstrabimus, negativam scilicèt extensionem, sive spatium, in quo corpora quaeque sint admitti oportere.

aving set forth the nature of place, it remains for us to say some things 244 H about the vacuum. Hence it will be more openly established, what we demonstrated in the preceding chapter, that a negative extension, namely space, in which each and every body is, must be admitted.

p. 86

245 Vacuum sive inane propriè sumptum dicitur: Spatium superficiebus comprehensum, ac veluti terminatum, in quo nullum penitùs corpus, sive fluidum, sive solidum, sive conspicuum, sive inconspicuum à quo repleatur, existat. Consultò dixi propriè sumptum, etenim, vulgò vacuum etiam vocari solet vas, quod, à nullo corpore nobis conspicuo occupatur, licet repleatur ab inconspicuo. Ex qua definitione sequentia Corollaria deducuntur. Primum. Nullum est vacuum, si nihil spatii, quod ab aliquo corpore non occupetur, intra universum existat. Secundum. Vacuum quoque non satis ex eo evincitur, quod sensibilia quaeque corpora in spatio existere demonstretur. Possunt enim omnia esse in spatio, quin aliquam illius portionem, quae à nullo corpore occupetur, intercipiant: at vicissim & esto Corollarium tertium. Evincitur dari spatium, si vacuum existere, aut esse possibile ostendatur Hoc enim ipso dari extensionem negativam manifestum est.

245 A vacuum or void, taken properly, is called a space comprehended by surfaces and as it were bounded, in which there exists absolutely no body, whether fluid or solid, whether conspicuous or inconspicuous, by which it is filled. I said deliberately taken properly, for in common speech a vessel is also wont to be called empty which is occupied by no body conspicuous to us, although it is filled by an inconspicuous one. From this definition the following Corollaries are deduced. First. There is no vacuum if no space exists within the universe which is not occupied by some body. Second. Nor is a vacuum sufficiently proved from the fact that all sensible bodies whatever are demonstrated to exist in space. For all can be in space without intercepting some portion of it which is occupied by no body: but conversely, and let this be the third Corollary, it is proved that space exists, if a vacuum is shown to exist or to be possible. For by this very fact it is manifest that a negative extension exists.

246 Dividi solet vacuum á Philosophis in coacervatum, & disseminatum. Primum est, notabile aliquod spatium intra universi ambitum, á nullo penitùs corpore occupatum. Disseminatum verò dicuntur spatiola corpusculis aquae, aëris ve intercepta, quae jam non aëre, alio ve corpore oppleta, sed penitùs inania, corpore ve omni prorsùs vacua sunt, sive vacuola minima insensibilia inter materiae texturam interclusa, ferè sicut inter plurima tritici grana intérjacent minima spatia in quibus nihil tritici inest. Tria circa vacuum coacervatum ad trutinam revocari solent à Philosophis. Primum: ¿An sit possibile? Secundum, ¿num re ipsa in mundo existat? Tertium ¿an illud possit solius naturae viribus obtineri? Vacuum coacervatum adeò repugnare, ut ne Divina quidem virtute haberi queat, apertissima sententia Cartesi est s1. Contrarium verò ii omnes Recentiores sentiunt, quibus solemne est, corpus à spatio distingui.

246 The vacuum is wont to be divided by Philosophers into the coacervate and the disseminate. The first is some notable space within the circuit of the universe, occupied by absolutely no body. Disseminate vacuums, on the other hand, is the name given to the little spaces intercepted by the corpuscles of water or of air, which are no longer filled with air or other body, but are wholly empty, or altogether devoid of every body; or very small, insensible little vacuums shut up within the texture of matter, almost as, between a great many grains of wheat, there lie very small spaces in which there is nothing of wheat. Three questions about the coacervate vacuum are wont to be weighed by Philosophers. First: is it possible? Second: does it really exist in the world? Third: can it be obtained by the forces of nature alone? That the coacervate vacuum is so repugnant that it cannot be had even by Divine power is the most open opinion of Descartes (n). The contrary, however, is held by all those Moderns with whom it is a settled principle that body is distinguished from space.

247 Cl. Newtonus docuisse minimè contentus, coacervatum vacuum non repugnare, putat vacuum illud, re ipsa in mundo existere, ut vidére est apud ipsum s2. His positis.

247 The celebrated Newton, by no means content with having taught that the coacervate vacuum is not repugnant, thinks that that vacuum really exists in the world, as may be seen in his own works (o). These things being laid down:

248 Dico 1.: non adeò repugnat vacuum coacervatum, ut Divina virtute haberi minimè possit. Est contra Cartesium. Prob.: potest Deus corpus omne in vase aliquo contentum rédigere in nihilum, simulque impedire, ne aliud succedat; sed hoc pacto daretur vacuum coacervatum: ergo. Major constat: nullum quippe vas adeò indiget à substantia repleri, ut nisi aliqua substantia in illo sit, existere in rerum natura minimè possit. Praeterea ex duabus rebus realiter entitativè distinctis, potest Deus anihilare unam, & aliam conservare, sic potest anihilare Petrum, conservato Paulo. Sed majorem negat Cartesius, propterea, nimirùm quia tunc

248 I say 1.: the coacervate vacuum is not so repugnant that it can by no means be had by Divine power. This is against Descartes. Proof: God can reduce to nothing every body contained in some vessel, and at the same time prevent another from succeeding; but in this way a coacervate vacuum would be had: therefore. The major is established: for no vessel so needs to be filled by a substance that, unless some substance is in it, it could by no means exist in the nature of things. Moreover, of two things really and entitatively distinct, God can annihilate one and conserve the other, just as He can annihilate Peter while conserving Paul. But Descartes denies the major, for this reason, namely, because then it would necessarily

Part. 2. Princip. n. 16.

Pt. 2 of the Principles, no. 16.

Lib. 2. Princip. Sect. 7. Schol. ad prop. 40. pag. 356, Edit. Londin. & pag. 371. Opt.

Bk. 2 of the Principia, sect. 7, Schol. to prop. 40, p. 356, London ed., and p. 371 of the Opticks.

p. 87

necessariò futurum sit, ut latera ipsa non distent à se mutuò, sed planè sese contingant. Contra tamen: Certum enim puto non posse illius vasis látera sese contingere, quin ejusdem figura pereat, ¿quis autem negabit posse Deum O. M. omnem substantiam in vase contentam in nihilum redigere, quin ejusdem vasis figura, vel minimè mutetur, quum á substantia, quae vas replet, nullo planè modo experientia teste, ipsius vasis figura dependeat?

come about that the sides themselves would not be distant from each other, but would plainly touch each other. On the contrary, however: for I hold it certain that the sides of that vessel cannot touch each other without its figure perishing; and who will deny that God, the Best and Greatest, can reduce to nothing all the substance contained in the vessel without the figure of that same vessel being changed in the least, since, as experience witnesses, the figure of the vessel itself depends in no way at all on the substance which fills the vessel?

249 Falsum etiam est, ea corpora sese mutuò tangere, quibus nullùm corpus re ipsa interjicitur. Ad physicum enim duorum corporum contactum non solùm requiritur, ut nullum corpus inter illa habeatur, verùm etiam, ut nullum, nè minimum quidem interjici illis posset, quin à suo loco dimoveantur. Id autem, ut constet apertiùs considerate Fig. XVI. Certum est, penitùs repugnare ut illa duo sphaerica corpora A B secundum convexas eorum superficies sese contingant: igitur sibi invicem contigua non erunt puncta a b, e d, m n, x y.; sed tunc nihil reale positivum inter illa haberetur: ergo falsum est duo corpora hoc ipso tangere sese mutuò, quòd nihil reale positivum, sive nullum corpus, re ipsa inter illa existat.

249 It is also false that those bodies touch each other between which no body is really interposed. For the physical contact of two bodies requires not only that no body be had between them, but also that none, not even the smallest, could be interposed between them without their being moved from their place. That this may be more openly evident, consider Fig. XVI. It is certain that it is wholly repugnant that those two spherical bodies A, B should touch each other along their convex surfaces: therefore the points a b, e d, m n, x y will not be contiguous to one another; but then nothing real and positive would be had between them: therefore it is false that two bodies touch each other by the very fact that nothing real and positive, or no body, really exists between them.

250 Fallitur ergo Vir Cl. Antonius Le Grand s1 quum ait: Substantiam possibilem non posse esse medium actuale dividens, ac séparans corpora, quum sit perspicuum, puncta a b globorum A B non nisi per substantiam possibilem futurum esse in illa hypothesi, ut re ipsa à se mutuo distent. Neque ipsum juvat, quod opponit, nihil scilicèt, in mundo tunc fore unitum, propterea nimirùm quod inter partes corporis, quae uniuntur, possibile sit aliquod medium, quod ea separet. Non juvat inquam, quia ut duo separata re ipsa sint à se mutuò non satis est, ut inter illa possibile sit aliquod medium, sed insupèr requiritur, ut medium aliquod inter ea sit possibile, quin si re ipsa illis interjiciatur, situm suum ea mutare cogantur. Sic distant re ipsa à se mutuò puncta a b globorum A B quia licet superiori facta hypothesi nihil reale interjiciant, intercipere tamen illud possunt, quin diversum ab eo, quem habent situm obtineant. Neque etiam Cartesianos juvat respondere, in proposito casu vasis, adhuc remanere corpus manente nimirùm extensione quae juxta ipsos est corporis essentia. Nam ut jam diximus [§. 4.] haec apertissima est petitio principii, & validissimè ex Tosca s2 impugnari potest hoc modo.

250 The celebrated Antoine Le Grand (p) is therefore mistaken when he says: A possible substance cannot be an actual medium dividing and separating bodies; since it is perspicuous that in that hypothesis the points a, b of the globes A, B would be really distant from each other only through a possible substance. Nor does what he objects help him, namely that nothing in the world would then be united, for this reason, to be sure, that between the parts of a body which are united some medium is possible which might separate them. It does not help, I say, because for two things to be really separated from each other it is not enough that some medium be possible between them; it is further required that some medium be possible between them such that, if it were really interposed between them, they would not be forced to change their situation. Thus the points a, b of the globes A, B are really distant from each other, because, although in the hypothesis made above they intercept nothing real, they can nevertheless intercept it without obtaining a situation different from the one they have. Nor does it help the Cartesians to reply that in the proposed case of the vessel body still remains, since extension, namely, remains, which according to them is the essence of body. For, as we have already said [§. 4.], this is a most open begging of the question, and it can be very strongly attacked, following Tosca (q), in this way.

251 Nam si ut vult Cartesius spatium illud, quod in praedicta hypothesi intra vas necessariò relinqueretur, esset corpus reale, certè vel de novo produceretur quando destrueretur aër, aut aliundè à Deo ibi adduceretur: aut jam ibi erat. Non primum, nec secundum, utrumque enim est contra hypothesim factam, supponitur

251 For if, as Descartes would have it, that space which in the aforesaid hypothesis would necessarily be left within the vessel were a real body, certainly it would either be produced anew when the air was destroyed, or be brought there by God from elsewhere, or else it was already there. Not the first, nor the second, for both are against the hypothesis made; for it is supposed

Institutio Philosophiae, pt. 4, ch. 13, no. 9.

Philosoph. Tom. 3. p. 254.

p. 88

enim, Deum intra vas, aliud corpus non subrogare: ergo fatendum erit, semper ibidem extitisse, & consequentèr penetratum erat cum aëre; sed penetratio unius corporis cum alio, etiam juxta Cartesium est naturaliter impossibilis: ergo & impossibile erit spatium illud relictum esse corpus reale: ergo est inane.

that God does not substitute another body within the vessel: therefore it will have to be admitted that it always existed there, and consequently that it was penetrated with the air; but the penetration of one body with another is, even according to Descartes, naturally impossible: therefore it will also be impossible that that space left behind is a real body: therefore it is void.

252 Dico 2.: re ipsa non datur in mundo vacuum coacervatum. Prob: existentia vacui coacervati in mundo neque experientia evinci potest: neque ratione demonstrari: ergo re ipsa non datur. Prob. antec.: non experientia: ea etenim experimenta, quae ad id suadendum adferri solent, minimè probant vacui existentiam, ut postea videbimus: neque ratione illius existentia ostenditur: nullius enim roboris sunt, quae censentur precipuae, ut ex solutione argumentorum patebit: ergo.

252 I say 2.: a coacervate vacuum does not really exist in the world. Proof: the existence of a coacervate vacuum in the world can neither be proved by experience nor demonstrated by reason: therefore it does not really exist. Proof of the antecedent: not by experience, for those experiments which are wont to be brought forward to persuade us of it by no means prove the existence of a vacuum, as we shall see later; nor is its existence shown by reason, for the arguments which are reckoned the principal ones are of no strength, as will be evident from the solution of the arguments: therefore.

253 Dico 3.: viribus naturae haberi nequit in mundo vacuum coacervatum. Prob.: nam quum ex proximè dictis nullum sit re ipsa intra ambitum universi notabile spatium â nullo corpore occupatum, nequit spatium aliquod notabile omni corpore privari, nisi vel corpus quod in illo erat, redigatur in nihilum, vel fiat, ut idem locus simul á duobus corporibus repleatur; sed manifestum est naturae viribus fieri neutrum posse: ergo naturae viribus haberi nequit in mundo vacuum coaecervatum.

253 I say 3.: a coacervate vacuum cannot be had in the world by the forces of nature. Proof: for since, from what has just been said, there is really no notable space within the circuit of the universe occupied by no body, no notable space can be deprived of every body unless either the body which was in it is reduced to nothing, or it comes about that the same place is filled at the same time by two bodies; but it is manifest that neither can be done by the forces of nature: therefore a coacervate vacuum cannot be had in the world by the forces of nature.

Argumenta solvuntur.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

254 Opp. 1. contra primam: nec Divina virtute potest fieri, ut detur vacuum, quando actu datur corpus; sed in casu vasis actu datur corpus: ergo. Prob. min. quod existit, & non est spiritus, ipsum est corpus; atqui spatium in vase existit, & spiritus non est: ergo. Dist. maj. quod existit neque spiritus est, ipsum est corpus, si physicè atque reali existentia existat, conc. Si aequivaleat duntaxat physicè existenti, nego, & conseq. Spatium verò ubi corpore omni vacuum ponitur, tametsi physica existentia corporibus competente non existat, eo tamen pacto existit, ut corpori re ipsa existenti quadam ratione aequivaleat, utpote ad quod recipiendum capacitate donatur.

bj. 1, against the first: not even by Divine power can it come about that 254 O there is a vacuum when there is actually a body; but in the case of the vessel there is actually a body: therefore. Proof of the minor: what exists and is not a spirit is a body; but space in the vessel exists and is not a spirit: therefore. I distinguish the major: what exists and is not a spirit is a body, if it exists by a physical and real existence, I grant; if it is only equivalent to a physically existing thing, I deny; and the consequence. Space, however, where it is posited as empty of every body, although it does not exist by the physical existence that belongs to bodies, nevertheless exists in such a way as to be in a certain manner equivalent to a really existing body, inasmuch as it is endowed with the capacity of receiving one.

255 Opp. 2. in illo casu, vasis latera jungerentur: ergo nec Divina virtute daretur vacuum. Prob. antec.: In illo casu nullum reale intervallum intercéderet; sed illa se realiter contingunt, inter quae nullum reale intervallum intérjacet: ergo Dist. maj: nullum intervallum reale intercederet, si hoc nomine intelligatur corpus reale existens, conc., si intelligatur capacitas corporis recipiendi, seu corpus quod interpóni queat, nego, & eisdem terminis distincta minori, nego conseq. Ad hoc ut duo corpora sese non contingant, atque ad invicem distent, satis est, ut ipsis manentibus immotis corpus aliquod interponi possit, quamtumvis nullum reaple

255 Obj. 2. In that case the sides of the vessel would be joined: therefore not even by Divine power would there be a vacuum. Proof of the antecedent: in that case no real interval would intervene; but those things really touch each other between which no real interval lies: therefore. I distinguish the major: no real interval would intervene, if by this name is understood a really existing body, I grant; if there is understood the capacity of receiving a body, or a body which could be interposed, I deny; and, the minor being distinguished in the same terms, I deny the consequence. In order that two bodies should not touch each other and should be distant from one another, it is enough that, while they remain unmoved, some body could be interposed, even though none is actually interposed;

p. 89

intejectum sit, eo namque ipso, illa in remotis, ac distantibus locis existant oportet, ut supra demonstratum á nobis est.

for by that very fact they must exist in remote and distant places, as has been demonstrated by us above.

256 Opp. 3. contra secundam cum magno Newtono: si actu non datur vacuum coacervatum, tunc caelorum spatia actu deberent esse plena; sed non possunt esse plena, nam sic cometarum, & planetarum motus retardaretur, imò jam inde á mundi principio, quo moventur, languéscere motus deberet: ergo. Nego min. & inclusam: etenim ut astra motum suum jugiter prosequantur, haudquaquam exposcitur aliud, praeter quam quod materia replens caelum planetarium non resistat sensibiliter astris. Adhaec: luminis substantia in qua undequaque per caeli ambitum diffussa, globi planetarum, & cometarum moventur, juxta ipsum eximium Newtonum non efficit, ut perturbentur illorum decursus, neque ut motus ipse paulatim languescat: ergo pari ratione poterunt spatia illa caelorum corpore alio fluidissimo, subtilissimoque repleri, quin perennis siderum motus, vel minimum, vel perturbetur, vel retardetur. Haec autem quae de vacuo coacervao diximus, non impediunt, quominus vacuum disseminatum cum Cl. Gassendo admittamus.

256 Obj. 3, against the second, with the great Newton: if there is not actually a coacervate vacuum, then the spaces of the heavens would have to be actually full; but they cannot be full, for thus the motion of the comets and planets would be retarded; nay, ever since the beginning of the world, from which they have been moving, their motion ought to have been growing languid: therefore. I deny the minor and its included proof: for in order that the stars may continually pursue their motion, nothing else whatever is required than that the matter filling the planetary heaven should not sensibly resist the stars. Moreover, the substance of light, diffused on every side through the circuit of heaven, in which the globes of the planets and comets are moved, does not, according to the excellent Newton himself, bring it about that their courses are disturbed, or that the motion itself grows gradually languid: therefore by the same reasoning those spaces of the heavens could be filled with another body, most fluid and most subtle, without the perennial motion of the stars being either disturbed or retarded even in the least. These things, however, which we have said about the coacervate vacuum do not prevent us from admitting the disseminate vacuum with the celebrated Gassendi.

257 Verosimiliùs namque est rebus corporeis spatia exilissima intérseri, quibus vacui disseminati nuncupationem impertímur, quum perspicuum sit subtilissimam ipsam materiam omnia pervadentem inanibus ejusmodi spatiis interrumpi. Etenim quum fluidissima sit, neque perfectè continua, constare debet particulis sese secundum paucissima puncta contingentibus, ac reipsa dissociatis; interstitia verò illa nullo replentur corpore. Si enim subtilior quaedam adstruatur substantia, altérutrum consequatur oportet, scilicèt, vel haec de qua agimus, subtilissima non est futura, vel quoniam hoc subtiliore fluido admisso difficultas eadem recurrit, admittenda erit doctrina materiae in infinitum divissae, & in fluiditate decrescentis. Postremò si nulla essent vacuola corporibus interspersa, nullus in rerum natura fieri posset motus localis. Ad hoc enim ut corpus aliquod moveatur, ex. gr. per aëra, necesse est corpus mobile protrudere aërem anteriorem in alium locum; sed illum non posset in alium locum protrúdere, si nulla essent vacuola corporibus interspersa: ergo. Major patet: neque enim (ut argumentatur Tosca), neque enim corpus moveri potest, quin in locum aëris anterioris subeat: nequit autem in eum subire persistente ibi anteriore aëre: aliter enim daretur naturaliter penetratio: oportet ergo corpus mobile anteriorem aërem protrúdere, ut moveri possit. Min. autem prob.: nam nequit corpus mobile anteriorem aërem in alium locum protrúdere, nisi adsit locus vel antrorsum, vel retrorsum, vel sursum, vel deorsum, vel ad látera occupabilis ab illo aëre protrudendo; sed si nulla dentur vacuola nullus est locus occupabilis, quum omnia sint plena: ergo.

257 For it is more probable that very slender spaces are interspersed among corporeal things, to which we give the name of disseminate vacuum, since it is perspicuous that the most subtle matter itself, which pervades all things, is interrupted by empty spaces of this kind. For since it is most fluid, and not perfectly continuous, it must consist of particles touching one another at very few points and really dissociated; and those interstices are filled by no body. For if some subtler substance is asserted, one of two things must follow: either this matter of which we are treating will not be the most subtle, or, since the same difficulty recurs once this subtler fluid is admitted, the doctrine of matter divided to infinity and decreasing in fluidity will have to be admitted. Finally, if there were no little vacuums interspersed among bodies, no local motion could take place in the nature of things. For in order that some body be moved, e.g. through the air, it is necessary that the moving body push the air in front of it into another place; but it could not push it into another place if there were no little vacuums interspersed among bodies: therefore. The major is evident: for (as Tosca argues) a body cannot be moved without entering into the place of the air in front of it; but it cannot enter into it while the air in front persists there, for otherwise there would naturally be penetration: the moving body must therefore push the air in front of it in order to be able to move. The minor is proved: for the moving body cannot push the air in front of it into another place unless there is a place, forward or backward, upward or downward, or at the sides, that can be occupied by that air which is to be pushed; but if no little vacuums exist, there is no occupiable place, since all are full: therefore.

258 Opp. 4. contra tertiam experimentum illud celebre quod

258 Obj. 4, against the third: that celebrated experiment which is called Torricellian

p. 90

Torricellianum adpellatur eo quod Evangelista Torricellius omnium primus adseratur hoc experimentum fecisse. Sit canaliculus vitreus A C.
