(Fig. XVII.) una sui parte hermeticè sigillatus, ejusque longitudo major sit duobus pedibus cùm dimidio; impleatur mercurio, tùm digito obturetur os illud per quod mercurio fuit impletus: invertatur canaliculus sic digito clausus, ac in vas aliquod etiam mercurio satis refertum, ejus extremitas simul cum digito obturante immitatur, post immersionem removeatur digitus, aperiaturque os canaliculi, & statim mercurius ex canaliculo in vas illud descendet, non tamen totus, sed permanebit in ipso canaliculo ad usque altitudinem A E variam, pro varietate temporis, & loci: ergo superior tubi pars E C à mercurio relicta omninò vacua est: ergo dari potest solius naturae viribus vacuum coacervatum.

because Evangelista Torricelli is asserted to have been the first of all to perform this experiment. Let there be a little glass tube A C (Fig. XVII.), hermetically sealed at one of its ends, and let its length be greater than two and a half feet; let it be filled with mercury, then let the mouth through which it was filled with mercury be stopped with a finger; let the tube, thus closed by the finger, be inverted, and let its end, together with the stopping finger, be put into some vessel also well filled with mercury; after the immersion let the finger be removed and the mouth of the tube opened, and at once the mercury will descend from the tube into that vessel, not, however, all of it, but it will remain in the tube itself up to the height A E, which varies with the variety of time and place: therefore the upper part of the tube, E C, left by the mercury, is altogether empty: therefore a coacervate vacuum can be had by the forces of nature alone.

259 Respondeo falsum esse superiorem tubi partem à mercurio relictam nulla penitùs substantia repleri. Enim verò quum vitrum innumeris porulis, ut jam diximus praeditum sit, nullam tubi partem delérere potest mercurius, quin subtilissima substantia aetherea poros vitri ingressa tubi partem repleat. Certè superior illa pars calorem concipit, si igni admoveatur, lumineque perfunditur, quod minimè contingeret si nulla ibi esset substantia: vacuum enim, quum nihil sit praeter corporis carentiam, non est capax caloris, neque luminis, neque lumen potest propagari, nisi vel substantia, per illud spatium diffunditur, vel quae jam in illo est, secundum rectam lineam validissimè à lucido corpore urgeatur, ut demonstrabimus quum de lumine nobis erit sermo. Caeterum si pars C E vacua omninò est, vellem scire ¿cur totus non depleatur tubus? Non enim adversatur naturae ut totus vacuus fiat, si contrarium legibus naturae non est, ut pars C E planè vacua existat.

259 I reply that it is false that the upper part of the tube left by the mercury is filled with no substance whatever. For since glass is furnished with innumerable little pores, as we have already said, the mercury cannot desert any part of the tube without the most subtle ethereal substance entering the pores of the glass and filling that part of the tube. Certainly that upper part takes on heat if it is brought near a fire, and is suffused with light, which would by no means happen if there were no substance there: for a vacuum, since it is nothing but the absence of body, is not capable of heat or of light; and light cannot be propagated unless either a substance is diffused through that space, or the substance which is already in it is most strongly urged in a straight line by the luminous body, as we shall demonstrate when we come to speak of light. Besides, if the part C E is altogether empty, I should like to know why the whole tube is not emptied? For it is not contrary to nature that the whole should become empty, if it is not contrary to the laws of nature that the part C E should exist plainly empty.

p. 91

PHYSICES

PHYSICS,

PARS ALTERA.

PA RT T WO.

DE MOTU. — ON MOTION

DISSERTATIO I. — DISSERTATION I

Agitur de Motu locali corporum.

On the local Motion of bodies.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De Motus natura, & obiter de Quiete.

On the nature of Motion, and incidentally on Rest.

260 De Tempore, Loco, & Vacuo jam satis: nunc motum localem adgredimur, de quo parum sollicita Scholastica Philosophia, ipsum vel cursìm duntaxat spectavit, vel penitùs etiam omisit, ut proindè nemini mirandum sit, si neglecta per tot aetates motûs scientia, nullos pene Physica progressus fecerit. Certè si quid est in rerum natura, quod à Philosophis omnibus maximè inquiri, & adcuratissimè pertractari debuerit, id certè sapientum omnium judicio est motus, cum necessarium sit, ut Aristoteles s1 fatetur: ignorato motu, naturam ignorari. Qua propter mirandum omninò est, quum praedictus Philosophus tanti fecisset motûs notitiam, tam negligenter ab his, qui Aristoteli nomen dedére investigari; quaedam enim in Scholis praevaluit consuetudo, ut non nisi sub aliquibus praecissionibus metaphysicis de motus constitutione, & natura pertractetur, admirandis ejus phaenomenis oblítis, quibus ignoratis omnem ferè Physicam in obscuro versari necesse est. Nos ergo in hac Physices Parte fusius cum Recentioribus Philosophis de motu agemus.

n Time, Place, and the Void we have now said enough: we now approach 260 O local motion, about which the Scholastic philosophy, little concerned, either looked at it only in passing or even omitted it altogether, so that it should therefore be a wonder to no one if, the science of motion having been neglected through so many ages, Physics made almost no progress. Certainly, if there is anything in the nature of things that ought to have been investigated above all by all Philosophers and treated most accurately, that, in the judgment of all the wise, is motion, since, as Aristotle (r) admits, it must be that if motion is unknown, nature is unknown. Wherefore it is altogether to be wondered at that, although the said Philosopher made so much of the knowledge of motion, it was investigated so negligently by those who enrolled themselves under Aristotle’s name; for a custom prevailed in the Schools that the constitution and nature of motion were treated only under certain metaphysical precisions, its admirable phenomena being forgotten, without knowledge of which nearly the whole of Physics must remain in darkness. We, therefore, in this Part of Physics shall treat of motion more fully, together with the Moderns.

261 Non defuisse olim, qui motus localis existentiam, non solùm in dubium vérterent, verùm etiam inficiarentur apertè, quales fuere Parménides, & Melissus, Sextus Empiricus testis est. At verò, motum re ipsa in natura contingere, quum certum adeò sit,

261 That there were once some who not only called the existence of local motion into doubt but even openly denied it, such as were Parmenides and Melissus, Sextus Empiricus is witness. But since it is so certain that motion really occurs in nature, and so evident

3. Phys. text. 1.

3 Phys., text 1.

p. 92

tamque evidens, ut ab eo tantum verti queat in dubium, qui loqui potest, quin linguam moveat, piaculum duco in demonstranda motus existentia aliquid vel minimum temporis insúmere, operamque vel levissimam collocare, illum imitatus; qui quum de motu interrogaretur, nihil quidem respondit, sed surgens ambulavit, per ipsam evidentiam sophistae fallaciam irrídens. Existentia, itaque motus localis citra omnem dubitationis aleam posita, illius naturam breviter inquiremus.

evident that it could be called into doubt only by one who can speak without moving his tongue, I consider it a sin to spend even the least bit of time, and to bestow even the slightest effort, on demonstrating the existence of motion, imitating that man who, when questioned about motion, answered nothing, but rose and walked, mocking the sophist’s fallacy by evidence itself. The existence of local motion being thus placed beyond all hazard of doubt, we shall briefly inquire into its nature.

262 Motus ab Aristotele definitur: actus entis in potentia ad novum locum, pro ut in potentia ad illum. Clarior verò describi potest: transitus corporis de loco in locum, sive: Status corporis quod actu fertur de loco in locum, aut continua loci adquisitio. Corpus enim dicitur localiter moveri, quum ita ab uno loco in alium transit, ut ideò in uno esse desinat, quia alteri praesens efficitur. Necesse est igitur ad motum localem, ut mobile ex eo desinat esse praesens uni loco, quia praesens alteri efficitur. Dividitur motus localis in absolutum, & relativum. Absolutus est, migratio corporis ab uno in alium locum absolutum, sive ab una spatii parte in aliam: relativus est migratio corporis ex vicinia eorum, quae circa ipsum sunt, ac veluti immobilia spectantur, in viciniam aliorum quae itidèm considerantur ut penitùs quiescentia.

262 Motion is defined by Aristotle: the act of a being in potency toward a new place, insofar as it is in potency toward it. It can, however, be described more clearly: the passage of a body from place to place, or: the state of a body which is actually carried from place to place, or the continual acquisition of place. For a body is said to be moved locally when it passes from one place into another in such a way that it ceases to be in the one because it is made present to the other. For local motion, therefore, it is necessary that the movable cease to be present to one place from the fact that it is made present to another. Local motion is divided into absolute and relative. Absolute motion is the migration of a body from one absolute place into another, or from one part of space into another; relative motion is the migration of a body from the vicinity of those things which are around it and are regarded as if immovable, into the vicinity of others which are likewise considered as entirely at rest.

263 Sic homo sedens in navi, movetur motu absoluto, dum navis à ventis defertur, minimè verò motu relativo, si ad partes navis referatur. Movetur motu absoluto, quum aliam atque aliam spatii partem successivè óccupet, at non movetur motu relativo, quum à partibus navis eandem distantiam servet. Cartesius sicuti non alium admittit locum, nisi relativum, ita non nisi relativum motum agnoscit. At verò praeter relativum, absolutum quoque motum esse admittendum iisdem evincitur rationibus, quibus ostensum est absolutum locum, nempè spatium, praeter relativum admitti oportere.

263 Thus a man sitting in a ship is moved with absolute motion while the ship is carried along by the winds, but not at all with relative motion, if he is referred to the parts of the ship. He is moved with absolute motion, since he successively occupies one part of space after another; but he is not moved with relative motion, since he keeps the same distance from the parts of the ship. Descartes, just as he admits no place other than the relative, so acknowledges no motion but the relative. But besides the relative, an absolute motion too must be admitted, as is proved by the same reasons by which it was shown that, besides the relative place, an absolute place, namely space, must be admitted.

264 Quies est permanentia corporis in eodem loco, & quidem si corpus permaneat semper in eodem loco relativo, corpus quiescit relativè; sin verò permaneat semper in eodem loco absoluto, corpus quiescit absolutè. Quapropter poterit corpus relativè quiescere, & moveri absolutè, ut accidit homini, qui sedet in navi dum ipsa velis impellitur. Vicissim poterit corpus moveri relativè, quamvis quiescat absolutè; veluti si quis ambulet in navi versùs partem unam, eadem prorsus velocitate, qua navis fertur in oppositam: nam ob duplicem hominis motum aequalem, alterum contrarium proprium, alterum communem, nempè alterum quo homo ambulat, qui est propriùs, alterum quo transfertur, qui est communis, fiet ut is in eodem loco absoluto semper cosistat.

264 Rest is the permanence of a body in the same place; and indeed, if a body remains always in the same relative place, the body rests relatively; but if it remains always in the same absolute place, the body rests absolutely. Wherefore a body can rest relatively and be moved absolutely, as happens to a man who sits in a ship while it is driven by its sails. Conversely, a body can be moved relatively although it rests absolutely: as if someone walks in a ship toward one part with exactly the same velocity with which the ship is carried toward the opposite part; for because of the man’s twofold equal motion, the one contrary and proper, the other common — namely the one by which the man walks, which is proper, and the other by which he is carried along, which is common — it comes about that he always stays in the same absolute place.

p. 93

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De proprietatibus motus, de que illius divisionibus.

On the properties of motion, and on its divisions.

265 Tres in motu omni proprietates, è quibus complures ejusdem differentiae derivantur discriminare possumus, scilicet, determinationem, celeritatem, & quantitatem: Determinatio est, directio corporis quod movetur, in unam potius, quàm aliam partem sivè ad certum terminum. Etenim quoniam quaquaversùs moveri potest corpus, ut moveatur necesse est dirigatur ad certam plagam. Directionem suam dum persequitur corpus, spatium conficit, quod spactari duplici modo potest: physicè, videlicet, ac mathematicè: Priori acceptione consideratum est totus locus, quem secundum omnem dimensionem suam, res mobilis succesivè occupat. Sic (Fig. XVIII.) sphaera A perpendiculariter ad lineam B C mota, spatium physicè conficit, quod concipitur instar corporis cylindrici recti D E. Posteriori sensu acceptum illud spatium, est linea directionis m n, in qua si habeatur ratio longitudinis, adeòque temporis, quo motus perágitur, per ipsam repraesentabitur spatium percursum.

265 There are three properties in all motion from which we can discern most of its differences: namely determination, celerity, and quantity. Determination is the direction of a body that is moved toward one part rather than another, or toward a certain term. For since a body can be moved in any direction whatever, in order that it be moved it must be directed toward a certain region. While a body pursues its direction it traverses a space, which can be regarded in two ways: physically, namely, and mathematically. In the former acceptation, what is considered is the whole place which the movable thing successively occupies according to its every dimension. Thus (Fig. XVIII.) the sphere A, moved perpendicularly to the line B C, traverses physically a space which is conceived as a right cylindrical body D E. Taken in the latter sense, that space is the line of direction m n, in which, if account is taken of the length, and so of the time in which the motion is performed, the space traversed will be represented by it.

266 Quemadmodùm corpus dicitur movéri motu simplici, quando una tantummodò est potentia quae illum ad motum determinat; movéri verò motu composito quum à pluribus simul potentiis & quidem secundum diversas directiones ad motum determinatur: ita directio duplex est; alia simplex, alia composita. Simplex ab una tantum impressione pendet, ut descensus globi A (Fig. citat) composita proficiscitur à pluribus impressionibus. Ita si globus E (Fig. XIX) simul à globo A directione A F, & à globo B directione B D impellatur, neutram ex his globus E sequetur, sed lineam E G diagonalem insistet.

266 Just as a body is said to be moved with simple motion when there is only one power that determines it to motion, but with compound motion when it is determined to motion by several powers at once, and indeed according to different directions, so direction is twofold: one simple, the other compound. The simple depends on one impression only, as the descent of the globe A (Fig. cited); the compound proceeds from several impressions. Thus if the globe E (Fig. XIX) is impelled at the same time by the globe A in the direction A F and by the globe B in the direction B D, the globe E will follow neither of these, but will keep to the diagonal line E G.

267 Celeritas, sive velocitas est illa mobilis adfectio qua dato tempore, datum spatium decurrit, unde & spatii, & temporis dimensioni ipsa respondet, adeòque est relatio, quam habet spatium ad tempus. Si enim duo corpora pertranseant idem spatium temporibus diversis, illud majori celeritate procedit, quod minori tempore metam adsequitur; illud verò quod tempore diuturniori ad eandem metam pervenit minori celeritate incédit. Contrà si duo corpora eodem prorsùs tempore emetiantur spatia inaequalia, illud quod majus spatium descripsit, velociùs; quod verò minus spatium peragravit, minus velociter incessisse pronunciamus.

267 Celerity, or velocity, is that affection of a movable by which it runs through a given space in a given time; whence it corresponds to the dimension both of space and of time, and so is the relation which space has to time. For if two bodies pass through the same space in different times, that one proceeds with greater celerity which reaches the goal in less time, while that which arrives at the same goal in a longer time goes with less celerity. Conversely, if two bodies measure out unequal spaces in exactly the same time, we declare that the one which described the greater space went more swiftly, and the one which traversed the smaller space less swiftly.

p. 94

268 Ex quo facilè intelligitur in conceptu velocitatis, duplicem alium conceptum contineri, alterum quidem spatii, alterum verò temporis, in tantum, ut eodem manente tempore, si spatium descriptum augeatur, vel minuatur, etiam velocitas motus proporcionaliter augeatur, vel minuatur, eodem verò manente spatio percurso, si tempus augeatur vel minuatur, vicissim velocitas augeatur vel minuatur in eadem ratione. Quapropter quaerentibus, ¿quid sit velocitas? Respondendum est, esse relationem quam habet spatium descriptum ad tempus intérea elapsum, adeoque ejus mensuram haberi si spatium descriptum dividatur per tempus in descriptione spatii consumptum, sive quod idem est. Quotus spatii quod certo tempore corpus aequabili motu percurrit, per ipsum tempus divisi, valorem celeritatis, qua corpus ipsum eo tempore movetur, optimè designat.

268 From this it is easily understood that in the concept of velocity two other concepts are contained, the one of space, the other of time, to such an extent that, the time remaining the same, if the space described is increased or diminished, the velocity of the motion is also proportionally increased or diminished; while, the space traversed remaining the same, if the time is increased or diminished, the velocity in turn is diminished or increased in the same ratio. Wherefore to those who ask, what is velocity? the answer must be that it is the relation which the space described has to the time elapsed meanwhile, and so its measure is had if the space described is divided by the time consumed in describing the space; or, what is the same, the quotient of the space which a body runs through with uniform motion in a certain time, divided by that time itself, best designates the value of the celerity with which the body is moved in that time.

269 Itaque si mobile A descripsit pedes 20 in tempore 4 minutorum, & mobile B descripsit pedes 40 in tempore 5 minutorum, velocitas mobilis A erit graduum 5, velocitas mibilis B erit gradum 8. Hoc est: spatium descriptum â mobili A in quavis temporis parte, est ad spatium descriptum à mobili B in eadem parte temporis, ut 5, ad 8. Suponamus etiam corpus A percurrisse 20 leucas, 2 horarum spatio, & corpus B 100, 4 horarum spatio: Dico: celeritatem corporis A esse ad celeritatem corporis B, ut est 10, (qui quotus est 20 divisi per 2.) ad 25 (qui quotus est 100 divisi per 4) hoc est: quantum 10 inferior est 25, tantum celeritas corporis A inferior est celeritate corporis B.

269 Thus if the movable A described 20 feet in a time of 4 minutes, and the movable B described 40 feet in a time of 5 minutes, the velocity of the movable A will be of 5 degrees, the velocity of the movable B of 8 degrees. That is: the space described by the movable A in any part of time is to the space described by the movable B in the same part of time as 5 to 8. Let us suppose also that the body A has run through 20 leagues in the space of 2 hours, and the body B 100 in the space of 4 hours: I say that the celerity of the body A is to the celerity of the body B as 10 (which is the quotient of 20 divided by 2) is to 25 (which is the quotient of 100 divided by 4); that is: by as much as 10 is less than 25, by so much is the celerity of the body A less than the celerity of the body B.

170 Quod tantum intelligendum est quum corpora moventur aequabiliter, nam si motus sit inaequabilis, quum corpus non moveatur eadem celeritate toto illo tempore, nequit variabilis illa celeritas, per constantem quantitatem designari. Corpus autem aequabiliter moveri dicitur; si eadem celeritate continuò moveatur, nempe, si aequalibus temporibus, aequales spatii partes percurrat. Dicitur verò moveri inaequabiliter, si non eadem semper sit sui motus celeritas, videlicèt si temporibus aequalibus, per inaequalia spatia abripiatur. Sic aequabilis erit motus corporis A si dum 1o. minuto pedes 5, deinde 2o. pedes 10, tum 3o. pedes 15. atque ita deinceps percurrat. Contrà verò inaequabilis erit illius motus si 1o. minuto per spatium pedale, reliquis verò per spatium non pedale, neque constanti semper lege, sed variata semper inaequabiliter spatii magnitudine abripiatur.

270 This is to be understood only when bodies are moved uniformly; for if the motion is non-uniform, since the body is not moved with the same celerity during that whole time, that variable celerity cannot be designated by a constant quantity. A body, moreover, is said to be moved uniformly if it is moved continually with the same celerity, namely, if in equal times it runs through equal parts of space. It is said to be moved non-uniformly if the celerity of its motion is not always the same, namely, if in equal times it is carried through unequal spaces. Thus the motion of the body A will be uniform if it runs through 5 feet in the 1st minute, then 10 feet by the 2nd, then 15 feet by the 3rd, and so on. Conversely, its motion will be non-uniform if in the 1st minute it is carried through the space of a foot, but in the remaining ones through a space not of a foot, and not by a constant law at all times, but with the magnitude of the space always varied non-uniformly.

271 Acceleratus est, cujus celeritas continuò augetur, Retardatus, cujus celeritas continuò minuitur. Si temporibus aequalibus aequalia accedant velocitatis incrementa, motus dicitur aequabiliter acceleratus, quemadmodum si ea proportione decedant, aequabiliter retardatus nuncupatur. Atque haec sunt praecipuae motus divisiones. Sequitur nunc tertia motus proprietas quae quantitas dicitur, sed antequam illam explicemus de Viribus aliquid dicendum est.

271 That motion is accelerated whose celerity is continually increased; retarded, that whose celerity is continually diminished. If in equal times equal increments of velocity are added, the motion is called uniformly accelerated, just as, if they fall away in that proportion, it is named uniformly retarded. And these are the chief divisions of motion. There follows now the third property of motion, which is called quantity; but before we explain it something must be said about Forces.

272 Vis est facultas sive potentia, quae vel motum in corpus

272 Force is the faculty or power which either induces motion in a body,

p. 95

inducit, vel remoto obstaculo induceret, eamque post doctissimum Leibnitzium dividunt Philosophi in vivam & mortuam. Vivam adpellant illam, quae actu inducit motum in corpus, ut est gravitas in lapide descendente, mortuam verò illam esse dicunt, quae actu quidem caret effectu, sed quae remoto obstaculo adigeret corpus ad motum, ut est eadem gravitas in globo, filo sustentato, qui quiescit usque donec sustinetur, at remoto sustentaculo statim déscendere incipit deorsùm. Eadem quoque, vis initialis, conatus seu nisus ad motum actualem compellatur.

or would induce it if an obstacle were removed; and this, following the most learned Leibniz, Philosophers divide into living and dead. They call that force living which actually induces motion in a body, as is gravity in a descending stone; that force, on the other hand, they say is dead which actually lacks its effect, but which, if an obstacle were removed, would drive the body to motion, as is the same gravity in a globe held up by a thread, which rests so long as it is held up, but when the support is removed at once begins to descend downward. This same force is also called initial force, conatus or nisus toward actual motion.

273 Per quantitatem motus (quam etiam momentum adpellant Recentiores) intelligimus, vim sive impetum, quem corpora extra quietis statum facere possunt contra obstacula objecta, adeòque ad definiendam quantitatem motus adtendendum est, & ad velocitatem cum qua corpus movetur, & ad massam sive quantitatem materiae ipsius corporis. Sint enim duo corpora A B habentia aequales materiae quantitates, eademque ferantur contra obstaculum oppositum aequali velocitate: utrumque corpus eundem impetum faciet adversus obstaculum, neque enim quidquam causae est, cur unum altero majorem vim facere debeat, quum & massae, & velocitates aequales ponantur; quòd si impetus aequales sunt, aequales pariter erunt motus, sive motuum quantitates.

273 By quantity of motion (which the Moderns also call momentum) we understand the force or impetus which bodies, out of the state of rest, can exert against obstacles set against them; and so, in defining the quantity of motion, attention must be paid both to the velocity with which the body is moved and to the mass, or quantity of matter, of the body itself. For let there be two bodies A B having equal quantities of matter, and let them be carried against an opposed obstacle with equal velocity: each body will exert the same impetus against the obstacle, for there is no cause why the one should exert a greater force than the other, since both the masses and the velocities are supposed equal; and if the impetuses are equal, the motions, or quantities of motions, will likewise be equal.

274 At manente massarum aequalitate fac corpus A velociùs ferri, corpus verò B ferri segniùs: tunc impetus corporum A & B facti contra obstaculum, minimè aequales erunt, sed major erit impetus corporis A, quod velocius movetur, eòque major erit, quò major est velocitas cum qua ipsum fertur in obstaculum. Et quoniam impetus, & motus, unum idemque sunt, sequitur, motus sive quantitatem motuum duorum corporum, A & B, quorum massae sunt aequales, esse inter se, ut sunt velocitates eorumdem corporum. Quod si manente aequalitate velocitatum ponantur massae corporum A & B inaequales, neque etiam impetus facti ab ipsis contra obstaculum erunt aequales, sed major erit impetus corporis, quod majorem continet materiae quantitatem, eòque major erit, quò major est quantitas materiae, unde tum impetus, tum motus corporum aeque velocium, erunt in ratione massarum.

274 But, the equality of the masses remaining, make the body A be carried more swiftly and the body B more sluggishly: then the impetuses of the bodies A and B exerted against the obstacle will by no means be equal, but the impetus of the body A, which is moved more swiftly, will be greater, and the greater, the greater the velocity with which it is carried against the obstacle. And since impetus and motion are one and the same, it follows that the motions, or quantities of motion, of two bodies A and B whose masses are equal are to each other as the velocities of those same bodies. But if, the equality of the velocities remaining, the masses of the bodies A and B are supposed unequal, neither will the impetuses exerted by them against the obstacle be equal, but the impetus of that body will be greater which contains the greater quantity of matter, and the greater, the greater the quantity of matter; whence both the impetuses and the motions of equally swift bodies will be in the ratio of the masses.

275 Ex quibus Theorématis consequitur modo tertium, quod ità se hàbet: momenta sive quantitates motuum corporum, quorum tùm velocitates, tùm massae sunt inaequales, rationem habent compositam ex rationibus simplicibus velocitatum, & massarum Ut itaque proposito duplici quorumcumque corporum motu, intelligi possit, quisnam ex illis motibus major, aut minor haberi debeat, priùs adcuratè deprehendi debet gravitas, seu massa utriusque corporis, deinde verò velocitas, seu celeritas, qua utrumque movetur, sive spatia, quae ab utroque corpore peraguntur, tùm multiplicata in singulis corporibus per celeritatem corporis massa, productum ex illis exhibebit motus quantitatem, quae singulis corporibus convenit: quod

275 From these Theorems there follows directly the third, which runs thus: the momenta, or quantities of motions, of bodies whose velocities as well as masses are unequal have a ratio compounded of the simple ratios of the velocities and of the masses. So that, therefore, when a twofold motion of any bodies whatever is proposed, it may be understood which of those motions must be held the greater or the smaller, first the gravity, or mass, of each body must be accurately ascertained, then the velocity, or celerity, with which each is moved, or the spaces which are traversed by each body; then, the mass of each body being multiplied by the celerity of the body, the product of them will exhibit the quantity of motion which belongs to each body: and this

p. 96

ipsum more Geometrico ita enunciatur. Quantitas motus, sive momentum corporis, rectè exprimitur per factum ex ductu celeritatis in massam.

very thing is stated thus in the geometric manner: The quantity of motion, or momentum, of a body is rightly expressed by the product of the celerity multiplied into the mass.

276 Quantitas ergò motus non ex sola mobilis celeritate aestimanda est. Quum enim motus, & toti corpori, & singulis ejusdem partibus competat, aliter, ut jam diximus aestimari non poterit, quàm si massam corporis in velocitatem ducamus. Sit enim ex. gr. massa corporis A, 4, velocitas seu celeritas 6. In hoc casu quaelibet pars corporis A, habebit 6 gradus celeritatis, & consequenter 6 item gradus impetus seu motus: impetus ergo seu vis totalis corporis, aequalis erit 6 gradibus impetus quater repetitis, seu quod idem est, si ducatur 4 in 6, quantitas motus in corpore A, erit 24. Similiter sit massa corporis B 3, velocitas 8, ducantur 3 in 8, erit quantitas in corpore B 24. Ex quo facilè intelligi poterit quod in utroque mobili, eadem quantitas motus reperitur. Spectari igitur potest momentum dati corporis veluti rectángulum, cujus basis referat massam ipsius corporis, altitudo verò illius celeritatem. Oritur enim rectangulum ex ductu baseos in altitudinem, ut dictum est in Geometria.

276 The quantity of motion, therefore, is not to be estimated from the celerity of the movable alone. For since motion belongs both to the whole body and to each of its parts, it cannot, as we have already said, be estimated otherwise than by multiplying the mass of the body into the velocity. For let, e.g., the mass of the body A be 4, its velocity or celerity 6. In this case each part of the body A will have 6 degrees of celerity, and consequently also 6 degrees of impetus or motion: the impetus, therefore, or force of the whole body will be equal to 6 degrees of impetus repeated four times; or, what is the same, if 4 is multiplied into 6, the quantity of motion in the body A will be 24. Likewise let the mass of the body B be 3, its velocity 8; let 3 be multiplied into 8: the quantity in the body B will be 24. From which it can easily be understood that the same quantity of motion is found in each movable. The momentum of a given body can therefore be regarded as a rectangle whose base represents the mass of the body itself, and its height the body’s celerity. For a rectangle arises from multiplying the base into the height, as was said in Geometry.

277 Quod si gravitas in corpore A sit 4, velocitas 5, massa autem in corpore B sit 3, velocitas 8, quantitas motus in corpore A, erit 20, in corpore B erit 24: unde quantitas motus major erit in B, quàm in A Inde verò facilè deduci potest, quod ipsa quantitas motus virtuti motrici respondére debet, ideòque si certa quaedam vis requiritur, ut corpus 1 librae ad 100 pedum distantiam projiciatur, duplo major virtus requiretur, ut illud eodem tempore ad spatium 200 pedum projici possit. Sicuti eadem ratione manifestissimè adparet, quod si corpus 10 librarum aliquo determinato tempore certa quadam vi ad 30 pedum distantiam projicitur, eadem prorsùs vis, & impetus requiretur, ut corpus 20 librarum per spatium 15 pedum projiciatur.

277 But if the gravity in the body A is 4, the velocity 5, and the mass in the body B is 3, the velocity 8, the quantity of motion in the body A will be 20, in the body B 24: whence the quantity of motion will be greater in B than in A. From this, moreover, it can easily be deduced that the quantity of motion itself must correspond to the motive power; and therefore, if a certain force is required for a body of 1 pound to be thrown to a distance of 100 feet, a power twice as great will be required for it to be thrown in the same time to a space of 200 feet. Just as, by the same reasoning, it appears most manifestly that if a body of 10 pounds is thrown in some determinate time by a certain force to a distance of 30 feet, exactly the same force and impetus will be required for a body of 20 pounds to be thrown through a space of 15 feet.

278 Ideòque universaliter tantò major futura est virtus motrix, quantò major est quantitas motus in corpore, quod movetur; quantitas verò motus tantò major erit, quantò major est gravitas seu massa corporis, simulque celeritas qua moveatur. Itaque in priori exemplo, quum eadem sit quantitas motus in utroque corpore, manifestè adparet, quod utrumque ex illis aequali vi, sive potentia movebitur; quod si ut in altero casu contingit, major sit in alterutro corpore quantitas motus, sive ex gravitate, sive potiùs ex celeritate haec inaequalitas oriatur, major quoque vis, sive potentia motrix requiretur. Quae omnia adcuratissimè observanda sunt, quum inde, velut ex uberrimo fonte tota ferè Statica, & Mechanica derivetur, ut in sequentibus data opera ostendemus.

278 And therefore, universally, the motive power will be the greater, the greater the quantity of motion in the body that is moved; and the quantity of motion will be the greater, the greater the gravity or mass of the body, and at the same time the celerity with which it is moved. Thus in the former example, since the quantity of motion is the same in each body, it manifestly appears that each of them will be moved by an equal force or power; but if, as happens in the other case, the quantity of motion is greater in one of the two bodies, whether this inequality arises from the gravity or rather from the celerity, a greater motive force or power is also required. All of which must be observed most accurately, since from this, as from a most abundant source, almost the whole of Statics and Mechanics is derived, as we shall show in what follows when occasion is given.

279 Ex dictis fit manifestum, vim sive impetum, sive motum, sive momentum (haec enim omnia unum, idemque sunt) alicujus corporis, tripliciter augeri posse. 1. Ex aucta velocitate, cujus rei habemus exemplum in globis ferreis, quos tormenta bellica vi

279 From what has been said it is manifest that the force or impetus, or motion, or momentum (for all these are one and the same) of any body can be increased in three ways. 1. By increased velocity, an example of which we have in the iron balls which engines of war, by the force of gunpowder,

p. 97

pulveris pyrii explodunt contra moenia oppidorum obsessorum, qui globi magno impetu ipsa moenia feriunt, ob magnam velocitatem, cum qua feruntur. 2: Ex aucta quantitate materiae; cujus rei habemus exemplum in arietibus, atque aliis machinamentis bellicis, quae apud Veteres obtinebant; ea enim quanquam tardissimè incederent, tamen immensam molem habebant, adeòque ad opugnanda moenia, magnum usum praestabant. 3.: Ex aucta tum velocitate, tum quantitate materiae, quo quidem casu impetus evadit immensus, quum incrementum duplici ex causa adveniat momento, ex velocitate scilicet, & ex massa.

discharge against the walls of besieged towns, which balls strike the walls themselves with great impetus because of the great velocity with which they are carried. 2: By increased quantity of matter; an example of which we have in battering rams and other machines of war which were in use among the Ancients; for these, although they advanced most slowly, yet had an immense mass, and so afforded great use for assaulting walls. 3.: By increased velocity and quantity of matter together, in which case the impetus becomes immense, since the increment comes to the momentum from a double cause, namely from the velocity and from the mass.

280 Quoniam autem non nullà quae in hoc capite dicta sunt difficultatem adferre possunt Adolescentibus, iccircò quaedam exempla aequalitatis, & inaequalitatis impetuum, oculis subjicere, & iterum demonstrare juvat, nec non regulas velocitatum, & quantitatis motuum clariùs propónere.

280 But since not a few of the things said in this chapter can cause difficulty for young students, it is helpful to set before their eyes some examples of the equality and inequality of impetuses, and to demonstrate them again, and also to propose more clearly the rules of velocities and of the quantity of motions.

281 Ad primum quod adtinet sint duae linae rectae A B, C D, (Fig. XX.) divisae in tot partes aequales, quot volueris, ex. gr. in novem. In prima linea supponatur corpus pedale, in secunda verò corpus aliud pedale priori perfectè homogeneum: tum haec corpora supponantur intra tempus idem, totidem linearum suarum partes percurrere. In hac hypothesi dico, vires motrices, mobilibus illis adplicatas, esse inter se perfectè aequales. Effectus enim producti sunt omninò similes, & consequenter eorum causae productivae judicari debent omninò similes.

281 As to the first, let there be two straight lines A B, C D (Fig. XX.), divided into as many equal parts as you like, e.g. into nine. On the first line let there be supposed a body of one foot, on the second another body of one foot, perfectly homogeneous with the former; then let these bodies be supposed to run through, within the same time, the same number of parts of their lines. In this hypothesis I say that the motive forces applied to those movables are perfectly equal to each other. For the effects produced are altogether alike, and consequently their productive causes must be judged altogether alike.

282 Sint rursùs alia duo corpora, per duas alias lineas aequales translata, ità ut corpus trium pedum, quale exhibetur per f g h moveatur per lineam A B, cum tribus gradibus velocitatis; alterum verò pedale, transferatur cum novem gradibus velocitatis per lineam C D.

282 Again, let there be two other bodies carried along two other equal lines, such that the body of three feet, such as is shown by f g h, is moved along the line A B with three degrees of velocity, while the other, of one foot, is carried along the line C D with nine degrees of velocity.

283 Dico, impetus corporibus illis adplicatos, esse pariter inter se aequales: quod sic ostendo. Tunc impetus, seu vires seu quantitates motuum sunt inter se aequales, quando eorum effectus sunt aequales: atqui in hoc exemplo effectus sunt aequales. Nam effectus primae virtutis, est transferre corpus trium pedum per tres partes aequales lineae A B, nimirum usque ad punctum 3. Effectus autem secundae virtutis motricis, est per tempus idem transferre corpus pedale per novem partes aequales lineae C D, seu usque ad punctum 9: atqui effectus ii sunt aequales:

283 I say that the impetuses applied to those bodies are likewise equal to each other: which I show thus. Impetuses, or forces, or quantities of motions are equal to each other when their effects are equal: but in this example the effects are equal. For the effect of the first power is to carry the body of three feet through three equal parts of the line A B, namely as far as the point 3; and the effect of the second motive power is to carry, in the same time, the body of one foot through nine equal parts of the line C D, or as far as the point 9: but these effects are equal.

284 Nam transferre corpus trium pedum per tres partes aequales lineae A B, est efficere, ut unumquodque corpus pedale componens corpus trium pedum, percurrat tres partes aequales; vel est efficere ut tria corpora pedalia percurrant singula, tres partes aequales illius lineae. Jam verò efficere, ut tria corpora pedalia percurrant singula, tres partes aequales spatii; idem est ac efficere, ut unicum corpus pedale percurrat novem partes aequales spatii; quandoquidem ex utráque parte, novem partes aequales spatii

284 For to carry a body of three feet through three equal parts of the line A B is to bring it about that each body of one foot composing the body of three feet runs through three equal parts; or it is to bring it about that three bodies of one foot each run through three equal parts of that line. Now to bring it about that three bodies of one foot each run through three equal parts of space is the same as to bring it about that a single body of one foot runs through nine equal parts of space; since on either side nine equal parts of space are traversed

p. 98

percurruntur à corpore pedali: ergo effectus sunt similes: ergo vires eorum productivae sunt aequales.

by a body of one foot: therefore the effects are alike: therefore their productive forces are equal.

285 Sint denique duo alia corpora homogenea, ita ut moles unius sit séxtupla molis alterius, & ambo pari velocitate transferantur. In hac hypothesi, evidens est, ad transferendum corpus séxtupedale, requiri virtutem séxtuplo intensiorem; quàm ad transferendum corpus séxtuplo mole minus. Sed Leges velocitatum, & quantitatis motum supra à nobis propositae, clarius iterum proponantur.

285 Finally, let there be two other homogeneous bodies, such that the bulk of the one is six times the bulk of the other, and let both be carried with equal velocity. In this hypothesis it is evident that, to carry the six-foot body, a power six times more intense is required than to carry the body six times smaller in bulk. But let the Laws of velocities and of the quantity of motions proposed by us above be set out again more clearly.

Regulae velocitatum.

RULES OF VELOCITIES .

286 I. Quando spatia á corporibus homogeneis decursa, inter se sunt aequalia, & tempora intra quae fuerunt translata, pariter sunt aequalia; tunc velocitates inter se sunt aequales. II. Quando spatia decursa, inaequalia sunt, tempora verò sunt aequalia, tunc velocitates inter se sunt; ut spatia decursa. III. Quando spatia decursa, aequalia sunt inter se, tempora verò sunt inaequalia; tunc velocitates sunt inter se reciprocè, ut tempora, hoc est, tempus breviùs majorem indicat velocitatem; & majus indicat minorem. IV. Quando spatia decursa inter se sunt inaequalia, & tempora sunt pariter inaequalia; tunc velocitates sunt inter se, ut quoti spatiorum, per tempora divisorum.

286 I. When the spaces run through by homogeneous bodies are equal to each other, and the times within which they were traversed are likewise equal, then the velocities are equal to each other. II. When the spaces run through are unequal, but the times equal, then the velocities are to each other as the spaces run through. III. When the spaces run through are equal to each other, but the times unequal, then the velocities are to each other reciprocally as the times; that is, the shorter time indicates the greater velocity, and the greater the smaller. IV. When the spaces run through are unequal to each other, and the times likewise unequal, then the velocities are to each other as the quotients of the spaces divided by the times.

Regulae pro quantitate motuum.

RULES FOR THE QUANTITY OF MOTIONS .

287 I. Si massae aut moles homogeneae inter se sint aequales, & earum velocitates sint pariter aequales, tunc quantitates impetuum mobilibus illis adplicatorum inter se sunt aequales: quia hoc in casu effectus sunt perfectè similes, sicut probatum fuit. II. Si moles, aut massae homogeneae, inter se sint aequales, & earum velocitates sint inaequales: tunc quantitates motuum, sive impetuum sunt inter se, ut velocitates III Si moles homogeneae, inter se sint inaequales, & earum velocitates sint aequales, tunc quantitates impetuum inter se sunt, ut massae, seu moles. IV. Si moles homogeneae, inter se sunt inaequales, & earum velocitates sint pariter inaequales; tunc quantitates impetuum sunt inter se, ut producta nata, ex multiplicatione cujusque molis per suam velocitatem.

287 I. If the masses or homogeneous bulks are equal to each other, and their velocities are likewise equal, then the quantities of the impetuses applied to those movables are equal to each other: because in this case the effects are perfectly alike, as was proved. II. If the homogeneous bulks or masses are equal to each other, and their velocities unequal, then the quantities of motions, or of impetuses, are to each other as the velocities. III. If the homogeneous bulks are unequal to each other, and their velocities equal, then the quantities of impetuses are to each other as the masses, or bulks. IV. If the homogeneous bulks are unequal to each other, and their velocities likewise unequal, then the quantities of impetuses are to each other as the products arising from the multiplication of each bulk by its velocity.

288 Regulae dudum praescriptae, tùm circa velocitates mobilium, tùm circa quantitates impetuum, spectari debent tanquam fundamenta totius scientiae machinalis, seu illius Philosophiae partis, quae mutuato à Geometria subsidio, variarum machinarum adparatum nobis suppeditat. Quàmverò utilis sit haec Physicae pars, quàmque multum inserviat ad complura naturae phaenomena

288 The rules just prescribed, both about the velocities of movables and about the quantities of impetuses, must be regarded as the foundations of the whole science of machines, or of that part of Philosophy which, with help borrowed from Geometry, supplies us with the apparatus of various machines. How useful this part of Physics is, and how much it serves for knowing very many phenomena of nature

p. 99

noscenda, & explananda, tantùm negare poterit, qui planè hospes in Geometria, & Physica sit, ut ea propter necessarium omninò existimarim utilissimam ac jocundissimam hanc Physices partem vobis trádere postquàm de Statica sermonem instituam. Nec vos harum rerum difficultates terreant; difficultas enim utilitate compensabitur. Praeterquam quod in id nervos omnes intendo, ut perexpeditam vobis commonstrem viam, nec scopulum offendetis, si adtenta, & seria meditatione ad veritates contemplandas animum adplicuéritis.

and explaining them, only one who is plainly a stranger to Geometry and Physics could deny; so that for this reason I have judged it altogether necessary to deliver to you this most useful and most delightful part of Physics once I take up the discussion of Statics. Do not let the difficulties of these matters frighten you, for the difficulty will be compensated by the usefulness. Besides which, I bend all my efforts to this, to show you a very easy road; nor will you strike any rock, if you apply your mind attentively and with serious meditation to contemplating the truths.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

De Naturae legibus Newtonianis.

On the Newtonian laws of Nature. 289

289 Naturae legem vocant Philosophi, regulam universalissimam, quae in omnibus rerum naturalium vicissitudinibus, atque commutationibus locum habet. Et quoniam omnis naturae vicissitudo proficiscitur à motu indè fit, ut naturae legum exercitium praecipuè in motionibus corporum se manifestèt. De his naturae legibus quum multa Philosophi disputassent, tandèm Newtonus omnia, quae antea de isto argumento dicta fuerant ad tria praecipua capita revocavit, quae quidem leges Naturae Newtonianae hodie passim à Philosophis vocantur.

Philosophers call a law of nature a most universal rule which has place in all the vicissitudes and changes of natural things. And since every vicissitude of nature proceeds from motion, it comes about that the exercise of the laws of nature shows itself chiefly in the motions of bodies. Since Philosophers had disputed much about these laws of nature, at length Newton reduced everything that had been said before on this argument to three principal heads, which today are commonly called by Philosophers the Newtonian Laws of Nature.

Lemma. — LEMMA

290 Motus quantum est ex se dirigitur per lineam rectam, nec eam deserit, nisi ab aliqua causa extrinseca ab ea detorqueatur. Ratio est, quia linea recta brevissima est ex his, quae à puncto ad punctum, sive à termino à quo ad terminum ad quem duci possunt, etiam simplicissima est; non enim quemadmodum linea curva in varias species dividitur: ergo motus per lineam rectam brevior est, ac simplicior; sed natura semper brevitatem, ac simplicitatem in omnibus adfectat, nihil frustra molítur, superflua rejicit, & quo maximo potest compendio cuncta operatur: ergo motus per lineam rectam potiùs quàm per aliam dirigitur. Hoc constituto antequàm Newtonianas motus Leges proponamus, quaedam de vi inertiae breviter à nobis dicenda sunt. Hujus nomine intelligimus, vim eam in unoquoque corpore, qua corpus unumquodque quantum in se est, perseverat in statu suo vel quietis, vel motus, sive vis quaedam materiae insita, qua fit ut unumquodque corpus proprium suum statum tueri, atque conservare nitatur.

290 Motion, so far as lies in itself, is directed along a straight line, nor does it desert it unless it is turned aside from it by some extrinsic cause. The reason is that the straight line is the shortest of those which can be drawn from point to point, or from the term from which to the term to which, and is also the simplest: for it is not divided into various species, as the curved line is: therefore motion along a straight line is shorter and simpler; but nature in all things affects brevity and simplicity, undertakes nothing in vain, rejects superfluities, and works all things with the greatest possible economy: therefore motion is directed along a straight line rather than along another. This being established, before we propose Newton’s Laws of motion, some things must briefly be said by us about the force of inertia. By this name we understand that force in each body by which every body, so far as lies in it, perseveres in its state either of rest or of motion, or a certain force implanted in matter, by which it comes about that each body strives to maintain and preserve its own state.

p. 100

291 Nam si corpus quiescit, quies illa in corpore foret in aeternum duratura, si nullus in ipsum impetus fiat. Et similiter corpus semel motum, perpetuò moveretur, si nullam retardationem à resistentia medii pateretur. Etenim omne corpus quod movetur, in medio illi resistente movetur, unde corpus, motum continuare nequit nisi in quantum hanc vincat resistentiam, eam autem vincere non potest, nisi dividendo & separando partes medii, nec potest has partes separare, nisi impendendo contra illas aliquam partem impetus, quem habebat ad se movendum; quum sensim ergo impetus diminuatur in mobili, ejus celeritas minui proportionaliter debet, & tandèm ad nihilum redúci.

291 For if a body rests, that rest in the body would last forever, if no impetus were made upon it. And likewise a body once moved would be moved perpetually, and would suffer no retardation from the resistance of the medium. For every body that is moved is moved in a medium resisting it; whence the body cannot continue its motion except insofar as it overcomes this resistance; and it cannot overcome it except by dividing and separating the parts of the medium, nor can it separate these parts except by spending against them some part of the impetus which it had for moving itself; since, therefore, the impetus is gradually diminished in the movable, its celerity must be diminished proportionally, and at length be reduced to nothing.

292 Sed ultra hanc resistentiam medii, datur etiam in corpore alia Resistentia, quatenus nempè corpus ad conservandum sibi statum suum, reluctatur vi impressae. Dum enim corpus B quiescens éxcipit ictum à corpore moto A, non movetur corpus B, quin corpus A amittat non nihil de vi sua, quare adest in B vis frangens impetum corporis A, quae vocatur vis resistentiae. His suppositis, prima lex Newtoniana ita proponi solet. Corpus omne perseverat in statu suo quietis, vel motus uniformiter, & in linea recta, nisi ab aliqua vi impressa cogatur statum illum mutare. Haec lex fundatur in vi inertiae, ob quam fit, ut singula corpora conentur conservare sibi eum statum, quo in statu actu sunt constituta.

292 But beyond this resistance of the medium there is also in the body another Resistance, namely insofar as the body, in order to preserve its own state, struggles against the impressed force. For when the body B at rest receives a blow from the moved body A, the body B is not moved without the body A losing something of its force; wherefore there is in B a force breaking the impetus of the body A, which is called the force of resistance. These things being supposed, the first Newtonian law is usually proposed thus: Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of moving uniformly and in a straight line, unless it is compelled by some impressed force to change that state. This law is founded on the force of inertia, because of which it comes about that individual bodies strive to preserve for themselves that state in which they are actually placed.

293 Corpus quiescens nunquam désinet quiescere ex se ipso, sed ad hoc ut constituatur in motu, necesse est, externam vim intervenire. Contrà corpus quod movetur, nunquam desinet moveri, si omnium circunstantium corporum resistentiam victam, & in nihilum redactam supponamus. Neque hìc audiendi sunt vulgares Peripatetici, qui doceat, corpora mota suaptè natura quietem adfectare, sive etiam ex motu ad quietem tendere, contra id quod docet eorum Princeps Aristoteles s1, ea praecipuè inducti ratione, quòd videant lapidum projectorum motum sensim languéscere, ac tandem omninò desinere[?]. Si enim lapides projecti aliquandò desistunt à motu, id quidèm duplici causae imputandum est. Prima quia à gravitate ipsa deorsum propulsi, tandèm in terram impingunt. Secunda quia aër eorum motui obsistit, nam si in vacuo lapis projectus esset, & praetereà si is omni gravitate destitueretur, proculdubiò ejus motus nunquàm languesceret, sed foret in aeternum duraturus.

293 A body at rest will never cease to rest of itself, but in order that it be placed in motion an external force must intervene. Conversely, a body that is moved will never cease to be moved, if we suppose the resistance of all the surrounding bodies overcome and reduced to nothing. Nor are the common Peripatetics to be heard here, who teach that moved bodies by their own nature affect rest, or also tend from motion to rest, contrary to what their Prince Aristotle (a) teaches, led chiefly by this reason, that they see the motion of thrown stones gradually grow languid and at length cease altogether. For if thrown stones at some time desist from motion, this must indeed be imputed to a double cause. The first, because, driven downward by gravity itself, they at length strike against the earth. The second, because the air resists their motion; for if a stone were thrown in a vacuum, and moreover if it were destitute of all gravity, without doubt its motion would never grow languid, but would last forever.

294 Seposita autèm cùm gravitatis, tùm resistentiae consideratione, projecta non modò moveri debent in aeternum, sed rectà, & aequabiliter moveantur óportet. Initio enim proculdubiò moventur per lineam rectam [§. 290.], quod si initio, cursus rectilineus est, ob vim inertiae, quae facit, ut corpora conservent sibi semper eum statum in quo constituta sunt, projecta corpora perpetuò

294 Setting aside, then, the consideration both of gravity and of resistance, projectiles must not only be moved forever, but must be moved in a straight line and uniformly. For at the beginning they are without doubt moved along a straight line [§. 290.]; and if at the beginning the course is rectilinear, then, because of the force of inertia, which makes bodies always preserve for themselves the state in which they are placed, projected bodies will perpetually persevere

Lib. IV. Phys. text. 69.

Bk. IV, Phys., text 69.

p. 101

persistent in eo cursu, neque unquam de semità rectilinea deflectent. Si enim curvam describerent jam mutarent singulis momentis directionem, quod repugnat inertiae materiae ob quam non potest sibi ullam determinationem tribuere. Quod autem aequabiliter moveri debeant, id fit ex eadem vi inertiae, nam ut motus acceleretur, vel retardetur, opus est, novam vim advenire, quae motui illi vel prosit vel officiat, quam tamen nos remotam suppónimus.

in that course, and will never deflect from the rectilinear path. For if they described a curve, they would then be changing their direction at every moment, which conflicts with the inertia of matter, because of which it cannot assign itself any determination. That they must be moved uniformly, moreover, comes from the same force of inertia; for in order that the motion be accelerated or retarded, a new force must come in which either helps or hinders that motion, a force which, however, we suppose removed.

295 Adhaec: corpus quàtenùs ex se indifferens est ad motum, & quietem, ut si semel quiescit, in aeternum quiescat, si verò semel positum sit in motu, ut moveatur perpetuò: ergo si semel sit ad motum determinatum, per se solum non redibit ad quietem, aut si quiescit, per se solum ad motum non concitabitur: ergo semel ad motum incitatum nova determinatione indigebit, ut ad quietem revocetur, & è contrariò. Praeterea corpus quod à Deo sphaericum cónditum est, semper sphaericum persevérat, & quod semel quadratum, semper suam figuram tuetur, donec ab aliqua causa haec figura mutetur: ergo similiter corpus quod semel quiescit, semper quiescer.

295 Besides: a body is of itself so indifferent to motion and rest that, if it once rests, it rests forever, but if it has once been placed in motion, it is moved perpetually: therefore, if it has once been determined to motion, it will not return to rest by itself alone; or if it rests, it will not be roused to motion by itself alone: therefore, once incited to motion, it will need a new determination in order to be called back to rest, and conversely. Moreover, a body which was created spherical by God always perseveres spherical, and one that is once square always maintains its figure, until this figure is changed by some cause: therefore likewise a body which once rests will always rest.

296 Ex dictis cólliges 1.: corpus intelligi non posse translatum, circa quadratum, pentágonum, aut aliud quodvis polygonum, quin in singulis angulis concipiantur causae occasionales mutatae determinationis ejusmodi corporis. Postquam enim corpus illud descripsit unum latus, per eandem lineam continuatam intelligeretur translatum, nisi foret obex ipsum detorquens per secundum latus; & sic consequenter, sub finem cujusque lateris. Quoniam igitur circulus concipi debet, tanquam polygonum constans lateribus numero indeterminatis, ideò si corpus aliquod circulariter agitetur, cóncipi debent, vel obices perpetui, vel idem continuatus, à quibus determinatio mobilis perpetuò mutetur.

296 From what has been said you will gather, 1.: that a body cannot be understood to be carried around a square, a pentagon, or any other polygon whatever, unless at each angle occasional causes of the changed determination of such a body are conceived. For after that body has described one side, it would be understood to be carried along the same line continued, unless there were an obstacle turning it aside along the second side; and so on consequently at the end of each side. Since, therefore, the circle must be conceived as a polygon consisting of sides indeterminate in number, if some body is moved circularly, there must be conceived either perpetual obstacles, or the same one continued, by which the determination of the movable is perpetually changed.

297 Sed ut clariùs intelligatis, circulum cóncipi debére veluti polygonum constantem lateribus infinitis, considerate circuli circunferentiam (& quod de ea dicturi sumus, idem nullo negotio ad reliquas omnes curvas aptari potest), atque in ea intelligite primùm descriptum triangulum, tùm quadratum, postea pentágonum, deinde exágonum denique decágonum omnia tamen regularia.

297 But that you may understand more clearly that the circle must be conceived as a polygon consisting of infinite sides, consider the circumference of a circle (and what we are about to say of it can be applied without any trouble to all the other curves), and understand described in it first a triangle, then a square, afterwards a pentagon, then a hexagon, and finally a decagon, all of them, however, regular.

298 Manifestum est omnium jam descriptarum figurarum, triangulum maximè deflectere à circuli ambitu; nam aliquantò plus ad eum accedit quadratum, aliquantò magis pentágonum, adhùc aliquantò magis exágonum, atque multò quidem magis decágonum. Quod si figuram regularem in circulo inscriptam intelligatis ex infinitis, hoc est indeterminatis lateribus constantem, quorum tamen singula sint quàm minima, jam declinatio ejus à circunferentia circuli erit nulla; adeòque circuli, aliarumque curvarum perimetri haberi possunt tanquam figurae rectilineae laterum infinitorum, quorum latera singula sint infinitè parva.

298 It is manifest that of all the figures now described the triangle departs most from the circumference of the circle; for the square comes somewhat nearer to it, the pentagon somewhat more, the hexagon still somewhat more, and the decagon indeed much more. But if you understand a regular figure inscribed in the circle consisting of infinite, that is, indeterminate sides, each of which is nevertheless as small as possible, then its declination from the circumference of the circle will be null; and so the perimeters of the circle and of the other curves can be held as rectilinear figures of infinite sides, each of whose sides is infinitely small.

299 Fingite nunc corpus in circuli circunferentia moveri, &

299 Imagine now a body moved in the circumference of a circle, and

p. 102

jam ipsum re vera movebitur in figura rectilinea infinitorum laterum, quorum singula sunt infinitè parva. Itaque si prima temporis particula corpus describit unum ex istis lateribus, deinceps, omni vi externa sépòsita, moveri aequabiliter debebit, ob vim inertiae, in eodem illo latere ulterius producto, quod latus circulum contingit. Quo circà, si cernimus corpus aliquod revolvi in circuli circunferentia, dicendum est adesse vim aliquam perpetuò agentem in corpus, quae ipsum rétrahit de cursu rectilineo, atque gradatim in reliqua polygoni latera flectit.

then it will in truth be moved in a rectilinear figure of infinite sides, each of which is infinitely small. Therefore, if in the first particle of time the body describes one of these sides, thereafter, every external force being set aside, it ought, because of the force of inertia, to be moved uniformly along that same side produced further, which side touches the circle. Wherefore, if we see some body revolve in the circumference of a circle, it must be said that there is some force acting perpetually on the body, which draws it back from its rectilinear course and gradually bends it into the remaining sides of the polygon.

300 Vis haec corporis recedendi à centro vocatur centrifuga: illa qua corpus centrum petit, centrípeta: ambae communi nomine centrales adpellantur. Hinc colliges 2. Corpus circulariter motum, & postea sibi relictum, seu remotis obicibus transferendum esse per tangentem circuli, quae sit exiguum latus continuatum; unde deducitur haec regula generalis, quae est totius systématis mundani fundamentum: Corpus circulariter motum, singulis momentis, nititur à centro sui motus récedere; & quidem eò vehementius, quo vehementius agitatur. Haec regula confirmatur experientia.

300 This force of a body of receding from the center is called centrifugal; that by which the body seeks the center, centripetal: both are called by the common name central. Hence you will gather 2. that a body moved circularly and afterwards left to itself, or with the obstacles removed, must be carried along the tangent of the circle, which is the small side continued; whence is deduced this general rule, which is the foundation of the whole system of the world: A body moved circularly strives at every moment to recede from the center of its motion; and indeed the more vehemently, the more vehemently it is agitated. This rule is confirmed by experience.

301 Si enim lapidem ex. gr. circulariter agitaveris in funda; ubi primum unum fundae funiculum demiseris, elabetur modò sursum, modò deorsum, modò horizontaliter, modò per aliam quamlibet determinationem, pro ut incipit tangens ab ea circunferentiae parte, in qua lapis sibi fuit relictus, & praeterea eò longius excurrit lapis ille, quò vehementius in orbem fuit agitatus. Quod si corpus moveatur in circulo infinito, sive etiam in linea recta, in quam utique migrat circulus infinitus, tunc quia deflèxus tangentis ab ejus circunferentia est nullus ut patet, nullus pariter erit conatus centrifugus, sive vis recendendi á centro.

301 For if you have whirled a stone, e.g., circularly in a sling, as soon as you let go one cord of the sling it will slip away now upward, now downward, now horizontally, now in any other determination, according as the tangent begins from that part of the circumference in which the stone was left to itself; and moreover that stone runs out the farther, the more vehemently it was whirled round. But if a body is moved in an infinite circle, or also in a straight line, into which an infinite circle in any case passes, then, since the deflection of the tangent from its circumference is null, as is plain, there will likewise be no centrifugal conatus, or force of receding from the center.

302 Sed dices: corpus in aliquo statu semel positum, de se perseverare debet in illo statu, atqui corpus circulariter agitatum, positum fuit in aliquo statu determinato: ergo sibi relictum semper movebitur circulariter. Nego min. Corpus enim, cujus determinatio jugiter mutatur, dici non debet in aliquo statu determinato positum, sed potius dici debet in perpetua mutatione status positum. Porrò determinatio mobilis circulariter agitati, perpetuò mutatur, sicut evidenter adparet, ubi corpus circa polygonum aliquod agitatur.

302 But you will say: a body once placed in some state must of itself persevere in that state; but a body moved circularly was placed in some determinate state: therefore, left to itself, it will always be moved circularly. I deny the minor. For a body whose determination is continually changed should not be said to be placed in some determinate state, but rather should be said to be placed in a perpetual change of state. Now the determination of a movable moved circularly is perpetually changed, as evidently appears when a body is moved around some polygon.

303 Instabis: tam determinatio mobilis per lineam circularem, dici debet unicus ejus status, quàm ipsius determinatio per lineam rectam. Nego propositionem: discrimen est, quia initium translationis est linea recta; non autem linea curva. Enimverò initium motus est translatio à puncto ad punctum. Porrò translatio illa fieri potest absque deflectione, adeòque per lineam rectam, sicut fuit probatum.

303 You will insist: the determination of a movable along a circular line should be called its single state just as much as its determination along a straight line. I deny the proposition: the difference is that the beginning of translation is a straight line, but not a curved line. For the beginning of motion is translation from point to point. Now that translation can be made without deflection, and so along a straight line, as was proved.

304 Ex dictis sequitur, quod quamvis naturale sit, id est legibus à Deo constitutis consentaneum, ut corpus aliquod translatum,

304 From what has been said it follows that, although it is natural, that is, consonant with the laws established by God, that some body carried

p. 103

& sibi relictum rectà moveatur, non minus tamen naturale est, corpus idem, linea recta primò translatum, à sua determinatione posteà dimoveri, quoties occurrunt obices ne rectà moveatur. Permanens itaque interturbatio, sive inflectio motus in corpore, qui per lineam circularem movetur, est contra exigentiam naturalem motus initialis secundum rectam lineam impressi, secundum quem corpus in unoquoque instanti se movere incipit; at interturbatio, sive inflectio haec, non est contra naturam, quia natura alicujus motus jam incepti non exigit, absolutè non interturbari, sed tantùm non interturbari deficiente obice aliquo qui interturbationem exigat. Sed secundam jam naturae legem proponamus.

and left to itself be moved in a straight line, it is nevertheless no less natural that the same body, first carried along a straight line, should afterwards be moved away from its determination as often as obstacles occur to prevent its being moved in a straight line. The permanent disturbance, therefore, or inflection of motion in a body which is moved along a circular line, is against the natural requirement of the initial motion impressed along a straight line, according to which the body at each instant begins to move itself; but this disturbance or inflection is not against nature, because the nature of a motion already begun does not require absolutely not to be disturbed, but only not to be disturbed in the absence of some obstacle which requires the disturbance. But let us now propose the second law of nature.

305 Secunda lex est: mutatio motus est semper proportionalis vi motrici impressae, & fit semper secundum rectam lineam, secundum quam vis illa imprimitur. Quoniam enim à vi motrice generatur motus in corporibus, illud certum est, motum in corpore génitum proportionalem esse ipsi vi motrici, usque adeò, ut si vis aliqua certum motum generet in corpore, dupla vis, duplum, tripla vis, triplum generabit, & generaliter vis una, quae sit ad aliam vim, ut numerus 100 ad 1, generabit motum, qui erit ad motum génitum ab alia vi, ut idem numerus 100 ad 1., sed ut id verum sit postulatur aequalitas temporum. Quod autèm motus fieri debeat per lineam rectam suprà demonstratum jam est.

305 The second law is: the change of motion is always proportional to the motive force impressed, and is always made along the straight line along which that force is impressed. For since motion is generated in bodies by motive force, this is certain, that the motion begotten in a body is proportional to the motive force itself, to such a degree that, if some force generates a certain motion in a body, a double force will generate a double motion, a triple force a triple one; and generally, one force which is to another force as the number 100 to 1 will generate a motion which will be to the motion begotten by the other force as the same number 100 to 1; but for this to be true, equality of the times is postulated. That the motion must be made along a straight line has already been demonstrated above.

306 Sequitur regula tertia: Actioni semper contraria, & aequalis est reactio. Hoc est, actioni destructae semper contraria & aequalis est resistentia. Ut haec lex intelligatur supponamus equum vim habentem ut 100, trahere lapidem funi adligatum, habentem resistentiam ut 50. Dico: equum non trahere lapidem cùm vi quam habet ut 100, sed cum vi ut 50. Sic intellecta regula, demonstratur: dum enim corpus aliquod in aliud agit, ejus vis eò tendit, ut superet secundi resistentiam. Non itaque vim omnem insúmet corpus agens, sed eam tantum partem, quae requiritur ad superandam[?] resistentiam secundi corporis. Portio vis motricis quam insúmit vocatur Actio, & resistentia, quam corpus alterum opponit, dicitur Reactio. Actio itaque reactionem habebit contrariam, & aequalem, quae ex lex 3. motus.

306 There follows the third rule: To action reaction is always contrary and equal. That is, to the action destroyed the resistance is always contrary and equal. That this law may be understood, let us suppose a horse having a force as 100 drawing a stone tied to a rope, which has a resistance as 50. I say: the horse does not draw the stone with the force which it has as 100, but with a force as 50. The rule, thus understood, is demonstrated: for while some body acts on another, its force tends to overcome the resistance of the second. The acting body, therefore, will not spend all its force, but only that part which is required for overcoming the resistance of the second body. The portion of the motive force which it spends is called Action, and the resistance which the other body opposes is called Reaction. Action, therefore, will have a contrary and equal reaction, which is the 3rd law of motion.

307 Sunt nonnulli qui falsitatem hujus legis indè ostendi posse arbitrantur, quod ea recepta, nullus unquam fieret motus in natura. Moveatur enim corpus A versùs corpus quiescens B. Jam verò si reactio corporis B in A tanta est, quanta est actio ipsius A in B, nullus sequetur motus in B; atqui videmus ipsum moveri; ergo falsum est actioni reactionem aequalem esse & contrariam. Vah putidum sophisma! Enim verò in ejusmodi ratiocinatione nihil est quod improbari non debeat. Isthaec enim naturae lex non vult resistentiam vi motrici aequalem esse, & contrariam, sed reactionem actioni, quae duo immáne quantùm distant inter se. Vis est omnis ea eficacia quae in corpore datur ad agendum absolutè loquendo.

307 There are some who think that the falsity of this law can be shown from this, that, if it were accepted, no motion would ever take place in nature. For let the body A be moved toward the body B at rest. Now, if the reaction of the body B on A is as great as the action of A on B, no motion will follow in B; but we see that it is moved; therefore it is false that reaction is equal and contrary to action. Bah, what a rotten sophism! For in reasoning of this kind there is nothing that ought not to be rejected. For this law of nature does not hold that the resistance is equal and contrary to the motive force, but the reaction to the action, two things which are enormously distant from each other. Force is all the efficacy which there is in a body for acting, speaking absolutely.

p. 104

Actio verò est solum ea portiò vis motricis, quam insúmit corpus dum agit. Non ergò semper corpora vim omnem quam habent in effectu producendo insúmunt, sed eam tantùm, quae requiritur ad coaequandam resistentiam corporis in contrarium tendentis; itaque motus fieri utique debet per vim tantam, quantus fuerit excessus actionis supra reactionem, aut resistentiam.

Action, however, is only that portion of the motive force which the body spends while it acts. Bodies, therefore, do not always spend all the force they have in producing an effect, but only that which is required for equalling the resistance of the body tending in the contrary direction; and so motion must indeed be made through a force as great as the excess of the action over the reaction, or resistance, has been.

308 Futilis itaque est objectio. Ut enim duo corpora in se invicèm agentia quiescant, requiritur ne dum, ut actiones sint aequales, sed etiam vires ab ipsis adhibitae. Tunc nempè quiescent, quum vires aequales habent, & vim omnem ádhibent, quam possident; in hoc enim casu, quum nihil iis supersit virium, & hae ponantur aequales, se mutuò destruent, & nullus orietur motus. Ita si equus trahere velit pondus aequale vi integrae, quam ipse possidet, hic profectò conabitur integra sua vi pondus transferre; quum tamen hoc sit aequale vi equi, eam destruet, & nullus orietur motus. Si verò pondus minus fuerit equi vi, tunc eam tantùm partem vis propriae adhibebit, quae superandam ponderis resistentiam adaequet, atque ita quum adhùc ipsi supersit portio vis, secum deferet pondus.

308 The objection, therefore, is futile. For in order that two bodies acting on each other should rest, it is required not only that the actions be equal, but also the forces applied by them. They will rest, namely, when they have equal forces and apply all the force they possess; for in this case, since nothing of their forces remains to them, and these are supposed equal, they will destroy each other mutually, and no motion will arise. Thus, if a horse wishes to draw a weight equal to the whole force which it possesses, it will certainly strive to move the weight with its whole force; but since this weight is equal to the force of the horse, it will destroy that force, and no motion will arise. But if the weight is less than the horse’s force, then it will apply only that part of its own force which equals the resistance of the weight to be overcome, and thus, since a portion of force still remains to it, it will carry the weight along with it.

309 Non incongruum erit hìc animadvertere, quoniam pluribus in locis elasticitatis nomen usurpabimus, quod motus elastici nomine innuimus eum, quo corpora tensa, compressa, flexa, sublata potentia tendente, comprimente, flectente in priorem figuram & situm restituuntur. Vim hanc sese in nativum statum reducendi: Elasticitatis, virtutis elasticae, elaterii nuncupatione donamus, quae restitutio si perficiatur eádem vi, qua corpus á suo statu dimotum fuit, elasticitas dicitur perfecta, secùs, imperfecta vocatur.

309 It will not be out of place to note here, since we shall use the name of elasticity in many places, that by the name of elastic motion we mean that by which bodies stretched, compressed or bent are restored to their former figure and situation once the power stretching, compressing or bending them is removed. This force of bringing itself back to its native state we honor with the name of Elasticity, elastic virtue, or elater; and if this restitution is accomplished with the same force by which the body was moved from its state, the elasticity is called perfect; otherwise it is called imperfect.

CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

De Motuum legibus, quae in corporum collisione locum habent.

On the Laws of Motions which have place in the collision of bodies.

310 Postquàm ad naturae phaenomena exquirenda seriò Physici animum adverterunt, illicò deprehensum est eam certo itinere, certisque semper legibus prógredi: praecipuè autem naturae constantia adparuit in collisione corporum, utpotè quae perpetuis quibusdam legibus perágitur. Harum legum notitiam, quum ad naturae occultissima arcana pervestiganda adprimè utilem censuisset Renatus Cartesius, non mediocre studium in iis perquirendis collocavit. ¡Atque utinam veriores nobis leges ipse dedisset! Stabilioribus enim fundamentis

s soon as Physicists seriously turned their minds to investigating the 310 A phenomena of nature, it was at once discovered that nature proceeds by a certain path and always by certain laws; but the constancy of nature appeared chiefly in the collision of bodies, inasmuch as this is carried on by certain perpetual laws. Since René Descartes had judged the knowledge of these laws exceedingly useful for tracking down the most hidden secrets of nature, he spent no mediocre study in searching them out.
