And would that he had given us truer laws! For he would have raised on more stable foundations the edifice

p. 105

superextruxisset aedificium, quod partìm nutare, partìm corruere, non sine aliquo nominis sui detrimento vidimus. Ejus exemplo admóniti veriora addúcere studebimus.

which we have seen partly totter, partly collapse, not without some detriment to his name. Warned by his example, we shall strive to bring forward truer ones.

311 Corpus unum ubi in aliud incurrit, motum huic in collisione impertit: id ipsum quibusdam legibus à natura perficitur, queis Dynámicae principia continentur. Advertendum verò collisionem duorum corporum triplici modo fieri posse. Primò: si unum in alterum prorsùs immotum incurrat. Secundò: si in eandem partem ferantur, sed inaequali velocitate sic, ut illud quod celeriùs movetur, motu suo alterum adsequatur, aut impellat. Tertiò: si ex oppositis partibus sibi mutuò occurrant. Jam quum alia sit motuum ratio in corporibus non elásticis, seu inertibus (quo nomine, & perfectè dura, & perfectè mollia comprehenduntur), alia in elasticis, leges utriusque generis in collisione animadversas próponemus. Ac de primis quidem pro triplici casu tres totidem Propositionibus á Nolleto s1 expressas damus.

311 When one body runs into another, it imparts motion to it in the collision: nature accomplishes this by certain laws, in which the principles of Dynamics are contained. It must be noted, however, that the collision of two bodies can take place in three ways. First: if one runs into the other entirely at rest. Second: if they are carried toward the same part, but with unequal velocity, such that the one which is moved faster overtakes the other with its motion, or impels it. Third: if they meet each other from opposite parts. Now since the ratio of motions is one in non-elastic, or inert, bodies (under which name both perfectly hard and perfectly soft bodies are comprehended), and another in elastic ones, we shall propose the laws of each kind observed in collision. And of the first, indeed, for the threefold case, we give three laws expressed in as many Propositions by Nollet (b).

Leges motus in collisione corporum elaterii expertium.

LAWS OF MOTION IN THE COLLISION OF BODIES DEVOID OF ELASTICITY.

Pro primo casu.

FOR THE FIRST CASE .

312 Si corpus quiescens impellitur ab alio, celeritas impingentis dispescitur inter utrumque pro ratione massarum.

312 If a body at rest is impelled by another, the celerity of the impinging body is divided between both in proportion to the masses.

313 Nempè quoniam corpus impellens quiescenti motum impertit ex eo unicè, ut impedimentum sui motus amoliatur: hoc verò ut fiat, necessum sit duntaxat, pro ratione massae utriusque vim dispertiri; si enim intelligantur corpora junctim sumpta in partes aequales, motus item totus in aequales totidem partes divisus, & aequalibus utriusque corporis partibus aequales motus partes tribuantur, patebit hoc pacto fieri, ut partes aequales duorum corporum aequali virium quantitate donatae, eandem directionem, aequali celeritate sint sequuturae, quin aliae aliis motus impedimentùm efficiant. Proinde, si corpus íncurrat in alterum quiescens, & sibi aequale in massa, dimidium velocitatis suae eidem communicabit: si subdúplum fuerit, duas tertias; si duplum, unam tertiam celeritatis partem largítur.

313 Namely, since the impelling body imparts motion to the one at rest solely in order to remove the impediment to its own motion, and since for this to happen it is necessary only to share out the force in proportion to the mass of each — for if the bodies taken together are understood to be divided into equal parts, and the whole motion likewise into as many equal parts, and equal parts of motion are assigned to equal parts of each body, it will be plain that in this way it comes about that equal parts of the two bodies, endowed with an equal quantity of forces, will follow the same direction with equal celerity, without some being an impediment to the motion of others — accordingly, if a body runs into another at rest and equal to it in mass, it will communicate to it half of its velocity; if the other is half as large, two thirds; if double, it bestows on it one third part of its celerity.

Pro secundo casu. — FOR THE SECOND CASE.

314 Si duo corpora eandem in partem inaequali celeritate ferantur, seu massae sint aequales, seu inaequales, collisione peracta, continuant motum, secundum directionem eandem, celeritate

314 If two bodies are carried toward the same part with unequal celerity, whether their masses are equal or unequal, when the collision is completed they continue their motion along the same direction with a common celerity

Leçons de Physique T. 1. Leç. IV. Sect. III.

Leçons de Physique, vol. 1, Leç. IV, sect. III.

p. 106

communi, quae tamen minor est, atque celeritas impellentis; major autem, quàm corporis impulsi ante impactionem fuerit.

which, however, is less than the celerity of the impelling body, but greater than that of the impelled body was before the impact.

315 Etenim si aequali prorsùs celeritate ferrentur, in eandem partem, atque adeò eandem inter se distantiam haberent, comparatè ad invicem duo corpora, velut quiescentia spectari deberent. Quum itaque celeritatibus inaequalibus ferri ponantur, non secùs haec corpora sese habent, ac si velociùs motum vi celeritatis respectivae, qua excedit alterum, in hoc prorsùs immotum tenderet. Quare idem, quod priori casu, cónsequi necesse est.

315 For if they were carried toward the same part with exactly equal celerity, and so had the same distance between them, the two bodies, compared with each other, would have to be regarded as if at rest. Since, therefore, they are supposed to be carried with unequal celerities, these bodies behave no otherwise than if the one moved faster tended, by the force of the respective celerity by which it exceeds the other, into this one as entirely at rest. Wherefore the same must follow as in the former case.

Pro tertio casu. — FOR THE THIRD CASE

316 Si duo corpora motu contrario sibi occurrant, motus, aut in utroque aut in uno, ad minimum extinguitur. Si post collisionem pars quaedam motus superstes fuerit, movebitur utrumque in eandem partem, secundum directionem illius, quod majori vi praeditum est, ita ut quantitas motus illis communis, sit aequalis excessui alterutrius ante collisionem.

316 If two bodies with contrary motion meet each other, the motion is extinguished either in both or at least in one. If after the collision some part of the motion has survived, each will be moved toward the same part, according to the direction of the one which was endowed with the greater force, such that the quantity of motion common to them is equal to the excess of the one over the other before the collision.

317 Nimirum si quantitates motus ante collisionem aequentur, quoniam ex diametro eae sibi adversantur, fiet, ut in ictu sese périmant. Eandem hanc regulam P. Regnault in mollibus duntaxat corporibus, at non in duris obtinére arbitràtur, eo quod haec videantur reflecti debere post ictum perindè, atque elastica, quum nulla partium compressio efficiatur. s1 Verum in utriusque generis corporibus id fieri cum Clariss. â Brixia putamus; s2 quamvis enim, si corpus perfectè durum in aliud simile prorsùs immotum incurrat, illud post impactum resiliat, ut supra diximus, multò tamen aliud est, quod hìc evenit; planum etenim durum, & immobile solummodo impedit, ne incurrens motum sua directione persequatur, efficitque[?], ut incidentis corporis directio in ictu mutetur; minimè verò impetus quidpiam per contrariam vim in eo extinguit: quemadmodum accidit, quum duo corpora sibi ex adverso occurrentia colliduntur. Si vires ante collisionem inaequales fuerint, earum partes aequales, quia opponuntur invicem, sese destruunt in collisione: idque circo corpus, quod validiùs est, excessu virium suarum in alterum tanquam immotum aget, ac proindè (per Legem primi casus) aequâ celeritate progredientur.

317 Namely, if the quantities of motion before the collision are equal, since they are diametrically opposed to each other, it will come about that in the impact they destroy each other. Hence Fr. Regnault thinks that this same rule holds only in soft bodies, but not in hard ones, because these seem to have to be reflected after the impact just like elastic ones, since no compression of the parts is effected. (c) But with the most illustrious Fortunato da Brescia we think that this happens in bodies of both kinds; (d) for although, if a perfectly hard body runs into another similar one entirely at rest, it rebounds after the impact, as we said above, what happens here is yet a very different thing; for a hard and immovable plane only prevents the incurring body from pursuing its motion in its own direction, and brings it about that the direction of the incident body is changed in the impact; but it by no means extinguishes any impetus in it by a contrary force, as happens when two bodies meeting each other from opposite sides collide. If the forces before the collision were unequal, their equal parts, since they are opposed to each other, destroy each other in the collision: and therefore the body which is the stronger will act with the excess of its forces on the other as on one at rest, and accordingly (by the Law of the first case) they will proceed with equal celerity.

Entret. Phys. Tom. I. X. Entret. IV. Regle. & XII. Entret. IV. Regle.

Entret. Phys., vol. I, Entret. X, Rule IV, & Entret. XII, Rule IV.

Phys. Gen. P. 1. §. 432.

Phys. Gen., pt. 1, §. 432.

p. 107

Leges motus in collisione corporum elasticorum.

LAWS OF MOTION IN THE COLLISION OF ELASTIC BODIES

Pro primo casu.

FOR THE FIRST CASE .

318 Corpus elasticum in alterum ejusdem naturae aequale, & quiescens dum incurrit, peracta collisione immotum persistit; illud verò quod quiescebat, secundum eam directionem, câque ipsâ celeritate movetur post ictum, quâ ante eundem incurrens ferebatur.

318 An elastic body, when it runs into another of the same nature, equal and at rest, remains immobile once the collision is completed; but the one which was at rest is moved after the impact along that direction, and with that very celerity, with which the incurring body was carried before.

319 Quum enim massae corporum aequentur, si incurrentis celeritas sit = 6, hujus dimidium quiescenti communicatur in ictu, altera parte impellenti remanente (per Legem primi casus): id quod fieret, si corpora destituerentur elaterio. At quoniam elasticus motus compressioni respondet, haec percussioni, percussio motui directo, quem in collissione corpus nanciscitur; idcirco celeritas dimidia in ictu acquisita, duplicatur partium compressarum aequali restitutione: proindè corpus impulsum peractâ collissione movebitur celeritate = 6 nimirum velocitate = 3 communicatâ in impactu, & celeritate = 3 ab elaterio profectâ. Corpus contrà incurrens celeritatis suae dimidium quum retineat; simul autèm partes compressae post ictum aequali celeritate, verùm directione oppositâ, se se restituant: ideo motum in eo extingui, & post impactum quiescere illud necesse est.

319 For since the masses of the bodies are equal, if the celerity of the incurring body is = 6, half of it is communicated to the one at rest in the impact, the other part remaining to the impelling body (by the Law of the first case): which is what would happen if the bodies were destitute of elater. But since the elastic motion corresponds to the compression, this to the percussion, and the percussion to the direct motion which the body obtains in the collision, therefore the half celerity acquired in the impact is doubled by the equal restitution of the compressed parts: accordingly the impelled body, once the collision is completed, will be moved with celerity = 6, namely with the velocity = 3 communicated in the impact, and with the celerity = 3 supplied by the elater. The incurring body, on the contrary, since it retains half of its celerity, while at the same time the compressed parts after the impact restore themselves with equal celerity but in the opposite direction, must therefore have its motion extinguished, and must rest after the impact.

320 Lex II. Si corpus elasticum A in alterum B similiter elasticum, sed minoris diametri quod quiescat, incurrat, utrumque ad eandem partem fertur, peracta collisione; sed celeritas ipsius B major futura est celeritate corporis A.

320 Law II. If an elastic body A runs into another, B, likewise elastic, but of smaller diameter, which is at rest, each is carried toward the same part once the collision is completed; but the celerity of B will be greater than the celerity of the body A.

321 Incurrat A celeritate = 6 in B, hoc sit subdúplum[?] quoad massam, & quiescat. Quoniam A impertítur ipsi B celeritatem pro ratione massae utriusque, atque adeò, quum duplum sit, de B, unam tertiam suae celeritatis, hoc est: celeritatem = 2. (per Legem primi casus corporum non elasticorum). Hi gradus, quia per elaterii restitutionem duplicantur, idcirco B post ictum celeritate = 4 secundum directionem ipsius A movebitur. Corpus A ex adversò celeritate = 2 in B translatâ tantundem motus elastici directione contraria amittit: insequitur proindè alterum non nisi celeritate = 2.

321 Let A run with celerity = 6 into B, which is half of it as to mass, and at rest. Since A imparts to B celerity in proportion to the mass of each, and so, since it is double of B, one third of its celerity, that is: the celerity = 2 (by the Law of the first case of non-elastic bodies), these degrees, because they are doubled by the restitution of the elater, will make B be moved after the impact with celerity = 4 along the direction of A. The body A, on the other hand, the celerity = 2 having been transferred into B, loses as much elastic motion in the contrary direction: it therefore follows the other only with celerity = 2.

322 Lex III. Si corpus elasticum A in alterum B majoris diametri, ejusdem naturae, & quiescens incurrat, concitabitur B ad directionem secundum quam ante ictum ferebatur A, verùm hoc post impactum regredietur.

322 Law III. If an elastic body A runs into another, B, of greater diameter, of the same nature, and at rest, B will be roused toward the direction along which A was carried before the impact, but A will go back after the impact.

323 Sit A subdúplum quoad massam ipsius B; & incurrat

323 Let A be half of B as to mass, and let it run in with celerity =

p. 108

celeritate = 6 (per legem dictam): tránsferet duas tertias celeritatis suae, hoc est: = 4 supersunt itaque duo gradus celeritatis in A. Jam quum elasticitas respondeat motui in collisione communicato, hicque sit quatuor graduum, idcircò vi motus elastici, celeritate quatuor graduum regrederetur. At quoniam duo ex his, per totidem gradus celeritatis, qui è motu directo supersunt, & secundum oppositam directionem cedunt, perimuntur; ea de causa corpus A celeritate duntaxat = 2 post ictum regredietur.

= 6 (by the said law): it will transfer two thirds of its celerity, that is: = 4; two degrees of celerity therefore remain in A. Now since the elasticity corresponds to the motion communicated in the collision, and this is of four degrees, by the force of the elastic motion A would therefore go back with a celerity of four degrees. But since two of these are cancelled by as many degrees of celerity which remain from the direct motion and yield in the opposite direction, for that reason the body A goes back after the impact with a celerity of only = 2.

Pro secundo casu. — FOR THE SECOND CASE

324 Lex I. Si corpus elasticum, aliud aequale sibi, ejusdemque naturae ad eandem partem insequatur, ferentur post collisionem eadem directione, celeritatibus permutatis.

324 Law I. If an elastic body follows another equal to itself and of the same nature toward the same part, they will be carried after the collision in the same direction, with their celerities exchanged.

325 Moveatur A celeritate = 4, & B eandem insequens directionem, celeritate = 12: quoniam haec corpora perindè se habent, ac si A quiesceret, & B moveretur in A celeritate = 8 seu illa celeritatis parte, qua celeritatem praecedentis excedit: idcircò in cóllisione corpus B dimidium hujus suae celeritatis, hoc est: quatuor gradus ipsi A impertiet (per Legem primi casus corp. non elast.) Celeritas haec = 4 vi elasticitatis duplicatur sitque = 8: eadem addita celeritati ante collisionem quatuor graduum est = 12. Corpus B contrà, communicatis in ictu quatuor celeritatis gradibus ex octo qui supererant, quatuor rursùm vi motus elastici in contrariam partem tendentis deperdit: ut adeo superstes ei duntaxat maneat celeritas = 4. Quare post ictum feretur A celeritate = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. B. celeritate = 12 — 4 — 4 = 4 hoc est: celeritatibus permutatis, motum eâdem directione persequentur.

325 Let A be moved with celerity = 4, and B, following the same direction, with celerity = 12: since these bodies behave just as if A were at rest and B were moved into A with celerity = 8, or with that part of its celerity by which it exceeds the celerity of the one going before, therefore in the collision the body B will impart to A half of this celerity of its own, that is: four degrees (by the Law of the first case of non-elast. bod.). This celerity = 4 is doubled by the force of elasticity and becomes = 8; the same, added to the celerity of four degrees before the collision, is = 12. The body B, on the contrary, having communicated in the impact four degrees of celerity out of the eight which were in excess, loses four again by the force of the elastic motion tending toward the contrary part, so that only the celerity = 4 remains to it as surviving. Wherefore after the impact A will be carried with celerity = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, B with celerity = 12 − 4 − 4 = 4; that is: with their celerities exchanged, they will pursue their motion in the same direction.

326 Lex II. Si corpus elasticum A in alterum B ejusdem naturae, sed minoris diametri, ac tardiùs motum incurrat; peractâ collisione, A motum tardiùs prosequetur, B verò, eandem describendo lineam, celeriùs.

326 Law II. If an elastic body A runs into another, B, of the same nature, but of smaller diameter and moved more slowly, once the collision is completed A will continue its motion more slowly, and B, describing the same line, more swiftly.

327 Ponatur A (quo ad massam duplum ipsius B,) ferri celeritate = 6; B autem celeritate = 3. Quoniam hujuscemodi corpora perindè se habent, ac si quiescerent, & corpus A celeritate duntaxat relativâ = 3 incurreret; idcircò A unam tertiam celeritatis hujùs partem = 1 in collisione largitur, quae celeritas vi elastici motus duplicatur sic, ut post ictum feratur corpus B celeritate = 3 + 1 + 1 = 5. Contrà corpus A, communicato uno gradu celeritatis per collisionem, & è residuis quinque, rursum per elaterii in oppositum restitutionem, uno extincto; movebitur post ictum celeritate = 6 — 1 — 1 = 4.

327 Let A (which as to mass is double of B) be supposed to be carried with celerity = 6, and B with celerity = 3. Since bodies of this kind behave just as if they were at rest and the body A ran in with only the relative celerity = 3, therefore A bestows in the collision one third part of this celerity, = 1, which celerity is doubled by the force of the elastic motion, so that after the impact the body B is carried with celerity = 3 + 1 + 1 = 5. The body A, on the contrary, having communicated one degree of celerity through the collision, and, of the remaining five, one being extinguished again through the restitution of the elater in the opposite direction, will be moved after the impact with celerity = 6 − 1 − 1 = 4.

328 Lex III. Si corpus elasticum A in alterum pariter elasticum B majoris diametri, tardiusque motum, incurrat: post ictum regredietur.

328 Law III. If an elastic body A runs into another, B, likewise elastic, of greater diameter and moved more slowly: after the impact it will go back.

329 Moveatur corpus A celeritate = 19 corpus B celeritate = 4, adeòque fiat relativa celeritas corporis A = 15. Sitque A quo ad

329 Let the body A be moved with celerity = 19, the body B with celerity = 4, and so let the relative celerity of the body A become = 15. And let A, as to

p. 109

massam subdúplum. Istud in ictu impertiet corpori B celeritatem = 10, duas nempè tertias [per legem dictam]: celeritas haec elaterii restitutione tantundèm aucta, efficiet, ut corpus B progrediatur celeritate = 4 + 10 + 10 = 24; corpus verò A retentos[?] post collisionem 4 + 5 celeritatis gradus motûs directi, vi motus elastici in contrariam partem tendentis, (qui quum aequetur percussioni, haecque sit = 10) eosdem 4 + 5 gradus motûs directi deperdit; & celeritate = 1 post ictum regreditur.

mass, half as great. In the impact this will impart to body B a velocity = 10, namely two thirds [by the law stated]: this velocity, increased by just as much again through the restitution of the spring, will cause body B to proceed with a velocity = 4 + 10 + 10 = 24; but body A, retaining after the collision 4 + 5 degrees of velocity of direct motion, loses those same 4 + 5 degrees of direct motion through the force of the elastic motion tending in the contrary direction (which equals the percussion, and the percussion is = 10), and after the impact goes back with a velocity = 1.

Pro tertio casu. — FOR THE THIRD CASE

330 Lex I. Corpora duo elastica ejusdem diametri, aequali celeritate sibi ex oppositis partibus occurrentia, post ictum eâdem celeritate resiliunt; idem obtinet, Si massae duorum corporum occurrentium sint in ratione inversa celeritatum.

330 Law I. Two elastic bodies of the same diameter, meeting each other from opposite sides with equal velocity, rebound after the impact with the same velocity; the same holds if the masses of the two bodies meeting are in the inverse ratio of their velocities.

331 Patet; tota enim earum vis in directum extinguitur; at in restitutione denuò restituitur. Resiliunt igitur eâ, qua ferebantur, celeritate. Si quoque corpus A, cujus massa sit = 3, & corpus B, cujus massa = 2, ita sibi occurrant, ut celeritas prioris sit = 4, posterioris = 6; quoniam vis tota utriusque in restitutione partium redditur: corpus A celeritate = 4, corpus B celeritate = 6 regredietur.

331 This is evident; for their whole force is extinguished in the direct line, but in the restitution it is restored again. They rebound, therefore, with the velocity with which they were borne. Again, if body A, whose mass is = 3, and body B, whose mass is = 2, meet each other in such a way that the velocity of the former is = 4, that of the latter = 6: since the whole force of each is given back in the restitution of the parts, body A will go back with a velocity = 4, body B with a velocity = 6.

332 Lex II. Duo corpora elastica aequalis diametri, ex oppositis partibus sibi occurrentia, celeritate inaequali, permutatis celeritatibus post ictum, resiliunt.

332 Law II. Two elastic bodies of equal diameter, meeting each other from opposite sides with unequal velocity, rebound after the impact with their velocities exchanged.

333 Incurrat corpus A celeritate = 6 B celeritate = 4. Quoniam celeritates aequales, quibus in oppositas partes feruntur corpora, sese elidunt: celeritas tota corporis B in ictu perimetur, eritque celeritas ipsius A = 6 — 4 = 2. Jam hujus dimidium communicatur corpori B tanquam quiescenti; sed in eam partem, quà movebatur ipsum A, hoc est; versùs quam reflectendum est B. Igitur post[?] ictum in eandem partem non nisi vis = 1 supererit in A. Porrò quia compressio = 4 + 1 est, eadem vi partium restitutio exigenda est; eâ tamen lege, ut quum in A superstes maneat versùs partem oppositam celeritas = 1, haec quintum celeritatis gradum, quo ad regrediendum polléret, périmat. Corpus B verò, quoniam quatuor ad resiliendum celeritatis gradus adeptum est vi celeritatis, quâ primum occurrit: unum versùs eandem regrediendo lineam, celeritatis gradum ab excessu majoris celeritatis alterius corporis obtinuit, & ob compressionem simplicis unius gradus factam, uno rursùs celeritatis versus eandem lineam gradu auctum sit; ea de causa corpus A resiliet celeritate = 4, corpus B celeritate = 6 adeòque permutatis.

333 Let body A run with a velocity = 6, B with a velocity = 4. Since the equal velocities with which the bodies are borne in opposite directions cancel each other, the whole velocity of body B will be destroyed in the impact, and the velocity of A itself will be = 6 − 4 = 2. Now half of this is communicated to body B, as though to a body at rest; but in the direction in which A itself was moving, that is, the direction in which B must be reflected. Therefore after the impact no more than a force = 1 will remain in A in the same direction. Further, since the compression is = 4 + 1, the restitution of the parts must be exacted with the same force; yet under this law, that since in A there remains a velocity = 1 toward the opposite side, this destroys the fifth degree of velocity which it would have had for going back. But body B, since it acquired four degrees of velocity for rebounding by the force of the velocity with which it first met the other: obtained one degree of velocity, going back along the same line, from the excess of the greater velocity of the other body, and, on account of the compression of one simple degree that was made, is increased once more by one degree of velocity along the same line; for that reason body A will rebound with a velocity = 4, body B with a velocity = 6, and so with the velocities exchanged.

334 Lex III. Si corpus A majoris, B minoris diametri, utrumque elasticum, aequali celeritate sibi directè occurrant: B semper post ictum resiliet; A verò interdum persequetur motum suum, quandoque post collisionem immotum consistet, nonnunquam reflectetur.

334 Law III. If body A, of greater, and B, of smaller diameter, both elastic, meet each other directly with equal velocity: B will always rebound after the impact; but A will sometimes continue its motion, sometimes stand motionless after the collision, sometimes be reflected.

p. 110

335 B resiliet, quoniam in partium restitutione vim amissam totam recuperat; duplo autem majore respectu illius, quàm corpus A in ictu communicavit, pollet. A interdum per eandem lineam movebitur; siquidem evenire potest, ut vis, quâ directè in alterum corpus incurrit, major sit viribus elaterii. Quandoque subsistet; fit enim, ut vis, quâ se partes compressae restituunt, aequetur motui directo post ictum superstiti, seque invicem extinguant omninò. Nonnunquam reflectetur: tum scilicet, quum evenit, ut partium vi elasticitatis restitutio exsuperet vim, quae post ictum è motu directo reliqua est.

335 B rebounds, since in the restitution of its parts it recovers the whole force it had lost; and it is endowed with a force twice as great as that which body A communicated in the impact. A will sometimes be moved along the same line; for it can happen that the force with which it ran directly into the other body is greater than the forces of the spring. Sometimes it stands still; for it happens that the force with which the compressed parts restore themselves is equal to the direct motion surviving after the impact, and that they extinguish each other altogether. Sometimes it is reflected: namely, when it happens that the restitution by the force of elasticity of the parts exceeds the force that is left over from the direct motion after the impact.

336 Plura de hisce motus regulis dedére Johann. Wallisius s1, pro corporibus duris: pro elasticis Wrenius, & Hugenius, confirmata subindè à Mariotto, cujus Machinam aptavit quoque Nolletus: Pater Regnault perspicuè pariter ista persequitur. s2 Cl. à Brixia denique diffusè pertractat s3 Legem III. secundi casus pro elasticis paulò amplius extendens.

336 More on these rules of motion was given by John Wallis (e), for hard bodies; for elastic ones by Wren and Huygens, confirmed afterwards by Mariotte, whose Machine Nollet also adapted: Father Regnault likewise pursues these matters perspicuously (f). Finally the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia treats them at length (g), extending Law III of the second case for elastic bodies somewhat more widely.

CAPUT V.

CHAPTER V.

De Motu Reflexo, ejusque legibus.

On Reflected Motion, and its laws.

337 Quum motus alicui corpori impressus non statim extinguatur, sed aliquo tempore in mobili perseveret, ut inferius explicabitur, fieri necessariò debet, ut si corpus ipsum antequàm motus, & impetus illi à causa impressus extinguatur, ac pereat, in corpus aliquod solidum, ac immobile, ut in parietem, incidat, motum quidem non amittat, sed quia ut ulteriùs juxta veterem motus directionem prógredi nequit, ad oppositas partes convertatur, haec autem motus adfectio Reflexio dicitur, sive regressus corporis mobilis resilientis ab alio corpore, quod neque penetrare, neque protrudere potest, ut si pila ex. gr. quae reflexionis quidem est capax in parietem immitatur; quum eum pervadere nequeat, neque propellere, statim reflectitur. Hujus autem reflexionis leges sunt.

ince the motion impressed on any body is not extinguished at once, but per337 S sists for some time in the mobile, as will be explained below, it must necessarily happen that if the body itself, before the motion and the impetus impressed on it by the cause is extinguished and perishes, falls upon some solid, immovable body, as upon a wall, it does not indeed lose its motion, but, since it cannot proceed any further according to the former direction of the motion, it is turned toward the opposite side; and this affection of motion is called Reflection, or the regress of a mobile body rebounding from another body which it can neither penetrate nor push forward; as if, e.g., a ball, which is indeed capable of reflection, is thrown against a wall: since it can neither pass through it nor drive it forward, it is at once reflected. And the laws of this reflection are these.

338 I. Si corpus aliquod in alterius corporis solidi immobilis superficiem perpendiculariter incidat per rectam G B (Fig. XXI.) perpendiculariter etiam, per eandem lineam G B rursùm resiliet, quum non sit major ratio, ut potiùs per aliam rectam á dicta deflectentem quam

338 I. If some body falls perpendicularly on the surface of another solid, immovable body along the straight line GB (Fig. XXI.), it rebounds, also perpendicularly, along the same line GB, since there is no greater reason why it should be directed rather along another straight line deflecting from the said one than along

Transact. Philos. N. XLIII.

Philosophical Transactions, no. XLIII.

Entret. Phys. T. 1. Entret. XI.

Entretiens physiques, vol. 1, Entretien XI.

Phys. Gen. P. I. Diss. II. Sect. V. Art. X.

Phys. Gen., pt. I, Diss. II, Sect. V, Art. X.

p. 111

per ipsam illam dirigatur. II. Si corpus illud in alterius corporis superficiem obliquè incidat, ut si pila ad angulum A B D (ead. Fig.) incidat in lineam, vel superficiem D B E, ita ex altera parte pila resiliet, per lineam B C, ut efformetur angulus E B C, qui dicitur angulus reflexionis, aequalis angulo D B A, qui vocatur angulus incidentiae. Unde celebre principium illud quod, angulus incidentiae semper aequalis est angulo reflexionis. Demonstratur: natura semper per lineas breviores operatur; ergo corpus quod movetur reflexionis capax íncidens in corpus resistens, incidit, & reflectitur per lineas breviores, sed lineae A B, C B quae sunt lineae incidentiae, & reflexionis, & angulos formant aequales sunt breviores duabus aliis A F, F C, & ceteris omnibus, quae inter eosdem terminos duci possunt [ex Geometr.]: ergo pila describet lineas breviores, & aequaliter inclinatas A B, C B, quàm longiores, & inaequaliter inclinatas A F, F C.

along that very one. II. If that body falls obliquely on the surface of another body, as if a ball falls at the angle ABD (same Fig.) on the line, or surface, DBE, it will so rebound on the other side, along the line BC, that there is formed the angle EBC, which is called the angle of reflection, equal to the angle DBA, which is called the angle of incidence. Hence that celebrated principle, that the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. It is demonstrated: nature always operates by shorter lines; therefore a body in motion that is capable of reflection, falling on a resisting body, falls and is reflected along shorter lines; but the lines AB, CB, which are the lines of incidence and of reflection and form equal angles, are shorter than the two others AF, FC, and than all the rest that can be drawn between the same end points [from Geometry]: therefore the ball will describe the shorter and equally inclined lines AB, CB, rather than the longer and unequally inclined AF, FC.

339 Perfecta angulorum incidentiae, & reflexionis aequalitas defendi tantùm potest, si reflexio in superficie admodùm polita fiat, nec asperitas, aut situs partium huic aequalitati obsit, neque corporis mobilis motus in contactu, seu percussione ullatenus imminuatur. Si enim scabra, & inaequabilis fuerit superficies, vel quacumque ratione sit distorta, ab ea corpus mobile pro vario partium suarum situ, aut asperitate variè resiliendo detorquebitur. At ubi de reflexione luminis in speculis agitur, quum ea reflexio in corporibus tersis, & politis fiat, id quasi principium adsúmi potest, angulum incidentiae aequalem esse angulo reflexionis.

339 The perfect equality of the angles of incidence and reflection can be maintained only if the reflection takes place on a very highly polished surface, and neither roughness nor the situation of the parts stands in the way of this equality, nor is the motion of the mobile body in any way diminished in the contact, or percussion. For if the surface is rough and uneven, or distorted in any way whatever, the mobile body will be twisted aside from it, rebounding in various ways according to the varied situation of its parts, or their roughness. But where it is a question of the reflection of light in mirrors, since that reflection takes place in clean and polished bodies, it can be taken as a principle, so to speak, that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.

CAPUT VI. — CHAPTER VI

De Motu refracto ejusque legibus.

On Refracted Motion and its laws.

340 Quae de reflexione motûs, ejusque legibus hactenùs exposuimus, plurimam certè lucem iis etiam allatura sunt, quae de altera motûs proprietate, nimirùm de refractione dicenda remanent. Quemadmodùm enim si corpus aliquod mobile in aliud corpus immobile, ac inpenetrabile íncidat, veterem motûs directionem amittit; ac novam prorsùs acquirit; ita quoque quum mobile ex uno corpore in aliud corpus inaequalis resistentiae vel densitatis transeundo incurrit, illud quidem pénetrat, sed ita reflectit, & inclinatur, ut novam motus directionem acquirat, undè optimè definiri solet refractio: inflectio, vel curvatio motus, qua corpus mobile, ob majorem, vel minorem corporis, quod obliquè subit, resistentiam, à recta linea, quam

hat we have so far set forth about the reflection of motion and 340 Wits laws will certainly bring a great deal of light also to the things that remain to be said about the other property of motion, namely refraction. For just as, if some mobile body falls on another body that is immovable and impenetrable, it loses its former direction of motion and acquires an entirely new one; so too, when a mobile, passing from one body, runs into another body of unequal resistance or density, it does indeed penetrate it, but is so bent and inclined that it acquires a new direction of motion; whence refraction is very well defined: the inflection, or curving, of motion by which a mobile body, on account of the greater or smaller resistance of the body which it enters obliquely, from the straight line which it was describing

p. 112

describebat deflectit. Diximus quod obliquè subit, quia si perpendiculariter incideret, nihil inflecteretur, sed rectà tenderet.

is deflected. We said which it enters obliquely, because if it fell perpendicularly, it would not be inflected at all, but would tend straight on.

341 Ut autem clariùs intelligi, & adcuratiùs id explicari possit concipiatur luminis radius A B (Fig. XXII.) qui in aëre propagatus incidat obliquè in superficiem aquae C D, hic enim quum primum aquam ingreditur, ita inflectitur, ut á linea recta B E, quam recto motu describeret, si eandem semper densitatem inveniret, deflectat, & accedat ad rectam B G quae superficiei C D perpendicularis concipitur.

341 But so that this may be understood more clearly and explained more accurately, let there be conceived a ray of light AB (Fig. XXII.), which, propagated in the air, falls obliquely on the surface of water CD; for this ray, as soon as it enters the water, is so inflected that it bends away from the straight line BE, which it would describe with straight motion if it always found the same density, and approaches the straight line BG, which is conceived as perpendicular to the surface CD.

342 Quod si radius ex puncto F in aqua posito prodiisset, ubi ad aëris superficiem pervenisset, non amplius rectam lineam F H describeret, sed ita potiùs per A B inflecteretur, ut non solùm â puncto H, sed etiam ab ipsa perpendiculari B I recéderet. Hinc in Dioptrica veluti certissimae refractionum leges adsumuntur, ac ostenduntur: Quod si radius ex corpore, vel medio rariori in corpus, ac medium densius transeat, ita motus inflectetur, ut ad perpendicularem accedat; si verò ex densiori in rarius, ab ipsa perpendiculari recedat.

342 But if the ray had issued from the point F, placed in the water, then on reaching the surface of the air it would no longer describe the straight line FH, but would rather be so inflected along AB as to recede not only from the point H, but also from the perpendicular BI itself. Hence in Dioptrics these are assumed and shown as the most certain laws of refractions: If a ray passes from a rarer body, or medium, into a denser body and medium, its motion will be so inflected as to approach the perpendicular; but if from a denser into a rarer, it recedes from the perpendicular itself.

343 Quod si non lucis radius, sed quodlibet corpus aliud, ut ex gr. plumbea, vel eburnea pila ex aëre in aquam obliquo motu descenderet, haec ita motum inflecteret, ut â perpendiculari recederet, sicut vicissim, si ex aqua in aërem prodiret ad perpendicularem accederet. Itaque lucis, alterius vè corporis motus adcuratissimè distingui debet, ne refractionem unâ eademque lege in lumine, aliisque corporibus péragi existimetur. Qua verò de causa quaecumque corpora, si lucem excéperis, ita refringi debeant, ut à perpendiculari recedant, facilè intelligetur, si observetur, aquam, utporè corpus densiùs magis motui resistere quàm aërem, qui levior est, ideoque motum pilae impressum aliqua ex parte dùm aquam subit, languidiorem fieri.

343 But if not a ray of light but any other body, as e.g. a ball of lead or of ivory, were to descend from the air into water with an oblique motion, it would so inflect its motion as to recede from the perpendicular, just as, conversely, if it came out of water into air, it would approach the perpendicular. Therefore the motion of light and that of another body must be distinguished most accurately, lest refraction be thought to be performed by one and the same law in light and in other bodies. But for what reason all bodies whatever, if you except light, must be so refracted as to recede from the perpendicular will easily be understood if it is observed that water, as a denser body, resists motion more than air, which is lighter, and that therefore the motion impressed on the ball becomes in some degree more sluggish while it is entering the water.

344 Quumque experimento facilè deprehendatur aquam motui magis perpendiculari, quàm horizontali resistere, ex duobus motibus, quibus obliquus[?] componitur, pendicularis languidor fiet, ac horizontalis augebitur, adeòque pila á perpendiculari recedet. At verò quum radius lucis faciliùs in aqua, crystallo aliisque corporibus, quorum pori, partes ve solidae stabiliores sunt, quàm in aëre moveatur, quippe quum partes aëris, atque interstitia ab iis formata perenni fluxu agitentur; radius ipse minorem in aqua, quàm in aëre resistentiam reperiet, adeòque refringetur accedendo ad perpendicularem.

344 And since it is easily detected by experiment that water resists perpendicular motion more than horizontal, of the two motions of which the oblique one is composed the perpendicular will become more sluggish, and the horizontal will be increased, and so the ball will recede from the perpendicular. But since a ray of light moves more easily in water, crystal and other bodies whose pores, or solid parts, are more stable, than in air, inasmuch as the parts of the air and the interstices formed by them are agitated by a perpetual flux, the ray itself will meet less resistance in water than in air, and so will be refracted by approaching the perpendicular.

p. 113

DISSERTATIO II. — DISSERTATION II

STATICA, sive

STATICS , or

De particularibus quibusdam motibus corporum solidorum.

On certain particular motions of solid bodies.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

Praeviae notiones proponuntur.

Preliminary notions are proposed.

345 Expensis motuum diversis generibus, peculiares quidam gravium solidorum motus sunt explanandi. Qua in tractatione quisque intelliget, quàm latè motus elementa, eorumque usus ad vitae humanae cómmoda pateat, neminique iccircò mirùm videri ut debeat, maximam hoc in argumento á Viris praestantissimis operam fuisse collocatam. Quibusdam proindè Mathematicorum innixi principiis, eorumdemque cognitione praevia, Staticam philosophico oculo perlustrabimus. Itaque sit notionum ex ordine evolutio.

aving set forth the various kinds of motions, we must explain certain 345 H peculiar motions of heavy solid bodies. In this treatment everyone will understand how widely the elements of motion, and their use for the conveniences of human life, extend, so that it ought to seem a wonder to no one that the greatest effort has been spent on this subject by most excellent men. Relying, therefore, on certain principles of the Mathematicians, and with a previous knowledge of them, we shall survey Statics with a philosophical eye. Let there be, then, an unfolding of the notions in order.

346 Statica est ea Physicae pars, quae de gravium aequilibrio disserit. Haec si circa solidorum corporum pondus versetur Geostatica, vel Statica citrà adjectionem vocatur; si de fluidis agat, Hydrostatica nuncupatur. De priore cum Clariss. Michaele Klaus agemus primùm, tùm alteram persequemur, notionibus generalibus antè indicatis.

346 Statics is that part of Physics which discourses on the equilibrium of heavy bodies. If it is concerned with the weight of solid bodies, it is called Geostatics, or Statics without any addition; if it treats of fluids, it is named Hydrostatics. We shall treat of the former first, with the most distinguished Michael Klaus, and then pursue the other, after general notions have first been indicated.

347 Potentia adpellatur quaevis causa motum efficiens. Pondus est, quod á potentia movetur, vel motui resistit. Vis viva, ac vis mortua quo significatu veniant, indigitavimus supra [§. 272.] Ut rem studiosiùs hic distiguant nonnulli, vim motricem cum motu actuali conjunctam, quaecumque illa sit, vim vivam dicunt; eam autèm quae pondus duntaxat sustinet, impresso solum aliquo ad motum nisu, pro vi mortua habent. Momentum adpellari solet vis massae gravitantis. Aequilibrium est, momentorum inter se aequalitas, & mutua compensatio.

347 Power is the name given to any cause producing motion. Weight is that which is moved by the power, or resists motion. In what sense living force and dead force are to be taken we indicated above [§. 272.]. To distinguish the matter more carefully here, some call the moving force joined with actual motion, whatever it may be, living force; but that which merely sustains a weight, with only some striving toward motion impressed on it, they hold for dead force. Momentum is usually the name given to the force of a gravitating mass. Equilibrium is the equality of momenta with one another, and their mutual compensation.

p. 114

348 Homogenea sunt corpora, quorum omnes partes sensibiles ejusdem sunt naturae; heterogenea ex adversò, quorum partes diversae sunt quoad naturam. Gravia, seu fluida, sive solida, homogenea habentur, quorum gravitates voluminibus proportionales sunt: gravia heterogenea verò, quae gravitates voluminibus proportionales non sortiuntur.

348 Homogeneous bodies are those all of whose sensible parts are of the same nature; heterogeneous, on the contrary, those whose parts are diverse as to nature. Heavy bodies, whether fluid or solid, are held to be homogeneous when their gravities are proportional to their volumes; but heterogeneous heavy bodies are those which are not allotted gravities proportional to their volumes.

349 Centrum aliud est gravium, aliud gravitatis, aliud magnitudinis, aliud motus. Primum est centrum commune universi, & comparatè ad corpora terrestria centrum telluris, ad quod illa feruntur. Alterum est punctum illud intra, vel extra corpus positum, circa quod undiquè partes aequalium momentorum, sive aequiponderantes consistunt, ut jam ante P. Schottum s1 Pappus Alexandrinus s2 & Stevinus s3 ferè explicuerunt. Ita in corporibus partes suas omnes unitas comprehendentibus centrum gravitatis intra ipsa illa positum est: at in annulo semiannulo, sphaera, aut semisphaera concava, extrinsecus constituitur ex. gr. in diametrorum intersectione, ex quo puncto, vel sola cogitatione suspensum corpus aequilibrium tuetur. Tertium quod etiam centrum figurae nuncupatur, est illud punctum, in magnitudine, seu extensione, per quod si plano aliquo gratis conficto transeunte, corpus dividatur, in partes aeque magnas secatur; sive ejusdem sint ponderis, sive diversi. Hoc cum centro gravitatis congruit in corporibus homogeneis regularibus; diversum verò est in irregularibus, & heterogeneis. Centrum motus paulò infra exponetur.

349 One center is that of heavy bodies, another of gravity, another of magnitude, another of motion. The first is the common center of the universe and, in comparison with terrestrial bodies, the center of the earth, to which they are borne. The second is that point, placed inside or outside the body, about which parts of equal momenta, or equiponderant parts, stand on every side, as, long before Father Schott (h), Pappus of Alexandria (i) and Stevin (j) had more or less explained. Thus in bodies that comprehend all their parts united, the center of gravity is placed within the bodies themselves; but in a ring, a half-ring, a concave sphere or hemisphere, it is constituted outside, e.g. at the intersection of the diameters, a point from which a body suspended, even by thought alone, maintains equilibrium. The third, which is also named the center of figure, is that point in the magnitude, or extension, such that, if some plane, freely imagined, passes through it, the body is divided and cut into equally great parts, whether they are of the same weight or of different. This coincides with the center of gravity in regular homogeneous bodies, but is different in irregular and heterogeneous ones. The center of motion will be set forth a little below.

350 Linea directionis gravium, est linea recta à centro gravitatis ipsius corporis ad centrum gravium, atque ad horizontem perpendiculariter ducta [§. 143] Nuncupationem hanc nacta est, quia dirigit gravium descensum, sic, ut ab ea gravitatis centrum, ipsumque grave nunquam recedat. Dicitur etiam diameter gravitatis, eò quod per centrum[?] gravitatis transeundo, corpus in duas partes equiponderantes dispescat.

350 The line of direction of heavy bodies is the straight line drawn from the center of gravity of the body itself to the center of heavy bodies, and perpendicularly to the horizon [§. 143]. It has obtained this name because it directs the descent of heavy bodies, so that the center of gravity, and the heavy body itself, never departs from it. It is also called the diameter of gravity, because, passing through the center of gravity, it divides the body into two equiponderant parts.

351 Jugum adpellatur linea recta, rigida, & inflexilis, quae circa unum punctum sui prorsus immobile liberrimè revolvi potest. Hujusmodi est linea A B (Fig. XXIII.) si planè rigida & ponderis expers concipiatur, ac circa immobile punctum F liberè volubilis.

351 The beam is the name given to a straight, rigid and inflexible line which can revolve most freely about one point of itself that is altogether immovable. Such is the line AB (Fig. XXIII.), if it is conceived as entirely rigid and void of weight, and freely revolvable about the immovable point F.

352 Centrum motus est illud immobile punctum, circa quod pondera ex rigidae linae extremis punctis suspensa, libere moveri queunt. Tale est (Fig. cit.) punctum F, si circum illud prorsùs immotum adplicita pondera A & B moveri possint. Punctum hoc dici etiam adsólet punctum suspensionis, eò quod ex illo prorsùs immobili adpensa corpora unà cum jugo libere dependeant. Idem illud centrum fulcri nomine venit, Graecis Hypomochlion sonat, quasi

352 The center of motion is that immovable point about which weights suspended from the extreme points of a rigid line can move freely. Such (Fig. cit.) is the point F, if the weights A and B applied about it, while it stays altogether unmoved, can be moved. This point is also usually called the point of suspension, because the bodies hung from it, altogether immovable as it is, hang freely together with the beam. The same point also goes by the name of center of the fulcrum; for the Greeks it is called Hypomochlion, as if you were to say:

Mag. universal. P. 3. L. 1. c. 1. Prop. 3.

Magia universalis, pt. 3, bk. 1, ch. 1, prop. 3.

Collect. Math. L. 8.

Mathematical Collection, bk. 8.

Static. L. 1. P. 1. Def. 4.

Statics, bk. 1, pt. 1, Def. 4.

p. 115

diceres: sub vecte positum; quia nempè ei linea rigida, quae etiam vectis Mathematicus, vel linea vectis adpellatur, innititur. Pondera ejusdem jugi extremis punctis adpensa, quum circa punctum suspensionis se ea lege sustinent, ut neutrum possit alterum vincere, locoque emovere, dicuntur in aequilibrio constitui. Hinc aequiponderantia indigitantur corpora, quae eidem jugo adpensa in aequilibrio consistunt; non aequiponderantia verò, si alteri unum praevaleat; undè istud praeponderans nominatur. Reliquorum notiones suis locis commodiùs adferentur. Ex his ducitur.

placed under the lever; because, namely, it rests upon a rigid line, which is also called the Mathematical lever, or line of the lever. Weights hung from the extreme points of the same beam, when about the point of suspension they sustain each other under such a law that neither can overcome the other and move it from its place, are said to be set in equilibrium. Hence bodies are designated equiponderant which, hung from the same beam, stand in equilibrium; but non-equiponderant if one prevails over the other: whence the latter is named preponderant. The notions of the rest will be presented more conveniently in their own places. From these is deduced the following

Corollarium.

COROLLARY.

353 Corpus ex immobili puncto suspensum non quiescit, nisi quum retinaculum lineae illi rectae congruerit, quae à puncto suspensionis ducta plano horizontali ad perpendiculum imminet. Recedat enim funependulum à perpendiculari A C (Fig. XXIV.) in B: quoniam recta A C transiens per punctum contactus C, & tangenti b d perpendicularis, producta per centrum e transit; s1 quumque sit omnium rectarum, quae eodem ex centro duci ad tangentem possunt, minima s2, minor erit quam recta a e: proindè etiam minor quam e B. Quo circa grave in B constitutum, longius absistet à centro gravium, quam in C. Nituntur autem gravia propiùs, quoad possunt, ad centrum gravium: Igitur funependulum non conquiescet in B, neque alio in loco, eandem ob causam, atque in C hoc est, non quiescet, nisi filum perpendiculari A C planè congruat.

353 Abody suspended from an immovable point does not rest unless its retaining cord coincides with that straight line which, drawn from the point of suspension, hangs perpendicularly over the horizontal plane. For let the pendulum recede from the perpendicular AC (Fig. XXIV.) to B: since the straight line AC, passing through the point of contact C and perpendicular to the tangent bd, passes, when produced, through the center e (k); and since it is the least of all the straight lines that can be drawn from the same center to the tangent (l), it will be less than the straight line ae: and therefore also less than eB. Wherefore a heavy body placed at B will stand farther from the center of heavy bodies than at C. But heavy bodies strive to come as near as they can to the center of heavy bodies: therefore the pendulum will not come to rest at B, nor, for the same reason, in any other place than at C; that is, it will not rest unless the thread coincides entirely with the perpendicular AC.

354 E converso autem gravi corpore quiescente; planum, cui ad perpendiculum insistit erit horizonti parallelum. Ex quo relucet artificium, penduli ope explorandi, an planum sit horizonti parallelum, num contrà inclinatum? Corpora gravia [?] planam superficiem horizontali plano insistentia, perstant immota, si linea directionis intra basim cadat; corruunt verò, si linea eadem extra basim incidat aberrando [§ 145] Ratio est manifesta: priori namque casu linea directionis à subjecto plano sustentatur; non item in altero. Adhaec: si in illo casu corpus A B D C prolaberetur (Fig. XXV.) dùm linea directionis E F intra basim C D continetur, deberet illud converti, ac revolvi circà extremum basis punctum D, atque adeò centrum gravitatis E ascendere per arcum E G supra horizontalem lineam E H, id, quod cum actione causae gravitantis pugnat, & non fit, nisi viribus gravitati adversantibus. At ubi (Fig XXVI.) linea directionis K L ultra basim D C excurrit, centrum gravitatis[?] K per arcum K M infra horizontalem rectam K N descendere

354 Conversely, moreover, when a heavy body is at rest, the plane on which it stands perpendicularly will be parallel to the horizon. From this shines forth the artifice of exploring, by means of a pendulum, whether a plane is parallel to the horizon or, on the contrary, inclined. Heavy bodies standing with a plane surface on a horizontal plane remain unmoved if the line of direction falls within the base; but they collapse if that same line strays and falls outside the base [§ 145]. The reason is manifest: for in the former case the line of direction is sustained by the underlying plane; not so in the other. Moreover: if in the former case the body ABDC were to topple (Fig. XXV.) while the line of direction EF is contained within the base CD, it would have to be turned and revolved about the extreme point D of the base, and so the center of gravity E would have to ascend along the arc EG above the horizontal line EH, which conflicts with the action of the gravitating cause, and does not happen except when forces opposing gravity are at work. But where (Fig. XXVI.) the line of direction KL runs out beyond the base DC, the center of gravity K can descend along the arc KM below the horizontal straight line KN, without

Euclid. Lib. 3. Prop. 19.

Euclid, bk. 3, prop. 19.

Idem Lib. 1. Prop. 19.

The same, bk. 1, prop. 19.

p. 116

potest, quin aliquid obsistat. Quoniam igitur á descensu non impeditur, per arcum eundem grave decidat necesse est.

without anything obstructing it. Since, therefore, it is not hindered from descending, the heavy body must necessarily fall along that same arc.

355 Ex consideratione centri gravitatis deducitur pariter, cur ea firmiùs erecta consistant, ac securius, quae basi latiore innituntur: atque adeò nosmet ipsi dum pedi utrique insistimus, tutò persistemus; contrá verò labamur facilè, uni duntaxat innixi; priori quippe casu basis sat ampla est, & fulcra gemina corpus sustentant; at in secundo angusta, multò angustior, ubi non nisi calcaneo pavimentum premimus, extra quam basim proindè directionis linea facilè excurrit. Hinc etiam regulae saltandi, incessus, motuumque corporis exigendorum derivantur. Ipsa corporis animalis conformatio eandem hanc aequilibritatis rationem commonstrat; partes geminae ex aequo distributae latera occupant, sic, ut á medio sejungantur intercapedine aequali, simplices verò medium obtinent locum. Neque in hominibus solum, sed in brutis quoque hoc aequilibrium patesit. Namque avium alae pondus utrinque ipsis aequale addunt; quae collum longius sortiuntur, pedibus etiam longioribus instructae sunt, quos volando retrorsum exporrigunt; dum uno pede nixae quietem capiunt, caput sub ala, quae transversim opposita est recondunt. Innumera hujus generis praetermittimus s1.

355 From the consideration of the center of gravity it is likewise deduced why those things stand erect more firmly and more securely which rest on a broader base; and so why we ourselves, while we stand on both feet, remain safely, but on the contrary totter easily when supported on one alone; for in the former case the base is ample enough, and twin props sustain the body; but in the second it is narrow, and much narrower still when we press the floor only with the heel, so that the line of direction easily runs out beyond the base. Hence too are derived the rules of dancing, of walking, and of regulating the motions of the body. The very conformation of the animal body shows this same principle of equilibrium: the paired parts, distributed equally, occupy the sides, so that they are separated from the middle by an equal interval, while the single parts hold the middle place. Nor is this equilibrium evident in men only, but in brutes as well. For the wings of birds add an equal weight to them on either side: those which are allotted a longer neck are also furnished with longer feet, which they stretch out backward in flying; while they take their rest supported on one foot, they hide the head under the wing that lies crosswise opposite. We pass over countless things of this kind (m).

356 Perspicitur ex hac doctrina similiter cur corpora horizontale planum, vel in puncto etiam contingentia, hoc loco tùm denique perstent, quum directionis linea per punctum illud transit. Hoc modo sphaera homogenea B C (Fig. XXVII.) super planum M N horizonti parallelum posita, immota consistit; centrum quippè magnitudinis a, congruit cum centro gravitatis, ac linea recta a E ducta ex centro ad punctum contactus E, tangenti, & plano M N est perpendicularis s2: hinc directionis linea per punctum contactus, seu basim, transit. At quoniam (Fig. XXVIII.) linea recta x a, quae ex centro ad punctum contactus, a ducitur, plano inclinato A B[?] perpendicularis est, atque adeò plano horizontali D B ad perpendiculum insistere nequit: iccircò recta x e, quae horizonti ad perpendiculum imminet, & linea directionis est, per punctum contactus a, seu basim, transire non potest: sphaera proindè nullo in puncto plani inclinati conquiescet. En vobis phaenomenon satis vulgare; causam autem non satis vulgò notam.

356 It is likewise seen from this doctrine why bodies touching a horizontal plane, even at a single point, remain in that place only when the line of direction passes through that point. In this way a homogeneous sphere BC (Fig. XXVII.), placed upon the plane MN parallel to the horizon, stands unmoved; for its center of magnitude a coincides with the center of gravity, and the straight line aE drawn from the center to the point of contact E is perpendicular to the tangent and to the plane MN (n): hence the line of direction passes through the point of contact, or base. But since (Fig. XXVIII.) the straight line xa, which is drawn from the center to the point of contact a, is perpendicular to the inclined plane AB, and so cannot stand perpendicularly on the horizontal plane DB: therefore the straight line xe, which hangs perpendicularly over the horizon and is the line of direction, cannot pass through the point of contact a, or base: the sphere therefore will come to rest at no point of the inclined plane. Here you have a phenomenon common enough, but a cause not commonly enough known.

Vid. Borellum de motu animal. Camus, des Forces mouvantes. Pardies. De viribus moventibus.

See Borelli, De motu animalium. Camus, des Forces mouvantes. Pardies, De viribus moventibus.

Euclid. Lib. 3. Prop. 18.

Euclid, bk. 3, prop. 18.

p. 117

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De Principiis sive Legibus fundamentalibus, & Instrumentis Staticae.

On the Principles, or fundamental Laws, and the Instruments of Statics.

357 Exponenda veniunt amplissimi quidem usus, Statices principia, sive Leges, è quibus corporum gravium adpensorum diversa inter se ratio derivatur. Princeps porrò illud, & ad Geostaticam juxtà atque Hydrostaticam pertinens fundamentum, videlicet: quantitatem motus dati corporis esse productum ex pondere, sive massa in velocitatem ducta, jam alias expendimus [§ 276]. Id unum superst, ut eo constituto, evolamus cetera, quae huic seu basi innituntur, & paucis complectamur omnia: eò duntaxat respicientes, ut ad intelligentiam Tironum adcommodatè, & pro Elementorum nostrorum ratione ac brevitate doctrinae summa potissimum capita pertractemus. Sint ergo per ordinem.

ext to be set forth are the principles, or Laws, of Statics, of very 357 N wide use indeed, from which is derived the diverse relation among themselves of heavy bodies hung up. The chief of them, moreover, and the foundation pertaining to Geostatics as well as to Hydrostatics, namely: that the quantity of motion of a given body is the product of the weight, or mass, multiplied into the velocity, we have already weighed elsewhere [§ 276]. One thing alone remains: that, this being established, we unfold the rest, which rest upon it as on a base, and embrace them all in few words, looking only to this, that we treat chiefly the principal heads of the doctrine, in a manner suited to the understanding of Beginners and in keeping with the plan and brevity of our Elements. Let them follow, then, in order.

Principium Statices I. — PRINCIPLE OF STATICS I

358 Celeritates duorum gravium solidorum, ex ejusdem jugi extremis liberè pendentium, sunt directè inter se, ut eorum distantiae à centro motus.

358 The velocities of two heavy solid bodies hanging freely from the extremities of the same beam are directly to each other as their distances from the center of motion.

359 In comperto quippe est corpus B (Fig. XXIX) moveri per arcum B D non posse, quin eodem ipso tempore corpus A deprimatur per arcum A C. Atqui celeritates duorum corporum motu[?] concitatorum, sunt inter se, ut spatia eodem tempore ab illis percursa. [Per Leges velocitatum]: Celeritas igitur corporis A est ad celeritatem corporis B, ut arcus A C ad arcum B D. Arcus autèm prior se habet ad posteriorem, ut distantia A E ad distantiam B E, sive ut radii circulorum, ut notum est ex Geometria: ergo velocitas corporis A est ad velocitatem corporis B, ut A E ad B E, hoc est: ut eorumdem distantiae à centro motus E.

359 For it is well established that body B (Fig. XXIX.) cannot be moved along the arc BD without body A being depressed at the very same time along the arc AC. But the velocities of two bodies set in motion are to each other as the spaces traversed by them in the same time [By the Laws of velocities]: therefore the velocity of body A is to the velocity of body B as the arc AC to the arc BD. But the former arc is to the latter as the distance AE to the distance BE, or as the radii of the circles, as is known from Geometry: therefore the velocity of body A is to the velocity of body B as AE to BE, that is, as their distances from the center of motion E.

Principium Statices II. — PRINCIPLE OF STATICS II

360 Corpora gravia, quorum pondera aequantur, & ad aequalem distantiam collocantur adpensa, respectivè ad centrum motus; in aequilibrio manent. Si pondera sint inaequalia, & distantiae aequales, non manent in aequilibrio, sed quod pondere majori

360 Heavy bodies whose weights are equal, and which are placed, hung up, at an equal distance with respect to the center of motion, remain in equilibrium. If the weights are unequal and the distances equal, they do not remain in equilibrium, but the one that is endowed with the greater weight

p. 118

donatum est, deprimetur. Si pondera sint aequalia, & distantiae inaequales, non consistunt aequilibrata, verùm quod à centro motus removetur magis, praeponderat.

will be depressed. If the weights are equal and the distances unequal, they do not stand balanced, but the one that is removed further from the center of motion preponderates.

361 Pars prima patet: quoniam corpora pondere aequalia ponuntur, & aequalis á centro motus distantia habetur, atque adeò aequalis utriusque celeritas (quum enim per Princip. I. celeritates sint, ut distantiae, si haec aequentur, etiam celeritates aequales sint est necesse) iccircò aequalis in utroque est motus quantitas, sive momenta sunt aequalia: immota proindè in aequilibrio consistent (per Def. aequilib.) Pars altera ostenditur: quum distantiae corporum ponuntur aequales, aequales itidèm sunt celeritates. Ergo momenta eorum sunt, ut pondera (nam quum pondera corporum sint, ut eorum massae, quantitates autèm motus duorum corporum, aequali celeritate actorum sint ut eorumdem massae; erunt quoque ut pondera ipsorum). Qua propter momentum illius, quod pondere majus est, excedet momentum alterius; & aequilibrio sublato, praeponderabit. Pars tertia quoque claret: quoniam distantia corporis unius major est distantia alterius; celeritas pariter illius, major erit celeritate hujus: Sunt autem corpora pondere aequalia. Majus ergo erit momentum corporis remotioris á centro motus; ac momentum alterius: aequilibrata proindè non persistent, verùm illud, quod removetur magis, magis quoque praeponderabit.

361 The first part is evident: since bodies equal in weight are posited, and an equal distance from the center of motion is had, and so an equal velocity of each (for since, by Princip. I, the velocities are as the distances, if these are equal the velocities too must be equal), therefore the quantity of motion in both is equal, or the momenta are equal: they will therefore stand unmoved in equilibrium (by the Def. of equilib.). The second part is shown: since the distances of the bodies are posited equal, the velocities are likewise equal. Therefore their momenta are as the weights (for since the weights of bodies are as their masses, and the quantities of motion of two bodies driven with equal velocity are as their masses, they will also be as their weights). Wherefore the momentum of the one that is greater in weight will exceed the momentum of the other; and, the equilibrium being removed, it will preponderate. The third part too is clear: since the distance of one body is greater than the distance of the other, the velocity of the former will likewise be greater than the velocity of the latter. But the bodies are equal in weight. Therefore the momentum of the body more remote from the center of motion will be greater than the momentum of the other: they will therefore not persist balanced, but the one that is removed further will also preponderate more.

Principium Statices III. — PRINCIPLE OF STATICS III

362 Corpora inaequalis ponderis, ex inaequalibus distantiis jugo adpensa, obtinent aequilibrium, si distantiae à centro motus fuerint, ut ipsa pondera reciprocè hoc est: si quod minori pondere donatum est, tantò magis distet à centro motus, quantò magis ponderosum est alterum (quo cum comparatur) minusque distat ab eodem centro.

362 Bodies of unequal weight, hung on a beam at unequal distances, obtain equilibrium if the distances from the center of motion are reciprocally as the weights themselves, that is: if the one that is endowed with the smaller weight is as much farther from the center of motion as the other (with which it is compared) is heavier and less distant from the same center.

363 Sit enim corpus A (Fig. cit.) duplò majoris massae quàm B, sintque hoc pacto adpensa, ut distantia A E sit ad distantiam E B, sicut corpus B ad A, id est: corpus B duplo sit minus altero, sed duplo remotiùs á puncto fixo E absistat: manifestò liquet A, & B in aequilibrio consistere, si quantitas motus in uno aequetur quantitati motus in altero, hoc est: si momenta sint aequalia. Atqui haec aequantur, eo ipso quod eorum distantiae á centro motûs sint in ratione ponderum reciprocâ; quum enim celeritates ponderum A & B sint directè inter se, ut eorumdem distantiae A E, & B E, celeritas corporis B, duplò major est celeritate corporis A. Dicatur illa = 2c haec = c: massa corporis A = 2m, corporis B = m. Ut reciproca indè haec necessariò obtineat proportio 2c : c = 2m : m, quoniam igitur momentum corporis B aequatur facto, quod ex dupla celeritate in simplicem massam ducta

363 For let body A (Fig. cit.) be of twice greater mass than B, and let them be so hung that the distance AE is to the distance EB as body B to A, that is: let body B be twice smaller than the other, but stand twice as far removed from the fixed point E: it is manifestly clear that A and B stand in equilibrium if the quantity of motion in the one equals the quantity of motion in the other, that is: if the momenta are equal. But these are equal by the very fact that their distances from the center of motion are in the reciprocal ratio of the weights; for since the velocities of the weights A and B are directly to each other as their distances AE and BE, the velocity of body B is twice as great as the velocity of body A. Let the former be called = 2c, the latter = c; the mass of body A = 2m, of body B = m. So that hence this reciprocal proportion necessarily holds, 2c : c = 2m : m; since, therefore, the momentum of body B equals the product that arises from the double velocity multiplied into the simple mass,

p. 119

consurgit; erit illud = 2c m. Momentum verò corporis A est productum ex multiplicata duplò majore massa per simplicem celeritatem, hoc est: = 2m c. quod evidenter idem est. In aequilibrio igitur corpora perstabunt. Ex his principiis ratio instrumentorum ponderatoriorum, seu Staticorum desumpta est: horum praecipua habentur Libra, & Statéra.

it will be = 2cm. But the momentum of body A is the product of the mass twice as great multiplied by the simple velocity, that is: = 2mc, which is evidently the same. The bodies will therefore stand in equilibrium. From these principles is taken the rationale of weighing instruments, or Statical ones: the chief of them are held to be the Balance and the Steelyard.

De Libra. — ON THE BALANCE

364 Libra seu bilanx, notissimum est Staticae instrumentum, quo ignotum dati corporis pondus, altero notae gravitatis adsumpto exploratur. Partes in ea plures distinguuntur. Prima est jugum A C (Fig. XXX.) rigida nempè virga, in duas partes A B & C B tum quoad longitudinem, tum quoad pondus, aequales, quae brachia dicuntur, divisa. Secunda est ansa D B, cui ope axiculi per centrum motûs B, & per foramina ansae transmissi, sic aptatur jugum, ut hoc circa ansae foramina tanquam centrum, liberè moveri possit. Tertia est lingula x, quae immobiliter ad angulos rectos medio jugi puncto adplicita est: nuncupatur quoque trutina, examen, vel argumentum librae eo, quod jugi vel parallelismum cum plano horizontali, vel inclinationem exhibeat. Quarta sunt lances E & F, quae extremis jugi partibus adpensae, pondera excipiunt.

364 The balance, or scales, is the best-known instrument of Statics, by which the unknown weight of a given body is explored by taking another of known gravity. Several parts are distinguished in it. The first is the beam AC (Fig. XXX.), namely a rigid rod divided into two parts AB and CB, equal both in length and in weight, which are called the arms. The second is the handle DB, to which the beam is so fitted, by means of a small axle passed through the center of motion B and through the holes of the handle, that it can move freely about the holes of the handle as about a center. The third is the tongue x, which is fixed immovably at right angles to the middle point of the beam: it is also called the trutina, examen, or argumentum of the balance, because it shows either the parallelism of the beam with the horizontal plane or its inclination. The fourth are the pans E and F, which, hung from the extreme parts of the beam, receive the weights.

365 Totum hoc organum Staticum, ut exactum sit primò non brachia solum, sed fila etiam, è quibus hae suspenduntur, pondere aequentur necesse est. Secundò lances quoque aequalis sint ponderis, exposcitur. Tertio adtritus super jugo, quoad fieri potest, sit exiguus ac propè nullus. Hinc ad minuendum adfrictum, axis trutinae insertus, cylindricus, & forámen in trutina rotundum sit, ut contactus minor evadat. Imò si axis ea parte, qua trutinam tangit[?], in aciem définat, motus jugi pernicior erit. Ad bilancis praeterea perfectionem haec fere pertinent. Brachia sint longiora; ponderum quippe inaequalitas, quae in brevioribus nonnumquam sensu vix discriminatur, in longioribus perfacilè se prodit. Língula pariter longior ob rationem haud absimilem fiat. Lances melius suspenduntur è catenulis metallicis, ac filis, utpote in quae aëris temperies quandoque diversimodè agit.

365 For this whole Statical organ to be exact, it is necessary, first, that not only the arms but also the threads from which the pans are suspended be equal in weight. Secondly, it is required that the pans too be of equal weight. Thirdly, that the friction upon the beam be, as far as can be done, slight and almost none. Hence, to lessen the friction, the axle inserted in the tongue is made cylindrical, and the hole in the tongue round, so that the contact may turn out smaller. Indeed, if the axle ends in an edge on the side where it touches the tongue, the motion of the beam will be quicker. Moreover, the following belong in general to the perfection of the balance. Let the arms be longer; for an inequality of the weights, which in shorter arms is sometimes scarcely discerned by sense, betrays itself very easily in longer ones. Let the tongue likewise be made longer, for a not dissimilar reason. The pans are better suspended from little metal chains than from threads, inasmuch as the temper of the air sometimes acts upon threads in various ways.

366 Quod ad praestantiorem adtinet usum ceteris praeferenda est libra, cujus centrum motus sit supra rectam, ex cujus extremis libranda corpora pendent: undè ceteris paribus postulant omnes, ut centrum gravitatis jugi detur paululum infra centrum motus. Usus librae notissimus est, de quo proindè nihil adtinet meminisse. Vitium in libram refundit potissimùm brachiorum inaequalitas; posita enim eorum inaequalitate, non ejusdem, sed inaequalis ponderis erunt corpora, quae lancibus imposita aequilibrantur, uti

366 As regards the more excellent use, that balance is to be preferred to the others whose center of motion is above the straight line from whose extremities the bodies to be weighed hang: whence, other things being equal, all require that the center of gravity of the beam be placed a little below the center of motion. The use of the balance is very well known, so that there is no need to mention anything about it. A defect is brought into the balance chiefly by the inequality of the arms; for, their inequality being posited, the bodies which, placed on the pans, are in equilibrium will be not of the same but of unequal weight, as

p. 120

(é Princip. III.) elúcet. Fraus haec (quin, & omnes) in dolosis libris deteguntur, facta ponderum in lancibus permutatione, docente P. Schotto: si enim (inquit) illud quod prius aequilibre erat in dextera lance adhuc in sinistra lance positum, servet aequilibrium; signum est libram exactam esse. Quod si contingat, ut ex hac lancium permutatione eadem corpora nunc quidem aequalia, nunc verò inaequalia adpareant; manifestum est, libram dolosam esse, & injustam. s1

(from Princip. III.) is clear. This fraud (indeed, every fraud) in deceitful balances is detected by making an exchange of the weights in the pans, as Father Schott teaches: for if (he says) that which was before in equilibrium in the right pan, when now placed in the left pan, preserves the equilibrium, it is a sign that the balance is exact. But if it happens that by this exchange of the pans the same bodies appear now equal, now unequal, it is manifest that the balance is deceitful and unjust. (o)

De Statéra. — ON THE STEELYARD

367 Statéra, Stater Romanus, aut Sinensis, est instrumentum ponderatorium brachiis inaequalibus comprehensum (Fig. XXXI.). Quatuor in eo partes numerantur, nimirùm virga rigida, sive jugum A B, in brachia inaequalia B D & A D divisum, ex quibus illud, quod longius est B D, in partes inter se aequales a b, b d, d e, &c. & quae singulae distantiam puncti D, á puncto A, seu longitudinem brachii minoris adaequent, dividitur. Partes hae rursùm in alias minores inter se aequales, pro minutiis determinandis dispescuntur. Ansa E D lingulam complexa, cui ope axis quemadmodum in libra aptatum est jugum. Lanx, vel uncus extremo brachii brevioris adpenditur, ut librandum corpus illi imponi, vel ex hoc suspendi possit. Aequipondium N est hùc illùc mobile, propterea cursor statérae dictus.

367 The steelyard, the Roman or Chinese Stater, is a weighing instrument comprised of unequal arms (Fig. XXXI.). Four parts are counted in it: namely the rigid rod, or beam, AB, divided into the unequal arms BD and AD, of which the longer, BD, is divided into parts equal among themselves, ab, bd, de, etc., each of which equals the distance of the point D from the point A, or the length of the shorter arm. These parts are divided again into other smaller parts, equal among themselves, for determining minute quantities. The handle ED, enclosing the tongue, to which the beam is fitted by means of an axle, as in the balance. The pan, or hook, is hung from the extremity of the shorter arm, so that the body to be weighed can be placed on it or suspended from it. The counterpoise N is movable hither and thither, and is therefore called the runner of the steelyard.

368 Quò instrumentum hoc exactum sit exposcitur, ut brevius brachium unà cum unco adaequet pondus brachii longioris ablato aequipondio: aut si id non fiat, brachium longiùs in partes proportionales dividatur, quae divisio tentando invenitur. Id commodi habent Staterae prae libra, quod pondus magnorum etiam corporum unico eoque satis exiguo pondere per eas explorari queat; quanquam in[?] eo praestent bilances, quòd in his exiguas etiam unciae particulas cognoscere possímus, & commodiùs, & in regionibus nostris plerumque soleamus, secus in statéris. Hac verò lege pondus dati corporis instrumento hoc examinatur: adpenso corpore M, cujus pondus exploratur; aequipondium N eo in loco brachii longioris constituitur, in quo cum librando corpore aequilibrium obtineat; aequilibrio jam posito, corpus adpensum, eam habet rationem ad aequipondium, quàm reciprocè distantia aequipondii á centro motus, ad distantiam corporis adpensi ab eodem, seu ad brachium brevius: scilicet si aequipondium N unius sit librae & distantia ejus D m ad distantiam D A ut 4 ad 1 erit corpus M quatuor librarum.

368 For this instrument to be exact it is required that the shorter arm, together with the hook, equal the weight of the longer arm when the counterpoise is removed: or, if that is not done, that the longer arm be divided into proportional parts, a division that is found by trial.
