Steelyards have this advantage over the balance, that the weight even of large bodies can be explored by means of them with a single weight, and that a fairly small one; although in this the scales excel, that in them we can discern even small particles of an ounce, and more conveniently, and in our regions we usually do so; not so with steelyards. The weight of a given body is examined with this instrument by the following law: the body M, whose weight is being explored, being hung on, the counterpoise N is set at that place of the longer arm at which it obtains equilibrium with the body to be weighed; equilibrium being now established, the hung body has the same ratio to the counterpoise that, reciprocally, the distance of the counterpoise from the center of motion has to the distance of the hung body from the same, or to the shorter arm: namely, if the counterpoise N is of one pound, and its distance Dm is to the distance DA as 4 to 1, the body M will be of four pounds.

369 Ratio hujus liquet adfatim (ex Princip. III. Stat.) Quod

369 The reason of this is abundantly clear (from Princip. III of Statics). But if

Mag. Universal. P. 3. Mag. Stat. Syntagm. 3. Prag. 3. sub finem.

Magia universalis, pt. 3, Mag. Stat., Syntagm. 3, Pragm. 3, toward the end.

p. 121

si porrò momentum in puncto m augeatur, ut si ea vis constitueretur, quae pondus centenarii exsuperaret, adtolleretur ab eo pondus quatuor centenariorum ex unco F suspensum: si momentum in remotiori parte collocaretur, faciliùs adhùc corpus adpensum extolleretur. Atque hìnc, quoniam potentia ad brachium staterae longius adplicata, eò vi majori pollet, quò longius illud porrigitur, patet, vires hoc pacto in immensum augeri posse: ut ea propter Syracusanus Mathematicus Archimedes, Hieroni, non citra fundamentum Staticae legibus constabilitum, pollicitus fuerit, se tellurem loco suo emoturum, si quis extra eam locus ad consistendum esset.

if, further, the momentum at the point m is increased, so that, if that force were made such as to exceed the weight of a hundredweight, a weight of four hundredweight suspended from the hook F would be lifted by it: if the momentum were placed in a more remote part, the hung body would be raised more easily still. And hence, since a power applied to the arm of the steelyard is endowed with so much greater force the farther that arm is stretched out, it is plain that forces can in this way be increased without limit: so that for this reason the Syracusan Mathematician Archimedes, not without a foundation established by the laws of Statics, promised Hiero that he would move the earth from its place, if there were some place outside it on which to stand.

370 Ceterum plura in stateram vitia irrepere queunt; si enim brachium breviùs cum unco vel lance acceptum, aequilibrium non tueatur cum altero brachio, sublato aequipondio: item si partes, in quas longius brachium dirimitur, sint inaequales, aut debitâ careant dimensione, dolosa semper statera futura est: quin aliis quoque ex capitibus fállere utentes quum possit, nec adeò in promptu sit fallaciam détegere, praestare ait Cl. Wolfius s1 ut è vita communi proscribatur.

370 Moreover, several defects can creep into the steelyard; for if the shorter arm, taken with the hook or pan, does not keep equilibrium with the other arm when the counterpoise is removed; likewise if the parts into which the longer arm is divided are unequal, or lack the due measure, the steelyard will always be deceitful: indeed, since it can deceive those who use it on other heads as well, and it is not so easy to detect the deceit, the distinguished Wolff says (p) it is better that it be banished from common life.

DISSERTATIO III. — DISSERTATION III

MECHANICA, sive

MECHANICS, or

De Machinis doctrina.

The doctrine of Machines.

371 Mechanica, seu Machinalis scientia tradit principia, ac leges, quibus potentia sustinendo, ac movendo corpori ex sese impar, machinarum quarundam adminiculo idonea sive ad sustinendum, sive ad movendum etiam illud reddi possit. Undè machina mechanica adpellatur, per quam potentia illi adplicata ad sustinendum vel movendum corpus, quorum neutrum praestare illa possit, apta redditur. Machina alia simplex dicitur, alia composita. Prior ex pluribus, quarum singulae seorsim ad edendum effectum sufficerent, non coalescit: posterior ex aliis simplicibus certa lege invicem aptatis consurgit.

echanics, or the Machinal science, hands down the principles and laws by 371 M which a power, of itself unequal to sustaining and moving a body, can be rendered fit by the aid of certain machines either to sustain it or even to move it. Whence a mechanical machine is the name for that through which a power applied to it is rendered fit for sustaining or moving a body, neither of which it could accomplish. One machine is called simple, another compound. The former does not coalesce out of several, each of which would separately suffice to produce the effect: the latter arises out of other simple ones fitted to each other by a fixed law.

372 Hoc jam loco unicum Machinalis scientiae principium, generale illud quidem, subjiciendum venit, quo uno plura ab aliis isthic constituta, libuit complecti.

372 In this place there now comes to be set down the single principle of the Machinal science, a general one indeed, by which alone it has pleased us to embrace the several principles that others have established here.

Elem. Mechan. §. 778.

Elem. Mechan., §. 778.

p. 122

Principium Mechanices. — PRINCIPLE OF MECHANICS

373 Potentia, & pondus ita machinae adplicentur necesse est, ut simul moveri nequeant, nisi potentia velocius moveatur, quàm pondus: & hac quidem lege, ut celeritas potentiae majorem habeat rationem ad celeritatem ponderis, quàm reciprocè pondus ipsum ad vim potentiae: quae ratio, quò major fuerit, eò facilius potentia exigua corpus ingens dimovebit.

373 Power and weight must be so applied to a machine that they cannot be moved together unless the power moves more swiftly than the weight: and indeed under this law, that the velocity of the power have a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than, reciprocally, the weight itself has to the force of the power: and the greater this ratio is, the more easily will a slight power move a huge body.

374 Ponatur enim vis potentiae = p & pondus movendum = P celeritas potentiae = C, & celeritas ponderis = c. Si celeritas potentiae majorem habeat rationem ad celeritatem ponderis, quàm reciprocè pondus ad vim potentiae, erit C : c > P : p factum proindè seu momentum potentiae p C, majus, quàm momentum ponderis resistentis P c. Corpus igitur ponderosum a potentia movebitur. Quum porrò productum p C eò majus evadat, quò magis ratio C c excedit rationem P : p consequitur, eò facilius ab exigua etiam potentia, ope machinae, corpus ingens moveri posse, quò ratio celeritatis, quâ potentia pollet, ad celeritatem ponderis major fuerit ratione, quae reciprocè pondus inter, & vim potentiae intercedit. Ex quo quidem elucet actutùm, hoc per machinas pondera levandi compendium cum aliquo temporis dispendio conjunctum esse, quod tamen jure in lucris reponi debet. Hoc constituto, machinas, prout ad Physicae rationem necesse est, tantispèr expendamus.

374 For let the force of the power be = p, and the weight to be moved = P, the velocity of the power = C, and the velocity of the weight = c. If the velocity of the power has a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than, reciprocally, the weight to the force of the power, it will be C : c > P : p; and therefore the product, or momentum, of the power, pC, will be greater than the momentum of the resisting weight, Pc. The heavy body will therefore be moved by the power. Since, further, the product pC turns out the greater the more the ratio C : c exceeds the ratio P : p, it follows that a huge body can be moved, by means of a machine, the more easily even by a slight power, the greater the ratio of the velocity with which the power is endowed to the velocity of the weight is than the ratio that holds reciprocally between the weight and the force of the power. From which indeed it at once shines out that this saving in lifting weights by machines is joined with some loss of time, which nevertheless ought rightly to be counted among the gains. This being established, let us weigh the machines for a while, so far as is necessary for the purpose of Physics.

De Vecte. — ON THE LEVER

375 Vectis, prima Mechanicae machina, est palus oblongus, materia solida constans, qui ad ingentia pondera faciliùs[?] movenda commodè adhibetur. Tria in eo distinguuntur, scilicet: potentia movens, sive momentum: resistentia, sive pondus sustinendum, vel movendum: punctum denique fixum, cui immobili vectis innititur: hoc latinè fulcrum, Graecis hypomochlion, Vitruvio pressio nuncupatur. Quoniam verò tria haec puncta triplici modo disponi in vecte possunt, idcircò triplex genus discriminari solet.

375 The lever, the first machine of Mechanics, is an oblong stake consisting of solid material, which is conveniently employed for moving huge weights more easily. Three things are distinguished in it, namely: the moving power, or momentum; the resistance, or weight to be sustained or moved; and finally the fixed point on which the lever rests, immovable: this is called in Latin fulcrum, by the Greeks hypomochlion, by Vitruvius pressio. But since these three points can be disposed in the lever in a threefold manner, a threefold kind is therefore usually distinguished.

376 Primum est, quando fulcrum inter potentiam, & pondus, medium locum tenet, cujus modi est vectis A B, (Fig. XXXII.) ubi inter potentiam B, & pondus A, intermedium est fulcrum C. Secundum genus est, quando fulcrum C, (Fig. XXXIII.) in parte una extrema reperitur, in extremo altero potentia A, & pondus B medium obtinet. Tertium habetur, in quo potentia A (Fig XXXIV) medium inter fulcrum B, & pondus C, occupat. Primi generis vectem heterodromum: Secundi homodromum adpellant: tertii generis ad homodromum révocant.

376 The first is when the fulcrum holds the middle place between the power and the weight, such as the lever AB (Fig. XXXII.), where the fulcrum C is intermediate between the power B and the weight A. The second kind is when the fulcrum C (Fig. XXXIII.) is found at one extremity, the power A at the other extremity, and the weight B holds the middle. The third is had when the power A (Fig. XXXIV.) occupies the middle between the fulcrum B and the weight C. The lever of the first kind they call heterodromous; of the second, homodromous; that of the third kind they refer to the homodromous.

p. 123

377 In primo vectis genere quantùm distantia C B superat distantiam A C, tantùm potentia B excedit resistentiam corporis A: atque adeò si inter punctum fixum, & potentiam, distantia sit decuplo major, quàm distantia ponderis ab eodem puncto, corpus A verò sit centum librarum; modò potentia B decem libris paulò plus aequivaleat, haec illud adtollet; ea tamen ratione, ut dum potentia spatium ferè decem digitorum descendendo cónficit, pondus unius duntaxat digiti intervallo extollatur. Idem est in vecte secundi generis, quantum enim distantia A C superat distantiam B C, tantò efficacius potentia resistentiam ponderis vincet. In tertio vectis genere id solum commodi est, quod potentia motrix pondus levius movere possit celeritate majori: id quod suâ non caret utilitate, dum temporis compendium quaeritur.

377 In the first kind of lever, by as much as the distance CB exceeds the distance AC, by so much does the power B exceed the resistance of the body A: and so, if the distance between the fixed point and the power is ten times greater than the distance of the weight from the same point, and the body A is of a hundred pounds, then, provided the power B is equivalent to a little more than ten pounds, it will lift it; yet in such a manner that while the power, in descending, covers a space of about ten inches, the weight is raised through an interval of only one inch. The same holds in the lever of the second kind; for by as much as the distance AC exceeds the distance BC, by so much more efficaciously will the power overcome the resistance of the weight. In the third kind of lever there is only this advantage, that the moving power can move a lighter weight with a greater velocity: which is not without its utility when a saving of time is sought.

De Axe in peritrochio. — ON THE WHEEL AND AXLE

378 Axis in peritrochio, secunda Mechanicae machina, est instrumentum ponderibus levandis aptum, in quo cylindrus h i (Fig. XXXV) quem axem vocant, fulcris k l utrimque sustentatus, circumpositum habet tympanum, m e, quod peritrochium compellant: in hujus ambitu baculi teretes, a c, b d, qui radii, seu scytalae dicuntur, infixi sunt, quibus adplicata potentia peritrochium cum axe versat, & pondus ope funis circumvoluti adtollit. Alias peritrochium dicitur ipsum illud orbiculatum planum, cujus in locum scytalae sufficiuntur. Si axi situm horizontalem obtinenti jungantur scytalae, Sucula nuncupatur; si verò ad perpendiculum erectus fuerit, Ergata nominatur. Sucularum usus maximus est in metallifodinis. Ergata id commodi habet, quod singulis scytalis plures unà homines adplicari possint, quin sese impediant.

378 The wheel and axle, the second machine of Mechanics, is an instrument suited to lifting weights, in which the cylinder hi (Fig. XXXV.), which they call the axle, sustained on either side by the props k, l, has placed around it a drum, me, which they call the peritrochium: in its circumference are fixed round rods, ac, bd, which are called spokes, or scytalae, by which the power applied turns the peritrochium with the axle, and lifts the weight by means of a rope wound round it. Elsewhere the name peritrochium is given to that circular plane itself, in place of which the scytalae are substituted. If the scytalae are joined to an axle having a horizontal position, it is called a Windlass; but if the axle is set up perpendicularly, it is named a Capstan. The use of windlasses is very great in mines. The capstan has this advantage, that several men together can be applied to each of the scytalae without hindering one another.

379 Machina haec ad vectem primi generis revocatur, imò re ipsa est vectis perpetuus. Hypomoclium enim est in medio[?] axis, videlicet in puncto m, vel f, quin per axem totum puncta ejusmodi rectè concipiuntur: potentia motrix in a vel b constituta distantiam a m, vel b m, à puncto fixo habet: resistentia in superficiei axis ipsius puncto è constituitur solaque semidiametro axis e f, à punto fixo f distat. Undè quantum distantia a m, excedit distantiam e f, tantò facilius potentia in a vincit resistentiam in e: quo proindè major futura est scytala, hoc magis vires potentiae crescunt. Atque ex eodem hoc principio deducitur vis & efficientia rotarum, quarum motus calcando exigitur, aut aquae adfluxu, alarum item, quae á vento circumaguntur in móletrinis, aliorumque id genus instrumentorum.

379 This machine is referred to the lever of the first kind; indeed, in reality it is a perpetual lever. For the hypomochlion is in the middle of the axle, namely at the point m, or f; indeed, points of this kind are rightly conceived through the whole axle: the moving power placed at a or b has the distance am, or bm, from the fixed point: the resistance is constituted at the point e of the surface of the axle itself, and is distant from the fixed point f only by the semidiameter of the axle, ef. Whence, by as much as the distance am exceeds the distance ef, by so much more easily does the power at a overcome the resistance at e: and therefore, the greater the scytala is to be, the more the forces of the power increase. And from this same principle are deduced the force and efficiency of wheels whose motion is driven by treading, or by the inflow of water, likewise of the sails that are turned round by the wind in mills, and of other instruments of that kind.

p. 124

De Trochlea.

ON THE PULLEY.

380 Trochlea tertia Mechanices machina, est instrumentum constans uno, vel pluribus orbiculis, circa axes suos alicubi fixos versatilibus, quibus circumvoluto fune, qui ductarius dicitur, pondera adducuntur. Si unus duntaxàt adhibeatur orbiculus adpellatur trochlea simplex, & monospastos; si è duobus, tribus, quatuor, aut pluribus coalescat; pro eorumdem numero dispastos, trispastos, tetraspastos aut polyspastos vocatur.

380 The pulley, the third machine of Mechanics, is an instrument consisting of one or several little wheels revolving about their axles, which are fixed somewhere, by which, with a rope wound round them, which is called the ductarius, weights are drawn in. If only one little wheel is employed, it is called a simple pulley, and monospastos; if it is composed of two, three, four or more, it is called, according to their number, dispastos, trispastos, tetraspastos or polyspastos.

381 Trochlea simplex circa axem immobilem volúbilis potentiae motricis vires non auget; quantùm enim ascendit pondus D (Fig. XXXVI.) tantum descendit A, adeòque motus tum ponderis, tum potentiae aequantur. Qua propter emolumentum omne hujus in eo situm est, quod directio potentiae mutetur, dum scilicet adminiculo trochleae illa deorsum movetur, quae alioquin sursum moveri deberet, ut pondus adtolleretur. Adhaec in descensu potentiae, vires ex ipso corporis moventis pondere crescunt. Demum funis circa orbem volutus minus adtéritur.

381 A simple pulley revolving about an immovable axle does not increase the forces of the moving power; for as much as the weight D ascends (Fig. XXXVI.), so much does A descend, and so the motions both of the weight and of the power are equal. Wherefore its whole advantage lies in this, that the direction of the power is changed, while, namely, by the aid of the pulley the power is moved downward which would otherwise have to be moved upward for the weight to be raised. Moreover, in the descent of the power, the forces grow from the very weight of the moving body. Finally, the rope rolled round the wheel is less worn by friction.

382 Patet verò trochleam B C vectem esse perpetuum heterodromum; axis quippè fixus L, circa quem revolvitur orbiculus, est instar fulcri, circum quod potentia, & pondus, quae se habent perindè, ac si essent extremis diametri C B adplicata, simul moventur. Si trochlea simplex (Fig. XXXVII.) mobilis fuerit, quoniam A extremum diametri A a D respondens puncto immobili F, est fulcrum, cui funis ope trochleae innititur; potentia in altero extremo diametri D; pondus demùm in medio a, constituuntur; àtque adeò trochlea sic comparata quum sit vectis secundi generis, ac distantia potentiae á fulcro, ad distantiam ponderis ab eodem, nempè D A ad A a[?] sit ut 2 ad 1; liquet (ex superiori Cap.) aequilibrium futurum, si potentia fuerit ad pondus, ut 1 : 2. Movebitur verò â potentia pondus, si illa ad hoc fuerit in majore ratione quam subdúpla; posito enim quod sit ut 4 : 6, quia distantia D A dupla est distantiae A a, deindè quia potentia duplo celerius movetur, quàm pondus (per Princip I. Stat.): celeritas iccircò potentiae majorem habebit rationem ad celeritatem ponderis, quàm reciprocè pondus ipsum ad vim potentiae, scilicet: 2 : 1 > 6 : 4, atque adeò pondus adminiculo trochleae mobilis tum movebitur (per Princip. Mechan.) Trochlea prior monospastos primi generis: altera haec secundi generis monospastos nuncupatur.

382 It is plain, moreover, that the pulley BC is a perpetual heterodromous lever; for the fixed axle L, about which the little wheel revolves, is like a fulcrum, around which the power and the weight, which behave just as if they were applied to the extremities of the diameter CB, are moved together. If the simple pulley (Fig. XXXVII.) is movable, since A, the extremity of the diameter AaD corresponding to the immovable point F, is the fulcrum on which the rope rests by means of the pulley, the power is placed at the other extremity of the diameter, D, and the weight, finally, in the middle, a; and so, since a pulley so arranged is a lever of the second kind, and the distance of the power from the fulcrum is to the distance of the weight from the same, namely DA to Aa, as 2 to 1, it is clear (from the preceding Chapter) that there will be equilibrium if the power is to the weight as 1 : 2. But the weight will be moved by the power if the latter is to it in a greater ratio than subduple: for supposing it is as 4 : 6, since the distance DA is double the distance Aa, and then since the power moves twice as fast as the weight (by Princip. I of Stat.), the velocity of the power will therefore have a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than, reciprocally, the weight itself to the force of the power, namely 2 : 1 > 6 : 4, and so the weight will then be moved by the aid of the movable pulley (by the Princip. of Mechan.). The former pulley is called monospastos of the first kind; this other, monospastos of the second kind.

383 In Dispasto cujus unus orbiculus immobilis, alter mobilis fuerit (Fig. XXXVIII.) duplo celerius movetur potentia P, quàm pondus M; nequit enim inferior orbiculus ex a in D ascendere, nisi potentia P per spatium = D a + b x, hoc est per duplum spatii à pondere confecti descendat. Proindè dispasti ope movebit

383 In the Dispastos, one little wheel of which is immovable and the other movable (Fig. XXXVIII.), the power P moves twice as fast as the weight M; for the lower little wheel cannot ascend from a to D unless the power P descends through a space = Da + bx, that is, through double the space covered by the weight. Therefore, by means of the dispastos, the power will move

p. 125

potentia pondus, si fuerit ad ipsum in majore ratione, quam sit 1 : 2, atque adeò dupla redditur per eundem potentia, tantundèmque juvatur, quantùm per monospastum secundi generis. Quapropter, quum incrementum omne motricis potentiae ab orbiculis mobilibus ducendum sit, tantùmque vis haec adcrescat quantùm velocitas ejusdem excedit velocitatem ponderis, ea de causâ in trispasto (Fig. XXXIX) triplicatur potentia, si quidem orbiculus M N, ex d in b adtolli nequit, nisi potentia P descendendo conficiat spatium altitudinis d b triplum, hoc est: nisi tria funis segmenta altitudini d b aequalia adducantur. Ita in tetraspasto quadruplicatur, in polyspasto multiplicatur pluries potentia.

the weight, if it is to it in a greater ratio than 1 : 2, and so the power is rendered double by it; and it is helped just as much as by the monospastos of the second kind. Wherefore, since all increase of the moving power is to be derived from the movable little wheels, and this force grows by as much as its velocity exceeds the velocity of the weight, for that reason in the trispastos (Fig. XXXIX.) the power is tripled, since indeed the little wheel MN cannot be raised from d to b unless the power P, in descending, covers a space triple the height db, that is: unless three segments of the rope equal to the height db are drawn in. Thus in the tetraspastos the power is quadrupled, in the polyspastos it is multiplied many times over.

384 Undè polyspasti ope adtolletur ingens pondus, adhibitâ exiguâ potentiâ, si ratio ipsius potentiae fuerit ad pondus major, quàm ratio unitatis ad numerum orbiculorum polyspastum constituentium. Quare dato valore potentiae, = 10 numero item orbiculorum = 6. (Fig. XL.) factum exprimet valorem ponderis á potentia huic machinae adplicata sustinendi = 60, sursum autem efferetur hoc pondus, si paulò major potentiae vis addatur. Speciatim pars polyspasti A B, trochlea superior; pars verò C D trochlea inferior; utraque Rechamus nominatur apud Vitruvium.

384 Whence by means of the polyspastos a huge weight will be lifted with a slight power employed, if the ratio of that power to the weight is greater than the ratio of unity to the number of little wheels constituting the polyspastos. Wherefore, given the value of the power = 10, and the number of little wheels likewise = 6 (Fig. XL.), the product will express the value of the weight to be sustained by the power applied to this machine, = 60; and this weight will be carried upward if a little greater force of the power is added. Specifically, the part AB of the polyspastos is the upper pulley, and the part CD the lower pulley; each is named rechamus in Vitruvius.

De Prancratio.

ON THE PANCRATIUM .

385 Prancratium quarta Mechanicae machina, est complexus plurium rotarum dentatarum certo artificio, eaque lege consociatarum, ut unius dentes denticulis alterius rotae circum axem suum volubilis inserantur, quo fiat, ut unâ motâ circa suum axiculum, ceterae omnes in motum cieantur. Machina haec Glossocomum â Pappo nuncupatur, s1 & eodem teste, seu inventa, seu explanata fuit ab Herone Alexandrino, qua de causâ Heronis Glossocomum vulgò dicitur. Varia est illius forma, & constructio[?]: suffecerit unam adumbrasse, quò pateat, quantoperè vires rotarum ejuscemodi compositione augeantur. s2

385 The Pancratium, the fourth machine of Mechanics, is a complex of several toothed wheels associated by a certain artifice and under such a law that the teeth of one are inserted into the little teeth of another wheel revolving about its own axis, whereby it comes about that, when one is moved about its little axle, all the others are set in motion. This machine is named Glossocomum by Pappus (q), and, on the same witness, it was either invented or explained by Hero of Alexandria, for which reason it is commonly called Hero’s Glossocomum. Its form and construction are various: it will be enough to have sketched one, from which it may appear how greatly the forces are increased by a composition of wheels of this kind (r).

386 Sit (Fig. XLI.) Pancratium é quatuor axibus cum rotis dentatis coalescens. Habeant rotae majores, quoad diametrum, rationem ad minores, ut 10 : 1, eademque sit ratio numeri dentium. Manubrium A B seu radius, cui adplicatur potentia sit decuplo longior radio rotulae C, erit velocitas potentiae ad velocitatem rotae C, ut 10 : 1. In altero axe rota major D, dentibus decuplo pluribus instructa, quàm rotula C, semel convertitur, dum interea C decies revolvitur. Eidem axi commitatur rotula E aequalis

386 Let there be (Fig. XLI.) a Pancratium composed of four axles with toothed wheels. Let the larger wheels have, as to diameter, the ratio to the smaller of 10 : 1, and let the ratio of the number of teeth be the same. Let the handle AB, or radius, to which the power is applied, be ten times longer than the radius of the little wheel C; the velocity of the power will be to the velocity of the wheel C as 10 : 1. On the second axle the greater wheel D, furnished with ten times more teeth than the little wheel C, is turned once while C meanwhile revolves ten times. To the same axle is joined a little wheel E, equal to the former

Collect. Mathem. Lib. 8. ad Prop 10.

Mathematical Collection, bk. 8, at prop. 10.

P. Schott. Mag. Univers. P 3. Magia Thaumaturga. Cap. 1. diversè constructa Pancrátia exhibet.

Father Schott, Magia universalis, pt. 3, Magia Thaumaturga, ch. 1, exhibits Pancratia constructed in various ways.

p. 126

priori C, quae eo tempore[?] [?] gyrum[?] absolvit[?], quo rota D circumagitur[?]. Dentes[?] in rota F sint pariter decuplo plures denticulis rotulae E, ut[?] ea[?] decies revolvi debeat, priusquam[?] F semel circa axem feratur[?], secumque[?] rotam adnexam G abripiat[?]. Rota demum H, ipsa[?] quoque dentes plures decuplo habens, vertetur[?] semel cum axe I H, & cylindro K, qui eadem[?] quâ[?] rota C, diametro continetur[?], atque funis ope pondus, revolvendo circa axem I H adtollit[?].

C, which completes its revolution in the time in which the wheel D is turned round. Let the teeth in the wheel F likewise be ten times more numerous than the little teeth of the little wheel E, so that the latter must revolve ten times before F is borne once round its axle and carries off with it the attached wheel G. Finally the wheel H, itself too having ten times more teeth, will turn once with the axle IH and the cylinder K, which is contained by the same diameter as the wheel C, and which, revolving about the axle IH, lifts the weight by means of a rope.

387 Posita igitur hac revolutionum serie ac proportione, erit celeritas potentiae A ad celeritatem rotulae C ut 10000 : 1000; hujus[?] ad velocitatem rotulae E, ut 1000 : 100: hujus[?] ad celeritatem G, ut 100 : 10: velocitas tandem G ad celeritatem cylindri, & ponderis L, ut 10 : 1. Quapropter obtinet[?] proportio haec (ex aequo ordinata[?]): velocitas potentiae A est ad velocitatem ponderis L, ut 10000 : 1, atque hinc machinae hujus adminiculo vis libram[?] unam potens elevare[?], ad 10000 libras adtollendas idonea redditur. Quin per Glossocomum, potentia tantis incrementis augeri potest[?], ut[?] calculo[?] subducto[?] demonstravit[?] Clariss. P. Schott, machinâ hac ex quatuor & viginti majoribus rotis coagmentatâ, tellurem, etiamsi[?] ex auro conflata foret, in altum extolli[?] suo è loco posse a potentia 125[?] libras ponderante. s1

387 This series and proportion of revolutions being posited, the velocity of the power A will be to the velocity of the little wheel C as 10000 : 1000; the velocity of the latter to the velocity of the little wheel E as 1000 : 100; that of this one to the velocity of G as 100 : 10; finally the velocity of G to the velocity of the cylinder, and of the weight L, as 10 : 1. Wherefore this proportion holds (ex aequo ordinata): the velocity of the power A is to the velocity of the weight L as 10000 : 1. And hence, by the aid of this machine, a force able to lift one pound is rendered fit for lifting 10000 pounds. Indeed, by means of the Glossocomum the power can be increased by such increments that, as the most distinguished Father Schott has demonstrated by calculation, with this machine compounded of twenty-four larger wheels the earth, even if it were made wholly of gold, could be raised on high from its place by a power weighing 125 pounds (s).

De Plano inclinato. — ON THE INCLINED PLANE

388 Planum inclinatum est superficies plana cum plano horizontali, cui insistit[?], angulos inaequales constituens. Recensetur[?] inter Mechanicas machinas eo nomine, quod ingentia in eo pondera faciliùs[?] vel[?] sustineantur[?], vel adtollantur[?]. Quapropter leges, quibus vires corporum moventium, [?] plani[?] hujus[?] augentur[?], paulisper[?] expendendae veniunt; sed ante hoc notetur[?] pondus illud[?], quo corpus plano inclinato superpositum descendere nititur, & superandum est, pondus respectivum[?]: integrum verò corporis nulli fulcro innixi pondus absolutum nuncupari[?].

388 An inclined plane is a plane surface forming unequal angles with the horizontal plane on which it stands. It is counted among the Mechanical machines on this account, that huge weights are either sustained or lifted on it more easily. Wherefore the laws by which the forces of moving bodies are increased by the aid of this plane come to be weighed a little; but before this let it be noted that the weight with which a body placed on an inclined plane strives to descend, and which must be overcome, is called the respective weight; but the whole weight of a body resting on no prop, the absolute weight.

389 Si corpus grave (Fig. XLII.) plano inclinato A B C impositum, sustineatur a potentia quae agit secundum directionem D K plano parallelam, erit potentia ad pondus absolutum corporis, ut altitudo plani A B ad longitudinem A C. Ductis enim lineis, alterâ D E ex centro gravitatis ad punctum contactus plani, alterâ verò D F exprimente directionem gravitatis, seu ponderis absoluti D H, & tandem E F perpendiculari ad lineam D F: tria resultant puncta vectis inflexi, sive angularis D E F, cujus hypomochlion est E, potentia D, & pondus F (perinde est quippe, sive in K, sive in D

389 If a heavy body (Fig. XLII.) placed on the inclined plane ABC is sustained by a power acting along the direction DK parallel to the plane, the power will be to the absolute weight of the body as the height of the plane AB to its length AC. For let lines be drawn: one, DE, from the center of gravity to the point of contact with the plane; another, DF, expressing the direction of gravity, or of the absolute weight, DH; and finally a third, EF, perpendicular to the line DF: there result the three points of the bent, or angular, lever DEF, whose hypomochlion is E, the power D, and the weight F (for it is all one whether the power at K or at D be

Loco cit. Mach. 2.

Place cited, Mach. 2.

p. 127

constituta[?] esse potentia, integrum[?] tamen[?] totum[?] pondus cogitetur[?] rectè[?] uno in puncto F lineae directionis D F collectum[?] esse[?]). Quare potentia in D est ad pondus in F, ut F E ad D E, atque ob similitudinem triangulorum D E F, & A B C, est D : F = A B : A C. At si potentia secundum directionem R I (Fig. XLIII.) basi[?] M N parallelam agat, quo ab ea pondus sustineatur[?], necessum[?] est, ut sit[?] potentia ad pondus, ut altitudo plani inclinati ad basim ejusdem[?].

be understood to be placed; yet let the whole weight be thought of as rightly collect‐ ed in the one point F of the line of direction D F). Therefore the power in D is to the weight in F as F E to D E, and, on account of the similarity of the triangles D E F and A B C, D : F = A B : A C. But if the power acts along the direction R I (Fig. XLIII.), parallel to the base M N, so that the weight may be sustained by it, it is necessary that the power be to the weight as the height of the inclined plane to its base.

390 Erecta enim in directionem R I, perpendiculari Q T, vectis rursum angularis T Q S habebitur, ita ut in T potentia I, in S pondus R concipi[?] mente possint[?], iisdem[?] nimirùm[?], quae supra sumpsimus[?], positis. Proinde potentia I erit ad pondus S, ut S Q ad T Q, hoc est ob similia triangula R Q S, S Q O, O P N, & L M N, erit T : S = L M : M N. Unde potentia exigua pondus adtollet per planum inclinatum, si ratio illius[?] ad absolutum corporis pondus fuerit major ea, quae currit[?] inter altitudinem ac longitudinem plani. Atque hinc generatim tanto magis vires potentiae ad sustinendum, vel adducendum corpus grave super planum inclinatum augentur, quanto plani longitudo est[?] quam altitudo major effecta[?]: adeoque si altitudo foret infinitè parva, sive planum horizontale, potentia sustinens infinitè parva [?]. Ex plano inclinato derivantur Cochlea, & Cuneus.

390 For when the perpendicular Q T has been erected upon the direction R I, the angular lever T Q S will again be had, so that the power I can be conceived to be in T and the weight R in S, the same things, namely, being supposed that we assumed above. Hence the power I will be to the weight S as S Q to T Q; that is, on account of the similar triangles R Q S, S Q O, O P N and L M N, T : S = L M : M N will hold. Hence a slight power will raise a weight along an inclined plane if its ratio to the absolute weight of the body is greater than that which holds between the height and the length of the plane. And hence, in general, the forces of the power for sustaining, or drawing, a heavy body upon an inclined plane are increased the more, the greater the length of the plane is made than its height: and so, if the height were infinitely small, or the plane horizontal, an infinitely small sustaining power is required. From the inclined plane are derived the Screw and the Wedge.

De Cochlea.

ON THE SCREW.

391 Cochlea est planum inclinatum circumductum in superficie cylindri, dum nempe cylinder in spiras[?], quas helices nuncupamus, aequales, ac parallelas sulcatur[?]. Duplex autem conjungitur[?], alia in exteriore superficie I K (Fig. XLIV.) alia in superficie interiore L M efformata, prior cochlea mas, posterior cochlea foemina[?] vocatur: utraque hoc modo conficitur[?], ut cavae hujus spirae, eidem incisae[?], prominentibus cylindri interioris spiris exactè[?] congruant, & mutuò helices se excipiant[?]. His porrò legibus continetur ratio, quâ vires, cochleae adminiculo adjuvantur[?].

391 The screw is an inclined plane carried round on the surface of a cylinder, namely when the cylinder is furrowed into equal and parallel spirals, which we call helices. It is joined, moreover, as a double one: one formed on the exterior surface I K (Fig. XLIV.), the other on the interior surface L M; the former is called the male screw, the latter the female screw: each is made in such a way that the hollow spirals of the latter, cut into it, fit exactly the projecting spirals of the inner cylinder, and the helices receive each other mutually. The ratio by which forces are aided by means of the screw is contained in the following laws.

392 Quoniam cochlea I K est planum inclinatum, cylindri superficiem ambiens, & potentiae, quae cochleae L M adplicatur, directio in planum[?] inclinatum[?] est basi ipsius cochleae parallela, aequilibrabitur potentia cum pondere, (per dicta de plano inclin.[?]) si illa fuerit ad hoc, ut distantia inter duas helices sibi proximas, ad circuitum cochleae, seu peripheriam circuli, quem potentia describit. Quocirca exiguae potentiae viribus cochleae adplicatis movebitur ingens corpus, si peripheria circuli à potentia percursi majorem rationem habeat ad distantiam helicum proximarum, quàm pondus ad potentiam: tum quippe celeritas potentiae majorem obtinebit[?] rationem ad celeritatem ponderis, quàm ipsum[?] pondus habeat[?] ad potentiam: atque adeo momentum potentiae, ponderis, ac

392 Since the screw I K is an inclined plane encircling the surface of a cylinder, and the direction of the power applied to the screw L M is parallel to the base of the inclined plane, the power will be in equilibrium with the weight (by what was said on the inclined plane) if the former is to the latter as the distance between two helices nearest each other is to the circuit of the screw, or the periphery of the circle which the power describes. Wherefore a huge body will be moved by the forces of a slight power applied to the screw, if the periphery of the circle run through by the power has a greater ratio to the distance of the nearest helices than the weight to the power: since, namely, the velocity of the power will then have a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than the weight itself has to the power: and so the momentum of the power will exceed the momentum of the weight and of the resistance.

p. 128

resistentiae momentum excedet. Quo fit, ut validiores sint cochleae, quò propiores iis helices inciduntur, eodem cylindri ambitu posito.

Whence it comes about that screws are the stronger, the closer to one another their helices are cut, the circuit of the cylinder remaining the same.

393 Cochlea, si rotae dentatae conjungatur, sic, ut illius revolutione impellantur denticuli rotae, haecque circumagatur, dicitur cochlea perpetua, sive infinita, quia sine fine gyrari potest. (Fig XLV.) Si potentia adplicetur in A, haec unam cochleae circuitionem perficiet, dum rota F E nonnisi unius dentis intervallo promovetur. Toties igitur revolvi potentia in A adplicata debet, quot dentibus rota F E instructa est, ut integra hujus rotae revolutio obtineatur: adeòque ut axis E H integram revolutionem perficiat, proindè ut pondus G ex eo dependens per spatium aequale peripheriae axiculi adtollatur. Quare si centum dentibus rota F E donata ponatur; peripheria radio A B descripta, decies contineat peripheriam axis H E, erit velocitas potentiae ad ponderis celeritatem; ut centies peripheria circuli radio B A descripti ad peripheriam axis H E semel, hoc est, ut 1000 ad 1. Unde machinae hujus adminiculo vis potens unam libram sustentare, cum pondere mille librarum aequilibrium constituet: adtollet verò, si ad illud majorem sortiatur rationem, ac sit 1 ad 1000.

393 If a screw is joined to a toothed wheel in such a way that by its revolution the little teeth of the wheel are driven and the wheel is turned round, it is called the perpetual or endless screw, because it can be turned without end. (Fig. XLV.) If the power is applied at A, it will complete one circuit of the screw while the wheel F E is advanced by the interval of only one tooth. The power applied at A must therefore be revolved as many times as the wheel F E is furnished with teeth, in order that a complete revolution of this wheel be obtained; and so that the axle E H may complete an entire revolution, and hence that the weight G hanging from it may be raised through a space equal to the periphery of the axle. Wherefore, if the wheel F E is supposed to be furnished with a hundred teeth, and the periphery described by the radius A B contains the periphery of the axle H E ten times, the velocity of the power will be to the speed of the weight as a hundred times the periphery of the circle described by the radius B A to once the periphery of the axle H E, that is, as 1000 to 1. Hence, by means of this machine, a force able to sustain one pound will establish equilibrium with a weight of a thousand pounds; and it will raise it if it obtains a greater ratio to it than 1 to 1000.

394 Cochlea demùm peculiaris hoc loco indigitari meretur, quae Archimedeae nuncupationem ab eodem illo auctore accepit. (Fig. XLVI.) Definitur ea cylindro A B, cui circumvolvitur spirarum instar tubus, qui opportunius è plumbo conflatur; extrema pars A manubrii ope versari circum axem potest, altera B orificium tubi adjunctum habens, sub aqua demergitur, totusque cylinder ad horizontem sub angulo circiter semirecto inclinatur. His constitutis, ubi cochlea circumagitur, aqua per tubi orificium subiens, ac revolutione ipsius machinae pedetentìm per spiras, veluti per totidem plana inclinata extolletur, tandemque in A profundetur.

394 Finally, a peculiar screw deserves to be pointed out in this place, which received the name Archimedean from that same author. (Fig. XLVI.) It is defined by the cylinder A B, around which a tube is wound in the manner of spirals, a tube more conveniently made of lead; the extreme part A can be turned about the axis by means of a handle; the other, B, having the orifice of the tube attached, is sunk under water, and the whole cylinder is inclined to the horizon at an angle of about half a right angle. These things being set up, when the screw is turned round, the water entering through the orifice of the tube is raised step by step, by the revolution of the machine itself, through the spirals as through so many inclined planes, and is at length poured out at A.

De Cuneo. — ON THE WEDGE.

395 Cuneus est pyramis quadrangula in aciem désinens. (Fig. XLVII.) Planum A D F B basis, A B latitudo, vel dorsum, a A vel a B altitudo, a C longitudo, C E acies cunei nuncupantur. Potentia huic machinae adplicari solita, vel est percutiens, vel premens, quae ope cunei findit, divellitque corpora etiam durissima.

395 The wedge is a quadrangular pyramid ending in an edge. (Fig. XLVII.) The plane A D F B is called the base, A B the breadth or back, a A or a B the height, a C the length, C E the edge of the wedge. The power usually applied to this machine is either striking or pressing, and by means of the wedge it splits and tears apart even the hardest bodies.

396 Vim cunei ex plano inclinato ducunt plerique (renuente in universum Cl. à Brixia s1 (de qua nos controversia nihil certi statuemus) spectando eum ceu compositum ex duobus planis inclinatis A C, B C: quumque perinde sit, sive corpus super planum inclinatum moveatur, sive sub corpore movendo planum

396 Most derive the force of the wedge from the inclined plane (the illustrious Fortunato da Brescia (t) objecting altogether, a controversy on which we shall settle nothing certain), regarding it as composed of two inclined planes A C, B C: and since it is all the same whether the body is moved over the inclined plane or the plane is thrust forward under the body to be moved and

p. 129

protrudatur; adhaec directio potentiae, quae ope cunei corpora dispescit, sit ad ejus longitudinem parallela: inferunt propterea potentiam esse ad vim obstaculi, uti est dimidia latitudo sive crassities cunei ad ejus longitudinem, hoc est: ½ A B: a C. Undè quia in acutiore cuneo altitudo minorem habet rationem ad longitudinem, eadem haec si ponatur manere, iccircò acutior validius dirimet partes obstaculi, quàm obtusus.

and moreover the direction of the power which drives bodies apart by means of the wedge is parallel to its length, they infer therefore that the power is to the force of the obstacle as half the breadth, or thickness, of the wedge is to its length, that is: ½ A B : a C. Hence, since in a sharper wedge the height has a smaller ratio to the length, if this same is supposed to remain, a sharper wedge will on that account separate the parts of an obstacle more strongly than a blunt one.

397 Haec de machinis vulgaribus dicta sint satis. Ex his componuntur innumerae aliae in usus diversos, quarum desiderium si quem teneat deinceps, consulat inter ceteros praecipuè Leupoldum, s1 Varignonium s2 & Machinarum ab Academ. Scient. Parisina adprobatarum descriptionem s3 fusè exaratam. Nostrum est, non artifices, machinarumque fabricatores, verùm Physicos docére ea, quae ab ipsis nec ignorari citra turpitudinem possunt, nec morari nimium properantes ad alia, debent. Paucula solum juverit ad horum cognitionem observare.

397 Let these things said about the common machines suffice. From them innumerable others are composed for various uses; if desire for these should hereafter take hold of anyone, let him consult, among others, chiefly Leupold (u), Varignon (x), and the description, drawn up at length, of the Machines approved by the Paris Academy of Sciences (y). It is our task to teach, not artisans and builders of machines, but Physicists, those things which they can neither be ignorant of without disgrace nor ought to dwell upon too long, hastening on to other matters. It will help only to observe a very few things for the knowledge of these.

Animadversio in Doctrinam de Machinis.

REMARK ON THE DOCTRINE OF MACHINES .

398 Quoniam ubi tria comperiuntur puncta in quorum uno potentia motrix sit adplicata, alteri pondus vincendum respondeat, tertium sit, circa quod motus perficitur, ibi vectem (seu incurvum in quo puncta per lineam curvam disponuntur, sive angularem, vel inflexum, ubi in rectis angulum componentibus puncta constituuntur) congruenter nobis mente sistere possumus, ibique tradita de eo doctrina locum habet; isthaec autèm in rebus multo plurimis quum obtineant, iccircò diversi prorsùs generis motiones ex natura vectis evolvi perspicuè possunt. Borellus certè é vectis cognitione omnes animalium motus explicari ostendit. s4 Vires profectò instrumentorum complurium hinc derivantur: fórfices, aut forcipes vectem duplicem primi generis referunt, cujus fulcrum est axiculus, potentia extremis brachiorum partibus admovetur, resistentiam corpus scindendum efficit.

398 Since, wherever three points are found, in one of which a moving power is applied, to another of which a weight to be overcome corresponds, while the third is that about which the motion is performed, there we can fittingly set a lever before our minds (either a curved one, in which the points are disposed along a curved line, or an angular or bent one, where the points are set in straight lines composing an angle), and there the doctrine handed down about it has its place; and since this holds in a great many things, motions of quite different kinds can therefore be clearly unfolded from the nature of the lever. Borelli certainly shows that all the motions of animals are explained from the knowledge of the lever (z). Indeed the forces of very many instruments are derived from this: scissors, or pincers, represent a double lever of the first kind, whose fulcrum is the little pin; the power is applied to the extreme parts of the arms; the body to be cut makes the resistance.

399 Baculus item super genu facile frangendus duplicem heterodromum vectem exhibet, utrique enim extremo manus imprimunt motum; fulcra sunt eae pedis partes, quibus baculus innititur; resistentia vincenda medium haec inter puncta contactus locum occupat. Undè consequitur, eò facilius forficibus discindi

399 Likewise a stick to be easily broken over the knee exhibits a double heterodromous lever. For the hands impress motion on each extremity; the fulcra are those parts of the leg on which the stick rests; the resistance to be overcome occupies the middle place between these points of contact. Whence it follows that bodies are cut apart by scissors the more easily,

Phys. P. 2. §. 2147. Vid. P. Schott. Mag. Mechan. Syntagm. 5.

Phys., pt. 2, §. 2147. See Fr. Schott, Mag. Mechan., Syntagm. 5.

Theatr. Machinar.

Theatrum Machinarum.

Nouvelle Mechanique.

Nouvelle Mechanique.

Machines approuvées par l' Academ. Royale des Scienc. de Paris VI. Tom. edit. Ex Gallico in Hispan. sermon. translat. prodeunt nunc Matriti.

Op. de motu animal.

Work De motu animal.

p. 130

corpora, tùm quo brachia manubrii longiora fuerint, tum quò corpus axiculo propiùs accesserit: rursumque baculum hoc promptius frangi, quò partes, quibus adprehenditur, magis protensae. Ratio quoque ex natura vectis heterodromi redditur, cur mola vento, vel aquae adfluxu concitata, eo volvatur celerius, quo alae vel radii longius porriguntur? Aëris quippe adlabentis, aut aquae impactus potentias motrices agunt, axis, quem alae, rotaevè ambiunt, hypomochlii vicem subit; lapis oneris rationem habet.

both the longer the arms of the handle are, and the closer the body comes to the little pin; and again, that this stick is broken the more readily, the farther out the parts by which it is grasped extend. The reason is also given, from the nature of the heterodromous lever, why a mill driven by the wind or by the inflow of water turns the faster, the farther the sails or spokes are stretched out. For the impact of the air flowing against them, or of the water, acts as the moving powers; the axle, which the sails or wheels surround, takes the place of the hypomochlion; the stone has the role of the load.

400 Neque absimili lege vectis homodromus perspicuam reddit nobis vim remórum; aquae enim ceu fulcro remus innititur, navis promovenda ponderis obtinet partes, manus potentiae: ea de causâ fit, ut faciliùs propellatur navigium quò remotior â scalmo est remigans, & quò scalmus aquae propiùs admovetur, hoc eodem ex principio derivantur guvernaculi vires: item deducitur, cur navis velociùs procurrat, quò altiùs antenna in malo adtollitur? Ventus namque comprimens vela, potentiae loco est, navis pro pondere, ima pars mali pro fulcro. Explicatur quoque, cur clavus tabulae firmiter infixus, bifido malleo excipiente caput illius prominens, facilè revellatur? Vectem namque secundi generis malleus refert, cujus manubrium potentia movens impellit; tabula, cui extremum alterum adprimitur, fulcrum est; clavus oneris adtollendi partes obtinet. Eamdem ob rationem culter una parte mensae adfixus eò scindit validiùs, quo propiùs ad punctum adfixionis res dividenda adplicatur. Similiter dentibus molaribus duriores etiam comminuimus cibos fortius, quàm incisoribus dictis; illi etenim à fulcro propiùs absunt, quam hi.

400 Nor by a dissimilar law does the homodromous lever make plain to us the force of oars; for the oar rests on the water as on a fulcrum, the ship to be moved forward holds the part of the weight, the hands that of the power: for that reason it happens that the vessel is propelled the more easily, the farther the rower is from the thole-pin and the closer the thole-pin is brought to the water. From this same principle the forces of the rudder are derived: likewise it is deduced why a ship runs forward the more swiftly, the higher the yard is raised on the mast. For the wind filling the sails stands in the place of the power, the ship for the weight, the lowest part of the mast for the fulcrum. It is explained also why a nail firmly fixed in a board is easily pulled out by a forked hammer taking hold of its projecting head. For the hammer represents a lever of the second kind, whose handle the moving power drives; the board, against which its other end is pressed, is the fulcrum; the nail holds the part of the load to be raised. For the same reason a knife fixed at one end to a table cuts the more strongly, the closer to the point of attachment the thing to be divided is applied. Similarly we grind even harder foods more strongly with the molar teeth than with the so-called incisors; for the former are nearer the fulcrum than the latter.

401 II. Ad axem in peritrochio referuntur elasticae horologiorum portatilium laminae, & cochlea conica, cui annectitur catena: atque é machinae hujus mechanicae principiis ingeniosè constructio partium automatón animantium excogitata fuit. Hac in compage artificiosa elaterium lamellae chalibeae S (Fig. XLVIII.) in gyrum convolutae, potentiae vices agit, dum illud ope catenulae rotam dentatam, quam in extremitate F, adjunctam habet cochlea A B, & â cujus rotae circuitione pendet reliquarum in horologio motus, impellit: resistentia proindè ab elaterio superanda est rotae E, atque adeò ceterarum revolutio; centrum motus, seu fulcrum in axe ipso A B, reperitur.

401 II. To the wheel and axle are referred the elastic springs of portable clocks, and the conical screw to which the chain is attached; and from the principles of this mechanical machine the construction of the parts of automaton animals was ingeniously devised. In this artful structure the spring of the steel lamina S (Fig. XLVIII.), coiled round in a spiral, plays the part of the power, while by means of the little chain it drives the toothed wheel which it has joined at the extremity F, the screw A B, and the wheel on whose revolution the motions of the rest in the clock depend: the resistance to be overcome by the spring is therefore the revolution of the wheel E, and so of the others; the center of motion, or fulcrum, is found in the axle A B itself.

402 Jam, quia lamella elastica plenè convoluta, utpotè validius tensa, quum sese evolvere incipit, vi pollet majore, haec verò continenter ipso evolutionis decursu imminuatur: resistentia ex adverso autem eadem jugiter maneat; (difficultas quippe in movendis horologii rotis non decrescit) iccircò axiculus cochleatus quem ambit catenula, non in cylindrum, sed in conicam formam aptatur, quo fit, ut dum elater sub suae evolutionis initium agit in axiculum, arctiorem hujus partem K L catena complectatur, at progressu evolutionis, catena in ampliorem axis ambitum F vel O

402 Now, since the elastic lamina, when fully coiled, being stretched more strongly, has a greater force when it begins to unwind itself, and this force is continually diminished in the very course of the unwinding, while the resistance, on the other hand, remains constantly the same (for the difficulty in moving the wheels of the clock does not decrease), the little screw-shaped axle which the chain surrounds is therefore fashioned not into a cylinder but into a conical form; whereby it comes about that, while the spring acts upon the axle at the beginning of its unwinding, the chain embraces its narrower part K L, but as the unwinding proceeds the chain reaches the wider circuit of the axle, F or O.

p. 131

pertingat. Quapropter ad eamdem semper vincendam resistentiam, idem jugiter momentum potentia retinet; quum scilicet aequa sit compensatio, sic ut integris elaterii viribus principio, ejus momentum temperetur velocitatis imminutione, dum nempè potentia per catenam adplicata, & agens, initio propiùs admovetur fulcro B: ubi contrà deinceps, amplitudo axiculi efficit, ut, decrescente quidem ex sese potentiâ, haec tamen à fulcro removeatur longiùs, radio videlicèt spirarum F, vel O, atque adeò celeritas augeatur.

Therefore, for overcoming the resistance, which is always the same, the power continually retains the same momentum; since, namely, there is an equal compensation, so that, while the forces of the spring are unimpaired at the beginning, its momentum is tempered by a diminution of velocity; while, that is, the power, applied through the chain and acting, is at the beginning brought nearer to the fulcrum B; whereas afterwards, on the contrary, the breadth of the axle brings it about that, though the power indeed decreases of itself, it is nevertheless removed farther from the fulcrum, by the radius, namely, of the spirals F or O, and so its speed is increased.

403 Axes in peritrochio haud dubiè sunt etiam claves, quibus utimur ad elateres horologiorum intorquendos, aut pondera eorumdem adtollenda, quae pro vario horologii situ modò suculam, modò ergatam dabunt. Terebra quoque generis hujus est instrumentum; quanquam hoc ob spíras circum cuspidem contortas, aliquid de cochlea; ob acumen, in quod desinit, quidpiam de cuneo admixtum habet.

403 Wheels and axles, without doubt, are also the keys which we use to wind the springs of clocks or to raise their weights, and which, according to the varying position of the clock, will give now a windlass, now a capstan. The gimlet too is an instrument of this kind; although, on account of the spirals twisted round its point, it has something of the screw mixed in, and on account of the sharpness in which it ends, something of the wedge.

404 III. Trochlea, in qua vectem quaerere ineptum sibi videri, audacter pronunciavit Cartesius s1 seorsum usurpata, vires potentiae perparùm quum augeat, consimilibus adjungitur, uti jam docuimus, idque fit ea lege, ut vel aliae aliis immineant, quod schemata superiora exhibuerunt, vel situ ad invicem parallelo juxta se constituantur orbiculi magnitudine aequales (Fig. XLIX.) quae constructio percommoda est, tunc maximè quum angustiae spatii, in quo machina locanda, coordinationem aliam non recipiunt. In usu trochlearum observandum monent, qui de his agunt, ut partes funis ductarii omnes semper sint sibi parallelae. Et quoniam funis in trochleis majoribus minus inflecti debet, quàm in minoribus; iccircò illae his praestant. Verùm quia numerus funium ex amplitudine trochlearum non augetur; adhaec quaedam in majoribus orbiculis sese offerunt incommoda, quae ex pondere eorumdem majori, ex adtritu validiore in axibus &c. oriuntur: iccircò legem illam in universum haud obtinere patescit. Porrò ad minuendam [?] frictionem seu trochleae circa axiculum suum, seu axis in peritrochio intra loculamentum, seu intra foramina, quae chelonia dicuntur; oportunum fuerit, foramina orbiculorum, aut loculamenta, non rotunda, sed ex tribùs, quatuorvè arcubus circularibus convexis efformare; has enim superficies arcuatas axiculus sese convertens, in paucioribus punctis continget s2. Trochleae cum axe in peritrochio junctae componunt machinam frequentissimi usus, quae Grus vocatur, & cujus fabrica commodissima a Musschenbroekio s3 describitur. Sucula cum polyspasto aliud machinae genus reddit, quam capram nuncupant.

404 III. The pulley, in which Descartes boldly declared (a) that it seemed to him foolish to look for a lever, since, used by itself, it increases the forces of the power very little, is joined to similar ones, as we have already taught; and this is done under the law that either some hang over others, as the figures above showed, or the little wheels, equal in size, are set beside one another in a position parallel to each other (Fig. XLIX.), a construction which is very convenient, especially when the narrowness of the space in which the machine is to be placed does not admit another arrangement. In the use of pulleys those who treat of them advise that it be observed that all the parts of the hauling rope always be parallel to one another. And since the rope must be bent less in larger pulleys than in smaller ones, the former are on that account superior to the latter. But since the number of ropes is not increased by the size of the pulleys, and besides certain inconveniences present themselves in larger little wheels, which arise from their greater weight, from the stronger friction on the axles, etc., it is therefore clear that that law does not hold universally. Further, to diminish the friction either of the pulley about its little axle, or of the wheel and axle within its case, or within the holes which are called chelonia, it will be expedient to form the holes of the little wheels, or the cases, not round but out of three or four convex circular arcs; for the little axle, turning round, will touch these arched surfaces in fewer points (b). Pulleys joined with the wheel and axle compose a machine of very frequent use, which is called the Crane, and whose most convenient construction is described by Musschenbroek (c). The windlass with a polyspast yields another kind of machine, which they call the gin.

405 IV. Rota dentata, si dentes secundum directionem radii promineant, Stellata; si ad radium perpendiculares fuerint, & deorsum versi, pectinata, si autèm verticales, coronata adpellatur.

405 IV. A toothed wheel, if its teeth project along the direction of the radius, is called stellate; if they are perpendicular to the radius and turned downward, pectinate; but if vertical, crowned.

406 Axis, qui rotam dentatam saepenumerò circumagit, dentibus, vel incisis, vel insertis, sivè paxillis instruitur, & laterna, vel curriculum rotae nominatur. Id in hoc instrumento advertendum, quum dentes axeos saepius functionem suam obire debeant, quàm rota dentata, plurium praesertim dentium, magisque propterea adterantur; firmiores illi constituendi sunt, quàm in rota dentata. Curandum praeterea, ne iidem dentes rotae cum eodem semper paxillo, aut dente ipsius axis committantur; sed diversi diversis dum inseruntur, fiat; ut diversimodè inter se adtriti ad aequalitatem motûs eò magis pertingant: id quod efficitur, si dentes in se invicem agentes eo sint numero, quorum unus alterum exactè non contineat, uti si rota 60, axis 7, vel 9, dentes comprehendat. s1

406 The axle which often turns a toothed wheel round is furnished with teeth, either cut into it or inserted, that is, with pegs, and is named the lantern, or the runner of the wheel. In this instrument it is to be noted that, since the teeth of the axle must perform their function more often than the toothed wheel, especially one of many teeth, and are on that account worn down more, they must be made firmer than in the toothed wheel. Care must besides be taken that the same teeth of the wheel are not always engaged with the same peg, or tooth of the axle itself; but that, different ones being inserted among different ones, it may come about that, being worn against one another in various ways, they may attain the more nearly to equality of motion: which is effected if the teeth acting on one another are of such a number that one does not exactly contain the other, as if the wheel comprises 60 teeth, the axle 7 or 9. (d)

407 V. Non experimenta modò, sed ratio etiam, antehàc stabilitis principiis nixa, evincit, gravia per planum inclinatum demissa motum accelerare uniformiter; nam per planum inclinatum neque gravitantis causae vis, neque motus continuus mobilis ipsius sistitur, proindè momentis singulis novus à fluido gravifico impulsus accedit, quibus celeritas respectiva continenter augeatur, eâ proportione, quae intercedit absolutam inter & respectivam gravitatem s2. Undè quemadmodum liberè labentia in fine lapsus eam vim nanciscuntur, quâ ad tantam adtolli possint altitudinem, è qua proruerunt; ita per planum inclinatum descendentia viribus iisdem polleant, necesse est, seclusâ medii, aliorumque corporum resistentiâ; his enim positis quum celeritas in fine lapsûs acquisita, non perimatur in corpore, si corpori deciduo aliud sese non offerat, quàm id duntaxat quod mutet directionem, consectarium est, ut vis in progressu descensûs obtenta in ascensum impendatur.

407 V. Not only experiments but reason too, relying on the principles established before, proves that heavy bodies let down along an inclined plane accelerate their motion uniformly; for along an inclined plane neither the force of the cause of gravitation nor the continued motion of the mobile itself is stopped; hence at each single moment a new impulse from the gravific fluid is added, by which the respective velocity is continually increased in the proportion which holds between the absolute and the respective gravity (f). Hence, just as bodies falling freely acquire at the end of their fall that force by which they could be raised to as great a height as that from which they fell, so it is necessary that bodies descending along an inclined plane possess the same forces, the resistance of the medium and of other bodies being set aside: for, these being supposed, since the velocity acquired at the end of the fall is not destroyed in the body if nothing presents itself to the falling body except that alone which changes its direction, it is a consequence that the force obtained in the progress of the descent is spent upon the ascent.

408 Hac [?] ex doctrina pendulorum motus, illiusque ratio physica derivatur; arcus etenim, quem funependulum in descensu percurrit, si spectetur ceu complexum ex infinitè parvis lineis rectis, hoc est: tanquàm plana inclinata sibi mutuo contigua C A, A B, (Fig. L.) infinitè parvae longitudinis, & quorum flexus, sive angulus A, directionem solummodò mutet, corpus grave arcum emetiendo, eam adipiscetur celeritatem, cujus vi ad altitudinem eidem aequalem ascendere queat. Frictio equidem fili in puncto suspensionis, ipsiusmet retinaculi partes non omnimodè flexiles, aëris renixus, aliquid sensim de vi motus decerpunt usque: eam ob rem, nisi oscillationum causa quaedam conservatrix accedat, arcus continuè decrescent; neque pondus adpensum ad altitudinem descensus prorsùs, sed, quod ad sensum, aequalem adtolletur.

408 From this doctrine the motion of pendulums, and its physical reason, are derived: for if the arc which a pendulum runs through in its descent is regarded as composed of infinitely small straight lines, that is, as of inclined planes contiguous to one another, C A, A B (Fig. L.), of infinitely small length, whose bend, or angle A, only changes the direction, the heavy body, in traversing the arc, will acquire that velocity by whose force it could ascend to a height equal to it. The friction of the thread at the point of suspension, indeed, the parts of the holder itself, which are not entirely flexible, and the resistance of the air gradually take something away from the force of the motion all the while: for that reason, unless some cause conserving the oscillations is added, the arcs continually decrease; nor is the hung weight raised altogether to the height of its descent, but only to one equal to it so far as the senses can tell.

Vid Krafftius. Praelect. Phys. P. 2. cap. 2. §. 83.

See Krafft, Praelect. Phys., pt. 2, ch. 2, §. 83.

Vid. Introduct. facil. in doctrin. de motu à P. Erasmo Froelich. cap [?] Prop. 4, & seqq.

p. 133

409 VI. Cochlea; quae multifariam aptari solet, in usus complures adhibetur. Permultùm augentur vires eaurundem ope, eo quidem incremento, ut P. Schottus integras domos ligneas cochlearum adminiculo translatas fuisse ex Munstero referat s1. Id praeterea emolumenti in iis deprehenditur, quod pondus, remotâ etiam potentiâ, sustineant per sese, modò helices utriusque mutuò se excipiant, & ad invicem comprimantur; possit proin potentia citrà dispendium interquiescere, ac recreari. Magnus tamen partium hac in machina adtritus, usum ejus minus commodum reddit: cui vitio occurritur pinguedinem spirarum convolutionibus interserendo. Observandum adhaec monet idem Schottus, quò durabilior sit cochlea, matrix plures spiras comprehendat; si enim unicam duntaxat habeat, tunc moles ponderis adtollendi uni illi innixa labem ei facilè infert s2.

409 VI. The screw, which is usually fitted up in many ways, is employed for a great many uses. Forces are increased very much by its means, and indeed with such an increase that Fr. Schott relates, from Münster, that whole wooden houses were moved by the help of screws (g). This advantage is besides found in them, that they sustain the weight by themselves even when the power is removed, provided the helices of each receive one another mutually and are pressed against each other; so the power can meanwhile rest and recover itself without loss. Yet the great friction of the parts in this machine makes its use less convenient: a defect which is remedied by putting grease between the windings of the spirals. The same Schott advises, besides, that it be observed that, so that the screw may be more durable, the nut should comprise several spirals; for if it has only one, then the mass of the weight to be raised, resting on that one alone, easily causes it damage (h).

410 VII. Ad cuneum pertinent artefacta varia: cultri, gladii, forfices, terebrae, aliaque similia; quin efficacia molecularum corpora naturalia componentium ex naturâ hujus machinae mechanicae derivatur: venenorum scilicet acrium, & corrosivorum, qualia sunt mercurius sublimatus, arsenicum, aqua fortis, &c. quae cuneorum instar agunt.

410 VII. To the wedge belong various manufactured things: knives, swords, scissors, gimlets, and others like them; indeed, the efficacy of the molecules composing natural bodies is derived from the nature of this mechanical machine: namely, of acrid and corrosive poisons, such as sublimate of mercury, arsenic, aqua fortis, etc., which act like wedges.

Adnotatio. — NOTE

411 In machinis mechanicis funes multiplici ratione usurpari solent, ac debent: hi uti adminicula sunt ad movendas machinarum ope moles corporum, ita impedimenti saepenumerò non exiguam partem addunt. Pro dignitate auxit hanc Mechanicae Tractationem P. de Lanis s3 eamdem Cl. Amontons s4 primus exegit methodo concinna, ostenditque multum interesse, resistentiae hujus mensuram nosse, commonstrans, plerumque ex rigiditate funium unicè augeri posse unâ parte tertiâ resistentiam, à motrice potentia superandam: id quod experimentis [?] commonstravit per sequentia theoremata. I. Resistentiam á funium rigore pendentem crescere in ratione directa ponderum, aut virium, eos tendentium. II. Eandem illam augeri praeterea, ceteris omnibus paribus, ea proportione, qua diameter funium accrescit. III. Funes eò complicari difficiliùs, quò cylindri, vel trochleae, quos ambiunt, sunt minores; quantumvis resistentia haec non augescat eâ ipsa proportione, quâ diametri minuuntur. His Auctoris animadversionibus experimenta, & illustrationes adjecit Clariss. Nolletus. s5

411 In mechanical machines ropes are wont to be, and must be, employed in manifold ways: and as they are aids for moving masses of bodies by means of machines, so they very often add no small part of hindrance. Fr. de Lana (i) worthily enlarged this treatment of Mechanics; the illustrious Amontons (j) was the first to work it out by an elegant method, and he showed that it matters greatly to know the measure of this resistance, pointing out that, for the most part, the resistance to be overcome by the moving power can be increased by one third part solely from the stiffness of the ropes: which he demonstrated by experiments through the following theorems. I. That the resistance depending on the stiffness of ropes increases in the direct ratio of the weights, or forces, stretching them. II. That this same resistance is increased besides, all other things being equal, in the proportion in which the diameter of the ropes grows. III. That ropes are folded with the more difficulty, the smaller the cylinders or pulleys which they surround: although this resistance does not grow in that very proportion in which the diameters are diminished. To these remarks of the Author the most illustrious Nollet added experiments and illustrations (k).

DISSERTATIO IV. — DISSERTATION IV

HYDROSTATICA. — HYDROSTATICS

Principia Hydrostaticae.

Principles of Hydrostatics.

412 Partem Staticae alteram, Hydrostaticam videlicet, quae de gravium fluidorum viribus agit, scitu dignissimam Physices partem paucis complectemur. Duplici autem spectari modo eorumdem pressio potest: altero dum fluida cum fluidis, altero dum illa cum solidis immersis conferuntur, de utroque adtingendum est aliquid: primum hoc loco, posterius exinde contemplabimur. Unum istic, priusquam rem à principio ordiamur, velut certum constituamus necesse est: fluidi cujuslibet partes superiores gravitare in partes inferiores, quibus illae incumbunt, fundumque vasis premi continenter atque urgeri à fluido contento. Scitum profectò, minimeque controversum habebitur, id, si ad materiae gravificae actionem tantisper mentem revocemus, atque (ut par est) cogitemus, corpus quoad naturam spectatum, aequè comparatum esse ad hunc illumve locum occupandum, neque verò locum ullum enti corporeo respectivè proprium [?] dici posse. Coeptum ex ordine prosequamur notionibus anteà expositis.

e shall embrace in a few words the other part of Statics, namely 412 W Hydrostatics, which treats of the forces of heavy fluids, a part of Physics most worth knowing. Their pressure, moreover, can be regarded in a twofold way: in one, when fluids are compared with fluids; in the other, when they are compared with solids immersed in them; something must be touched upon concerning each: the first we shall contemplate in this place, the second afterwards. One thing we must here lay down as certain before we begin the matter from its beginning: that the upper parts of any fluid gravitate upon the lower parts on which they rest, and that the bottom of the vessel is continually pressed and urged by the fluid contained in it. This will surely be held as known and not at all controverted, if we recall our minds for a little to the action of the gravific matter, and consider (as is right) that a body, regarded as to its nature, is equally disposed to occupy this place or that, and that no place can be called respectively proper to a corporeal being. Let us pursue in order what we have begun, the notions having first been set out.

413 Fluidorum pressionem dum hic spectamus, gravitatem in iis specificam consideramus, quo nomine intelligimus illam, quae corpori competit, quatenus in entium corporeorum certa classe, sive specie reponitur, hoc est: Si materiae duae, ratione ponderis, inter se conferantur, (utraque eodem volumine comprehensa); pondus hoc comparatum gravitas specifica nuncupatur. Ita gravitatem aquae, specificam videlicet, ad gravitatem mercurii esse dicimus, ut 1 ad 14, quo innuimus, alterum hoc fluidum (aequali sub volumine) decies, & quater plus appendere, quam illud. Vas uniforme dicitur illud cujus omnes sectiones fundo ipsi parallelae sunt figura similes, & amplitudine aequales: cujusmodi habentur vasa cylindrica, & prismatica; secus ex adverso cujus sectiones inaequales erunt vas difforme vocatur. Hujus amplitudo, si ad basim minor fuerit quam versus apicem, divergens dicitur; si contrà indè ab altiori vertice continuè ad fundum usque amplitudo crescat, vas convergens nominatur. Tubi communicantes vocitantur, qui eo pacto sunt connexi, ut fluidum immissum ex uno in alium liberè excurrat.

413 While we here regard the pressure of fluids, we consider in them their specific gravity, by which name we understand that which belongs to a body inasmuch as it is placed in a certain class, or species, of corporeal beings; that is: if two matters are compared with each other in respect of weight (each comprised in the same volume), this compared weight is called specific gravity. Thus we say that the gravity of water, namely its specific gravity, is to the gravity of mercury as 1 to 14, by which we indicate that the latter fluid (under an equal volume) weighs fourteen times more than the former. A uniform vessel is said to be one all of whose sections parallel to the bottom itself are similar in figure and equal in breadth: such are cylindrical and prismatic vessels; on the contrary, one whose sections are unequal is called a nonuniform vessel. If its breadth is smaller at the base than toward the top, it is called divergent; if, on the contrary, the breadth grows continually from the higher top down to the bottom, it is named a convergent vessel. Those are called communicating tubes which are so connected that a fluid let in runs freely from one into the other.

p. 135

Leges de pressione fluidorum.

LAWS OF THE PRESSURE OF FLUIDS .

414 Lex I. Fluida vasis comprehensa ea ipsa premunt in ratione altitudinis, quâ super planum horizontale eminent, & latitudinis baseos, quae illorum descensui opponitur: aestimanda est proindè eorundem pressio secundum rationem compositam altitudinis, & baseos.

414 Law I. Fluids comprised in vessels press them in the ratio of the height by which they stand above a horizontal plane, and of the breadth of the base which is opposed to their descent: their pressure is therefore to be estimated according to the compound ratio of the height and the base.

415 Primò quippè, fluidum vase uniformi A B C D (Fig. LI.) ad perpendiculum erecto contentum, urgetur secundum directionem horizonti, seu fundo vasis perpendicularem: neque partes duntaxat fundo proximae, sed summa omnium, quae ex amplitudine basis B D, & altitudine a B resultat, vim suam exserit (per §. 412.). Quare pressio in fundum à tota mole, hoc est, ab altitudine in basim ductâ aestimetur, necesse est.

415 Firstly, a fluid contained in a uniform vessel A B C D (Fig. LI.) set up perpendicularly is urged along the direction perpendicular to the horizon, or to the bottom of the vessel: and not only the parts nearest the bottom, but the sum of all, which results from the breadth of the base B D and the height a B, exerts its force (by §. 412.). Therefore it is necessary that the pressure on the bottom be estimated from the whole mass, that is, from the height multiplied into the base.

416 Secundò: Quod si fluidum vase ad horizontem inclinato M E N O (Fig. cit.) comprehendatur: tametsi major sit massa; quoniam tamen fluidi partes velut incumbunt plano inclinato a N, iccircò gravitatis partem in latus sive longitudinem plani éxserunt. Ea igitur vis duntaxat in fundum E N agit, quae aequalis est altitudini a b, habita ratione basis. Id quod dilucidè menti sistetur, fluidi molem, ductis ad perpendiculum a b parallelis, in columnas dispescendo.

416 Secondly: but if the fluid is comprised in a vessel M E N O inclined to the horizon (Fig. cit.), although the mass is greater, yet, since the parts of the fluid rest as it were upon the inclined plane a N, they therefore exert part of their gravity against the side, or length, of the plane. That force alone, therefore, acts on the bottom E N which is equal to the height a b, account being taken of the base. This is clearly set before the mind by dividing the mass of the fluid into columns, lines parallel to the perpendicular a b being drawn.

417 Tertiò: In vase divergente (Fig. LII.) basis c d haud aliter premitur, quam si foret cylindro e c d f, fluidum contentum; perspicuum est etenim, columnas m m, l l, &c. vasis ipsius parietibus inniti ceu fulcris, basi verò eas solum incumbere, quae ad perpendiculum eidem impendent. Atqui hae, altitudine e c = f d, ac diametro e f = c d, definiuntur. Fundus itaque vasis divergentis aequè premitur, atque si cylindro aequalis altitudinis, & baseos fluidum committeretur.

417 Thirdly: in a divergent vessel (Fig. LII.) the base c d is pressed no otherwise than if the fluid contained in it were in the cylinder e c d f: for it is clear that the columns m m, l l, etc. rest upon the walls of the vessel itself as on supports, and that only those rest upon the base which hang perpendicularly over it. But these are defined by the height e c = f d and the diameter e f = c d. The bottom of a divergent vessel is therefore pressed just as if the fluid were committed to a cylinder of equal height and base.
