418 Quartò: In convergente demùm vase commonstrandum superest, fundum K H (Fig. LIII.) non minus urgeri ab ipso fluido, quàm si vas aequabilem ubivis amplitudinem K Q T H servaret. Libet praecipuum hoc, Hydrostaticae caput, pereleganti ratiocinio Cl. Varignon s1 stabilire: Demittantur ex marginibus superioribus, & secundum diametrum oppositis (B & C) ad fundum perpendiculares B M, & C O; tum portio baseos K M in partes aequales, aut minores dimidiae lineae M O dirimatur, ac tali in numero, qui semper aequetur summae terminorum progressionis duplae, incipientis ab unitate ex. gr. in 3, in 7, in 15, in 31, in 63 &c. Nempè K M dividatur, si lubet in K U, U L, L M; acceptisque M N, & O N aequalibus, cuique harum partium, agantur K Q, L R, A N, T H parallelae, & aequales ipsi B M, vel C O.

418 Fourthly: it remains, finally, to be shown that in a convergent vessel the bottom K H (Fig. LIII.) is urged by the fluid itself no less than if the vessel kept everywhere an even breadth K Q T H. I wish to establish this principal head of Hydrostatics by the very elegant reasoning of the illustrious Varignon (l): let the perpendiculars B M and C O be let fall to the bottom from the upper margins (B and C), opposite each other along the diameter; then let the portion K M of the base be divided into parts equal to, or smaller than, half the line M O, and in such a number as is always equal to the sum of the terms of a double progression beginning from unity, e.g. into 3, into 7, into 15, into 31, into 63, etc. Namely, let K M be divided, if you please, into K U, U L, L M; and, M N and O N having been taken equal to each of these parts, let K Q, L R, A N, T H be drawn parallel and equal to B M or C O.

Memoires de l' Academ. 1692. p. 16. edit. Holland.

Memoires de l’Academ. 1692, p. 16, Holland ed.

p. 136

419 His constitutis, columna fluidi B N, libramentum exercebit super fulcro M adversus columnam E M, quae basis margine E D coercetur: exercebit (inquam) perindè ac faceret pondus Z super bilance E X, cujus hypomoclion foret in Y, & brachii extremum E per marginem tubi K E D retineretur. Igitur quoniam hoc pacto onus à fulcro Y sustentatum duplum foret ponderis Z; brachia quippè vectis E X aequantur, aut ab aequalitate parum deerrant, sustineret utique proindè fulcimentum, & pondus, & alioquin simul resistentiam huic aequalem; iccircò punctum M, aut portio L N ipsiusmet fundi, duplo columnae B N praematur, necesse est, seu perindè urgebitur pars L N, atque si R N, columna foret integra fluidi, ac fundo immineret.

419 These things being set up, the column of fluid B N will exert a balancing action upon the fulcrum M against the column E M, which is confined by the margin E D of the base: it will exert it (I say) just as the weight Z would do upon the balance E X, if its hypomochlion were at Y and the extremity E of its arm were held back by the margin of the tube K E D. Since, therefore, in this way the load sustained by the fulcrum Y would be double the weight Z (for the arms of the lever E X are equal, or depart little from equality), the support would accordingly sustain both the weight and, at the same time, a resistance equal to it; therefore it is necessary that the point M, or the portion L N of the bottom itself, be pressed by double the column B N; or the part L N will be urged just as if R N were an entire column of fluid and hung over the bottom.

420 Quapropter si spectetur A N L E D tanquàm columna hujuscemodi, comperietur similiter, quod, dum fluidum sese librat super fulcimento L contra fluidi K E L portionem, retentam obstante vasis margine K E, pars fundi K N premenda sit à fluido A N K D B; haud secùs, atque à columna aequali Q N. Pari modo fluidum A N, H, F C, fundi partem N H premet perindè, ac si columna aequalis N T insisteret. Quocirca fluidi tota moles B D K H F C, totum fundum K H ea praecise virium quantitate premet, qua is gravaretur per fluidum Q K H T, paris altitudinis, & latitudinis ubique aequalis basi K H. Atque hoc pressionis fluidorum fundamentum inter alia firmatur experimento, quo tubi plures aequè alti constituuntur, singulorumque fundus aequali apertura pertunditur, aequalibus obturamentis arcenda; eventus namque palam faciet, vim eandem ad sustinenda singulorum obturamenta adhiberi oportere, quamcumque figuram, aut situm vasa haec sortiantur.

420 Wherefore, if A N L E D is regarded as a column of this kind, it will be found similarly that, while the fluid balances itself upon the support L against the portion K E L of the fluid, held back by the margin K E of the vessel standing in its way, the part K N of the bottom must be pressed by the fluid A N K D B no otherwise than by the equal column Q N. In like manner the fluid A N, H, F C will press the part N H of the bottom just as if an equal column N T stood upon it. Wherefore the whole mass of the fluid B D K H F C will press the whole bottom K H with precisely that quantity of forces with which it would be weighed down by the fluid Q K H T, of equal height and of a breadth everywhere equal to the base K H. And this foundation of the pressure of fluids is confirmed, among other things, by an experiment in which several equally high tubes are set up and the bottom of each is pierced with an equal opening, to be closed with equal stoppers; for the outcome will make plain that the same force must be applied to sustain the stoppers of each, whatever figure or position these vessels may have.

Lex II. Fluida in omnem partem premunt.

LAW II. FLUIDS PRESS IN EVERY DIRECTION .

421 Fluida deorsum versùs niti, quemadmodum gravia cetera, dubium est [?] nemini. In latera verò conniti, ex ipso pressu, qui secundum gravitatis directionem efficitur, partium habilitate ad motum, earumdem figurâ, exilitate, ac dissociatione répeti perfacilè explicarique potest. Intelligatur enim massa fluidi in columnas, conflatas ex exilissimis sphaerulis, & secundum paucula plana se contingentibus, divisa. (Fig. LIV.) Quoniam partes columnae 3a. impressioni cuivis cedunt promptissimè, & in motum facillimè cientur, dum directione perpendiculari premuntur, locum hunc situmque suum nequaquam servarent, nisi à moleculis columnae ab, & 4c, atque omni ex parte retinerentur. Premuntur igitur sphaerulae minimae secundum latera, & puncta contactuum: id quod de omnibus columnis est concludendum.

421 That fluids strive downward, as do other heavy bodies, no one doubts. But that they also strive against the sides can very easily be traced back to, and explained from, the very pressure which is produced along the direction of gravity, and from the aptness of their parts for motion, their figure, minuteness and disconnection. For let a mass of fluid be understood to be divided into columns composed of most minute spherules touching one another in a very few planes. (Fig. LIV.) Since the parts of the column 3a yield most promptly to any pressure, and are very easily set in motion while they are pressed in a perpendicular direction, they would by no means keep this place and position of theirs unless they were held back by the molecules of the columns ab and 4c, and on every side. The smallest spherules are therefore pressed along their sides and points of contact: which must be concluded of all the columns.

422 Demùm ex pressu, quo urgentur vi gravitatis, consequitur, fluida quoque ex imo premere in sublime, dum scilicet aliis prementibus deorsum, adtolluntur, ferè ut in bilance gravius solidum suomet descensu alterum sublevat. Stabiliunt Legem hanc plurima

422 Finally, from the pressure by which they are urged by the force of gravity, it follows that fluids also press from below upward, namely when, others pressing downward, they are raised up, almost as in a balance the heavier solid lifts the other by its descent. Many indications establish this law, phenomena

p. 137

indicia occurrentia phaenomena. Ex vase ad horizontem inclinato liquor non profluèret, si corporum firmorum instar in subjectum duntaxat planum vim suam exsereret: navis è latere hians aquam hoc loco excipit, ac tantò quidem celerius, quò altius circumfusa navigio supra foramen aqua eminet: dolium quacumque parte pertusum liquori exitum praebet.

that occur daily. From a vessel inclined to the horizon the liquid would not flow out if, like firm bodies, it exerted its force only on the underlying plane; a ship gaping at the side takes in water at that place, and the more quickly, the higher the water surrounding the vessel stands above the hole: a cask pierced in any part whatever affords an exit to the liquid.

423 Uno tentamine omnigenam fluidorum pressionem explorare licebit. Si namque plura inserantur vasi foramina, aliud imminens horizonti ad perpendiculum, aliud verticale eidem, aliud lateri committatur, aperturae obturamentum è subere aptetur, ea lege, ut foramini exactè quidem congruat, leviori tamen impressione queat dimoveri; tunc enim, immisso liquore, observabitur, ab aqua ad altitudinem aperturae pertingente suber protrudi; seu imo, seu laterali, sive in verticem prorrecto foramini, fuerit insertum.

423 By a single trial one may explore the pressure of fluids in every direction. For if several holes are made in a vessel, one looking perpendicularly down toward the horizon, another vertical to it, another let into the side, and a stopper of cork is fitted to each opening under the condition that it fit the hole exactly, yet can be removed by a rather light impression; then, the liquid being let in, it will be observed that the cork is pushed out by the water reaching the height of the opening, whether it was inserted in the bottom hole, the lateral one, or the one stretched out toward the top.

Lex III. Fluida homogenea se componunt ad libellam, sive ad eandem horizontalem lineam.

LAW III. HOMOGENEOUS FLUIDS ARRANGE THEMSELVES AT A LEVEL, OR ALONG THE SAME HORIZONTAL LINE .

424 Nimirùm omnes fluidi partes sese mutuò, non secundum perpendiculares lineas tantùm, verùm & secundum obliquas in aequilibrio sustinent. Atque de primo indubium est; scilicet secundum perpendiculares lineas, fluida aequilibrare semet; una quippè è columnis, in quas divisum cogitatur, nequit descendere, quin vicinae, & contingentes ascendant: quemadmodùm pondus in lance una deprimi non potest, quin alterum in altera eodem ipso tempore adtollatur. In homogeneis certè patescit, momenta columnarum fluidi aequari; partium enim ad descensum nisus, ac velocitas est omnium aequalis, massa quoque ejusdem inter eas generis; vis igitur ad motum in singulis par habetur.

424 Namely, all the parts of a fluid sustain one another mutually in equilibrium, not only along perpendicular lines but also along oblique ones. And as to the first there is no doubt, namely that fluids balance themselves along perpendicular lines; for one of the columns into which the fluid is thought to be divided cannot descend unless the neighboring and contiguous ones ascend: just as a weight in one pan cannot be depressed without the other in the other pan being raised at that very same time. In homogeneous fluids, certainly, it is evident that the momenta of the columns of the fluid are equal; for the striving of the parts toward descent, and their velocity, is equal in all, and so also is the mass, being of the same kind among them; the force for motion is therefore held to be equal in each.

425 Deindè, quoniam (per Legem II.) pressio fluidorum in omnem partem porrigitur, columnae perpendiculares ab obliquis librantur. Quo circa inter omnes fluidi homogenei partes aequilibratio obtinebitur: neque una ejus portio supra horizontalem lineam altius exsurget, quàm altera. Quod quidem experientiae haud adversatur, quâ notum, liquorem ad labia vasis paululum adsurgere: aut, si spatium, quo fluidum comprehenditur protendatur amplius, in convexam abire superficiem eas partes, quae ab extremis versùs medium protenduntur; primum namque ab ipsa liquoris, & laterum vasis proportione, atque adeò adhaesione proficiscitur: alterum ab aequilibrij lege pendet omninò; si quidem telluris superficiei, dum fluida sese adaptant, necessum est, ut quamvis in minore spatio rectam, quoad sensum, lineam tueantur, in majori tamen, superficiem versus centrum suam aequabiliter extrorsum flectant.

425 Next, since (by Law II.) the pressure of fluids extends in every direction, the perpendicular columns are balanced by the oblique ones. Wherefore equilibrium will be obtained among all the parts of a homogeneous fluid; nor will one portion of it rise higher above the horizontal line than another. This indeed is not contrary to experience, by which it is known that a liquid rises a little at the lips of the vessel; or that, if the space in which the fluid is comprised is extended more widely, those parts which stretch from the extremes toward the middle go off into a convex surface; for the first proceeds from the very proportion of the liquid and of the sides of the vessel, and so from adhesion; the second depends entirely on the law of equilibrium, since, while fluids adapt themselves to the surface of the earth, it is necessary that, though in a smaller space they keep a straight line so far as the senses go, yet in a larger one they bend their surface evenly outward with respect to the center.

426 Lex IV. Fluida homogenea in tubis communicantibus [quemcumque hi situm obtineant; & quâcumque perimetro definiantur] ad eandem altitudinem suspensa aequilibrantur.

426 Law IV. Homogeneous fluids in communicating tubes (whatever position these may hold, and by whatever perimeter they may be defined) are balanced when suspended to the same height.

427 In primis si aequali perimetro donentur tubi, & ad perpendiculum erigantur, res in comperto est. Deindè si ad

427 In the first place, if the tubes are endowed with an equal perimeter and are erected perpendicularly, the matter is ascertained. Next, if they are supposed to be inclined to the horizon,

p. 138

horizontem inclinari ponantur, aequilibrii ratio non minus elucet (ex Lege I.) si demùm perimetri tuborum sint inaequales, ex Geostaticis eruitur principiis, fluida in aequilibrio futura, si obtineat quidem, ut reciproca molis in uno, & in altero velocitatis ratio habeatur. Atqui haec ratio est molis, ac velocitatis in fluido tubis ejusmodi contento. Statuatur enim tubus a b (Fig. LV.) amplitudine alterum C d, centies superare: fieri nequit, ut fluidum in illo deprimatur versus e, altitudine unius pollicis, quin motus in angustiore fiat ad altitudinem centum digitorum.

the reason of the equilibrium shines out no less (from Law I.). If, finally, the perimeters of the tubes are unequal, it is derived from the principles of Statics that the fluids will be in equilibrium if it holds that the ratio of the mass in the one is reciprocal to the ratio of the velocity in the other. But this ratio of mass and velocity is had in a fluid contained in tubes of this kind. For let the tube a b (Fig. LV.) be supposed to exceed the other, C d, a hundred times in breadth: it cannot happen that the fluid in the former is depressed toward e by the height of one inch without a motion taking place in the narrower one to the height of a hundred digits.

428 Est igitur sicuti moles fluidi ampliore tubo comprehensi ad molem in arctiore, ita reciprocè velocitas in hoc ad velocitatem in illo: momenta proindè utrinque sunt aequalia; atque hinc aequilibrium fluidi in utroque. Jam verò in homogeneis fluidis id tunc fieri, quum eandem ipsa altitudinem obtinent, patet: quum enim pressio sit in ratione composita altitudinis, & basis (ex Lege I.) si verticalis sectio e f, tanquam basis communis, spectetur & per eam horizontalis linea m n agatur, eriganturque perpendicula m a, n d, erit pressio versùs basim, ceu fundum parte una = e f m a, ex altera = e f n d. Quoniam verò momenta aequantur fluidi (ex dictis) & gravitas specifica (ex hypoth.) est eadem; ac propterea in mutuae pressionis ad invicèm comparatione hujus, ceu diversa foret, nulla sit ratio habenda: consequitur, pressum in crure utróque versùs e f, secundum directiones oppositas tendentem aequari, hoc est: e f m a = e f n d atque per e f dividendo facta, erit m a = n d, sive altitudines aequales, ac proindè m n, & a d, perpendicula aequalia intercipiunt. Est autem m n (ex construct.) horizontalis linea. Ergo a d, sivè superficies geminae fluidi in utroque tubo ad libellam constituuntur.

428 As, therefore, the mass of the fluid comprised in the wider tube is to the mass in the narrower, so reciprocally is the velocity in the latter to the velocity in the former: the momenta are therefore equal on both sides; and hence the equilibrium of the fluid in both. Now, that in homogeneous fluids this comes about when they obtain the same height is clear: for since the pressure is in the compound ratio of height and base (from Law I.), if the vertical section e f is regarded as a common base, and the horizontal line m n is drawn through it, and the perpendiculars m a, n d are erected, the pressure toward the base will be, on the one part, = e f m a, on the other = e f n d. But since the momenta of the fluid are equal (from what has been said), and the specific gravity (by hypothesis) is the same, and therefore in the mutual comparison of the pressure no account need be taken of it as though it were different, it follows that the pressure in each leg toward e f, tending in opposite directions, is equal, that is: e f m a = e f n d; and, division by e f being made, m a = n d will hold, or the heights are equal, and hence m n and a d intercept equal perpendiculars. But m n (by construction) is a horizontal line. Therefore a d, or the twin surface of the fluid in each tube, is settled at a level.

429 Lex V. Fluida heterogenea in tubis communicantibus cujuscumvis [?] figurae atque perimetri, & quomodolibet ad horizontem inclinatis, in aequilibrio persistunt, quum illorum altitudines fuerint reciprocè, ut eorum gravitates specificae.

429 Law V. Heterogeneous fluids in communicating tubes of any figure and perimeter whatever, and inclined to the horizon in any manner whatever, persist in equilibrium when their heights are reciprocally as their specific gravities.

430 Sint enim in tubis fluida hoc modo comparata, ut altitudo a E (Fig. LVI.) sit ad altitudinem b F, sicut est reciprocè gravitas specifica fluidi G ad gravitatem fluidi g: futurum assero, ut in aequilibrio conquiescant, quum etenim gravitatis diversae isthic habenda sit ratio, contrà atque in homogeneis momenta utriusque ac pressio versùs communem sectionem B D eo pacto inter sese conferri debent, ut gravitatis discrimen in considerationem adducatur: quamvis ubi seorsim spectantur, & citrà comparationem, pressio (per Legem I.) fluidorum duntaxat ex altitudine, & basi aestimetur; iccirco momentorum aequalitas obtinebitur, & aequilibrium consistet, quum eadem fuerit à centro motus distantiarum ratio, quae est reciprocè gravitatum (per Princip. Stat. III.)

430 For let fluids be so arranged in the tubes that the height a E (Fig. LVI.) is to the height b F as, reciprocally, the specific gravity of the fluid G is to the gravity of the fluid g: I assert that they will rest in equilibrium. For since account must here be taken of the diverse gravity, contrary to what holds in homogeneous fluids, the momenta of each, and the pressure toward the common section B D, must be compared with each other in such a way that the difference of gravity is brought into consideration: although, where they are regarded separately and without comparison, the pressure of fluids (by Law I.) is estimated only from height and base; therefore equality of momenta will be obtained, and the equilibrium will stand, when the ratio of the distances from the center of motion is the same as that which is reciprocally the ratio of the gravities (by Princip. Stat. III.)

431 At sectio communis, seu basis, velut centrum motus rectè intelligitur, altitudines verò sunt ipsae ab eodem distantiae; si

431 But the common section, or base, is understood as the center of motion; and the heights themselves are the distances from it; since

p. 139

quidem (per Legem dictam) pressio, libramentumque fluidorum, quum ex se expectantur, ab his pendeat, ac repetatur, oportet. Aequilibrium igitur fluida heterogenea component, si altitudines fuerint reciprocè, ut specificae ipsorum gravitates.

indeed (by the Law cited) the pressure and balancing of fluids, when they are regarded in themselves, must depend upon these and be derived from them. Heterogeneous fluids will therefore compose an equilibrium if their heights are reciprocally as their specific gravities.

432 Lex VI. Fluida actu fluentia, quum ex ampliore spatio in arctiùs transeunt, motum in ipso transfluxu accélerant.

432 Law VI. Fluids in actual flow, when they pass from a wider space into a narrower one, accelerate their motion in the very passage.

433 Ponatur fluidum ex vase profluere hac lege, ut amplitudo spatii ex. gr. cylindri, decuplo sit major, quàm apertura, quae lumen tubi vocatur, ex qua fluidum erumpit: dico, fluidum decuplo majori celeritate ad aperturam erupturum, quàm movebatur in spatio latiore. Adigatur enim fluidum cylindro comprehensum vi quadamumcumque versùs angustiorem partem, eo quidem pacto, ut intervallo momenti unius pollicem spatii emetiri debeat. Perspicuum est fluidi massam decuplam, relatè ad diametrum orificii, promoveri non posse hac ratione, quin eodem simul tempore per arctiorem partem, fluidi portio digiti spatium altitudine aequans, & decuplo major latitudine orificii, indè propellatur. Atqui fluidi quantitas pollicem unum alta, & latitudine aperturam decies continens, nequit data temporis intercapedine spatium decuplo minus permeare, quin celeritas decuplo augescat; necessum igitur est, ut decem partes, quas longitudo vel altitudo digiti complectitur, totidem partibus, in quas latitudo foraminis dirimitur, per ordinem respondeant, sive adplicentur momento temporis eodem. Id, quod citra incrementum celeritatis ad decuplum fieri haud potest: quum ad motus celeritatem perindè sit omnino, sive corpus = 1/10 spatii dato tempore percurrat spatium coporis decuplum, seu moles corporea decuplo major, quam sit extensio spatii, eodem tempore per spatium = 1/10 parti corporis feratur.

433 Let a fluid be supposed to flow out of a vessel under this condition, that the breadth of the space, e.g. of a cylinder, is ten times greater than the opening, which is called the lumen of the tube, from which the fluid bursts out: I say that the fluid will burst out at the opening with a velocity ten times greater than that with which it moved in the wider space. For let the fluid comprised in the cylinder be driven by any force whatever toward the narrower part, in such a way that in the interval of one moment it must traverse an inch of space. It is clear that a tenfold mass of fluid, relative to the diameter of the orifice, cannot be moved forward in this way without a portion of the fluid, equaling in height the space of a digit and ten times greater than the breadth of the orifice, being at the same time driven out thence through the narrower part. But a quantity of fluid one inch high, and containing the opening ten times in breadth, cannot pass through a space ten times smaller in the given interval of time unless its velocity grows tenfold; it is therefore necessary that the ten parts which the length or height of the digit comprises correspond in order to as many parts into which the breadth of the hole is divided, or be applied to them in the same moment of time. This cannot be done without an increase of the velocity to tenfold: since, as regards the velocity of motion, it is altogether the same whether a body = 1/10 of the space runs through, in a given time, a space ten times the body, or a corporeal mass ten times greater than the extension of the space is carried in the same time through a space = 1/10 part of the body.

434 Deindè res eadem hoc etiam momento nititur, quòd quum fluidum ex latiore spatio transit in arctius, partes laterales constrictos aperturae parietes offendant, atque adeò impedimentum suimet effluxus habeant; à fluido autèm urgente identidem, & liberiùs sese per spatium largius infundente constringantur arctiori tramite: hoc verò pacto fit, ut fluentis liquidi partes per orificium rectà libereque fluxurae, impetum faciant majorem, atque facilem sibi exitum nactae illicò foras profiliant: quam obrem necesse est, ut motus celeritas capiat incrementum.

434 Next, the same thing rests also on this ground, that when a fluid passes from a wider space into a narrower, the lateral parts strike against the narrowed walls of the opening and so meet with a hindrance to their own outflow; but, the fluid continually urging them and pouring itself more freely through the larger space, they are squeezed into the narrower path; and in this way it comes about that the parts of the flowing liquid that are to flow straight and freely through the orifice make a greater impetus and, having found an easy exit, at once leap out: for which reason it is necessary that the velocity of the motion receive an increase.

p. 140

De Fluidorum cum solidis immersis aequilibrii ratione.

ON THE RATIO OF THE EQUILIBRIUM OF FLUIDS WITH IMMERSED SOLIDS .

435 Modò fluidorum inter se pressione considerata, explicanda [?] superest eorum cum solidis immersis aequilibrii ratio. De hoc argumento post Archimedem s1 Galilaeus, Stevinus, Mersennus, Boylius, Varignonius, Mariottus, Newtonus, aliique permulti egerunt: nos rem summatim expendemus, paucis legibus doctrinam complectendo: quas priusquam per ordinem connectamus, immersionis librationisque solidorum in fluidis corporum veluti naturam contemplemur paululum est necesse. Nimirum grave solidum fluido gravi nequit immergi, nisi volumen fluidi par ipsi solido, quod per immersionem recipitur, sua de statione dimoveatur [?].

435 Having just considered the pressure of fluids among themselves, there remains to be explained the ratio of their equilibrium with immersed solids. On this subject, after Archimedes (m), Galileo, Stevin, Mersenne, Boyle, Varignon, Mariotte, Newton and very many others have treated: we shall weigh the matter summarily, embracing the doctrine in a few laws; before we connect these in order, it is necessary to contemplate a little what is, as it were, the nature of the immersion and balancing of solid bodies in fluids. Namely, a heavy solid cannot be immersed in a heavy fluid unless a volume of the fluid equal to the solid itself, which is received by the immersion, is moved from its station.

436 Excipe tamen, nisi corpus sit spongiosum: tunc enim fluidum magna parte subit poros solidi; aut nisi hoc immersum dissolvatur facilè: eo quippe casu particulae à solido avulsae fluidi poris se insinuabunt. Quamobrem, ut immersio reapse consequatur, solidum pondere suo resistentiam massae fluidi, suo loco excludendae vincat necesse est: unde fit, ut tanta praecisè corporis solidi pars intra fluidum sit recipienda, quantum est volumen seu moles, quam solidum suomet pondere dimovere loco suo potest: atque ut immersio eo usque pergat, donec idem volumen immerso corpori pondere sit aequale [?]. Luculenter ista intelligentur, si fluidum in partes, seu columnas aequales mente dispescatur, unique earum corpus solidum respondere atque incumbere cogitetur. Hoc intellecto consequuntur pro triplici conditione, totidem leges.

436 Except, however, if the body is spongy: for then the fluid in great part enters the pores of the solid; or unless, being immersed, it is easily dissolved; for in that case the particles torn from the solid will insinuate themselves into the pores of the fluid. Wherefore, in order that immersion actually follow, the solid must by its weight overcome the resistance of the mass of fluid to be excluded from its place: whence it comes about that precisely so great a part of the solid body is to be received within the fluid as is the volume, or mass, which the solid can move from its place by its own weight; and that the immersion proceeds until that same volume is equal in weight to the immersed body. These things will be clearly understood if the fluid is divided in the mind into equal parts, or columns, and the solid body is thought to correspond to, and rest upon, one of them. This being understood, there follow, for a threefold condition, as many laws.

Leges de motu libratorio solidorum fluidis immersorum.

LAWS OF THE BALANCING MOTION OF SOLIDS IMMERSED IN FLUIDS .

437 Lex I. Si corpus solidum ejusdem fuerit gravitatis specificae cum fluido, in quo immergitur, sistet intra fluidi superficiem ubivis, & in quo fuerit constitutum loco, immotum persistet [?].

437 Law I. If a solid body is of the same specific gravity as the fluid in which it is immersed, it will remain unmoved anywhere within the surface of the fluid, and in the place in which it has been set.

438 Quoniam solidum ac fluidum sub aequalibus dimensionibus eadem pollent gravitate, eo prorsus modo se habet solidum, quo illud fluidi volumen, cujus locum illud occupat. Atqui fluidi volumen hoc ante immersionem cum ceteris fluidi partibus suo in loco immotum aequilibrium servaverat. Solidum ergo immersum etiam cum illis in aequilibrio conquiescit. Id clarè percipietur, si fluidum in columnas aequales illi, cui solidum innititur, divisum concipiatur, ac fluidi volumen loco suo expulsum, à reliqua sua mole avelli, substituto illic solido immerso [?].

438 Since the solid and the fluid have the same gravity under equal dimensions, the solid behaves in altogether the same way as that volume of the fluid whose place it occupies. But this volume of the fluid, before the immersion, had kept its equilibrium with the other parts of the fluid, unmoved in its place. Therefore the immersed solid also rests in equilibrium with them. This will be clearly perceived if the fluid is conceived to be divided into columns equal to that on which the solid rests, and the volume of fluid expelled from its place is supposed to be torn away from the rest of its mass, the immersed solid being substituted there.

Libri duo qui vulgò nuncupantur De insidentibus humido, commentariis illustrati à Federico Commandino [?].

The two books commonly called De insidentibus humido, illustrated with commentaries by Federico Commandino.

p. 141

439 Lex II. Si corpus solidum specificè sit levius fluido, cum immergitur, illud aliqua solùm parte demergetur.

439 Law II. If a solid body is specifically lighter than the fluid in which it is immersed, it is sunk in it with only some part of itself.

440 Fluidum namque (ex hypoth.) est specificè gravius solido. Igitur fluidum, minori sub volumine acceptum pondere adaequat ipsum solidum, sic ut volumen hoc fluidi unam duntaxat solidi partem exaequet. At immersio corporis solidi eo usquè tantùm pertingit, donec fluidi volumen expulsum tanti sit ponderis, quanti est immersum corpus (per §. 435.) ergo solidum specificè levius fluido, aliqua sui parte solum illi immergitur.

440 For the fluid (by hypothesis) is specifically heavier than the solid. Therefore the fluid, taken under a smaller volume, will equal the solid itself in weight, so that this volume of the fluid equals only one part of the solid. But the immersion of the solid body reaches only so far, until the volume of fluid expelled is of as great a weight as the immersed body (by §. 435.); therefore a solid specifically lighter than the fluid is sunk into it with only some part of itself.

441 Lex III. Si corpus solidum specificè sit gravius fluido, huic illud totum immergitur, ejusque fundum petit.

441 Law III. If a solid body is specifically heavier than the fluid, it is wholly immersed in it and seeks its bottom.

442 Solidum eo usque immergitur, donec volumen fluidi loco suo extrusum, illi pondere sit aequale, (per §. 435.) Itaque si volumen expulsum minus ponderis contineat, quàm corpus solidum, hoc totum immergetur. At vero fluidi volumen illud minoris est ponderis, ponitur quippè corpus solidum specificè graviùs: fluidum proindè suo aequali volumine minus ponderis comprehendit. Solidum ergo totum immergetur. Porrò immersum hac lege ubi fuerit, quum in quavis à fundo distantia obtineat, illam fluidi columnam, quae solido est subjecta, majori pondere atque ad pressum majore nisu pollere, quàm ceteras; illa cum his aequilibrium non constituet: proindè fiet, ut nuspiam immotum consistat corpus solidum, sed in vasis fundum praecipitet sese. Hinc

442 The solid is immersed until the volume of fluid thrust out of its place is equal to it in weight (by §. 435.). Therefore, if the expelled volume contains less weight than the solid body, the latter will be wholly immersed. But that volume of fluid is of less weight; for the solid body is supposed to be specifically heavier: the fluid therefore comprises less weight in a volume equal to it. The solid will therefore be wholly immersed. Further, once it is immersed by this law, since at any distance whatever from the bottom it holds that the column of fluid which is placed under the solid has a greater weight, and is able to press with a greater striving than the others, that column will not establish equilibrium with these: hence it will come about that the solid body nowhere stands unmoved, but hurls itself to the bottom of the vessel. Hence

Corollarium.

COROLLARY. 443

443 Quum solidum immersum fluidi volumen loco excludat, hoc autem à ceteris ejusdem partibus suo in situ fuerit sustentatum: necessum est, ut ubi solidum in expulsi voluminis locum succedit, ab iisdem fluidi partibus tantumdem ponderis, quantum in ipso solido est sustentetur, nempè quantum suo de situ dimota fluidi portio continet: ac proindè, ut solidum tanto sui ponderis veluti privetur, quanti est volumen fluidi, quod immersione facta loco suo exclusum fuit. Pondus hoc solidi diminutum respectiva, comparativa, aut adparens gravitas nuncupari adsolet; quum altera, quae corpori in spatio penitùs vacuo competeret, vera, & absoluta rectè adpelletur.

Since the immersed solid excludes a volume of the fluid from its place, and this had been sustained in its position by the other parts of the same fluid, it is necessary that, where the solid succeeds into the place of the excluded volume, as much weight is sustained in the solid itself by those same parts of the fluid as the portion of the fluid moved from its position contains; and hence that the solid is, as it were, deprived of as much of its weight as is the volume of fluid that was excluded from its place when the immersion was made. This diminished weight of the solid is wont to be called respective, comparative, or apparent gravity; while the other, which belongs to the body in a space altogether void, is rightly called true and absolute.

444 Unde quia gravitas haec à sola differentia, quae est inter specificam gravitatem utriusque, hoc est, à densitatis discrimine proficiscitur, iccircò ejusdem solidi immersi respectiva gravitas eadem est, sive immersum corpus fluidi superficiem coaequet, seu profundiùs agatur, posita fluidi ubivis aequabili densitate. Porrò id quod absolutae gravitati decedit, sive jactura ponderis, quam facit idem solidum in diversis fluidis eam rationem habet, quàm gravitates specificae fluidorum. Jacturae verò, quas diversa solida eodem in fluido accipiunt sunt inter se, ut ipsa volumina solidorum.

444 Hence, since this gravity proceeds solely from the difference which exists between the specific gravity of each, that is, from the difference of densities, the respective gravity of the same immersed solid is therefore the same whether the immersed body is level with the surface of the fluid or is driven more deeply, the density of the fluid being supposed everywhere equal. Further, that which departs from the absolute gravity, or the loss of weight which the same solid suffers in different fluids, has the same ratio as the specific gravities of the fluids. But the losses which different solids undergo in the same fluid are to one another as the volumes themselves of the solids.

p. 142

PHYSICES

PHYSICS,

PARS III.

PART III .

ELECTROLOGIA seu

ELECTROLOGY, or

De Virtute Electrica.

ON ELECTRIC VIRTUE .

445 Nihil fortassè est, quod nostra hac aetate majus Naturali scientiae studio decus, atque incrementum adtulerit, aut acrius Philosophorum excitarit ingenia, quàm vis electrica, ut proindè turpe videatur Naturae arcana inquirentibus pulcherrimam hanc Philosophiae partem aut neglexisse penitùs, quod fecerunt Veteres, aut vix leviter adtigisse, quod & Recentiores plurimi, nescio qua de causa fecére. Quapropter, ne quidquam quod ad rem hanc pertineat praetermittam, Clarissimis ex universa Europa Philosophis, praecipuè verò Cl. Pauliano s1 facem praeferentibus, quaestionem hanc utilissimam sanè ac jocundissimam, primus omnium in America nostra, adcuratiori methodo, majorique quâ possim claritate tradere decrevi.

here is perhaps nothing which in this age of ours has brought 445 T greater honor and increase to the study of Natural science, or has more keenly roused the wits of Philosophers, than the electric force, so that it seems shameful for those who inquire into the secrets of Nature either to have entirely neglected this most beautiful part of Philosophy, as the Ancients did, or to have barely touched it lightly, as very many of the Moderns too have done, for I know not what reason. Wherefore, so as not to pass over anything that pertains to this matter, with the most illustrious Philosophers of all Europe, and especially the illustrious Paulian (n), carrying the torch before me, I have resolved to hand down this question, truly most useful and most pleasant, first of all in our America, by a more accurate method and with the greatest clarity I can.

446 In hac ergò de causis electricae virtutis pertractandâ quaestione, de qua maximâ cum animorum contentione ab annis fermè sexaginta disputatur apud Recentiores Physicos, methodum selegimus sequentem. I. Praemittemus definitiones aliquot, quae jure vocantur primae notiones Electricitatis. II. Electrica referemus experimenta, quae necessariò debent exponi in qualibet hypothesi physicâ. III. Varias trademus celebriorum Physicorum sententias circa materiam electricam, ipsarumque naevos indicabimus. IV. Sententiam Cl. Pauliani, quae & nostra est, aperiemus, in eaque phaenomena jam relata tentabimus exponere. V denique. Proponemus & solvere conabimur praecipua argumenta, quae contra nostram sententiam fieri ab adversariis solent.

446 In treating, then, this question of the causes of electric virtue, about which there has been dispute, with the greatest contention of minds, among the Modern Physicists for nearly sixty years, we have chosen the following method. I. We shall set down beforehand some definitions, which are rightly called the first notions of Electricity. II. We shall report the electric experiments which must necessarily be explained in any physical hypothesis. III. We shall hand down the various opinions of the more celebrated Physicists concerning electric matter, and shall point out their blemishes. IV. We shall disclose the opinion of the illustrious Paulian, which is ours too, and in it we shall attempt to explain the phenomena already reported. V. Finally, we shall propose, and try to answer, the principal arguments that are usually brought by adversaries against our opinion.

Grand Dictionnaire de Physique, Verb. Electricité, ex quo, paucis immutatis, universam hanc excerpsimus Dissertat.

Grand Dictionnaire de Physique, under the word Electricité, from which, with a few changes, we have excerpted this whole Dissertation.

p. 143

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De notionibus ad quaestionem virtutis Electricae praeámbulis.

On the notions preliminary to the question of electric virtue.

447 Notio I. Componitur Electrica machina primò, globo vitreo, cujus diameter potest esse major vel minor: secundò, rota lignea, cujus ope motus rotationis imprimitur vitreo globo, quem manus sicca ádfricat: tertiò, tubo ferreo, qui per tenuissimas orichalci laméllas cum vitreo globo communicationem habet: quartò, funículis sericis, qui ferreum tubum suspensum tenent horizontaliter: quintò deniquè, scabéllo resináceo in modum placentae confecto, in quo possit homo suis stans pedibus, facilè, commodèque constitui. Exactè admodum repraesentatur haec machina per Fig LVII.

447 Notion I. An electric machine is composed, first, of a glass globe, whose diameter can be larger or smaller; second, of a wooden wheel, by whose means a rotary motion is impressed on the glass globe, which a dry hand rubs; third, of an iron tube, which has communication with the glass globe through very thin plates of brass; fourth, of silk cords, which hold the iron tube suspended horizontally; fifth, finally, of a stool of resin made in the shape of a cake, on which a man can easily and conveniently be placed standing on his feet. This machine is represented quite exactly by Fig. LVII.

448 Notio II. Corpus actu electricum, est corpus versus quod eunt, & à quo redeunt corpora quaeque levissima, qualia sunt tabaccum tritum, orichalci folia tenuissima, avium plúmulae &c. Virtus namque electrica manifestari solet per adtractiones, repulsiones, scintillas, inflammationes, motitationes &c. Sese prodit etiam virtus electrica per flammam caeruleam, quae cum crepitu excitatur ex corpore electrico. Lóquimur hìc de hac electricitatis specie, quam in pósterum totalem, & perfectam adpellabimus. Notio III. Ex corporibus alia sunt per se, & alia per communicationem electrica. Cera obsignatoria (vulgò lacre), súccinum, alúmen, ádamas, crystállum, ac praecipuè vitrum sunt córpora per se electrica. Metalla autèm & corpora viventia sunt corpora per communicationem electrica.

448 Notion II. A body actually electric is a body toward which all very light bodies go, and from which they come back, such as ground tobacco, very thin leaves of brass, the little feathers of birds, etc. For electric virtue is usually manifested by attractions, repulsions, sparks, inflammations, agitations, etc. Electric virtue betrays itself also by a blue flame, which is excited with a crackling from the electric body. We speak here of that species of electricity which we shall hereafter call total and perfect. Notion III. Of bodies, some are electric in themselves, and others by communication. Sealing wax (commonly lacre), amber, alum, diamond, crystal, and especially glass are bodies electric in themselves. Metals, however, and living bodies are bodies electric by communication.

449 Notio IV. Corpora per se electrica virtutem suam manifestant, quotiescumque panno, vel papyro, vel manu sicca fricantur. Corpora autèm per communicationem electrica vim electricam perfectam concipiunt, quotiescumque per filum ferreum, aut per funiculum cannábinum communicationem habent cum corporibus per se, & actu eléctricis. Notio V. Corpora per se electrica nullam, aut quasi nullam virtutem electricam per communicationem, & vice versa: corpora per communicationem electrica nullam, aut quasi nullam virtutem electricam per frictionem acquirunt. Notio VI. Omnia omninò orbis hujus corpora sunt verosimiliter, aut per se, aut per communicationem electrica.

449 Notion IV. Bodies electric in themselves manifest their virtue whenever they are rubbed with cloth, or paper, or a dry hand. Bodies electric by communication, however, receive a perfect electric force whenever they have communication, through an iron wire or a hempen cord, with bodies electric in themselves and in act. Notion V. Bodies electric in themselves acquire no electric virtue, or as good as none, by communication; and conversely, bodies electric by communication acquire no electric virtue, or as good as none, by friction. Notion VI. All the bodies of this world without exception are, in all likelihood, electric either in themselves or by communication.

p. 144

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De Praecipuis experimentis electricis.

On the principal electric experiments. 450

450 Historicè tantùm in hoc Cap. referemus experimenta praecipua, quae fieri solent ope electricae machinae, ipsisque per modum observationum subjiciemus experimenta, minus praecipua, & quasi secundaria.

In this Chapter we shall only report, historically, the principal experiments which are usually made by means of the electric machine, and to them we shall subjoin, by way of observations, the less principal and, as it were, secondary experiments.

451. Experimentum I. Motus circularis imprimatur ope rotae, globo vitreo, intereadùm adfricatúr manu sicca. Suspendatur horizontaliter funiculorum sericorum ope, tubus ex albo ferro (vulgò oja de lata) confectus, qui cum vitreo globo per tenues aliquot orichalci láminas communicationem habeat. Tantam vim electricam cóncipiet ferreus tubus, ut statím flammulam caeruleam ex ipsius sinu cum crépitu prosilientem videas, si ad ipsum admoveas digitum, clavim, uno verbo, corpus quodcumque per communicationem electricum.

451 Experiment I. Let a circular motion be impressed by means of the wheel on the glass globe, while meanwhile it is rubbed with a dry hand. Let a tube made of white iron (commonly oja de lata), which has communication with the glass globe through some thin plates of brass, be suspended horizontally by means of silk cords. The iron tube will receive so great an electric force that you will at once see a little blue flame leaping out with a crackling from its bosom if you bring near it your finger, or a key, or, in a word, any body electric by communication.

452 Observationes I. Tubus idem ferreus funiculorum cannàbinorum ope suspensus vim electricam, vel nullam, vel admodùm exiguam cóncipit, quantòcumque motu rotationis donetur vitreus globus. II. Ex tubo ferreo electrica virtute donato, nullam omninò flammam excitabis, si versùs ipsum admoveas ceram obsignatoriam, túbulum vitreum, vel quodcumque aliud corpus per se electricum. III. Ex tubo ferreo nondùm eléctrica virtute donato pendeant duo fila cannábina sibi invicem parallela, à se invicèm haec duo fila recedent, atque ángulum efficient, statim ut vim electricam concipiet ferreus tubus. Imò quidem eò major erit angulus à duobus filis effectus, quò vividior erit electricitas tubi. Hinc Electrometri nomen habent haec duo cannábina fila.

452 Observations. I. The same iron tube, suspended by means of hempen cords, receives either no electric force or very little, however great the motion of rotation with which the glass globe is endowed. II. From an iron tube endowed with electric virtue you will excite no flame at all if you bring near it sealing wax, a little glass tube, or any other body electric in itself. III. If two hempen threads, parallel to each other, hang from an iron tube not yet endowed with electric virtue, these two threads will recede from each other and form an angle as soon as the iron tube receives electric force. Indeed, the angle made by the two threads will be the greater, the livelier the electricity of the tube. Hence these two hempen threads have the name of Electrometer.

453 Experimentum II. Super corpus per se electricum; qualis est placenta resinácea, collocetur animal quodcumque, & ope fili ferrei communicationem habeat hoc animal cum tubo de quo loquebamur in experimento I: tantam vim electricam quasi subitò concipiet, ut si digitum admoveas, ex ipso cum crepitu prorumpat flamma caerulea, quae tùm tibi, tùm ipsi dolorem pariat adeò sensibilem, ut vos aciculam leviter pupugisse statim credidêritis.

453 Experiment II. Upon a body electric in itself, such as a cake of resin, let any animal be placed, and let this animal have communication, by means of an iron wire, with the tube of which we spoke in experiment I: it will receive so great an electric force, almost suddenly, that if you bring your finger near, a blue flame will burst out from it with a crackling, which will cause both you and it a pain so sensible that you would at once believe you had been lightly pricked with a needle.

454 Observationes. I Ad quamcumque distantiam ex tubo ferreo reperiatur placenta resinacea, is qui fuit super illam collocatus, virtutem electricam statim acquiret dummodò per filum ferreum, aut per funiculum cannábinum mádidum cum eléctrico tubo communicationem habeat. II Qui super placentam resinaceam collocatur, is flammam non éxcitat ex electrico tubo quo

454 Observations. I. At whatever distance from the iron tube the cake of resin is found, he who has been placed upon it will at once acquire electric virtue, provided he has communication with the electric tube through an iron wire or a wet hempen cord. II. He who is placed upon the cake of resin does not excite a flame from the electric tube with which

p. 145

cum habet communicationem III Si quis humi consistens manu teneat vas aliquod metallicum in quo reperiatur spiritus vini calidus, ipsumque offerat homini super placentam resinaceam collocato, liquorem hunc homo jam electricus inflammabit, quotiescumque ignem ex illo tentabit excitare. IV. Idem prorsùs phaenomenum accidit, quum homo jam electricus vas metallicum manu tenet, & homo electricâ virtute destitutus flammam tentat excitare.

he is in communication. III. If someone standing on the ground holds in his hand some metal vessel containing warm spirit of wine, and offers it to a man placed on the resin cake, this man, now electric, will set the liquor on fire as often as he tries to draw fire from it. IV. Exactly the same phenomenon occurs when the man who is now electric holds the metal vessel in his hand, and a man destitute of electric virtue tries to draw the flame.

455 Experimentum III. Corpora quaeque levissima, qualia sunt tabacum tritum, auri vel argenti laminae tenuiores, avium plúmulae, furfur &c. nunc adtrahuntur versus corpus electrica virtute donatum, nùnc repelluntur ab hoc corpore, nùnc adhaerent huic eidem córpori. Imò quidem sese manifestat electrica virtus per itus, & reditus corporum hujusmodi levissimorum.

455 Experiment III. All the lightest bodies, such as ground tobacco, the thinner leaves of gold or silver, small bird feathers, bran, etc., are now attracted toward a body endowed with electric virtue, now repelled from this body, now cling to this same body. Indeed, electric virtue manifests itself by the goings and returnings of bodies of this kind, the lightest ones.

456 Observationes. I: electricae máchinae tubo ferreo superimponatur pátera quaedam metallica in qua reperiantur corpora levissima, tubum ferreum fugient haec omnia corpuscula statìm, ut virtutem electricam tubus concipiet. II. Si tubo ferreo subjecta fuisset haec eadem pátera, versùs tubum adtracta fuissent corpora levissima ipsi imposita, statím ut virtutem electricam tubus concepisset.

456 Observations. I. If on the iron tube of the electric machine there is placed some metal dish containing the lightest bodies, all these little bodies will flee the iron tube as soon as the tube receives the electric virtue. II. If this same dish had been placed under the iron tube, the lightest bodies put on it would have been attracted toward the tube as soon as the tube received the electric virtue.

457 Experimentum IV. Sit lagéna vitrea aquis semipléna, & folio metallico exteriùs cooperta. Sit in hac lagéna filum ferreum perpendiculariter erectum, quod ad fundum usque protendatur. Filo huic ferreo communicetùr éléctrica virtus; experientia constat, quod si quis lagénam hanc unâ manu per partem ipsius inferiorem sustineat, & alterâ manu flammam éxcitet ex supradicto filo, violentè commovebuntur duo ipsius cúbiti, & pectus (Fig. LVIII.)

457 Experiment IV. Let there be a glass flask half full of water and covered on the outside with metal foil. In this flask let an iron wire be set up perpendicularly, reaching down to the bottom. Let electric virtue be communicated to this iron wire; experience establishes that if someone holds up this flask with one hand by its lower part, and with the other hand draws a flame from the aforesaid wire, both his elbows and his chest will be violently shaken (Fig. LVIII.).

458 Observationes. I. Lagéna de qua loquimur, communicationem habeat cum tubo ferreo electrico, & quispiam unâ manu partem inferiorem lagénae tenens, aut etiam tangens, alterâ manu flammam excitet ex tubo, is eandem omninò commotionem experietur. II. Junctis manibus catenam efforment homines non pauci. Primus ex illis, partem inferiorem lagénae manu sustineat; ultimus verò flammam excitet ex electricae machinae tubo, omnes simul, & eodem instanti percutientur eâdem commotione, tùm in cúbitis, tùm in péctore. Ejusmodi experimentum primum Lugduni Batavorum factum fuit ideò vulgò experimentum primum, dicitur La experiencia de Léyden.

458 Observations. I. Let the flask of which we speak be in communication with the electric iron tube, and if anyone, holding or even touching the lower part of the flask with one hand, draws a flame from the tube with the other hand, he will feel exactly the same shock. II. Let a good many men form a chain with joined hands. Let the first of them hold up the lower part of the flask with his hand, and the last draw a flame from the tube of the electric machine; all will be struck together, and at the same instant, with the same shock, both in the elbows and in the chest. An experiment of this kind was first made at Leiden; therefore this first experiment is commonly called La experiencia de Léyden [the Leyden experiment].

459 Experimentum V. Involvatur chartâ quadam densiori pars aliqua tubi ferrei machinae electricae. Super páteram metallicam collocetur lagéna vitrea cum tubo ferreo communicans. Lagénae fundum inter, & páteram metallicam reperiatur filum ferreum; experientia constat, quod si quis ex eadem hac manu qua filum ferreum tenet, flammam éxcitet ex charta, électrici tubi partem aliquam involvente, maximo cum fragóre perforábitur charta haec densissima.

459 Experiment V. Let some part of the iron tube of the electric machine be wrapped in a rather thick paper. On a metal dish let a glass flask be placed communicating with the iron tube. Between the bottom of the flask and the metal dish let there be an iron wire; experience establishes that if someone, with the same hand with which he holds the iron wire, draws a flame from the paper wrapping some part of the electric tube, this very thick paper will be pierced with a very great crack.

460 Observationes. I. Si chartae loco ponatur avis aliqua,

460 Observations. I. If in place of the paper some bird is put,

p. 146

mortem ipsi certissimam adferent aliquot scintillae ex ipsius implumi capite excitatae. II. Loco lagénae aquis semiplenae, de qua loquebamur in experimento IV & V possumus uti quadrato vitreo, cujus operiantur pars superior, & pars inferior folio quodam metallico ad extremitates usque vitri vix sese extendente. Notum est hoc experimentum sub nomine tabellae magicae, vel speculi Frankliniani.

most certain death will be brought upon it by a few sparks drawn from its featherless head. II. In place of the flask half full of water, of which we were speaking in Experiments IV and V, we can use a square of glass whose upper part and lower part are covered with some metal foil, extending, however, scarcely to the edges of the glass. This experiment is known under the name of the magic picture, or of Franklin’s pane.

461 Experimentum VI. super tectum alti cujusdam aedificii constituatur placenta resinacea, aut vitrea. Hanc super placentam perpendiculariter erigatur aliqua virga ferrea; experientiâ constat quod si nubes aliqua, fulmen in sinu suo déferens, virgae huic ferreae superimmineat, ex ea excitabuntur scintillae eodem prorsùs modo, ac si virga communicationem habuisset cum vitreo globo actu fricato eximiae cujusdam éléctricae machinae.

461 Experiment VI. On the roof of some high building let a cake of resin, or of glass, be placed. On this cake let some iron rod be set up perpendicularly; experience establishes that if some cloud bearing lightning in its bosom hangs over this iron rod, sparks will be drawn from it in exactly the same way as if the rod had been in communication with the glass globe, actually being rubbed, of some excellent electric machine.

462 Experimentum VII. Super placentam resinaceam constituatur globi vitrei Fricator, is non modò vim electricam sensibilem concipiet, sed etiam flammam excitabit ex tubo machinae jam éléctrico ad quem digitum suum admovet. Ex memoria vestra non éxcidat ultimum hoc experimentum.

462 Experiment VII. Let the rubber of the glass globe be placed on a cake of resin: he will not only receive a sensible electric force, but will also draw a flame from the tube of the machine, now electric, to which he brings his finger. Let this last experiment not slip from your memory.

463 Observatio. Fricator idem nudo pavimento insistens extra placentam, non concipit vim electricam sensibilem. Haec sunt experimenta praecipua â Viris Clariss. Nolleto, Franklino, Beccaría, Pauliano, & aliis relata, quorum conabimur in sequenti capite explicationem adferre.

463 Observation. The same rubber, standing on the bare floor outside the cake, does not receive a sensible electric force. These are the principal experiments reported by the most distinguished men Nollet, Franklin, Beccaria, Paulian, and others, of which we shall try to give the explanation in the following chapter.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

De Causis Electricae Virtutis.

On the Causes of Electric Virtue. 464

464 Veras electricae virtutis adsignare causas, hoc opus, hic labor semper fuit in Physica quemadmodùm adparebit enumeratione sequenti.

To assign the true causes of electric virtue: this has always been the task, this the toil, in Physics, as will appear from the following enumeration.

Sententia Philosophorum Antiquiorum.

THE OPINION OF THE MORE ANCIENT PHILOSOPHERS .

465 Nullum omninò negotium, Philosophis antiquioribus facessebant electrica phaenómena. In promptu enim ipsis erant, vel qualitas quaedam occulta corporibus electricis essentialis, & intrinseca, vel innatus quidam horror vacui. Praevalebat in Scholis haec ultima sententia; plurimi enim apud antiquos adfirmabant aëra per effluvium electricum expelli, & metu vacui adduci corpora quaecumque levissima. Risu potiùs quàm seriis rationibus debet haec sententia confutari.

465 Electric phenomena gave the more ancient Philosophers no trouble at all. For they had ready at hand either some occult quality, essential and intrinsic to electric bodies, or else an innate horror of the vacuum. This last opinion prevailed in the Schools; for very many among the ancients affirmed that the air is expelled by the electric effluvium, and that any of the lightest bodies whatever are drawn in through fear of a vacuum. This opinion ought to be refuted with laughter rather than with serious reasons.

p. 147

Sententia Cartesii.

THE OPINION OF DESCARTES .

466 De causis electricae virtutis ex instituto egit Cartesius; sic enim loquitur s1. „ Ex modo quo vitrum generari dictum est, facilè colligitur praeter illa majuscula intervalla per quae globuli secundi elementi versùs omnes partes transire possunt, multas etiam rimulas oblongas inter ejus particulas reperiri, quae quum sint angustiores, quàm ut istos glóbulos recipiant, soli materiae primi elementi tránsitum praebent, putandumque est hanc materiam primi elementi omnium meatuum quos ingreditur figuras induere assuetam, per rimulas istas transeundo, in quasdam quasi fásciolas tenues, & oblongas efformari, quae quum similes rimulas in aëre circumjacente non inveniant, intra vitrum se continent, vel certè ab eo non multum evagantur, & circa ejus particulas convolútae, motu quodam circulari ex unis ejus rimulis in alias fluunt. Quamvis enim materia primi elementi fluidissima sit, quia tamen constat minutiis inaequaliter agitatis, ratione consentaneum est, ut credamus ex maximè concitatis ejus minutiis, â vitro in aërem assiduè migrare, aliasque ab aëre in vitrum earum loco reverti; sed cùm eae quae revertuntur, non sint aeque concitatae, illas quae minimùm habent agitationis, versùs rimulas, quibus nulli meatus in aëre correspondent, expelli, atque ibi unas aliis adhaerentes, fásciolas istas componere, quae fasciolae iccircò successu temporum figuras acquirunt determinatas, quas non facilè mutare possunt.

466 Descartes treated of the causes of electric virtue expressly; for thus he speaks (o): “From the manner in which glass was said to be generated, it is easily gathered that, besides those larger intervals through which the globules of the second element can pass in all directions, many small oblong chinks are also found between its particles, which, since they are too narrow to receive those globules, afford passage to the matter of the first element alone; and it must be thought that this matter of the first element, being accustomed to put on the shapes of all the passages it enters, is formed, in passing through those chinks, into certain thin and oblong little ribbons, as it were, which, since they do not find similar chinks in the surrounding air, keep themselves within the glass, or at least do not wander far from it, and, wound about its particles, flow with a certain circular motion from some of its chinks into others. For although the matter of the first element is most fluid, yet because it consists of minute parts unequally agitated, it is consonant with reason for us to believe that some of its most strongly agitated minute parts continually migrate from the glass into the air, and that others return from the air into the glass in their place; but that, since those which return are not equally agitated, those which have the least agitation are driven toward the chinks to which no passages in the air correspond, and there, clinging one to another, compose those little ribbons, which ribbons for that reason acquire in the course of time determinate shapes, which they cannot easily change.

467 „ Undè fit, ut si vitrum satis validè fricetur, ita ut non nihil incalescat, ipsae hoc motu foras excussae, per aërem quidem vicinum se dispergant, aliorumque etiam corporum vicinorum meatus ingrediantur, sed quia non tam faciles ibi vias inveniunt, statim ad vitrum revolvantur, & minutiora corpora quorum meatibus sunt implicitae, secum adducant::::: Quod autem hic de vitro notavimus, de plerisque aliis corporibus etiam credi debet; nempè quod interstitia quaedam inter eorum particulas reperiantur, quae quum nimis angusta sint ad glóbulos secundi elementi admittendos, solam materiam primi recipiunt„. Ex dictis sequitur Cartesium admisisse tanquàm principia totidèm, ea quae sequuntur.

467 “Whence it comes about that if the glass is rubbed strongly enough to grow somewhat warm, they, shaken out by this motion, disperse indeed through the neighboring air, and enter also into the passages of other neighboring bodies; but because they do not find such easy ways there, they at once roll back to the glass, and draw along with them the smaller bodies in whose passages they are entangled … And what we have noted here about glass must also be believed of most other bodies: namely, that certain interstices are found between their particles which, since they are too narrow to admit the globules of the second element, receive only the matter of the first.” From what has been said it follows that Descartes admitted as so many principles the things that follow.

468 I. in vitro quolibet éxtant pori majores, & pori minóres. Isti materiae primi elementi, illi verò glóbulis secundi elementi tránsitum praebent. II. Materia primi elementi dificiliùs movetur in aëre, quàm in poris minoribus vitri. III. Propter hanc resistentiam aëris, materia primi elementi citò revertitur in vitrum ex quo

468 I. In any glass whatever there are larger pores and smaller pores; the latter afford passage to the matter of the first element, the former to the globules of the second element. II. The matter of the first element moves with more difficulty in the air than in the smaller pores of the glass. III. Because of this resistance of the air, the matter of the first element quickly returns into the glass from which it had come

Part. 4. Princip. art. 185.

Pt. 4, Principles, art. 185.

p. 148

fuerat propter frictionem egressa. IV. Materia primi elementi, & materia electrica nullomodo distinguuntur inter se. V. Juxta Cartesium electrica phaenomena pendent à successiva quadam effluentia materiae primi elementi ex poris minoribus vitri, & adfluentia ejusdem materiae versùs poros minores ejusdem vitri, sicca manu fricati.

come out on account of the friction. IV. The matter of the first element and the electric matter are in no way distinguished from each other. V. According to Descartes, electric phenomena depend on a certain successive outflow of the matter of the first element from the smaller pores of the glass, and inflow of the same matter toward the smaller pores of the same glass, when it is rubbed with a dry hand.

469 Adnotationes. I. Gratis, & absque fundamento tanquàm principia ponuntur ea quae fuerunt enunciata numero 1. 2. 3. 4. §. 468. II. Effluentia, & adfluentia materiae electricae videtur esse potius simultanea, quàm successiva, ut adnotabitur inferiùs. III. Peculiaris haec sententia Cartesii circa materiam electricam pendet evidenter ab ipsius systemate generali quod falsum esse, à nobis demonstratum fuit §§. 45, & 46. IV. Eas omnes ob causas nobis esse rejicienda videtur Cartesii sententia circà materiam electricam.

469 Remarks. I. The things that were stated in nos. 1, 2, 3, 4 of §. 468 are laid down as principles gratuitously and without foundation. II. The outflow and inflow of the electric matter seem to be simultaneous rather than successive, as will be noted below. III. This peculiar opinion of Descartes about the electric matter evidently depends on his general system, which we have shown to be false, §§. 45 and 46. IV. For all these reasons the opinion of Descartes about the electric matter seems to us one to be rejected.

Sententia Honorati Fabri.

THE OPINION OF HONORÉ FABRI .

470 Neque profectò sententiam probabiliorem proposuit Honoratus, Fabri qui eodem quo Cartesius aevo floruit. Sic enim loquiturs1. ,, Súccinum & cera Hispanica multo igne constant, & pingui succo, quod vel ex filaminibus súccini liquescentis constat: nempè in longum ducuntur illa filámina quorum lentor, & tenacitas ín dubium revocari non possunt :::::: Partes ignis quae súccino ínsunt continuò águnt in humidum illud viscósum, & lentum, quod deindè caloris vi rarescit, ávolatque in hálitum, qui etiam lentus & viscosus est; hinc in filamina ducitur quantumvis insensibilia :::: Porro emittitur praedictus hálitus ad instar jaculi:::::

470 Nor indeed did Honoré Fabri, who flourished in the same age as Descartes, propose a more probable opinion. For thus he speaks (p): “Amber and Spanish wax consist of much fire and of a fat juice, which consists, as it were, of filaments of melting amber: namely, those filaments are drawn out in length, and their viscosity and tenacity cannot be called into doubt … The parts of fire that are in the amber act continually on that viscous and pliant moisture, which then, by the force of heat, is rarefied and flies off in an exhalation, which is itself also pliant and viscous; hence it is drawn out into filaments, however insensible … Further, the aforesaid exhalation is emitted in the manner of a dart …

471 ,, Quia proptèr lentórem materiae, filum emissum poro adhaeret, indè fit prae impetus violentia, ut filum quod plus aequo in longum ducitur, & valdè adtenuatur, vel tandèm rumpatur circà medium, vel non rumpatur quidèm, sed post validam tensionem ex prima illa emissione derivatam statim redeat etiam cum impetu :::: Analogiam habes in chorda tensa, quae si dimittatur, vel frangatur prae nimia tensione, segmenta reducuntur versùs alteram extremitatem, cui affixa est; hinc si segmentum illud cujus extremitas poro adhaeret, & non sine aliqua vi versùs porum, & succinum reducitur, incidat in minutissima corpuscula, quae facilè moveri possint, en secum rapit & ipsi succino adfigit ,, Et alibi ,, Corpus scabrum maleo dúctile vi electrica caret ,,. Sic centum, & triginta ab hinc annis de electricitate sentiebat Honoratus Fabri.

471 “Because, owing to the viscosity of the matter, the emitted thread clings to a pore, it comes about, through the violence of the impulse, that the thread, drawn out in length more than is due and greatly attenuated, either at length breaks about the middle, or indeed does not break, but after the strong tension derived from that first emission at once returns, likewise with impetus … You have an analogy in a stretched string: if it is let go, or breaks from excessive tension, its segments are drawn back toward the other extremity, to which it is fixed; hence if that segment whose extremity clings to the pore, and which is drawn back with some force toward the pore and the amber, falls upon very minute little bodies that can easily be moved, it carries them off with it and fastens them to the amber itself.” And elsewhere: “A rough body that is ductile under the hammer lacks electric force.” So, a hundred and thirty years ago, did Honoré Fabri think about electricity.

472 Adnotationes. In hac sententiâ non explicantur

472 Remarks. In this opinion the phenomena of

Tom. 4. Physic.

Vol. 4, Physics.

p. 149

phaenomena corporum per communicationem electricorum: volebat enim P. Fabri, nullum omninò corpus nequidem metalla fieri posse per communicationem electrica, ut ex postremis ipsius verbis jam citatis manifestum fit. II. Non explicatur in hac sententia undenàm oriatur in vitro tanta vis electrica. Adfirmat enim auctor hujus hypotéseos ceram obsignatoriam, & súccinum esse corpora omnium maximè electrica, de vitri autèm electricitate ne verbum quidem ullum fécerat hoc loci. III denique. Non explicantur in hac sententia phaenomena, quorum hâc tempestate tanta est copia, ut stupendum electrica machina spectaculum praebet: ergo rejicienda est sententia Honorati Fabri tanquàm insufficiens ad exponenda electrica phaenomena.

of bodies electric by communication are not explained: for Father Fabri held that no body at all, not even metals, can become electric by communication, as is manifest from his last words, already cited. II. It is not explained in this opinion whence so great an electric force arises in glass. For the author of this hypothesis affirms that sealing wax and amber are the most electric bodies of all, but in this place had not said even a single word about the electricity of glass. III, finally. In this opinion the phenomena are not explained, of which there is in this age so great an abundance that the electric machine affords an astonishing spectacle: therefore the opinion of Honoré Fabri is to be rejected as insufficient for setting forth electric phenomena.

Sententia D. DuFay.

THE OPINION OF MR. DU FAY.

473 Primus fuit in Gallia D. DuFay qui virtutis electricae quaestionem ordine quodam, & methodo perpenderit. Experimenta ipsius praecipua consignantur in Monumentis Academiae scientiarum Paris.s1 Is adfirmat duplicem esse electricitatem specificè diversam, vitream nempè, & recinaceam. Si duplex est electricitas specificè diversa, (inquit ille) duplex erit materia electrica specificè diversa; si autem duplex est materia electrica specificè diversa facilè admodùm exponentur electrica phaenomena per conflictum scilicet duplicis hujus materiae. Vult etiam D. DuFay materiàm electricam omnem vorticosè gyrare circa corpus electricum, tanquam circà centrum proprium.

473 The first in France who weighed the question of electric virtue with a certain order and method was Mr. Du Fay. His principal experiments are recorded in the Memoirs of the Paris Academy of Sciences (q). He affirms that there is a twofold electricity, specifically different, namely vitreous and resinous. If there is a twofold electricity specifically different (he says), there will be a twofold electric matter specifically different; and if there is a twofold electric matter specifically different, electric phenomena will be very easily set forth, namely through the conflict of this twofold matter. Mr. Du Fay also holds that all the electric matter whirls in the manner of a vortex about the electric body, as about its proper center.

474 Adnotationes. I. Vis electrica vitri videtur tantùm intensior esse vi electrica resínae: ergo specificè non disferunt electricitas vitrea, & resinacea electricitas: alioquin dicendum foret specificè differre fervidissimum ignem ab igne minus férvido. II. Nullum est experimentum adsignabile quo probabiliter etiam innuatur motum aliquem vorticosum existere in electrica materia: ergo tanquàm falsa rejicienda est sententia D. DuFay circà materiam electricam.

474 Remarks. I. The electric force of glass seems only to be more intense than the electric force of resin: therefore vitreous electricity and resinous electricity do not differ specifically; otherwise one would have to say that the most fervent fire differs specifically from a less fervent fire. II. There is no assignable experiment by which it is even probably intimated that some vortical motion exists in the electric matter: therefore the opinion of Mr. Du Fay about the electric matter is to be rejected as false.

Sententia D. de Molieres. — THE OPINION OF MR. DE MOLIÈRES

475 Versùs finem Lectionis suae XIV. sententiam suam exposuit D. de Molieres; haec quinque quasi capitibus comprehenditur. I. Non differt electrica materia à vorticulis olei intra quodcumque corpus electricum contentis. II. Per adfrictum manus siccae coguntur ex electrico corpore in aërem égredi oleosi vorticuli, quorum plerique sese per modum atmosphaerae disponunt circà corpus electricum. III. Sese in aëre extendunt

475 Toward the end of his Lesson XIV Mr. de Molières set forth his opinion; it is comprised under five heads, as it were. I. The electric matter does not differ from the little vortices of oil contained within any electric body whatever. II. By the rubbing of a dry hand the oily little vortices are forced to go out of the electric body into the air, and most of them dispose themselves in the manner of an atmosphere about the electric body. III. There spread themselves out in the air the

Ann. 1733. 1734. 1737.

Years 1733, 1734, 1737.

p. 150

oleosi vorticuli atque propter plenum perfectum ab initio mundi perseverans in natura, vorticuli similes versùs corpus electricum adfluunt. IV. Plures sunt oleosi vorticuli in metallis, & in aliis corporibus per communicationem electricis, quàm in vitro & in corporibus electricis per adfrictum. V denique. Ex corporibus non electricis égreditur insensibilis materia, quae cum atmosphaera corporum electricorum fermentescit, atque ex illa fermentatione oritur scintilla, quàm ex corporibus actu electricis solemus excutere.

the oily little vortices, and, on account of the perfect plenum that has persisted in nature from the beginning of the world, similar little vortices flow toward the electric body. IV. There are more oily little vortices in metals and in other bodies electric by communication than in glass and in bodies electric by rubbing. V, finally. From non-electric bodies there issues an insensible matter which ferments with the atmosphere of electric bodies, and from that fermentation arises the spark which we are accustomed to strike out of bodies actually electric.

476 Adnotationes. I. Demonstrabimus inferiùs igneam esse materiam electricam; ergo distinguitur haec materia ab oleo. II. Nihil probat oleum corpus tenax ac lentum in vorticulos adeò rápidos gyrari, & agi posse. III. Probabile non est plùs esse electricae materiae in corporibus per communicationem electricis, quàm in corporibus electricis per se. Imò quidem indicare videntur experimenta, exiguam admodùm esse electricae materiae quantitatem in corporibus quae sola communicatio potest electrica réddere; haec enim corpora calefacta, & sicciori manu fricata nullum unquam signum praebent electricitatis. IV. Fermentatio de qua loquitur D. de Molieres videtur esse merum commentum: ergo rejicienda est ipsius sententia tanquam hypothesis ex omni fermè parte peccans.

476 Remarks. I. We shall demonstrate below that the electric matter is fiery; therefore this matter is distinguished from oil. II. Nothing proves that oil, a tenacious and viscous body, can be whirled and driven in such rapid little vortices. III. It is not probable that there is more electric matter in bodies electric by communication than in bodies electric per se. Indeed, experiments seem to indicate that the quantity of electric matter is very small in bodies which communication alone can render electric; for these bodies, when heated and rubbed with a rather dry hand, never give any sign of electricity. IV. The fermentation of which Mr. de Molières speaks seems to be a mere fiction: therefore his opinion is to be rejected as a hypothesis faulty in almost every part.

Sententia D. Jallabert.

THE OPINION OF MR. JALLABERT.

477 Haec sibi concedi postulavit D. Jallabert in Opusculo suo de Electricitate.s1 I. Existit fluidum aliquod elasticum, & tenue, nonmodò replens orbem hunc universum, sed & poros corporum etiam densissimorum. II Partes hujus fluidi, sicut partes fluidorum omnium tendunt ad aequilibrium, ac proindè tendunt ad implenda spatia in quibus derelinquuntur aliqua vacuola. III. Fluidum hoc ab igne elementari prorsùs indistinctum, atque per adfrictum ex sinu corporum per se electricorum excússum, sese plerumque per modum atmosphaerae disponit circà corpora, quae sunt in statu actuali electricitatis. IV. Fluidum hoc non est homogeneae densitatis; densius enim est in corporibus raris, quàm in densis: densiùs enim est ex. gr. in aëre, quàm in aqua. V. Corpus actu electricum tot accipit ab aëre circumdante particulas igneas, quot ipsi suppeditat. VI denique Ignis elementaris per se ipsum invisibilis secum abripit particulas corporum, ex quibus égredi cogitur, sicque se manifestum reddit.

477 These things Mr. Jallabert asked to be granted him in his little work on Electricity (r). I. There exists a certain elastic and thin fluid, filling not only this whole universe but also the pores of even the densest bodies. II. The parts of this fluid, like the parts of all fluids, tend to equilibrium, and therefore tend to fill the spaces in which some little voids are left. III. This fluid, wholly undistinguished from elemental fire, and shaken out by rubbing from the bosom of bodies electric per se, disposes itself for the most part in the manner of an atmosphere about bodies that are in a state of actual electricity. IV. This fluid is not of homogeneous density: for it is denser in rare bodies than in dense ones; it is denser, e.g., in air than in water. V. A body actually electric receives from the surrounding air as many fiery particles as it supplies to it. VI, finally. Elemental fire, of itself invisible, carries off with it the particles of the bodies from which it is forced to go out, and thus renders itself manifest.

478 Adnotationes. Plura sunt in hac hypothesi veritati cónsona, quàm à veritate aliena. Hoc unum falsum est, materiam electricam densiorem esse in corporibus raris, quàm in densis; densior

478 Remarks. There are more things in this hypothesis consonant with the truth than foreign to it. This one thing is false, that the electric matter is denser in rare bodies than in dense ones; for this matter is denser in

Experiences sur l' Electricitè avec quelques conjectures sur la cause de ses effets.

Experiences sur l’Electricité avec quelques conjectures sur la cause de ses effets.

p. 151
