enim est haec materia in súccino, vitro, adamante, quàm in aëre, aqua, &c. Nisi fortè velit Cl. Auct pro densitate intelligi majorem materiae electricae copiam, quod non adeò absurdum videtur. Cetera omnia sunt in hac hypothesi aut vera, aut saltèm probabilia; sed haec sententia falso innititur fundamento si pro certo statuit materiam electricam densiorem esse in corporibus raris, quàm in densis; ergo ex hoc capite rejicienda est.

in amber, glass, diamond, than in air, water, etc. Unless perhaps the distinguished Author wishes a greater abundance of electric matter to be understood by density, which does not seem so absurd. All the other things in this hypothesis are either true or at least probable; but this opinion rests on a false foundation if it lays down as certain that the electric matter is denser in rare bodies than in dense ones; therefore on this head it is to be rejected.

Sententia D. Franklin. — THE OPINION OF MR. FRANKLIN

479 In sententia Franklinis1 haec sunt capita notatu digna. I. Materia electrica non solùm ab igne elementari, sed etiam à materia quacumque communi specificè distinguitur. II. Existit vis repulsiva inter particulas electricae materiae, & vis adtractiva inter particulas materiae electricae, & particulas materiae non electricae. III. Corpus electricum angulósum facilè admodùm per angulos suos materiam electricam amittit. IV. Corpus acuminatum non electricum facilè admodùm electrico corpori 10, aut 12 pollicibus distans, materiam electricam éripit.

479 In the opinion of Franklin (s) these are the heads worth noting. I. The electric matter is specifically distinguished not only from elemental fire but also from any common matter whatever. II. There exists a repulsive force between the particles of the electric matter, and an attractive force between the particles of the electric matter and the particles of non-electric matter. III. An angular electric body very easily loses its electric matter through its angles. IV. A pointed non-electric body very easily snatches the electric matter from an electric body 10 or 15 inches distant.

480 Adnotationes. I Nihil probat ignem electricum ab igne elementari specificè distingui. II. Datur evidenter causa physica & immediata phaenomenorum electricorum, quam inferiùs determinabimus: ergo non licet recurrere ad qualitates adtractivas & repulsivas, de quibus in Opúsculo suo Franklinus loquitur.

480 Remarks. I. Nothing proves that electric fire is specifically distinguished from elemental fire. II. There is evidently a physical and immediate cause of electric phenomena, which we shall determine below: therefore it is not permissible to have recourse to the attractive and repulsive qualities of which Franklin speaks in his little work.

Sententia D. Nollet.

THE OPINION OF MR. NOLLET.

481 Hic est proprius sententiae Nolletianae character, simultanea, scilicet effluentia, & adfluentia materiae cujusdam subtilissimae. Sic rem hanc totam exposuit Vir ille Clariss. atque de Electricitate, totaque Physica optimè merituss2. I. Materia electrica nihil est aliud, quàm ignis elementaris, qui plùs, minùsve abundanter reperitur in omnibus omninò corporibus. II Omne corpus electricum sive per frictionem, sive per communicationem virtutem hanc conceperit, donatur atmosphaerâ quadam igneâ, quae ad majorem minoremvè densitatem sese extendit, prout intensior, vel remissior est corporis electricitas. III. Ex sinu corporis electrici continuò effluunt ignea corpuscula, quibus componitur hujusmodi atmosphaera. IV Non solum ex aëre, sed etiam ex omni circumstanti corpore continuò adfluit versùs corpus

481 This is the proper character of the Nolletian opinion: the simultaneous effluence and affluence, namely, of a certain most subtle matter. Thus did that most distinguished Man, who has deserved excellently of Electricity and of the whole of Physics, set forth this entire matter (t). I. The electric matter is nothing other than elemental fire, which is found more or less abundantly in absolutely all bodies. II. Every electric body, whether it has received this virtue by friction or by communication, is endowed with a certain fiery atmosphere, which extends itself to a greater or lesser density according as the electricity of the body is more intense or more remiss. III. From the bosom of the electric body fiery corpuscles continually flow out, of which an atmosphere of this kind is composed. IV. Not only from the air, but also from every surrounding body, there flows continually toward the electric

In Oper. cui titul. Experiences & Observations sur l' Electricitè, faites a Philadelphie, traduites par Mr. d' Alibard.

In the work entitled Experiences & Observations sur l’Electricité, faites a Philadelphie, translated by M. d’Alibard.

p. 152

electricum, ex. gr. versùs globum vitreum siccâ manu fricatum, ignea materia, quae jacturas abundè réparat, quas ob frictionem vitreus globus patitur. V. Conflictus existit inter materiam electricam effluentem, & materiam electricam adfluentem, atque ex eo conflictu Nolletus deducit phaenomenôn electricorum explicationem, ut videre est in operibus, quae fuerunt ab ipso hanc obrem in lucem édita.

body, e.g. toward a glass globe rubbed with a dry hand, a fiery matter which abundantly repairs the losses that the glass globe suffers on account of the friction. V. A conflict exists between the effluent electric matter and the affluent electric matter, and from that conflict Nollet deduces the explanation of electric phenomena, as may be seen in the works which he published for this purpose.

482 Adnotationes. I. Propter resistentiam, & elaterium aëris, pars aliqua, neque sanè exigua, electricae materiae quae per adfrictum & motum rotationis, fuerat ex sinu vitrei globi effluens, in ipsummet globum redit, seu fit adfluens: vix enim aliter exponi potest, cur tempore frigido & sicco vividior existat electrica virtus, quàm tempore calido & húmido II. In sententia Nolletiana non videtur exponi posse cur homo super placentam resinaceam more solito constitutus, non possit flammulam excitare ex tubo ferreo electrico ad quem digitum ádmovet; tunc enim conflictus maximus existit inter materiam exeuntem ex electrico digito, & materiam effluentem ex tubo pariter electrico: ergo non exponuntur in sententia Nolletiana omnia omninò electrica phaenómena.

482 Remarks. I. On account of the resistance and the elasticity of the air, some part, and that not a very small one, of the electric matter which, through rubbing and the motion of rotation, had been effluent from the bosom of the glass globe returns into the globe itself, or becomes affluent: for scarcely otherwise can it be explained why the electric virtue is livelier in cold and dry weather than in warm and humid weather. II. In the Nolletian opinion it does not seem possible to explain why a man placed in the usual way on a cake of resin cannot draw a little flame from the electric iron tube to which he brings his finger: for then a very great conflict exists between the matter going out of the electric finger and the matter flowing out of the tube, which is likewise electric: therefore not absolutely all electric phenomena are explained in the Nolletian opinion.

Sententia Clariss. Paulian, quae et nostra est. — THE OPINION OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED PAULIAN, WHICH IS ALSO OURS .

483 Duobus veluti principiorum generibus innititur nostra haec Electricitatis Theoria, quorum alia recipiuntur ab omnibus omninò Physicis, alia verò nobis sunt prorsùs peculiaria. I. Datur materia quaedam electrica. Et verò dantur electrica corpora: ergo datur materia quaedam hanc ipsis virtutem concilians. II. Materia electrica est materia quaedam subtilissima, & fluidissima: pénetrat enim intra corpora densissima, qualia sunt metalla, lapides, &c. III. Materia electrica est materia ignea, quoniàm, materiae hujus ope, inflammatur spiritus vini accenditur candéla, &c. IV. Materia electrica non est homogeneae densitatis; dantur enim corpora quae sunt alia aliis magis electrica. V. Omne corpus electricum, sivè per frictionem, sivè per communicationem virtutem hanc concéperit, emittit ex sinu suo ignea corpuscula, quorum plurima in modum atmosphaerae sese disponunt. Et verò eo prorsùs modo formatur atmosphaera corporum electricorum, quo formatur atmosphera corporum odoriferorum, sed atmosphaera corporum odoriferorum per veram emissionem efformatur, ut omnes consentiunt: ergo per veram emissionem pariter efformatur atmosphaera corporum electricorum.

483 Our present Theory of Electricity rests, as it were, on two kinds of principles, of which some are received by absolutely all Physicists, while others are altogether peculiar to us. I. There is a certain electric matter. For indeed there are electric bodies: therefore there is a certain matter that confers this virtue on them. II. The electric matter is a certain most subtle and most fluid matter: for it penetrates within the densest bodies, such as metals, stones, etc. III. The electric matter is a fiery matter, since by the help of this matter spirit of wine is inflamed, a candle is lit, etc. IV. The electric matter is not of homogeneous density; for there are bodies of which some are more electric than others. V. Every electric body, whether it has received this virtue by friction or by communication, emits from its bosom fiery corpuscles, most of which dispose themselves in the manner of an atmosphere. And indeed the atmosphere of electric bodies is formed in exactly the same way in which the atmosphere of odoriferous bodies is formed; but the atmosphere of odoriferous bodies is formed by a true emission, as all agree: therefore the atmosphere of electric bodies is likewise formed by a true emission.

484 VI. Tot ignea corpuscula adfluunt versùs corpus electricum, quot effluxerant ex ipsius sinu Suam enim electricitatem non amittit globus vitreus, post frictiones innumeras, & jacturas immensas,

484 VI. As many fiery corpuscles flow toward the electric body as had flowed out of its bosom. For the glass globe does not lose its electricity after innumerable frictions and immense losses,

Essai sur l' Electricitè, & alibi in variis Opusculis.

Essai sur l’Electricité, and elsewhere in various small works.

p. 153

quas passus est, ergo jacturas suas evidenter réparat. Non potest autem corpus electricum resarcire jacturas, quin tot ignea corpuscula versùs ipsum adfluant, quot effluxerant ex ipsius sinu: ergo &c. Jam verò quòd spectat ad principia quae nobis sunt hac in re peculiaria, illa sunt numero quinque.

which it has suffered; therefore it evidently repairs its losses. But the electric body cannot make good its losses unless as many fiery corpuscles flow toward it as had flowed out of its bosom: therefore, etc. Now as regards the principles that are peculiar to us in this matter, they are five in number.

485 I. Pars aliqua tantùm igneorum corpusculorum ex vitreo globo sicca manu fricato exeuntium, ingreditur ferreum tubum electricae machinae; pars alia verò eorundem corpusculorum sese communicat vel aëri, vel corporibus hinc indè circumstantibus. Constat enim experientiâ non solum Electricae machinae tubum, sed & ipsum vitrei globi Fricatorem vim electricam sensibiliter concipere, dummodò super placentam resinaceam constituatur.

485 I. Only some part of the fiery corpuscles going out of the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand enters the iron tube of the electric machine; another part of the same corpuscles communicates itself either to the air or to the bodies standing round about on every side. For experience establishes that not only the tube of the electric machine, but also the very Rubber of the glass globe sensibly receives electric force, provided he is placed on a cake of resin.

486 II. Ignea corpuscula, quae exeunt ex sinu vitrei globi, & quae tubum ferreum electricae machinae non ingrediuntur, reddunt initialiter electrica ea omnia corpora, quae machinam hinc indè circumdant, etiamsi super resinam, aut vitrum, aut simile quidpiam non constituantur, dummodò sint haec corpora per communicationem electrica. Et verò Fricator super placentam resinaceam, aut vitream constitutus, sensibiliter, seu perfectè electricus redditur per ignea corpuscula, quae exeunt ex sinu vitrei globi, & quae tubum ferreum electricae machinae non ingrediuntur: ergo per haec eadem corpuscula imperfectè, seu initialiter electricus reddi debet Fricator idem in pavimento positus: rétinet enim in hoc situ veram & expedítam potentiam electricitatem recipiendi per viam communicationis. Quod autèm de Fricatore posito in pavimento dicitur, hoc & dicatur proportionaliter de corporibus hinc inde machinam circumdantibus, quae sunt per communicationem electrica, & quae super resinam, aut vitrum non collocantur.

486 II. The fiery corpuscles which go out of the bosom of the glass globe, and which do not enter the iron tube of the electric machine, render initially electric all those bodies which surround the machine on every side, even if they are not placed on resin, or glass, or anything similar, provided these bodies are electric by communication. And indeed the Rubber, placed on a cake of resin or of glass, is rendered sensibly, or perfectly, electric by the fiery corpuscles which go out of the bosom of the glass globe and which do not enter the iron tube of the electric machine: therefore by these same corpuscles the same Rubber, when placed on the floor, must be rendered imperfectly, or initially, electric: for in this situation he retains a true and ready power of receiving electricity by way of communication. And what is said of the Rubber placed on the floor, let it be said proportionally also of the bodies surrounding the machine on every side which are electric by communication and are not set on resin or glass.

487 III Circumdantur atmosphaerâ densâ corpora perfectè, seu totaliter electrica, & atmospaerâ rara, corpora imperfectè, seù initialiter electrica: dénsitas enim atmospherae electricae est in ratione directa electricitatis corporum IV. Multa ignea corpuscula ex sinu vitrei globi exeuntia in ipsum globum continuò redeunt propter resistentiam & elaterium ambientis aëris. Eam ob causam vividior est vis electrica tempore frigido, & sicco, quàm calido, & humido tempore: eandem etiam ob causam vividior est electricitas in pleno, quàm in vacuo. Hinc sequitur igneorum corpusculorum ex sinu vitrei globi effluentiae respondére simultaneam quamdam versùs eundem globum adfluentiam, partìm eorundem, partìm similium corpusculorum quae suppedditantur ab aëre, & circumstantibus corporibus. V. Verissima est, quanquàm minimè sensibilis simultanea affluentia, & effluentia corpusculorum igneorum. Non datur enim etiam in atmosphaera terrestri plenum perfectum (§. 257.), quod evidenter requireretur ut physicè sensibiliter patefieret synchrona illa affluentia, & effluentia materiae electricae. His praemissis sit conclusio.

487 III. Bodies perfectly, or totally, electric are surrounded by a dense atmosphere, and bodies imperfectly, or initially, electric by a rare atmosphere: for the density of the electric atmosphere is in the direct ratio of the electricity of the bodies. IV. Many fiery corpuscles going out of the bosom of the glass globe continually return into the globe itself on account of the resistance and the elasticity of the surrounding air. For that reason the electric force is livelier in cold and dry weather than in warm and humid weather; for the same reason, too, electricity is livelier in a plenum than in a vacuum. Hence it follows that to the effluence of the fiery corpuscles from the bosom of the glass globe there corresponds a certain simultaneous affluence toward the same globe, partly of the same corpuscles, partly of similar corpuscles supplied by the air and by the surrounding bodies. V. Most true, although very little sensible, is the simultaneous affluence and effluence of the fiery corpuscles. For not even in the terrestrial atmosphere is there a perfect plenum (§. 257.), which would evidently be required for that synchronous affluence and effluence of the electric matter to become physically and sensibly manifest. These things premised, let this be the conclusion.

p. 154

488 In sententia nostra rectè exponuntur omnia electricitatis phaenomena. Probatur enumeratione sequenti, revocando scilicèt ad causas suas physicas experimenta praecipua quae fuerunt in cap. II. relata.

488 In our opinion all the phenomena of electricity are rightly explained. This is proved by the following enumeration, namely by referring to their physical causes the principal experiments that were related in ch. II.

489 Explicatio Experimenti I Ex globo vitreo siccâ manu fricato, & motu circulari donato exeunt ignea corpuscula, quorum alia ingrediuntur ferreum tubum, funiculorum sericorum ope suspensum horizontaliter, alia verò sese communicant aëri, & corporibus hinc indè circumstantibus Per hanc emissionem, totaliter electricus redditur ferreus tubus horizontaliter suspensus, & initialiter tantùm electrica redduntur aer, & corpora hinc indè circumstantia. Quo supposito sic ratiócinor. Quum versùs tubum ferreum totaliter electricum admoveo digitum initialiter duntaxàt electricum, tunc juxta leges aequilibrii, debet atmosphaera electrica densa tubum ferreum circumdans deferri versùs atmosphaeram electricam raram digitum meum ambientem, non secùs atque aer exterior fertur in cubiculum, cujus fuit aër interior igne accenso rarefactus. In ea mixtione, conflictus vehemens existit inter materiam electricam tubum ferreum circumdantem, & materiam electricam ambientem digitum, atque per hunc conflictum excitatur flammula caerulea cum crepitu prosiliens.

489 Explanation of Experiment I. From the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand and endowed with circular motion there go out fiery corpuscles, of which some enter the iron tube suspended horizontally by means of silk cords, while others communicate themselves to the air and to the bodies standing round about on every side. By this emission the iron tube suspended horizontally is rendered totally electric, while the air and the bodies standing round about are rendered only initially electric. This supposed, I reason thus. When I bring my finger, which is only initially electric, toward the totally electric iron tube, then, according to the laws of equilibrium, the dense electric atmosphere surrounding the iron tube must be carried toward the rare electric atmosphere surrounding my finger, just as the outer air is carried into a room whose inner air has been rarefied by a lighted fire. In that mixing a vehement conflict exists between the electric matter surrounding the iron tube and the electric matter surrounding the finger, and through this conflict a little blue flame is excited, leaping forth with a crackle.

490 Explicatio Experimenti II. Tubus machinae electricae, filum ferreum quod manu tenetur, & homo super placentam resinaceam collocatus sunt tria corpora per communicationem electrica, quorum ultimum separatur ope resinae à reliquo pavimento per communicationem tantùm electrico: ergo quum imprimitur globo vitreo sicca manu fricato motus aliquis rotationis, debent tubus, filum ferreum, & homo super placentam resinaceam collocatus vim electricam concipere maximam debet & dolorem sensibilem procreare flamma caerulea ex corpore viventi excitatâ; ¿quis enim non videt flammam hanc caeruleam esse verum, & propriè dictum ignem?

490 Explanation of Experiment II. The tube of the electric machine, the iron wire which is held in the hand, and the man placed on the resin cake are three bodies electric by communication, of which the last is separated by means of the resin from the rest of the floor, which is electric only by communication: therefore, when some motion of rotation is impressed on the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand, the tube, the iron wire and the man placed on the resin cake must receive a very great electric force, and the blue flame drawn from the living body must produce a sensible pain; for who does not see that this blue flame is a true fire, and properly so called?

491 Explicatio Experimenti III. Admittimus & nosmetipsi simultaneam quandam effluentiam particularum ignearum ex sinu corporum electricorum, & adfluentiam particularum ignearum versùs eadem electrica corpora. Per particulas igneas adfluentes adtrahuntur corpora quaecumque levissima versùs electrica corpora, & per particulas igneas effluentes repelluntur corpora quaecumque levissima ab iisdem corporibus electricis: ergo in nostra sententia rectè exponuntur itus, & reditus levissimorum corporum.

491 Explanation of Experiment III. We ourselves also admit a certain simultaneous effluence of fiery particles from the bosom of electric bodies, and affluence of fiery particles toward the same electric bodies. By the affluent fiery particles any of the lightest bodies whatever are attracted toward the electric bodies, and by the effluent fiery particles any of the lightest bodies whatever are repelled from the same electric bodies: therefore in our opinion the goings and returnings of the lightest bodies are rightly explained.

492 Explicatio Experimenti IV. Violenta commotio de qua fit mentio in Experim. IV. óritur à conflictu vehementi duorum profluviorum igneorum, quorum unum ingreditur per manum, quae partem inferiorem lagénae vitreae sustinet, alterum verò per manum quae flammam excitat ex filo ferreo.

492 Explanation of Experiment IV. The violent shock mentioned in Experim. IV arises from the vehement collision of two fiery outflows, one of which enters through the hand that holds up the lower part of the glass flask, and the other through the hand that draws the flame from the iron wire.

493 Explicatio Experimenti V. Conflictus vehemens duorum profluviorum igneorum, quorum unum viam habet per filum

493 Explanation of Experiment V. The vehement conflict of two fiery outflows, one of which has its way through the iron wire,

p. 155

ferreum, álterum verò per tubum electricum causa est, cur maximo cum fragóre perforetur charta densissima de qua fit mentio in Experim. V.

the other through the electric tube, is the cause why the very thick paper mentioned in Experim. V is pierced with a very great crack.

494 Explicatio Experimenti VI. Nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens est corpus actu electricum, quemadmodùm exponetur inferiùs: ergo scintillae debent excitari ex virga ferrea de qua agitur in Experim. VI.

494 Explanation of Experiment VI. A cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is a body actually electric, as will be set forth below: therefore sparks must be drawn from the iron rod treated of in Experim. VI.

495 Explicatio Experimenti VII. Pars aliqua corpusculorum igneorum ex vitreo globo sicca manu fricato exeuntium, sese communicat corporibus machinam electricam circumstantibus: ergo vim electricam sensibilem Fricator concipere debet, dummodò sit super placentam resinaceam constitutus. Debet & Fricator idem flammam excitare ex tubo ferreo ad quem digitum ádmovet: in illo enim vis electrica multò debilior est, quàm in tubo ferreo.

495 Explanation of Experiment VII. Some part of the fiery corpuscles going out of the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand communicates itself to the bodies standing about the electric machine: therefore the Rubber must receive a sensible electric force, provided he is placed on a cake of resin. And the same Rubber must also draw a flame from the iron tube to which he brings his finger: for in him the electric force is much weaker than in the iron tube.

Solvuntur argumenta, cùm á Cl. Nolleto, tùm ab aliis opposita contra sententiam nostram.

THE ARGUMENTS OPPOSED AGAINST OUR OPINION , BOTH BY THE DISTINGUISHED NOLLET AND BY OTHERS , ARE ANSWERED.

496 Opp. I. Explicatio Experim. I non est in hac novâ sententia conformis legibus sanae Physicae: ergo. Prob. antec.: si tubus ferreus per funiculos séricos suspensus vim electricam concipit propter causas adsignatas, pariter & vim electricam concipere debet tubus idem ferreus per funiculos cannábinos suspensus; falsum consequens: ergo & antec. Prob. sequela: tám communicat cum globo vitreo tubus ferreus per funiculos cannábinos suspensus, quàm quum suspenditur per funiculos sericos; ergo si &c.

496 Obj. I. The explanation of Experim. I in this new opinion is not conformable to the laws of sound Physics: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: if the iron tube suspended by silk cords receives electric force on account of the causes assigned, the same iron tube suspended by hempen cords must likewise receive electric force; the consequent is false: therefore the antecedent also. Proof of the sequel: the iron tube suspended by hempen cords communicates with the glass globe just as much as when it is suspended by silk cords; therefore, if, etc.

497 Dist. antec.: tam & eodem modo communicat, nego; tam & longè diverso modo communicat tubus ferreus, &c. conc. antec. & neg. conseq. Tubus ferreus per funiculos sericos suspensus, ita concipit vim electricam, ut illam omninò, aut quasi omninò retineat; suspenditur enim ope funiculorum per se electricorum; contra verò tubus ferreus per funiculos cannábinos suspensus, ita concipit vim electricam, ut illam magnâ ex parte amittat; suspénditur enim per funículos, qui sunt per communicationem electrici.

497 I distinguish the antecedent: it communicates just as much and in the same manner, I deny; just as much, and in a far different manner, the iron tube communicates, etc., I concede the antecedent and deny the consequence. The iron tube suspended by silk cords receives electric force in such a way that it retains it wholly, or almost wholly; for it is suspended by means of cords electric per se; on the contrary, the iron tube suspended by hempen cords receives electric force in such a way that it loses it in great part; for it is suspended by cords that are electric by communication.

498 Inst. 1. Si versùs tubum electrica virtute donatum admoveatur obsignatoria cera, nulla omninò excitatur scintilla. Quo supposito sic ratiocinor: ex hac sententia nova sequitur, quod in eo casu flammula cum crépitu debeat excitari ex tubo ferreo; sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: obsignatoria cera non longè distans ab electrica machina fieri debet initialiter electrica: ergo. Prob. antec.: Ferrum quodcumque non longè distans ab electrica machina fit initialiter electricum: ergo pariter obsignatoria cera non longè distans ab electrica machina, fieri debet initialiter electrica.

498 Inst. 1. If sealing wax is brought toward the tube endowed with electric virtue, no spark at all is excited. This supposed, I reason thus: from this new opinion it follows that in that case a little flame with a crackle must be drawn from the iron tube: but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: sealing wax not far distant from the electric machine must become initially electric: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: any iron whatever not far distant from the electric machine becomes initially electric: therefore likewise sealing wax not far distant from the electric machine must become initially electric.

p. 156

Nego paritatem: Ferrum non longè distans ab electrica machina acquisivit atmosphaeram electricam raram; est enim ferrum per communicationem electricum: contra verò obsignatoria cera per adfrictum duntaxat, electrica nullam acquirit atmosphaeram electricam, quamvis non distet ab electrica machina.

I deny the parity: iron not far distant from the electric machine acquires a rare electric atmosphere; for iron is electric by communication: whereas sealing wax, which is electric only by rubbing, acquires no electric atmosphere, although it is not far distant from the electric machine.

499 Inst. 2. Ex hac sententia nova saltèm sequitur quod flammula debeat excitari ex tubo ferreo electrico versùs quem admovetur obsignatoria cera sicciori manu fricata, sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: obsignatoria cera sicciori manu fricata, atmosphaeram electricam acquisivit: ergo. Dist. antec.: atmosphaeram electricam acquisivit, quae aequè densa est, ac atmosphaera tubi ferrei electrici, conc.; quae rarior est, quàm atmosphaera tubi ferrei electrici, nego antec., & consequens. Flammula non excitatur nisi per mixtionem, & consequentem conflictum atmosphaerae densae cum atmosphaera rara: ergo flammula non debet excitari, quum admovetur cera totaliter electrica versùs tubum ferreum totaliter electricum.

499 Inst. 2. From this new opinion it at least follows that a little flame must be drawn from the electric iron tube toward which sealing wax rubbed with a rather dry hand is brought; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: sealing wax rubbed with a rather dry hand has acquired an electric atmosphere: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: it has acquired an electric atmosphere which is just as dense as the atmosphere of the electric iron tube, I concede; one which is rarer than the atmosphere of the electric iron tube, I deny the antecedent and the consequent. A little flame is not drawn except through the mixing, and the consequent conflict, of a dense atmosphere with a rare atmosphere: therefore a little flame ought not to be drawn when wax totally electric is brought toward an iron tube totally electric.

500 Inst. 3. Saltèm in hac nova sententia non explicatur cur ex tubo ferreo electrico cum crepitu quodam flammula soleat excitari: ergo tanquam insufficiens rejicienda est. Prob. antec.: mixtio materiae electricae tubum ferreum circumdantis, & materiae electricae digitum ambientis, deberet fieri sine crepitu: ergo &c. Prob. antec.: duae flammae contiguae sese immiscent sine crepitu: ergo pariter duae atmosphaerae electricae sese deberent sinè crepitu immiscere. Nego conseq. Duo atmosphaerae electricae de quibus loquimur, expellunt aërem intermedium, vel nullomodo, vel mediocriter duntaxat dilatatum, ac proindè expellunt aërem elasticum, crepitum edendi capacem: contrà vero duae flammae contiguae sese immiscentes expellunt aërem nimis rarefactum, quàm ut crepitum edere queat.

500 Inst. 3. At least in this new opinion it is not explained why a little flame is usually drawn from the electric iron tube with a certain crackle: therefore it is to be rejected as insufficient. Proof of the antecedent: the mixing of the electric matter surrounding the iron tube and of the electric matter surrounding the finger ought to take place without a crackle: therefore, etc. Proof of the antecedent: two contiguous flames mingle with each other without a crackle: therefore likewise two electric atmospheres ought to mingle with each other without a crackle. I deny the consequence. The two electric atmospheres of which we speak expel the intermediate air, which is either not dilated at all or only moderately, and therefore they expel elastic air, capable of producing a crackle: whereas two contiguous flames mingling with each other expel air too much rarefied to be able to produce a crackle.

501 Opp. 2. Experimenti II explicatio non videtur esse conformis Physicae legibus: ergo. Prob. antec.: haec explicatio supponit hominem super placentam resinaceam constitutum eodem praecise instanti concipere virtutem electricam, sive placenta resinacea multùm, sive parùm distet ab electrica machina: atqui hoc non videtur conforme Physicae legibus: ergo. Prob. min.: juxta Physicae leges, non debet electrica materia ex globo vitreo exiens, eodem tempore spatia diversa percurrere: ergo. Dist. antec.: eodem tempore reali, & vero, concedo; eodem tempore sensibili & adparente, subdist. supponendo quod spatia differant aliquot millibus leucarum, conc. supponendo quod differant aliquot pedibus, nego, & conseq. Incredibili quadàm velocitate donatur electrica seu ignea materia: debet igitur haec materia eodem sensibiliter tempore ad pedem centesimum, & ad pedem vigesimum pervenire.

501 Obj. 2. The explanation of Experiment II does not seem conformable to the laws of Physics: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: this explanation supposes that a man placed on a resin cake receives electric virtue at precisely the same instant, whether the resin cake is far or but little distant from the electric machine: but this does not seem conformable to the laws of Physics: therefore. Proof of the minor: according to the laws of Physics, the electric matter going out of the glass globe ought not to traverse different spaces in the same time: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: in the same real and true time, I concede; in the same sensible and apparent time, I subdistinguish: supposing that the spaces differ by some thousands of leagues, I concede; supposing that they differ by some feet, I deny, and I deny the consequence. The electric, or fiery, matter is endowed with a certain incredible velocity: this matter must therefore arrive at the hundredth foot and at the twentieth foot in the same sensible time.

502 Inst. ex hac sententia sequitur, quod homo super placentam resinaceam more solito collocatus deberet flammam excitare ex tubo ferreo electrico, quo cum communicationem habet: sed hoc

502 Inst. From this opinion it follows that a man placed in the usual way on a resin cake ought to draw a flame from the electric iron tube with which he is in communication: but this

p. 157

est falsum: ergo. Prob. major.: homo pavimento innixus, flammulam excitat ex tubo ferreo quocum non communicat: ergo à fortiori homo super placentam collocatus deberet &c. Nego conseq: Homo super placentam collocatus aequè electricus est, ac tubus ferreus, ac proindè circúmdatur atmosphaera electrica aequè densa, ac atmosphaera ferrei tubi. Contràverò homo pavimento innixus initialiter tantùm est electricus, & consequenter circumdatur atmosphaerâ electrica rara, intereà dùm ferreus tubus cingitur atmosphaera electrica densa: ergo juxta principia superiùs exposita debet hic ex tubo ferreo aliquam, ille verò nullam flammulam excitare. At inquies: ¿quonam mechanismo inflammatur spiritus vini, de quo fit mentio in Observatione III experimenti II? Respondeo: eodem prorsùs modo inflammatur spiritus vini, quo ex tubo ferreo flammula quaedam excitatur.

is false: therefore. Proof of the major: a man resting on the floor draws a little flame from the iron tube with which he does not communicate: therefore a fortiori a man placed on the cake ought, etc. I deny the consequence. The man placed on the cake is just as electric as the iron tube, and is therefore surrounded by an electric atmosphere just as dense as the atmosphere of the iron tube. Whereas the man resting on the floor is only initially electric, and is consequently surrounded by a rare electric atmosphere, while the iron tube is girded by a dense electric atmosphere: therefore, according to the principles set forth above, the latter must draw some little flame from the iron tube, but the former none. But, you will say, by what mechanism is the spirit of wine inflamed, which is mentioned in Observation III of Experiment II? I reply: the spirit of wine is inflamed in exactly the same way in which a certain little flame is drawn from the iron tube.

503 Opp. 3.: non datur in hac nova sententia causa physica adfluentiae particularum ignearum versùs corpora actu electrica: ergo admittenda non est explicatio Experimenti. III. Prob. antec: antequàm imprimeretur globo vitreo motus aliquis rotationis, materia electrica, quae reperiebatur in aëre, non adfluebat versùs globum vitreum, aut versùs tubum ferreum: ergo neque adfluere debet, postquàm vitreo globo fuit motus aliquis rotationis impressus. Nego primum antec.: Datur in atmosphaera inferiori plenum sensibile, & aer est elasticus. Quibus praesuppositis sic ratiocinor: Globus vitreus fieri non potest electricus, quin ignea multa corpuscula ex sinu suo emittat, & quin novum motum acquirat materia electrica, quae reperitur in aëre, & in corporibus machinam electricam hinc indè circumstantibus. Haec autem omnia non possunt accidere, quin, propter aërem elasticum, & propter plenum sensibile, effluentiae particularum ignearum ex sinu vitrei globi, correspondeat adfluentia earumdem, aut similium particularum ignearum versùs eundem globum vitreum. Quod de globo vitreo dictum est, hoc de tubo ferreo dicatur proportionaliter: ergo in hac sententia datur causa physica adfluentiae particularum ignearum versus electrica corpora.

503 Obj. 3. In this new opinion there is no physical cause of the affluence of fiery particles toward bodies actually electric: therefore the explanation of Experiment III is not to be admitted. I prove the antecedent: before some motion of rotation was impressed on the glass globe, the electric matter which was found in the air did not flow toward the glass globe or toward the iron tube: therefore neither ought it to flow toward them after some motion of rotation has been impressed on the glass globe. I deny the first antecedent: in the lower atmosphere there is a sensible plenum, and the air is elastic. These things presupposed, I reason thus: the glass globe cannot become electric without emitting many fiery corpuscles from its bosom, and without a new motion being acquired by the electric matter which is found in the air and in the bodies standing round the electric machine on every side. But all these things cannot happen without there corresponding, on account of the elastic air and on account of the sensible plenum, to the effluence of fiery particles from the bosom of the glass globe an affluence of the same, or of similar, fiery particles toward the same glass globe. What has been said of the glass globe, let it be said proportionally of the iron tube: therefore in this opinion there is a physical cause of the affluence of fiery particles toward electric bodies.

504 Nego ultimam conseq: In primo casu jacturam nullam patiebatur vitreus globus, & novum motum non acceperat electrica materia, quae reperitur in aëre, & in corporibus machinam electricam hinc indè circumstantibus. In 2. autèm casu immensam ferè jacturam particularum ignearum pátitur vitreus globus: & novum motum acquisivit electrica materia, quae reperitur in aëre, & in corporibus machinam electricam hinc indè circumstantibus. At inquies: ¿Quaenam est causa physica effluentiae particularum ignearum ex sinu vitrei globi sicca manu fricati? Respondeo: effluentia haec debetur frictioni junctae motui rotationis. Dices iterùm: ¿Quanam igitur de causa ex globo metallico sicca manu fricato, & vehementissimo motu rotationis donato non effluunt igneae particulae? Respondeo: existere phaenomeni hujus causam geminam: nam I. multò

504 I deny the last consequence: in the first case the glass globe was suffering no loss, and the electric matter which is found in the air and in the bodies standing round the electric machine on every side had not received a new motion. But in the 2nd case the glass globe suffers an almost immense loss of fiery particles, and the electric matter which is found in the air and in the bodies standing round the electric machine on every side has acquired a new motion. But you will say: what is the physical cause of the effluence of fiery particles from the bosom of the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand? I reply: this effluence is owed to friction joined to the motion of rotation. You will say again: for what cause, then, do no fiery particles flow out of a metal globe rubbed with a dry hand and endowed with a most vehement motion of rotation? I reply that there exists a twofold cause of this phenomenon: for I. there are far fewer

p. 158

pauciora sunt ignea corpuscula in metallis, & in corporibus per communicationem electricis, quàm in vitro, & in corporibus electricis per se. II. Habent metalla partes rigidiusculas[?], quibus frictio motum illum non imprimit, ex quo enascitur[?] corpusculorum igneorum effluentia.

fiery corpuscles in metals, and in bodies electric by communication, than in glass and in bodies electric of themselves. II. Metals have somewhat rigid parts, on which friction does not impress that motion from which the effluence of fiery corpuscles arises.

505 Opp. 4. Ex nostra sententia sequitur, quod si filum ferreum, de quo fit mentio in Experimento IV includeretur in lagena metallica, commotio foret multò vehementior, quàm quum filum ferreum includitur in lagena vitrea: sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: si filum ferreum includeretur in lagena metallica, profluvium igneum ingrediens per manum, quae partem inferiorem lagenae metallicae sustinet, multò majus foret, quàm quum experimentum fit ope[?] lagenae vitreae: ergo ex nostra sententia sequitur &c. Prob. antec.: electrica materia multò facilius permeat lagenam metallicam, quàm lagenam vitream: ergo si &c. Nego secundum antec. tanquam falsum supponens. Filum ferreum inclusum in lagena metallica non fieret sensibiliter electricum, per poros enim metalli evaporaretur materia electrica filo ferreo communicata. Hinc concedo ultimum antec. & nego conseq.

505 Obj. 4. From our opinion it follows that if the iron wire mentioned in Experiment IV were enclosed in a metal flask, the shock would be much more vehement than when the iron wire is enclosed in a glass flask; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: if the iron wire were enclosed in a metal flask, the fiery outflow entering through the hand that holds up the lower part of the metal flask would be much greater than when the experiment is made by means of a glass flask; therefore from our opinion it follows, etc. Proof of the antecedent: the electric matter permeates a metal flask much more easily than a glass flask: therefore, if, etc. I deny the second antecedent, as supposing something false. The iron wire enclosed in a metal flask would not become sensibly electric; for the electric matter communicated to the iron wire would evaporate through the pores of the metal. Hence I concede the last antecedent and deny the consequence.

506 Opp. 5. non datur in sententia nostra causa physica fragóris de quo fit mentio in Experimento V: ergo. Prob. antec.: conflictus vehemens duorum profluviorum electricorum non deberet fragorem tantum excitare: ergo non datur &c. Dist. antec.: conflictus vehemens duorum profluviorum electricorum in loco fere[?] vacuo non deberet fragorem tantum excitare, concedo; conflictus vehemens duorum profluviorum electricorum, quae rarefaciunt, & expellunt aërem intermedium fragorem tantum non deberet excitare, nego & conseq. Quum de sono agemus omnis penitus evanescet difficultas[?].

506 Obj. 5. In our opinion there is no physical cause of the crash mentioned in Experiment V: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: the vehement conflict of two electric outflows ought not to excite so great a crash; therefore there is not, etc. I distinguish the antecedent: the vehement conflict of two electric outflows in an empty place ought not to excite so great a crash, I concede; the vehement conflict of two electric outflows which rarefy and expel the intermediate air ought not to excite so great a crash, I deny, and I deny the consequence. When we treat of sound, every difficulty will vanish entirely.

507 Opp. 6. nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens, non est corpus electricum: ergo non valet explicatio Experimenti VI. Prob. antec.: nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens est corpus aqueum: ergo non est corpus electricum. Dist. antec.: est corpus aqueum totaliter, nego; partialiter tantum, concedo, & nego conseq. Nubes fulmen deferens, est corpus continens particulas aqueas, sulphureas, bituminosas, nitrosas &c. Exponemus in articulo fulminis, quonam mechanismo nubes haec vim electricam acquirat.

507 Obj. 6. A cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is not an electric body: therefore the explanation of Experiment VI does not hold. Proof of the antecedent: a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is a watery body: therefore it is not an electric body. I distinguish the antecedent: it is a body totally watery, I deny; partially only, I concede, and I deny the consequence. A cloud bearing lightning is a body containing watery, sulphurous, bituminous, nitrous particles, etc. In the article on lightning we shall set forth by what mechanism this cloud acquires electric force.

508 Opp. 7. Ex nostra sententia sequitur, quod Fricator de quo fit mentio in Experimento VII non deberet flammam excitare ex tubo ferreo ad quem digitum suum admovet, sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: homo super placentam resinaceam more solito collocatus flammam non excitat ex tubo quocum communicat per filum ferreum: ergo pariter Fricator super placentam collocatus non debet flammam excitare ex tubo ferreo quocum per globum vitreum communicationem habet. Nego conseq. Homo super placentam collocatus tam est electricus, quàm tubus ferreus

508 Obj. 7. From our opinion it follows that the Rubber mentioned in Experiment VII ought not to draw a flame from the iron tube to which he brings his finger; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: a man placed in the usual way on a resin cake does not draw a flame from the tube with which he communicates through the iron wire: therefore likewise the Rubber placed on the cake ought not to draw a flame from the iron tube with which he has communication through the glass globe. I deny the consequence. The man placed on the cake is just as electric as the iron tube with

p. 159

quocum per filum ferreum communicat: contrà verò Fricator multò minus est electricus quàm tubus ferreus, licet constituatur[?] super placentam resinaceam: ergo debet hic ex tubo ferreo aliquam, ille verò nullam flammulam excitare.

which he communicates through the iron wire: whereas the Rubber is much less electric than the iron tube, even though he is placed on a cake of resin: therefore the former must draw some little flame from the iron tube, but the latter none.

CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

Dubia aliqua circa electricitatem quàm brevissimè explicantur.

Some doubts about electricity are explained very briefly.

509 Quaeres I. ¿Quanam de causa vis electrica debilior[?] est humido, aut calido tempore, & vis eadem electrica vividior est tempore sicco, aut frigido? Respondeo: humido, aut calido tempore aërem multò minus esse elasticum, quàm tempore sicco, aut frigido: ergo tempore sicco aut frigido, debent ignea corpuscula ex sinu corporis electrici primùm emissa, meliùs in idem corpus repercuti[?], quàm quum tempus est humidum, aut calidum: ergo vis electrica debet vividior esse tempore sicco, aut frigido, quàm tempore humido, aut calido.

ou will ask, I.: for what cause is the electric force weaker in humid or 509 Y warm weather, and the same electric force livelier in dry or cold weather? I reply: in humid or warm weather the air is much less elastic than in dry or cold weather; therefore in dry or cold weather the fiery corpuscles first emitted from the bosom of the electric body must be better beaten back onto the same body than when the weather is humid or warm: therefore the electric force must be livelier in dry or cold weather than in humid or warm weather.

510 Quaeres II. ¿Quanam de causa Homo initialiter electricus scintillam vividam excitat ex tubo ferreo ad quem digitum suum ádmovet, & idem Homo flammam debiliorem excitat ex globo vitreo ad quem digitum eundem admovet? Respondeo: quod phaenomenon hoc nobis indicare videtur materiam electricam multò puriorem exire ex globo vitreo, quàm ex tubo ferreo.

510 You will ask, II.: for what cause does a man initially electric draw a lively spark from the iron tube to which he brings his finger, while the same man draws a weaker flame from the glass globe to which he brings the same finger? I reply: this phenomenon seems to indicate to us that a much purer electric matter goes out of the glass globe than out of the iron tube.

511 Quaeres III. Utrùm materia electrica possit esse contra paralysim remedium praesens? Narratur enim non modò Paralyticum unum Genevae à D. Jallaberts1, sed etiam Paralyticos multos Monspelii fuisse à D. de Sauvages curatos ope electricae machinae. Respondeo affirmative. Et verò juxta Medicos Paralysis est motus animalis, & tactûs in parte quadam corporis abolitio, vel diminutio vehemens, cum ejusdem quandoque atrophia, pulsu debili, aliisque symptomatis, proveniens à partium nervosarum relaxatione propter deficientem spirituum animalium praesentiam, aut activitatem ab oborta obstructione nervorum. Materia electrica est materia quaedam ignea subtilissima, quae motu velocissimo donatur. Debet hic ignis sese insinuare per poros materiae, tubulos

511 You will ask, III.: whether the electric matter can be a present remedy against paralysis? For it is related not only that a Paralytic at Geneva was cured by Mr. Jallabert (u), but also that many Paralytics at Montpellier were cured by Mr. de Sauvages by means of the electric machine. I reply in the affirmative. And indeed, according to the Physicians, Paralysis is the abolition, or vehement diminution, of animal motion and of touch in some part of the body, sometimes with atrophy of the same, a weak pulse and other symptoms, arising from a relaxation of the nervous parts on account of the deficient presence, or activity, of the animal spirits, through an obstruction of the nerves that has arisen. The electric matter is a certain most subtle fiery matter, which is endowed with a most rapid motion. This fire must insinuate itself through the pores of the matter obstructing the tubules of the nerves,

p. 160

nervorum obstruentis, paulatimque obstructionem omnem dissipare, & consequenter praesens esse remedium contra paralysin.

and little by little dissipate every obstruction, and consequently be a present remedy against paralysis.

512 Quaeres IV. ¿Ad quam distantiam vapor electricus propagetur? Respondeo: incredibile videri posse maximam distantiam ad quam veluti momento temporis hujusmodi vápor propagatur. Nam Fayus ad pedes 1256, Maffejus ad 2220, Watson ad 8000, ad 10600, ad 12276, pedes in filis ferreis virtutem electricam tanta celeritate propagatam fuisse testantur, ut eodem ferè instanti in altera catenae extremitate succusio perciperetur. At non iccircò putamus instantaneam esse hujusmodi propagationem, quum Beccarias1 adcuratissimis experimentis deprehenderit, vaporem electricum in 500 pedibus Parisiens. percurrendis, sensibile aliquod temporis intervallum insúmere.

512 You will ask, IV.: to what distance is the electric vapor propagated? I reply: the very great distance to which a vapor of this kind is propagated, as it were in a moment of time, may seem incredible. For Du Fay at 1256 feet, Maffei at 2220, Watson at 8000, at 10600, at 12276 feet, testify that the electric virtue was propagated along iron wires with such speed that the shock was perceived at the other extremity of the chain at almost the same instant. But we do not on that account think that a propagation of this kind is instantaneous, since Beccaria (x) discovered by most accurate experiments that the electric vapor, in traversing 500 Paris feet, takes up some sensible interval of time.

513 Quaeres V. ¿Quid sint Phosphori? Respondeo: Phosphoros omnes jure spectari à Recentioribus Physicis tanquàm corpora per adfrictum electrica. Hinc 1. Phosphorus artificiales ex sulphureis, & salinis urinae partibus constans non modò coruscare debet in ténebris, sed & partium adfrictu accendi ac obvia corpora comburere. Hinc 2. mare agitatum, saccharum celeri motu concussum, ligna putrida, squammae piscium, quum putrescere incipiunt &c. scintillas emittere debent. Hinc 3. certa barometra lucent quum agitantur in ténebris. Hinc 4. scintillas habebitis si dorsa felium pilis adversis fricuéritiss2.

513 You will ask, V.: what are Phosphori? I reply: all phosphori are rightly regarded by the Modern Physicists as bodies electric by rubbing. Hence 1. artificial phosphorus, consisting of the sulphurous and saline parts of urine, must not only glitter in the dark, but also be kindled by the rubbing of its parts and burn the bodies in its way. Hence 2. the agitated sea, sugar shaken with a quick motion, rotten wood, the scales of fish when they begin to putrefy, etc., must emit sparks. Hence 3. certain barometers shine when they are agitated in the dark. Hence 4. you will have sparks if you rub the backs of cats against the lie of the hair (y).

Experiences sur l' electricitè par Mr. Jallabert.

Experiences sur l’électricité, by Mr. Jallabert.

Dell' Elettricismo Naturale, & Artificiale.

Dell’Elettricismo Naturale, & Artificiale.

Alii naturales sunt phosphori, alii artificiales reperiuntur. Inter naturales haberi etiam solent lampyrides (vulgò alumbradores) oculi catórum, lingua Viperae irritatae, &c. Artificiales arte parantur, suntque vel sicci, vel liquidi. Siccus est inprimis lapis Bononiensis, qui ex monte Paterno propè Bononiam pétitur, hic ubi post calcinationem aëri exponitur lucem ita haurit, ut in obscuriorem locum posteà translatus aliquandiù instàr carbonis accensi luceat. Cl. Homberg, & Lemeri parare norunt phosphoros fluidos, & consistentes. (Memoires de l'Acad. 1711. & 1715.) Verùm nobis otium non súppetit, aut methodum conficiendi phosphoros, aut phaenomena plura, eorumque magis distinctam explicationem dandi; pluribus hoc persequuntur Regnault (Entret. Phys. tom. 2. Ent. 17.) & Ozanam (Recreat. Math. & Phys. tom. 4. Lib. 1. 2.) Id in universùm pro ratione horum phaenomenorum animadvertendum; motum, agitationemque subtilium partium accidere in observationibus phosphóricis: ita phosphorus Bononiensis radiis luminis agitatur, aut potius partes lapidis sulphureae igne evolutae, & exaltatae, nitrosis, aëris, cui exponuntur particulis per potentiores illius meatus ingressis sic agitantur, ut elucescere in tenebris possint.

Some phosphori are natural, others are found to be artificial. Among the natural are usually counted also fireflies (commonly alumbradores), the eyes of cats, the tongue of an irritated Viper, etc. The artificial are prepared by art, and are either dry or liquid. Dry, above all, is the Bologna stone, which is fetched from Monte Paterno near Bologna; when, after calcination, it is exposed to the air, it so drinks in the light that, carried afterwards into a darker place, it shines for some while like a lighted coal. The distinguished Homberg and Lemery knew how to prepare fluid and solid phosphori (Memoires de l’Acad. 1711 & 1715.) But we have not the leisure to give either the method of making phosphori, or more of their phenomena and a more distinct explanation of them; several authors pursue this: Regnault (Entret. Phys., vol. 2, Ent. 17.) and Ozanam (Recreat. Math. & Phys., vol. 4, bk. 1, 2.) As the account of these phenomena, this is to be noted in general: that a motion and agitation of subtle parts occurs in phosphoric observations; thus the Bologna phosphorus is agitated by the rays of light, or rather the sulphureous parts of the stone, unfolded and exalted by fire, are so agitated by the nitrous particles of the air to which it is exposed, entering through its more open passages, that they can shine out in the dark.

p. 161

CAPUT V.

CHAPTER V.

De Tonitru prout electricitati connexo.

On Thunder as connected with electricity.

514 Tria distinguimus in tonitru fulgur nempè, fragorem, & fulmen. Repentina coruscatio subitò perstringens oculos, nomen habet fúlguris. Sonus quidam hórridus in atmosphaera boans, & reboans dicitur fragor. Denique accensa quaedam exhalatio, quae saepè ingenti cum stráge ad terram usquè detrúditur, vocatur fulmen. Quaenam sint causae physicae fulgóris, id facile determinabimus, postquàm sedulò perpendérimus, undenam oriatur fulmen.

e distinguish three things in thunder, namely the flash, the crash 514 Wand the lightning. The sudden glitter that suddenly strikes the eyes has the name of flash. A certain horrid sound booming and re-echoing in the atmosphere is called the crash. Finally, a certain kindled exhalation, which is often thrust down even to the earth with huge destruction, is called lightning. What the physical causes of the flash are we shall easily determine after we have carefully weighed whence lightning arises.

515 Dico igitur I: materia electrica est causa physica fulminis. Demonstratur experientia sequenti quam in Cap. II retulimus, & quam hìc in probationem adferre necesse est. Super tectum alti cujusdam aedificii constituatur placenta resinacea, aut vitrea. Super hanc erigatur perpendiculariter aliquis ferreus tubus; constat experientiâ, quod si aliqua nubes déferens in sinu suo fulmen superimmineat huic ferreo tubo, ex illo excitabuntur scintillae, eodem prorsùs, modo ac si tubus hic ferreus, horizontaliter suspensus funiculorum sericorum ope, communicationem habuisset cum vitreo globo eximiae cujusdam electricae machinae: ergo materia electrica est causa physica fulminis.

515 I say, therefore, I.: the electric matter is the physical cause of lightning. It is demonstrated by the following experiment, which we related in Ch. II, and which it is necessary to bring forward here as proof. On the roof of some high building let a cake of resin, or of glass, be placed. On it let some iron tube be set up perpendicularly; experience establishes that if some cloud bearing lightning in its bosom hangs over this iron tube, sparks will be drawn from it in exactly the same way as if this iron tube, suspended horizontally by means of silk cords, had been in communication with the glass globe of some excellent electric machine: therefore the electric matter is the physical cause of lightning.

516 Dico 2: particulae bituminosae, sulphurae, nitrosae, &c. sunt alimenta fulminis. Demonstratur 1. Ibi fulmen est frequens, ubi reperiuntur fodinae sulphuris, bituminis, nitri, &c: ergo particulae bituminosae; sulphureae, nitrosae sunt alimenta fulminis. 2. Si quis versetur in loco, qui casu quodam misero fuerit fulmine tactus, is bituminis, sulphuris, & nitri tetrum spirabit odórem: ergo particulae bituminosae, sulphureae, nitrosae sunt alimenta fulminis.

516 I say, 2.: bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous particles, etc., are the food of lightning. It is demonstrated 1. Lightning is frequent where mines of sulphur, bitumen, niter, etc., are found: therefore bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous particles are the food of lightning. 2. If anyone is in a place which by some miserable chance has been struck by lightning, he will breathe a foul smell of bitumen, sulphur and niter: therefore bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous particles are the food of lightning.

Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

517 Opp. 1. Si materia electrica foret causa physica fulminis, sequeretur quod nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens esset actu electrica, sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: nihil est quod nubem hujusmodi reddat electricam: ergo falsum est quod actu electrica sit nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens. Nego conseq. Particulae bituminosae, sulphureae, & nitrosae per actionem solis in atmosphaeram elevatae, reddunt electricam nubem, quam videmus fulmen in sinu suo deferentem.

517 Obj. 1. If the electric matter were the physical cause of lightning, it would follow that a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is actually electric; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: there is nothing that renders a cloud of this kind electric: therefore it is false that a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is actually electric. I deny the consequence. Bituminous, sulphureous and nitrous particles, raised into the atmosphere by the action of the sun, render electric the cloud which we see bearing lightning in its bosom.

p. 162

518 Inst. Particulae sulphureae, bituminosae, & nitrosae de quibus hìc agitur, non sunt in statu actuali electricitatis: ergo non possunt electricam reddere nubem, quae fulmen defert in sinu suo. Prob. antec: particulae bituminosae &c, quae vólitant in atmosphaera, frictionem nullam patiuntur: ergo non sunt in statu actuali electricitatis. Dist. antec.: frictionem nullam patiuntur, neque patiuntur aliquid, quod aequivaleat frictioni, nego, & patiuntur aliquid, concedo, & nego conseq. Saepè áccidit, ut particulae bituminosae &c. regnantibus ventis contrariis eleventur in atmosphaeram. Hae particulae jam calidae, maximam tunc patiuntur agitationem. Frictioni validissimae aequivalet haec agitatio, sicque facilè pervenitur ad statum actualis electricitatis. Non potest autem nubes aliqua bitumen, sulphur, & nitrum actu electricum in sinu suo continére, quin pars ipsiùs aquea fiat per communicationem electrica. Ea igitur sola nubes fulmen in sinu suo defert, quae est actu electrica; & ea sola nubes est actu electrica, quae continet particulas bituminosas, sulphureas, & nitrosas regnantibus ventis contrariis in atmosphaeram terrestrem elevatas.

518 Inst. The sulphureous, bituminous and nitrous particles treated of here are not in a state of actual electricity; therefore they cannot render electric the cloud which bears lightning in its bosom. Proof of the antecedent: the bituminous particles, etc., which flit about in the atmosphere, undergo no friction: therefore they are not in a state of actual electricity. I distinguish the antecedent: they undergo no friction, nor do they undergo anything equivalent to friction, I deny; they undergo no friction, but they undergo something, I concede, and I deny the consequence. It often happens that bituminous particles, etc., are raised into the atmosphere when contrary winds prevail. These particles, being already warm, then undergo a very great agitation. This agitation is equivalent to a most vigorous friction, and thus they easily arrive at a state of actual electricity. But a cloud cannot contain in its bosom bitumen, sulphur and niter actually electric without its watery part becoming electric by communication. That cloud alone, therefore, bears lightning in its bosom which is actually electric; and that cloud alone is actually electric which contains bituminous, sulphureous and nitrous particles raised into the terrestrial atmosphere when contrary winds prevail.

519 Opp. 2. Multa sunt phaenomena fulmen spectantia, quae non possunt exponi in sententia nostra: ergo rejicienda est. Prob. antec: non potest exponi in hac sententiâ quaenam sit causa physica fúlguris: ergo. Prob antec.: non datur in regione nubium, conflictus atmosphaerae electricae densae, cum atmosphaera electrica rara: ergo. Nego secundum antec., & expono phaenomenon propositum: quum nubes minus electrica fertur in nubem magis electricam, tum fulgur habetur eodem prorsùs mechanismo, quo excitatur electrica scintilla, de qua loquebamur in Experimento IV. Cap. II. Nego etiam tertium antec.: nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens est corpus totaliter electricum, & consequenter corpus atmosphaerâ electricâ densissima circúmdatum, quod redit initialiter electricas nubes vicinas, quae fulmen in sinu suo non habent: ergo in sententia nostra datur in regione nubium, conflictus atmosphaerae electricae densae, cum atmosphera electrica rara.

519 Obj. 2. There are many phenomena regarding lightning which cannot be explained in our opinion: therefore it is to be rejected. Proof of the antecedent: it cannot be explained in this opinion what the physical cause of the flash is: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: in the region of the clouds there is no conflict of a dense electric atmosphere with a rare electric atmosphere: therefore. I deny the second antecedent, and I explain the proposed phenomenon: when a less electric cloud is borne into a more electric cloud, then the flash occurs by exactly the same mechanism by which the electric spark is excited of which we spoke in Experiment IV, Ch. II. I deny also the third antecedent: a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is a body totally electric, and consequently a body surrounded by a very dense electric atmosphere, which renders initially electric the neighboring clouds that do not have lightning in their bosom: therefore in our opinion there is, in the region of the clouds, a conflict of a dense electric atmosphere with a rare electric atmosphere.

520 Inst. 1. ex dictis sequitur quod nullum fulgur esse deberet, quum nubes totaliter electrica habet in vicinia sua nubes totaliter electricas, sed hoc repugnare videtur; ergo. Dist. major.: sequitur &c. si nubes omnes eundem habeant gradum totalis electricitatis, concedo, si gradum habeant diversum totalis electricitatis, nego maj., & conseq Fricator super placentam resinaceam constitutus fit totaliter electricus: is tamen scintillam éxcitat ex tubo ferreo totaliter etiam electrico, quia scilicet vis electrica multò debilior est in Fricatore, quàm in tubo: ergo pariter ex duabus nubibus totaliter electricis scintilla debet excitari, dummodò una sit magis vel minus electrica, quàm altera.

520 Inst. 1. From what has been said it follows that there ought to be no flash when a totally electric cloud has totally electric clouds in its vicinity; but this seems repugnant; therefore. I distinguish the major: it follows, etc., if all the clouds have the same degree of total electricity, I concede; if they have a different degree of total electricity, I deny the major, and the consequence. Let the Rubber placed on a resin cake be totally electric: he nevertheless draws a spark from the iron tube, which is also totally electric, because, namely, the electric force is much weaker in the Rubber than in the tube: therefore likewise a spark must be excited from two totally electric clouds, provided one is more or less electric than the other.

521 At inquies ¿Quaenam est in nostra sententia causa physica fragoris in atmosphaera boantis, & reboantis? Respondeo:

521 But, you will say, what in our opinion is the physical cause of the crash booming and re-echoing in the atmosphere? I reply: the flash

p. 163

Fulgur dilátat aërem contentum inter nubem magis electricam, & nubem minus electricam, quae sibi mutuo occurrunt. Hic aër subitò dilatatus cómprimit aërem vicinum, aër vicinus eximio elaterio donatus, sese restituit in primam suam figuram, atque sese restituendo fragorem hórridum éxcitat quem audímus in atmosphaera boantem, & reboantem. Ex hac physica explicatione haec necessariò sequuntur 1. Nonnunquam dari debent fulgura, quin fragor audiatur; quum scilicet, vel nimiùm distamus à loco in quo versatur nubes electrica, vel quum aër contentus inter nubem magis electricam, & nubem minus electricam sufficientem non acquisivit dilatationem. II. Nonnunquam audiri debet fragor, quin fulgur habeatur, quod accidit, quum terram inter, & nubem electricam reperitur nubes aliqua crassior; nubes enim hujusmodi, radios luminis absorbet ex quibus fulgura constant.

dilates the air contained between the more electric cloud and the less electric cloud which run against each other. This air, suddenly dilated, compresses the neighboring air; the neighboring air, endowed with an excellent elater, restores itself to its first figure, and in restoring itself excites the horrid crash which we hear booming and re-echoing in the atmosphere. From this physical explanation the following necessarily follow: I. There must sometimes be lightning flashes without any crash being heard; namely, when we are too far distant from the place in which the electric cloud is moving, or when the air contained between the more electric cloud and the less electric cloud has not acquired sufficient dilatation. II. Sometimes a crash must be heard without any lightning flash being seen, which happens when some thicker cloud is found between the earth and the electric cloud; for a cloud of this kind absorbs the rays of light of which lightning flashes consist.

522 III. Non raro judicare debemus, sonum intra nubium viscera quasi discurrere; sonus enim saepè reflectitur, vel á diversis nubium partibus, vel á diversis montibus, & cautibus, &c. IV. Fragor non auditur ex magna distantia; sonus enim non secùs, ac motus, hoc est per incursum in alia corpora tùm debilior fit, tùm etiam quandoque perit. V. Facilè cognosci potest, quantum distet á nobis nubes, quae fulmen in sinu suo continet. Et verò lumen fulguris ad nos usque intra spatium insensibile temporis, transmittitur; sonus autem intra unum minutum secundum temporis 173 hexapedas parisinas tantummodò percurrit: si igitur fulgur inter, & fragorem numerentur quatuor minuta secunda temporis, inde inferetur evidenter nubem electricam 692 hexapedis Parisinis á nobis esse distantem. VI. Si fragor audiatur eodem instanti praecisè, quo micat fulgur, tùm inferendum erit propiorem esse nubem electricam.

522 III. Not rarely must we judge the sound to be, as it were, running about within the bowels of the clouds; for the sound is often reflected either from different parts of the clouds, or from different mountains and crags, etc. IV. The crash is not heard from a great distance; for sound, no otherwise than motion, that is, through running into other bodies, both becomes weaker and sometimes even perishes. V. It can easily be known how far distant from us is the cloud which holds the thunderbolt in its bosom. And indeed the light of the lightning flash is transmitted all the way to us within an insensible space of time, whereas sound runs through only 173 Paris toises within one second of time: if, therefore, four seconds of time should be counted between the flash and the crash, it will evidently be inferred from this that the electric cloud is 692 Paris toises distant from us. VI. If the crash is heard at precisely the same instant at which the flash gleams, then it will have to be inferred that the electric cloud is nearer.

523 Quaeres iterum: ¿Quandonam, & quânam de causa frángitur nubes, fulmen in sinu suo deferens? Respondeo: tùnc frangi nubem fulmen in sinu suo continentem, quum validior est ventus, qui fert nubem minus electricam contra nubem magis electricam, vel quum vividior est electricitas, quae viget intra nubis electricae viscera. Neque profectò ullus erit, qui vim, & efficaciam hujus ultimae causae révocet in dubium; nemo enim nescit propter nimiam electricitatem, hiberno praecipuè tempore, confractos fuisse vitreos globos; ergo á fortiori nimiam propter electricitatem saepius frangi debent electricae nubes.

523 You will ask again: When, and for what cause, is the cloud carrying the thunderbolt in its bosom broken? I reply: the cloud containing the thunderbolt in its bosom is broken then, when the wind which carries the less electric cloud against the more electric cloud is stronger, or when the electricity which thrives within the bowels of the electric cloud is more vigorous. Nor indeed will there be anyone who calls into doubt the force and efficacy of this last cause; for no one is unaware that, on account of excessive electricity, especially in wintertime, glass globes have been shattered; therefore a fortiori electric clouds must more often be broken on account of excessive electricity.

524 Ex dictis haec evidenter sequuntur. I. Exhalationes bituminosas, sulphureas, & nitrosas quae reperiuntur intra viscera nubium electricarum, & quae sunt alimenta fulminis accendi debere per ignem electricum. II. Ex his exhalationibus alias esse crassas, alias tenuiores: exhalationes crassae agunt in corpora, quorum ampliores sunt pori; & intacta relinquunt corpora, quorum pori arctiores sunt. Eam ob causam fulmina quaedam nonnunquam vaginam, intacto ense, consumpsére. Tenues autèm exhalationes agunt

524 From what has been said the following evidently follow. I. The bituminous, sulphureous and nitrous exhalations which are found within the bowels of electric clouds, and which are the fuel of the thunderbolt, must be kindled by the electric fire. II. Of these exhalations some are thick, others thinner: the thick exhalations act on bodies whose pores are wider, and leave untouched bodies whose pores are narrower. For that reason certain thunderbolts have sometimes consumed the scabbard, leaving the sword untouched. Thin exhalations, on the other hand, act only

p. 164

in sola corpora compacta. Exhalationibus hujus speciei constabant fulmina, quae liquaverunt ensem intacta vagina.

on compact bodies alone. Of exhalations of this species were formed the thunderbolts which melted the sword, leaving the scabbard untouched.

525 Quaeres deniquè ¿Undenam oriatur vis stupenda exhalationis accensae? Respondeo: oriri primum ab ipsa velocitate ignis, quam incredibilem esse, norunt omnes; deinde ab ipso elaterio aëris, qui reperitur intra particulas sulphureas, bituminosas, & nitrosas ex quibus exhalatio constat. Hic autem est diligenter adnotandum non omne fulmen, seu non omnem exhalationem accensam in terram décidere. Ea tantum exhalatio cadit, cui nubes superiores resistentiam majorem opponunt, quàm nubes inferiores.

525 You will ask, finally: Whence does the stupendous force of the kindled exhalation arise? I reply: it arises first from the very velocity of fire, which all know to be incredible; then from the very elater of the air which is found within the sulphureous, bituminous and nitrous particles of which the exhalation consists. Here, however, it is to be diligently noted that not every thunderbolt, or not every kindled exhalation, falls to the earth. That exhalation alone falls to which the upper clouds oppose a greater resistance than the lower clouds.

526 Opp. deniquè: in sententia nostra exponi non potest, undenam oriatur lapis fulmineus, ergo sunt phaenomena fulmen spectantia quae in hac sententia non possunt exponi. Prob. antec: lapis neque est materia neque alimentum fulminis: ergo. Nego totum argumentum, tanquam falsum supponens. Quaecumque narrantur de lapide fulmineo, haec habentur â Physicis Recentioribus, Viris nempè sanae mentis, tanquam aniles fabulae. Lapis fulmineus nihil est aliud quam lapis existens in loco ad quem fulmen pervenit, & ab accensa exhalatione sensibiliter immutatus. Haec circà tonitru tradenda habuimus. Jam verò postulat naturalis ordo, ut pauca dicamus de terraemotibus, quibus cum tonitru magnam analogiam esse, jure videtur.

526 Obj. finally: in our opinion it cannot be explained whence the thunderstone arises; therefore there are phenomena regarding the thunderbolt which cannot be explained in this opinion. Proof of the antec.: the stone is neither the matter nor the fuel of the thunderbolt: therefore. I deny the whole argument, as supposing what is false. Whatever is related about the thunderstone is held by the more recent Physicists, men, namely, of sound mind, as old wives’ tales. The thunderstone is nothing other than a stone existing in the place to which the thunderbolt has come, and sensibly altered by the kindled exhalation. This is what we had to set forth concerning thunder. Now, however, the natural order demands that we say a few things about earthquakes, with which thunder is rightly seen to have a great analogy.

CAPUT VI. — CHAPTER VI

De Terraemotibus prout ab Electricitate pendentibus.

On Earthquakes, as Depending on Electricity.

527 Si quis unquam in dubium revocaverit diversos terrae tractus validis aliquandò motibus succuti, is interrogare poterit miseros Olysiponenses, quorum urbs praeclara fuit violentem propter terrae concussionem, die 1 Novembris anni 1755, non solum subversa, sed & quasi absorpta.s1 Ut autem funesti hujus phaenomeni causas physicas certius, & facilius inveniamus, haec mihi videntur esse necessariò praemittenda. Primo: praeter ignem quem in centro terrae admittunt non pauci Physici, & quem ideo centralem adpellant, dantur

f anyone has ever called into doubt that various tracts of the earth have at 527 I times been shaken by violent motions, he may question the wretched people of Lisbon, whose most illustrious city, on account of a violent concussion of the earth, on the 1st of November of the year 1755, was not only overturned but, as it were, swallowed up. (z) But in order that we may find the physical causes of this deadly phenomenon more surely and more easily, the following seem to me necessarily to be premised. First: besides the fire which not a few Physicists admit at the center of the earth, and which for that reason they call central, there are in addition many

p. 165

insuper in ejusdem terrae sinu ignes multi subterranei. Hinc oriuntur flammae, quas évomunt mons Aetna in Sicilia, mons Vesubius in tractu Neapolitano, &c. II. Sine pábulo non servantur ignes isti subterranei. Pábulum autèm ignium istorum commune sunt sulphur, bitumen, nitrum, ceteràque corpora fossilia, quorum plurima sunt per adfrictum electrica. Hinc non mirum est quod frequentes sint sulphuris, & bituminis fodinae in iis terrarum tractibus sub quibus subterranei ignes látitant.

many subterranean fires in the bosom of the same earth. Hence arise the flames which Mount Etna in Sicily, Mount Vesuvius in the territory of Naples, etc., vomit forth. II. These subterranean fires are not kept up without fuel. The common fuel of these fires, moreover, is sulphur, bitumen, niter and the other fossil bodies, most of which are electric by friction. Hence it is no wonder that mines of sulphur and of bitumen are frequent in those tracts of land beneath which subterranean fires lie hidden.

528 III. Accenduntur in ipso terrae sinu particulae sulphureae, bituminosae, & nitrosae jam calidae per motum impressum electricae materiae quam continent. Excitatur autem hic novus motus, seu potiùs aequivalens haec frictio, nùnc à ventis contrariis in intima terrae viscera per ingentes ipsius meatus quos aerophilacios vocant penetrantibus, nùnc ab electrica scintilla intùs excitata. Hinc sequitur dari corpora per se electrica inflammabilia, & corpora per se electrica non inflammabilia. Primi generis sunt materiae omnes sulphureae, secundi generis materiae vitreae. IV. Dantur in sinu terrae specus subterraneae, quibus ut plurimùm ingentes montium moles incumbunt. V. In specubus subtérraneis reperiuntur, ignis, aqua, aër, ita tamen ut ignis, seu potiùs materia combustibilis, nempè sulphurea, bituminosa accensa locum inferiorem occupet, aqua verò locum medium, aër autem locum superiorem. His praemissis, & quasi totidèm principiis positis.

528 III. Within the very bosom of the earth sulphureous, bituminous and nitrous particles, already hot through the motion impressed by the electric matter which they contain, are kindled. This new motion, however, or rather this equivalent friction, is excited now by contrary winds penetrating into the inmost bowels of the earth through its huge passages, which they call aërophylacia, now by an electric spark excited within. Hence it follows that there are bodies electric per se that are inflammable, and bodies electric per se that are not inflammable. Of the first kind are all sulphureous materials, of the second kind vitreous materials. IV. There are in the bosom of the earth subterranean caves, upon which for the most part huge masses of mountains rest. V. In subterranean caves are found fire, water and air, in such a way, however, that the fire, or rather the combustible matter, namely sulphureous and bituminous matter, when kindled, occupies the lowest place, the water the middle place, and the air the uppermost place. These things being premised, and laid down as so many principles,

529 Dico: Principiorum mox traditorum ope facilè admodùm exponuntur terreaemotus. Prob. conclusio explicatione sequenti. Sit ingens specus subterranea, cui regio, vel urbs aliqua superincumbat. In inferiori parte hujus specus accendantur per ignem electricum, materiae sulphureae, bituminosae, nitrosae, &c. Partem mediam specus ejusdem occupet aqua, & partem superiorem aër. Quibus suppositis sic ratiocinor. Res in hoc statu esse non possunt, quin ab igne subterraneo incalescant aqua, & aër: incalescere non possunt aqua, & aër, quin mirum in modum rarefiant; rarefieri non possunt, quin majorem locum occupare conentur.
