Quò faciliùs igitur ab iis angustiis liberentur atque sese expediant, proprium carcerem adtollent, ipsum disrumpent, atque vehementi cum fragóre indè erumpent; ¿quid mirum igitur quòd terra validis tunc succutiatur motibus?

529 I say: By means of the principles just set forth earthquakes are explained very easily. The conclusion is proved by the following explanation. Let there be a huge subterranean cave over which some region or city lies. In the lower part of this cave let sulphureous, bituminous, nitrous materials, etc., be kindled by electric fire. Let water occupy the middle part of the same cave, and air the upper part. These things supposed, I reason thus. Things cannot be in this state without the water and the air growing hot from the subterranean fire: the water and the air cannot grow hot without being rarefied in a wonderful manner; they cannot be rarefied without striving to occupy a greater space. Therefore, in order to free themselves from those straits and extricate themselves the more easily, they will lift up their own prison, burst it asunder, and break out from it with a violent crash: what wonder, then, that the earth is at that time shaken by violent motions?

530 Ea fuit probabiliter causa physica non solum violentae hujus concussionis qua subversa fuit Urbs Olysiponensis, & Guathimalensis, sed etiam omnium omninò terraemotuum de quibus ampla fit apud Historicos mentio. Funesti hujus phaenomeni sensibilem vobis praebent imagines cuniculi militares. Et verò si pulvere pyrio selecto cuniculum instruas, & probè majores omnes meatus obstruas; pulvis pyrius accensus certum terrae tractum non movebit modò, sed penitùs subvertet:s1 ergo principiorum traditorum ope rectè, & facilè admodum exponitur, quidquid ad terraemotus adtinet.

530 This was probably the physical cause not only of the violent concussion by which the City of Lisbon was overturned, and that of Guatemala, but also of absolutely all the earthquakes of which ample mention is made among the Historians. Military mines afford you sensible images of this deadly phenomenon. And indeed, if you furnish a mine with choice gunpowder and duly stop up all the larger passages, the kindled gunpowder will not merely move a certain tract of earth but will utterly overturn it: (*) therefore by means of the principles set forth, whatever pertains to earthquakes is explained rightly and very easily.

Idem infortunium passa est Guathimala praeclara Urbs hujus nostrae Americae violentam propter terrae concussionem subversa, die 29 Julii Anni proximè elapsi 1773.

The same misfortune was suffered by Guatemala, an illustrious City of this our America, overturned on account of a violent concussion of the earth on the 29th of July of the year just past, 1773.

Vid. Memoir. de l' Academ. Royal, ad ann. 1700.

See Memoir. de l’Academ. Royal, for the year 1700.

p. 166

Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

531 Opp. 1. Tota haec explicatio terraemotuum falsum supponit: ergo & ipsa falsa est. Prob. antec.: Supponit ignes accensos existere in fundo subterranearum specuum; sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. minor.: si existerent ignes accensi, existeret, & aer in eodem fundo, atqui ibi non existit: ergo. Prob. minor: aër occupat partem superiorem specus: ergo non existit in ejus fundo. Dist. ultimum antec.: omnis aër subterraneus occupat &c, nego, maxima pars illius, concedo & nego conseq. Quemadmodùm in excipulo machinae pneumaticae ex quo fuit aër exhaustus, existere non potest accensus ignis, ita similiter non existerent ignes accensi in fundo subterranearum specuum, si fundum hoc esset prorsùs aëre vacuum. Quamvis igitur maxima pars aëris subterranei reperiatur in parte superiori specus, non dubium est, quin multus aër existat in ejus fundo.

bj. 1. This whole explanation of earthquakes supposes what is false: 531 O therefore it is itself false as well. Proof of the antec.: It supposes that kindled fires exist at the bottom of subterranean caves; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the minor: if kindled fires existed, air also would exist at the same bottom; but it does not exist there: therefore. Proof of the minor: air occupies the upper part of the cave: therefore it does not exist at its bottom. I distinguish the last antecedent: all subterranean air occupies, etc., I deny; the greatest part of it, I grant, and I deny the consequence. Just as kindled fire cannot exist in the receiver of the pneumatic machine from which the air has been exhausted, so likewise kindled fires would not exist at the bottom of subterranean caves if this bottom were altogether empty of air. Although, therefore, the greatest part of the subterranean air is found in the upper part of the cave, there is no doubt that much air exists at its bottom.

532 Opp. 2. Si terraemotus pendérent à causis superiùs adsignatis, sequeretur quod loca maritima non deberent esse terraemotibus magis obnoxia, quàm loca non maritima, sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: in nostra sententia, maris proximitas non fuit adsignata tanquam una ex causis physicis terraemotuum: ergo loca maritima non deberent esse magis obnoxia terraemotibus, quàm loca mediterranea. Dist. antec.: non fuit adsignata directè, concedo antec.: indirectè, nego, & conseq. Mare suppeditat ignibus subterraneis materiam combustibilem: ergo loca maritima debent esse magis obnoxia terraemotibus, quàm loca non maritima.

532 Obj. 2. If earthquakes depended on the causes assigned above, it would follow that maritime places ought not to be more subject to earthquakes than places not maritime; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the maj.: in our opinion the nearness of the sea was not assigned as one of the physical causes of earthquakes: therefore maritime places ought not to be more subject to earthquakes than inland places. I distinguish the antec.: it was not assigned directly, I grant the antec.; indirectly, I deny, and the conseq. The sea supplies combustible matter to the subterranean fires: therefore maritime places must be more subject to earthquakes than places not maritime.

533 At inquies, ¿quomodo fieri potest, ut quum terra tremit, tùm saepè mare intumescat? Respondeo: Quum terra tremit, saepè maris fundum elevatur. Non mirum est igitur, quod mare tunc intumescat; non mirum est etiam quod ipsius aquae hùc illùc in utramque partem non sine quodam terrarum diluvio excurrant. Hinc explicabis I. Cur in terraemotu tractus maris absorptis undis, siccus aliquandò remanserit; tunc enim apertis quae sub mari erant subterraneis specubus, tanta voragine aquae exhaustae sunt, ut tractus siccus remanserit. Explicatur II. Cur intumescentia, & inundatio fluminum saepè fuerit terraemotuum effectus. Et verò quoties habemus magnum aliquem terraemotum, totiès fundum maris adtollitur, & ipsius aquae intumescunt; quoties fundum maris adtollitur, totiès fluminum aquae non possunt maris alveum ingredi, quod quum accidit, tum aquae fluviatiles necessariò hùc illùc in utramque partem non sine terrarum diluvio excurrunt.

533 But you will say: how can it come about that, when the earth trembles, the sea then often swells? I reply: When the earth trembles, the bottom of the sea is often raised. It is no wonder, therefore, that the sea then swells; no wonder, too, that its waters run out hither and thither in both directions, not without a certain deluge of the land. Hence you will explain I. Why in an earthquake a tract of the sea, its waves swallowed up, has sometimes remained dry; for then, the subterranean caves which were under the sea being opened, the waters were drained off by so great an abyss that the tract remained dry. There is explained II. Why the swelling and flooding of rivers has often been an effect of earthquakes. And indeed, as often as we have some great earthquake, so often the bottom of the sea is raised and its waters swell; as often as the bottom of the sea is raised, so often the waters of the rivers cannot enter the bed of the sea; and when this happens, then the river waters necessarily run out hither and thither in both directions, not without a deluge of the land.

534 Explicabis III: cur in quibusdam terraemotibus adsurrexerint insulae novae. Tunc enim aër per ignes subterraneos dilatatus, ita terram sub aquis delitescentem adtollit, ut haec eadem terra

534 You will explain III: why in certain earthquakes new islands have risen up. For then the air, dilated by the subterranean fires, so lifts up the land lying hidden under the waters that this same land comes out higher

p. 167

sublimior evadat aquarum superficie. Ea fuit probabiliter origo certarum insularum quae in Archipelago, & in Oceano Atlantico adsurrexerunt.

than the surface of the waters. This was probably the origin of certain islands which have risen up in the Archipelago and in the Atlantic Ocean.

535 Inst. 1. Si terraemotus penderent à solis causis superiùs memoratis, sequeretur quod loca montuosa frequentiores terraemotus pati non deberent, quàm loca non montuosa; sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. major.: in sententia nostra montes non adnumerantur inter causas terraemotuum: ergo. Dist. antec.: non adnumerantur directè, concedo; indirectè, nego, & conseq. Ideo loca montuosa frequentiores motus patiuntur, quia ut plurimùm sub montibus specus reperiuntur, ut superiùs diximus. Hinc explicatur facilè cur tremat, nunc major, nunc minor terrae tractus. Id enim pendet ceteris paribus á majore, vel minore cavernae profunditate, & latitudine, quò profundior enim, & latior est subterranea caverna, eò majus evidenter debet esse spatium terrae quod adtollitur.

535 You will insist 1. If earthquakes depended on the causes mentioned above alone, it would follow that mountainous places ought not to suffer more frequent earthquakes than places not mountainous; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: in our opinion mountains are not numbered among the causes of earthquakes: therefore. I distinguish the antec.: they are not numbered directly, I grant; indirectly, I deny, and the conseq. Mountainous places suffer more frequent motions for this reason, that for the most part caves are found under mountains, as we said above. Hence it is easily explained why now a greater, now a lesser tract of earth trembles. For this depends, other things being equal, on the greater or lesser depth and breadth of the cavern; for the deeper and broader the subterranean cavern is, the greater, evidently, must be the space of earth which is lifted up.

536 Inst. 2. Ex dictis sequitur quod idem terraemotus non posset duas urbes concútere, quin & concúteret omnia loca intermedia, sed hoc est falsum, nam ultimus terraemotus, quem Olysiponensem vocare possumus, plurimas Europae urbes, aut concussit, aut subvertit; nec tamèn omnia loca intermedia detrimentum aliquod passa fuerunt: ergo. Dist. majorem: quin & concúteret omnia loca intermedia, supponendo quod hic terraemotus pendeat ab unico igne in unica specu subterranea accenso, concedo; supponendo quod pendeat à pluribus ignibus accensis, nego, & conseq. Ultimus terraemotus pendebat evidenter á pluribus ignibus accensis in diversis specubus subterraneis, quae per venas sulphureas inter se communicabant.

536 You will insist 2. From what has been said it follows that the same earthquake could not shake two cities without also shaking all the places in between; but this is false, for the last earthquake, which we can call that of Lisbon, either shook or overturned very many cities of Europe; and yet not all the places in between suffered some damage: therefore. I distinguish the major: without also shaking all the places in between, supposing that this earthquake depends on a single fire kindled in a single subterranean cave, I grant; supposing that it depends on several kindled fires, I deny, and the conseq. The last earthquake evidently depended on several fires kindled in different subterranean caves, which communicated with one another through sulphureous veins.

537 Opp. 3. multa sunt phaenomena ad terraemotus pertinentia quae non possunt exponi in sententia nostra: ergo insufficiens est. Prob. antec. enumeratione sequenti. In nostra sententia non videtur exponi posse phaenomenum sequens: visi sunt terraemotus[?] per quos novae scaturigines apertae sunt, & antiquae scaturigines siccatae fuerunt: ergo &c. Nego antec., & expono phaenomenon propositum. Terraemotus per quos rupti fuerunt ággeres, qui prius aquas quasi inclusas detinebant, novas scaturigines aperire debuerunt. Contrà verò terraemotus per quos novi ággeres fluentibus aquis oppositi fuerunt, antiquas debuerunt siccare scaturigines, ipsasque à pristinâ via, apertis aliis meatibus avértere; ergo in nostra sententia rectè exponitur phaenomenum propositum.

537 Obj. 3. There are many phenomena pertaining to earthquakes which cannot be explained in our opinion: therefore it is insufficient. Proof of the antec. by the following enumeration. In our opinion the following phenomenon does not seem able to be explained: earthquakes have been seen through which new springs were opened, and old springs were dried up: therefore, etc. I deny the antec., and I explain the phenomenon proposed. Earthquakes through which dikes were broken which formerly held back the waters as though shut in must have opened new springs. On the other hand, earthquakes through which new dikes were set against the flowing waters must have dried up the old springs, and turned the waters themselves aside from their former course, other passages being opened: therefore in our opinion the phenomenon proposed is rightly explained.

538 At inquies: quomodo fieri potuit, ut in quibusdam terraemotibus aquae prius frigidae, evaserint calidae, in aliis verò aquae prius calidae frigefactae fuerint? Respondeo: motus omnes, qui juxta látices aliquot novum ignem accendunt, debent aquas calefacere quae prius erant frigidae, nemo autem dubitat, quin per motum accendi possint materiae combustibiles. Quotiescumque verò per aliquem terraemotum extinguuntur ignes antiqui, sive per

538 But you will say: how could it come about that in certain earthquakes waters formerly cold became hot, while in others waters formerly hot were made cold? I reply: all motions which kindle a new fire near some springs must heat the waters which were formerly cold; and no one doubts that combustible materials can be kindled by motion. But as often as the old fires are extinguished through some earthquake, whether they are extinguished through evaporation

p. 168

evaporationem, sive per aliam quamcumquè causam extinguantur, toties frigescere debent aquae quas prius calefaciebant ignes recens extincti. Dices iterum. ¿Quomodo ex certis terraemotibus pestilentia procedere potuit? Respondeo. In quibusdam terraemotibus exeunt ex ipso terrae sinu exhalationes bituminosae, sulphureae, nitrosae &c., quae inficiunt aërem: ergo ex certis terraemotibus debuit procedere pestilentia.

or through any other cause whatever, so often must the waters grow cold which the fires lately extinguished used to heat. You will say again: How could pestilence proceed from certain earthquakes? I reply. In certain earthquakes bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous exhalations, etc., come forth from the very bosom of the earth, which infect the air: therefore pestilence must have proceeded from certain earthquakes.

CAPUT VII. — CHAPTER VII

De Fluiditate corporum prout electricitati connexa.

On the Fluidity of Bodies, as Connected with Electricity.

539 Ea sunt corpora fluida, quae partium suarum sensibilium divisioni non resistunt, & quorum partes insensibiles sunt in motu continuo, & perturbato. Ex hac descriptione haec videntur necessario sequi. Primò. Corpora fluida constare particulis exiguis. Si enim partes ipsorum essent majusculae, & crassiores, non possent hùc illùc facilè moveri. Secundò: Plerumque rotunda est figura particularum ex quibus fluida constant. Et verò particulae hujusmodi facilè separantur aliaé ab aliis: ergo aut parum, aut nihil inter se cohaerent: ergo illas plerumque rotundas esse adfirmari potest. Dixi plerumque; non enim negaverim nonnullas, ex his partibus oblongas esse, conicas nonnullas, nonnullas cylindricas, aut alterius cujuscumque figurae. Tertiò: Fluida communia penetrantur á fluido subtiliori, quod ab igne electrico indistinctum esse credimus. His praemissis.

hose bodies are fluid which do not resist the division of their sensi539 T ble parts, and whose insensible parts are in continual and disordered motion. From this description the following seem necessarily to follow. First: Fluid bodies consist of tiny particles. For if their parts were rather large and rather thick, they could not easily be moved hither and thither. Second: For the most part the figure of the particles of which fluids consist is round. And indeed particles of this kind are easily separated one from another: therefore they cohere among themselves either little or not at all: therefore it can be affirmed that they are for the most part round. I said for the most part; for I would not deny that some of these parts are oblong, some conical, some cylindrical, or of any other figure whatever. Third: Common fluids are penetrated by a subtler fluid, which we believe to be not distinct from the electric fire. These things premised,

540 Dico: I. Partes insensibiles corporum fluidorum sunt semper in motu perturbato. Prob: sublato motu continuo, & perturbato in partibus insensibilibus corporum fluidorum, explicari non possunt pléraque naturae phaenomena; admisso autem hoc motu, facilè admodùm explicantur haec eadem phaenomena: ergo partes insensibiles corporum fluidorum sunt semper in motu perturbato. Prob. antec.: sublato motu continuò, & perturbato in partibus insensibilibus corporum fluidorum, explicari non potest ex. gr. cur sales exsolvantur in aqua frigida; cur metalla dissolvantur in aquis stygiis &c; admisso autèm hoc motu, negotium nullum facessit horum effectuum explicatio, quemadmodùm vel leviter consideranti patebit: ergo.

540 I say I: The insensible parts of fluid bodies are always in disordered motion. Proof: if continual and disordered motion in the insensible parts of fluid bodies is taken away, most of the phenomena of nature cannot be explained; but if this motion is admitted, these same phenomena are explained very easily: therefore the insensible parts of fluid bodies are always in disordered motion. Proof of the antec.: if continual and disordered motion in the insensible parts of fluid bodies is taken away, it cannot be explained, for example, why salts are dissolved in cold water, why metals are dissolved in Stygian waters, etc.; but if this motion is admitted, the explanation of these effects gives no trouble at all, as will be plain to anyone considering it even lightly: therefore.

541 Dico 2: Ignis intra fluida látitans est causa motus continui, & perturbati, quò agitantur partes insensibiles corporum

541 I say 2: The fire lying hidden within fluids is the cause of the continual and disordered motion by which the insensible parts of fluid bodies are agitated.

p. 169

fluidorum. Prob.: motus continuus & perturbatus quò agitantur partes insensibiles corporum fluidorum repetendus est ab illo corpore, cujus partes sunt semper in motu perturbato, ut fatentur omnes Physici: ergo repetendus est ab igne intra hujusmodi corpora latitante.

Proof: the continual and disordered motion by which the insensible parts of fluid bodies are agitated is to be traced back to that body whose parts are always in disordered motion, as all Physicists acknowledge: therefore it is to be traced back to the fire lying hidden within bodies of this kind.

542 Dico 3: Ignis producens motum continuum, & perturbatum in partibus insensibilibus corporum fluidorum non videtur esse distinctus ab igne electrico. Probatur: Ignis augens fluiditatem corporum, non videtur esse distinctus ab igne hanc eandem fluiditatem producente, sed ignis electricus est ignis augens fluiditatem corporum: ergo ignis electricus est ignis hanc eandem fluiditatem producens. Prob. min.: sint duo vasa perfectè aequalia A, & B (Fig. LIX.) quae adimpleantur eâdem aquâ. Electrica fiat aqua in vase A contenta, remaneatque nonelectrica aqua in vase B comprehensa. Duobus istis vasis succesivè adplicetur idem sipho capillaris experientia constat, quod aqua electrica multò velocius fluet, quàm aqua non electrica, seu quod idem est, experientiâ constat, quod aqua electrica fluidior erit, quàm aqua non electrica; ergo ignis electricus, est ignis augens fluiditatem corporum.

542 I say 3: The fire producing the continual and disordered motion in the insensible parts of fluid bodies does not seem to be distinct from the electric fire. Proof: The fire increasing the fluidity of bodies does not seem to be distinct from the fire producing this same fluidity; but the electric fire is a fire increasing the fluidity of bodies: therefore the electric fire is the fire producing this same fluidity. Proof of the min.: let there be two perfectly equal vessels, A and B (Fig. LIX.), which are filled with the same water. Let the water contained in vessel A be made electric, and let the water held in vessel B remain non-electric. To these two vessels let the same capillary siphon be applied in succession: experience establishes that the electric water will flow much more swiftly than the non-electric water, or, what is the same, experience establishes that the electric water will be more fluid than the non-electric water: therefore the electric fire is a fire increasing the fluidity of bodies.

Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

543 Opp. I. Si corpora fluida semper essent in motu perturbato sequeretur quod omnia fluida, forent sensibiliter calida, sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: natura caloris sensibilis consistit in motu perturbato partium corporis calidi: ergo si &c. Antec. rotundè negari debet â nobis, qui ut Dissertatione sequenti videbimus oppositam sententiam contra Cartesium defendimus. Sed claritatis gratia dist. antec.: in motu perturbato partium sensibilium, ut postea, explicabimus, concedo; partium duntaxat insensibilium corporis calidi, nego, & conseq. Solutio melius explicabitur quum de calore agemus. Sed dices: hoc posito nunquam dici potest fluida esse in quiete. Dist. esse in quiete partium earundem insensibilium, concedo; sensibilium, nego. Ea fluida quiescere dicuntur, quorum pártes sensibiles existunt in quiete respectivâ, hoc est quoad sensum nostrum.

bj. I. If fluid bodies were always in disordered motion, it would follow 543 O that all fluids would be sensibly hot; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the maj.: the nature of sensible heat consists in the disordered motion of the parts of the hot body: therefore if, etc. The antec. must be roundly denied by us, who, as we shall see in the following Dissertation, defend the opposite opinion against Descartes. But for clarity’s sake I distinguish the antec.: in the disordered motion of the sensible parts, as we shall explain afterwards, I grant; of the insensible parts only of the hot body, I deny, and the conseq. The solution will be better explained when we treat of heat. But you will say: this being supposed, it can never be said that fluids are at rest. I distinguish: that they are at rest as to those same insensible parts, I grant; as to the sensible parts, I deny. Those fluids are said to be at rest whose sensible parts exist in respective rest, that is, as far as our sense is concerned.

544 Opp. 2. Ignis non est in motu continuo: ergo non est causa fluiditatis corporum. Prob. antec.: motus perpetuus non existit in rerum natura: ergo. Dist. antec.: non existit in rerum natura; hoc est, non existit, motus semel impressus, qui constanter idem, & in eodem praecisè gradu perseveret, concedo; hoc est, non existunt in rerum natura corpora quae semper sint in aliquo motu nunc majore, nec minore, nego, & conseq. Sic autem explicamus, & ad Mechanicae leges redúcimus motum ignis quem liberum supponimus. Primò. Dantur in rerum natura moleculae infinitè parvae, aut quasi infinitè parvae primi, secundi, tertii ordinis &c. à Geometris representari solent hujusmodi moleculae per hos characteres [?]

544 Obj. 2. Fire is not in continual motion: therefore it is not the cause of the fluidity of bodies. Proof of the antec.: perpetual motion does not exist in the nature of things: therefore. I distinguish the antec.: it does not exist in the nature of things, that is, there does not exist a motion, once impressed, which perseveres constantly the same and in precisely the same degree, I grant; that is, there do not exist in the nature of things bodies which are always in some motion, now greater, now lesser, I deny, and the conseq. Thus, moreover, we explain the motion of fire, which we suppose free, and reduce it to the laws of Mechanics. First. There exist in the nature of things molecules infinitely small, or as it were infinitely small, of the first, second, third order, etc. Molecules of this kind are customarily represented by Geometers by these characters:

p. 170

545 Secundò: Molecula infinitè parva primi ordinis est infinitè major, quàm molecula infinitè parva secundi ordinis; item molecula infinitè parva secundi ordinis est infinitè, aut quasi infinitè major, quàm molecula infinitè parva tertii ordinis &c: molecula A ex. gr. vorticosè gyrabit versùs moleculam B (Fig. LX.) si donetur eodem tempore, & perseveranter motu perpendiculari, seu centrípeto, juxta lineam A B, & motu horizontali seu projectionis, juxta lineam A C. Non alio mechanismo Luna gyrat circa terram, & planétae circa Solem periodicè moventur.

545 Second: A molecule infinitely small of the first order is infinitely greater than a molecule infinitely small of the second order; likewise a molecule infinitely small of the second order is infinitely, or as it were infinitely, greater than a molecule infinitely small of the third order, etc.: the molecule A, for example, will whirl round in a vortex toward the molecule B (Fig. LX.) if it is endowed at the same time, and perseveringly, with a perpendicular or centripetal motion along the line A B, and with a horizontal motion, or motion of projection, along the line A C. By no other mechanism does the Moon revolve about the earth, and the planets move periodically about the Sun.

546 Centrípeta vis juxta eximium Newtonum s1 est quâ corpora versùs punctum aliquod tanquàm ad centrum undique trahuntur, impelluntur, vel utcumque tendunt. Demonstravit itaque Cl. Newtonus quod molecula A. infinitè parva secundi ordinis sensibiliter tendet, seu motum centrípetum habebit in moleculam B infinitè parvam primi ordinis, dummodò istae duae moleculae non multum distent à se invicèm. Sic igitur expono motum continuum & vorticosum elementaris ignis. Ignis elementaris seu igneus quicumque vorticulus componitur ex molecula infinitè parva ordinis superioris, circà quam vorticosè gyrant moleculae infinitè parvae inferioris ordinis, simul & perseveranter donatae vi projectionis, & vi centrípeta. Si moleculà centralis sit quantitas infinitè parva primi ordinis, moleculae gyrantes erunt quantitates infinitè parvae secundi ordinis. Si molecula centralis sit quantitas infinitè parva secundi ordinis, moleculae gyrantes erunt quantitates infinitè parvae tertii ordinis &c.

546 Centripetal force, according to the eminent Newton (a), is that by which bodies are drawn, impelled, or in any way tend from all sides toward some point as toward a center. The celebrated Newton has accordingly demonstrated that a molecule A, infinitely small of the second order, will sensibly tend, or will have a centripetal motion, toward a molecule B, infinitely small of the first order, provided these two molecules are not far distant from each other. Thus, therefore, I explain the continual and vortical motion of elementary fire. Elementary fire, or any fiery little vortex whatever, is composed of a molecule infinitely small of a higher order, about which molecules infinitely small of a lower order whirl round in a vortex, endowed simultaneously and perseveringly with the force of projection and with centripetal force. If the central molecule is a quantity infinitely small of the first order, the whirling molecules will be quantities infinitely small of the second order. If the central molecule is a quantity infinitely small of the second order, the whirling molecules will be quantities infinitely small of the third order, etc.

547 Opp. denique: Si per electricitatem fluidior fieret aqua jam fluida, pariter per electricitatem augeretur mercurii fluiditas; sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. minor.: Si per electricitatem augeretur mercurii fluiditas, sequeretur quod mercurius altior esse deberet in thermometro (de quo cum de frigore agemus) cui communicata fuit vividior electricitas, quàm in simili thermometro, quod nullam acquisivit electricitatem, sed hoc est falsum ut experientiâ constat: ergo. Prob. major.: si per electricitatem augetur mercurii fluiditas, sequitur quod major ipsi communicatur ignis quantitas; sed si mercurio thermometri communicatur major ignis quantitas, profectò altior debet esse in thermometro mercurius: ergo si &c.

547 Obj. finally: If water already fluid were made more fluid through electricity, the fluidity of mercury would likewise be increased through electricity; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the minor: if the fluidity of mercury were increased through electricity, it would follow that the mercury ought to stand higher in a thermometer (of which we shall speak when we treat of cold) to which a livelier electricity has been communicated than in a similar thermometer which has acquired no electricity; but this is false, as experience establishes: therefore. Proof of the major: if the fluidity of mercury is increased through electricity, it follows that a greater quantity of fire is communicated to it; but if a greater quantity of fire is communicated to the mercury of the thermometer, the mercury must surely stand higher in the thermometer: therefore if, etc.

548 Dist. majorem, si per electricitatem augetur mercurii fluiditas, sequitur quod major ipsi communicatur quantitas ignis electrici & quasi elementaris, concedo, ignis mixti, & quasi usualis, nego, & dist. minorem: si mercurio thermometri communicatur major quantitas ignis mixti, & quasi usualis, profectò altior esse debet in thermometro mercurius, concedo minorem: major quantitas ignis electrici, & quasi elementaris, altior esse debet &c., nego, & conseq. Ignis elementaris constituitur à vorticulis: usualis verò

548 I distinguish the major: if the fluidity of mercury is increased through electricity, it follows that a greater quantity of electric and, as it were, elementary fire is communicated to it, I grant; of mixed and, as it were, usual fire, I deny; and I distinguish the minor: if a greater quantity of mixed and, as it were, usual fire is communicated to the mercury of the thermometer, the mercury must surely stand higher in the thermometer, I grant the minor; if a greater quantity of electric and, as it were, elementary fire, it must stand higher, etc., I deny, and the conseq. Elementary fire is constituted by little vortices; usual fire, on the other hand,

Princip. Lib. 1. Def. [?]

Principia, bk. 1, Def. 5.

p. 171

efformatur ab iisdem vorticulis, qui secum abripnerunt particulas bituminosas, sulphureas, oleosas, nitrosas &c. A majori vel minori dilatatione pendet altitudo mercurii in thermometro. Haec autem dilatatio, effectus est ignis mixti, & quasi usualis, non verò ignis electrici, & quasi elementaris; ergo mercurius altior esse non debet in thermometro, cui communicata fuit vividior electricitas, quàm in simili thermometro, quod nullam acquisivit electricitatem. Atque hactenùs de Electricitate.

is formed by those same little vortices, which have swept along with them bituminous, sulphureous, oily, nitrous particles, etc. On the greater or lesser dilatation depends the height of the mercury in the thermometer. This dilatation, moreover, is an effect of mixed and, as it were, usual fire, not of electric and, as it were, elementary fire: therefore the mercury ought not to stand higher in a thermometer to which a livelier electricity has been communicated than in a similar thermometer which has acquired no electricity. And so much for Electricity.

PHYSICES — PHYSICS

PARS IV.

PART IV.

DE QUALITATIBUS CORPORUM.

ON THE QUALITIES OF BODIES.

DISSERTATIO I. — DISSERTATION I

De Physica natura qualitatis sensibilis.

On the Physical Nature of Sensible Quality.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

Notiones necessariae praemittuntur.

The Necessary Notions Are Set Forth First.

549 Suas corpus quodcumque habere qualitates, quibus formaliter, ut Scholae verbo utar, sensibile redditur, nescius nemo est: at quae sit physica illarum natura, inter Philosophos acriter disputatur. Scholastici namque, sive Peripatetici, quos vocant rigidiores ratum fixumque habent, eas esse, entitates talis naturae, quae à corporea substantia cui insunt, quamque nobis sensibilem reddunt, separari divinitùs possint, & sine illa existere, illas iccircò accidentia absoluta adpellant, contrà verò Recentioribus persuasum est, nullam sensibilem qualitatem esse accidens absolutum prout illud sumunt Scholastici, sed ex magnitudine, figura, motu, quiete, atque textura corpusculorum; quibus sensibilia quaeque corpora componuntur eas omnes immediatè provenire. Ut verò ordine quo possit magis adcuratiori procedamus, definitiones aliquot praemittendae sunt.

hat every body has qualities by which, formally, to use the word of the 549 T Schools, it is rendered sensible, no one is unaware: but what their physical nature is, is keenly disputed among Philosophers. For the Scholastics, or Peripatetics, those whom they call the stricter, hold it settled and fixed that they are entities of such a nature that they can be separated by divine power from the bodily substance in which they inhere and which they render sensible to us, and can exist without it; for that reason they call them absolute accidents. The Moderns, on the contrary, are persuaded that no sensible quality is an absolute accident as the Scholastics take it, but that all of them proceed immediately from the magnitude, figure, motion, rest and texture of the corpuscles of which all sensible bodies are composed. But in order that we may proceed in the more accurate order possible, some definitions must be set out first.

p. 172

550 Sensibile dicitur, quod quia tale formaliter, ita nostra[?] sensoria [?] afficit, ut sensum in nobis excitet. Sic lignum quia durum est, vel coloratum, dicitur sensibile, quia si sensoriis nostris adplicetur, ita ea afficit, quatenus tale, ut hinc animus sentiat. Ex quo infertur, quod corpus per id formaliter est sensibile, per quod formaliter ejusmodi est, ut adplicatum externis sensoriis, ita ipsa afficiat, ut hinc animus ad sentiendum determinetur. Nomine sensibilis qualitatis ea corporis adfectio intelligitur, per quam formaliter corpus est sensibile, sic color, sapor &c. dicuntur qualitates sensibiles corporum, quatenùs per illas formaliter habet corpus, ut externorum sensuum ministerio à nobis percipiatur. Ex quo infertur, quod qualitas sensibilis in eo physicè posita est, per quod formaliter habet corpus, ut eam in organo sensorio, cui adplicatur immutationem faciat, ad quam in anima sensatio quaedam determinata, consequitur, quae in cogitatione consistit.

550 That is called sensible which, because it is formally such, so affects our sense organs as to excite sensation in us. Thus wood, because it is hard or colored, is called sensible, because, if it is applied to our sense organs, it so affects them, inasmuch as it is such, that the mind thereupon feels. From this it is inferred that a body is formally sensible by that through which it is formally of such a kind that, when applied to the external sense organs, it so affects them that the mind is thereupon determined to feel. By the name of sensible quality is understood that affection of a body by which the body is formally sensible; thus color, taste, etc., are called sensible qualities of bodies, inasmuch as through them a body formally has it that it is perceived by us through the ministry of the external senses. From this it is inferred that a sensible quality is physically placed in that by which a body formally has it that it produces in the sense organ to which it is applied a change upon which there follows in the soul a certain determinate sensation, which consists in thought.

551 Existentia sensibilium qualitatum in corporibus certissima est. Qui negant accidentia absoluta in sensu Scholastico, qualitatum sensibilium existentiam non iccircò inficiantur: & ipsi namque fatentur, id verè esse in corporibus per quod habent formaliter, ut externorum sensuum organa pro sensationis negotio immutent, certoque modo afficiant. Nervi sunt tenuissimi quidam veluti funiculi, qui ex intima cerebri substantia, tum etiam ex membranis cerebrum circumdantibus, tanquam ex radice prodeuntes, per totam animalis machinam praecipuè sensationis gratia[?] diffunduntur. Filamenta ex quibus nervi componuntur non omnino solida sunt: sed (ut demonstrat Cl. Heister) intùs cava, ut proindè tanquam vera vascula haberi possint.

551 The existence of sensible qualities in bodies is most certain. Those who deny absolute accidents in the Scholastic sense do not on that account deny the existence of sensible qualities: for they too acknowledge that there truly is in bodies that by which they formally have it that they change the organs of the external senses for the business of sensation and affect them in a certain way. Nerves are certain very slender little cords, as it were, which, proceeding as from a root out of the inmost substance of the brain, and also out of the membranes surrounding the brain, are spread through the whole machine of the animal, chiefly for the service of sensation. The filaments of which the nerves are composed are not altogether solid, but (as the celebrated Heister demonstrates) hollow within, so that they can accordingly be regarded as true little vessels.

552 Spirituum animalium nomine intelligitur substantia summè fluida, & maximè mobilis in cerebro secreta. Ex his quae in Logica, & in Metaphysica dicta sunt persuasum nobis est: ex immutatione, quae ex rei sensibilis adpulsu in organo sensorio efficitur, nullam in nobis sensationem contingere, nisi immutatio ipsa cerebro communicetur. Certum itidem est, organum externi cujusque sensus positum esse in tenuissimis quibusdam nervorum fibris, dissimili artificio pro specifico sensuum discrimine simul intextis, eisque nostri corporis parti exteriori insertis, quae dum ab re sensibili adficitur, sensatio in animo contingit. Positum est itaque ex. gr. organum visûs in ea oculi membrana, quae opticorum nervorum expansio est, & vulgo retina nuncupatur. His positis, veluti principium fundamentale sequens adsertio haberi debet.

552 By the name of animal spirits is understood a substance supremely fluid and most mobile, secreted in the brain. From what was said in the Logic and in the Metaphysics we are persuaded that from the change which is produced in the sense organ by the impulse of a sensible thing no sensation occurs in us unless that change is communicated to the brain. It is likewise certain that the organ of each external sense is placed in certain very slender fibers of the nerves, interwoven with a dissimilar artifice according to the specific difference of the senses, and inserted in the outer part of our body; while this part is affected by the sensible thing, sensation occurs in the mind. Thus, for example, the organ of sight is placed in that membrane of the eye which is the expansion of the optic nerves and is commonly called the retina. These things being laid down, the following assertion must be held as a fundamental principle, as it were.

553 Immutatio externi sensorii ex sensibilis rei adpulsu proveniens, quam sensatio ipsius rei in anima consequitur, non est physicè loquendo, nisi certa quaedam motio in iis nervorum fibris, quae externum sensorium constituunt, ex rei ipsius adpulsu excitata. Agens namque corporeum non agit, nisi per motum localem, videlicet nonnisi quatenùs localiter movet id, in quod agit. Nulla certè corporea actio est, quae partium motu, (ut patebit consideranti)

553 The change of the external sense organ arising from the impulse of a sensible thing, upon which the sensation of that thing follows in the soul, is nothing else, physically speaking, than a certain motion in those fibers of the nerves which constitute the external sense organ, excited by the impulse of the thing itself. For a bodily agent does not act except through local motion, namely, only insofar as it locally moves that on which it acts. Certainly there is no bodily action which by the motion of its parts (as will be plain to anyone who considers it) is

p. 173

non absolvatur. Ergo nullum quoque corpus pátitur aliquid ab agente corporeo, nisi quatenùs ab illo movetur. Patiuntur autem sensoria à rebus sensibilibus, dum illa ab hisce pro sensationis negotio excitantur: ergo in sola motione fibrarum nervearum, ex quibus ipsa sensoria composita sunt, illorum passio consistit.

not accomplished. Therefore no body, either, undergoes anything from a bodily agent except insofar as it is moved by it. But the sense organs undergo something from sensible things while they are excited by them for the business of sensation: therefore their undergoing consists in the motion alone of the nervous fibers of which the sense organs themselves are composed.

Objectiones diluuntur.

THE OBJECTIONS ARE DISPELLED.

554 Opp. 1. Ex nostra adsertione sequitur: organum illud, cujus est omnes impressiones discernere, nempè cérebrum, praeditum esse tactu exquisitissimo; sed tantum abest, ut cérebrum gaudeat exquisito tactu, quin potius sit penè stupidum: ergo impressiones sensibilium non sunt merè locales motiones. Argumentum ab ipsis Peripateticis responderi etiam debet: nam juxta ipsos: sensus communis in cérebro résidet. Dist. major. tactu exquisitissimo, si hoc vult dicere quod medullaris illius substantia ejus, sit naturae, ut valeat externorum omnium sensuum motiones recipere, concedo; si vult dicere quod tota ejus substantia capax sit sensûs, si vel levissimè à re externa tangatur, nego, & dist. minor.: cérebrum caret tactu, hoc est, intima illius substantia nequit omnium sensuum impressiones recipere, nego, hoc est nullus fit sensus, si tantum pars illius éxtima, hoc est cérebri cortex in quo nulli sunt nervi, tangatur, concedo minor., & nego conseq.

bj. 1. From our assertion it follows that that organ whose office it is 554 Oto discern all impressions, namely the brain, is endowed with a most exquisite touch; but so far is the brain from enjoying an exquisite touch that it is rather almost insensible: therefore the impressions of sensible things are not merely local motions. The argument must be answered by the Peripatetics themselves as well: for according to them the common sense resides in the brain. I distinguish the major: with a most exquisite touch, if this means that its medullary substance is of such a nature that it is able to receive the motions of all the external senses, I grant; if it means that its whole substance is capable of sensation if it is touched even very lightly by an external thing, I deny; and I distinguish the minor: the brain lacks touch, that is, its inmost substance cannot receive the impressions of all the senses, I deny; that is, there is no sensation if only its outermost part, that is, the cortex of the brain, in which there are no nerves, is touched, I grant the minor, and I deny the conseq.

555 Praeterea argumentum peccat fallacia dictionis. Est nempè error in voce tactus, quae dupliciter sumi potest 1 pro sensu qui ex contactu nervi sensorii à re sensibili á nobis excitatur. 2 pro sensu quo calida, frigida, humida &c. à nobis percipiuntur. 1. modo sumpta vox illa tactus ad quemlibet sensationis speciem referri potest, quia omnis sensus contactu perficitur, ut expressè docet magnus Boerhaavius s1: secundo modò sumpta: tactus pecularis sensus est, id tantum commune habens cum sensibus reliquis, ut quemadmodùm illi, ita etiam ipse in nobis non excitetur, nisi nervi, qui ei peragendo inserviunt à proprio objecto contingantur. Quâ distinctione posita, non est cur Peripatetici vitio vertant Recentioribus quod omnes sensus externos ad unum tactum révocent, quasi nempè, ipsi tunc sumant tactum, pro eo speciali sensu quo calor & frigus &c. percipiuntur, quod falsum omninò est.

555 Moreover, the argument sins by the fallacy of diction. There is, namely, an error in the word touch, which can be taken in two ways: 1. for the sensation which is excited in us by the contact of a sensory nerve with a sensible thing; 2. for the sense by which hot, cold, moist, etc. things are perceived by us. Taken in the first way, that word touch can be referred to any species of sensation whatever, because every sensation is accomplished by contact, as the great Boerhaave expressly teaches (b); taken in the second way, touch is a particular sense, having only this in common with the other senses, that, just like them, it too is not excited in us unless the nerves which serve it in performing its office are touched by their proper object. This distinction laid down, there is no reason why the Peripatetics should turn it into a fault in the Moderns that they reduce all the external senses to touch alone, as if, namely, they then took touch for that special sense by which heat and cold, etc., are perceived, which is altogether false.

556 Opp. 2. Si immutatio externorum organorum, id est, sensuum ex contactu oritur, frustranea est specifica organorum diversitas, sed Deus Opt. M. nihil egit frustrà: ergo. Argumentum contra ipsum Aristotelem urgeri potest. Pluribus enim locis tradit apertissimè, gustum esse speciem tactus. Lib. 2. de anima ait;

556 Obj. 2. If the change of the external organs, that is, of the senses, arises from contact, the specific diversity of the organs is in vain; but God, Best and Greatest, did nothing in vain: therefore. The argument can be pressed against Aristotle himself. For in many places he teaches most openly that taste is a species of touch. In bk. 2 On the Soul he says: Taste is

Praelect. in suas Inst. Med. ad n. 566.

Praelect. in suas Inst. Med., at no. 566.

p. 174

Sapor unum quid est rerum, quae tactu percipiuntur. Directè ad argumentum respondeo, quod quum maximè inter se differant sensibilia ea corpora, à quibus externa sensoria immutantur, & planè dissimilis sit modus, quo sensoria ipsa ab illis adficiuntur, factum non est frustra, sed summo Divini Opificis consilio, maximáque necessitate naturae, ut notabiliter quoque diversa sit externorum ipsorum sensoriorum structura, ex quo sequitur ad omnes rerum sensibilium impressiones suscipiendas, & cérebro communicandas, unum tactus organum, sumpto tactu pro speciali sensu nequaquàm sufficere.

is one of the things which are perceived by touch. To the argument I reply directly that, since the sensible bodies by which the external sense organs are changed differ very greatly among themselves, and the manner in which the sense organs themselves are affected by them is plainly dissimilar, it was not done in vain, but by the supreme counsel of the Divine Maker, and by the greatest necessity of nature, that the structure of the external sense organs themselves should also be notably diverse; from which it follows that for receiving the impressions of all sensible things and communicating them to the brain, a single organ of touch, touch being taken for a special sense, would by no means suffice.

557 Opp. 3. instando: quaecumque diversitas contingit in impressionibus rerum sensibilium, communicatur cerebro per nervos, fibras nerveas, & spiritus animales; sed in omni corporis parte hae res omnes reperiuntur & quidem ejusdem rationis: ergo in omni corporis parte extant organa quae possunt recipere sensibilium rerum impressionem, seu mutationem: ergo nostra opinione posita in solo tactu sensitiva vis consistit, & hoc uno sensu lucem, saporem, &c. percipiemus: ergo superflua erunt reliqua organa humani corporis. Nego min. argumenti: etenim humani corporis partes, quae sensationibus instrumentaliter peragendis inserviunt maximè differunt inter se, quamvis ex nervorum filamentis singulae componantur: non potest ergo dici, eas esse ejusdem rationis, hoc est, nullum planè essentiale discrimen inter eas interesse. Nego itaque fibras in omnibus corporis partibus eodem artificio simul esse intextas: hoc enim artificium, ipsâ teste experientia planè dissimile est pro specifico ipsarum partium discrimine.

557 Obj. 3, by insisting: whatever diversity occurs in the impressions of sensible things is communicated to the brain through the nerves, the nervous fibers and the animal spirits; but in every part of the body all these things are found, and indeed of the same nature: therefore in every part of the body there exist organs which can receive the impression, or change, of sensible things: therefore, our opinion being laid down, the sensitive power consists in touch alone, and by this one sense we perceive light, taste, etc.: therefore the remaining organs of the human body would be superfluous. I deny the min. of the argument: for the parts of the human body which serve instrumentally for performing sensations differ greatly among themselves, although each of them is composed of filaments of nerves: it cannot, therefore, be said that they are of the same nature, that is, that there is no essential difference whatever between them. I deny, therefore, that the fibers are interwoven with the same artifice in all parts of the body: for this artifice, as experience itself attests, is plainly dissimilar according to the specific difference of those parts.

558 Hinc enim fit, ut corpuscula solùm, ex quibus species colorum constant penetrare possint per visum, ipsumque sensorium commovere, non item verò corpuscula, quae sola, ac solummodò subire possunt, ac movere auditum, atque ita de ceteris Itaque etsi omnia externa organa ex nervorum fibris componantur, verumtamèn quia illorum structura planè diversa est, fit ut non nisi à rebus dissimilibus immutari pro sensatione ipsa possint, videlicèt, ut à lucis radiis eae tantum nervorum fibrae valeant commoveri, quae reticularem oculi membranam constituunt. Immeritò ergo interrogat P. de Benedictis, quamobrem quum in pede, ut in membris reliquis sint nervi, & fibrae, non propterea sensibilia quaeque, unius pedis ministerio à nobis discernantur? Supervacanea namque est istaec interrogatio, cui hac alterâ interrogatione responderi optimè potest. si manu ex gr. tantas, tamque mirabiles operationes facimus, ut scribere, pingere, sculpere, &c. quia manus instructa est digitis, musculis, nervis, & fibris, eccur easdem operationes nequeunt fieri pede in quo etiam digiti, musculi, nervi, & fibrae reperiuntur?

558 For hence it comes about that only the corpuscles of which the species of colors consist can penetrate through the sight and move its sense organ, but not likewise the corpuscles which alone, and only they, can strike and move the hearing, and so of the rest. Therefore, although all the external organs are composed of nerve fibers, nevertheless, because their structure is plainly different, it comes about that they cannot be changed for sensation except by dissimilar things; namely, that only those nerve fibers which constitute the reticular membrane of the eye can be set in motion by the rays of light. Wrongly, therefore, does Father de Benedictis ask why, since there are nerves and fibers in the foot as in the other members, not every sensible thing is therefore discerned by us through the ministry of the foot alone. For this question is superfluous, and can best be answered by this other question: if with the hand, for example, we perform so many and such wonderful operations, such as writing, painting, sculpting, etc., because the hand is furnished with digits, muscles, nerves and fibers, why can the same operations not be done with the foot, in which digits, muscles, nerves and fibers are also found?

559 Opp. 4. Si nulla sensatio potest sine motu pércipi, sequitur nullam esse memoriam aut sensationem in dormientibus, quum

559 Obj. 4. If no sensation can be perceived without motion, it follows that there is no memory or sensation in those who are asleep, since

p. 175

nulla detur impressio facta ab objectis tunc absentibus; sed hoc est contra experientiam: ergo. Dist. maj.: nullam esse sensationem ab occasione externa (de qua procedit quaestiò), concedo; mere internam, nego, & conseq.

no impression is made by objects then absent: but this is contrary to experience: therefore. I distinguish the maj.: that there is no sensation on an external occasion (which is what the question concerns), I grant; a merely internal one, I deny, and the conseq.

560 Opp. 5. Si adsertio nostra vera est, anima sentit eo ipso temporis puncto, quo in organo sensorio mutatio aliqua producitur; sed hoc esse non potest, si motus nervis sensoriis impressus ad cérebrum usque propagari debeat, ut anima percipiat: ergo, &c. Major constat. Nam si arbori oculos clausos obvertas, dum eosdem aperis, illicò lumen oculos ingreditur, & illicò vides, nec minima quidem mórula inter mutationem oculi, & animae perceptionem intercedit. Minor verò patet, quia quum motus in tempore fiat, aliquod temporis intervallum necessarium est, ut motus retinae fibrillis impressus ad cerebrum usque propagetur: ergo &c. Resp. disting. maj.: anima sentit eo ipso temporis puncto quo mutatio fit in organo sensorio, hoc est, inter motum nervis sensoriis impressum, & animae perceptionem nulla intercedit mora observabilis, conc. Nulla absolutè, nego maj., & sic distinct. min. neg. conseq. Si motus per exiguum spatium magna celeritate propagetur, tempus, quo per illud spatium propagatur, á nobis non percipitur seu non distinguitur. Sic quamvis certum sit, (ut postea videbimus) sonum successivè propagari, non verò in instanti; nullam tamèn possumus observare moram inter momentum, quo quis nobis proximus loquitur, & momentum, quo vox ipsius ad aures nostras pérvenit. Idem quoquè patet in propagatione lucis; statim ac accenditur candela in tenebroso loco, illicò objecta omnia etiam remota, lumine videntur perfusa, quamvis lux in instanti propagari non possit. Igitur experimentum, quod nobis objicitur, id unum probat, motum à nervis sensoriis ad cerebrum usquè magna celeritate transmitti.

560 Obj. 5. If our assertion is true, the soul feels at the very point of time at which some change is produced in the sense organ; but this cannot be, if the motion impressed on the sensory nerves must be propagated all the way to the brain in order that the soul may perceive: therefore, etc. The major is evident. For if you turn your closed eyes toward a tree, while you open them the light at once enters the eyes, and at once you see, nor does even the least little delay intervene between the change of the eye and the perception of the soul. The minor, however, is plain, because, since motion takes place in time, some interval of time is necessary for the motion impressed on the little fibers of the retina to be propagated all the way to the brain: therefore, etc. Reply: I distinguish the maj.: the soul feels at the very point of time at which the change takes place in the sense organ, that is, between the motion impressed on the sensory nerves and the perception of the soul no observable delay intervenes, I grant. None absolutely, I deny the maj., and, the min. being distinguished in the same way, I deny the conseq. If motion is propagated through a very small space with great velocity, the time in which it is propagated through that space is not perceived, or is not distinguished, by us. Thus, although it is certain (as we shall see afterwards) that sound is propagated successively and not in an instant, we can nevertheless observe no delay between the moment at which someone very near us speaks and the moment at which his voice reaches our ears. The same is also plain in the propagation of light: as soon as a candle is lit in a dark place, all objects, even distant ones, are at once seen bathed in light, although light cannot be propagated in an instant. Therefore the experiment which is objected to us proves this one thing only, that the motion is transmitted from the sensory nerves to the brain with great velocity.

561 Inst. 1. Motus ad cerebrum non propagatur per nervos, qui ad cerebrum non pertingunt; sed sensorii nervi complures, nimirum 6[?], qui ex medulla spinali prodeunt ad cerebrum non protenduntur: ergo &c. Respondeo, conc. maj. neg. min. Nam medulla spinalis est cerebri ipsius, seu medullae oblongatae productio, & nervis constat ad cerebrum usque protensis, undè fit, ut in vertebrarum s1 dorsi luxationibus, membra corporis infra luxationem posita, & motum, & sensibilitatem, quae à nervis infra luxationem constitutis pendent, amittant. Sunt itaque nervi, veluti cerebrum in omnes corporis partes diffusum.

561 You will insist 1. Motion is not propagated to the brain through nerves which do not reach the brain; but several sensory nerves, namely 60, which come out of the spinal marrow, do not extend to the brain: therefore, etc. I reply: I grant the maj., I deny the min. For the spinal marrow is a prolongation of the brain itself, or of the medulla oblongata, and consists of nerves extended all the way to the brain; whence it comes about that in dislocations of the vertebrae (a) of the back, the members of the body placed below the dislocation lose both the motion and the sensibility which depend on the nerves situated below the dislocation. The nerves are thus, as it were, the brain diffused into all parts of the body.

Vertebrae dicuntur ossa intus excavata, superius, & inferius plana, exterius variis processibus donata, quorum in collo septem, dorso, duodecim, lumbis, quinque, numerant Anatomici. Dicuntur vertebrae, quia per eas corpus variè inflectitur, vertiturque.

Vertebrae is the name given to bones hollowed within, flat above and below, and furnished on the outside with various processes, of which Anatomists count seven in the neck, twelve in the back, and five in the loins. They are called vertebrae because through them the body is variously bent and turned.

p. 176

562 Inst. 2. Reperti sunt homines, qui sine cerebro vivebant, ac sentiebant: ergo ad animae sensationem necesse non est, ut motus nervis sensoriis impressus ad cerebrum usque propagetur. Respond. dist. antec. Vivebant, & sentiebant sine maxima cerebri parte, conc. prorsùs sine illa tota parte, nego antec. & conseq. In illis erat spinalis medulla, & in ipsius principio potuit esse specialis quaedam structura, qua pars illa apta[?] redderetur[?], ut cerebri munere aliquatenùs fungeretur. Ceterùm verisimile est, homines illos stupidos admodum, atque hebetes fuisse. Si autem in aliquibus etiam deesset spinalis medulla, necessariò hujus partis vices gerere debuit pars alia quaecumque fuerit. Tandem partes has suppletorias adfuisse, ex ipsa cadaverum sectione, & observatione anatomica innotuit; fieri autem potuit, ut partes illae vi ipsius morbi corruptae, & obliteratae perierint.

562 You will insist 2. Men have been found who lived and felt without a brain: therefore for the sensation of the soul it is not necessary that the motion impressed on the sensory nerves be propagated all the way to the brain. Reply: I distinguish the antec.: they lived and felt without the greatest part of the brain, I grant; altogether without that whole part, I deny the antec. and the conseq. In them there was the spinal marrow, and at its beginning there could have been some special structure by which that part was fitted to discharge in some measure the office of the brain. For the rest, it is likely that those men were very stupid and dull. If, however, in some the spinal marrow too was lacking, some other part, whatever it may have been, must necessarily have taken the place of this part. Finally, that these supplementary parts were present became known from the very dissection of the corpses and from anatomical observation; it could also have happened, however, that those parts, corrupted and obliterated by the force of the disease itself, perished.

563 Inst. 3. Si serpentes, lacerti, aliaque animalia, quae circularibus incisuris distinguuntur, transversim secentur, singulae illorum partes ad acûs puncturam, aut aliam quamcumque irritationem variis modis torquentur, & agitantur: ac proindè adhuc sentiunt sine cerebro: ergo per analogiam, quae est inter corpora hominis, & bruti, idem dicendum est de homine. Respondeo, nego conseq. & parit. Alia enim est corporis humani structura, alia serpentum, & lacertorum, in quibus medullae spinalis partes considerari possunt tanquam totidem minora cerebra. Hinc fit, ut partes corporis humani resectae, post brevissimum tempus omni motu destituantur.

563 You will insist 3. If serpents, lizards and other animals which are marked by circular incisions are cut crosswise, the single parts of them are twisted and agitated in various ways at the prick of a needle or any other irritation whatever: and accordingly they still feel without a brain: therefore, by the analogy which exists between the bodies of man and of brute, the same must be said of man. I reply: I deny the conseq. and the parity. For the structure of the human body is one thing, that of serpents and lizards another; in these the parts of the spinal marrow can be considered as so many smaller brains. Hence it comes about that parts of the human body, when cut off, are deprived of all motion after a very short time.

564 Inst. 4. Incertum omninò est, an motus ex organo sensorio ad cerebrum propagetur fibrillarum nervearum oscillatione, an fluidi nervei, aut spirituum animalium ope, aut alio quocumque modo: ergo &c. Respond. permitto antec. & nego conseq. Etsi non investigemus modum, quo illa motus propagatio absolvitur, satis est ratione, atque experientia constare in organo sensorio motum quemdam excitari, qui ad cerebrum usque nervorum auxilio propagatur, dum anima sentit. Eodem modo respondendum est, si quis objiciat, à nobis intelligi non posse, qua ratione fieri queat, ut propter motum nervis impressum anima, quae est substantia simplex, & spiritualis percipiat objectum sensibile: factum hic statuimus, rationem facti non quaerimus. Porrò adversus facta indubitata, objectiones quaecumque nihil valent.

564 You will insist 4. It is altogether uncertain whether motion is propagated from the sense organ to the brain by the oscillation of the nervous fibrils, or by means of the nervous fluid or the animal spirits, or in any other way whatever: therefore, etc. Reply: I allow the antec. and deny the conseq. Even if we do not investigate the manner in which that propagation of motion is accomplished, it is enough that it is established by reason and experience that some motion is excited in the sense organ which is propagated all the way to the brain by the help of the nerves while the soul feels. In the same way one must reply if anyone objects that it cannot be understood by us how it can come about that, on account of the motion impressed on the nerves, the soul, which is a simple and spiritual substance, perceives the sensible object: here we establish the fact; we do not seek the reason of the fact. Moreover, against indubitable facts objections of whatever kind have no force.

565 Inst. 5. Qui organo sensorio destituuntur, sentiunt tamen, & contrà sensatione carent aliqui, in quorum nervis sensoriis motus etiam validus producitur. Ergo ut anima sentiat, necesse non est, motum nervis sensoriis imprimi. Prob. antec. ii, quibus abscissa sunt membra, dolorem aliquando in iisdem membris sentire sibi videntur, ut contigit puellae de qua Cartesius meminit s1

565 You will insist 5. Those who are deprived of a sense organ nevertheless feel, and, on the contrary, some lack sensation in whose sensory nerves even a strong motion is produced. Therefore, in order that the soul may feel, it is not necessary that motion be impressed on the sensory nerves. Proof of the antec.: those whose limbs have been cut off sometimes seem to themselves to feel pain in those same limbs, as happened to the girl whom Descartes mentions (c).

p. 177

Furiosi, & delirantes homines objecta sibi videri videntur, quae praesentia non sunt, quaeque proinde nullam, in eorum organis sensoriis mutationem producunt. S. Augustinus s1 hoc factum narrat: Presbyter quidam fuit nomine Restitutus, qui quando ei placebat ita se auferebat à sensibus, & jacebat simillimus mortuo, ut non solum vellicantes, atque pungentes minimè sentiret, sed aliquando igne ureretur admoto sine ullo doloris sensu. Respondeo: his observationibus conclusionem adprimè confirmari. Nam in omni sensatione quatuor ut diximus in Log. sunt accuratè distinguenda; duo quae pertinent ad nostrum corpus, scilicet, motus organo sensorio ab objecto sensibili impressus, & motus inde ad cerebrum propagatus; ac tertium, quod animae est nempè, his motibus respondens objecti sensibilis perceptio. Si motus organo sensorio impressus ad cerebrum usque non propagetur, anima non sentit, ut accidit in nobis dormientibus, & contingebat in Presbytero Restituto, qui mortuo simillimus jacebat.

Madmen and delirious persons seem to themselves to see objects which are not present, and which accordingly produce no change in their sense organs. St. Augustine (e) relates this fact: There was a certain priest named Restitutus who, whenever it pleased him, so withdrew himself from his senses, and lay so very like a dead man, that he not only felt nothing at all of those who plucked and pricked him, but was sometimes even burned with fire applied to him without any sense of pain. I reply: by these observations our conclusion is confirmed most excellently. For in every sensation four things, as we said in the Logic, are to be accurately distinguished; two which pertain to our body, namely, the motion impressed on the sense organ by the sensible object, and the motion thence propagated to the brain; and a third, which belongs to the soul, namely, the perception of the sensible object corresponding to these motions. If the motion impressed on the sense organ is not propagated all the way to the brain, the soul does not feel, as happens in us when we sleep, and as happened in the priest Restitutus, who lay most like a dead man.

566 Si verò sine actione objecti sensibilis externi, fibrae cerebri à causis internis eodem prorsùs modo agitentur; quo moventur, ubi objectum sensibile sua in organum extrinsecum actione eosdem motus producit, tum anima easdem habet perceptiones, quas haberet objecto sensibili in organum extrinsecum agente, & perceptiones suas vi imaginationis productas, à sensationibus non distingueret; uti accidit furiosis, & delirantibus hominibus, in quorum cerebro irregulares, ac vehementiores motus excitantur: & hoc pacto, quae sibi imaginantur confundunt cum his quae vident. Simili modo explicatur, cur ii, quibus membrum aliquod abscissum est, dolorem in eodem membro aliquandiu sentire sibi videantur; nimirùm in nervis illis, qui ad partem corporis amputatam pertingebant iidem aliquando à causis extrinsecis motus oriuntur, quos objecta externa excitarent, si nulla pars fuisset resecta.

566 But if, without the action of an external sensible object, the fibers of the brain are agitated by internal causes in exactly the same way in which they are moved when a sensible object by its action on the external organ produces the same motions, then the soul has the same perceptions which it would have if the sensible object were acting on the external organ, and it does not distinguish its perceptions, produced by force of imagination, from sensations; as happens to madmen and delirious men, in whose brain irregular and more vehement motions are excited: and in this way they confuse what they imagine with what they see. In the same way it is explained why those whose limb has been cut off sometimes seem to themselves to feel pain in that same limb for a while; namely, because in those nerves which reached the amputated part of the body the same motions sometimes arise from extrinsic causes which external objects would excite if no part had been cut off.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

Stabilitur physica natura qualitatis sensibilis.

The Physical Nature of Sensible Quality Is Established.

567 His suppositis quae à nobis dicta sunt in Logica: adsero: Qualitates sensibiles corporis naturalis, ex mechanicis adfectionibus particularum materiae, ex quibus illud compositum est, unicè provenire. Prob. In eo posita est sensibilis corporis qualitas, per quod

hese things being supposed which were said by us in the Logic, I assert: 567 T The sensible qualities of a natural body arise solely from the mechanical affections of the particles of matter of which that composite consists. Proof. The quality of a sensible body is placed in that by which

Princip. P. [?]

Principles, pt. IV.

Lib. XIV. de Civ. Dei, cap. 24.

Bk. XIV of The City of God, ch. 24.

p. 178

formaliter habet corpus aptum, ut sit sensibile [§. 550], sed à mechanicis adfectionibus particularum materiae, quibus compositum est, habet corpus ut specificè, (quemadmodùm ab illarum soliditate, ut genericè) sit sensibile: ergo. Prob. min.: Naturale quodcumque corpus per id formaliter est sensibile, per quod habet formaliter, ut externis sensoriis adplicatum nerveas illorum fibras movere certa ratione valeat [§. 550.] sed hóc praestare potest quodcumque corpus, hoc ipso, quod ex solidis corpusculis certâ magnitudine, & figurâ praeditis, certo artificio simul intextis intrinsecus componatur.

a body formally has it that it is fit to be sensible [§. 550]; but from the mechanical affections of the particles of matter of which it is composed a body has it that it is specifically sensible (just as from their solidity it is so generically): therefore. Proof of the min.: Any natural body whatever is formally sensible by that through which it formally has it that, applied to the external sense organs, it is able to move their nervous fibers in a certain manner [§. 550.]; but any body whatever can achieve this by the very fact that it is intrinsically composed of solid corpuscles endowed with a certain magnitude and figure and interwoven together with a certain artifice.

568 Et certè hoc ipsum adfirmare debent Peripatetici, nisi dicere velint eodem eos adfici modo eandem prorsùs qualitatem sensibilem haberi in lapide ex altitudine pedis unius, & ex apice turris praealtae in caput delapso, ubi lapis idem est, mechanica solum adfectio, motus, nempè, diversus est. In fine adverte, quod an Gratia, lumen gloriae atque id genus aliae spirituales animae qualitates sint accidentia absoluta in sensu Peripatetico, viderint Theologi. Moneo tantùm, etsi qualitates istae pro hujusmodi accidentibus habeantur, id ipsum non propterea de qualitatibus sensibilibus (de quibus tota quaestio est) dici oportere. Sunt enim genere diversae. Falli iccircò eos putò, qui ut evincant qualitates sensibiles corporum esse entitates absolutas, ad spirituales animae qualitates confugiunt, easque hujus esse naturae demonstrare nituntur; ut optimè advertit Clarissim. à Brixia.

568 And certainly the Peripatetics must affirm this very thing, unless they wish to say that we are affected in the same way, and that exactly the same sensible quality is found in a stone that has fallen on the head from a height of one foot and from the top of a very high tower, where the stone is the same and only the mechanical affection, namely the motion, is different. Finally, note that whether Grace, the light of glory, and other spiritual qualities of the soul of that kind are absolute accidents in the Peripatetic sense, let the Theologians see. I only point out that, even if these qualities are held to be accidents of this kind, it does not on that account follow that the same must be said of sensible qualities (which the whole question concerns). For they are diverse in genus. I therefore think those are mistaken who, in order to prove that the sensible qualities of bodies are absolute entities, take refuge in the spiritual qualities of the soul and strive to demonstrate that these are of this nature; as the most celebrated Fortunato da Brescia excellently observes.

DISSERTATIO II. — DISSERTATION II

De Qualitatibus tactilibus.

On Tactile Qualities.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De Calore.

On Heat.

569 Partes corporis dicuntur perturbatè moveri, quum ita moventur singulae, ut nulla sit loci differentia, secundum quam non abripiantur. Dicuntur verò moveri motu expansivo, quum tendunt motu suo ab ipsius corporis centro ad illius circumferentiam, adeò nimirùm ut illius tendentiae causâ, corporis extensio secundum omnem dimensionem, nisi impedimentum adsit, augeatur. Hinc veluti Principium fundamentale sequens propositio haberi debet. Dilatatio corporis, motusque perturbatus, qui in

he parts of a body are said to be moved in a disordered way when they are 569 T moved singly in such a way that there is no difference of place toward which they are not carried away. They are said to be moved with an expansive motion when they tend with their motion from the center of the body itself toward its circumference, so that, by reason of that tendency of theirs, the extension of the body is increased in every dimension unless an impediment is present. Hence the following proposition must be held as a fundamental Principle, as it were. The dilatation of a body, and the disordered motion which is excited in the parts

p. 179

partibus illius internis, quum calorem concipit, excitatur sunt caloris effectus principes, ejusque veluti charactéres. Expansivus quippè ille, perturbatusque motus partium corporis incalescentis, ita á calore, quo adficitur corpus dependet, eaque ratione ipsum consequitur, ut non secùs dependeat effectus á sua efficiente causa, illumque consequatur. Posito enim calore in corpore, in eodem ponitur, & ipse motus, illo aucto, & hic augetur, sublato verò, aut imminuto, motus quoque tollitur penitùs vel sensim decrescit, atque imminuitur.

within it when it conceives heat, are the principal effects of heat, and, as it were, its characteristics. For that expansive and disordered motion of the parts of a body growing hot so depends on the heat by which the body is affected, and follows it in such a way, that it depends on it and follows it no otherwise than an effect depends on its efficient cause and follows it. For when heat is posited in a body, the motion itself is also posited in it; when the former is increased, the latter too is increased; but when it is taken away or diminished, the motion also is either taken away entirely or gradually decreases and is diminished.

570 Calor itaque in ea entitate positus formaliter est, cujus vi dilatantur corpora quaeque, eorumque internae partes perturbatè agitantur. Deinceps itaque, ut loquar cum Doctissimo Boerhaavio s1 calorem, sive ignem adpellabo illam rem, quae istam in se proprietatem habet, ut corpora omnia consistentia, & fluentia penetret atque eò ipsò eadem dilatet in spatia majora. Non placet ergo nobis ea caloris definitio quae à Peripateticis traditur, calorem scilicet, esse, id, quo congregantur homogenea, & heterogenea disgregantur. Ut enim egregiè observat Mallebranchius s2 calor partes aquae non congregat, illas potius in vapores dissipat. Non congregat partes vini, imò nec partes argenti vivi. Contrà, omnia corpora solida, & fluida homogenea, & heterogenea resolvit, & disgregat. Ac si quaedam sint quorum partes, ignis non possit dissipare, id non fit quod sint ejusdem naturae, sed quia sunt crassiores, & solidiores, quàm ut possint ábripi motu partium. Adhaec: massam ex auro, argento, & aere conflatam nullus calor ita segregare poterit ut metalla etiam imperfecta seorsim ab auro & argento remaneant, imò si diversae auri, argenti, & aeris portiones in vase contineantur, ignique subjiciantur, post aliquod tempus vi caloris in unam congregantur massam. His positis.

570 Heat, therefore, is formally placed in that entity by force of which all bodies are dilated and their internal parts are agitated in a disordered way. Henceforth, then, to speak with the most learned Boerhaave (f), I shall call heat, or fire, that thing which has in itself this property, that it penetrates all bodies, solid and fluid, and by that very fact dilates them into greater spaces. We are not pleased, therefore, with the definition of heat which is handed down by the Peripatetics, namely that heat is that by which homogeneous things are gathered together and heterogeneous things separated. For, as Malebranche excellently observes (g), heat does not gather together the parts of water; rather it dissipates them into vapors. It does not gather together the parts of wine, nor even the parts of quicksilver. On the contrary, it resolves and separates all bodies, solid and fluid, homogeneous and heterogeneous. And if there are some whose parts fire cannot dissipate, this does not happen because they are of the same nature, but because they are too thick and too solid to be carried away by the motion of the parts. Moreover, no heat will be able so to segregate a mass melted together from gold, silver and copper that even the imperfect metals remain apart from the gold and silver; nay, if different portions of gold, silver and copper are contained in a vessel and placed over the fire, after some time they are gathered by the force of heat into one mass. These things laid down,

571 Dico 1. Calor non consistit in motu céleri, perturbato, & expansivo partium corporis incalescentis. Est contra Cartesium. Probatur: In eo non consistit calor, quod caloris effectus est; sed motus celer, perturbatus, & expansivus partium corporis, quum calorem concipit est caloris effectus [§. 569.] ergo. Confirmatur: certum omninò est, calorem esse omninò aliud ab ea sensorii passione, quam ipsius caloris sensatio in animo consequitur; sed passio sensorii, non est nisi dilatatio quaedam fibrarum nervearum quibus illud constat, & perturbata motio spirituum animalium quibus illae turgent: ergo calor est aliud ab illo celeri, perturbato, expansivoque motu, qui in particulis corporis quum calorem concipit excitatur.

571 I say 1. Heat does not consist in the swift, disordered and expansive motion of the parts of the body growing hot. This is against Descartes. Proof: Heat does not consist in that which is an effect of heat; but the swift, disordered and expansive motion of the parts of a body, when it conceives heat, is an effect of heat [§. 569.]: therefore. It is confirmed: it is altogether certain that heat is something entirely other than that undergoing of the sense organ upon which the sensation of heat itself follows in the mind; but the undergoing of the sense organ is nothing but a certain dilatation of the nervous fibers of which it consists, and a disordered motion of the animal spirits with which they swell: therefore heat is something other than that swift, disordered and expansive motion which is excited in the particles of a body when it conceives heat.

572 Dico 2: Calor in actu primo, sive prout est in corporibus, aptissimè constituitur in corpusculis mole exilissimis, celerrimo, expansivo perturbatoque motu adfectis, in fibras corporis animalis

572 I say 2: Heat in first act, or as it is in bodies, is most fitly constituted in corpuscles extremely slight in bulk, endowed with a most rapid, expansive and disordered motion, which into the fibers of the animal body
