Elem. Chem. tom. 1. p. 69.

Elem. Chem., vol. 1, p. 69.

Recherche de la Verité. Cap. 5.

Recherche de la Verité, ch. 5.

p. 180

irruentibus, similique illas motu incitantibus. Prob. per partes: 1. Certum est, calorem esse corpus, & ejus conditionis, ut pervadere queat corpora omnia: sed nequit calor, si corpus est, pervadere omnia corpora, nisi quatenùs subeat illorum poros; neque potest poros subire, & per totam ipsorum corporum molem sese diffundere, nisi quatenùs calor nihil sit diversum à corpusculis, ut est perspicuum: ergo. Secundò: nullum penitus in rerum natura existit corpus adeò compactum, ut illius poros calor subire minimè possit, ut testatur magnus Boerhaave s1: ergo adeò exilia sunt caloris corpuscula, ut jure dixerit idem ille Auctor, modò laudatus, illorum subtilitatem si ad imaginationem nostram referatur, esse infinitam.

rush, and stir them up with a similar motion. Proof by parts: 1. It is certain that heat is a body, and of such a condition that it can pervade all bodies; but heat, if it is a body, cannot pervade all bodies except insofar as it enters their pores; nor can it enter the pores and diffuse itself through the whole mass of those bodies unless heat is nothing different from corpuscles, as is evident: therefore. Second: there exists absolutely no body in the nature of things so compact that heat cannot enter its pores, as the great Boerhaave testifies (h): therefore the corpuscles of heat are so slight that the same Author, just praised, has rightly said that their subtlety, if it is referred to our imagination, is infinite.

573 Tertiò: Necesse est ut caloris particulae moveantur celerrimè motu perturbato, & expansivo. Certum est enim, fieri nullatenùs posse ut vi caloris omnia corpora dilatentur, ebulliant fluida, dura liquescant, omniumque demùm minimae partes expansivum, perturbatumque motum quum incalescunt concipiant, nisi particulae exilissimae in quibus calor consistit, urgeant parietes pororum corporis, quos subeunt, vincant momentum, quo illius moleculae adhaerent sibi mutuò, easque iccircò divellant, propellantque multiplici directione, simulque impediant, quandiu cum illis permixtae sunt, ne ad pristinum contactum partes ipsae corporis revertantur; sed hoc non possunt praestare caloris particulae, nisi expansivo, perturbatoque motu praeditae sint, ut per se patet: ergo.

573 Third: It is necessary that the particles of heat be moved most swiftly with a disordered and expansive motion. For it is certain that it can in no way come about that by force of heat all bodies are dilated, fluids boil, hard things liquefy, and finally the smallest parts of all things conceive an expansive and disordered motion when they grow hot, unless the extremely slight particles in which heat consists press upon the walls of the pores of the body which they enter, overcome the momentum by which its molecules adhere to one another, and therefore tear them apart and drive them in manifold directions, and at the same time prevent, as long as they are mixed with them, the parts of the body itself from returning to their former contact; but the particles of heat cannot accomplish this unless they are endowed with an expansive and disordered motion, as is self-evident: therefore.

574 Ad haec: motum esse celerrimum constat, quum enim dictae particulae sint mole exilissimae, nec agant nisi per motum, certumque sit ex dictis, vim quâ moventur seu quantitatem motus earum, aequare factum ex ductu massae singularum in celeritatem earumdem: apertum manet vim illarum particularum non posse esse maximam (qualis necessaria est quum valeant etiam corpora durissima dilatare), nisi maxima sit celeritas, qua motum suum perficiunt. Confirmatur adsertio: Hac caloris naturâ posita, omnes illius effectus ac phaenomena aptè explicantur. Explicatur enim primò. Cur calor non aequè facilè corpora dura pervadat ac fluida; quum enim particulae fluidi corporis solutae sint, atque ad motum magis expeditae, exigua resistentia á caloris corpusculis superanda est, ut in fluidum corpus sese insinuent, & per totam illius molem dispergantur: oppositum est de duris sentiendum.

574 Moreover: it is established that the motion is most swift; for since the said particles are extremely slight in bulk and do not act except through motion, and it is certain from what has been said that the force with which they are moved, or their quantity of motion, equals the product of the mass of each into their celerity, it remains plain that the force of those particles cannot be the greatest (such as is necessary, since they are able to dilate even the hardest bodies) unless the celerity with which they perform their motion is the greatest. The assertion is confirmed: This nature of heat being laid down, all its effects and phenomena are fitly explained. For there is explained first why heat does not pervade hard bodies as easily as fluids; for since the particles of a fluid body are loose and more ready for motion, a slight resistance has to be overcome by the corpuscles of heat in order that they may insinuate themselves into a fluid body and be dispersed through its whole mass: the opposite is to be thought of hard bodies.

575 Secundò: Rarefactio corporum cur per calorem fiat ratio redditur, quia quum caloris particulae motu expansivo praeditae sint; eae corporum poros subire nequeunt, quin contra illorum parietes vim faciant, partes urgeant, easque cogant ad recedendum á se mutuò, atque adeò ad majus spatium occupandum. Tertiò exponitur induratio, & exsiccatio luti, contra verò emollitio cerae eodem calore effecta: ibi enim partes aqueae, ac fluidiores, quae tractabilem

575 Second: The reason why the rarefaction of bodies takes place through heat is given because, since the particles of heat are endowed with expansive motion, they cannot enter the pores of bodies without exerting force against their walls, pressing upon the parts and compelling them to recede from one another, and so to occupy a greater space. Third, the hardening and drying of mud, and on the other hand the softening of wax, by the same effect of heat, is explained: for in mud the watery and more fluid parts, which

Elem. Chem. Tractat. de Igne.

Elem. Chem., Tract. de Igne.

p. 181

limum reddiderant, avolantes, faciunt ut aliae terrestres, tenaciores, & graviores propius coeant, & implicentur: in cera verò particulae viscosae, minusque evaporationi obnoxiae á vehementi motu ac vario deducuntur, hinc minus inter se compactae, minus resistunt manui prementi. Ex his autèm complura alia cognoscere poteritis, & facilè explanare.

had made it tractable, fly off and cause the other parts, earthy, more tenacious and heavier, to come closer together and become entangled; in wax, on the other hand, the viscous particles, less liable to evaporation, are drawn apart by the vehement and varied motion; hence, being less compacted with one another, they resist less the hand that presses them. From these things, moreover, you will be able to understand and easily explain many others.

Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

576 Opp. 1. Calor consistit in motu celerrimo perturbato, & expansivo corporis incalescentis, ergo Prob. antec.: illo motu posito, & aucto in corpore, in eodem ponitur, & augetur calor, & vicissim, eo motu sublato vel imminuto ipse quoque calor tollitur penitus, vel sensim decrescit: ergo. Dist. antec.: & hoc tantùm probat motum perturbatum, & expansivum corporis incalescentis esse caloris effectum principem, ac illius veluti charactérem, concedo; & probat aliquid contra adsertionem nostram, nego. Profectò verò: motio quoque similis in fibrillis sensorii tactus, quum caloris sensus in nobis fit, excitata, hac ipsâ proportione calori respondet, neque tamen in illa motione statuendus calor est, nisi velímus de nomine, ut ajunt Scholastici, disputare.

576 Obj. 1. Heat consists in a very swift, perturbed and expansive motion of the body growing hot: therefore. Prob. antec.: when that motion is posited and increased in a body, heat is posited and increased in it, and conversely, when that motion is removed or diminished, the heat itself too is either wholly removed or gradually decreases: therefore. Dist. antec.: and this proves only that the perturbed and expansive motion of the body growing hot is the principal effect of heat, and as it were its character, I grant; and it proves anything against our assertion, I deny. And indeed a similar motion too, excited in the fibrils of the sensorium of touch when the sensation of heat arises in us, answers to heat in this very proportion, and yet heat is not to be placed in that motion, unless we wish to dispute about a name, as the Scholastics say.

577 Opp. 2.: Ignis sive calor saepè donatur motu recto: ergo non donatur motu perturbato, aut vorticoso. Prob. antec.: Ignis saepè lucet, ergo donatur motu recto. Dist. antec.: motu recto inconjungibili cum motu perturbato, aut vorticoso, nego; conjungibili cum motu perturbato, conc. Vorticulus idem igneus eodem tempore motu recto, motuque perturbato donari poterit. Dum enim vel centrum vorticuli, vel etiam totalis vorticulus feretur per lineam rectam, perturbatè, necessariò gyrabunt moleculae quae constituuntur in ipsius circumferentia. ¿Nonne globus idem super planum quodcumque volutus, donatur eodem tempore, & motu per lineam rectam, & motu rotationis circa centrum suum? Ergo motus rectus non est inconjungibilis cum motu perturbato. Caloris motum varium esse posse penès pabuli, aut subjecti in quod vim suam exerit varietatem, aut juxta obices, & impedimenta, quae illius motum inhibent, fatentur omnes. Sic fieri potest, ut motus caloris sit vorticosus, aut rotationis, sed hoc non impedit quo minus perturbatus dicatur. Dum enim sulphureae particulae vertigine abreptae circa se gyrant, & aliae alias impellunt, fit quidam motus perturbatus, ut omnes consentiunt.

577 Obj. 2. Fire, or heat, is often endowed with a straight motion: therefore it is not endowed with a perturbed or vortical motion. Prob. antec.: fire often shines; therefore it is endowed with a straight motion. Dist. antec.: with a straight motion incompatible with a perturbed or vortical motion, I deny; with one compatible with a perturbed motion, I grant. The same small fiery vortex can be endowed at the same time with a straight motion and with a perturbed motion. For while either the center of the small vortex, or even the whole small vortex, is carried along a straight line, the molecules placed at its circumference will necessarily whirl in a perturbed way. Is not the same globe, rolled upon any plane whatever, endowed at the same time both with motion along a straight line and with a motion of rotation about its center? Therefore straight motion is not incompatible with perturbed motion. All admit that the motion of heat can be varied according to the variety of the fuel, or of the subject on which it exerts its force, or according to the obstacles and impediments that check its motion. Thus it may happen that the motion of heat is vortical, or rotatory, but this does not prevent its being called perturbed. For while the sulphureous particles, carried off in a whirl, spin about themselves, and some drive others, there arises a certain perturbed motion, as all agree.

578 Opp. 3: Fluida quaeque corpora, cujus generis sunt aqua, aër, mercurius &c, partes habent motu vario, & indeterminato agitatas, nec tamen sunt actu calida: ergo. Respondeo 1. Nullum fluidum esse omnis caloris expers, licet fortè cum corpore nostro comparatum frigidum videatur: quum scilicet partes sanguinis, aut spirituum celeriùs agitantur, quàm corporis fluidi particulae.

578 Obj. 3. All fluid bodies, of which kind are water, air, mercury, etc., have their parts agitated with a varied and indeterminate motion, and yet they are not actually hot: therefore. I reply 1. that no fluid is wholly devoid of heat, although perhaps, compared with our body, it seems cold: namely, since the parts of the blood or of the spirits are agitated more swiftly than the particles of the fluid body. I reply

p. 182

Respondeo 2: non satis esse ad calorem sensibilem, ut motus partium corporis sit varius, & perturbatus sed praeterea necessè est, ut sit celerrimus. Hinc fit ut partes aquae leni motu agitatae frigus potiùs quàm calorem in corporibus nostris procreent: nam ingenitum nobis calorem, aut motum magis minuunt, quàm augeant

2.: that for sensible heat it is not enough that the motion of the parts of the body be varied and perturbed, but it is necessary besides that it be very swift. Hence it comes about that the parts of water, agitated with a gentle motion, produce cold rather than heat in our bodies: for they rather diminish our innate heat, or motion, than increase it.

579 Inst. Multa sunt ad motum proclivia, quae in calidorum censu non habentur, ut nitrosi, & acidi liquores qui copioso abundant spiritu, & fermentationem multum promovent: ergo. Resp. non solum motum, sed & varium, & perturbatum, & celerrimum ad caloris naturam pertinere. Hinc liquores acidi licet fermentationem promoveant, tamen soli, calorem vix procreant, quod motu illo perturbato eorum particulae non agitentur, nisi quum salibus alkalicis permiscentur: ut quum spiritus nitri sali fixo alkalico adfunditur. Sic aër tenui ore vibratus frigidior est, sed patulo ore erumpens est calidior: quum enim ore contracto expellitur, céleri quidem motu, sed directo, & non perturbato emittitur.

579 Inst.: There are many things prone to motion which are not held in the number of hot things, such as nitrous things and acid liquors, which abound in copious spirit and greatly promote fermentation: therefore. Resp.: not motion alone, but a varied, perturbed and very swift motion belongs to the nature of heat. Hence acid liquors, although they promote fermentation, yet by themselves scarcely produce heat, because their particles are not agitated with that perturbed motion except when they are mixed with alkaline salts: as when spirit of niter is poured onto a fixed alkaline salt. Thus air blown out with a narrow mouth is colder, but bursting out of a wide-open mouth is hotter: for when it is expelled with the mouth contracted, it is emitted with a swift motion indeed, but a direct and not a perturbed one.

580 Opp. 4: dantur fermentationes in quibus conspicua est perturbata partium motio sine ullo calore, imò cum ingenti frigore, ut testantur Viri Clariss. Muschembroekius, Slare, Amontonsius, Gulielminus, Geoffroy, aliique plurimi Physici: ergo expansivus, perturbatusque motus partium corporis non est adeò proprius caloris effectus, ut calor ipse statui in eo legitimè possit, cujus vi, & energia ille motus in corporibus excitatur. Nego conseq.: ebullitio namque, sive perturbata etiam partium motio in frigidis fermentationibus, non sine calore est, licet propter magnam salinae substantiae copiam, quae in illis exsolvitur, calor ipsae non sit conspicuus. Observatum hoc est in fermentatione quadam ex qua teste Clariss. Muschembroek fumi adeò calidi erumpebant, ut liquor thermometri ad fumos adplicati per plures gradus ascenderet; intereadùm thermometri alterius liquor in ipsum liquidum fermentans immersum, deprimeretur.

580 Obj. 4.: There are fermentations in which a perturbed motion of the parts is conspicuous without any heat, nay, with intense cold, as the most distinguished men Musschenbroek, Slare, Amontons, Guglielmini, Geoffroy and very many other physicists testify: therefore the expansive and perturbed motion of the parts of a body is not so proper an effect of heat that heat itself can legitimately be placed in it, by whose force and energy that motion is excited in bodies. I deny the conseq.: for the ebullition, or perturbed motion of the parts, even in cold fermentations, is not without heat, although, on account of the great quantity of saline substance that is dissolved in them, their heat is not conspicuous. This was observed in a certain fermentation from which, as the most distinguished Musschenbroek testifies, fumes so hot burst forth that the liquor of a thermometer applied to the fumes rose through several degrees, while meanwhile the liquor of another thermometer, immersed in the fermenting liquid itself, was depressed.

581 Observandum est igitur, duo esse fermentationum genera, alterum scilicet earum in quibus praevalet substantia sulphurea, earum verò alterum in quibus salina praedominatur. Fermentationes primi generis dicuntur calidae, quia ob sulphuris praedominium ea in illis praevalent corpuscula in quibus calor consistit. Fermentationes secundi generis frigidae nuncupantur, quatenùs ob praedominium salinarum particularum quae in illis exsolvuntur principem in ipsis locum tenent corpuscula in quibus, ut dicemus, frigus résidet. Fermentationes frigidas esse omninò salinas, vel maximam partem salis complecti, experimenta ipsa frigidarum fermentationum luculentissimè demonstrant observante Cl. Gulielmino.

581 It is to be observed, then, that there are two kinds of fermentations: the one, namely, of those in which a sulphureous substance prevails, the other of those in which a saline one predominates. Fermentations of the first kind are called hot, because, owing to the predominance of sulphur, the corpuscles in which heat consists prevail in them. Fermentations of the second kind are named cold, inasmuch as, owing to the predominance of the saline particles that are dissolved in them, the chief place in them is held by the corpuscles in which, as we shall say, cold resides. That cold fermentations are wholly saline, or contain for the most part salt, the very experiments on cold fermentations most clearly demonstrate, as the distinguished Guglielmini observes.

582 Opp. 5. manifestum est, experientiâ, excitari posse calorem sine ullo motu partium perturbato, & expansivo, ut testatur auctor supra laudatus: ergo: Dist. antec.: sine motu, &c. partium insensibilium, nego, Sensibilium, conc. & nego conseq. Potest haberi calor in

582 Obj. 5.: It is manifest from experience that heat can be excited without any perturbed and expansive motion of the parts, as the author praised above testifies: therefore. Dist. antec.: without motion etc. of the insensible parts, I deny; of the sensible parts, I grant; and I deny the conseq. Heat can be present in a body

p. 183

corpore, quin aliquis sensibilis motus in illo adpareat, quia potest contingere, ut in ipso corpore ea non exsolvatur copia corpusculorum caloris, quae ad sensibiles illius partes perturbatè agitandas sufficiat. Verùm in corpore nequit esse calor sine ullo prorsùs partium insensibilium motu, quia calor in illo esse non potest, quin ea corpuscula in ipso sint, & moveantur in quibus calor consistit, & sanè quum liquor thermometri in illas fermentationes de quibus auctor loquitur immissi, per plures gradus ascendat, apertum manet, in ipsis tenuissima corpuscula existere, quae acta in motum vitri poros subeant, contentumque liquorem expansivo, perturbatoque motu exagitent, nisi velimus liquorem ipsum dilatari, quin aliquid existat cui illa dilatatio accepta referatur.

without any sensible motion appearing in it, because it can happen that there is not released in that body such a quantity of corpuscles of heat as suffices to agitate its sensible parts in a perturbed way. But there cannot be heat in a body without any motion whatever of the insensible parts, because heat cannot be in it unless those corpuscles in which heat consists are in it and are moved; and surely, since the liquor of a thermometer immersed in those fermentations of which the author speaks rises through several degrees, it remains plain that very fine corpuscles exist in them which, driven into motion, enter the pores of the glass and agitate the contained liquor with an expansive and perturbed motion; unless we wish the liquor itself to be dilated without anything existing to which that dilatation may be ascribed.

583 Opp. 6. boreas vehementi motu fertur & tamèn frigidus est: ergo. Secundò: aquae in fluminum gurgitibus perturbato, & celeri motu praecipitantur; sed nullum in iis calorem observamus: ergo. Ad primum respondeo, quod licet boreas vehementi motu feratur, quia tamen recto agitur frigidus est, praesertim quum è partibus septentrionalibus particulas, quae partium insensibilium motum concitatum sistere queunt advehat. Ad secundum dico: ideo non observari calorem in aquae gurgitibus, quia partes aquae sensibiles hoc motu abripiuntur, ad caloris autem naturam, non solum motus vehemens, ac perturbatus quarumcunque partium, sed agitatio requiritur tenuissimarum, & insensibilium: quae à particulis potissimum igneis abreptae, alia corpora, fibrasque penetrare similique motu incitare queant.

583 Obj. 6. The north wind is carried with a vehement motion, and yet it is cold: therefore. Secondly: waters in the whirlpools of rivers rush headlong with a perturbed and swift motion; but we observe no heat in them: therefore. To the first I reply that, although the north wind is carried with a vehement motion, yet because it is driven in a straight line it is cold, especially since it brings from the northern regions particles which can check the excited motion of the insensible parts. To the second I say: heat is not observed in the whirlpools of water because the sensible parts of the water are carried off by this motion; but for the nature of heat there is required not merely a vehement and perturbed motion of any parts whatever, but an agitation of very fine and insensible parts, which, carried off above all by the fiery particles, can penetrate other bodies and fibers and stir them with a similar motion.

584 Opp. 7: Metalla aliaque dura corpora quandoque calent, quin corpuscula tumultuario motu adfecta in illis existant: ergo. Nego antec.: Ut enim omittam nullum corpus, quantumvis durum calorem posse concipere, quin illius extensio augeatur; manifestum est, metalla, si quum summè calent, frigidae aquae immergantur, insignem in illa ebullitionem cum strepitu excitare: ergo in illorum poris tenuissima corpuscula existunt, quae particulis aquae tumultuarium illum motum communicant, unde non dissimili motu ipsa pollére, videtur perspicuum.

584 Obj. 7: Metals and other hard bodies are sometimes hot without corpuscles affected with a tumultuous motion existing in them: therefore. I deny the antec.: For, to pass over the fact that no body, however hard, can take on heat without its extension being increased, it is manifest that metals, if they are immersed in cold water when they are extremely hot, excite in it a notable ebullition with a hissing noise: therefore very fine corpuscles exist in their pores which communicate that tumultuous motion to the particles of the water; whence it seems evident that they themselves are possessed of a not dissimilar motion.

585 Opp. denique ovi albúmen in consistentem massam, caloris actione concrescit: ergo calor non consistit in corpusculis motu celerrimo, perturbato, & expansivo adfectis: concipi enim nullatenus potest, quomodo ab eo, quod celerrime movetur, consistentia, atque adeò partium quies oriri possit. Dist. antec.: concrescit ita ut illa consistentia sit caloris effectus per se nego; ita ut sit caloris effectus per accidens, conc. & nego conseq. Consistentiam acquirit albúmen ovi, non quia caloris natura per se valeat consistentiam corporibus tribuere, sed quia corporum quorundam partes ejus sunt magnitudinis, & figurae, eoque artificio intextae, ut moveri nequeant á caloris corpusculis, quin implicentur inter se, & in duram massam concrescant. Profectò ipsum ovi

585 Obj. finally: the white of an egg congeals into a consistent mass by the action of heat: therefore heat does not consist in corpuscles affected with a very swift, perturbed and expansive motion; for it can in no way be conceived how consistency, and hence rest of the parts, could arise from that which is moved most swiftly. Dist. antec.: it congeals in such a way that that consistency is an effect of heat per se, I deny; in such a way that it is an effect of heat per accidens, I grant; and I deny the conseq. The white of an egg acquires consistency not because the nature of heat is of itself able to bestow consistency on bodies, but because the parts of certain bodies are of such a size and figure, and woven together with such artifice, that they cannot be moved by the corpuscles of heat without becoming entangled with one another and congealing into a hard mass. Indeed the very white of the egg,

p. 184

albúmen, quod primò caloris actione durescit, planè dissolvitur si calor ipse augeatur, maximo sanè argumento, illius consistentiam, non directè, & per sese, sed per accidens à calore provenire.

which at first hardens by the action of heat, is wholly dissolved if the heat itself is increased: a very strong argument indeed that its consistency comes from heat not directly and of itself, but by accident.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De Frigore.

On Cold.

586 Proprium frigoris est densare corpora, dura reddere quae mollia sunt, liquores plurimos, in consistentem massam mutare, motumque perturbatum, & expansivum internarum partium corporis tardare, atque etiam planè sistere[?]. Necesse est enim ut contrarii sint effectus caloris, & frigoris. Hinc necessariò sequitur, quod frigus in eo formaliter consistat, cujus causâ constringuntur corpora, rigescunt mollia, liquores plurimi in duram abeunt massam, motusque perturbatus, & expansivus partium internarum corporis retardatur, & sistitur. In eo enim statuendum est frigus, à quo effectus qui vulgo frigori tribuuntur, proveniunt. Hinc frigus non optimè definitur à Peripateticis, qualitas quae congregat, tum homogenea, & heterogenea[?]. Certum enim est, non esse constantem frigoris effectum, ut heterogenea congreget. Si enim vehementiori frigori subjiciantur vinum, acetum, spiritus vini, separantur atque dissolvuntur liquores illi, pars vini aquea in glaciem concrescit, spiritus suam fluiditatem retinet, & tartarum praecipitatur. His positis.

t is proper to cold to condense bodies, to make hard those that are soft, to 586 I change very many liquors into a consistent mass, and to retard, and even wholly to stop, the perturbed and expansive motion of the internal parts of a body. For it is necessary that the effects of heat and of cold be contrary. Hence it necessarily follows that cold formally consists in that by whose agency bodies are constricted, soft things stiffen, very many liquors pass into a hard mass, and the perturbed and expansive motion of the internal parts of a body is retarded and stopped. For cold must be placed in that from which the effects commonly attributed to cold proceed. Hence cold is not well defined by the Peripatetics as a quality that gathers together both homogeneous and heterogeneous things. For it is certain that it is not a constant effect of cold to gather heterogeneous things together. For if wine, vinegar and spirit of wine are subjected to a rather intense cold, those liquors are separated and dissolved: the watery part of the wine congeals into ice, the spirit retains its fluidity, and the tartar is precipitated. These things being laid down,

587 Dico 1: Frigus in partium quiete haud rectè collocatur. Est contra Cartesium. Prob.: non rectè explicatur calor, per motum partium corporis incalescentis [§. 573.] ergo neque frigus per partium quietem rectè exponitur. Secundò: In eo quod frigoris effectus est, statui frigus rectè non potest: sed quies partium est frigoris effectus [§. 586.] ergo non nisi perperam potest frigus in partium quiete consistere. Confirmatur: Ratum enim est, frigus ab ea distingui realiter organi tactus passione, quam frigoris sensatio in anima consequitur; sed passio organi tactus non est nisi privatio motus in iis nervorum fibris, quae organum ipsum constituunt: ergo. Tertiò: Si frigus nihil esset à partium quiete diversum, nullum haberi posset corpus vel minimè frigidum[?], nisi ejus partes quoad sensum quiescerent: sed hoc est, prorsùs falsum, ut ex fermentationibus frigidis constat: ergo. Adhaec: illud corpus erit frigidissimum, cujus partes nulla prorsùs ratione moventur: ergo corpora quaeque durissima erunt frigidissima, glaciesque ipsa ex qua frigidus halitus cumulatim erumpit. intestinoque partium motu donata est,

587 I say 1: Cold is not rightly placed in the rest of the parts. This is against Descartes. Prob.: heat is not rightly explained by the motion of the parts of the body growing hot [§. 573.]; therefore neither is cold rightly expounded by the rest of the parts. Secondly: Cold cannot rightly be placed in that which is an effect of cold: but the rest of the parts is an effect of cold [§. 586.]: therefore only wrongly can cold be made to consist in the rest of the parts. It is confirmed: It is settled that cold is really distinguished from that passion of the organ of touch which the sensation of cold in the soul follows; but the passion of the organ of touch is nothing but a privation of motion in those fibers of the nerves which constitute the organ itself: therefore. Thirdly: If cold were nothing different from the rest of the parts, no body could be had that is in the least cold unless its parts were at rest as far as sense can tell: but this is altogether false, as is clear from cold fermentations: therefore. Moreover: that body will be the coldest whose parts are moved in no way at all: therefore all the hardest bodies will be the coldest, and ice itself, from which a cold exhalation bursts forth abundantly, and which is endowed with an intestine motion of its parts,

p. 185

[?]

would not be a supremely cold body. Although, therefore, a body whose parts are at rest is not hot, it is not on that account, by this very fact, to be judged cold.

588 Dico secundò[?] cum magno Boerhaavio s1 [?]

588 I say secondly, with the great Boerhaave (i): cold by no means consists in the mere privation of heat. This is against very many of the Moderns, among whom the distinguished ’s Gravesande is numbered. Prob.: Since water is dilated in congelation [§. 571. ff.], if it passed into ice on account of the withdrawal of heat, the water would be dilated solely on account of that withdrawal; and hence, conversely, it would be condensed by heat, as the hypothesis of our adversaries supposes; we should have to say that water has from the efficient cause by which it is condensed that very thing, namely that it is fluid: but it is against the nature of heat that water affected by it should be reduced to a smaller space than it possesses of itself [§. 567.]: therefore water is not changed into ice for this cause alone, that it is deprived of heat; but it is converted into ice when something is added to it: therefore it does not grow cold through the mere withdrawal of heat, and consequently cold does not consist in the mere privation of heat. Hence, by the very fact that a body is not hot, it cannot be judged cold, unless other things are equal.

589 Dico 3: [?] C. s' Gravesande s2 [?]

589 I say 3: Cold, even in its cause, is something real and positive. Prob.: For if cold is neither motion nor the privation of heat, as we have already demonstrated, it certainly remains that, since it is opposed to heat, it too, just as heat does, consists in a positive entity. Secondly: It is proved from an observation of the distinguished ’s Gravesande (k). Let snow be taken, mixed in equal parts with sea salt, contained in a vessel, and surrounding a glass filled with water. If this mixture is placed on the fire, at the moment at which it melts, that is, at which its heat is increased, it does not, as other bodies do, communicate heat to the water, but the water is converted into ice. No other reason can be given for this phenomenon except that the corpuscles of heat which penetrate that vessel and dissolve the snow drive something positive out of the snow into the water, which makes the water change into ice: therefore cold consists in something positive.

590 Dico 4: [?]

590 I say 4: Cold in first act consists in corpuscles extremely slender in bulk, and these slender corpuscles are the most subtle primitive particles of salts, but chiefly of niter. The first part can be proved aptly enough from what we have said about heat. The second part is established by experience; for the most subtle particles of every salt contribute to producing cold in bodies, and cold increases or decreases according to the greater or smaller quantity of them, as the Florentine Academicians testify; for all salts placed round a vessel containing water assist its congelation. The most subtle parts of salt, therefore, even though they are few, seem to penetrate through the pores of vessels, to put the fire to flight, to fix the parts of the water, and hence to be those very

Elem. Chem. Tom. 1. p. 73.

Elem. Chem., vol. 1, p. 73.

Elem. Phy[?]. §. 2460, & seq.

Elem. Phys., §. 2460 ff.

p. 186

ipsa esse corpuscula in quibus diximus frigus consistere. Quod autem nitrosae particulae principem locum teneant argumento est frigus illud intensissimum quod nitri ope producitur. Thermometro si quidem ex mercurio confecto in nivem immisso, cum nitri spiritus adfusus fuerat, deprehendit toties laudatus Muschembroek, tubi mercurium infra terminum, qui glaciei frigus indicat, descendisse. Invenit quoque fortissimum aceti spiritum in eandem nivem immersum abiisse in glaciem. Quod autem aqua non habeat in glaciem, etiam si nitrum illi admisceatur, causa est, quia ut hoc accideret, nitrum deberet in sua primitiva corpuscula resolvi, ita autem ab aqua solvi nequit, ut omnes fatentur. Ex hoc ergo non sequitur nitrum non esse congelationis causam, neque in illius potissimum particulis frigus residere; quippè non in quibuscumque, sed in primitivis salium corpusculis frigus collocavimus.

corpuscles in which we have said that cold consists. That the nitrous particles hold the chief place is argued by that very intense cold which is produced by means of niter. For the often-praised Musschenbroek found that, when a thermometer made with mercury was immersed in snow onto which spirit of niter had been poured, the mercury descended below the mark that indicates the cold of ice. He found also that very strong spirit of vinegar, immersed in the same snow, passed into ice. But that water does not pass into ice even if niter is added to it, the cause is that, for this to happen, the niter would have to be resolved into its primitive corpuscles; but it cannot be so dissolved by water, as all admit. From this, therefore, it does not follow that niter is not the cause of congelation, nor that cold does not reside chiefly in its particles; since we have placed cold not in any corpuscles whatever, but in the primitive corpuscles of salts.

591 Neque silentio praeterire possum celebre experimentum ab Accademicis Florentinis peractum: quemadmodum nempe calor ignis, aut solis in speculo collectus, & ad proximum thermometrum reflexus, ejusdem thermometri liquorem rarefacit, & altius illum cogit ascendere; ita si loco solis, glacies substituatur, thermometri liquor descendit, & condensatur; sed in primo casu etiam juxta adversarios corpuscula quaedam egrediuntur ab igne, quae spiritum vini thermometro inclusum rarefaciunt: ergo corpuscula quaedam ex glacie prodire debent, quae à speculo collecta in thermometrum reflectantur, ejusque liquorem condensent, ac propterea frigus non in caloris absentia tantummodò constitui debet, ut inter alios ostendere conatur D. de Ratte s1 non animadvertens contra ipsum probare experimenta, quae adfert ut nostram sententiam infirmet.

591 Nor can I pass over in silence the celebrated experiment performed by the Florentine Academicians: namely, that just as the heat of a fire, or of the sun, collected in a mirror and reflected onto a nearby thermometer, rarefies the liquor of that same thermometer and forces it to rise higher, so, if ice is substituted in place of the sun, the liquor of the thermometer descends and is condensed; but in the first case, even according to our adversaries, certain corpuscles come out from the fire which rarefy the spirit of wine enclosed in the thermometer: therefore certain corpuscles must come out of the ice which, collected by the mirror, are reflected onto the thermometer and condense its liquor; and consequently cold must not be made to consist only in the absence of heat, as, among others, Mr. de Ratte (l) tries to show, not noticing that the experiments he brings forward to weaken our opinion prove against himself.

592 Quid quòd in sententia nostra optimè exponuntur frigoris phaenomena. Referunt Scriptores in Ukrania Poloniae Provincia esse acerrimum frigus, longèque intensius, quàm in Normanna Galliae Provincia; cum tamen in globo terrestri idem sit respectivus locorum situs. Fluvius qui Regiam Sinarum Urbem Pekin alluit, circa mensem Novembris tanta vi frigoris intra diem unum concrescit, & induratur, ut quatuor mensium spatio currus, & ingentia pondera sustineat, illae tamen Sinensis fluvius eandem habet respectivam in globo terrestri positionem, quàm obtinet Romae Tyberis, in quo non viget haec frigoris vis.

592 What of the fact that on our opinion the phenomena of cold are explained excellently? Writers report that in the Ukraine, a province of Poland, the cold is very keen, and far more intense than in Normandy, a province of France, although the respective situation of the places on the terrestrial globe is the same. The river that washes Peking, the royal city of the Chinese, congeals about the month of November within a single day with such force of cold, and hardens so, that for the space of four months it sustains carriages and huge weights; yet that Chinese river has the same respective position on the terrestrial globe as the Tiber at Rome holds, in which this force of cold does not prevail.

593 Hinc dicendum est, ventos quosdam aliis frigidiores esse, qui salinos, nitrosos halitus secum deferant, & ipsis referti, ac permixti corporum poros pervadant, praedictosque effectus producant. In nostrâ sententiâ intelligitur etiam, cur rivuli quidam hiberno tempore liberrimè fluant, tempore autem aestivo in durissimam glaciem concrescant: Observatum enim est, rivulorum illorum litora, plurimis nitri, salisque particulis abundare, quae quidem particulae

593 Hence it must be said that certain winds are colder than others, which carry saline and nitrous exhalations with them and, filled with them and mixed with them, pervade the pores of bodies and produce the aforesaid effects. On our opinion one understands also why certain streams flow most freely in wintertime, but in summertime congeal into the hardest ice: for it has been observed that the banks of those streams abound in a great deal of niter and in saline particles, which particles indeed

L' Encyclopedie, verb. Froid.

L’Encyclopédie, s.v. Froid.

p. 187

aestivo calore solvuntur, & in rivuli aquas defluunt, iisque permiscentur. Ultra ea quae diximus [§ 201] de glacie, dicendum nunc etiam est aquam dum in glaciem abit dilatari, quia primitivae aquae partes ejus sunt texturae, ut corpuscula itidem primitiva nitri, aliorumque salium à quibus congelatio peragitur, nequeant cum illis intimè misceri, quemadmodùm ad indurandam aquam requiritur, quin magna effervescentia contingat. Glaciei ergo expansiva virtus, ait toties laudatus Musschembroek s1, oritur à corpusculis subtilissimis in atmosphaera volitantibus, aquae admixtis, cum ea effervescentibus, eamque figentibus in firmam solidamque massam.

are dissolved by the summer heat and flow down into the waters of the stream and are mixed with them. Besides what we have said [§. 201] about ice, it must now also be said that water is dilated while it passes into ice because the primitive parts of water are of such a texture that the likewise primitive corpuscles of niter, and of the other salts by which congelation is effected, cannot be mixed intimately with them, as is required for hardening water, without a great effervescence taking place. The expansive force of ice, therefore, says the often-praised Musschenbroek (m), arises from very subtle corpuscles flitting in the atmosphere, mixed with the water, effervescing with it, and fixing it into a firm and solid mass.

594 Adversus sententiam nostram plurima opponi solent argumenta, quae facilè solvuntur. Unum tantummodò vobis proponam. Experientia constat, frigidam sentiri aquam, si ab eo calore quo sensorium nostrum adfectum est, ipsius aquae calor deficiat: ergo frigus non consistit in corpusculis frigorificis, sed in caloris tantummodò diminutione. Nego conseq.: Frigida enim nobis ea aqua adparet, quae minus quàm tactus organum calida est, quia quum motus in aquae partibus à caloris corpusculis, quae in illa sunt, productus, sit illo remissior, quo tunc pollent nerveae tactus fibrae; aqueae ipsae particulae illis fibris adplicatae, earum motum retardant, & sistunt, simulque eas densant, atque constringunt, uno verbo, eam passionem in illis excitant, quàm frigoris sensatio in anima comitatur.

594 Against our opinion very many arguments are usually opposed, which are easily answered. I shall propose to you only one. Experience shows that water is felt as cold if the heat of the water falls short of that heat by which our sensorium is affected: therefore cold does not consist in frigorific corpuscles, but only in a diminution of heat. I deny the conseq.: For that water appears cold to us which is less hot than the organ of touch, because, since the motion produced in the parts of the water by the corpuscles of heat that are in it is more remiss than that with which the nervous fibers of touch are then endowed, the watery particles themselves, applied to those fibers, retard and stop their motion, and at the same time condense and constrict them; in a word, they excite in them that passion which the sensation of cold in the soul accompanies.

595 Ceterum haec objectio, vel nulla est, vel certè probat etiam calorem in sola frigoris diminutione consistere. Enim verò: quemadmodum frigidum nobis adparet corpus, quod minus quàm sensorium nostrum calidum est; ita experientiâ teste, corpus illud nobis calidum se prodit, quod debiliore, quàm ipsum sensorium, est frigore adfectum. Tepidum, dicimus, (inquit Cl. Boerhaavius) s2 quod eodem cum corpore humano calore gaudet; calidum quando calorem corporis nostri superat, frigidum, quod minus calidum est.

595 Moreover, this objection either is worthless or certainly proves that heat too consists in the mere diminution of cold. For indeed, just as that body appears cold to us which is less hot than our sensorium, so, as experience witnesses, that body shows itself hot to us which is affected with a weaker cold than the sensorium itself. We call tepid (says the distinguished Boerhaave) (n) that which enjoys the same heat as the human body; hot, when it exceeds the heat of our body; cold, what is less hot.

596 Non superfluum erit hic data occasione in vestram utilitatem animadvertere perniciosissimum atque saluberrimum esse posse frigidi potus usum pro diversâ corporis nostri conditione. Si vehementiori exercitatione, & qualibet alia corporis agitatione aliquis aestuaverit, id summoperè vitare debet, quod refrigerationem interius, vel exterius adferre possit. Ex imprudenti in his casibus balneorum frigidorum usu subitaneam mortem non raròoriginem, habuisse, Doctissimus Medicus Lancissi s3 testatur. Etenim frigoris impressio, solidas corporis animalis partes constringit, fluidas autem condensat, atque talis esse potest effectus, ut partium solidarum actio, fluidarum autem motus nimis minuatur. Hinc maximè turbari potest tota corporis machina. Hinc nascuntur in canalibus obstructiones, &

596 It will not be superfluous here, the occasion being given, to point out for your benefit that the use of cold drink can be most pernicious and most wholesome according to the diverse condition of our body. If anyone has grown heated by rather vehement exercise, or by any other agitation of the body, he must avoid above all whatever could bring on a cooling, inwardly or outwardly. That sudden death has not rarely had its origin in the imprudent use of cold baths in these cases, the most learned physician Lancisi (o) testifies. For cold, when impressed, constricts the solid parts of the animal body and condenses the fluid ones, and the effect can be such that the action of the solid parts and the motion of the fluids are too greatly diminished. Hence the whole machine of the body can be thrown into the greatest disorder. Hence arise obstructions in the canals, and

frequentissima in humorum secretionibus impedimenta, & ex imminuta, aut penitùs sublatâ transpiratione inuumera morborum genera, tum ipsa mors eveniat.

very frequent impediments in the secretions of the humors, and from diminished or wholly suppressed transpiration there ensue innumerable kinds of diseases, and even death itself.

597 Ex potionis frigidioris abusu intelligitur quoque illius usus. Si nempè nimia sit in fibris extensio, relaxatio, nervorumque atonia, in his casibus utilissimè adhibentur potiones frigidae. Quae quum ita sit, mirum esse non debet, quod Vir Clariss. Hoffmannus duo ediderit opuscula, quorum unum inscribitur. De frigido potu vitae, & sanitati hominum inimicissimo: alterum verò de aquae frigidae potu salutari.

597 From the abuse of cold drink its use too is understood. Namely, if there is excessive extension and relaxation in the fibers, and atony of the nerves, in these cases cold drinks are most usefully applied. This being so, it ought not to be a wonder that the most distinguished Hoffmann published two little works, of which one is entitled On Cold Drink, Most Hostile to the Life and Health of Men; the other, however, On the Wholesome Drinking of Cold Water.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

DE CALORIS ET FRIGORIS CRITERIO.

ON THE CRITERION OF HEAT AND COLD.

Et obiter de criterio humiditatis, & siccitatis, nec non de Barometro gravitatis aëris criterio.

AND INCIDENTALLY ON THE CRITERION OF HUMIDITY AND DRYNESS , AND ALSO ON THE BAROMETER, THE CRITERION OF THE WEIGHT OF THE AIR .

598 Ut tactûs vitio in explorando corporum calore, & frigore occurrerent Recentiores Philosophi instrumentum illud invenere, quod vulgò Thermometrum, aut thermoscopium adpellatur, quo utimur veluti criterio ad discernendum in corporibus gradum caloris ac frigoris. Hujus plures sunt formae, ac veluti species. Prima ejus inventio tribuitur Cornelio Drebbel, Bátavo, eum ad meliorem conditionem reduxit postea Sanctorius, majorem perfectionem addiderunt Academici Florentini, â quibus thermometra Florentina nuncupantur. Hi omnes constructi sunt cum spiritu vini rectificatissimo. Thermometrum mercuriale inventum est â Daniele Fahrenheyt, dictum propterea Thermometrum Fahrenheytianum. Clariss. Reaumurius invenit methodum conficiendi thermometra ex vini spiritu, quae ea constanti lege sibi mutuò respondeant, ut in eodem loco posita eundem caloris gradum designent. In explicanda constructione thermometri nollumus immorari. Eam quam clarissimè explicavit in suis foliis Periodicis s1 American. noster D. Joseph. Ignatius Bartolache, Medicinae Doct., atque in Reg. Pont. Mex. Acad. Primariae Medicinae Cathedrae ad quadrienium Moderat. &c. Vir de Mathematica totaque Medicinâ optimè meritus, Scientiarum, Bonarumque Artium Cultor egregius. Fig. LXI. exactè repraesentat thermomentrum Fahrenheyt.

o remedy the defect of touch in exploring the heat and cold of bodies, 598 T the more recent Philosophers invented that instrument which is commonly called the Thermometer, or thermoscope, which we use as a criterion for discerning the degree of heat and cold in bodies. There are several forms of it, and as it were species. Its first invention is attributed to Cornelis Drebbel, a Dutchman; Sanctorius afterwards brought it to a better condition; the Florentine Academicians added greater perfection, after whom they are named Florentine thermometers. All these are constructed with most highly rectified spirit of wine. The mercurial thermometer was invented by Daniel Fahrenheit, and is therefore called the Fahrenheit Thermometer. The most distinguished Réaumur found a method of making thermometers of spirit of wine which correspond to one another by so constant a law that, placed in the same spot, they mark the same degree of heat. We do not wish to dwell on explaining the construction of the thermometer. It has been explained most clearly in his periodical sheets (p) by our fellow American Don José Ignacio Bartolache, Doctor of Medicine, and for a four-year term Holder of the Principal Chair of Medicine in the Royal and Pontifical Academy of Mexico, etc., a man who has deserved excellently of Mathematics and of the whole of Medicine, an outstanding cultivator of the Sciences and of the Liberal Arts. Fig. LXI exactly represents the Fahrenheit thermometer.

Lib. 2. de mortis subitaneis.

Bk. 2, De mortibus subitaneis.

Mercurio Volante sobre asuntos de Fisica y Medicina n. 3.

Mercurio Volante sobre asuntos de Física y Medicina, no. 3.

p. 189

599 Ne vobis aliquid utilitatis deesit, aliqua de Hygroscopio & Barometro subjungam. Hygroscopium quod & Hygrometrum dici solet, est instrumentum, quo aëris humiditas, atque siccitas explorantur, earumque incrementa, & decrementa palam fiunt. Hoc autèm modo construi solet. Cannábinus funis, aut nervea chorda A B (Fig. LXII.), cujus alterum extremum A sit muro infixum, extendatur super rotulam B ex altero chordae extremo, pondus D pendeat cum annexo indice E. Eidem parieti adfixa sit lamina a b in partes aequales divisa cui index ille respondeat: quum teste experientiâ minuatur longitudo funis cannábini, & nerveae chordeae dum humorem contrahunt, contrà verò dum exsiccantur, longiores fiant, altius ascendet index D auctâ aëris humiditate, ea verò iminutâ, descendet. Hoc itaque ascensu & descensu incrementum, & decrementum humiditatis, & siccitatis, quibus aër adficitur, nobis innotescent.

599 That nothing of use may be lacking to you, I shall add something on the Hygroscope and the Barometer. The Hygroscope, which is also usually called the Hygrometer, is an instrument by which the humidity and dryness of the air are explored, and their increases and decreases are made manifest. It is usually constructed in this way. Let a hempen rope, or a gut string A B (Fig. LXII), whose one end A is fixed in the wall, be stretched over the small wheel B; from the other end of the string let a weight D hang, with an attached index E. To the same wall let there be fixed a plate a b divided into equal parts, to which that index corresponds: since, as experience testifies, the length of a hempen rope and of gut strings is diminished while they take up moisture, and on the contrary they become longer while they are dried out, the index D will rise higher when the humidity of the air is increased, and will descend when it is diminished. By this ascent and descent, therefore, the increase and decrease of the humidity and dryness by which the air is affected will become known to us.

600 Aërem ponderosum esse, nemo prorsùs Recentiorum est qui vel minimùm dubitet. Nimis enim videtur apertum suspensionem mercurii in Torricellanis tubis ab externo premente aëre provenire. Accedit: certissimè constare globum vitreum ex. gr. aëre plenum, se ipso aëre vacuo esse graviorem. Neque ab hac opinione Aristoteles ipse abhorruit. Dixerat enim Lib. 4. de Caelo text. 29. Omnia gravitatem habere praeter ignem, & ibid. textu 30, cuncta in sua regione, etiam aërem ipsum gravitare. Erit fortassé qui putet ponderosum esse aërem propter vapores, & exhalationes quibus aër ipse abundat. Verùm animadvertat is velim, si vapores, exhalationesque graves sunt, debere etiam aërem esse ponderosum, ut nempè vapores ipsi atque exhalationes in eo suspendi, illique innatare liberrimè possint. Non enim potest fluidum, quod omni caret pondere, solida graviaque corpora sustinére.

600 There is no one at all among the Moderns who doubts even in the least that air is heavy. For it seems all too plain that the suspension of mercury in Torricellian tubes comes from the external pressing air. Add that it is most certainly established that a glass globe, for example, full of air, is heavier than itself emptied of air. Nor did Aristotle himself shrink from this opinion. For he had said, bk. 4 On the Heavens, text 29: all things have gravity except fire; and ibid., text 30: all things in their own region, even the air itself, gravitate. There will perhaps be someone who thinks that the air is heavy on account of the vapors and exhalations with which the air itself abounds. But I should like him to notice that, if vapors and exhalations are heavy, the air too must be heavy, so that, namely, the vapors themselves and the exhalations can be suspended in it and float in it most freely. For a fluid which lacks all weight cannot sustain solid and heavy bodies.

601 Ex aëris itaque pondere originem suam sumpsit Barómetrum, instrumentum scilicet, quo ad mutationes gravitatis aëris explorandas velut criterio uti solémus. Constat autem Barómetrum tubo inflexo A C D (Fig. LXIII.) mercurio pleno, planaeque tabulae A D immobiliter adfixo. Ad tubi latus habetur scala, cujus una portio est E F in pollices divisa, sumpto initio divisionis â superficie a b mercurii stagnantis in aperto tubi orificio inferiori C D. Hinc enim altitudo illa comparatur, ad quam vi pressionis, quam in stagnantis mercurii superficiem b externus aër exercet, mercurius ipse per tubum ad tractum A C sustinetur. Singuli porrò scalae pollices in suas lineas subdividi solent, ut exiguae etiam mutationes, quas mercurii altitudo patitur, exactius discernantur.

601 From the weight of the air, therefore, the Barometer took its origin: that is, an instrument which we are accustomed to use as a criterion for exploring the changes in the gravity of the air. The Barometer consists of an inflected tube A C D (Fig. LXIII) full of mercury and immovably fixed to a flat board A D. At the side of the tube there is a scale, of which one portion E F is divided into inches, the beginning of the division being taken from the surface a b of the mercury standing in the open lower orifice C D of the tube. For from here is reckoned that height to which, by the force of the pressure which the external air exerts on the surface b of the standing mercury, the mercury itself is sustained through the tube up to the stretch A C. Further, the single inches of the scale are usually subdivided into their lines, so that even the small changes which the height of the mercury undergoes may be discerned more exactly.

602 Barometri usus in eo totus est, ut quanta sit incumbentis atmosphaerae gravitas quotidiè dignoscatur. Quo itaque altius in Barometro haeserit mercurius, eò gravior atmosphaera censenda est, eò autem levior, quò depressior in illo mercurius fuerit. Eritque hodierna atmosphaerae gravitas ad externam ejusdem gravitatem, quemadmodùm ad hesternam mercurii in Barometro

602 The use of the Barometer lies wholly in this, that it may be recognized day by day how great the gravity of the incumbent atmosphere is. Therefore the higher the mercury has stood in the Barometer, the heavier the atmosphere is to be judged, and the lighter, the lower the mercury has been in it. And today’s gravity of the atmosphere will be to its yesterday’s gravity as today’s height of the mercury in the Barometer is to yesterday’s

p. 190

altitudinem, hodierna se habuerit, ut si ex. gr. heri suspensus manserit mercurius in Barometri tubo A C (Ead. Fig.) ad altitudinem a e, hodie verò ad altitudinem a B in illo suspensus existat, gravitas hodierna atmosphaerae erit ad externam, quemadmodùm se habet altitudo a e, ad altitudinem a B. Sed de his hactenùs.

height; so that if, for example, yesterday the mercury remained suspended in the tube A C of the Barometer (same Fig.) at the height a e, but today it stands suspended in it at the height a B, today’s gravity of the atmosphere will be to yesterday’s as the height a e is to the height a B. But enough of these things.

DISSERTATIO III. — DISSERTATION III

De Qualitatibus olfactilibus, gustabilibus, & audibilibus.

On the Qualities perceived by Smell, Taste, and Hearing.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

¿In quonam consistat odor corporum?

In what does the smell of bodies consist?

603 His supositis, quae de odoribus dicta sunt [§. 158. & seq.] Dico: odor in actu primo, seu prout est in corporibus, in substantiali subtilissimo odori corporis efluvio consistit, & hoc efluvium sunt particulae volatilis substantiae sulphureo-mercurialis corporis odori, quae certo modo configuratae, ac determinatae atque â corporibus odoratis avulsae, cum aëre tanquam vehiculo narium cavitates dum inspiramus subeunt, fibrillasque nerveas per organum olfactus distributas variè impellunt, ac cómmovent. Prob. per partes. Prima constat ex eo, quod concipi nequeat, quomodo organum corporeum, sine reali partium contactu possit adfici, & commoveri; sed fibrae nervorum irritantur, premuntur, & vellicantur ab odoribus: ergo. Feminae etenim (ut ait Boerhaavius s1 ad solum odorem moschi, ambrae, continuò animo linquuntur. Eadem odorata in epilepticis exacervationes faciunt. Clariss. Boyle s2 refert se novisse hominem firmae valetudinis, sed perquàm sanguineae temperiéi, qui violentos ex odore moschi percipiebat capitis dolores, alium qui haud dissimile incommodum patiebatur, ob suavem damascenarum

hese things being supposed which have been said about smells [§. 158. 603 T ff.], I say: smell in first act, or as it is in bodies, consists in a substantial and most subtle effluvium of the odorous body, and this effluvium is the particles of the volatile sulphureo-mercurial substance of the odorous body, which, configured and determined in a certain manner and torn away from odorous bodies, enter the cavities of the nostrils with the air as their vehicle while we breathe in, and variously push and stir the nervous fibrils distributed through the organ of smell. Prob. by parts. The first is established from this, that it cannot be conceived how a bodily organ could be affected and stirred without a real contact of parts: but the fibers of the nerves are irritated, pressed and plucked by smells: therefore. For women (as Boerhaave says (q)) at the mere smell of musk and amber at once fall into a faint. The same odorous things cause exacerbations in epileptics. The most distinguished Boyle (r) reports that he knew a man of firm health, but of a very sanguine temperament, who felt violent headaches from the smell of musk; another who suffered a not dissimilar discomfort from the sweet fragrance of damask roses (s).

p. 191

rosarum fragrantium s1 haec autem, & alia plurima explicari néqueunt nisi per substantiale odori corporis effluvium.

(s). These things, however, and very many others cannot be explained except through a substantial effluvium of the odorous body.

604 Secunda pars probatur: nam ex experimentis chymicis constat ea tantum corpora esse odora quae volátili sulphureo-mercuriali substantia praedita sunt, eaque olére intensiùs, quae hujuscemodi substantia magis abundant: ergo. Tertia pars, nempè has particulas configuratas esse, constat apertissimè. Certum enim omninò est, corpuscula odori efluvii per id formaliter esse odora, per quód nerveas olfactus fibras titillare possunt; constat autem nerveas has fibras non moveri â corpusculis odoriferi effluvii, nisi quatenùs ipsa corpuscula magnitudine certa donata sunt, certâque figurâ adfectâ, ratione demonstrante, effectum purè mechanicum, cujusmodi est illa fibrarum motio, nonnisi mechanicae causae posse acceptum referri: ergo.

604 The second part is proved: for it is established from chemical experiments that only those bodies are odorous which are endowed with a volatile sulphureo-mercurial substance, and that those smell more intensely which abound more in a substance of this kind: therefore. The third part, namely that these particles are configured, is most plainly established. For it is altogether certain that the corpuscles of the odorous effluvium are formally odorous through that by which they can tickle the nervous fibers of smell; but it is established that these nervous fibers are not moved by the corpuscles of the odoriferous effluvium except inasmuch as the corpuscles themselves are endowed with a certain size and affected with a certain figure, since reason demonstrates that a purely mechanical effect, such as that motion of the fibers is, can be ascribed only to a mechanical cause: therefore.

605 Postrema pars probatur: nullus enim odor percipitur, nisi aër naribus adtrahatur. Spiritus salis ammoniaci, qui validissimè nares nostras adficit, (inquit laudatus Boerhaavius s2 adpositus naso nihil omninò faciet, quandiu, vel exspiramus, vel certè non inspiramus. Nisi enim aër naribus adtrahatur nequeunt odoriferi effluvii corpuscula, quae per aërem dispersa sunt, eique innatant, in nerveas narium fibras incurrere easque prout ad excitandum sensum olfactus requiritur, titillare. Praeterea in nostra sententiâ clarissimè explicantur odorum phaenomena. Primo: calor odorem in corporibus excitat, frigus prohibet. Calore enim separatur â crassioribus particulis sulphureo-mercurialis substantia, qua corpus constat, & plurimum adtenuatur. Dilatantur itidem pori corporis, unde quae in illo est volatilis substantiae portio facilè erumpit, & quoquoversùs diffunditur. Contra verò frigus poros corporis constringit, motumque intestinum partium retardat, & prohibet.

605 The last part is proved: for no smell is perceived unless air is drawn in through the nostrils. Spirit of sal ammoniac, which most powerfully affects our nostrils, (says the praised Boerhaave (t)) placed at the nose will do nothing at all as long as we either breathe out, or at any rate do not breathe in. For unless air is drawn in through the nostrils, the corpuscles of the odoriferous effluvium, which are dispersed through the air and float in it, cannot run into the nervous fibers of the nostrils and tickle them as is required for exciting the sense of smell. Moreover, on our opinion the phenomena of smells are explained most clearly. First: heat excites smell in bodies, cold prevents it. For by heat the sulphureo-mercurial substance of which the body consists is separated from the coarser particles and is very greatly attenuated. The pores of the body are likewise dilated, whence the portion of volatile substance that is in it easily bursts out and is diffused in every direction. On the contrary, cold constricts the pores of the body and retards and prevents the intestine motion of the parts.

606 Secundò: Confricatione atque adtritu ea dura corpora fiunt odora, quae inodóra videntur, quae verò odora sunt, intensiorem odorem spargunt. Confricatione enim laxatur corporis textura, ejusque pori dilatantur, quaeque in illis est sulphureo-mercurialis substantia ad magnum sanè motum concitatur. Tertio: Quamplura quae divisim sumpta minimè olent, validum, si misceantur odorem diffundunt, Sal ammoniacus. & sal alkalinus inodórus uterque, in ipsa commistione odorem validissimum spirant. Ex mistione enim sequitur fermentatio, atque hinc subtilium illarum particularum dissolutio, & evaporatio in quibus odor consistit. Sic etiam auripigmentum, & calx viva utrumq̃ inodórum corpus in aqua permixta, & cocta tetrum atque adversum odorem spirant. Ut autem

606 Secondly: By rubbing and friction those hard bodies become odorous which seem inodorous; and those which are odorous breathe out a more intense smell. For by rubbing the texture of the body is loosened and its pores are dilated, and the sulphureo-mercurial substance that is in them is stirred to a truly great motion. Thirdly: Very many things which, taken separately, smell very little, give off a powerful smell if they are mixed. Sal ammoniac and alkaline salt, each of them inodorous, breathe out a most powerful smell in the very mixing. For from the mixture there follows a fermentation, and hence the dissolution and evaporation of those subtle particles in which smell consists. So also orpiment and quicklime, each an inodorous body, when mixed in water and boiled, breathe out a foul and repugnant smell. But, to say a few words

Praelect. Academ. de olfact.

Praelect. Academ., on smell.

De insig. efficacia effluvior. cap. 6.

De insig. efficacia effluvior., ch. 6.

Plura alia tradit Clariss. P. de Lanis in Magisterio Naturae, & Artis (ex quo velut thesauro suam haud pauci Physicorum absterserunt inopiam quàm faciles ad usurpanda aliena, tàm officiosi utinam ad reddendum auctori meritum honorem!)

The most distinguished Fr. Lana Terzi reports many other things in the Magisterium Naturae et Artis (from which, as from a treasury, not a few Physicists have relieved their own poverty: would that they were as dutiful in rendering the author his deserved honor as they are ready to appropriate what belongs to others!)

Loco citat.

Loc. cit.

p. 192

paucis dicamus de specifico odorum discrimine, duo tantum genera distingui possunt, suave nempè, & molestum.

about the specific difference of smells, only two kinds can be distinguished, namely the pleasant and the troublesome.

607 Suavis est odor, si odori effluvii corpuscula ita respondeant olfactus organo, ut ejus fibrae ordinatè, placidèque ab illis moveantur. Contra verò odor est molestus, si nerveae olfactus fibrae perturbatè ab odori effluvii corpusculis vexentur, & distorqueantur. Hinc non nisi ex diversa dispositione organi olfactus repetenda videtur ratio, cur idem odor uni gratus sit, alteri ingratus, sicuti etiam cur idem odor nobis nec placeat semper, neque semper displiceat. Dubium non est enim, quin mutatâ temperie vel texturâ nervearum fibrarum olfactus, fieri necessario debeat, ut ex eorumdem corpusculorum adpulsu [?] fibrae ipsae non eodem semper modo moveantur.

607 A smell is pleasant if the corpuscles of the odorous effluvium so answer to the organ of smell that its fibers are moved by them in an orderly and gentle way. On the contrary, a smell is troublesome if the nervous fibers of smell are harassed and twisted in a perturbed way by the corpuscles of the odorous effluvium. Hence the reason why the same smell is agreeable to one person and disagreeable to another, as also why the same smell neither always pleases us nor always displeases us, seems to be sought only in the different disposition of the organ of smell. For there is no doubt that, when the temper or texture of the nervous fibers of smell is changed, it must necessarily come about that the fibers themselves are not always moved in the same way by the impact of the same corpuscles.

608 Sed dices contra nostram conclusionem: si odor consistit in profluvio substantiali, &c., pondus corporis longa odoris emissione continuè minueretur; sed hoc experientiae adversatur: ergo. Nego min.: quia ipsa teste experientiâ pondus odori corporis camphorae ex. gr. sensibiliter etiam decrescit ut observavimus cum Clariss. Boyle [§. 185.]. Neque decrescere potest pondus odori corporis odorae evaporationis causâ, nisi corporis materia hanc ob causam minuatur, ac proinde nisi odor corporis in substantiali illius effluvio consistat. Ceterùm posse odorem, quem corpus spargit in effluvio consistere, quin ipsius pondus sensibiliter decrescat, inficias ibit nemo, cui perspecta fuerit subtilitas illorum corpusculorum ex quibus sensibilia quaeque corpora primo consurgunt. Plurima hac de re à nobis dicta sunt §§. 158. & seqq. & §. 185.

608 But you will say against our conclusion: if smell consists in a substantial outflow, etc., the weight of a body would be continually diminished by a long emission of smell; but this is contrary to experience: therefore. I deny the min.: because, as experience itself testifies, the weight of an odorous body, of camphor for example, does decrease even sensibly, as we have observed with the most distinguished Boyle [§. 185.]. Nor can the weight of an odorous body decrease on account of the odorous evaporation unless the matter of the body is diminished for this cause, and consequently unless the smell of the body consists in a substantial effluvium of it. For the rest, no one will deny that the smell which a body spreads can consist in an effluvium without its weight decreasing sensibly, if he has clearly seen the subtlety of those corpuscles from which all sensible bodies first arise. Very many things on this matter have been said by us in §§. 158 ff. and §. 185.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

¿In quonam consistat sapor corporum?

In what does the taste of bodies consist?

609 Observatio prima. Ea corpora sapida sunt, quae sale abundant, & quo majorem salis copiam continent, eò sunt sapidiora. Contra verò planè insipida sunt illa quae nihil planè, aut ferme nihil salinae substantiae complectuntur. Comprobare id vel ex eo licet, quod sapidum nihil sit, ex quo extrahere sal non detur, quod extracto sale non reddatur insipidum, nihil itidem insipidum, quod commixto sale sapidum non fiat. Observatio secunda: nullius solidi corporis sapor percipitur, nisi corpus ipsum dentibus conteratur, & salivae beneficio dissolvatur. Hinc insipida planè sunt, quae dentibus conteri nequeunt, & saliva dissolvi, ut metalla, lapides, &c.

bservation first. Those bodies are savory which abound in salt, and the 609 O greater the quantity of salt they contain, the more savory they are. On the contrary, those are altogether insipid which contain nothing at all, or almost nothing, of saline substance. This can be confirmed even from the fact that there is nothing savory from which salt cannot be extracted and which, once the salt is extracted, is not rendered insipid; likewise nothing insipid which does not become savory when salt is mixed in. Observation second. The taste of no solid body is perceived unless the body itself is ground by the teeth and dissolved by the help of the saliva. Hence those things are altogether insipid which the teeth cannot grind and the saliva cannot dissolve, such as metals, stones, etc. Observation

p. 193

Observatio tertia: solidorum corporum etsi sapida ea sint, nullus planè sapor percipitur, si lingua vel nimis arida fuerit, vel nimio humore túrgida. Observatio quarta: sapida corpora calore fiunt sapidiora, contra verò insipida planè evadunt, si nimiè frigescant. Quae frigidissima sunt, inquit Doctiss. Boerhaavius, ea non gustantur, neque gustus ullus superest, quando lingua exquisitè friget. His positis.

third: although solid bodies are savory, no taste at all is perceived if the tongue is either too dry or swollen with too much moisture. Observation fourth: savory bodies become more savory with heat, but on the contrary become altogether insipid if they grow excessively cold. Things that are very cold, says the most learned Boerhaave, are not tasted, nor does any taste remain when the tongue is exquisitely cold. These things being laid down,

610 Dico: Sapores in actu primo, & prout in corpore existunt consistunt primariò in salinis sapidi corporis particulis certâ magnitudine ac figurâ adfectis, quae â saliva dissolvi, cuticulam gustatus organum vestientem pervádere, nerveàs papillas sub ea protuberantes agitare varia ratione, vellicare, stringere, compungere, aut demulcere pro varia modificatione possint. Prob. per partes. Prima, ex observatione prima: nam si corporum sapor â salinis particulis non oriretur, neque insipida ea essent corpora quae sale destituta sunt, neque illa essent sapida quae sale abundant. Dixi primario consistere sapores in salinis particulis. Dubium enim non est, quin etiam sulphurea substantia ad sapores plurimum conferat, experientiâ demonstrante salinarum particularum vim non parùm â sulphure minui: proinde ab illo effici, ut gustus organum non eodem semper modo â salinis corpusculis immutetur

610 I say: Tastes in first act, and as they exist in the body, consist primarily in saline particles of the savory body, affected with a certain size and figure, which, dissolved by the saliva, can pervade the cuticle that clothes the organ of taste and agitate in various ways the nervous papillae protruding beneath it, and pluck, squeeze, prick or soothe them according to their various modification. Prob. by parts. The first, from observation first: for if the taste of bodies did not arise from saline particles, neither would those bodies be insipid which are destitute of salt, nor would those be savory which abound in salt. I said that tastes consist primarily in particles of salt. For there is no doubt that a sulphureous substance too contributes very much to tastes, since experience demonstrates that the force of the saline particles is diminished not a little by sulphur: hence it is brought about by it that the organ of taste is not always changed in the same way by the saline corpuscles.

611 Quod autem certam magnitudinem, ac figuram habere debeant. Prob. Etenim non nisi ratione magnitudinis, & figurae quibus donata sunt, linguae pórulos subire possunt illa corpuscula, easque nervorum fibras vellicare, quae gustatus organum immediatè constituunt. Mechanici siquidem effectus non nisi mechanicam esse causam, manifestum est; constat autem salina corpuscula ab eo habere formaliter, ut sint sapida, â quo habent formaliter, ut nerveas gustatus fibras titillare possint: ergo. Quod autem sint hujusmodi ut salivâ dissolvi possint constat ex observatione secunda. Saporum varietates gemino hoc carmine comprehenduntur.

611 But that they must have a certain size and figure, Prob. For only by reason of the size and figure with which they are endowed can those corpuscles enter the little pores of the tongue and pluck those fibers of the nerves which immediately constitute the organ of taste. It is manifest indeed that a mechanical effect has only a mechanical cause; but it is established that the saline corpuscles have formally that they are savory from that from which they have formally that they can tickle the nervous fibers of taste: therefore. But that they are of such a kind as to be able to be dissolved by the saliva is established from observation second. The varieties of tastes are comprised in this pair of lines:

Sunt Salsus, Pinguis; Dulcisque, Acidusque sapores:

The tastes are Salty, Fatty, Sweet and Acid;

Acer, & Insipidus, Austerus, Acerbus, Amarus.

Sharp, and Insipid, Austere, Harsh, Bitter.

Aliqui volunt, Insipidum propriè non esse saporem, sed saporis negationem.

Some hold that Insipid is not properly a taste, but the negation of taste.

612 Confirmatur conclusio: in nostra sententia ratio redditur eorum quae de saporibus in limine observavimus. Primo: Sapor consistentis corporis non percipitur, nisi corpus ipsum conteratur dentibus, & saliva dissolvatur. Salinae siquidem cujus [?] corporis particulae immutare non possunt gustus organum, nisi ab iis, quibus in ipso corpore permixtae sunt sejunctae fuerint, atque ita saliva dissolutae, ut linguae poros subire queant. Secundo: nullius solidi corporis sentitur sapor, si lingua nimis arida fuerit, vel nimio humore turgida. Humore siquidem deficiente deest menstruum, quo salina corporis

612 The conclusion is confirmed: on our opinion a reason is given for those things which we observed about tastes at the threshold. First: the taste of a consistent body is not perceived unless the body itself is ground by the teeth and dissolved by the saliva. For the saline particles of a body cannot change the organ of taste unless they are separated from those with which they are mixed in the body itself, and are so dissolved by the saliva that they can enter the pores of the tongue. Secondly: the taste of no solid body is felt if the tongue is too dry or swollen with too much moisture. For when moisture is lacking, the menstruum is wanting by which the saline substance of the body

p. 194

substantia dissolvatur, & ad gustus organum deducatur. Nimius verò humor minuit rationem corporis soluti ad vehiculum solvens, ideoque parva, aut propè nulla fit organi sensorii immutatio. Praeterea si nerveae linguae papillae nimio humore turgescant ineptae sunt, ut ex salinarum particularum adpulsu motum concipiant, atque hinc, ut gustus sensatio in nobis excitetur.

may be dissolved and conducted to the organ of taste. But excessive moisture diminishes the ratio of the dissolved body to the dissolving vehicle, and therefore little or almost no change of the sense organ takes place. Moreover, if the nervous papillae of the tongue swell with excessive moisture, they are unfit to take on motion from the impact of the saline particles, and hence for the sensation of taste to be excited in us.

613 Redditur etiam ratio observationis quartae. Calor enim efficit ut non solum dissolvantur particulae salinae, verùm etiam ut fortiùs irruant in gustus sensorium, idque validiùs moveant. Contra verò frigus non solum prohibet dissolutionem salinarum particularum, verùm etiam motum earum, quae solutae sunt, retardat, & etiam sistit, constrictisque linguae porulis, impedit insupèr, ne illae porulos ipsos subeant, nerveasque gustatus fibras premant, & vellicent. Advertendum est in fine, quod sapor agit pro ratione variae dispositionis organi. Proindè quia non omnium eadem est temperies hominum, nec eadem in omnibus nervearum fibrillarum textura, idem sapor neque omnibus grátus est, neque omnibus molestus. Similiter ob mutatam organi dispositionem fit, ut sapor, qui gratus nobis antea fuerat, non amplius placeat. Undè obtinuit hispanica pároemia: sobre gustos no hai disputas.

613 A reason is also given for observation fourth. For heat brings it about not only that the saline particles are dissolved, but also that they rush more strongly into the sensorium of taste and move it more powerfully. On the contrary, cold not only prevents the dissolution of the saline particles, but also retards and even stops the motion of those which have been dissolved, and, by constricting the little pores of the tongue, prevents them moreover from entering those very pores and pressing and plucking the nervous fibers of taste. It is to be noted at the end that taste acts according to the various disposition of the organ. Hence, because not all men have the same temperament, nor is the texture of the nervous fibrils the same in all, the same taste is neither agreeable to all nor troublesome to all. Similarly, because of a changed disposition of the organ, it happens that a taste which had been agreeable to us before pleases no longer. Whence the Spanish proverb has gained currency: sobre gustos no hai disputas [there is no disputing about tastes].

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

De Sono, & ejus praecipuis adfectionibus.

On Sound, and its principal affections.

614 Qui clarè soni naturam explicare cupiunt, sonum alium in corpore sonóro, alium in medio per quod transmittitur considerant. Priorem sonum primitivum, secundum derivativum adpellant. Centrum soni dicitur illud punctum, ex quo sonus diffunditur, atque ad aures pérvenit. Sonus directus est ille qui â corpore sonoro rectâ fertur ad auditum. Sonus reflexus, vocatur ille, qui ab obstaculo, in quod incurrit, regéritur, atque ex illo ad aures pérvenit. Certum est, ea tantùm corpora sonora esse, quae tremorem concipiunt, si percutiantur. Motus hicce tremulus extra omne dubium est in chordis, ex quibus agitatione tremula, sonus elicitur. In campanis majoribus, & in multis aliis corporibus motus hicce tremulus admodùm sensibilis est. Sublato aëre nullum percipi sonum, tametsi corpus sonorum validis percusionibus urgeatur, dictum jam â nobis est in Logica (§. 107). His constitutis.

hose who wish to explain clearly the nature of sound consider one sound 614 Tin the sonorous body, another in the medium through which it is transmitted.
