The former they call primitive sound, the latter derivative. The center of sound is said to be that point from which the sound is diffused and reaches the ears. Direct sound is that which is carried straight from the sonorous body to the hearing. Reflected sound is called that which is thrown back from an obstacle into which it runs, and from it reaches the ears. It is certain that only those bodies are sonorous which take on a tremor if they are struck. This tremulous motion is beyond all doubt in strings, from which sound is drawn out by a tremulous agitation. In larger bells, and in many other bodies, this tremulous motion is quite sensible. That when the air is removed no sound is perceived, although the sonorous body be plied with strong blows, has already been said by us in the Logic (§. 107). These things being established,

615 Dico: Sonus prout spectatur in corpore sonóro, sive primitivus, consistit in motu tremulo minimarum corporis sonori

615 I say: Sound as it is regarded in the sonorous body, or primitive, consists in a tremulous motion of the smallest parts of the sonorous body;

p. 195

partium: ut autem est in medio, per quod transmittitur, adeòque sonus derivativus, potissimum in tremulo aëris motu, qui â tremóre & fremitu corporum sonantium oritur, & ad auditus usque organum propagatur, positus est. Pars prima demonstratur. Ea tantùm corpora sonora sunt, quae percussa, aut vibrata tremorem concipiunt, atque adeò quae partibus elasticis atque aptis ad celerrimas vibrationes peragendas constant; sed eo ipso sonus primitivus consistit in motu tremulo minimarum corporis sonori partium: ergo. Major constat, si quidem experimentis compertum habemus, ea corpora quae sunt magis elastica, adeòque ad motum tremulum aptiora, etiam esse magis sonóra. Sic quia stannum praeplumbo riget, argentum magis quàm aurum, chalybs prae ferro, iccircò alterum altero magis est sonorum; & nimiùm flexilibus partibus constantia corpora, sono destituta esse, vulgò notum est. Adhaec: novimus campanas solo contactu manûs, dum sonant admotae, sonum reddere diminutum, quia motus trémulus aliquo ex parte impeditur.

but as it is in the medium through which it is transmitted, and hence derivative sound, it is placed chiefly in a tremulous motion of the air, which arises from the tremor and quivering of sounding bodies and is propagated all the way to the organ of hearing. The first part is demonstrated. Only those bodies are sonorous which, when struck or vibrated, take on a tremor, and hence which consist of elastic parts fit for performing very swift vibrations; but by that very fact primitive sound consists in a tremulous motion of the smallest parts of the sonorous body: therefore. The major is established, since we have found by experiments that those bodies which are more elastic, and hence fitter for tremulous motion, are also more sonorous. Thus, because tin is stiffer than lead, silver more than gold, steel than iron, for that reason the one is more sonorous than the other; and it is commonly known that bodies consisting of excessively flexible parts are destitute of sound. Moreover: we know that bells, by the mere contact of a hand applied while they are sounding, give back a diminished sound, because the tremulous motion is in some part impeded.

616 Prob. altera pars: scilicet corpora non esse sonora per tremorem, seu vibrationes totales, sed particulares, id est, per motum tremulum exiguarum partium, id quód detexerunt Viri Cl. Perrault s1 Carrè s2 & de La Hire s3, quum antea corpora per vibratione totales sonora esse putarentur. Res vulgaribus experimentis comprobata est. Duo tantùm adhibeam. Si fides musica plectro sebo uncto vehementiùs percutiatur, tametsi vibrationes totales futurae sint, sonum non edit, plectrum verò pice vel resina asperum si per eamdem ducatur, sonus clarè percipitur; sed hujus reddi ália ratio nequit, quàm quod plectrum resinâ obductum exasperetur, & denticulos velut obtineat, quibus minimas partes chordae cónfricet, & ágitet, quas perstringere non potest plectrum sebo lúbricum: ergo. Secundo: Forcipis focariae flexilis, elasticae si extrema digitis compressa repentè dimittantur, aut nullus auditur sonus, aut modicus, etsi elasticitate sua in motum vibratorium concitentur forcipis brachia, clarum tamen sonant, si corpore duro percutiantur: ergo exiguarum partium motus tremulus sonum efficit primitivum.

616 The second part is proved: namely, that bodies are not sonorous through a tremor, or vibrations, that are total, but through particular ones, that is, through a tremulous motion of small parts; which the distinguished men Perrault (u), Carré (x) and de La Hire (y) discovered, whereas formerly bodies were thought to be sonorous through total vibrations. The thing is proved by common experiments. I shall use only two. If a musical string is struck rather vehemently with a bow greased with tallow, even though total vibrations are bound to occur, it gives no sound; but if a bow made rough with pitch or resin is drawn over the same string, a sound is clearly perceived: but no other reason can be given for this than that the bow coated with resin is roughened and as it were obtains little teeth, with which it rubs and agitates the smallest parts of the string, which the bow made slippery with tallow cannot graze: therefore. Secondly: if the ends of a pair of flexible, elastic fire tongs, pressed together by the fingers, are suddenly released, either no sound is heard or a moderate one, although the arms of the tongs are set into a vibratory motion by their elasticity; yet they sound clearly if they are struck with a hard body: therefore the tremulous motion of small parts produces primitive sound.

617 Prob. 3. pars: per motum derivativum intelligimus id quod aptum est ad percellendum organum auditus: sed talis est motus tremulus medii, potissimùm autem aërearum particularum: ergo. Major constat: quum enim soni sensatio in nobis non fiat, nisi auditus organum á corpore sonante immutetur, immutari autèm immediatè ab eo nequeat, quum ab illo immediatè non tangatur, iccircò immutari debet per interjectum medium. Medium verò

617 The 3rd part is proved: by derivative motion we understand that which is apt to strike the organ of hearing: but such is the tremulous motion of the medium, and chiefly of the aerial particles: therefore. The major is established: for since the sensation of sound does not arise in us unless the organ of hearing is changed by the sounding body, and it cannot be changed by it immediately, since it is not immediately touched by it, for that reason it must be changed through an interposed medium. But that this medium

Essai de Physique.

Essai de Physique.

Memoir de l' Academ. 1709 [?].

Mémoires de l’Académie, 1709.

Memoir de l' Academ. 1716.

Mémoires de l’Académie, 1716.

p. 196

hoc esse in primis aërem, patet primò ex natura ejus, qui quoniam insigni est elasticitate praeditus aptitudine gaudet, ut ejus particulae corpori sonoro proximae â vibratis hujus partibus exiguis repellantur, hae alias, & alias remotiores urgeant, dum tandem impressio fiat in ipsum organum ac sonus percipiatur; deinde liquet id ipsum ex eo, quod nullus sonus sublato aëre percipiatur: ergo sonus derivativus, &c.

is above all the air is plain, first, from its nature: for since it is endowed with a notable elasticity, it has the aptitude that its particles nearest the sonorous body are repelled by the small vibrated parts of that body, and these urge others, and still others more remote, until at length an impression is made on the organ itself and the sound is perceived; next, the same is clear from the fact that no sound is perceived when the air is removed: therefore derivative sound, etc.

618 Diximus sonum derivativum in motu tremulo aërearum potissimum particularum positum esse: aërem enim non esse unicum medium per quod sonus transferatur experimenta plurima â D. Nollet s1, aliisque capta, planè evincunt. Sic aqua aptum satis videtur corpus ad motum tremulum concipiendum, experientiâ testante pisces campanae sonitu saepe saepius in piscinis ad escam paratam convocari.

618 We have said that derivative sound is placed in the tremulous motion chiefly of aerial particles: for that air is not the only medium through which sound is transferred, very many experiments made by Mr. Nollet (z) and others clearly prove. Thus water seems a body quite fit for taking on a tremulous motion, since experience testifies that fish in fishponds are very often called together by the sound of a bell to food prepared for them.

619 Naturâ soni perspectâ, adfectiones principes, quoad licet expendamus. Celeritas soni, diffusio illius determinato tempore per certum spatium, inter adfectiones praecipuas meritò referuntur. Hanc Eruditi diversi studiosè observare conati sunt, ut videre est apud Muschembroekium s2 Tandèm juxta celebriores observationes, 180 perticarum Gallicarum, intervallo unius minuti secundi constituta fuit; quia tamen de hoc ipso producto adhùc controversia erat, iccircò ab Academia Regia Scientiarum Parisina, rei hujus exactior inquisitio commissa fuit ann. 1738. Viris Clariss. De Tury, Maraldi, & de la Caille. Hi itaque lineam pro suis operationibus delegeruut 14636 perticas, sive hexapedas longam, expertique sunt primò.

619 The nature of sound having been examined, let us weigh its principal affections, as far as we may. The celerity of sound, or its diffusion through a certain space in a determinate time, is rightly reckoned among its principal affections. Various learned men have tried to observe it carefully, as can be seen in Musschenbroek (a). At length, according to the more celebrated observations, it was fixed at 180 French perches in the interval of one second; but because there was still controversy about this very result, a more exact inquiry into this matter was for that reason entrusted by the Royal Academy of Sciences of Paris, in the year 1738, to the most distinguished men de Thury, Maraldi and de La Caille. These, then, chose for their operations a line 14636 perches, or toises, long, and found, first:

620 Sonum spatio 1 minut. 2di, tam interdiù, quàm noctu, pluvio aeque, ac sereno tempore conficere 173 perticas sive Hexapedas, ut alibi diximus. 2: quod ventus secundum eadem lineam, quam sonus percurrit, spirans, vel retardet, vel acceleret eum pro ratione suae celeritatis, hoc est; ventus adversus retardat, secundus promovet sonum. 3: celeritatem soni ea semper lege comparatam esse, ut is aequalibus temporibus, aequalia spatia percurrat. 4: quod intensio soni, sive ejus vis nihil de celeritate mutet; ut enim vehementior sonus longius diffundatur, quàm debilior; iste tamèn per 1 minut. 2dum perindè, atque alter 173 perticas percurrit. s3

620 That sound, in the space of 1 second, both by day and by night, in rainy as in clear weather, covers 173 perches or toises, as we have said elsewhere. 2: that a wind blowing along the same line which the sound runs through either retards or accelerates it in proportion to its own celerity, that is: a contrary wind retards the sound, a following wind furthers it. 3: that the celerity of sound is always constituted by such a law that it runs through equal spaces in equal times. 4: that the intensity of sound, or its force, changes nothing in its celerity; for although a more vehement sound is diffused farther than a weaker one, the latter nevertheless runs through 173 perches in 1 second just as the other does (b).

621 Cujus ratio haec esse videtur, quod quum impressio ex. gr. á tormento bellico validior sit, proximae aëreae particulae ob majorem vim ad vicinas magis accedendo, majus quidem conficiunt spatium, adtamen ut se suis locis iterum restituant, necesse sit, tantundèm spatii habeant rursum: at aëris particulae á sclopo pugillari minus impulsae, sicut minus spatium ob vim minorem progrediendo faciunt, ita regrediendo minus percurrunt. Ex his jam sequitur.

621 The reason of which seems to be this: that since the impression, e.g., from a cannon, is stronger, the nearest aerial particles, by approaching the neighboring ones more on account of the greater force, do indeed cover a greater space; yet in order to restore themselves to their places again, they must have just as much space once more: but the particles of air less impelled by a pistol, just as they make less space in going forward on account of the smaller force, so in going back they run through less. From these things it now follows:

Leçons de Physique Tom. 3. Leç. 11. Exp. 4.

Leçons de Physique, vol. 3, lesson 11, exp. 4.

Comment. Acad. del Cimento P. 3. p. 113.

Comment. Acad. del Cimento, pt. 3, p. 113.

Memoir. de l' Acadm. 1738.

Mémoires de l’Académie, 1738.

p. 197

622 Celeritatis aequabilis, quâ sonus fertur, perutilem cognitionem esse ad distantias locorum definiendas, ubi operationes Geometricae adhiberi nequeunt, videlicèt: ad mensuranda freta marium, ostia fluminum, distantiam fossae obsidionariae â propugnaculo &c. Nempè si inter tormenti, vel sclopi exonerationem, & sonum auditum numerentur minuta secunda; quum singula respondeant distantiae 173 perticarum, atque hae per numerum minutorum secundorum multiplicentur, habebitur distantia loci (intelligendo distantiam in linea recta, secundum quam sonus diffunditur) in quo tormentum exoneratum est; ita si 10 minut. 2d. elabantur inter visum ignem, & sonum perceptum: distantia erit 1730 perticarum. Ad haec, dimetiri etiam licebit venti celeritatem; quum enim ventus secundus promoveat sonum, si â celeritate per ventum adaucta 173 perticas, singulis minutis secundis respondentes subtraxeris, residuum celeritatem venti exhibebit.

622 The knowledge of the uniform celerity with which sound is carried is very useful for determining the distances of places where geometrical operations cannot be applied: namely, for measuring straits of the seas, mouths of rivers, the distance of a siege trench from a bulwark, etc. That is, if between the discharge of a cannon or of a musket and the hearing of the sound the seconds are counted, then, since each corresponds to a distance of 173 perches, and these are multiplied by the number of seconds, the distance of the place in which the cannon was discharged will be had (understanding the distance along the straight line along which the sound is diffused); thus, if 10 seconds elapse between the fire seen and the sound perceived, the distance will be 1730 perches. Moreover, it will also be possible to measure the celerity of the wind; for since a following wind furthers the sound, if from the celerity increased by the wind you subtract the 173 perches corresponding to each second, the remainder will show the celerity of the wind.

623 Reflexio est singularis soni adfectio. Nempè sonus non secùs, ac motus alius, directionem suam, ubi in obstaculum impingit, mutat, & juxta motus legem generalem sic reflectitur ut angulus reflexionis aequalis sit angulo incidentiae. Nihil autem admirabilius in soni reflexione est quàm resonantia, quae Echo dicitur, tumque habetur, quum aër variè agitatus á corpore sonante, in oppositum corpus incidens eádem prorsùs modificatione regeritur, ut auribus eundem ferè sonum exhibeat haec repercussio, quàm directi radii sonori efficiunt. Verùm non omnis sonus reflexus, & ab obice in aurem remissus id praestat, ut Echo sistatur: certae scilicèt, conditiones adsint necesse est.

623 Reflection is a singular affection of sound. That is, sound, no otherwise than any other motion, changes its direction when it strikes an obstacle, and according to the general law of motion is so reflected that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. But nothing is more admirable in the reflection of sound than the resonance which is called Echo, and which takes place when the air, variously agitated by the sounding body and falling on an opposite body, is thrown back with exactly the same modification, so that this repercussion presents to the ears almost the same sound as the direct sonorous rays produce. But not every reflected sound, sent back from an obstacle into the ear, brings it about that an Echo is formed: certain conditions, namely, must be present.

624 Ac primo quidem exposcitur, ut ea sit distantia audientis ab obstaculo, ex quo sonus redit, ut antecedenter ab sono directo auditus organum perfectè immutetur, priusquàm sonus reflexus ad illud perveniat: cujus quidem ratio est, quia si non sit discretum tempus, quod inter adpulsum soni directi, & soni reflexi intercedit, una tantum motio, & immutatio organi excitabitur ab utroque sono, vel certè consequens, priorem tanta festinatione excipiet, ut discriminari minimè possint, adeòque etiam unus tantùm â nobis percipietur sonus, facit tamen haec coincidentia soni directi, & soni reflexi, ut melius corpus sonans exaudiatur.

624 And first, indeed, it is required that the distance of the hearer from the obstacle from which the sound returns be such that the organ of hearing is perfectly changed beforehand by the direct sound before the reflected sound reaches it: the reason of which is that, if the time which intervenes between the impact of the direct sound and that of the reflected sound is not distinct, only one motion and change of the organ will be excited by both sounds, or at least the subsequent one will follow the prior with such haste that they can by no means be discriminated; and hence also only one sound will be perceived by us. This coincidence of the direct sound and the reflected sound nevertheless makes the sounding body heard better.

625 Requiritur secundo: non solum reflexio vocis, & sonantis corporis ex debita distantia, sed etiam ut sit reflexio ejusmodi, vi cujus vox resiliat, ex quibusdam quasi concameratis meatibus, anfractibus, & cavernosis antris, ita, ut vibrationes sonorae per ejusmodi obstacula collectae, perveniant ad aurem, postquàm priores, quae aërem primo commoverant, jam cessarint: cujus iterùm ratio est, quia si qualiscumque & omnis omninò reflexio sufficeret ad hanc resonantiam, Echo semper existeret; at experientiâ constat, tunc solum fieri repercusionem, quum vox directa fertur in obices variis meatibus, ductibus, & anfractibus horridos. Memorabilis est

625 It is required, secondly, not only that there be a reflection of the voice and of the sounding body from a due distance, but also that the reflection be of such a kind that by its force the voice leaps back from certain as it were vaulted passages, windings and cavernous grottoes, so that the sonorous vibrations, collected through obstacles of this kind, reach the ear after the prior ones, which first set the air in motion, have already ceased: the reason of which again is that, if any reflection whatsoever, and every one at all, sufficed for this resonance, an Echo would always exist; but it is established by experience that a repercussion occurs only when the direct voice is carried into obstacles bristling with various passages, ducts and windings. Memorable is the

p. 198

Echo Villae Simonettae propè Mediolanum, ubi vox è fenestra in oppositum parallelè murum, passibus 33. distantem emissa, quater, & vigesies, imò etiam trigesies repetitur. Haec adnotare placuit ex P Klaus. Celebria per orbem terrarum de Echo exempla referunt P. Kirker s1, Sturmius s2, aliique.

Echo of the Villa Simonetta near Milan, where a voice sent from a window against the opposite parallel wall, 33 paces distant, is repeated twenty-four times, nay even thirty times. It has pleased me to note these things from Fr. Klaus. Celebrated examples of Echo throughout the world are reported by Fr. Kircher (c), Sturm (d) and others.

Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

626 Opp. 1: Tubae sonus ex plusquam centum passibus auditur; quum tamen aëris motus â tuba commoti vix ex duobus passibus percipiatur: ergo sonus eò usque diffunditur, quo usque motus aëris pervenire non potest. Respondeo negando conseq. & dico: insonante tuba, aëris tremorem ad eandem distantiam pervenire ad quam ejusdem sonus extenditur: hic autem aëris motus quum tremulus tantùm sit, & ex minutissimis vibrationibus componatur, sensui tactus est omninò imperceptibilis, neque enim ad eum immutandum ob ejus tenuitatem sufficit, percipitur tamen ab auditus sensorio, ob exquisitam ad idque proportionatam texturam, quam habet, ratione cujus â tam tenuibus percusionibus adficitur.

626 Obj. 1: The sound of a trumpet is heard from more than a hundred paces, although the motion of the air stirred by the trumpet is scarcely perceived from two paces: therefore sound is diffused as far as the motion of the air cannot reach. I reply by denying the conseq., and I say: when a trumpet sounds, the tremor of the air reaches the same distance to which its sound extends; but this motion of the air, since it is only tremulous and composed of very minute vibrations, is altogether imperceptible to the sense of touch, for on account of its tenuity it does not suffice to change that sense; it is perceived, however, by the sensorium of hearing, on account of the exquisite texture, proportioned to this, which it has, by reason of which it is affected by such slight percussions.

627 Quod autèm aëris tremor ad eandem distantiam excurrat, ad quam pérvenit sonus, experientiâ patet; quum enim tormentum bellicum exploditur, fenestrae praesertim vitreae, etiam mille, aut bis mille passus distantes, tremunt, nec antè tremunt, quàm explosionis sonus audiatur; quumque talis tremor, nonnisi ab aëre impellente possit provenire, perspicuum fit, aëris tremorem esse â sono inséparabilem & ad eandem distantiam cum ipso pervenire.

627 But that the tremor of the air runs out to the same distance which the sound reaches is plain from experience; for when a cannon is fired, windows, especially glass ones, even a thousand or two thousand paces distant, tremble, and they do not tremble before the sound of the explosion is heard; and since such a tremor can only come from air impelling them, it becomes evident that the tremor of the air is inseparable from sound and reaches the same distance with it.

628 Opp. 2: Si intra ampullam vitream hermeticè sigillatàm tintinnabulum aliquo artificio pulsetur, sonus percipitur; sed hoc néquaquam ita eveniret, si sonus in aëris motu vibratorio consisteret: nam aër intra ampullam inclusus, vitrum pertransire nequit ut aërem externum ad aurem usque impellat: ergo. Respondeo: quod quoties sonus aliquis excitatur, non modò aërem, verùm & cetera corpora motu quodam trémulo cieri: frequenter enim experímur sonantibus crassioribus chordis instrumenti musici, ac canentibus majoribus orgáni pneumatici fistulis, ábacos, sedilia, imò & solum ipsum, cui dicta instrumenta insistunt, trémere. Quid ergo mirum si in casu objectionis, vibrante aëre in ampulla incluso vitrum ipsum simili tremore concitetur, quod experientia testatur: nam si ampulla manu stringatur, quasi surdus, & valde obtusus sonus auditur eò scilicet, quod vitri vibrationes ab adplicata manu ex parte prohibeantur.

628 Obj. 2: If, inside a glass phial hermetically sealed, a little bell is struck by some artifice, the sound is perceived; but this would by no means happen if sound consisted in a vibratory motion of the air: for the air enclosed within the phial cannot pass through the glass so as to drive the external air all the way to the ear: therefore. I reply that whenever any sound is excited, not only the air but also the other bodies are stirred with a certain tremulous motion: for we frequently experience that, when the thicker strings of a musical instrument sound and the larger pipes of a pneumatic organ sing, the tables, the seats, nay even the very floor on which the said instruments stand, tremble. What wonder, then, if, in the case of the objection, when the air enclosed in the phial vibrates, the glass itself is stirred with a similar tremor, as experience testifies? For if the phial is gripped by the hand, a deaf, as it were, and very dull sound is heard, namely because the vibrations of the glass are in part prevented by the applied hand.

629 Opp. 3: Si vera esset nostra opinio, non possémus simul, &

629 Obj. 3: If our opinion were true, we could not at once and at the same time

In Phonurgia.

In the Phonurgia.

Phys. Elect. tom. 1. p. 659. & seqq.

Phys. Elect., vol. 1, p. 659 ff.

p. 199

eodem tempore diversos sonos percipere, ut vocum, campanarum &c sed hoc est contra experientiam: ergo. Prob. maj.: Nam aër nequit eodem tempore simul diversis motibus concitari, idemque dicendum de auriculari tympano. Respondeo negando propositionem: Nam motus aëris tremulus suis etiam constat mótulis, undè alternantibus percusionibus diversorum corporum, eidem organo communicatis, potest ipsum diversis motibus eodem sensibili tempore cieri, quod idem dicendum est de tympano auris, & consequenter possunt diversi soni eodem tempore sensibili percipi.

time perceive different sounds, as of voices, bells, etc.; but this is contrary to experience: therefore. Proof of the major: the air cannot be set in motion at the same time by different motions together; and the same must be said of the drum of the ear. I reply by denying the proposition. For the tremulous motion of the air also consists of its own small motions; hence, when the alternating percussions of different bodies are communicated to the same organ, the air can be stirred by different motions in the same sensible time; and the same must be said of the drum of the ear, and consequently different sounds can be perceived in the same sensible time.

630 Exemplum habetis in stagnante aqua, cui si lapillos in diversis ejus partibus simul injiciatis, profectò videbitis totam in protuberantes undulas in circuli morem crispari, qui continuò sese dilatantes, invicem intersecantur absque ulla prorsùs perturbatione: similiter ergo in nostro casu vibrationes â diversis corporibus per sonum concitatae absque ulla perturbatione ad aurem usque excurrunt, eamque diversimodè adficiunt, quo fit ut simul diversi soni percipiantur.

630 You have an example in standing water: if you throw little stones into different parts of it at the same time, you will surely see the whole of it ruffled into swelling ripples in the manner of a circle, which, continually spreading themselves out, intersect one another without any disturbance whatever. Likewise, therefore, in our case the vibrations excited by different sounding bodies run all the way to the ear without any disturbance, and affect it in different ways, whence it comes about that different sounds are perceived at the same time.

631 Opp. 4. Si sonus in praefatis vibrationibus consisteret non possemus per auditum, corporis sonantis distantiam emetiri: ergo. Respondeo: quod vibrationes in aëre in modum circuli efformantur, & aër undulatim crispatur quaquaversus, in cujus circuli centro corpus sonans existit: hinc, quò plus hujusmodi vibrationes â centro recedunt, eo majores peripherias efficiunt, & consequenter minor illarum portio, seu minor arcus aërem remotiorem adficit, quàm propiorem; hinc particulae aëris ferientes pauciores sunt, simulque minus unitae, minorem ergo adfectionem imprimunt sensui, remotiùs â corpore sonante existenti, & ope hujus majoris, aut minoris adfectionis, objecti sonantis distantia percipitur.

631 Obj. 4. If sound consisted in the aforesaid vibrations, we could not measure the distance of a sounding body by hearing: therefore. I reply: since the vibrations in the air are formed in the manner of a circle, and the air is rippled in waves in every direction, at the center of which circle the sounding body stands, hence the farther vibrations of this kind recede from the center, the greater the circumferences they make, and consequently a smaller portion of them, or a smaller arc, affects the more remote air than the nearer; hence the particles of air that strike are fewer, and at the same time less united; they therefore impress a smaller affection on the sense the farther one stands from the sounding body; and by means of this greater or smaller affection the distance of the sounding object is perceived.

632 Opp. tandem: juxta probabiliorem sententiam: sonus gravis in tardioribus, acutus verò in velocioribus vibrationibus consistit; sed vibrationes tympani auris debent esse Isochronae, seu ejusdem durationis, ut sunt vibrationes ejusdem chordae aequè tensae: ergo semper audiretur idem sonus in ratione gravis, vel acuti, quod experientiae repugnat, praesertim quum idem corpus eadem servatâ tensione non possit modò in tardiores, modò in velociores vibrationes concitari. Resp. negando suppositum nempè, quod auris tympanum eamdem semper servet tensionem. Auriculare namque typanum id fermè muneris praestat auditui, quod lens crystallina visui.

632 Obj. finally: according to the more probable opinion, a low sound consists in slower vibrations, a high one in swifter vibrations; but the vibrations of the drum of the ear must be isochronous, or of the same duration, as are the vibrations of the same string equally stretched: therefore the same sound would always be heard as to low or high, which is contrary to experience, especially since the same body, keeping the same tension, cannot be set now into slower, now into swifter vibrations. Reply: by denying the supposition, namely that the drum of the ear always keeps the same tension. For the drum of the ear performs for hearing nearly the same office that the crystalline lens performs for sight.

633 Quemadmodum enim crystallina lens ita luminis radios excipit, ut vi suae convexitatis eos in basim retíneae debita distinctione projiciat, quod ut efficiat, convexitatem suam in majorem, aut minorem mutat, pro diverso radiorum illapsu, diversaque incidentia; ita & tympanum auris ita constitutum est, ut pro diverso aëris vibrantis illapsu, modò tensionem augeat, modò minuat; ita ut quemadmodum crystallina lens convexitatem auget, aut minuit

633 For just as the crystalline lens receives the rays of light in such a way that by the force of its convexity it projects them onto the base of the retina with due distinctness, and to accomplish this changes its convexity to greater or smaller according to the different falling-in and different incidence of the rays: so also the drum of the ear is so constituted that, according to the different falling-in of the vibrating air, it now increases its tension, now diminishes it; so that, just as the crystalline lens increases or diminishes its convexity by

p. 200

sese explicando, aut contrahendo, operâ delicatissimi musculi, ita & tympanum auriculare suam tensionem auget, aut minuit operâ gemini musculi, quo typanum vel adducitur, vel laxatur: analogiam habetis in militari tympano, cujus membrana funiculorum operâ magis tenditur, aut làxatur.

or contracting itself through the action of a most delicate muscle, so also the drum of the ear increases or diminishes its tension through the action of a twin muscle, by which the drum is either drawn tight or slackened: you have an analogy in the military drum, whose membrane is stretched more or less by means of cords.

634 Praeterea quemadmodùm crystállina lens ad majorem, aut minorem contractionem determinatur â primâ radiorum projectione, quibus suscipiendis, & intus projiciendis confestim aptatur; ita auris tympanum ad tensionem augendam, aut minuendam á primis aëris impulsionibus determinatur, quo fit ut facillimè celerioribus, aut diuturnioribus sese adcommodet, sonorumque differentias in ratione etiam gravis, & acuti percipiat.

634 Moreover, just as the crystalline lens is determined to a greater or smaller contraction by the first projection of the rays, to receiving which and to projecting them inward it straightway adapts itself, so the drum of the ear is determined to increasing or diminishing its tension by the first impulses of the air; whence it comes about that it very easily accommodates itself to swifter or longer-lasting ones, and perceives the differences of sounds also as to low and high.

DISSERTATIO IV. — DISSERTATION IV

De Qualitatibus visibilibus, sive de Luce & ejus proprietatibus.

On visible Qualities, or on Light and its properties.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

Lucis tàm primitivae, quàm derivativae natura inquiritur.

The nature of light, both primitive and derivative, is inquired into.

635 Corpus lucidum dicitur illud, quod ipsâ suâ naturâ tale est, ut lumen emittat. Illud verò illuminatum vocatur, quod lumen, quo fulget non habet ex se, sed illud totum ab extrinseco recipit. Sic flamma ex. gr., carbones accensi & praecipuè Sol sunt corpora lucida. Illuminata verò ea omnia, quae praesente sole aut flammâ nobis conspicua sunt; inconspicua, luminoso aut sublato aut extincto. Lux primitiva est illa adfectio, per quam formaliter corpus est luminosum. Lux derivativa est adfectio illa quae per medium â lucido corpore diffusa, atque ad oculos usque propagata, efficit ut circumstantia corpora, alioquin inconspicua, videantur. His explicatis.

luminous body is said to be that which is such by its own nature that it 635 A emits light. That, on the other hand, is called illuminated which does not have from itself the light with which it shines, but receives it wholly from without. Thus flame, for example, burning coals, and above all the Sun are luminous bodies. Illuminated, on the other hand, are all those things which are visible to us when the sun or a flame is present, invisible when the luminous body is taken away or extinguished. Primitive light is that affection through which a body is formally luminous. Derivative light is that affection which, diffused through a medium from a luminous body and propagated all the way to the eyes, brings it about that surrounding bodies, otherwise invisible, are seen. These things explained,

636 Dico primo: Lux prout spectatur in corpore lucido, seu primitiva in concitatissimo quodam motu subtilium partium ejusdem rectè constituitur. Prob.: Lux primitiva rectè constituitur in eo,

636 I say first: light as it is regarded in a luminous body, or primitive light, is rightly made to consist in a certain most agitated motion of the subtle parts of that body. Proof: primitive light is rightly made to consist in that

p. 201

quod cum ipsa luce semper in corpore conjunctum est, & â quo lux sic dependet, ut illo posito in corporibus, ipsa illicò in iis habeatur, eaque lucida efficiantur, quo contra sublato, lux statim pereat; sed cum luce semper conjunctus est subtilium corporis partium concitatissimus motus, sic ut nullum sit corpus lucidum, in quo motus ejusmodi non deprehendatur, & quàmprimum subtiliores corporum partes in motum concitatum aguntur, lux ab eis emittitur, ea verò extinguitur simul ac partes agitatae ad quietem rediguntur: ergo Lux primitiva in concitatissimo quodam motu subtilium corporis partium consistit. Minor per partes apertissimè demonstratur.

which is always joined with light itself in a body, and on which light so depends that, when it is posited in bodies, light is at once had in them and they are made luminous, whereas when it is taken away light straightway perishes; but always joined with light is a most agitated motion of the subtle parts of the body, so that there is no luminous body in which a motion of this kind is not detected; and as soon as the subtler parts of bodies are driven into agitated motion, light is emitted by them, but it is extinguished as soon as the agitated parts are brought back to rest: therefore primitive light consists in a certain most agitated motion of the subtle parts of a body. The minor is demonstrated part by part most plainly.

637 Et ad primam quod adtinet, scilicet, corpora omnia lucicida tali motu donari, certissimum omninò est. In flamma enim, & carbonibus accensis vehemens partium motio conspicua est, corpora item putrescentia, pisces putridi, ligna putredine corrupta, lucem emittentia intestino partium motu agitari ex alibi dictis manifestum est, quum fermentatio, & putrefactio sine partium motu & agitatione explicari nequeat. Pars quoque altera liquet, videlicèt: corpora lucem emittere, quàmprimum subtiliores particulae ad motum concitantur.

637 And as to the first part, namely that all luminous bodies are endowed with such a motion, it is altogether most certain. For in flame and in burning coals a vehement motion of the parts is visible; likewise that putrefying bodies, putrid fish, wood corrupted by rot, which emit light, are agitated by an intestine motion of the parts is manifest from what has been said elsewhere, since fermentation and putrefaction cannot be explained without motion and agitation of the parts. The other part too is clear, namely that bodies emit light as soon as their subtler particles are set in motion.

638 „¿An non corpora omnia, (inquit Clariss. Newtonus s1 quae partibus abundant terrestribus, & praesertim sulphurosis lumen emittunt; quotiescumque partes istae satis sint agitatae, sive id calore fiat, sive adtritu, sive percussu, sive putrescendo, sive motu aliquo vitali, sive alia quavis de causâ? Ut aqua marina, felis dorsum manu obliquè in loco tenebricoso affrictum, ligna, carnes, & pisces dum putrescunt, vapores ex aquis putridis, qui ignes fatui vulgò appellantur, cicindelae, & animalium quorundam oculi, motu quodam vitali, phosphorus Bononiensis radiis luminis agitatus, & certi liquores inter se permixti, quorum particulae cum impetu concurrunt, ut oleum vitrioli, á nitro pari pondere destillatum, dein dupla portione mixtum cum oleo garyophillorum, sive anisi?„

638 “Do not all bodies (says the most distinguished Newton (e)) which abound with terrestrial parts, and especially with sulphureous ones, emit light as often as those parts are sufficiently agitated, whether this be done by heat, or by friction, or by percussion, or by putrefying, or by some vital motion, or by any other cause whatever? As sea water, the back of a cat stroked obliquely with the hand in a dark place, wood, flesh and fish while they putrefy, the vapors from putrid waters which are commonly called ignes fatui, glowworms and the eyes of certain animals by a certain vital motion, the Bononian phosphorus agitated by the rays of light, and certain liquors mixed with one another whose particles come together with an impetus, as oil of vitriol distilled from an equal weight of niter, and then mixed with a double portion of oil of cloves or of aniseed?”

639 Sed infinita sunt, quae veritatem hanc manifestam reddunt, & phaenomenorum electricorum consideratio ad evidentiam demonstrat. Postrema pars facilè admodùm ostenditur: motu nempè partium cessante, lucem á corporibus non spargi, nemo quippè ignorat, flammam extingui dum inflammatum corpus comprimitur, lucem in accensis corporibus carbonibus ex. gr. ignitoque ferro disperire, dum aquae immerguntur, quâ partium agitatio sistitur.

639 But there are countless things that make this truth manifest, and the consideration of electrical phenomena demonstrates it to evidence. The last part is shown quite easily: for no one is unaware that, when the motion of the parts ceases, light is not spread from bodies; that flame is extinguished when the inflamed body is compressed; that light in burning bodies, for example in coals and in red-hot iron, vanishes when they are plunged into water, by which the agitation of the parts is stopped.

640 Dico secundo: lux derivativa sive lumen est substantia subtilissima, motu celerrimo secundum rectam lineam adfecta. Prob. per partes. Et in primis lumen esse corpoream substantiam, ex eo

640 I say second: derivative light, or lumen, is a most subtle substance, affected with a very swift motion along a straight line. Proof, part by part. And first, that light is a corporeal substance is made

Optic. quaest. 9.

Opticks, query 9.

p. 202

redditur perspicuum, quod adfectiones corporis participet: nam primò dum ex uno in alium medium transit, refringitur. Secundo: in superficiem opacam incidens in adversam partem reflectitur. Tertio: lux propagata colligi in unum punctum ac quasi condensari potest, si concavo speculo, vel convexa lente exceptum fuerit in puncto quod focum vocant, in quo intensum adeò calorem producit, ut combustibilia quaeque corpora eo in loco posita post pauca minuta incendat, metalla, omniaque liquabilia fundat, dissolvat; quae liquefactioni minimè obnoxia sunt, quaeque sale abundant in vitrum mutet, ut videre est in Actis Eruditorum Lipsiae s1, ubi plurima referuntur de concavo speculo quod ab illius inventore D. Tschirnhause, Tschirnhausianum vocatur. s2

evident from this, that it shares in the affections of a body: for, first, while it passes from one medium into another, it is refracted. Second: falling upon an opaque surface, it is reflected toward the opposite side. Third: propagated light can be gathered and, as it were, condensed into one point, if it is received by a concave mirror or a convex lens, in the point which they call the focus, in which it produces a heat so intense that it sets on fire, after a few minutes, any combustible bodies placed in that spot, melts and dissolves metals and all fusible things, and turns into glass those which are least liable to liquefaction and abound in salt, as may be seen in the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig (f), where a great many things are related of the concave mirror which, from its inventor D. Tschirnhaus, is called the Tschirnhausian. (g)

641 Quarto organum visus perstringit lumen, illudque copia sua, aut vehementia (non secus ac nimius fragor aurem offendit) disturbat, imò laedit magnoperè, sed haec omnia manifestè arguunt substantiam corpoream, sive impenetrabilem: ergo. Et sanè ut optimè argumentatur Cl. Gassendus s3 sicuti impacta in parietem pila, ab ea resilit, quia corpus quum sit, transire per locum â corpore occupatum non potest; ita lucis radius in corpus impactus ab ipso repercutitur, quia illud suâ corpulentiâ locum occupat, nam effectuum naturalium ejusdem generis easdem esse causas regula constans est, ut diximus [§. 22.]. Deinde substantiam esse subtilissimam ex eo patescit, quod vitri poros subeat facillimè. Quid quod structura exilissimorum animalculorum luminis exilitatem demonstret? Si enim animalcula ipsa, ut diximus jam [§. 164.] tantae sint exilitatis, si tam exiguae molis sunt oculi, & eorum pupillae, quàm longè minor debet esse luminis materia, ut in oculos ac pupillam illabatur, facilèque haec organa permeet?

641 Fourth: light strikes the organ of sight, and by its abundance or vehemence (just as an excessive crash offends the ear) it disturbs it, nay hurts it greatly; but all these things manifestly prove a corporeal, or impenetrable, substance: therefore. And indeed, as the distinguished Gassendi argues very well (h), just as a ball driven against a wall rebounds from it, because, since it is a body, it cannot pass through a place occupied by a body, so a ray of light driven against a body is struck back by it, because that body occupies the place with its bulk; for it is a constant rule that natural effects of the same kind have the same causes, as we have said [§. 22.]. Next, that it is a most subtle substance is evident from this, that it enters the pores of glass most easily. What of the fact that the structure of the tiniest animalcules demonstrates the tenuity of light? For if the animalcules themselves, as we have already said [§. 164.], are of such tenuity, if their eyes and the pupils of them are of so slight a bulk, how much smaller must the matter of light be, so that it may glide into the eyes and the pupil and easily permeate these organs?

Ad ann. 1687. Mens. Jan. pag. 53.

For the year 1687, month of January, p. 53.

Quoniam verò radiorum collectio, atque adeò vires speculorum subsidio auctae, pendent â figura eorundem cóncava, iccircò materia quaevis speculo caustico opportuna est, modò poliri exactè queat. Hinc Wolfio teste celeber Dresdae artifex Gaertnerus magna specula ustoria ex ligno construxit, quae efficiendi habilitate Tschirnhausianis superaria [?] dicebantur. Quin Zannius [?] [apud Wolf. Elem. Catoptr. §. 223.] refert confectum fuisse â Neumanno speculum, quo metalla fluida reddebantur ex charta duriore, & stramine ei adglutinato. Adtamen complexus matériae ex qua parantur specula comparatus ea lege sit oportet, ut luminis radios regerat non vero absorbeat, ut fit in corporibus nigris. Ea de causa Cl. Boyle, ope speculi, quod in formam caustici ex nigro marmore confecit, lignum in foco adstitutum, sole etiam diutiùs in speculum illapso comburere non potuit, ut refert Muschenbroeck [Essai de Physique §. 975.].

But since the gathering of the rays, and hence the powers of mirrors, increased by their aid, depend on their concave figure, therefore any material whatever is suitable for a burning mirror, provided it can be polished exactly. Hence, on Wolff’s testimony, the celebrated Dresden craftsman Gärtner constructed great burning mirrors of wood, which were said to surpass the Tschirnhausian ones in effectiveness. Indeed Zahn [in Wolff, Elem. Catoptr. §. 223.] relates that a mirror was made by Neumann by which metals were rendered fluid, out of rather hard paper with straw glued onto it. Nevertheless, the texture of the material from which mirrors are prepared must be so constituted that it sends back the rays of light and does not absorb them, as happens in black bodies. For that reason the distinguished Boyle, by means of a mirror which he made in the form of a burning glass out of black marble, could not burn wood set in the focus, even though the sun had fallen upon the mirror for quite a long time, as Musschenbroek relates [Essai de Physique §. 975.].

Sect. 1. Phys. Lib. 6. cap. 2.

Sect. 1, Phys., bk. 6, ch. 2.

p. 203

642 Quod verò celerrimus sit motus illorum corpusculorum evincitur. Primò ex celerrima luminis diffusione. Secundò: demonstratur ex stupenda vi illa speculi caustici ut diximus [§. 640.]; quum enim vis hujusmodi sit ea ipsa, quâ illa corpuscula moventur, & haec oriatur ex ductu massae in celeritatem [§. 275.]; exilissima nequit esse, ut re verá est massa singulorum illorum corpusculorum, nisi ut eorum vis sit tanta, quantam esse vidimus, atque adeò celeritate maxima moveantur necesse est. Denique motum hunc rectilineum esse experimento compertum habemus, radius enim luminosus per exiguum forámen in cámeram obscuram immissus jugiter lineâ rectâ propagatur, & in punctum foraminulo juxta rectam lineam oppositum, incidit: ergo lumen est substantia subtilissima, motu celerrimo secundum rectam lineam adfecta.

642 That the motion of those corpuscles is very swift is proved, first, from the very swift diffusion of light. Second, it is demonstrated from that astonishing force of the burning mirror of which we have spoken [§. 640.]: for since a force of this kind is that very force by which those corpuscles are moved, and this arises from the product of the mass into the celerity [§. 275.], the mass of each of those corpuscles, being most slight, as indeed it is, cannot give them a force as great as we have seen it to be unless they are moved with the greatest celerity; and so it is necessary that they be moved with the greatest celerity. Finally, we have it ascertained by experiment that this motion is rectilinear: a luminous ray let in through a very small hole into a dark chamber is always propagated in a straight line, and falls upon the point opposite the little hole along a straight line: therefore light is a most subtle substance, affected with a very swift motion along a straight line.

643 Dico 3: Lucis propagatio seu lux derivativa, sive lumen non rectè explicatur per igneum profluvium ex corporibus lucidis dimanans. Est contra Cl. Gassendum, & Newtonum. Prob.: Si ita esset, medium semel illustratum etiam sublato lucido corpore, illuminatum manéret. Non enim luminis corpuscula lucidi corporis praesentia indigent, ut in ipso medio conserventur, etsi lucidum corpus â quo emissa fuere non amplius illi praesens existat; sed falsum est illuminatum manere medium sublato lucido corpore â quo illustratur: ergo. Deinde, lumen sparsum â candela in cubiculo vel â sole per aërem eò intensiùs fieri deberet, quò longiore tempore corpus illic praesens est; quum enim corpus lucidum nova luminis corpuscula singulis momentis emittat, necesse est, ut in eadem parte medii per quod lumen diffunditur, corpuscula semper fiant copiosiora, ac proindè lumen intensiùs, quod tamen utrumque cum experientia pugnat.

643 I say 3: the propagation of light, or derivative light, or lumen, is not rightly explained by a fiery outflow emanating from luminous bodies. This is against the distinguished Gassendi and Newton. Proof: if it were so, a medium once lit up would remain illuminated even when the luminous body was taken away. For the corpuscles of light do not need the presence of the luminous body in order to be preserved in the medium itself, even though the luminous body from which they were emitted is no longer present to it; but it is false that the medium remains illuminated when the luminous body by which it is lit up is taken away: therefore. Next, the light spread by a candle in a small room, or by the sun through the air, ought to become the more intense the longer the body is present there; for since the luminous body emits new corpuscles of light at every moment, it is necessary that in the same part of the medium through which the light is diffused the corpuscles always become more abundant, and therefore the light more intense; yet each of these conflicts with experience.

644 Utraque haec ratio firmatur similitudine, quâ utitur Cl. Gassendus ad explicandam suam de lumine opinionem: ait enim, lumen produci non secùs atque odores, emissione videlicèt exilium corpusculorum; sed certum est odorem conservari sublato etiam corpore, odoras moleculas spargente; certum item est, odorem intensiorem vividioremque reddi continuò in eadem medii parte, quò diuturnior est praesentia eorum corporum á quibus odorata corpuscula emanant: ergo in substantiali lucidi corporis effluvio lumen non rectè collocatur.

644 Each of these reasons is strengthened by the comparison that the distinguished Gassendi uses to explain his opinion about light: for he says that light is produced just as odors are, namely by the emission of slender corpuscles; but it is certain that an odor is preserved even when the body spreading the odorous molecules is taken away; it is likewise certain that an odor is made continually more intense and more lively in the same part of the medium the longer the presence of the bodies from which the odorous corpuscles emanate lasts: therefore light is not rightly placed in a substantial effluvium of the luminous body.

645 Dicunt Newtoniani: illuminatum non manere medium, quod semel illustratum est, lucido corpore sublato: quia licet luminis corpuscula non indigeant praesentiâ corporis lucidi, ut in medio, per quod diffusa sunt conserventur; ea tamen indigent, ut in illo moveri non cessent; ac proindè, ut ipsum medium nobis illustratum exhibeant.

645 The Newtonians say that the medium, once lit up, does not remain illuminated when the luminous body is taken away: because, although the corpuscles of light do not need the presence of the luminous body in order to be preserved in the medium through which they have been diffused, they do need it in order not to cease being moved in it, and therefore in order to show the medium itself lit up to us.

646 Contra tamen, arguit Clariss. Fort. â Brixia: etenim nullum corpus projectum indiget praesentiâ projicientis, ut in motu quem ab illo recepit perseveret; sed pergit moveri, & si

646 But against this, argues the most distinguished Fortunato da Brescia: for no projected body needs the presence of the projector in order to persevere in the motion that it received from it; but it goes on being moved even if the projector

p. 204

ciens post impressum illi motum deficiat: ergo neque luminis corpuscula non [?] indigent praesentiâ corporis lucidi, ne motus quem ab illo receperunt [?] in ipsis pereat. Praeterea neque soni, neque odoris corpuscula ita dependent â sonoro, aut odoro corpore, ex quo emanant, ut nonnisi illius praesentiâ moveri queant, & sensationem in nobis excitare: ergo neque corpuscula luminis ita dependent [?] â lucido corpore, ut in motu sistantur [?], atque ad luminis sensationem in nobis excitandam planè inepta evadant, statim ac lucidum corpus non amplius nobis praesens existit.

fails after impressing the motion on it: therefore neither do the corpuscles of light need the presence of the luminous body, lest the motion which they received from it should perish in them. Moreover, neither the corpuscles of sound nor those of odor so depend on the sounding or odorous body from which they emanate that they can be moved, and excite sensation in us, only in its presence: therefore neither do the corpuscles of light so depend on the luminous body that they should come to a halt in their motion and be rendered wholly unfit for exciting the sensation of light in us as soon as the luminous body is no longer present to us.

647 Quod si quis dicat soni corpuscula moveri posse etiam absente sonoro corpore â quo emissa fuere, quia illorum motus perturbatus est, & per aërem quaquaversus diffunditur [?], non nisi praesente lucido, â quo fuerint [?] vibrata, moveri posse corpuscula luminis, quia illorum motus est rectilineus: contra est, quod sicut perturbatus corpusculorum motus non indiget ut conservetur, praesentiâ corporis perturbatè moventis, ita neque motus corpusculorum rectilineus opus habere deberet, ne pereat, praesentiâ corporis vibrantis secundum rectam lineam. Utriusque namque motus eadem omninò ratio est, independentia [?] scilicet corporis moti â movente, ut eum, quem semel accepit, quemcumque motum retineat. Imò tantum abest durationem motus rectilinei semel corpori impressi, â moventis duratione dependere, ut inter naturae leges ea sit una, omne corpus semel in motum concitatum semper moveri secundum rectam lineam, quamdiu non cogitur â causa externa directionem suam mutare [§. 294.].

647 But if someone should say that the corpuscles of sound can be moved even when the sounding body from which they were emitted is absent, because their motion is perturbed and spreads through the air in every direction, whereas the corpuscles of light can be moved only when the luminous body by which they were darted forth is present, because their motion is rectilinear: against this it is urged that, just as the perturbed motion of corpuscles does not need, in order to be preserved, the presence of a body moving them in a perturbed way, so neither should the rectilinear motion of corpuscles need, lest it perish, the presence of a body vibrating them along a straight line. For the reason of each motion is altogether the same, namely the independence of the body moved from the mover, so that it retains the motion it has once received, whatever that motion may be. Nay, so far is the duration of a rectilinear motion once impressed on a body from depending on the duration of the mover, that among the laws of nature this is one: every body once set in motion is always moved along a straight line, so long as it is not compelled by some external cause to change its direction [§. 294.].

648 At hinc nemo eorum, qui pro certo habent, substantiale lucidi corporis effluvium in quo lumen constituunt, notabili aliquo temporis intervallo indigere, ut â sole, ceterisque astris ad nos perveniat, inficiari poterit [?], fore, ut lumen maneat in medio, per quod diffusum est, etiam lucido sublato corpore, â quo producitur. Evidens est enim in hac hypothesi, lumen independenter â corpore lucido in medio conservari toto illo temporis spatio, quod labitur [?] dum transit [?] â lucido ipso corpore ad nos perveniens [?]. Nam si ponatur unam horam requiri, ut lumen â Sole S ad terram T (Fig. 117.), propagetur, evidens est lumen â S diffusum manere per spatium â S ad T, etiamsi intra illud unius horae intervallum, Sol S, â quo lumen ipsum emissum, non amplius existat.

648 But hence none of those who hold for certain that the substantial effluvium of the luminous body, in which they make light consist, needs some notable interval of time in order to reach us from the sun and the other stars, can deny that it will come about that light remains in the medium through which it has been diffused, even when the luminous body by which it is produced is taken away. For it is evident on this hypothesis that light is preserved in the medium independently of the luminous body for that whole time which elapses while it travels from the luminous body itself to us. For if it is supposed that one hour is required for light to be propagated from the Sun S to the earth T (Fig. 117.), it is evident that the light diffused from S remains in the space from S to T even if, within that interval of one hour, the Sun S, which emitted that light, ceases to exist.

649 Quum igitur Vir Cl. Newtonus s1, s' Gravesandius s2, Musschenbroekius s3, aliique praeterea multi ponunt, lumen spatio septem, vel octo minutorum primorum â sole ad terram venire,

649 Since, then, the distinguished Newton (i), ’s Gravesande (k), Musschenbroek (l) and many others besides hold that light comes from the sun to the earth in the space of seven or eight minutes, and hence

p. 205

adeoque indigere spatio aliquot horarum, ut à sole ad Saturnum, tum à Saturno ad nos perveniat, spatio vero aliquot mensium, ut à fixis stellis ad terram usque propagetur; arbitror, hos omnes facile concessuros, in substantiali corporis effluvio minimè posse lumen constitui, quum simul ab illis detur, quod experientiae apertè contrarium est, fore scilicet, ut lumen ipsum notabili temporis spatio conservetur in medio, per quod semel diffusum est, etiam lucido absente corpore, à quo fuit productum.

that it needs the space of some hours in order to reach Saturn from the sun, and then us from Saturn, and the space of some months in order to be propagated from the fixed stars all the way to the earth, I think that all these will readily grant that light can by no means be made to consist in a substantial effluvium of a body, since at the same time it would be granted by them, what is plainly contrary to experience, namely that light itself is preserved for a notable space of time in the medium through which it has once been diffused, even when the luminous body by which it was produced is absent.

650 Dico quarto: Luminis propagatio explicanda videtur per aethereae substantiae, motu vibratorio donatae pressionem rectilineam à corporis lucidi motu profectam, & visus organum impellentem. Prob. Materia namque aetherea corporeae substantiae affectiones sibi vendicat, & frangi, reflecti, movere organum potest, & subtilissima quum sit, motum recipere à lucidi corporis particulis potest; quumque ubivis diffusa habeatur, motus propagatio per eam quàm optime explicatur. Praeterea constat à solo tremulo motu aëris, aurium cavitatem subeuntis ita affici organum auditus, ut in nobis fiat soni sensatio; sed juxta omnes inter lumen, & sonum maxima analogia habetur: ergo à solo motu vibratorio aethereae subtilissimae substantiae, quae oculi pupillam penetret, potest visus organum ita immutari, ut sensatio luminis in nobis excitetur.

650 I say fourth: the propagation of light seems to be explained by a rectilinear pressure of an ethereal substance endowed with vibratory motion, a pressure proceeding from the motion of the luminous body and impelling the organ of sight. Proof: for the ethereal matter claims for itself the affections of a corporeal substance, and can be refracted, reflected and move the organ; and since it is most subtle, it can receive motion from the particles of the luminous body; and since it is had diffused everywhere, the propagation of motion through it is explained in the best possible way. Moreover, it is established that the organ of hearing is so affected by the tremulous motion of the air alone, entering the cavity of the ears, that the sensation of sound arises in us; but among all things there is the greatest analogy between light and sound: therefore by the vibratory motion alone of a most subtle ethereal substance, which penetrates the pupil of the eye, the organ of sight can be so altered that the sensation of light is excited in us.

Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

651 Opp. 1. contra primam: rationes quibus conclusio nostra innititur, nihil aliud evincunt, nisi lucem primitivam à motu partium corporis lucidi, tamquam à necessaria conditione dependere: ergo lux primitiva tantum veluti à conditione, non tamquam à formali sua ratione dependet à agitatissimo[?] motu subtilium partium corporis lucidi. Nego totum argumentum: quoniam nihil prorsus praeter tremorem communicatur corpori sonoro dum percutitur, & sonum edit, nullo [?] ex Philosophorum repugnante, tremor hujusmodi, non conditio ad sonum praerequisita, sed ipse sonus est: ergo eadem ratione si dum corpus efficitur lucidum, nihil aliud, praeter motum in subtilioribus ejus partibus excitatur, motus ipse non mera est conditio ad primitivae lucis productionem necessariò requisita, sed ipsa lux.

bj. 1 against the first: the reasons on which our conclusion rests prove 651 O nothing else than that primitive light depends on the motion of the parts of the luminous body as on a necessary condition: therefore primitive light depends on the most agitated motion of the subtle parts of the luminous body only as on a condition, not as on its formal reason. I deny the whole argument: since nothing whatever except a tremor is communicated to a sounding body while it is struck and gives forth a sound, therefore, with none of the Philosophers objecting, a tremor of this kind is not a condition prerequired for sound, but is sound itself: therefore by the same reason, if, while a body is made luminous, nothing else is excited but motion in its subtler parts, that motion is not a mere condition necessarily required for the production of primitive light, but is light itself.

652 Opp. 2. contra 2. non bene probatur ex reflexione luminis, ipsam esse corpus: ergo. Prob. antec. Nam reflexio luminis non est sicut pilae reflexio, nam reflexio dicitur de luce metaphoricè, & impropriè: ergo. Nego antec. probationem: nam ut evincatur, eo modo non resilire lumen, quemadmodum requiritur, ut corpus idcirco dicatur, satis non est ostendere ipsum, non sicut pilam ex speculo reflecti. Etenim neque sonus resilit ut pila, quum fit Echo, & tamen corporeae sunt aereae illae particulae in quarum tremore

652 Obj. 2 against the 2nd: it is not well proved from the reflection of light that it is a body: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: for the reflection of light is not like the reflection of a ball, since reflection is said of light metaphorically and improperly: therefore. I deny the proof of the antecedent: for in order to prove that light does not rebound in the way that is required for it therefore to be called a body, it is not enough to show that it is not reflected from a mirror like a ball. For neither does sound rebound like a ball when an Echo occurs, and yet those aerial particles in whose tremor

Princip. Philosoph. Mathem. Lib. 1. Schol. ad prop. 96, nec non Optic. Lib. 2. Prop. 11.

Princip. Philosoph. Mathem., bk. 1, Schol. to prop. 96, and also Optic., bk. 2, prop. 11.

Elem. Phys. §. 2155 [?].

Elem. Phys. §. 2155.

Comment. in Exp. Acad. del Cimento Part. 2. p. 184 [?].

Comment. in Exp. Acad. del Cimento, pt. 2, p. 184.

p. 206

consistit sonus[?], etiam juxta Peripateticos, corporeae sunt, & certum est ideo[?] reflecti sonum[?], quia corporeae sunt illae particulae[?]: ergo & lumen non metaphoricè, sed verè, & propriè reflectitur, quamvis non ut pila â pariete resiliat.

sound consists, even according to the Peripatetics, are corporeal, and it is certain that sound is reflected because those particles are corporeal: therefore light too is reflected not metaphorically, but truly and properly, even though it does not rebound like a ball from a wall.

653 Opp. 3. Luminis particulae sunt tenuissimae: ergo non possunt [?] resistentiam[?], ut reflecti, & refringi possint: [?] lux [?] in [?]: ergo refractio de luce dicitur tantùm[?] metaphoricè. Nego conseq.[?] [?] tenuitas[?] particularum luminis[?] [?] motu [?] & reflecti[?] [?] quàm à lucido corpore impelluntur[?] [?]. Quum enim[?] illae particulae sint corporeae, [?] nemo non videt in iis esse posse texturam, in qua corporum [?] posita est, & ex qua [?] dependet.

653 Obj. 3: the particles of light are most tenuous: therefore they cannot meet with [such resistance] that they can be reflected and refracted: for since light […] in […]: therefore refraction is said of light only metaphorically. I deny the consequence. For just as […] the tenuity of the particles of light, and […] by motion […], since among them they can […] and be reflected, since […] than they are impelled by the luminous body […]. For since those particles are corporeal, […] no one fails to see that there can be in them the texture in which the […] of bodies is placed, and on which their […] depends.

654 Opp. 4. Corpora quae refringuntur ex raro in densum medium transeuntia[?], recedunt â perpendiculari, quoniam eorum motus ex duobus componitur, ex perpendiculari scilicet[?], qui â gravitate oritur[?], & ex horizontali extrinsecus impresso; sed lux non ita refringitur, quum[?] ad perpendicularem accedat: ergo non est corpus. Nego conseq.[?] Nam quamvis globus plumbeus ex. gr.[?] ita refringatur[?] in transitu ex aëre in aquam, quia corpus est, non rectè inde infertur[?], lumen ideo non esse corpus, quia non eodem modo, quo plumbeus globulus, refringitur[?]; sed dicendum est, lucem non in eamdem partem refringi[?], ac globum illum, non quia ille globus est corpus, sed quia lux refringitur non cum recessu, sed cum accessu ad perpendicularem, sive ob rationem allatam jam â nobis [§. 3[?]], sive quia fortius ab aqua quam ab aëre attrahatur, ut Cl. Newtonus censuit. Ut ergo evincant Peripatetici non bene â Recentioribus probari luminis corporeitatem ex ipsius refractione, demonstrare deberent[?] eam solam[?] refractionem ex corporeitate oriri, quae in transitu ex medio rariori in densius cum recessu â perpendiculari perficitur.

654 Obj. 4: bodies which are refracted in passing from a rare medium into a dense one recede from the perpendicular, because their motion is compounded of two, namely of the perpendicular one, which arises from gravity, and of a horizontal one impressed from without; but light is not so refracted, since it approaches the perpendicular: therefore it is not a body. I deny the consequence. For although a leaden ball, for example, is refracted in this way in passing from air into water because it is a body, it is not rightly inferred from this that light is not a body because it is not refracted in the same way as a leaden ball; but it must be said that light is not refracted toward the same side as that ball, not because the ball is a body, but because light is refracted not with a recession from, but with an approach to, the perpendicular, either for the reason already brought forward by us [§. 3…], or because it is attracted more strongly by water than by air, as the most distinguished Newton held. In order, then, to prove that the corporeality of light is not well proved by the Moderns from its refraction, the Peripatetics ought to demonstrate that only such a refraction arises from corporeality as is performed, in the passage from a rarer medium into a denser one, with a recession from the perpendicular.

655 Neque valet dicere, lumen non refringi ex se, sed ratione subjecti, aëris scilicet[?] in quo producitur. Primò etenim explicare Peripatetici deberent, quamobrem aër illuminatus, licet sit corpus, non tamen ut corpora solida, nempe[?] cum recessu â perpendiculari, dum aquam subire cogitur, refringatur. 2. Danda ab eis causa est, cur aër lumine perfusus vitrum possit subire[?], non possit lumine carens[?]: ergo stat[?] â Recentioribus firmissimè[?] corporeitatem luminis ex illius reflexione, & refractione contra Peripateticos demonstrari.

655 Nor does it avail to say that light is not refracted of itself, but by reason of its subject, namely the air in which it is produced. For, first, the Peripatetics ought now to explain why illuminated air, although it is a body, is nevertheless not refracted as solid bodies are, namely with a recession from the perpendicular, while it is forced to enter water. 2. They must give the cause why air suffused with light can enter glass, while air lacking light cannot. It stands, then, that the corporeality of light is most firmly demonstrated by the Moderns against the Peripatetics from its reflection and refraction.

656 Opp. 5. Lux compenetratur[?] cum toto corpore diaphano; sed corpora nequeunt naturaliter compenetrari[?]: ergo lux non est substantia

656 Obj. 5: light is compenetrated with the whole diaphanous body; but bodies cannot be naturally compenetrated: therefore light is not a corporeal substance. Dist.

p. 207

corporea. Dist. maj.[?] [?]

I distinguish the major: it is compenetrated in such a way that it truly enters and passes through the solid particles of that body, I deny the major; inasmuch as it enters its pores and runs freely through them, I grant the major, and I deny the consequence: for the pores with which a diaphanous body abounds are set in a straight line and communicate with one another, so that light is diffused through them in such a way that it passes through the body itself and runs freely beyond it. The whole body, moreover, seems to be occupied by light, that is, there seems to be no part at all in it which is not suffused with light, because the pores of that body are not only innumerable, but also so close to one another that we ourselves can discern no interval whatever between them. And just as […] it does not follow that glass is compenetrated with water, so must it be said of light […] illuminating the glass.

657 Inst.[?] [?]

657 Inst.: those parts of the glass which exist between the pores are either opaque or diaphanous. Not the first, because then the whole glass would be opaque, since the pores are not glass but empty spaces, which are nothing. But if those parts are diaphanous, they are then receptive of light: therefore light is received not only in the pores of the glass, but also in the very body of the glass. I reply that those parts are opaque, and I deny that it will therefore come about that the whole glass is opaque. For although the pores are nothing but empty spaces, yet if they are so disposed as to be set in a straight line and to communicate with one another, they constitute a diaphanous body, although they do not constitute the light which falls into it, but make the free passage of the rays. The Peripatetics themselves […] two bodies […]. A body, then, is porous, and is rightly called a body, although its pores are not a body but the empty spaces of a body, which are nothing: therefore by the same reason a body is rightly called diaphanous, although the pores, from whose right disposition its diaphaneity is derived, are not a body.

658 [?]

658 Moreover, although the particles which bound the pores of a body are entirely solid and the pores are not a body, the Peripatetics do not on that account infer that the body is altogether solid: therefore by the same reason a body can be diaphanous although those particles of it are not diaphanous, but opaque. […] it is necessary that the particles be solid from whose position and mutual adhesion we call a body solid […]. A body, then, can truly be, and be called, fluid, although the particles which constitute it are solid: therefore it can also be, and be called, a diaphanous body, although the particles of which it is composed are opaque; and just as from this alone, that the component particles of a body are solid, it cannot be inferred that the whole body is solid, so from this alone, that the particles of which a body is made up are opaque, it is not rightly deduced that it is opaque.

659 [?]

659 You will say: these reasons have no weight, since it is certain that no body is wholly porous, that none can […]

p. 208

[?]

[…] be called, just as on the contrary the whole body is called diaphanous […]. But against this: for it is asserted gratuitously and without foundation that the whole glass is diaphanous. For since, as every new experiment plainly demonstrates, […] light […] innumerable […] it is evident that light does not so pervade the whole glass that nothing […] to which light denies passage.

660 [?]

660 You will say: the whole glass is denominated luminous, just as the whole […] is said to receive light, which is by no means affirmed of a sieve pierced with very small holes, whose parts are not diaphanous, but receive light only through the holes. But I reply very easily: the whole glass is called luminous because both its pores, through which light passes, and the very particles which bound them and […] reflect it, are of so small a magnitude that they altogether escape the senses. But in a sieve the matter stands the other way. For however many the holes may be which […] light in it, and give it passage, they are nevertheless far […], just as also the parts in it […] by which the incident rays of light are sent back to us.

661 [?] s1 [?]

661 Obj. 6: if what has been said were true, light, being a most subtle substance, […] through the pores […] of the substance would fly away and vanish; but light […]: therefore light is not a most subtle substance. […] since […] is let in only through the pores […] water […] with a varied and diverse motion […] is refraction. For from this, that light is constantly propagated along a straight line, […] passes through the pores […] in the bodies […] in a straight line […] communicate […]. And this reply is that of […] Newton (m), […]

662 [?]

662 To the second it is said that […] because the motion […] is varied and diverse, […] since […] in the same straight line […] communicated […]. And although water also is agitated with a varied and diverse motion […] the Peripatetics […] in which its diaphaneity consists […] nothing hinders […] in a most subtle substance affected with a rectilinear motion […].

Lib. [?] quaest. [?]

Bk. 2, […] quaest. […].

p. 209

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De Luminis reflexione[?], & refractione[?].

On the reflection and refraction of light.

663 R[?]

he reflection of light is its going back from the surface of the opaque body 663 Ton which it falls. Thus light is said to be reflected when it goes back from the surface of a mirror toward the opposite side. The incident ray of light is the straight line along which light is propagated in falling; the reflected ray, on the other hand, is the straight line along which it is propagated in being reflected: so that, if light falls on the surface A B (Fig. LXV.) along the straight line a b, and rebounds along the straight line b d, the straight line a b will be the direct ray of light, and the straight line b d the reflected ray. Recall to memory what we said when we spoke of the reflection of motion.

664 [?]

664 A ray of light falling on the polished surface of an opaque body is reflected by this constant law, that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. For it is most evidently established that light let in through a very small hole of a darkened room, if it is received on the polished surface of a mirror, always rebounds from it in such a way that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence; and this proposition is so certain that it is assumed as an axiom in Catoptrics by common consent. Light falling obliquely on the polished surface of an opaque body makes the angles of inclination of the direct and the reflected ray equal. So, if light falls from the radiant point a (same Fig.) on the point b, and rebounds to d, then, the perpendicular z b being erected, the angles a b z and d b z will be equal. For since the angles z b A and z b B are equal, being right angles, the angles of reflection and incidence, a b A and d b B, cannot be equal unless the angles of inclination a b z and d b z are also equal.

665 [?]

665 Light itself is reflected […], keeping after reflection the [celerity] with which it fell. For if it were otherwise, the angle of reflection would not be equal to the angle of incidence. Nor does the heat which is communicated by the incident light to the bodies from which it is reflected stand in the way. For since those bodies are heated more which […] a greater quantity of light, […] the heat arises not from that part of the light which is reflected, but from the other part which is refracted, it is also easily understood that […] the reflected light is propagated not with a different [celerity], and that hence, in a perfect reflection of light, the angles of incidence and of reflection are equal to each other.

666 [?]

666 The refraction of light is the departure and deflection of a luminous ray, passing through different

p. 210

diversa media transeuntis, à directione quam habuerat abscessio detorsioque[?]. Haec deviatio locum non habet ubi radius ad perpendiculum illabitur, verùm requiritur obliquitas incidentiae. Recólere juvat, quae de refractione motùs à nobis dicta sunt. Principium universale refractionis radiorum luminis hujusmodi est: Lumen obliquè transiens ex medio rariore in densius, ex aëre nempè in aquam, vel vitrum, refringitur accedendo ad perpendicularem: at ex medio densiore in rarius, ex vitro nimirum, aut aqua in aërem commeans, refringitur à perpendiculari linea recedendo.

media, from the direction which it had. This deviation has no place where the ray falls along the perpendicular; rather, obliquity of incidence is required. It is helpful to recall what we have said of the refraction of motion. The universal principle of the refraction of the rays of light is this: Light passing obliquely from a rarer medium into a denser one, namely from air into water or glass, is refracted by approaching the perpendicular: but passing from a denser medium into a rarer one, namely from glass or water into air, it is refracted by receding from the perpendicular line.

667 Prob. prima pars. Esto vas vitreum plani fundi D F H E (Fig. LXVI) opacâ laminâ tenuissimè in B perforata coopertum. Fiat ut luminis radius A B per foramen B vas ipsum subeat. Compertum experientiâ est, dùm vas solo repletur aëre, radium A B rectâ prógredi in b, contra verò pergere in a, si eodem penitùs manente vasis situ, vas ipsum aqua repleatur. Igitur ad perpendicularem B e accedit radiùs A B dum ab aëre in aquam obliquè transit. Quod ad secundam partem spectat, vulgatissima res est, nummum A (Fig. LXVII.) positum in fundo vasis C A B videri ex loco a si vas aqua repleatur, conspici vero eodem ex loco non posse si solo aëre vas ipsum plenum fuerit. Radius ergo A B erumpens è vase aquâ pleno, declinat à recto tramite ac proindè refringitur recedendo à perpendiculari B E dum ab aqua in aërem transit: ergo lumen &c.

667 Proof of the first part. Let there be a glass vessel with a flat bottom D F H E (Fig. LXVI), covered with an opaque plate very finely perforated at B. Let a ray of light A B enter the vessel itself through the hole B. It is ascertained by experience that, while the vessel is filled with air alone, the ray A B proceeds straight to b, but on the contrary goes on to a if, the position of the vessel remaining entirely the same, the vessel itself is filled with water. Therefore the ray A B approaches the perpendicular B e while it passes obliquely from air into water.
