As to the second part, the matter is very well known: a coin A (Fig. LXVII.) placed on the bottom of the vessel C A B is seen from the spot a if the vessel is filled with water, but cannot be seen from the same spot if the vessel itself is full of air alone. The ray A B, therefore, breaking out of the vessel full of water, turns aside from the straight path and is therefore refracted by receding from the perpendicular B E while it passes from water into air: therefore light, etc.

668 Sed animadversione dignum est, quod licet verissimum sit, lumen hac ratione refringi, dum ex aëre in aquam aut vitrum, & vicissim dum ex aqua, aut vitro in aërem obliquè transit: non propterea verum est, quod vulgò dici solet, nempe universaliter refringi lumen, accedendo, ad perpendicularem, vel ab ea recedendo, dum ex uno medio in aliud diversae densitatis obliquè progreditur; neque est universaliter verum, refringi lumen accedendo ad perpendicularem, dum transit obliquè ex quocumque medio rariore in quodcumque densius: contra verò frangi recedendo a perpendiculari, dum ex quocumque medio densiore in quodcumque rarius itidèm obliquè transit: contrarium enim observavit certoque deprehendit solertissimus S Gravesandus s1.

668 But it is worth noting that, although it is most true that light is refracted in this way while it passes obliquely from air into water or glass, and conversely from water or glass into air, it is not therefore true, as is commonly said, that light is universally refracted by approaching the perpendicular, or by receding from it, while it proceeds obliquely from one medium into another of different density; nor is it universally true that light is refracted by approaching the perpendicular whenever it passes obliquely from any rarer medium into any denser one, or on the contrary is refracted by receding from the perpendicular whenever it likewise passes obliquely from any denser medium into any rarer one: for the most ingenious ’s Gravesande observed and certainly detected the contrary (n).

669 Observavit namque lumen nullam prorsùs refractionem pati, sed transire tramite recto, ex oleo olivarum in boracem, & ex borace in oleum olivarum licet hujusmodi corpora densitate differant. Densitas siquidem olei olivarum est ad densitatem bóracis, ut 6 ad 2. Lumen refringi perpendicularem versùs in transitu ex alumine in vitriolum Gedanense[?] quamvis eadem planè sit horum corporum densitas. Lumen refringi accedendo itidèm ad perpendicularem in transitu ex aqua in spiritum Terebinthinae, adeòque ex medio densiore in rarius. Est enim densitas aquae ad densitatem spiritus Terebinthinae ut 8 ad 7.

669 For he observed that light suffers no refraction at all, but passes in a straight path, from olive oil into borax, and from borax into olive oil, although bodies of this kind differ in density. For the density of olive oil is to the density of borax as 6 to 2. That light is refracted toward the perpendicular in the passage from alum into Danzig vitriol, although the density of these bodies is entirely the same. That light is likewise refracted by approaching the perpendicular in the passage from water into spirit of turpentine, and hence from a denser medium into a rarer one. For the density of water is to the density of spirit of turpentine as 8 to 7.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

Nonnulla ad Opticam, Catoptricam, & Dioptricam spectantia quam brevissimè exponuntur.

Some things pertaining to Optics, Catoptrics and Dioptrics are set forth as briefly as possible.

670 Complura hunc in locum referenda forent instrumenta, quae vel utilitate sua, vel jucunditate spectaculi, quod praebent, sese commendant: adtamen, quia; per angustias temporis, diffusioribus exindè nobis esse haud licet, iccircò admonitione hac, uti nostrum isthaec persequendi desiderium exprimimus, ita, quod jure debemus, tempus causamur. Quaedam igitur delibabimus duntaxat.

ery many instruments ought to be brought into this place which com670 V mend themselves either by their usefulness or by the pleasure of the spectacle they afford; nevertheless, since the narrowness of time does not allow us to be more expansive about them, by this notice, just as we express our desire to go through these things, so too, as we rightly ought, we plead the lack of time. We shall therefore merely touch on some of them.

671 Optica, est scientia visionis directae, sive scientia Physico-Mathematica qua docemur, quo mechanismo objecta quae ex omnibus punctis radios lucis ad oculum mittunt, à nobis videantur. Catoptrica est scientia visionis reflexae. Principium universale reflexionis radiorum ex superficiebus politis, minime diversum est à lege illa, quam cetera corpora in reflexione servant, scilicèt ut angulus reflexionis sit angulo incidentiae aequalis. Porrò superficies ejusmodi, in quibus regularis isthaec luminis reflexio deprehenditur, Specula adpellantur. Dividuntur autèm specula potissimùm in plana, convexa, & concava: planum vocatur quod plana, convexum, quod convexa; concavum, quod concava superficie terminatur.

671 Optics is the science of direct vision, or the Physico-Mathematical science by which we are taught by what mechanism objects which send rays of light from all their points to the eye are seen by us. Catoptrics is the science of reflected vision. The universal principle of the reflection of rays from polished surfaces is not at all different from the law which other bodies keep in reflection, namely that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. Further, surfaces of this kind, in which this regular reflection of light is detected, are called mirrors. Mirrors, moreover, are divided chiefly into plane, convex and concave: that is called plane which is bounded by a plane surface, convex that which is bounded by a convex one, concave that which is bounded by a concave one.

672 Ut aequalitas angulorum incidentiae, ac reflexionis in speculis seu concavis, sive convexis innotescat, ducenda est per punctum in quod radius luminosus incidit, recta linea tangens superficiem curvam. Hujusmodi est (Fig. LXVIII., & LXIX.) linea F C ducta per punctum D, in quod radius directus I D, perpendiculariter illapsus, in se ipsum reddit: radius verò A D obliquè in idem punctum incidens sic reflectitur in E, ut angulus incidentiae C D A aequetur angulo reflexionis F D E. Idem de ceteris radis intelligendum est.

672 In order that the equality of the angles of incidence and of reflection in mirrors, whether concave or convex, may become known, a straight line tangent to the curved surface must be drawn through the point on which the luminous ray falls. Such (Fig. LXVIII. and LXIX.) is the line F C drawn through the point D, on which the direct ray I D, falling perpendicularly, returns into itself; but the ray A D, falling obliquely on the same point, is so reflected to E that the angle of incidence C D A equals the angle of reflection F D E. The same is to be understood of the other rays.

673 Dioptrica est scientia visionis refractae, quae radiorum luminosorum flexionem in vitris praecipuè considerat. Dispesci verò adsolent vitra in classes varias, à diversâ eorumdem figura discretas. Vitrum planum superficiebus planis inter se parallelis terminatur. Lens est vitrum formae lenticularis: haec alia est convexo-convexa, quae nempè convexâ sphaericâ superficie duplici comprehenditur, alia plano-convexa, quae una superficie planâ, altera convexâ definitur. Vitrum concavo-concavum est, cujus utraque superficies

673 Dioptrics is the science of refracted vision, which considers chiefly the bending of luminous rays in glasses. Glasses, moreover, are usually divided into various classes, distinguished by their different figure. A plane glass is bounded by plane surfaces parallel to each other. A lens is a glass of lenticular form: one is convexo-convex, namely that which is enclosed by a double convex spherical surface; another plano-convex, which is bounded by one plane surface and the other convex. A concavo-concave glass is that each of whose surfaces shows a cavity;

p. 212

cavitatem [?]

a plano-concave one, one of whose surfaces is plane, while the other presents a cavity. Finally, a glass concave on one side and convex on the other is called a meniscus.

674 [?]

674 It is the task of Dioptrics to contemplate all these things distinctly, to examine the properties of the different media, and to form from glasses, having obtained either a convex or a concave form, telescopes, microscopes and spectacles, by all of which our sight is wonderfully helped, whether for the viewing of remote things, or for detecting the more minute secrets of nature, or for discerning more easily and better any new bodies whatever. We shall touch on a few things.

675 [?] s1 [?]

675 Glasses, or spectacles, for the eyes are most useful to the myopic, or those who […] see distant things confusedly; for since, owing to the too convex conformation of the eye, […] they need light with diverging rays, they therefore use concave glasses, which render parallel rays diverging: on the contrary, to presbyopes, or those who see distant things more clearly and distinctly and near things confusedly, convex glasses are of great help: for the rays from […] near objects […] are fixed in their […]; for which reason they fittingly use glasses of this kind, which gather the rays, or at least promote their convergence. The distinguished Redi (o) affirms that the [invention] of these spectacles is owed to Alessandro della Spina, and […] about the year […].

676 [?]

676 Further, from the combination of both kinds of glass the Telescope came forth, its author being (as seems to most) Zacharias Jansen, toward the end of the sixteenth century. It was constructed on this plan: that a convex glass should be turned toward the objects and a concave one toward the eye […]. This telescope is also called the Galilean, because […] for observing the phenomena of the heavens by Galileo. […] first perfected this instrument […]; the Astronomical telescope derived its origin from the same source, consisting of two glasses convex on both sides; but since it seemed somewhat inconvenient that […] the object […] inverted, […] added two further glasses, which should set upright what the former had inverted; and then, for viewing terrestrial objects, a telescope […] with four convex glasses […].

677 [?] s2 [?]

677 Finally, from glasses which swell out with a convex surface […], since they enlarge the images of minute objects, microscopes, or engyscopes, are constructed by the fit composition of various glasses […]. The first of those who […] this instrument is said to be, as Musschenbroek (p) [relates], Francesco Stelluti, who in the year […] published a description of the parts of the […] which he discovered with this aid. Then followed Power, Hooke, Grew,

Grew, [?]

Malpighi, Leeuwenhoek, Bonanni, Hartsoeker, Joblot, Réaumur and very many others, who have shown, as it were, a new world of minute things. A microscope consisting of only one lens is called simple; one of several is called compound, whose inventor is said to be Cornelis Drebbel, in the year […], as Huygens relates in his Dioptrics.

678 [?] s1 [?]

678 James Gregory in the year 1663 invented and described a catadioptric telescope composed of lenses and mirrors. A few years afterwards the most distinguished Newton (q) published a catadioptric telescope of a somewhat different structure, very well suited to celestial observations, called Newtonian from the name of its author, just as the former was named Gregorian. Both, however, at length, after an interval of some years, […] namely John Hadley brought them to perfection.

679 [?]

679 From the combination of a lens and a mirror the Polemoscope was likewise made: namely an instrument by whose aid one can view objects while looking in another direction. Its chief part is a plane mirror […] inclined, from which the image of the object is sent back toward the eye of the beholder, since he himself cannot have it along a straight line. In this way it will be possible to observe without danger the movements of the enemy, […] behind the defenses of bulwarks, […] and to […] who […], etc.

680 [?]

680 Here too belongs the camera obscura, which represents on a flat ground external objects expressed in their own colors, so that they can conveniently be drawn. The Magic Lantern, too, is reckoned among these instruments, in which, by the aid of a concave mirror, minute things are enlarged to […] form.

681 [?] s2 [?] s3 [?]

Lieberkühn, Academician of Berlin, to which the name solar microscope […] differs from the magic lantern […] in a darkened room […] the rays of the sun […] glasses […]. But […] with P. Para [du Phanjas], who most recently published in French a very clear Physics under this title: Théorie des Êtres sensibles, ou Cours complet de Physique, à Paris 1772, from which we have excerpted a great many things.

DISSERTATIO V. — DISSERTATION V

De Qualitatibus insensibilibus.

On insensible Qualities.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De Sympathia, Antipathia, Idiosyncrasia, & Antiperístasi.

On Sympathy, Antipathy, Idiosyncrasy and Antiperistasis.

682 Qualitates insensibiles, sive occultae vocantur illae, quae non agunt ipsae immediatè in sensus nostros, sed ex effectibus, & ratione cognoscuntur, quibus tamen immeritò occultarum nomen tribui existimant Recentiores Philosophi, qui rectam philosophandi rationem insequuntur, nec abstractis pèrperam vocibus, quibus summoperè Peripatetici delectantur, facultatis nempè, aut qualitatis, aut formae aliisque similibus contenti sunt, verùm causas inquirunt rerum, quas non oculis quidem, sed animo complecti licet. Inter hujusmodi qualitates recensentur Sympathia, Antipathia, & aliae omnes supra memoratae, de quibus hoc loco acturi sumus.

hose qualities are called insensible, or occult, which do not themselves act 682 T immediately on our senses, but are known from their effects and by reason; the name of occult, however, is held to be undeservedly given to them by the Modern Philosophers, who follow the right method of philosophizing and are not content with abstract words wrongly used, in which the Peripatetics delight exceedingly, namely faculty, or quality, or form, and others like them, but they inquire into the causes of things, which can be grasped not indeed with the eyes, but with the mind. Among qualities of this kind are reckoned Sympathy, Antipathy and all the others mentioned above, of which we are to treat in this place.

683 Simpathia autem dicitur illa rerum consensio, quá fit, ut una adfectâ, sentiente, motâ, patiente, adficiatur, sentiat, moveatur, patiatur etiam altera. Quo pariter refertur amicitia quaedam aut potius cônvenientia inter homines, & amor quidam naturalis. Antipathiam ex adverso vocant repugnantiam, & quandam velut inimicitiam inter res, ita, ut una alteram respuat, & aversetur Idiosyncrasiam dicunt quando vel res innoxias, imò salutares aversamur, & ferre non possumus, vel res noxias, & adversas ceteròqui adpetimus, facilèque toleramus. Antiperistasis deffinitur in Scholis resistentia unius corporis adversus corpus contrariu à quo circumquaque obsidetur, invalescentis, & intensio qualitatis propter qualitatem contrariam.

683 Sympathy, then, is the name for that agreement of things by which it comes about that, when one is affected, feels, is moved or suffers, the other too is affected, feels, is moved and suffers. To this likewise is referred a certain friendship, or rather fitness, between men, and a certain natural love. Antipathy, on the contrary, is the name they give to a repugnance and, as it were, a certain enmity between things, such that one rejects and turns away from the other. They speak of idiosyncrasy when we either turn away from harmless, nay salutary, things and cannot bear them, or seek and easily tolerate things harmful and otherwise adverse. Antiperistasis is defined in the Schools as the resistance of one body against a contrary body by which it is besieged on every side, growing in strength, and the intensification of a quality on account of the contrary quality.

684 Qualitatum harum explanatio Physicis Recentioribus tam recondita haud videtur, ut si ad omnes quae circumstant, conditiones animum maturè ac circunspecto judicio advertamus, eae ex genuinis, claris, verisque principiis exponi non possint, advertendo tamen, dandam esse operam, ut de re ipsa certiores facti, illud in primis adcuratè inquiramus, num quidquid narratur, ita re vera, sub iis circunstantiis & conditionibus se habeat. Plurimae enim sublestae fidei observationes, & fabulae hic se ingerunt, plurimaque

684 The explanation of these qualities does not seem so recondite to the Modern Physicists that, if we turn our mind with mature and circumspect judgment to all the attendant conditions, they cannot be set forth from genuine, clear and true principles; observing, however, that care must be taken that, in order to be made more certain of the thing itself, we first of all inquire accurately whether whatever is narrated is really so under those circumstances and conditions. For very many observations of doubtful credit, and fables, intrude themselves here, and very many things are narrated

p. 215

narrantur quae si experientiam consulamus, & adcuratissimè omnia pervestigemus, vel prorsùs non ita se habere, pro certo comperiemus, vel eo quo perhibentur modo, nunquam contingere. Hoc animadverso.

which, if we consult experience and investigate everything most accurately, we shall find for certain either not to be so at all, or never to happen in the way in which they are reported. This having been noted,

685 Dico primo: Sympathia, Antipathia, Idiosyncrasia, & Antiperistasis, profluviis substantialibus, & motui, quieti, figurae, situi partium, aliisque mechanicis adfectionibus, item consuetudini, moribus, temperamento, aut imaginationi rectè tribuuntur. Prob. per partes. Primò effectus sympathicos ex dictis principiis quámclarissimè exponendo. Sic ex. gr. pulvis ex vitriolo calcinato, qui sympathicus dicitur, injectusque in sanguinem recens emissum è vulnere, fluxum hujus sistere, & vulneri, mederi deprehenditur: non aliter hunc effectum praestare concipietur, quàm per vitrioli corpuscula, quae calentibus adhùc sanguinis particulis admixta, & cum iisdem in fermentationem concitata, ad vulnus unde expressus est sanguis, feruntur (non secùs, ac transpiratio contingit) & quidem tanquam cunei apertos meatus, quibus sanguis profluit, penitùs obstruunt.

685 I say first: Sympathy, Antipathy, Idiosyncrasy and Antiperistasis are rightly attributed to substantial outflows, and to the motion, rest, figure and situation of the parts, and to other mechanical affections; likewise to custom, to manners, to temperament, or to imagination. Proof, part by part. First, by explaining sympathetic effects most clearly from the said principles. Thus, for example, the powder from calcined vitriol which is called sympathetic, and which, when thrown into blood freshly let out of a wound, is found to stop its flow and to heal the wound, will be conceived to produce this effect in no other way than through the corpuscles of the vitriol, which, mixed with the still warm particles of the blood and set into fermentation together with them, are carried to the wound from which the blood was pressed out (just as transpiration takes place), and indeed, like wedges, entirely block up the open passages through which the blood flows forth.

686 Effectuum id genus aliorum item in hominibus, & animalibus ratio redditur ex conclusione nostra. Sic quod oscitante uno, oscitet alter, cane uno latrante, latret & alter, canentibus aviculis aliis. incitentur aliae ad modulandum, ex eo est, quod homines, & animalia quae idoneam habent corporis dispositionem ad ea facilè excitentur, quae ab aliis geruntur, excitatis quippè certis ideis, conspirant corporis membra, facilèque motibus secundum certam ideam determinatis incitantur. Multum quoque ad effectus sympathicos confert vis consuetudinis, quando per eam peculiaris dispositiò & habilitas corporibus inducitur. Denique propensio unius hominis erga alium enascitur ex morum in primis convenientia, temperamenti congruentia, ex elegantiis item in sermone, corpore, vita, moribusque. Ista quippè amorem próvocant, & conciliant, tacitisque velut vinculis adstringunt. Effectus antipathici oppositam suo modo causam habent. Sic aversionis inter homines causae facilè sunt detegendae: etenim in vultu, moribus, vita, sermone, aut actionibus, reperitur semper aliquid, quo unus alteri non potest esse non adversus. Effectus quoque hujusmodi in animalibus congruè ex stabilitis jam principiis ducuntur. Sic agni fugam, praesente lupo; hujus impetum in agnum; gallinarum clangórem praetervolante milvo, à quibusdam impressionibus duci, quis negaverit?

686 The reason of other effects of this kind, likewise in men and animals, is given from our conclusion. Thus, that when one yawns another yawns, that when one dog barks another barks too, that when some little birds sing others are stirred to warble, comes from this, that men and animals which have a fit disposition of body are easily stirred to the things that are done by others: for when certain ideas are excited, the members of the body conspire, and are easily stirred to motions determined according to a certain idea. The force of custom also contributes much to sympathetic effects, when through it a particular disposition and aptitude is induced in bodies. Finally, the inclination of one man toward another arises above all from the agreement of manners, the congruence of temperament, and likewise from elegance in speech, body, life and manners. For these provoke and win love, and bind men as with silent chains. Antipathetic effects have, in their own way, the opposite cause. Thus the causes of aversion between men are easily detected: for in the face, manners, life, speech or actions something is always found by which the one cannot but be averse to the other. Effects of this kind in animals too are fittingly derived from the principles already established. Thus who will deny that the flight of the lamb when the wolf is present, the wolf ’s rush upon the lamb, and the clucking of hens when the kite flies past, are brought about by certain impressions?

687 Ex structura & dispositione partium mira phaenomena herbae mimosae, vel pudicae (vulgò la vergonzosa) manu adpropinquante expallescentis, folia contrahentis, & velut se substrahentis contactui, manumque aversantis, eleganter deduxit Cl. Camerarius s1

687 From the structure and disposition of the parts the distinguished Camerarius (t) has elegantly deduced the wonderful phenomena of the herb mimosa, or pudica (commonly la vergonzosa), which grows pale when a hand approaches, contracts its leaves and, as it were, withdraws itself from contact and shuns the hand,

p. 216

Praeviè[?] scilicet posita anatomia hujuscemodi plantae, animadversa foliorum ex varii generis fibris, utriculis, vasculis, & vésiculis aëre turgidis reticulari compositione, vasculorum succiferorum, & trachearum aequilibrio expenso, rem illustrat: nempè, manu adpropinquante ab emissis calidis halitibus aër in vesiculis contentus rarefit, atque expanditur, hinc vascula succifera aliquo modo comprimuntur, his compressis uberior influxus succi, à quo folia vigorem, & extensionem obtinebant, reprimitur, unde folia expallescunt, flaccida redduntur, & contrahuntur. Manu deindè retractâ, non mirum est, herbae vigorem restitui, quando cessante expansionis, causâ aëris rarefactio à succo per vascula influente superatur.

having, namely, first set out the anatomy of this kind of plant, having noted the reticular composition of the leaves out of fibers, utricles, small vessels and little vesicles swollen with air of various kinds, and having weighed the equilibrium of the sap-bearing vessels and of the tracheae, he illustrates the matter: namely, when a hand approaches, the air contained in the vesicles is rarefied and expanded by the warm exhalations emitted, hence the sap-bearing vessels are in some measure compressed; when these are compressed, the more abundant inflow of the sap, from which the leaves obtained their vigor and extension, is checked, whence the leaves grow pale, become flaccid and contract. When the hand is then withdrawn, it is no wonder that the vigor of the herb is restored, since, the cause of the expansion ceasing, the rarefaction of the air is overcome by the sap flowing in through the vessels.

688 Idiosyncrasiarum ratio potissima in eo est, quod ob singularem organum dispositionem, constitutionem, similitudinem, cùm primis vero fibrarum nervearum, vel teneriorem, molliorem, laxiorem, vel rigidiorem &c. constitutionem, certae impressiones animum adficiant, & prout illae menti, vel gratae sunt, vel adversae, ea variis modis adficiatur, vel placidè, vel ingratè, aut impetuosè: unde communis sensorii & nervorum, qui indè ad partes, & per eas protensi, ac distributi sunt, determinati motus sequuntur. Explicatur proindè cur quidam homines timeant feles, canes, mures, aliaque animalia horreant, abominentur atque ad nomen etiam illorum expallescant, & contremiscant.

688 The chief reason of idiosyncrasies lies in this, that, owing to a singular disposition, constitution and likeness of the organs, and above all a more tender, softer, looser or more rigid etc. constitution of the nervous fibers, certain impressions affect the mind, and according as they are either agreeable or adverse to the mind, it is affected in various ways, either calmly, or unpleasantly, or impetuously; whence there follow determinate motions of the common sensorium and of the nerves which are stretched out and distributed from there to the parts and through them. It is accordingly explained why certain men fear cats, dogs, mice, and shudder at and abominate other animals, and grow pale and tremble even at their name.

689 Si enim infantes rebus ejusmodi à vetulis imperitis terrefacti, & offensi fuerint, (ut saepius contingit non sine magno salutis detrimento, imò etiam vitae periculo), quum fibrae cerebri in infante adhuc tenellae, vehementi impressione fuerint nimis exagitatae, & labefactatae, iccircò per reliquam deinceps vitam reducta, ac denuo exorta simili idea materiali, sive imaginatione, impressio, & agitatio in fibris labefactatis est justò vehementior; in mente verò idea immaterialis ingratissima, & adversa existit. Atque è dictis ferè fundamentis redditur ratio Idiosyncrasiarum haereditariarum, adventitiarum, seu quae post nativitatem vario modo contrahuntur, & consuetudine acquisitarum.

689 For if infants have been frightened and offended by things of this kind by ignorant old women (as happens very often, not without great harm to health, nay even with danger to life), since the fibers of the brain, still tender in the infant, have been too much agitated and weakened by the vehement impression, therefore, through the rest of life thereafter, when a similar material idea, or imagination, is brought back and arises anew, the impression and agitation in the weakened fibers is more vehement than is right; and in the mind an immaterial idea arises that is most disagreeable and adverse. And from the foundations stated, more or less, the reason is given of idiosyncrasies that are hereditary, adventitious, or contracted in various ways after birth, and acquired by custom.

690 Similiter si advertatur ad diversos modos, quibus ab objectis variis organa nostra, & per nervos diffusi spiritus animales adficiuntur, hosque spiritus ope imaginationis tàm in brutis, quàm hominibus celerrimè per totum corpus moveri posse, difficile non erit illos effectus exponere, qui per matris nervos ob vivam imaginationem in tenellum, atque adeò facilè mutabile fetus corpusculum propagantur.

690 Likewise, if attention is paid to the different ways in which our organs, and the animal spirits diffused through the nerves, are affected by various objects, and to the fact that these spirits, by the aid of the imagination, can be moved very swiftly through the whole body, in brutes as well as in men, it will not be difficult to explain those effects which, through the nerves of the mother, on account of a lively imagination, are propagated into the tender, and hence easily changeable, little body of the fetus.

691 Effectus illi, qui Antiperistasi tanquam qualitati occultae tribuuntur à Peripateticis, sine metaphorica illa qualitatum pugna per mechanicas adfectiones explicari non secus possunt, ut quòd loca subterranea aestivo tempore frigidiora sint, quàm hiemali, & profectò experimenta, quae ad occultae hujus qualitatis

691 Those effects which are attributed by the Peripatetics to Antiperistasis as to an occult quality can just as well be explained by mechanical affections, without that metaphorical battle of qualities: as, for instance, that underground places are colder in summer than in winter. And indeed the experiments which, for the proof of this occult quality,

In Diss. peculiar. de herba mimosâ.

In a special dissertation on the herb mimosa.

p. 217

probationem adferuntur, vel ex sensuum fallacia oriuntur, vel insufficientia sunt ad eam qualitatem adstruendam. Siquidem idem locus temperatus pro diversa sensorii constitutione, modò calidus, modò frigidus sensu judice videtur, ut in Logica explanatum à nobis fuit.

are adduced either arise from the deception of the senses or are insufficient to establish that quality. For the same place, though equally tempered, seems to the judgment of sense now hot, now cold, according to the different constitution of the sensorium, as was explained by us in the Logic.

692 Unde quando hieme ex aëre frigidiore sensorio jam frigoris vi occupato, in minus frigidum, qualis est in locis subterraneis (in quibus causis frigorificis minus liber accessus patet) transimus, calidus hic judicatur; contrà verò ubi ex calidiore per aestatem, organo calore jam occupato in minus calidum, qualis est caverna (quae solaribus radiis non illustratur) frigoris sensus nobis obrépere videtur. Sensuum quippè judicium fallax esse circa calorem & frigus, quis non novit?

692 Hence, when in winter we pass from the colder air, the sensorium being already taken over by the force of cold, into a less cold one, such as there is in subterranean places (into which a less free access lies open to the causes producing cold), the place is here judged hot; but contrariwise, when in summer we pass from a hotter place, the organ being already taken over by heat, into a less hot one, such as is a cave (which is not lit by the rays of the sun), a sensation of cold seems to steal over us. For who does not know that the judgment of the senses about heat and cold is deceptive?

693 Diffusius hujus capitis argumenta exsequuntur Verulamius s1, Kircherus. s2 P. de Lanis s3, Schott s4 aliique Recentiores, quos consulere potestis. De Viribus medicamentorum pauca dicamus.

693 The arguments of this chapter are pursued more at length by Bacon (u), Kircher (x), Fr. de Lana (y), Schott (z) and other Moderns, whom you may consult. Let us say a few things about the Powers of medicines.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De Viribus medicamentorum, venenorum, & Alexipharmacorum.

On the Powers of medicines, poisons, and Alexipharmics.

694 Medicamenta in multiplices classes dispescunt Medici, nos aliquas innuemus, hoc potissimum consilio, ut quoad Physicos decet eorum agendi rationem pervestigemus. Evacuantia generatim alia sunt cathartica lenitiva, alia emetica, quae per vomitum purgant, alia diaphoretica, quae per sudorem discutiunt malignitatem, alia diuretica, quae per urinam, errhina, quae per nares, salivantia, quae per salivam corpus perpurgant. Venena alia distinguuntur mineralia, ut arsenicum, vitrum in fragmenta redactum &c.: alia quae constringendo, nimis incrassando, obstruendo, corporis animalis constitutionem perturbant Alexiphármaca demùm dicuntur, quibus venena arcentur, & expelluntur. De his jam similiter inquiritur; ¿ an earum qualitatum agendi ratio inter occultas referri jure possit? Cui quaestioni ut fiat satis.

edicines are divided by Physicians into manifold classes; we shall indi694 M cate some of them, chiefly with this design, that we may investigate their manner of acting so far as befits Physicists. Evacuants, generally speaking, are some cathartic or laxative; others emetic, which purge by vomiting; others diaphoretic, which dispel malignity through sweat; others diuretic, which purge the body through the urine; errhines, through the nostrils; salivants, through the saliva. Poisons are distinguished into some mineral, such as arsenic, glass reduced to fragments, etc.; others, which disturb the constitution of the animal body by constricting, by thickening too much, by obstructing. Alexipharmics, finally, are those by which poisons are warded off and expelled. Concerning these it is now likewise asked whether their manner of acting can rightly be referred among occult qualities. To satisfy this question,

In Hist. Nat.

In Hist. Nat.

Mag. Nat. & Art. vol. 3.

In Magia Univers. & in Mag. Sympath.

In Magia Univers. and in Mag. Sympath.

p. 218

quam subeunt radii solares multò maximam, dum adprimè densam locorum illorum atmosphaeram permeant; quo fit, ut Sol diebus aliquot supra horizontem illorum emicare videatur, quamvis infra eundem deprimatur. Bátavi profectò qui ann. 1597 in nova Zembla hiemarunt, Solem disparuisse ferunt 4 Novembris die, rursum die 24 Jannuarii conspicuum fuisse, ac proindè sex circitèr dierum intervallo calculi Astronomici rationibus antevertisse.

which the solar rays undergo, by far the greatest, while they pass through the exceedingly dense atmosphere of those places; whence it comes about that the Sun seems to shine above their horizon for some days, although it is depressed below it. Indeed the Dutch who wintered in Nova Zembla in the year 1597 report that the Sun disappeared on the 4th day of November and was visible again on the 24th day of January, and so had anticipated the reckonings of astronomical calculation by an interval of about six days.

731 Adhaec: quoniam diuturna illis protrahuntur crepuscula, sic, ut duobus circitèr mensibus Solis ortus ab altero velut occupetur, alterùm verò tandiù perduret à Solis occasu, iccirco nocturna illis calígo nonnisi duos circiter menses tenet. Quin ut observat Wolffius s1 haec duorum mensium caligo temperatur, plusquam dimidio temporis illius spatio, Lunae splendore.

731 Moreover: since long-lasting twilights are drawn out for them, so that for about two months the rising of the Sun is as it were forestalled by the one, while the other lasts so long after the setting of the Sun, therefore the darkness of night holds them for no more than about two months. Nay, as Wolff observes (d), this darkness of two months is tempered, for more than half of that space of time, by the splendor of the Moon.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

Mundi systemata strictim exponuntur.

The systems of the world are briefly set out.

732 Systematis nomine intelligunt hic Philosophi ordinem, sive dispositionem hujus universi, praecipuarumque illius partium, explicandis motibus, ac phaenomenis caelestibus adcommodatam. Tria hactenùs in Scholis, tùm astronomicis, tùm physicis celebrantur systemata, atque etiamnum vigent. Juvat proinde singula strictim persequi.

y the name of system Philosophers here understand the order, or disposi732 B tion, of this universe and of its principal parts, adapted to explaining the motions and the celestial phenomena. Three systems have hitherto been celebrated in the Schools, both astronomical and physical, and they still flourish. It is fitting, therefore, to go through each of them briefly.

733 I. Ptolemaicum sic dictum à Claudio Ptolemaeo. Ejus sistema terrae in universi medio collocatae aërem primùm, tùm ignem circumdare facit, septem deindèt Caelos pro singulis Planetis solidos construit, & mundi circulo concentricos, hoc ordine, ut in 1. hoc est in supremo omnium Saturnus, in 2. Jupiter, in 3. Mars, in 4. Sol, in 5. Venus, in 6. Mercurius, in 7. Luna decurrat: super his demùm Caelis, firmamentum cum stellis fixis locat, quod primum mobile nuncupavit, quoniam ipsius motu inferiorum Planetarum orbes ábripi ab ortu in occasum putavit spatio 23 horarum, 56 minutorum, 4 secundorum.

733 I. The Ptolemaic, so called from Claudius Ptolemy. His system makes first air, then fire, surround the earth, which is placed in the middle of the universe; it then constructs seven solid Heavens, one for each Planet, concentric with the circle of the world, in this order: that in the 1st, that is, in the highest of all, Saturn runs its course, in the 2nd Jupiter, in the 3rd Mars, in the 4th the Sun, in the 5th Venus, in the 6th Mercury, in the 7th the Moon. Above these Heavens, finally, it places the firmament with the fixed stars, which he called the primum mobile, because he thought that by its motion the orbs of the lower Planets are carried from east to west in the space of 23 hours, 56 minutes, 4 seconds.

734 II. Systema Tichonicum à Tichone Brahe constructum Hic relicta terrà pro universi centro, unà cum atmosphaera immobili suprà[?], & circum ipsam primo loco statuit Lunam, deindè Solem, circa hunc verò tanquàm reliquorum Planetarum centrum reposuit Mercurium, Venerem, Martem, tum Jovem cum quatuor Satellitibus à Galilaeo detectis, ac tandem Saturnum cum binis lateronibus,

734 II. The Tychonic system, constructed by Tycho Brahe. This, leaving the earth as the center of the universe, together with the immobile atmosphere, sets the Moon in the first place around it, then the Sun; around this, as the center of the remaining Planets, he placed Mercury, Venus, Mars, then Jupiter with the four Satellites discovered by Galileo, and at length Saturn with its two attendants; finally he

Elem. Geograph. §. 131.

Elem. Geograph. §. 131.

p. 219

denique his omnibus firmamentum, terrae concentricum superaddidit.

he added on top of all these the firmament, concentric with the earth.

735 III. Systema Copernicanum à Nicolao Copernico, post 30 annorum studium, quod illustrandae huic hypothesi impendit, nomen sumpsit. Juxta eum Sol in mundi centro immobilis constituitur: circa quem proximè movetur Mercurius, tùm Venus, deindè Tellurem cum Luna sibi circumgyrante posteà Martem, tùm Jovem, denique Saturnum revolvi arbitratur: ultrà omnes Planetas verò, & quidem ad immensam paenè distantiam ponit Spheram Stellarum fixarum omni penitùs motu destitutam. Planetis singùlis, unico Sole excepto, quem propterea è Planetarum numero expungit, motum periodicum tribuit, nempè sub Zodiaco secundum signorum seriem.

735 III. The Copernican system took its name from Nicolaus Copernicus, after the thirty years’ study which he spent on illustrating this hypothesis. According to it the Sun is set immobile in the center of the world; he holds that around it Mercury moves nearest, then Venus, next the Earth with the Moon circling about it, afterwards Mars, then Jupiter, and finally that Saturn revolves; beyond all the Planets, and indeed at an almost immense distance, he places the Sphere of the fixed Stars, wholly destitute of all motion. To the single Planets, the Sun alone excepted, which he therefore strikes out of the number of the Planets, he assigns a periodic motion, namely under the Zodiac, following the series of the signs.

736 Tellurj triplicem adsignat motum, videlicèt: primum vertiginis circa proprium axem ab Occasu in ortum, quo declarare volunt Copernicani vicissitudinem noctis & diei; siquidem posito hoc motu Sol nobis ab ortu in Occasum gyrari videtur, ac tellus aliam semper faciem illumninandam Soli objectat: motum hunc diurnum vocat, quòd intervallo unius diei perficiatur. Alterum periodicum dicit in orbe magno circa Solem sub ecliptica, quo motu tellus per signa ita progreditur, ut Sol nobis in eo signo, quod tegit, esse videatur, adeoque dum terra est in signis borealibus, ipse nobis in australibus, & contrà, versari adpareat: motum hunc annuum adpellat, qui anni unius spatio absolvitur.

736 To the Earth he assigns a threefold motion, namely: first, that of turning about its own axis from west to east, by which the Copernicans mean to explain the alternation of night and day; for once this motion is supposed, the Sun seems to us to be whirled from east to west, and the earth always presents another face to the Sun to be illuminated: this motion he calls diurnal, because it is completed in the interval of one day. The second he calls periodic, in the great orb around the Sun under the ecliptic, by which motion the earth so advances through the signs that the Sun appears to us to be in the sign which it covers, and hence, while the earth is in the northern signs, the Sun appears to us to dwell in the southern ones, and the reverse: this motion he names annual, as it is completed in the space of one year.

737 Postremum parallelismi motum adstruit, quo axis ipse telluris in sua circa Solem revolutione, tùm axi ipsius mundi, túm sibimetipsi parallelus semper existit: hoc motu phaenomena vicissitudinis in anni tempestatibus evolvunt Copernicani. Adtamen axis terrestris inclinationem talem ad planum eclipticae, ut cum eo conficiat angulum 66 graduum, 30 minutorum, in rei hujus explanationem quoque adsciscunt. „Hac ipsa aetate nostra (ait Cl. Theologus Hyacinthus Serry) s1 „ Viri plerique pietate, ac religione praestantes, nonnulli etiam Purpurâ eminentes cum Gallilaeo, cum Copernico sentire liberè permittuntur, modò certum, indubitatumque Systema non dicant; sed commodum Astronomiae usibus hypothesim faciant, ut ex Decreto S. Congreg. S. Officii anno 1620[?] perspectum est.„ Hactenùs ille. (Fig LXX. oculis subjicit Systema Copernicanum).

737 Lastly he establishes the motion of parallelism, by which the axis of the earth itself, in its revolution around the Sun, always remains parallel both to the axis of the world itself and to itself: by this motion the Copernicans unfold the phenomena of the alternation of the seasons of the year. To explain this matter, moreover, they also adopt such an inclination of the earth’s axis to the plane of the ecliptic that it makes with it an angle of 66 degrees, 30 minutes. “In this very age of ours (says the distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry) (e) very many men eminent in piety and religion, some even distinguished by the Purple, are freely permitted to hold with Galileo and with Copernicus, provided they do not call it a certain and undoubted System, but make it a hypothesis convenient for the uses of Astronomy, as was provided by the Decree of the Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office in the year 1620.” Thus far he. (Fig. LXX sets the Copernican System before your eyes.)

Praelect. Theolog. Tom. 1. Praelect. 1. de Opificio mundi pag. 130 edit. Venet. Ann. 1742.

Praelect. Theolog. vol. 1, Praelect. 1, On the Workmanship of the World, p. 130, Venice edition, year 1742.

p. 220

[?]mis rarefaciendo, aut mixturam illius naturalem dissolvendo, malignam fermentationem in eo excitando, vel nimium adstringendo, partes condensando, vigorem proindè eorum & actiones naturales cohibendo.

rarefying it too much, or dissolving its natural mixture, exciting a malignant fermentation in it, or constricting too much, condensing the parts, and hence restraining their vigor and natural actions.

704 Nappellus nimio calore sanguinem cui admiscetur extenuat, agitat, tenuemque viscerum substantiam exurit; cicuta verò aquatica nimio frigore sanguinis particulas in subtilioribus extremisque venis paulatim sistit, ut ibi veluti congelatus torpeat, tùm quiete ac frigore sensim ad cor accedentibus, sanguinem in ipso corde stagnantem reddit, undè mors consequitur. Omittimus ea quae de basilisco ajunt; scilicet aspectum illius esse mortiferum, de rémora item pisciculo, qui naves remoratur, quae quidem à melioris notae Criticis inter aniles fabulas recensentur. Motus verò qui ex morsu tarantulae (quae est araneae species in Calabria propè Tarentum satis obvia) in quibusdam hominibus excitantur postea explicabimus.

704 Monkshood, by excessive heat, thins and agitates the blood with which it is mixed, and burns up the delicate substance of the viscera; water hemlock, on the other hand, by excessive cold gradually halts the particles of the blood in the finer and extreme veins, so that there it grows torpid as though congealed; then, as these approach the heart little by little with rest and cold, it renders the blood stagnant in the heart itself, whence death follows. We omit what they say of the basilisk, namely that its look is deadly, and likewise of the remora, the little fish that holds ships back, things which indeed are reckoned among old wives’ tales by critics of better note. The motions, however, which are excited in certain men by the bite of the tarantula (which is a species of spider well known in Calabria near Tarentum), we shall explain later.

705 Alexipharmacorum agendi ratio in his posita est, vel quod spicula veneni acri obtundant, & infringant, ut oleosa, vel quod ordinatum motum sanguinis restituant, vel resolvendo partes spissiores, spiritus debiles excitando, ut theriaca &c, vel ob pororum ac partium proportionem mutuam venenata corpuscula in se recipiendo. Sic vulnus à Scorpione (vulgò alacran) inflictum sanatur, si scorpius ipse contritus vulneri statim imponatur, dum venenatae particulae à morsu in manu relictae à particulis homogeneis, quae in contrito scorpionis corpore reperiuntur, tanquam à spongia exsuguntur vel demum antidota vim suam contra singulare aliquod venenum habent sitam in motu, qui sit oppositus motui ipsiusmet veneni.

705 The manner of acting of Alexipharmics consists in this: either that they blunt and break the sharp points of the poison, as oily things do; or that they restore the ordered motion of the blood, by resolving the thicker parts and rousing the weak spirits, as theriac etc. does; or by receiving the poisoned corpuscles into themselves on account of the mutual proportion of the pores and parts. Thus a wound inflicted by a Scorpion (commonly alacrán) is healed if the scorpion itself, crushed, is at once laid on the wound, since the poisonous particles left in the hand by the bite are sucked out, as by a sponge, by the homogeneous particles which are found in the crushed body of the scorpion; or, finally, antidotes have their force against some particular poison placed in a motion which is opposite to the motion of the poison itself.

706 Sic remedium adversus tarantulae morsum efficacissimum, sunt motus ac vibrationes instrumenti musici; sanguine enim per venenum condensato, vasculisque obstructis, adfluxus spirituum animalium impeditur, nervi proindè laxantur; vibrationibus verò harmonicis musicae, agitatur sanguis, spiritus vigorem recipiunt, hi per fibras, & nervos discurrunt, fibrae, nervique ad unisonam cum chordis, vel instrumentis sonoris constitutionem perducti, vibrationes chordarum recipiunt; hinc motus membrorum, ac denique saltus; saltandi contentione agitatio sanguinis augetur, sudorque elicitur, unde venenum etiam adtenuatum, & agitatum, transpiratione sensim dissipatur; pro mensurà autem veneni dissipati aeger melius habet, & haec sanitatis recuperatio ad continuandum saltum incitat, quo fit, ut venenum omne exspiret, sanguis fluorem, & cursum pristinum recipiat.

706 So the most effective remedy against the bite of the tarantula is the motions and vibrations of a musical instrument; for when the blood has been condensed by the poison and the little vessels obstructed, the inflow of the animal spirits is impeded, and the nerves are consequently relaxed; but by the harmonic vibrations of the music the blood is agitated, the spirits receive vigor, these run through the fibers and nerves, and the fibers and nerves, brought to a constitution in unison with the strings or sounding instruments, receive the vibrations of the strings; hence the motion of the limbs, and finally leaping; by the exertion of leaping the agitation of the blood is increased and sweat is drawn out, whence the poison too, thinned and agitated, is gradually dissipated by transpiration; and in proportion as the poison is dissipated the sick man is better, and this recovery of health spurs him on to continue the leaping, whence it comes about that all the poison breathes out and the blood recovers its fluidity and its former course.

707 Neque mirandum est, particularem concentum musicum, ut notat P. Schott. ad curandum quemlibet sic adfectum exposci. Quum enim spiritus animales, fibrae, nervi, particulae venenatae diversam habeant consistentiam, magnitudinem in diversis hominibus, diversa etiam harmonica conformatio requiritur ad commovendos spiritus, fibras, ac nervos, ad venenum proindè dissipandum per agitationem,

707 Nor is it to be wondered at that a particular musical harmony, as Fr. Schott notes, is demanded to cure each person so affected. For since the animal spirits, fibers, nerves and poisonous particles have a different consistency and size in different men, a different harmonic conformation too is required to move the spirits, fibers and nerves, and hence to dissipate the poison by agitation,

p. 221

& saltum. Qui plura de hoc argumento desiderat consulat erudita Recentiorum Medicorum volumina, haec inter gloriam sibi vendicant opera Cl. Hermanni Boerhaave, & ejusdem Commentatoris Illustrissimi D. Vanswieten.

leaping. Whoever desires more on this subject should consult the learned volumes of the more recent Physicians; among these the works of the distinguished Herman Boerhaave, and of his Commentator, the most illustrious Dr. van Swieten, claim glory for themselves.

708 Ex dictis omnibus perspicuum redditur, naturalium rerum cognitionem ad miros effectus explicandos conferre plurimum, multa quae vulgus stupet, pandere; naturae arcana manifestare, & quod caput est, ad Auctoris Naturae cognitionem ducere, quem tota mente venerabundi adoramus.

708 From all that has been said it becomes clear that the knowledge of natural things contributes a great deal to explaining wonderful effects, lays open many things at which the common people are amazed, makes manifest the secrets of nature, and, what is chief, leads to the knowledge of the Author of Nature, whom we adore in reverence with our whole mind.

Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED. 709

709 Opp. 1. contra primam: eadem est partium textura in vivo corpore quam in mortuo, sed pleraque medicamina aut venena vim suam nullomodo exerunt in cadavera: sic cantharides ex. gr. in vivo corpore vesicas excitant, non in mortuo: ergo medicamentorum agendi ratio non congrue deducitur ex partium textura &c. Resp. negando antec. & conseq. cantharides, aut cauteria calore corporis vivi accensae, & humore dilútae, effervescentiam procreant & vivi corporis pellem crispant.

Obj. 1. against the first: the texture of the parts is the same in the living body as in the dead, but most medicines or poisons in no way exert their force on corpses: thus cantharides, e.g., raise blisters on the living body, not on the dead: therefore the manner of acting of medicines is not fittingly deduced from the texture of the parts etc. Reply, by denying the antec. and the conseq.: cantharides, or cauteries, kindled by the heat of the living body and diluted by its moisture, produce an effervescence and wrinkle the skin of the living body.

710 Opp. 2. Nullomodo potest per partium texturam &c. explicari cur cortex Peruvianus qui Quina vulgò dicitur quartanam plerumque aut sanet, aut ad tempus sistat, cur cantharides vesicam ipsam non alia laedunt organa: ergo. Resp. pluribus modis facilè explicari posse, quomodo cortex Peruvianus operetur.

710 Obj. 2. It can in no way be explained by the texture of the parts etc. why the Peruvian bark, which is commonly called Quina, mostly either cures a quartan fever or stops it for a time, or why cantharides injure the bladder itself and not other organs: therefore. Reply: it can easily be explained in several ways how the Peruvian bark operates.

711 Nam 1. pulvis Quinae humorem illum qui quartanam efficit, quiquè viribus suis veneno est simillimus, aut figit, aut illius motum inhibet, aut novam in sanguine fermentationem promovet, aut per occultam sive insensibilem transpirationem virus illud diffiat. Sic cantharidum pulvis quandiu sanguine, & aliis humoribus diluitur, manet innoxius, sed postquam in renibus à sanguinis massâ secretus est, tum vi sua causticâ aut renes ipsos, aut vesicam exulcerat.

711 For 1. the powder of Quina either fixes that humor which causes the quartan, and which in its powers is most like a poison, or checks its motion, or promotes a new fermentation in the blood, or drives out that venom through an occult, or insensible, transpiration. So the powder of cantharides, as long as it is diluted with the blood and the other humors, remains harmless; but after it has been secreted from the mass of the blood in the kidneys, by its caustic force it ulcerates either the kidneys themselves or the bladder.

712 Opp. demum: ejusmodi phaenomena, & alia quam plurima commodius explicantur per formas substantiales Peripateticas, quàm per texturam partium, & effluvia substantialia, quum incredibile sit effluvia indesinenter manare à duris & solidis corporibus: ergo. Dist. antec. commodius & adcommodatiùs ad naturam verae Physicae nego & non ita conc. Inclusa antecedentis soluta manet in pluribus locis nostrae Physicae, ubi de effluviis sermonem habuimus. Adhaec: nemo hactenùs negavit pleraque gemmae, tum ipsos adamantes corpora certè durissima vi electricâ pollére, quae citra substantialem effluxum intelligi minimè potest. Quid plura? Ex regulo antimonii parantur vascula, quae vino aut cerevisiae infusae vim emeticam tribuunt, & per multos annos in hunc usum adhibentur citra ponderis sensibilem imminutionem. Sic etiam mercurius paululùm aquae incoctus, vim illi tribuit, qua vermes enecet, ut alia complura omittam.

712 Obj. finally: such phenomena, and very many others, are explained more conveniently by the Peripatetic substantial forms than by the texture of the parts and substantial effluvia, since it is incredible that effluvia should flow unceasingly from hard and solid bodies: therefore. Dist. antec.: more conveniently and more suitably to the nature of true Physics, I deny; not so, I grant. What is included in the antecedent stands answered in several places of our Physics where we spoke of effluvia. Moreover: no one has hitherto denied that most gems, and diamonds themselves, bodies certainly very hard, are powerful in electric force, which can by no means be understood without a substantial efflux. What more? From the regulus of antimony little vessels are made which give an emetic force to wine or beer poured into them, and they are used for this purpose for many years without any sensible diminution of their weight. So too mercury, boiled a little in water, gives it a force by which it kills worms, to omit very many other things.

AND TERRESTRIAL BODIES,

On the Composition of the World.

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

Summaria de adspectabilis Sphaerae mundanae compáge doctrina proponitur.

A summary doctrine of the structure of the visible world-sphere is set forth.

713 Triplex distinguitur artificialis sphera; caelestis una, quae caelum & sidera, terrrestris altera, quae molem terraqueam exhibet, tertia armillaris, sic dicta, quod sit complexum ex variis circulis & armillis globum repraesentans.

hree kinds of artificial sphere are distinguished: one celestial, which dis713 T plays the heaven and the stars; another terrestrial, which displays the terraqueous mass; the third armillary, so called because it is a complex of various circles and rings representing a globe.

714 Spherae hujus, qua velut obtutu constitutio universi, & varietas motuum, quos exigunt corpora mundi praecipua conspiciatur, partes principes sunt. I. Axis, seu linea diametralis, sphaerae centrum transiens, sic, ut circa ipsam volvatur; puncta ejusdem extrema, poli dicuntur. II. Sphaerula in axis meditullio constituta, quae terraquei globi positum adumbret. III. Circuli partim majores, partim minores. Majores sphaeram omnem uti & reliquos circulos majores, in partes geminas aequales secant, suntque hi: Aequator, Meridianus, Horizon, Zodiacus duo Coluri. Minores circuli sphaeram in partes inaequales secant. Hi quatuor habentur: duo Tropici, totidemque polares. Omnes in 360 aequales inter se partes, seu gradus

714 The principal parts of this sphere, in which, as at one glance, the constitution of the universe and the variety of the motions which the chief bodies of the world require are beheld, are: I. The Axis, or diametral line, passing through the center of the sphere in such a way that the sphere turns about it; its extreme points are called the poles. II. A small sphere set in the middle of the axis, which represents the position of the terraqueous globe. III. Circles, partly greater, partly lesser. The greater cut the whole sphere, as also the other greater circles, into two equal parts, and they are these: the Equator, the Meridian, the Horizon, the Zodiac, the two Colures. The lesser circles cut the sphere into unequal parts. Four of these are counted: the two Tropics, and as many polar circles. All are divided into 360 parts equal among themselves, or degrees;

p. 223

dirimuntur; hi rursum in 60 alias, quae minuta nuncúpantur. Spectari adhaec adsolent in sphaerae totius ambitu puncta quaedam, & cardinalia dici. Quorum quidem omnium singillatim notiones distinctè persequimur.

these in turn into 60 others, which are called minutes. Besides, certain points in the circuit of the whole sphere are usually considered and called cardinal. We shall go through the notions of all of these distinctly, one by one.

715 Polus indicat punctum mundani axis circa quod prorsùs immotum machina universi circumagatur. Gemina sunt hujusmodi puncta sive poli, Arcticus unus, qui etiam Borealis & Aquilonius vocatur ob ventum indè spirantem. Alter Antarcticus compellatur, & etiam Meridionalis, sive Australis dicitur. Uterque inter puncta cardinalia principe loco refertur.

715 The Pole indicates the point of the world’s axis around which, itself wholly unmoved, the machine of the universe is turned. There are two such points, or poles: one the Arctic, which is also called Boreal and Aquilonian from the wind that blows from there. The other is called the Antarctic, and is also named Meridional, or Austral. Both are counted in the first place among the cardinal points.

716 Aequator, seu aequinoctialis, aut aequidialis circulus est, in quo dum Sol constituitur, dies nocti aequatur. Anni unius decursu bis in eo Sol versatur, dum principium signi Arietis adtingit circa 20 Martii, & ubi signum Librae ingreditur circa 23 Septembris. Distat aequator ab utroque polo mundi quadrante, sphaeram proindè in partes geminas aequales Borealem, & Australem dispescit. Usus ejus his paenè definitur I. Mundum omnem dividit in hemisphaeria duo nunc dicta. II. Indicat gemina anni aequinoctia; vernum scilicet, atque autumnale. III. Metitur dies, & horas; illius quippè 360 gradus, spatio 24 horarum praeterlabuntur, adeòque singuli 15 gradus, unam horam conficiunt. IV. Terminus est, á quo Solis, Lunae, caeterorumque Astrorum declinationes sumuntur; declinatio siquidem cujusvis sideris, est ejus ab aequatore versùs alterutrum polum distantia, quam arcus circuli per polos mundi, & centrum Astri transiens mensurat. V. Orientis & Occidentis cardines in horizonte definit. VI. Diverso ad horizontem situ efficit, ut rectus, obliquus, parallelus horizon se praebeat.

716 The Equator, or equinoctial or equidial circle, is that in which, while the Sun is placed in it, day is equal to night. In the course of one year the Sun is in it twice: when it touches the beginning of the sign Aries, about the 20th of March, and when it enters the sign Libra, about the 23rd of September. The equator is distant from each pole of the world by a quadrant; it therefore divides the sphere into two equal parts, the Boreal and the Austral. Its use is defined in a manner by these points: I. It divides the whole world into the two hemispheres just named. II. It indicates the two equinoxes of the year, namely the vernal and the autumnal. III. It measures days and hours; for its 360 degrees pass by in the space of 24 hours, and so each 15 degrees make one hour. IV. It is the boundary from which the declinations of the Sun, the Moon and the other Stars are taken; for the declination of any star is its distance from the equator toward one or the other pole, which is measured by the arc of a circle passing through the poles of the world and the center of the Star. V. It defines the cardinal points of East and West on the horizon. VI. By its different position with respect to the horizon it brings it about that the horizon presents itself as right, oblique, or parallel.

717 Horizon describi intelligitur ex puncto verticali, quod Arabicè Zenith, & altero ex adversa parte constituto, quod Nadir, dicitur (utrumque inter cardinalia habentur), sphaeramque in partes aequales secat, superiorem & inferiorem, sic ut planum circuli per mundi centrum transeat. Undè quum puncta haec ex diametro opposita, dum ab alio loco in alium commeamus, quìn relatè ad quemvis hominem, alia sint atque alia, patet horizontem mutari identidèm, eosque totidèm diversos esse, quot puncta in sphaerae superficie cogitari possunt. Atque haec de horizonte Astronomico, vel rationali, sic dicto, quia ab Astrónomis Caeli motus observantibus consideratur, & ratione duntaxat, non sensu percipitur. Etenim alius est horizon sensibilis, vel physicus, quem unusquisque in vasta aliqua planitie, aut in medio, & tranquillo mari constitutus, visu circumacto definit. Quapropter mathematicè loquendo, horizon sensibilis neque circulum reapse maximum conformat, quia per mundi centrum nequaquàm porrigitur, neque proindè in partes aequales Caeli sphaeram secernit, horizonti tamen rationali semper est parallelus.

717 The Horizon is understood to be described from the vertical point, which in Arabic is called Zenith, and from another set on the opposite side, which is called Nadir (both are counted among the cardinal points), and it cuts the sphere into equal parts, the upper and the lower, in such a way that the plane of the circle passes through the center of the world. Hence, since these diametrically opposite points, as we travel from one place to another, nay, relatively to each man, are different and different again, it is plain that the horizon changes again and again, and that there are as many different horizons as there are points that can be thought on the surface of the sphere. And this concerns the Astronomical, or rational, horizon, so called because it is considered by Astronomers observing the motions of the Heavens, and is perceived by reason only, not by sense. For there is another horizon, sensible or physical, which everyone set in some vast plain, or in the middle of a calm sea, defines by turning his sight round. Wherefore, mathematically speaking, the sensible horizon neither actually forms a greatest circle, since it in no way extends through the center of the world, nor consequently does it separate the sphere of the Heaven into equal parts; yet it is always parallel to the rational horizon.

718 Usus horizontis hi sunt. I. Sphaeram mundanam in partes geminas distribuit, & rationalis quidem in aequales, seu in

718 The uses of the horizon are these. I. It distributes the world-sphere into two parts, and the rational horizon indeed into equal ones, or hemispheres:

p. 224

hemisphaerium superum, quod supra horizontem rationalem eminet, & inferum, quod eidem horizonti subjicitur: sensibilis autem partem Caeli nobis conspicuam ab inconspicua discriminat. II. Determinat ortus & occasus siderum. III. Stellas plagae cuivis particulari nunquam orientes, aut occidentes designat. IV. Quantitatem diei artificialis, & noctis definit, illud quippè intervallum, quo Sol supra horizontem moratur, artificialis dies adpellatur, uti nox habetur spatium hoc, quo infra horizontem deprimitur. V. Est terminus á quo Astrorum altitudo reperitur: tanta enim est altitudo sideris supra horizontem, quantus est circuli, qui per polos horizontis, & ipsum Astri centrum ducitur, arcus, inter idem centrum & punctum horizontis comprehensus. Idem est de Astrorum profunditate, quam infra horizontem sortiuntur. VI. Horizon pro diverso positu sphaeram nunc rectam nunc parallelam, nunc obliquam constituit. Circulus hic in Tabulis Geographicis notari haud consuevit. In Sphaera armillari vices illius obit capax & immobilis limbus in quo tria inscribuntur, gradus nempè, quos in Zodiaco Sol percurrit, antiquum, & novum Calendarium, ac venti principes.

the upper, which rises above the rational horizon, and the lower, which lies beneath that same horizon; the sensible horizon, on the other hand, distinguishes the part of the Heaven visible to us from the invisible. II. It determines the risings and settings of the stars. III. It designates, for each particular region, the stars that never rise or never set. IV. It defines the length of the artificial day and of the night: for that interval during which the Sun remains above the horizon is called the artificial day, as the night is taken to be this space during which it is depressed below the horizon. V. It is the boundary from which the altitude of the Stars is found: for the altitude of a star above the horizon is as great as the arc of the circle drawn through the poles of the horizon and the very center of the Star, comprehended between that center and the point of the horizon. The same holds of the depth of the Stars which they have below the horizon. VI. The Horizon, according to the different position of the sphere, makes it now right, now parallel, now oblique. This circle is not usually marked on Geographical Maps. In the armillary Sphere its office is performed by a broad and immovable rim, on which three things are inscribed: namely the degrees which the Sun runs through in the Zodiac, the old and the new Calendar, and the cardinal points of the winds.

719 Zodiacus circulus est, sub quo Planetae perpetuò moventur, & qui in oppositis duobus aequinoctialibus punctis ad angulos obliquos aequatorem intersecat, in aliis verò ex diametro pariter oppositis, & solstitialibus tropicos adtingit, aestivum quidem in Cancri principio, hibernum in Capricorno: polos proinde a mundanis & ipsius aequatoris diversos habet spatio 23 grad. ac 30 minutor. circiter. s1

719 The Zodiac is the circle under which the Planets are perpetually moved, and which cuts the equator at oblique angles in two opposite, equinoctial points, while in two others, likewise diametrically opposite, the solstitial, it touches the tropics: the summer tropic at the beginning of Cancer, the winter one at the beginning of Capricorn; its poles are therefore distant from the poles of the world and of the equator itself by a space of about 23 degrees and 30 minutes (c).

720 Dividitur secundum latitudinem, quae juxta Veteres 12, juxta Recentiores 16, quin & 20 gradus complectitur, in tres circulos quorum medius idemque maximus via Solis, via regia adpellatur, eo, quod Solis centrum motu periodico hanc viam constanter describat; ecliptica item a Solis, Lunaeque eclipsibus, quae nonnisi in ea, aut propè eandem lineam contingunt: reliqui duo circuli minores á medio aequidistantes, termini latitudinis vocantur. Secundum longitudinem dividitur ordine signorum in 12 partes aequales, quarum quaelibet 30 grad. complectitur, & á vicino signo nomen accipit. Signa porrò Zodiaci alia dicuntur stellata, alia signata: illa sunt asterismi, ac potissimùm animalium figurae é pluribus stellis compositae, ut symbolicè naturam anni per menses significent: haec verò sunt priorum characteres. Signa quibus characteres adscribi solent[?], duobus versibus comprehensa sunt, quorum primo borealia, altero australia exprimuntur, videlicet:

720 It is divided according to its latitude, which according to the Ancients comprises 12 degrees, according to the Moderns 16, nay even 20, into three circles, of which the middle and greatest is called the way of the Sun, the royal road, because the center of the Sun constantly describes this path by its periodic motion; it is likewise called the ecliptic from the eclipses of the Sun and Moon, which occur only in it or near that same line; the remaining two lesser circles, equidistant from the middle one, are called the limits of latitude. According to its longitude it is divided, in the order of the signs, into 12 equal parts, each of which comprises 30 degrees and takes its name from the neighboring sign. The signs of the Zodiac, further, are some called starry, others marked: the former are asterisms, and chiefly figures of animals composed of several stars, so that they symbolically signify the nature of the year through the months; the latter are their characters. The signs to which the characters are usually added are comprised in two verses, by the first of which the northern ones, by the other the southern ones are expressed, namely:

In definienda eclipticae declinatione, qua ab aequatore dimovetur, haud convenit inter Eruditos. Pytheas ann. ante Christ. nat. 324. declinationem statuit 23°. 52'. 41". (hoc est 23 grad. 52 minut. prim. 41 min. secund.[?]) ann. post Christ. 1715. Clariss. de Louville 23°. 28'. 24". (hoc est 23 grad. 28 minut. prim. 24 secund.[?]) Vide Wolf. Elem. Astron. §. 165.

In defining the declination of the ecliptic, by which it is removed from the equator, there is no agreement among the Learned. Pytheas, in the year 324 before the birth of Christ, fixed the declination at 23°. 52′. 41″ (that is, 23 degrees, 52 first minutes, 41 seconds); in the year after Christ 1715 the most distinguished de Louville at 23°. 28′. 24″ (that is, 23 degrees, 28 first minutes, 24 seconds). See Wolff, Elem. Astron. §. 165.

p. 225

♈ ♉ ♊ ♋ ♌ ♍

♈ ♉ ♊ ♋ ♌ ♍

Sunt Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo.

They are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo,

♎ ♏ ♐ ♑ ♒ ♓

♎ ♏ ♐ ♑ ♒ ♓

Libraque, Scorpius, Arcitenens, Caper, Amphora, Pisces.

and Libra, Scorpio, the Archer, the Goat, the Jar, Pisces.

721 Usus Zodiaci his continetur I. Sicut aequator diurnum, ita Zodiaci medium sive ecliptica periodicum astrorum, & solis praecipuè motum metitur, tum enim motus periodicus absolvi dicitur, quum revolutio integra ab Astris sub ecliptica completur. II. Eclipses Solis & Lunae sub eodem circulo peraguntur. III. Dierum, & noctium inaequalitatem efficit; siquidem propterea neque dies inter sese, neque hi cum noctibus aequantur, quod Sol in ecliptica deferatur. IV. Tempestatum, quarum una alteram per vices annuo quovis curriculo excipit, constans vicissitudo ab eclipticae positu dependet. V. Latitudinis Astrorum terminus est ecliptica; latitudo namque sideris, est arcus circuli (qui propterea latitudinis circulus vocatur, & maximus est) ducti per polos eclipticae, ac per centra ipsorum Astrorum, interceptus inter hoc centrum, ipsamque eclipticam. VI. Longitudines siderum in ea numerantur: arcus enim eclipticae, à principio Arietis in consequentia, sive secundum signorum seriem progrediendo, usque ad latitudinis circulum comprehensus, longitudo est sideris.

721 The use of the Zodiac is contained in these points: I. As the equator measures the diurnal motion, so the middle of the Zodiac, or ecliptic, measures the periodic motion of the stars, and chiefly of the sun; for the periodic motion is said to be completed when an entire revolution under the ecliptic is completed by the Stars. II. The eclipses of the Sun and Moon take place under this same circle. III. It causes the inequality of days and nights; for neither are the days equal among themselves, nor these to the nights, for the reason that the Sun is carried along in the ecliptic. IV. The constant alternation of the seasons, of which one succeeds another in turn in every yearly course, depends on the position of the ecliptic. V. The ecliptic is the boundary of the latitude of the Stars; for the latitude of a star is the arc of the circle (which is therefore called the circle of latitude, and is a greatest circle) drawn through the poles of the ecliptic and through the centers of the Stars themselves, intercepted between this center and the ecliptic itself. VI. The longitudes of the stars are numbered in it: for the arc of the ecliptic, proceeding from the beginning of Aries in consequentia, or according to the series of the signs, comprehended as far as the circle of latitude, is the longitude of the star.

722 Meridianus est circulus descriptus ex punctis duobus ortus & Occasus veri, sive illis, in quibus aequinoctii tempore Sol oritur & occidit, quae rursùm cardinalia vocantur, atque per polos tùm mundi, tùm horizontis, seu puncta Zenith, & Nadir transiens, ac propterea horizontem ad angulos rectos secans, ad quem quum Sol pervenit suo in ascensu, meridiem efficit. Hinc ea omnia Sphaerae puncta eundem habent meridianum quae non distant inter se, nisi secundum rectam ab uno mundi polo ad alterum ductam; diversum contrà sortiuntur loca illa, quae ab ortu in Occasum, vel vicissìm dissita sunt: ut adeò mutetur meridianus, dum progredimur ab ortu occasum versùs aut vice versa: minimè verò ubi à septentrione in austrum, vel è converso proficiscimur. Tot proin meridiani reapse numerantur, quot puncta verticalia ab ortu in occasum designari queunt. Adtamen ab uno primordium capimus, qui primus nominatur, sic ut ab eo reliqui in numerum veniant, computatione ab Occidente in Orientem facta. Hic alius ab aliis constituitur. Galli eum in ultima ex Insulis Canariis, quae Insula Ferri dicitur, fixerant antequam Recentiores ejus Gentis Astronomi in ipso Astronomico Parisiensi Observatorio primum meridianum constituerent, uti hodienum adsolent. Meridiani circuli usum strictìm damus.

722 The Meridian is the circle described from the two points of true rising and setting, or those in which, at the time of the equinox, the Sun rises and sets, which again are called cardinal, and passing through the poles both of the world and of the horizon, or the points Zenith and Nadir, and therefore cutting the horizon at right angles; when the Sun reaches it in its ascent, it makes midday. Hence all those points of the Sphere have the same meridian which are not distant from one another except along a straight line drawn from one pole of the world to the other; on the contrary, those places obtain a different one which are distant from east to west, or vice versa: so that the meridian changes while we travel from east toward west, or vice versa, but not at all when we proceed from north to south, or conversely. As many meridians, therefore, are really reckoned as there are vertical points that can be designated from east to west. Yet from one we take the beginning, which is named the first, so that from it the rest come into the count, the reckoning being made from West to East. This is fixed by some in one place, by others in another. The French had fixed it in the last of the Canary Islands, which is called the Island of Ferro, before the more recent Astronomers of that Nation established the first meridian in the Astronomical Observatory of Paris itself, as is customary today. We give the use of the meridian circle briefly.

p. 226

723 I. Caelum in hemisphaeria duo, Orientale, & Occidentale partitur. II. Maximam Astrorum supra horizontem metitur altitudinem, sidus enim supra horizontem tandiu adtollitur, dum ad Meridianum perveniat, ab hoc dein recedens, deprimitur: culminare dicitur, ubi eundem adtingit. III. Toto anni tempore punctum determinat meridiei & mediae noctis: eos namque circulos omnes, quos diurno suo motu Sol pecurrit, bisecat. Cetera meridiani munia Astrónomis nota mittimus: non enim ut Astrónomi, sed Physicorum ex munere ista persequimur.

723 I. It divides the Heaven into two hemispheres, the Eastern and the Western. II. It measures the greatest altitude of the Stars above the horizon, for a star is raised above the horizon until it reaches the Meridian; then, receding from it, it is depressed: it is said to culminate when it reaches it. III. Throughout the whole year it determines the point of midday and of midnight: for it bisects all those circles which the Sun runs through by its diurnal motion. The other offices of the meridian, known to Astronomers, we pass over: for we go through these things not as Astronomers but by the office of Physicists.

724 Coluri sunt circuli duo maximi, qui dum transeunt per polos mundi, in illis sese ad angulos rectos dividunt, aequatorem autem unàque eclipticam quadrifariam aequa partitione dividunt. Colurus aequinoctiorum per ea traducitur Zodiaci puncta, in quibus quum Sol versatur, aequinoctia contingunt, nempè per Arietis & Librae initia. Colurus Solstitiorum per puncta Solstitialia, (sic dicta quòd Sol ad ea pertingens consistere, sive stationem facere, quòdammodò videatur, id est: per dies aliquot suam ab aequatore declinationem nullatenùs mutare, Cancri videlicèt principium, & Capricorni producitur.

724 The Colures are two greatest circles which, while they pass through the poles of the world, divide each other there at right angles, and divide the equator, and likewise the ecliptic, into four by an equal partition. The colure of the equinoxes is drawn through those points of the Zodiac in which, when the Sun is there, the equinoxes occur, namely through the beginnings of Aries and Libra. The colure of the solstices is drawn through the solstitial points (so called because the Sun, on reaching them, seems in some manner to stand still, or to make a station, that is: for some days not to change its declination from the equator at all), namely through the beginning of Cancer and of Capricorn.

725 Utriusque coluri usus in his reponitur. I. Determinant quatuor puncta cardinalia Zodiaci, ea nimirùm, in quibus quum Sol constituitur conversiones tempestatum exiguntur; in Ariete quidem verna, in Capricorno biemalis, in Cancro aestiva, in Libra auctumnalis. Hinc singulis anni partibus terna respondent signa, veri Aries, Taurus, Gemini &c. II. Quemadmodùm colurus aequinoctiorum definit in Zodiaco gemina illa puncta, quae dum Sol occupat, dies nocti aequatur; ita colurus solstitiorum duo in eodem illo puncta signat, in quibus existente Sole tùm maxima dies, & minima nox, tùm è conversò maxima nox, & minima dies agitur. III. Sicut colurus aequinoctiorum signa Zodiaci in borealia sex: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, totidemque australia: Libra, Scorpius, Arcitenens, Caper, Amphora, Pisces, dispescit; sic alter è coluris ascendentia, quae à Capricorni initio ad Cancri primum gradum continentur, à descendentibus, seu à reliquis secernit &c.

725 The use of each colure consists in these points. I. They determine the four cardinal points of the Zodiac, namely those in which, when the Sun is placed there, the turnings of the seasons are brought about: in Aries the vernal, in Capricorn the winter, in Cancer the summer, in Libra the autumnal. Hence three signs correspond to each part of the year: to spring Aries, Taurus, Gemini, etc. II. As the colure of the equinoxes defines in the Zodiac those two points while the Sun occupies which day is equal to night, so the colure of the solstices marks two others in that same circle, in which, when the Sun is there, now the longest day and the shortest night, now conversely the longest night and the shortest day take place. III.
