As the colure of the equinoxes divides the signs of the Zodiac into six northern ones: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, and as many southern ones: Libra, Scorpio, the Archer, the Goat, the Jar, Pisces; so the other colure separates the ascending signs, which are contained from the beginning of Capricorn to the first degree of Cancer, from the descending ones, or the rest, etc.

726 Tropici sunt minores duo in Sphaera circuli, ad quos quum Sol pertingit, longiùs seu ad borëam, seu ad austrum non excurrit, sed ad Aequatorem revertitur Solstitiales quoque nuncupari solent, propterea, quòd per solstitialia Zodiaci puncta traducantur: hinc alter tropicus Cancri, alter tropicus Capricorni vocatur. Distant hi circuli ab aequatore 23 grad. & fere 30 minut. prim. ab invicem 47 grad à polo viciniore 60 grad. & ferè 30 minut. prim. Eorum usus triplex distinguitur. I. Viam Solis terminant. II. Maximam, minimamque diem in obliquo horizonte definiunt. III. Zonam torridam claudunt, & ordiuntur temperatam.

726 The Tropics are two lesser circles in the Sphere, at which, when the Sun reaches them, it does not run out further either to the north or to the south, but turns back to the Equator. They are also usually called Solstitial, because they are drawn through the solstitial points of the Zodiac: hence one is called the tropic of Cancer, the other the tropic of Capricorn. These circles are distant from the equator 23 deg. and about 30 first minutes, from each other 47 deg., from the nearer pole 66 deg. and about 30 first minutes. Their use is distinguished as threefold. I. They bound the path of the Sun. II. They define the longest and the shortest day on an oblique horizon. III. They close the torrid zone and begin the temperate.

727 Polares gemini, pariter minores circuli, à polis, quibus admoventur, nomen habent, alter arctici, antarctici alter, adtamen

727 The Polar circles are twin, likewise lesser circles; they have their name from the poles toward which they are moved, the one being of the arctic, the other of the antarctic, yet as far

p. 227

tanta ab his intercapedine sejuncti, quanta tropici ab aequatore, nimirùm 23 grad. ferè 30 minut. prim. Circuli hi cum tropicis & aequatore ipso paralleli vulgò dicuntur, eo quod hi omnes à se mutuò in singulis ambitus sui punctis eaquali intervallo absistant. Usus polarium circulorum est I. Quod sidera intra arcticum conclusa, his quibus sphaera, vel obliqua, vel parallela est occidant, intra antarcticum comprehensa, nunquam oriantur. II. Eorum interjectu Zonae temperatae à frigidis discreminantur. Haec omnia ex inspecta sphaera aliqua armillari dilucidius intelligentur.

removed from these as the tropics are from the equator, namely 23 deg., about 30 first min. These circles, together with the tropics and the equator itself, are commonly called parallels, because all of them stand apart from one another by an equal interval at every point of their circuit. The use of the polar circles is: I. That the stars enclosed within the arctic circle never set for those to whom the sphere is either oblique or parallel, and those comprehended within the antarctic never rise. II. By their interposition the temperate Zones are distinguished from the frigid. All these things will be understood more clearly by inspecting some armillary sphere.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De triplici Sphaerae positione.

On the threefold position of the Sphere.

728 In triplici situ spectari sphaera potest nempè in recto, obliquo, & parallelo, prout diversa est scilicèt aequatoris ad horizontem positio. Sphaera recta est, dum aequator horizonti ad perpendiculum imminet, ipsumque ad angulos rectos secat, sic ut poli ejusdem in horizonte constituantur. Hanc nancisci dicuntur, qui sub aequatore habitant; ubi proindè toto anni tempore dies noctibus aequantur. Sphaera obliqua est, in qua aequator obliquè sive ad angulos inaequales in horizontem inclinatur. Hac ii gaudent, quorum latitudo, sive distantia ab aequatore versùs alterutrum polum in meridiano loci computata, ad 90 grad. non pertingit, hoc est: ii omnes, qui aequatorem inter, ac polos habitant: his propterea dies noctibus inaequales aguntur.

n a threefold situation the sphere can be viewed, namely in the right, the 728 I oblique and the parallel, according as the position of the equator with respect to the horizon is different. The sphere is right when the equator stands perpendicularly over the horizon and cuts it at right angles, so that its poles are set in the horizon. Those who dwell under the equator are said to have this position; where, therefore, throughout the whole year the days are equal to the nights. The sphere is oblique in which the equator is inclined to the horizon obliquely, or at unequal angles. Those enjoy this whose latitude, or distance from the equator toward one or the other pole computed on the meridian of the place, does not reach 90 degrees, that is: all those who dwell between the equator and the poles; for them, therefore, the days are unequal to the nights.

729 Sphaera demùm parallela illa nuncupatur, in qua aequator cum horizonte parallelismum servat. Hac sphaerae positione potiuntur illi, quorum vertex cum altero polorum mundi coincidit, atque adeò quorum latitudo 90 grad. exaequat, seu iis, qui sub polis degunt: sub ea habitantibus una duntaxat dies annuo decursu est, una & nox, tanto utraque temporis intervallo definita, quantum in sex Zodiaci figuris peragrandis Sol insumit; quum enim horizon eorum & aequator congruant, Zodiaci signa sex supra horizontem perpetuò eminent, totidèm infra eundem delitescunt, ea causâ tanto tempore Sol ipsis adfulgeat supra horizontem necesse est, quantum exposcitur, ut signa Zodiaci sex percurrat, tanta rursùs temporis intercapedine lateat infra horizontem, quantum requiritur, ut per totidem inferiora signa moveatur hoc est 6 mensium spatium.

729 The sphere, finally, is called parallel in which the equator keeps parallelism with the horizon. This position of the sphere is had by those whose vertex coincides with one of the poles of the world, and so whose latitude equals 90 deg., or by those who live under the poles: for those who dwell under it there is in the yearly course only one day and one night, each bounded by as great an interval of time as the Sun takes in traversing six figures of the Zodiac; for since their horizon and the equator coincide, six signs of the Zodiac stand perpetually above the horizon, and as many lie hidden below it; for that reason it is necessary that the Sun shine upon them above the horizon for as long a time as is demanded for it to run through six signs of the Zodiac, and again lie hidden below the horizon for as great an interval of time as is required for it to be moved through as many lower signs, that is, the space of 6 months.

730 Tametsi verò sex mensium spatio circumscribi deberet iisdem nox, non secus, atque dies, haec tamen satis iis porrigitur longiùs, nox contrà imminuitur, ob ipsam videlicèt refractionem,

730 Although, however, night as well as day ought to be circumscribed for them by the space of six months, yet for them the day is extended longer, while the night is on the contrary diminished, namely on account of the very refraction

p. 228

quam subeunt radii solares multò maximam, dum adprimè densam locorum illorum atmosphaeram permeant; quo fit, ut Sol diebus aliquot supra horizontem illorum emicare videatur, quamvis infra eundem deprimatur. Bátavi profectò qui ann. 1597 in nova Zembla hiemarunt, Solem disparuisse ferunt 4 Novembris die, rursum die 24 Januarii conspicuum fuisse, ac proindè sex circitèr dierum intervallo calculi Astronomici rationibus antevertisse.

which the solar rays undergo, by far the greatest, while they pass through the exceedingly dense atmosphere of those places; whence it comes about that the Sun seems to shine above their horizon for some days, although it is depressed below it. Indeed the Dutch who wintered in Nova Zembla in the year 1597 report that the Sun disappeared on the 4th day of November and was visible again on the 24th day of January, and so had anticipated the reckonings of astronomical calculation by an interval of about six days.

731 Adhaec: quoniam diuturna illis protrahuntur crepuscula, sic, ut duobus circitèr mensibus Solis ortus ab altero velut occupetur, alterùm verò tandiù perduret à Solis occasu, iccirco nocturna illis caligo nonnisi duos circiter menses tenet. Quin ut observat Wolffius s1 haec duorum mensium caligo temperatur, plusquam dimidio temporis illius spatio, Lunae splendore.

731 Moreover: since long-lasting twilights are drawn out for them, so that for about two months the rising of the Sun is as it were forestalled by the one, while the other lasts so long after the setting of the Sun, therefore the darkness of night holds them for no more than about two months. Nay, as Wolff observes (d), this darkness of two months is tempered, for more than half of that space of time, by the splendor of the Moon.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

Mundi systemata strictim exponuntur.

The systems of the world are briefly set out.

732 Systematis nomine intelligunt hic Philosophi ordinem, sive dispositionem hujus universi, praecipuarumque illius partium, explicandis motibus, ac phaenomenis caelestibus adcommodatam. Tria hactenùs in Scholis, tùm astronomicis, tùm physicis celebrantur systemata, atque etiamnum vigent. Juvat proinde singula strictim persequi.

y the name of system Philosophers here understand the order, or disposi732 B tion, of this universe and of its principal parts, adapted to explaining the motions and the celestial phenomena. Three systems have hitherto been celebrated in the Schools, both astronomical and physical, and they still flourish. It is fitting, therefore, to go through each of them briefly.

733 I. Ptolemaicum sic dictum à Claudio Ptolemaeo. Ejus sistema terrae in universi medio collocatae aërem primùm, tùm ignem circumdare facit, septem deinde Caelos pro singulis Planetis solidos construit, & mundi circulo concentricos, hoc ordine, ut in 1. hoc est in supremo omnium Saturrus, in 2. Jupiter, in 3. Mars, in 4. Sol, in 5. Venus, in 6. Mercurius, in 7. Luna decurrat: super his demùm Caelis, firmamentum cum stellis fixis locat, quod primum mobile nuncupavit, quoniam ipsius motu inferiorum Planetarum orbes abripi ab ortu in occasum putavit spatio 23 horarum, 56 minutorum, 4 secundorum.

733 I. The Ptolemaic, so called from Claudius Ptolemy. His system makes first air, then fire, surround the earth, which is placed in the middle of the universe; it then constructs seven solid Heavens, one for each Planet, concentric with the circle of the world, in this order: that in the 1st, that is, in the highest of all, Saturn runs its course, in the 2nd Jupiter, in the 3rd Mars, in the 4th the Sun, in the 5th Venus, in the 6th Mercury, in the 7th the Moon. Above these Heavens, finally, it places the firmament with the fixed stars, which he called the primum mobile, because he thought that by its motion the orbs of the lower Planets are carried from east to west in the space of 23 hours, 56 minutes, 4 seconds.

734 II. Systema Tychonicum à Tichone Brahe constructum Hic relicta terrà pro universi centro, unà cum atmosphaera immobili suprà, & circum ipsam primo loco statuit Lunam, deindè Solem, circa hunc verò tanquàm reliquorum Planetarum centrum reposuit Mercurium, Venerem, Martem, tum Jovem cum quatuor Satellitibus à Galilaeo detectis, ac tandem Saturnum cum binis lateronibus,

734 II. The Tychonic system, constructed by Tycho Brahe. This, leaving the earth as the center of the universe, together with the immobile atmosphere, sets the Moon in the first place around it, then the Sun; around this, as the center of the remaining Planets, he placed Mercury, Venus, Mars, then Jupiter with the four Satellites discovered by Galileo, and at length Saturn with its two attendants; finally he

Elem. Geograph. §. 131.

Elem. Geograph. §. 131.

p. 229

denique his omnibus firmamentum, terrae concentricum superaddidit.

he added on top of all these the firmament, concentric with the earth.

735 III. Systema Copernicanum à Nicolao Copernico, post 30 annorum studium, quod illustrandae huic hypothesi impendit, nomen sumpsit. Juxta eum Sol in mundi centro immobilis constituitur: circa quem proximè movetur Mercurius, tùm Venus, deindè Tellurem cum Luna sibi circumgyrante posteà Martem, tùm Jovem, denique Saturnum revolvi arbitratur: ultrà omnes Planetas verò, & quidem ad immensam paenè distantiam ponit Spheram Stellarum fixarum omni penitùs motu destitutam. Planetis singulis, unico Sole excepto, quem propterea è Planetarum numero expungit, motum periodicum tribuit, nempè sub Zodiaco secundum signorum seriem.

735 III. The Copernican system took its name from Nicolaus Copernicus, after the thirty years’ study which he spent on illustrating this hypothesis. According to it the Sun is set immobile in the center of the world; he holds that around it Mercury moves nearest, then Venus, next the Earth with the Moon circling about it, afterwards Mars, then Jupiter, and finally that Saturn revolves; beyond all the Planets, and indeed at an almost immense distance, he places the Sphere of the fixed Stars, wholly destitute of all motion. To the single Planets, the Sun alone excepted, which he therefore strikes out of the number of the Planets, he assigns a periodic motion, namely under the Zodiac, following the series of the signs.

736 Telluri triplicem adsignat motum, videlicèt: primum vertiginis circa proprium axem ab Occasu in ortum, quo declarare volunt Copernicani vicissitudinem noctis & diei; siquidem posito hoc motu Sol nobis ab ortu in Occasum gyrari videtur, ac tellus aliam semper faciem illumninandam Soli objectat: motum hunc diurnum vocat, quòd intervallo unius diei perficiatur. Alterum periodicum dicit in orbe magno circà Solem sub ecliptica, quo motu tellus per signa ita progreditur, ut Sol nobis in eo signo, quod tegit, esse videatur, adeoque dum terra est in signis borealibus, ipse nobis in australibus, & contrà, versari adpareat: motum hunc annuum adpellat, qui anni unius spatio absolvitur.

736 To the Earth he assigns a threefold motion, namely: first, that of turning about its own axis from west to east, by which the Copernicans mean to explain the alternation of night and day; for once this motion is supposed, the Sun seems to us to be whirled from east to west, and the earth always presents another face to the Sun to be illuminated: this motion he calls diurnal, because it is completed in the interval of one day. The second he calls periodic, in the great orb around the Sun under the ecliptic, by which motion the earth so advances through the signs that the Sun appears to us to be in the sign which it covers, and hence, while the earth is in the northern signs, the Sun appears to us to dwell in the southern ones, and the reverse: this motion he names annual, as it is completed in the space of one year.

737 Postremum parallelismi motum adstruit, quo axis ipse telluris in sua circa Solem revolutione, tùm axi ipsius mundi, tùm sibimetipsi parallelus semper existit: hoc motu phaenomena vicissitudinis in anni tempestatibus evolvunt Copernicani. Adtamen axis terrestris inclinationem talem ad planum eclipticae, ut cum eo conficiat angulum 66 graduum, 30 minutorum, in rei hujus explanationem quoque adsciscunt. „Hac ipsa aetate nostra (ait Cl. Theologus Hyacinthus Serry) s1 Viri plerique pietate, ac religione praestantes, nonnulli etiam Purpurâ eminentes cum Gallilaeo, cum Copernico sentire liberè permittuntur, modò certum, indubitatumque Systema non dicant; sed commodum Astronomiae usibus hypothesim faciant, ut ex Decreto S. Congreg. S. Officii anno 16[?]0 perspectum est.„ Hactenùs ille. (Fig LXX. oculis subjicit Systema Copernicanum).

737 Lastly he establishes the motion of parallelism, by which the axis of the earth itself, in its revolution around the Sun, always remains parallel both to the axis of the world itself and to itself: by this motion the Copernicans unfold the phenomena of the alternation of the seasons of the year. To explain this matter, moreover, they also adopt such an inclination of the earth’s axis to the plane of the ecliptic that it makes with it an angle of 66 degrees, 30 minutes. “In this very age of ours (says the distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry) (e) very many men eminent in piety and religion, some even distinguished by the Purple, are freely permitted to hold with Galileo and with Copernicus, provided they do not call it a certain and undoubted System, but make it a hypothesis convenient for the uses of Astronomy, as was provided by the Decree of the Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office in the year 1620.” Thus far he. (Fig. LXX sets the Copernican System before your eyes.)

Praelect. Theolog. Tom. 1. Praelect. 1. de Opificio mundi pag. 130 edit. Venet. Ann. 1742.

Praelect. Theolog. vol. 1, Praelect. 1, On the Workmanship of the World, p. 130, Venice edition, year 1742.

p. 230

CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

Censura systematum mundi.

A judgment on the systems of the world.

738 Dico: Systema Copernicanum, ut mera hypothesis ad explicandos Astrorum motus ac phaenomena multò adcommodatius videtur, quàm Ptolemaicum & Tychonicum. Universè primùm id commostramus. Etenim Copernici hypothesis non adversatùr Physicae & Astronomiae quemadmodum systema Ptolemaicum. ¿Quis enim intelligat in hoc, quo pacto primum mobile sphaeras omnes inferiores ab ortu in occasum abripiat, unà tamen eo motu hae gaudeant, ut contraria ratione ab occasu in ortum simul quotidiè secundum seriem signorum sub Zodiaco progrediantur? Nam superficies, quibus hae sphaerae semet contingunt, convexa nempè inferioris, & concava superioris, si laevigatae sunt fiet, ut superior nihil motûs impertiatur sphaerae inferiori, atque adeò illa revolvi possit, quin haec secum raptet; si verò asperae statuantur, in quibus partes prominentes se se mutuo excipiant, patet liquidò, unum eundemque tam superiorum, quam inferiorum motum perfectum iri, ut rectè arguit Gassendus. s1

say: the Copernican System, as a mere hypothesis for explaining the mo738 I tions of the Stars and the phenomena, seems much more suitable than the Ptolemaic and the Tychonic. We show this first in general. For the hypothesis of Copernicus is not opposed to Physics and Astronomy as the Ptolemaic system is. For who could understand, in the latter, how the primum mobile carries away all the lower spheres from east to west, while these nevertheless enjoy that motion in such a way that, by a contrary reckoning, they at the same time advance daily from west to east according to the series of the signs under the Zodiac? For if the surfaces by which these spheres touch one another, namely the convex surface of the lower and the concave of the upper, are smooth, it will come about that the upper imparts no motion to the lower sphere, and so the former can revolve without carrying the latter along with it; but if they are made rough, so that their projecting parts fit into one another, it is clearly evident that one and the same motion will be effected both of the upper and of the lower spheres, as Gassendi rightly argues (f).

739 Cum Astronomicis observationibus multò minimè congruere Ptolemaei systema commostrant luculentè phaenomena. Compertum namque est, Mercurium, & Venerem nunc ad latera Solis, nunc supra eundem à nobis ex tellure conspici. Atqui hâc in hypothesi infra Solem, & ipso propiores jugiter adparere deberent. Ut nihil dicam de stellarum fixarum inconcinno situ, dum omnes in una adfixae superficie constituuntur, quum in propátulo sit apud Astronomos alias aliis remotiores diversis in planis locari.

739 The phenomena clearly show that the Ptolemaic system agrees very little with Astronomical observations. For it has been found that Mercury and Venus are seen by us from the earth now at the sides of the Sun, now above it. But in this hypothesis they ought always to appear below the Sun and nearer to us. Not to speak of the awkward position of the fixed stars, since they are all set fixed in one surface, whereas it is manifest among Astronomers that they are located in different planes, some more remote than others.

740 Secundò: Copernicana hypothesis est ordinata magis, & concinna serie caelestium corporum situm ac dispositionem nectit; siquidem in ea nullus ex Planetis primariis orbitam s2 alterius secat, ut in Tychonis systemate; deindè Planetarum omnium revolutiones circa idem centrum exiguntur, Solem nempè, contra atque in Tychonico. Adhaec Copernici hypothesis motum telluri tribuendo, dum interea Sol stellaeque fixae suis locis consistunt, multò simplicius, & paucioribus ex principiis phaenomena Caeli

740 Second: the Copernican hypothesis is more orderly, and weaves together the position and disposition of the celestial bodies in a neater series; for in it none of the primary Planets cuts the orbit (g) of another, as in the system of Tycho; then the revolutions of all the Planets are performed about the same center, namely the Sun, contrary to what happens in the Tychonic. Moreover, the hypothesis of Copernicus, by attributing motion to the earth while meanwhile the Sun and the fixed stars stand in their places, explains the phenomena of the Heaven much more simply and from fewer principles than

Phys. Sect. 2. Lib. 1. Cap. 1.

Phys. sect. 2, bk. 1, ch. 1.

p. 231

explicat, atque Tychonicum, in hoc quippè globi omnes caelestibus spatiis comprehensi, dempto terraqueo, motu cientur, & quidem, quo 24 horarum intervallo suum quique ambitum conficiant, ut ea propter celeritate paenè incredibili moveri debeant: ergo praeferenda est hypothesis Copernicana (Axiom. II. §. 32.)

than the Tychonic does; for in the latter all the globes contained in the celestial spaces, the terraqueous one excepted, are set in motion, and indeed in such a way that each completes its circuit in the interval of 24 hours, so that for that reason they must be moved with an almost incredible velocity: therefore the Copernican hypothesis is to be preferred (Ax. II, §. 32).

741 Ea de causa multò est facilius, multòque aptius ad observationes Astronomicas, & demonstrationes condendas: ut proinde Tychoniani Astronomi quoque ad suas observationes perficiendas, tabularumque constructiones expediendas Copernicana hypothesi utuntur. Quinimò, ut observat Clariss. Serry s1 ab Ecclesia ipsa ad emendationem Calendarii Romani quondam posita fuit.

741 For this reason it is much easier, and much more apt, for Astronomical observations and for constructing demonstrations: so that the Tychonian Astronomers too make use of the Copernican hypothesis to complete their observations and to carry out the construction of their tables. Nay, as the most distinguished Serry observes (h), it was once adopted by the Church herself for the emendation of the Roman Calendar.

742 Diurnus quidem motus, quo terra ipsa ab occasu in ortum convertitur, efficit, ut Sol; Planatae ipsi, ac Stellae fixae nobis ab ortu in occasum videantur revolvi: proindè diei noctisque vicissitudo consequitur; nam, ut omnes, qui motus rationem norùnt, fateri coguntur, quùm omnia, quae moveri loco nobis adparent, conspiciantur hoc pacto propterea, quod vel reapse suum ipsa locum mutent. vel quod spectator in adversam partem progrediatur, corporibus illis immotis, juxta illud Virgilii s2.

742 The diurnal motion, indeed, by which the earth itself is turned from west to east, brings it about that the Sun, the Planets themselves and the fixed Stars seem to us to revolve from east to west; hence the alternation of day and night follows; for, as all who know the nature of motion are forced to admit, since all things which appear to us to be moved in place are perceived in this way because either they themselves really change their place, or the spectator proceeds in the opposite direction while those bodies are unmoved, according to that line of Virgil (i):

743 Provehimur portu, terraeque urbesque recedunt, iccircò necessum est, perindè omnia motûs diurni phaenomena nobis adpareant, sive Astris ipsis revolutio tribuatur diurna in Occidentem, sive telluri atque oculo nostro motus in partem oppositam, videlicet Orientem versùs, Sole atque stellis loco suo haud dimotis, competere dicatur. Sed haec innuisse satis fuerit.

743 We are borne forth from the harbor, and lands and cities fall away, therefore it is necessary that all the phenomena of the diurnal motion appear to us in just the same way, whether the diurnal revolution toward the West is attributed to the Stars themselves, or the motion in the opposite direction, namely toward the East, is said to belong to the earth and to our eye, the Sun and the stars not being moved from their place. But it will be enough to have hinted at these things.

744 Princeps adversùs Copernicanam hypothesim momentum ex Sacris Literis Tychonici conformant. Nempè, contendunt doctrinam Copernici verbis illarum adversari, utpote quae manifestè Solem moveri, terram autem stare docent. Genesis scilicet 19. Sol egressus est super terram. Psalm. 92. Firmavit Orbem terrae qui non commovebitur. Ecclesiastes cap. 1. Terra autem in aeternum stat: oritur Sol, & occidit, & ad locum suum revertitur, & Josue cap. 10. (jubente Judaeorum Duce ne Sol contra Gabaon moveretur) stetit Sol in medio Caeli, & non festinavit occumbere spatio unius diei. Isai. cap. 38. Et reversus est Sol decem lineis per gradus, quos descenderat. Atque ex his plurimi deducunt, systema Copernicanum telluris motum, & quietem Solis adstruens, Scripturarum Sanctarum auctoritati oppositum videri.

744 The Tychonians frame their chief argument against the Copernican hypothesis from the Sacred Scriptures. They contend, namely, that the doctrine of Copernicus is opposed to their words, inasmuch as these manifestly teach that the Sun moves, but that the earth stands still. Thus Genesis 19: The sun was risen upon the earth. Psalm 92: He hath established the world which shall not be moved. Ecclesiastes ch. 1: But the earth standeth for ever. The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place; and Josue ch. 10 (when the Leader of the Jews commanded that the Sun should not move over against Gabaon): So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down the space of one day. Isaias ch. 38: And the sun returned ten lines by the degrees by which it was gone down. And from these very many conclude that the Copernican system, which asserts the motion of the earth and the rest of the Sun, seems to be opposed to the authority of the Holy Scriptures.

745 At enim doctrinâ perindè, atque in verbum Divinum reverenti pietate insignes Copernicani opinionem suam cum his testimoniis neutiquam pugnare reponunt. Ajunt namque, haec & id genus alia verba, intelligi haud oportere in sensu literali, physico, proprio, & absoluto, verùm in sensu populari duntaxat, optico, improprio,

745 But the Copernicans, distinguished alike in learning and in reverent piety toward the Divine word, reply that their opinion in no way conflicts with these testimonies. For they say that these and other words of the kind must be understood not in the literal, physical, proper and absolute sense, but only in the popular, optical, improper

Orbita Planetae dicitur ea curva linea in se ipsam rediens, quam in motu suo periódico describit.

The orbit of a Planet is the name given to that curved line, returning into itself, which it describes in its periodic motion.

Loco suprà cit.

In the place cited above.

Aeneid. Lib. III. ℣. 72.

Aeneid, bk. III, v. 72.

p. 232

& quoad adparentiam. Respondent Scripturam Divinam adtemperare sese ad captum vulgi. Rationem isthaec adserendi reddunt quod „Deo, (ut Cl. Muratorius ait s1 per suas Scripturas loquenti non is fuerit scopus, ut inanem erga res scitu non necessarias, erga mundi elementa, & corpora, hominum curiositatem pasceret, sed ut verè utilia ad aeternam beatitudinem consequendam traderet. Neque enim in doctis humanae sapientiae verbis ipse loquitur, sed sese demittit ad earum locutionum usum, quae quanquam minus accuratae, & ad humanae sapientiae trutinam impropriae dignoscuntur, rudi tamen populo veritatem quampiam utilem ac salutarem commodius exponunt„. Profitentur in reliquo, se à communibus loquendi modis nolle recedere, adcommodatè ad id, quod sensuum testimonio adparet, à se dictum iri: Sol oritur; ad meridiei punctum adtolliur; ad Occasum vergit &c.

and according to appearance. They answer that Divine Scripture tempers itself to the capacity of the common people. The reason they give for asserting this is that “God (as the distinguished Muratori says (k)), speaking through his Scriptures, did not have this aim, to feed men’s vain curiosity about things not necessary to know, about the elements of the world and about bodies, but to hand down things truly useful for attaining eternal happiness. For He does not speak in the learned words of human wisdom, but lowers Himself to the use of those expressions which, although they are recognized as less accurate and as improper when weighed in the balance of human wisdom, yet set forth some useful and salutary truth more conveniently to an unlearned people.” For the rest, they profess that they do not wish to depart from the common ways of speaking, and that they will speak in accommodation to what appears by the testimony of the senses: The Sun rises; it is raised to the point of midday; it declines toward the West, etc.

746 Cl. etiam Theologus Hyacinthus Serry postquam supra laudata Sacrarum Literarum testimonia adducit, in adversarium Copernicanae hypotheseos ita insurgit s2 „¿Ob ea paucula Scripturae verba censoriam virgam exerces? ¿Quidni potiùs, si Theologus es, donec ingeniosum Systema damnet Ecclesia, laudata Scripturae verba ad commodum sensum inflectis? Ut quae pro immobili terrae stabilitate jactantur, ea de firmitate duntaxat, consistentia, perduratione, localem motum nequaquam excludente, intelligantur: namque & Caelos, seu Aethera firmasse sursum Divina Sapientia dicitur Proverb. 8. cùm tamen ab ea caelorum firmitate motus juxta Ptolomaei Systema nequaquam abhorreat: Quae verò pro Solis mobilitate ex Sacris Literis proferuntur, haec non ex rei veritate, sed ex vulgi opinione, communique more loquendi sint dicta; ut ad rudis populi sensum sese accommodarent Scriptores Sacri: quod aliis tàm multis exemplis dedimus manifestum: atque in hoc ipso, quod de Josue praesertim objicitur, certissimum est; ex vulgi scilicèt opinione id esse dictum, si tota rei gestae narratio diligentius adtendatur. Sol, inquit Josue, contra Gabaon ne movearis: & tamen cùm tellus Solis comparatione exigua moles sit, & Gabaon in eodem terrae globo veluti minutissimum punctum; quid quaeso Soli praecipitur, ne moveatur contra Gabaon? ¿Ita ne huic puncto respondere potuit ingens Solis globus, ut contra illud aut moveretur aut staret? Ad vulgare igitur oculorum judicium allusit Josue: nostris enim oculis Sol apparet veluti discus duobus ad summum palmis dimetiendus, ac super exiguum caeli spatium decurrens„.

746 The distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry too, after adducing the testimonies of Sacred Letters cited above, rises up thus against the adversary of the Copernican hypothesis (l): “Do you wield the censor’s rod on account of those few little words of Scripture? Why not rather, if you are a Theologian, until the Church condemns the ingenious System, bend the words of Scripture cited to a convenient sense? So that those words which are paraded in favor of the immobile stability of the earth may be understood only of firmness, consistency and duration, in no way excluding local motion: for Divine Wisdom is also said to have established the Heavens, or the sky above, Prov. 8, though motion according to Ptolemy’s System is in no way at odds with that firmness of the heavens: while those which are brought forward from Sacred Letters in favor of the mobility of the Sun were said not according to the truth of the thing, but according to the opinion of the common people and the common manner of speaking, so that the Sacred Writers might accommodate themselves to the understanding of an unlearned people: which we have made manifest by so many other examples; and in this very one which is especially objected, about Josue, it is most certain, namely that it was said according to the opinion of the common people, if the whole narration of the deed is attended to more diligently. Move not, O sun, says Josue, toward Gabaon: and yet, since the earth is a small mass in comparison with the Sun, and Gabaon on that same globe of the earth is as a most minute point, what, I ask, is the Sun commanded, that it should not move toward Gabaon? Could the huge globe of the Sun so correspond to this point as either to move or to stand still over against it? Josue therefore alluded to the common judgment of the eyes, for to our eyes the Sun appears as a disk to be measured by two palms at most, running over a small space of the sky.

747 „Additur in historica narratione: Stetit itaque Sol in medio caeli: at caelestes orbes, utpotè sphaerici (si exactè loqui velimus) ut extremis, ita quoque medio carent; nullumque in

747 “It is added in the historical narration: So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven: but the celestial orbs, being spherical (if we wish to speak exactly), as they lack extremities, so also they lack a middle; and no middle can be devised in a circular path

De moderamine Ingenior. cap. 22.

De moderamine Ingenior. ch. 22.

Loco supra citat.

In the place cited above.

p. 233

semita, aut linea circulari excogitari medium potest. Illud itaque ad vulgi sensum interpretari necesse est; quòd illi medius videatur caelorum locus, qui ab Oriente, & Occidente aequaliter distat. Clauditur tandem narratio his verbis: non fuit antea, nec postea tam longa dies. Ita ne verò nulla unquam in toto terrarum orbe longior dies illuxit? At regiones sub utroque Polo sitas peragrantibus exploratum est, Solem illic lucere diutiùs, longioresque contingere dies: imo hoc ipsum demonstrativa, & evidentissima ratione ab Astronomicae Scientiae peritis probari, certissimum est. Judaici itaque populi, cui Solis effectus in polaribus regionibus erant ignoti, accommodata narratio fuit.

or line. That, therefore, must be interpreted according to the understanding of the common people: that that place of the heavens seems to them the middle which is equally distant from the East and the West. The narration is finally closed with these words: there was not before nor after so long a day. Has then no longer day ever shone in the whole world? But it is well ascertained by those who travel through the regions situated under either Pole that the Sun shines longer there and that longer days occur: nay, it is most certain that this very thing is proved by a demonstrative and most evident reasoning by those skilled in Astronomical Science. The narration, therefore, was accommodated to the Jewish people, to whom the effects of the Sun in the polar regions were unknown.

748 „Id ni dicamus, Sacrosque Scriptores in his de Solis motu, Terraeque stabilitate loquendi formulis non ex vulgi more locutos fateamur, periculum est, ne & pari licentiâ, parique Divinarum Scripturarum abusu hoc ipsum Copernici, & Galilaei de Terrae mobilitate systema, quod suis inconsideratè censuris inúrunt plerique Theologi Recentiores, demonstrare aggrediatur morosus quidam Sacrorum Verborum exactor. Cùm enim tam saepè Sacris in Literis orbis terrae cardinibus dicatur impositus, Regum. 1. cap. 2. Domini sunt cardines terrae; Proverb. 8. Adhuc terram non fecerat, & flumina, & cardines orbis terrae; cárdines verò, si pressè loqui velimus, rem versatilem, mobilemque impositam sonent, quae super iis volvatur, vertaturque; quid indè, rogo vos, consequetur, nisi mobilem esse tellurem, atque versátilem, quae suis imposita cardinibus certâ lege volvitur, agiturque? Eo vel maximè, quòd & Job. Cap. 9. ℣. 6. Deus terram de loco suo commovere dicatur; quòd citra figuram & Katàlexim (certum morem loquendi vulgò adcommodatum) dictum volet morosus verborum exactor„. Hactenùs Cl. Serry.

748 “Unless we say this, and confess that the Sacred Writers, in these formulas of speech concerning the motion of the Sun and the stability of the Earth, spoke according to the custom of the common people, there is danger lest, with equal license and an equal abuse of the Divine Scriptures, some morose exactor of the Sacred Words should set about demonstrating this very system of Copernicus and Galileo on the mobility of the Earth, which most of the more recent Theologians brand with their inconsiderate censures. For since the world is so often said in Sacred Letters to be set upon its cardines [poles, hinges]: 1 Kings ch. 2: For the poles of the earth are the Lord’s; Proverbs 8: He had not yet made the earth, nor the rivers, nor the poles of the world; and since cardines, if we wish to speak strictly, denote a turning and movable thing set upon them, which is revolved and turned upon them: what, I ask you, will follow from this, except that the earth is movable and turning, which, set upon its hinges, is revolved and driven by a fixed law? All the more because in Job ch. 9, v. 6, God is said to move the earth out of its place; which the morose exactor of words will want to have been said without figure and katalexis (a certain manner of speaking accommodated to the common people).” Thus far the distinguished Serry.

749 Sed sint haec obiter dicta, non ut Copernici, & Galilaei systema velut ratum fixumque habeamus, quum jam indè á principio dixerimus, velut meram hypothesin ad explicanda phaenomena illum tantùm nos adoptare.

749 But let these things be said in passing, not so that we may hold the system of Copernicus and Galileo as ratified and fixed, since we said from the very beginning that we adopt it only as a mere hypothesis for explaining the phenomena.

ADPENDIX. — APPENDIX

Quid de Astrorum influxu sentiendum sit?

What is to be thought of the influence of the Stars?

750 Pervulgata est quaestio: an sidera ad productionem effectuum in tellure observatorum concurrant, sive, ut vulgò proponitur, in sublunaria influant. Sol praecipuè, & Luna effluviorum cum tellure nostra communionem sortiri videntur quibusdam: quod argumentum á duobus his Astris ad reliqua proferunt; neque contenti sunt dicere, sidera per calorem, & lucem agere in sublunaria, sed diversos alios

ublicly debated is the question whether the stars concur in producing the 750 P effects observed on the earth, or, as it is commonly put, whether they influence sublunary things. The Sun chiefly, and the Moon, seem to some to share a communion of effluvia with our earth: an argument which they extend from these two Stars to the rest; nor are they content to say that the stars act on sublunary things through heat and light, but they think that various other influences

p. 234

influxus in tellurem praestari putant, dum Astris diversas proprietates specificas tribunt: Lunam adprime humidam, humores in tellure excitare; Saturnum frigidum; Martem siccum, & calidum, &c. ut proinde quorumdam ortus pluviam concitet, aliorum siccitatem inducat &c. Haec & plura id genus persequi porrò non libet: compendio nostrum de influxu Astrorum sensum proferemus. Quo circa sequitur conclusio.

are exerted upon the earth, while they attribute different specific properties to the Stars: that the Moon, being exceedingly moist, excites the humors on the earth; that Saturn is cold; Mars dry and hot, etc.; so that, accordingly, the rising of some brings on rain, that of others induces drought, etc. It is not our pleasure to pursue these and more things of the kind any further: we shall set forth our view of the influence of the Stars in brief. Wherefore the conclusion follows.

751 Praeter actionem lucis nullum alium influxum astrorum in tellurem agnoscimus: excipe tamen Solem qui calore suo satis sensibili terram nostram fovet, tum etiam Lunam quae sinminus calore, frigoreve, at certè pondere suo in subjectam atmosphaeram pro vario situ, variè nostrum globum premere potest. In primis enim effluvia quaedam substantialia humida, sicca &c. in terram ab astris transmitti nequeunt; ¿quae enim causa proferri potest, à qua ejusmodi effluvia ultrà sui astri atmosphaeram ad aliquod solum milliaria porrectam per longissima spatia propellatur? Certè de effluviis terrestribus inter omnes convenit, ea minimè ultra atmosphaeram in Lunae regionem excurrere; deindè tametsi effluvia extruderentur, ¿quid tamen fingi potest, quod ea ad nostram potius tellurem, quàm ad aliud spatium & corpus caeleste determinet? Deniquè si Luna in qua adversarii vim maximam reponunt, effluvia sua sphaericè spárgeret, qnum haec, quò ampliùs recedunt à corpore lunari, eò magis divergant ab invicem, & in tanta distantia, quantam Luna à tellure habet, divaricari possint, ac debeant plurimum, minimè possunt hoc tam avaro & exiguo effluviorum rore effectus ii produci, qui lunae influxui tribuuntur.

751 Apart from the action of light we acknowledge no other influence of the stars upon the earth: except, however, the Sun, which by its heat, sensible enough, warms our earth, and also the Moon, which, if not by heat or cold, yet certainly by its weight upon the atmosphere beneath it, can press upon our globe variously according to its varying position. For, in the first place, certain substantial effluvia, moist, dry, etc., cannot be transmitted from the stars to the earth; for what cause can be adduced by which such effluvia should be propelled through the longest spaces beyond the atmosphere of their star, which extends only some miles? Certainly about terrestrial effluvia all agree that they by no means run out beyond the atmosphere into the region of the Moon: then, even if effluvia were thrust out, what can be imagined that would direct them to our earth rather than to some other space and celestial body? Finally, if the Moon, in which our adversaries place the greatest force, scattered its effluvia spherically, then, since these diverge from one another the more, the further they recede from the lunar body, and at so great a distance as the Moon has from the earth can and must be spread very far apart, those effects which are attributed to the influence of the moon can by no means be produced by so stingy and meager a dew of effluvia.

752 Ostenditur secundò. Luminis actio causa esse potest omnium effectuum; lumen enim consistit in presione rectilinea aethereae substantiae ad nos usque propagata. Ergo alius potest excitari motus particularum minimarum, vehemens nempè, varius, ac perturbatus, hoc autem motu posito, alius sequi effectus, hoc cessante, rursus alius, absque eo, ut ad noctium humiditatem explicandam, ad Lunae, nescio, quae profluvia recurratur. Quapropter dùm totam naturam foveri, ac propagari, plantas adolescere, frumentum flavescere, fructus maturescere, verbo promoveri, generationes, alterationes, augmentationes cernimus, dùm tempestates anni certo moderamine recurrere, magis peculiares aëris mutationes saepè multum diversas pro aliarum causarum concursu fieri experimur, Solis actioni tribuamus haec necesse est, sed non alia ratione agentis, quàm luce sua, atque hinc consequente calore.

752 It is shown, secondly. The action of light can be the cause of all the effects; for light consists in the rectilinear pressure of the ethereal substance, propagated all the way to us. Therefore a different motion of the smallest particles can be excited, namely a vehement, varied and perturbed one; and once this motion is posited, one effect follows, and when it ceases, again another, without any need to have recourse, in order to explain the moisture of the nights, to I know not what outflowings of the Moon. Wherefore, when we see the whole of nature cherished and propagated, plants growing up, grain turning yellow, fruits ripening, in a word, generations, alterations and augmentations promoted; when we experience the seasons of the year recurring with a fixed regulation, and more particular changes of the air, often very diverse, taking place according to the concurrence of other causes, it is necessary that we attribute these things to the action of the Sun; but to the Sun acting in no other way than by its light and the heat consequent upon it.

753 Unde licet sideribus ceteris vis insit, exigua nervorum opticorum capillamenta concutiendi, & agitandi, atque adeo, quum his capillamentis tenuiores & ad motum aptiores in aëre, aqua, & terra particulae contineantur, vis agitandi movendique has particulas, ac proindè effectus aliquos (quantum vero sub sensum casuros, quisque arbitrabitur ex distantia ferè immensa fixarum, ex

753 Hence, although there is in the other stars a force of striking and agitating the slender fibrils of the optic nerves, and so, since particles thinner than these fibrils and more apt for motion are contained in the air, water and earth, a force of agitating and moving these particles, and consequently of producing some effects (how far these will fall under sense, each will judge from the almost immense distance of the fixed stars, and from the

p. 235

lumine languido Planetarum) edendi, iis tamen nullus omninò adscribendus est, nisi pro luminis ratione, cujus actio pro demonstrata haberi debet. Et quoniàm siderum universorum lumine fortius est, lumen Solis unius, ideò ei horum effectuum omnium, causa praecipuè est tribuenda. Quod si fortè observatum fuerit, non eandem esse temperationem aëris quotiescumque Sol eodem modo radios in tellurem vibrat: id non in reliquo Astra, sed peculiarem tùm aëris aut terrae habitudinem refundendum est. Ex his manat.

faint light of the planets), nevertheless none at all is to be ascribed to them except in proportion to their light, whose action must be held as demonstrated. And since the light of the Sun alone is stronger than the light of all the stars together, therefore the cause of all these effects is chiefly to be attributed to it. But if it should perhaps be observed that the temper of the air is not the same whenever the Sun darts its rays upon the earth in the same way, this is to be referred not to the other heavenly bodies, but to some peculiar condition, at that time, of the air or of the earth. From these things it follows:

Corollarium I.

COROLLARY I .

754 Astrologiam Judiciariam tanquam imposturam vanissimam, & Philosopho indignam repudiandam esse, tùm quod á Sacris Litteris reprobetur, damnetur á Conciliis Bràcarensi, & Toletano, reprehendatur á Patribus, Summorum Pontificum auctoritate, legibus Canonicis, & Civilibus interdicatur; tùm quòd â sapientibus omnibus risu explodatur. Certè divisio illa Caeli in 12 domos, in qua fundatur horoscopus, sive figura constitutionis caelestis, quae in momento nativitatis existit, commentitia est. Praeterea nec eadem fata eveniunt omnibus, qui eodem sidere nati sunt, ut patet exemplo geminorum Esau, & Jacob, qui & propensionem, & fortunam habuerunt diversissimam: nec eodem gaudent horoscopo, qui similia fata experiuntur, pro ut manifestum est; quia multi simul pereunt naufragio, incendio, peste, pugnâ, quum tamen diversissimis temporibus in lucem editi sint. Ut nihil dicam suppositum totum artis hujus, adsumptum â numero septenario Planetarum, & â situ domorum caelestium, falsum esse. Primum ostenditur â Satellitibus Jovis, & Saturui, imò, & Veneris uno; alterum, quia Constellationes quae tribuerunt nomen 12 Signis Zodiaci, juxta quorum ordinem 12 domos suas reperiri in Caelo ponunt, dudùm â pristino loco jam 30 gradibus recesserunt. Sed nugis immorari non vacat.

754 Judicial astrology is to be repudiated as a most empty imposture, unworthy of a Philosopher, both because it is reproved by the Sacred Scriptures, condemned by the Councils of Braga and Toledo, censured by the Fathers, and forbidden by the authority of the Supreme Pontiffs and by the canon and civil laws, and because it is hissed off with laughter by all the wise. Certainly that division of the Heaven into 12 houses, on which the horoscope is founded, or the figure of the celestial configuration that exists at the moment of birth, is a fiction. Moreover, neither do the same fates befall all who are born under the same star, as is plain from the example of the twins Esau and Jacob, who had the most different propensity and fortune; nor do those who experience similar fates enjoy the same horoscope, as is manifest: since many perish together by shipwreck, fire, plague, or battle, although they were brought into the light at the most different times. Not to mention that the whole supposition of this art, taken from the septenary number of the planets and from the situation of the celestial houses, is false. The first is shown by the satellites of Jupiter and Saturn, indeed even by the single one of Venus; the second, because the constellations to which they gave the name of the 12 Signs of the Zodiac, in whose order they hold that their 12 houses are found in the Heaven, have long since already receded 30 degrees from their original place. But there is no leisure to dwell on trifles.

Corollarium II.

COROLLARY II .

755 Astrologiam Aëroscopicam, seu quae tempestates, & aëris mutationes ex Astris vaticinatur, Philosopho respuendam esse; neque enim ars haec vel ratione ulla, aut experientia firmatur, etenim quasdam ponunt Planetis inesse proprietates, hujusmodi vaticinatores: Saturnum frigidum, & siccum, Venerem Planetam calidum, & humidum, &c., quae suppositiones, non conjecturae sunt philosophicae, sed fabulosae; ¿cur enim unus calidus sit, humidus alter, quando omnes sunt massa opaca, â tellure nostra non multum abludentes? Experientiâ suam artem

755 Aeroscopic astrology, or that which foretells storms and changes of the air from the stars, is to be rejected by the Philosopher: for this art is confirmed neither by any reason nor by experience; for soothsayers of this kind posit certain properties in the planets: Saturn cold and dry, Venus a hot and moist planet, etc., which suppositions are not philosophical conjectures but fabulous ones; for why should one be hot, another moist, when all are opaque masses not much unlike our earth? By experience they cannot establish their art;

p. 236

stabilire nequeunt; haec enim nititur repetita saepius observatione, Astrologi vero nec habent, nec habere possunt observationem, ubi ex simili stellarum positu similis fuerit secutus eventus in rebus sublunaribus: quando per Astronomos certum est; eorundem siderum aspectum in compluribus annorum millionibus non redire; etsi positio etiam ejusmodi rediisset, ea quoad omnia sidera ignota fuisset imperitis illis, quum ii antè praeteritum saeculum Planetas secundarios ignoraverint.

for this rests on frequently repeated observation, whereas the astrologers neither have nor can have an observation in which, from a similar position of the stars, a similar event has followed in sublunary things: since it is certain from the astronomers that the same aspect of the same stars does not return within many millions of years; and even if such a position had returned, it would have been unknown, as regards all the stars, to those unskilled men, since until the past century they were ignorant of the secondary planets.

756 Neque faciunt pro veritatis praesumptione quidpiam praedictiones quandoque verae: quis est enim, inquit Cicero, qui totum diem jaculans non aliquando collimet, praeterquam quod longè plures falsae ad derogandam Astrologis fidem plurimùm momenti habeant, innumera ejus rei sunt exempla. Sic anno 1524 ob magnas Planetarum Conjunctiones in Aquario praedicebantur integra, ac certa diluvia, annus tamen erat serenissimus, anno 1586 venti & procellae propter Conjunctiones omnium Planetarum, quum tamen annus totus pacatè exactus sit. Ipsi certè Astrologi non conveniunt inter se suis in praedictionibus: hinc Gallus quidam sibi coemit tot Calendaria, ut singulis diebus potuerit unum seligere conforme Caelo, quo factum, ut diceret, suum Calendarium toto anno esse conforme Caelo, ac licet vaticinia haec nonnumquam Calendariis inserantur, minimè tamen evincitur sapientum consilio ista fieri, aut ab iis fidem his ineptiis tribui, quando nullum facile quis in toto Orbe doctum Astronomum reperiet, qui non simplicitatem hanc indignanter respuat indignam docto, ut ait Amort. s1

756 Nor do predictions that sometimes come true do anything for a presumption of truth; for who is there, says Cicero, who, hurling darts all day long, does not sometimes hit the mark? Besides the fact that the far more numerous false ones carry very great weight toward detracting from the astrologers’ credit, there are innumerable examples of this. Thus in the year 1524, on account of great conjunctions of the planets in Aquarius, entire and certain deluges were predicted, yet the year was most serene; in the year 1586, winds and storms on account of conjunctions of all the planets, although the whole year was passed in calm. Certainly the astrologers themselves do not agree among themselves in their predictions: hence a certain Frenchman bought himself so many calendars that for each single day he could choose one conformable to the heavens, whereby it came about that he said his calendar was conformable to the heavens the whole year round; and although these prophecies are sometimes inserted in calendars, it is by no means proved that this is done by the counsel of the wise, or that credence is given by them to these follies, since one will hardly find in the whole world a learned astronomer who does not indignantly reject this simplicity, unworthy of a learned man, as Amort says. (m)

757 Fiunt nempe haec, ut consuetudini serviatur non aliter, ac dum medici ipsi tabulae phlebotomicae se accommodant, cujus fundamentum non aliud est, quàm ordo numericus dierum à novilunio computatorum, qui nullam vim habet. Certè Amort ait: tabula pro sectione venae, quae solet esse in Calendariis est tantum pro pueris, rusticis, & simplici plebe. Ob eandem inefficacem numerorum relationem de diebus criticis, annis climactericis opiniones fabulis accensendae sunt.

757 These things, namely, are done so that custom may be served, not otherwise than as physicians themselves accommodate themselves to the phlebotomic table, whose foundation is nothing other than the numerical order of the days counted from the new moon, which has no force at all. Certainly Amort says: the table for the letting of a vein, which is usually in calendars, is only for boys, rustics, and the simple common people. On account of the same inefficacious relation of numbers, the opinions about critical days and climacteric years are to be counted among fables.

Corollarium III.

COROLLARY III .

758 Effectus Lunae falsò, nimiaque credulitate adtribui. Ita creditur Luna lapides vi quadam peculiari corrodere, animalium ossa crescente Luna medullae plena, senescente autem medulla vacua, & sanguine ferè repleta esse putantur. Astaci, ostrea, multique alii pisces pleniores esse nova aut plena Luna, quàm dimidiata existimantur. Verùm haec inter temere vulgata meritò reponantur; veri enim simillimum est, ait Cl.

758 Effects are falsely, and with excessive credulity, attributed to the Moon. Thus the Moon is believed to corrode stones by a certain peculiar force; the bones of animals are thought to be full of marrow while the Moon is waxing, but empty of marrow while it is waning, and almost filled with blood. Lobsters, oysters, and many other fish are judged to be fuller at the new or the full moon than at the half moon. But these things are deservedly placed among things rashly spread abroad; for it is most likely, says the distinguished Rohault (n)

Phys. Partic. P. 1. q. 10.

Phys. Partic., pt. 1, q. 10.

p. 237

Rohaultius s1 solis calorem plurium annorum spatio haec, & saxa torrere, & conficere posse, quae igne paucis horis conficiuntur, quod quum contingit, minimè mirum videri debet, si aëris humor tam saxa haec quàm calcem in pulverem redigit. Similiter, prosequitur ille, falsò existimatur, animalium ossa crescente Luna medullae plena esse, vacua senescente, hanc enim rem quum amplius 25 annos observaverit ille, alia ossa medullae plena, alia vacua crescente Luna atque senescente semper comperuit.

(n), that the heat of the sun in the space of many years can torrefy and consume these stones, which are consumed by fire in a few hours; and when this happens, it ought to seem no wonder at all if the moisture of the air reduces these stones, just as it does lime, to powder. Similarly, he continues, it is falsely thought that the bones of animals are full of marrow while the Moon waxes and empty while it wanes; for when he had observed this for more than 25 years, he always found some bones full of marrow and others empty, both while the Moon was waxing and while it was waning.

759 Quamobrèm alia adsignanda causa: illud verisimillimum quorundam animalium ossa medulla vacua esse, vel quia alimento defecerint, vel quia labore defessa fuerint: Falsò quoque, & omninò adversante experientia creditum est, astacos, ostrea &c. se pro varia Lunae acie implere, aut extenuare. Quod si piscium corpora aliquandò minui videantur, hoc evenit vel ob alimenti defectum, vel undis tempestate commotis, aut etiam propria contentione nimium agitati, id quod iis verosimillimum videbitur, qui norint pisces in freto Caletensi, ubi aqua maximè agitatur, captos, plerumque minus plenos esse, quàm eos, qui propè Bononiam, ubi mare paulò magis tranquillum conquiescit, capiuntur. Ceteri demùm effectus non humido Lunae influxui, sed praesenti tunc atmosphaerae constitutioni, nempè, vel nimio humore vel noxiis aliis effluviis refertae, tribuendi sunt.

759 Wherefore another cause is to be assigned: it is most likely that the bones of certain animals are empty of marrow either because the animals have lacked nourishment or because they have been worn out by labor. Falsely too, and wholly against experience, has it been believed that the Moon, according to her various phases, fills out or thins lobsters, oysters, etc. If the bodies of fish sometimes seem diminished, this happens either from a lack of nourishment, or because they are too much agitated, the waves being stirred up by a storm, or even by their own exertion; which will seem most likely to those who know that the fish caught in the Strait of Calais, where the water is most agitated, are generally less full than those caught near Boulogne, where the sea rests somewhat more tranquil. Finally, the other effects are to be attributed not to a moist influence of the Moon, but to the constitution of the atmosphere present at the time, filled, namely, either with excessive moisture or with other noxious effluvia.

DISSERTATIO II. — DISSERTATION II

De Terra elementari.

ON THE ELEMENTAL EARTH .

CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

De Natura Terrae.

On the Nature of the Earth.

760 De natura Elementorum tractaturi primò nobis occurrit Terra; ea est enim, quae, ut ait Plinius, nos nascentes excipit, natos alit, semelque editos sustinet. Quare sit conclusio.

760 As we are about to treat of the nature of the Elements, the Earth first presents itself to us; for it is she that, as Pliny says, receives us when we are born, nourishes us once born, and, once we are brought forth, sustains us. Let the conclusion therefore be:

761 Terra verosimiliter est corpus compositum ex crassioribus, atque ad motum minus aptis particulis, irregulari potissimùm figurâ adfectis. Prob. ex eo quia hoc optimè congruere videtur inertiae,

761 The earth is in all likelihood a body composed of coarser particles, less apt for motion, affected for the most part with an irregular figure. Proof: from the fact that this seems to agree best with the inertia, gravity, and

Phys. Part. II. c. 27.

Phys., pt. II, ch. 27.

p. 238

gravitati, soliditati terrae. Adhaec: quum ignis vi difficillimè solvatur terra, nec particulae ejus in auram difflari possint, crassiores eae sint, est necesse: quumque simul unitae massam consistentem fixamque efficiant, atque lumini transitum intercludant, irregularis figurae verosimiliter sunt, quae variè inter se impliceantur, & anfractuosos meatus forment. Quum demùm terra reliquorum miscibilium velut basis & fundamentum habeatur, necnon durities, fixitas, soliditas, gravitas corporum magna ex parte, à terra ducatur, non tantum crassiores illius particulas esse cónvenit, magisque invicem implexas, sed minus etiam ad motum aptas.

and solidity of the earth. Further: since the earth is dissolved with the greatest difficulty by the force of fire, and its particles cannot be blown off into the air, they must be coarser; and since, united together, they make a consistent and fixed mass and shut off the passage of light, they are in all likelihood of an irregular figure, such as to be variously entangled with one another and to form winding passages. Finally, since the earth is held to be, as it were, the basis and foundation of the other miscible bodies, and since the hardness, fixity, solidity, and gravity of bodies is derived in great part from the earth, it is fitting that its particles be not only coarser and more entangled with one another, but also less apt for motion.

Adnotatio. — REMARK

762 Cartesius terram ex tertii elementi partibus, corpusculis nempè striatis inter sé implexis, & invicem contortis componit [§. 44.]. Gassendus cum Epicureis ex anlulis, & atomis hamatis, sibique mutuò adhaerentibus, ut reliqua corpora firma & arida, constare vult. P. Regnault ramosas esse terrae particulas adserit, quae lucem non transmittant, massamque consistentem efficiant. Cl. à Brixia ait, cujus figurae sint corpuscula terrae primitiva divinare certò non possumus. Probabile est, subdit deindè, primitivas particulas affectas esse figura cubica: quòd haec, ut ait Plato, firmissimas, tutissimasque bases possideat, ac propterea maximè propria illorum corpusculorum videatur, quae ad aridum, iners, fixumque constituendum corpus, sunt à natura destinata. De hoc verò nos nihil certi constituimus.

762 Descartes composes the earth from parts of the third element, namely from striated corpuscles entangled among themselves and twisted together [§. 44.]. Gassendi, with the Epicureans, would have it made up, like the other firm and dry bodies, of little rings and hooked atoms mutually adhering to one another. Fr. Regnault asserts that the particles of earth are branching, such as do not transmit light and make a consistent mass. The distinguished da Brescia says that we cannot divine with certainty of what figure the primitive corpuscles of earth are. It is probable, he then adds, that the primitive particles are affected with a cubic figure: since this, as Plato says, possesses the firmest and safest bases, and therefore seems most proper to those corpuscles which are destined by nature to constitute a dry, inert, and fixed body. On this, however, we determine nothing certain.

CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

De figura, situ, & magnitudine, globi terraquei.

On the Figure, Situation, and Magnitude of the Terraqueous Globe. 763

763 Tellurem tanquam corpus mundanum, quod orbis, vel globus terraqueus dici solet, hic contemplamur. Tellus igitur est, corpus mundanum ex terra & aqua, sparsim interjecto fluido igneo, in vastam molem compactum, aëre undique cinctum, hominum ac brutorum commune habitaculum. Terrae nomine imprimis hìc venit congeries varii generis corporum solidorum crassiorum sabuli, argillae, terrarum pinguium diversi colorum, lapidum, salium, &c.: quam congeriem in

We here contemplate the Earth as a mundane body, which is usually called the orb, or the terraqueous globe. The Earth, then, is a mundane body compacted of earth and water, with a fiery fluid interspersed here and there, into a vast mass, surrounded on every side by air, the common habitation of men and of brutes. Under the name of earth there comes here first of all the heap of solid and coarser bodies of various kinds: sand, clay, fat earths of diverse colors, stones, salts, etc.: a heap which is found in the Earth,

p. 239

tellure reperiri, nemo, nisi ignarus, & historiae, & narrationum negaverit. Aqua intelligitur substantia illa fluida, & humida, quam Deus O. M. in prima creatione á solido, ac sicco separavit, atque in mare, magnam superficiei terrestris partem occupans congessit.

as no one, unless he were ignorant both of history and of narratives, would deny. By water is understood that fluid and moist substance which God, Best and Greatest, in the first creation separated from the solid and dry, and gathered into the sea, which occupies a great part of the terrestrial surface.

764 Ignem per interiores terrae partes diffundi patet, tùm ex eo, quod in mixtis corporibus comprehendatur, tùm ex thermis, calore fodinarum, exhalationibus variis, montibus ignivomis. Compactum esse in molem vastam corpus telluris, nemo nescit; suam autem compactionem, & firmitatem á causa gravitatis habet, quâ nempe partes circumquaque comprimuntur, & compelluntur. Illud verò difficilius resolvitur, in quam figuram moles haec compacta sit: an videlicèt sphaericam contineat? Vel sphaeroidicam, atque hanc, an ad polos depressam, & ad aequatorem elevatam, num contrà ad polos adsurgentem, subsidentem in aequatore.

764 That fire is diffused through the interior parts of the earth is plain, both from the fact that it is contained in mixed bodies, and from hot springs, the heat of mines, various exhalations, and fire-vomiting mountains. That the body of the Earth is compacted into a vast mass, no one is unaware; and it has its compaction and firmness from the cause of gravity, by which, namely, its parts are compressed and driven together on every side. But this is more difficult to resolve: into what figure this mass has been compacted: whether, namely, it holds a spherical one? Or a spheroidal one; and this, whether depressed at the poles and raised at the equator, or, on the contrary, rising at the poles and sinking at the equator.

765 Tellurem esse quoad sensum, & physicè sphaericam commonstrare nituntur Physici. Primò ex ipsis Lunae eclipsibus, haec enim eclipsim patitur, quia telluris umbram ingreditur, eamque sic dividit, perindè, atque si esset planum basi ipsius umbrae parallelum: quum nempè circa tellurem Luna revolvatur. Atqui umbra terrae in omnibus eclipsibus lunaribus hucusque per tot secula observatis, semper adparuit rotunda: ergo. Secundò quia omnes adparentiae tàm caelestes, quàm terrestres aptissimè, ac citra errorem sub figura telluris Sphericâ explicantur, ut patet in globis & Sphaeris artefactis. Tertio quia iter facientes vident priùs, & quidem aequaliter versùs omnem partem, montium culmina, & turrium apices, quàm bases. Diximus Physico sensu, non Mathematico rotundam esse tellurem. Figurae verò quoad sensum sphericae nequaquam officiunt praealti montes, nam terra ut ait Seneca, se habet ad montes, sicut ingens pila ad pilum. Neque obstat etiam camporum planities, dum terra nobis in planum excurrere videtur: id enim provenit partim ab ejus magnitudine, partim ab horizonte viso, qui relatè ad totum globum, est pars valdè exigua, neque sensibilem curvaturam habet.

765 Physicists endeavor to demonstrate that the Earth is spherical as regards sense, and physically. First, from the very eclipses of the Moon; for she suffers an eclipse because she enters the shadow of the Earth, and divides it just as if she were a plane parallel to the base of that shadow: since, namely, the Moon revolves around the Earth. But the shadow of the earth in all the lunar eclipses observed hitherto through so many centuries has always appeared round: therefore. Secondly, because all appearances, celestial as well as terrestrial, are explained most aptly and without error under a spherical figure of the Earth, as is plain in artificial globes and spheres. Thirdly, because those who travel see the summits of mountains and the tops of towers sooner than their bases, and that equally in every direction. We have said that the Earth is round in the physical sense, not the mathematical. Very high mountains in no way hinder its figure from being spherical as regards sense, for the earth, as Seneca says, is to the mountains as a huge ball to a hair. Nor does the flatness of the plains stand in the way, when the earth seems to us to stretch out into a plane: for this comes partly from its magnitude, partly from the visible horizon, which, relative to the whole globe, is a very small part and has no sensible curvature.

766 Hinc telluris figurae quoad sensum sphaericae non officit neque Newtoni, Hugenii, S Gravesandi, aliorumque opinionem, existimantium terraqueam molem non sphaerae instar conformatam, sed sphaeroidis sub aequatore turgescentis, ad polos autem subsidentis figuram referre; neque Cassini utriusque, Maraldi, Mairani, Eisenschmidii, ac plurium hypothesim, quâ telluri oblonga versus polos, depressa sub aequatore figura tribuitur. Nam praeterquàm quod argumenta supra exposita Figuram telluri rotundam sensu physico adstruant, certum est, neutram harum opinionum physicae, ac sensibili telluris rotunditati magnopere adversari.

766 Hence the figure of the Earth, spherical as regards sense, is not hindered either by the opinion of Newton, Huygens, ’s Gravesande, and others, who think that the terraqueous mass is not formed like a sphere but presents the figure of a spheroid swelling under the equator and sinking at the poles; or by the hypothesis of both Cassinis, of Maraldi, Mairan, Eisenschmidt, and many more, by which a figure oblong toward the poles and depressed under the equator is attributed to the Earth. For besides the fact that the arguments set out above establish a round figure for the Earth in the physical sense, it is certain that neither of these opinions is greatly opposed to the physical and sensible roundness of the Earth.

767 Etenim excessus ille majoris diámetri supra minorem tam est exiguus, ut nihil impediat, quominus habeantur pro diámetris physicè aequalibus, adeòque terraquea moles pro physicae sphaerica. Newtonus

767 For that excess of the greater diameter over the lesser is so slight that nothing prevents their being held as physically equal diameters, and hence the terraqueous mass as physically spherical. Newton

p. 240

quippe majorem telluris diametrum, ad minorem esse ponit, ut 230 ad 229, adeoque terra sub aequatore altior foret, quam sub polis 17 milliaribus & [?] parte. Hugenius verò eandem fere diametrorum rationem statuit, quae est numeri 578 ad 577: quae si deindè ratio, ut solet, per regulas proportionum in milliaribus investigetur, patebit, excessum majoris semidiametri telluris supra minorem, nec 7 quidem milliaria aequare; quae tam exigua differentia tellurem utique quoad sensum sphaericam relinquit.

indeed holds that the greater diameter of the Earth is to the lesser as 230 to 229, and hence that the earth would be higher under the equator than under the poles by 17 miles and a sixth part. Huygens, on the other hand, establishes almost the same ratio of the diameters, namely that of the number 578 to 577; and if this ratio is then worked out in miles by the rules of proportion, as is usually done, it will be plain that the excess of the greater semidiameter of the Earth over the lesser does not equal even 7 miles; and so slight a difference leaves the Earth, at any rate as regards sense, spherical.

768 Neque argumentum pro prima opinione, à telluris diurno motu desumptum, evincit quidpiam, ex qua revolutione consequi putant Patroni hujus hypotheseos, ut partes per vim centrifugam sub aequatore majorem, quàm versus polos, longius à telluris axe recedant, atque adeò elevatiores sint sub aequatore, quàm sub polis, molemque sphaeroidicam telluris efforment. Non, inquam, evincit quidpiam: posito enim telluris circa axem motu, non sequitur evidenter, partes circa aequatorem turgescere, versus polos comprimi: massa quippe telluris non mollis, sed firmiter compacta est, nec conforme experientiae videtur, Sphaeram circa axem circumvolutam in sphaeroidem ad cardines revolutionis compressum mutari, quantacumque celeritate convertatur.

768 Nor does the argument for the first opinion, taken from the daily motion of the Earth, prove anything; from this revolution the patrons of this hypothesis think it follows that the parts, by a greater centrifugal force under the equator than toward the poles, recede farther from the axis of the Earth, and so are more elevated under the equator than under the poles, and form the spheroidal mass of the Earth. It does not, I say, prove anything: for, granting the motion of the Earth about its axis, it does not evidently follow that the parts about the equator swell out and are compressed toward the poles: for the mass of the Earth is not soft but firmly compacted, nor does it seem conformable to experience that a sphere revolved about its axis should be changed into a spheroid compressed at the poles of the revolution, with whatever speed it be turned.

769 Situm telluris quod adtinet, communis opinio est, eam in ipso universi centro minimum quoad sensum, collocatam esse. Quamvis enim per Copernicanam hypothesim Sol in universi centro constituatur, tellus autem in orbe magno circa Solem convertatur; ex mente tamen Astronomorum semidiameter orbis magni, si ad semidiametrum caeli stelliferi referatur, veluti evanescit, efficitque, ut tellus à centro universi nullo sensibili intervallo distet.

769 As regards the situation of the Earth, the common opinion is that it is placed in the very center of the universe, at least as regards sense. For although, by the Copernican hypothesis, the Sun is set in the center of the universe and the Earth is turned in the great orb around the Sun, yet in the judgment of the astronomers the semidiameter of the great orb, if it is compared with the semidiameter of the starry heaven, as it were vanishes, and brings it about that the Earth is distant from the center of the universe by no sensible interval.

770 Rationes porro situm hunc telluris evincentes sunt. Prima quia in utroque aequinoctio tempus, quo Sol supra horizontem moratur, penitus adaequat tempus, quo is sub aequatore moratur. Secunda quia nobis in telluris superficie existentibus quamcunque demum regionem incolamus, Stellae semper sub eadem magnitudine seu in ortu, seu in occasu, seu in medio Caeli adparent, dummodo absint vapores, nebulae, atque exhalationes, visum impedientes, & figuram corporum mutantes. Tertia, quia in quacunque terrae parte seclusis montium & vallium impedimentis semper videmus Caeli dimidium: ita ex 12 Zodiaci signis, 6 supra horizontem perpetuo conspiciuntur, & ex Stellis diametraliter oppositis, quales ferè sunt oculus Tauri, & cor Scorpii, quando una in horizonte orientali ascendit, altera in occidentali descendit.

770 The reasons, moreover, that establish this situation of the Earth are these. The first, because at either equinox the time during which the Sun stays above the horizon exactly equals the time during which it stays below the horizon. The second, because to us who exist on the surface of the Earth, whatever region at last we may inhabit, the stars always appear of the same magnitude, whether at their rising, or at their setting, or in the middle of the heaven, provided there are absent vapors, mists, and exhalations, which impede the sight and change the figure of bodies. The third, because in whatever part of the earth, setting aside the hindrances of mountains and valleys, we always see half of the heaven: thus of the 12 signs of the Zodiac, 6 are perpetually seen above the horizon, and of stars diametrically opposite, such as are, more or less, the Eye of the Bull and the Heart of the Scorpion, when one rises on the eastern horizon, the other sets on the western.

771 Magnitudo telluris si cum Caelo stellifero comparetur, adeò exigua est, ut perinde, ac punctum ad illud se habeat. Absoluta verò ejus magnitudo incerta est omnino. Profectò in definienda magnitudine unius gradus è maximis circulis orbis terraquei, plurimum inter se discrepant Auctores. Unde mirum non est, si in telluris magnitudine stabilienda dissentiant: ex valore siquidem unius

771 The magnitude of the Earth, if it is compared with the starry heaven, is so slight that it stands to it just as a point. Its absolute magnitude, however, is altogether uncertain. Indeed, in determining the magnitude of one degree of the great circles of the terraqueous orb, authors disagree very much among themselves. Hence it is no wonder if they dissent in establishing the magnitude of the Earth: since from the value of one degree

p. 241

gradus colligitur valor peripheriae circuli maximi, atque hinc quantitas diametri, & semidiametri, tùm convexae superficiéi, ac demùm soliditas, ut Geómetrae norunt. Plurium hic mensuras adferre non licet; unam & alteram ad communiorem ferè calculum exactam subjicio. Telluris diameter continet milliaria germanica ferè 1720. Superficies, milliaria quadrata ferè 92,880,000. Soliditas, ferè 26,563,680,000. Gradus unus caelestis continet 25 leucas communes Galliae: leuca autem communis continet 2400 passus geometricos.

is gathered the value of the periphery of a great circle, and hence the quantity of the diameter and of the semidiameter, as well as of the convex surface, and finally the solidity, as geometers know. It is not possible to bring forward many measures here; I submit one or two, worked out, nearly, to the more common calculation. The diameter of the Earth contains nearly 1720 German miles. The surface, nearly 92,880,000 square miles. The solidity, nearly 26,563,680,000. One celestial degree contains 25 common leagues of France: and a common league contains 2400 geometric paces.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

De nonnullis corporibus terrestribus, ac primum de petrificationibus.

On Certain Terrestrial Bodies, and First on Petrifications.

772 Non possum mentionem non facere de certo corporum terrestrium genere, scilicèt de conchis, óstreis, aliisque testaceis corporibus, quae inter quorundam montium strata occurrunt. De horum origine triplex est Physicorum opinio. Wooduardus ex diluvio universali hoc phaenomenon derivat, scilicèt: quando aquis operiebantur omnes terrae; tùm quidem petrae, marmora, metalla, corpora omnia, in minutas particulas, & moleculas dividebantur, divisa confusim in illa aquarum vi ferebantur hùc illùc, sub finem autem corpora haec aquae immixta secundum gravitatis leges praecipitabantur: hinc factum, ut corpora ista marina testacea conchilia, utpotè non nihil graviora, eam partem peterent, quae petris, lapidibus, & aliis convenit, inter quae ea etiam hodie inveniuntur ipsam hanc ob causam. Altera hypothesis, quam nuper Leibnitzius propugnavit, adserit in omnibus illis locis olim mare fuisse, in quibus conchae, ostreae reperiuntur, ab illis locis verò mare ipsum in praesens recessisse corporibus ibidem relictis.

cannot fail to make mention of a certain kind of terrestrial bodies, 772 I namely of shells, oysters, and other testaceous bodies, which occur among the strata of certain mountains. On their origin the opinion of physicists is threefold. Woodward derives this phenomenon from the universal deluge, namely: when all the lands were covered by the waters, then indeed rocks, marbles, metals, all bodies were divided into minute particles and molecules; thus divided, they were carried confusedly hither and thither by that force of the waters, but toward the end these bodies, immersed in the water, were precipitated according to the laws of gravity: hence it came about that those marine testaceous shells, being somewhat heavier, sought the part that belongs to rocks, stones, and the like, among which they are found even today for this very reason.
