That fire is a fluid body is plain from this, that it communicates fluidity to other bodies, as to metals, and in others also preserves their fluidity, and brings itself back to equilibrium, as we observe in a room, where the heat is at length evenly diffused. That the molecules of fire are most subtle and most hard we gather from this, that it pervades all bodies, however compact, whereas the other fluids, even supremely volatile ones, can be kept in glasses or other vessels; then from this, that, as a universal solvent, it so tears apart and dissolves almost all bodies that by no industry of ours can they be restored to their former state; whence it is proven that the greatest mobility is in fire: it is necessary too that, to effect the motions of rarefaction, dissolution, combustion, etc., the quantity of motion in fire be very great.

Scholion. — SCHOLIUM

828 Ignis non consistit in particulis sulphureis & nitrosis á materia subtili agitatis, ut Cartesiani opinantur, ut enim praeteream plura, patet hoc ex eo, quod in foco speculi caustici, ubi tantus est ignis, ut metalla saltem imperfecta brevi in vitrum abeant nihil sulphuris aut nitri reperiatur, nec ad aërem his corpusculis impraegnatum refugere licet; quum in exhausto recipiente idem eveniat; nec effugium in metallis quaeratur, quia per chymicos, ex auro, silice, adamante, sulphur nullum extrahitur.

828 Fire does not consist in sulphurous and nitrous particles agitated by the subtle matter, as the Cartesians suppose; for, to pass over many things, this is plain from this, that in the focus of a burning mirror, where the fire is so great that the imperfect metals at least turn in a short time into glass, nothing of sulphur or nitre is found; nor may one take refuge in air impregnated with these corpuscles, since the same thing happens in an exhausted receiver; nor let an escape be sought in the metals, since no sulphur is extracted by the chemists from gold, flint or diamond.

Corollarium.

COROLLARY.

829 Flamma est congeries bullularum sive particularum sulphurearum, terrearum, salinarum, rigidarum, & acuminatarum á fluido subtilissimo igneo, motu vehementi, & confuso exagitatarum, atque ab aëre circumfuso, ne continuò dissipentur, condensatarum. Flamma enim respectivè ad alia corpora ignita parum urit, quòd minus ignis, & multum alienae materiae relatè ad ista corpora ignita complectatur. Figura ejus conica ex

829 Flame is an aggregate of little bubbles, or of sulphurous, earthy, saline, rigid and pointed particles, agitated with a vehement and confused motion by the most subtle igneous fluid, and condensed by the surrounding air, so that they are not continually dissipated. For flame, relatively to other ignited bodies, burns little, because it embraces less fire, and much foreign matter, relatively to those ignited bodies. Its conical figure arises from

p. 258

eo nascitur quod in unico loco aërem findat: ibi nempè ubi aër debilius resistit, & flamma magis est activa, siquidem partes subtilissimae illùc extruduntur.

this, that it cleaves the air in a single place: namely, there where the air resists more weakly and the flame is more active, since the most subtle parts are thrust out thither.

830 Colores flammae à materia ejus diversa oriuntur, caeruleus circa basim ex humore oleagino non dum benè execocto, & dissipato; flamma enim quò est purior & in majori copia igniculos continet, eò candidior est; in medio rubrum colorem paticulae multae terreae igni permixtae efficiunt, si enim lamella mediam in flammam ingeratur, multa fuligine inficitur, non ita in basi & apice. Quod apex flammae albescat, ex depurata flammae materia habetur: adhaec lanugo veluti circa flammam adparet, quae nihil esse aliud videtur, nisi humor adtenuatus & non benè accensus atque adeo aëri, ex parte autem igni admixtus, non secus, ac ex. gr. gutta vini aquae immixta, velut in filamina quaedam sese dispergit. Nullus hactenùs (quod viderim) melius de igne tractavit, quàm toties & nunquam satis laudatus Boerhaave, in Elementis Chemiae. Ipsum consulite si plura vultis.

830 The colors of flame arise from its diverse matter: the blue around the base, from an oily humor not yet well concocted and dissipated; for the purer the flame is, and the greater the quantity of little fires it contains, the whiter it is; in the middle, many earthy particles mixed with the fire produce the red color, for if a small plate is thrust into the middle of the flame, it is stained with much soot, not so at the base and the tip. That the tip of the flame whitens is owing to the purified matter of the flame: besides, a kind of down appears, as it were, round the flame, which seems to be nothing else but an attenuated humor, not well kindled, and hence mixed partly with the air, partly with the fire, no otherwise than, e.g., a drop of wine mixed with water disperses itself, as it were, into certain filaments. No one hitherto (that I have seen) has treated of fire better than Boerhaave, so often and never sufficiently praised, in the Elementa Chemiae. Consult him, if you want more.

CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

De Meteoris in universum.

On Meteors in General.

831 Meteorum idem notat, ac in sublimi adparens, unde quae à Graecis meteora seu pressius metarsia dicuntur, ea latinè communiter sublimia vocantur. Dispescuntur commodè in tria genera sive classes. Primam aërea vel aquea obtinet, in quibus nempè aër vel aqua exsuperat. Secunda complectitur ignita, in quibus praevalent halitus subtilissimi ac spirituosi. Tertia classis meteora lucida seu emphatica sunt, in quibus vel unicè vel saltem potiori parte lux, & splendor sub considerationem cadunt. Universim meteorum dicitur mixtum imperfectum ex halitibus quibusdam adtenuatis seu ut Chymici loquuntur sublimatis constans & in superiori aëre formatum. De singulis pauca delibabimus, & generalem hanc definitionem ac naturam meteori singillatim ostendemus.

eteor means the same as appearing on high; whence the things that 831 Mare called by the Greeks meteora, or more precisely metarsia, are commonly called in Latin sublimia [lofty things]. They are conveniently divided into three kinds, or classes. The first contains the aërial or aqueous ones, in which, namely, air or water predominates. The second embraces the fiery ones, in which most subtle and spirituous exhalations prevail. The third class are the luminous or emphatic meteors, in which either solely, or at least for the greater part, light and splendor fall under consideration. A meteor, universally, is said to be an imperfect mixture consisting of certain attenuated (or, as the Chemists speak, sublimated) exhalations, and formed in the upper air. Of each we shall touch on a few things, and we shall show this general definition and nature of a meteor in each one singly.

832 Nubes est congeries vaporum in sublimi suspensa. Oritur ex vaporibus, qui in principio ita sunt tenues, ut non sint sensibiles, deinde verò accessu aliarum ad alias particulas mutua conjunctione moleculas majores constituunt, & hae aliis adhaerentes nubem vastissimam efformant, ut adeò nubes, congeries quaedam exiguarum bullularum in quibus aquei vapores consistunt, dicenda sit. A nube nebula non nisi densitatis gradu & loco differt; utraque enim ex

832 A cloud is an aggregate of vapors suspended on high. It arises from vapors which at the beginning are so tenuous that they are not sensible, but which then, by the accession of some particles to others, constitute larger molecules by mutual conjunction; and these, adhering to others, form a very vast cloud, so that a cloud is accordingly to be called an aggregate of minute little bubbles in which aqueous vapors consist. Mist differs from a cloud only in its degree of density and in place; for each arises from little bubbles of humid

p. 259

humidorum halituum bullulis simul in magna copia adglomeratis nascitur: in illo tamen discrepant, quod bullulae nubem constituentes longè latiores adeòque respectu ad aërem leviores sint iis, quae nebulam efficiunt, ut illi veluti incumbant: mutatur nebula in nubes, hoc ipso quod inferior aër eas rarefactas ac propterea leviores redditas dissipatasque extrudat: hinc patet cur sole ad meridianum accedente, nebulae in nubes plerumque transeant.

exhalations agglomerated together in great quantity: they differ, however, in this, that the little bubbles constituting a cloud are far wider, and hence lighter with respect to the air, than those which make a mist, so that they lie, as it were, upon them: mist is changed into clouds by the very fact that the lower air thrusts out the bubbles, rarefied and therefore made lighter and dissipated: hence it is plain why, as the Sun approaches the meridian, mists for the most part pass into clouds.

833 Pluvia ex diffractis nubium bullulis oritur, quae diffringuntur pluribus è causis, nempè, vel ob nimium solis calorem, per quem plurimum dilatantur, vel si contrariorum ventorum impetu inter se collidantur, vel si contra montium latera urgeantur, vel demum si ab intenso aëris frigore nimis constringantur. Aura Seròtina, est humor quidam instar pluviae subtilissimae, & insensibilis, ingruente nocte ex alto deciduus, oriturque ex tenuissimis aqueis bullulis, quae in altum evectae diffringuntur, abeuntque in guttas insensibiles, quamprimùm aër post Solis occasum frigore aliquo corripitur: hinc nulla est hiemis tempore, sed aestate tantum ac potissimum vere, & autumno, nulla quoque flante vento Caeloque nimboso, & pluvio, hieme etiam crassiores illae guttuleae à ventis dissipantur, aut in tam exiguas per rarefactionem non dilatantur.

833 Rain arises from the broken little bubbles of the clouds, which are broken from several causes: namely, either on account of the excessive heat of the Sun, by which they are very greatly dilated; or if they collide with one another by the force of contrary winds; or if they are pressed against the sides of mountains; or, finally, if they are too much constricted by an intense cold of the air. The evening damp is a certain humor, like a most subtle and insensible rain, falling from on high as night comes on; and it arises from most tenuous aqueous little bubbles, which, carried on high, are broken and turn into insensible drops as soon as the air, after sunset, is seized by some cold: hence there is none in wintertime, but only in summer, and chiefly in spring and autumn, when, moreover, no wind is blowing. And when the sky is stormy and rainy, and in winter too, those thicker droplets are dissipated by the winds, or are not dilated by rarefaction into such minute ones.

834 Ros matutinus ratione temporis differt solum: labitur enim paulò ante ortum Solis, eo quod humidior tunc aër sit, proindè halitus illi concrescant, qui in aëre supererant, quare minus vera est illorum sententia, qui censent, quod ros nihil sit aliud quam plantarum sudor ex vasculorum orificio continuò exspirans & frigoris vi concretus; etsi etenim hanc transpirationem non negemus, aliud tamen de rore adfirmandum est, quum constet lineos laneosque pannos ceteraque corpora, vitrum item quae nihil hujusmodi sudoris transmittunt, si tempore roris decidui aperto aëri exponantur, sensibiliter madefieri. Pruina nihil est aliud, quàm ros acriori frigore gelatus, decoquit illa & exsugit teneriores fruges, & folia, uti gemmas vitium, imo non raro vites ipsas, nam alimentitius succus qui è terra extrusus ac diffusus in omnes plantae fibras est, frigore pruinae densatur: hinc textura fibrillarum constringitur ac mutatur.

834 The morning dew differs only in respect of time: for it falls a little before the rising of the Sun, because the air is then more humid, and hence those exhalations which remained over in the air concrete; wherefore the opinion of those is less true who think that dew is nothing else than the sweat of plants, continually breathing out from the orifice of their little vessels and congealed by the force of cold; for although we do not deny this transpiration, yet something else must be affirmed of dew, since it is established that linen and woolen cloths and other bodies, glass likewise, which transmit nothing of a sweat of this kind, are sensibly wetted if they are exposed to the open air at the time when the dew is falling. Hoarfrost is nothing other than dew frozen by a sharper cold; it scorches and sucks out the tenderer crops and leaves, such as the buds of vines, indeed not seldom the vines themselves; for the nutritive juice, which, thrust out from the earth, is diffused into all the fibers of the plant, is condensed by the cold of the hoarfrost: hence the texture of the little fibers is constricted and changed.

835 Grando est pluvia congelata à frigidissima aëris regione: fit tunc, quando tenues vaporum flocci ab aëre calido in minimas liquaefacti guttas, & deorsum jam nitentes alteri frigido occurrunt, & ab eo confestim coagulati durantur, accedentibus subindè novis quasi tunicis ob vapores, quos in lapsu contingunt. Hinc patet cur hieme non grandinet, nàm tunc sunt nubes telluri viciniores, quàm ut plurimae ex illis mininis guttulis, in quas primae ille abeunt, coire in unam possint; priusquam à frigore corripiantur, item cur quò altior fuerit nubes, ex qua resoluta grando formatur, eò grana grandinis sint majora.

835 Hail is rain congealed by the very cold region of the air: it is made when thin flakes of vapors, liquefied by warm air into very small drops and already tending downward, meet another, cold air, and are at once coagulated and hardened by it, new coats, as it were, being thereupon added on account of the vapors which they touch in falling. Hence it is plain why it does not hail in winter: for then the clouds are too near the Earth for very many of those very minute droplets, into which the first ones turn, to be able to come together into one before they are seized by the cold; likewise why, the higher the cloud from whose resolution the hail is formed, the larger the grains of hail are.

836 Nix efficitur si dum bullulae humidi halitus in pluviam

836 Snow is produced if the little bubbles of a humid exhalation, while turning into rain,

p. 260

abeuntes frigore glacientur; flocci enim nivium nihil aliud sunt, quàm tenuissimae aquae guttulae, quae frigore correptae uniuntur. Primum inter se filorum instar, tum diversa ratione sibi in descensu implicantur. Figura nivis quandoque regularis est, nonnunquam irregularis, saepè stellam hexagonam, interdum lilium, nec raro rosam si microscopio inspiciatur, exhibet, quae figurae pendere videntur ex diversis exhalationibus conglaciatis. Ex his facilè intelligitur quìd mel, manna, capillitium Veneris seu fila virginea, quae velut fila aranearum super saepes, & gramina adparent sint, & unde originem ducant.

are frozen by cold; for the flakes of snow are nothing else than most tenuous droplets of water, which, seized by cold, are united first among themselves like threads, when they become entangled with one another in diverse ways in their descent. The figure of snow is sometimes regular, sometimes irregular; often, if it is examined with a microscope, it shows a hexagonal star, at times a lily, and not seldom a rose; which figures seem to depend on the diverse exhalations frozen together. From these things it is easily understood what honeydew, manna, and the hair of Venus, or virgin threads, which appear like spiders’ threads over hedges and grasses, are, and whence they draw their origin.

837 Meteora ignita sunt primò fulgur, secundò tonitru, tertiò fulmen, de quibus satis dictum in Electrologia est, quartò Helena, Pollux, sunt ignes, qui navigantibus adparent in infima aëris regione, & ex spirituosis fumis, quos mare tempestatibus agitatum transpirat, paululùm evecti, coadunatis atque succensis formatur. Si unus adparuit, Helena, dum duo videbantur, Castor & Pollux dicebantur. Quintò: stellae cadentes, & discurrentes sunt ignei quidam globuli in sublimi aëre accensi, & ita per illum moti, ut interdum rectà incedere, quandoque praecipite de caelo labi nobis adpareant. Sextò: ignis lambens, & fatuus, est pinguis ex hominum vel corporum carne, & pinguiori materia exsudans halitus, qui ex compressione vel adtritu accenditur, & equis vel hominibus adhaeret citra damnum.

837 The fiery meteors are, first, the flash; second, thunder; third, lightning, of which enough has been said in the Electrology; fourth, Helen and Pollux, which are fires that appear to those sailing, in the lowest region of the air, and are formed from spirituous fumes, which the sea, agitated by storms, transpires, carried up little by little, gathered together and kindled. If one appeared, it was called Helen; when two were seen, Castor and Pollux. Fifth: falling and shooting stars are certain fiery globules kindled in the upper air, and so moved through it that at times they appear to us to proceed straight, at other times to glide headlong from the sky. Sixth: the licking fire, and the foolish fire, is a fat exhalation sweating out from the flesh of men or of bodies, and from fattier matter, which is kindled by compression or friction, and clings to horses or men without harm.

838 Ignis fatuus est halitus quidam uliginosus ex putrefactis plantis, cadaveribus aliisque oleaginosis dissolutis corporibus diurno solis calore praeparatus, qui accedente adtritione, vel fermentatione accenditur, lucet, & ac velut ardet. Fatui dicuntur ignes, quòd non solum huc illucque more fatui hominis nullâ certa lege discurrant, verum etiam quod sequantur, qui eos fugiunt, & ex adverso fugiant, qui illos sequuntur, unde à simplicibus metuuntur, non intelligentibus scilicet, ea causa id fieri, quod qui ignem insequitur, tum motu sui corporis, tum halitu suo aërem ante se, & cum hoc ignem fatuum impellat, qui verò ab igne fugit aërem post se, & cum aëre ignem fatuum adducat, dum locum à suo corpore relictum aëri implendum cedit.

838 The foolish fire is a certain marshy exhalation from putrefied plants, corpses and other oily dissolved bodies, prepared by the daily heat of the Sun, which, upon the onset of friction or fermentation, is kindled, shines, and, as it were, burns. They are called foolish fires because not only do they run hither and thither by no certain law, in the manner of a foolish man, but also because they follow those who flee them, and in turn flee those who follow them; whence they are feared by simple folk, who do not understand, namely, that this happens for the reason that he who pursues the fire, both by the motion of his body and by his breath, drives the air before him, and with it the foolish fire; while he who flees from the fire draws the air after him, and with the air the foolish fire, while he yields the place left by his body to be filled by the air.

839 Septimo: eadem est ratio, quae ferè praedictorum meteororum, phaenomenorum, quae sola diversa figura inter se discriminantur; si enim uliginosus, aut bituminosus halitus unà cum nitrosis spiritibus collectus, & in sublimi aëre fermentationis, adtritionis, aut compressionis ope repentè accensus, globi ignei speciem referat, habeatque penès se pensiles quasi floccos, ac saltatorio motu feratur, Capra saltans dicitur: si oblonga, & horizonti parallela, Trabs: si in sui medio intumescat, Draco: si sit rotunda, & plana, Clypeus: si teres, & cylindrica, columna: si desinat in mucronem, Pyramis si latè dispersa sit, & incensas veluti paleas ostendat, Stipula nuncupatur. Octavo: Aurora Borealis sive lux septentrionalis est

839 Seventh: nearly the same is the account of the phenomena of the aforesaid meteors, which are distinguished among themselves only by their diverse figure; for if a marshy or bituminous exhalation, gathered together with nitrous spirits and suddenly kindled in the upper air by means of fermentation, friction or compression, presents the appearance of a fiery globe, and has about it hanging flakes, as it were, and is borne with a leaping motion, it is called the Leaping Goat; if it is oblong and parallel to the horizon, the Beam; if it swells in its middle, the Dragon; if it is round and flat, the Shield; if smooth and cylindrical, the Column; if it ends in a point, the Pyramid; if it is widely dispersed and shows, as it were, kindled straws, it is named the Stubble. Eighth: the Aurora Borealis, or northern light, is

p. 261

fulgor ille, qui nocturno tempore in Septentrionali caeli plaga ita nobis interdum adparet, ut caelum ipsum ea in parte velut ardere videatur. Hujus phaenomeni historia diffusa est, quae passim apud Recentiores quum reperiatur, brevitatis causâ necessaria solum adduco.

that glow which in the nighttime at times appears to us in the northern quarter of the sky in such a way that the sky itself seems, as it were, to burn in that part. The history of this phenomenon is extensive; since it is found everywhere among the Moderns, for brevity’s sake I adduce only what is necessary.

840 In primis in telluris atmosphaera, ut cetera ignita meteora, suam habet sedem, in eaque producitur; nam infra nubes interdum visa haec lux fuit, testante Mayero: deinde si ultra atmosphaeram porrigeretur, ea foret altissima, adeòque conspiceretur è locis etiam aequatori vicinis, quod tamen est contra experientiam, praesertim quum contingat saepè, ut in uno loco videatur, in alio paucis milliaribus dissito non observetur. Quapropter ex halitu, & vapore in altum è terra delatis sive ex materia fulminum, ac fulgurum nondum benè matura, ut ita dicam, & ad fulmineos fulgurisque effectus nondum praeparata lucem hanc, uti reliqua meteora ignita, provenire existimamus.

840 In the first place, it has its seat in the atmosphere of the Earth, like the other fiery meteors, and is produced in it; for this light has at times been seen below the clouds, as Mayer testifies: then, if it extended beyond the atmosphere, it would be very high, and hence would be seen even from places near the equator, which, however, is contrary to experience, especially since it often happens that it is seen in one place and is not observed in another a few miles distant. Wherefore we think that this light, like the remaining fiery meteors, comes from an exhalation and vapor carried on high from the earth, or from the matter of lightning and of flashes not yet well ripened, so to speak, and not yet prepared for the effects of lightning and of flashes.

841 Meteora lucida seu Emphatica sunt. Primo Iris quae est arcus multicolor in nube rorida ex oppositi solis refractione reflexioneque formatus, unde vel devehit, vel naturaliter indicat pluviam, sed sine magna aquarum eluvione, nubes enim nimium gravidae ad reflectendos sicque refringendos solis radios non sunt idoneae. Colores iridis magis conspicui sunt: ruber seu puniceus, flavus, viridis, caeruleus, ac demum purpureus seu violaceus, & hi quidem in Iride primaria ordinem memoratum obtinent, & vivaciores sunt; in secundaria verò conversum, sic ut extima illius parte reluceat purpureus, deinde caeruleus &c. Qui etiam debiliores magisque diluti conspiciuntur.

841 The luminous or Emphatic meteors are: first, the Rainbow, which is a many-colored arc formed in a dewy cloud by the refraction and reflection of the Sun opposite; whence it either brings down or naturally indicates rain, but without a great flood of waters; for clouds too heavily laden are not fit for reflecting and thus refracting the rays of the Sun. The more conspicuous colors of the rainbow are: red or crimson, yellow, green, blue, and finally purple or violet; and these in the primary rainbow hold the order mentioned and are more vivid; but in the secondary the reverse, so that in its outermost part the purple shines, then the blue, etc.; which are also seen weaker and more diluted.

842 Dicitur autem Iris primaria, quae post duas radiorum refractiones, & unam reflexionem ad oculum pervenit, ac ferè sub angulo circiter 42 gradum videtur. Secundaria verò quae post duas refractiones totidemque reflexiones sub angulo circiter 52 graduum in oculum incidit. Illud advertendum Iridem non videri, nisi visus inter Solem & nubem roridam intermediet, sic quando ad lucem per fenestras immissam ex ore aquam spargis, & medius inter Solem, & guttas consistis, Iridem conspicis, cujus alias etiam analogias in fonticulis salientibus, in telis aranearum, in collo columbae, floribus vel herbis sub Solis ortum rore conspersis ac debito situ locoque aspectis habes.

842 That rainbow, moreover, is called primary which reaches the eye after two refractions of the rays and one reflection, and is seen at an angle of about 42 degrees; and the secondary, that which falls into the eye after two refractions and as many reflections, at an angle of about 52 degrees. It is to be noticed that the rainbow is not seen unless the sight is between the Sun and the dewy cloud; so when you sprinkle water from your mouth toward the light let in through windows, and stand between the Sun and the drops, you behold a rainbow, of which you also have other analogies in little leaping fountains, in spiders’ webs, on the neck of a dove, in flowers or grasses sprinkled with dew about sunrise and viewed in the due situation and place.

843 Porrò cur idem colores semper esse, & permanere videantur, ex eo est, quod continuò aliae atque aliae nubis roridae partes, seu novae identidem guttulae eodem situ ac dispositione prioribus succedant, non secus ac in ardente cereo eadem flamma perdurare creditur, ob alias, & alias ignis particulas continuò succedentes. Secundo Halo sive corona, vel area est circulus coloratus, & communius subalbicans, quandoque tamen colores Iridis, sed obscuriores referens, qui non nunquam circa Solem, crebrius circa Lunam adparet, formatur in nube rorida inter astrum, & oculum

843 Further, why the same colors seem always to be and to remain is from this, that continually other and other parts of the dewy cloud, or new droplets again and again, succeed the earlier ones in the same situation and disposition, no otherwise than in a burning taper the same flame is believed to endure, on account of other and other particles of fire continually succeeding. Second: the Halo, or crown, or area, is a colored circle, more commonly whitish, sometimes however showing the colors of the rainbow, but more obscure, which appears now and then around the Sun, more often around the Moon; it is formed in a dewy cloud placed between the star and the eye,

p. 262

interjecta cum plexu ad duplicem refractionem idoneo vi cujus radii cum axe seu linea per centrum sideris, & oculum ducta angulum fere 23 graduum efficiunt.

with a texture suited to a double refraction, by virtue of which the rays make with the axis, or the line drawn through the center of the star and the eye, an angle of nearly 23 degrees.

844 Si Halo semper major, ac major addensetur, pluviam praesagit, quia sensim in imbrem nubes concrescunt: si à multis, vel etiam ab una parte dissipetur, ventos, vel à pluribus, vel una ex parte exortos indicat, si totus evanescat, serenitatem praenunciat, tum enim vi caloris nubes dissipantur. Tertiò: Parhelium, & Paraselene sunt meteora lucida juxta Solem, vel Lunam consistentia, horumque astrorum imagines exhibentia; quoties enim Soli non infra versus terram neque è regione, sed ad latera, & ex obliquo sive ad boream sive ad austrum nubes adcurrit proximè in aquas resolvi apta, & versus solem etiam diaphana, ex altera verò parte instar speculi terminata, toties suam ipsi imaginem imprimit, quae indè ad oculos nostros reflexa nobis solem in nube repraesentat, ut ita geminos lucere Soles ignari arbitrentur. Insuper fieri potest ut imago Solis simili ratione in unam nubem impressa aliam rursus imaginem in nubem alteram inducat, & haec rursus in aliam, idem de Luna cum proportione sentiendum.

844 If the Halo is condensed ever larger and larger, it presages rain, because the clouds gradually concrete into a shower; if it is dissipated on many sides, or even on one side, it indicates winds arising either from several quarters or from one; if it vanishes wholly, it foretells fair weather, for then the clouds are dissipated by the force of heat. Third: the Parhelion and Paraselene are luminous meteors standing beside the Sun or the Moon and showing the images of those stars; for as often as a cloud apt to be resolved very soon into waters, diaphanous, too, toward the Sun, but terminated on the other side like a mirror, runs up to the Sun, not below it toward the earth, nor directly opposite, but at the sides and obliquely, either toward the north or toward the south, so often the Sun impresses its own image upon it, which, reflected thence to our eyes, represents the Sun to us in the cloud, so that the ignorant judge that twin Suns are shining. Moreover, it can happen that the image of the Sun, impressed in like manner on one cloud, induces again another image on a second cloud, and this again on another; the same is to be thought, proportionally, of the Moon.

845 Quarto: Virgae formantur in aëre, quum vel rectus nubium tractus diversos exhibet colores eam ob causam, ob quam in iride vel corona formantur. Quinto: Voraginem, hiatum, vel foveam adpellamus, quando serena nocte exhalationes sursum evectae in medio quidem densiores, reliqua parte rariores inter astrorum lucem & oculum nostrum sunt collocatae, si enim multae fuerint, voraginem, si pauciores, hiatum, si in longum protensae, foveam, vel lacum exhibent; siquidem propter densitatem in medio minus illustrantur, omne verò obscurum licet aequè vicinum, & in eadem superficie positum, semper remotius videtur, ac depressius, nitidum verò propinquius magisque elevatum. Haec de uberrima materia compendio dixisse sufficiat.

845 Fourth: Rods are formed in the air when a straight tract of clouds shows diverse colors, for the same cause for which these are formed in the rainbow or the crown. Fifth: we call it a Chasm, a Gap, or a Pit, when on a clear night exhalations carried upward, denser in the middle and rarer in the remaining part, are placed between the light of the stars and our eye; for if they are many, they show a chasm; if fewer, a gap; if extended lengthwise, a pit or lake; since on account of the density in the middle they are less illuminated, and everything dark, although equally near and placed in the same surface, always seems more remote and more depressed, while what is bright seems nearer and more elevated. Let it suffice to have said this, in compendium, on a most copious matter.

CAPUT POSTREMUM.

CHAPTER THE LAST.

Quid de Plantis dicendum sit.

What is to be said of Plants.

846 Plantae, quo nomine stirpium omne genus, quod ex terra erumpit, intelligitur: sunt corpora organica vario partium organicarum sapientissimè coordinatarum, & conjunctarum adparatu constantia, radicibus suis terrae inhaerentia, atque succi convenientis in orbem euntis ac redeuntis influxu animata. Adparatum mirabilem organicorum horum corporum

lants, by which name every kind of growth that bursts forth from the 846 P earth is understood, are organic bodies consisting of a varied apparatus of organic parts most wisely co-ordinated and joined together, adhering to the earth by their roots, and animated by the influx of a suitable juice going round and returning in a circuit. The wonderful apparatus of these organic bodies was investigated

p. 263

perquisivére, & explicuere Malpighius Italus, & Grevius Anglus. Vita quodammodo, & actiones in plantis absolvuntur fluidi vitalis per organa solida sapientissimè disposita jugi & in orbem redeunte motu, quem aetheris aërisque agitatio, impulsus, pressio mediante simul vi elastica efficiunt, ut ea propter rectè dicantur machinae Hydraulico-Pneumaticae, quae ut penitius intelligantur breviculam earum Anatomen subdo.

and explained by Malpighi the Italian and Grew the Englishman. Life, in a manner, and its actions are accomplished in plants by the continual motion, returning in a circuit, of the vital fluid through solid organs most wisely disposed; which motion the agitation, impulse and pressure of the ether and the air bring about, the elastic force mediating at the same time; so that on that account they are rightly called Hydraulic-Pneumatic machines; and that these may be understood more deeply, I subjoin a very brief Anatomy of them.

847 Plantarum partes aliae sunt fluidae, aliae solidae. Fluida pars est humor ille vel succus, qui instar sanguinis in homine, per solidas plantae partes diffunditur. Succum hunc, & verum ac genuinum plantarum nutrimentum, probabilissimè dicunt esse partes salinas, terreas, oleosas, quae in succo aqueo praeparatae, extenuatae, subactae, & cum hoc succo tanquàm vehiculo in plantarum totam structuram distributae circumferuntur, sic ut singulae partes, quod earum substantiae nutriendae, & augendae idoneum est, recipere possint. Partes solidae organicum ipsarum corpus constituunt & sunt: truncus, radices, rami, folia, flores, fructus. Truncus qui in arboribus caudex & stipes, in floribus & herbis caulis, scapus, & thyrsus in tritico, & similibus calmus, vel culmus, dicitur, est veluti corpus plantae quod è terra erumpens ei supereminet, atque in ramos frondes &c. se explicat. Radix est ea plantae pars, quae tota infra terram posita, ei adhaerescens suum plantae alimentum trahit. Rami quemadmodum ortus ex corpore animalis, ita ex plantae corpore sive trunco plerumque inordinatè, quandoque eleganti ordine erumpunt, & quaquaversus se difundunt; ejus prorsùs naturae, cujus truncus, ex quo nascuntur, cortice uti ille muniti, medullam continent in medio iisdemque vasculis, fibris nempè, utriculis atque tracheis componuntur. Folia duas praecipuè partes complectuntur: pediculum nempè quo folium est plantae annexum, & ipsum folii corpus.

847 Of the parts of plants, some are fluid, others solid. The fluid part is that humor or juice which, like the blood in man, is diffused through the solid parts of the plant. This juice, and the true and genuine nourishment of plants, they say most probably to be saline, earthy and oily parts, which, prepared in the aqueous juice, attenuated, worked up, and distributed with this juice, as with a vehicle, into the whole structure of the plants, are carried round, so that the single parts can receive what is suitable for nourishing and increasing their substance. The solid parts constitute their organic body, and are: the trunk, roots, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits. The trunk, which in trees is called the bole and stock, in flowers and herbs the stalk, scape and thyrsus, in wheat and the like the straw or haulm, is, as it were, the body of the plant, which, bursting forth from the earth, rises above it and unfolds itself into branches, fronds, etc. The root is that part of the plant which, placed wholly below the earth and adhering to it, draws its nourishment for the plant. The branches, just as the limbs from the body of an animal, so burst forth from the body, or trunk, of the plant, for the most part without order, sometimes in an elegant order, and spread themselves in every direction; being of altogether the same nature as the trunk from which they arise, and furnished like it with bark, they contain pith in the middle, and are composed of the same little vessels, namely fibers, utricles and tracheae. The leaves embrace chiefly two parts: namely, the petiole, by which the leaf is attached to the plant, and the very body of the leaf.

848 Flores sunt velut primus plantae partus, in iis quatuor partes distinguntur, nempè, calix qui est floris basis & fulcimentum: foliola quae supra calicem adsurgunt à dilatato caule propagata, constant ex lignosis fistulis sivè fibris, tracheis quoque, & simul multiplici utriculorum ordine; stamina ex imâ floris parte erumpunt varia numero atque figura: constant pedunculo, & adpensa capsula, quae lignosis fistulis tracheis atque utriculis per longum locatis integratur: stylus demum est ea floris pars, quae illius centrum occupans plantae semen cavitate sua recondit, & fovet. Fructus est ultimum plantarum opus, cui producendo, & perficiendo reliquae omnes partes sunt destinatae, constat autem involúcro atque semine, illud pro specifico fructuum discrimine differt; & multiplex est, ac diversae consistentiae, & firmitatis in fructibus diversis; semen ad ortum plantarum pertinet: de quo breviter.

848 The flowers are, as it were, the first offspring of the plant; in them four parts are distinguished, namely: the calyx, which is the base and support of the flower; the petals, which rise above the calyx, propagated from the dilated stalk, and consist of woody tubes, or fibers, of tracheae too, and at the same time of a manifold order of utricles; the stamens burst forth from the lowest part of the flower, various in number and figure: they consist of a filament and an attached capsule, which is made up of woody tubes, tracheae and utricles placed lengthwise: the style, finally, is that part of the flower which, occupying its center, hides and cherishes the seed of the plant in its cavity. The fruit is the last work of plants, to the producing and perfecting of which all the remaining parts are destined; it consists, moreover, of an envelope and the seed; the former differs according to the specific difference of the fruits, and is manifold, and of diverse consistency and firmness in diverse fruits; the seed pertains to the origin of plants: of which briefly.

849 Semen dicitur illud granulum seu nucleus, ex quo veluti ex ovo planta progerminat, quatuor in eo distinguuntur involúcra;

849 That little grain, or kernel, is called the seed, from which, as from an egg, the plant germinates; four things are distinguished in it: the envelopes;

p. 264

primum sive omnium extimum ceteris duriùs est, eo detracto duae occurrunt pelliculae, quatum exterior crassa, ac fermè cartilaginosa est, interior valdè subtilis, sic ut in exsiccato semine vix ab exteriori sejungi possit. Post haec integumenta, quae secundinae vocantur, duo vel etiam plures lobi in conspectum veniunt tenui admodum pellucidaque membrana, quae ordine quarta est, comprehensi, complectuntur autem in quadam veluti fossula utrinque in lobis excavata germen futurae plantae, quod nihil est aliud quàm ipsa tota planta ex semine nascitura partibus omnibus, trunco nempè, caule, radicibus, ramis, &c. absoluta adeò, ut seminalis plantula in germine delitescens, non nisi penès partium magnitudinem ab adulta differat.

the first, or outermost of all, is harder than the rest; when it is removed, two little skins are met, of which the exterior is thick and almost cartilaginous, the interior very subtle, so that in a dried seed it can scarcely be separated from the exterior. After these integuments, which are called secundines, two or even more lobes come into view, enclosed in a certain thin and pellucid membrane, which is fourth in order; and they embrace, in a kind of little ditch, as it were, hollowed out on either side in the lobes, the germ of the future plant; which is nothing else than the whole plant itself that is to arise from the seed, complete in all its parts, namely trunk, or stalk, roots, branches, etc., so that the seminal plantlet lying hidden in the germ does not differ from the adult except in the size of its parts.

850 Ortus porrò ex semine hac ratione peragitur; semine idoneo terrae commisso, ejus, & Solis calore leniter laxantur fibrae membranarum earumque meatus dilatantur, quo fit ut humor, quo terra abundat, eos paulatim subeat, in illis variè percoletur, fermentet, aptusque nutritioni efficiatur: nutritius succus in membranis percolatus loborum substantiam ingreditur, ubi cum specifico succo plantulae miscetur, fermentescit ac novas partes adsciscit: is debita ratione in lobis praeparatus, radiculae ipsius germinis subtilissimos poros subit, & in ejus fibrillas se insinuat, quae hoc succo nutrita, & aucta extra prorrumpit, capillitium spargit, & terrae illorum filamentorum ope inseritur, aucta sufficienter radice vividior nutritii liquoris portio in reliquam germinis partem transit, ejusque partes irradians, & impellens motum ipsis communicat: hinc evolvuntur, & explicantur partes futurae plantae, quae in germine inter se convolutae complicataeque delitescunt, tum sensim eaedem ipsae augentur, & suo ordine in conspectum veniunt: ut adeò ex prima hac seminis evolutione reliqua plantae adcretio facilè intelligatur.

850 The rising from the seed, further, is accomplished in this way: when the seed is committed to suitable earth, the fibers of its membranes are gently loosened by the heat of the earth and of the Sun, and their passages are dilated; whence it comes about that the humor in which the earth abounds gradually enters them, is variously strained in them, ferments, and is made apt for nutrition: the nutritive juice, strained in the membranes, enters the substance of the lobes, where it is mixed with the specific juice of the plantlet, ferments, and takes on new parts; this juice, prepared in due manner in the lobes, enters the most subtle pores of the radicle of the germ itself and insinuates itself into its little fibers; and the radicle, nourished and increased by this juice, bursts forth outward, spreads out its hair, and by means of those filaments is inserted into the earth; the root being sufficiently increased, a more lively portion of the nutritive liquor passes into the remaining part of the germ, and, irradiating and impelling its parts, communicates motion to them; hence are evolved and unfolded the parts of the future plant, which lie hidden in the germ, rolled up and folded together among themselves; then by degrees these same parts are increased and come into view in their order: so that from this first evolution of the seed the remaining growth of the plant is easily understood.

Corollarium.

COROLLARY.

851 Nullae adeò plantae sunt quae ex semine non generentur. Certè peculiaris plantarum dispositio miro ordine, & distinctione partium collocatio, vénulae, utriculi, tracheae, ad flores fructus ejusdem speciei producendos manifestum faciunt, non ex fortuito elementorum concursu aut ex putri plantas enasci. Id ipsum Malpighii experimento ostenditur, qui terram ex profundiore voragine érutam vasi ita incluserat, ut superiorem partem telis delicatissimis obduceret sic ut aëri pluviaeque ingressus in vas pateret, non vero aliis minimis corpusculis per aërem delatis; atque ita Solis radiis exposuit. Reperit post longissimum tempus nullam herbam, aut plantae indicium adparere; ut ea propter intulerit, quod quum nullum semen vel antea in terra

851 There are therefore no plants that are not generated from seed. Certainly the peculiar disposition of plants, the collocation of their parts in wonderful order and distinction, the little veins, utricles and tracheae, for producing flowers and fruits of the same species, make it manifest that plants are not born from a fortuitous concourse of the elements, or from putrid matter. This very thing is shown by an experiment of Malpighi, who had enclosed earth dug out of a rather deep pit in a vessel in such a way as to cover its upper part with very delicate cloths, so that entrance into the vessel lay open to the air and the rain, but not to other very minute corpuscles carried through the air; and so he exposed it to the rays of the Sun. He found that after a very long time no herb, or sign of a plant, appeared; so that on that account he inferred that, since no seed had either lain hidden before in the earth

p. 265

profundius eruta latuerit vel per aerem in vas incidere potuerit, plantae suam genesim ex semine habeant.

dug out from deeper down, or could have fallen into the vessel through the air, plants have their genesis from seed.

852 Nutritionem & augmentum plantarum quod adtinet, ea convenientis succi admissione, elaboratione, depuratione, & ejus per organa plantae jugi circulatione absolvitur; radices enim humorem adtrahunt, is receptus per lignosas plantae fistulas ascendit eo, quod ab altero â dilatatione, & constructione trachearum, quae lignosis fistulis interseruntur, sursum indesinenter urgeatur; è quibus in ceteras partes dispensatur. Circulari verò succum alimentitium ostenditur imprimis, quia non nisi hâc ratione videtur absolvi posse plantarum nutritionem; si quidem haec fieri nequit, nisi utile & quod conveniens plantae alimentum est, ab inutili secernatur, hocque ad eas iterùm partes retrudatur, ut idoneum nutritioni per novam depurationem, & elaborationem reddatur: deinde patet experientia; Malpighius enim cortice in orbem secto avulsaque annulari portione deprehendit, superioris corticis limbum notabiliter intumescere atque etiam augeri, inferioris verò nullum obtinuisse incrementum, sed gemmas duntaxat suo tempore praetulisse. Atque haec, quae ex P. Klaus excerpta sunt dicta sufficiant, ut Physicae cùm Generali tum Particulari supremam manum imponamus.

852 As regards the nutrition and growth of plants, it is accomplished by the admission, elaboration and purification of a suitable juice, and by its continual circulation through the organs of the plant; for the roots draw in moisture; this, once received, ascends through the woody tubes of the plant, because it is urged upward unceasingly by the alternate dilatation and constriction of the tracheae which are interspersed among the woody tubes; and from these it is dispersed into the other parts. That the nutritive juice circulates is shown, first of all, because only in this way does it seem that the nutrition of plants can be accomplished; since indeed this cannot take place unless that which is useful, and is suitable nourishment for the plant, is separated from the useless, and this is thrust back again to those parts, so that it may be rendered fit for nutrition through a new purification and elaboration; and then it is plain from experience; for Malpighi, when the bark had been cut round in a circle and a ring-shaped portion torn away, found that the edge of the upper bark swelled notably and also increased, but that the lower obtained no increase, but only put forth buds in their season. And let these things, which have been excerpted from Fr. Klaus, suffice to have been said, so that we may put the finishing hand to the Physics, both General and Particular.

853 Quod si cui fortassè aliqua, quae in hisce Recentioris Philosophiae Elementis adtuli breviora quàm oporteret videantur, eum cogitare velim, me solis Adolescentibus scripsisse. Prostant in aliorum commodum eruditi multorum, longèque ampliora volumina. Nec tamen propterea muneri meo defuisse putem, qui utilius judicarem quidquid negotium tironibus facessere posset, planum facere, atque Elementis hisce Americanos Juvenes juvare potius, quàm majore mole disputationum ipsos onerare. Philosophia namque, & meditatione & experimentis acquirenda est, nec magni commodi quicquam in prolixitate situm habet.

853 But if to anyone perhaps some of the things which I have brought forward in these Elements of the Newer Philosophy should seem briefer than was fitting, I would wish him to consider that I have written for Young Men alone. Many large volumes of learned men, far fuller ones, are available for the convenience of others. Nor yet would I think on that account that I have failed in my office, since I judged it more useful to make plain whatever could cause trouble to beginners, and with these Elements rather to help the American Youth than to burden them with a greater mass of disputations. For Philosophy is to be acquired both by meditation and by experiments, and it has nothing of great advantage placed in prolixity.

O. S. C. S. M. E. C. A. R.
